Correct, complete alternatives depend on intended meaning: use 'il y a une chose que je...' for 'there is one thing that I...'; use 'j'ai une chose que...' rarely — more natural is 'j'ai quelque chose que...' for 'I have something that...'. If you mean 'there's one thing I (want/need/say)', follow with a verb: 'Il y a une chose que je veux dire.'
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: There is one thing I want to tell you.

meaning: has a difference / makes a difference.
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase formed with avoir (a = has) + une différence. Depending on context it can mean 'there is a difference' (someone/something 'has a difference') or 'it makes a difference' when used with impersonal subjects or rephrased (e.g., 'ça fait une différence' is more natural for 'it makes a difference'). Word order and contraction matter: 'a' is the third-person singular of avoir (il/elle a).
target_language_example: Il a une différence d'opinion avec son collègue.
native_language_example: He has a difference of opinion with his colleague.

meaning: has an explanation / there is an explanation (for something).
additional_notes: From the verb avoir (a) + noun explication. Used to say that something can be explained or that there is a reason for it. You will often see it in sentences like «Il a une explication» (He has an explanation) or «Ça a une explication» (There is an explanation for that). If referring to a past event or object, context determines what 'it' is. Pronunciation: [a yn ɛksplikasjɔ̃].
target_language_example: Ça a une explication logique.
native_language_example: There is a logical explanation for that.

meaning: in one minute; one minute away (time until something happens)
additional_notes: Commonly used to say something will happen very soon or to tell someone to wait a short time. Depending on context, it can mean "in one minute" (from now) or be part of expressions like "à une minute de" meaning "one minute from" a place or event. Use the accented à. Neutral/informal contexts.
target_language_example: Attends ici, je reviens à une minute.
native_language_example: Wait here, I'll be back in one minute.

meaning: has a door / there is a door (literally: 'has a door')
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb avoir (a = has) and 'une porte' (a door). It appears in descriptions of places or objects (e.g., 'La maison a une porte' = 'The house has a door'). Watch spelling: in full sentence you usually write 'a une' (without apostrophe). If you mean 'to a door' or 'at a door', use prepositions (à la porte, à une porte).
target_language_example: La maison a une porte rouge.
native_language_example: The house has a red door.

meaning: there is a reason for (that); there's a reason behind (it/that).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has an explanation or cause. Commonly appears as 'Il y a une raison à ...' or informally 'Y a une raison à ...'. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or demonstrative (cela/ça/tout).
target_language_example: Il y a une raison à ce comportement.
native_language_example: There is a reason for that behavior.

meaning: in one week; one week from now
additional_notes: This phrase is composed of 'à' (to/at) + 'une semaine' (one week). It indicates a point exactly one week ahead of a reference time. Standard written French uses the accented form 'à une semaine' — in casual typing the accent may be omitted but accents are preferred. For talking about a week ago, use 'il y a une semaine'. Depending on context, French speakers more commonly say 'dans une semaine' for 'in one week'.
target_language_example: Le rendez-vous est fixé a une semaine.
native_language_example: The appointment is set for one week from now.

meaning: likely a mistaken or incomplete fragment — not a standard French phrase
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'a à peu'. It appears to be a typographical error or misordering of parts from correct expressions such as 'à peu près' (meaning 'approximately') or 'a peu' (incorrectly missing the accent). If you encounter 'a à peu' in text, check the surrounding context; the author probably intended 'à peu près' or another standard phrase.
target_language_example: Dans cette phrase, 'a à peu' semble être une coquille et ne veut rien dire.
native_language_example: In this sentence, 'a à peu' seems to be a typo and does not mean anything.

meaning: they abandoned the / they left the (something).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé simple) of 'abandonner' for 'ils/elles' — formal/literary written form meaning to leave behind, give up on, or abandon someone/something. Often followed by a direct object (le/la/les + noun). In spoken French, the passé composé (ils ont abandonné le...) is more common.
target_language_example: Ils abandonnèrent le navire en flammes.
native_language_example: They abandoned the burning ship.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragmentary or ungrammatical sequence literally meaning 'absolutely that I'. It can appear as part of a longer sentence but is not used alone as a set expression.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the adverb 'absolument' (absolutely/definitely) with the subordinating conjunction 'que' followed by the subject 'je' (I). It's typically the result of breaking a subordinate clause (e.g. «... absolument que je ...») but by itself is awkward. Preferred constructions: «Je veux absolument que...», «Il est absolument certain que je...», or rephrase to avoid the split 'absolument que je'.
target_language_example: Il est absolument que je doive partir n'est pas correct — on dira plutôt «Il est absolument certain que je doive partir» ou «Je dois absolument partir».
native_language_example: 'Il est absolutely that I must leave' is not correct — better: 'It is absolutely certain that I must leave' or 'I absolutely must leave.'

meaning: accepted on (a specific date) — used to indicate the date on which something was accepted
additional_notes: This phrase is typically followed by a date (e.g., accepté le 12 mars) and is often found in formal or administrative contexts (emails, letters, records). It uses the past participle accepté with the definite article le to mark the day. If indicating who accepted, use "accepté par" (accepted by).
target_language_example: Le dossier a été accepté le 3 avril.
native_language_example: The file was accepted on April 3.

meaning: accepted my (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'accepté' (accepted) followed by the possessive adjective 'mon' (my) used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., mon idée, mon cadeau). Use with a singular masculine object; for feminine nouns use 'ma' (ma idée → mon idée because idée begins with vowel: note exception). In spoken and written French, agreement of 'accepté' is not required here because it's used with 'avoir' (il/elle a accepté).
target_language_example: Elle a accepté mon invitation.
native_language_example: She accepted my invitation.

meaning: accepted a (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: The phrase is the past participle 'accepté' (accepted) followed by the indefinite article 'un' (a). It appears before a masculine singular noun: e.g. 'accepté un emploi' = 'accepted a job'. Word order and agreement: 'accepté' agrees with a preceding direct object only when using être or in passive/compound constructions with agreement rules; in most simple uses with avoir, no visible agreement is needed. This is not a fixed phrase—it's just the verb 'accepter' in past participle form plus 'un'.
target_language_example: Il a accepté un poste à l'étranger.
native_language_example: He accepted a position abroad.

meaning: part of the phrase 'accident de la circulation' — 'traffic/road accident'.
additional_notes: In these examples 'accident de la' appears as the beginning of the fixed expression 'accident de la circulation' meaning a traffic or road accident. Alone 'accident de' can combine with other nouns (accident de travail, accident de la route). Use 'un/son/sa' before the full noun phrase (un accident de la circulation).
target_language_example: Il a eu un accident de la route hier soir.
native_language_example: He had a road accident last night.

meaning: road traffic accident; car crash (an accident that happens on the road).
additional_notes: Used to refer to accidents involving vehicles on roads (cars, motorcycles, trucks). Common in news and everyday speech. Can describe anything from minor collisions to fatal crashes. Often interchangeable with 'accident de la circulation' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il y a eu un accident de la route sur l'autoroute ce matin.
native_language_example: There was a road accident on the highway this morning.

meaning: '... shopping for' or 'purchases for' (used with a noun to specify what the shopping/purchases are for).
additional_notes: Achats is the plural noun 'purchases' or 'shopping'. Followed by de + noun to indicate purpose or occasion (e.g., achats de Noël = Christmas shopping). Common in questions and statements about having started, finished, or gone to do that shopping.
target_language_example: As-tu commencé tes achats de rentrée ?
native_language_example: Have you started your back-to-school shopping?

meaning: to buy the (masculine singular direct object)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb acheter (to buy) followed by the definite article le before a masculine singular noun: e.g. acheter le livre = to buy the book. In spoken French the article may contract with a following vowel (l' for vowel-starting nouns). Remember that with a pronoun object you would use l'acheter (to buy it) or l'acheter (to buy him/her/it) depending on context. For feminine nouns use acheter la; plural uses acheter les.
target_language_example: Je vais acheter le pain cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy the bread this afternoon.

meaning: This is not a correct or complete French expression; likely a mistake. 'Acheter' means 'to buy'. 'Quelque' is an indefinite adjective meaning 'some' or 'a few' but must be followed by a noun (e.g. 'quelque chose', 'quelques livres').
additional_notes: You will not see 'acheter quelque' by itself in correct French. To say 'to buy something' use 'acheter quelque chose'. To say 'to buy some [plural noun]' use 'acheter quelques + noun' (note the plural form 'quelques' with an -s). Example errors to avoid: 'acheter quelque livres' (wrong) → correct: 'acheter quelques livres'.
target_language_example: Je vais acheter quelque chose au supermarché.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy something at the supermarket.

meaning: 'bought two' — past participle acheté + the number deux (i.e. purchased two of something).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short sequence: acheté is the past participle of acheter (to buy) and agrees in gender/number with a preceding direct object when used with the auxiliary avoir only if the object is placed before the verb (e.g. 'les pommes que j'ai achetées'). In simple statements you will more often see forms like 'J'ai acheté deux pommes.' Here 'acheté deux' typically appears followed by a noun (what was bought).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté deux livres hier.
native_language_example: I bought two books yesterday.

meaning: 'bought some' or 'bought (part of something)' (past participle + partitive/article)
additional_notes: Acheté is the past participle of acheter (to buy). When followed by du (the contraction of de + le, a partitive article), acheté du indicates someone bought some of an uncountable item or a portion of something (e.g., acheté du pain = bought some bread). It often appears in sentences like «J'ai acheté du…» (I bought some…). Word order and agreement depend on the full sentence (e.g., with direct objects or quantities).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté du fromage pour le dîner.
native_language_example: I bought some cheese for dinner.

meaning: 'bought the' (past participle + definite article: someone bought a specific thing).
additional_notes: From the verb acheter (to buy) in the passé composé: subject + avoir (ai/as/a/avons/avez/ont) + acheté. 'Le' is the masculine singular definite article ('the'). Use 'achetée' when the direct object is feminine and agreement is required (with preceding direct object pronoun). Common in everyday past tense statements and questions about purchases.
target_language_example: Il a acheté le livre hier.
native_language_example: He bought the book yesterday.

meaning: bought everything / bought it all
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the past participle 'acheté' (bought) and 'tout' (everything/it all). Used to say someone purchased all items or everything available. Word order can vary depending on emphasis: 'tout acheté' or 'il a tout acheté' are common. If referring to a specific object, context or a pronoun is usually added (e.g. 'je l'ai acheté tout' is uncommon; prefer 'je l'ai tout acheté' only in certain constructions).
target_language_example: Il a acheté tout dans le magasin.
native_language_example: He bought everything in the store.

meaning: an act of faith; a gesture or decision made on trust or belief rather than proof.
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe doing something that requires trust, courage, or belief (not necessarily religious). Can mean a symbolic gesture showing confidence or commitment. Often followed by pour/à or used with verbs like faire (faire acte de foi).
target_language_example: Accepter ce projet sans garanties est un vrai acte de foi.
native_language_example: Accepting this project without guarantees is a real act of faith.

meaning: secret admirer (someone who admires you but keeps their identity hidden).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has romantic or admiring feelings but hasn't revealed themselves. Can refer to someone sending anonymous notes, gifts, or simply keeping their feelings private. Gender-specific: 'admirateur' is masculine; use 'admiratrice secrète' for a female admirer (or 'admirateur(se) secret(ète)' in inclusive contexts).
target_language_example: Elle a reçu une lettre d'un admirateur secret.
native_language_example: She received a letter from a secret admirer.

meaning: to love/like this (emphatic), literally 'love this'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; 'adore' is the verb 'to adore/love' and 'ce' is the demonstrative 'this/that'. In French you'd normally see 'j'adore ce ...' followed by a noun (J'adore ce livre = I love this book) or 'J'adore ça/je l'adore' to refer to something previously mentioned. Alone 'adore ce' is incomplete and should be followed by a noun or noun phrase.
target_language_example: J'adore ce film, il est excellent.
native_language_example: I love this movie; it's great.

meaning: 'address of' (shows possession or relation: the address belonging to someone or something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate whose address it is or the address for a place/object (e.g. adresse de Marie, adresse de l'entreprise). Common in written and spoken French. If giving someone's email address you can say "adresse e‑mail de...". For the phrase 'the address of' in general contexts, use 'l'adresse de ...'.
target_language_example: Donne-moi l'adresse de ton frère, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your brother's address, please.

meaning: email address
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask for or give someone's electronic mail address. Can be written also as "adresse email" or "adresse électronique". Used with possessive adjectives (mon/ton/votre) and question words (Quelle est...).
target_language_example: Voici mon adresse e-mail : julie.dupont@example.com.
native_language_example: Here is my email address: julie.dupont@example.com.

meaning: Let whatever will happen happen; come what may.
additional_notes: An impersonal, somewhat literary/fixed expression used to accept an uncertain outcome — similar to English 'come what may' or 'whatever happens'. Often used after a decision or determination to act despite possible consequences. Can be standalone or follow another clause.
target_language_example: Je signe le contrat — advienne que pourra.
native_language_example: I'll sign the contract — come what may.

meaning: part of the expression 'l'affaire est (quelque chose)' — often used to say 'the matter/case is (done/settled/serious/etc.)' or in set phrases like 'l'affaire est dans le sac' ('the thing is done').
additional_notes: Alone 'affaire est' is not a standalone fixed phrase in French; it's usually seen inside longer expressions: e.g. 'l'affaire est réglée' (the matter is settled), 'l'affaire est dans le sac' (it's in the bag / it's done), or 'l'affaire est sérieuse' (the matter is serious). 'Affaire' means 'matter, case, business' and 'est' is the third-person singular of être ('is'). Useful to recognise as 'the matter is...'.
target_language_example: L'affaire est réglée, vous pouvez y aller.
native_language_example: The matter is settled, you can go.

meaning: matters/affairs relating to; things to do with (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate topics, business, or matters concerning something. Often appears in phrases like "affaires de famille" (family matters), "affaires de cœur" (matters of the heart), or "affaires de business" (business affairs). Requires a noun after "de". Can be formal or neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Ce sont des affaires de famille, nous devons en parler entre nous.
native_language_example: Those are family matters; we must discuss them among ourselves.

meaning: 'business to' or 'things to (do) for' — used as part of expressions meaning someone has matters/errands to attend to.
additional_notes: affaires à usually appears in phrases like avoir des affaires à régler/faire (to have matters to deal with / errands to do). It is not a complete phrase by itself; you need a verb (e.g., avoir) and an infinitive or qualifier after à. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: J'ai des affaires à régler avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have matters to settle before leaving.

meaning: 'in order to' or 'so as to' (expresses purpose).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to state the purpose or intention of an action. More formal than just 'pour' but functionally similar in many contexts. Example: 'afin de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Il travaille tard afin de réussir ses examens.
native_language_example: He works late in order to pass his exams.

meaning: 'so that' / 'in order that' (expresses purpose or intended result; followed by a subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose clause and usually requires the subjunctive verb mood in the subordinate clause (e.g. afin que tu comprennes). Can be slightly more formal than "pour que," which has the same meaning and is more common in speech. Use "afin de" + infinitive when followed by an infinitive instead of a finite verb.
target_language_example: Je ferme la fenêtre afin que le bruit ne nous dérange pas.
native_language_example: I close the window so that the noise doesn't bother us.

meaning: security guard; a person who protects property or people.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's job. Can be used with verbs like être (Je suis agent de sécurité), travailler comme, trouver, or être au chômage. Neutral, formal/common workplace term. Plural: agents de sécurité.
target_language_example: Elle travaille comme agent de sécurité au musée.
native_language_example: She works as a security guard at the museum.

meaning: secret agent; spy.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who works undercover or clandestinely for intelligence services. In French the adjective follows the noun (agent secret). Can be used as a short label (Agent secret!) or in a full sentence (Je suis un agent secret).
target_language_example: Elle rêve de devenir agent secret.
native_language_example: She dreams of becoming a secret agent.

meaning: 'is about' or 'concerns' (short for "il s'agit de")
additional_notes: Commonly used in the impersonal expression "il s'agit de" to introduce the subject or to say what something is about/concerns. Often contracted in speech and writing as "il s'agit d'" before a vowel (e.g. "il s'agit d'un problème"). Use when explaining what something is or what the matter is.
target_language_example: Il s'agit d'une erreur.
native_language_example: It's about/a mistake.

meaning: Oh really? / Is that so? (expression of surprise, interest, or to prompt confirmation).
additional_notes: Very common conversational phrase. Tone and intonation change the nuance: neutral curiosity, mild surprise, doubt, or irony. Often used alone or followed by a question (e.g. 'Ah bon ?' or 'Ah bon, pourquoi ?'). Not strongly formal or informal — fine in most everyday situations.
target_language_example: Ah bon, tu pars déjà ?
native_language_example: Oh really, you're leaving already?

meaning: I bought
additional_notes: Passé composé of acheter with je. It often means either "I bought" or "I've bought." The final -e in achetée appears when the direct object comes before the verb and is feminine singular, as in la robe que j'ai achetée. Otherwise, you would usually see j'ai acheté.
target_language_example: La robe que j'ai achetée hier est très belle.
native_language_example: The dress I bought yesterday is very beautiful.

meaning: changed
additional_notes: From the verb changer (to change). 'J'ai changé' = 'I changed' or 'I have changed'. Often followed by de + noun to indicate what changed (d'avis, de travail, de nom) or a direct object (les serrures). Use for personal change (opinion, job, name) or changing things.
target_language_example: J'ai changé d'avis.
native_language_example: I changed my mind.

meaning: I advised/recommended (to) — used with an infinitive verb after 'de'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of conseiller + the preposition de. Use it when saying you advised someone to do something: j'ai conseillé de + infinitive (or j'ai conseillé à quelqu'un de + infinitive to specify who). If you want to name the person advised, include 'à' before the person (e.g., je lui ai conseillé de partir).
target_language_example: Je leur ai conseillé de consulter un médecin.
native_language_example: I advised them to see a doctor.

meaning: 'I believed that it...' (short for "j'ai cru que c'") — expresses a past belief or impression about something
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause using the passé composé of croire (j'ai cru) followed by 'que' and a contraction of 'ce' + vowel-starting verb/pronoun (c'). It usually introduces a mistaken or temporary belief (e.g. 'I thought that...'). In speech and informal writing, 'j'' is often dropped and you may see 'ai cru que...' as part of a sentence after a subject pronoun (e.g. 'Je ai cru...' is not standard; the full form is 'j'ai cru que c'...' ). Common continuations: 'c'était', 'c'était fini', 'ça allait', 'c'était la bonne adresse', or 'c'était impossible.'
target_language_example: J'ai cru que c'était fermé, mais il y avait encore du monde.
native_language_example: I thought it was closed, but there were still people there.

meaning: 'asked (someone) to (do something) for me' — part of a past-tense request structure.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in the passé composé: 'J'ai demandé de + infinitive' with an indirect object pronoun 'me' when you asked someone to do something for you. More fully: 'J'ai demandé à [quelqu'un] de [faire quelque chose] (pour) moi.' In speech the 'à [quelqu'un]' can be omitted if context makes the person clear. Use 'me' before the infinitive to indicate the action benefits or affects the speaker (e.g. 'de me ramener' = 'to bring me back').
target_language_example: Je lui ai demandé de me prévenir si le vol est annulé.
native_language_example: I asked him/her to let me know if the flight is canceled.

meaning: 'asked (someone) not to' — part of the verb phrase used when saying you asked someone not to do something.
additional_notes: This is a fragment: 'ai demandé' is the first-person passé composé of 'demander' (I asked). When followed by 'de ne' it begins a negative request construction like 'Je leur ai demandé de ne pas...' (I asked them not to ...). Always complete with an infinitive and 'pas' after 'ne' to form the full negation: 'de ne pas + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Je leur ai demandé de ne pas fumer ici.
native_language_example: I asked them not to smoke here.

meaning: I asked (someone) not to ...
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé with 'avoir' + demander + infinitive construction plus negation 'ne pas' before the infinitive. It expresses that the speaker requested that someone refrain from doing something. Depending on context the subject of 'demander' can be explicit (je, je l'ai demandé) or implied. In full sentences you often see: 'J'ai demandé de ne pas + infinitive' or 'Je lui ai demandé de ne pas + infinitive.'
target_language_example: Je lui ai demandé de ne pas fumer ici.
native_language_example: I asked him/her not to smoke here.

meaning: 'I told you' (emphatic repetition: speaker reminding or insisting).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the past tense 'je (t')ai dit' ('I told you') often followed by a short reinforcing phrase (e.g. 'je ne peux pas', 'je vais bien'). In natural French the clause order is usually 'Je te l'ai dit' or 'Je vous l'ai dit' — the example form 'ai dit, je' shows the core words but is not the normal standalone order. Used to remind, insist, or conclude after having already given information.
target_language_example: Je te l'ai dit, je n'ai rien à cacher.
native_language_example: I told you, I have nothing to hide.

meaning: 'told (to) the' — a sequence from the passé composé of dire plus the preposition au (à + le), e.g. 'I told the ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but part of a sentence: ai dit = first person singular passé composé of dire (j'ai dit = I said/told). 'au' is the contraction of à + le ('to the' or 'at the'). Together they appear when you say you told something to a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'j'ai dit au professeur'). You will usually see the full form 'j'ai dit au/à la/aux/à + name'.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit au revoir avant de partir.
native_language_example: I said goodbye to him/her before leaving.

meaning: 'told (someone) not to' (part of the construction 'j'ai dit de ne pas ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but part of the perfect tense with the verb dire (j'ai dit = I told) followed by 'de ne pas' + infinitive to express telling someone not to do something. The full pattern: [person] + dire (past) + de ne pas + infinitive. Pronouns (te/vous/lui) can appear before 'ai' (Je vous ai dit) or after context. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de ne pas entrer.
native_language_example: I told you not to enter.

ai dit de ne pas le

target_language_multi_word_term: ai dit de ne pas le
meaning: 'told (someone) not to do it'.
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé construction with dire (avoir + dit) + de + infinitive and a direct object pronoun le (it). It appears in examples like «Je lui ai dit de ne pas le faire» = I told him/her not to do it. The pronoun order in French: subject + (ne) + avoir (ai) + past participle (dit) + object pronoun(s) + infinitive (faire). In casual speech you may hear contractions (Je t'ai dit de pas le faire) but standard written form uses «ne ... pas».
target_language_example: Je leur ai dit de ne pas le dire aux enfants.
native_language_example: I told them not to tell the children.

meaning: I said that it/this/that (contracted form: 'J'ai dit que c'était...' = 'I said that it was...').
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase 'J'ai dit que c'était...' (literally 'I said that it was...') used to report what you said earlier. 'ai dit' is the passé composé of 'dire' for 'je' (I said). 'c'' is the contracted form of 'ce' before a vowel or mute h (here in 'c'était'). Common in spoken and written French. Replace 'c'' + verb with the appropriate clause: e.g. 'c'était', 'c'est', 'c'était fini', 'c'est ton tour'.
target_language_example: J'ai dit que c'était prêt.
native_language_example: I said that it was ready.

meaning: 'I told (someone) that you...'.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of dire (ai dit) plus que tu = 'that you...'. Used to report what the speaker told a third person about 'you'. The subject (Je) and indirect object (lui/leur) often appear before « ai dit ». The rest of the sentence completes what was said (e.g. feelings, situation). Pronunciation context: « ai dit » is pronounced roughly like "eh dee".
target_language_example: Je leur ai dit que tu viendrais demain.
native_language_example: I told them that you would come tomorrow.

meaning: 'told (to)' — past tense structure meaning 'I told (to)'.
additional_notes: Formed from the passé composé of dire (j'ai dit) followed by à + person. Use to indicate who was told something: J'ai dit à + [person] + que... or Je l'ai dit à + [person]. Equivalent to 'I told [someone]'. Replace subject (je) and verb tense as needed.
target_language_example: J'ai dit à mon frère de ne pas s'inquiéter.
native_language_example: I told my brother not to worry.

meaning: had to
additional_notes: 1st-person singular passé composé of devoir, usually followed by an infinitive. Most often it expresses necessity in the past ('I had to'), but in some contexts it shows a guess about the past ('I must have').
target_language_example: J'ai dû appeler un médecin.
native_language_example: I had to call a doctor.

meaning: 'I heard that...' or 'I heard what...'.
additional_notes: This is part of the expression "J'ai entendu ce que..." used to report something you heard. It is followed by a clause introduced by que/qui (ce que, ce qui) or by an informal 'ce que' with spoken contractions (e.g. 't'as'). The full phrase is typically "J'ai entendu ce que..." = "I heard what/that..."
target_language_example: J'ai entendu ce que tu as dit hier soir.
native_language_example: I heard what you said last night.

meaning: 'I heard some' or 'I've heard (some)' (first-person singular, passé composé + partitive/plural)
additional_notes: This is the verb entendre (to hear) in the passé composé: j'ai entendu. When followed by des it indicates hearing some (objects, people, things) or a plural/indefinite quantity. Use for reporting something you heard. Structure: j'ai entendu des + noun. Pronunciation: [ɛ ɑ̃tɑ̃dy de].
target_language_example: J'ai entendu des bruits étranges la nuit dernière.
native_language_example: I heard some strange noises last night.

meaning: 'I tried to (you)...' — short for "j'ai essayé de te..." meaning 'I tried to [do something to/for you]' or 'I tried to [do something and involve you]'.
additional_notes: This is the contracted start of the phrase "j'ai essayé de te..." (j'ai = I have; essayé de = tried to; te/t' = you). It precedes a verb (e.g. appeler, en parler). Common in spoken and written French. The contraction t' appears before a vowel sound (t'appeler, t'en parler). English equivalent: "I tried to [verb] you" usually translated as "I tried to [verb] you" or more naturally "I tried to [verb] you/ talk to you/ tell you."
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de t'appeler hier soir, mais tu n'as pas répondu.
native_language_example: I tried to call you last night, but you didn't answer.

meaning: have had to / had to (followed by an infinitive or noun phrase) — expresses having experienced or been obliged to do/receive something
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of avoir + the preposition de: 'j'ai eu de ...'. It often appears in expressions like 'j'ai eu de la chance' (I was lucky / I had luck) or 'j'ai eu de la peine' (I was saddened / I had trouble). When followed by an infinitive after 'de' it can mean 'I had to' in contexts like 'j'ai eu de travailler' (rare/colloquial) — more commonly use 'j'ai dû' for 'I had to'. 'Ai eu de' literally means 'have had (of)'.
target_language_example: J'ai eu de la chance hier.
native_language_example: I was lucky yesterday.

meaning: 'I had the' (past tense: j'ai eu le ...)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence: ai (1st-person singular present of avoir used in compound past), eu (past participle of avoir), and le (definite article). It appears in sentences like "J'ai eu le temps" (I had the time) or "J'ai eu le mal de mer" (I experienced seasickness). It indicates that the speaker experienced/possessed something in the past. Make sure the full sentence begins with "J'ai eu le..."; other subjects change the auxiliary (e.g., "Il a eu le...").
target_language_example: J'ai eu le temps de finir le rapport.
native_language_example: I had time to finish the report.

meaning: I did what / I have done what (followed by clause).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of the passé composé (avoir + fait) followed by 'ce que' ('what' / 'that which'). Use it when saying you performed the action described in the following clause: e.g. «J'ai fait ce que tu as demandé.» Note word order: 'ai fait' is auxiliary + past participle; 'ce que' introduces the thing/action.
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que tu m'as demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you asked me.

meaning: I've done what you (asked/did) — a fragment of a sentence meaning 'I did what you ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own; it's the start or middle of a sentence using the passé composé (ai fait = j'ai fait). The full sentence would usually be 'J'ai fait ce que tu as demandé' (I did what you asked) or 'J'ai fait ce que tu as fait' (I did what you did). Note subject 'j’' is normally written before 'ai' (j'ai fait).
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que tu as demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you asked.

meaning: have/made (something); did some — used with 'faire' in passé composé plus partitive/article 'du' to indicate making, doing, or producing some of something or doing (a job) to some degree.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of faire (j'ai fait) followed by 'du' (de + le) used in different ways: 1) with nouns to mean 'made some' (Je t'ai fait du café = I made you some coffee); 2) with abstract nouns to mean 'did/made' as in 'did a good job' (J'ai fait du bon boulot); 3) in fixed expressions like 'faire du mieux' meaning 'did the best' (J'ai fait du mieux que je pouvais). 'Du' is partitive or an article and not always literal 'some' in English. Word order: subject + ai fait du + noun.
target_language_example: Je t'ai fait du chocolat chaud ce matin.
native_language_example: I made you some hot chocolate this morning.

meaning: 'I did everything that...' (start of a clause meaning you completed all that someone wanted/asked)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a sentence where the speaker says they did everything someone asked or wanted. It's normally followed by a relative clause starting with 'que' + subject + verb (e.g. 'que tu as dit', 'qu'ils ont demandé'). Common in past tense (passé composé: 'J'ai fait...').
target_language_example: J'ai fait tout ce que tu as demandé.
native_language_example: I did everything that you asked.

meaning: 'I did that for...' (used to say why or for whom you did something).
additional_notes: Common structure: subject + 'ai fait ça pour' + (person or reason). 'Ai fait' is the passé composé of 'faire' (j'ai fait = I did/made). Followed by a person (toi, nous, vous) or a purpose/reason (te protéger, ton bien). Use to explain motive or beneficiary.
target_language_example: J'ai fait ça pour t'aider à réussir.
native_language_example: I did that to help you succeed.

meaning: I've finished with / I'm done with (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you have ended your involvement, relationship, or patience with someone or something. Often preceded by 'j'en' (J'en ai fini avec...) to mean 'I'm done with that' or 'I've had enough of it/him/her/you.' Can express finality or emotional closure. Tone can be neutral or strong depending on context.
target_language_example: J'en ai fini avec ses mensonges.
native_language_example: I'm done with his lies.

meaning: 'have never had' (first-person singular, past experience).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé negative construction: Je n'ai jamais eu de + noun. Use to say you have never experienced or possessed something. Note that in spoken French the 'ne' is often omitted: J'ai jamais eu de. The 'de' is the partitive/indefinite article after negation and remains before singular/plural nouns (e.g. je n'ai jamais eu de réponse, je n'ai jamais eu de fils).
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais eu de voiture.
native_language_example: I have never had a car.

meaning: ‘I read in’ or ‘I read it in’ (used to say you saw/read something in a source or perceived something in someone's expression).
additional_notes: Combines the past tense of lire (j'ai lu) with the preposition dans + source or location (journal, livre, yeux, pensées). Use to cite where you read information (Je l'ai lu dans le journal) or metaphorically to say you 'read' something in someone's eyes/thoughts (J'ai lu dans ses yeux). The object (ce, ça, l') may be explicit before 'ai lu'.
target_language_example: Je l'ai lu dans un article hier.
native_language_example: I read it in an article yesterday.

meaning: adds emphasis: 'I even' (used to stress that something surprising or extreme happened).
additional_notes: Combines the auxiliary 'ai' (from 'avoir') with 'même' to emphasize the verb. Common in spoken and informal French. Often followed by a past participle (J'ai même pensé) or another verb form depending on tense. Can express surprise, contradiction, or an unexpected action.
target_language_example: J'ai même oublié son anniversaire.
native_language_example: I even forgot his birthday.

meaning: didn't
additional_notes: informal spoken French for "n'ai pas" after je/j'. In everyday speech, the ne is often dropped: j'ai pas = je n'ai pas. It is usually part of a negative past tense with avoir, so English often uses "didn't" rather than a literal "haven't." Not used in formal writing.
target_language_example: J'ai pas compris.
native_language_example: I didn't understand.

meaning: I spent/ I took/ I passed a (depends on context) — first-person singular past of 'passer' plus an object (e.g. 'ai passé un examen' = I took an exam; 'ai passé un bon moment' = I had a good time).
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé: 'ai' (auxiliary avoir) + past participle 'passé'. The meaning changes with the object that follows: - 'passé un examen' = took an exam; - 'passé un moment' = spent/had a time; - 'passé un appel' = made/placed a call. Use with an object (un/une/les, etc.).
target_language_example: J'ai passé un examen hier.
native_language_example: I took an exam yesterday.

meaning: I thought that... (short for "J'ai pensé que c'était...").
additional_notes: This is part of the past-tense phrase "J'ai pensé que c'était..." used to express a past opinion or assumption. In spoken and written French you often see the contraction "c'" before a vowel (c'était). The full phrase is "J'ai pensé que c'était..." and is followed by what you thought (a fact, a person, an opinion, etc.).
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que c'était trop tôt pour appeler.
native_language_example: I thought that it was too early to call.

meaning: I thought that you / I thought you would
additional_notes: Part of the passé composé construction "J'ai pensé que vous..." used to introduce what the speaker believed or expected about the listener. Often followed by verbs in the conditional (auriez, voudriez) or an infinitive (aimeriez, savoir) to express expectations, assumptions, or polite reasoning. Use 'J'ai pensé que vous...' for 'I thought you...' (formal or plural 'you'). For informal singular use 'j'ai pensé que tu...'.
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que vous aimeriez ce livre.
native_language_example: I thought you would like this book.

meaning: 'may have' or 'might have' (used to express possibility about something that happened).
additional_notes: Formed with the auxiliary verb (ai = j'ai) + adverb peut-être. Used to indicate uncertainty about a past action or event (often followed by a past participle or clause). Can appear in negative or polite contexts (e.g. Je n'ai peut-être pas..., Je vous ai peut-être...).
target_language_example: Je l'ai peut-être déjà vu quelque part.
native_language_example: I might have already seen him somewhere.

meaning: I no longer have
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of "je n'ai plus" (I no longer have / I don't have anymore). In writing you should use the full form "je n'ai plus"; in speech the "ne" is often dropped and pronunciation links "ai" and "plus". Use to say you stopped having or possessing something or that something has ended (e.g. time, patience, money).
target_language_example: J'ai plus de pain.
native_language_example: I don't have any bread anymore.

meaning: 'I have put/placed' or 'I asked (a question)' depending on context (past participle of poser with avoir: je + ai + posé).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé (perfect) form of the verb poser. 'Poser' can mean 'to put/place', 'to set down', 'to lay', 'to ask' (a question), 'to pose' (a problem), or 'to place (a call)'. The exact translation depends on the object: e.g. 'J'ai posé la valise' = I put down the suitcase; 'J'ai posé une question' = I asked a question. Use with an object or reflexive form changes meaning ('je me suis posé' = I asked myself / I wondered).
target_language_example: J'ai posé la tasse sur la table.
native_language_example: I put the cup on the table.

meaning: I put/placed a (female noun) / I asked a (question).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of poser + a feminine noun: 'j'ai posé une...' Depending on context, poser means 'to place' (an object) or 'to ask' (a question). The subject is 'je' contracted with the auxiliary 'ai' (avoir). You will need the feminine noun after 'une' (e.g. 'une question', 'une chaise', 'une lettre').
target_language_example: J'ai posé une question pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: I asked a question during the meeting.

meaning: 'I took' or 'I have taken' followed by a plural noun (e.g. I took some...).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present perfect (passé composé) of prendre: j'ai pris + plural noun (des = some). Used to say you took, had, or consumed several items. Context determines translation (took, had, bought, ate, photographed, etc.). Watch liaison: j'ai pris des + noun.
target_language_example: J'ai pris des photos pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: I took some photos during the trip.

meaning: 'I have taken my' or 'I took my' (used before a feminine noun), often in expressions like 'I made my decision' or 'I took my day off'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person passé composé of 'prendre' + the feminine possessive 'ma'. It appears before a feminine noun (ma décision, ma journée). Common uses: 'J'ai pris ma décision' = I've made my decision; 'J'ai pris ma journée' = I took the day off. Context determines whether it's a physical taking, making a choice, or taking time off.
target_language_example: J'ai pris ma décision hier soir.
native_language_example: I made my decision last night.

meaning: 'I took a' or 'I had a' (feminine singular object) — past tense using prendre.
additional_notes: Combines the first-person singular passé composé of prendre (j'ai pris = I took/had) with the feminine indefinite article une. Used before feminine nouns: une douche (a shower), une photo (a photo), une place (a seat). Depending on context, prendre can mean 'take', 'have' (a meal/shower), 'capture' (a photo), or 'get/secure' (a place).
target_language_example: J'ai pris une photo du coucher de soleil.
native_language_example: I took a photo of the sunset.

meaning: 'met/encountered a' (I have met a... / I met a...)
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé form of the verb rencontrer (rencontrer = to meet/encounter). It combines the auxiliary avoir (ai) + past participle rencontré and is followed by an indefinite article + noun (un/une). Use it to say you met someone or encountered something: e.g. J'ai rencontré un ami / J'ai rencontré un problème. For spoken French, the passé composé is commonly used to describe past events.
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai rencontré un collègue au marché.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I met a colleague at the market.

meaning: have/had ... nothing
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the combination of the auxiliary verb form ai (from avoir) plus rien (nothing) used in negative past (passé composé) or perfect tense constructions: Je n'ai rien + past participle = I didn't ... anything / I haven't ... anything. In spoken French the ne is often dropped, so you'll hear "j'ai rien" instead of "je n'ai rien." Examples in the input show both indirect object pronouns (leur, vous) and past participles: Je ne leur ai rien donné = I didn't give them anything.
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien vu hier soir.
native_language_example: I didn't see anything last night.

meaning: 'I found some' (incomplete/unnatural fragment)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a natural, complete French phrase by itself. It looks like part of a sentence using the passé composé of trouver (j'ai trouvé = I found) followed by quelque(s) + noun (e.g. «j'ai trouvé quelques livres» = I found some books). Alone, 'ai trouvé quelque' is missing the subject pronoun (j') and the noun after 'quelque/quelques'. Use 'j'ai trouvé' + a noun or 'j'ai trouvé que' (meaning 'I found that') depending on intended meaning.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé quelques idées intéressantes.
native_language_example: I found some interesting ideas.

meaning: really (have)
additional_notes: Combines the auxiliary verb 'ai' (1st/3rd person singular of 'avoir' in passé composé contexts) with the adverb 'vraiment' meaning 'really' or 'truly'. Used to add emphasis to a past action or state: 'I really did', 'I really enjoyed', 'I really believed it'. In English you usually place 'really' before the main verb or after the auxiliary ('I really did', 'I have really...').
target_language_example: Je l'ai vraiment fait.
native_language_example: I really did it.

meaning: have seen (something/someone) in (a place, medium, or someone's expression).
additional_notes: Form of the verb voir in passé composé (j'ai vu) followed by dans + noun. Used to say you saw someone or something inside/within a location or figuratively 'in someone's eyes/look'. Context determines whether 'dans' is literal (in the newspaper, in the park) or figurative (in his eyes/regard). Change subject/pronouns as needed (Je vous ai vu, Nous l'avons vu).
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu dans la vitrine ce matin.
native_language_example: I saw it in the shop window this morning.

meaning: 'have seen' + partitive/indefinite 'de' (seen some/seen a lot of/seen ...)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb avoir (j'ai) + vu (past participle of voir) followed by de (partitive or indefinite). Depending on context, 'vu de' can mean 'seen some' (e.g. 'de la lumière' = some light) or appear in expressions like 'j'ai vu de tout' (I've seen it all / I've seen many things). It can also be followed by a possessive phrase ('de mes yeux' = with my own eyes). Pay attention to gender/number and article after de (de la, du, des) and to word order.
target_language_example: J'ai vu de très belles choses pendant mon voyage.
native_language_example: I saw some very beautiful things during my trip.

meaning: I saw the ... (past tense: j'ai vu + masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of voir (to see). J'ai vu le is followed by a masculine singular noun (le dossier, le juge, le futur, etc.). Use j'ai vu la for feminine nouns and j'ai vu les for plurals. It can be literal (I saw the file) or figurative/idiomatic (I saw the future, I saw the face of God).
target_language_example: J'ai vu le film hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw the movie last night.

meaning: 'saw his/her/its' (perfect tense: I saw his/her/its ...).
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular passé composé form of 'voir' (j'ai vu) followed by a possessive adjective (son). It appears in sentences like "J'ai vu son chien" = "I saw his/her dog." The gender of the possessed noun determines whether 'son' refers to his, her, or its in French; context tells which. In speech and writing, the 'j'' in 'j'ai' is often elided before a vowel sound (j'ai vu).
target_language_example: J'ai vu son frère au café.
native_language_example: I saw his/her brother at the café.

meaning: 'I saw a' or 'I have seen a' (past tense: first person singular of 'voir' + indefinite article 'une').
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form: 'j'ai vu une ...' = 'I saw a ...' or 'I have seen a ...'. Use 'une' for feminine singular nouns. The example 3 ('Je l'ai vu une fois') uses the same verb form 'ai vu' but with an object pronoun ('l'') and 'une fois' (once); note agreement: with direct object preceding the verb, past participle can agree (here 'vu' stays masculine because 'l'' refers to a masculine object).
target_language_example: J'ai vu une voiture rouge hier.
native_language_example: I saw a red car yesterday.

meaning: 'saw (someone/something) at' — first-person singular passé composé of voir (j'ai vu) followed by the preposition à to indicate location or event.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the structure j'ai vu + à used when saying you saw someone or something at a place or during an event. Usually appears within a full sentence with an object and a place/event: e.g. «J'ai vu Paul à la gare.» Conjugation reminder: voir → j'ai vu (passé composé).
target_language_example: J'ai vu à la fenêtre ce chat blanc.
native_language_example: I saw that white cat at the window.

meaning: have been
additional_notes: first-person singular form used with « j’ »: « j’ai été ». Literally « have been ». It often appears before another past participle to make a passive meaning like « I was acquitted / bitten / robbed ».
target_language_example: J'ai été surpris par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: I was surprised by the news.

meaning: 'also have' or 'I also have' when used after the subject pronoun 'J'' (I).
additional_notes: Combines the first-person singular of avoir (j'ai = I have) with 'aussi' (also). Used to add that the speaker, in addition to someone else or to previous statements, possesses or needs something, or wants to say something. Word order: 'J'ai aussi ...' (I also have ... / I also need ... / I also want to tell you ...). In spoken/written French the contraction 'J'' is required before 'ai'.
target_language_example: J'ai aussi des questions à poser.
native_language_example: I also have some questions to ask.

meaning: I have something else / I have other things (to say, to do, etc.).
additional_notes: Used after 'J' (je) as in 'J'ai autre chose...' to indicate you have something different, additional, or other plans/ideas/requests. Often completed with prepositions or verbs (de prévu, en tête, à te dire, à te demander) but can stand alone ('J'ai autre chose.') to mean 'I have something else' or 'I have other matters.' Neutral register; common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: J'ai autre chose à te demander demain.
native_language_example: I have something else to ask you tomorrow.

meaning: 'I need a little' or 'I need some'.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'J'ai besoin d'un peu...' used to ask for a small amount of something (air, water, time, space, etc.). In normal speech you usually include the subject 'J'' (J'ai besoin d'un peu de...) — the input omits 'J'' but examples show full form. After 'd'un peu' you often say 'de' + noun (e.g. d'un peu d'eau) or simply 'd'un peu' + whatever is understood from context. Use for modest requests or to soften a need.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un peu de calme, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a little peace and quiet, please.

meaning: 'need to' (reflexive: I need to do something for myself).
additional_notes: This is the conjugated form of 'avoir besoin de' with a reflexive verb following (je + ai besoin de + me + infinitive). Use it to express a personal need to do an action for yourself (e.g., rest, relax, concentrate). In English it corresponds to 'I need to [verb]' when the verb is reflexive ('to rest', 'to relax'). The pronoun 'me' agrees with the subject (je).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de me détendre ce soir.
native_language_example: I need to relax tonight.

meaning: 'I need to (you)...' — part of the phrase 'J'ai besoin de te...' meaning 'I need to (do something) to/with you' or 'I need to (verb) you'.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of sentences where the speaker expresses a need involving the listener. In full form it appears as 'J'ai besoin de te + infinitive' (e.g. 'J'ai besoin de te parler' = 'I need to talk to you'). In spoken French the subject 'Je' + 'ai' are often contracted to 'J'' (J'ai). The construction requires an infinitive verb after 'te' and 'te' is the object pronoun meaning 'you' (informal singular). For formal or plural you would use 'vous' instead: 'J'ai besoin de vous parler.'
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de te demander quelque chose d'important.
native_language_example: I need to ask you something important.

meaning: contraction appearing in spoken/written French meaning 'I have what he...' or part of a clause like 'j'ai ce qu'il...' (I have what he/it ...).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence of words: 'ai' (1st/2nd person singular of avoir in present: j'ai / tu as), 'ce' (this/that/what), 'qu'il' (that he/it). You'll most commonly see it inside a larger sentence such as 'J'ai ce qu'il faut' (I have what is needed) or 'J'ai ce qu'il me faut' (I have what I need). Alone, 'ai ce qu'il' is incomplete and must be part of a full clause. For beginners, learn common complete phrases: 'J'ai ce qu'il faut' = I have what it takes / what is needed.
target_language_example: J'ai ce qu'il me faut pour réparer la porte.
native_language_example: I have what I need to fix the door.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment (e.g. from 'j'ai ce que...' = 'I have what...').
additional_notes: This is not a common standalone expression. More likely a piece of a sentence combining the verb 'avoir' (ai) and the demonstrative 'ce que' (what/that which). For example: 'J'ai ce que tu veux' = 'I have what you want.' Beginners should treat 'ai' as the 1st-person singular present of 'avoir' (I have) and 'ce que' as 'what/that which'.
target_language_example: J'ai ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I have what you want.

meaning: have some
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of j’ai de..., where ai is the first-person singular of avoir ("have"). It often introduces an indefinite amount, as in j’ai de l’eau ("I have some water"), but de can also be part of a longer expression, so this is not really a fixed phrase on its own.
target_language_example: J’ai de la chance aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I'm lucky today.

meaning: I have some good (plural).
additional_notes: This is the tail of the common phrase 'J'ai de bonnes + [noun]' meaning 'I have good + plural noun' (e.g., nouvelles, raisons). 'De' is used after 'avoir' when describing an unspecified quantity of plural nouns. Use 'de bonnes' before a feminine plural noun; before masculine plural use 'de bons'.
target_language_example: J'ai de bonnes idées pour le projet.
native_language_example: I have some good ideas for the project.

meaning: I have (some) — used before a singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of 'avoir' (j'ai) followed by the partitive/article 'de l'' (de + l') used when talking about having an unspecified amount or possession of something that begins with a vowel or mute h (de l'argent, de l'espoir, de l'expérience). In many cases in spoken French, 'de' is used after expressions of quantity; with 'j'ai' it often simply means 'I have' + noun. Use 'du' before masculine consonant nouns and 'de la' before feminine consonant nouns. After negation, 'de' usually replaces the partitive (e.g. je n'ai pas d'argent).
target_language_example: J'ai de l'eau dans la bouteille.
native_language_example: I have some water in the bottle.

meaning: I have (some) [feminine noun]
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of avoir + partitive article 'de la' used before feminine singular nouns to mean 'some' or an indefinite amount, or in certain expressions (e.g. 'avoir de la chance' = 'to be lucky'). In everyday speech the 'de' can contract or be omitted in some fixed expressions (e.g. 'j'ai la visite' is possible but 'j'ai de la visite' means 'I have visitors'). Use 'j'ai du' for masculine nouns and 'j'ai des' for plural nouns.
target_language_example: J'ai de la chance aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have some luck today / I'm lucky today.

meaning: have some
additional_notes: Usually appears as j'ai des... before a plural noun. des is the plural indefinite article ('some'), but English often leaves it untranslated: j'ai des choses à faire = 'I have things to do.'
target_language_example: J'ai des idées pour le week-end.
native_language_example: I have some ideas for the weekend.

meaning: have two
additional_notes: This looks like the conjugated verb avoir (ai = I have) + the number deux (two). It's not a fixed idiom — it's simply the first-person present form 'I have' followed by the number 'two' (e.g., 'j'ai deux...'). Note that 'ai deux' alone is uncommon in writing because the subject pronoun j' (or je) usually appears before 'ai'.
target_language_example: J'ai deux livres.
native_language_example: I have two books.

meaning: have some
additional_notes: Usually appears as j'ai du + an uncountable noun, as in j'ai du pain or j'ai du temps. Here du is the partitive article, often translated as 'some'. Don't confuse it with dû: j'ai dû means 'I had to'.
target_language_example: J'ai du temps ce soir.
native_language_example: I have some time tonight.

meaning: 'I already have a' (first-person singular, present tense)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression but a sequence: ai (avoir, 1st person singular present) + déjà (already) + un (indefinite article). It begins a statement saying the speaker already possesses or has something (masculine singular noun follows). For feminine nouns use 'une' (j'ai déjà une...). Contraction: written as 'j'ai déjà un...' in full.
target_language_example: J'ai déjà un vélo, merci.
native_language_example: I already have a bike, thanks.

meaning: still have
additional_notes: Formed from the verb avoir (j'ai) + encore. Used to say you still possess or have remaining something (time, work, questions, etc.). In English often translated as "still have" or "have ... left". Placement: encore follows the verb. Examples: "J'ai encore le temps" = "I still have time"; "J'ai encore quelques questions" = "I have a few questions left."
target_language_example: J'ai encore une heure avant le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I still have an hour before the appointment.

meaning: 'have faith' or 'have faith in' (I have faith in...).
additional_notes: Used with a subject (J'ai = I have) plus 'foi en' + person or thing to express trust, confidence, or religious faith. Common in both personal and religious contexts. In these examples 'J'ai foi en nous/vous' means 'I believe in us/you' — I trust our/your ability or future.
target_language_example: J'ai foi en toi, tu peux y arriver.
native_language_example: I have faith in you; you can make it.

meaning: 'have just' (I have just / I just did).
additional_notes: Combination of the auxiliary verb avoir in first-person singular (ai) + juste meaning 'just' (recently). Used in compound tenses (passé composé) to indicate a very recent action when followed by a past participle: j'ai juste fini = I just finished. Can also appear alone in speech to soften or limit a statement (e.g., je n'ai juste pas le temps).
target_language_example: J'ai juste mangé il y a cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I just ate five minutes ago.

meaning: have time (I have time / I've got time).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present form of the verb phrase 'avoir le temps'. Used to say you are available or not rushed. Common responses: 'J'ai le temps' (I have time) and 'Je n'ai pas le temps' (I don't have time). Can be followed by an infinitive: 'J'ai le temps de t'aider' (I have time to help you).
target_language_example: J'ai le temps de boire un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have time to drink a coffee before leaving.

meaning: might have
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb avoir (j'ai = I have) with the adverb peut‑être (maybe/might). Use it to express uncertainty about possessing or obtaining something (e.g. an object, a job, an opportunity). Word order: j'ai peut‑être + noun or j'en ai peut‑être + quantity. In spoken French, the pronunciation can run together.
target_language_example: J'ai peut-être une idée pour le projet.
native_language_example: I might have an idea for the project.

meaning: have a lot of / have plenty of
additional_notes: Informal way to say you have many things, much of something, or are very busy. Used before a noun (plenty of X) or phrase (plenty to do). Common in spoken French; 'plein' is invariable when followed by 'de'.
target_language_example: J'ai plein de rendez-vous cette semaine.
native_language_example: I have a lot of appointments this week.

meaning: have only
additional_notes: This is the contraction of "ai" (from "avoir") + "que" used in constructions meaning "to have only" or "to have nothing but." It commonly appears in negative or restrictive sentences where French uses "ne... que" to mean "only." In spoken and written French the "ne" is often dropped: "J'ai qu'une chose" = "Je n'ai qu'une chose." The pronoun/phrase after can be singular or gendered (un/une).
target_language_example: Je n'ai qu'un seul livre.
native_language_example: I only have one book.

meaning: 'only need (timewise)' or 'I'll just be (time amount)'.
additional_notes: Used in expressions like 'J'en ai que pour + time' to say you only need or will take a short amount of time. Common colloquial structure; the full form is often 'Je n'en ai que pour une minute' meaning 'I only need one minute (for that)'. 'En' refers to the task/situation mentioned earlier. Negative 'ne' is often dropped in spoken French: 'J'en ai que pour...'.
target_language_example: J'en ai que pour deux minutes, attendez-moi.
native_language_example: I only need two minutes, wait for me.

meaning: I have someone / I have someone (with me) / I have someone to see (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the verb 'avoir' (j'ai) + 'quelqu'un' (someone). Meaning depends on context and additional words: 'J'ai quelqu'un d'autre' = 'I have someone else' (often about a relationship or another person); 'J'ai quelqu'un à voir' = 'I have someone to see' (meaning an appointment or person to visit). Use with context words (e.g. 'd'autre', 'à voir', 'avec moi') to clarify exact meaning.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir, j'ai quelqu'un à la maison.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out tonight, I have someone at home.

meaning: I have something
additional_notes: Usually appears as j'ai quelque chose, because ai is the je form of avoir and je contracts to j' before a vowel. It can mean literally having something, or more broadly having something to say, do, show, etc., depending on what follows.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

meaning: I have something important (to say / to do / to ask).
additional_notes: This phrase is the tail of full sentences that start with J' (J'ai quelque chose d'important...). Use it to announce that you possess/need to communicate or do an important thing. Often followed by an infinitive and an indirect object: à dire, à faire, à te demander, à vous dire, etc. Polite/formal distinction: use 'te' for informal singular you and 'vous' for formal or plural you.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you.

meaning: 'I have a few' (used before a plural noun)
additional_notes: Formed from the verb avoir in the first person singular (j'ai = I have) plus quelques ('a few'). Used to indicate a small, indefinite number of things. Always followed by a plural noun (quelques idées, quelques questions). Neutral register.
target_language_example: J'ai quelques livres à lire.
native_language_example: I have a few books to read.

meaning: 'have nothing' / 'don't have anything' (informal negation used in spoken French)
additional_notes: This is the contracted, informal spoken form of je n'ai rien (I have nothing / I don't have anything). In casual conversation the ne is often dropped: J'ai rien instead of Je n'ai rien. Use the full form in formal writing. It can appear in phrases like J'ai rien à dire (I have nothing to say) or J'ai rien d'autre (I don't have anything else).
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai rien à ajouter.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have anything to add.

meaning: 'I don't have any...' (colloquial/informal shortened form of 'je n'ai rien de...')
additional_notes: This is a contracted, colloquial fragment used in spoken French when the subject 'je' and the negation 'ne' are dropped: '(je) n'ai rien de...' meaning 'I don't have anything (that)...' or 'there is nothing (that) ... for me'. It's incomplete on its own and needs a following adjective, noun or clause: e.g. 'ai rien d'intéressant' = '(I) don't have anything interesting'. Common in casual conversation; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: J'ai regardé le menu, mais j'ai rien d'intéressant à commander.
native_language_example: I looked at the menu, but I don't have anything interesting to order.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase; it's likely a fragment: 'ai' is the first‑person singular present of 'avoir' (I have) and 'sur' is the preposition 'on/over/about'.
additional_notes: You will not find 'ai sur' as a standalone idiomatic expression. It can appear when 'ai' (j'ai) is followed by 'sur' in a sentence, for example in constructions like 'j'ai sur moi' (I have on me / I am carrying) or 'j'ai des doutes sur...' where 'ai' and 'sur' are separated by other words. Remember: in speech and writing you normally use the contracted form 'j'ai' instead of 'je ai'.
target_language_example: J'ai sur moi mon passeport.
native_language_example: I have my passport on me.

meaning: I have so much / I have so many (colloquial/incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone standard phrase in French. It looks like the first-person singular present of avoir (j'ai) followed by 'tant' ('so much' / 'so many'). In natural French you would say 'j'ai tant (de)...' or 'j'ai tellement (de)...' For countable nouns use 'j'ai tant de livres' (I have so many books). For uncountable use 'j'ai tant d'argent' (I have so much money) or 'j'ai tellement faim' (I'm so hungry) when using adverbial 'tellement'. Without 'de' or following noun, 'j'ai tant' sounds incomplete or poetic (e.g. 'J'ai tant à dire' = I have so much to say).
target_language_example: J'ai tant de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have so many things to do today.

meaning: I have so many / I have so much
additional_notes: Use with a noun after 'de' to express a large quantity (tant de + noun). 'Ai' is the first-person singular present of 'avoir' (j'ai). With adjectives or numbers, word order may change. Example: « J'ai tant de travail » = I have so much work. Can convey frustration or emphasis.
target_language_example: J'ai tant de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have so many things to do today.

meaning: I have so many things (to do) / I have a lot going on.
additional_notes: A partial phrase built from the verb avoir (ai = I have) + tant de choses (so many things). Often used to say you have many tasks, responsibilities or matters on your mind; usually completed in a full sentence like «J'ai tant de choses à faire» (I have so many things to do). Informal/formal-neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai tant de choses à régler cette semaine.
native_language_example: I have so many things to sort out this week.

meaning: I have/I'm so (much) — used to intensify feelings, desires, needs, or quantities.
additional_notes: Always follows "J'" or "Je" + verb (here "ai" = "have"). "Tellement" intensifies whatever comes after: chance, faim (hunger), envie (desire), hâte (eagerness), etc. Can be translated as "so," "so much," or "such" depending on context (e.g., "J'ai tellement faim" = "I'm so hungry"; "J'ai tellement de choses" = "I have so many things" ). Be aware that it can modify polite or vulgar phrases (examples include sexual language); tone depends on the noun or phrase it intensifies.
target_language_example: J'ai tellement hâte de te revoir.
native_language_example: I'm so eager to see you again.

meaning: 'I have everything (that)...' or 'I have all I need.'
additional_notes: This is a common shortened form used in sentences starting with J'ai tout ce qu'il/ce/il me faut/il vous faut etc. It means you possess everything required or needed. The full phrase is usually J'ai tout ce qu'il faut or J'ai tout ce qu'il me faut. Use il faut to express necessity (what is needed).
target_language_example: J'ai tout ce qu'il me faut pour cuisiner ce soir.
native_language_example: I have everything I need to cook tonight.

meaning: I have something to (ask/tell/show/propose) you; 'truc' = something/thing (informal).
additional_notes: Used in casual speech to introduce that you want to ask, tell, show, or propose something to the listener. 'Truc' is a vague, informal word meaning 'thing' or 'something.' The full phrase is usually: 'J'ai un truc à te...' + verb (demander, dire, montrer, proposer). Contraction: 'ai' follows 'J'' (J'ai).
target_language_example: J'ai un truc à te demander : peux-tu m'aider ce soir ?
native_language_example: I have something to ask you: can you help me tonight?

meaning: 'have a' (first-person singular of 'avoir' + indefinite article 'un') — 'I have a ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the present-tense form 'j'ai un' split after a pronoun 'en' in examples (e.g. 'j'en ai un' = 'I have one of them'). Here 'ai' is the verb 'avoir' (to have) for 'je' (I) and 'un' is the masculine indefinite article or 'one'. When used with 'en' (a pronoun), 'j'en ai un' means 'I have one (of them)'. Without 'en', 'j'ai un' simply means 'I have a/an'.
target_language_example: J'ai un livre intéressant.
native_language_example: I have an interesting book.

meaning: have a (feminine noun following)
additional_notes: This is the verb form j'ai (I have) followed by the indefinite article une. It's used before a feminine singular noun: e.g. j'ai une question, j'ai une idée. In examples where the subject is spoken, the full phrase is usually "j'ai une". The meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: J'ai une question pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a question for you.

meaning: 'have a question' (as in: I have a question).
additional_notes: This is part of the sentence Je/J' ai une question (I have a question). Use when you want to ask something or get someone's attention to ask. Common polite follow-ups: «Puis-je poser une question ?», «J'ai une question à propos de…». Contraction: Je becomes J' before a vowel (J'ai).
target_language_example: J'ai une question sur le devoir.
native_language_example: I have a question about the homework.

meaning: have a question for (someone).
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase "(J')ai une question à + [person]" meaning "I have a question for [person]." Often followed by a verb or a noun phrase: e.g. "J'ai une question à vous poser" (I have a question to ask you). The subject is usually "j'" or "je" (J'ai) but the construction can be adapted: "Il a une question à te poser."
target_language_example: J'ai une question à vous poser.
native_language_example: I have a question for you.

meaning: 'I have one' or 'I have (a) ...' depending on context; often used to introduce news, information, or an item.
additional_notes: Ai une is the part of the verb phrase j'ai une (I have a/one). When combined as j'en ai une, en replaces a previously mentioned noun (of them/one of those): 'I have one of those' or 'I have another'. Commonly used to introduce news or something to tell someone (J'ai une nouvelle = I have news). Context determines whether it's 'one', 'another', 'a piece of news', or 'a good one'.
target_language_example: J'en ai une intéressante à te raconter.
native_language_example: I have an interesting one to tell you.

meaning: adds emphasis to 'avoir' (to have); means 'really have' or 'truly' (e.g. 'I really need', 'I'm really hungry').
additional_notes: Used to intensify a statement with the verb avoir (J'ai...). 'Vraiment' is an adverb meaning 'really' or 'truly' and usually follows the conjugated verb (J'ai vraiment...). Common in expressions like J'ai vraiment besoin de..., J'ai vraiment faim, J'en ai vraiment envie. Word order: subject + avoir + vraiment + rest.
target_language_example: J'ai vraiment besoin d'aide maintenant.
native_language_example: I really need help right now.

meaning: with the help of; assisted by
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something provides help or assistance. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (aide de quelqu'un / aide de quelque chose). In everyday French you may also hear 'avec l'aide de' which is slightly more explicit. Can introduce a means or an assistant.
target_language_example: Il a réussi l'examen grâce à l'aide de son professeur.
native_language_example: He passed the exam with the help of his teacher.

meaning: to help with (something).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate assisting someone by using or dealing with a thing or task: aider quelqu'un avec quelque chose. Can be followed by a noun, a verb in the -ing sense in English (French uses an infinitive), or a pronoun. Example: Je peux t'aider avec tes devoirs / Je vais l'aider avec le déménagement.
target_language_example: Je peux t'aider avec ton projet si tu veux.
native_language_example: I can help you with your project if you want.

meaning: to help her / to help the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Aider = to help. When followed by a feminine singular noun or the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (meaning 'her' or 'it' for a feminine noun), it becomes 'aider la...' or 'aider la' + pronoun. Context shows whether 'la' means 'her' (person) or 'the' (feminine thing). In spoken French 'aider la' as two words is often the start of a phrase (e.g. 'aider la voisine', 'aider la faire' is incorrect — use 'l'aider' for verb pronoun). Use l'aider instead of aider la + verb pronoun.
target_language_example: Peux-tu aider la voisine à porter ses sacs ?
native_language_example: Can you help the neighbor (female) carry her bags?

meaning: to help one's (something); 'aider' = to help, 'sa' = his/her/its (feminine singular possessive).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the start of a verb + possessive structure: 'aider' (to help) followed by 'sa' (her/his/its) + a feminine noun (e.g. 'mère', 'voiture', 'carrière'). The gender of the noun determines using 'sa' (feminine) rather than 'son'. Context will complete the meaning (who is being helped and what is being helped). Pronunciation note: 'sa' is pronounced /sa/.
target_language_example: Je veux aider sa sœur à réviser pour l'examen.
native_language_example: I want to help his/her sister study for the exam.

meaning: to help your (someone).
additional_notes: Common structure: aider + possessive (ton/ta/tes) + person (père, frère, etc.). Means to give assistance to the named person or help them with something. Imperative forms are frequent (Va aider ton frère = Go help your brother). Use appropriate possessive: ton (masculine singular or before a vowel), ta (feminine singular), tes (plural).
target_language_example: Va aider ton frère à finir ses devoirs.
native_language_example: Go help your brother finish his homework.

meaning: 'to help your' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Aider means 'to help'. 'Votre' is the formal or plural possessive adjective meaning 'your'. Together they are not a fixed phrase but appear when telling someone to help or assist something belonging to them (e.g., aider votre enfant, aider votre équipe). Use 'ton' (informal singular) instead of 'votre' with friends/family. Verb must agree in context (e.g., 'pour vous aider' = 'to help you').
target_language_example: Je peux aider votre enfant avec ses devoirs.
native_language_example: I can help your child with his/her homework.

meaning: kind/friendly toward; willing to do something for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who is pleasant, polite or willing to help someone. Commonly follows a noun or pronoun: aimable pour + verb or + quelqu'un. Can mean 'kind to' or 'nice enough to' (do something). Tone is neutral/polite.
target_language_example: Il a été aimable pour nous aider avec les bagages.
native_language_example: He was kind enough to help us with the luggage.

meaning: 'likes what' or 'likes that which'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb aimer (to like/love) with the relative phrase ce que (what/that which). Used to say someone likes something described by a clause that follows. Word order: subject + aime ce que + clause. Can express preference for actions, qualities or things.
target_language_example: Elle aime ce que tu as préparé.
native_language_example: She likes what you prepared.

meaning: 'likes (someone) for (a quality) at'; used to say what someone likes about another person or thing
additional_notes: This construction combines the verb aimer (to like/love) with chez to specify the trait, place, or aspect in which the liking is focused. It's common in phrases like « J'aime chez toi ta patience » (I like your patience) or « J'aime chez elle son humour » (What I like about her is her sense of humor). In everyday speech, French speakers more often say « ce que j'aime chez + quelqu'un » or « j'aime chez + quelqu'un + (son/sa...) » rather than the two-word fragment alone. Use with a noun or clause describing the admired quality.
target_language_example: Ce que j'aime chez lui, c'est sa gentillesse.
native_language_example: What I like about him is his kindness.

meaning: 'likes ... like' or 'loves ... as' (comparison structure)
additional_notes: Formed from the verb aimer followed by the comparative connector comme. Used to compare how someone likes or loves something/someone, or to introduce an example or manner (e.g. 'aime comme un fou' — loves like a madman).
