Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Elle aime comme une folle la musique classique.
native_language_example: She loves classical music like a madwoman.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in modern French; appears to be the verb 'aime' (from 'aimer') followed by the preposition 'de' — context-dependent and usually incorrect as a standalone sequence. 'Aimer' typically takes a direct object or an infinitive without 'de'.
additional_notes: 'Aime de' is not a normal construction by itself. You will see 'aime de' only inside larger, grammatically correct sequences where 'de' belongs to the following phrase (e.g., « il aime de tout son cœur » in literary/archaic style) or in errors by learners. To express liking + verb use 'aimer' + infinitive (j'aime nager). To express liking that something happens use 'aimer que' + subjunctive (j'aime que tu viennes).
target_language_example: Il aime de parler en public, selon certains, mais la tournure est maladroite.
native_language_example: He likes to speak in public, according to some, but the phrasing is awkward.

meaning: has liked/loves (something or someone) since (a time or event).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'aimer' (to like/love) in the appropriate conjugated form with the preposition 'depuis' (since/for). Use 'depuis' to indicate when a feeling or action started in the past and continues into the present: e.g., 'Il aime depuis 2010' (He has loved/supported since 2010) or 'Elle aime depuis le lycée' (She has loved since high school). Remember to conjugate 'aimer' to match the subject (j'aime, tu aimes, il/elle aime, nous aimons, etc.). Note that context determines whether 'aimer' means 'to like' or 'to love'.
target_language_example: Il aime depuis toujours.
native_language_example: He has loved/liked since always (for as long as anyone can remember).

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; it's the conjugated verb 'aime' (he/she/it likes or loves; also 'I like' in subjunctive contexts) followed directly by the conjunction 'et' ('and'). It appears when 'aime' connects to another element introduced by 'et' in a sentence.
additional_notes: 'Aime et' by itself is grammatically incomplete and must be followed by another noun, verb phrase, or clause. You will find it inside longer sentences, e.g. 'Elle aime et respecte son professeur.' (She likes and respects her teacher.) Context determines whether 'aime' expresses liking or loving.
target_language_example: Elle aime et respecte son professeur.
native_language_example: She likes and respects her teacher.

meaning: 'likes my' (he/she/one likes my...)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb aimer (to like/love) in the third-person singular (il/elle/on aime) followed by the possessive adjective mon (my). You'll normally see it inside a sentence, e.g. «Il aime mon livre» = 'He likes my book.' Context determines whether aimer means 'to like' or 'to love'. Remember French agreement: mon is used before masculine singular nouns and also before any singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h (e.g. mon ami, mon école).
target_language_example: Elle aime mon chien.
native_language_example: She likes my dog.

meaning: no longer likes / doesn't like anymore
additional_notes: Combines the verb aimer (to like/love) with plus (no more). In spoken French, meaning depends on pronunciation: 'plus' pronounced /ply/ = 'more', pronounced /plys/ or with silent s (often /ply/) usually means 'no longer' when used after a verb. Context and intonation determine whether it means 'likes more' (comparative) or 'doesn't like anymore' (negation). For clear negation, French often uses 'n'aime plus'.
target_language_example: Elle n'aime plus le café.
native_language_example: She doesn't like coffee anymore.

meaning: loves/likes (someone or something) more than (another).
additional_notes: Used to compare degrees of liking or love. Structure: subject + 'aime plus que' + object preferred + 'que' + object compared. In informal speech, 'aime mieux' or 'préfère' can be used for 'prefer'. Context determines whether it implies romantic love or general liking; verb agreement and word order follow normal French rules.
target_language_example: Il aime plus que tout sa famille.
native_language_example: He loves his family more than anything.

meaning: 'likes all the' or 'loves all the' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Combination of aimer (to like/love) + tous les (all the). Used before a plural noun: aime tous les + [noun]. Meaning depends on context and intensity (aimer can mean like or love). Word order: subject + aime tous les + noun. Example: 'Il aime tous les chiens.' = 'He likes all dogs.'
target_language_example: Elle aime tous les livres de science-fiction.
native_language_example: She likes all the science-fiction books.

meaning: literally 'likes everything' — used to say someone likes everything or everything pleases them
additional_notes: Made of the verb aimer (to like/love) + tout (everything). Can describe a person who likes many things, or be used hyperbolically to mean 'likes everything' about something (e.g., 'il aime tout' = he likes everything; 'elle aime tout dans ce film' = she likes everything about this film). Context determines whether it means 'likes everything' generally or 'likes all parts/aspects' of something. Conjugate aimer to match the subject (j'aime tout, tu aimes tout, il/elle aime tout, etc.).
target_language_example: Elle aime tout ce qui est sucré.
native_language_example: She likes everything that is sweet.

meaning: 'likes very' (literal literal grouping; not standard in French)
additional_notes: This combination is unidiomatic on its own. French normally uses 'aime beaucoup' to mean 'likes a lot'. 'Très' is typically used with adjectives (très bon) and adverbs (très vite), or with adjectives after a noun phrase—it can appear after a verb only in colloquial/emphatic constructions with an adverb or adjective following (e.g., 'aime très fort'), but 'aime très' by itself is incomplete. Prefer 'aime beaucoup' or 'l'aime beaucoup'.
target_language_example: Il aime très fort son chien.
native_language_example: He really loves his dog.

meaning: used with verbs to mean 'tends to' or 'is wont to' (habitual or repeated action).
additional_notes: Followed by an infinitive; expresses a habitual tendency or inclination (similar to 'aimer + infinitive' but with a slightly more literary or formal tone). Common in written French or more formal speech: 'Il aime à penser...' = 'He tends to think...'. Not the same as 'aimer' meaning 'to like' when used alone.
target_language_example: Elle aime à se promener le soir.
native_language_example: She tends to take a walk in the evening.

meaning: likes to listen to (something) — used with partitive 'de' + noun to indicate listening to some/unspecified amount or type (e.g. de la musique, du jazz).
additional_notes: Combines 'aime' (from aimer = to like) + infinitive 'écouter' + preposition 'de' used before a partitive/article + noun. In practice you often see 'aime écouter de la/du/des' + noun (Elle aime écouter de la musique). With a specific item or artist you'd drop the partitive and use definite article or name (Elle aime écouter la symphonie, Elle aime écouter Mozart). Word order: subject + aime écouter de + partitive/article + noun.
target_language_example: Elle aime écouter de la musique.
native_language_example: She likes to listen to music.

meaning: 'they like' (followed by a feminine singular noun or feminine noun phrase: 'they like the...')
additional_notes: Aiment = third-person plural of aimer (to like / to love). La is the feminine singular definite article 'the' or can be used before a feminine noun phrase. Together, aiment la = 'they like the...'. If the noun is plural use 'les' (Ils aiment les chiens). Use 'il/elle aime la...' for he/she likes. Pronunciation: [ɛm la].
target_language_example: Ils aiment la cuisine italienne.
native_language_example: They like Italian cuisine.

meaning: 'they like/enjoy a' (plural subject + indefinite feminine noun)
additional_notes: Combines the verb aimer (to like/love) conjugated for ils/elles (aiment) with the indefinite article une before a feminine singular noun. Useful to describe what people or things like. In many cases English omits the article (e.g. "they like happy endings"), but French uses the article ("ils aiment une fin heureuse"). Context determines whether the subject is people, animals, or things.
target_language_example: Ils aiment une promenade au parc le dimanche.
native_language_example: They like a walk in the park on Sundays.

meaning: to like (used to express mild or friendly liking; less strong than "aimer" meaning to love)
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb (aimer bien + infinitive) or by a noun. Conveys a friendly or casual liking rather than deep romantic love. Common in spoken and written French. Example nuance: "Je t'aime" (I love you) vs "Je t'aime bien" (I like you / I care for you in a friendly way).
target_language_example: J'aime bien aimer bien la musique classique.
native_language_example: I like to like classical music.

meaning: I'd like some / I would like (of it/them).
additional_notes: Combination of conditional of aimer (aimerais = 'I would like') plus partitive pronoun/en meaning 'of it', 'of them', or 'some'. Used to say you'd like some of something mentioned before: e.g. "J'en aimerais" or with quantity: "J'aimerais en prendre deux." The en refers back to a noun introduced earlier (du pain → j'aimerais en).
target_language_example: Si vous avez des biscuits, j'aimerais en prendre deux, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: If you have cookies, I'd like to take two of them, please.

meaning: 'I would like (to) you' — part of the polite conditional construction meaning 'I would like to (do something) to/for you' or 'I would like you to...'.
additional_notes: Aimerais is the conditional form of aimer (je aimerais = I would like). When followed by the pronoun te (informal 'you'), it commonly appears in constructions like «J'aimerais te parler» (I would like to talk to you) or «J'aimerais te demander...» (I would like to ask you...). The pronoun te is placed before the main verb in affirmative sentences and replaced by 'vous' for formal/plural. This phrase is polite and slightly tentative because of the conditional.
target_language_example: J'aimerais te voir demain si tu es libre.
native_language_example: I'd like to see you tomorrow if you're free.

meaning: polite conditional 'I would like (to) you' — used to begin requests or offers (je vous aimerais is uncommon; correct form is 'je voudrais' or 'je vous aimerais bien' in some contexts).
additional_notes: This phrase looks like the conditional of 'aimer' plus the object pronoun 'vous'. In modern polite requests English speakers usually use 'je voudrais' or 'j'aimerais' + infinitive (e.g. 'J'aimerais vous parler' = 'I would like to speak to you'). Standalone 'aimerais vous' without a verb that follows is incomplete. If you mean 'I would like you to...' use 'Je souhaiterais que vous...' or 'J'aimerais que vous...'.
target_language_example: J'aimerais vous parler un instant.
native_language_example: I would like to speak to you for a moment.

meaning: 'you like to do' (informal singular)
additional_notes: Second-person singular (tu) of aimer + infinitive faire. Used to ask or say what someone likes doing: Tu aimes faire du sport ? / Tu aimes faire ça ? In spoken French the 'tu' is often dropped in casual questions (Aimes faire...? is less common on its own). Remember pronunciation: 'aimes' is pronounced like /ɛm/ and 'faire' like /fɛʁ/.
target_language_example: Tu aimes faire du vélo le week-end ?
native_language_example: Do you like to ride a bike on weekends?

meaning: 'you like' + plural noun (informal singular 'tu' form).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb aimer (to like/love) in the second-person singular present (tu aimes) followed by the plural definite article les and a plural noun: tu aimes les films = you like films. Used in informal spoken and written French with 'tu'. For formal or plural 'you' use 'vous aimez les'.
target_language_example: Tu aimes les vacances à la plage ?
native_language_example: Do you like beach vacations?

meaning: like
additional_notes: aimez is the vous form of aimer, so it means 'you like' or, in a question, 'do you like' (for one person formally or for several people). le is the masculine singular article before a noun. With foods, drinks, and activities, French often uses le for things in general: aimez le café = 'like coffee,' not usually 'like the coffee.'
target_language_example: Vous aimez le chocolat noir ?
native_language_example: Do you like dark chocolate?

meaning: ‘do you like them’ or 'you like the...' (formal/plural 'you')
additional_notes: Form is from the verb aimer (to like/love) with the direct object pronoun or article 'les' (them/the). In questions with inversion or intonation, 'Vous aimez les... ?' means 'Do you like ...?' When 'les' stands before a noun (les animaux, les pâtes) it is the definite plural article 'the' and the sentence asks if you like that category. When 'les' refers to people/things previously mentioned, it can mean 'them.' 'Vous' is formal or plural 'you.'
target_language_example: Vous aimez les films français ?
native_language_example: Do you like French films?

meaning: 'do you like your...' or 'you like your...'
additional_notes: Combines the verb aimer (to like/love) in the second-person plural/formal question form (aimez) with the possessive adjective votre (your). In questions, 'Est-ce que vous aimez votre ... ?' = 'Do you like your ...?' As a statement, 'Vous aimez votre ...?' is a more informal/questioning way to ask the same. Use votre for 'your' when speaking to one person formally or to multiple people.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous aimez votre nouvelle maison ?
native_language_example: Do you like your new house?

meaning: liked this / liked that (past participle + demonstrative).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase — it's the past participle 'aimé' (from aimer = to like/love) followed by the demonstrative 'ce' used before a noun (e.g. ce livre) or in questions with inversion/est-ce que. In sentences it's usually part of a compound past (il/elle a aimé ce livre) or simple past contexts. Use 'as-tu aimé ce...' or 'avez-vous aimé ce...' to ask if someone liked something. Agreement: 'aimé' does not change for masculine/feminine when used with avoir unless a direct object pronoun precedes the verb.
target_language_example: Tu as aimé ce film ?
native_language_example: Did you like this movie?

meaning: would have liked (that)... / liked that... (used with a subordinate clause)
additional_notes: Formed from the past participle aimé of aimer plus que introducing a clause. Commonly appears in conditional or past conditional constructions: e.g. « J'aurais aimé que... » (I would have liked that...). On its own 'aimé que' is not a complete phrase; you usually need a helping verb (aurais, aurait, etc.) or context to show tense and subject. Use with the subjunctive when expressing wishes about something that did not happen: « J'aurais aimé que tu sois là » (subjunctive: sois).
target_language_example: J'aurais aimé que tu viennes à la fête.
native_language_example: I would have liked you to come to the party.

meaning: liked that you / would have liked you to
additional_notes: 'aimé que tu' appears as part of a larger expression with aimer in the conditional or past conditional (e.g. 'j'aurais aimé que tu...' or 'j'aurais aimé que tu viennes') to express regret or a wish about someone's action. It's followed by a subjunctive or an infinitive depending on construction: after 'j'aurais aimé que' use the subjunctive (j'aurais aimé que tu sois venu), while 'j'aurais aimé te voir' uses an infinitive. In spoken French you may also hear 'j'aurais aimé que tu viennes' to say 'I wish you had come.'
target_language_example: J'aurais aimé que tu sois là pour fêter ça avec moi.
native_language_example: I would have liked you to be there to celebrate this with me.

meaning: like this / such / in this way (used to introduce an example or to link to what follows)
additional_notes: Ainsi de is less common on its own than simply 'ainsi' and often appears in formal or written contexts before a noun or phrase to give an example or to introduce a consequence (similar to 'for example' or 'thus'). It can be followed by '...' + noun (e.g. 'ainsi de nombreux cas') or used in constructions like 'ainsi de suite' (and so on). For everyday speech, 'ainsi' or 'comme' are more frequent.
target_language_example: Il y a des retards, ainsi de nombreux trains ont été annulés.
native_language_example: There are delays, thus many trains were canceled.

meaning: to say like this / to put it this way (used to introduce or paraphrase a statement)
additional_notes: Rare or literary construction. 'Ainsi' means 'thus/like this' and 'dire' means 'to say'. Together they can introduce a reformulation: 'ainsi dire' = 'to say it this way' or 'so to speak'. In everyday French you'd more often hear 'dire ainsi', 'autrement dit', or 'en d'autres termes'. Use in formal or written contexts.
target_language_example: Autrement dit, ainsi dire, il faut attendre.
native_language_example: In other words, so to speak, we must wait.

meaning: as well as; just as; and also.
additional_notes: Common connector used to add an item or make a comparison. In many contexts it means "as well as" (adding something: A ainsi que B). It can also mean "just as" or "in the same way as" when comparing. Formal/register-neutral; useful in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Il aime le chocolat ainsi que les fruits.
native_language_example: He likes chocolate as well as fruit.

meaning: seems/appears (to be) good; gives a good impression
additional_notes: air (masculine noun) means 'appearance' or 'look'. Combined with an adjective like bien, 'air bien' can describe the way something or someone appears (e.g., 'il a l'air bien' = 'he seems fine'). More commonly used with 'avoir l'air' (to look/seem): 'avoir l'air bien/bon/mal/etc.'. Standalone 'air bien' without 'avoir' is uncommon in modern spoken French; beginners should learn the full phrase 'avoir l'air bien' or simply 'sembler/paraître'.
target_language_example: Il a l'air bien après la conversation.
native_language_example: He seems fine after the conversation.

meaning: 'look' or 'appearance of' (followed by a noun or adjective)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or adjective to describe someone's/something's appearance, manner, or the impression they give. Often contracted as air d' before a vowel (e.g., air d'innocent). Common constructions: avoir l'air de + noun/infinitive or simply 'air d' + adjective/noun in descriptive phrases. Not a complete phrase on its own — needs more words.
target_language_example: Il avait un air d'innocent malgré la situation.
native_language_example: He had the look of an innocent person despite the situation.

meaning: an impression of a / a sort of (gives a sense or appearance of something)
additional_notes: Used to describe the way someone or something seems to be, often followed by a noun or infinitive phrase. Commonly appears in expressions like "il a l'air d'un/une + noun" (he/she looks like a ...). Note the contraction: l'air + de + un → l'air d'un. It's formal/neutral and used to comment on appearance or apparent role.
target_language_example: Il a l'air d'un professeur quand il parle.
native_language_example: He looks like a teacher when he speaks.

meaning: to seem or appear to be (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun (often after "avoir l'air de") to say how someone seems. Common spoken structure: "(Tu) as l'air d'être + [adjective/noun phrase]" or short form "t'as l'air d'être...". Can express appearance, impression, or perceived state (e.g., "au bout du rouleau" = exhausted).
target_language_example: Il a l'air d'être très fatigué.
native_language_example: He seems to be very tired.

meaning: a delightful/pleasant (air or melody); can also describe a charming or delightful feeling/atmosphere.
additional_notes: Literally 'delicious air' — used poetic or evaluative contexts. Most often describes a tune, melody, or the general mood/atmosphere that is very pleasant. Not a common everyday collocation for speaking about literal air (like fresh air); more likely found in literary, musical or expressive descriptions.
target_language_example: L'air délicieux de cette mélodie m'apaise.
native_language_example: The delightful tune of this melody soothes me.

meaning: an expression meaning 'a look of' or 'an air of' (used to describe someone's expression or general appearance).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe someone's expression, mood, or the general impression they give: 'un air en ...' often followed by an adjective or phrase (e.g. 'un air en colère' = 'an angry look'). It is slightly formal/neuter and common in written and spoken French. You will often see 'avoir un air...' to say 'to have an air/appearance...'.
target_language_example: Elle avait un air en colère quand elle est arrivée.
native_language_example: She had an angry look when she arrived.

meaning: 'in great shape' / 'very well' (about health, energy, mood)
additional_notes: Used after avoir l'air (to look/seem) or être to describe someone as very fit, healthy, energetic, or in high spirits. Common in everyday conversation. When used with avoir l'air, the full pattern is avoir l'air en pleine forme = to look/appear very well.
target_language_example: Tu as l'air en pleine forme aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You look in great shape today.

meaning: 'to look/appear happy' (used after forms of avoir: avoir l'air + adjective).
additional_notes: Common construction: avoir l'air + adjective means 'to seem' or 'to look' a certain way. Conjugate avoir for the subject: J'ai l'air, Tu as l'air, Il/Elle a l'air, Nous avons l'air, Vous avez l'air, Ils/Elles ont l'air. Can describe temporary appearance or impression. Informal spoken forms may contract (T'as l'air).
target_language_example: Il a l'air heureux.
native_language_example: He looks happy.

meaning: premium (grade) gasoline; 'super' petrol (higher-octane fuel)
additional_notes: Used at petrol stations to indicate a higher-octane fuel option (often labeled 'Super' or 'SP95/98'). 'Air super' is less common than simply 'super' or 'essence super' — in many contexts you will see 'sans plomb 95' or 'sans plomb 98' instead. Use when asking for or selecting premium fuel for a car.
target_language_example: Je vais mettre de l'air super dans la voiture.
native_language_example: I'll put premium (super) petrol in the car.

meaning: 'looks/appearance very...' — used to emphasize how something or someone appears (followed by adjective).
additional_notes: Combine with an adjective to say someone/something looks very [adjective]: e.g. "il a l'air très fatigué" = "he looks very tired." "Air" here is short for "avoir l'air" (to look/seem). In written French you usually see the full structure: "avoir l'air très + adjective," or in spoken French: "il a l'air très..."
target_language_example: Elle a l'air très contente aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She looks very happy today.

meaning: seems/looks very good (colloquial phrasing)
additional_notes: Literal words: air = look/appearance, très bien = very good. In French, 'avoir l'air' or 'ça a l'air' are standard to say 'to look/seem'. By itself 'air très bien' is not a complete phrase; you'd usually say 'il a l'air très bien' (he looks very well/good) or 'ça a l'air très bien' (that looks very good). Used to give a positive impression about a person, thing, or situation. Informal but common in speech when combined with a verb (avoir l'air).
target_language_example: Ça a l'air très bien, cette idée.
native_language_example: That idea looks/seems very good.

aliments que tu manges habituellement avec

target_language_multi_word_term: aliments que tu manges habituellement avec
meaning: 'foods that you usually eat with' (used to ask which foods you normally pair with something)
additional_notes: This is a fragment likely used in questions about food pairings (e.g., "Quels sont les aliments que tu manges habituellement avec ... ?"). tu (you, informal) indicates casual speech. habituellement = usually / normally. The phrase will typically be completed by naming an ingredient or dish (avec + noun).
target_language_example: Quels sont les aliments que tu manges habituellement avec du fromage ?
native_language_example: Which foods do you usually eat with cheese?

aliments que vous mangez habituellement avec

target_language_multi_word_term: aliments que vous mangez habituellement avec
meaning: 'foods that you usually eat with' (used to ask about typical accompaniments)
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment often used when asking someone what foods they normally pair with something (e.g., 'aliments que vous mangez habituellement avec le fromage' = 'foods you usually eat with cheese'). It uses the polite/formal 'vous' and the adverb 'habituellement' (usually). You can replace 'vous' with 'tu' in informal situations: 'aliments que tu manges habituellement avec...'.
target_language_example: Quels sont les aliments que vous mangez habituellement avec du poisson ?
native_language_example: What foods do you usually eat with fish?

meaning: went to do (something) — indicates someone went somewhere to carry out an action (past historic form).
additional_notes: ‘Alla’ is the third-person singular past historic (passé simple) of aller (to go). It is literary/formal and mostly appears in written narratives. In everyday spoken French, the passé composé (est allé(e)) is used instead. 'Alla faire + noun/infinitive' means 'went to do [shopping, errands, etc.]' — context decides the action (e.g. faire des courses = grocery shopping).
target_language_example: Il alla faire une promenade dans le parc.
native_language_example: He went to take a walk in the park.

meaning: the imperfect 'I was going to' used before 'vous' (polite 'you'); expresses an intended action in the past (I was about to / I was going to tell/ask you).
additional_notes: This is part of the verb phrase 'J'allais vous ...' (je + aller in the imparfait + object pronoun vous + infinitive). It conveys a past intention or near-future action from a past perspective (e.g. I was going to tell/ask you). Often used politely to introduce something you were about to do or say. In speech the subject and verb contract (J'allais). Replace 'vous' with other object pronouns as needed (je t'allais is not used; use 'je t'allais' is incorrect — for informal singular use 'je t'allais' isn't used; instead say 'j'allais te...').
target_language_example: J'allais vous prévenir, mais vous étiez déjà parti.
native_language_example: I was going to warn you, but you had already left.

meaning: to go to bed; to go to sleep (go to one's bed).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to tell someone to go to bed. Often used with a subject (je/tu/il/elle/nous) and can be followed by a time or reason. Can mean simply 'go to bed' (physically) or imply 'go to sleep.'
target_language_example: Il est tard, je vais aller au lit.
native_language_example: It's late, I'm going to go to bed.

meaning: 'to also go' or 'to go as well' (go + also)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb aller (to go) with the adverb aussi (also/as well). Placement typically follows the conjugated verb or infinitive: with a conjugated verb + infinitive, aussi often follows the infinitive (e.g. «aller aussi»). Used to indicate someone will go in addition to others. In negative contexts use forms like «ne ... pas ... non plus» or «ne ... pas ... non plus» depending on nuance (e.g. «Je ne veux pas y aller non plus»). Word order can change for emphasis; 'aussi aller' is unusual in modern spoken French.
target_language_example: Ils vont partir, et je vais aller aussi.
native_language_example: They are going to leave, and I will go too.

meaning: to match
additional_notes: Used when two things look good together or are compatible (clothing, colors, objects). Can also mean 'to go along with' in the sense of being consistent or compatible (e.g. something doesn't go with/fit with something else). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ces chaussures vont bien aller avec ta robe.
native_language_example: Those shoes will go well with your dress.

meaning: to go get
additional_notes: Used to say you are going somewhere to fetch, pick up or bring back something or someone. Common with objects (aller chercher le portefeuille) and people (aller chercher Maria). Can be followed by a noun or a person. Informal everyday expression.
target_language_example: Je vais aller chercher du pain.
native_language_example: I'll go get some bread.

meaning: 'to fit perfectly' (used for clothing or figuratively for something that suits someone exactly)
additional_notes: Used for garments, shoes, or figuratively for roles/situations that suit someone very well. Equivalent to English 'to fit like a glove.' Often appears in constructions like 'Ça lui va comme un gant' or with an infinitive 'aller comme un gant' after a subject.
target_language_example: Cette veste va aller comme un gant pour toi.
native_language_example: That jacket will fit you like a glove.

meaning: 'to go like' or 'to fit/turn out like' (used to compare how something goes/turns out)
additional_notes: Used to compare the way something 'goes' or 'turns out' to something else. Often appears in phrases like "Ça va comme..." or "Aller comme + noun/pronoun" to say one thing suits or corresponds to another, or to introduce a comparison of manner. This is not a fixed idiom by itself; its exact sense depends on context. For many contexts speakers prefer constructions such as "aller (bien/mal)" for fit/condition or "ressembler à" for resemblance.
target_language_example: Ça va aller comme prévu.
native_language_example: It will go as planned.

meaning: 'to go from' (indicates movement or range from one point/thing to another) or used in expressions meaning 'to vary from... to...' or 'to be up to' in impersonal constructions.
additional_notes: Used with nouns to indicate movement or range: aller de X à Y = to go from X to Y / to range from X to Y. Also appears in impersonal expressions like "il va de soi" (it goes without saying) where it contributes to a fixed phrase. Requires a following preposition (often à) or is part of an expression; not a standalone verb phrase meaning simply 'to go'.
target_language_example: Les températures vont aller de 10 à 20 degrés cette semaine.
native_language_example: Temperatures will range from 10 to 20 degrees this week.

meaning: to move forward; to move on (emotionally or in life)
additional_notes: Used to say someone should progress, stop dwelling on the past, or continue with life/projects. Common in both personal and professional contexts. Often followed by no object. Literal components: 'aller' = to go, 'de l'avant' = of/from the front.
target_language_example: Après cette mauvaise nouvelle, il faut aller de l'avant.
native_language_example: After that bad news, we must move on.

meaning: 'to go without saying' — to be obvious or taken for granted
additional_notes: Used impersonally to say that something is obvious or naturally expected. Often appears in constructions like "Il va de soi que..." (It goes without saying that...). Formal or neutral register; common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Il va de soi que cela doit aller de soi dans une situation professionnelle.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that this should go without saying in a professional situation.

meaning: 'to go then' / a prompt or mild exclamation used to encourage action, urge someone to go, express impatience or surprise depending on context.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom with one meaning. More commonly used in conjugated imperatives (va/allez donc) rather than the infinitive phrase 'aller donc' in isolation; however 'aller donc' can appear in spoken or literary contexts to urge someone to go or to comment on someone's going. Tone, context and verb form determine force (e.g., encouragement, dismissal, surprise).
target_language_example: Si tu veux changer d'air, tu devrais aller donc voir ta famille pour un week-end.
native_language_example: If you want a change of scenery, you should go then see your family for a weekend.

meaning: 'to go together' (physically or match) or 'to be dating' / 'to be a couple' (when referring to people).
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: with people it commonly means 'to be in a romantic relationship' (e.g., Ils vont ensemble); with objects or ideas it can mean 'to go together' or 'to match' (e.g., ces couleurs vont ensemble). Can be used in present, past, etc. Not a false cognate; literal translation is possible but context determines nuance.
target_language_example: Ils aiment aller ensemble au cinéma chaque samedi.
native_language_example: They like to go together to the cinema every Saturday.

meaning: 'go and' — literal combination of the verb aller (to go) + conjunction et (and); can appear when two actions are linked in sequence, though it's not a fixed idiom in modern French.
additional_notes: 'Aller et' is compositional: it simply joins 'aller' and 'et'. This sequence can occur in narrative or colloquial speech when listing successive actions (e.g. « Il va et ... » or past « Il est allé et ... »), but native speakers more often use constructions like 'aller + infinitive' (aller faire) or separate clauses ('Il est allé, puis il a...'). Use caution: many English 'go and' usages translate differently into French. The phrase can be grammatically correct when the verb forms and agreement are appropriate (e.g. 'Il est allé et a...'), but the exact contiguous tokens 'aller et' are less common in standard written French than alternative constructions.
target_language_example: Pour accomplir la tâche, il a dû aller et revenir plusieurs fois.
native_language_example: To complete the task, he had to go and come back several times.

meaning: to come and go; to move back and forth or move freely between places.
additional_notes: Used to describe the ability to move freely, to go back and forth, or to circulate within a place or situation. Often appears in expressions meaning 'as one pleases' (aller et venir à son gré / comme bon te semble). Literal components are transparent (aller = to go, venir = to come).
target_language_example: Tu peux aller et venir librement dans la maison.
native_language_example: You can come and go freely in the house.

meaning: to go immediately; to go right away
additional_notes: A simple verb phrase: aller (to go) + immédiatement (immediately). Used to tell someone to go somewhere at once or to say you are leaving right now. Formality: neutral; suitable in most contexts. Immediately can be strengthened with other adverbs (tout de suite).
target_language_example: Je dois aller immédiatement à la pharmacie.
native_language_example: I must go to the pharmacy immediately.

meaning: to go as far as / to go so far as to (do something); to reach a point or limit
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb (infinitive) or a complement introduced by 'à' or 'jusqu'à' to indicate reaching a physical point or taking an action to an extreme. Common constructions: 'aller jusqu'à [lieu]' (reach a place) and 'aller jusqu'à + infinitive' (go so far as to do something). Contraction: 'jusqu'' appears before a vowel (e.g. 'aller jusqu'à').
target_language_example: Il a décidé d'aller jusqu'à mentir pour obtenir le poste.
native_language_example: He decided to go so far as to lie to get the job.

meaning: 'to go as far as' or 'to go up to' (can be literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used with a noun introduced by 'au' (à + le). Can describe physical distance (going as far as a place) or degrees/limits (going as far as doing something). Often followed by an infinitive or noun: aller jusqu'au bout, aller jusqu'au mensonge, or aller jusqu'au café du coin. For feminine nouns use 'aller jusqu'à la' and for plural 'aller jusqu'aux'.
target_language_example: Il est prêt à aller jusqu'au bout pour réussir.
native_language_example: He is ready to go all the way to succeed.

meaning: go and ... him/it
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own. This usually appears before another infinitive, with le as a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it”: for example, aller le voir = “go see him” and aller le chercher = “go get him/it”. There is normally another verb after le.
target_language_example: Je vais aller le voir cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see him this afternoon.

meaning: to go far; literally to travel a long distance, figuratively to get far in life, career, a project, or to achieve great success.
additional_notes: Used both literally and figuratively. Common conjugations: aller loin (infinitive), il/elle ira loin (future), tu es allé(e) loin (past). Often used with modalities or reasons (e.g., « avec ce talent, tu vas aller loin »). Can be followed by context specifying area of success (career, studies, projet).
target_language_example: Avec ton travail et ta détermination, tu vas aller loin.
native_language_example: With your work and determination, you're going to go far.

meaning: a sequence combining the verb 'aller' (to go; auxiliary for near future) and the indirect object pronoun 'lui' (to him/to her); commonly appears in constructions like 'aller + infinitive' where 'lui' is the indirect object (e.g. 'aller lui dire' = 'to go to tell him/her'). The exact meaning depends on context (movement toward someone, or future action directed at someone).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; 'aller' is often used as an auxiliary for the near future (je vais) and the pronoun 'lui' marks the indirect object. In standard word order the pronoun appears before the verb (je lui parle) but in the periphrastic future you typically have 'aller' + infinitive with the pronoun either before the infinitive (je vais lui parler) or attached with a hyphen in affirmative imperative constructions in older/written forms. 'Aller lui' by itself is uncommon; it appears when 'aller' is followed immediately by 'lui' (e.g. in inverted or poetic word order) or in reduced transcriptions, but learners will mainly see 'aller + infinitive' with 'lui' before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Aller lui parler maintenant serait utile.
native_language_example: Going to talk to him/her now would be useful.

meaning: to go there (to that place).
additional_notes: Simple phrase combining the verb aller (to go) with là (there). Used to indicate movement toward a place that is near in the conversation or already known. Can be followed by a destination: aller là-bas (more emphatic 'go over there') or by context: 'Tu veux aller là ?' (Do you want to go there?).
target_language_example: On peut aller là pour déjeuner.
native_language_example: We can go there for lunch.

meaning: to go nowhere / to be unable to go anywhere
additional_notes: Usually appears with 'part' as 'aller nulle part' meaning 'to go nowhere' or in negative sentences ('ne ... nulle part') to mean 'nowhere'. In everyday French, speakers often say 'nulle part' alone after a verb (Je ne peux aller nulle part) or prefer 'part' with 'nulle' omitted in casual speech ('Je ne peux aller nulle part' is common). Affirmative sentence 'Je peux aller nulle part' is uncommon and sounds odd — normally you'd say 'Je peux aller n'importe où' (I can go anywhere).
target_language_example: Avec ce temps, on ne peut aller nulle part.
native_language_example: With this weather, we can't go anywhere.

meaning: 'to go where' — used to ask or talk about the destination or place someone is going to.
additional_notes: Common in questions and embedded clauses. Word order: aller (to go) + où (where). In spoken French you may hear 'où est-ce que tu vas ?' or 'tu vas où ?' instead of using the infinitive phrase 'aller où' in isolation. Use with conjugated forms of aller for grammatical sentences: e.g. 'Je ne sais pas où aller' (I don't know where to go).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas où aller ce week-end.
native_language_example: I don't know where to go this weekend.

meaning: 'to go by' or 'to go via' (indicating a route or means); can also mean 'to proceed by/through' in a figurative sense.
additional_notes: Used to indicate traveling via a place or using a particular route/mode: aller par Paris (to go via Paris), aller par la mer (to go by sea). In more abstract contexts, it can appear in phrases like aller par étapes (to proceed in stages). The verb phrase is compositional and usually followed by a place, route, or method. Register: neutral.
target_language_example: Nous devons aller par Lyon si nous voulons éviter l'autoroute.
native_language_example: We need to go via Lyon if we want to avoid the highway.

meaning: to go (somewhere) to speak or to go and talk (to someone).
additional_notes: aller + infinitive expresses a near-future or purpose ('to go to do something'). 'Aller parler' is not an idiom by itself but the verb construction appears in phrases like 'aller parler à quelqu'un' (go and speak to someone) or 'aller parler de...' (go to talk about...). Use with a person after 'à' or a topic after 'de'.
target_language_example: Je vais aller parler à mon professeur cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to go and talk to my teacher this afternoon.

meaning: 'to be acceptable for / to suit / to be intended for' or 'to go for' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Aller pour is used in related senses: 1) to suit or fit (e.g. Cette robe va pour une fête = This dress is suitable for a party); 2) to be intended for or destined for (Ce cadeau va pour toi = This gift is for you); 3) to indicate reputation or category (Il va pour un expert = He is regarded as an expert). It is not the most common fixed phrase and may sound slightly formal or regional in some contexts; often appears as aller + pour + noun/pronoun. Conjugate aller to match the subject and choose meaning from context.
target_language_example: Ce manteau va pour l'hiver : il va pour protéger contre le froid.
native_language_example: This coat is suitable for winter: it serves to protect against the cold.

meaning: to go and get/take a (something) — expresses going somewhere to pick up, obtain, or have something (follow with a noun).
additional_notes: Construction: aller (to go) + prendre (to take/get) + an object. It implies moving with the intention of obtaining or consuming something (e.g., aller prendre un café). Conjugate aller as needed: je vais aller prendre un is the future-ish periphrasis but commonly use aller + prendre directly (je vais prendre un, nous allons prendre un, il/elle va prendre un). Often used for food/drink, quick errands, appointments, or actions where you go to get something. Use the appropriate article (un/une/des/le/la) and noun after it. Informal and neutral registers both use it.
target_language_example: Je vais aller prendre un café avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get a coffee before the meeting.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete fragment (no fixed meaning).
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'aller quelque' by itself. You might see 'aller quelque part' (to go somewhere) or 'aller quelque chose' is incorrect. If you intended 'aller quelque chose', use 'il va y avoir quelque chose' (there will be something) or for 'to go somewhere' use 'aller quelque part'. For beginners: check the full phrase — 'aller' is the verb 'to go' and needs a complement (e.g., 'aller à Paris', 'aller quelque part').
target_language_example: Je veux aller quelque part ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to go somewhere this weekend.

meaning: to go without saying; to be obvious or unnecessary to state
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is so obvious it doesn't need to be said. Often appears in expressions like "aller sans dire" or the more common fixed phrase "ça va sans dire". Formality: neutral; common in both spoken and written French. Note: "aller sans dire" is less commonly used on its own than "ça va sans dire", but it is grammatically correct in contexts where the verb "aller" refers to a situation or conclusion.
target_language_example: Que cela aille sans dire, je respecterai votre décision.
native_language_example: Let it go without saying, I will respect your decision.

meaning: A fragment used before an infinitive in reflexive constructions meaning 'to go and have/get [something done to oneself]' (neutral) or as part of idiomatic/rude expressions 'aller se faire + [infinitive]' telling someone to 'go and [do something to yourself]' (offensive).
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase by itself; it precedes an infinitive (e.g. aller se faire opérer, aller se faire voir, aller se faire foutre). In neutral contexts it describes going to obtain a service or undergo something (aller se faire opérer = to go to have surgery). In colloquial/insulting contexts it forms vulgar commands and should be used with caution. Register varies from neutral (medical/services) to highly informal and offensive (insults).
target_language_example: Il lui a dit d'aller se faire voir après la dispute.
native_language_example: He told her to go and get lost after the argument.

meaning: literally 'to go so' or 'to be so' when 'aller' (to go/ to be, in some contexts) combines with 'si' (so/that); not a fixed standalone verb — usually part of a larger clause (e.g. comparisons, conditions, or emphatic constructions).
additional_notes: Alone 'aller si' is uncommon as an independent multiword unit. It appears when 'aller' and 'si' are adjacent in a sentence (e.g. 'aller si bien', 'aller si vite', or in constructions like 'aller si + adjective/adverb'). Learners should treat it as compositional: understand 'aller' and 'si' separately and parse the full phrase. Register is neutral; usage depends on the surrounding words.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas aller si vite.
native_language_example: You must not go so fast.

meaning: to go by oneself; to go alone (without company)
additional_notes: Used when someone goes somewhere without other people. Can refer to a person going alone (no companion) or a child going alone depending on context. Commonly used in conversational French. Verb aller is conjugated; e.g. Il va tout seul = He goes alone.
target_language_example: Je peux y aller tout seul.
native_language_example: I can go there by myself.

meaning: to go too far; to exceed acceptable limits (in words or actions).
additional_notes: Used when someone crosses a boundary — e.g., says something offensive, takes an action that's excessive, or pushes a situation beyond what's acceptable. Can refer to literal excess but most commonly figurative. Common responses: «Tu vas trop loin» (You're going too far) or «Il a tout simplement été trop loin».
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas aller trop loin dans ces accusations.
native_language_example: You must not go too far with these accusations.

meaning: go see
additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase meaning to go and see someone or something. With a person, it often means "go see" or "go visit"; with a film or show, it means "go watch"; and without a direct object, it can mean "go check" or "go see for oneself."
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir le médecin demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to go look elsewhere; to leave and seek something/someone in another place. Often used figuratively to tell someone to go away or to suggest finding alternatives.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning either (1) literally go look somewhere else, or (2) figuratively tell someone to go away or advise seeking alternatives. Tone depends on context — can be neutral (advice) or blunt/rude (dismissal). Can be followed by a noun (aller voir un autre médecin) or stand alone (Va/Allez voir ailleurs).
target_language_example: Si le magasin n'a pas ta taille, tu peux aller voir ailleurs.
native_language_example: If the store doesn't have your size, you can go look elsewhere.

meaning: not a standalone expression; a sequence meaning roughly 'go and [verb] you' when followed by another infinitive, as in aller vous chercher
additional_notes: As written with a space, aller vous is not the same as the formal inverted question form allez-vous. In standard French, aller vous usually appears only as part of a longer construction such as aller vous voir, aller vous aider, or aller vous chercher.
target_language_example: Je vais aller vous chercher à la gare.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick you up at the station.

meaning: to go there
additional_notes: In standard French, the usual form is « y aller », not « aller y ». The sequence « aller y » is generally not used in normal sentence word order, so this entry is best understood as a reference to the components of the expression rather than a standard standalone phrase. In commands, related forms like « vas-y » or « allez-y » can mean « go ahead ».
target_language_example: On dit « y aller », pas « aller y » en français standard.
native_language_example: People say "y aller," not "aller y" in standard French.

meaning: to go to the gym / to go to the sports hall
additional_notes: Used when talking about going to a place for exercise — 'la salle' is short for 'la salle de sport' (the gym). Commonly used in everyday speech. You can change the article and noun for other places (e.g. aller au stade, aller à la piscine).
target_language_example: Je vais aller à la salle cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I am going to go to the gym this afternoon.

meaning: 'go there' or colloquial 'come on, there' depending on context
additional_notes: Literal imperative of aller + la (là without accent sometimes omitted in rapid typing). As an instruction it can mean 'go there' (vous-form or plural imperative). In colloquial spoken French, 'allez' alone is used as encouragement ('come on') and 'allez la' can add emphasis or point to a place; however the standard written form is 'allez là' with accent. For addressing one person informally use 'va là' or just 'là'.
target_language_example: Allez la, mets-toi derrière la barrière.
native_language_example: Go there, stand behind the barrier.

meaning: will be
additional_notes: A future construction using the present tense of aller + infinitive être. Used to say someone will become or will be in a certain state or situation (emotion, condition, location, role). Common in spoken and written French to express near future. Use with different subjects by conjugating aller (e.g., je vais être, il/elle va être, nous allons être).
target_language_example: Ça va bien se passer — vous allez être surpris.
native_language_example: It will go well — you are going to be surprised.

meaning: go ahead
additional_notes: A polite/neutral imperative form meaning 'go' or 'go ahead'. Used with vous (plural or formal you). Can encourage someone to start, to proceed, to go somewhere, or to give permission. Often repeated for emphasis (allez-y, allez-y). If speaking informally to one person, use 'vas-y'.
target_language_example: Allez-y, faites-le !
native_language_example: Go ahead, do it!

meaning: Who knows / go figure / nobody knows (used to express uncertainty or resignation).
additional_notes: Informal expression often used conversationally to shrug off a question or admit you don't know the reason. Literally 'go know', but functionally equivalent to English 'who knows', 'beats me', or 'go figure'. Can stand alone or be followed by a clause (e.g. 'allez savoir pourquoi' = 'who knows why').
target_language_example: Allez savoir pourquoi il est parti si tôt.
native_language_example: Who knows why he left so early.

meaning: come on
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression used to encourage someone, to urge them to do something, or to express impatience/disbelief. Combines allez (imperative of aller) and va (imperative of aller) — redundant but common in casual speech for emphasis (similar to 'oh, come on' or 'go on then'). Tone and context determine whether it's encouraging, dismissive, or incredulous.
target_language_example: Allez va, dis-lui ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: Come on, tell her what you think.

meaning: 'go fuck yourself' (very strong insult)
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to angrily tell someone to go away or express extreme contempt. Should not be used in polite company. Literal components: 'allez' (go, imperative plural/formal), 'vous' (you), 'faire foutre' (to get fucked) — the phrase is emphatic and directed at one or more people.
target_language_example: Allez vous faire foutre, je ne veux plus vous voir.
native_language_example: Go fuck yourself, I never want to see you again.

meaning: Let's go / come on / let's do it (encouraging others to start moving or begin an action).
additional_notes: Contraction of 'allons' (we go) + 'y' (there/it). Common informal expression used to urge people to leave, begin something, or encourage action. Tone depends on context: can be enthusiastic, impatient, or dismissive (e.g. 'laisse tomber' = 'never mind, let's go'). Often used with an exclamation mark or a short pause.
target_language_example: Allons-y, il est déjà tard.
native_language_example: Let's go, it's already late.

meaning: lit/has lit some (something) — past participle of allumer + indefinite article 'des' (some).
additional_notes: Used with a past tense (here passé composé) to say someone lit/turned on plural or uncountable items (e.g., candles, lights). 'Allumer' means 'to light' or 'to turn on' (a lamp, stove, cigarette). 'Des' is the plural/indefinite article meaning 'some' and has no direct singular equivalent. Conjugation agrees with the subject (elle a allumé, nous avons allumé, etc.).
target_language_example: Ils ont allumé des lampes dans le jardin.
native_language_example: They lit some lamps in the garden.

meaning: lit/turned on the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: From the verb allumer (to turn on, to switch on, to light). 'Allumé le' is the start of a sentence where the following word is a masculine noun or device (e.g. 'allumé le poste', 'allumé le chauffage'). In spoken French you may hear contractions or different word order (e.g. 'j'ai allumé la lumière' rather than 'allumé le lumière' — remember 'la lumière' is feminine). For past actions use the compound past: 'j'ai allumé le ...' (I turned on the ...).
target_language_example: J'ai allumé le chauffage ce matin.
native_language_example: I turned on the heater this morning.

meaning: went into
additional_notes: Past participle aller (allé) + preposition dans. Used to say someone went to or into a place. In spoken/written French you'd normally include the subject and auxiliary (être) for past tense (il est allé). Can be followed by a location (une chambre, un endroit, un pays) or a building; implies motion toward and entering or visiting the place.
target_language_example: Je suis allé dans le jardin ce matin.
native_language_example: I went into the garden this morning.

meaning: went to do
additional_notes: Past form of aller faire, usually used with être: je suis allé(e) faire..., nous sommes allé(e)s faire.... It means someone went somewhere in order to do an activity, errand, or pastime. In natural English, it is often translated more idiomatically as 'went shopping', 'went surfing', 'went for a walk', etc., rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Je suis allé faire du vélo ce matin.
native_language_example: I went biking this morning.

meaning: went to
additional_notes: Usually appears in a structure like « je suis allé me + infinitive », where « me » belongs to the following reflexive verb, not to « aller ». For example, « je suis allé me coucher » means « I went to bed ». « allé » is the past participle of « aller », so the form may change to « allée », « allés », or « allées » depending on who is speaking.
target_language_example: Je suis allé me promener après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: I went for a walk after lunch.

meaning: went to bed / went to sleep.
additional_notes: A reflexive construction: aller + se coucher (here in past: 'je suis allé me coucher' for a male speaker; a female speaker would say 'je suis allée me coucher'). Used to say you went to bed or went to sleep, often after something else. Can include details (e.g. 'avec mes vêtements' = went to bed with my clothes on).
target_language_example: Après la fête, je suis allé me coucher très tard.
native_language_example: After the party, I went to bed very late.

meaning: went to (to) — reflexive/participle + infinitive structure
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but looks like the past participle allé followed by a reflexive clitic se before an infinitive (e.g. «être/allé se coucher» in some constructions) or as part of a pronominal infinitive construction after verbs: in correct modern usage you usually see forms like «aller se + infinitive» (present infinitive construction meaning 'to go and [do something]') or «est allé se + past participle» in reported contexts. More commonly you will encounter «aller se + infinitive» meaning 'to go (to) [do something]' (e.g. «Il est allé se promener» = 'He went for a walk'). Note word order: in infinitive constructions the reflexive pronoun se appears before the infinitive (aller se coucher). In compound tenses with a pronominal verb the auxiliary is être (elle s'est allée is uncommon — pronominal verbs with aller are rare); better examples use «aller» + se + infinitive.
target_language_example: Il est allé se promener dans le parc.
native_language_example: He went for a walk in the park.

meaning: went to a (masculine or general) — past participle of 'aller' used with the auxiliary être + the indefinite article 'un'. Indicates that someone went to a masculine or unspecified place/event.
additional_notes: 'Allé' appears with the correct agreement (allé / allée / allés / allées) depending on the subject when used in compound tenses (e.g., Il est allé, Elle est allée). In casual speech you may hear the full form with the auxiliary (je suis allé(e) à un ...). If the noun is masculine and definite you would use 'au' instead (au concert). Use 'à une' for feminine nouns (à une réunion).
target_language_example: Il est allé à un centre islamique hier.
native_language_example: He went to an Islamic center yesterday.

meaning: went to buy (feminine subject).
additional_notes: Compound of the past participle/allé (from aller) + infinitive acheter. Used to say someone (she/it) 'went to buy' something. Because allé agrees with a preceding feminine subject (or clitic 'la'/'elle'), it appears as allée. In spoken French you may also hear 'elle est allée acheter...' or 'je suis allé(e) acheter...'. Specify the object after the phrase: allée acheter du pain, allée acheter des billets, etc.
target_language_example: Elle est allée acheter du pain ce matin.
native_language_example: She went to buy bread this morning.

meaning: 'went to buy a' (used with a feminine subject: she went somewhere to purchase a ...).
additional_notes: This phrase is the passé composé construction using être + allé(e) + infinitive acheter and the indefinite article un for a masculine singular noun. It requires agreement of the past participle with a feminine subject (elle est allée). Change the article and noun as needed (une, des) and adjust past-participle agreement for gender/number (il est allé, ils sont allés, elles sont allées).
target_language_example: Elle est allée acheter un cartable.
native_language_example: She went to buy a schoolbag.

meaning: literally 'gone to do some...' — used as part of a phrase meaning someone went somewhere to do (plural) tasks/errands/activities
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the beginning of expressions like «elle est allée faire des courses» (she went to do some shopping) or «il est allé faire des réparations» (he went to do some repairs). Use with a noun (usually plural) indicating the activity (courses, photos, réparations, etc.). The auxiliary past form «allé(e)» agrees in gender/number when used with être in compound tenses (elle est allée). In informal speech you may hear «aller faire + [noun]» to mean 'to go do [something]'.
target_language_example: Elle est allée faire des courses cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: She went to do some shopping this afternoon.

meaning: a conversational prompt: 'so, what...' used to ask what (we/you) have, do, say, or will do next.
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase that combines 'alors' (so/then) with the start of 'qu'est-ce que' (what). Often used to move a conversation forward, ask for the next step, or request information/decisions. Informal to neutral spoken register; in writing you might see the full form 'Alors, qu'est-ce que...' or shorter 'Alors, qu'est-ce qu'on...'. The phrase usually continues with a verb or noun (ex.: '...on fait ?' = '...we do?').
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce qu'on fait ce soir ?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing tonight?

meaning: short for 'alors ce/ça' used to start a sentence or reaction: 'so, it/that...' or 'well, ...'
additional_notes: This is an informal clipped form you'll see in speech or casual writing where the next word begins with a vowel or is 'est' (e.g. 'alors c'est...'). Often used to introduce a comment, reaction, conclusion, or to resume/redirect a conversation. The full forms are 'alors ce...' or 'alors ça...' depending on meaning (ce/ça).
target_language_example: Alors c'est comme ça que tu veux faire ?
native_language_example: So that's how you want to do it?

meaning: A spoken way to begin a comment, reaction, conclusion, or summary — similar to 'so, it's...' or 'well, it's...' in English.
additional_notes: Common in informal and neutral conversation to introduce an opinion, explanation, or decision. 'Alors' means 'so' or 'then'; adding 'c'est' emphasizes what follows. Tone and context can make it neutral, dismissive, emphatic, or conversational. Often followed by an adjective, clause, or evaluation.
target_language_example: Alors c'est décidé, on part demain.
native_language_example: So, it's decided — we're leaving tomorrow.

meaning: 'then' or 'so' in certain fixed expressions (rare/formal); often part of larger phrases like «alors de + noun» meaning 'at the time of' or 'during'.
additional_notes: Alone, "alors" means 'then', 'so', or 'at that time'. The sequence "alors de" is less common by itself and typically appears inside fixed or formal expressions (e.g. «alors de la réunion» = 'during the meeting' / 'at the time of the meeting'). In everyday spoken French you'd more often hear "lors de" (more standard for 'during') or simply "pendant". Use "alors de" only in contexts where a formal written tone is appropriate or when copying a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Il a parlé alors de la situation économique.
native_language_example: He then spoke about the economic situation.

meaning: then she / so she (used to continue or comment on a story about a female person)
additional_notes: Combines alors (then/so/therefore) + elle (she). Used to sequence events, draw a conclusion, or introduce what a woman/person did next. Tone and exact meaning depend on context: can be temporal ('and then she...'), causal ('so she...'), or conversational filler ('well, she...'). Not an idiom—literal composition applies.
target_language_example: Il a expliqué la situation, alors elle a décidé de partir.
native_language_example: He explained the situation, so she decided to leave.

meaning: A sequence of the discourse marker 'alors' followed immediately by 'en' (pronoun or preposition). Not a fixed idiom on its own; it functions as part of larger constructions to introduce a consequence, transition, or to refer back to something represented by 'en'. Meaning depends on context and the role of 'en'.
additional_notes: 'Alors' is a discourse marker meaning 'so/then/then again'. 'En' can be a pronoun replacing a quantity or phrase introduced earlier, or part of prepositional phrases (e.g. 'en ce qui concerne'). The two words can appear together (often with a comma: 'Alors, en...') or consecutively without a comma when 'en' is the pronoun: e.g. 'Alors en as-tu?' Pay attention to punctuation and intonation in speech. For learners: study 'alors' and the uses of 'en' separately; the combined sequence does not have an independent fixed meaning.
target_language_example: Alors en as-tu parlé avec elle ?
native_language_example: So, have you talked to her about it?

meaning: 'so' or 'then' when followed by 'he/it' (il) — used to link and continue a sentence about 'he' or 'it'.
additional_notes: Combines the adverb 'alors' (so/then/therefore/then) with the subject pronoun 'il' (he/it). Used to continue or draw a conclusion about a previously mentioned situation. Depending on context, 'alors' can indicate a result (so), a moment in time (then), a conversational filler (well), or to resume a story. Example patterns: 'Alors il a dit…' (So he said...), 'Alors il faut...' (So it is necessary...).
target_language_example: Il a fini son travail, alors il est parti.
native_language_example: He finished his work, so he left.

meaning: 'so I' or 'then I' — the phrase 'alors' followed by 'je' starts a statement that links to what came before (so, then, therefore) + 'I'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'alors' is a very common discourse word meaning 'so', 'then', 'at that time' or 'therefore'. When followed by a subject pronoun ('alors je...') it often appears in spoken or written French to continue, explain, or conclude an action or thought (e.g. 'alors je lui ai dit...' = 'so I told him...'). It is compositional (the parts keep their meanings). Neutral register — used in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Alors je suis parti(e) parce que c'était tard.
native_language_example: So I left because it was late.

meaning: "so the" or "then the" (literal combination of alors + le); not a fixed idiom.
additional_notes: This is simply the adverb/connector alors ('so', 'then', 'therefore', 'in that case') followed by the definite article le ('the'). It can appear in spoken or written French when 'alors' introduces or links to a noun phrase introduced by 'le' (e.g. 'Alors le problème...'). Not a special phrase—meaning depends on the sentence. Watch word order and contractions (e.g. 'alors que' is different: 'while').
target_language_example: Alors le problème, c'est que nous n'avons pas assez de temps.
native_language_example: So the problem is that we don't have enough time.

meaning: 'alors' = then/so; 'ne' = particle used in negation (not) — together they are not a fixed phrase
additional_notes: Not a set expression. 'Alors' is a common adverb meaning 'then', 'so', 'well' and can introduce consequence or transition. 'Ne' is the particle used in negation (usually paired with 'pas', 'jamais', 'plus', etc.). 'Alors ne' can appear when 'alors' is followed immediately by a negation (e.g. « alors ne fais pas ça »). In spoken French, the 'ne' is often omitted: « alors, fais pas ça ». Do not treat 'alors ne' as a single lexical unit; learn each word separately.
target_language_example: Alors ne fais pas ça maintenant.
native_language_example: So, don't do that now.

meaning: 'so, then' used before 'we' (nous) — roughly 'so we' or 'then we'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'alors' can mean 'then', 'so', 'at that time' or be a filler word. Paired with 'nous' it typically introduces what 'we' will do next, summarizes a conclusion, or moves the conversation forward (e.g. 'Alors nous...'). In writing a comma after 'alors' is common but not required. Tone can be neutral; context determines formality.
target_language_example: Alors nous partons à huit heures demain.
native_language_example: So, we are leaving at eight o'clock tomorrow.

meaning: so/then where (used to introduce a question or point about location or situation)
additional_notes: Combines alors (so/then/therefore) + où (where). Used to connect ideas, ask for clarification, or transition to asking 'where' something is or will happen. Can be spoken alone as a lead-in: «Alors, où...?». Tone depends on context: neutral to slightly prompting.
target_language_example: Alors où est la réunion demain ?
native_language_example: So where is the meeting tomorrow?

meaning: while / whereas / even though (contrast or simultaneous actions)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast (whereas) or to indicate two actions happening at the same time (while). Context determines meaning: often contrasts two facts (Mes chaussures sont vieilles, alors que les siennes sont neuves) or points out simultaneity or surprise (Tu es resté planté alors que mon fils me mentait). Can be followed by indicative tense. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il travaille tard, alors que sa sœur rentre tôt.
native_language_example: He works late, whereas his sister comes home early.

meaning: 'while' or 'whereas' (introduces a contrast or simultaneous action)
additional_notes: Used to link two clauses: to contrast two facts (whereas) or to indicate that something happens at the same time as something else (while). Standard French form is 'alors que'; 'alors qui' is less common and may be a regionalism, colloquial usage, or typo. For formal writing prefer 'alors que'.
target_language_example: Il prétendait travailler, alors qui passait son temps à regarder la télévision.
native_language_example: He claimed to be working, whereas he spent his time watching television.

meaning: 'so/then' + 'you' — phrase used to address someone, often to follow up, prompt, or react
additional_notes: Combines alors ('so/then/therefore') with the informal pronoun tu ('you'). Common in spoken French to continue a conversation, express surprise, prompt action, or ask a follow-up question. Tone and punctuation change meaning: with a question mark it's a prompt (e.g., 'Alors tu viens ?'); with an exclamation it can show surprise or impatience (e.g., 'Alors tu !' — rare, often needs more context); as an opening it can lead into a longer sentence. Informal and typical in speech; usually followed by a verb or clarification.
target_language_example: Alors tu viens ce soir ?
native_language_example: So, you coming tonight?

meaning: Literal sequence 'alors un' — 'so a' or 'then a'. Not a fixed idiom; appears when 'alors' (so/then) is immediately followed by 'un' (a/one) starting the next phrase.
additional_notes: The two words are common individually: 'alors' introduces what follows (so/then/at that time) and 'un' is the indefinite article or numeral. 'Alors un' is not an established expression — you will see it when 'alors' is directly followed by a noun phrase beginning with 'un'. In writing a comma after 'alors' is often used ('Alors, un...'), but the exact contiguous sequence without punctuation ('alors un') can also occur in spoken or rushed writing. Do not treat as an idiom.
target_language_example: Il a hésité, alors un homme s'est levé pour intervenir.
native_language_example: He hesitated, so a man stood up to intervene.

meaning: 'so you' or 'then you' (used to address or pivot to the listener(s), introducing a question, conclusion, or contrast).
additional_notes: Alone, alors means 'so', 'then', or 'therefore'. Paired with vous it introduces a comment or question about the listener(s). Meaning depends on context and intonation and may be followed by a comma in writing: e.g. Alors vous, qu'en pensez-vous ? It is compositional (straightforward combination of words), not a fixed idiom, and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Alors vous, qu'est-ce que vous en dites ?
native_language_example: So you, what do you think about it?

meaning: a spoken/colloquial way to introduce what happens next or to mean 'so, at' (often part of larger expressions like 'alors à + time/place' or a casual filler 'alors, à ...').
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence is not a fixed idiom; it typically appears when 'alors' (so/then/then well) is followed by a preposition 'à' starting the next part of the sentence (e.g. 'alors à demain' = 'so, see you tomorrow'). In speech it can act as a connector or filler: 'alors, à...' to introduce a plan, time or place. Don't treat it as a single lexical item — learn 'alors' and common collocations (alors que, alors ça, alors voilà, alors à + [time/place]).
target_language_example: Bon, alors à demain pour le déjeuner.
native_language_example: Alright, so see you tomorrow for lunch.

meaning: a conversational filler meaning roughly 'so, that...' or 'well, that...'; often introduces a reaction or conclusion about something just mentioned.
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase: 'alors' is a common discourse marker ('so', 'then', 'well') and 'ça' ('that/it') can follow to refer back to something. Used to express surprise, emphasis, to start a comment, or to prompt continuation. Tone and context determine meaning — can be followed by a clause, an exclamation, or left hanging. Example continuations: 'alors ça...', 'alors ça va?', 'alors ça, c'est...', or 'alors ça!' as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Alors ça, je ne m'y attendais pas du tout !
native_language_example: Well, that I did not expect at all!

meaning: 'fine for' (a penalty given because of something)
additional_notes: Used to say someone received or paid a monetary penalty for a specific offense (e.g. 'amende pour excès de vitesse' = fine for speeding). Typically followed by the reason introduced by a noun or an infinitive phrase (pour + noun / pour + infinitive). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a reçu une amende pour stationnement interdit.
native_language_example: She received a fine for illegal parking.

meaning: a friend of (someone); indicates the person to whom someone is a friend. This spelling uses 'a' (without accent) but note standard French requires 'à' with accent.
additional_notes: The correct French preposition is 'à' with an accent ('ami à'). 'ami a' (without accent) is a common misspelling when typing quickly or omitting diacritics. In spoken French you might hear constructions like 'C'est l'ami à Paul' (colloquial/regional); the most standard form is 'l'ami de Paul'. Use 'à' for informal/regional usage and 'de' for standard written French.
target_language_example: C'est l'ami a Paul.
native_language_example: He's Paul's friend.

meaning: Not a complete fixed phrase in French; likely part of a larger phrase meaning "friend at/on/to" (e.g. ami au travail = friend at work).
additional_notes: By itself, "ami au" is unfinished: "au" is the contraction of "à + le" and needs a following noun (au cinéma, au travail, au téléphone, etc.). You will usually see "ami au/à la/aux" when specifying where or in what role someone is a friend (e.g. "un ami au travail" = a friend from work). Use the correct contraction (au for masculine singular nouns, à la for feminine singular, à l' before a vowel, aux for plural).
target_language_example: C'est un ami au travail.
native_language_example: He is a friend from work.

meaning: literally 'friend in'; often part of a phrase meaning 'a friend in (a place or group)' or 'a friend at (a location)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'ami dans' is the sequence of the noun ami (friend) followed by the preposition dans (in/inside). It appears in larger expressions like 'un ami dans la police' (a friend in the police) or 'un ami dans le quartier' (a friend in the neighborhood). Use it when specifying where or within which group someone is your friend or contact. Word order and articles are important: 'un ami dans la maison' (a friend in the house) vs. 'l'ami dans la maison' (the friend in the house).
target_language_example: J'ai un ami dans l'équipe de foot.
native_language_example: I have a friend on the soccer team.

meaning: 'friend in' — used before a noun to indicate someone is a friend in a particular context or role (e.g. ami en commun = mutual friend).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; 'ami en' appears when followed by a noun or adjective to specify the domain (ami en commun, ami en ligne, ami en qui j'ai confiance). Often you'll see 'ami' followed by 'de' instead (ami de la famille). Make sure to include the following word to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: C'est un ami en qui j'ai confiance.
native_language_example: He's a friend I trust.

meaning: "ami est" is not a standard fixed French phrase; it looks like two words meaning 'friend is' (ami = friend, est = is).
additional_notes: This sequence would appear when describing someone (e.g. « mon ami est… » = 'my friend is…'). Alone, 'ami est' is incomplete and not used by itself. Remember to include a subject or possessive (mon/ton/son) or continue the sentence with an adjective, profession, age, etc. 'Ami' is masculine singular; use 'amie' for a female friend. If the subject is plural use 'amis sont'.
target_language_example: Mon ami est avocat.
native_language_example: My friend is a lawyer.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistake or two separate words 'ami' (friend) + 'et' (and).
additional_notes: There is no common multiword expression 'ami et' in French. If you see 'ami et' in text, it is probably two separate words: 'ami' (a male friend) or 'une amie' (female friend), followed by the conjunction 'et' meaning 'and'. Check the surrounding words to determine the intended phrase (for example 'ami et collègue' = 'friend and colleague').
target_language_example: Il est mon ami et collègue au travail.
native_language_example: He is my friend and colleague at work.

meaning: This looks like two words 'ami' (friend) + 'ne' (part of negation), but as written 'ami ne' is not a correct standalone French phrase.
additional_notes: Possibly a typo or mis-segmentation. In French, 'ami' means 'friend'. 'Ne' is used with 'pas' (or other negatives) to form negation (e.g. 'ne ... pas'). If you meant 'ami(e)' with parentheses, that indicates the feminine form 'amie'. If you meant 'amis' (plural) or a phrase like 'ami ne... pas' you need the verb to complete the negation (e.g. 'Mon ami ne vient pas' = 'My friend is not coming').
target_language_example: Mon ami ne comprend pas.
native_language_example: My friend does not understand.

meaning: 'a friend of' or 'a friend associated with' (used to indicate possession or association, often before a possessive phrase like 'moi' or a name).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; this is the noun 'ami' plus the preposition 'à' used colloquially to indicate belonging/association (e.g. 'une amie à moi' = 'a friend of mine'). Standard written French more often uses 'de' for simple possession ('un ami de Paul'), while 'à' appears in more familiar or emphatic expressions ('une amie à moi', 'un ami à Paul' in some regional/colloquial uses).
target_language_example: C'est un ami à Paul qui habite là-bas.
native_language_example: He's a friend of Paul's who lives over there.

meaning: appears to be two separate words: 'amie' = (female) friend; 'a' = has (3rd person singular of avoir) or preposition 'to/at' depending on context.
