additional_notes: Used for video (slow motion) and figuratively to say something is happening slowly or at reduced pace. Common in both literal (film) and metaphorical contexts. Can appear as 'mettre/voir qch au ralenti' or 'fonctionner/travailler au ralenti.'
target_language_example: Ils regardent la vidéo au ralenti pour voir le détail.
native_language_example: They watch the video in slow motion to see the detail.

meaning: goodbye
additional_notes: A standard, polite way to say goodbye when parting. It is more neutral/formal than salut. Literally, it comes from the idea of 'until we see each other again,' but it is used like ordinary 'goodbye.'
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, au revoir !
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, goodbye!

meaning: "help!" / "to help" (call for help)
additional_notes: Used to shout for immediate help or to draw urgent attention. Can be an exclamation alone (Au secours !) or part of a sentence (crier au secours = to cry for help). Formality: neutral; common in urgent situations. Literal translation: "to (the) help" but functions as an urgent plea.
target_language_example: Au secours ! Quelqu'un m'a volé mon sac.
native_language_example: Help! Someone stole my bag.

meaning: within; inside; at the heart of (used figuratively to mean 'in' an organization, group, family, etc.).
additional_notes: Common formal phrase used to say something exists or happens inside an institution, group, family, or body. Often followed by a noun (au sein de + [nom]). Equivalent to 'within' or 'as part of' in English. More formal than 'dans'.
target_language_example: Elle travaille au sein de l'équipe marketing.
native_language_example: She works within the marketing team.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely incorrect or a fragment (possibly intended: «en dessous», «au sous-sol», or «au-dessus»).
additional_notes:
There is no common standalone expression «au sous» in French. Possible intended meanings depending on context:
- «au sous-sol» = in the basement (can be shortened mistakenly to «au sous» in speech/writing but incorrect).
- «en dessous» = underneath / below.
- «au-dessus» = above.
If you saw «au sous» in text, check for a typo or missing word. Ask the speaker/writer for clarification or look for surrounding words that complete the phrase.
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il y a une faute — on voulait dire «au sous-sol» : Le stockage est au sous-sol.
native_language_example: I think there's a mistake — they meant «au sous-sol»: The storage is in the basement.

meaning: 'about' or 'regarding' (on the subject of).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of what you're going to say or write. Formal to neutral register; common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (au sujet de ce rapport / au sujet de toi).
target_language_example: Je t'appelle au sujet de ta candidature.
native_language_example: I'm calling you about your application.

meaning: at the time of
additional_notes: Used to place something in a past era, often before a person, period, or generation: au temps de Napoléon, au temps de mes grands-parents. It often refers to 'back when' something was the case.
target_language_example: Au temps de mes grands-parents, il n'y avait pas d'internet.
native_language_example: In my grandparents' time, there was no internet.

meaning: in total; altogether; overall.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the final sum, total number, or overall amount. Common in questions (Au total ? / Combien au total ?) and statements (Il y en a X au total). Neutral register and very frequent in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Nous avons trois livres et deux cahiers, dix au total.
native_language_example: We have three books and two notebooks, ten in total.

meaning: at work
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate location (at one's workplace) or being engaged in work. Can mean 'to work' when describing the action of starting work (e.g. se mettre au travail = to get to work). Use depending on context: 'Je suis au travail' = I'm at work; 'aller au travail' = to go to work; 'se mettre au travail' = to begin working.
target_language_example: Je suis au travail, on en parlera ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm at work, we'll talk about it tonight.

meaning: at work at (a time or place) — used before specifying when or where someone is at work
additional_notes: This construction combines 'au travail' (at work) with a following preposition phrase introduced by 'à' (e.g., a time or a location). It's not a fixed idiom by itself; you will usually see 'au travail' alone or followed by 'à' + time/location: 'au travail à 9h' (at work at 9:00) or 'au travail à Paris' (at work in Paris). For simple usage, beginners can use 'au travail' to mean 'at work' and add 'à' plus the time/place as needed.
target_language_example: Je serai au travail à 9 heures.
native_language_example: I will be at work at 9 o'clock.

meaning: across, through, or over (something); indicating movement or viewpoint passing from one side to the other or through something
additional_notes: Used to describe physical crossing (across the road, through a city) or figurative perspective ('through someone's eyes'). Can mean 'across' or 'through' depending on context. Often followed by a noun. Synonyms: 'à travers' (more common), both are largely interchangeable though 'au travers de' can sound slightly more formal or literary.
target_language_example: Il a marché au travers de la forêt jusqu'au village.
native_language_example: He walked through the forest to the village.

meaning: on the phone
additional_notes: Used to say someone is using the telephone or that something happened via a phone call. Can be used with verbs like être (être au téléphone), parler (parler au téléphone), répondre (répondre au téléphone) and with a person: parler à quelqu'un au téléphone = speak to someone on the phone.
target_language_example: Je suis au téléphone, je te rappelle après.
native_language_example: I'm on the phone, I'll call you back later.

meaning: 'at the wheel' / 'driving' (in the driver's seat)
additional_notes: Used to say someone is driving or in control of a vehicle. Common in everyday spoken and written French. Can refer literally to being behind the steering wheel or more figuratively to being in control. Often follows verbs like être, être au volant de, or appears after a noun (le type au volant).
target_language_example: Qui est au volant ?
native_language_example: Who is driving?

meaning: at least
additional_notes: Used to express a minimum number, amount, or duration. It can also mean that something is the minimum acceptable option, as in requests or suggestions: Tu peux au moins répondre. = You could at least reply.
target_language_example: On peut au moins essayer.
native_language_example: We can at least try.

meaning: above; over; higher than (in position or level).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is physically higher than something else or higher in level/amount. Followed by a noun or pronoun (au-dessus de la table, au-dessus de moi). Can also be used figuratively (au-dessus des attentes). The opposite is « au-dessous de ».
target_language_example: Le tableau est accroché au-dessus de la cheminée.
native_language_example: The painting is hung above the fireplace.

meaning: no case; not in any case; under no circumstances
additional_notes: Used after a negative idea to emphatically say that something does not apply in any situation. Commonly appears in expressions like "en aucun cas" (in no case/under no circumstances) or alone after a verb/negation: "Ce n'est aucun cas acceptable" (less common) — more natural: "En aucun cas". Formal/register-neutral.
target_language_example: En aucun cas tu ne dois divulguer ce mot de passe.
native_language_example: Under no circumstances should you disclose this password.

meaning: 'increase in' or 'rise of' (used before a noun).
additional_notes: A common formal phrase used to talk about a rise or growth in something (augmentation de prix, augmentation de salaire, augmentation de la température). It must be followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by de. In English word order it's often 'an increase in X' or 'the rise of X'.
target_language_example: L'augmentation de salaire sera annoncée demain.
native_language_example: The increase in salary will be announced tomorrow.

meaning: near, beside, with; or in the context of someone (toward/with someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical closeness (beside/near) or relational/communicative context (with/about someone). Common with people or institutions: 'auprès de quelqu'un' = with/near someone, 'auprès de' + noun. Often interchangeable with 'près de' for physical proximity but 'auprès de' emphasizes relation or interaction.
target_language_example: Il a appris beaucoup auprès de ses professeurs.
native_language_example: He learned a lot from/with his teachers.

meaning: 'I would have liked (that)...' — expresses a wish or regret about something that did not happen.
additional_notes: Used to talk about wishes, regrets, or unrealized desires in the past. Followed by a subordinate clause with the imperfect or past subjunctive (in speech often the imperfect) or the conditional + past depending on structure: here it's conditional present + que + (imperfect/subjunctive). Common in polite complaints or expressing disappointment.
target_language_example: J'aurais aimé que tu m'appelles avant de venir.
native_language_example: I would have liked you to call me before coming.

meaning: 'would never' (conditional negative: expresses something you would not have expected or would not do)
additional_notes: Combination of the conditional form of 'avoir' (tu/je/etc. + 'aurais') plus 'jamais' for negation. Often appears with 'ne' (Je ne l'aurais jamais fait) but in spoken/written French the 'ne' is sometimes dropped (Je n'aurais jamais...). Used to express surprise about something that did happen (I would never have thought) or to say someone should not have done something (you should never have... / you ought not to have...). Context determines whether it's about expectation ('would never have believed') or regret/criticism ('shouldn't have').
target_language_example: Je n'aurais jamais imaginé ça.
native_language_example: I would never have imagined that.

meaning: 'would never have thought' (expression of surprise or disbelief about something imagined in the past or about a hypothetical past).
additional_notes: Often appears in the conditional perfect (je n'aurais jamais pensé...) to express that the speaker did not expect or cannot imagine something. Frequently followed by que + clause. The full negative form usually includes ne (Je n'aurais jamais pensé...), but in spoken French the ne is often dropped: J'aurais jamais pensé.... Used to react to surprising news or to state an unexpected possibility.
target_language_example: Je n'aurais jamais pensé qu'elle accepterait l'invitation.
native_language_example: I would never have thought that she would accept the invitation.

meaning: you should have been (conditional past of obligation + être).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone ought to have been or behaved a certain way in the past (regret or criticism). Formal/plural or polite form (vous). Structure: vous + auriez dû + être + adjective/place/etc. Can change gender/number in the adjective after être (e.g., prudent/prudente/prudents/prudentes).
target_language_example: Vous auriez dû être ici hier.
native_language_example: You should have been here yesterday.

meaning: you too; you as well (addressing 'vous').
additional_notes: Used to tell or ask someone (formal/plural 'vous') that they are included in an action, quality, or feeling. Often placed before or after 'vous' for emphasis: 'Vous aussi...' or '...vous aussi'. Common in questions and exclamations (e.g. surprise, disappointment, solidarity).
target_language_example: Vous aussi, vous pouvez participer si vous voulez.
native_language_example: You too can take part if you want.

meaning: 'also has' or 'has as well' (sequence of the adverb aussi followed by the verb form a of avoir)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common sequence where aussi ('also') appears immediately before the verb form a (3rd-person singular of avoir). Standard neutral word order in French places aussi after the verb (Il a aussi...). Placing aussi before the verb (Il aussi a...) is less common and used for emphasis, contrast, or stylistic effect; it may sound marked or poetic in everyday speech. Ensure subject-verb agreement and be aware of register.
target_language_example: Il aussi a une voiture.
native_language_example: He also has a car.

meaning: literally "also this"; rare/marked expression used to link or emphasize an additional point — often formal or written; in everyday speech speakers prefer alternatives like "ça aussi" or just "aussi"
additional_notes: "Aussi ce" is uncommon as a standalone phrase in spoken French. When it appears, it's typically in formal, literary, or legal writing, often at the start of a clause to add or emphasize an additional point. Word order and punctuation matter: when "Aussi" begins a sentence it can signal a conclusion or continuation and may be followed by a comma. In most contexts, native speakers use "ça aussi", "aussi" elsewhere in the sentence, or rephrase the clause for clarity.
target_language_example: Aussi ce constat mérite-t-il d'être examiné avec attention.
native_language_example: Also, this finding deserves to be examined carefully.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a confusion or incorrect combination (no clear meaning).
additional_notes: The sequence "aussi ce que" does not form a common French expression. Native speakers would not use it as a set phrase. Possible intended alternatives depending on context: "aussi que" (as... as / also that), "aussi" + clause (meaning "also"), or "ce que" (meaning "what/that which"). If you see "aussi ce que" in writing, check whether one of those corrections fits the sentence. Example correct alternatives: "aussi... que" — Il est aussi grand que toi. "ce que" — Dis‑moi ce que tu veux. "aussi" used alone — Elle vient aussi.
target_language_example: Incorrect: *Je veux aussi ce que tu as.* — Better: Je veux aussi ce que tu as dit. / Je veux ce que tu as.
native_language_example: Incorrect: *I want also what you have.* — Better: I also want what you have. / I want what you have.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a sequence of words that can appear inside a larger sentence meaning 'also what I...' or 'as well what I...'.
additional_notes: This is not a stand-alone idiom. It combines 'aussi' (also/as well), 'ce que' (what/that which) and 'je' (I). It will usually be followed by a verb or clause. Punctuation and word order affect naturalness — e.g. 'Aussi ce que je dis...' or 'Ce que je veux aussi...' are more common. For learners: treat 'aussi' and 'ce que' separately and insert them into full sentences.
target_language_example: Aussi ce que je dis est important pour le groupe.
native_language_example: Also what I say is important for the group.

meaning: 'also in' or 'too in' (adds that something applies/exists in another place, time, or context)
additional_notes: 'Aussi' means 'also' or 'too'; 'dans' means 'in' (inside, within, in a time period). Together they are used when stating that something is true in another location, context, or time (e.g. "also in Paris", "also in the report"). Word order: 'aussi' comes before 'dans'.
target_language_example: Cette règle s'applique à Lyon, et aussi dans le sud de la France.
native_language_example: This rule applies in Lyon, and also in the south of France.

meaning: 'also of' or 'too much to' depending on context; often part of constructions meaning 'as well as' or 'also has/contains'.
additional_notes: Aussi by itself commonly means 'also' or 'too'. In combination with de, the meaning depends on the surrounding words and grammar. Examples: 'aussi de' can appear when listing items ('Il y a du pain, aussi de la confiture' = 'There is bread, and also jam'), or within phrases like 'aussi de la peine' (colloquial emphasis). It can also occur in comparative or causative structures ('C'est aussi de la faute de...' ≈ 'It is also the fault of...'). Pay attention to articles (de, du, de la) and word order to determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Il y a des pommes, aussi de la salade si tu veux.
native_language_example: There are apples, and also some salad if you want.

meaning: also some/also any (feminine singular partitive) — adds or includes something in addition
additional_notes: Aussi de la combines 'aussi' (also/as well) with the partitive article 'de la' used before feminine singular uncountable nouns (e.g., 'aussi de la salade' = also some salad). It's used to say you want/there is/there will be more of something, or to add an item to a list. Word order: 'aussi de la' usually appears before a noun. When the noun is masculine use 'aussi du', and with plural use 'aussi des'. In negative constructions the partitive often becomes 'de' (e.g., 'pas de').
target_language_example: Je prendrai aussi de la soupe.
native_language_example: I'll have some soup too.

meaning: also some / also any (adds 'des' after 'aussi' when listing additional plural nouns)
additional_notes: Aussi means 'also' or 'too'. When you add it before a plural noun with the partitive/indefinite article des (some), you get 'aussi des' to say 'also some' or 'also [plural items]'. Common in sentences that list additional items or causes: e.g. 'Il y a des fruits, et aussi des légumes' = 'There are fruits, and also some vegetables.' Word order: 'aussi' comes before 'des'.
target_language_example: Elle a apporté des gâteaux, et aussi des boissons.
native_language_example: She brought cakes, and also some drinks.

meaning: 'also in' or 'as well in' (used to add that something applies in a particular place, time, or context).
additional_notes: Aussi means 'also' or 'too'. When followed by a preposition like en, it links the previous idea to a specific context introduced by en (e.g. 'aussi en France' = 'also in France'). It often appears in sentences like 'Il est connu aussi en ville' or 'Cette règle vaut aussi en entreprise.' Word order matters: 'aussi' usually comes before the context word or phrase.
target_language_example: Cette loi s'applique aussi en France.
native_language_example: This law applies also in France.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a sequence where 'aussi' (also/so) precedes the verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed expression in French. More often you will see 'aussi' used before an adjective or at the start of a clause (e.g. 'Il est aussi grand' = 'He is also tall', or 'Aussi, ...' = 'Therefore/so' in formal written French when followed by an inversion: 'Aussi arrive-t-il...' ). 'Aussi est' can appear in sentences like 'Il aussi est...' (colloquial, but incorrect word order) or in structures such as 'Aussi est-il...' (formal: 'Therefore he is...'). For beginners: learn 'aussi' = 'also' or 'too' (placed before the adjective or after the subject: 'Elle aussi' = 'her too') and 'est' = third-person singular of 'être' ('is').
target_language_example: Elle aussi est contente.
native_language_example: She is happy too.

meaning: 'also I' or 'I also' — used to add that the speaker does something or feels the same (rare/uncommon word order in modern French)
additional_notes: Aussi normally means 'also' or 'too'. Placing 'aussi' directly before the subject pronoun ('aussi je') is uncommon in contemporary spoken French and can sound literary, formal, or archaic. More natural alternatives are 'moi aussi' (Me too) or 'je aussi' (colloquial, better: 'moi aussi' or 'moi aussi, je...'). In written/formal French, 'Aussi' at the start of a sentence can mean 'therefore' and is followed by inversion: 'Aussi, je...' meaning 'Therefore, I...'. Be careful: word order changes meaning and register — to express 'me too' use 'moi aussi'.
target_language_example: Aussi je souhaite préciser que je suis d'accord.
native_language_example: Also, I wish to clarify that I agree.

meaning: literally 'also the' — used when adding emphasis or linking information; often part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'aussi, le ...' or 'aussi le/la/les ...').
additional_notes: ‘Aussi’ means 'also' or 'too' and normally sits before the element it modifies. When written as 'aussi le' it simply combines 'also' + the definite article and will appear before a noun or a clause introduced by 'que'/'qui' etc. Depending on context, punctuation changes meaning: 'Aussi, le...' at the start of a sentence can mean 'Therefore/So, the...' in formal/written French (inverted use), while 'aussi le chat' just means 'the cat as well'. Check surrounding words to determine whether 'aussi' means 'also' or is used in a formal connective sense.
target_language_example: Marie vient aussi le soir.
native_language_example: Marie also comes in the evening.

meaning: literally 'also my' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment used when adding something belonging to the speaker (e.g. 'also mine').
additional_notes: This combination is not a set expression in French. You'll more commonly see 'aussi' (also/too) and possessives like 'mon' (my) used together in a sentence (e.g. 'C'est aussi mon livre' = 'It's also my book'). Word order matters: 'aussi mon' by itself is incomplete and should be part of a full sentence. 'Aussi' can go before the verb or before the adjective/noun it modifies depending on meaning.
target_language_example: C'est aussi mon sac.
native_language_example: It's also my bag.

meaning: as clear/notable (feminine singular) — 'aussi' = as/too, 'nette' = clear/distinct/noticeable
additional_notes: Phrase compares equality using 'aussi + adjective + que' (as ... as). 'Nette' is the feminine singular form of 'net' and can mean clear, distinct, sharp, definite, or marked depending on context. Without 'que' and a comparison target, it may appear in fragments (e.g. 'aussi nette que sa sœur' = 'as clear as her sister'). Make sure adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes (net, nette, nets, nettes).
target_language_example: Sa décision est aussi nette que la tienne.
native_language_example: Her decision is as clear as yours.

meaning: also for / as well for
additional_notes: Used to add another purpose, recipient, reason, or item to something already mentioned. It combines aussi (also) with pour (for). Common in sentences like « C'est aussi pour... » or « Je l'achète aussi pour... ». Word order: aussi usually precedes the element it modifies; with pour it often appears together before a noun or verb phrase.
target_language_example: Je l'ai pris aussi pour ma sœur.
native_language_example: I took it also for my sister. / I also got it for my sister.

meaning: as clean; equally clean
additional_notes: Aussi ... (adjective) is used to compare equality: 'aussi propre' means something is 'as clean' as something else. Usually appears with que (aussi propre que...) to say 'as clean as'. Without context it can also appear in exclamations (e.g. 'aussi propre !') but the typical use is comparative. Word order: adjective after subject or with être (Il est aussi propre que...).
target_language_example: Cette table est aussi propre que la tienne.
native_language_example: This table is as clean as yours.

meaning: as... as (used in comparisons); can also appear in formal/literary clauses meaning 'also that' or 'just as'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in comparisons with the pattern 'aussi + adjective/adverb + que' (e.g. 'aussi grand que' = 'as tall as'). In everyday use it marks equality in degree. In formal/registerd contexts it can link clauses with a meaning like 'also that' or 'just as'. Do not confuse with 'aussi' alone (meaning 'also'/'too'). Word order: 'aussi' before the adjective/adverb, 'que' before the comparison target.
target_language_example: Cette voiture est aussi rapide que la sienne.
native_language_example: This car is as fast as his/hers.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French. Appears to be an incomplete or mistaken sequence combining 'aussi' (also/too/so) and 'quelque' (some/a few/about). It can occur in informal speech if followed by other words (e.g. 'aussi quelque part' or 'aussi, quelque ...'), but as a standalone two-word unit it has no established meaning.
additional_notes:
Avoid using 'aussi quelque' as a fixed expression. Correct forms you might mean include:
- 'aussi... que' (comparison: 'as... as'),
- 'quelque chose' (something),
- 'quelque' + number (about/around),
- 'aussi' alone to mean 'also/too'.
If you see 'aussi quelque' it is likely a typo, elision, or part of a larger construction and needs context to be interpreted.
target_language_example: Il a dit, aussi quelque chose, mais je n'ai pas bien entendu.
native_language_example: He said, also something, but I didn't hear well.

meaning: 'you too' or 'also you' (used to include the person addressed).
additional_notes: Aussi + subject pronoun (like tu) is less common in everyday spoken French than 'toi aussi'. 'Aussi tu' can appear in formal or written contexts, or with a pause/intonation (e.g., 'Aussi, tu...') and sometimes before inversion in questions ('Aussi tu viens ?' — somewhat marked). For learners, use 'toi aussi' in casual speech. Word-for-word translation is possible but the natural ordering differs from English.
target_language_example: Aussi tu viens ce soir ?
native_language_example: You too are coming tonight?

meaning: also a / also one (feminine).
additional_notes: Combines aussi (also) + une (the feminine indefinite article). Used to add an additional feminine noun or item. Word order: 'aussi' usually comes before the article/noun. Context determines whether it means 'also a' or 'as well a' — English often omits 'a' (e.g., 'also one' vs 'also a').
target_language_example: Je veux aussi une pomme.
native_language_example: I also want an apple.

meaning: literally 'also you'; rare word order in French. Can occur when 'aussi' (meaning 'also' or 'therefore') begins a clause and is followed by the subject 'vous' — e.g. 'Aussi, vous...' meaning 'Therefore, you...'. Not the normal way to say 'you too' (use 'vous aussi').
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon as a standalone reply. For 'you too' in responses or wishes, prefer «vous aussi». The order 'aussi vous' appears when 'aussi' is clause-initial (often written with a comma) meaning 'therefore' or 'also' followed by the subject pronoun, or in certain emphatic or literary constructions. Avoid using 'aussi vous' to mean 'you too' in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Aussi vous, si vous signez, devrez respecter les règles.
native_language_example: Also you, if you sign, will have to respect the rules.

meaning: also at / also to (used to add another place, time, person, or thing)
additional_notes: aussi means 'also' or 'too'. When followed by à + noun or pronoun, 'aussi à' adds another indirect object or location (e.g. 'also at the office', 'also to Paul'). Word order can vary: français often places 'aussi' before the verb or before the element it modifies. Be careful: 'aussi' has other uses (comparisons: 'as...as', or 'therefore' in inverted constructions), so context matters.
target_language_example: Elle pense aussi à sa famille.
native_language_example: She also thinks of her family.

meaning: as soon as; immediately when
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action that happens immediately after another. Often followed by a clause with a verb in the future (in French speech) or present depending on context. Can also appear in the set phrase "aussitôt que possible" meaning "as soon as possible".
target_language_example: Aussitôt que tu arrives, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: As soon as you arrive, call me.

meaning: as much/so much (of it/that); used to refer back to a quantity or degree previously mentioned
additional_notes: Often appears in constructions like «autant en ...» followed by a clause or pronoun (e.g. «autant en profiter», «autant en dire»). It points back to an amount, degree, or the thing just mentioned and can introduce a suggestion or consequence ("might as well / so there's no point not to"). Context determines exact translation: sometimes means "as much as", other times "so much of it" or idiomatic "might as well". Not a standalone phrase; normally part of a larger expression.
target_language_example: Il ne reste qu'une part de gâteau, autant en profiter maintenant.
native_language_example: There is only one piece of cake left, we might as well enjoy it now.

meaning: as much as
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or degrees (as much as / as ... as) and also in permissive phrases meaning 'as much as you want' or 'for as long as you want'. Often followed by a clause introduced by que (e.g. 'autant que tu veux') or by a verb/quantity. Can be used with verbs of possession, use, eating, etc.
target_language_example: Prends autant que tu veux.
native_language_example: Take as much as you want.

meaning: 'as much as possible' / 'as ... as possible'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate doing something to the greatest feasible extent. Can modify verbs (e.g., read, see, accept). Common in instructions and suggestions. Equivalent to 'as...as you can' in English.
target_language_example: Visite le musée autant que possible.
native_language_example: Visit the museum as much as possible.

meaning: around; surrounding; about (spatial or figurative).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position around something (e.g., sitting around a table, putting an arm around someone) or figuratively (e.g., 'the world doesn't revolve around you'). Often followed by a noun or pronoun. Pronunciation note: 'autour' sounds like /o.tuʁ/.
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes tous assis autour de la table.
native_language_example: We all sat around the table.

meaning: something else
additional_notes: Used to refer to a different thing. In questions, especially with vouloir or désirer, it often means "anything else?"
target_language_example: Je voudrais autre chose à boire.
native_language_example: I'd like something else to drink.

meaning: 'something else in' (part of a larger phrase meaning 'something else in [something]').
additional_notes: This fragment is not a standalone phrase; it appears inside longer expressions like "autre chose en tête" (something else on one's mind) or "autre chose en magasin" (something else in store). You will usually need the following noun or expression to complete the meaning. 'Autre chose' = 'something else'; 'en' links to the following noun or phrase.
target_language_example: J'ai autre chose en tête en ce moment.
native_language_example: I have something else on my mind at the moment.

meaning: on the other side of / the other side of
additional_notes: Used to indicate the opposite side or the far side of something (a street, table, mountain, etc.). Often appears with a definite article: de l'autre côté de (of the other side of). Can be used literally (physical location) or more loosely (across/from the other person).
target_language_example: La boulangerie est de l'autre côté de la place.
native_language_example: The bakery is on the other side of the square.

meaning: on the other side of (the)
additional_notes: Used to indicate location on the opposite side of something. Usually followed by a definite article + noun (e.g. 'autre côté du pont' = the other side of the bridge). In everyday French you'd more commonly say "de l'autre côté de" (e.g. "de l'autre côté du pont"). "Autre côté du" by itself is incomplete; expect the full form to include the preposition 'de' before 'l\'autre' or the article contraction (du/de la/des).
target_language_example: De l'autre côté du parc, il y a un café.
native_language_example: On the other side of the park, there is a café.

meaning: somewhere/someplace else; another place
additional_notes: Used to indicate a different location. Can mean 'somewhere else' (autre part) or in casual contexts 'another piece' when part is 'part'/'slice' (but note: for 'another piece' of food, French more commonly uses 'une autre part' or 'une autre part de...' depending on context). In most of the example sentences it means 'elsewhere' (do it somewhere else; sit somewhere else).
target_language_example: Allons discuter autre part, c'est trop bruyant ici.
native_language_example: Let's go talk somewhere else, it's too noisy here.

meaning: another cup of (something)
additional_notes: Used to ask for or state having an additional cup/serving of a drink (usually coffee, tea). Grammatically, 'autre' must agree with the noun: for feminine singular 'une autre tasse de', for masculine 'un autre verre de'. In question 3 the correct form is 'une autre tasse' (agreement).
target_language_example: Je prendrai une autre tasse de thé, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have another cup of tea, please.

meaning: literally 'other to' — not a fixed phrase; appears in constructions like 'un autre à...' meaning 'another (one) to.../another person to...'.
additional_notes: This is not a set expression on its own. 'autre' is an adjective or pronoun meaning 'other' or 'another', and 'à' is a preposition. They appear together in sentences such as 'un autre à appeler' (another one to call) or 'Il y en a un autre à côté' (there is another one next to it). Beginners should treat 'autre' and 'à' separately and learn common patterns: 'un/une autre' (another), 'd'autres' (others), and verb phrases with 'à' (à + infinitive = to + verb, or à + location/person).
target_language_example: Il y a un autre à appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: There is another one to call tonight.

meaning: literally 'other is' — not a standalone phrase in French; likely a fragment where 'autre' (other) is followed by a verb.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression. 'Autre' is an adjective or pronoun meaning 'other' or 'another'. It must agree in gender/number with the noun it modifies (un autre, une autre, d'autres). You will normally see 'autre' before a noun (un autre livre) or as a pronoun (je n'en veux pas d'autre). 'Autre est' could appear only as part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'L'autre est...' meaning 'the other one is...'). Do not use 'autre est' by itself.
target_language_example: L'autre est plus grand que celui-ci.
native_language_example: The other one is taller than this one.

meaning: This phrase is not a correct or natural French expression.
additional_notes: In French, 'autre' means 'other'. It is normally used before a noun (une autre idée), after a definite article with contraction (l'autre = the other), or with a pronoun (un autre, les autres). 'Autre le' is not a valid combination: the article 'le' and the adjective/pronoun 'autre' do not pair in that order. Possible correct forms depending on meaning: 'l'autre' (the other), 'un autre' (another/one other), 'une autre' (another, feminine), 'les autres' (the others). Any instance of 'autre le' should be rewritten using a correct structure.
target_language_example: *autre le* n'est pas une expression correcte en français ; on écrirait plutôt « l'autre » ou « un autre ».
native_language_example: *autre le* is not a correct expression in French; you would write « l'autre » or « un autre » instead.

meaning: This sequence is not a standalone French phrase; likely a fragment where 'autre' (other) appears before a negation or is part of a larger expression.
additional_notes: There are no common French expressions 'autre ne' by itself. 'Autre' means 'other' and is used before nouns (un autre livre), after definite articles (les autres), or in comparisons (autre chose). 'Ne' is the first part of negation (ne ... pas, ne ... plus, ne ... jamais) and must pair with a second element. If you see 'autre ne' in text, it's probably a cut-off fragment: e.g. 'autre ne ...' could continue as 'autre ne veut pas' (the other does not want) or be a typo. Learn 'autre' and common 'ne ... pas' negation separately.
target_language_example: Il y a un autre livre, mais l'autre ne m'intéresse pas.
native_language_example: There is another book, but the other one does not interest me.

meaning: in other words; that is to say.
additional_notes: Used to restate, clarify, or summarize what was just said in simpler or more explicit terms. Common in spoken and written French; can introduce a paraphrase, conclusion, or a rephrasing. Often followed by a comma. Can be used alone as a prompt ("Autrement dit ?") to ask for clarification.
target_language_example: Il est souvent en retard; autrement dit, on ne peut pas compter sur lui.
native_language_example: He's often late; in other words, you can't rely on him.

meaning: a short sequence meaning 'others in' or 'other (ones) in', not a standalone fixed phrase
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression in French. It usually appears as part of a larger phrase, for example when talking about 'other people in (the room, the group)' — e.g. «les autres en salle» (the others in the room) or in constructions like «les autres en ont parlé» (the others talked about it). Alone, 'autres en' is incomplete and requires context (a noun, clause, or verb).
target_language_example: Les autres en ont déjà discuté.
native_language_example: The others have already discussed it.

meaning: 'the others have' or 'others have' (third-person plural of avoir after 'autres').
additional_notes: Combines 'autres' (others) with the auxiliary verb 'ont' (they have). Used to say that other people did or experienced something when followed by a past participle (compound past) or to indicate possession or actions in simple constructions. Agreement: 'autres' can be masculine/feminine and singular/plural context affects preceding words (e.g. 'tous les autres', 'toutes les autres').
target_language_example: Les autres ont fini avant nous.
native_language_example: The others finished before us.

meaning: near the outskirts or edge of; around (a place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate proximity to the outskirts or surrounding area of a place (city, planet, structure). Often followed by a noun. Slightly formal/neutral; common in written and spoken French to mean 'around' or 'on the outskirts of.'
target_language_example: Ils campent aux abords de la forêt.
native_language_example: They are camping on the outskirts of the forest.

meaning: for/to the needs of his family; to support his family (financially).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like subvenir (subvenir aux besoins de ...) to indicate providing for someone's basic needs, usually financially. Pronoun sa can change (ma/tes/nos) to match the possessor. Commonly used in contexts about income, work, and support.
target_language_example: Elle travaille pour subvenir aux besoins de sa famille.
native_language_example: She works to provide for her family's needs.

meaning: 'in charge' or 'at the controls' (of a group, organization, vehicle, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has control or authority. Can be literal (at the controls of a plane/vehicle) or figurative (in charge of a company, government, situation). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Quand il est aux commandes, l'équipe travaille mieux.
native_language_example: When he's in charge, the team works better.

meaning: next to; alongside; beside (in the sense of 'together with' or 'by the side of').
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate physical position (beside) or figurative support/partnership (working alongside someone). Followed by a noun or pronoun introduced with de: ex. aux côtés de mon ami / aux côtés du président. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Elle a travaillé aux côtés de son mentor pendant trois ans.
native_language_example: She worked alongside her mentor for three years.

meaning: under the orders of; at the command of
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone is acting under someone's authority or direction (often in military, formal, or workplace contexts). Can be followed by a person or organization: «aux ordres de + nom». Formal phrasing; not common in casual speech except in set expressions (e.g. «être aux ordres de» = to be under someone's command).
target_language_example: Il a agi aux ordres de son supérieur pendant l'opération.
native_language_example: He acted under the orders of his superior during the operation.

meaning: with apples; made with apples (used after food names).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe dishes containing apples (e.g., tarte aux pommes = apple pie). 'Aux' is the contraction of à + les and agrees with plural noun 'pommes'. Also used in comparisons like 'préférer X aux pommes' meaning 'prefer X to apples.'
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une tarte aux pommes pour le dessert.
native_language_example: I bought an apple pie for dessert.

meaning: 'on someone's heels' or 'hot on the trail of' — chasing closely
additional_notes: Used to say someone is pursuing or chasing someone else closely (literally 'at the scruffs' historically). Common with police, pack/pack of animals, or figurative pursuits. Often follows the pursuer: "La police est aux trousses du voleur."
target_language_example: La police est aux trousses du suspect.
native_language_example: The police are hot on the suspect's trail.

meaning: in the eyes of; from the viewpoint of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone's perspective, judgment, or point of view. Can be literal (referring to actual eyes/appearance) or figurative (legal, moral, social opinion). Often followed by a person, institution, or abstract entity (e.g., Dieu, Rome, tous).
target_language_example: Aux yeux de la loi, elle est coupable.
native_language_example: In the eyes of the law, she is guilty.

meaning: 'had the' (imperfect tense of avoir + definite article)
additional_notes: Used to describe past continuous or habitual possession/qualities in the third-person plural (they/these people). 'Avaient' is the imperfect of 'avoir' (to have); 'le' is the masculine singular definite article that begins a noun phrase (e.g. le même âge, le choix, le don). Use 'avaient' for plural subjects (ils/elles).
target_language_example: Elles avaient le sourire aux lèvres.
native_language_example: They had smiles on their faces.

meaning: How old were you when you ... (did something in the past)?
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect question 'Quel âge avais-tu' (How old were you) with a past action introduced by 'quand tu as' + past participle (passé composé). Use to ask about someone's age at the time of a specific past event. The verb after 'tu as' is in passé composé (tu as fait, tu as commencé, etc.).
target_language_example: Quel âge avais-tu quand tu as déménagé à Boston ?
native_language_example: How old were you when you moved to Boston?

meaning: contraction of 'avais le/la/l'' used to mean 'had the...' or 'was seeming/appeared to...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb 'avoir' (imperfect, 'je/tu/il avais') followed by a definite article 'le/la/l'' + noun. Contexts: 'avoir l'air' = to seem/appear; 'avoir l'intention' = to intend; 'avoir l'esprit ailleurs' = to be distracted. In spoken French the subject pronoun is often dropped (e.g. 'T'avais' = 'Tu avais'). The imperfect (avais) describes past habitual state or ongoing past action. Pay attention to gender/liaison after l'.
target_language_example: J'avais l'impression que tu n'étais pas bien.
native_language_example: I had the impression that you weren't feeling well.

meaning: was right about (something).
additional_notes: Past-imperfect form of 'avoir raison' used with 'à' + noun or 'de' + verb in some regional or informal uses; more commonly you'd say 'avoir raison' with 'sur' or 'de' (e.g. 'tu avais raison' / 'tu avais raison de partir' / 'tu avais raison sur ce point'). 'Avais raison à' can appear in spoken French meaning 'you were right about (that)'.
target_language_example: Tu avais raison à propos de la météo.
native_language_example: You were right about the weather.

meaning: 'had just' or 'had barely' (used with 'à peine' to mean something happened only a moment before).
additional_notes: Often appears in the structure 'avait à peine + verb' to mean 'had barely/just (done) something' or 'had hardly (done) something' — equivalent to 'had just' or 'had barely' in English. It uses the imperfect 'avait' + 'à peine' + past participle or infinitive construction. Common in narrative to show one action happened immediately before another.
target_language_example: Elle avait à peine terminé son travail quand on a frappé.
native_language_example: She had barely finished her work when someone knocked.

meaning: was there a / was there an (used to ask if something existed or happened).
additional_notes: This is the inversion question form of 'il y avait un...' (there was a...). 'Y avait-il un...?' is slightly formal; in spoken French you might hear 'Est-ce qu'il y avait un...?' or 'Y a-t-il un...?' for present. Use to ask whether something (a problem, a fire, a word, a scandal) existed or occurred.
target_language_example: Y avait-il un témoin hier soir ?
native_language_example: Was there a witness last night?

meaning: there were lots of people / it was very crowded
additional_notes: Literally: 'there was a lot of people'. Used to describe places or events with many people present. Commonly appears with locations (au concert, dans le stade, à la fête) or alone as a general statement. The neutral past-imperfect tense (il y avait) describes a past situation or ongoing background condition.
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y avait beaucoup de monde au marché.
native_language_example: Last night, there were lots of people at the market.

meaning: 'had the heart' — used to describe someone's emotional state or willingness (often in past tense).
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'had the heart' (avoir le cœur + infinitive or + à + noun) is used to say someone felt able/unable emotionally to do something (e.g. 'il n'avait pas le cœur de partir' = he didn't have the heart to leave). Can describe sympathy, courage, or emotional readiness. Often appears in past tenses ('avait', 'n'avait pas').
target_language_example: Il avait le cœur lourd après la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He had a heavy heart after the news.

meaning: 'was homesick' (literally: 'had the sickness of')
additional_notes: Used with 'pays' (le mal du pays) to mean 'homesick'. The phrase is commonly formed with the verb 'avoir' in past tenses (avait = he/she/it had, was) or other persons (j'avais, tu avais, nous avions). You can also say 'avoir le mal du pays' in infinitive or other tenses (e.g., 'il a le mal du pays', 'ils auront le mal du pays').
target_language_example: Après quelques mois à l'étranger, elle avait le mal du pays.
native_language_example: After a few months abroad, she was homesick.

meaning: in advance of; ahead of (time) / an advance of (money) when followed by an amount
additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: 1) followed by a time expression to mean 'in advance of' or 'ahead of' (e.g. "avance de trois jours" = "three days in advance"); 2) used with a monetary amount to mean an "advance payment" (e.g. "une avance de 500 €" = "an advance of €500"). Word order and articles matter: you often see "une avance de" for payments and phrases like "à l'avance" or "en avance" for time. Not a fixed idiom by itself — meaning depends on the words that follow.
target_language_example: Il a versé une avance de 500 € pour réserver l'appartement.
native_language_example: He paid an advance of €500 to reserve the apartment.

meaning: 'before the storm' — used figuratively as 'the calm before the storm'.
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed expression 'le calme avant la tempête' to describe a quiet or peaceful period that comes just before trouble, activity, or sudden change. Can be used literally (weather) or figuratively (tense situation).
target_language_example: C'est le calme avant la tempête.
native_language_example: It's the calm before the storm.

meaning: before the falling; usually 'before the fall of (night)' — i.e., before it gets dark.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'avant la tombée de la nuit' meaning 'before night falls' or simply 'before dusk'. Alone, 'la tombée' can mean the falling (of night, of rain, etc.), so context matters. Use to indicate something happening shortly before darkness or an event's 'fall'.
target_language_example: Finissons le travail avant la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: Let's finish the work before night falls.

meaning: before the (falling of) — used with night: before night falls / before dark.
additional_notes: Almost always followed by 'la nuit' (avant la tombée de la nuit) meaning 'before nightfall' or 'before it gets dark'. Used to indicate doing something before darkness arrives. Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Rentre à la maison avant la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: Come home before night falls.

meaning: 'for a long time' or 'not for a long time' depending on context (usually: 'not anytime soon').
additional_notes: Often used with negation to mean 'not for a long time' or 'not anytime soon' (e.g., "tu ne reverras pas... avant longtemps" = you won't see... for a long time / not anytime soon). Without negation it can mean 'in a long time' or 'after a long time', but most everyday uses imply delay. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Tu ne partiras pas avant longtemps.
native_language_example: You won't leave anytime soon.

meaning: before my (female speaker) — used to indicate something happened earlier than the speaker's birth or earlier than something belonging to the speaker.
additional_notes: Avant + possessive (ma) is followed by a noun (e.g., naissance). It literally means 'before my ...'. Use ma for feminine singular nouns (ma naissance, ma carrière). For masculine singular nouns beginning with a vowel sound, use mon (e.g., avant mon anniversaire). The phrase often appears in time expressions (events that happened before the speaker's birth) or to say you prioritize something before your own.
target_language_example: Ils ont déménagé avant ma naissance.
native_language_example: They moved before I was born.

meaning: 'before us' or 'before we (do something)'.
additional_notes: Can mean spatially or temporally 'in front of us' / 'earlier than us' depending on context. Often used in sentences like 'c'était avant nous' (it was before us) or in constructions with verbs: 'avant que nous ...' is different — that uses 'avant que' + subjunctive. 'Avant nous' on its own is followed by a noun or implies a time/event happening earlier than our involvement.
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés avant nous.
native_language_example: They arrived before us.

meaning: 'before a' (used before a masculine singular noun or numeral).
additional_notes: Avant = 'before' (in time or position). When followed by the indefinite article 'un' or a masculine noun, it literally means 'before a' or 'before one'. In many contexts speakers use 'avant de' + infinitive (before doing something). Use 'avant un' when referring to a concrete noun: e.g. 'avant un match' = 'before a match.'
target_language_example: Nous devons arriver avant un match important.
native_language_example: We must arrive before an important match.

meaning: before you (in time or order).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something happened or came earlier than 'you' — can refer to time (arriving earlier) or order/sequence (going ahead in line). Common in spoken and written French. If addressing a group, 'vous' may be plural or formal singular.
target_language_example: Ils sont partis avant vous.
native_language_example: They left before you.

meaning: above all; first and most importantly
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the most important point or priority. Can start a sentence or appear parenthetically (avec des virgules). Common in formal and informal contexts. Pronunciation: [avɑ̃ tu].
target_language_example: Avant tout, prends soin de toi.
native_language_example: Above all, take care of yourself.

meaning: before (followed by a subordinate clause, often with subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause meaning 'before' in time. In formal grammar it is typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., avant que tu partes → before you leave). In spoken French the indicative is sometimes heard, but learners should use the subjunctive after avant que. Can appear in negative or imperative contexts (e.g., pars avant qu'ils arrivent).
target_language_example: Pars maintenant avant que la pluie n'arrive.
native_language_example: Leave now before the rain arrives.

meaning: with this
additional_notes: Literal combination of avec (with) + demonstrative ce (this/that). Used before a noun or clause introduced by que/qui/etc. In spoken French ce becomes c' before a vowel (avec c' + vowel). Common in phrases like «avec ce livre» (with this book) or «avec ce que tu dis…» (with what you say…). Tone and exact translation (this/that) depend on context and speaker's distance to the thing.
target_language_example: Avec ce film, je me suis beaucoup amusé.
native_language_example: With this movie, I had a lot of fun.

meaning: with what / with that which
additional_notes: Combines 'avec' (with) + 'ce qui' (what/that which). Used to refer to a thing or situation already mentioned: 'avec ce qui...' introduces a clause explaining what exists or happens along with something else. Often followed by a verb clause (e.g. 'avec ce qui reste', 'avec ce qui se passe').
target_language_example: Avec ce qui reste, on pourra préparer deux tartes.
native_language_example: With what is left, we can make two pies.

meaning: with this; together with this (thing or document).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something being given, included, or accompanying another item (physical or in writing). Often appears in contexts like receipts, emails, or when handing over documents: 'avec ceci' = 'along with this' or 'with this one.' Can be followed by a noun or stand alone when the thing is clear from context.
target_language_example: Je vous envoie le contrat avec ceci la liste des pièces à fournir.
native_language_example: I am sending you the contract along with this list of required documents.

meaning: with that
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to something previously mentioned. Can mean 'with that' (physically or in combination) or 'about/regarding that' depending on context. In spoken French 'à propos de cela' or 'en rapport avec cela' may be used for 'about that'.
target_language_example: Fais attention avec cela, c'est fragile.
native_language_example: Be careful with that, it's fragile.

meaning: 'with how much' or 'with how many' — used to ask about quantity or price in combination with another verb or phrase.
additional_notes: Often used in questions to ask how much of something is used/needed or how many people/items accompany something. Context determines whether it means 'how much' (amount/price) or 'how many' (count). You will usually see it followed by a noun or implied context: e.g. 'Avec combien de personnes ?' (How many people?) or 'Avec combien ça revient ?' (How much does it cost with that?).
target_language_example: Avec combien de personnes venez-vous ?
native_language_example: How many people are you coming with?

meaning: 'with' used before a noun introduced by 'de' (often after quantities, expressions, or negation)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; 'avec' means 'with' and can be followed by 'de' in contexts such as: after quantities (beaucoup de, peu de) where you still need 'avec' (e.g. «avec peu de temps» = with little time), after negation or expressions using 'de' (e.g. «avec rien de spécial» — though 'rien de spécial' more commonly stands alone), or to link 'with' + a noun phrase that begins with 'de' (possession, partitive, or descriptive). Word order and contraction rules still apply (no contraction between 'avec' and 'de').
target_language_example: Je pars avec de l'argent et quelques papiers importants.
native_language_example: I'm leaving with some money and a few important papers.

meaning: with them
additional_notes: Refers to a group of people or feminine nouns (elles = they, feminine). Use 'avec eux' for mixed or all-male groups. Context determines whether 'them' refers to people or feminine objects.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec elles ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the cinema with them (feminine) tonight.

meaning: over time; with time; as time passes.
additional_notes: Used to say that something changes, improves, or becomes clearer as time goes by. Common in spoken and written French. Can introduce a gradual process or a future result that will happen given enough time.
target_language_example: Avec le temps, sa douleur s'est atténuée.
native_language_example: Over time, his pain lessened.

meaning: with the
additional_notes: A common combination of avec + the plural article les. It is used before plural nouns, whether masculine or feminine: avec les amis, avec les filles.
target_language_example: Je vais au parc avec les enfants.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with the children.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; looks like a fragment meaning 'with him at this/that...' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a common set expression. It appears to be three separate words that might occur together in a longer sentence (e.g. 'avec lui, à ce moment-là' or 'avec lui à ce prix'). Beginners should treat them separately: 'avec' = with, 'lui' = him/it (indirect object or disjunctive pronoun), 'à ce' = 'at this' or 'to this' as the start of a phrase (usually followed by a noun or demonstration like 'moment', 'prix', 'propos'). The exact meaning depends on the words that follow. Watch for punctuation: 'avec lui, à ce...' often introduces an explanation or detail.
target_language_example: Je suis allé au concert avec lui à ce moment-là.
native_language_example: I went to the concert with him at that moment.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment or incorrect word order meaning roughly 'with us this...' or the start of a clause ('with us, this...').
additional_notes:
The sequence "avec nous ce" is not a conventional French set phrase. It typically results from a word-order error or an unfinished clause. Possible correct alternatives depending on intent:
- "avec nous" = "with us"
- "ce qui est avec nous" = "what/that which is with us"
- "ce que nous avons" = "what we have"
If you intend emphasis or a parenthetical insertion, French would usually reorder the words (e.g. "Ce, avec nous, ..." is very marked and rare).
target_language_example: Avec nous ce projet a plus de chances de réussir.
native_language_example: With us, this project has a better chance of succeeding.

meaning: 'with or' (literal combination of 'avec' = with and 'ou' = or); not a fixed idiom by itself.
additional_notes: This is simply the sequence of the preposition 'avec' and the conjunction 'ou'. It can appear in choices or lists (e.g. 'avec ou sans' = 'with or without') but 'avec ou' alone is incomplete and depends on surrounding words. For beginners, recognize 'avec' (with) and 'ou' (or) and expect more words after them to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Tu veux le café avec ou sans sucre ?
native_language_example: Do you want the coffee with or without sugar?

meaning: a nonstandard/informal way to say 'without' (standard: 'sans').
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'avec' (with) + 'pas de' (not any) and is considered colloquial or regional; it's grammatically incorrect in standard French. Native speakers might hear it in casual speech or dialects, meaning 'without' (e.g. 'avec pas de sucre' = 'without sugar'). Use 'sans' in formal writing and careful speech.
target_language_example: Je prends mon café avec pas de sucre.
native_language_example: I take my coffee without sugar.

meaning: 'with pleasure' — used to say 'you're welcome' or 'I'd be happy to' / 'gladly'.
additional_notes: Common polite response to thanks or an offer to help. Can be used alone (short reply) or in full sentences: present/future/past (Ce sera avec plaisir / C'était avec plaisir). Neutral/formal register.
target_language_example: Si tu veux, je peux t'aider — avec plaisir.
native_language_example: If you want, I can help you — with pleasure.

meaning: with more / including more
additional_notes: Literally 'with more'. Used to add quantity, intensity or additional elements to something. In natural French 'avec plus' often appears in longer phrases (e.g. 'avec plus de' + noun: 'avec plus de temps') or in comparative contexts. Alone it can sound incomplete; learners will usually see it followed by 'de' + noun, a number, or an adjective/adverb in context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec plus de sucre, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with more sugar, please.

meaning: with what / with which (used to ask or emphasize the means, instrument, amount, or quality).
additional_notes: Combines avec (with) + quel (which/what). Used in questions about means, money, instrument, or to introduce an exclamatory clause emphasizing manner or degree (often with emotion). Agrees in gender/number with the noun when followed by one (e.g. avec quelle, avec quels, avec quelles). Can be followed directly by a noun (Avec quel argent ?) or used before a clause for emphasis (Avec quel enthousiasme ils travaillent !).
target_language_example: Avec quel courage elle a parlé devant tout le monde !
native_language_example: With what courage she spoke in front of everyone!

meaning: 'with whom are' — beginning of a question phrase (appears in informal or colloquial word orders, or as part of inversion constructions)
additional_notes: This exact sequence ('avec qui es') is not a complete standard written sentence by itself; it typically appears within a larger question (e.g. 'Avec qui es-tu ?') or in colloquial speech when rearranged ('Tu es avec qui ?'). It can occur in spoken fragments or in poetic/elliptical contexts. For learners, prefer full forms like 'Avec qui es-tu ?' (inversion) or 'Tu es avec qui ?' (colloquial).
target_language_example: Avec qui es-tu ce soir ? — but the fragment 'avec qui es' appears in the inverted clause 'Avec qui es-tu ?'
native_language_example: With whom are you tonight? — demonstrating the phrase 'avec qui es' as part of 'Avec qui es-tu ?'

meaning: 'with whom I' — used when the speaker refers to the person(s) with whom they perform or will perform an action.
additional_notes: Built from 'avec' (with) + 'qui' (who) + subject pronoun 'je' (I). Commonly appears in relative clauses or embedded questions: e.g. 'La personne avec qui je travaille...' (The person with whom I work) or 'Je me demande avec qui je vais y aller.' Word order can change in speech, but this exact sequence 'avec qui je' is used when continuing the clause with the first-person subject.
target_language_example: La collègue avec qui je travaille est en congé.
native_language_example: The colleague with whom I work is on leave.

meaning: 'with whom' (note: this exact sequence is ungrammatical in French).
additional_notes:
This sequence is not a correct French phrase. Possible intended/related correct forms:
- "avec qui" = with whom (used in questions and relative clauses).
- "qui que ce soit" = whoever it may be (indefinite pronoun phrase).
- "avec n'importe qui" = with anyone.
The string "avec qui que ce" mixes elements of these phrases and should be avoided. If you see it, replace with one of the correct alternatives above depending on meaning.
target_language_example: (non standard/incorrect) *Avec qui que ce* veux-tu y aller ?
native_language_example: (non standard/incorrect) *With whom* do you want to go there?

meaning: 'with everything' or 'including everything'
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining avec (with) + tout (everything/all). Used to indicate inclusion of all items or aspects. Can appear in contexts like: packing (j'ai pris la valise avec tout = I took the suitcase with everything), describing something that comes complete (le menu, avec tout = the menu, with everything), or emphasizing completeness. Tone is neutral and can be used in spoken and written French. Depending on word order and context, it may contract or be expanded (e.g. 'avec tout ça' = 'with all that').
target_language_example: Il est parti avec tout ce dont il avait besoin.
native_language_example: He left with everything he needed.

meaning: with a pain / suffering (literally 'with a pain')
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom in French by itself; it looks like the literal combination of avec (with) + un mal (a pain, an ailment, or harm). You will more commonly see mal used alone (J'ai mal = I'm in pain) or in expressions like 'avoir mal à...' (to have pain in...), 'un mal de tête' (a headache), or figurative uses such as 'faire du mal' (to harm). 'Avec un mal' would appear in a larger context (e.g. « avec un mal incurable » = with an incurable illness) rather than as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Il vit avec un mal chronique depuis des années.
native_language_example: He has been living with a chronic pain for years.

meaning: 'with a little' or 'with a bit (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate adding a small quantity of something (often food or drink). Common in recipes and everyday speech. Can be followed by a noun introduced by de (e.g. 'avec un peu de lait') or by a noun without de in some contexts (less common).
target_language_example: Je prends mon café avec un peu de sucre.
native_language_example: I take my coffee with a little sugar.

meaning: with you at / with you in (followed by a place or time)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the preposition 'avec' (with) + the pronoun 'vous' (you, plural/formal) + the preposition 'à' (at/to/in). It will normally be followed immediately by a place, event, or time: e.g. 'avec vous à la réunion' (with you at the meeting) or 'avec vous à 18h' (with you at 6 PM). Make sure to include the noun or time after 'à'.
target_language_example: Je serai avec vous à la conférence demain.
native_language_example: I will be with you at the conference tomorrow.

meaning: 'blind with' or 'blinded by' (used figuratively to say someone is overcome by an emotion or condition).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun (aveugle de + [nom]) to indicate being figuratively 'blinded' by something (love, rage, jealousy, fear, pride, etc.). Example: aveugle d'amour = blinded by love. Not used for literal blindness (use aveugle seul or être aveugle).
target_language_example: Il est aveugle de jalousie.
native_language_example: He is blinded by jealousy.

meaning: you have (so/then); adds emphasis or inference to a question or statement.
additional_notes: Avez is the 2nd-person plural/formal of 'avoir'. 'Donc' here doesn't mean 'therefore' in a formal logical sense but adds emphasis, surprise, inference or draws a conclusion from prior information. Common in questions (Have you, then...?/So you have...?) and in accusatory or surprised statements (So you have lied.). Tone depends on context and intonation. Use 'as donc' for tu form.
target_language_example: Vous avez donc oublié mon message ?
native_language_example: So you forgot my message?

meaning: 'have heard the' (formal/plural you + past participle + masculine singular article).
additional_notes: This is the formal/plural second-person past form of the verb entendre (vous avez entendu) followed by the masculine singular definite article le + noun. Used to say that 'you (formal or plural) heard the/the [man, captain, doctor, etc.]'. If addressing one person formally or multiple people, use 'vous'. For feminine nouns use 'la' (e.g. 'vous avez entendu la femme').
target_language_example: Vous avez entendu le professeur parler ?
native_language_example: Did you hear the professor speaking?

meaning: 'have had' (you have had / did you have...)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb avoir in the passé composé (vous avez eu) plus the indefinite plural article des. Used to ask or state that someone experienced, received, or acquired plural things or events in the past. Context determines translation: as a question it can mean 'Did you have...?' or 'Have you had...?' In statements it means 'you have had' (e.g. problems, children, news). Formal subject pronoun vous is shown here.
target_language_example: Vous avez eu des rendez-vous cette semaine ?
native_language_example: Did you have any appointments this week?

meaning: had a
additional_notes: Literally the passé composé of avoir (vous avez eu) + indefinite article un. Used to say someone 'had' or 'has had' something (often an event or experience) — e.g. 'vous avez eu un accident' = 'you had an accident' or 'you have had an accident'. Context determines English tense (simple past or present perfect). The pronoun vous is shown in the examples but the phrase structure applies with other subjects (j'ai eu un, il a eu un, etc.).
target_language_example: Vous avez eu un problème avec la voiture ?
native_language_example: Did you have a problem with the car?

meaning: 'you have had a' (formal/plural 'you')
additional_notes: Combines the polite/plural subject 'vous' (implied), the present perfect auxiliary 'avez eu' (have had), and the feminine indefinite article 'une'. Used to talk about something someone has experienced or possessed (a year, an adventure, a long day, etc.). Context determines translation (experience, possession, relationship). This is formal/plural; the informal singular equivalent is 'tu as eu une'.
target_language_example: Vous avez eu une belle surprise hier ?
native_language_example: Did you have a nice surprise yesterday?

meaning: have never
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of ne ... jamais: n'avez jamais = 'you have never'. Avez is the vous form of avoir ('have'), so this is used with formal singular you or plural you. In casual speech, ne is often dropped, so you may hear avez jamais instead of n'avez jamais.
target_language_example: Vous n'avez jamais vu ce film ?
native_language_example: You've never seen this movie?

meaning: have lost the (you, formal/plural).
additional_notes: Form of the passé composé: vous (formal/plural) + avez (auxiliary 'avoir') + perdu (past participle of 'perdre') + definite article + noun. Used to say someone has lost something (la clé, la bataille, la partie) or in idiomatic questions ('Vous avez perdu la tête ?' = 'Have you lost your mind?'). Context determines the noun that follows 'la'.
target_language_example: Vous avez perdu la montre ?
native_language_example: Have you lost the watch?

meaning: 'have' + 'nothing' — used in negative constructions to mean 'didn't ... anything' or 'haven't ... anything'.
additional_notes: This appears as part of the negative expression 'ne ... rien' with the auxiliary verb (here 'avez' for vous). In spoken or informal French the 'ne' is often dropped, so you'll hear 'vous avez rien' instead of the full 'vous n'avez rien'. It can be used with different verbs: 'vous n'avez rien dit' = you didn't say anything; 'vous n'avez rien fait' = you didn't do anything. Remember in written/formal French include 'ne'.
target_language_example: Vous n'avez rien compris ?
native_language_example: You didn't understand anything?

meaning: 'you (plural or formal) all have' or 'you have all' (present perfect/context-dependent)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb avoir (vous avez) + the pronoun tous (all). Used to address a group (vous) meaning 'all of you' did or have something. Depending on the sentence it can appear with past participles (vous avez tous été / eu / passé) or with verbs like comprendre (vous avez tous compris). In spoken French, vous can be formal singular or plural; tous clarifies 'everyone'. tous is pronounced /tu/ when used adverbially and often follows the verb.
target_language_example: Vous avez tous fait un bon travail.
native_language_example: You have all done a good job.

meaning: 'have you seen/seen that' used to introduce or ask about something seen or what happened.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the polite/plural form of 'avoir' (vous avez) + 'vu' (seen) + 'ce' (this/that). It's commonly used to ask if someone has seen something or to introduce a clause with 'ce que/ce qui' (what/that which): e.g. 'Vous avez vu ce que...' = 'Did you see what...?' In spoken French you may also hear 't'as vu ce...' (informal singular).
target_language_example: Vous avez vu ce que le chien a trouvé ?
native_language_example: Did you see what the dog found?

meaning: 'have you seen what' (used to ask if someone noticed or saw something, or to introduce what was seen)
additional_notes: This is the inversion/part of polite/plural 'vous' question form: 'Vous avez vu ce que...?' = 'Have you seen what...?' It can be used to ask if someone noticed something, to report what someone saw, or to introduce a clause describing an action or result. In casual speech you may also hear 't'as vu ce que...' (tu as vu ce que...) for 'you (sing./informal) have you seen what...'.
target_language_example: Vous avez vu ce que j'ai trouvé au marché ?
native_language_example: Have you seen what I found at the market?

meaning: 'have you seen this/that' (polite/plural 'you')
additional_notes: Combines the polite/plural form of 'to have' (avez) + past participle 'vu' (seen) + demonstrative 'cette' (this/that for feminine nouns). Used to ask if someone (vous) has seen a particular feminine noun (fille, femme, émission). For masculine nouns use 'avez-vous vu ce' or 'avez-vous vu cet' before a vowel sound. Word order in questions can vary (Est-ce que vous avez vu..., Avez-vous vu...).
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous avez vu cette voiture rouge ?
native_language_example: Have you seen this red car?

meaning: 'have you seen the' (polite/formal 'you').
additional_notes: Combines the formal/plural subject pronoun 'vous' with the compound past of 'voir' (avez vu) followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by 'le'. Used to ask if someone has seen something (a thing, person, film, time, work, etc.). In spoken French the word order can be the same with rising intonation for a question: «Vous avez vu le... ?» Can replace 'le' with other articles/pronouns (la, les, l', ce, ça).
target_language_example: Vous avez vu le match hier soir ?
native_language_example: Did you see the match last night?

meaning: 'have you seen the' (plural definite object) — polite/formal or plural 'you'.
additional_notes: Used in questions with 'vous' (formal singular or plural) to ask if someone has seen specific things (plural noun after 'les'). Structure: 'Vous avez vu les + [plural noun] ?' Common in spoken and written French. If addressing one informal person, use 'Tu as vu les...?' or to ask about a singular item use 'le/la'.
target_language_example: Vous avez vu les photos de la fête ?
native_language_example: Have you seen the photos from the party?

meaning: 'have you seen my...?' (polite/formal or plural 'you')
additional_notes: A polite/formal or plural way to ask if someone has seen something or someone that belongs to you. 'Vous' + 'avez vu' is the passé composé of 'voir'. Change 'mon' to match the possessed noun's gender/number (ma/mes). For informal singular 'you' use 'tu as vu mon/ma/mes...'.
target_language_example: Vous avez vu mon livre quelque part ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my book anywhere?

meaning: you have a lot of
additional_notes: "avez" is the vous form of avoir, so this is used with you plural or formal singular. It often appears as "vous avez beaucoup de + noun" for 'you have a lot of ...', as in "vous avez beaucoup de livres". It can also be followed by another phrase, like "vous avez beaucoup en commun" ('you have a lot in common').
target_language_example: Vous avez beaucoup d'énergie aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You have a lot of energy today.

meaning: what do you need?
additional_notes: Informal spoken question used to ask someone (tu or vous depending on context) what they need. Literally 'have need of what'. Often heard as 'tu as besoin de quoi ?' or 'vous avez besoin de quoi ?' In writing, more polite forms: 'De quoi avez-vous besoin ?' or 'Qu'est-ce dont vous avez besoin ?'.
target_language_example: Vous avez besoin de quoi pour le projet ?
native_language_example: What do you need for the project?

meaning: 'how many do you have?' (asking quantity)
additional_notes: Common way to ask how many of something someone has. Often used with vous/tu/il/etc. and followed by de + noun (Vous avez combien de livres ?). Can also stand alone (Vous avez combien ?) or appear with pronouns (Vous en avez combien ?) — the pronoun en replaces the noun phrase. Slightly informal/neutral; polite with 'vous'.
target_language_example: Vous avez combien de frères et sœurs ?
native_language_example: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

meaning: you have (some)... — plural or partitive; used to ask or state that someone possesses or has some of something.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb avoir (vous avez) + the plural/partitive article des. Used before plural nouns or unspecified quantity (some). In questions it often means "do you have any...". 'Vous' can be formal singular or plural. Watch agreement: 'avez du', 'de la', 'de l’' for singular/partitive.
target_language_example: Vous avez des livres à me prêter ?
native_language_example: Do you have any books to lend me?

meaning: 'have...still' or 'do you still have...?' (present tense of 'avoir' + 'encore' meaning 'still' or 'more')
additional_notes: Used with 'vous' here: 'avez' is the present-tense form of 'avoir' (to have). 'Encore' can mean 'still' (continuing state) or 'more/again' depending on context. Common uses: asking if someone still possesses something (Vous avez encore du sable?), if they still feel something (Vous avez encore faim?), if they still have time (Vous avez encore du temps?) or if there is more to do/learn (Vous en avez encore à apprendre...). Word order: 'avez encore' when 'avoir' is directly followed by 'encore'.
target_language_example: Vous avez encore des questions ?
native_language_example: Do you still have questions?

meaning: 'you have done your' (polite/plural 'vous' form)
additional_notes: Combines the polite/plural subject 'vous' + past tense 'avez fait' (have done) + a possessive 'votre' (your). It introduces what the person has done (e.g. votre boulot, votre devoir, votre part). Use with a noun after 'votre'. In English this is typically translated as 'you have done your...' or 'you did your...' depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous avez fait votre part, merci.
native_language_example: You have done your part, thank you.

meaning: 'do not have' or part of the negative 'you do not' (informal/colloquial omission of ne).
additional_notes: Avez pas is the contracted form found in spoken or informal French where the negative particle 'ne' is dropped: 'vous n'avez pas' becomes 'vous avez pas' or 'vous n'avez pas' in writing.
