It appears in questions and statements (e.g. 'Vous n'avez pas envie?' = 'Don't you feel like it?'). In careful/written French include 'ne' (vous n'avez pas). The phrase combines 'avez' (2nd-person plural of avoir) with 'pas' (negation).
target_language_example: Vous avez pas fini vos devoirs?
native_language_example: Haven't you finished your homework?

meaning: 'do not need' (spoken/informal negative with vous)
additional_notes: This is an informal or colloquial way to say 'vous n'avez pas besoin' (you do not need). In standard written French the negative particle 'ne' is usually included: 'vous n'avez pas besoin de...'. In speech, the 'ne' is often dropped, so 'vous avez pas besoin' is common. Use with 'vous' (formal/plural). Followed by 'de' + noun or 'de' + infinitive (or sometimes nothing).
target_language_example: Vous avez pas besoin de venir si vous êtes fatigué.
native_language_example: You don't need to come if you're tired.

meaning: don't have (any)
additional_notes: This is the negative form of "avoir" in the present for vous (formal/plural): "vous n'avez pas de + noun" means "you don't have (any) + noun". In questions, it's often used to ask if someone lacks something (e.g. "Vous n'avez pas de monnaie ?" = "Don't you have change?"). When followed by a noun, the partitive/indefinite article (un/une/des/du/de la) typically becomes "de" after negation: "pas de voiture" (not "pas une voiture").
target_language_example: Vous n'avez pas de clé pour la porte ?
native_language_example: Don't you have a key for the door?

meaning: 'do not have to' (you don't need to / it's not necessary for you to)
additional_notes: Colloquial/informal negative form of 'avoir à' used with 'vous' (standard written form is 'vous n'avez pas à'). Means there is no obligation or need to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'le savoir', 'répondre'). Can be softened to tell someone they don't need to worry or act.
target_language_example: Vous n'avez pas à vous excuser.
native_language_example: You don't have to apologize.

meaning: just have to / all you need to do is (simply do...)
additional_notes: Used in the structure « vous n'avez qu'à + infinitive » (or other person: « tu n'as qu'à ») to give a simple suggestion or instruction: 'all you need to do is...'. Often implies an easy or obvious action; tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context. Can be translated as 'just (do)...' or 'you only have to...'.
target_language_example: Si vous êtes en retard, vous n'avez qu'à appeler pour prévenir.
native_language_example: If you're late, you just have to call to let them know.

meaning: 'have nothing' (part of the negative construction 'n'avez rien' = 'you have nothing' / 'you don't have anything').
additional_notes: In standard French the negative is formed with 'ne ... rien' (e.g. 'Vous n'avez rien'). In spoken/informal French 'ne' is often dropped, producing phrases like 'vous avez rien' or 'avez rien' in questions. Can appear with additions like 'd'autre' (nothing else) or 'à...'(nothing to + verb). Also used in constructions like 'n'avoir rien à craindre' (have nothing to fear).
target_language_example: Vous n'avez rien à perdre si vous essayez.
native_language_example: You have nothing to lose if you try.

meaning: 'have three' (you have three ...).
additional_notes: Combines the verb avoir (vous avez = you have) with the number trois (three). Used to say someone has/gets three of something or is given three units (choices, seconds, messages, etc.). Formal/plural subject form (vous). For informal singular use say 'tu as trois'. Order is verb + number + noun: 'Vous avez trois choix.'
target_language_example: Vous avez trois minutes pour répondre.
native_language_example: You have three minutes to answer.

meaning: 'have your' (formal/plural 'you have your')
additional_notes: Combination of the verb avoir (vous avez) + possessive adjective vos (your, plural). Used in questions and statements to ask if someone possesses something or to state they hold certain things/opinions. 'Vous' is formal or plural. In casual speech with one person you might hear 'tu as tes...'. Context determines the noun that follows (convictions, papiers, règles, ordres).
target_language_example: Vous avez vos clés ?
native_language_example: Do you have your keys?

meaning: you really have / you truly have (formal/plural 'vous').
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'avoir' (to have) in the present ('avez' for vous) with the adverb 'vraiment' (really/truly). Used to emphasize the statement that follows (need, appearance, possession, etc.). In spoken French 'vous' can be formal singular or plural. For casual singular use with a friend, use 'tu as vraiment'.
target_language_example: Vous avez vraiment besoin de repos.
native_language_example: You really need some rest.

meaning: 'have to' or 'need to' (you have to/you need to ... me)
additional_notes: This is part of the construction 'avoir à + infinitive' meaning 'to have to' or 'to need to' do something. When combined with a pronoun like 'me' it indicates the action is directed toward or affects the speaker (e.g. 'vous avez à me répondre' = 'you have to answer me'). In everyday speech, 'avoir à' is less common than 'devoir' for obligation; context and verb choice determine naturalness. Word order: subject + avoir (conjugated) + à + pronoun + infinitive or verb phrase.
target_language_example: Vous avez à me dire la vérité.
native_language_example: You have to tell me the truth.

meaning: 'you had' (imperfect) + 'a' — used to describe something someone used to have or had in the past (formal/plural or polite 'you').
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect form of 'avoir' (vous aviez) and the indefinite article 'une'. Used with the polite or plural 'vous'. Common in past descriptions (ongoing or habitual past) or to report past facts. Can introduce nouns (copine, théorie, semaine) or actions/relationships (liaison). Context determines translation (e.g., 'you had a girlfriend,' 'you had a week').
target_language_example: Vous aviez une voiture avant de déménager.
native_language_example: You had a car before moving.

meaning: 'plane of' or '... plane' (part of noun phrases like 'avion de chasse' = 'fighter plane').
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase: 'avion' means 'airplane' and 'de' is the preposition 'of'/'from' used to link to another noun or descriptor (type, purpose, origin, possession). You'll usually see it in longer noun phrases (avion de ligne, avion de chasse, avion de transport). Word order is 'avion de + noun'.
target_language_example: C'est un avion de ligne moderne.
native_language_example: It's a modern airliner.

meaning: This looks like two separate words: 'avion' = 'plane' and 'est' = 'is' (third-person singular of 'être').
additional_notes: The sequence 'avion est' by itself is not an established fixed phrase in French; it's simply the noun 'avion' followed by the verb 'est' and would appear inside a sentence (e.g. 'L'avion est en retard' = 'The plane is late'). Remember to include the definite article 'le' or contraction 'l'' before 'avion' in many sentences: 'L'avion est...'.
target_language_example: L'avion est en retard.
native_language_example: The plane is late.

meaning: notice of / opinion of / warning of (depends on context)
additional_notes: Short phrase used before a noun to indicate a formal notice, announcement, or opinion about something. Common in fixed expressions like "avis de décès" (death notice), "avis de convocation" (notice of meeting), "avis de passage" (delivery notice). Can also appear in phrases meaning 'to someone's opinion' when used with "à l'" as in "à l'avis de" (in the opinion of). The exact translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: J'ai reçu un avis de passage du facteur.
native_language_example: I received a delivery notice from the postman.

meaning: wanted notice; bulletin seeking a person (usually by police) or information about a missing person.
additional_notes: Commonly used for police 'wanted' posters or public notices asking for help locating a person. Can refer to missing-person notices or criminal 'wanted' notices depending on context. Formal/neutral register; often appears in newspapers, police bulletins and official communications.
target_language_example: La police a publié un avis de recherche pour retrouver le suspect.
native_language_example: The police issued a wanted notice to locate the suspect.

meaning: to have doubted (past infinitive phrase)
additional_notes: Literally 'to have doubted'. This is the perfect infinitive form: 'avoir' + past participle 'douté'. Used after expressions that require an infinitive in the past (e.g., after certain verbs, prepositions like 'après', or to talk about a doubt that occurred before another action). The simple infinitive is 'douter' (to doubt).
target_language_example: Après avoir douté, elle a finalement accepté.
native_language_example: After having doubted, she finally agreed.

meaning: to have done
additional_notes: A perfect infinitive: avoir + past participle. It is used to talk about an action already completed before another action or feeling, often after verbs like être content de, regretter, or after certain expressions.
target_language_example: Je suis content d'avoir fait ce travail hier.
native_language_example: I'm happy to have done this work yesterday.

meaning: to have walked for a while
additional_notes: Literally: "to have walked a moment." Used with passé composé (avoir + marché) to indicate someone walked for a short period. "Un moment" here means "a little while" or "for a bit." Common in everyday speech and narration to describe a brief walk.
target_language_example: Après le déjeuner, nous avons marché un moment.
native_language_example: After lunch, we walked for a while.

meaning: 'to have saved the' (past tense fragment).
additional_notes: Not a complete sentence by itself; it's the auxiliary avoir + past participle sauvé followed by the feminine singular definite article la and a following noun (e.g. la vie, la situation). In French, past participle sauvé generally does not agree when the auxiliary is avoir, unless a preceding direct object requires agreement. Commonly appears in phrases such as avoir sauvé la vie. Functions as a fragment indicating a completed action affecting a feminine noun.
target_language_example: Il prétend avoir sauvé la vie du marin.
native_language_example: He claims to have saved the sailor's life.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment intended to mean 'to have seen something' (avoir vu quelque chose) or 'to have seen some...' followed by a noun.
additional_notes: This string is not standard French on its own. 'Quelque' must be followed by a noun (e.g. 'quelque chose' = something, or 'quelques' = some (plural)). Correct alternatives: 'avoir vu quelque chose' (to have seen something) or 'avoir vu + noun' (e.g. 'avoir vu le film'). If you encounter 'avoir vu quelque' it is probably a typo or incomplete phrase and should be completed or corrected.
target_language_example: Il semble que j'aie avoir vu quelque, mais la phrase est incomplète.
native_language_example: It seems that I have 'avoir vu quelque', but the phrase is incomplete.

meaning: to have access (to something)
additional_notes: Used with 'à' to indicate ability or permission to reach, use, see, or enter something (physical or digital). Common construction: 'avoir accès à + noun' (avoir accès à Internet, à un dossier, à un bâtiment). Can express permission (I am allowed) or availability (I can connect). Often conjugated (j'ai accès, tu as accès, il/elle a accès, nous avons accès, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir si je peux avoir accès au dossier.
native_language_example: I want to know if I can have access to the file.

meaning: 'to have to deal with' or 'to deal with' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when you must confront, handle, or interact with a person, problem, or situation. Often followed by a noun or pronoun. Can imply a difficult or formal interaction depending on context: e.g. J'ai affaire à un client exigeant (I have to deal with a demanding client).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas envie d'avoir affaire à ce dossier maintenant.
native_language_example: I don't want to deal with this file right now.

meaning: 'to do something in vain' or 'despite doing something (without result)'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: avoir beau + infinitive. Expresses that someone tries or does something but it has no effect. Often translated as "even though/although someone does X, it doesn't help" or "no matter how much one does X". Typical structure: (il) a beau + infinitive or subject + avoir beau + infinitive. Tends to be more formal/literary but is also common in spoken French.
target_language_example: J'ai beau avoir beau essayer, rien ne change.
native_language_example: No matter how much I try, nothing changes.

meaning: to need
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or need. It is followed by a noun or by an infinitive: avoir besoin de quelque chose / avoir besoin de faire quelque chose. Literally, it is closer to 'to have need of.'
target_language_example: Tu pourrais avoir besoin de ceci.
native_language_example: You might need this.

meaning: (colloquial) to taste/smell good; used in some informal/regional contexts to mean 'to be right' or 'to fare well' in a particular respect.
additional_notes: Not a standard written construction by itself; more common, clearer alternatives include 'avoir bon goût', 'ça a bon goût', 'sent bon', or 'être bon'. 'Avoir bon' appears in spoken/regional French and fixed expressions (e.g. 'avoir bon coeur' is non-equivalent). Beginners should prefer the clearer phrases above. Register: informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Ce plat a bon — j'ai l'impression qu'il a bon.
native_language_example: This dish tastes good — I feel like it tastes good.

meaning: to look healthy, well, or in good spirits (appearance).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's physical appearance or facial expression when they look well, rested, or lively. Often used with people (elle/il a bonne mine) but can also describe food or plants in some contexts (e.g., une salade qui a bonne mine). The expression focuses on outward appearance, not necessarily actual health.
target_language_example: Après les vacances, elle semble avoir bonne mine.
native_language_example: After the holidays, she really looks well.

meaning: 'to be hot' (to feel warm).
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels warm or hot. Often used with a subject pronoun and conjugated (j'ai chaud, il a chaud). Can describe physical temperature or discomfort from heat. Can combine with reflexive or informal/vulgar phrases (e.g. "je me suis mis à avoir chaud", "avoir chaud au cul").
target_language_example: Je me suis mis à avoir chaud pendant la randonnée.
native_language_example: I started to feel hot during the hike.

meaning: 'to trust' or 'to have confidence (in someone/something)'
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing: avoir confiance en quelqu'un/quelque chose. Often followed by en + noun/pronoun (e.g. en lui, en ses capacités). Can also appear in constructions like «faire confiance» or reflexive contexts such as «se faire confiance».
target_language_example: Il faut avoir confiance en ses collègues pour réussir.
native_language_example: You need to trust your colleagues to succeed.

meaning: to be aware of; to have knowledge of (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone knows about or has been informed of something. Often appears in formal or administrative/legal contexts and commonly followed by de (avoir connaissance de quelque chose). Not interchangeable with "avoir conscience" or the simpler verb "connaître" in all contexts.
target_language_example: Nous devons déclarer que nous avons connaissance des faits.
native_language_example: We must state that we are aware of the facts.

meaning: 'to be aware' or 'to have awareness/conscience of (something)'
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone recognises or is aware of a fact, situation, or feeling. Often followed by de + noun or que + clause: avoir conscience de quelque chose / avoir conscience que + clause. Can also refer to moral conscience in other constructions (e.g. avoir la conscience tranquille).
target_language_example: Il faut avoir conscience des conséquences avant d'agir.
native_language_example: You must be aware of the consequences before acting.

meaning: to take place; to be in effect or in session
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an event, class, rule or practice occurs or is in force. Common in formal or neutral contexts (e.g., classes, meetings, laws). Not the same as "avoir un cours" which means "to have a class" (as in to attend).
target_language_example: Ce type de sanction a encore cours dans certains pays.
native_language_example: This type of sanction is still in effect in some countries.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Common expression used to say someone experiences good fortune or luck. Conjugate like the verb avoir (e.g., j'ai de la chance, elle a de la chance). Can describe a one-time fortunate event or general luck. Often followed by an explanation: J'ai de la chance d'avoir des amis formidables.
target_language_example: Elle pense avoir de la chance d'avoir trouvé ce travail.
native_language_example: She thinks she is lucky to have found this job.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck
additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning to have good fortune or happen to be fortunate. Often used in spoken French. Similar to 'avoir de la chance' but a bit more colloquial. You can use it about people or situations (Il a de la veine, Tu as de la veine).
target_language_example: Il faut avouer qu'il a de la veine d'avoir gagné au tirage au sort.
native_language_example: You have to admit that he's lucky to have won the raffle.

meaning: 'to have the right' or 'to be entitled to' (to be allowed or permitted to have/receive something).
additional_notes: Often followed by 'à' plus a noun or infinitive: avoir droit à quelque chose (to be entitled to something). Used to express legal, social, or personal entitlement or permission. Do not confuse with 'avoir raison' (to be right). Conjugated forms (j'ai droit, tu as droit, il/elle a droit, nous avons droit, etc.) are commonly used in context.
target_language_example: J'ai droit à des congés payés après un an de travail.
native_language_example: I am entitled to paid leave after one year of work.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say someone was fortunate or got lucky (often by chance). Common in spoken French. Can describe a single lucky event (J'ai eu du bol) or general luck. Similar to English 'to be lucky' or colloquial 'to have good luck'.
target_language_example: J'ai eu du bol hier soir: j'ai gagné au tirage et ça prouve que j'ai du bol en ce moment.
native_language_example: I was lucky last night: I won the raffle and it proves I'm having good luck right now.

meaning: to be good; to have a beneficial aspect or positive qualities
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something has a positive side or is useful/effective in some way. Common in spoken and written French, often in constructions like "ça a du bon" or with a noun/infinitive: "avoir du bon + noun/infinitive". Not very formal; idiomatic rather than literal.
target_language_example: Ça a du bon d'avoir du bon réseau quand on voyage.
native_language_example: It's good to have a good signal when traveling.

meaning: to have difficulty (doing something); to struggle
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or a noun to say someone finds something hard. Most commonly appears as "avoir du mal à + infinitive" (to have trouble doing X). Common in everyday and formal speech; can be used in various tenses and persons.
target_language_example: Je vais avoir du mal à trouver le sommeil, maintenant.
native_language_example: I am going to have difficulty falling asleep now.

avoir du pain sur la planche

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du pain sur la planche
meaning: to have a lot of work or tasks to do; to be busy
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say someone has many things to do or a heavy workload. Common in casual and neutral contexts. Not about literal bread or a board. Can refer to current or upcoming tasks.
target_language_example: En ce moment, j'ai du pain sur la planche avec trois projets à finir.
native_language_example: Right now, I have a lot on my plate with three projects to finish.

avoir du sang sur les mains

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du sang sur les mains
meaning: to be responsible for someone's death or for serious harm (to have blood on one's hands).
additional_notes: Figurative expression used to accuse someone of causing death, violence, or serious wrongdoing. Often used in moral, legal, or political contexts. Not literal: it doesn't mean physically having blood on your hands. Strong/accusatory language; use with care.
target_language_example: Il aura du sang sur les mains si les autorités restent muettes.
native_language_example: He will have blood on his hands if the authorities remain silent.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical or understandable
additional_notes: Used to say that something is reasonable, coherent, or easy to understand. Often appears in impersonal constructions: "Ça a du sens" (That makes sense). Can follow clauses: "Ça n'a pas de sens" (That doesn't make sense).
target_language_example: Il est important que ça ait du sens si on va investir du temps.
native_language_example: It's important that it makes sense if we're going to invest time.

meaning: to have (something) in mind; to be thinking of or considering something
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is thinking about, planning, or keeping something in mind. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., 'avoir une idée en tête', 'avoir en tête de + infinitive'). Common in everyday speech. Components are fairly compositional — not an idiom with a completely different meaning.
target_language_example: J'ai toujours avoir en tête ce projet de livre.
native_language_example: I always have this book project in mind.

meaning: to want; to feel like (doing something); to have a desire for
additional_notes: Used with a noun (avoir envie de quelque chose = to want something) or with an infinitive (avoir envie de + infinitive = to feel like doing something). Literally 'to have desire'. Common everyday expression for desires, cravings, or intentions (less formal than vouloir for simple wants but very common). Conjugate avoir before envie (j'ai envie, tu as envie, il/elle a envie, nous avons envie, etc.).
target_language_example: J'ai envie d'utiliser l'expression avoir envie pour dire ce que je veux.
native_language_example: I want to use the expression avoir envie to say what I want.

meaning: to be hungry
additional_notes: Literally 'to have hunger' in French; used to express being hungry. Conjugate according to subject (j'ai faim, tu as faim, il/elle a faim, nous avons faim, vous avez faim, ils/elles ont faim). Often used with modal verbs (Il doit avoir faim = He must be hungry) and in past tenses (Nous avions faim = We were hungry).
target_language_example: Il doit avoir faim après avoir couru.
native_language_example: He must be hungry after running.

meaning: 'to have faith' or 'to place trust/confidence (in someone, something, or an outcome).
additional_notes: Used for religious faith or general trust/confidence. Often followed by 'en' + noun or pronoun (avoir foi en Dieu, avoir foi en quelqu'un) or used with a clause introduced by 'que' to indicate belief. Slightly more formal or literary than 'croire'.
target_language_example: Nous devons avoir foi en nos capacités pour réussir.
native_language_example: We must have faith in our abilities to succeed.

meaning: to be cold; to feel cold (physically).
additional_notes: Common French expression formed with avoir + noun to describe physical sensations (like avoir chaud, avoir faim). Conjugate avoir with the subject: J'ai froid, Tu as froid, Il/Elle a froid, Nous avons froid, Vous avez froid, Ils/Elles ont froid. Can be used in various tenses and constructions (e.g., Vous allez avoir froid = you are going to be cold; Vous devez avoir froid = you must be cold / you probably are cold).
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir froid si tu restes dehors sans manteau.
native_language_example: You must be cold if you stay outside without a coat.

meaning: 'to be ashamed' or 'to feel ashamed'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels ashamed or should feel ashamed for something. Commonly followed by de + noun/infinitive (e.g. honte de ton comportement / honte d'avoir menti). Often appears with deverbal expressions like devoir (tu devrais avoir honte).
target_language_example: Tu devrais avoir honte de ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: You should be ashamed of what you said.

meaning: 'to hate' or 'to detest' (strong dislike).
additional_notes: Literally 'to have horror'; used with 'de' + noun or infinitive: avoir horreur de quelque chose / de faire quelque chose. Stronger than 'ne pas aimer' and expresses intense aversion.
target_language_example: J'ai horreur de tomber en panne sur l'autoroute.
native_language_example: I hate breaking down on the highway.

meaning: 'to be eager' or 'to look forward to' (to be excited about something that will happen).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or de + noun. Common structure: avoir hâte de + verb (e.g. J'ai hâte de partir = I can't wait to leave). When referring to another person as the object, use que + clause (J'ai hâte que tu viennes is less common; French often prefers avoir hâte de + infinitive). Expresses positive anticipation. Not particularly informal but common in spoken register.
target_language_example: J'ai hâte d'utiliser ce guide parce que j'ai vraiment hâte de maîtriser le français.
native_language_example: I can't wait to use this guide because I'm really eager to master French.

meaning: 'to be wise to' / 'to have good reason to' / 'to be in one's interest (to do something)'
additional_notes: Used to say someone would do well to do something or has a reason/advantage to do it. Common constructions: avoir intérêt à + infinitive (You should / you'd better), or avoir intérêt de + noun. Can express advice, warning or a logical consequence (e.g. Tu as intérêt à partir = you'd better leave).
target_language_example: Tu as intérêt à étudier si tu veux réussir l'examen. (contains avoir intérêt)
native_language_example: You'd better study if you want to pass the exam.

meaning: to look; to seem (based on appearance or impression)
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone or something appears or seems. Typically followed by an adjective, a noun phrase, or de + infinitive. Constructions include: "avoir l'air + adjectif" (Il a l'air fatigué), "avoir l'air de + infinitif" (Elle a l'air de vouloir partir). Conveys perception or impression rather than an objective fact.
target_language_example: Il a l'air fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He looks tired after the trip.

meaning: 'to have the' (literal); used as part of fixed expressions meaning 'to receive/obtain/experience something' or in polite imperatives.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase with a single meaning — it's the verb avoir + the feminine definite article la. Meaning depends on the noun that follows: e.g. avoir la garde (to have custody), avoir la gentillesse de (please be kind enough to), avoir la fessée (to get a spanking), avoir la prison à vie (to receive a life sentence), avoir la bonne approche (to have the right approach). Can introduce an obligation, a future event, or a polite request when used in set phrases. Pay attention to gender: with masculine nouns you'd see avoir le; plural = avoir les.
target_language_example: Elle va avoir la responsabilité du projet.
native_language_example: She is going to have responsibility for the project.

meaning: An idiomatic fragment meaning to feel a strong appetite/drive for something or to be inclined to be harsh/critical; often used as part of fixed expressions such as 'avoir la dent dure' (to be harsh/critical) or 'avoir la dent contre quelqu'un' (to hold a grudge against someone).
additional_notes: On its own 'avoir la dent' is normally incomplete and appears in fixed phrases. Common completions: 'avoir la dent contre' (bear a grudge), 'avoir la dent dure' (be severe/critical), regional uses may pair it with an object to mean a strong appetite. Avoid using the fragment alone in formal writing — prefer the complete expression.
target_language_example: Il semble avoir la dent contre elle depuis l'entretien.
native_language_example: He seems to hold a grudge against her since the interview.

meaning: to have a hangover (feel sick after drinking alcohol).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Literally 'to have the wooden mouth/face' but means suffering from headache, nausea, sensitivity to light/sound after drinking too much. Used with avoir (j'ai la gueule de bois). Common in everyday spoken French.
target_language_example: J'ai la gueule de bois ce matin après la soirée d'hier — j'aurais dû moins boire.
native_language_example: I have a hangover this morning after last night's party — I should have drunk less.

meaning: 'to feel dizzy' or 'to be light-headed'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a physical sensation of dizziness, vertigo, or light-headedness (e.g., after standing up quickly, being sick, or when overwhelmed). Often conjugated normally: J'ai la tête qui tourne, Il avait la tête qui tournait, etc. Not literal; it describes a feeling, not that the head is actually turning.
target_language_example: J'ai la tête qui tourne après être resté debout trop longtemps.
native_language_example: After standing for too long, I feel dizzy.

meaning: to have a crush (on someone); to be infatuated
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say you like someone romantically, often mildly or briefly. Commonly followed by 'pour' or 'sur' + person (e.g. 'avoir le béguin pour quelqu'un'). Can be used in present or past (j'ai le béguin, j'ai eu le béguin).
target_language_example: Il avoue qu'il a le béguin pour elle.
native_language_example: He admits that he has a crush on her.

meaning: to have the last word; to be the final person to speak or to win an argument.
additional_notes: Used when someone insists on making the final remark or winning a discussion. Can be literal but is usually idiomatic about arguments or conversations. Often implies annoyance or stubbornness. Common in expressions describing people who always insist on concluding a discussion.
target_language_example: Elle aime avoir le dernier mot, même quand elle a tort.
native_language_example: She likes to have the last word, even when she's wrong.

meaning: to take place; to happen (used for events, incidents, actions occurring or scheduled)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an event will occur or has occurred. Common tenses: "va avoir lieu", "a eu lieu", "aura lieu", "pouvait/peut avoir lieu", and conditional/subjunctive forms (e.g., "si cela devait avoir lieu"). Typically neutral or formal; often used for meetings, ceremonies, incidents, deployments, etc. Not literal — "avoir" + "lieu" does not mean "to have a place" in English.
target_language_example: Le déploiement du produit ne peut avoir lieu avant janvier.
native_language_example: The product deployment cannot take place before January.

meaning: 'to feel pain' or 'to hurt' (something hurts someone).
additional_notes: Used with a body part introduced by 'à' (e.g. J'ai mal à la tête = I have a headache). Can also be followed by an infinitive to mean 'to have difficulty' or 'to hurt to do something' in certain constructions (e.g. J'ai du mal à comprendre / Ça me fait mal de le dire). Conjugate 'avoir' for tense/person: J'ai mal, Tu as mal, Il/Elle a mal, Nous avons mal, etc. When indicating whose pain it is, use indirect object pronouns or names (Ça lui fait mal = It hurts him/her).
target_language_example: Quand j'ai mal, je dis 'J'ai mal' pour expliquer où j'ai mal.
native_language_example: When I'm in pain, I say 'I'm in pain' to explain where it hurts.

meaning: to have among; to include someone/something among a group or list.
additional_notes: Used when stating that someone or something is part of a set, group, list, or collection. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by "parmi" (e.g., "avoir X parmi ses amis" = to have X among one's friends). More common constructions use verbs like "être" or "compter" with "parmi"; "avoir parmi" is less frequent but acceptable in contexts like "Il a parmi ses collaborateurs plusieurs experts."
target_language_example: Il aime avoir parmi ses invités des personnes de divers horizons.
native_language_example: He likes to have among his guests people from diverse backgrounds.

meaning: to take part in; to have a share or involvement in something.
additional_notes: Somewhat formal or literary; typically used with de (avoir part de quelque chose) or in expressions like avoir sa part. Common everyday alternatives: participer à, prendre part à, avoir sa part de. Often implies contributing to or sharing responsibility for an outcome.
target_language_example: Il a voulu avoir part à la décision.
native_language_example: He wanted to have a part in the decision.

meaning: to be afraid; to feel fear
additional_notes: Common expression meaning to feel fear. Usually followed by de + noun or de + infinitive to indicate the object/cause of the fear (e.g. avoir peur de l'orage, avoir peur de parler). Appears in various tenses and constructions (il a peur, il a eu peur, il va avoir peur, commencer à avoir peur).
target_language_example: Il commença à avoir peur.
native_language_example: He began to be afraid.

meaning: to be able to stand (because the water or ground is shallow); to have firm footing; to be not out of one's depth
additional_notes: Used mainly about water or other situations where depth/height matters: 'avoir pied' means you can touch the bottom with your feet (the water is shallow enough). Commonly used in the negative 'ne pas avoir pied' = 'to be in deep water / unable to touch ground' (can be literal or figurative: overwhelmed, out of one's depth).
target_language_example: Je peux avoir pied ici, l'eau n'est pas très profonde.
native_language_example: I can stand here (I can touch the bottom), the water is not very deep.

meaning: 'to feel pity' or 'to have mercy' (to feel compassion for someone or to show mercy).
additional_notes: Used both to describe feeling compassion (avoir pitié de quelqu'un = to pity someone) and to ask for mercy (Aie pitié !/Ayez pitié !). Common structure: avoir pitié de + personne/quelque chose. Can be used with indirect object: 'J'ai pitié de lui.' Formal imperative 'Ayez pitié' for pleading or moral appeal.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas d'avoir pitié de ceux qui souffrent.
native_language_example: Don't forget to have pity on those who suffer.

meaning: to have (as) / to be intended for; used to indicate purpose, role, aim, or target
additional_notes: Followed by a noun phrase or infinitive clause (e.g. «avoir pour but», «avoir pour mission», «avoir pour objectif de…»). Common in formal or neutral registers. Context determines whether it means 'to have as' (a role/aim) or 'to be intended for' (an audience/recipient).
target_language_example: Ce projet a pour but d'améliorer la qualité de l'air.
native_language_example: This project has the aim of improving air quality.

meaning: to have some...
additional_notes: This is usually not a complete standalone phrase. quelque normally needs a noun after it (for example, avoir quelque difficulté = 'to have some difficulty'). If you mean 'to have something,' French usually says avoir quelque chose.
target_language_example: Il semble avoir quelque difficulté à comprendre.
native_language_example: He seems to have some difficulty understanding.

meaning: to be right
additional_notes: Used to say someone is correct. Because this entry is listed under the infinitive form, example sentences often place it after another verb, as in "Tu dois avoir raison." Although it looks like "to have reason," that literal translation is usually not how the expression is understood; for "to have a reason," French more often uses "avoir une raison de ...". The opposite is "avoir tort".
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir raison.
native_language_example: You must be right.

meaning: to be right to (do something); to have good reason to
additional_notes: Used when saying someone is justified in doing something or that a belief/opinion is correct. Common structures: avoir raison de + infinitive (e.g. Il a raison de s'inquiéter = He is right to worry) or avoir raison (without "de") to mean "to be right" about something (Il avait raison = He was right).
target_language_example: Il a raison de partir tôt.
native_language_example: He is right to leave early.

meaning: 'to have an appointment' or 'to have a date/meeting'.
additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting, appointment, or a date with someone. Can refer to formal appointments (doctor, interview) or informal meetings/dates. Commonly conjugated with avoir (e.g., j'ai rendez-vous, nous avons rendez-vous). To specify time or person, add details: J'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin à 10h / J'ai rendez-vous avec Paul.
target_language_example: Nous allons dire 'avoir rendez-vous' : j'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin à 15 heures.
native_language_example: We say 'avoir rendez-vous': I have an appointment at the doctor's at 3 PM.

meaning: 'to have one's period' (to be menstruating).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say a woman/girl is on her menstrual cycle. Polite and standard everyday expression. Can be used with a subject: J'ai mes règles / Elle a ses règles. Alternative, slightly more formal phrasing: 'être indisposée' (to be indisposed).
target_language_example: Elle ne veut pas nager parce qu'elle a ses règles.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to swim because she has her period.

meaning: to be thirsty / to feel thirst
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something needs a drink. Literally 'to have thirst' (avoir = to have, soif = thirst). Can be used literally (people, animals) or figuratively (e.g., 'avoir soif de sang' = 'to thirst for blood'). Present tense example: j'ai soif = I'm thirsty.
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir soif après la course.
native_language_example: You must be thirsty after the run.

meaning: to be sleepy / to feel sleepy
additional_notes: Avoir sommeil uses the verb avoir (to have) + sommeil (sleep) to express that someone is sleepy. Commonly used in everyday speech and can be used with different subjects (tu, vous, il/elle). Often appears with devoir (tu dois avoir sommeil) to suggest the speaker's assumption: "you must be sleepy."
target_language_example: Je commence à avoir sommeil, je vais me coucher.
native_language_example: I'm starting to feel sleepy; I'm going to bed.

meaning: to have had enough; to be fed up (with someone/something)
additional_notes: Used when someone has reached their limit or is tired of a situation or person. Often followed by 'de' + noun or verb infinitive: J'ai mon compte de + noun/infinitive. Can appear in constructions like 'en avoir son compte' or simply 'avoir son compte' in spoken French. Tone is neutral to slightly colloquial.
target_language_example: J'ai enfin eu ma dose, j'ai mon compte — je pars.
native_language_example: I've had enough, I'm done — I'm leaving.

meaning: to be wrong (to be incorrect).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is mistaken. Often appears with modal verbs (devoir, pouvoir, avoir dû) to express probability or past inference: "doit avoir tort" = "must be wrong"; "a dû avoir tort" = "must have been wrong." Common opposite: "avoir raison" (to be right).
target_language_example: Il doit avoir tort sur ce point.
native_language_example: He must be wrong about that point.

meaning: 'to hear about' or 'to learn of' (something, often indirectly or via rumor).
additional_notes: Used with 'de' before the thing heard about: avoir vent de + noun/that-clause. Implies learning through hearsay, rumor, or indirect information rather than official/confirmed sources. Common in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai eu vent de son départ la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I heard about his departure last week.

meaning: to have to; to be obliged to; to need to (do something). Can also appear in fixed expressions like "avoir à faire à" meaning "to have to deal with" someone/something.
additional_notes: Often used with an infinitive: avoir à + infinitive = 'to have to (do something)'. Similar in meaning to devoir but sometimes less strong or more neutral. In the phrase "avoir à faire à", it means 'to have to deal with' or 'be faced with'. Negation works as in other verbs: Je n'ai pas à + infinitive = 'I don't have to...'.
target_language_example: Nous pouvons nous y rendre sans avoir à les informer.
native_language_example: We can get there without having to inform them.

meaning: to keep an eye on; to watch closely (often suspiciously or protectively).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to monitor or watch someone/something carefully. Can imply suspicion, caution, or guardianship. Common in spoken and written French. Conjugate avoir as usual: j'ai à l'œil, il a à l'œil, etc.; often used with a direct object: 'avoir qn/qc à l'œil'.
target_language_example: Je dois avoir à l'œil la nouvelle recrue pendant sa période d'essai.
native_language_example: I need to keep an eye on the new recruit during their probation period.

meaning: 'to have to do with' or 'to be related to / connected with'
additional_notes: Used to indicate a relationship or relevance between things or people. Commonly appears in constructions like "avoir quelque chose à voir avec" (to have something to do with). Can be used in affirmative or negative forms: e.g. "Ça a à voir avec..." or "Ça n'a rien à voir avec..."
target_language_example: Est-ce que ça a quelque chose à voir avec ton travail ?
native_language_example: Does that have anything to do with your work?

meaning: To have that; used colloquially to refer to possessing or experiencing something just mentioned (an object, symptom, quality, etc.). Context supplies what 'ça' refers to.
additional_notes: Literal translation: 'to have that'. The phrase is usually incomplete on its own and appears in context or as a brief answer. Common in informal speech (e.g., confirming possession or a condition). Examples: confirming you possess something ('Tu as un plan ? — J'ai ça.') or reporting a symptom ('J'ai ça depuis hier').
target_language_example: Tu as le document ? — Oui, j'ai ça.
native_language_example: Do you have the document? — Yes, I have that.

meaning: 'we have (done) a lot' — part of the compound past or present structure meaning 'we ... a lot' (e.g. we liked/learned/drank a lot).
additional_notes: This is the first-person plural (nous) form of avoir + 'beaucoup' (a lot). 'Beaucoup' modifies the verb when used with a past participle or infinitive: e.g. nous avons beaucoup aimé = we liked (it) a lot; nous avons beaucoup bu = we drank a lot. Context determines the verb tense: 'avons' is present of avoir and is used here as an auxiliary for the passé composé (nous avons + past participle). It can also appear with an infinitive in structures like 'nous avons beaucoup à faire' (we have a lot to do) but in the examples it marks quantity/frequency/intensity of the action.
target_language_example: Nous avons beaucoup voyagé l'été dernier.
native_language_example: We traveled a lot last summer.

meaning: have said
additional_notes: Part of the passé composé of dire with nous: nous avons dit means "we said" or "we have said." In natural English, it is often translated simply as "we said."
target_language_example: Nous avons dit non à cette idée.
native_language_example: We said no to that idea.

meaning: we heard the / we have heard the
additional_notes: Simple past meaning (passé composé) using 'avoir' + 'entendre' (to hear). 'Le' is the definite article that agrees with the noun that follows (le bruit, le président, le garçon, etc.). Use it to report a sound or that you heard someone speak or play an instrument. For other subjects replace 'avons' with the correct form of 'avoir' (j'ai entendu, tu as entendu, il/elle a entendu, nous avons entendu, vous avez entendu, ils/elles ont entendu).
target_language_example: Nous avons entendu le chat miauler cette nuit.
native_language_example: We heard the cat meowing last night.

meaning: 'we had a lot' or 'we've had a lot' (of something).
additional_notes: This is the first-person-plural passé composé of avoir + an adverb: nous avons eu + beaucoup (de...). It means that 'we' experienced, received, or possessed a large amount of something in the past. You will usually see it followed by a noun or 'de' + noun (e.g. avons eu beaucoup de travail, avons eu beaucoup de pluie). In spoken French, the subject pronoun nous is often dropped or replaced by on (on a eu beaucoup...).
target_language_example: Nous avons eu beaucoup de pluie cet été.
native_language_example: We had a lot of rain this summer.

meaning: 'we had' or 'we have had' + plural noun (past experience or occurrence).
additional_notes: Combination of the present-tense form of 'avoir' (nous avons) with the past participle 'eu' to form the passé composé: nous avons eu = we had / we have had. Followed by 'des' and a plural noun. Used to report past events, experiences or occurrences. In English can be translated as 'we had' or 'we have had' depending on context. Pronunciation tip: the 's' in 'avons' is silent; liaison may occur with a following vowel (nous avons entendu).
target_language_example: Nous avons eu des problèmes avec la voiture la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: We had problems with the car last week.

meaning: 'we spent (some amount of time) ...' (past tense of passer du temps).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression (des heures, des jours, etc.) to say 'we spent (hours) doing something.' Construction: Subject (nous) + avons passé + des + [time period] + (à + verb / sur + object). Common in spoken and written French. 'Passer' here means to spend time, not to pass something to someone.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé des heures à étudier pour l'examen.
native_language_example: We spent hours studying for the exam.

meaning: 'we spent / we crossed the' (we passed the).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect (passé composé) form of 'passer' with 'nous' + feminine singular object introduced by 'la'. Depending on context, 'passer' can mean 'to spend (time)' (e.g. passer la journée/la nuit/la soirée) or 'to cross/pass' (e.g. passer la frontière). Translate according to the noun that follows. Common pattern: 'nous avons passé + la/le/l' + time period or place.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé la journée à visiter la ville.
native_language_example: We spent the day visiting the city.

meaning: 'we spent a (time period)'.
additional_notes: Part of the passé composé of the verb passer used with a direct object meaning 'to spend' (time). The full verb form is 'nous avons passé' + a time expression or event (une soirée, une journée, une nuit, une semaine...). Use to describe how time was spent (good, bad, quiet, interesting...).
target_language_example: Nous avons passé une après‑midi agréable au musée.
native_language_example: We spent a pleasant afternoon at the museum.

meaning: 'we thought' (first-person plural past tense of penser).
additional_notes: Avons pensé is the passé composé form used with nous (we) and the auxiliary avoir: nous avons pensé = we thought / we have thought. It expresses a completed thought or opinion in the past. Context determines whether to translate it as simple past ('we thought') or present perfect ('we have thought'). For negative or question forms, invert or add ne...pas: nous n'avons pas pensé / avons-nous pensé ?
target_language_example: Nous avons pensé que tu viendrais.
native_language_example: We thought that you would come.

meaning: 'we watched a' / 'we watched an' (past tense)
additional_notes: Combination of the auxiliary verb avoir (nous avons) + past participle regarder → passé composé: 'we watched'. Followed by an indefinite article (un/une) and a noun. Used for a completed action in the past. Change 'avons' to other subject forms as needed (j'ai regardé, tu as regardé, ils ont regardé).
target_language_example: Hier soir, nous avons regardé un documentaire sur les animaux.
native_language_example: Last night we watched a documentary about animals.

meaning: 'we stayed in' (past tense: nous avons séjourné dans ...)
additional_notes: A compound past form using the auxiliary avoir + past participle 'séjourné' (to stay, to reside temporarily). Used to say where a group including the speaker stayed. Often followed by a place: un hôtel, une maison, un village, etc. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous avons séjourné dans un petit hôtel près du port.
native_language_example: We stayed in a small hotel near the harbor.

meaning: 'we found a' (first-person plural, past tense).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé (past tense) of trouver for 'nous' + the indefinite article 'une' (feminine singular). Used to say 'we found a...' or 'we have found a...'. Change 'une' to 'un' for masculine nouns (nous avons trouvé un). If the sentence uses 'nous sommes tombés sur' it means 'we came across' or 'we ran into' — interchangeable in some contexts with 'avons trouvé'.
target_language_example: Nous avons trouvé une clé sous le paillasson.
native_language_example: We found a key under the doormat.

meaning: 'we have seen the' or 'we saw the' (perfect/simple past meaning depends on context).
additional_notes: Formed from the first-person plural of 'avoir' (nous avons) + past participle 'vu' + definite article 'le'. Used to say that 'we' saw a specific masculine noun (le + noun). In spoken French, context and time expressions determine whether it's translated as present perfect ('we have seen') or simple past ('we saw'). Replace 'le' with 'la', 'les' or 'l'' to match the noun's gender/number.
target_language_example: Nous avons vu le chien au parc hier.
native_language_example: We saw the dog at the park yesterday.

meaning: 'we were attacked' (past passive of 'attaquer').
additional_notes: Formal/perfect passive: subject 'nous' + auxiliary 'avoir' in present (avons) + past participle 'été' (être) + past participle 'attaqués' agrees in gender/number with 'nous'. Used to say that 'we' were the victims of an attack by someone/something. Replace 'avons' with other forms for different subjects/tenses (e.g., 'a été attaqué', 'ont été attaqués').
target_language_example: Après la tempête, nous avons été attaqués par des pillards.
native_language_example: After the storm, we were attacked by looters.

meaning: have enough
additional_notes: Most commonly means "have enough" (nous avons assez de ... = we have enough of ... / enough ...). When used with the pronoun en (nous en avons assez), it means "we've had enough" or "we're fed up" (i.e. tired of something). Can be followed by nouns (de + noun) or expressions of time/quantity.
target_language_example: Nous avons assez d'argent pour payer le loyer.
native_language_example: We have enough money to pay the rent.

meaning: 'we need your' (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: A form of the verb phrase avoir besoin de (to need). Avons besoin de is the first-person plural (we need). Ton is the masculine singular possessive adjective (your). Together they introduce something the speakers need that is masculine singular (e.g., ton aide, ton avis, ton avis). In spoken French you may also hear 'on a besoin de ton...' instead of 'nous avons besoin de ton...'.
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de ton aide pour déménager samedi.
native_language_example: We need your help to move on Saturday.

meaning: we have things (to do/say/etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an infinitive or complement to mean 'we have things to [do/say/discuss]'. 'Des choses' is vague — translates as 'things' or 'matters'. The subject is usually 'nous' (we) so full phrase is 'nous avons des choses...'.
target_language_example: Nous avons des choses importantes à régler.
native_language_example: We have important things to sort out.

meaning: 'we still have a lot (of...)' or 'we still need a lot (of...)'.
additional_notes: Used with nouns or infinitives to say there remains a large amount or many things to do/cover. Usually appears as 'nous avons encore beaucoup de [noun]' or 'nous avons encore beaucoup à [infinitive]'. Common in everyday and formal contexts. Contraction/variation: 'on a encore beaucoup' in informal speech.
target_language_example: Nous avons encore beaucoup de travail à faire.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do.

meaning: we made a
additional_notes: avons fait un is the first‑person plural passé composé (nous) of faire + indefinite article. It literally means "we made/did a...". Use it to describe actions completed in the past (we made a fire, we did a tour, we took a trip, etc.). The noun that follows (feu, barbecue, château de sable, tour, voyage...) completes the idea. English choice between "made" and "did" depends on the noun (made a fire/made a sandcastle, did a tour/did a long journey → more natural: "took a tour" or "went on a trip").
target_language_example: Nous avons fait un pique-nique au parc.
native_language_example: We had/took a picnic in the park.

meaning: 'we have the right' or 'we are allowed to'.
additional_notes: Used to express permission or a legal/right entitlement for 'nous' (we). Often appears in questions and negatives: "Avons-nous le droit de... ?" (Are we allowed to...?) or "Nous n'avons pas le droit de..." (We are not allowed to...). Contraction with inversion or negation follows normal French grammar (e.g. "n'avons pas"). Can be used in declarative sentences: "Nous avons le droit de...".
target_language_example: Nous avons le droit d'exprimer notre opinion.
native_language_example: We have the right to express our opinion.

meaning: we have little / we don't have much
additional_notes: Combines the first-person plural of avoir (avons = we have) with peu (little/not much). Used to say that a group has a small amount of something. Often followed by a noun (avons peu de temps) or used alone with context (Nous avons peu). In spoken French you may hear contractions or alternative word order (on a peu).
target_language_example: Nous avons peu de temps pour finir.
native_language_example: We have little time to finish.

meaning: have something (in) — part of a larger expression meaning 'we have something in [a place/state]'.
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it appears as part of sentences like «nous avons quelque chose en...», often followed by a noun or location (ex.: en stock, en tête, en commun). The verb form 'avons' is first-person plural (we). Choose the word after 'en' to complete the meaning (location, state, possession, etc.).
target_language_example: Nous avons quelque chose en réserve pour vous.
native_language_example: We have something in reserve for you.

meaning: 'we still have' or 'we always have' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Form: first-person plural (nous) of avoir + toujours. Can mean 'we still have' (continuing possession/situation) or 'we always have' (habitual). Context and tense determine which sense fits. Use with nouns (un problème, faim) or abstract nouns (le choix).
target_language_example: Nous avons toujours du temps pour aider.
native_language_example: We still have time to help.

meaning: were able to
additional_notes: Combination of the present subjunctive of avoir (vous ayez) + past participle pu (from pouvoir). Used after expressions of emotion, opinion, or necessity (e.g. content que, heureux que) to talk about someone's ability to do something in the past. Often translated as "that you were able to" or simply "you could". Fits formal and informal contexts; the pronoun is usually vous but same structure exists for other persons (que j'aie pu, qu'il/elle ait pu, etc.).
target_language_example: Je suis content que vous ayez pu venir hier soir.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you were able to come last night.

meaning: babysitter; someone who looks after children temporarily (sits for the kids).
additional_notes: Used for a person (male or female) hired to care for children for a short period (evening, few hours). Common in spoken and written French; sometimes written baby sitter or babysitter. Can be a teenage sitter or a professional. Informal contexts may include stronger language around them, as in example 3.
target_language_example: On a besoin d'une baby-sitter pour samedi soir.
native_language_example: We need a babysitter for Saturday night.

meaning: magic wand
additional_notes: Literally 'wand (stick) magical'. Used to refer to a small stick used by magicians or in fantasy to cast spells. Also sometimes used figuratively for a simple tool or solution that would magically fix a problem (informal/metaphorical).
target_language_example: Le magicien a brandi sa baguette magique et a fait apparaître une colombe.
native_language_example: The magician waved his magic wand and made a dove appear.

meaning: a (figurative or literal) 'bath of' or 'immersed in' — used to describe being covered by or experiencing a large amount of something (e.g., light, soleil, foule).
additional_notes: Commonly used in French to form short phrases like 'un bain de soleil' (a sunbath), 'un bain de foule' (being in a crowd), or 'un bain de lumière' (flooded with light). Can be literal (taking a bath) or figurative (an intense experience or immersion). Usually follows a noun: 'un bain de + noun'.
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, nous avons profité d'un bain de soleil au bord du lac.
native_language_example: After the hike, we enjoyed a sunbath at the lakeside.

meaning: a bloodbath; a situation with a lot of violence or many casualties.
additional_notes: Used figuratively or literally to describe extreme violence, mass killing, or a chaotic situation with heavy losses (e.g., in battles, fights, competitions). Strong, dramatic expression — common in news, literature, or emphatic speech. Not polite; avoid in formal/neutral contexts unless reporting violence.
target_language_example: Si les négociations échouent, ce sera un bain de sang.
native_language_example: If the negotiations fail, it will be a bloodbath.

meaning: sunbathe; a sunbath (to lie in the sun to get a tan).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is sunbathing or took a sunbath. Can be used reflexively with prendre (prendre un bain de soleil = to sunbathe). Not literal bathing—it's about lying in the sun. Suitable for beach, poolside, or garden contexts.
target_language_example: Cet après-midi, je vais prendre un bain de soleil à la plage.
native_language_example: This afternoon I'm going to sunbathe on the beach.

meaning: This looks like two words 'bain' (bath) and 'est' (is). As written, 'bain est' is not a standard French phrase; it likely results from a fragment or a typo (e.g., 'le bain est...' meaning 'the bath is...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. If you see 'bain est' in text, it's probably part of a sentence where 'bain' is the noun 'bath' and 'est' is the verb 'is' (3rd person singular of être). For a complete thought you need the rest of the sentence: e.g. 'Le bain est chaud.' ('The bath is hot.'). If you intended another phrase (like 'bien est' or 'bain de...' or 'Bain Est' as a place name), check the source.
target_language_example: Le bain est prêt.
native_language_example: The bath is ready.

meaning: 'bath' combined with 'tous' to indicate a recurring frequency (e.g. 'tous les matins' = 'every morning').
additional_notes: 'Bain' means 'a bath'. 'Tous' is used to express recurrence and is typically followed by 'les' plus a plural time expression (e.g. 'tous les matins', 'tous les soirs', 'tous les deux jours'). Word order in examples may place 'bain' before the frequency ('prendre un bain tous les soirs') or after with an article ('le bain tous les soirs'). Pronunciation: 'tous' is pronounced /tu/ when followed by a consonant-starting word like 'les' in speech; in writing it remains 'tous'.
target_language_example: Il prend un bain tous les matins.
native_language_example: He takes a bath every morning.

meaning: 'to kiss (someone) on' (a part of the body).
additional_notes: Used with a body part after 'sur' (e.g. sur la joue, sur le front). 'Baiser' as a verb can be formal/literary for 'to kiss' but note: in modern spoken French, 'baiser' is often vulgar meaning 'to screw' — preferred everyday verb for 'to kiss' is 'embrasser'. In contexts like these (romantic or affectionate brief contact), it is understood as 'to place a kiss on'.
target_language_example: Il lui a donné un baiser sur la joue avant de partir.
native_language_example: He gave her a kiss on the cheek before leaving.

meaning: 'to give up' or 'to stop trying (physically or mentally)'
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression literally meaning 'to lower the arms.' Used when someone stops making an effort, resigns themselves, or loses hope. Can be used for both physical action (dropping one's arms) and figurative situations (giving up on a task or situation). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Après plusieurs échecs, il a fini par baisser les bras.
native_language_example: After several failures, he finally gave up.

meaning: 'ball with' — used to say a dance/ball is held with someone or includes something (literally "ball with").
additional_notes: bal means a formal dance or ball. bal avec is not a fixed idiom by itself; you will more often see phrases like "un bal avec des musiciens", "un bal avec mon partenaire", or "aller à un bal avec quelqu'un" (to go to a ball with someone). Use "aller à un bal" to say 'go to a ball' and add "avec" + person/thing to indicate accompaniment or inclusion.
target_language_example: Je vais au bal avec Marie ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the ball with Marie tonight.

meaning: 'the ball is' (literal); often appears in the idiom 'La balle est dans ton camp' meaning 'it's your move / it's up to you'.
additional_notes: As a standalone two-word sequence, 'balle est' is simply the noun 'balle' (ball/bullet) followed by the verb 'est' (is). In everyday use you'll most often encounter this in the fixed expression 'La balle est dans ton/votre camp' meaning 'it's your move / the decision is yours'. Be careful: 'balle' can also mean 'bullet' in contexts about injuries (e.g. 'blessure de balle' = gunshot wound). Word order matters: 'La balle est là-bas' = 'The ball is over there.'
target_language_example: La balle est dans votre camp maintenant.
native_language_example: The ball is in your court now.

meaning: introduces the type or purpose of a ball (e.g. 'balle à neige' = snowball) or marks a compound noun formed with 'balle' + noun.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; 'balle à' is the start of compound nouns where 'à' connects 'balle' (ball or projectile) to its use, content, or characteristic. Common examples: 'balle à neige' (snowball), 'balle à blanc' (blank cartridge/blank round), 'balle à zéro' is not standard. The gender stays feminine (la balle). Pronunciation: the 'e' in balle is pronounced; 'à' is stressed lightly. Use when naming specific kinds of balls or cartridges.
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent avec une balle à neige pendant l'hiver.
native_language_example: The children play with a snowball during winter.

meaning: 'ball of' or 'balloon of' — a part of a noun phrase introducing what the ball/balloon is made of, used for sports balls (ballon de football) or containers (ballon de baudruche).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the start of many noun phrases: 'ballon de football' (soccer ball), 'ballon de basket' (basketball), 'ballon de baudruche' (party balloon). In French the noun 'ballon' can mean a large ball (used in sports) or an inflated balloon; 'de' links to the specification (type, material, purpose). Remember agreement and word order: the descriptive noun usually follows 'ballon de'.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté un ballon de football pour le parc.
native_language_example: I bought a football for the park.

meaning: a rude way to address a group: 'you lot' / 'bunch of' (insulting).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to insult or strongly criticize a group (e.g. bande de connards = 'bunch of assholes'). Very informal and vulgar. Tone depends on the noun that follows; often followed by insults. Not appropriate in polite contexts. It functions like 'bunch of' or 'you lot' but with hostile intent.
target_language_example: Bande de menteurs, tais‑toi !
native_language_example: You bunch of liars, shut up!

meaning: comic strip / comic book (comics).
additional_notes: Refers to illustrated stories in panels; in French often shortened to BD. Can mean a single comic strip, a comic book, or the medium of comics in general.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une nouvelle bande dessinée ce matin.
native_language_example: I bought a new comic book this morning.

meaning: This combination is not a standard French phrase; it appears to be two words (banque = bank, est = is) placed together and would literally mean "bank is".
additional_notes: Likely a fragment rather than a complete expression. In French, 'banque' means a financial institution; 'est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). To form a full sentence, you need a subject and complement (e.g. "La banque est fermée" = "The bank is closed"). Don't use 'banque est' alone as a set phrase.
target_language_example: La banque est fermée le dimanche.
native_language_example: The bank is closed on Sundays.

meaning: 'the bar is' (simple present of être used to describe the bar)
additional_notes: This is the verb être (est = 'is') used after the noun 'bar'. It forms simple statements about the bar's state, location, or restrictions (e.g., open/closed, location, allowed/prohibited). Use subject + est for il/elle/on (here: 'le bar est' = 'the bar is').
target_language_example: Le bar est fermé ce soir.
native_language_example: The bar is closed tonight.

meaning: front lower part; the front bottom (of something).
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining bas (low/bottom) + avant (front). Used to indicate the lower/front area of an object or body (e.g., 'le bas avant de la jupe' = the front bottom of the skirt). It’s compositional and literal; not an idiom. Context matters—could describe position on clothing, vehicles, or body parts.
target_language_example: Regarde le bas avant de la porte, il est endommagé.
native_language_example: Look at the front bottom of the door; it's damaged.

meaning: down in; low in (literal spatial sense) or 'deep in' (figurative), depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it combines the adjective/ adverb 'bas' (low/down) with the preposition 'dans' (in/into). You'll typically see 'bas' before a noun/adverbial or after a verb (e.g. 'regarder bas', 'tomber bas') and 'dans' introduces a place, container, or time. Together they can appear in sentences like 'en bas, dans la cave' (down in the cellar) or 'bas dans la liste' (low down in the list). Because it's compositional, translate each part literally and adjust word order to natural English: 'down in', 'low in', or 'at the bottom of'.
target_language_example: Il est bas dans la liste des candidats.
native_language_example: He is low down in the list of candidates.

meaning: 'bottom of' or 'lower part of' (used before a noun)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase combining bas (low/bottom) + de. It is used before a noun to indicate the lower part of something (e.g., le bas de la page = the bottom of the page). Remember to use the correct article after de (du, de la, de l', des) when needed: le bas de la porte, le bas du mur, le bas de l'escalier. Not to be confused with 'bas' alone (meaning 'low' or 'stockings').
target_language_example: Regarde le bas de la page pour les notes.
native_language_example: Look at the bottom of the page for the notes.

meaning: the bottom of (feminine noun phrase) — used before a feminine noun or noun phrase to indicate the lower part of something.
additional_notes: Literal phrase: bas = bottom/low part; de la is the feminine singular partitive/possessive connector. It appears before a feminine noun (e.g. bas de la page = bottom of the page). If the following noun is masculine use "bas du" (bas du mur). For plural use "bas des". In spoken French you may also see "au bas de la" (at the bottom of the...).
target_language_example: Regarde le bas de la page pour les notes.
native_language_example: Look at the bottom of the page for the notes.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase on its own; likely two words appearing together where 'bas' = 'low' or 'bottom' and 'et' = 'and'.
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'bas et' as a set phrase. Most likely this is just the adjective/noun 'bas' (meaning low, bottom, stockings) followed by the conjunction 'et' (and) that connects to another element. Pay attention to context: 'bas' can be an adjective (un niveau bas), a noun (des bas = stockings), or an adverb in some set phrases (en bas = downstairs). 'et' simply means 'and'.
target_language_example: Les bas et les chaussures sont dans l'armoire.
native_language_example: The stockings and the shoes are in the closet.

meaning: 'down the' or part of expressions meaning 'lower' or 'bottom' (depends on context)
additional_notes: On its own, "bas les" is incomplete: "bas" means 'low'/'bottom' and "les" is the plural definite article 'the'. You will see "bas les" inside fixed expressions like "bas les masques" (remove the masks) in informal slogans or in constructions such as "les bas les plus..." in descriptive phrases. You need the rest of the phrase to understand the full meaning; do not use "bas les" alone.
target_language_example: Bas les masques !
native_language_example: Off with the masks! (or: Take off your masks!)

meaning: Hands off! / Don't touch (something).
additional_notes: An informal, somewhat forceful expression used to tell someone to stop touching or taking something. Literally 'down the paws' — compares the person to an animal with 'paws'. Common in spoken French; can be rude depending on tone. Use with friends or in confrontations, not in formal situations.
target_language_example: Bas les pattes de mon téléphone !
native_language_example: Hands off my phone!

meaning: baseball (the sport).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the sport baseball. Often preceded by the preposition 'jouer à/au' when saying to play baseball (jouer au base-ball). Pronunciation similar to English; hyphenated in French. Plural: les base-balls is rare — usually use context or 'des matchs de base-ball'.
target_language_example: On joue au base-ball ce dimanche au parc.
native_language_example: We're playing baseball this Sunday at the park.

meaning: 'baseball à' is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun 'baseball' followed by the preposition 'à' used to introduce purpose, style, a person associated with baseball, or a skill (e.g. 'casquette de baseball à visière' or 'match de baseball à 7 joueurs').
additional_notes: Alone, 'baseball' = the sport 'baseball' or items related to it (e.g. une casquette de baseball = a baseball cap). When you see 'baseball à ...' the 'à' links baseball to a characteristic, purpose, or complement and must be completed (e.g. 'baseball à manches longues' = baseball [shirt] with long sleeves; 'match de baseball à domicile' = home baseball game). It's not a fixed idiom. Use a full phrase to be clear.
target_language_example: Nous avons acheté une casquette de baseball à visière plate.
native_language_example: We bought a baseball cap with a flat visor.

meaning: boat + auxiliary 'a' (he/she/it has) — indicates a boat has done something (e.g., capsized, sunk).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase: 'bateau' means 'boat' and 'a' is the third-person singular of 'avoir' used as an auxiliary in the passé composé (has ... / did ...). In the examples it introduces past actions performed by a boat (chavirer = to capsize; couler = to sink). For beginners: focus on recognizing 'bateau' (boat) and that 'a' + past participle forms the past tense.
target_language_example: Le bateau a coulé près du port.
native_language_example: The boat sank near the harbor.

meaning: 'boat of' or 'boat for' — used to describe a boat belonging to someone or used for a purpose (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination of bateau (boat) + de (of/for). It will be followed by a noun or noun phrase indicating possession (bateau de pêche = fishing boat / boat belonging to a fisherman) or purpose (bateau de plaisance = pleasure boat). Word order: bateau de + noun. Use l' or le/la + owner when specifying a person (le bateau de Paul = Paul's boat).
target_language_example: Le bateau de pêche est au port.
native_language_example: The fishing boat is in the harbor.

meaning: 'to retreat' or 'to withdraw' (often from a fight, battle, or difficult situation).
additional_notes: Used both literally (armies retreat) and figuratively (people back down from an argument, give up a position). More formal than slang. Similar to 'se retirer' but specifically implies pulling back under pressure or after a setback.
target_language_example: Après l'échec de l'offensive, les troupes ont dû battre en retraite.
native_language_example: After the failed offensive, the troops had to retreat.

meaning: 'battu' = beaten/defeated; 'battu le' appears as part of a verb phrase like 'battu le record' meaning 'beat the...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword idiom; it's the past participle 'battu' (from battre) followed by a definite article 'le'. Commonly used in constructions like 'battre le record' (to beat the record) in the past: 'a battu le record' = 'beat the record'. Word order and agreement: 'battu' agrees in compound tenses with a preceding direct object when formed with 'être' in pronominal uses, but with 'avoir' (most common) it stays 'battu'.
target_language_example: Il a battu le record hier.
native_language_example: He beat the record yesterday.

meaning: Good job; well done.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's work or effort. Can be said directly (Beau boulot!) or in sentences (T'as fait du beau boulot). Tone can be sincere or ironic depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken and informal contexts; also fine in neutral registers.
target_language_example: Beau boulot, tu as tout réparé rapidement.
native_language_example: Good job, you fixed everything quickly.

meaning: handsome guy; attractive/pretty boy (casual compliment).
additional_notes: Informal, used to compliment or address a man (often casually or flirtatiously). Can be said directly to someone ('Bonjour, beau gosse') or about someone ('C'est un beau gosse'). Tone can be playful; not suitable for very formal situations.
target_language_example: Salut, beau gosse, tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Hi handsome, do you want a coffee?

meaning: 'the best/most beautiful day of' (used to say 'the best day of [someone's] life')
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'le plus beau jour de (ma/ta/sa/notre) vie' meaning 'the happiest/most memorable day of someone's life' (often about weddings, births, special events). 'Beau jour de' by itself is not commonly used without 'le plus' or a possessive and 'vie'.
target_language_example: C'est le plus beau jour de ma vie.
native_language_example: This is the best day of my life.

meaning: a beautiful day of my life / a very happy day in my life
additional_notes: This phrase is a slightly unusual or poetic way to say that a particular day is one of the happiest or most memorable in someone's life. More common expressions include «le plus beau jour de ma vie» (the best day of my life) or «un des plus beaux jours de ma vie» (one of the best days of my life). Without «le plus», the phrase still conveys strong positive emotion about a day. Use in spoken French may sound emphatic or literary.
target_language_example: C'était un beau jour de ma vie quand j'ai rencontré mes amis d'enfance.
native_language_example: It was a beautiful day in my life when I met my childhood friends.

meaning: the middle; the very center (often 'the heart' of something).
additional_notes: Literally 'beautiful middle'. Used to emphasize the central point or exact center of a place, time, or situation (e.g., 'au beau milieu de' = 'in the very middle of'). Common in written and spoken French. You usually see it in the fixed phrase 'au beau milieu de...'.
target_language_example: Nous nous trouvions au beau milieu de la forêt.
native_language_example: We were in the very middle of the forest.

meaning: literally 'beautiful for' but not a fixed phrase; 'beau' followed by 'pour' introduces what something is good/pleasant for (or appropriate/useful for).
additional_notes: Not a single idiomatic expression in French. You will see 'beau pour' when 'beau' (nice/beautiful/good) modifies a noun or situation and 'pour' introduces a purpose or beneficiary: e.g. 'C'est beau pour toi' (that's nice for you) or 'une journée belle pour se promener' (a beautiful day for walking). Word order and agreement still apply (beau/belle/beaux/belles). If you meant another fixed phrase (like 'bon pour' or 'beaucoup pour' etc.), use that instead.
target_language_example: C'est beau pour les enfants de jouer dehors aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It's nice for the children to play outside today.

meaning: 'more beautiful than' (used in comparisons: '...beau que...' = '...more beautiful than...').
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people. Structure: [adjective in comparative form] + que (e.g. plus beau que = more beautiful than). Alone 'beau que' appears in examples as part of the comparative 'plus beau que' or for poetic comparisons ('aussi beau que' = as beautiful as). Remember agreement: 'beau' becomes 'bel' before a vowel (plus bel que).
target_language_example: Ton sourire est plus beau que le mien.
native_language_example: Your smile is more beautiful than mine.

meaning: Nice job; good work; well done.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's work or effort. Can be said directly ("Beau travail!") or inside a sentence ("Tu as fait du beau travail."). Polite and neutral—suitable in informal and formal contexts. "Du beau travail" emphasizes the quality ("some fine work").
target_language_example: Bravo, tu as fait du beau travail sur ce projet.
native_language_example: Well done, you did a great job on this project.

meaning: literally 'nice to' — used before an infinitive or noun to express that something is pleasant/beautiful to do or to look at (often followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase).
