additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'beau' is an adjective and 'à' is a preposition that combine in contexts like 'beau à voir', 'beau à entendre', or 'beau à regarder' to say that something is pleasant/beautiful to see/hear/watch. Depending on the verb or noun that follows, use the appropriate infinitive or article. Examples: 'C'est beau à voir' = 'It's beautiful to see.' 'Beau à regarder' = 'nice to look at.'
target_language_example: C'est beau à regarder au coucher du soleil.
native_language_example: It's nice to look at at sunset.

meaning: 'many people are' (or 'many people were' depending on tense).
additional_notes: Beaucoup de gens = many people. Followed by a verb (here 'sont' = 'are' in present). In your examples the context is past (they died), so French uses past tense (sont morts = they died; note: 'sont morts' is passé composé with être). Use 'beaucoup de gens' with different verbs: 'beaucoup de gens sont heureux' = many people are happy. If you want to say 'many people were', use a past tense: 'beaucoup de gens ont été' or use 'étaient' for imperfect depending on meaning. Word order is the same as in English.
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens sont contents de la nouvelle.
native_language_example: Many people are happy about the news.

meaning: heard a lot (about something or someone)
additional_notes: Literally 'much heard'. Used to say you've heard a lot about someone or something (e.g., J'ai beaucoup entendu parler de ce restaurant → I've heard a lot about this restaurant). Alone 'beaucoup entendu' is incomplete in French; it's usually part of a larger phrase like 'J'ai beaucoup entendu (parler de...)' or 'On en a beaucoup entendu parler.'
target_language_example: J'ai beaucoup entendu parler de ce film.
native_language_example: I've heard a lot about this movie.

meaning: not a fixed phrase; 'beaucoup' means 'a lot' or 'much' and 'et' means 'and' — used separately in sentences (e.g. 'a lot and...').
additional_notes: This is not an idiom — it's simply the adverb beaucoup ('a lot', 'much') followed by the conjunction et ('and'). In French you can say 'ils travaillent beaucoup et...' to link two ideas. Word order is the same as in English: verb + beaucoup + et + next clause. Pay attention to agreement: beaucoup doesn't change with number or gender.
target_language_example: Ils mangent beaucoup et restent en forme.
native_language_example: They eat a lot and stay in shape.

meaning: literally 'much done' — not a standard fixed phrase in French; would be interpreted as part of a clause meaning 'a lot (has) been done' or 'many things are done' depending on context.
additional_notes: Not a common standalone idiom. In natural French the structure usually includes an auxiliary or noun: e.g. 'beaucoup a été fait' (a lot has been done) or 'beaucoup de choses ont été faites' (many things have been done). 'Beaucoup' is an adverb ('a lot') and 'fait' is the past participle of 'faire' or an adjective meaning 'done'. The bare sequence 'beaucoup fait' can appear within a larger sentence but is ungrammatical by itself; ensure correct auxiliary and agreement when forming full sentences.
target_language_example: Il y a eu beaucoup fait dans ce projet depuis le début.
native_language_example: A lot has been done on this project since the beginning.

meaning: 'beaucoup le' is not a standard fixed phrase in French; it can appear when 'beaucoup' (an adverb) precedes a clitic or determiner in informal or dialectal speech, but grammatically the sequence is unusual. In most cases the correct forms are 'beaucoup' + verb (j'aime beaucoup), 'beaucoup de' + noun (beaucoup de gens), or constructions like 'beaucoup le/la/les + verb' only in colloquial elisions or emphatic contexts.
additional_notes: This sequence is generally nonstandard. If encountered, it often reflects spoken or regional usage, a clipping, or a mis-segmentation (e.g., 'beaucoup, le ...' with a pause). Do not treat 'beaucoup le' as a standalone idiom. Prefer standard alternatives: 'beaucoup' (adverb), 'beaucoup de' (quantity), or 'le beaucoup' only in rare literary/emphatic contexts. Translation depends on context; usually rendered as 'a lot', 'much', or 'many'.
target_language_example: Il y en a beaucoup, le village change vite.
native_language_example: There are a lot of them; the village is changing quickly.

meaning: talked a lot; spoke much about (someone/something).
additional_notes: Beaucoup modifies the verb parler and indicates frequency or quantity of speaking. Often appears as 'a beaucoup parlé (de ...)' = 'talked a lot (about ...)'. Use with de + object to say who/what was talked about. Past participle form here (parlé) implies passé composé or other past contexts.
target_language_example: Ils ont beaucoup parlé de leurs projets.
native_language_example: They talked a lot about their plans.

meaning: much larger / a lot bigger (feminine singular)
additional_notes: Used to compare sizes/extent: 'beaucoup' intensifies 'plus grande' (more big). Matches the gender and number of the noun described—'grande' is feminine singular. For masculine use 'beaucoup plus grand'; for plural add 's' as needed. Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Cette maison est beaucoup plus grande que la nôtre.
native_language_example: This house is much larger than ours.

meaning: a fragment meaning "a lot for your" or "many for your" (incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed expression by itself. "Beaucoup" means "a lot/many" and "pour votre" means "for your" (formal or plural 'your'). You will usually see them as part of a larger sentence, e.g. "beaucoup pour votre patience" (thank you very much for your patience) or "beaucoup pour votre aide" (thank you very much for your help). In spoken French, after "merci", people often say "merci beaucoup pour votre..." when addressing someone formally or politely. If speaking informally to someone you know well, use "ton" instead of "votre" (e.g. "merci beaucoup pour ton aide").
target_language_example: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: 'the beauty of' (used to talk about what is beautiful about something).
additional_notes: A common way to point out the attractive or admirable quality of someone or something. Often followed by a noun or a clause introduced by 'la chose', 'la simplicité', 'ce paysage', etc. Can be used in general statements ('C'est la beauté de la chose') or to emphasize a particular quality ('toute la beauté de...').
target_language_example: C'est la beauté de cette idée : elle est simple et efficace.
native_language_example: That's the beauty of this idea: it's simple and effective.

target_language_multi_word_term: être dans de beaux draps / être dans de beaux draps
meaning: to be in trouble; to be in a difficult or awkward situation.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression. Used to say someone is (or will be) in a problematic, embarrassing, or complicated situation. Often used with "être" in the present: "on est dans de beaux draps" = "we're in trouble." Not literal (doesn't involve sheets). Can be used jokingly or seriously depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si tu oublies le passeport, on sera dans de beaux draps.
native_language_example: If you forget your passport, we'll be in trouble.

meaning: fine weather; nice days (often used to refer to sunny, pleasant days)
additional_notes: Literally 'beautiful days'. Common in expressions about the weather or good times. Can be used generally ('les beaux jours arrivent' = the nice days are coming) or figuratively to mean better times. Plural only in typical use.
target_language_example: Les beaux jours arrivent, on pourra enfin manger dehors.
native_language_example: The nice days are coming; we can finally eat outside.

meaning: sweet dreams; (literally) beautiful dreams
additional_notes: A friendly farewell or wish said to someone before they go to sleep. More common is the singular phrase "fais de beaux rêves" (informal) meaning "have sweet dreams." "Beaux rêves" alone is short and less common but understandable. Use in informal or familiar contexts.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit et fais de beaux rêves.
native_language_example: Good night and have sweet dreams.

meaning: indeed / really / in fact (adds emphasis that something truly happened)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a statement is true or really happened; stronger than just 'bien' or 'vraiment'. Often placed between subject and verb or before the past participle. Common in spoken and written French. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Elle a bel et bien quitté son travail la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: She really did quit her job last week.

meaning: 'daughter-in-law' (or 'stepdaughter' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used for both 'daughter-in-law' (the spouse's daughter by marriage) and 'stepdaughter' (the child from a partner after remarriage). Which meaning applies depends on context; you can clarify with possessive words (ma belle-fille = my daughter-in-law/stepdaughter). Feminine form; masculine equivalent is 'beau-fils'.
target_language_example: Ma belle-fille vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: My daughter-in-law is coming for dinner tonight.

meaning: literally 'beautiful in' — used before naming a style, color, material or situation to say 'beautiful in [something]'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the adjective belle followed by the preposition en. You will see it in sentences like «belle en rouge» (beautiful in red) or «belle en soie» (beautiful in silk). Remember agreement: belle is feminine singular; for masculine use beau, and for plural use beaux/belles as appropriate. The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Elle est belle en bleu.
native_language_example: She looks beautiful in blue.

meaning: need of something/someone else; (usually appears in broader expressions)
additional_notes: On its own 'besoin d'autre' is incomplete/uncommon in French. Native speakers normally say 'besoin d'autre chose' (need something else) or 'besoin d'un autre/une autre' (need another one or someone else). Use a noun or demonstrative after 'autre' to complete the idea: e.g. 'J'ai besoin d'autre chose' or 'Elle a besoin d'un autre médecin.'
target_language_example: Tu as besoin d'autre chose ou ça va ?
native_language_example: Do you need anything else or is it okay?

meaning: need of a quick action/help; need a short boost or intervention
additional_notes: Informal phrase often used in spoken French. 'Coup' here means a quick action, push, boost, or hand (e.g., 'un coup de main' = a hand). 'Besoin d'un coup' is usually followed by a noun or implied context: e.g., 'besoin d'un coup de main' (need a hand) or shortened in casual speech when the rest is understood. Alone it sounds colloquial and may be ambiguous without context.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un coup pour finir ce déménagement.
native_language_example: I need a hand to finish this move.

meaning: 'need to (me)' or part of expressions meaning 'there's no need to (do something to/for me)'
additional_notes: This combination appears when someone says whether an action is necessary with respect to the speaker. Common negative phrase: "Pas besoin de me..." = "No need to... (for me)" (e.g. "Pas besoin de me remercier" = "No need to thank me"). In questions it can mean "Do you need to... me?" ("Tu as besoin de me demander ça ?"). Word order: English uses infinitive after 'need to', French often uses 'avoir besoin de' + noun or verb infinitive; the pronoun 'me' goes before the verb (or after in some imperative/infinitive constructions: e.g. "me le dire").
target_language_example: Pas besoin de me le dire, je suis déjà au courant.
native_language_example: No need to tell me, I'm already aware.

meaning: 'to need some' or 'to need a (bit of)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not complete on its own — 'quelque' must be followed by a noun (quelque chose = something; quelque chose de = something that is…) or combined as 'quelques' (plural) before a plural noun. More common: 'avoir besoin de' + noun or infinitive (e.g. 'avoir besoin de quelque chose' = to need something; 'avoir besoin de quelque chose de spécial' = to need something special). For beginners, learn the full pattern 'avoir besoin de + noun' and 'avoir besoin de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de quelque chose pour réparer la porte.
native_language_example: I need something to fix the door.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment appearing in colloquial speech when asking or wondering what is needed, typically incomplete and followed by a clause introduced by 'que' (e.g. 'besoin de quoi que je...' ). Literally 'need of what that', but best expressed in full forms like 'De quoi as-tu besoin ?'
additional_notes: This sequence is usually incomplete and informal. It often appears in spoken fragments such as 'T'as besoin de quoi que je fasse ?' or 'Besoin de quoi que je t'aide ?' The standalone 'besoin de quoi que' should be followed by a clause (subject/pronoun + verb). For learners, prefer full, grammatical alternatives: 'De quoi as-tu besoin ?' or 'Tu as besoin que je fasse quoi ?'
target_language_example: T'as besoin de quoi que je fasse pour t'aider ?
native_language_example: What do you need me to do to help you?

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken or jumbled form of expressions with 'besoin de' or 'quoi que ce soit' meaning 'need something' or 'need anything'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a correct or idiomatic French phrase. Learners probably mean either: 'avoir besoin de' (to need) + a noun/object, or 'quoi que ce soit' (anything/whatever it may be). Correct combinations include 'Tu as besoin de quelque chose ?' (Do you need something?) or 'si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit' (if you need anything). Avoid using 'besoin de quoi que ce' as-is.
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

meaning: need (of) the / need for the (plural or after de + definite article).
additional_notes: Combines besoin (need) with the plural definite article des (de + les). Used to talk about needing something (plural) or needing a type of thing. Often appears as besoin de + noun; when the noun is plural or preceded by a definite article it becomes besoin des. Example: «J'ai besoin des documents» = I need the documents. For general statements about needing something indefinite, use besoin de + noun (e.g., besoin d'aide).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin des clés pour ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: I need the keys to open the door.

meaning: used to compare who needs something more: '...more than I do'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears after a verb phrase with en/avoir and besoin (e.g. Tu en as plus besoin que moi) and compares the need between two people. The pronoun 'en' refers back to something previously mentioned (something needed). You can change the subject: 'tu...que moi', 'vous...que moi', 'il...que moi'. Word order: subject + en + avoir (conjugated) + plus + besoin + que + moi.
target_language_example: Elle en aura plus besoin que moi.
native_language_example: She will need it more than I will.

meaning: 'I need you to...' (followed by a verb in subjunctive or infinitive depending on construction).
additional_notes: Used to express a need for someone to do something. In spoken French you often see 'J'ai besoin que tu...' followed by the subjunctive (e.g., 'sois') when the clause has its own subject. If the verb directly follows the speaker's need without subordinate subject change, French can also use 'J'ai besoin que tu' + verb (subjunctive) or an infinitive construction like 'J'ai besoin que tu viennes' (subjunctive) vs. 'J'ai besoin de toi' (I need you — noun). Use 'J'ai besoin que tu...' to ask or insist that the person do or be something.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin que tu m'écoutes maintenant.
native_language_example: I need you to listen to me now.

meaning: urgent need; something needed immediately
additional_notes: Used to describe a pressing or immediate requirement (e.g., medical, financial, logistical). Can modify nouns (un besoin urgent) or be used in phrases like 'avoir un besoin urgent de...' ('to have an urgent need for...'). Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous avons un besoin urgent de fournitures médicales.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for medical supplies.

meaning: 'urgent need of' or 'in urgent need of'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something requires something immediately. Followed by a noun or an infinitive verb introduced by 'de' (e.g. besoin urgent de soins, besoin urgent de parler). Tone is neutral — common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Nous avons un besoin urgent de volontaires.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for volunteers.

meaning: '... butter' (compound noun: butter made from X, e.g. beurre de cacahuètes = peanut butter).
additional_notes: Used to form names of spreads or butters made from a specific ingredient: beurre de + noun (often a food). In French the full phrase usually includes the ingredient (beurre de cacahuètes, beurre de noix, beurre de cacao). In spoken French you may hear 'du beurre de...' when asking for or offering some (du = some). Word order differs from English for some compound names (peanut butter = beurre de cacahuètes).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté du beurre de noix pour les tartines.
native_language_example: I bought some nut butter for the slices of bread.

meaning: peanut butter (spread made from ground peanuts).
additional_notes: Common food item used as a spread on bread, toast, or in recipes. 'Cacahuète' = peanut. In some French-speaking regions 'beurre de cacahuète' is also called 'beurre d'arachide' (especially in parts of Africa).
target_language_example: J'aime le beurre de cacahuète sur mes tartines le matin.
native_language_example: I like peanut butter on my toast in the morning.

meaning: 'the library is' (a subject + verb phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but simply the noun 'bibliothèque' (library) followed by the verb 'est' (is). Use to state facts about the library: location, condition, hours, etc. Replace 'bibliothèque' with another place noun to make similar sentences. Pronunciation tip: bibliothèque = bee-bli-oh-tek.
target_language_example: La bibliothèque est ouverte jusqu'à 18h.
native_language_example: The library is open until 6 PM.

meaning: to (go) to the library in order to / for (doing something).
additional_notes: bibliothèque = library. When followed by pour + infinitive, it indicates purpose: why someone goes to or comes to the library (e.g., pour lire, pour étudier). Common verbs with this phrase: aller (aller à la bibliothèque pour...), venir (venir à la bibliothèque pour...). Note the preposition: on says 'à la bibliothèque' (feminine) for 'to the library.'
target_language_example: Nous allons à la bibliothèque pour emprunter des livres.
native_language_example: We are going to the library to borrow books.

meaning: 'okay, I'll...' — a way to agree or accept and say you'll do something or go somewhere.
additional_notes: Often used after someone gives instructions, permission, or information. 'Bien' (or 'Très bien', 'Eh bien') signals acceptance or readiness; 'je vais' begins a statement of intent ('je vais le faire' = I'll do it; 'je vais y aller' = I'll go'). Common in spoken and polite contexts. Can be shortened to 'Très bien, j'y vais' or 'Bon, je vais...'.
target_language_example: Très bien, je vais préparer les documents tout de suite.
native_language_example: Okay, I'll prepare the documents right away.

meaning: 'beloved' — dearly loved person or thing (masculine form); often used as an adjective or noun.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something deeply loved or cherished. Feminine form is bien-aimée. Can be used as an adjective before or after a noun (mon bien-aimé, la bien-aimée). Common in literary, religious, or emotional contexts.
target_language_example: Mon frère est mon bien-aimé.
native_language_example: My brother is my beloved.

meaning: 'very' or 'quite' before a noun or adjective (adds emphasis); can also mean 'well at' in literal combinations.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own but a combination where bien (very/well) is followed by the contraction au (à + le) when referring to a masculine singular noun: e.g. bien au chaud (very warm/well tucked in), bien au courant (well informed). It adds emphasis or describes state. Depending on context, bien = 'very' (adverb intensifier) or 'well' (adverb of manner). Remember au is used before masculine singular nouns (à + le).
target_language_example: Il est bien au chaud près du feu.
native_language_example: He is very warm by the fire.

meaning: goes well with / matches (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing looks or tastes good together with another (colors, clothes, food, etc.). Often appears as 'va bien avec' or 'se marie bien avec'. The definite article (le/la/les) agrees with the second noun: 'va bien avec le costume', 'va bien avec la robe', 'va bien avec les chaussures'.
target_language_example: Cette chemise va bien avec le pantalon.
native_language_example: This shirt goes well with the pants.

meaning: 'very' or 'well' used for emphasis before demonstratives/pronouns (colloquial; regional).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard fixed phrase in contemporary standard French. It can appear in informal or regional speech as an emphatic marker (e.g., 'bien ce' before a demonstrative like 'ça' or a relative pronoun) to strengthen what follows — similar to 'really' or 'quite' in English. Because it's nonstandard, you will rarely see it in written French and it may be omitted or replaced by 'bien' alone, 'vraiment', or 'tout à fait' in standard usage.
target_language_example: Il a bien ce truc qui m'énerve.
native_language_example: He really has that thing that annoys me.

meaning: 'that's exactly what I (or someone) ...' / 'that's indeed what I ...'
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences like "C'est bien ce que j'ai dit/entendu/compris/espère." It emphasizes confirmation or agreement: "that's exactly/indeed what I said/heard/understood/hope." The full phrase usually begins with "C'est" (It is) and the verb follows the j' (j'ai, j'avais, j'espère, etc.). Use to confirm or affirm information.
target_language_example: C'est bien ce que j'ai compris.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I understood.

meaning: emphasis on 'what you...' — 'indeed/really what you.../I see what you...'
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or confirm the content of what the other person said, wants, or did. Often appears in questions for confirmation (C'est bien ce que vous avez dit ? = 'Is that really what you said?') or in statements to show understanding (Je vois bien ce que vous faites = 'I clearly see what you're doing'). 'Bien' adds emphasis or clarity. Word order varies (bien can come before or after other elements); this entry highlights common patterns with 'vous'.
target_language_example: C'est bien ce que vous avez prévu ?
native_language_example: Is that really what you planned?

meaning: an emphatic phrase meaning 'indeed that' or 'very well, that (is so)'; used to stress or confirm something already said
additional_notes: Rare/less common combination. 'Bien' can mean 'well', 'very', or 'indeed'; followed by 'cela' ('that') it emphasizes or confirms a statement (similar to 'c'est bien cela' = 'that's right'). On its own 'bien cela' is unusual in everyday speech — more natural forms: 'c'est bien ça', 'c'est bien cela', or simply 'bien sûr' depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est bien cela que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That's indeed what I meant.

meaning: 'as' or 'just like' (used to compare or introduce an example).
additional_notes: Rare/limited usage: 'bien comme' can appear in literary or formal contexts to mean 'truly/just as' or 'just like' when comparing two things (similar to 'comme' or 'tout comme'). It is not a common everyday collocation; in spoken French you'd more often hear 'comme', 'tout comme', or 'bien que' (which has a different meaning: 'although'). Watch for confusion with 'bien que' (concessive) — 'bien comme' is comparative/emphatic, not concessive.
target_language_example: Il parle bien comme son frère quand il était jeune.
native_language_example: He speaks just like his brother did when he was young.

meaning: 'well done' (cooked thoroughly), used for meat or food.
additional_notes: Common phrase in restaurants when ordering meat. Opposites include 'saignant' (rare) and 'à point' (medium). Can be used alone as a short answer (e.g., when confirming how you want your steak).
target_language_example: Je veux mon steak bien cuit, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want my steak well done, please.

meaning: comfortable, at ease in (used with nouns: e.g. bien dans sa peau = comfortable in one's skin).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of fixed expressions like « bien dans sa peau » (to feel good about oneself) or « bien dans son rôle » (comfortable in one's role). It describes being comfortable, confident, or well-adjusted in a situation or in oneself. Often followed by a possessive phrase (sa peau, son rôle, sa tête) or a noun introduced by « ... ». Not used alone without context.
target_language_example: Depuis qu'elle a changé de travail, elle est bien dans son rôle.
native_language_example: Since she changed jobs, she feels comfortable in her role.

meaning: 'a lot of' or 'many' (used before a noun to emphasize quantity).
additional_notes: Used in informal and neutral registers to stress a large number or amount. Follows determiners and precedes a noun or noun phrase: e.g. « bien de la patience », « bien des gens ». With de + definite article it can contract (bien des). Often interchangeable with 'beaucoup de' but can feel slightly more emphatic or colloquial depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a bien de la nourriture pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: There is plenty of food for everyone.

meaning: 'enough of something' or 'plenty of'
additional_notes: This is a somewhat formal/neutral French expression used to indicate a large quantity or plenty of something (similar to 'beaucoup de' or 'plein de'). It often appears before a noun: bien de quoi + noun. Can also be used with verbs to mean 'more than enough to...': 'bien de quoi faire...' Note: not very common in everyday spoken French compared with 'beaucoup de' or 'plein de', but you'll see it in written or slightly formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il y a bien de quoi nourrir toute la famille.
native_language_example: There is more than enough to feed the whole family.

meaning: 'exactly what I'm talking about' (part of the phrase "(tu) sais bien de quoi je parle")
additional_notes: This fragment appears inside sentences like «(tu) sais bien de quoi je parle» or «je sais très bien de quoi je parle». It literally contains "bien" (emphasis) + "de quoi je (parle/veux parler)" meaning "what I (am talking/want to talk) about." Use it to stress that the listener already knows the topic being referred to. Common completions: «je parle», «je veux parler».
target_language_example: Tu sais bien de quoi je parle, alors réponds.
native_language_example: You know exactly what I'm talking about, so answer.

meaning: 'well said' or 'I told you so' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone for expressing something clearly or appropriately ('well said'). Also used after a prior warning or prediction to mean 'I told you so' (often with past-tense verbs: je l'avais bien dit / je vous avais bien dit). Tone can be neutral, approving, or mildly reproachful depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vous avais bien dit de vérifier la porte.
native_language_example: I did tell you to check the door.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; a sequence where 'bien' (well/very) appears next to 'elle' (she/her). Meaning depends on context — e.g. 'bien, elle...' as a spoken connector ('well, she...') or in uncommon juxtaposition like 'bien elle...' used for emphasis in colloquial speech or truncated sentences.
additional_notes: 'Bien elle' is not a standard fixed phrase in French. You will more commonly see 'eh bien, elle...' or 'elle est bien...'. When 'bien' and 'elle' appear together without other words, it usually reflects informal speech or a clipped sentence where 'bien' functions as a discourse marker before referring to 'elle'. Pay attention to punctuation and intonation — written 'bien elle' can feel abrupt or colloquial.
target_language_example: Bien elle, je ne sais pas ce qu'elle attend.
native_language_example: Well, her — I don't know what she's waiting for.

meaning: 'very' or 'well' + adjective/phrase — used to intensify or qualify (e.g. bien en avance = quite/very early).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before adjectives, participles or noun phrases to mean 'quite', 'very', 'well' or 'rather' depending on context. It can combine with time expressions (bien en avance = well in advance), states (bien en forme = very fit), or to stress extent (bien en colère = very angry). Placement is before the word it modifies. Not a fixed idiom on its own—meaning depends on the following word.
target_language_example: Il est bien en avance pour la réunion.
native_language_example: He is well in advance / very early for the meeting.

meaning: 'of course' / 'naturally' (used to confirm or emphasize agreement or that something was heard).
additional_notes: Common phrase with two main uses: 1) to mean 'of course' or 'naturally' when agreeing or reacting (e.g. 'Bien entendu, voyons !' or 'Mais bien entendu.'); 2) in contexts about hearing, used to emphasize that someone heard something clearly ('Tu m'as bien entendu' = 'You heard me'). Tone depends on context and intonation — can be neutral, emphatic, or slightly sarcastic.
target_language_example: Bien entendu, je t'aiderai demain.
native_language_example: Of course, I'll help you tomorrow.

meaning: 'nice try' or 'good attempt' (often used to acknowledge an attempt, sometimes sarcastically).
additional_notes: Used to praise or acknowledge someone's attempt. Tone depends on context and intonation—can be sincere encouragement or polite/sarcastic dismissal (like 'nice try, but no'). Common in spoken French after someone makes an effort that fails or is close to succeeding.
target_language_example: Tu as presque répondu juste — bien essayé !
native_language_example: You almost answered correctly — nice try!

meaning: a short linking phrase meaning 'well and...' or 'so, and...'; used to connect ideas or introduce a follow-up comment
additional_notes: Used conversationally to continue a thought, introduce a consequence, or shift topics. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause (e.g., "Bien, et..." or "Bon, et...") and may be followed by a question or new point. Tone can be neutral or slightly informal depending on context. Not a fixed idiom; it's simply the adverb 'bien' plus the conjunction 'et'.
target_language_example: Bien et si on partait maintenant ?
native_language_example: Well, and if we left now?

meaning: well done
additional_notes: Multiple uses: 1) Literally 'well made' or 'well done' to describe something done correctly or constructed nicely (C'est bien fait; Il est bien fait). 2) As an expression of schadenfreude—'serves you right' or 'serves them right'—often said after someone gets what they deserve (Bien fait pour toi ! / Bien fait !). 3) Can appear in proverbs (Vite fait, bien fait = quickly done, well done). Tone depends on context—neutral for quality, mocking when used as 'serves you right.'
target_language_example: Bien fait pour toi, tu aurais dû écouter le conseil.
native_language_example: Serves you right, you should have listened to the advice.

meaning: used to say someone did the right thing / it was wise to (do something).
additional_notes: Followed by an infinitive verb: 'bien fait de' + infinitive. Used to express approval or that an action was a good/wise decision (equivalent to 'you were right to...' or 'it's a good thing that...'). Common in both formal and informal speech. Conjugate the preceding verb as needed (e.g. 'Tu as bien fait de ...', 'Nous avons bien fait de ...').
target_language_example: Tu as bien fait de partir tôt.
native_language_example: You were right to leave early.

meaning: 'well played' / 'good job' (praise for something done well).
additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone for a good performance, clever action, or successful result. Can be used sincerely for achievements (games, performances, tasks) or lightly/ironically. Often said alone as an interjection: "Bien joué !"
target_language_example: Bien joué pour ton exposé, c'était clair et intéressant.
native_language_example: Well played on your presentation, it was clear and interesting.

meaning: adds emphasis to a following noun or phrase, meaning 'quite the' / 'very' / 'really', or can confirm something like 'indeed' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This short sequence appears in spoken French to strengthen or confirm a statement. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. 'bien la maison', 'bien la preuve') or used in expressions like 'c'est bien la...' to mean 'that is indeed the...'. Usage and exact sense depend on context: it can express surprise, confirmation, or intensification. It's not a fixed idiom on its own; learners commonly see it inside larger phrases.
target_language_example: C'est bien la voiture que j'ai vue hier.
native_language_example: That's indeed the car I saw yesterday.

meaning: really the
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a standalone phrase. 'Bien' here intensifies the following definite article + noun phrase (le/la/les) or a clause introduced by 'le' (e.g. le fait). In natural French you'd usually see it as 'bien le + noun' or 'bien le fait que...' meaning 'really the...' or 'quite the...'. Can also appear in expressions like 'c'est bien le...' = 'it's really the...'.
target_language_example: C'est bien le problème.
native_language_example: That's really the problem.

meaning: for his/her part; as far as he/she is concerned (emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the person referred to (lui = him/her/it depending on context). Often appears in sentences like «Bien lui en prit» (old-fashioned) meaning 'it served him well' or in contrasts: «Pour moi, c'est différent; bien lui, il...». It can also appear after a verb to stress that something is good/right for that person. Tone can be formal or neutral depending on context; not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: Pour moi c'est risqué, bien lui, il assume le choix.
native_language_example: For me it's risky; as for him, he stands by the choice.

meaning: right here; definitely here / really present
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone or something is present, visible, or definitely the case. Tone depends on context: can be neutral (pointing out presence) or emphatic (confirming something clearly). Often follows a noun or pronoun: e.g. « Il est bien là » = "He is indeed here."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, le cadeau est bien là.
native_language_example: Don't worry, the gift is definitely right here.

meaning: 'well, I...' — an informal clipped spoken start where 'bien' introduces or emphasizes and 'm'' is the beginning of a pronominal element referring to 'me' (e.g. m' + verb)
additional_notes: Colloquial, appears in fast or hesitating spoken French as the start of a sentence (transcripts, dialogues). Incomplete on its own — usually followed immediately by a verb or continuation (e.g. 'bien m'entends', 'bien m'en souvienne' in rapid speech), or used when the speaker trails off. Not standard written French; mainly conversational. Signals hesitation, emphasis, or a shift to a personal comment.
target_language_example: Bien m'entends — je ne savais pas quoi dire.
native_language_example: Well, I mean — I didn't know what to say.

meaning: used to emphasize contrast about oneself; roughly 'as for me' or 'well, me' (introducing a personal reaction or opinion).
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to mark a shift to the speaker's perspective or reaction; similar to 'pour ma part' or 'quant à moi'. It can appear alone as an interjection ('Bien moi…') or followed by a clause ('Bien moi, je préfère...'). Tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Bien moi, je préfère rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: Well, as for me, I prefer to stay home tonight.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; typically a fragment combining the adverb 'bien' and the possessive 'mon'. Depending on context it can appear as (1) part of a larger phrase where 'bien' modifies something belonging to 'mon' (rare/awkward), (2) a transcription with omitted words, or (3) within a spoken pause e.g. 'Bien, mon...' meaning 'Well, my...'.
additional_notes: 'Bien mon' on its own is uncommon and usually indicates missing words or informal speech with a pause/comma. For direct address use 'mon ami', 'ma chère', etc. If you encounter 'bien mon' in text, read surrounding context — it often belongs to a longer clause (e.g. 'bien mon ...' followed by a noun or clause) or is a colloquial hesitative sequence ('Bien, mon ...').
target_language_example: Il disait « bien mon dieu », mais c'était mal écrit — il voulait dire « mon dieu ».
native_language_example: He wrote 'bien mon dieu', but that was incorrect — he meant 'mon dieu'.

meaning: indeed / even / in fact (used to reinforce or emphasize a statement)
additional_notes: Used to strengthen or emphasize what follows; often appears before a contrasting or surprising idea. Similar to «même» or «bien» used for emphasis. Tone is neutral; common in written and spoken French but not an everyday fixed expression — context determines exact nuance (even, indeed, actually).
target_language_example: Il a réussi, bien même sans beaucoup d'entraînement.
native_language_example: He succeeded, even without much training.

meaning: 'well for us' / 'that suits us' OR as discourse 'well, we... (transition)'.
additional_notes: Two words: bien (well/good) + nous (we/us). Not a fixed standalone idiom; appears in contexts like comparisons or after verbs/adjectives (e.g. « Cela ferait bien nous [something] » is rare). More commonly part of larger phrases (e.g. « ça nous va bien »). Can also occur in discourse sequences as « Bien, nous... » meaning 'Well, we...'. Check surrounding words to determine whether it's evaluative ('good for us') or transitional.
target_language_example: Bien nous accueille la chance aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Luck welcomes us well today. / Today luck is good for us.

meaning: 'of course' / a stronger 'yes' (emphatic agreement).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize agreement or surprise at the idea of saying no. More emphatic than a simple 'oui' and can imply 'but of course' or 'naturally'. Often spoken in informal or neutral contexts; intonation matters (rising or stressed).
target_language_example: Tu viens ce soir ? — Bien oui, j'arrive !
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight? — Of course I am, I'm coming!

meaning: well (by) / good for; used before expressions indicating how well something is done or who benefits
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; 'bien' (well/very) followed by 'par' (by/per) appears in constructions like 'bien par…' or 'bien par X' to qualify an action or distribution (e.g. 'bien par personne' = well per person). It can also occur in phrases such as 'bien paré' (well prepared) where 'par' is part of a past participle construction—so watch the full context. Not common as an isolated two-word chunk; learners will mostly see 'bien' and 'par' in larger expressions.
target_language_example: La portion est bien par personne pour le dîner.
native_language_example: The portion is good per person for dinner.

meaning: respectable, conventional, or politically correct (often with a critical or ironic tone)
additional_notes: Used to describe people, opinions, or attitudes that follow mainstream, socially acceptable views—often implying they are self-satisfied, conformist, moralizing, or out of touch. Frequently used pejoratively: «les bien-pensants» = 'the respectable/mainstream people'.
target_language_example: Il critique sans cesse les artistes, comme tout bien pensant.
native_language_example: He constantly criticizes artists, like any self-satisfied conformist.

meaning: well placed; in a good position or situation
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone located, timed, or positioned advantageously (physically or figuratively). Can refer to a person (well positioned in a company), an object (a sign well placed), or an idea/comment (a well-timed remark). Agreement: 'bien' doesn't change but the noun may require adjectives elsewhere (e.g., 'une affiche bien placée').
target_language_example: Le panneau est bien placé près de l'entrée.
native_language_example: The sign is well placed near the entrance.

meaning: much more / far more / a lot more
additional_notes: Used to intensify comparison or degree. Can modify adjectives, adverbs, nouns, or clauses (e.g. 'bien plus chaud' = 'much hotter', 'bien plus que' = 'much more than'). Common in both spoken and written French. Not informal.
target_language_example: Ce problème est bien plus compliqué que je ne pensais.
native_language_example: This problem is much more complicated than I thought.

meaning: healthy, in good health (usually describes a person).
additional_notes: Adjective phrase used to describe someone who is physically well. Often used after the noun: il est bien portant / elle est bien portante. Can also be written with a hyphen (bien-portant) in some older texts but modern usage separates the words. Not typically used to describe objects; for that, use 'en bon état' or 'en bonne santé' for people as well.
target_language_example: Mon grand-père est encore bien portant à quatre-vingt-dix ans.
native_language_example: My grandfather is still healthy at ninety years old.

meaning: 'good for' or 'suitable for'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is beneficial, appropriate or suitable for a person, purpose or situation. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g. bien pour la santé, bien pour étudier). Can also be used more generally to approve something (C'est bien pour toi).
target_language_example: Boire de l'eau est bien pour la santé.
native_language_example: Drinking water is good for health.

meaning: well, why? / okay, why?
additional_notes: A short conversational phrase combining 'bien' (well/okay) + 'pourquoi' (why). Used to react, ask for reasons, or prompt someone to explain—often with surprise, skepticism, or to ask 'and why is that?'. Tone depends on context and intonation. Not a fixed idiom; it's compositional.
target_language_example: — Bien pourquoi ?
native_language_example: — Well, why?

meaning: a way to say 'it's good when' or 'nice when' (introduces a favorable condition)
additional_notes: Used to comment that something is pleasant, convenient, or helpful in a certain situation. Followed by a clause introduced by que or by a verb in the indicative/subjunctive depending on nuance. Informal spoken French may prefer « c'est bien quand » or simply « bien » + clause. Not a fixed idiom—compositional from bien (well/good) + quand (when).
target_language_example: C'est bien quand il fait beau pour se promener.
native_language_example: It's nice when the weather is good for walking.

meaning: An adverbial combination used to intensify an approximate quantity, meaning roughly "a good/quite [number]" or "as many as..." when followed by a numeral or quantity word (e.g. "bien quelque vingt personnes" ≈ "as many as twenty people").
additional_notes: Used to emphasize an amount; somewhat literary or formal and less common in everyday speech. More frequently speakers say "bien une vingtaine de", "au moins", or simply "bien vingt". Structure: 'bien' (intensifier) + 'quelque' (approximate determiner before a number). Because this exact sequence is rare, word order and presence of prepositions may vary in actual usage.
target_language_example: Il y avait bien quelque vingt personnes à la réunion.
native_language_example: There were as many as twenty people at the meeting.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom on its own; 'bien' (well/indeed/very) followed by the relative pronoun 'qui' (who/that). Appears inside larger sentences where 'bien' adds emphasis or modality before a clause introduced by 'qui'.
additional_notes: Use context to translate: 'bien' can mean 'indeed', 'certainly', 'quite', or intensify; 'qui' introduces a relative clause. 'bien qui' is compositional and not a standalone expression—it's simply the juxtaposition of an adverb or intensifier and a relative pronoun. Example translations depend on sentence structure (e.g., 'there are indeed who', 'it's certainly that ...' rendered naturally in English).
target_language_example: Il est bien qui parle fort pendant les réunions.
native_language_example: There are indeed people who speak loudly during meetings.

meaning: 'to oneself' or part of reflexive verbs meaning 'well' (as adverb + reflexive pronoun)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a sequence where bien (well) appears before a reflexive verb pronoun (se). It often appears in expressions like "bien se sentir" (to feel well), "bien se débrouiller" (to manage well), or "s'en sortir bien" (to get out of something well). Word order: in infinitive forms you often see "bien se + infinitive" (e.g. "bien se reposer"). For conjugated verbs the reflexive pronoun moves (e.g. "Il se sent bien").
target_language_example: Il est important de bien se reposer après une maladie.
native_language_example: It's important to rest well after an illness.

meaning: to properly/fully (do) one's ... / to make sure something sounds good
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it appears as 'bien' + a noun or verb form related to 'son' (sound) or as part of expressions where 'son' is a possessive (e.g. 'bien son travail' is incorrect — correct would be 'bien sonné' or 'bien sonorisé'). Alone, 'bien son' is uncommon in French. More likely you will see: 'bien sonner' (to sound good/well), 'son bien' (one's good/benefit), or 'bien à son...' in formal closings. Don't use 'bien son' by itself — check the surrounding words. 'Bien sonner' is useful: 'La chanson sonne bien' = 'The song sounds good.'
target_language_example: La guitare bien sonne après le réglage.
native_language_example: The guitar sounds good after tuning.

meaning: of course; certainly
additional_notes: Common French expression used to agree, confirm, or emphasize that something is obvious or true. Standard spelling is « bien sûr » with a circumflex on sûr, but the user asked for the form without the accent. Pronunciation: [bjɛ̃ syʁ]. Can be used alone as a short reply ("Bien sur !") or within a sentence ("Bien sur que oui").
target_language_example: Tu veux venir ce soir ? — bien sur !
native_language_example: Do you want to come tonight? — Of course!

meaning: of course
additional_notes: Used to agree, confirm something, or say something is obvious or expected. It often appears at the start of a sentence, but it can also come after the noun or answer it refers to.
target_language_example: Tu peux compter sur moi, bien sûr.
native_language_example: You can count on me, of course.

meaning: Not a standard written French form. "bien t'" represents an informal, elided sequence where "bien" is followed by the clitic object pronoun "te" that has been apostrophized before a following vowel or clitic (e.g. in rapid speech within larger colloquial sequences). It does not have an independent lexical meaning beyond the meanings of "bien" (well/really) + "te" (you).
additional_notes: This form is very uncommon in writing and mainly appears in transcriptions of informal spoken French. You will typically encounter the full forms instead (e.g. "bien te" or constructions like "ça te va bien"). When you see "bien t'", check surrounding words to determine the intended phrase (for example, "bien t'en parler" would be a transcriptional elision of "bien te en parler", though that particular sequence is nonstandard — correct spoken forms use different word order: "t'en parler" or "te le dire"). Avoid using "bien t'" in formal writing. Classify this entry as informal and compositional: it combines two normal words but is an elided, spoken-only surface form.
target_language_example: Je te l'avais bien t' dit, mais tu n'as pas écouté.
native_language_example: I did tell you that, really, but you didn't listen.

meaning: an emphatic phrase meaning 'really your' or 'quite your' used to reinforce a noun or quality (colloquial/idiomatic).
additional_notes: Rare and informal. 'Bien' here intensifies the following noun or possessive (ton). Often appears in spoken French in expressions like 'bien ton style' or 'bien ton truc' to mean 'that really suits you' or 'that's so you'. Usage is regional/colloquial — not standard written French. Word order and context matter: 'bien ton' precedes the noun it modifies.
target_language_example: C'est bien ton style, ce pull te va super bien.
native_language_example: That's really your style; that sweater suits you very well.

meaning: very, completely (informal/emphatic) — used to intensify an action or adjective
additional_notes: Rare and informal phrase; 'bien' means 'well' or 'very' and 'tout' means 'all' or 'completely'. Together they emphasize completeness or intensity (similar to 'bien complètement' or 'tout à fait'). Usage is colloquial and may vary by region; more common alternatives: 'tout à fait', 'vraiment', 'complètement'.
target_language_example: Il a bien tout expliqué pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He explained everything very thoroughly during the meeting.

meaning: 'well thought out' / 'clever (idea)'.
additional_notes: Used to praise an idea, remark, solution or joke — similar to 'good one' or 'well done' in English. Can be used alone (Bien trouvé !) or with a name (Bien trouvé, Jimmy). Tone ranges from sincere praise to light ironic approval depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as réparé la porte avec ce bout de bois ? Bien trouvé !
native_language_example: You fixed the door with that piece of wood? Well thought out!

meaning: really a / truly a (used to emphasize the noun that follows)
additional_notes: Used before an article + noun to add emphasis or to stress that something is indeed that thing. Often interchangeable with 'vraiment un' or 'bien un(e)' in spoken French. Placement: 'bien' precedes the article and noun (bien un/une + noun). Tone is neutral; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: C'est bien un problème sérieux.
native_language_example: It is really a serious problem.

meaning: polite closing meaning 'yours sincerely' or 'yours faithfully' (formal ending of a letter/email).
additional_notes: Used as part of formal written closings in French correspondence, usually followed by a comma and the sender's name (e.g. « bien votre, »). Note the more common variants: « Bien à vous » (less formal) and « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame/Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées » (very formal). "Bien vôtre" with a circumflex is also used; modern usage may omit the accent. Capitalization of the first letter can vary depending on style (Bien vôtre / bien vôtre).
target_language_example:
Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
bien votre,
Jean Martin
native_language_example:
Please accept, Madam, the expression of my distinguished salutations.
Yours faithfully,
Jean Martin

meaning: 'well you' or 'you well' — a sequence of words that can appear in French sentences, usually not a fixed standalone phrase; meaning depends on context and word order (e.g., part of constructions expressing that something suits someone, that someone is well treated, or in set phrases like 'prenez bien soin de vous').
additional_notes: Alone, 'bien vous' is not a common fixed expression; it typically appears within a larger clause (e.g., 'cela vous va bien' or 'nous vous traitons bien'). Inverted orders like 'bien vous' can occur for emphasis or in certain syntactic constructions (e.g., 'Bien vous en fasse' — archaic/formal). For learners, treat 'bien' as 'well' and 'vous' as the formal/plural 'you'. Word order and surrounding verbs determine the precise meaning.
target_language_example: Je souhaite bien vous aider dans ce projet.
native_language_example: I truly want to help you with this project.

meaning: 'well seen' → 'good point' / 'nice observation' / 'good catch'.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's observation, remark, or action — like saying "good point", "well noticed" or "nice catch" in English. Can be standalone (Bien vu.) or used in a sentence (C'est bien vu.). In context 3 and 4, it can also mean "I saw it well" / "Did you see it clearly?" depending on intonation; context determines whether it's a comment on perception (I saw it) or evaluation (good observation).
target_language_example: Tu as remarqué l'erreur — bien vu !
native_language_example: You noticed the mistake — good catch!

meaning: emphasis/confirmation meaning 'indeed' or 'certainly' when paired with a verb or expression (colloquial).
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken phrase used to reinforce or confirm what was just said; often appears as part of a larger expression (e.g., "bien y penser", "bien y croire") or as a short reply meaning 'yes, indeed' depending on region. It is not a fixed grammatical unit on its own and may sound regional or conversational. Use with caution in formal writing.
target_language_example: Ah oui, bien y penser avant de partir!
native_language_example: Ah yes, definitely think about it before leaving!

meaning: (emphatic) to be/there is indeed one; to really exist one (in a given context)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed idiom by itself but is a combination: adverb 'bien' (emphasis), pronoun 'y' (there), infinitive 'avoir' or conjugated form 'il y a' (there is/have) and indefinite article 'un'. In natural French the usual order is 'bien + il y a + un' (e.g. 'Il y a bien un...'). Use to stress the existence of a single item or person. It is compositional and not a false cognate; it cannot be translated literally word-for-word into natural English without rephrasing.
target_language_example: Il faut bien y avoir un leader dans l'équipe.
native_language_example: There must really be a leader in the team.

meaning: used in letters/emails to sign off politely (short for "bien à vous" / "bien à toi").
additional_notes: A closing phrase used before a name in correspondence. It’s an abbreviated, slightly formal/polite version of "bien à vous" (yours sincerely/with kind regards) or "bien à toi" (informal). You will typically see it at the end of an email or letter, followed by the sender's name. Not commonly used alone in spoken everyday conversation.
target_language_example:
Bien à vous,
Marie Dupont
native_language_example:
Yours sincerely,
Marie Dupont

meaning: well-mannered; polite (describes a person or their behavior).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who shows good manners, respect, and proper behavior. Can modify a person (Il est bien élevé) or behavior (un enfant bien élevé). Opposite: mal élevé (rude, badly brought up). Not used for objects.
target_language_example: Elle est très bien élevée et dit toujours «s'il vous plaît» et «merci».
native_language_example: She is very well-mannered and always says 'please' and 'thank you.'

meaning: good about
additional_notes:
Has several uses depending on context:
- "dire du bien de [qqn]" = to speak well of someone / say good things about someone ("du bien" ≈ "good about").
- "pour le bien de [qqn/qqch]" = for the good of / for the benefit of.
- "ça fait du bien de [infinitive]" = it feels good to / it's good to (do something).
"bien de" here is not a fixed single meaning but part of set phrases. Use context to choose the correct English equivalent.
target_language_example: Elle a toujours dit du bien de son ancien professeur.
native_language_example: She always said good things about her former teacher.

meaning: for the good of; the well-being of / 'good' (as in moral good) when used in 'le bien du mal' contrast.
additional_notes: Context matters: 'bien' can mean 'good' (opposite of 'mal') in phrases like 'distinguer le bien du mal' (to distinguish right from wrong). As a phrase 'pour le bien de' or 'pour le bien du/de la' means 'for the benefit of' or 'for the good of' (e.g. 'pour le bien du public' = for the public good). 'Bien du' itself is not a fixed idiom but a sequence appearing before a masculine noun (du = de + le).
target_language_example: Nous agissons pour le bien du village.
native_language_example: We act for the good of the village.

meaning: "bien est" is not a common fixed French expression. It is simply the adverb "bien" (well/quite) followed immediately by the third-person singular of the verb "être" (est = is). In standard French word order, this sequence is rare and often signals unusual syntax, poetic/literary inversion, or an error; more typical is "est bien" (is indeed/is well).
additional_notes: You will rarely see "bien est" as a standalone phrase. It can occur in poetic or archaic constructions where inversion is used for emphasis (e.g., "Bien est l'âme qui..."), or inside clauses where word order differs from everyday speech. In most contexts, use "est bien" instead (e.g., "Cela est bien" or "Il est bien"). The sequence is compositional (meaning follows from its parts) and can be translated literally when it does appear, but watch for likely incorrectness in casual usage.
target_language_example: Bien est la mémoire qui garde nos joies passées.
native_language_example: Well is the memory that keeps our past joys. (Literary: "The memory that keeps our past joys is good.")

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French. It is most likely a fragment resulting from sentence structure (the adverb 'bien' followed by the conjunction/coordination 'et' and the definite article 'le'), a typo, or an unusual juxtaposition in informal/ironic speech. It has no independent idiomatic meaning.
additional_notes: 'Bien et le' will not appear as an established expression. You might see these three words adjacent in running text by chance (e.g., 'bien et le' as part of a longer clause), but their meanings are derived compositionally from the separate words: 'bien' (well/very), 'et' (and), 'le' (the). If you intended a different phrase (e.g., 'bien sûr', 'bien que', 'bien le bonjour'), check spelling or provide context.
target_language_example: Il parle bien et le public l'écoute attentivement.
native_language_example: He speaks well and the audience listens to him attentively.

meaning: the most valuable (possession) / the most precious thing
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often implied) to say that something is someone's most valuable possession or asset (e.g., 'bien le plus précieux' = 'most precious possession'). Often followed by an adjective like 'précieux' or by a noun (e.g., 'bien le plus précieux', 'bien le plus important'). Commonly used in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Ma famille est mon bien le plus précieux.
native_language_example: My family is my most precious possession.

meaning: although
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause expressing a concession (contrasting idea). Followed by the subjunctive in formal written French when the clause has a different subject (e.g. bien que ce soit). In casual spoken French you may also hear the indicative. Can appear at the start or in the middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Bien que ce soit difficile, je vais essayer.
native_language_example: Although it's difficult, I will try.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; 'bientôt' means 'soon' and 'de' is a preposition — together they only appear when followed by more words in a larger construction, not as an independent expression.
additional_notes: You will rarely see 'bientôt de' by itself in correct, standard French. 'Bientôt' is used alone (e.g. 'à bientôt' = 'see you soon'). When 'de' follows 'bientôt' it must connect to additional words (e.g. in some informal or headline-like contexts you might encounter fragments such as 'bientôt de nouvelles mesures' meaning 'new measures soon' — note this is elliptical). For clear, grammatical phrasing prefer structures like 'de nouvelles mesures bientôt' or 'bientôt, des nouvelles mesures'. If you intended a different fixed expression, provide more context.
target_language_example: Bientôt de nouvelles mesures seront annoncées.
native_language_example: New measures will be announced soon.

meaning: 'soon to' or 'it will soon be' (used with weather/time expressions and also 'be about to' with verbs like faire + noun).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in fixed expressions with faire + daypart: "faire jour" (to become daylight) and "faire nuit" (to become night) meaning "it will soon be day/night." With other verbs like "faire des affaires" it means "to do/make" and combined with "bientôt" simply indicates the action will happen soon (we will soon do business). Not idiomatic as a single chunk—meaning depends on the verb phrase that follows.
target_language_example: Il va bientôt faire jour.
native_language_example: It will soon be daylight.

meaning: 'soon the' (literal), but not a fixed phrase — 'bientôt' means 'soon' and 'le' is the definite article 'the'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression. You'll most often see 'bientôt' used alone (e.g. 'à bientôt' = 'see you soon', 'bientôt' = 'soon'). If 'le' follows, it's because 'bientôt' modifies a specific noun phrase introduced by 'le' (e.g. 'bientôt le printemps' = 'spring will be here soon'). Pay attention to word order and agreement in the full sentence.
target_language_example: Bientôt le printemps, les fleurs vont revenir.
native_language_example: Spring will be here soon; the flowers will come back.

meaning: 'soon' + reflexive marker: indicates that an action will happen soon (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: bientôt means 'soon'. When used before a reflexive verb (se + infinitive), it expresses that the subject will experience or undergo the action shortly (e.g., 'va bientôt se terminer' = 'will soon end'). In English you usually translate the whole phrase (will soon + verb) rather than literally 'soon oneself'. Place bientôt before the verb phrase: subject + (aller) + bientôt + se + infinitive or subject + bientôt + se + conjugated verb.
target_language_example: La fête va bientôt se terminer.
native_language_example: The party will soon end.

meaning: soon at / coming soon to (used before a time or place)
additional_notes: Combines bientôt (soon) with the preposition à. Often appears before a time, date, place or event to say that something will happen there or then soon: e.g. 'bientôt à la télévision' (coming soon on TV) or 'bientôt à Paris' (soon in Paris). Not a fixed idiom by itself — its exact sense depends on the noun or phrase that follows. Use à or other prepositions according to the noun that follows (bientôt en, bientôt chez, etc.).
target_language_example: Le film sera bientôt à l'affiche dans notre cinéma.
native_language_example: The movie will be coming soon to our cinema.

meaning: welcome to (a place or event).
additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving at a place or joining an event. Often followed by a location or event name (e.g. bienvenue à Paris / bienvenue à la réunion). Can be used in welcome signs and spoken greetings. If addressing one person informally you might also hear "bienvenue" alone; for formal or plural use, context is unchanged because "bienvenue" does not vary for number or gender when used as an interjection.
target_language_example: Bienvenue à Paris, profitez bien de votre séjour.
native_language_example: Welcome to Paris, enjoy your stay.

meaning: 'beer with' — used to specify what goes with a beer (e.g., an ingredient, a mixer, or a food accompaniment).
additional_notes: A simple, compositional phrase: bière = beer, avec = with. Commonly used in ordering: 'Une bière avec...' then add e.g. du citron, du sirop, des glaçons, ou 'une bière avec les frites' to indicate accompaniment. Context determines whether the following noun is an additive (mixer/garnish) or a side/dish. In spoken French you might hear contractions or omissions (e.g. 'Une bière, avec...').
target_language_example: Une bière avec du citron, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A beer with lemon, please.

meaning: 'beer and' — the noun bière (beer) followed by the conjunction et (and).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the word bière followed by et. It appears in sentences where someone mentions beer and then adds another action or item (e.g., 'beer and another one' or 'beer and sausages'). Useful to recognize the noun + et structure for linking items or actions. Note pronunciation: bière [bjɛʁ], et [e].
target_language_example: Il a acheté une bière et un sandwich.
native_language_example: He bought a beer and a sandwich.

meaning: a way to describe a beer flavored with or served with (something) — 'beer with' or 'beer flavored with'.
additional_notes: Used before an ingredient or style to indicate a beer that includes that flavor or accompaniment: bière à la cerise (cherry beer), bière à la vanille (vanilla-flavored beer), bière à la pression sometimes used regionally for draft beer. Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Not a fixed phrase by itself — it requires the following word(s).
target_language_example: Je prends une bière à la framboise, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a raspberry-flavored beer, please.

meaning: injury caused by (e.g. 'blessure par balle' = gunshot wound).
additional_notes: Used with a cause or instrument introduced by 'par' (balle, coup, arme, etc.). Common phrase: 'une blessure par balle' (gunshot wound). Often appears in medical, police or news contexts. Follows normal French noun phrase order: 'une blessure par X'.
target_language_example: Il a été hospitalisé pour une blessure par arme blanche.
native_language_example: He was hospitalized for a stab wound (an injury caused by a bladed weapon).

meaning: wounded/injured in (used to specify where or during what incident someone was hurt).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun or noun phrase indicating the event, location or context (e.g. un accident, la bataille, un accident de la circulation). Often appears with passive construction (il a été blessé dans...) or as an adjective (blessé dans l'accident). Use 'légèrement blessé' for 'slightly injured' and 'gravement blessé' for 'seriously injured'.
target_language_example: Il a été blessé dans un accident de vélo.
native_language_example: He was injured in a bicycle accident.

meaning: wounded/injured in (a specific body part).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has an injury to a particular part of the body. Followed by a body part: e.g. 'blessé à la jambe' (injured in the leg). Often used in news or medical contexts. The subject can be 'être blessé à' (to be injured in).
target_language_example: Il a été blessé à l'épaule pendant le match.
native_language_example: He was injured in the shoulder during the match.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely just the colour 'bleu' followed by the conjunction 'ou' meaning 'blue or'.
additional_notes: This is not an established multiword expression. In ordinary French, 'bleu ou' would appear inside a larger phrase to offer a choice (e.g. 'bleu ou vert' = 'blue or green'). If you saw 'bleu ou' alone, it is incomplete — expect another option after 'ou' or a continuation. 'Bleu' = blue (colour) and 'ou' = or (conjunction).
target_language_example: Tu veux la chemise bleu ou rouge ?
native_language_example: Do you want the blue or red shirt?

meaning: to drink a lot; to be a heavy drinker (literally: to drink like a hole).
additional_notes: Informal idiomatic expression used to describe someone who drinks excessively, typically alcohol. Often pejorative. Commonly used with a subject (e.g., Il boit comme un trou). Not literal; avoid using in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il boit comme un trou depuis son divorce.
native_language_example: He has been drinking like a fish / he drinks heavily since his divorce.

meaning: 'to drink (some/of)'.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean drinking something (boire de l'eau, boire du vin). In French the partitive article (du, de la, de l') or an indefinite (un, une) usually follows boire. After a negative construction use de (Je ne bois pas de café). When specifying quantity use expressions like 'boire un verre de...' or 'boire beaucoup de...'.
target_language_example: Il aime boire de l'eau après le sport.
native_language_example: He likes to drink water after exercising.

meaning: to drink (some) — used with feminine singular partitive nouns (e.g. boire de la bière = to drink some beer).
additional_notes: This is the verb boire (to drink) followed by the partitive article de la, which indicates an unspecified amount of a feminine noun. Use 'boire du' for masculine nouns, 'boire de l\'' before vowels, and 'boire des' for plural. In negative sentences the partitive often becomes 'de' (e.g. Il ne boit pas de bière).
target_language_example: Elle veut boire de la soupe ce soir.
native_language_example: She wants to drink some soup tonight.

meaning: to drink the (masculine singular object)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but simply the verb boire (to drink) followed by the definite article le, used before a masculine singular noun or to refer to a specific thing already mentioned. You will usually see it completed by a noun (e.g. boire le café) or by a pronoun (e.g. le boire → to drink it). Word order and contractions apply: before a vowel sound, le becomes l' (boire l'eau).
target_language_example: Il va boire le café ce matin.
native_language_example: He is going to drink the coffee this morning.

meaning: 'to drink something' (informal, incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete standard French phrase by itself. It looks like the combination of the verb boire (to drink) and the indefinite pronoun quelque (meaning 'some' or part of a compound like 'quelque chose' = 'something'). Alone, 'boire quelque' is ungrammatical; in correct usage you would say 'boire quelque chose' (to drink something) or 'boire un peu de' (to drink some/of). Beginners should use complete forms: 'boire quelque chose' or 'boire un verre' etc.
target_language_example: Je veux boire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I want to drink something.

meaning: 'never drink' (first‑/second‑/third‑person singular form of 'boire' with 'jamais')
additional_notes: This combines the verb boire (to drink) in a conjugated form (bois) with jamais (never). In full sentences you usually include a subject and partitive/article: e.g. Je ne bois jamais d'alcool. Remember French negation uses ne ... jamais around the verb (ne is often dropped in spoken French). The exact article after jamais depends on the noun (d' before a vowel, de/du/de la for partitives).
target_language_example: Je ne bois jamais de soda.
native_language_example: I never drink soda.

meaning: not a natural standalone phrase; appears to be three words that together would mean 'drink never any' but is ungrammatical in French
additional_notes: This exact sequence is not correct French. To express 'never drink any' you would say 'ne bois jamais de' (informal singular imperative/statement missing 'ne' in some spoken forms) or 'ne bois jamais de [quelque chose]'. In spoken French, the 'ne' is often dropped: 'Bois jamais de lait ?' is casual but still uncommon; better: 'Ne bois jamais de lait.' For commands (don't drink): 'Ne bois pas de...' or for general habit: 'Il ne boit jamais de...' Remember 'de' (not 'des') is used after negation before a noun.
target_language_example: Ne bois jamais de boissons alcoolisées si tu conduis.
native_language_example: Never drink alcoholic drinks if you are driving.

meaning: 'bois' can be either the verb form (je bois/tu bois = I/you drink) or the noun 'bois' (wood). With 'à' the meaning depends on which it is and the context: as verb + à before a noun or infinitive it indicates the thing/location/way related to drinking (e.g. boire à la paille = drink through a straw; boire à la santé de = drink to someone's health). As noun + à it forms compound phrases meaning 'wood for ...' (e.g. bois à brûler = wood for burning). Determination depends on surrounding words and sentence structure.
additional_notes: The exact written form 'bois à' is ambiguous without context because 'bois' looks like the verb but is spelled the same as the noun. Pronunciation differs slightly in connected speech. When functioning as a verb, the infinitive is normally 'boire' and typical constructions use 'boit/bois' depending on subject; 'bois à' as verb + preposition is less common in isolation. When noun + à, it introduces purpose or intended use of the wood. Watch for contractions with articles (à + le = au, à + les = aux) which will change surface form.
target_language_example: Il bois à la fontaine n'est pas grammatical — on dirait «Il boit à la fontaine.» mais la séquence écrite «bois à» peut apparaître dans «Le bois à brûler est empilé.»
native_language_example: Il boit à la fontaine is ungrammatical — you would say «Il boit à la fontaine.» but the written sequence «bois à» can appear in «Le bois à brûler est empilé.» (The wood for burning is piled up.)

meaning: atomic bomb; a nuclear explosive weapon.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a nuclear weapon (very large explosive power, often with historical or political context). Formal/neutral term. Can be used literally (weapon) or metaphorically in speech to describe something extremely powerful or shocking.
target_language_example: La bombe atomique a changé le cours de l'histoire.
native_language_example: The atomic bomb changed the course of history.

meaning: 'bombe à' is the start of a compound phrase meaning 'spray/pressurized container for...' or 'bomb for...'; it needs a noun after 'à' to complete the meaning (e.g. bombe à aérosol = aerosol can, bombe à eau = water bomb).
additional_notes: Alone, 'bombe à' is incomplete. In French it commonly appears in fixed compounds formed as 'bombe à + noun' to describe a container or device that uses/contains something (aérosol, peinture, eau, gaz) or a type of explosive/device (bombe à fragmentation, bombe à retardement). For everyday usage, 'bombe' can mean 'spray can' (bombe de peinture) or 'bomb' (explosive) depending on context. Pay attention to the noun that follows to determine the meaning.
target_language_example: Il a acheté une bombe à peinture pour retoucher le mur.
native_language_example: He bought a spray paint can to touch up the wall.

meaning: time bomb; something dangerous that will cause trouble later
additional_notes: Literally a 'time-delayed bomb'. Used both for a literal explosive device and figuratively to describe a situation/problem that will have serious negative consequences in the future (e.g., social, economic, political). Context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Cette dette publique est une bombe à retardement pour l'économie.
native_language_example: This public debt is a time bomb for the economy.

meaning: an exclamation meaning 'good God!' or 'for heaven's sake!'.
additional_notes: Used as a strong interjection to express surprise, anger, frustration or emphasis. Can be considered mildly blasphemous or rude by some because it invokes God; avoid in very formal or religious contexts. Often appears in stronger forms with swear words (e.g. « bon Dieu de merde ») or with repeated/emphatic structure (« Bon Dieu ! », « Mais bon Dieu ! »).
target_language_example: Mais bon Dieu, pourquoi as-tu fait ça ?
native_language_example: Good God, why did you do that?

meaning: 'happy birthday'.
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy birthday. Can be addressed to people of any age and formal or informal depending on context (use names or titles to adjust politeness). Often said on the person's birthday or in cards/messages. The word 'bon' is masculine singular; the full fixed phrase is always 'bon anniversaire'.
target_language_example: Bon anniversaire, Sophie !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Sophie!

meaning: 'enjoy your meal' or 'good appetite'.
additional_notes: Commonly said before someone starts eating to wish them an enjoyable meal. Also used descriptively in the phrase "avoir un bon appétit" (to have a good appetite). Formality: neutral — appropriate in most situations. Pronunciation note: the phrase is often said with liaison: [bɔ̃ napɛti].
target_language_example: Bon appétit ! Profitez bien de votre repas.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! Make the most of your meal.

meaning: Have a good afternoon / good afternoon (as a wish).
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a pleasant afternoon or as a polite greeting/farewell in the afternoon. Can be formal or neutral; tone depends on context. In sentence 1 it's used sarcastically/irritated (with strong language). The phrase is compositional and directly translates to English.
target_language_example: Bon après-midi, à bientôt !
native_language_example: Have a good afternoon, see you soon!

meaning: 'good at' (masculine subject) used before a masculine singular noun introduced by 'au' (à + le).
additional_notes: Used to describe that a (masculine or contextually masculine) person is skilled at a sport, game or activity whose noun is masculine singular. Agreement: 'bon' changes with the subject's gender/number (bonne, bons, bonnes). For feminine or plural nouns/use, use 'bonne à/aux/à la/à l'' as appropriate. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il est bon au foot.
native_language_example: He is good at football (soccer).

meaning: kind/good to (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone treats another person well or kindly. Typically appears after être (être bon avec quelqu'un) or in past forms (a été bon avec). Usually followed by a person (moi, toi, lui, etc.). Corresponds to English 'be good to' or 'be kind to'.
target_language_example: Il a été bon avec moi.
native_language_example: He was good to me.

meaning: Good luck / Hang in there — an encouragement said before a difficult or unpleasant task.
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone facing a challenge (exam, work, illness, tasks). Polite and common in spoken and written French; not a literal 'have courage' order but a supportive phrase. Can be used alone or followed by a specific situation: "Bon courage pour ton examen."
target_language_example: Bon courage pour ton entretien demain !
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow!

meaning: the bright side of (things).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the expression «Regarde/Regardez le bon côté des choses» meaning 'look on the bright side.'
