Usually followed by "choses" but can pair with other nouns (e.g. «le bon côté des événements»). Works with various imperatives and persons (Regarde/Regardez/Vois/Voyez/Voyons).
target_language_example: Regarde le bon côté des choses.
native_language_example: Look on the bright side of things.

meaning: good at or comfortable in (used before a noun to say someone is good in/at a particular area or feels at ease in a situation).
additional_notes: Often used as 'être bon dans + [nom]' to say someone is skilled in a subject or role (e.g. bon dans les maths). Can also express feeling comfortable 'être bien dans + [quelque chose]' but note 'bien dans' is more common for 'comfortable'. 'Bon dans' focuses on ability or suitability. Use with definite/plural articles as required (bon dans la classe, bon dans les matchs).
target_language_example: Il est bon dans les langues étrangères.
native_language_example: He is good at foreign languages.

meaning: a voucher, coupon, ticket, or certificate for something (e.g., a 'bon de réduction' = discount voucher).
additional_notes: Usually appears before a noun to specify the type of voucher or document: bon de réduction (discount coupon), bon de commande (order form/ purchase order), bon de livraison (delivery note). Not used alone as a complete noun in many contexts; it needs the following noun to show what kind of 'bon' it is. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: J'ai reçu un bon de réduction pour mon prochain achat.
native_language_example: I received a discount voucher for my next purchase.

meaning: This is not a complete or standard French phrase; likely a misordering or partial phrase. It appears to combine 'bon endroit' (good/right place) and 'au bon...' (at the right...), but as written it is ungrammatical and does not occur in standard French.
additional_notes: As written, 'bon endroit au bon' is incorrect. Correct alternatives include 'au bon endroit' (at the right place) or 'au bon moment' (at the right time). If you need to keep these words in sequence for emphasis or stylistic reasons, rewrite the sentence so the phrase becomes grammatical (for example: 'être au bon endroit au bon moment' — to be in the right place at the right time). The entry's example uses the exact sequence requested but note it remains ungrammatical in normal usage.
target_language_example: Il répétait 'bon endroit au bon' en plaisantant, mais tout le monde savait que la phrase était incorrecte.
native_language_example: He kept saying 'bon endroit au bon' jokingly, but everyone knew the phrase was incorrect.

meaning: Literally "good and"; not a fixed standalone phrase in French. Usually appears as two separate words ('bon,' as an interjection or adjective, and 'et' meaning 'and') rather than a single idiom. Often results from a punctuation-less transcription of spoken 'bon, et...' used to continue or change the topic.
additional_notes: By itself 'bon et' is uncommon as a fixed expression. In writing you should check punctuation: 'bon, et...' or 'bon et...' with comma/ellipsis reflects spoken connectors. It may also appear when 'bon' is an adjective directly followed by 'et' linking to another adjective (e.g. 'bon et loyal' — 'good and loyal'), in which case it's compositional and literal.
target_language_example: C'est un bon et fidèle ami.
native_language_example: He is a good and faithful friend.

meaning: 'good exercise' (a worthwhile physical activity or practice).
additional_notes: Used to describe an activity that is beneficial for fitness, health, or learning (e.g., a physical workout or a practice task). Can apply to sports (jogging, swimming, walking) or to exercises in class. Common, neutral phrase.
target_language_example: Faire du vélo est un bon exercice pour le coeur.
native_language_example: Cycling is a good exercise for the heart.

meaning: cheap; inexpensive.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that costs little money. Agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies when placed after it: bon marché (masc. sing.), bonne marché is incorrect — the phrase is invariable in form for the adjective 'bon marché' itself but you may see agreement on determiners (e.g., une jupe bon marché, des chaussures bon marché). Often used neutrally (not necessarily low quality) but can imply low quality depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté ce manteau bon marché pendant les soldes.
native_language_example: I bought this coat cheaply during the sales.

meaning: 'witty remark' or 'clever/funny comment'.
additional_notes: Refers to a brief, clever or humorous remark (a quip). Used for something said to amuse or show wit. Note: in sentence 1, 'mot de passe' (password) uses 'mot' meaning 'word' — different context. 'Bon mot' is idiomatic and not literal 'good word' in this sense.
target_language_example: Il a lancé un bon mot qui a fait rire toute la salle.
native_language_example: He made a witty remark that made the whole room laugh.

meaning: a good idea, a good deal, or a smart plan/opportunity
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say something is a good idea, a useful tip, a bargain, or a smart opportunity. Common in spoken French: can refer to a practical plan (un projet) or to a great deal/offer (une bonne affaire).
target_language_example: Allons-y ce soir — c'est un bon plan.
native_language_example: Let's go tonight — that's a good plan.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'so good that' when part of a larger construction (e.g. 'si bon que' or 'tellement bon que').
additional_notes: On its own 'bon que' is uncommon and sounds incomplete. French uses comparative or result connectors such as 'si... que', 'tellement... que' or 'assez... pour que' to express 'so good that' or 'good enough that'. You may see 'bon que' inside sentences after modifiers (e.g. 'trop bon que' is still informal/ungrammatical — prefer 'trop bon pour que' or 'si bon que'). If you find 'bon que' in writing, check surrounding words: it may be part of a longer idiom or a spoken fragment.
target_language_example: Le gâteau était si bon que tout le monde en a repris.
native_language_example: The cake was so good that everyone had seconds.

meaning: common sense; good judgment.
additional_notes: Used to describe practical intelligence or sound judgment. Can refer to a person (une personne de bon sens), a quality (avoir du bon sens), or be used in expressions like "dans le bon sens du terme" (in the proper sense). Neutral register — suitable in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Il faut du bon sens pour gérer cette situation.
native_language_example: You need common sense to manage this situation.

meaning: 'good time' or 'a good moment/enjoyment'.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'good time'. Often used in expressions like 'passer un bon temps' (to have a good time) or in fixed phrases such as 'le bon temps' to refer to pleasant times. On its own it can describe a pleasant period or experience; context may require a verb (e.g., 'passer') to be natural in French.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé un bon temps au festival.
native_language_example: We had a good time at the festival.

meaning: literally 'good wind'; used to wish someone well or to ask what brings them here ('what brings you?').
additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: as a farewell or good wish (similar to 'good luck' or 'safe travels') — e.g. simply 'Bon vent.' — and in the question form 'Quel bon vent (t')amène ?' meaning 'What brings you here?' or 'What wind has brought you?'. Slightly literary or old-fashioned but still heard in conversation. Not offensive.
target_language_example: Bon vent et prends soin de toi.
native_language_example: Good winds and take care of yourself.

meaning: 'the good old days' (nostalgic reference to the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer nostalgically to an earlier time perceived as better or simpler. Often preceded by 'le' or used in expressions like 'au nom du bon vieux temps' (for old times' sake). Informal/colloquial but common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: On devrait ressortir les photos du bon vieux temps.
native_language_example: We should bring out the photos from the good old days.

meaning: 'have a good trip' / 'safe journey' (a wish said to someone who is traveling).
additional_notes: Common, polite phrase used to wish someone well before a journey. Can be used standalone (Bon voyage !) or in a sentence (Je vous souhaite bon voyage). Also appears in questions about someone's trip (Tu as fait bon voyage ? = Did you have a good trip?). Not informal slang.
target_language_example: Bon voyage et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Have a good trip and see you soon!

meaning: good/fit/ready for (followed by an infinitive or noun) — indicates suitability or readiness
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or noun to say something is suitable, ready, or okay to do. Common patterns: "bon à + infinitive" (e.g. bon à savoir — good to know; bon à manger — fit to eat) or "bon à + noun" in some fixed phrases. Not a complete phrase by itself — needs context. Tone is neutral.
target_language_example: Ce fromage n'est pas bon à manger.
native_language_example: This cheese is not fit to eat.

meaning: useful, handy, worth taking or accepting
additional_notes: Used to say that something (information, an offer, an opportunity, an item) is useful or can be taken/accepted — even if not perfect. Often appears in general statements (e.g. "C'est toujours bon à prendre" = "That's always useful"). Context decides if literal (physically taking) or figurative (accepting/benefiting).
target_language_example: Si tu as des conseils, c'est toujours bon à prendre.
native_language_example: If you have any tips, they're always useful to have.

meaning: good-for-nothing; useless person
additional_notes: Pejorative expression used to insult someone's competence or worth. Often used alone as an exclamation ("Bon à rien !") or with descriptors (e.g. "espèce de bon à rien"). Common in spoken French. Gender/number can change (e.g. "bonne à rien" for a feminine target, "bons/bonnes à rien" for plural), though masculine form is frequently used generically.
target_language_example: Arrête de l'insulter, ce n'est pas un bon à rien.
native_language_example: Stop insulting him, he's not a good-for-nothing.

meaning: a good student (well-behaved or academically strong).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who performs well at school or behaves properly in class. Can mean academically successful, diligent, or well-mannered depending on context. Often used with an article (un/une) but can appear without in spoken or informal contexts (e.g., 'John est bon élève').
target_language_example: Elle est un bon élève en mathématiques.
native_language_example: She is a good student in mathematics.

meaning: as you please / wherever you like (used with verbs like 'aller', 'venir' or 'sembler').
additional_notes: Always appears in the fixed expression 'comme bon te semble' or 'où bon te semble'. It means 'as you see fit' or 'wherever you want' and is somewhat formal/literary; in everyday French you might hear 'comme tu veux' or 'où tu veux'. 'Te' is the informal singular object pronoun (tu). For polite/plural use replace 'te' with 'vous' → 'bon vous semble' (usually 'comme bon vous semble' or 'où bon vous semble').
target_language_example: Va où bon te semble, je te fais confiance.
native_language_example: Go wherever you like, I trust you.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'well, you...' or 'okay, you...'.
additional_notes: This combination is not an established multiword expression. In spoken French, 'bon' is often used as a filler meaning 'well' or 'okay' (e.g. 'Bon, vous...'), followed by a verb or question addressed to 'vous' (formal/plural 'you'). Expect it to appear before a directive, question or transition: 'Bon, vous...' should be followed by additional words. It should not be treated as a single idiom.
target_language_example: Bon vous, qu'en pensez-vous ?
native_language_example: Well, you, what do you think?

meaning: Used to start a question or change the subject; roughly 'So, what...' or 'Well, what...'.
additional_notes: A conversational connector: 'Bon' (well/okay) + 'qu'est-' beginning of 'qu'est-ce que' (what). Used to prompt action, ask what happened, or move the conversation forward. Very common in spoken French. Often followed by 'on' (we) + verb: e.g. 'Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on fait ?' = 'So, what do we do?'.
target_language_example: Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on fait maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

meaning: Well then; so; alright (used to start, resume, or close a conversation or to prompt a response).
additional_notes: A common conversational filler that can introduce a comment, signal a transition, prompt someone (often with a question), or close a discussion. Tone and context change its nuance: friendly ('Well then, good night'), impatient ('Well then?'), or decisive ('Well then, I'll get revenge'). Not formal but widely used in spoken and written dialogue.
target_language_example: Bon alors, on y va ?
native_language_example: Well then, shall we go?

meaning: an exclamation like 'damn' / 'for heaven's sake' used to express surprise, frustration, or emphasis.
additional_notes: Informal and can be strong depending on context; similar to 'bon Dieu' but milder than outright curses. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence: 'Bon sang, ...' or '..., bon sang !'. Tone and situation determine politeness — avoid in very formal settings.
target_language_example: Bon sang, fais attention !
native_language_example: Damn, be careful!

meaning: "happiness is" (literal), typically the start of a fuller phrase: 'happiness is ...'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase in French; it's simply the noun 'bonheur' (happiness) followed by the verb 'est' (is). You will usually see it as the beginning of a sentence that defines or describes happiness (e.g. "Le bonheur est de...", "Le bonheur est lorsque..."). Remember to include the definite article 'le' in most sentences: 'Le bonheur est...' Compositional and literal: meaning comes directly from the words.
target_language_example: Le bonheur est simple quand on partage.
native_language_example: Happiness is simple when you share.

meaning: snowman
additional_notes: A compound noun meaning a figure made of snow. Used in everyday speech; feminine/masculine agreement: typically 'un bonhomme de neige' (masculine). Plural: 'des bonhommes de neige'. Can be used literally (made of snow) or playfully in stories.
target_language_example: Nous avons construit un bonhomme de neige dans le jardin.
native_language_example: We built a snowman in the garden.

meaning: a casual way to say 'hello everyone' (short for «bonjour les...») — used before a group or addressing people informally
additional_notes: Often appears as the start of a greeting followed by a group identifier (e.g. «bonjour les amis», «bonjour les enfants», «bonjour les collègues»). By itself 'bonjour les' is incomplete in formal writing; in speech or informal contexts people may pause or leave the group word implied. Use 'bonjour' alone for a neutral hello, and 'bonjour à tous' or 'bonjour tout le monde' for 'hello everyone'.
target_language_example: Bonjour les amis, prêts pour la sortie ?
native_language_example: Hello friends, ready for the outing?

meaning: a good deed; an act of kindness or moral/positive action.
additional_notes: Used to describe a helpful, charitable, or morally positive act. Can refer to a single gesture (e.g., helping someone) or a larger act (e.g., charitable work). Commonly used in everyday and formal contexts. Plural: bonnes actions.
target_language_example: Il a fait une bonne action en aidant la voisine à porter ses courses.
native_language_example: He did a good deed by helping the neighbor carry her groceries.

meaning: 'a good year' or used as 'Happy New Year' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'good year'. Used to wish someone a Happy New Year when said alone or as a greeting around New Year's. In other contexts it describes a period of a year that was good (une bonne année) or roughly 'for about a year' in informal uses (e.g. 'pendant une bonne année' = 'for a good year/about a year').
target_language_example: Nous avons passé une bonne année ensemble.
native_language_example: We had a good year together.

meaning: good luck
additional_notes: Used to wish someone success or luck in a situation. Commonly said when parting or before an event (exam, trip, challenge). Polite and neutral — appropriate in most contexts. Can be addressed to one person or a group (bonne chance à tous).
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton examen demain.
native_language_example: Good luck for your exam tomorrow.

meaning: 'a good thing to' (used before an infinitive to say something is good to do)
additional_notes: This phrase is usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., bonne chose à faire) and means that doing that action is a good idea or beneficial. It appears in expressions like "C'est une bonne chose à savoir" (It's a good thing to know). Use it to give mild approval or advice. Not an idiom or slang.
target_language_example: C'est une bonne chose à apprendre pour ton travail.
native_language_example: It's a good thing to learn for your job.

meaning: informal/pejorative: 'woman' or 'wife' (often dismissive; can mean 'old woman' or 'mistress' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in informal or colloquial speech. Can be neutral in some contexts to mean 'woman' or 'wife' (e.g., 'sa bonne femme' = his wife), but often carries a dismissive, derogatory, or old-fashioned tone ('la bonne femme' = some woman/old woman). Context determines whether it means 'wife', 'some woman', 'old woman', or 'mistress'. Avoid in polite speech.
target_language_example: Il est parti avec une bonne femme, et ils ne sont jamais revenus.
native_language_example: He left with some woman, and they never came back.

meaning: a good/good-natured girl; used to describe a well-behaved, kind, or obedient girl.
additional_notes: Commonly used to praise behavior (kindness, obedience, politeness). Can be literal (a well-behaved girl) or used playfully/affectionately by adults toward children. Tone depends on context — sometimes slightly patronizing if said to an adult. Agreement: 'bonne' matches feminine singular 'fille'.
target_language_example: Sois une bonne fille et aide ta sœur.
native_language_example: Be a good girl and help your sister.

meaning: Happy [holiday/celebration] or Happy birthday (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy celebration. In many contexts in France it commonly means "Happy birthday" when said to a person; in other contexts it means "Happy [name of holiday]" (e.g. Bonne fête du Canada = Happy Canada Day). Can be followed by the name of the holiday (Bonne fête de la lune) or directed at a person (Bonne fête à toi). Tone is neutral and appropriate in both formal and informal settings.
target_language_example: Bonne fête, profite bien de ta journée !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, enjoy your day!

meaning: good mood; cheerful mood.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is cheerful, in a pleasant or positive mood. Often used with être (être de bonne humeur / être en bonne humeur). Can be used generally (Il est de bonne humeur) or about a specific time (être en très bonne humeur). The opposite is 'mauvaise humeur' (bad mood).
target_language_example: Elle est de bonne humeur ce matin.
native_language_example: She is in a good mood this morning.

meaning: a good idea to / it's a good idea to
additional_notes: Used to say that doing something is advisable or wise. Followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase: bonne idée de + infinitive (e.g. bonne idée de partir) or bonne idée de + nom (e.g. bonne idée de cadeau). Can be used with expressions like « C'est une bonne idée de... » or simply « bonne idée » in informal speech.
target_language_example: C'est une bonne idée de partir tôt.
native_language_example: It's a good idea to leave early.

meaning: 'have a good day' (a polite farewell) or 'a good day' (noun phrase).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite goodbye: 'Bonne journée.' = 'Have a good day.' Can also describe a day as being good: 'une bonne journée.' Context tells whether it's a farewell or a description. Formality: neutral/polite and appropriate in most situations. Pronunciation tip: the final 'e' in 'bonne' is pronounced, and 'journée' stresses the -ée.
target_language_example: Bonne journée, à demain !
native_language_example: Have a good day, see you tomorrow!

meaning: good news; a piece of positive information
additional_notes: Used to announce or react to positive information. Can stand alone as an exclamation ("Bonne nouvelle!") or be followed by details. Gender: 'nouvelle' is feminine, but English translation is invariant. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Bonne nouvelle : le train est à l'heure.
native_language_example: Good news: the train is on time.

meaning: good news for (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that some information is positive or beneficial to a person, group, or situation. Commonly followed by a noun or a pronoun (toi, vous, le clan, etc.). Can be used as 'Il y a une bonne nouvelle pour...' (There is good news for...) or 'J'ai une bonne nouvelle pour...' (I have good news for...).
target_language_example: J'ai une bonne nouvelle pour toi : ton examen est réussi.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: you passed your exam.

meaning: good night
additional_notes: Used to say farewell in the evening or before someone goes to sleep. Commonly used alone or followed by a name/term of address (e.g., "Bonne nuit, Marie"). Can be polite or familiar depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, à demain.
native_language_example: Good night, see you tomorrow.

meaning: good for; suitable for; ready for (something).
additional_notes: Used after a feminine noun or adjective (bonne) + preposition 'pour'. Commonly means 'suitable/useful for' (e.g. une solution bonne pour tout le monde = a solution good for everyone) or 'ready/fit for' in informal contexts (e.g. bonne pour la casse = ready to be junked). If referring to a masculine noun, use 'bon pour'. Agreement depends on the noun/adjective before 'pour'.
target_language_example: Cette chaise est bonne pour la terrasse.
native_language_example: This chair is good for the terrace.

meaning: Safe travels / Have a good trip (literally: 'good road').
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a pleasant or safe journey when they are traveling by road or leaving on a trip. Can be said informally to friends, family or acquaintances. Also appears in questions when talking about the correct route (e.g. "C'est la bonne route ?" = "Is this the right road?").
target_language_example: Bonne route et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Safe travels and see you soon!

meaning: Have a good evening / Enjoy the rest of your evening.
additional_notes: Polite farewell used in the evening or at night. Appropriate in both formal and informal contexts; you can say it to one person or a group. Often said when parting ways or ending a conversation (in person, by phone, or in messages). If addressing a single male you might also hear "bonne soirée, monsieur"; for friends you can use simply "bonne soirée !"
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide — bonne soirée !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — have a good evening!

meaning: good manners; polite behavior
additional_notes: Used to refer to polite behavior, etiquette, or social rules. Often plural in French. Can be used generally (les bonnes manières) or in questions/addresses to scold someone (e.g. Où sont tes bonnes manières ? meaning 'Where are your manners?').
target_language_example: Apprends les bonnes manières à table.
native_language_example: Learn good manners at the table.

meaning: 'have a good holiday' / 'have a nice vacation' (wished to someone).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to wish someone an enjoyable holiday or vacation period. 'Bonnes' agrees in gender/number with 'vacances' (always plural). Use 'Passe de bonnes vacances' (informal singular you) for friends/family, and 'Passez de bonnes vacances' (formal or plural you) for polite or multiple people. Often said as a short goodbye before a holiday.
target_language_example: Passez de bonnes vacances et profitez bien du soleil !
native_language_example: Have a nice vacation and enjoy the sun!

meaning: an exclamation like 'good heavens!' or 'goodness gracious!'.
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, shock, disbelief or strong emotion. Polite/old-fashioned tone — not vulgar; can be emphatic on its own. Equivalent to English mild oaths such as 'good heavens' or 'for heaven's sake'.
target_language_example: Bonté divine, tu as vu la taille de ce gâteau ?
native_language_example: Good heavens, did you see the size of that cake?

meaning: an intense swear/exclamation like 'fucking hell' or 'goddamn it'.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and strong. Used to express anger, frustration, shock or to insult someone. Avoid in polite company or formal situations. Can be directed at a person (as an insult) or used alone as an exclamation. Equivalent to combining 'bordel' (mess/whorehouse, used as strong expletive) with 'merde' (shit).
target_language_example: Bordel de merde, j'ai encore perdu mes clés !
native_language_example: Fucking hell, I lost my keys again!

meaning: to kick someone's butt; to beat someone up (informal, aggressive).
additional_notes: Very informal/colloquial and vulgar. Used to threaten or promise physical punishment or a strong beating; can also be used figuratively to mean 'defeat' or 'dominate' someone. Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Si tu continues, je vais te botter le cul.
native_language_example: If you keep going, I'm going to kick your butt.

meaning: 'speechless' or 'open-mouthed' (astonished, unable to speak).
additional_notes: Used as an adjective or fixed expression after a noun/pronoun (often with être or rester) to describe someone so surprised or impressed that they can't speak. Literally 'mouth open.' Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle est restée bouche bée devant le spectacle.
native_language_example: She stood there speechless in front of the show.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase on its own; likely part of a larger expression (e.g., 'bouche-à-bouche' or 'bouche et...' as start of a clause).
additional_notes: On its own 'bouche et' is incomplete and not used as a standalone idiom. 'Bouche' means 'mouth'. Common related expressions: 'bouche-à-bouche' (mouth-to-mouth/CPR), 'ferme ta bouche' / 'tais-toi' (shut your mouth/be quiet), or phrases like 'bouche et oreilles' when listing body parts. If you saw 'bouche et' in text, check the surrounding words — it's probably connecting 'bouche' with another noun or part of a compound expression.
target_language_example: Il a parlé de la bouche et des oreilles du bébé pendant l'examen.
native_language_example: He talked about the baby's mouth and ears during the check-up.

meaning: move (away) from; get away from (someone/something)
additional_notes: Imperative or present-tense form of the verb bouger followed by de + noun/pronoun. Used to tell someone or something to move away or to indicate moving away from a place or person. Common in spoken French: e.g. «Bouge de là!» = “Get out of the way!” or «Il bouge de sa chaise» = “He moves from his chair.”
target_language_example: Bouge de la porte, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Move away from the door, please.

meaning: 'job of' / 'work of' used to describe a type of job or a task related to something.
additional_notes: Boulot is an informal word for 'job' or 'work' (more casual than travail or emploi). When followed by de + noun, it describes the kind of job or the task (e.g. boulot de nuit = night shift job, boulot de bureau = office job). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé un boulot de nuit pour cet été.
native_language_example: I found a night job for this summer.

meaning: Not a set phrase; it's simply the noun 'boulot' (job/work) followed by the verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This combination isn't an idiom on its own. 'Boulot' is informal for 'job/work' (more casual than 'travail'). 'Est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). You'll usually see them in full sentences like 'Le boulot est difficile' (The job is hard) or 'Le boulot, c'est important' (Work is important). Pay attention to articles and contractions (le boulot, un boulot).
target_language_example: Le boulot est fatigant cette semaine.
native_language_example: The job is tiring this week.

meaning: 'boulot' = job/work; 'et' = and. (Together they are not a fixed phrase.)
additional_notes: This is not a set expression — it's simply the noun 'boulot' (colloquial for 'job' or 'work') followed by the conjunction 'et' ('and'). 'Boulot' is informal; use 'travail' for more formal situations. Expect it in lists or phrases like 'boulot et famille' (work and family) or 'boulot et école' (work and school).
target_language_example: Entre le boulot et la vie privée, j'ai peu de temps libre.
native_language_example: Between work and private life, I have little free time.

meaning: a job/work at (somewhere) or 'work to' (something) depending on context.
additional_notes: Boulot = informal for 'job' or 'work'. With 'à' it can mean: 1) 'un boulot à faire' = 'a job/task to do' (à + infinitive or faire = to be done); 2) 'un boulot à New York' = 'a job in/at New York' (location); or 3) in colloquial imperatives it can appear in phrases like 'demande du boulot à X' = 'ask X for a job'. 'Boulot' is informal — prefer 'emploi' or 'travail' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il cherche un boulot à Paris cet été.
native_language_example: He's looking for a job in Paris this summer.

meaning: a bunch/cluster of (used with flowers or figuratively to mean a group of things or a set of qualities).
additional_notes: Commonly used with fleurs (un bouquet de fleurs = a bouquet of flowers). Can also be used figuratively (un bouquet de saveurs, un bouquet d'arômes). Followed by a noun; choose the appropriate article/number after 'de' (de, du, des) depending on context (e.g. un bouquet de fleurs, un bouquet de laurier).
target_language_example: Il m'a offert un bouquet de fleurs pour mon anniversaire.
native_language_example: He gave me a bouquet of flowers for my birthday.

meaning: 'shortness of breath' or 'out of breath'.
additional_notes: Used to describe the physical state of being breathless after exertion or from a medical condition. Can be used literally (e.g., after running) or in expressions like 'à bout de souffle' meaning exhausted or worn out. Not the title of the film — when capitalized and used as a title (À bout de souffle) it refers to the famous 1960 French movie.
target_language_example: Après la course, j'étais complètement bout de souffle.
native_language_example: After the run, I was completely out of breath.

meaning: the end/result (informal: 'in the end' or 'ultimately').
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'au bout du compte' meaning 'in the end' or 'when all is said and done'. It's used to state the final outcome after considering everything. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Au bout du compte, nous avons décidé de partir.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to leave.

meaning: 'the end of the world' or 'a very remote place'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a place that is extremely far away or isolated. Can be literal (the end of the world) but is commonly used figuratively in everyday speech to mean 'in the middle of nowhere' or 'the back of beyond'. Often appears in phrases like «au bout du monde» (at the end of the world / in a very remote place).
target_language_example: Ils habitent au bout du monde, il faut des heures pour y arriver.
native_language_example: They live at the end of the world; it takes hours to get there.

meaning: mailbox; the physical receptacle for receiving mail (also email inbox in some contexts).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a physical mailbox at home or on the street (letterbox). Can also mean an email inbox in modern contexts, but in everyday spoken French 'boîte aux lettres' usually means the physical box for postal mail. Feminine noun phrase: 'la boîte aux lettres'. Plural: 'les boîtes aux lettres'.
target_language_example: J'ai relevé le courrier dans la boîte aux lettres.
native_language_example: I collected the mail from the mailbox.

meaning: nightclub; a place for dancing, music and late-night socializing.
additional_notes: Commonly shortened to "boîte" in spoken French. Often implies late hours, DJs or live music, dancing and drinks. Used as a feminine noun: "une boîte de nuit". To enter some clubs you may need to meet age or dress requirements.
target_language_example: On va en boîte de nuit ce soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we go to a nightclub tonight?

meaning: glove compartment (the small storage compartment in a car dashboard).
additional_notes: Commonly shortened in speech to "boîte" in some contexts, but full form is clear. Used to indicate where items (gloves, documents, keys, etc.) are stored in a car. Masculine or feminine? "La boîte à gants" (feminine).
target_language_example: La clé de secours est dans la boîte à gants.
native_language_example: The spare key is in the glove compartment.

meaning: 'toolbox' — a container for tools.
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to a physical box that holds tools (hammer, pliers, etc.). Can also be used metaphorically in contexts like software or skill sets (e.g., "une boîte à outils numérique"), but examples here are literal. Feminine noun phrase (la boîte à outils).
target_language_example: La boîte à outils est sous l'établi.
native_language_example: The toolbox is under the workbench.

meaning: literally 'box was' — two-word sequence combining boîte (box/company) and était (was); not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the noun boîte followed by the past-tense verb être (imparfait). Boîte can mean 'box' (literal) or informally 'company'/'club' (familiar). The sequence boîte était would appear inside a larger sentence (e.g., "La boîte était fermée" = "The box/company was closed"). Pay attention to context to choose the correct translation. For beginner learners, learn boîte as 'box' and the imparfait était as 'was'.
target_language_example: La boîte était vide.
native_language_example: The box was empty.

meaning: literally 'arm of' — used to show possession, part of, or a branch/extension of something (e.g., bras de mer = arm of the sea).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in compound geographic or anatomical phrases (bras de mer, bras de rivière, bras de la chaise) or to indicate a part/extension belonging to something. It is not a complete phrase on its own; it needs a noun after 'de' to say 'arm/branch of X'. 'Bras' can be literal (body part) or figurative (branch, inlet, wing).
target_language_example: Le bras de la rivière traverse la forêt.
native_language_example: The arm (branch) of the river runs through the forest.

meaning: 'right arm' (literal) / 'right-hand man' or 'assistant' (figurative)
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to the physical right arm. Figuratively, it means a trusted helper or key assistant (English: 'right-hand man/woman'). Context tells which meaning applies. Gender agreement: bras is masculine; 'bras droit' stays the same for a male or neutral referent, but you may see 'sa bras droit' (incorrect) — correct: 'son bras droit' because 'bras' is masculine. Can refer to either gender as the assistant (e.g., 'Elle est son bras droit').
target_language_example: Le ministre a présenté sa nouvelle collaboratrice comme son bras droit.
native_language_example: The minister introduced his new collaborator as his right-hand person.

meaning: Literally 'arms for' — combination of bras ('arms') + pour ('for'). Not an idiom; appears when specifying that something is intended for the arms or related to arms.
additional_notes: Not a fixed multiword expression in French. Used compositionally in phrases like 'outil/attelle/vêtement bras pour [usage]' though more natural French usually places 'pour' before the noun phrase (e.g., 'pour les bras'). When 'bras pour' appears it will typically be inside a longer noun phrase (e.g., 'manchon bras pour cyclisme') or in product labels. Translate literally in most contexts.
target_language_example: Manchon bras pour cyclisme — conçu pour protéger les bras.
native_language_example: Arm sleeve for cycling — designed to protect the arms.

meaning: to break someone's heart; to deeply hurt or sadden someone emotionally.
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe causing strong emotional pain, disappointment, or sadness. Commonly followed by an indirect object (e.g., me, la, lui) or a clause describing what caused the hurt. Not literal (not about physically breaking a heart). Can be used in both serious and emotional everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Cette trahison a vraiment réussi à briser le cœur de Marie.
native_language_example: This betrayal really succeeded in breaking Marie's heart.

meaning: toothbrush.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun meaning the tool used to clean teeth. Always feminine singular: 'une brosse à dents' (a toothbrush), 'la brosse à dents' (the toothbrush). Use with reflexive verb 'se brosser les dents' to say 'to brush one's teeth' (e.g., 'Je me brosse les dents').
target_language_example: J'ai pris ma brosse à dents avant de partir.
native_language_example: I took my toothbrush before leaving.

meaning: 'noise at' or 'noise from' (preposition à indicating location or source of a noise).
additional_notes: This entry treats the sequence bruit + à (noun followed by preposition). It commonly appears in contexts like «bruit à la porte», «bruit à l'étage», or with contractions: à + le = au, à + les = aux, and à + vowel = à l'. The standalone sequence bruit à without a following noun is uncommon in isolation and usually appears as part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: Il y avait un bruit à l'étage; on parlait du «bruit à» juste au-dessus de nous.
native_language_example: There was a noise upstairs; we were talking about the «bruit à» just above us.

meaning: noise/sound in (somewhere); used to say there is or isn't noise inside a place, or figuratively that something will make a public stir.
additional_notes: Common collocation: faire du bruit dans + lieu = to make noise in a place. Can be literal (physical sound inside a room or building) or figurative (an event causing attention or gossip: ça a fait du bruit dans le monde). Often appears with négation: pas un bruit dans la maison = not a sound in the house.
target_language_example: Il n'y avait pas un bruit dans la salle pendant la conférence.
native_language_example: There wasn't a sound in the hall during the lecture.

meaning: 'noise of' or 'sound of' (used to describe the noise produced by something).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to indicate the source or type of a sound (e.g. bruit de moteur = engine noise). Can be used in literal descriptions and in figurative expressions (bruit de couloir = rumor, though that uses the full phrase). Common in descriptions and reports.
target_language_example: J'entends un bruit de moteur dehors.
native_language_example: I hear an engine noise outside.

meaning: This looks like two words 'bruit' (noise) and 'est' (is); by itself it isn't a fixed phrase — likely part of a sentence meaning 'the noise is...'.
additional_notes: Not a standalone idiom. 'bruit' = 'noise, sound'; 'est' = third-person singular of 'être' ('is'). You will usually see them together in sentences like 'Le bruit est fort' (The noise is loud) or 'Le bruit est venu de la rue' (The noise came from the street) though for 'came from' a different verb is used. Use gender/number agreement with adjectives: 'Le bruit est fort', 'Les bruits sont forts'.
target_language_example: Le bruit est trop fort dans cette pièce.
native_language_example: The noise is too loud in this room.

meaning: 'burned the' (past participle + definite article) — used when saying something or someone burned (something) or was burned, followed by a masculine noun.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a fragment: brûlé is the past participle of brûler (to burn) and le is the masculine singular definite article. It can appear in different grammatical constructions (e.g., passé composé with avoir/être, or as an adjective). You will usually see it inside a full sentence, e.g. il a brûlé le gâteau (he burned the cake) or la maison brûlée (the burned house) — note the article may attach differently depending on word order. Watch agreement: when used adjectivally after a feminine noun, brûlé becomes brûlée.
target_language_example: Il a brûlé le papier par accident.
native_language_example: He burned the paper by accident.

meaning: drank a
additional_notes: Past participle + indefinite article: 'bu' is the past participle of boire (to drink). 'bu un' commonly appears before a beverage or 'verre' (glass). In English you would usually say 'drank a' or 'had a (drink)'. Context determines what was drunk: e.g. 'bu un verre (de vin)' = 'had a glass (of wine)'.
target_language_example: Hier soir, j'ai bu un verre de jus d'orange.
native_language_example: Last night I had a glass of orange juice.

meaning: 'bubble of' or 'balloon of' — used to describe a small enclosed area, a speech/thought bubble, or a figurative bubble (e.g., social or economic).
additional_notes: Literally 'bubble of'. Often followed by a noun to indicate what the bubble contains or describes: bulle de savon (soap bubble), bulle de texte (text/speech bubble), bulle immobilière (housing bubble). Can be used both literally and figuratively. Word order: 'bulle de' + noun.
target_language_example: Ils vivent dans une bulle de confort.
native_language_example: They live in a comfort bubble.

meaning: 'office of' / 'desk of' / 'agency of' — a prepositional phrase used to indicate possession, function or affiliation (e.g. office/department belonging to or dedicated to ...).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to specify which office, desk, department or agency (bureau de poste = post office; bureau de direction = management office; bureau de renseignements = information desk). Can indicate physical desk (bureau) or an administrative unit. Use de + definite article when needed (le/la/les) depending on the noun: "le bureau de poste" or often just "bureau de poste" in fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Le bureau de poste est fermé le dimanche.
native_language_example: The post office is closed on Sundays.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French multi-word expression; appears to be a fragment meaning 'office/desk of my...' and is incomplete without a following noun.
additional_notes: 'Bureau' can mean 'office' or 'desk'. In French you normally say 'mon bureau' for 'my office'/'my desk'. If you use possession with 'de' you need a noun after 'mon' (e.g. 'le bureau de mon père' = 'my father's office/desk'). The sequence 'bureau de mon' alone is ungrammatical as a complete noun phrase.
target_language_example: Le dossier est posé sur le bureau de mon père.
native_language_example: The file is placed on my father's desk.

meaning: post office
additional_notes: Used to refer to the local post office building or branch. Common in directions and when asking where to send/collect mail or buy stamps. 'Bureau' here means 'office' and 'de poste' specifies postal service.
target_language_example: Le bureau de poste est ouvert jusqu'à 17h.
native_language_example: The post office is open until 5 PM.

meaning: the phrase 'bureau en' isn't a fixed expression by itself; it's 'bureau' (office/desk) followed by a preposition like 'en' to form phrases such as 'au bureau en voiture' or 'bureau en partant' — meaning depends on the following word (e.g. 'bureau en voiture' = 'office by/with car' is actually ungrammatical; more common patterns are 'se rendre au bureau en voiture' = 'go to the office by car', or 'le bureau en dessous' = 'the office below').
additional_notes: There is no standalone idiom 'bureau en'. In your examples 'bureau' (office/desk) combines with different structures: - 'au/au bureau' (to/at the office) + mode of transport introduced by 'en' (en voiture, en train) → 'go to the office by car/train'. - 'le bureau en dessous' uses 'en dessous' (below) to mean 'the office below'. - 'quitter le bureau en toute hâte' and 'en partant' use 'en' to form adverbial phrases ('in/with great haste', 'upon leaving'). Learn 'bureau' (office/desk) and the various uses of 'en' separately; then combine: 'aller au bureau en train' = 'go to the office by train', 'quitter le bureau en toute hâte' = 'leave the office in great haste', 'le bureau en dessous (de notre appartement)' = 'the office below (our apartment)'.
target_language_example: Elle est allée au bureau en bus ce matin.
native_language_example: She went to the office by bus this morning.

meaning: 'desk with' / 'office at' (part of a phrase that links 'bureau' to a function, location or object using 'à')
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own; it's the start of many common expressions such as 'bureau à domicile' (home office), 'bureau à partager' (shared office), or 'bureau à vendre' (office for sale). The preposition à links 'bureau' to what follows (purpose, location, feature). You will always need the next word(s) to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: J'ai installé un bureau à domicile dans le salon.
native_language_example: I set up a home office in the living room.

meaning: 'the bus is' (used to describe the bus — its state, location, or condition).
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase: bus (le bus) + est (3rd person singular of être). Use to state facts about the bus (late, broken down, full, dirty, expensive ticket, present, etc.). Replace 'bus' by another noun to form similar sentences. For negative or different tenses, modify the verb (n'est pas, était, sera, etc.).
target_language_example: Le bus est arrivé en retard ce matin.
native_language_example: The bus arrived late this morning.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; appears to be a fragment meaning 'the bus is in...' but incomplete.
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a complete or idiomatic French expression by itself. In French, to say where a bus is you would say either "Le bus est en retard" (The bus is late), "Le bus est arrivé" (The bus has arrived), or use "Le bus est en (...)" followed by a noun like a vehicle state or location expressed with a noun (rare) or a gerund/participle: "Le bus est en route" (The bus is on its way) or "Le bus est en service" (The bus is in service). Do not use "bus est en" alone; include the article "le" and complete the phrase.
target_language_example: Le bus est en route, il arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The bus is on its way; it will arrive in five minutes.

meaning: 'don't drink' (plural/formal or polite imperative + negation)
additional_notes: A negative imperative formed with the verb boire (to drink): 'Ne buvez pas' is the standard command telling one or more people (or one person formally) not to drink something or not to drink alcohol. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped, giving ' buvez pas' or 'N'oubliez pas' style; writing should keep 'Ne buvez pas'. Use 'Ne bois pas' for one person in informal singular, and 'Ne buvons pas' for 'let's not drink.'
target_language_example: Ne buvez pas cette eau, elle est contaminée.
native_language_example: Don't drink this water, it's contaminated.

meaning: building A (label for a specific building, e.g. in a complex or campus).
additional_notes: Used to identify a particular building by letter (A, B, C...). Common in signs, maps, campus directions, apartment complexes, offices. Pronounce the letter as in French: « bâtiment A » = [ba.ti.mɑ̃ a]. You may also see « bâtiment B », « bâtiment principal », or abbreviations like « bât. A » on schedules and plans.
target_language_example: La réunion a lieu dans le bâtiment A, salle 203.
native_language_example: The meeting takes place in building A, room 203.

meaning: 'the baby has' (third-person singular of avoir used in present or as auxiliary in compound tenses).
additional_notes: bébé = the baby. a is the third-person singular present of avoir (to have). Used to describe what the baby has or to form compound past tenses (e.g., 'le bébé a crié' = the baby cried / the baby has cried). In simple present contexts it means 'the baby has' (possession) or functions as an auxiliary: 'le bébé a commencé...' = the baby has started / the baby started. Pronunciation: [be-be a].
target_language_example: Le bébé a faim et pleure.
native_language_example: The baby is hungry and is crying.

meaning: 'the baby has' or 'the baby did' (bébé + third-person singular of avoir).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun bébé followed by the verb avoir (to have) in the 3rd person singular: "bébé a" = "the baby has". In French, avoir is also used in some expressions where English uses different verbs (e.g. "a fait" = "did/made", "a droit à" = "is entitled to/has the right to"). Context determines the English translation.
target_language_example: Le bébé a faim et veut manger.
native_language_example: The baby is hungry and wants to eat.

meaning: "a baby with" (literal) — appears in two uses: 1) talking about having a baby with someone (romantic/parenting meaning); 2) as part of the idiom "jeter/le bébé avec l'eau du bain" meaning "to throw the baby out with the bathwater."
additional_notes: This pair of words can occur simply as the literal combination "a baby with [someone]" (e.g., "avoir un bébé avec toi" = "to have a baby with you"). However, many example sentences show the fixed idiom "jeter le bébé avec l'eau du bain," meaning to discard something valuable along with the undesirable. The idiom is not compositional (its figurative meaning doesn't follow from the words). When used literally, it's neutral; when used in the idiom, it's a common proverb-like expression.
target_language_example: Elle veut avoir un bébé avec lui, mais ils attendent d'être prêts.
native_language_example: She wants to have a baby with him, but they're waiting until they're ready.

meaning: literally 'baby in' — used when describing where a baby is (e.g., in a car seat, in arms, in a room); not a fixed expression on its own.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's the noun bébé followed by the preposition dans ('in'). You will usually see it as part of a longer phrase: bébé dans la poussette (baby in the stroller), bébé dans les bras (baby in someone's arms), bébé dans la voiture (baby in the car). Make sure to include the article or possessive after dans (dans la, dans le, dans mes, etc.).
target_language_example: Il y a un bébé dans la poussette.
native_language_example: There is a baby in the stroller.

meaning: 'the baby is' — simple present phrase used to describe a baby (state, age, condition, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun bébé (baby) followed by the verb être (to be). Use it to start sentences like «Le bébé est malade» (The baby is sick) or «Le bébé est né hier» (The baby was born yesterday — note past meaning with passé composé is more common for birth). Remember to add the subject determiner (le/un/mon) when needed: «Mon bébé est...»
target_language_example: Le bébé est fatigué.
native_language_example: The baby is tired.

meaning: the baby (with negation or emphasis using 'ne'); appears as 'the baby does not...' or in expressions about the baby
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the word bébé followed by the negative particle ne (often paired with pas, plus, que, or another negative word). In spoken French, the 'ne' is frequently dropped (e.g. «Le bébé ne parle pas» → «Le bébé parle pas»). Sometimes examples show 'bébé ne' inside a clause or sentence where the rest of the negative element comes later (e.g. ne...pas, ne...que). Also watch for informal/special uses like 'Ne dis pas' directed at the baby.
target_language_example: Le bébé ne mange pas encore de solides.
native_language_example: The baby does not eat solids yet.

meaning: used to describe something as very childish, babyish or suited for a baby (literally 'baby of/for'); often appears in expressions like 'bébé à ...' to qualify an object or style as infantile.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase; 'bébé' is noun 'baby' and 'à' can be used to link it to another noun or quality (e.g. 'bébé à bord', 'bébé à la mer' or informal descriptions like 'une voix bébé à' meaning a babyish voice). Use depends on context; it's compositional and literal. Not slang, but can be informal depending on use.
target_language_example: Un siège bébé à fixer dans la voiture.
native_language_example: A baby seat to attach in the car.

meaning: this is
additional_notes: Very common expression used to identify, present, or point out someone or something. Depending on context, it can mean 'this is', 'that is', or 'it's'. It is the contracted form of 'ce est'.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami.
native_language_example: This is my friend.

meaning: 'that is' / 'that is to say' — used to clarify, restate, or give a more precise explanation.
additional_notes: Use to introduce a clarification, explanation, rephrasing, or specification of what was just said. Can precede a simple restatement (C'est-à-dire moi = that is, me) or a more detailed explanation. Often contracted in speech (c'est-à-dire → 'c'est-à-dire' pronounced quickly).
target_language_example: Il arrivera demain, c'est-à-dire vers midi.
native_language_example: He will arrive tomorrow, that is to say around noon.

meaning: a shortened phrase meaning 'it's up to' or 'it's (someone's) turn to' when followed by a person or decision (e.g., c'est au tour de..., c'est au chef de...).
additional_notes: Alone 'c'est au' is incomplete — it needs what follows: usually 'tour de' (turn of), a person, or an infinitive/nominal phrase explaining responsibility or whose turn it is. Common in spoken and written French as part of phrases like 'c'est au tour de...' (it's ...'s turn) or 'c'est au client de décider' (it's up to the customer to decide). Word order: c'est + au + [role/person] or c'est + au + [infinitive phrase].
target_language_example: C'est au professeur de décider qui présente en premier.
native_language_example: It's up to the teacher to decide who presents first.

meaning: 'it's also this' / 'this is also...'.
additional_notes: Rarely used as a fixed phrase on its own. Combines c'est (it is/this is) + aussi (also) + ce (this/that/which). Usually appears in longer sentences to add an additional item, reason, or point: e.g. « C'est aussi ce que je pense » = "That's also what I think." Word order and surrounding words determine the exact sense.
target_language_example: C'est aussi ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That's also what I meant.

meaning: it's something/someone else; it's a different matter
additional_notes: Used to contrast or say that something is different from what was just mentioned. Often appears in longer expressions like "c'est une autre histoire" (that's another story) or "c'est autre chose" (that's something else). By itself, "c'est autre" is incomplete in standard French and sounds colloquial or truncated; learners should prefer full expressions (e.g., "c'est autre chose").
target_language_example: Il semble calme maintenant, mais avant c'était différent — là, c'est autre chose.
native_language_example: He seems calm now, but before it was different — now, that's something else.

meaning: that's it
additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with something, or to indicate that something just said is correct. Can be used alone as a short response (like "exactly" or "that's it"). Tone and context determine whether it is emphatic or neutral.
target_language_example: — Tu veux dire que le train partira à six heures ? — C'est cela.
native_language_example: — You mean the train leaves at six? — That's it.

meaning: it's this
additional_notes: A compositional phrase made of c'est ('it is/this is/that is') + cette ('this/that' before a feminine singular noun). It is usually followed by a feminine singular noun, so on its own it often feels incomplete: c'est cette robe = 'it's this dress'.
target_language_example: C'est cette robe que je préfère.
native_language_example: It's this dress that I prefer.

meaning: it's about
additional_notes: This short sequence appears in different contexts. Most commonly c'est de + noun or infinitive is used to mean "it's about" (e.g. c'est de la musique = it's music / c'est de parler de = it's about speaking) or to introduce the origin/author with de (c'est de Paul = it's from Paul). Be careful: French usually uses c'est + de only when followed by a noun phrase or to indicate source; many verbs require different constructions (e.g. "il s'agit de" = "it's about" for topics). The exact meaning depends on the words that follow.
target_language_example: C'est de la poésie, pas une explication.
native_language_example: It's poetry, not an explanation.

meaning: This exact phrase is not a fixed French expression; literal meaning: 'it's of the other' or 'it's from the other one.'
additional_notes: Without context, this sequence is not a common set phrase in French. It could appear in sentences like "C'est de l'autre côté" (it's on the other side) with a missing word, or in contrasts: "Ce livre est à Paul, c'est de l'autre" (colloquial/incomplete) — but that latter would be nonstandard. If you encounter it, check surrounding words: likely a word is missing (e.g. côté, part, personne). Do not use 'c'est de l'autre' by itself as a set phrase.
target_language_example: Ce sac n'est pas à moi, c'est de l'autre côté du magasin.
native_language_example: This bag isn't mine; it's on the other side of the store.

meaning: it's/that’s (followed by plural noun)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of "c'est" + "des" used before a plural noun or adjective + plural noun. In standard written French you might see "ce sont des" for formal/grammatical agreement (ce sont des livres = those are books), but spoken French often uses "c'est des": "C'est des amis." Translate as "it's/that's" or "those are" depending on context. Be careful with agreement: verbs and adjectives after may still be plural even though the phrase looks singular.
target_language_example: C'est des étudiants sympathiques.
native_language_example: They're nice students.

meaning: 'that is to say' / 'which means' (used to rephrase or emphasize what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clarification, explanation, consequence or to emphasize a point already mentioned. Often followed by a short clause or a phrase giving the effect/implication of the previous statement. Common in spoken and written French. Not literal 'it is to say' in English—use 'which means' or 'meaning' or 'that is to say'.
target_language_example: Il n'a pas dormi de la nuit, c'est dire à quel point il était stressé.
native_language_example: He didn't sleep all night, which shows how stressed he was.

meaning: literally 'it is in' — usually the start of a phrase like 'c'est en + verb/participle' to mean 'it's by/while/in doing ...' or part of fixed expressions (incomplete by itself).
additional_notes: Alone, 'c'est en' is not a complete expression in French; it typically begins a clause such as 'c'est en faisant X que ...' (It's by doing X that ...) or 'c'est en + noun/adjective' used within a larger sentence. Expect a verb in the -ant (present participle) after it when expressing 'by/while doing ...'. Example patterns: 'C'est en pratiquant que l'on progresse.' (It's by practicing that one improves.) Also appears in locative phrases like 'C'est en ville' ('It's in town'), where 'en' is a preposition — again requiring more context to be grammatical.
target_language_example: C'est en travaillant tous les jours que j'ai appris rapidement.
native_language_example: It's by working every day that I learned quickly.

meaning: it's out / it's excluded / it's outside (something)
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase often followed by a noun or prepositional phrase (e.g. « c'est hors de prix », « c'est hors sujet »). Alone, "c'est hors" is uncommon in spoken French; you normally add what it's outside of. Can express that something is beyond a limit, excluded, irrelevant, or too expensive depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est hors de prix — je ne peux pas l'acheter.
native_language_example: It's overpriced — I can't buy it.

meaning: it's just at/near (a place or time).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining c'est (it is), juste (just/exactly/near), and au (to the/at the). Used to point out that something is located very close to or occurs right at a specific place/time. You'll usually hear it followed by a location or time (e.g., 'c'est juste au coin' or 'c'est juste au début'). Informal and conversational; tone and exact meaning depend on context.
target_language_example: C'est juste au coin, tu verras le café.
native_language_example: It's just around the corner, you'll see the café.

meaning: 'that's life' — used to accept or resign oneself to something disappointing or unchangeable.
additional_notes: A common French expression used to shrug off misfortune, setbacks, or inevitabilities. Can be used on its own (Mais c'est la vie) or with a question tag (C'est la vie, hein?) to invite agreement. Tone ranges from resigned to slightly humorous. Not formal or slang — it's neutral and widely used in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Il a raté le train, mais c'est la vie.
native_language_example: He missed the train, but that's life.

meaning: it's the
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French before a plural noun, but in more formal or careful French, "ce sont les" is usually preferred. It is often used to identify plural people or things, or in common expressions like "c'est les vacances".
target_language_example: C'est les vacances !
native_language_example: It's the holidays!

meaning: 'it's now' or 'now is the time' (used to say that something should happen immediately or starts now).
additional_notes: A combination of c'est (it is/this is) + maintenant (now). Used to indicate that the present moment is the time for something. Can introduce a statement about urgency or timing: e.g. c'est maintenant que... (it's now that...). Tone depends on context; not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: C'est maintenant qu'il faut décider.
native_language_example: Now is the time to decide.

meaning: these are my...
additional_notes: colloquial, non-standard French sometimes used before a plural noun, instead of standard ce sont mes.... You may hear it in speech, but beginners should usually learn and use ce sont mes... in careful French.
target_language_example: C'est mes amis là-bas.
native_language_example: Those are my friends over there.

meaning: it's me
additional_notes: Used to identify oneself as the person responsible or involved; often followed by a clause introduced with qui or qu' to emphasize 'I' did something (e.g. "c'est moi qui l'ai fait" = "I'm the one who did it"). Can be used simply to answer "Who?" ("C'est moi." = "It's me.").
target_language_example: C'est moi qui ai oublié les clés.
native_language_example: I'm the one who forgot the keys.

meaning: it's a no / that's a refusal
additional_notes: Used to give a firm negative answer or to emphasize that something is not allowed or accepted. Slightly more emphatic than a simple "non"; common in spoken French. Can follow or replace a full sentence (e.g., "C'est non, on ne peut pas") and may sound a bit blunt.
target_language_example: Tu peux emprunter ma voiture ? — C'est non, j'en ai besoin aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Can you borrow my car? — It's a no, I need it today.

meaning: It's us / We're the ones (responsible or present).
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining 'c'est' (it is/this is) + 'nous' (us/we). Often used to identify people ('It's us'), to claim responsibility ('we're the ones who did it'), or to say 'we're next' in informal contexts. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation. Can be used as an answer to a door, in introductions, or when taking credit.
target_language_example: Qui vient chercher les billets ? — C'est nous.
native_language_example: Who is coming to pick up the tickets? — It's us.

meaning: It's a yes / that's a yes (used to confirm an affirmative decision).
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to state or confirm that the answer or decision is 'yes'. Often used in conversation to emphasize that something has been accepted or agreed to. Context determines tone (casual, decisive, sometimes playful).
target_language_example: Après réflexion, c'est oui, j'accepte ton invitation.
native_language_example: After thinking about it, it's a yes, I accept your invitation.

meaning: 'it's by' or 'it's through' (usually the start of a phrase: c'est par + [quelque chose])
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase on its own — French speakers normally use 'c'est par' as the beginning of a clause meaning 'it is by/through [something]' or to indicate cause, means, or authorship (e.g. 'C'est par amour' = 'It's out of love', 'C'est par lui que...'). You will almost always see it followed by a noun, pronoun, or relative clause. Not used alone as a full sentence.
target_language_example: C'est par lui que la décision a été prise.
native_language_example: It was through him that the decision was made.

meaning: 'let's go' / 'here we go' / 'it's started'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is starting or that you're ready to begin. Common in spoken French: can announce the start of an action, a trip, a meeting, or that something happened on its own (depending on context). Tone can be enthusiastic or neutral.
target_language_example: OK, c'est parti pour la réunion !
native_language_example: OK, let's go for the meeting!

meaning: that's why; therefore; for that reason.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result or explanation. Common in spoken and written French. It connects a cause (previous idea) to its consequence. Can be followed by a clause or a short phrase. Formality: neutral—works in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, c'est pourquoi nous sommes restés à la maison.
native_language_example: It was raining, that's why we stayed home.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation or reason (equivalent to "it's just that" / "the thing is that").
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in spoken French as "c'est que..." followed by a clause. The sequence "c'est que ce" is less common by itself; when it occurs it's typically followed by a negation or a demonstrative clause (e.g. "c'est que ce n'est pas..." or "c'est que ce...
target_language_example: C'est que ce n'est pas si simple que tu le crois.
native_language_example: It's just that it's not as simple as you think.

meaning: This phrase as written is incomplete/ungrammatical in French; likely an error. 'C'est' means 'it is/this is' and needs a noun, adjective, or clause after it. 'Quelque' means 'some' or 'somewhat' but must be followed by a noun (quelque chose) or used as an adverb (quelque peu).
additional_notes: You will rarely (if ever) see 'c'est quelque' by itself. Possible intended phrases: "c'est quelque chose" (that's something), "c'est quelque part" (it's somewhere), or "c'est quelque peu" (it's somewhat — more formal). If you want to say 'it's something,' use "c'est quelque chose." If you want 'some' before a noun, use "c'est quelque + noun" but be careful: spoken French often uses "quelque" before a noun without agreement (quelque chose is fixed).
target_language_example: C'est quelque chose qui m'inquiète.
native_language_example: It's something that worries me.

meaning: It's started again / here we go again.
additional_notes: Used when something restarts or repeats (often with a sense of resignation, amusement, or inevitability). Commonly appears as the fuller phrase "C'est reparti pour un tour." Can be used for events restarting, repetitive situations, or when something happens again unexpectedly.
target_language_example: Oh non, la réunion dépasse encore le temps prévu — c'est reparti.
native_language_example: Oh no, the meeting is running over again — here we go again.

meaning: literally 'it/this is without' — used to indicate something lacks or is provided without something (often followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining c'est (it is/this is) + sans (without). It must be completed by the thing that is missing or absent: e.g. "C'est sans intérêt" (it's without interest / it's pointless) or "C'est sans gluten" (it's gluten-free). Alone it feels incomplete in many contexts and is usually followed by a noun or adjective. Not an idiom; purely compositional.
target_language_example: C'est sans gluten, vous pouvez le manger.
native_language_example: It's gluten-free, you can eat it.

meaning: 'it's certain' / 'for sure' / 'definitely'.
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to express certainty or agreement. Standard spelling is "c'est sûr" (with circumflex on sûr). Writing it as "c'est sur" without the accent is a common mistake in informal contexts but may be encountered. Can be used alone as a short answer or within a sentence.
target_language_example: Tu viens demain ? — C'est sur.
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? — Definitely.

meaning: 'it's all about' / 'it's only for' (depends on context) — part of phrases like "c'est tout à fait" or "c'est tout à [infinitive]".
additional_notes: Alone, "c'est tout à" is incomplete and needs more words to form a full expression. Common completions: "c'est tout à fait" (it's completely/absolutely), "c'est tout à fait normal" (that's completely normal), or "c'est tout à [infinitive]" in informal speech to mean "it's just to/for [verb]" (e.g. "c'est tout à essayer" — it's just to try). Don't use "c'est tout à" by itself in formal writing.
target_language_example: C'est tout à fait possible.
native_language_example: It's completely possible.

meaning: that's all
additional_notes: Used to indicate that nothing more needs to be said or done, or to downplay/explain something briefly. Can be added at the end of a sentence to close a topic or to minimize an explanation ('I'm just... that's all'). Tone depends on context and intonation: neutral, dismissive, or final.
target_language_example: Je voulais juste aider, c'est tout.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help, that's all.

meaning: literally 'it's about' or 'it's roughly' (used to introduce an approximate amount or description)
additional_notes: This is an informal abbreviated phrase often completed as 'c'est à peu près' meaning 'it's about/approximately'. On its own 'c'est à peu' feels incomplete in standard French; learners will usually hear or read the full expression 'c'est à peu près'. Use to indicate approximation (time, quantity, estimate).
target_language_example: C'est à peu près dix minutes pour y aller.
native_language_example: It's about ten minutes to get there.

meaning: that's appropriate / that's timely / that is relevant
additional_notes: Used to say something is suitable, well-timed, or relevant to the situation. Can comment on a remark, an action, or timing. Tone is neutral; not idiomatic slang. Close to 'c'est pertinent' (it's relevant) or 'c'est bienvenu' (it's welcome).
target_language_example: Ta remarque arrive juste — c'est à propos.
native_language_example: Your comment comes at the right time — that's timely/appropriate.

meaning: that's it
additional_notes: Very common conversational phrase. Can confirm something ("that's right"), indicate you've identified something or finished ("that's it"), or emphasize what you mean ("that's what I mean"). Context and intonation determine the exact sense. Often used alone as a short response.
target_language_example: C'est ça, tu as compris.
native_language_example: That's right, you understood.

meaning: 'ça vous' is used when 'ça' (that/it) is followed by 'vous' (formal or plural 'you') as object — commonly appears in questions like 'ça vous va ?' (does that suit you?) or 'ça vous dérange ?' (does that bother you?).
additional_notes: Written form normally uses the cedilla: 'ça vous'. 'Ça vous' by itself isn't a complete sentence; it's typically followed by a verb or clause. 'Vous' here is the formal singular or plural 'you'. Informal singular equivalent is 'ça te'. Pronunciation: 'ça' /sa/ and 'vous' /vu/.
target_language_example: Ca vous va si on décale la réunion ?
native_language_example: Does that work for you if we move the meeting?

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase — looks like part of a verb phrase meaning 'hides something' (literally 'hides + something').
additional_notes: This is not a complete set phrase in French; it's the verb 'cacher' conjugated in the present (cache) followed by an unspecified object (quelque = 'some' / part of 'quelque chose'). By itself 'cache quelque' is incomplete and uncommon. You will more often see: 'il/elle cache quelque chose' (he/she hides something) or 'il/elle cache quelqu'un' (he/she hides someone). 'Quelque' before a noun means 'some' (quelque chose = something, quelque part = somewhere when combined with part). Use the full constructions rather than 'cache quelque' alone.
target_language_example: Elle cache quelque chose sous la table.
native_language_example: She is hiding something under the table.

meaning: 'to hide the' (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Verbe 'cacher' (to hide) + article 'la' (feminine singular). Use 'cacher le' for masculine, 'cacher les' for plural. Can refer to hiding physical objects or abstract things (la vérité). Verb appears in different tenses (essayer de cacher, a caché, essaya de cacher, etc.). Ensure correct agreement and placement of pronouns and negation (e.g. je ne vais pas cacher la vérité).
target_language_example: Tom a essayé de cacher la vérité.
native_language_example: Tom tried to hide the truth.

meaning: 'a gift from my' (used before a male family member or masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that something was given to the speaker by a male person (e.g., mon père, mon mari, mon grand-père). Follow with the person who gave the gift. If the giver is feminine, use 'cadeau de ma'. For plural or formal constructions you might use 'cadeau de mes' or 'cadeau de M.' (Monsieur). Commonly appears in spoken and written French to indicate origin/possession.
target_language_example: C'est un cadeau de mon frère.
native_language_example: It's a gift from my brother.

meaning: 'café' followed by the preposition 'à' (written without accent here) — typically used to link 'café' to another word indicating purpose, flavor, location, or style (e.g. café à emporter, café à la vanille). Note: correct French spelling uses the accented 'à'.
additional_notes: The sequence 'café à' is not a fixed idiom by itself. It is compositional: 'à' connects 'café' to a noun, adjective, or infinitive to express purpose, flavor, origin, or location. Common correct forms include 'café à emporter' (coffee to take away), 'café à la vanille' (vanilla-flavored coffee), 'café à Paris' (coffee in Paris). The entry uses the unaccented form 'café a' because the user requested that exact token; in actual French writing the preposition should be 'à' with a grave accent.
target_language_example: Je prendrai un café a emporter ce matin.
native_language_example: I'll take a coffee to go this morning.

meaning: 'coffee with' — the start of a phrase like 'café au lait' (coffee with milk).
additional_notes: By itself 'café au' is incomplete; it normally appears before a noun (e.g. lait) to mean 'coffee with [that ingredient]'. The most common collocation is 'café au lait' (coffee with milk). Pronunciation: [ka.fe o].
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café au lait, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

meaning: 'coffee in' or 'coffee at' (literal — typically part of a larger phrase like 'un café dans...' meaning a coffee inside/at a place).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun "café" (coffee or café/coffee shop) followed by the preposition "dans" (in/inside). You will usually see it as part of longer expressions, for example "un café dans le salon" (a coffee in the living room) or "prendre un café dans un bistrot" (to have a coffee at a bistro). Use "dans" to indicate being inside or within something. For location at/in a place, French also commonly uses "au/à la/aux" before a place name (e.g. "un café au coin de la rue").
target_language_example: On prend un café dans ce petit café du quartier ?
native_language_example: Shall we have a coffee in this little neighborhood café?

meaning: Not a standard French expression; likely a typo or a mixing of French and English. 'café' means 'coffee' or 'coffee shop' in French; 'me' is English and not used after nouns in French.
additional_notes: 'café me' is ungrammatical in French. Possible intended French alternatives: 'un café pour moi' or 'un café, s'il vous plaît' (a coffee for me / a coffee, please). If 'café me' appears in informal bilingual contexts, it may reflect code-switching or an English speaker inserting 'me' after a French noun. Use the proper French construction with 'pour moi' or a polite request form.
target_language_example: Café me ne veut rien dire en français — dites plutôt «un café pour moi».
native_language_example: "Café me" doesn't mean anything in French — say "a coffee for me" instead.

meaning: black coffee (coffee without milk or cream).
additional_notes: Common phrase in cafés and everyday speech. Implies coffee served without milk; sugar may or may not be added depending on context (you can say 'sans sucre' to specify no sugar). Also used as a short request: 'Un café noir' = 'I'll have a black coffee.'
target_language_example: Je prendrai un café noir, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a black coffee, please.

meaning: coffee without (something); usually short for 'café sans sucre' or 'café sans lait' — 'coffee without...'.
additional_notes: This is an abbreviated way to order coffee without an ingredient. In spoken French you might hear 'un café, sans' when context makes clear what is omitted (sugar, milk, etc.). Better to specify: 'un café sans sucre' (no sugar) or 'un café sans lait' (no milk).
target_language_example: Un café sans sucre, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A coffee without sugar, please.

meaning: Not a correct fixed phrase. It appears to combine 'café' (coffee) and 'tous' (every).
additional_notes: French does not use 'café tous' as a set phrase. In the example sentences you would say 'café tous les matins' (coffee every morning) or 'tous les matins, je bois du café' (every morning I drink coffee). 'Tous' must be followed by a time period with the definite article (e.g., 'tous les matins', 'tous les jours').
