By itself it is incomplete; you normally need the rest of the sentence to identify what 'la' refers to.
target_language_example: Il a oublié de me dire la vérité avant de partir.
native_language_example: He forgot to tell me the truth before leaving.

meaning: 'to tell me something' (incomplete fragment)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own. It appears as part of longer constructions like «de me dire quelque chose» (to tell me something) or «de me dire quelque part» (to tell me somewhere) depending on context. Alone, 'quelque' is anomalous and typically requires completion (e.g., 'quelque chose', 'quelque part', 'quelquefois'). The fragment 'de me dire quelque' can occur in spoken hesitation or in clipped text but is grammatically incomplete by itself.
target_language_example: Il vient de me dire quelque, mais je n'ai pas bien entendu la fin.
native_language_example: He just told me something, but I didn't hear the end clearly.

meaning: to take me / to pick me up (depends on context); literally 'of/to take me'.
additional_notes: A fragment often seen after verbs that require 'de' + infinitive (e.g. 'arrêter de me prendre', 'essayer de me prendre'). Can mean 'to take me' (physically pick up/transport) or figuratively 'to catch/take advantage of me' depending on the verb and context. Not a standalone phrase — it must be attached to another verb.
target_language_example: Il a proposé de me prendre à la gare.
native_language_example: He offered to pick me up at the station.

meaning: of/about a guy; (used after nouns/adjectives to indicate 'guy' type or belonging to a guy).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Mec' = guy/bloke. 'de mec' often appears in phrases like 'une copine de mec' (a guy's girlfriend) or 'un truc de mec' (a guy thing). It can indicate possession/association (belonging to a man) or describe something typical of men. Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: C'est un cadeau de mec, pas pour moi.
native_language_example: It's a guy's present, not for me.

meaning: of better / better (as part of a comparative phrase)
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase on its own. 'De meilleur' commonly appears before a noun to express that something is better than something else (e.g. 'un produit de meilleur qualité' — though note that standard French prefers 'de meilleure qualité' with adjective agreement). More commonly used forms for comparisons are 'meilleur(e)(s)' after the noun (un film meilleur) or 'meilleur que' (better than). Pay attention to gender and number: 'meilleur' (masc. sing.), 'meilleure' (fem. sing.), 'meilleurs' (masc. pl.), 'meilleures' (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Elle cherche un sac de meilleure qualité.
native_language_example: She is looking for a bag of better quality.

meaning: a vulgar intensifier meaning 'fucking' or 'damn' (expresses contempt toward the noun it follows).
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Placed after a noun to insult it or show strong negative emotion about the person/thing (e.g., 'enflure de merde' = 'fucking bastard' / 'shitty bastard'). Can be added after exclamations for emphasis ('Bon Diable de merde!' — strong curse). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Sale menteur de merde !
native_language_example: You filthy lying bastard!

meaning: 'my balls' used as a vulgar intensifier expressing contempt or dismissal (English equivalents: 'my ass', 'yeah right')
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Attaches after a noun or phrase to mock, belittle, or show disbelief/anger about what was said (e.g. 'X de mes couilles' ≈ 'X my ass'). Common in spoken/informal contexts among people who use strong profanity; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Tu es un expert, de mes couilles !
native_language_example: You're an expert, my ass!

meaning: an ironic or dismissive interjection like 'yeah, right' / 'as if' / 'my foot' used to express disbelief or contempt.
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat rude; used after a noun or phrase to show scorn, sarcasm or to mock what was just said. Not literal — it doesn't mean 'of my two'. Tone and context convey the insult. Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Tu vas devenir médecin, de mes deux !
native_language_example: You’re going to become a doctor, yeah right!

meaning: part of the expression 'de mieux en mieux' meaning 'more and more' or 'better and better' (used to show increasing intensity or improvement).
additional_notes: Alone 'de mieux en' is incomplete; it appears in the fixed expression 'de mieux en mieux' (or less commonly 'de pire en pire' for worsening). Use to say something is improving or happening increasingly: 'Il va de mieux en mieux' = 'He is getting better and better.'
target_language_example: Sa santé va de mieux en mieux.
native_language_example: His health is getting better and better.

meaning: 'better and better' / 'improving more and more'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, person, or thing is progressively improving over time. Can be used alone as a short reaction (like 'even better' or 'getting better'). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Après la pause, tout va de mieux en mieux.
native_language_example: After the break, everything is getting better and better.

meaning: of minutes / minutes of (time) — used to indicate a quantity or duration in minutes after a number (e.g. '10 de minutes' is nonstandard; see notes).
additional_notes: Alone, 'de minutes' is not a standard standalone phrase in French. French normally expresses minutes with the noun 'minute(s)' directly after a number: '10 minutes', 'il reste 5 minutes'. 'de minutes' can appear as part of longer constructions after certain quantifiers or expressions that require 'de' + plural noun: e.g. 'une dizaine de minutes' (about ten minutes), 'quelques dizaines de minutes'. Do not say 'dix de minutes' — say 'dix minutes'.
target_language_example: Une dizaine de minutes suffira.
native_language_example: About ten minutes will be enough.

meaning: appropriate, fitting, or advisable in a given situation
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that something is customary, suitable, or expected in the circumstances (often with abstract nouns like 'solidarité', 'remerciements', 'égalité'). Common in formal or neutral registers. Structure: [noun] + est/sont + de mise or quelque chose serait de mise.
target_language_example: Un peu de prudence serait de mise aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: A bit of caution would be appropriate today.

meaning: 'of me' or 'from me' when followed by a demonstrative or clause — marked/emphatic word order; roughly 'as for me, this...'/literally 'of/from me this'
additional_notes: This sequence (de moi ce) is uncommon in neutral everyday French and often appears in literary, poetic, or highly emphatic contexts where the speaker isolates 'de moi' before continuing with 'ce ...'. More natural alternatives for most contexts are 'de moi', 'pour moi', or 'quant à moi'. Use with care; preserves literal translation in certain constructions but sounds marked.
target_language_example: De moi ce que j'affirme, c'est que la vérité doit prévaloir.
native_language_example: Of me, what I assert is that the truth must prevail.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase in French; literally 'of/from me a/one' and usually occurs where 'de moi' is followed by 'une' as part of a larger sentence (possession, source, or partitive).
additional_notes: This sequence does not function as an independent idiom. It appears when 'de moi' (of/from me) is immediately followed by the feminine indefinite article 'une' and a noun: e.g. in a longer clause where word order or punctuation places 'de moi une' together. Always check the full sentence — the words are compositional rather than an established phrase. Avoid using 'de moi une' as a standalone expression.
target_language_example: Il a pris de moi une réponse honnête.
native_language_example: He took from me an honest answer.

meaning: from me to (someone/thing) — indicates movement, transfer, or direction starting at 'me'.
additional_notes: Used when specifying the origin of an action, object, or message that goes from the speaker to someone or something else. Often followed by a person or place: de moi à toi (from me to you), de moi à la réception (from me to the front desk). In spoken French 'moi' may be replaced by a subject pronoun depending on sentence structure (e.g., 'de moi' after a preposition).
target_language_example: Le cadeau est parti de moi à toi.
native_language_example: The gift went from me to you.

meaning: part of a comparative expression meaning 'by less and less' or 'with decreasing ...' (used in phrases like 'de moins en moins' = 'less and less').
additional_notes: This fragment usually appears in the full expression 'de moins en moins' to indicate a gradual decrease (e.g., 'de moins en moins populaire' = 'less and less popular'). It can combine with adjectives, adverbs or nouns. Alone it's incomplete and not used by itself; learners should learn the full phrase 'de moins en moins'.
target_language_example: Il devient de moins en moins patient.
native_language_example: He is becoming less and less patient.

meaning: less and less; gradually decreasing over time.
additional_notes: Used to describe a progressive decline in quantity, frequency, intensity, or degree. Placed after a verb (Il dort de moins en moins) or before an adjective/adverb (de moins en moins nombreux / vite). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je vois mes amis de moins en moins.
native_language_example: I see my friends less and less.

meaning: literally "of months"; a fragment used in larger expressions to indicate a period measured in months or to link months to another noun (e.g., "une période de mois"). Often incomplete on its own and normally appears within constructions like "un mois de...", "des mois de...", or after a number as "X mois".
additional_notes: "De mois" by itself is uncommon and typically requires a determiner or number before/after to be grammatically correct in normal usage. It appears in phrases such as "un mois de congé" (a month of leave), "des mois de travail" (months of work), or as part of time expressions extended by "de" (e.g., "une série de mois secs"). Do not confuse with "deux mois" (two months) where "de" is not the preposition but part of a numeral phrase. Context determines whether you need a determiner or number.
target_language_example: Il a passé des mois de maladie, et ces de mois ont été difficiles.
native_language_example: He spent months being ill, and those months were difficult.

meaning: 'to show' (infinitive form introduced by the preposition 'de')
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb 'montrer' preceded by 'de'. In French, 'de' commonly appears before an infinitive after certain expressions (e.g., 'c'est le moment de...', 'demandez-lui de...'). It means 'to show' or 'to point out' depending on context. Watch for constructions: 'de montrer' itself doesn't add meaning beyond linking the verb to the preceding expression. 'Montrer' can mean to display something, to point at someone ('montrer du doigt'), or to demonstrate an action or feeling.
target_language_example: Ils ont décidé de montrer les photos au public.
native_language_example: They decided to show the photos to the public.

meaning: of mule / made of mule (literal); used in compound nouns or expressions referring to something related to a mule (animal) or a mule-style shoe
additional_notes: Alone, 'de mule' is just the preposition 'de' + noun 'mule'. It can appear in phrases like 'chaussure de mule' (mule shoe) or 'selle de mule' (mule saddle). Not a fixed idiom by itself. Pay attention to context and gender/number agreement (de la mule / des mules) when needed.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté une paire de mules en cuir.
native_language_example: She bought a pair of leather mules (backless shoes).

meaning: of (one's) mother; indicating origin, relation, or attribution to the mother
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show that something belongs to, comes from, or is characteristic of the mother (e.g., 'le nom de mère' = mother's name). Often appears in longer phrases like 'du côté de ma mère' (on my mother's side) or in possessive constructions with 'la mère de...' In French, possession more commonly uses 'la mère de [person]' rather than 'de mère' alone; 'de mère' without context is unusual and typically part of a larger expression.
target_language_example: Je connais la tradition de mère en fille dans cette famille.
native_language_example: I know the mother-to-daughter tradition in this family.

meaning: from memory; by memory; relating to memory (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- 'de mémoire' alone or after a verb means 'from memory' or 'by heart' (e.g. drawing, reciting without looking). 
- In phrases about 'trous de mémoire' or 'perte de mémoire' it relates to memory (memory lapses, memory loss). 
Context decides translation: literal 'from memory' for actions done without reference; when used in medical/psychological contexts it links to 'memory' (e.g. memory loss).
target_language_example: Il a récité le poème de mémoire.
native_language_example: He recited the poem from memory.

meaning: 'in the same way', 'likewise', or 'also'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate similarity or to suggest doing the same action. Can mean 'likewise' when responding (e.g., 'Same to you') or 'in the same manner' when comparing actions. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Si tu m'aides, je ferai de même pour toi.
native_language_example: If you help me, I'll do the same for you.

meaning: 'by birth' / 'from birth' (indicates something present or true since the time of birth)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that the quality, condition, place, or thing relates to someone's birth (e.g., lieu de naissance = place of birth; aveugle de naissance = blind from birth). Common in descriptions (medical, legal, biographical). Not idiomatic — literal and transparent.
target_language_example: Il est citoyen français de naissance.
native_language_example: He is a French citizen by birth.

meaning: to not
additional_notes: Not usually a fixed expression by itself. It most often appears in structures like de ne pas + infinitive after verbs or expressions that take de, and it corresponds to English "not to" or "to not": essayer de ne pas oublier = "to try not to forget."
target_language_example: J'essaie de ne pas oublier mes clés.
native_language_example: I'm trying not to forget my keys.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase — sequence of words that can appear together in negative constructions with a pronoun (e.g. "de" + "ne" + "le").
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression. It can occur when a clause contains a negation with "ne" and a direct object pronoun "le" and another word "de" appears nearby (for example after certain verbs or prepositions). Word order in French is important: object pronouns (le, la, les) usually come before the verb (Je le vois), while negation wraps the verb with "ne...pas" (Je ne le vois pas). "De" is often a preposition or part of an infinitive construction (avoir besoin de, décider de). Beginners should not treat "de ne le" as a single unit; instead learn negation (ne...pas, ne...plus, ne...jamais) and pronoun placement separately.
target_language_example: Il a décidé de ne le dire à personne.
native_language_example: He decided not to tell it to anyone.

meaning: to not say it / to not tell it
additional_notes: This phrase is the infinitive construction with negation: de + ne + le + dire. It appears after verbs like promettre, devoir, or se souvenir (e.g. promettre de ne le dire à personne). 'Le' refers to 'it' (a secret or piece of information). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: promettre de ne le dire → promettre de le dire (with ne omitted) is common but less formal; however dropping 'ne' changes meaning if not careful. The full negative construction is 'ne ... pas/plus/etc.' here only 'ne' plus the object pronoun expresses 'not to tell it'.
target_language_example: Il a juré de ne le dire à personne.
native_language_example: He swore not to tell it to anyone.

meaning: relating to a wedding; of the wedding (used in phrases like 'lune de noces' = honeymoon)
additional_notes: A formal/literary adjective phrase used after a noun to specify that something is connected to a wedding. Common in set phrases such as 'lune de noces' (honeymoon) or 'voile de noces' (wedding veil). Often appears in fixed expressions rather than used productively.
target_language_example: Ils partiront en lune de noces la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: They will leave on their honeymoon next week.

meaning: nowadays; these days; in the present time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the present era or current habits/conditions, often to contrast with the past. Common in both formal and neutral registers. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: De nos jours, beaucoup de gens travaillent à distance.
native_language_example: Nowadays, many people work remotely.

meaning: literally 'of/from us it' — not a fixed phrase; a sequence that appears in sentences where 'le' refers back to something and 'de nous' marks a relationship with 'us' (e.g. possession, source, or object of a preposition).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. You will encounter 'de nous le' inside larger sentences where 'de nous' (of/from us) links something to 'us' and 'le' is a direct object pronoun referring to a masculine singular thing already mentioned. Word order in French often places object pronouns (like 'le') before the verb: e.g. 'Il nous le donne' = 'He gives it to us.' In other contexts 'de nous' may follow a noun (la décision de nous) and 'le' could be a separate pronoun; make sure to analyze the whole sentence to understand the role of each part.
target_language_example: Ils l'ont pris de nous le lendemain.
native_language_example: They took it from us the next day.

meaning: again
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens another time or is restored to a previous state. Slightly more formal/neutral than 'encore' in some contexts; interchangeable with 'à nouveau' in many cases. Follows verb or adjective phrases (e.g., 'être de nouveau', 'arriver de nouveau').
target_language_example: Il est de nouveau heureux.
native_language_example: He is happy again.

meaning: 'news' (information about someone or something) or 'some new [things]' (part of a noun phrase using the adjective 'nouvelles').
additional_notes: Appears in contexts like "prendre des nouvelles" (to ask after someone's well-being) or as part of a noun phrase (e.g. "de nouvelles idées"). Alone, "de nouvelles" requires surrounding words to determine if "nouvelles" is a noun (news) or adjective (new). The sequence includes the preposition/article form "de" and the plural feminine adjective/noun "nouvelles"; watch for agreement and the presence of "des" vs "de" depending on negation, quantity, or modification.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas encore eu de nouvelles de Paul.
native_language_example: I haven't received any news from Paul yet.

meaning: at night / nighttime (used to describe something happening or used during the night).
additional_notes: Used to indicate night-time occurrence or a night-related object. When describing jobs or activities, 'de nuit' means 'night' as in night shift (e.g., 'travaille de nuit' = works at night). In compounds like 'table de nuit' it means an object related to the bedroom/night (a bedside table). Word order: usually follows the noun ('équipe de nuit', 'service de nuit', 'lampe de nuit').
target_language_example: Elle fait des gardes de nuit à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: She does night shifts at the hospital.

meaning: from nowhere; appearing or coming from no recognizable place or origin
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something appears suddenly with no clear origin, or to describe a very remote/isolated place (le centre de nulle part). Common in narratives: 'il est sorti de nulle part' = he appeared out of nowhere. Can be literal (remote location) or figurative (ideas, people).
target_language_example: Une voiture est arrivée de nulle part.
native_language_example: A car came out of nowhere.

meaning: of/from nowhere; (part of expressions meaning 'no ...' or 'from no ...')
additional_notes: Alone, 'de nulle' is not a complete phrase in French; it appears as the start of expressions like 'de nulle part' (from nowhere) or 'de nulle utilité' (of no use). It usually combines with another word (e.g., 'part', 'utilité', 'importance') to form a negative or negating idea. Pay attention to agreement and article use in full expressions.
target_language_example: Cette information vient de nulle part.
native_language_example: This information comes from nowhere.

meaning: of number / number's (possession or specification)
additional_notes: A short prepositional phrase combining 'de' (of/from) with 'numéro' (number). Used to show possession, origin, specification (e.g. le titre de numéro — the title of the issue/number) or to link a noun to a numbered item (le chapitre de numéro 3 → chapter number 3). In many contexts French prefers 'numéro de' (number of) rather than 'de numéro'; word order matters (e.g. 'le numéro de téléphone' = the phone number). 'De numéro' may appear when 'numéro' follows and is modified: 'la maison de numéro 5' (the house numbered 5).
target_language_example: La maison de numéro 5 se trouve au bout de la rue.
native_language_example: The house with number 5 is at the end of the street.

meaning: of pairs; used to count or refer to pairs of items (e.g., shoes, socks).
additional_notes: Used after an expression of quantity (combien de, trop de, etc.) to specify 'pairs' as the unit. Common with items that naturally come in pairs (chaussures, chaussettes, gants). Grammar: in questions use 'combien de paires de X' or 'de combien de paires de X' (both are correct).
target_language_example: J'ai trois de paires de chaussettes dans mon tiroir.
native_language_example: I have three pairs of socks in my drawer.

meaning: of parents / from parents (shows possession or origin related to parents)
additional_notes: A short phrase using the preposition de + plural noun parents. Commonly appears in contexts indicating possession (les conseils de parents = parents' advice), origin (une lettre de parents = a letter from parents), or composition (un foyer de parents = a parents' household). Use appropriate article or determiner as needed (les parents, des parents).
target_language_example: Nous avons reçu une lettre de parents d'élèves.
native_language_example: We received a letter from parents of students.

meaning: 'please' (polite/formal request: 'I beg/ask you')
additional_notes: Used to make polite or formal requests or commands. Often follows an imperative or is included in phrases like 'Arrêtez de parler, je vous prie' (Please stop talking). Tone is formal/polite; common in written or polite spoken French. Not used for casual requests with friends—use 's'il te plaît' instead.
target_language_example: Arrêtez de parler, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Please stop talking.

meaning: of (one's) word; trustworthy—keeps promises.
additional_notes: Used after nouns like "homme" or "femme" to say someone keeps their word (reliable, trustworthy). Common fixed expression: "être un homme de parole" = to be a man of one's word / to be trustworthy. Not used literally as 'of speech'.
target_language_example: Elle est une femme de parole : quand elle promet quelque chose, elle le fait.
native_language_example: She is a woman of her word: when she promises something, she does it.

meaning: 'something specific' / 'anything particular' (used in questions like "anything in particular that…")
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions: "Y a-t-il quelque chose de particulier que... ?" which asks if the person wants or prefers anything specific (to eat, drink, watch, etc.). Often used with vouloir (tu/vous vouliez/veux) or other verbs. Polite and neutral register.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose de particulier que tu voudrais manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is there anything particular you'd like to eat tonight?

meaning: 'of particular that you' — not a standalone fixed phrase; a fragment that can appear inside longer constructions such as quelque chose de particulier que vous ... (something specific that you ...).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common fixed phrase by itself. It typically appears as part of a larger clause (e.g., quelque chose de particulier que vous cherchez / que vous voulez). For expressing "especially you," use en particulier vous or tout particulièrement vous. For "something specific that you...", use quelque chose de particulier que vous + verb. The fragment should be followed by a verb or noun to complete the sentence.
target_language_example: Avez-vous quelque chose de particulier que vous voudriez montrer ?
native_language_example: Do you have something specific that you would like to show?

meaning: Not a standalone negation in modern standard French; 'pas' is the common negative particle used with 'ne' (ne ... pas). 'De pas' as a two-word sequence is uncommon and usually appears only inside specific constructions or regional/colloquial uses; it does not function as an independent phrase meaningfully apart from contexts where 'de' and 'pas' are adjacent for grammatical reasons.
additional_notes: 'De pas' is not a separate negation like 'ne ... pas'. You will rarely see 'de pas' as an intentional fixed expression in standard French. It can appear when 'de' precedes a negative phrase or in some fixed or archaic expressions, or through elision/liaison across words (e.g., after certain prepositions). For learning purposes, focus on 'ne ... pas' (and on hearing 'pas' alone in spoken French). Avoid treating 'de pas' as a single lexical item.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de pas dans cette phrase.
native_language_example: There are no 'steps' (or no 'pas') in this sentence.

meaning: passing through; just visiting temporarily.
additional_notes: Used to say you are only staying briefly or are temporarily at a place (e.g., traveling, on a short trip, at someone's home or at work for a short time). Common in phrases like 'je suis de passage' (I'm just passing through/visiting). Not formal or slang—neutral everyday expression.
target_language_example: Je suis de passage en ville pour deux jours.
native_language_example: I'm just passing through town for two days.

meaning: a truncated/informal fragment of "passer à autre chose" meaning 'to move on to something else' or 'to switch to another thing'. As given, it is incomplete and normally requires a noun (e.g., "chose") after "autre"; it can appear in casual speech or clipped forms when context supplies the missing word.
additional_notes: This form is elliptical and not standard on its own; more correct full form: "passer à autre chose". You may hear "de passer à autre" in spoken French when the remainder is implied. Use with care in writing. Context usually supplies the omitted noun.
target_language_example: Il est temps de passer à autre, on a trop parlé de ce sujet.
native_language_example: It's time to move on to something else, we've talked about this topic too much.

meaning: of the country / from the country; used to indicate origin or belonging to a country (often follows a noun).
additional_notes: Literally 'of/from country'. Commonly appears after nouns to show origin, nationality, or relation to a country (e.g., 'produit de pays' = product of the country, 'habitant de pays' = inhabitant of a country). It can combine with definite/indefinite articles (du, de la, des) depending on the noun: e.g., 'du pays' (masculine/singular), 'de la pays' is incorrect—use 'du' or 'de' + country name. When used before a country name beginning with a vowel, 'de' becomes 'd'' (d'Italie).
target_language_example: C'est un produit de pays.
native_language_example: It's a product of the country.

meaning: to think about something/someone else; to stop thinking about the current subject
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete as written in French. A more natural expression is "penser à autre chose" meaning "to think about something else" or "penser à quelqu'un d'autre" for "think of somebody else." Used to indicate changing your thoughts or distracting yourself. Often appears in constructions like "essayer de penser à autre chose" (try to think of something else) or "arrête de penser à autre chose" (stop thinking about something else).
target_language_example: Essaie de penser à autre chose pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Try to think about something else during the meeting.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment that can appear in sentences where 'de personne' (of/from/no one) is followed by 'est' (is) due to clause boundaries. Meaning depends on context and full sentence.
additional_notes: This sequence is likely a mistaken or fragmentary string. 'de personne' can mean 'of the person' (possession) or appear in negation 'de personne' in some constructions, while 'est' is the verb 'is'. Examples where the pieces appear together usually involve clause boundaries or omitted words (e.g. 'le nom de la personne est...' = 'the person's name is...'). To determine exact meaning, check surrounding words and articles ('de la personne est...' vs 'de personne est...' in negation is unusual). Common learner points: • 'personne' can be a noun ('person') or mean 'nobody' in negative contexts with 'ne...personne'. • 'de' indicates possession, origin, or partitive relationships. • 'est' is third-person singular of 'être' = 'is'.
target_language_example: Le nom de la personne est inconnu.
native_language_example: The person's name is unknown.

meaning: nobody
additional_notes: Often used after expressions with negation (e.g. ne … pas de personne is less common; more frequently used in fixed phrases like « personne » alone or « ne … personne »). When used with 'de' it can appear in contexts like « rien de personne » (rare) or set phrases; beginners will most often encounter 'personne' as 'personne' or 'ne … personne'. 'De personne' can also appear as part of possessive/statements like « ce n'est pas de personne » meaning 'it doesn't belong to anyone' but this usage is less common.
target_language_example: Il n'y avait de personne dans la salle.
native_language_example: There was nobody in the room.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct French expression. Likely a mistaken combination: 'de personnes' is valid (meaning 'of people' or 'people' after a quantity), while 'as' is English or could be a fragment of another French word. Treat as an error rather than a standard phrase.
additional_notes: 'de personnes' is the correct French multi-word unit. 'as' does not belong in standard French after 'de personnes'. Possible causes: typo, mistaken copy-paste, or mixing languages (English 'as'). If you meant a complete sentence or phrase, provide context (e.g., 'de personnes âgées' = 'of elderly people').
target_language_example: *This sequence is incorrect in French:* «de personnes as» ne figure pas dans une phrase correcte.
native_language_example: *This sequence is incorrect in French:* "de personnes as" does not appear in a correct sentence.

meaning: of small / small (used in combinations; literal meaning 'of small' or 'small')
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase in French. 'De petit' can appear before a noun to mean 'of small [size/amount]' (e.g. 'une boîte de petit format') or inside expressions like 'de petit...' (e.g. 'de petit âge' is uncommon). More often French uses 'petit' directly before the noun (petit chien = small dog) or uses constructions like 'de petite taille' or 'de petite taille/importance'. Watch gender/number agreement: petit → petite (feminine), petits/petites (plural).
target_language_example: une maison de petite taille
native_language_example: a house of small size / a small house

meaning: by a small margin; barely; narrowly.
additional_notes: Used to say something almost happened or was narrowly avoided. Often follows verbs like 'échapper', 'manquer', or the impersonal expression 'il s'en est fallu de peu'. Translates to 'by a little', 'by a narrow margin', 'barely'.
target_language_example: J'ai raté le bus de peu.
native_language_example: I missed the bus by a little / I barely missed the bus.

meaning: of photo / photographic (used to indicate relation to photos or photography)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a prepositional fragment: 'de' + 'photo' appears in compounds or descriptions (e.g. 'appareil de photo' = camera, 'album de photos' = photo album, 'repro de photo' = photo reproduction). Agreement and plural may vary: often you'll see 'photo' or 'photos' depending on noun. It can mean 'made for photos' or 'related to photos' depending on context.
target_language_example: Je cherche un album de photos pour nos vacances.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a photo album for our vacation.

meaning: A non-standalone sequence of words that can appear across multi-word expressions involving the foot and direction/placement (literally 'from/of foot into'). It is not a fixed phrase by itself; it appears as part of larger verbs or constructions (e.g., "mettre le pied dans", "entrer de pied dans").
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase on its own — usually found inside longer expressions describing setting foot into/onto something or movement by foot. For learners, study full expressions (e.g., "mettre le pied dans la porte", "mettre le pied dans la bouche" figuratively) rather than using 'de pied dans' alone. Context determines whether the sense is literal (physical entry) or idiomatic (e.g., "mettre le pied dans la bouche" = 'put one's foot in one's mouth').
target_language_example: Il est entré de pied dans la pièce sans dire un mot.
native_language_example: He came into the room with his foot first without saying a word.

meaning: 'from ... to' used in expressions indicating a range in feet (unit of length) — requires numbers and usually the plural 'pieds' (e.g. 'de 10 pieds à 20 pieds').
additional_notes: The fragment 'de pied à' by itself is incomplete; in practice you will see 'de X pied(s) à Y pied(s)' or 'de pied en pied' (different idiom). 'pied' = foot (unit). Not a cognate. Compositional in that it literally links 'from foot to', but must include numbers or explicit 'pied(s)'. Can be translated literally when used with measurements.
target_language_example: La corniche s'étend de pied à pied sur toute la façade.
native_language_example: The cornice runs from foot to foot along the whole facade.

meaning: 'of feet' or 'from feet' — literal part of expressions about feet or measurement (e.g. nombre de pieds = number of feet).
additional_notes: Alone, 'de pieds' is not a complete phrase; it appears as the complement in larger expressions (e.g. 'nombre de pieds', 'douleur de pieds', 'à quatre pattes sur les pieds', or in measurements like 'pieds' for feet). Pay attention to the surrounding words and articles (des, les, mes) which normally appear: 'des pieds', 'les pieds', 'mes pieds'.
target_language_example: Il compte le nombre de pieds du meuble.
native_language_example: He counts the number of feet (legs) of the piece of furniture.

meaning: worse and worse; getting progressively worse.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, condition, or behavior that is deteriorating over time. Equivalent to English 'worse and worse' or 'going from bad to worse.' Common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Depuis la panne, tout va de pire en pire.
native_language_example: Since the breakdown, everything is getting worse and worse.

meaning: literally 'of pieces of' — a word sequence that appears when the noun pièces (pieces/coins/parts/rooms) is linked to a following noun introduced by de (e.g. pièces de monnaie, pièces de rechange). It expresses possession or specification (pieces of X).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a compositional sequence: 'pièces' followed by 'de' + noun. Meaning of pièces depends on context (coins, spare parts, rooms, plays, etc.). Articles/pluralization follow normal French (une pièce de, des pièces de). In English it often becomes 'pieces/coins/parts of X' or 'X pieces/parts'.
target_language_example: Combien de pièces de monnaie as-tu dans ta collection de pièces de monnaie ?
native_language_example: How many coins do you have in your coin collection?

meaning: literally 'of plan'; not a standard standalone phrase in French — when seen, it usually appears in fixed expressions meaning 'according to the plan' or 'as planned'
additional_notes: 'de plan' by itself is uncommon or nonstandard in modern French. Learners should prefer 'selon le plan', 'comme prévu' or 'd'après le plan'. You may encounter 'de plan' in informal speech or shorthand contexts (e.g. notes, headlines) or in fixed compounds, but it is not a regular idiomatic phrase.
target_language_example: Rien n'a été fait de plan, tout s'est improvisé.
native_language_example: Nothing was done according to a plan; everything was improvised.

meaning: voluntarily; of one's own free will
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something willingly, without being forced or obliged. Often appears in formal or neutral registers (legal, administrative, spoken French). Can modify verbs: e.g. 'il a quitté son poste de plein gré' = he left voluntarily.
target_language_example: Elle a accepté l'offre de plein gré.
native_language_example: She accepted the offer voluntarily.

meaning: more
additional_notes: Often used after a quantity, noun, or question word to mean an additional amount: une heure de plus = "one more hour", quelques jours de plus = "a few more days", que dire de plus ? = "what more is there to say?" It does not translate literally word-for-word into natural English.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une minute de plus.
native_language_example: I'd like one more minute.

meaning: part of the construction 'de plus en plus' meaning 'more and more' (progressively increasing).
additional_notes: Alone 'de plus en' is incomplete; the full phrase is 'de plus en plus'. It's used before adjectives, adverbs, verbs or nouns to indicate an increasing degree or frequency: 'de plus en plus difficile' = 'more and more difficult'. Can appear at start or mid-sentence. Keep the full phrase together; don't split it.
target_language_example: Il devient de plus en plus confiant.
native_language_example: He is becoming more and more confident.

meaning: more and more
additional_notes: Used to describe a gradual increase over time or becoming more of a quality/degree. Often placed before adjectives, adverbs, verbs (with surrounding context) or noun phrases. Can be repeated with comparatives (e.g., « de plus en plus chaud », « de plus en plus difficile »).
target_language_example: Il devient de plus en plus patient chaque année.
native_language_example: He is becoming more and more patient every year.

meaning: 'pocket' or 'pocket-sized'; also 'pocket money' when used as 'argent de poche'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean small enough to fit in a pocket (édition de poche = paperback/pocket edition; lampe de poche = flashlight/torch). When paired with 'argent' (argent de poche) it means allowance/pocket money. Word order is noun + de poche. Context determines whether it refers to size or to money.
target_language_example: Il a acheté une édition de poche du roman.
native_language_example: He bought a pocket edition of the novel.

meaning: of weight; (figuratively) of importance or influence
additional_notes: Used literally to talk about physical weight (perdre du poids = lose weight; une unité de poids = unit of weight). Used figuratively in expressions like "manquer de poids" or "avoir du poids" to mean lacking or having influence/importance (e.g. "son argument manque de poids" = his argument lacks weight/force). Often appears after a quantity (un peu de poids, beaucoup de poids) or after verbs like perdre, prendre.
target_language_example: Son opinion a beaucoup de poids dans l'entreprise.
native_language_example: His opinion carries a lot of weight in the company.

meaning: used to describe a punch (a blow) aimed at someone or something; 'a punch to/at'.
additional_notes: This phrase is built from 'poing' (fist) and the preposition 'à' and is used in expressions like 'un coup de poing à [quelqu'un]' or 'frapper de poing à [quelque chose]' to indicate the target of a punch. It's relatively literal and somewhat formal/literary; in everyday speech French speakers more often say 'donner un coup de poing à quelqu'un' or simply 'frapper quelqu'un'.
target_language_example: Il a donné un coup de poing à son adversaire.
native_language_example: He gave a punch to his opponent.

meaning: 'state-of-the-art' / 'peak' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used in two main senses: 1) 'de pointe' after a noun = 'state-of-the-art', 'cutting-edge' (e.g. technologie de pointe). 2) In the fixed expression 'heure(s) de pointe' it means 'peak (hour)', 'rush hour' (traffic). Placement: usually follows the noun. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: La société utilise des équipements de pointe.
native_language_example: The company uses state-of-the-art equipment.

meaning: part of the phrase 'points de suture' meaning 'stitches' (lit. 'of points of'); on its own it's not a complete expression but appears within constructions like 'avoir besoin de points de suture'
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase; appears as the middle of 'avoir besoin de points de suture' or 'avoir X points de suture'. Use with verbs such as 'avoir', 'avoir besoin de', 'recevoir', 'mettre' (mettre des points de suture). Plural 'points de suture' is common. Agreement: number precedes 'points' (e.g. 'trois points de suture').
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de points de suture.
native_language_example: I need stitches.

meaning: out of children's reach / beyond the reach of children
additional_notes: Used to describe objects (medicines, cleaning products, small items) that should be kept where children cannot reach them. You will often see this phrasing on labels and warnings. A more common shorter form is "hors de portée des enfants."
target_language_example: Gardez ce produit de portée des enfants.
native_language_example: Keep this product out of children's reach.

meaning: 'of the post' or 'relating to a job/position' (used after a noun to indicate the job/role) or part of expressions referring to mail/post office
additional_notes: Short phrase that appears in different contexts. As a modifier after a noun, de poste often relates to a job/position (e.g. 'chef de poste' = station/shift leader, 'poste' = job or post). It can also appear in compounds about mail or the post office (e.g. 'bureau de poste' = post office). Alone it is not a complete phrase; you usually see it attached to another word.
target_language_example: Il a été promu chef de poste.
native_language_example: He was promoted to station leader (chief of the post).

meaning: Not a standard standalone French phrase; likely a fragment within a larger sentence. Literally: 'of post is' or 'of position is'.
additional_notes: You will not commonly see 'de poste est' by itself in correct French. It looks like three words taken from a larger structure (for example: 'la localisation de poste est...' or 'la description de poste est...'). 'Poste' can mean 'job/position', 'mail/post', or 'station'. To be correct, include the full noun phrase around 'de poste' (e.g. 'la description de poste est claire' — 'the job description is clear').
target_language_example: La description de poste est publiée sur le site de l'entreprise.
native_language_example: The job description is published on the company's website.

meaning: 'first-year' (describing someone in their first year) or 'top-quality' in informal exclamation
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of the phrase 'de première année' (first-year student). Alone, 'de première' often appears in shortened descriptions (e.g. 'un étudiant de première') to mean 'a first-year'. In informal speech or exclamations (e.g. 'Quel/Quand il y a un chien de première !'), it can emphasize something remarkable or top-quality; this usage is colloquial and context-dependent. When used with a field (piano, année, classe), it qualifies the level/grade as first.
target_language_example: Elle est en histoire, étudiante de première année.
native_language_example: She is in history, a first-year student.

meaning: 'to take care (of)'; used with an object to mean caring for someone/something or ensuring something is looked after
additional_notes: Usually appears after verbs or expressions that require an infinitive with 'de' (e.g., 'avoir besoin de', 'essayer de') so you get constructions like 'avoir besoin de prendre soin de...'. The full common construction is 'prendre soin de [quelqu'un/quelque chose]'; 'de prendre soin' is the infinitive preceded by the preposition 'de' linking from another verb or phrase. Can mean both physical care and general attention/maintenance.
target_language_example: Elle a demandé à son voisin de prendre soin de ses plantes pendant ses vacances.
native_language_example: She asked her neighbor to take care of her plants during her vacation.

meaning: 'of problem' or part of phrases meaning 'problem(s)' (e.g. 'pas de problème' = 'no problem')
additional_notes: Alone 'de problème' is not a complete phrase; it appears after quantifiers or negation (pas, sans, aucun) or in constructions like 'il n'y a pas de problème' or 'aucun problème'. Common useful phrases: 'pas de problème' (no problem), 'sans problème' (without trouble), 'aucun problème' (no problem/none). Note: after negation in French, 'de' replaces 'des/du' before a noun.
target_language_example: Pas de problème, je peux t'aider.
native_language_example: No problem, I can help you.

meaning: 'of relevance' or 'pertaining to' when appearing inside certain fixed expressions; not a standalone common phrase meaning 'about' (contrast with 'à propos'/'à propos de').
additional_notes: 'De propos' by itself is uncommon. Learners should use 'à propos' or 'à propos de' to mean 'by the way' or 'about'. 'De propos' appears inside set phrases like 'hors de propos' (out of place) or 'sans propos' in older usage. Use 'à propos de X' for 'about X'.
target_language_example: Cette remarque est hors de propos dans cette réunion.
native_language_example: This remark is out of place in this meeting.

meaning: closely; up close; closely watched/followed.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity (up close) or figurative closeness (closely following, closely monitoring). Common with verbs like voir (voir de près = see up close), suivre (suivre de près = follow closely), surveiller (surveiller de près = monitor closely).
target_language_example: Les médecins ont surveillé le patient de près.
native_language_example: The doctors monitored the patient closely.

meaning: preferably; if possible; rather.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a preference or the preferred option. Can stand alone as an answer (meaning 'preferably' or 'ideally'). Often followed by the preferred item or circumstance (e.g., 'de préférence + noun' or 'de préférence + verb phrase').
target_language_example: Je prendrai du thé, de préférence sans sucre.
native_language_example: I'll have tea, preferably without sugar.

meaning: of/a psychopath; (informal) extremely crazy or intense (often used jokingly after a noun to exaggerate).
additional_notes: Literally means 'of a psychopath' and can describe a person (quelqu'un de psychopathe) or be used as an informal intensifier after a noun to emphasize extreme quality or behaviour (e.g., 'une énergie de psychopathe' = 'insane energy'). Tone is informal and can be strong; avoid in formal situations. Agreement follows normal grammar when used in phrases (de + noun/adjective).
target_language_example: Il a une mémoire de psychopathe.
native_language_example: He has a psychopath's memory (i.e., an insane memory).

meaning: 'of a whore' — vulgar insult or intensifier; roughly equivalent to 'fucking' or 'of a bitch' in English depending on context.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. 'Pute' means 'whore' and 'de pute' is not a neutral expression; it can appear in crude insults (e.g. 'fils de pute' = 'son of a bitch') or as a coarse intensifier in spoken French. Avoid in polite conversation. Use only to recognize or understand strong profanity.
target_language_example: Il m'a traité de fils de pute.
native_language_example: He called me a son of a bitch.

meaning: of/from father; a prepositional fragment used to indicate paternal origin or relation to a father
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase; it appears inside longer expressions (e.g. describing parentage: 'enfant de père inconnu'). Watch agreement and articles: 'de père' after indefinite/partitive, 'du père' when 'de + le' is required. Common in formal/descriptive contexts about lineage or origin.
target_language_example: L'enfant est de père inconnu.
native_language_example: The child is of unknown father.

meaning: about when / from when (asking or referring to the date or time of something)
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the time or date something is from. Common in questions like "De quand date-ce ?" (When is it from?) or "De quand est-ce ?" In casual speech it often appears in longer phrases: "Tu sais de quand ça date ?" (Do you know how old that is / when that's from?).
target_language_example: De quand date ce bâtiment ?
native_language_example: When is this building from?

meaning: 'by what right' / 'who do you think you are?'.
additional_notes: Used to challenge someone's authority or behavior — often confrontational. Can be literal (asking on what legal or moral basis) or rhetorical (expressing indignation). Common in formal and informal contexts; tone determines politeness.
target_language_example: De quel droit parlez-vous ainsi à ma sœur ?
native_language_example: By what right do you speak to my sister like that?

meaning: which (plural, after de)
additional_notes: Used before a plural feminine or mixed plural noun after the preposition "de" to ask about or specify which ones. Often appears in questions (e.g., "De quelles couleurs?" = "Which colors?") and relative clauses ("les choses de quelles tu parles" → normally rephrased as "les choses dont tu parles"). Agreement is with the plural noun that follows. In spoken French, "des quelles" is uncommon; use "de quelles" when "de" is required by the verb or phrase.
target_language_example: De quelles villes viens-tu ?
native_language_example: Which cities are you from?

meaning: of/from someone (used before an adjective or past participle that begins with a vowel sound)
additional_notes: This is a contracted form used when saying something belongs to or is characteristic of someone, and the next word begins with a vowel or mute 'h'. It appears in constructions like « de quelqu'un d'important » (of someone important) or « de quelqu'un d'heureux » (of someone happy). In English it corresponds to 'of someone' or 'from someone' followed by an adjective or participle. Remember the contraction d' replaces de before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: C'est l'avis de quelqu'un d'intelligent.
native_language_example: It's the opinion of someone intelligent.

meaning: of a few / some (a small number of)
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate an unspecified small number. Equivalent to 'some' or 'a few' in English. Often appears in expressions like 'de quelques jours', 'de quelques personnes'. When used after certain quantifiers or negations, 'de' may replace 'des' (e.g. 'quelques' normally stands alone: 'quelques personnes'; 'de quelques' appears in contexts like 'parmi de quelques...' or in more formal constructions).
target_language_example: J'ai reçu des nouvelles de quelques amis.
native_language_example: I received news from a few friends.

meaning: 'of question' — not a standalone phrase in French; appears within larger fixed expressions (e.g. forming part of 'il n'en est pas question' meaning 'there is no question of it' or occurring in constructions like 'pas de question de...')
additional_notes: Alone, 'de question' is incomplete and uncommon; French typically uses 'il n'en est pas question' or constructions like 'pas de question de...' (e.g. 'pas de question de partir maintenant' = 'no question of leaving now'). Also note the related but different pattern 'question de' (word order reversed) meaning 'a matter of' (e.g. 'question de temps'). Do not use 'de question' by itself; learn the full expressions.
target_language_example: Pas de question de partir maintenant — nous devons attendre.
native_language_example: No question of leaving now — we must wait.

meaning: 'of whom has' or 'from whom has' (part of a larger clause)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a complete phrase on its own; it appears inside longer sentences (e.g. questions or relative clauses) where 'qui' refers to a person and 'de' expresses possession, origin, or relation. Word order in French often places 'de qui' before a verb like 'a' (has) to form clauses such as 'de qui a hérité...' (whose [person] has inherited...). For beginners: expect this pattern inside longer structures (questions: 'De qui a-t-il reçu...?' or relative clauses: 'la femme de qui a parlé...').
target_language_example: De qui a-t-elle reçu ce cadeau ?
native_language_example: From whom did she receive this gift?

meaning: literally 'of whom would make' — part of a conditional/relative construction; used to introduce what someone/something would do or cause (often in hypothetical or reported contexts).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence of words that appears in sentences combining a relative pronoun (qui), the preposition de, and the conditional/conditional-like verb ferait (from faire). It often follows a noun or expression and introduces a clause describing what that person/thing would do or cause. Example structures: « X, de qui ferait … » or « quelque chose de qui ferait … » — however such word order is relatively formal/rare; more common alternatives are « qui ferait » or « de quoi ferait » depending on meaning. Pay attention to context to determine the correct translation.
target_language_example: C'est une décision de qui ferait changer beaucoup de choses, si elle était prise.
native_language_example: It's a decision that would change many things, if it were made.

meaning: of which would make a / that would make a (feminine noun)
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase. It combines de (of/from), qui (which/who) and ferait (conditional of faire: would make/do) followed by une (feminine indefinite article). It would appear inside a larger sentence modifying a feminine noun: e.g. «un propos de qui ferait une belle histoire» (not a natural example — see realistic example below). In practice you'd more often see structures like «qui en ferait une…» or «de quoi faire une…» depending on intended meaning. Watch agreement and context: «ferait» is conditional (would), and «une» signals a feminine noun follows.
target_language_example: C'est une situation de qui ferait une belle histoire si on la raconte correctement.
native_language_example: It's a situation that would make a great story if told properly.

meaning: 'about whom' or 'who it is (about)'.
additional_notes: Used in the fixed expression 'de qui il s'agit' meaning 'who/whom is being referred to'. Often appears in questions or statements to ask/confirm the identity of a person previously mentioned or implied. Word order: 'Sais-tu de qui il s'agit ?' Note that 'il s'agit de + quelqu'un' is another common form (e.g., 'Il s'agit de Marie').
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas encore de qui il s'agit.
native_language_example: I don't know yet who it's about.

meaning: 'who it is about' or 'whom it concerns' (used to ask or say who is meant/being referred to).
additional_notes: Short for 'de qui il s'agit'. Common in questions and statements to ask/confirm the identity of a person previously mentioned or implied. Structure: 'savoir/devoir/être + de qui il s'agit'. In spoken French the full form is 'de qui il s'agit' (often contracted in speech). Use with 'sais-tu', 'savez-vous', 'je sais', etc.
target_language_example: Tu sais de qui il s'agit ?
native_language_example: Do you know who it is about?

meaning: 'of whom' or 'about whom' (used to link to a person previously mentioned)
additional_notes: Used after a noun or clause to introduce a relative or interrogative clause referring to a person. Appears in phrases like «la personne de qui je parle» (the person of whom I speak) or in questions «De qui parles-tu ?» (Who are you talking about?). In everyday speech, French often prefers 'qui' alone in subject position ('qui a fait ça?') but uses 'de qui' when the verb or preposition requires 'de'.
target_language_example: C'est la femme de qui je t'ai parlé.
native_language_example: That's the woman I told you about.

meaning: 'about whom' or 'of whom' (used in questions or relative clauses).
additional_notes: Literal components: de (of/about) + qui (who) + tu (you). Often appears in questions or clauses asking or referring to the person about whom something is said. In standard French, word order usually places the pronoun before the verb (e.g. «De qui parles-tu?»). Alone, the sequence 'de qui tu' is incomplete in written French; you will commonly see 'De qui tu parles ?' in informal speech (less standard) or the correct inversion 'De qui parles-tu ?' in formal/written style.
target_language_example: De qui tu parles ici ?
native_language_example: Who are you talking about here?

meaning: of what
additional_notes: Literally "of what." After verbs or adjectives followed by de, English often says "what ... about/of?" instead: De quoi parlez-vous ? = What are you talking about? Before an infinitive, it often means "something to" or "enough to" do something: de quoi manger, de quoi vivre.
target_language_example: Tu as de quoi écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to write with?

meaning: Not a standalone fixed phrase; fragment of constructions where 'de quoi' is followed by 'a' (third-person singular of 'avoir' or the preposition 'à' contracted with a following vowel in some contexts). Typically signals 'something to/that ...' or 'enough to ...' and is incomplete without additional words.
additional_notes: 'De quoi' commonly means 'something' or 'enough (to...)'. The sequence 'de quoi a' can appear when 'de quoi' is followed by a verb phrase starting with 'a' (often 'a' = 'à' + vowel or 'a' = third-person singular of 'avoir' in certain verb forms). Alone it is incomplete and requires more context (e.g., a relative clause or infinitive). Examples: 'Il n'a pas de quoi se vanter' (here 'de quoi' + infinitive), or in a clause like 'c'est de quoi a surpris tout le monde' (nonstandard; more likely 'qui a surpris'). Watch for word order and agreement; many occurrences are idiomatic.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas de quoi a peur cet enfant.
native_language_example: I don't know what this child is afraid of.

meaning: 'de quoi' = 'about what / of what / enough to' (depends on context); 'es' is the 2nd-person singular of 'être' ('you are').
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'de quoi es' is not a standalone fixed phrase in French. It may appear at the start of questions or clauses like 'De quoi es-tu sûr ?' (What are you sure of?) or in constructions such as 'Il y a de quoi être...'. Pay attention to word order and punctuation: when forming questions with inversion use 'es-tu'. 'De quoi' can mean 'about what', 'what... about', or 'enough to' depending on context.
target_language_example: De quoi es-tu sûr ?
native_language_example: What are you sure of?

meaning: 'what (about) they' — part of a question or clause meaning 'what they (have/are/need/etc.)' or 'what about them'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase; it combines de quoi ('what' / 'of what' / 'enough to') with the subject pronoun ils ('they'). It typically appears in questions or relative clauses: e.g. «De quoi ils parlent?» (What are they talking about?) or «Je ne sais pas de quoi ils ont besoin» (I don't know what they need). Word order in French often places de quoi before the verb or auxiliary. For informal spoken French you may also hear «c'est de quoi... ?» constructions, but standard written uses full clauses.
target_language_example: De quoi ils ont peur ?
native_language_example: What are they afraid of?

meaning: 'of/about which I' or part of a larger clause meaning 'something I...'
additional_notes: This sequence is incomplete on its own. In French, 'de quoi' means 'of/about which' or 'enough (to...)' depending on context; when followed by a subject pronoun like 'je' it typically begins a relative or subordinate clause (e.g. 'de quoi je parle' = 'what I am talking about') or an expression with a verb (e.g. 'de quoi je doute' = 'what I doubt'). Beginners will most often see 'de quoi' used in questions ('de quoi parles-tu ?' = 'what are you talking about?') or in structures like 'avoir de quoi + infinitive' (to have enough to ...).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas de quoi je parle.
native_language_example: I don't know what I'm talking about.

meaning: 'de quoi' = 'enough/what for' or 'something to' depending on context; with 'le' it likely begins a clause referring back to a masculine noun (e.g. "de quoi le/ la/les + infinitive/phrase").
additional_notes: This fragment combines 'de quoi' (literally 'of what' but used to mean 'something to', 'enough to', or 'what for') with the definite article/pronoun 'le'. On its own 'de quoi le' is incomplete — you will see forms like 'de quoi le remercier' (something to thank him for) or 'de quoi le convaincre' (something to convince him). 'De quoi' often introduces a complement with an infinitive or a subordinate clause. Pay attention to gender/number: 'de quoi le' vs 'de quoi la' vs 'de quoi les'.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé de quoi le convaincre.
native_language_example: I found something to convince him with.

meaning: 'what are you talking about' (informal, partial form)
additional_notes: This is an informal, shortened fragment of the question "De quoi parles-tu ?" or "De quoi est-ce que tu parles ?" used when asking what someone is talking about. In writing you should include the full form or add the subject/verb ending (parles-tu, est-ce que tu parles, il/elle parle). Without the subject it sounds like a clipped spoken phrase. Use to ask for clarification about the topic of conversation.
target_language_example: De quoi parles-tu ? Je n'ai pas bien compris.
native_language_example: What are you talking about? I didn't quite understand.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; most often a mistaken combination of two separate expressions ('de quoi' and 'quoi que'). It does not have an independent, accepted meaning in standard French.
additional_notes:
Common confusions:
- 'de quoi' can mean 'something to / enough to / what for' depending on context (e.g., 'Tu as de quoi écrire ?' = 'Do you have something to write with?').
- 'quoi que' is a conjunction meaning 'whatever / although' and is followed by the subjunctive: 'Quoi que tu fasses, je serai là.' = 'Whatever you do, I'll be there.'
- If you encounter 'de quoi que' in writing or speech, it is likely an error, a regional or colloquial blend, or a typo. To convey a correct idea, choose either 'de quoi' or 'quoi que' (or restructure the sentence).

Possible intended meanings and correct alternatives:
- If the speaker meant 'something to [verb]': use 'de quoi' (e.g., 'Tu as de quoi manger ?').
- If the speaker meant 'whatever/although': use 'quoi que' + subjunctive (e.g., 'Quoi que tu dises...' should be 'Quoi que tu dises...' with subjunctive 'dises').
- If 'de quoi que' appears inside a longer clause, check whether words were omitted or word order is wrong; rewrite the sentence for clarity.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas « de quoi que tu parles » — il faut dire « de quoi tu parles ? » ou « à quoi tu penses ? ».
native_language_example: It's not 'de quoi que tu parles' — you should say 'de quoi tu parles?' or 'à quoi tu penses?'.

meaning: 'what is it about' / 'what is this concerning'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full question form 'De quoi s'agit-il ?' meaning 'What is this about?' or 'What is the matter?' Used to ask for the subject or nature of something. Formal/neutral register. Can be followed by words like 'vraiment', 'au juste', or 'alors' for emphasis.
target_language_example: De quoi s'agit-il exactement dans ce dossier ?
native_language_example: What is this file about exactly?

meaning: 'reasonable' / 'sensible' when used after certain nouns or adjectives (literally 'of reason')
additional_notes: Often appears in fixed expressions like 'quelque chose de raison' or 'agir de raison' to mean 'reasonable' or 'sensible'. More commonly French uses 'raisonnable' for 'reasonable'; 'de raison' is less frequent and can sound formal or literary. It follows a noun (quelque chose de raison) or is part of a phrase meaning 'by reason' or 'for good reason' depending on context. Not used alone as a standalone adjective.
target_language_example: C'est une décision de raison, pas d'impulsion.
native_language_example: This is a decision of reason, not of impulse.

meaning: 'to watch the' (part of the infinitive phrase 'de regarder la télévision' — 'to watch the television').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the start of an infinitive clause introduced by 'de' followed by the verb 'regarder' and the feminine definite article 'la' (usually before 'télévision' or 'télé'). Commonly appears in constructions like 'avant de regarder la télévision', 'préférer ... que de regarder la télé', or as part of a noun phrase 'un plaisir est de regarder la télé'.
target_language_example: Avant de regarder la télévision, éteins ton téléphone.
native_language_example: Before watching the television, turn off your phone.

meaning: of an appointment / appointment (part of a phrase, e.g. 'carte de rendez-vous' = appointment card).
additional_notes: This phrase is not standalone: it's the preposition 'de' + 'rendez-vous' (appointment, meeting). It appears in compounds or genitive constructions (e.g. 'heure de rendez-vous' = appointment time, 'confirmation de rendez-vous' = appointment confirmation). 'Rendez-vous' is masculine in French: un rendez-vous. Use 'de' to link a noun to 'rendez-vous' to show possession or type.
target_language_example: Heure de rendez-vous : 14h00.
native_language_example: Appointment time: 2:00 PM.

meaning: 'to give back', 'to return' or part of verbs meaning 'to make/return' depending on context (infinitive construction with 'de').
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed phrase by itself but often appears as 'de' + infinitive 'rendre' after certain verbs, adjectives or nouns (e.g., 'essayer de rendre', 'capable de rendre'). 'Rendre' alone means 'to give back/return' or 'to make (someone/something + adjective)'. When you see 'de rendre' it usually links a previous word that requires 'de' before an infinitive. Pay attention to context to know whether 'rendre' means 'return' (rendre un livre) or 'make/leave' (rendre heureux = make happy).
target_language_example: Elle a promis de rendre le livre à la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: She promised to return the book to the library.

meaning: to go back/return to (a place) — used before a feminine place name or a noun with 'la'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment that appears in sentences like «Je viens de rentrer à la maison» (I just returned home) or «Il est rentré à la fac» (He returned to the university). It combines the verb rentrer (to return/go home) with the preposition à and the feminine definite article la. You will usually see a location after it (maison, fac, ville, bibliothèque, etc.). If the place is masculine use 'au' (rentrer au) or plural 'aux'. For expressing 'just returned', use 'venir de' + infinitive: 'Je viens de rentrer à la maison.'
target_language_example: Je viens de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just returned home.

meaning: 'to remain at the (feminine noun) / to stay at the (feminine noun)' — part of a phrase meaning to stay in or at a place or situation
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the combination of the preposition 'de' + infinitive 'rester' + the preposition 'à' + the feminine definite article 'la' that introduces a following feminine noun (e.g. la maison, la maison, la gare). You'll usually see it as part of a larger clause: 'decide de rester à la maison' = 'to decide to stay at home'. Word order and meaning depend on the verbs and nouns around it. If the place is masculine use 'au' (de rester au ...) or plural 'aux'.
target_language_example: J'ai décidé de rester à la maison aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I decided to stay at home today.

meaning: back
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has come back or returned. Commonly follows the subject (e.g., "Il est de retour") or appears after a name. Can be used for people, objects, or services (e.g., "Le site est de retour").
target_language_example: Je suis de retour.
native_language_example: I'm back.

meaning: of retirement; relating to retirement (e.g., 'pension de retraite' = retirement pension)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase composed of 'de' + 'retraite'. Often appears after a noun to specify that something is related to retirement (e.g., 'pension de retraite', 'âge de retraite', 'fonds de retraite'). Use depends on the noun it modifies. Not used alone as a full noun phrase without context.
target_language_example: Il a pris sa pension de retraite l'année dernière.
native_language_example: He took his retirement pension last year.

meaning: 'you're welcome' (or literally 'of nothing').
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a polite reply to 'merci' to mean 'you're welcome.' It can also appear in negative constructions with verbs like 'se souvenir' or 'douter' to mean 'anything' or 'nothing' (e.g. 'ne ... de rien' = 'not ... anything/remember nothing'). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: — Merci pour ton aide. — De rien !
native_language_example: — Thanks for your help. — You're welcome!

meaning: required, customary, expected (socially or officially).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is customary, considered necessary, or required in a given situation (e.g., a polite behavior, social norm, or official policy). Often appears in expressions like "c'est de rigueur" or "être de rigueur." Not to be confused with "rigueur" alone meaning strictness or rigor.
target_language_example: Dans ce restaurant, une tenue correcte est de rigueur.
native_language_example: In this restaurant, proper dress is required.

meaning: 'as a rule', 'normally', 'usually'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a general rule or usual situation. Often appears in phrases like "en règle générale" or alone after a statement: "De règle, ..." is less common in everyday spoken French than "en général" but is acceptable in written or formal contexts. Can be followed by a clause describing the usual outcome.
target_language_example: De règle, les trains arrivent à l'heure le matin.
native_language_example: As a rule, the trains arrive on time in the morning.

meaning: of/any answer; used to talk about a reply or response (often in negative phrases).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like 'pas', 'délai', or 'personne' to indicate lack or absence of a reply. In English it often corresponds to 'any answer/response' or 'a reply' depending on context. Typical constructions: 'Je n'ai pas eu de réponse' (I didn't get a reply) and 'délai de réponse' (response time/response delay).
target_language_example: J'attends toujours de réponse de sa part.
native_language_example: I'm still waiting for a response from them.

meaning: of meeting / meeting (used as an adjective or part of a noun phrase)
additional_notes: Literally 'of meeting' or 'meeting's'. Commonly used to describe something related to a meeting, e.g. salle de réunion (meeting room), compte rendu de réunion (meeting minutes), organisation de réunion (meeting organization). It usually follows a noun to form a noun phrase (noun + de réunion). Not a standalone phrase; needs a head noun.
target_language_example: Nous avons réservé la salle de réunion pour demain.
native_language_example: We booked the meeting room for tomorrow.

meaning: 'dream' as an adjective: fantastic, perfect, ideal
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as wonderful, ideal, or like a dream (e.g., un corps de rêve = a dream body; un couple de rêve = an ideal couple). Common in informal and neutral registers. Translate depending on context: 'dream', 'dreamlike', 'fantastic', 'ideal'.
target_language_example: Ils ont trouvé une maison de rêve près de la plage.
native_language_example: They found a dream house near the beach.

meaning: of role / role-related (used to indicate belonging to or concerning a role)
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase but the sequence de + rôle. Appears when specifying something that pertains to a role (e.g. "les responsabilités de rôle"). Word order matters: normally you say "le rôle de X" rather than "de rôle X"; however the substring "de rôle" can occur inside longer noun phrases like "les exigences de rôle" or "un problème de rôle".
target_language_example: Les exigences de rôle sont clairement définies.
native_language_example: The role requirements are clearly defined.

meaning: used as part of an adjective phrase to mean 'dirty' or 'filthy' (literally 'of dirty'); often appears in phrases like 'des trucs de sale' (colloquial/pejorative).
additional_notes: Alone 'de sale' is not a fixed standalone phrase; 'sale' means 'dirty' or 'nasty' and 'de' is the preposition/partitive linking it to a noun. You will commonly see 'sale' after a noun with 'de' in colloquial expressions (e.g. 'un type de sale' — rude/insulting). Be careful: word order usually is noun + 'sale' (un homme sale = a dirty man). 'De sale' can appear in constructions like 'plein de sale boulot' in casual speech but this is informal. Context determines whether it’s literal (physically dirty) or figurative (nasty, mean).
target_language_example: C'est un travail de sale, mais il faut le faire.
native_language_example: It's a dirty job, but it has to be done.

meaning: of science; relating to science (used in formal/academic contexts).
additional_notes: A formal expression used to indicate that something belongs to, concerns, or is derived from the field of science. Often appears in combinations like 'connaissances de science', 'discipline de science', or in institutional names. Not common in everyday spoken French on its own; more likely replaced by phrases like 'scientifique' or 'en science(s)'.
target_language_example: Il a une formation de science et de technologie.
native_language_example: He has training in science and technology.

meaning: 'of the stage' or 'stage (as an adjective)'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate a relation to the stage, theatre, or performance (e.g. décor de scène = stage set; artiste de scène = stage performer). It often functions like the English adjective 'stage' or the prepositional phrase 'of the stage'. Word order: in French the structure is 'noun + de scène'.
target_language_example: Le décor de scène est prêt pour la représentation.
native_language_example: The stage set is ready for the performance.

meaning: backup / emergency (used to describe something kept or used in case of failure or danger).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to indicate an emergency or spare version (plan de secours = backup plan; clé de secours = spare key; hélicoptères de secours = rescue helicopters). Can be short as 'secours' in some contexts (aller aux secours = go to help/rescue).
target_language_example: J'ai une copie de secours de tous mes fichiers.
native_language_example: I have a backup copy of all my files.

meaning: 'of the week' or 'weekday' (used to describe something relating to the week or a weekday).
additional_notes: Commonly used in compound expressions to contrast week vs. weekend or to describe regular weekday items (e.g., 'tenue de semaine' = weekday outfit, 'repas de semaine' = weekday meal). Often follows a noun: 'vêtement de semaine', 'travail de semaine'. Not a standalone phrase — needs a noun before it.
target_language_example: Repas de semaine: des plats rapides et faciles.
native_language_example: Weekday meals: quick and easy dishes.

meaning: 'on duty' / 'service-related' / 'service'
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something related to work duty, service, or support. Context determines exact sense: 'être de service' = to be on duty; 'porte de service' = service/utility door; 'numéros de service' = service phone numbers (customer service, emergency lines); 'carte de service' could mean an ID or a work/service card. Not a standalone verb phrase — it modifies a noun.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je suis de service à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm on duty at the hospital.

meaning: 'of (a) situation' — indicates something related to or belonging to a situation.
additional_notes: Commonly used after nouns like 'genre', 'type', 'rapport' to describe the situation being referred to (e.g., 'ce genre de situation' = 'this kind of situation'). Also appears in set phrases like 'rapport de situation' (situation report). Grammar: 'de' links the preceding noun to 'situation' (possession/relationship).
target_language_example: Fais attention pour éviter ce genre de situation.
native_language_example: Be careful to avoid this kind of situation.

meaning: at his/her best; doing as well as one can
additional_notes: Used after a noun or verb phrase to say someone is performing at their highest ability. Often follows a verb like 'faire', 'être' or expressions like 'au mieux de'. Context determines gender/possessive (son can refer to il/elle/one). Commonly used in phrases such as 'faire de son mieux' (to do one's best) — note word order difference: 'de son meilleur' emphasizes 'at one's best' rather than the idiomatic 'de son mieux'.
target_language_example: Elle était de son meilleur pendant la compétition.
native_language_example: She was at her best during the competition.

meaning: completely; fully; of one's own accord/intention (depends on context)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in expressions like «de son plein gré» (of one's own free will) and «de plein (son)» rarely. Alone, «de son plein» is not a common fixed phrase; it's usually part of a larger phrase (e.g. «de son plein gré»). If you see «de son plein gré», it means 'voluntarily' or 'of one's own accord'. Do not use «de son plein» by itself in formal writing unless it's clearly part of a longer expression.
target_language_example: Il a démissionné de son plein gré.
native_language_example: He resigned of his own accord.

meaning: 'so that' / 'in such a way (that)'.
