additional_notes: Used to introduce a result or purpose clause. Often appears as part of the expression 'de sorte que' followed by indicative (result) or subjunctive (purpose/intent) depending on nuance. Can also be used alone before a clause: 'de sorte que...'. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a parlé lentement de sorte que tout le monde comprenne.
native_language_example: He spoke slowly so that everyone understands.

meaning: so that / in such a way that (expresses purpose or result)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose or result clause. Followed by an infinitive (de sorte de + infinitive) to express purpose, or followed by que + subjunctive/indicative (de sorte que) to express result. In everyday speech 'pour que' is more common for purpose; 'de sorte de' is slightly more formal and often written.
target_language_example: Il a modifié le texte de sorte de clarifier l'idée.
native_language_example: He modified the text so as to clarify the idea.

meaning: 'so that' / 'in such a way that' (introduces a result or purpose).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result (so that/as a result) or a purpose (so that/to ensure). Can be followed by indicative (for result/fact) or subjunctive (for purpose/possibility) depending on nuance. Common in formal and neutral registers; interchangeable with 'pour que' for purpose but 'pour que' always takes the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Venez tôt, de sorte que nous puissions en parler tranquillement.
native_language_example: Come early so that we can talk about it calmly.

meaning: 'to go out of' or 'to come out of' (used before a word starting with a vowel or mute h)
additional_notes: This is the partitive/infinitive construction combining the preposition de + the verb sortir followed by d' when the next word begins with a vowel or mute h (e.g., sortir d'une pièce, sortir d'ici). Depending on context, sortir de means 'to leave' (a place), 'to take out' (an object from something), or 'to go/come out of' (an enclosure or situation). The contraction d' appears before a vowel sound: sortir d' + vowel word. Remember subject and tense determine conjugation (je sors de, il est sorti de, etc.).
target_language_example: Elle vient de sortir d'une réunion.
native_language_example: She has just come out of a meeting.

meaning: 'of breath' or 'breathless' (depends on context); literally related to breathing or breath.
additional_notes: Often appears after a noun to describe something related to breathing (e.g., 'manque de souffle' = shortness of breath) or in set phrases meaning 'breathless' or 'gasping'. By itself it's not a complete phrase and needs a noun or verb around it. Context determines whether it's literal (breathing) or figurative (exertion, astonishment).
target_language_example: Après la course, j'avais un manque de souffle.
native_language_example: After the run, I had shortness of breath.

meaning: 'from a reliable source' or 'reliably/surely sourced'.
additional_notes: Used to say information comes from someone or somewhere trustworthy. Common in news, conversations, and reports. Often follows verbs like savoir, tenir, or apprendre: e.g. « Je sais / On tient de source sûre ». Can be used to signal confidence but not absolute proof.
target_language_example: On tient de source sûre que la réunion est annulée.
native_language_example: We have reliable information that the meeting is canceled.

meaning: of/from under, from beneath (literally 'from under')
additional_notes: Rare as a standalone sequence; usually appears as part of longer expressions (e.g. 'la poussière de sous les meubles' would be non-idiomatic — more common: 'sous' alone or 'au-dessous de', 'en dessous de', or constructions like 'provenant de dessous'). 'De sous' can occur in poetic or colloquial contexts to mean 'coming from beneath' but beginners will mostly use 'sous' or 'en dessous de' to say 'under' or 'below'.
target_language_example: Le chat est sorti de sous la chaise.
native_language_example: The cat came out from under the chair.

meaning: 'sufficiently' or 'enough' used in constructions where an adverbial phrase follows 'de' (e.g. to qualify a noun phrase or after verbs/expressions requiring 'de' + adjective/adverbial phrase).
additional_notes: Suffisamment is normally an adverb (Il est suffisamment grand). The sequence 'de suffisamment' appears in more complex syntactic contexts, for example before adjectives modifying a noun phrase (de suffisamment grand taille) or after nouns/verbs that take 'de' plus an adjectival/adverbial phrase. It is compositional: the meaning follows from 'de' + 'suffisamment'. For most beginners, use 'suffisamment' alone in simple sentences.
target_language_example: Elle manque de suffisamment d'expérience pour réussir dans ce rôle.
native_language_example: She lacks sufficient experience to succeed in this role.

meaning: right away
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) meaning "right away/at once" to ask for immediate action (Je m'en occupe de suite = I'll take care of it right away). 2) meaning "consecutively/in a row" when used with a time expression (cinq jours de suite = five days in a row). Context tells which meaning applies. Informal tone is fine in spoken requests.
target_language_example: Viens ici de suite !
native_language_example: Come here right away!

meaning: 'to stay' (used after verbs like prévoir, compter, espérer — infinitive form with 'de').
additional_notes: This is the infinitive 'séjourner' preceded by the particle 'de' because it follows certain verbs (e.g. prévoir de, décider de, compter de) or expressions that require 'de' before another verb. It means to stay (somewhere) for a period of time. In questions about duration or location it commonly appears after verbs like prévoir/prévoirz/compter. Use without 'de' after other verbs that take a different connector (e.g. 'vouloir séjourner', 'aimer séjourner' — no 'de').
target_language_example: Nous prévoyons de séjourner deux semaines à Paris.
native_language_example: We plan to stay two weeks in Paris.

meaning: to ... you
additional_notes: contraction of de te before a vowel or mute h. It usually appears as part of a larger expression before an infinitive, for example de t'aider ('to help you') or de t'inquiéter ('to worry'). The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows, and t' can mean either 'you' or reflexive 'yourself'.
target_language_example: J'essaie de t'aider.
native_language_example: I'm trying to help you.

meaning: of/at the table; used to indicate possession, association, or position related to a table.
additional_notes: Commonly follows a noun to show relation to a table (e.g., 'serviette de table' = table napkin). Also appears in expressions about being at the table or leaving the table ('se lever de table'). Can mean 'of the table' (possession) or 'from the table' (position/association) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont laissé leurs assiettes sur la table, pas de table à débarrasser ?
native_language_example: They left their plates on the table, no table to clear?

meaning: 'of size' / 'big/significant' or idiomatically 'up to the task' (able/able to compete).
additional_notes: Has both literal and idiomatic uses. Literally follows a noun or adjective to describe physical size (e.g., de taille moyenne = of medium size). Idiomatically, used in negative or affirmative constructions to mean 'able' or 'up to the task' (ne pas être de taille = not good/strong enough; être de taille can imply being a worthy opponent or of considerable importance: une surprise de taille = a major surprise). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas de taille pour ce poste.
native_language_example: He is not up to the job.

meaning: an incomplete fragment; not a correct standalone French expression. It appears as a misordered or truncated piece of a sentence that intends to mean 'to tell you something' but is missing or misplacing words (correct: «à te dire quelque chose» or «quelque chose à te dire»).
additional_notes: This sequence is nonstandard and should not be used by itself. The correct constructions are «J'ai quelque chose à te dire» (I have something to tell you) or «Il y a des choses à te dire» depending on context. The fragment «de te dire quelque» might arise from speech errors, poetic inversion, or transcription mistakes. Pay attention to the preposition «à» after «quelque chose» when expressing telling someone something; using «de» here is incorrect.
target_language_example: ...de te dire quelque chose, mais je n'ai pas le temps maintenant.
native_language_example: ...to tell you something, but I don't have time right now.

meaning: A contracted sequence appearing before a vowel: combination of 'de' + object pronoun 'te' + contraction of a following 'le'/'la' as 'l'' (e.g. 'de te l'...' = 'of/from you it/her/him'), but this exact string is uncommon on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a possible written contraction where 'de' (of/from), the stressed/tonic pronoun 'te' (you, rarely used after prepositions), and a contracted article/pronoun 'le'/'la' appear together before a vowel. In normal French, you are more likely to see 'de toi', 'te le' (spoken), or constructions like 'de te l'annoncer' only in informal or poetic contexts. Be careful: written sequences like this are rare; pronoun order and contractions follow strict rules (e.g. 'te le' becomes 'te le' (no contraction) and 'le' contracts to l' only before a vowel in the following word).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de te l'annoncer, mais le concert est annulé.
native_language_example: I'm sorry to tell you it, but the concert is canceled.

meaning: A fragment that appears in fixed expressions meaning 'from time to' or 'occasionally' when completed (e.g., in 'de temps à autre'). By itself it is incomplete and not used alone.
additional_notes: This sequence is normally part of set phrases such as 'de temps à autre' (from time to time) or archaic/poetic uses. The common modern equivalent is 'de temps en temps'. Do not use 'de temps à' alone in formal writing — include the rest of the expression. It is not a cognate of any single English phrase and cannot be translated literally without the rest of the expression.
target_language_example: Parfois, de temps à autre, je relis de vieux poèmes.
native_language_example: Sometimes, from time to time, I reread old poems.

meaning: 'how long' (used in questions about duration, embedded in inversion with 'il/elle/on').
additional_notes: This sequence appears inside questions formed with inversion and 'combien' to ask about duration: 'Combien de temps a-t-il ... ?' The '-t-' is an inserted liaison consonant used when verb ends with a vowel and followed by 'il' (e.g. 'a' + 'il' → 'a-t-il') for pronunciation and grammar; it doesn't change meaning. You can also ask 'Combien de temps est-ce qu'il...' or 'Depuis combien de temps...' for similar senses. 'Pour combien de temps...' asks 'for how long' (planned or expected duration).
target_language_example: Combien de temps a-t-il étudié au Canada ?
native_language_example: How long did he study in Canada?

meaning: how much time it takes / how long it takes
additional_notes: This looks like a non-standard or slightly mixed phrasing. The usual French expressions are « combien de temps cela prend » or « combien de temps ça prend » (informal) to ask how long something will take. Use « ça » in speech; use « cela » or « cela prend » in more formal contexts. Word order matters: include 'combien' to form a proper question.
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend pour finir le projet ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to finish the project?

meaning: This sequence is not a correct or standard French expression as written; it appears to be a mistake or misordering of words (no established meaning).
additional_notes: Possible corrections and intended phrases: - "de temps en temps" (meaning "from time to time" / "occasionally"). - "comptez (le) temps" or "comptez le temps" (imperative/statement with verb "compter", meaning "count the time"). - If "comptez" is intended as 2nd person plural imperative, the correct order depends on context: e.g., "Comptez le temps". The exact string "de temps comptez" does not occur in standard French and should be corrected for clarity. Use context to choose the right phrase.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas pourquoi vous écrivez « de temps comptez » ; cette formulation n'est pas correcte.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you write "de temps comptez"; that wording is not correct.

meaning: This phrase is not a correct or standard French expression.
additional_notes:
Likely a typo or mistaken combination. Possible intended phrases include:
- "de temps en temps" (meaning "from time to time / occasionally").
- "devoir" forms like "dois" are from the verb devoir (to have to / must): e.g. "je dois" = "I must / I have to". "de temps dois" mixes parts of different expressions and is not grammatical. If you meant "occasionally," use "de temps en temps." If you intended "I must," use "je dois."
target_language_example: *De temps dois* n'est pas correct en français ; vous voulez peut‑être dire « de temps en temps » ou « je dois ».
native_language_example: "De temps dois" is not correct in French; you might mean "de temps en temps" or "je dois."

meaning: from time to time
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens at irregular, infrequent intervals. Interchangeable with 'parfois' or 'occasionnellement' in many contexts. Can appear at the start, middle or end of a sentence: 'De temps en temps, ...', '... fait ça de temps en temps.'
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema from time to time.

meaning: This appears to be a typo or misspelling of the correct French expression "de temps en temps", which means "from time to time" or "occasionally".
additional_notes: The correct phrase is "de temps en temps". "De temps es" is not standard French and will be misunderstood by native speakers. If you see "de temps es" in written text, it's almost certainly an error. Use "de temps en temps" to say that something happens occasionally; it can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence (formal and informal contexts).
target_language_example: De temps es, je vais au cinéma.
native_language_example: (Intended meaning) From time to time, I go to the cinema.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment, typo, or incorrect word order. It does not have an established meaning. Possible intended phrases include 'de temps en temps' (occasionally) or 'il y a du temps' / 'il y a longtemps' (a long time ago).
additional_notes: As written, 'de temps il' is ungrammatical. If encountered, treat it as an error or a fragment of a sentence (e.g., words reordered when trying to say 'il y a du temps' or 'de temps en temps'). Provide corrected alternatives to convey common meanings. Example corrections: 'De temps en temps' = occasionally; 'Il y a longtemps' = a long time ago.
target_language_example: De temps il manque des mots dans cette phrase — on dirait une erreur.
native_language_example: 'De temps il' is missing words in that sentence — it looks like a mistake.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a mistaken word order or a fragment produced when mixing 'de temps en temps' with a clause containing 'je'.
additional_notes: The sequence 'de temps je' does not occur in standard French. It may result from misordering words: the correct idiom is 'de temps en temps' ('from time to time'), and in sentences with 'je' the subject normally precedes the verb (e.g. 'Je le fais de temps en temps.'). If you see 'de temps je' it is almost certainly an error and should be rewritten (for example, 'je... de temps en temps' or 'de temps en temps, je...').
target_language_example: De temps je faisais des erreurs, mais j'ai appris.
native_language_example: From time to time I made mistakes, but I learned.

meaning: 'from time to time' / 'occasionally'.
additional_notes: Use to say that something happens occasionally or not regularly. Commonly placed before or after the verb: 'Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.' Not to be confused with the incorrect fragment 'de temps on'.
target_language_example: Parfois j'écris 'de temps on' par erreur quand je tape vite.
native_language_example: Sometimes I type 'de temps on' by mistake when I'm typing fast.

meaning: '(amount) of time that you' — part of expressions about duration (often appears as "autant de temps que tu veux" or in questions like "ça fait combien de temps que tu...?")
additional_notes: This fragment appears in duration expressions. Common patterns: "autant de temps que tu veux" (as much time as you want) and "Ça fait combien de temps que tu... ?" (How long have you been...?). In spoken French the full phrase often omits 'de' or reorders words (e.g. "combien de temps" + "que tu..."). Use it to talk about how long someone has done or been doing something.
target_language_example: Tu peux rester autant de temps que tu veux.
native_language_example: You can stay as long as you want.

meaning: '(period) of time that you' — part of expressions asking or stating how long (something has lasted) involving 'you'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in common constructions like «Ça fait combien de temps que vous... ?» (How long have you...?) or in statements like «autant de temps que vous pourrez» (as much time as you can). The full phrase often needs surrounding words (Ça fait, autant, etc.). Use with verbs to ask duration: work, live, be together, etc.
target_language_example: Ça fait combien de temps que vous habitez ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living here?

meaning: This phrase as written is not a correct or natural French expression; likely a word order or form error. It seems intended to ask or state how long someone will stay (e.g. « combien de temps resterez-vous ? » or « combien de temps tu restes ? »).
additional_notes:
Beginners should use standard, correct forms to ask about duration of a stay: 
- Formal or polite question: « Combien de temps resterez-vous ? » (How long will you stay?)
- Informal: « Tu restes combien de temps ? » or « Combien de temps tu restes ? »
- Alternative (present): « Tu restes jusqu'à quand ? » (How long are you staying / until when?)
The sequence « de temps resterez » by itself is ungrammatical because French asks about duration with « combien de temps » and the verb (rester) must be conjugated properly and placed after the subject or with inversion for questions.
target_language_example: Combien de temps resterez-vous à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long will you stay in Paris?

meaning: 'de temps en temps' mistakenly written; intended to mean 'from time to time' / 'occasionally' if corrected.
additional_notes: This entry treats 'de temps te' as a misspelling or typo of the correct French phrase 'de temps en temps'. The correct expression is 'de temps en temps' and is neutral, used to say something happens occasionally; it is placed after the verb or at the end of a sentence (e.g., Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps). Do not use 'de temps te' in standard French.
target_language_example: Nous faisons une promenade de temps te.
native_language_example: We take a walk from time to time (intended meaning; note the French contains a typo).

meaning: Not a standard or grammatically correct French phrase; likely a typo or misordering. It may result from mixing parts of phrases like 'de temps en temps' (from time to time) or 'tu as le temps' (do you have time?).
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'de temps tu' does not occur in correct French. If encountered, check the surrounding text for missing words or inversion. Possible intended phrases:
- 'de temps en temps' = occasionally
- 'tu as le temps ?' / 'as-tu le temps ?' = do you have time?
Keep in mind 'de temps tu' cannot be translated literally into natural English.
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il y a une faute ici : 'de temps tu' ne veut rien dire en français.
native_language_example: I think there's a mistake here: 'de temps tu' doesn't mean anything in French.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo or misordering of 'de temps en temps' (meaning 'from time to time' or 'occasionally').
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'de temps va' in French. Learners seeing this sequence should check for typos or incorrect word order. The intended phrase is probably 'de temps en temps' (occasionally) or 'au fil du temps' (over time), depending on context. The example below deliberately uses the exact sequence to show how it would look, but it is ungrammatical and should be avoided.
target_language_example: Cette phrase contient l'expression incorrecte « de temps va » qui n'est pas utilisée en français.
native_language_example: This sentence contains the incorrect expression 'de temps va' which is not used in French.

meaning: part of questions about duration (how long) when addressing 'vous'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions asking about time or duration, usually as part of fixed phrases like "Combien de temps vous a-t-il fallu...?" or "Depuis combien de temps vous... ?" Use the full question forms: "Combien de temps... ?" (How long?) and "Depuis combien de temps... ?" (How long has it been / How long have you been...). The pronoun "vous" makes the question formal or plural. Word order may change in more formal inversion (e.g. "Depuis combien de temps êtes-vous là ?").
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps vous habitez ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living here?

meaning: occasionally; from time to time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens now and then, not regularly. Similar to 'parfois' or 'de temps en temps' (very close). Neutral register and common in spoken and written French. Can appear at start, middle or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Je téléphone à mes parents de temps à autre.
native_language_example: I call my parents from time to time.

meaning: 'how long' (asking about duration).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions about duration, usually as part of 'combien de temps ça va durer/prendre' — literally 'how much time is it going to last/take'. Common in spoken and written French to ask how long something will continue or require.
target_language_example: Combien de temps ça va durer, selon toi ?
native_language_example: How long will it last, in your opinion?

meaning: of terrible / very bad (used to describe something as awful or shocking).
additional_notes: This is a simple combination of the preposition 'de' + adjective 'terrible'. In French, adjectives usually follow the noun, so you would more commonly see 'terrible' after a noun (e.g. 'une nouvelle terrible' = 'a terrible/awful piece of news'). 'De terrible' can appear after certain expressions (e.g. 'rien de terrible' = 'nothing terrible') or in contracted phrases. Pay attention to agreement: 'terrible' does not change in form for gender when used attributively in many contexts, but may vary in meaning depending on context.
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien de terrible, tout va bien.
native_language_example: There's nothing terrible, everything is fine.

meaning: from you for (or to) — indicates something given, intended, or about someone (you) in relation to something else
additional_notes: This short sequence appears inside larger phrases such as «un cadeau de toi pour moi» (a gift from you for me) or «ton message de toi pour l'entreprise» (your message from you for the company). Word-for-word: de = from/of, toi = you (stressed/after preposition), pour = for/to. It is compositional and used in everyday French when specifying the sender/owner (de toi) and the intended recipient or purpose (pour). Make sure word order and context are clear; often you'll see possessive forms instead (ton, ta) which are more natural: «un cadeau de ta part pour moi» or «ton cadeau pour moi».
target_language_example: C'est un dessin de toi pour maman.
native_language_example: It's a drawing from you for mom.

meaning: part of constructions meaning 'make you a ...' or 'what makes you a ...' (literally 'of you a ...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears in the structure 'faire de + quelqu'un + (quelque chose)' meaning 'to make someone (something)' or in questions 'Qu'est-ce qui fait de toi...?' meaning 'What makes you...?' Word order in French places the person between 'de' and the noun: faire de toi une star = make you a star. Also watch examples like 'J'ai besoin de toi une seconde' — here 'de toi' is separate: 'I need you for a second.' So context matters: 'de toi une ...' specifically signals 'faire de toi une ...' constructions.
target_language_example: Ils vont faire de toi une meilleure personne.
native_language_example: They are going to make you a better person.

meaning: from you to (used to indicate direction, range, or a relationship starting with 'you')
additional_notes: This phrase is a sequence of prepositions and a pronoun: 'de' (from/of) + 'toi' (you, stressed/tonic form) + 'à' (to/at). It appears in expressions like 'de toi à moi' (between you and me) or when specifying a range/direction involving 'you' (e.g. 'de toi à lui' = from you to him). By itself 'de toi à' is incomplete and usually part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: De toi à moi, je trouve ce film ennuyeux.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I find this movie boring.

meaning: of/for always; indicating something that lasts forever or is habitual.
additional_notes: Used after nouns or verbs with 'de' + 'toujours' to mean 'of all time' (timeless) or 'always' (habitual). Context determines nuance: with verbs it often means 'always' (Je promets de toujours...), though more common French places 'toujours' after the infinitive (promets de toujours dire → promets de toujours dire is acceptable but 'promets de toujours dire' is less common than 'promets de dire toujours'). With nouns, 'compagnon de toujours' means 'lifelong/everlasting companion.' Can sound slightly literary or emphatic in some uses.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami de toujours.
native_language_example: He's my lifelong friend.

meaning: to go around (something); to circle around; often used in the expression "tourner autour de" meaning to avoid the main point or to hesitate.
additional_notes: Alone 'de tourner autour' is incomplete; the common construction is 'tourner autour de + [quelque chose/quelqu'un]'. It can be literal (physically circling) or figurative (avoiding an issue, hesitating, beating around the bush). In spoken French the phrase 'arrête de tourner autour du pot' means 'stop beating around the bush.'
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-nous la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell us the truth.

meaning: 'to beat around the bush' — avoid saying something directly.
additional_notes: Used in the phrase 'arrêter de tourner autour du pot' meaning 'stop beating around the bush' / 'stop avoiding the main point'. 'Tourner autour de' literally means 'to turn around', and 'pot' is 'pot' — but the expression as a whole means to dodge the main topic. Common in spoken and written French. You can change 'pot' to refer to a specific thing (e.g., 'tourner autour du sujet'), but 'tourner autour du pot' is the fixed idiom.
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi ce que tu veux vraiment.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what you really want.

meaning: everyday; ordinary; used daily
additional_notes: Used to describe something common, routine, or typical in daily life (e.g., language, objects, habits). Can modify nouns (la vie de tous les jours, le vin de tous les jours) or activities (conversation de tous les jours). Equivalent to 'everyday' or 'day-to-day.'
target_language_example: C'est une tenue de tous les jours, confortable et simple.
native_language_example: It's an everyday outfit, comfortable and simple.

meaning: of all time; ever (used to say someone/something is the best or greatest in history).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to express that someone or something ranks highest across all eras. Common in superlative expressions (le meilleur de tous les temps, le plus grand de tous les temps). Often used in discussions about artists, athletes, works, etc.
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur film de tous les temps.
native_language_example: It's the best film of all time.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; a sequence of two common words meaning roughly 'of all' + 'in' — depending on context it can function like 'of all in' or 'among all in'. Often appears as part of a larger clause rather than standing alone.
additional_notes: The sequence 'de tous dans' is uncommon as an independent fixed phrase. Treat it compositionally: learn 'de tous' (of all/everyone) and 'dans' (in/inside) separately. When you see 'de tous dans' it will usually be followed by a noun phrase or clause that specifies the group and location (e.g. 'de tous dans la salle...'). Do not memorize it as an idiom; interpret based on surrounding words.
target_language_example: De tous dans la salle, c'est lui qui connaît le mieux la réponse.
native_language_example: Of all in the room, he is the one who knows the answer best.

meaning: a sequence of words ('de' + 'tout' + masculine demonstrative adjective 'cet') that would mean 'of all this' or 'from all this' when followed by a masculine singular noun, but it's unusual — normally you'd use 'de tout ce' or 'de tout cela'.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'de tout cet' is rare and often incorrect in modern French because 'tout' + demonstrative adjective usually appears as 'tout ce' (for masculine singular before consonant) or 'tout cet' is possible before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound only when 'tout' is used adverbially (e.g. 'tout est prêt', 'tout ce que'). For 'of all this' you normally say 'de tout cela' or 'de tout ça' or 'de tout ce' + noun (e.g. 'de tout ce projet'). If you see 'de tout cet', check that a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel follows (e.g. 'de tout cet effort' would be nonstandard; better: 'de tout cet effort' is sometimes heard but 'de tous ces efforts' (of all these efforts) or 'de tout cet effort' — use with care).
target_language_example: Je doute de tout cela, pas de tout cet idée.
native_language_example: I doubt all of that, not of this whole idea.

meaning: with all my heart; sincerely/wholeheartedly
additional_notes: Used to express strong emotional support, gratitude, or sincerity. Common in phrases like "je suis de tout cœur avec vous" (I'm with you wholeheartedly) or "merci de tout cœur" (thank you from the bottom of my heart). Formal and informal contexts; can be used with je/tu/nous/vous.
target_language_example: Je te souhaite bonne chance de tout cœur.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck with all my heart.

meaning: for all time; since always; throughout history (i.e. for as long as anyone can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true for a very long time or forever. Common in formal and neutral registers. Can be synonymous with "depuis toujours" or "toujours" depending on context. Often followed by a verb: « Cela a été vrai de tout temps. »
target_language_example: Les hommes ont raconté des histoires de héros de tout temps.
native_language_example: People have told stories of heroes for all time.

meaning: anyway / in any case / regardless
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that remains true regardless of previous information or to dismiss objections. Common in spoken and written French. Can start a sentence or follow a clause (e.g., «... de toute façon.»). Tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: De toute façon, je n'aurais pas pu venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Anyway, I couldn't have come tonight.

meaning: anyway / in any case / regardless
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that is true despite other information or to dismiss previous comments. Commonly interchangeable with 'de toute façon' or 'en tout cas'. Can be placed at the start or middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: De toute manière, je viendrai même s'il pleut.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'll come even if it rains.

meaning: obviously; clearly
additional_notes: Used to state that something is evident or obvious from the situation or facts. Can stand alone as an answer (e.g. "De toute évidence.") or modify a sentence before or after the verb. Neutral register — suitable for spoken and written French.
target_language_example: De toute évidence, elle a oublié notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Obviously, she forgot our appointment.

meaning: from all sides; from everywhere; on all fronts.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something comes or happens from every direction or from many sources (physical sides, critics, threats, etc.). Common in both literal (surrounded) and figurative (widely criticized) contexts. Can be used with passive constructions (être cerné de toutes parts) or active verbs (se faire critiquer de toutes parts).
target_language_example: Ils ont été attaqués de toutes parts.
native_language_example: They were attacked from all sides.

meaning: with all one's strength; as hard as one can
additional_notes: Used to say someone is using their full physical (or sometimes emotional) effort. Commonly follows verbs like crier, pousser, tirer, se débattre. Equivalent to 'as loud as possible' when used with crier, or 'with all one's might' for physical actions.
target_language_example: Il a soulevé la porte de toutes ses forces.
native_language_example: He lifted the door with all his strength.

meaning: 'of all your' or 'from all your' (used before a feminine plural noun)
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the preposition de + the adjective toutes (feminine plural of 'all') + the possessive tes (your, for plural noun). It appears before a feminine plural noun: e.g. «de toutes tes idées», «de toutes tes amies». In speech it can introduce a part of a larger expression (de toutes tes X) and often follows verbs or nouns that take de. Word order: de + toutes + tes + [feminine plural noun].
target_language_example: Je me souviens de toutes tes histoires.
native_language_example: I remember all your stories.

meaning: Not a common standalone French multi-word expression; typically a fragment within phrases like 'pas de trace', 'aucune trace de', or 'trace de' (e.g. 'aucune trace de sang'). It doesn't function independently to convey a complete meaning.
additional_notes: 'De trace' is usually part of larger constructions. You may encounter it in contexts such as 'pas de trace', 'aucune trace de', or when followed by a noun as in 'trace de sang' ('trace of blood'). If you see 'de trace' alone, it's likely clipped or a typo. Use full phrases for clarity.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de trace de pas sur le sentier.
native_language_example: There are no footprints on the trail.

meaning: to work more / to work harder (more hours or with more effort).
additional_notes: Appears after verbs like conseiller (to advise) or demander (to ask/request) with the preposition 'de' plus an infinitive. 'Travailler plus' can mean 'work more' (increase hours) or 'work harder' (put in more effort); context (e.g. 'dur' = 'hard') clarifies meaning. Common structure: [verb] + de + infinitive.
target_language_example: Ils m'ont demandé de travailler plus la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: They asked me to work more next week.

meaning: wrong, askew, or not going as planned (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can describe something physically crooked or misaligned (Le tableau est de travers). Used idiomatically to say something went wrong or is going badly (Quelque chose a dû aller de travers; Tout va de travers). In the fixed expression «Pas un cheveu de travers !» it means 'not a single thing out of place' (i.e., perfectly tidy or well-behaved).
target_language_example: Depuis ce matin, tout semble aller de travers.
native_language_example: Since this morning, everything seems to be going wrong.

target_language_multi_word_term: de traverser la rivière à la nage
meaning: to cross the river by swimming
additional_notes: Literal components: 'traverser la rivière' = to cross the river; 'à la nage' = by swimming. Often used after verbs or expressions of ability or possibility (pouvoir, être capable de, être en mesure de) to indicate the method of crossing.
target_language_example: Il a été en mesure de traverser la rivière à la nage.
native_language_example: He was able to cross the river by swimming.

meaning: too many / unnecessary / out of place (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: 1) after verbs to mean 'too much' or 'from doing too much' (often appears as 'trop' or 'de trop' after a past participle: 'malade de trop manger' = sick from overeating). 2) to say someone/something is unnecessary or makes things awkward: 'se sentir de trop' = feel out of place/like a fifth wheel. 3) 'un mot de trop' = one word too many, i.e. an unnecessary or harmful remark. 4) with numbers, 'de trop' = too many (one or more extra). Note: not informal; meaning is compositional in some uses but idiomatic in others.
target_language_example: Il a apporté trois chaises, une était de trop.
native_language_example: He brought three chairs — one was too many.

meaning: of stuff / of thing (vague, colloquial; used when 'truc' is linked to another word or in clipped spoken expressions)
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase. 'Truc' = 'thing'/'stuff' (informal). 'de truc' occurs in phrases like 'une boîte de truc(s)' in very casual speech or in expressions where 'de' links 'truc' to another noun or adjective (e.g., 'un truc de ouf' / 'truc de fou' in colloquial speech). Spelling and agreement vary in fast speech: people often say 'des trucs' or drop plural marking in speech. Avoid in formal writing; use 'chose(s)' or more precise terms in formal contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé une boîte de truc dans le grenier.
native_language_example: I found a box of stuff in the attic.

meaning: of the type (of), like, similar to — used to describe category or kind
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to indicate that something belongs to a certain type or is similar to a given example. Often followed by the noun or an adjective (e.g., « de type familial », « de type sportif ») or by a noun phrase with no article (e.g., « un bâtiment de type administratif »). Neutral register and widely used in descriptions, reports, or everyday speech.
target_language_example: C'est un appareil de type industriel.
native_language_example: It's an industrial-type device.

meaning: 'of the head' or part of fixed expressions; literal meaning 'of the head' but used in several contexts
additional_notes: Literally means 'of the head' and appears in different contexts: 1) literal anatomy (la voiture de tête = lead car; la statue dépourvue de tête = without a head), 2) as part of set phrases (from memory = 'par cœur' rather than 'de tête' in French; note: 'de tête' alone can appear colloquially like 'pas de tête' to mean 'no head' or 'no brains' depending on context), 3) in culinary terms 'fromage de tête' is a head cheese (a terrine made from a pig's head). The meaning depends on the noun that follows or the expression as a whole.
target_language_example: Il a acheté du fromage de tête au marché.
native_language_example: He bought head cheese at the market.

meaning: from one
additional_notes: Usually seen when un is the numeral 1 in a larger expression, especially for counting ranges: de un à dix = 'from one to ten'. It can also appear in counting or score phrases like et de un ! ('and that's one!'). In most other contexts, de + un is normally contracted to d'un.
target_language_example: Les enfants apprennent à compter de un à vingt.
native_language_example: The children are learning to count from one to twenty.

meaning: 'of value' / 'valuable' (used to indicate worth or importance)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe its worth or value. Can be literal (monetary value) or figurative (importance, usefulness). In some contexts it may be part of a longer phrase (e.g., 'avoir de la valeur' = 'to be valuable'). Word order: 'de valeur' follows the noun it qualifies in the examples.
target_language_example: Cette médaille est un objet de valeur pour moi.
native_language_example: This medal is an object of value to me.

meaning: to unlock (used after another verb or as part of an infinitive phrase)
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb 'verrouiller' (to lock) with the particle 'de' before it, often appearing after certain verbs or expressions that require 'de' + infinitive (e.g., 'arrêter de verrouiller', 'avoir besoin de verrouiller'). Alone, 'verrouiller' means 'to lock'; with 'de' it simply links the infinitive to the preceding verb. It is not a fixed phrase by itself.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de verrouiller la porte avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to lock the door before leaving.

meaning: to lock (the) — infinitive with the definite feminine object after 'de' (e.g., 'to lock the [door]').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but part of a verb phrase: 'oublier de verrouiller la porte' = 'to forget to lock the door'. 'La' is the feminine definite article referring to a specific feminine noun (e.g., 'la porte'). The structure 'oublier de + infinitive' means 'to forget to [do something]'.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de verrouiller la porte avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don't forget to lock the door before leaving.

meaning: literally 'of lives are' — a sequence of words that can appear when a noun phrase using 'de vies' (of lives) is followed by the verb 'sont' (are). It is not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on the full sentence.
additional_notes: Not a standalone expression. 'De vies' often appears in contexts like 'manque de vies' or part of a longer noun phrase; 'sont' is 3rd person plural of être. The sequence 'de vies sont' typically occurs where a possessive/partitive or prepositional phrase referring to lives is immediately followed by a clause with 'sont'. Always check the surrounding sentence for precise meaning and agreement.
target_language_example: Les conséquences de vies sont souvent difficiles à mesurer après une catastrophe.
native_language_example: The consequences of lives are often difficult to measure after a disaster.

meaning: 'lives are at stake' (part of the phrase used to say lives are at risk)
additional_notes: This is not a complete standalone phrase; it appears inside sentences like "Des milliers/millions de vies sont en jeu." which means "Thousands/millions of lives are at stake." Use with a quantifier before "vies" (des centaines, des milliers, des millions, trop, etc.).
target_language_example: Des milliers de vies sont en jeu.
native_language_example: Thousands of lives are at stake.

meaning: of the city / city (as in 'for city use' or 'urban').
additional_notes: Literally 'of the city'. Often used after a noun to describe something related to the city or intended for urban use (e.g. 'voiture de ville' = town/city car, 'chaussures de ville' = dress shoes). Also appears in names/expressions like 'centre-ville' (city centre) but standalone 'de ville' is a modifier that follows the noun. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Il conduit une voiture de ville pour se rendre au travail.
native_language_example: He drives a city car to get to work.

meaning: 'from town to town' / 'from city to city' (traveling from one town/city to another repeatedly).
additional_notes: Used in the expression 'de ville en ville' to describe moving or traveling from one town/city to another, often repeatedly or as a pattern. Usually appears as 'de ville en ville' (complete phrase). Can be followed by verbs like aller, voyager, parcourir. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Il est parti de ville en ville à la recherche d'un emploi.
native_language_example: He went from town to town looking for a job.

meaning: from your point (of view) / from your position
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase "de votre point de vue" (from your point of view) or "de votre point de départ/placement". On its own, "de votre point" is incomplete and needs a following noun (vue, départ, vue de vue, etc.). It indicates perspective, origin, or location belonging to the person you're addressing (formal/plural "votre"). Formal register because of "votre"; use "ton point" in informal singular.
target_language_example: De votre point de vue, que devrions-nous changer ?
native_language_example: From your point of view, what should we change?

meaning: to want to do (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'de' with the infinitive construction 'vouloir faire' following expressions of certainty/doubt (e.g. 'être sûr de'). It appears in questions like 'Are you sure you want to do that?' The speaker may change gender/number of 'sûr' (sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres) to match the subject. 'De' is required after certain adjectives and verbs (e.g. 'décider de', 'avoir peur de', 'être sûr de').
target_language_example: Il n'est pas sûr de vouloir faire ce voyage.
native_language_example: He is not sure he wants to make this trip.

meaning: 'to want to (do) it' — part of the phrase used to ask or state whether someone wants to do something (le = it / the action).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a sequence: 'être sûr de vouloir le faire' = 'to be sure you want to do it'. 'De' follows expressions like 'sûr de' or 'certain de'. 'Le' is a direct object pronoun meaning 'it' (refers to an action or thing already mentioned). Word order: subject + être sûr(e) de + vouloir + le + verb infinitive (faire). Agreement: 'sûr' varies by speaker gender (sûr/sûre) and formality (tu/vous).
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de vouloir le tenter ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to try it?

meaning: to want to leave (as part of a larger phrase: 'sure/l'absolutely certain to want to leave')
additional_notes: This construction combines 'vouloir partir' (to want to leave) with the preposition 'de' after adjectives like 'sûr(e)(s)' or verbs expressing certainty/doubt: e.g. 'être sûr de vouloir partir' = 'to be sure that one wants to leave.' Used when asking or stating whether someone really wants to leave. Conjugation/agreement (sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres) depends on the subject, but 'de vouloir partir' stays the same.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr de vouloir partir si tôt.
native_language_example: I'm not sure I want to leave so early.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; the sequence 'de' + 'vouloir' + 'y' can occur in complex sentences where an infinitive clause introduced by 'de' contains 'vouloir' followed by the pronoun 'y' (often before an infinitive). It does not form a standalone expression with a unique meaning beyond its components.
additional_notes: 'de' can introduce an infinitive after certain verbs (or be part of other constructions). 'vouloir' means 'to want'. 'y' is a pronoun meaning 'there' or 'to it/there' (often replacing à + thing or a place). In natural French, 'y' usually precedes a conjugated verb or an infinitive (e.g. 'je veux y aller'). The exact sequence 'de vouloir y' may appear in embedded clauses (for example: «Il a cessé de vouloir y croire.») but such sequences are not learned as single units — learn the components and word order rules instead.
target_language_example: Il a cessé de vouloir y croire.
native_language_example: He stopped wanting to believe in it/there.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself; literally 'of/from you and'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom in French. It looks like part of a longer phrase where 'de vous' (of/from you; polite/plural 'you') is followed by 'et' (and). You will encounter it inside sentences, e.g. in lists or compound expressions: 'de vous et de votre famille' (of you and your family). Pay attention to context and to required contractions (e.g. 'de' becomes 'd'' before a vowel).
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de vous et de vos documents.
native_language_example: We need you and your documents.

meaning: 'of it to you' part of the clitic combination used before entendre/entendre dire: literally 'to hear you say it' (as in 'heureux de vous l'entendre dire' = 'happy to hear you say that').
additional_notes: This fragment appears when the object pronoun 'le/la/les' (here contracted to l') and the indirect object pronoun 'vous' appear before an infinitive verb like 'entendre' or the semi-auxiliary phrase 'entendre dire'. In full order the idea is 'être heureux de + [infinitive phrase]' with the pronouns placed before the infinitive: 'heureux de vous l'entendre dire' = 'happy to hear you say it' (literally 'happy of you it to-hear to-say'). The sequence is formal/neutral and common in written and spoken French. The phrase 'de vous l'' by itself is incomplete — it always attaches to a verb (e.g. l'entendre, l'avoir, etc.).
target_language_example: Je suis content de vous l'entendre dire.
native_language_example: I'm glad to hear you say that.

meaning: to hear it from you / to hear you say it
additional_notes: This fragment appears in French sentences where someone expresses that they will hear (or have heard) 'it' from the person addressed. It usually follows verbs or expressions like « content » (heureux) or « désolé » or constructions such as « Je serai content de vous l'entendre dire » (I'll be happy to hear you say that). Alone it is incomplete; it needs a verb before it and an object reference for « l' » (it).
target_language_example: Je serai heureux de vous l'entendre dire.
native_language_example: I'll be happy to hear you say that.

meaning: 'of it to you' or 'about you it' — a sequence of words that can appear in larger sentences where 'de' links a noun/verb and 'vous' is an object or prepositional object, followed by the direct object pronoun 'le'. The precise meaning depends on context and surrounding words.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase. Appears when a clause uses 'de' + 'vous' (prepositional or partitive) and then the direct object pronoun 'le' referring back to a masculine singular noun. Word order may vary in spoken/written French and with different pronoun combinations (e.g., je vais vous le donner). Be careful: in many cases 'de vous le' will be split across clause boundaries and its interpretation requires the whole sentence.
target_language_example: Il s'agit de vous le dire avant la réunion.
native_language_example: It's a matter of telling it to you before the meeting.

meaning: a fragment meaning "to ask you" or part of constructions with the infinitive "poser" following a preposition "de"; often appears after verbs that govern "de + infinitive" or in reflexive/modal contexts (context decides exact sense).
additional_notes: Not a standalone sentence — it's an infinitive phrase fragment. "Poser" means "to put" or "to ask" (e.g. "poser une question" = "to ask a question"). "De vous poser" can appear in clauses like "J'hésite de vous poser..." (rare/incorrect) but correctly after verbs requiring "de + infinitive": e.g. "J'ai peur de vous poser cette question." It also appears inside infinitive relative clauses: "J'ai besoin de vous poser une question." Context decides whether it directly targets "you" (vous) or is part of a reflexive construction when combined differently (e.g. "se poser" for "to arise/ask oneself").
target_language_example: J'ai peur de vous poser cette question.
native_language_example: I'm afraid to ask you this question.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French multiword expression; it is most likely a fragment or mistaken word order and has no clear standalone meaning.
additional_notes:
This sequence of words does not form a correct phrase in French. It could appear as a fragment inside a longer, incorrect sentence or as part of a transcription error. Possible intended correct forms include:
- 'de vous' (of/about you)
- 'un de vous' (one of you)
To salvage meaning, check word order and surrounding context. Example corrections:
- 'Parlez-moi de vous.' (Talk to me about you.)
- 'Un de vous doit venir.' (One of you must come.)
target_language_example: *de vous un* (fragment — not a grammatical sentence in French)
native_language_example: *de vous un* (fragment — not a grammatical phrase in English)

meaning: part of a reflexive or passive-like verbal structure meaning 'to be (for) you' or 'to have been for you' depending on context
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's a sequence that appears inside larger verb constructions with infinitives or past participles, for example after verbs like 'sembler', 'paraître', 's'agir de', or in perfect infinitive forms (e.g. 'avoir été de vous être' rarely). More commonly you will see 'vous être' (to be for you) or 'être de + personne' (to belong to someone). The exact meaning depends on the main verb and tense. Pay attention to word order and surrounding words to understand the full sense.
target_language_example: Il semble important de vous être utile.
native_language_example: It seems important to be useful to you.

meaning: real, genuine; used after a noun or adjective to mean 'truly' or 'real' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Often used in spoken French to emphasize authenticity or degree. Common patterns: 'un ami de vrai' (a true friend), 'c'est du lourd de vrai' (it's really heavy/serious) or placed after adjectives: 'beau de vrai' (really beautiful). It's informal and more frequent in some regional speech; in formal contexts prefer 'vrai' before the noun ('un vrai ami') or adverbs like 'vraiment'.
target_language_example: C'est un ami de vrai, toujours là quand j'ai besoin.
native_language_example: He's a true friend, always there when I need him.

meaning: adds emphasis: 'really' or 'truly' (used after certain words or expressions).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the preposition/partitive 'de' plus the adverb 'vraiment'. It often appears after adjectives or verbs in colloquial speech to intensify meaning (e.g. 'beaucoup de vraiment' is rare — more commonly you'll see constructions like 'c'est vraiment…' or 'rien de vraiment…'). Standalone 'de vraiment' is less common than 'vraiment' by itself; when present it usually connects to a noun phrase introduced by 'de' (e.g. 'rien de vraiment intéressant' = 'nothing really interesting'). Use 'vraiment' alone to mean 'really' in most contexts.
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien de vraiment urgent.
native_language_example: There is nothing really urgent.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; a fragment that can occur when words like 'de', 'vue' and 'est' appear consecutively in a sentence (usually across clause boundaries) rather than forming a single expression.
additional_notes: The sequence 'de vue est' does not form a conventional multi-word expression in French. It may appear in running text when a phrase ending with 'de vue' (e.g. 'du point de vue') is followed by a verb phrase starting with 'est'. Example: 'Du point de vue est...' would be incorrect, but 'Du point de vue, est-ce que...' or 'Du point de vue moral, il est...' are correct. If you encounter 'de vue est', check punctuation and surrounding words: it's likely part of a longer, correct construction where punctuation or word order was changed. For learners, prefer established phrases like 'du point de vue' (from the point of view) or 'de vue d'oiseau' (bird's-eye view).
target_language_example: Du point de vue est-il nécessaire de préciser cela ?
native_language_example: From the point of view, is it necessary to specify that?

meaning: of/from bike, or used to describe something related to a bicycle (e.g., 'riding a bike').
additional_notes: This is a prepositional phrase combining 'de' with the noun 'vélo' (bicycle). Its exact translation depends on context: it can mean 'of a bike' (possession), 'from a bike' (origin), or appear in expressions like 'faire du vélo' where 'du vélo' means 'biking'/'to ride a bike'. Alone, 'de vélo' is not a complete phrase; you commonly see it after another noun (un casque de vélo — a bike helmet) or after verbs that require 'de' + noun.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté un panier de vélo pour l'avant.
native_language_example: She bought a bike basket for the front.

meaning: of that
additional_notes: Literally combines de + ça. The exact English translation depends on the verb or expression: it can mean of that, about that, from that, or with that. Very common in spoken French; de cela is more formal or written.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus parler de ça.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about that anymore.

meaning: 'about that' (used to refer back to something previously mentioned; literally 'of that of which I...').
additional_notes: This sequence appears when a speaker refers back to a thing or topic already mentioned and then uses a relative construction with 'dont' plus a verb referring to the speaker (je, je veux te, etc.). In natural French you'd usually say 'c'est de ça dont je parle' or more simply 'c'est de ça que je parle' (the latter is more common). 'Dont' replaces 'de + [thing]' and links the noun to the verb; the full phrase emphasizes 'that (thing) is what I'm talking about.' Use with verbs that govern 'de' (parler de, vouloir parler de, rêver de, avoir besoin de, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est de ça dont je voulais te parler hier.
native_language_example: That's what I wanted to talk to you about yesterday.

meaning: of this here / about this here (informal, pointing to something nearby)
additional_notes: A colloquial sequence used when referring to something physically or contextually close. It combines de (of/about), ça (this/that), and ici (here). In careful French you'd more often hear «de ça» or «ici» alone, or a more precise phrase like «à propos de ça» (about this) or «de ceci ici». «De ça ici» is casual and emphasizes both the thing (ça) and its proximity (ici).
target_language_example: Je veux plus d'informations de ça ici.
native_language_example: I want more information about this here.

meaning: an informal colloquial way to mean 'more than that' or 'besides that' (adds something extra).
additional_notes: This is a spoken/colloquial sequence combining de + ça + plus. It can be used to add information or say 'on top of that' / 'besides that' but it's informal and quite conversational. Depending on context intonation and word order, speakers might instead say 'en plus' (more standard) or 'de plus' (written). Use 'en plus' or 'de plus' in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il est déjà en retard, de ça plus il a oublié ses clés.
native_language_example: He's already late, and on top of that he forgot his keys.

meaning: 'about that' or 'that's what it's about' (used in questions/confirmations).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expressions «c'est de ça qu'il s'agit» or «c'est de ça qu'il est question», meaning 'that's what it's about' or 'is that what this is about?'. Often used to confirm or ask if the subject under discussion is that thing. Informal contractions may elide the vowel (qu' + il/est). The phrase relies on the preceding context (ça = that/this).
target_language_example: C'est de ça qu'il s'agit ?
native_language_example: Is that what this is about?

meaning: from this to (that) / ranging from ... to ... (informal, often in spoken French)
additional_notes: Used to indicate a range or list of examples, similar to 'from ... to ...' in English. Often appears in spoken French as part of an enumeration: 'de ça à ça' = 'from this to that'. When followed by a verb it can mean 'from ... to (doing) ...' (context matters). It's informal and commonly used in conversation.
target_language_example: Il y a de ça à ça dans son discours : humour, sérieux et émotion.
native_language_example: There is everything from this to that in his speech: humor, seriousness and emotion.

meaning: 'outside after' or 'outside later' (indicates something will happen outside at a later time)
additional_notes: This is a combination of dehors (outside) and après (after/later). It's not a fixed idiom — it simply places an event or action outside and specifies it will occur afterward. Word order in French is normally 'dehors' and 'après' can follow to mean 'afterwards/outside afterwards' or be part of a larger time expression (e.g. 'dehors, après, ...'). Depending on context you might instead hear 'après, dehors' or more natural phrases like 'on le fera dehors après' or 'plus tard, dehors'.
target_language_example: On discutera dehors après.
native_language_example: We'll talk outside later.

meaning: outside after the (time/event).
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a fixed idiom. 'Dehors' = outside; 'après' = after; 'le' is the definite article that will be followed by a time expression or event (e.g. 'déjeuner', 'film', or a time like 'déjeuner' -> 'le déjeuner'). In a full sentence you might see: 'dehors après le film' (outside after the movie) or 'dehors après le déjeuner' (outside after lunch). Word order: de hors (location) + après le (temporal relation).
target_language_example: On se retrouve dehors après le film.
native_language_example: Let's meet outside after the movie.

meaning: outside of / out of (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate being or moving outside of something. More common in spoken French is simply 'dehors' (outside) or 'à l'extérieur de' for formal contexts; 'dehors de' can sound awkward in many constructions and is less frequent than 'en dehors de' (meaning 'apart from' or 'except for')—don't confuse them. Use 'sortir de' for 'to go out of (a place)'.
target_language_example: Il y a des chaussures dehors de la porte.
native_language_example: There are shoes outside the door.

meaning: 'outside of the' or 'outside the' (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is a less common combination—French usually uses either "dehors" alone (meaning "outside") or "en dehors de" (meaning "outside of" / "apart from"). "Dehors de la" can appear in spoken or regional usage before a feminine noun (e.g., "dehors de la maison") but standard French prefers "à l'extérieur de la" or "en dehors de la". Use "dehors" by itself when saying someone/something is outside: "Il est dehors."
target_language_example: En dehors de la ville, il y a beaucoup d'espaces verts.
native_language_example: Outside the city, there are many green spaces.

meaning: 'outside of my' or 'outside my' (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a fragment: dehors means 'outside' and de + ma ('of my') links it to a feminine noun (e.g. 'dehors de ma maison' = 'outside my house'). In natural French you more often say 'à l'extérieur de ma...' or simply 'devant ma...' or 'chez moi' depending on context. Use 'dehors de ma...' when emphasizing 'outside of my [something]' but check the noun that follows (must be feminine).
target_language_example: Il y a de la neige dehors de ma maison.
native_language_example: There is snow outside my house.

meaning: aside from that; besides that; other than that
additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception or to add a comment about something different from what was just mentioned. Less common than alternatives like "à part ça", "à part cela" or "en dehors de ça", but understood in conversational French. Often followed by a comma and a contrasting statement.
target_language_example: Dehors de ça, tout s'est bien passé.
native_language_example: Aside from that, everything went well.

meaning: 'outside of the' or 'outside the'
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located or happening outside a specific place or thing. 'Dehors' means 'outside'; when followed by 'du' (contraction of 'de le') it specifies 'outside the' + masculine singular noun (e.g. 'dehors du bâtiment' = 'outside the building'). For feminine nouns use 'dehors de la' (or 'dehors de l'' before a vowel) and for plural use 'dehors des'.
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent dehors du jardin.
native_language_example: The children are playing outside the garden.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French. It is simply the adverb 'dehors' (outside) followed by the article 'une' (a/an) and will only occur in specific syntactic contexts; as a standalone sequence it usually indicates a word order or typing error.
additional_notes: Native speakers do not use 'dehors une' as a set expression. If you encounter it, check sentence structure—'une' should directly precede a feminine noun (une chaise) and 'dehors' typically appears before or after the verb or after the noun phrase (La chaise est dehors or une chaise dehors). Example contexts where the two words might appear adjacent: dialog or poetic inversion, or when punctuation separates clauses ("Dehors, une..." meaning "Outside, a..."). For learners: treat 'dehors' and 'une' separately and be careful with word order.
target_language_example: Dehors, une pluie soudaine a commencé.
native_language_example: Outside, a sudden rain began.

meaning: 'outside at' (used to indicate being located or happening outside at a particular time or place)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the preposition 'dehors' (outside) followed by 'à' (at/to) and typically requires a following time, place, or verb phrase (e.g. 'dehors à midi', 'dehors à la porte', 'dehors à regarder le ciel'). More common patterns are simply 'dehors' (outside) or 'à l'extérieur de' (outside of). Use 'dehors à' when you want to specify 'outside at [time/place]'.
target_language_example: Nous serons dehors à midi pour le pique-nique.
native_language_example: We will be outside at noon for the picnic.

meaning: beyond; on the other side of (figurative or literal)
additional_notes: Used to indicate something is beyond a limit, boundary, or concept. Often appears in expressions like "au-delà de" (beyond, in addition to). Alone as "delà de" is less common; learners will most often see "au-delà de" meaning "beyond" or "more than" (e.g., au-delà de mes attentes = beyond my expectations). Can be used for physical distance, time, limits, or abstract ideas.
target_language_example: Au-delà de la montagne, il y a un village.
native_language_example: Beyond the mountain, there is a village.

meaning: 'tomorrow is' (the start of a sentence: used to talk about what will happen or be the case tomorrow).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the noun 'demain' (tomorrow) plus the verb 'est' (is). You will normally see it at the beginning of a sentence followed by a description (e.g. 'Demain est férié' = 'Tomorrow is a holiday'). Conjugation changes with the subject: for 'tomorrow will be' in near future you can also say 'demain ce sera' or use other verbs as needed.
target_language_example: Demain est férié, on n'a pas cours.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is a public holiday, we don't have class.

meaning: 'tomorrow it' — the start of a sentence referring to something happening or being the case tomorrow (often followed by a verb or clause).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the word 'demain' (tomorrow) followed by the subject pronoun 'il' (it/he). In French, 'il' is often used as an impersonal subject (like 'il pleut' = 'it is raining') or to refer to a masculine noun mentioned earlier. Expect a verb or clause after 'demain il', e.g. 'demain il fera beau' (tomorrow it will be sunny) or 'demain il vient' (tomorrow he/it is coming).
target_language_example: Demain il fera plus chaud.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it will be warmer.

meaning: 'tomorrow I' — the beginning of a sentence stating what the speaker will do or feel tomorrow.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the adverb 'demain' (tomorrow) followed by the subject pronoun 'je' (I). You will normally complete it with a verb: e.g. 'Demain je vais...' (Tomorrow I will...), 'Demain je pars.' (Tomorrow I'm leaving.). Use the inverted or contracted forms as usual: 'Demain, j'arriverai...' (note the apostrophe when the verb begins with a vowel).
target_language_example: Demain je vais au marché.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I am going to the market.

meaning: Literally 'tomorrow us' — not a standalone fixed phrase in French; typically appears at the start of a sentence as 'Demain nous...' meaning 'Tomorrow we...' when followed by a verb or clause.
additional_notes: On its own 'demain nous' is incomplete. 'Demain' = 'tomorrow' and 'nous' = 'we/us'. In written French it's common to put a comma after 'Demain' (Demain, nous...) but in speech the pause may be omitted. Use it to introduce plans or actions that will happen the next day: 'Demain nous partirons', 'Demain nous allons voir...'.
target_language_example: Demain nous partirons tôt le matin.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we will leave early in the morning.

meaning: 'tomorrow for' — used when specifying a purpose, recipient, time or appointment relating to tomorrow (often followed by a noun or verb phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the adverb 'demain' (tomorrow) followed by the preposition 'pour' (for). It introduces the purpose, intended recipient, deadline or scheduled time connected to tomorrow. Make sure to complete the phrase with a noun, infinitive verb, or clause (e.g. 'demain pour la réunion', 'demain pour signer', 'demain pour toi'). Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar.
target_language_example: Je viendrai demain pour la réunion.
native_language_example: I'll come tomorrow for the meeting.

meaning: 'tomorrow at' (used to specify a time or place the next day).
additional_notes: Combine demain (tomorrow) with à to introduce a time or place: «demain à 9h» = tomorrow at 9, «demain à la gare» = tomorrow at the station. Used in schedules, plans, or meeting arrangements. Note that times often use «à» + hour; for days you can say just «demain» without à.
target_language_example: On se retrouve demain à 18h au café.
native_language_example: Let's meet tomorrow at 6 PM at the café.

meaning: 'I was wondering' (used to introduce a question or curiosity in the past).
additional_notes: This is part of the impersonal reflexive phrase "Je me demandais..." (literally "I was asking myself...") used to politely express wondering about something in the past. It is followed by a subordinate question introduced by "ce que" (what/that which) or "ce qui" (what/which when the clause is subject). Common in spoken and written French to soften questions.
target_language_example: Je me demandais ce que tu ferais demain.
native_language_example: I was wondering what you would do tomorrow.

meaning: 'asked where' (imperfect tense: I/he/she/you was/were asking where)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb demander (to ask) in the imperfect (demandais) plus the interrogative où (where). Used to report or describe ongoing or repeated past asking about location. Subject is understood from context (je demandais, tu demandais, il/elle demandais is incorrect—note: il/elle demandait). Common in indirect questions: «Je demandais où...».
target_language_example: Hier, je demandais où était la gare.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was asking where the train station was.

meaning: '(I) was asking where you (were)'. Used in reported or interrupted speech to introduce a question about someone's location or plans.
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the verb demander (imperfect) plus an indirect question introduced by où + subject tu. In full sentences you'd normally see it in contexts like «Je demandais où tu étais» or «Je demandais où tu allais». The imperfect (demandais) gives a past, repeated, or polite/backstory sense. Word order in reported questions is different from direct questions: subject follows the question word (où tu étais, not où étais-tu).
target_language_example: Hier, je demandais où tu allais avant de partir.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was asking where you were going before leaving.

meaning: 'was wondering why' (I was wondering why...)
additional_notes: Used with 'je me' as part of the imperfect reflexive phrase 'je me demandais pourquoi' to politely express wondering about a past situation. Followed by a clause explaining what was wondered (often with 'tu/es arrivé', 'vous êtes arrivé(s)'). Can be used to soften questions or introduce a reason request. In spoken French, many speakers might use the present tense in the subordinate clause (e.g. 'tu es arrivé') even though the main clause is imperfect.
target_language_example: Je me demandais pourquoi tu as choisi ce livre.
native_language_example: I was wondering why you chose that book.

meaning: I was wondering when…
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the imperfect tense with 'je me' (je me demandais) to politely express curiosity or expectation about the timing of something. Followed by a clause introduced by 'tu', 'vous', or a verb in conditional/conditional-past: e.g. 'tu allais', 'tu viendrais'. Can be used to soften questions or express that you had been thinking about something for a while.
target_language_example: Je me demandais quand tu rentrerais à la maison.
native_language_example: I was wondering when you would come home.

meaning: asked if
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of demander + si. Used to report a past request/question about whether something was true or would happen. Common in reported speech: «Je demandais si...» = 'I asked if/whether...'. Can also mean 'I was asking whether' (ongoing/polite). 'Si' here means 'if/whether', not 'yes'.
target_language_example: Je demandais si vous pouviez m'aider.
native_language_example: I asked if you could help me.

meaning: 'the request has' (part of the passive construction 'demande a été ...' = 'the request was ...')
additional_notes: This appears as part of the passive perfect form 'la demande a été + past participle' meaning 'the request was ...' (accepted/rejected/etc.). 'Demande' = request; 'a' is the third-person singular of 'avoir' used to form compound tenses. Not a complete phrase by itself — you will commonly see 'la demande a été acceptée/rejetée'.
target_language_example: La demande a été acceptée hier.
native_language_example: The request was accepted yesterday.

meaning: a marriage proposal; the act of asking someone to marry you.
additional_notes: Used for the formal proposal or request to marry. Can refer to the moment, the offer itself, or the request letter/gesture. Commonly used with verbs like accepter (accept), refuser (refuse), faire (make/perform) or recevoir (receive).
target_language_example: Il a fait sa demande en mariage au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: He proposed to her by the sea.

meaning: 'wonder(s) what' or 'ask(s) what' (used in expressions like je me demande ce qu')
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the impersonal/reflexive phrase je me demande (I wonder) followed by ce qu' + clause. Ce qu' is the contraction of ce que before a vowel/ mute h. Used to introduce a subordinate question (what ...). Translate as "what" or "what ... like/has/did" depending on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Je me demande ce qu'il fait demain.
native_language_example: I wonder what he is doing tomorrow.

meaning: 'asks what he/it...'/ 'asks what he's/it's...'
additional_notes: This is a fragment of a longer sentence: demande (il/elle/on) + ce qu'il + verb. It introduces an indirect question: someone 'asks what' followed by a clause starting with 'il' (he/it) + verb. In English this becomes 'asks what he/it + verb' or 'asks what he's/it's + verb'. To form a complete sentence, add who asks and the rest of the clause (e.g. 'demande ce qu'il veut').
target_language_example: Elle demande ce qu'il veut.
native_language_example: She asks what he wants.

meaning: 'asks how much' or 'asks how many' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb demander (to ask) + combien (how much/how many). Use when reporting or describing that someone asks about a quantity or price. Followed by a noun (combien de pommes) for 'how many' or by a verb (combien ça coûte) for 'how much'. Can appear in different tenses (il demande combien, elle a demandé combien).
target_language_example: Il demande combien ça coûte.
native_language_example: He asks how much it costs.

meaning: '(one) wonders/how many' — used to ask or wonder about the number of something.
additional_notes: Often appears in the structure 'Je me demande combien de ...' (I wonder how many ...). Followed by a plural noun or plural verb construction. Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about a quantity. For direct questions you can use 'Combien de ... ?' without 'Je me demande'.
target_language_example: Je me demande combien de livres elle a lus.
native_language_example: I wonder how many books she has read.

meaning: 'asks where he' / 'asks where it (masculine) ...' — beginning of a reported question clause
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself. It's typically part of a larger sentence reporting what someone asks, e.g. «Il demande où il est» (He asks where he is) or «Elle demande où il habite» (She asks where he lives). The verb after 'où il' completes the meaning (est, habite, travaille, etc.). Use it when reporting or quoting a question introduced by 'demander'.
target_language_example: Elle demande où il travaille.
native_language_example: She asks where he works.

meaning: asks why he/it ... (introduces a question about the reason for something involving 'il').
additional_notes: Literal sequence: demande (asks/request) + pourquoi (why) + il (he/it). This appears as part of longer sentences (e.g. «Il demande pourquoi il...») meaning 'He asks why he/it ...' or in reported speech: 'She asks why he...'. You will usually see it followed by a verb or clause explaining what 'il' did or should do. Useful for forming reported questions or describing someone asking for a reason.
target_language_example: Il demande pourquoi il doit partir si tôt.
native_language_example: He asks why he has to leave so early.

meaning: 'asks why the' (used to report that someone asks for the reason for something plural)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb demande (asks/request) + pourquoi (why) + les (the, plural). It's typically part of a longer sentence: subject + demande pourquoi les + [noun/plural clause]. Not a fixed idiom — it's a compositional sequence used when reporting a question about plural things or a plural situation. Word order: [Il/Elle] demande pourquoi les + [nom/pluriel or clause].
target_language_example: Elle demande pourquoi les enfants sont en retard.
native_language_example: She asks why the children are late.

meaning: 'asks which' or 'asks what (kind of)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb demander (to ask/request) and the interrogative quel (which/what + noun). Used when someone asks about which one or what kind of something — it must be followed by a noun (e.g. 'demande quel livre', 'demande quelle heure').
