additional_notes: Used to mean saying farewell; can imply a permanent or emotional parting (not just a casual 'see you later'). Often followed by 'à' + person or place (dire adieu à quelqu'un/à quelque chose). Can be used reflexively (se dire adieu) for mutual farewells.
target_language_example: Je suis venue pour te dire adieu.
native_language_example: I came to say goodbye to you.

meaning: tell (to)
additional_notes: A common combination of the verb dire (to tell/say) plus the contraction au (à + le) meaning 'to the' before a masculine singular noun. Used when telling something to someone or instructing someone. Structure: dire au + [person/noun] + [ce que / de + infinitive]. For example: « Je vais dire au professeur. » = I will tell the teacher. If the person is feminine, use dire à la (or dire à l' before a vowel) or dire aux for plural. "Dire au" itself is not a fixed phrase but a regular verb + article/contraction.
target_language_example: Je dois dire au médecin ce qui m'inquiète.
native_language_example: I need to tell the doctor what worries me.

meaning: to say goodbye
additional_notes: Common expression used when leaving or parting from someone or something. Often followed by à + person (dire au revoir à quelqu'un) or can be used alone. Not formal slang.
target_language_example: Je dois dire au revoir à mes collègues avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to say goodbye to my colleagues before leaving.

meaning: to say the same (about oneself) / to be able to say the same (about one's situation).
additional_notes: Used with 'en' (en dire autant) to compare one's situation or opinion to someone else's. Often follows a statement about someone else, meaning 'I (or someone) can say the same' or 'I cannot say the same.' Common in spoken and written French to express agreement or contrast. Typical patterns: 'J'aimerais en dire autant' (I wish I could say the same) and 'Je ne peux pas en dire autant' (I can't say the same).
target_language_example: Il a réussi son examen, mais je ne peux pas en dire autant.
native_language_example: He passed his exam, but I can't say the same.

meaning: 'to say something different' or 'to say otherwise' (very rare/unnatural as a standalone phrase).
additional_notes: Not a common fixed expression by itself; speakers normally use «dire autre chose», «dire le contraire», or add an object or clause after «dire autre». If encountered, it will usually be part of a larger structure (e.g. «dire autre [chose/que…]») — avoid dropping the object in natural speech.
target_language_example: Il ne sait pas dire autre sans préciser quoi.
native_language_example: He doesn't know how to say 'something else' without specifying what.

meaning: 'to say with' — used to indicate saying something accompanied by a particular tone, gesture, word, or accompaniment.
additional_notes: Literally 'to say with'. Often appears when describing how something is said (e.g., 'dire avec un sourire', 'dire avec colère') or what accompanies the speech (music, echo, etc.). Not a fixed idiom on its own; typically followed by a noun or phrase describing the manner, tone, or accompaniment. Use 'dire' for 'to say' and 'avec' for 'with'.
target_language_example: Il aime dire avec un sourire ce qu'il pense.
native_language_example: He likes to say with a smile what he thinks.

meaning: say what
additional_notes: Used before clauses introduced by 'que' or relative pronouns (qui/que) to mean 'to say what/that...'. Often appears in expressions like 'dire ce qui est' (say what is true) or 'dire ce qu'il faut' (say what is necessary). The exact translation depends on the following clause (e.g. 'dire ce qu'il veut' = 'say what he wants').
target_language_example: Dis-moi de dire ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: Tell me to say what you think.

meaning: 'to say what's going on' or 'to say what is happening' (informal, colloquial order of words)
additional_notes: This is an informal/conversational word order found in spoken French: the standard form is "dire ce qui se passe" (to say what is happening) or "dire ce qu'il se passe" in some regional/colloquial uses. It often appears in questions or requests (e.g., "Tu peux dire ce qu'il se passe ?"). Use the standard "ce qui se passe" in formal writing. The phrase includes the impersonal "se" used with "passer" (to happen).
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire ce qu'il se passe ici ?
native_language_example: Can you say what's happening here?

meaning: to say what (something) is / to state what ... is
additional_notes: This is a contracted beginning of phrases like « dire ce que c'est » (to say what it is) or « dire ce que c'était » (to say what it was). You will typically see the full forms (c'est, c'était, ça) in speech and writing. Used when asking or reporting someone stating the identity, nature, or content of something. The contraction c' appears before vowel sounds.
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire ce que c'est ?
native_language_example: Can you say what it is?

meaning: start of a phrase meaning 'to say what happens' or 'to say what is being done/said', usually continued with a verb (e.g. 'dire ce qui se passe').
additional_notes: This fragment is incomplete on its own and normally appears before a reflexive verb: 'dire ce qui se passe' (to say what is happening), 'dire ce qui se dit' (to say what people are saying). Use it only as part of a full clause. Word-for-word: 'to say what oneself/itself ...' (se is a reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: Il est difficile de dire ce qui se passe en ce moment.
native_language_example: It's hard to say what is happening right now.

meaning: to tell someone to; to ask someone to
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the pattern dire à quelqu’un de + infinitive to report an instruction, order, or request: On m’a dit de partir = 'I was told to leave.' When the recipient is already understood or left unstated, you can also see dire de + infinitive, as in the example below. Depending on context, it can sound like a firm instruction ('tell') or a softer request ('ask').
target_language_example: Le patron va dire de commencer sans moi.
native_language_example: The boss is going to tell them to start without me.

meaning: 'to say some' or 'to say (some) ...' — part of a construction used before a plural noun or partitive idea (e.g. dire des choses).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; 'dire' (to say) followed by 'des' (the plural partitive/indefinite article) introduces what is said about multiple things or an unspecified amount. You will usually see it as 'dire des choses', 'dire des mensonges', 'dire des bêtises', etc. Word order: dire + des + plural noun. 'Des' contracts from 'de + les' in some contexts but here functions as an indefinite plural article ('some').
target_language_example: Il aime dire des mensonges.
native_language_example: He likes to tell some lies.

meaning: to say 'two' / to say two (words); literally "to say two".
additional_notes: This is a literal combination of the verb dire (to say) and the numeral deux (two). It is not a common fixed idiom in French on its own and is ambiguous without context. Possible interpretations: instructing someone to pronounce the numeral 'deux' (dire « deux »), saying two words (dire deux mots), or—less naturally—referring to saying something twice (French normally uses "deux fois" for "twice"). To avoid ambiguity, add context or a noun: dire « deux » (say the word 'two'), dire deux mots (say two words), dire deux fois (say twice).
target_language_example: Il m'a demandé : « Peux-tu dire deux pour le test ? »
native_language_example: He asked me, "Can you say 'two' for the test?"

meaning: to say something about (someone/something); often appears in phrases like "dire du mal de" (to speak ill of) or "dire du bien de" (to speak well of).
additional_notes: Construction: verb 'dire' followed by preposition 'de' + article 'le' contracted to 'du' when part of set expressions (e.g., 'dire du mal de', 'dire du bien de'). Typically requires an object introduced by a following 'de' phrase (une personne, une chose). Can be neutral, positive or negative depending on context and qualifiers (bien/mal).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas toujours dire du mal des collègues sans connaître toute l'histoire, mais on peut aussi ne rien dire.
native_language_example: One should not always say bad things about colleagues without knowing the whole story, but one can also say nothing.

meaning: 'to speak ill (of someone)'; to say negative or bad things about someone.
additional_notes: Used with de + person/people (dire du mal de quelqu'un). Common expression meaning to criticize, gossip negatively, or slander. Can be general (complain about) or stronger (badmouth). Often appears in negative constructions (ne ... jamais) or warnings.
target_language_example: Ne dis pas dire du mal de tes collègues sans les connaître.
native_language_example: Don't speak ill of your colleagues without knowing them.

meaning: to say in (a given language or wording); to express something by using a particular phrase or language.
additional_notes: Used when specifying how something is said or expressed (often followed by a language, a tone, or a paraphrase). Common pattern: dire + en + [language/terme/quelque sorte de mot]. Example: « dire en français », « dire en d'autres termes ». Not a fixed idiom on its own—needs context (e.g., a language or a rephrasing) to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Comment dit-on 'apple' en français? / Je vais le dire en d'autres mots.
native_language_example: How do you say 'apple' in French? / I'll say it in other words.

meaning: to say is / to state that (literary or formal word order; rare in modern spoken French).
additional_notes: This word order (dire est) is not the normal contemporary structure in French. In modern usage you would usually say 'il est dit' (it is said), 'on dit' (people say), or 'dire que'/'dire + clause' (to say that...). 'Dire est' can appear in formal, poetic, or archaic constructions where the infinitive follows the verb as a noun-like phrase (similar to Latin-influenced word order). Beginner learners will rarely need this form; prefer more common alternatives.
target_language_example: Dire est une chose, mais agir en est une autre.
native_language_example: To say is one thing, but to act is another.

meaning: to say the same (thing).
additional_notes: Used when two or more people express the same idea or comment. Often appears in phrases like «dire la même chose» (say the same thing) or in shorter forms where «chose» is implied. Common in responses like «J'allais vous dire la même chose» (I was going to tell you the same thing).
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'il a tort ? — Je pourrais dire la même.
native_language_example: You think he's wrong? — I could say the same.

meaning: to say the...
additional_notes: This is usually not a complete fixed expression on its own. Here, le is normally the masculine singular article ('the'), so it usually needs a noun after it: dire le nom = 'to say the name'. If you mean 'to say it', French normally uses le dire, not dire le.
target_language_example: Il faut dire le mot exact.
native_language_example: You have to say the exact word.

meaning: intended to mean “tell me” but nonstandard in French; literal words 'to say me'
additional_notes: This word order is nonstandard in modern French. The correct imperative form with the object pronoun is "dis‑moi" (or "dites‑moi" in formal/plural). "dire moi" may appear in informal writing, mistakes, or dialectal/colloquial contexts, but it is considered ungrammatical in standard French. Use "dis‑moi" for informal singular address and "dites‑moi" for formal/plural.
target_language_example: Je t'ai entendu dire moi que tu partais demain — est‑ce vrai ?
native_language_example: I heard you say to me that you were leaving tomorrow — is that true?

meaning: to say 'my' — literally the verb dire followed by the possessive mon; used when reporting or quoting speech that begins with 'mon'
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiomatic phrase by itself. 'Dire mon' typically appears inside larger reported-speech constructions (e.g. Il a dit mon + noun/clause). In natural French you will more often encounter the full quoted clause (e.g. « il a dit 'mon père...' ») or dire + que. This entry highlights the sequence of verb + possessive as it can appear when reproducing someone's words.
target_language_example: Il a répété : « dire mon histoire ainsi, ce n'est pas juste », mais il ne voulait pas vraiment dire mon nom.
native_language_example: He repeated: "to say my story like that isn't fair," but he didn't really mean to say my name.

meaning: to ask someone to tell you where you are or where you should go (literally: 'tell me where I...').
additional_notes: Used when asking someone for location or directions. Usually followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'dois changer', 'me situe', 'suis', 'peux prendre'). Common in polite questions: 'Pouvez-vous me dire où je ... ?' or 'Peux-tu me dire où je ... ?'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire où je dois descendre pour aller au musée ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where I should get off to go to the museum?

meaning: 'say where you' / 'tell where you' (start of a clause asking someone to say where they are or where they will do something)
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it's the beginning of a request or instruction: dire où tu (es, vas, habites, travailles, etc.). Common completions: «dire où tu es» (tell where you are), «dire où tu vas» (tell where you are going). Used in informal and neutral contexts when asking someone to give a location or destination.
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire où tu es maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can you tell where you are now?

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; literally 'to say for' — arises when the verb dire (to say/tell) is followed by the preposition pour. Can occur in reported speech where someone 'says for' something, or in colloquial turns like « dire pour + infinitive » meaning 'to say (that) in order to.../to say for the purpose of...'. Often replaced by dire que or dire à depending on meaning.
additional_notes: This combination is compositional (dire + pour) rather than an established multiword expression. It is uncommon as a standalone pattern; French prefers constructions like « dire que » (to say that), « dire à » (to tell someone), or « pour + infinitive » for purpose. Context determines whether « dire pour » is natural. Example uses include reporting a message intended for someone/something or explaining purpose ('he said for the meeting that...').
target_language_example: Elle a dit pour Paul qu'elle ne pouvait pas venir.
native_language_example: She said for Paul that she couldn't come.

meaning: 'to tell (someone) when' — ask or refer to the time/date of something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with an object (me, nous, etc.) or a question word to ask for the time or moment of an event. In casual speech negative or surprised rhetorical questions like "Tu comptais me le dire quand ?" mean "When were you planning to tell me that?" — expressing surprise or annoyance at a late disclosure. Can appear with different subjects and polite/formal forms (tu, vous).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire quand commence la réunion ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me when the meeting starts?

meaning: say that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause after dire. Most often it means "say/tell that" (often as dire à quelqu’un que = "tell someone that"), but after verbs like vouloir it can mean "mean that". Very common for reporting information, opinions, or messages.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je pars demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I'm leaving tomorrow.

meaning: 'to say that I ... you' (beginning of a clause where the speaker reports saying something about 'you' or to 'you')
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: 'dire que je t'' is the start of a reported speech or a clause where the verb 'dire' ('to say') is followed by a subordinate introduced by 'que' and then 'je t'' which is the contraction of 'je te' before a vowel or mute h (e.g. 'je t'aime', 'je te dis'). You will normally see it completed, for example: 'dire que je t'aime' (to say that I love you) or 'dire que je t'ai vu' (to say that I saw you). The structure can be used for direct object ('je te ...') or reflexive constructions depending on the following verb. Watch for elision: 'te' becomes 't'' before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Il m'a dit de ne pas dire que je t'aime si vite.
native_language_example: He told me not to say that I love you so quickly.

meaning: 'to say that you' (start of a clause reporting what 'you' said)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the combination of the verb dire (to say) plus a subordinating conjunction que and the subject pronoun vous. You'll usually see it as part of a larger sentence: dire que vous + verb/phrase (e.g. dire que vous êtes d'accord = 'to say that you agree'). Use it when reporting or quoting what someone (you) said. Word order and verb tense follow normal French grammar after que.
target_language_example: Elle va dire que vous êtes arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: She will say that you arrived late.

meaning: to say something
additional_notes: This is a shortened or conversational form of 'dire quelque chose' (to say something). Alone, 'quelque' is incomplete — standard French uses 'quelque chose' for 'something'. You may hear 'dire quelque' in casual spoken fragments or lyrics where the 'chose' is omitted, but for beginners use 'dire quelque chose'.
target_language_example: Je voulais dire quelque, mais je n'ai pas osé.
native_language_example: I wanted to say something, but I didn't dare.

meaning: to say something
additional_notes: A common verb phrase used when someone speaks or expresses an idea. Can mean a brief remark ('say something') or to convey information ('tell something'). Often used with indirect objects (dire quelque chose à quelqu'un) to mean 'tell someone something'.
target_language_example: Je veux dire quelque chose au sujet de ce projet.
native_language_example: I want to say something about this project.

meaning: 'to say who' (to tell who someone is or who did something)
additional_notes: A common short phrase combining the verb dire (to say/tell) + qui (who). Used when asking or instructing someone to identify a person or indicate who performed an action: e.g. «Tu peux dire qui a fait ça?» = 'Can you say who did that?'. Often appears inside longer sentences (dire + interrogative or clause).
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire qui a appelé ?
native_language_example: Can you say who called?

meaning: what (to say)
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase used to ask or refer to what was said or what should be said. Often appears in questions like "Dire quoi?" meaning "What did you say?/Say what?" or in indirect contexts: "J'aurais dû dire quoi?" = "What was I supposed to say?" Can be used alone as a surprised/clarifying reaction. "Tu veux dire quoi ?" = "What do you mean?"
target_language_example: Tu veux dire quoi par ça ?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: to say whatever / to tell (someone) anything (often part of a larger clause)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed standalone idiom; it combines the verb dire (to say) with an interrogative/relative sequence quoi que or with an object. Alone 'dire quoi que' is incomplete and will usually be followed by additional words (e.g. 'dire quoi que ce soit' = 'to say anything/whatever') or rephrased as 'dire quoi' (= 'to say what'). Note: 'quoi que' by itself can mean 'whatever' + subjunctive (quoi que tu fasses).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi dire quoi que je tente, les mots me manquent.
native_language_example: I don't know what to say — whatever I try, I can't find the words.

meaning: 'to say about' or 'to tell about' (used to introduce what is said regarding someone/something).
additional_notes: Often used with indirect speech or opinions (dire quelque chose sur + noun). Common constructions: « dire quelque chose sur quelqu'un/quelque chose » (to say something about someone/something). Can also appear in questions: « Qu'est-ce que tu peux dire sur… ? » = "What can you say about…?" Verb is conjugated normally (dire).
target_language_example: Que peux-tu dire sur ce film ?
native_language_example: What can you say about this movie?

meaning: to always say; to repeatedly state (habitually say something).
additional_notes: Literal composition: verb dire + adverb toujours. Not a fixed idiom — used to indicate habitual or repeated speech. Can be followed by a noun phrase or a clause (e.g. dire toujours la même chose / dire toujours que...). Contexts: neutral descriptive, can be slightly critical if emphasizing repetition.
target_language_example: Il a tendance à dire toujours la même chose.
native_language_example: He tends to always say the same thing.

meaning: to tell everything; to reveal all (often the whole truth or all the details).
additional_notes: Used when someone reveals all information, confesses fully, or doesn't hide anything. Can be used literally (to tell every fact) or more generally (to confess). Context determines whether it's serious (a full confession) or casual (sharing all the details).
target_language_example: Il a fini par dire tout ce qu'il savait.
native_language_example: He ended up telling everything he knew.

meaning: literally 'to say/tell all this' — not a common fixed phrase in French; can occur as part of larger structures meaning 'to say all this' or 'to tell all of this'
additional_notes: Word order 'dire tout ce' is unusual on its own; typically appears followed by a relative clause or complement (e.g. 'dire tout ce que je sais'). Often better expressed as 'dire tout' or 'dire tout à quelqu'un' depending on intent. Use with complement: 'dire tout ce que...' (to say all that/what...). Can be literal and is compositional.
target_language_example: Je vais dire tout ce que je sais; je ne peux pas dire tout ce sans précision.
native_language_example: I will say everything I know; I cannot 'dire tout ce' without clarification.

meaning: literally "to say a"; the verb dire followed by the indefinite article un, used as the start of a noun phrase (e.g. to say/tell a [something]).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own. Appears when dire is followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by un: dire un mot, dire un mensonge, dire un compliment, dire un secret. Conjugate dire as needed (je dis, tu dis, il/elle dit, nous disons, etc.). Context determines the full meaning; the construction is compositional and usually can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Je veux dire un mot avant de partir.
native_language_example: I want to say a word before leaving.

meaning: to say your / to tell your (literally).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom in French; it's simply the verb dire ('to say/tell') followed by the possessive adjective votre ('your', formal or plural). It needs an object or continuation (e.g. dire votre nom = to say your name). On its own it is incomplete and uncommon without context. Use depending on formality: 'votre' is formal or plural. For informal singular, use 'ton'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous dire votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you say your name, please?

meaning: an interjection meaning roughly 'well, hey' or 'wow/you know' used to express surprise, emphasis, mild reproach, or to get attention.
additional_notes: Very common spoken phrase. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation: can show surprise (Wow!), mild reproach or teasing (Come on/Now then), draw attention (Hey!), or add emphasis to a comment. Informal but widely used in everyday speech. Not literally 'say then' despite the words.
target_language_example: Dis donc, tu as fini si vite !
native_language_example: Well, you finished so quickly!

meaning: 'never say' (imperative/negative expression with the verb dire).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb dire (to say/tell) with jamais (never). In examples it appears both in imperatives (Ne dis jamais = Never say) and in present tense negatives (Je ne dis jamais = I never say; Tu ne me dis jamais rien = You never tell me anything). Remember: in standard French the negative structure places ne before the verb and jamais after it (or ne...jamais around the verb). In spoken informal French speakers sometimes drop the 'ne'.
target_language_example: Ne dis jamais ça à personne.
native_language_example: Never say that to anyone.

meaning: 'say that' / 'tell (me) that' (informal spoken French)
additional_notes: Colloquial combination of the imperative or present of dire + the adverb là. Used in spoken French to ask someone to state or repeat something, to point to a specific point in a conversation, or to emphasize a clause. Tone is informal; context determines nuance (instruction, request for confirmation, or filler). Note: written French prefers 'dis-le/dites-le' or more explicit phrasing.
target_language_example: Si tu sais la vérité, dis là maintenant.
native_language_example: If you know the truth, say that now.

meaning: Don't say that / don't say this (colloquial, contracted form of 'ne dis pas ça' or 'ne dis pas ceci').
additional_notes: Informal spoken French: 'ne' is dropped and 'ça' or 'ce' may be shortened; very casual. More standard forms are 'ne dis pas ça' or 'ne dis pas ceci'. Use with friends or in speech; avoid in formal writing. 'Ce' here is a reduced form of 'ça' or part of 'ceci'.
target_language_example: Dis pas ce que tu crois.
native_language_example: Don't say what you think.

meaning: shortened/informal way to say 'ne dis pas ce que...' → 'don't say what...'
additional_notes: This looks like a fragment: it's the informal omission of the subject and sometimes the negation particle 'ne' (e.g. 'Ne dis pas ce que...'). Common in casual spoken French. It begins a warning or instruction telling someone not to say something or not to reveal what follows. To be a complete sentence you usually need a subject (tu, vous) or continuation: 'Ne dis pas ce que tu sais.'
target_language_example: Ne dis pas ce que tu as entendu hier.
native_language_example: Don't say what you heard yesterday.

meaning: 'don't say what I...' — an incomplete/colloquial fragment used when someone asks another not to say something about them (elliptical form of "(Ne) dis pas ce que je...")
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone idiom but an informal, elliptical fragment you might hear in spoken French. Standard full form is "Ne dis pas ce que je..." or more commonly "Ne dis pas que je..." The fragment "dis pas ce que je" may appear in rapid speech before the speaker completes the clause (e.g. "dis pas ce que je t'ai fait"), or as an interrupted request. Use in written French is uncommon; prefer the full negative form with "ne" in formal contexts. Note: "dis pas ce que je" is compositional (literal meaning) and informal.
target_language_example: Dis pas ce que je t'ai raconté à propos de son projet.
native_language_example: Don't say what I told you about his project.

meaning: 'say more' or 'tell me more' (imperative/command form or informal request).
additional_notes: From the verb dire (to say). Used to ask someone to say more, give more details, or speak further. Can be a direct imperative (tu form) telling someone to speak more: «Dis plus» = 'Say more.' In spoken French you might more often hear «Dis‑m'en plus» (Tell me more about it) or «Raconte‑m'en plus.» Alone, 'dis plus' is brief and can sound informal or abrupt.
target_language_example: Dis plus sur ton voyage, j'aimerais connaître les détails.
native_language_example: Say more about your trip; I'd like to know the details.

meaning: you were saying that
additional_notes: Imperfect tense + que + subject pronoun tu. Used to report what someone was repeatedly saying or what they said in the past (ongoing or habitual past). Can translate as 'you were saying that...' or in many contexts simply 'you said that...'. Followed by a clause describing what was said.
target_language_example: Tu disais que tu viendrais ce week-end.
native_language_example: You were saying that you would come this weekend.

meaning: 'speech by' or 'talk by' (introduces who gave a speech or the type of speech).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone gave a speech (discours de + person's name) or to indicate the subject/type of speech (discours de clôture = closing speech). 'Discours' = speech; 'de' links to the speaker or the speech's function or topic. For a full sentence you may need an article or name: le discours de Marie, un discours de bienvenue. Word order: discours de + noun/name.
target_language_example: Le discours de la directrice a duré vingt minutes.
native_language_example: The principal's speech lasted twenty minutes.

meaning: '(that) the ... say' — third-person plural present of 'dire' + definite article (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used when reporting what multiple people or sources say (e.g., les journaux, les gens, les appareils). In English you'd usually translate as 'the ... say' or 'what the ... say.' The structure often appears in clauses introduced by 'ce que' or 'que' (e.g., ce que disent les gens = what people say). Word order: verb (disent) comes before the noun with article (les) in these constructions.
target_language_example: Écoute ce que disent les experts.
native_language_example: Listen to what the experts say.

meaning: 'gone from' or 'disappeared from' (someone/something no longer there or no longer has something).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that a person or thing is no longer present at a place or that something has been removed from something. Can refer to people (il a disparu de la maison), objects (le livre a disparu de la bibliothèque) or abstract things (la couleur a disparu de la photo). Common past participle construction: [quelqu'un/quelque chose] + a/est + disparu + de + [lieu/objet].
target_language_example: Mon portable a disparu de ma chambre.
native_language_example: My phone disappeared from my room.

meaning: 'disappeared in' or 'missing since' (used to indicate something/someone vanished during or at a time/place).
additional_notes: Formed from the past participle disparu (disappeared) + preposition en. Often followed by a time period, location or condition: e.g. « disparu en mer » (disappeared at sea), « disparu en 1999 » (disappeared in 1999). Used in reporting or narration. The verb être (Il/elle est disparu(e)) or avoir (less common) may appear in full sentences; here the phrase fragment specifies where or when the disappearance occurred.
target_language_example: Le bateau a disparu en mer la nuit dernière.
native_language_example: The boat disappeared at sea last night.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment likely resulting from inversion, punctuation, or omission of an auxiliary. Typically corresponds to 'il a disparu' (he disappeared) or appears in constructions like 'Disparu, il...' (having disappeared, he...).
additional_notes:
This exact two-word sequence is uncommon as a standalone sentence. Possible contexts:
- Typo/omission: missing auxiliary verb (should be 'il a disparu').
- Headline or telegraphic style: verbs/subjects compressed.
- Participle phrase: 'Disparu, il...' where 'disparu' is used adverbially or adjectivally before a comma.
When you see 'disparu il', check surrounding punctuation and context to determine intended meaning.
target_language_example: Disparu il fut retrouvé le lendemain — la police avait mal compris l'indice.
native_language_example: Missing, he was found the next day — the police had misunderstood the clue.

meaning: Not a correct or standard French phrase as written; likely a misordering of words such as 'il y a disparu' or 'il a disparu', which mean respectively 'he/it disappeared there' and 'he/it disappeared'.
additional_notes:
The sequence 'disparu il y' is ungrammatical in French. Possible intended correct forms:
- 'Il a disparu' = 'He/it disappeared' or 'He/it has disappeared'. Use this for general statements about disappearance.
- 'Il y a disparu' = 'He/it disappeared there' (adds a locative 'there'). This form places 'il y' before the verb auxiliary: 'Il y a disparu en 1940.'
For learners, prefer 'Il a disparu' for most situations. If you must preserve the given sequence in a full sentence it would only occur as part of a larger, reordered clause (and still be nonstandard), e.g. in poetic inversion or an error.
target_language_example: Ceci est une phrase incorrecte : « disparu il y » ne se dit pas en français.
native_language_example: This is an incorrect sentence: 'disparu il y' is not said in French.

meaning: 'disappeared without' or 'gone without (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Combines the past participle disparu (disappeared/gone/missing) with the preposition sans (without). Commonly followed by an infinitive, a noun, or a determiner phrase to say someone/something disappeared without doing something or without something. Often used in expressions like « disparu sans laisser de trace ». Agreement: when subject is feminine singular, use disparue; here 'disparu' as given is masculine or neutral masculine form.
target_language_example: Il est disparu sans laisser de trace.
native_language_example: He disappeared without leaving a trace.

target_language_multi_word_term: ne dispose pas de / je ne dispose pas de
meaning: 'I don't have' or 'I do not have at my disposal'.
additional_notes: Used to say you do not have something available (time, information, an object, etc.). In French the full negative form is 'ne ... pas' around the verb: 'je ne dispose pas de...' Often in spoken French the 'ne' is dropped: 'je dispose pas de...' or 'j'ai pas...' For formal written French use 'je ne dispose pas de'. The verb 'disposer (de)' means 'to have at one's disposal' or 'to possess/avail oneself of'.
target_language_example: Je ne dispose pas de suffisamment de temps pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: I don't have enough time to finish the project.

meaning: 'do not have' or 'does not have' (negation of 'disposer de' = to have at one's disposal)
additional_notes: This is the negative form of the verb phrase 'disposer de', used to say that someone lacks something. In correct French it appears as 'ne ... pas de' around the verb: e.g. 'Je ne dispose pas de...' or in spoken/written dropping 'ne': 'Je dispose pas de...'. Followed by a noun: 'de' contracts to 'd'' before a vowel. For possession use 'avoir' more commonly in conversation ('Je n'ai pas de...').
target_language_example: Je ne dispose pas de suffisamment d'informations pour répondre.
native_language_example: I do not have enough information to answer.

meaning: we have / let us have (available); we possess
additional_notes: From the verb disposer de. In the present tense 'nous disposons de' means 'we have' or 'we possess' (formal). In commands or suggestions, 'disposons de' (rare) can mean 'let's have' or 'let us use' when followed by something (e.g. 'Disposons de ces ressources' = 'Let's use these resources'). More commonly, English speakers will hear 'nous avons' for 'we have'. 'Disposer de' emphasizes availability or possession of resources, time, information, etc.
target_language_example: Nous disposons de suffisamment de temps pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We have enough time to finish the project.

meaning: 'distance from my' (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: This is a short phrase composed of distance (f.) + de + ma (my, feminine). It needs a following feminine noun (or an implied noun) to be complete, e.g. 'distance de ma maison' = 'distance from my house'. In speech you might also see contractions or possessives change depending on the noun (mon for masculine nouns, mes for plural).
target_language_example: La distance de ma maison au travail est de 10 km.
native_language_example: The distance from my house to work is 10 km.

meaning: used in questions to ask how far something is (lit. 'at what distance is [it] located').
additional_notes: Common construction: 'À quelle distance se trouve ... ?' = 'How far is ...?' Use with places or things. You can replace 'se trouve' with 'est' in casual speech ('À quelle distance est la bibliothèque ?'). 'À quelle distance' asks for a measurement (kilometers, meters).
target_language_example: À quelle distance se trouve la gare la plus proche ?
native_language_example: How far is the nearest train station?

meaning: vendor of / distributor of / machine that dispenses (something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate someone or something that distributes or sells that item. Often refers to vending machines (distributeur de boissons = drink vending machine) or companies/people who distribute products (distributeur de pièces détachées). Grammar: 'de' contracts with le/la/les when followed by definite article (du, de la, des).
target_language_example: Il y a un distributeur de billets près de la gare.
native_language_example: There is an ATM near the station.

meaning: ATM; cash machine (machine that dispenses banknotes).
additional_notes: Commonly used in France to refer to an automated teller machine where you withdraw cash or use bank cards. Often shortened in speech to «distributeur» or «DAB» (distributeur automatique de billets). Useful when asking for nearby machines or describing problems (card retained, machine out of service, card rejected).
target_language_example: Le distributeur de billets est en panne, pouvons-nous aller à un autre ?
native_language_example: The ATM is out of order; can we go to another one?

meaning: uses of the verb 'dire' (to say) in short sequences where 'dit' and 'je' appear near each other in phrases like 'Après ce que tu as dit, je…', 'Je me suis dit…' or 'Ceci dit, je…' — idiomatic ways to report speech, thoughts, or introduce a contrast.
additional_notes: This entry groups common patterns where 'dit' (past participle or third-person present) appears in constructions with 'je' (first-person pronoun). Typical uses: reporting what someone said ('Après ce que tu as dit, je…'), expressing an internal thought ('Je me suis dit…'), or making a transition/contrast ('Ceci dit, je…'). Verb form and punctuation vary: 'dit' can be part of a compound tense (tu as dit), a past participle (après ce que tu avais dit), or a fixed phrase (ceci dit).
target_language_example: Après ce que tu avais dit, je pouvais venir vers toi ?
native_language_example: After what you had said, could I come to you?

meaning: 'tells (to)' — third-person singular of dire + the preposition 'to' (used before a plural or plural-sounding indirect object)
additional_notes: Dit aux is the form of the verb dire (to say/tell) in the present tense for il/elle/on (il dit) when followed by the preposition à + a plural or plural-sounding object (e.g., 'dit aux enfants' = tells the children). In French you normally say 'dit à' + indirect object; 'aux' is the contraction of 'à + les'. Use dit aux for 'he/she/one tells (to) the ...'. For other subjects or tenses, the verb form changes (je dis, tu dis, nous disons, ils disent, etc.).
target_language_example: Elle dit aux étudiants d'écouter attentivement.
native_language_example: She tells the students to listen carefully.

meaning: 'says a lot' or 'reveals a lot' (literally 'says a lot')
additional_notes: Used to comment that something (a fact, gesture, object, situation) reveals a lot of information or is significant. Often appears after a subject: « ça dit beaucoup » or « cela en dit beaucoup » and in phrases like « ça en dit beaucoup sur… ». Tone can be neutral or evaluative (positive or negative) depending on context.
target_language_example: Son silence en dit beaucoup.
native_language_example: His silence says a lot.

meaning: says that
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger clause (e.g. «il dit ce que...», «elle dit ce que...») meaning someone 'says that' or 'says what' followed by reported speech or a clause. Can introduce reported content: «il dit ce que tu as fait» = 'he says that you did it'. Word order and use depend on the surrounding sentence.
target_language_example: Elle dit ce que tout le monde pense.
native_language_example: She says what everyone is thinking.

meaning: ‘said what I…’ — the start of a clause meaning 'I said what I [did/was going to do/etc.]'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears when reporting what the speaker said; it's usually completed by a verb (e.g., ai vu, avais à dire, allais faire). Common construction: «J'ai dit ce que j'ai vu» = I said what I saw. The pronoun and verb following the apostrophe depend on tense/person: j'ai, j'avais, j'allais, etc. Useful for reported-information phrases like 'I told you what...'.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit ce que j'allais faire.
native_language_example: I told you what I was going to do.

meaning: "says what I..." (start of a clause meaning 'says what I [do/think/mean]').
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself — it's the beginning of a reported-speech or relative clause: e.g. «il dit ce que je pense» = 'he says what I think'. Often followed by a verb or clause (pense, veux, veux dire, fais, etc.). The order is subject + dit + ce que + subject (je) + verb. Useful for reporting what someone says matches the speaker's thought or action.
target_language_example: Elle dit ce que je pense vraiment.
native_language_example: She says what I really think.

meaning: 'says what' or 'says which/that which' (third-person singular of dire + 'ce qui').
additional_notes: Combines the verb dire (to say) in the third person singular (dit) with the relative expression ce qui ('what' / 'that which'). Common in reported speech or clauses: e.g. 'Il dit ce qui...' = 'He says what.../He says that which...'. Often followed by a verb: dit ce qui est arrivé, dit ce qui s'est passé. Not a fixed idiom—it's a compositional phrase.
target_language_example: Elle dit ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: She says what happened last night.

meaning: 'told (me/you/etc.) not to (do) it'.
additional_notes: Part of a larger reported-speech construction with the verb dire (to tell). Common pattern: [person] + a + dit + de + ne + pas + [infinitive] (and sometimes a direct object pronoun like le). Example shows le referring to an action or thing previously mentioned. Pronouns (me, lui, te, on) indicate the indirect object who was told. The exact subject and pronoun can change (e.g. 'm'a dit de ne pas le faire' = 'told me not to do it').
target_language_example: Il m'a dit de ne pas le toucher.
native_language_example: He told me not to touch it.

meaning: 'told (someone) not to' (colloquial omission of standard negation)
additional_notes: This construction is informal and commonly heard in spoken French. It replaces the standard 'dire de ne pas + infinitive' (e.g. 'je t'ai dit de ne pas venir'). Grammatically, it's a contraction where the 'ne' is dropped: 'je t'ai dit de pas venir'. Use in casual conversation; avoid in formal writing or speech. The subject is the person who said it (je, je t'avais, je vous ai...), followed by 'dire de pas' + verb infinitive.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de pas le faire.
native_language_example: I told you not to do it.

meaning: short for 'dit de te...' used before a reflexive or pronominal verb: 'told you to (do something)'.
additional_notes: This is a contracted sequence found when someone reports an order or instruction: Je t'ai dit de t' + verb (e.g. t'asseoir, t'habiller, t'en débarrasser). The first 't'' is the indirect object 'te' (to you) after 'dire' (to tell). The second 't'' is the reflexive or pronominal pronoun attached to the verb (te + verb). In spoken and written French the pronouns often contract: 'Je t'ai dit de t'asseoir' = 'I told you to sit down.'
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de t'occuper de la valise.
native_language_example: I told you to take care of the suitcase.

meaning: literally 'said about you' — a fragment meaning 'said of/about you' used in reported speech or descriptions
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own; it's the combination of the past participle 'dit' (said) + preposition 'de' + object pronoun 'te' (you). You'll find it inside longer sentences like «On a dit de te prévenir» (informal/colloquial) or more grammatically «Il a été dit de te contacter». Word order and register can vary: formal French often uses passive constructions ('Il a été dit de...') while spoken French uses active constructions with 'on' or omits auxiliary verbs. The phrase requires context to be grammatical and natural.
target_language_example: On a dit de te prévenir avant midi.
native_language_example: They said to warn you before noon.

meaning: 'said about you' or 'spoken of you' (referring to what someone says about you)
additional_notes: This is a short phrase built from the past participle 'dit' (said) + preposition 'de' + object 'vous'. It often appears in sentences like «Qu'est‑ce qu'on dit de vous?» (What do people say about you?) or «On a dit de vous que…» (They said about you that…). In spoken French you might also hear 'on dit de toi' (informal singular 'you'). Verb agreement and context matter: 'dit' can be part of a passive-like construction or reported speech.
target_language_example: On a dit de vous que vous étiez très compétent.
native_language_example: They said about you that you were very competent.

meaning: says (to) give you / tells (someone) to give you
additional_notes: This fragment is part of a larger sentence and uses the verb dire (to say/tell) followed by an infinitive construction (dire de + infinitive) meaning 'to tell to do something'. 'Vous' is the indirect object or polite direct object 'you'. Depending on context it can mean 'he/she says to give you' or 'tells you to give'. The exact subject and object roles depend on surrounding words. Commonly appears in reported speech: « Il m'a dit de vous donner ceci. » (He told me to give this to you.)
target_language_example: Il m'a dit de vous donner la clé.
native_language_example: He told me to give you the key.

meaning: says the same (thing) / expresses the same opinion
additional_notes: A short phrase built from the verb dire (to say) in the third person singular (dit) plus la même (the same). It usually appears in contexts like «il/elle dit la même chose» or «tu dis la même» to mean someone repeats or holds the same statement or opinion as another. On its own ('dit la même') is informal and elliptical — speakers often omit words (e.g. 'chose') in casual speech.
target_language_example: Elle dit la même que lui, donc ils sont d'accord.
native_language_example: She says the same as him, so they agree.

meaning: 'says where' or 'tells where'.
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb dire (to say/tell) in the 3rd person singular (dit = he/she/it says; or past participle in compounds) plus the interrogative/relative où (where). Commonly appears in sentences like « il dit où c'est » (he says where it is) or in reported speech: « elle m'a dit où aller » (she told me where to go). Context determines tense and subject. Note: "dit où" on its own is not a full sentence; it's part of a clause.
target_language_example: Elle m'a dit où se trouve la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: She told me where the library is.

meaning: has/have said where she was going (or going to go).
additional_notes: This is a fragment used in questions or statements about whether a female person (elle) reported her destination or plans. It appears in different tenses and word orders depending on question form (inversion A-t-elle dit..., est-ce qu'elle a dit..., or rising intonation). Useful for asking/confirming where a woman went or will go.
target_language_example: A-t-elle dit où elle allait avant de partir ?
native_language_example: Did she say where she was going before leaving?

meaning: said where he (would/were) — introduces reported information about a man's location or plans
additional_notes: Used in reported speech or questions to ask whether someone (he) told another person about his location, destination, or plans. Tense of the verb after 'où il' (allait, était, etc.) shows time (future/intent vs past/state). In English it's often rendered as "said where he was/was going/would go."
target_language_example: Elle m'a dit où il partait demain ?
native_language_example: Did she tell me where he was leaving tomorrow?

meaning: said that I (it/her/him/…)
additional_notes: This is a truncated clip of reported speech: 'dit que' = 'said that', 'je' = 'I', and 'l'' is a contracted object pronoun (le/la/les or l' before a vowel). The full phrase depends on the next word: e.g. 'dit que je l'aimais' = 'said that I loved/liked him/her/it'. Often appears in past tenses (j'ai dit que...). Context determines whether l' = him, her, it. Can also be used with adjectives: 'dit que je l'étais' = 'said that I was (it/that)'.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que je l'aimais.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I loved him/her/it.

meaning: '(he/she) said that I would do it' (literal fragment: 'said that I it')
additional_notes: This is a fragment built from the verb dire (to say) in the past (dit) plus a subordinate clause introduced by que. In examples it appears as part of sentences like "J'ai dit que je le ferais" (I said that I would do it). The pronoun le refers to a masculine object or action already mentioned. Word order: subject + ai/ai/ai etc. + dit + que + je + le + verb. Tense inside the clause can be conditional (ferais) or future (ferai) depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que je le ferais demain.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I would do it tomorrow.

meaning: 'says that I ...' (beginning of a clause where someone reports what the speaker does)
additional_notes: This is a clipped piece of reported speech: dit que (he/she says that) + je m' + verb starting with a vowel or mute h (e.g., je m'appelle, je m'intéresse). It cannot stand alone; it needs the rest of the verb. Common in spoken or written reports: «Il dit que je m'appelle…», «Elle dit que je m'intéresse…».
target_language_example: Il dit que je m'appelle Sophie.
native_language_example: He says that my name is Sophie.

meaning: 'says that I/you...' (beginning of a reported speech phrase; often followed by a verb or object)
additional_notes: This is a fragment used when reporting what someone says about the speaker or the listener (je/te). In French spoken/colloquial style, contractions like "je t'" appear before a vowel (e.g. "je t'aime", "je t'appelle"). Alone it is incomplete — expect a verb or rest of phrase after the apostrophe. Often appears in longer sentences: "Il dit que je t'aime" (He says that I love you).
target_language_example: Il dit que je t'aime.
native_language_example: He says that I love you.

meaning: 'says nothing about' or 'doesn't say anything about'
additional_notes: A short phrase formed from the verb dire (to say) in third person singular (dit) followed by rien (nothing) and du (de + le). It typically appears in sentences like «Il ne dit rien du...», meaning 'He says nothing about...' The negative ne is often present in full sentences (Il ne dit rien du projet). In spoken French the ne is frequently omitted.
target_language_example: Elle ne dit rien du problème au directeur.
native_language_example: She says nothing about the problem to the manager.

meaning: 'says his/her/its' (literally 'says his') — part of reported speech or description.
additional_notes: This is the verb dire (to say) in the 3rd person singular (dit) followed by a possessive adjective (son). It usually appears as part of a larger phrase, e.g. «il dit son nom» (he says his name) or «elle dit son opinion» (she expresses her opinion). The exact possessive (son/sa/ses) agrees with the thing owned, not the speaker (son is used before masculine nouns or before feminine nouns starting with a vowel). Not a standalone fixed phrase — it's compositional and used in normal speech/writing.
target_language_example: Il dit son adresse au livreur.
native_language_example: He gives/says his address to the delivery driver.

meaning: Literal: 'says your' or fragment 'say your' depending on context; not a standard fixed phrase. Usually a fragment formed by the verb dire in 3rd person singular ('dit' = he/she says) followed by the possessive adjective 'ton' ('your', familiar). Can be part of a larger sentence (e.g., « il dit ton nom »). It may also result from an incorrect form of the imperative (correct is « dis ton … »).
additional_notes:
Not a conventional standalone phrase. Possible uses:
- As 3rd-person present: « il dit ton… » (he says your… ) must be followed by a noun (e.g., nom, prénom).
- As an incorrect written imperative: someone might write 'dit ton' but the correct imperative for 'tu' is 'dis'.
Avoid using 'dit ton' alone; include the noun or correct the verb form.
target_language_example: Il dit ton prénom quand il raconte l'histoire.
native_language_example: He says your first name when he tells the story.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase; appears to be a mistaken juxtaposition of 'dit' (says/said) and 'vous' (you). It does not occur as a grammatical unit in standard French.
additional_notes:
Possible intended/correct forms depending on meaning and context:
- 'dites-vous' (with hyphen or space in inversion/questions) — e.g. 'Dites-vous cela ?' ('Do you say that?').
- 'je vous dis' — 'I tell you'.
- 'il vous dit' — 'he tells you'.
- 'dit : «vous...»' — reported speech where 'dit' is followed by a colon and then 'vous' as the start of a quotation. 
As written, 'dit vous' is ungrammatical; correct structure requires proper conjugation, word order, or punctuation. Choose the intended verb form and pronoun placement to correct it.
target_language_example: Il dit vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici. (INCORRECT — should be 'Il vous dit que vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici' or 'Il dit : «Vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici.»')
native_language_example: He says you cannot enter here. (INCORRECT as written in French; see corrected forms above.)

meaning: tells everyone / says to everyone
additional_notes: Literal phrase built from the verb dire (to say/tell) + à tout (to everyone). Used when someone tells or informs all people (often 'dit à tout le monde'). Alone 'dit à tout' is informal/elliptical; more complete form is 'dit à tout le monde' or 'dit à tout le monde que...'.
target_language_example: Il dit à tout le monde qu'il part en voyage.
native_language_example: He tells everyone that he's going on a trip.

meaning: an exclamation meaning roughly 'well, well' / 'wow' / 'say, now' used to express surprise, emphasis, or to call attention.
additional_notes: Polite/formal second-person plural imperative of dire + 'donc' used conversationally as an interjection. Tone depends on context: can show surprise (Mais dites donc !), mild admiration (Dites donc, il est très classe), incredulity (Enfin, dites donc !), or to draw attention before addressing someone (Dites donc, Doinel). Not strongly informal, but familiar in speech.
target_language_example: Dites donc, tu as changé de coupe de cheveux !
native_language_example: Well, you've changed your haircut!

meaning: 'eighteen' (the number 18).
additional_notes: Used to name the number 18 in counting, dates, ages, math, phone numbers, prices, etc. Hyphenated in French numbers from 17–99 (with some variations). Pronunciation: /dis‿ɥit/.
target_language_example: Elle a dix-huit ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She is eighteen years old today.

meaning: 'nineteen' (the number 19).
additional_notes: Used as the cardinal number 19. Can appear alone, before nouns (e.g., 'dix-neuf ans' = nineteen years old), or in time expressions: 'pour dix-neuf heures' means 'by 7 p.m.' (24-hour clock). Pronounced /di.nəf/.
target_language_example: Il a dix-neuf ans.
native_language_example: He is nineteen years old.

meaning: seventeen (the number 17).
additional_notes: Used to give an age, a quantity, a time (minutes), or to count. Written with a hyphen in French numerals (dix-sept). Pronounced [dees-set]. Common in everyday speech and formal writing.
target_language_example: Elle a dix-sept ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She is seventeen years old today.

meaning: literally 'doctor has' — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a sentence (docteur + verb 'a' meaning 'has').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase. It looks like two separate words: docteur (doctor) and a (third-person singular of avoir = 'has' or the preposition 'to' in names like 'Docteur A.'). Depending on context it can mean 'the doctor has...' (docteur a + past participle) or be the start of a title/label (Docteur A. as an initial). For beginners: learn 'docteur' (a medical doctor) and the verb form 'a' separately.
target_language_example: Le docteur a prescrit des médicaments.
native_language_example: The doctor prescribed medication.

meaning: literally 'doctor is' — not a standalone phrase; likely part of a sentence (e.g. 'Le docteur est...' = 'The doctor is...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression in French. It appears to be two words that would appear together when describing a doctor (docteur) followed by the verb être (est). Beginners should treat 'docteur' (doctor) and 'est' (is) separately. Example full uses: 'Le docteur est là.' ('The doctor is here.') or 'Le docteur est gentil.' ('The doctor is kind.'). Remember to include the definite article (le/la) or possessive when needed: 'Le docteur est...' or 'Mon docteur est...'.
target_language_example: Le docteur est en retard.
native_language_example: The doctor is late.

meaning: literally 'fingers in his/her/its' — part of expressions describing someone sticking their fingers into something (often metaphorical: meddling, investigating, or touching).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's a fragment used when saying someone has their fingers in something (e.g. 'avoir les doigts dans le nez' is idiomatic, but more commonly 'mettre les doigts dans' + object for literal actions like 'put fingers in the jar'). Can be used literally (physical touching) or figuratively (meddling). You will usually see it as part of verbs like 'mettre/mettre ses doigts dans', 'avoir les doigts dans', or in idioms. Adjust possessive (ses) to match the subject (mes/tes/ses/nos...).
target_language_example: Ne mets pas tes doigts dans ses affaires.
native_language_example: Don't stick your fingers in his/her things (or don't meddle in his/her business).

meaning: literally 'fingers of' — used to show possession or association with fingers; appears in expressions describing things related to fingers or a light touch.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination of the plural noun doigts (fingers) followed by de (of). It will be completed by another noun (e.g., doigts de pied = toes, doigts de fée = delicate fingers/skilled touch). Pay attention to context: it can form idioms (doigts de fée = very skillful/delicate fingers) or literal descriptions (les doigts de la main).
target_language_example: Elle a des doigts de fée quand elle joue du piano.
native_language_example: She has 'fairy fingers' when she plays the piano (i.e., very delicate/skillful fingers).

meaning: I must / I have to buy (some)...
additional_notes: Combines devoir (conjugated «je dois» = I must/have to) + acheter (to buy) + des (partitive/plural indefinite article = some). Used to say you need to purchase unspecified items. Change 'des' to a specific article or quantity when needed (e.g. 'acheter le', 'acheter des tomates', 'acheter cinq pommes'). For other subjects, conjugate devoir (tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons...).
target_language_example: Je dois acheter des fruits pour la semaine.
native_language_example: I have to buy some fruit for the week.

meaning: 'I must/need to buy a (masculine singular item)'.
additional_notes: Combines: devoir (conjugated: je dois = I must/need to) + acheter (to buy) + un (masculine indefinite article). Use for expressing obligation/need to purchase one masculine singular noun. Change 'un' to 'une' for feminine nouns, plural 'des' for plural. If you want softer necessity, use 'je dois' or 'il faut que'.
target_language_example: Je dois acheter un nouveau livre pour le cours.
native_language_example: I need to buy a new book for the class.

meaning: 'I must/should really' or 'I really have to' (emphatic form of devoir).
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (conjugated: je dois) with the adverb bien to add emphasis or insistence. Used to strengthen an obligation or intention: e.g. 'Je dois bien...' = 'I really must...' or 'I suppose I must...' Depending on context and intonation, it can sound stronger (necessity) or more resigned/polite. Common in spoken and written French. Followed by an infinitive or a clause.
target_language_example: Je dois bien finir ce travail ce soir.
native_language_example: I really must finish this work tonight.

meaning: 'I must say that I...' or 'I have to say that I...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal comment, often an opinion, reaction, or feeling. Conveys a mild admission or emphasis (e.g., surprise, admiration, curiosity). Commonly followed by an adjective, feeling, or clause about the speaker. Formality: neutral — suitable in spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Je dois dire que je suis agréablement surpris par le résultat.
native_language_example: I must say that I am pleasantly surprised by the result.

meaning: 'must still' or 'have to still' (first or second person singular of devoir + encore)
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (to have to/must) in the present tense (je dois, tu dois) with encore (still/yet). Used to say that someone still has to do something. Context determines subject (je/tu) — alone 'dois encore' is incomplete and normally appears inside a sentence: e.g. «Je dois encore finir mes devoirs.»
target_language_example: Tu dois encore préparer la présentation ce soir.
native_language_example: You still have to prepare the presentation tonight.

meaning: 'must do' or 'have to do' followed by a clause introduced by 'ce' (what/that).
additional_notes: This construction pairs a conjugated form of devoir (here 'dois') + faire + 'ce' + a relative clause (que/qui/qu'il faut, etc.). It expresses obligation: 'you/I must do what...'. The exact translation depends on the clause that follows (ce que = what; ce qui = what/that which). Common in advice, commands, or moral statements.
target_language_example: Tu dois faire ce qui te rend heureux.
native_language_example: You must do what makes you happy.

meaning: 'must do' or 'have to do' (part of phrases meaning to perform or give effort toward something).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the modal verb devoir (dois = you/I/one must) + faire de. Meaning depends on what follows: often followed by un/ton/mon + noun or expressions like 'mon mieux' (my best). Can also appear in questions 'Que dois-je faire de...?' meaning 'What should I do with...?' Not a fixed idiom by itself; interpret according to the full phrase.
target_language_example: Tu dois faire de ton mieux pour l'examen.
native_language_example: You must do your best for the exam.

meaning: 'must do the' / 'have to do the' (informal fragment)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's a fragment combining the verb devoir (conjugated: je/tu dois) + faire + the feminine definite article la. It means someone (you/I) must do something feminine that would follow 'la' (e.g., la vaisselle, la lessive). In spoken French you may hear similar fragments; supply the noun after 'la' to complete the idea. For other subjects use the appropriate conjugation of devoir (je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils/elles doivent).
target_language_example: Tu dois faire la vaisselle ce soir.
native_language_example: You must do the dishes tonight.

meaning: 'I/you must + him/her/it' (contraction of 'dois le' or 'dois la').
additional_notes: Combination of the verb devoir (conjugated: je dois = I must / I have to; tu dois = you must) with the direct object pronoun 'le' or 'la' contracted before a vowel: l' + verb that follows (e.g. l'appeler = call him/her/it). Used to say you must do something to someone or something. Word order: subject + devoir + object pronoun + infinitive (Je dois l'appeler = I must call him/her/it).
target_language_example: Je dois l'écouter avant de décider.
native_language_example: I must listen to him/her/it before deciding.

meaning: 'I must/I've got to (do) it' — first-person singular of devoir + direct object pronoun 'la' (feminine 'it').
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (to have to/must) in the present (je dois = I must) with the feminine direct object pronoun la (it/her). Used when the speaker refers to a feminine noun previously mentioned (la clé, la lettre, la voiture, etc.). Word order: subject + devoir + object pronoun (je dois la + infinitive) or je dois la + verb (je dois la saisir). In spoken French the pronoun stays before the infinitive (je dois la retrouver).
target_language_example: Je dois la réparer avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I must fix it before tonight.

meaning: 'I must/need to (do something) to them' or 'I have to (do something) them' — combines the verb devoir (first/second/third person forms vary) with the direct object pronoun les (them).
additional_notes: dois = first-person singular present of devoir (je dois = I must/have to) or second-person singular (tu dois). Here it's je dois = I must. les is the plural direct object pronoun meaning 'them' (people or things). In French the pronoun comes before the main verb: Je dois les avertir = I must warn them. With infinitive verbs, the pronoun stays before the infinitive (les avertir, les rejoindre, les trouver).
target_language_example: Je dois les appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to call them tonight.

meaning: 'I must / I have to' + reflexive pronoun (short form).
additional_notes: Dois is the 1st or 2nd person singular present of devoir (je dois = I must, tu dois = you must). The m' is the elided reflexive pronoun (me) used before a vowel or muted h (m'excuser, m'habiller, m'occuper, m'y remettre). Together they start reflexive or pronominal verbs: Je dois m'excuser = I must excuse myself / I have to apologize. In spoken French the pronoun stays attached to the verb that follows. Use m' for je/tu with verbs beginning with a vowel or h muet.
target_language_example: Je dois m'excuser pour être en retard.
native_language_example: I must apologize for being late.

meaning: 'I must (do something) about it' / 'I have to (do something) with/about it' (first-person singular obligation + 'en' referring to something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (dois = I must / you must in informal tu) with the pronominal sequence m' + en. m' = me (to/for me or reflexive pronoun), en = 'of it', 'about it', 'from it', or 'about them' depending on context. Common patterns: 'm'en débarrasser' (get rid of it), 'm'en occuper' (take care of it), 'm'en souvenir' (remember it), 'm'en dire' (tell me about it). Word order: the pronouns come before the infinitive (dois m'en + infinitive).
target_language_example: Je dois m'en occuper demain.
native_language_example: I have to take care of it tomorrow.

meaning: 'I must / I have to get ready' (first-person singular, informal spoken word order).
additional_notes: Combination of devoir (must/have to) in the present (je dois) + reflexive verb se préparer (to get ready). Used to say you need to prepare or get yourself ready for something (school, work, an event, prayer, etc.). In full grammatically complete form you might say "je dois me préparer"; in casual speech the subject pronoun (je) is often dropped when context is clear. You can change the object of preparation by adding "pour" + noun or an infinitive (e.g. "pour l'école", "pour partir").
target_language_example: Je dois me préparer pour la soirée de ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to get ready for tonight's party.

meaning: 'I must/should speak' (first person singular of devoir + infinitive parler).
additional_notes: Combines the present tense of the modal verb devoir (je dois = I must/should/have to) with the infinitive parler (to speak). Used to express obligation, necessity, or strong recommendation that the speaker needs to speak. Context determines force (must vs. should). Contraction: in speech, je dois often sounds like /ʒə dwa/ or /ʒə dwa/ and may be followed directly by the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je dois parler au professeur demain.
native_language_example: I must speak to the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: 'must not say' / 'should not say' (negative obligation; you mustn't say)
additional_notes: Informal spoken structure: standard written form is 'ne dois pas dire' (often contracted to 'dois pas dire' in speech). Use with 'je/tu/il/etc.' and an object (de mensonge, ça, du mal de...). Conveys prohibition or advice not to say something. For formal/written French include the 'ne' before the verb: 'tu ne dois pas dire...'.
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas dire ça devant les enfants.
native_language_example: You mustn't say that in front of the children.

meaning: 'you must not' (informal negative with 'tu') — used to tell someone (tu) not to do something.
additional_notes: This is the negative form of devoir with the informal singular pronoun 'tu' plus a reflexive or other verb: 'tu ne dois pas te...' (you must not ... yourself). Common in commands or strong advice. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'tu dois pas te...'. Replace 'te' with another object pronoun if needed (me, nous, vous, se).
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas te moquer d'eux.
native_language_example: You must not make fun of them.

meaning: 'I/you must know what' — part of phrases meaning someone needs to know something specific.
additional_notes: This is composed of the modal verb devoir (conjugated: je dois, tu dois, etc.) + savoir (to know) + ce (introducing a clause: ce que / ce qui). It appears before clauses like ce que (what + direct object) or ce qui (what + subject). Use it to express obligation or necessity to find out information: "I must know what happened," "You must know what you're doing." Conjugate devoir to match the subject (je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils/elles doivent).
target_language_example: Je dois savoir ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: I must know what you said.

meaning: I must tell you (it) / I have to tell you (it).
additional_notes: This combination is part of a larger verb phrase: from devoir (to have to) + indirect object pronoun te (to you) + direct object pronoun le (it/him). Used when the speaker says they need to tell someone something (or repeat it). Word order: subject + devoir conjugated + te + le + (dire/répéter/etc.). Informal/register: neutral; common in speech. Pronunciation note: the pronouns link to the verb (dois-te-le pronounced quickly).
target_language_example: Je dois te le dire maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to tell you (it) now.

meaning: literally 'owe everything' or 'must do everything' — not a standard fixed phrase on its own
additional_notes: This sequence combines the verb 'devoir' (conjugated 'dois' = 'I/you must' or 'I/you owe') with the adverb 'tout' ('all', 'everything'). By itself 'dois tout' is incomplete and depends on context: it can mean 'I/you must do everything' when followed by an infinitive or object (e.g. 'Je dois tout faire' = 'I must do everything'), or 'I/you owe everything' in a financial or metaphorical sense (e.g. 'Je te dois tout' = 'I owe you everything'). Beginners should not treat 'dois tout' as a fixed idiom — include the verb object or infinitive to be clear.
target_language_example: Je dois tout finir avant demain.
native_language_example: I must finish everything before tomorrow.

meaning: 'dois' = 'must' or 'have to' (1st/2nd person singular of devoir); 'des' = plural indefinite article ('some') — together they often appear when devoir is followed by a noun phrase beginning with 'des'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase. 'Dois' is the singular present form of the verb devoir (je dois, tu dois) meaning obligation or necessity. When devoir is followed by a plural noun, the article 'des' (some) appears: e.g. 'Tu dois des explications' (You owe some explanations) or more commonly 'Tu dois des excuses' (You owe an apology). More frequently, devoir is followed by an infinitive ('Tu dois partir' = You must leave). Pay attention: 'dois des' can also occur when devoir means 'to owe' (e.g. 'Je dois des euros à Marie' = I owe Marie some euros).
target_language_example: Tu dois des explications à ta sœur.
native_language_example: You owe your sister some explanations.

meaning: 'must never' or 'has to never' (negated obligation).
additional_notes: This construction combines doit (3rd person singular of devoir: 'must/has to/ought to') with jamais ('never'). In standard French, a negative obligation is usually expressed with ne ... jamais: il ne doit jamais. Omitting ne is informal/spoken and common in casual speech, but considered grammatically incorrect in written/standard French. Use "ne doit jamais" in formal contexts. Also note: placement of jamais follows the verb (doit jamais / ne doit jamais).
target_language_example: Il ne doit jamais toucher à ce bouton.
native_language_example: He must never touch that button.

meaning: must not
additional_notes: informal spoken form of "ne doit pas", with the "ne" dropped. It uses doit, the 3rd-person singular present of devoir, so you hear it with il/elle/on/ça. It expresses prohibition, advice, or what is not supposed to happen; with être, it can also mean "can't be" in the sense of what is probably not the case ("ça doit pas être facile").
target_language_example: On doit pas faire ça ici.
native_language_example: You shouldn't do that here.

meaning: there must be something / there has to be something
additional_notes: Used to express a logical conclusion or expectation that 'something' exists, is present, or should be done. Complete phrase usually appears as "Il doit y avoir quelque chose" (there must be something) or followed by a complement: "quelque chose" (something), "quelque part" (somewhere), or "quelque + infinitive" (something to do). "Doit" here is the present of devoir and indicates probability or necessity.
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir quelque chose sous la table.
native_language_example: There must be something under the table.

meaning: This exact sequence is not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or fragmented string (possibly parts of 'doit', 'y', 'en' appearing together).
additional_notes: The words individually: 'doit' = third-person singular of 'devoir' ('must' / 'owes'); 'y' = pronoun meaning 'there' or replaces 'à + thing'; 'en' = pronoun meaning 'of it / some / from there'. In correct French, these pronouns have a fixed order before the conjugated verb: me/te/se/nous/vous > le/la/les > lui/leur > y > en. Example combinations would be 'il doit y aller' (he must go there) or 'il en doit' (he owes some). The sequence 'doit y en' as given is not grammatical — you'd usually say 'il doit y en avoir' (there must be some) or split differently: 'il doit en avoir' (he must have some) or 'il doit y aller' (he must go there).
target_language_example: Il doit y en avoir dans le placard.
native_language_example: There must be some in the cupboard.

meaning: 'must not' / 'do not have to' (negation of obligation) — context determines whether it's prohibition or lack of obligation
additional_notes: Formed from devoir (to have to / must) in third-person plural (ils/elles doivent) plus ne ... pas for negation. In most of the example sentences it expresses prohibition: 'they must not' / 'you must not'. In some contexts devoir can also mean 'to have to' (obligation) and with negation it can mean 'do not have to' (no obligation), but that reading is less common with devoir; context and intonation decide the sense. For informal spoken French the ne is often dropped (ils doivent pas).
target_language_example: Ils ne doivent pas entrer dans cette salle.
native_language_example: They must not enter this room.

meaning: 'dollars of' — French sequence where the plural noun 'dollars' is followed by the preposition 'de' before another noun; appears in quantified expressions (e.g. 'millions de dollars') or noun phrases like 'dollars de papier'.
additional_notes: In French, the currency usually follows the number (e.g. 10 dollars). 'Dollars de' occurs when 'dollars' is followed by 'de' + noun, often after a quantifier: 'des millions de dollars', 'des centaines de dollars', or in descriptive phrases like 'des dollars de papier'. The exact string 'dollars de' may be part of larger phrases rather than a standalone unit.
target_language_example: Ils ont compté des dollars de papier retrouvés dans le sac.
native_language_example: They counted dollars of paper found in the bag.

meaning: 'so' or 'therefore' followed by 'to the' (masculine singular) — used when linking a conclusion to a place or thing: 'so/to the (masculine noun)'.
additional_notes: This is just the sequence of the adverb 'donc' (therefore/so) plus the contraction 'au' (à + le = to the/at the for masculine singular nouns). It appears when you draw a conclusion or continue a thought and then refer to a masculine singular noun/place. Example contexts: donc au centre, donc au marché, donc au travail. Word order is typical: 'donc' comes before the preposition. Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional.
target_language_example: Il a raté le bus, donc au marché je vais y aller à pied.
native_language_example: He missed the bus, so I'll go to the market on foot.

meaning: a short sequence where 'donc' (so/therefore) is followed by 'de' — usually part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'donc de la', 'donc de le' -> 'donc du'); by itself it's not a fixed expression.
additional_notes: You will rarely use 'donc de' alone. 'Donc' means 'so', 'therefore', or can add emphasis in spoken French. It is often followed by an article or pronoun ('donc le', 'donc la', 'donc du', 'donc de la', 'donc des', 'donc d'') when connecting to a noun phrase: e.g. 'Donc du pain' (so bread / therefore some bread). In casual speech 'donc' can also soften a question or add impatience: 'Alors, donc… ?' If you see 'donc de' in writing, check the following word — it usually forms part of a larger noun phrase.
target_language_example: Il faut donc de l'eau pour la plante.
native_language_example: So you need water for the plant.

meaning: 'so' or 'therefore' + 'he/it' (used to draw a conclusion about a masculine subject).
additional_notes: donc is a common connector meaning 'so', 'therefore', or 'then'. When followed by il, it links a previous idea to a conclusion about 'he' or 'it' (il). In speech it can also add emphasis or mark a reaction: e.g. «Donc il a dit ça ?» (So he said that?). Word order remains subject after donc: 'donc il...'.
target_language_example: Tu as oublié ton passeport, donc il faudra en acheter un autre.
