The sequence 'déjà vu quelque' without a following word is incomplete and should be avoided in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Il a dit 'déjà vu quelque' par erreur en parlant; c'était une phrase incomplète.
native_language_example: He said 'déjà vu quelque' by mistake while speaking; it was an incomplete phrase.

meaning: 'to have a feeling of having already experienced something' (to feel that something is familiar as if it happened before).
additional_notes: Literally 'already seen something'. Used to describe the sensation that a current situation or event has already happened. The fixed noun 'déjà vu' is often used alone (un déjà vu). You can say 'j'ai déjà vu quelque chose' or 'j'ai un déjà vu' to express the same idea. Not used for literal prior knowledge—it's about the feeling of familiarity.
target_language_example: En regardant la scène, j'ai eu l'impression d'un déjà vu quelque chose que je ne pouvais pas expliquer.
native_language_example: Watching the scene, I had the impression of a déjà vu quelque chose that I couldn't explain.

meaning: 'already at' or 'already' used with a time/place/amount
additional_notes: Déjà means 'already.' When followed by à + noun or number, it emphasizes that something is already at a certain time, place, level, amount, etc. Common in expressions like "déjà à 10 heures" (already at 10 o'clock), "déjà à moitié plein" (already half full) or "déjà à 50 %". Used in neutral registers.
target_language_example: Il est déjà à la maison.
native_language_example: He is already at home.

meaning: That's something; at least that's a start (expresses partial satisfaction or relief).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge a positive point or small progress when the overall situation isn't ideal. Often follows a statement or stands alone. Tone can be resigned, mildly grateful, or ironic depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as réussi à réparer la porte ? — Non, mais j'ai trouvé la vis. — Déjà ça.
native_language_example: Did you manage to fix the door? — No, but I found the screw. — Well, that's something.

meaning: to already be (in a certain state or situation).
additional_notes: Combination of déjà (already) + être (to be). Used to say that someone/something is already in a given condition or has already arrived at a state. You would normally follow with an adjective, noun with article, or a past participle (e.g. déjà être prêt, déjà être au courant, déjà être parti). It's not a fixed idiom — it's compositional and used in the same way as 'already be' in English.
target_language_example: Il est déjà être prêt à partir.
native_language_example: He is already ready to leave.

meaning: an offense of / the crime of (used to name a specific wrongdoing)
additional_notes: Used to introduce the type of minor or major offense someone committed. Common in legal contexts. Often followed by a noun (e.g. délit de fuite = hit-and-run; délit d'initié = insider trading). Not used alone; requires the specific offense after 'de'.
target_language_example: Il a été condamné pour un délit de fuite.
native_language_example: He was convicted for a hit-and-run.

meaning: 'hit-and-run' (the crime of leaving the scene after causing an accident).
additional_notes: Refers to leaving an accident scene without stopping to help or exchange information; used in police/reports and everyday speech. Often appears with verbs like 'commettre', 'signaler', 'être victime de'.
target_language_example: La voiture a pris la fuite — c'était clairement un délit de fuite.
native_language_example: The car fled the scene — it was clearly a hit-and-run.

meaning: common denominator; something shared by different things (literal: math denominator).
additional_notes: Used both in math (lowest common denominator) and figuratively to mean a shared characteristic or cause among different items or problems. In math: "plus petit dénominateur commun" = least common denominator. Can be singular or plural depending on context.
target_language_example: Le dénominateur commun entre ces deux projets est le manque de budget.
native_language_example: The common denominator between these two projects is a lack of budget.

meaning: departure at (a specific time or place)
additional_notes: Used to indicate when or from where something/someone departs. Often followed by a time (départ à 9 h) or a place (départ à la gare). Common in schedules, travel contexts, and announcements. If indicating starting point, use 'départ de' for 'departure from'.
target_language_example: Le départ à 14 h est confirmé.
native_language_example: The departure at 2 PM is confirmed.

meaning: to go too far; to cross the line (behave in an unacceptable or excessive way).
additional_notes: Used when someone's words or actions are beyond what is acceptable. Often used in spoken French to express that a limit of politeness or propriety has been crossed. Can apply to insults, rude behaviour, excessive demands, etc.
target_language_example: Il a vraiment dépassé les bornes en parlant ainsi à sa collègue.
native_language_example: He really went too far by speaking to his colleague like that.

meaning: expresses annoyance, disappointment or spite — often part of phrases like «au dépit de» or «au grand dépit de» meaning “to the annoyance/disappointment of”.
additional_notes: Dépit is a noun meaning disappointment, chagrin or spite. The construction 'dépit de' is usually seen in fixed phrases such as 'au dépit de' or 'au grand dépit de' rather than alone; 'par dépit' is another common related phrase meaning 'out of spite'. Use 'dépit de' to indicate that something occurred to the annoyance or disappointment of someone (e.g. 'au dépit de ses parents').
target_language_example: Au grand dépit de ses amis, il a choisi de partir seul.
native_language_example: To the great annoyance of his friends, he chose to leave alone.

meaning: to drop off (someone or something) at a place; to leave, deliver, or file at a location.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a person or object and a destination (déposer quelqu'un/quelque chose à [lieu]). Can mean physically dropping someone off (by car), leaving an item somewhere, or formally submitting/fileing documents (déposer un dossier à la mairie). Context determines whether it's casual (give a ride) or formal (submit).
target_language_example: Je peux te déposer à la gare ce soir.
native_language_example: I can drop you off at the train station tonight.

meaning: to drop off at (a specific place/female noun).
additional_notes: Used with a place introduced by the feminine definite article la (e.g. la gare, la mairie). Equivalent to déposer quelque chose ou quelqu'un à + lieu. Common when talking about leaving a person, a package or a vehicle at a location. Conjugate déposer as needed: je dépose, il a déposé, etc.
target_language_example: Je peux te déposer à la gare cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I can drop you off at the train station this afternoon.

meaning: asks whether an action would bother or inconvenience someone ("does it bother you if...").
additional_notes: Commonly used to politely request permission or check for objection. Often appears as "Ça te/vous dérange si je... ?" with informal "te" or formal/plural "vous". Can be followed by verbs in the present or subjunctive (colloquially present). Equivalent to "Est-ce que ça vous dérange si... ?"
target_language_example: Ça vous dérange si j'ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Does it bother you if I open the window?

meaning: private detective; private investigator.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person hired to investigate private matters (infidelity, missing persons, fraud, etc.). Agreement: 'détective' is masculine; used without article in short IDs ("Arbogast, détective privé"). Can be used with verbs like engager (to hire) or être (to be).
target_language_example: Elle a engagé un détective privé pour retrouver son frère.
native_language_example: She hired a private detective to find her brother.

meaning: 'hate these' (verb + demonstrative; used to say you dislike specific plural things)
additional_notes: Déteste is the 1st/2nd/3rd person singular present form of détester (to hate). Ces is the plural demonstrative adjective meaning 'these' or 'those' used before a plural noun (ces livres, ces films). Together, 'déteste ces' would appear before a plural noun: e.g. Je déteste ces chansons. For correct conjugation, match the subject (Je déteste, Tu détestes, Il/Elle déteste, Nous détestons, Vous détestez, Ils/Elles détestent).
target_language_example: Je déteste ces chaussures, elles me font mal.
native_language_example: I hate these shoes, they hurt me.

meaning: 'hates me' — verb détester with object pronoun me (me) in sequence as requested but note this is not standard word order in French
additional_notes: This exact token sequence 'déteste me' is not grammatically correct in standard French prose. In normal French the object pronoun precedes the conjugated verb: 'il me déteste'. The sequence 'déteste me' can occur only in some nonstandard contexts (e.g., poetic inversion, line breaks, or when reproducing spoken errors) or in reversed word order for emphasis in very marked styles. For imperative affirmative with object pronouns the pronoun follows with a hyphen: 'Déteste-moi' (rare). Use standard constructions for correct French: 'il me déteste', 'elle me déteste', 'je me déteste'.
target_language_example: Dans son journal intime, on peut lire la phrase reconstruite mot à mot: «déteste me» comme reproduction d'un discours confus.
native_language_example: In his diary, you can read the word-for-word reconstructed phrase: "déteste me" as a reproduction of confused speech.

meaning: 'I hate my...' (first-person singular + 'my')
additional_notes: Déteste = 'hate' (verb, je déteste = I hate). 'Mon' is the masculine singular possessive used before masculine nouns and before feminine nouns that begin with a vowel sound (e.g. mon amie). Together they start phrases like 'Je déteste mon ...' to express dislike or strong negative feeling about something you own or are related to (job, body, father, country in example 4). Use 'ma' for feminine nouns without a vowel (ma voiture), 'mes' for plural (mes amis). Tone can be strong — in polite contexts consider milder verbs like 'n'aime pas'.
target_language_example: Je déteste mon travail en ce moment.
native_language_example: I hate my job at the moment.

meaning: 'hate everything' or 'hate it all' (present tense, emphatic).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb détester (to hate) and the pronoun tout (everything). Used to express strong dislike for everything or for a situation as a whole. Tone can be hyperbolic or literal depending on context. If referring to a person one hates, you'd use 'déteste tout le monde' (hates everyone). For negative general statements, other constructions like 'je déteste ça' (I hate that) or 'je déteste tout ça' (I hate all that) are common.
target_language_example: Après cette journée, il dit qu'il déteste tout.
native_language_example: After that day, he says he hates everything.

meaning: 'hates all the' or 'hates the whole...'
additional_notes: This sequence is incomplete on its own: 'déteste tout le...' needs a noun or phrase after 'le' (e.g. 'déteste tout le monde' = 'hates everyone', or 'déteste tout le temps' = 'hates all the time' but that specific example means 'always hates'). More common complete phrases are 'déteste tout' (hates everything) and 'déteste tout le monde' (hates everyone). Use with a following noun or expression; watch gender/number agreement (le/la/les).
target_language_example: Il déteste tout le monde dans ce livre.
native_language_example: He hates everyone in that book.

meaning: 'hate to see' or 'really dislike seeing' (followed by noun / clause).
additional_notes: Common construction: détester + voir + [noun/infinitive/that-clause implied]. Expresses strong emotional dislike at witnessing something (people, images, situations). Often followed by direct object (des animaux, des enfants, sa photo) or a verb phrase (voir quelqu'un + infinitive/participle). Tone is neutral to strong; not slang.
target_language_example: Je déteste voir des animaux blessés.
native_language_example: I hate to see injured animals.

meaning: 'you hate' (literal) — note: this exact word order is not standard French; it's ungrammatical in most contexts.
additional_notes: The correct word order for expressing 'you hate' is 'vous détestez' (formal/plural) or 'je vous déteste' (I hate you). 'Déteste vous' may appear only in very specific constructions with inversion for questions or in poetic/archaic word order, e.g. 'Déteste-vous... ?' (Do you hate...?) where a hyphen and inversion are used. Without inversion or hyphen, 'déteste vous' is generally incorrect. Use proper conjugation and word order: 'Vous détestez' (you hate), 'Il vous déteste' (he hates you), 'Je vous déteste' (I hate you).
target_language_example: Déteste vous ce que j'ai fait ?
native_language_example: Do you hate what I did?

meaning: 'I hate to be' / 'I hate being'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb détester (to hate) with the infinitive être (to be). Used to state dislike of a state or situation. In English you can translate as 'I hate being ...' or 'I hate to be ...'. Conjugate détester to match the subject (e.g., Je déteste, Tu détestes, Il/Elle déteste).
target_language_example: Je déteste être en retard au travail.
native_language_example: I hate being late for work.

meaning: 'destroyed the' (past/past-participle form of détruire used with a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: Détruit is the past participle of détruire (to destroy). In sentences like the examples it functions as the passé composé (e.g. a détruit = has/—destroyed) or as an adjective/past participle agreeing when necessary. Here 'le' is the masculine singular definite article before the noun (le château, le canapé, le jardin, le bâtiment). For feminine nouns use 'la' (a détruit la maison). To form the passé composé: avoir + détruit (elle a détruit, ils ont détruit).
target_language_example: Le vent a détruit le toit.
native_language_example: The wind destroyed the roof.

meaning: to have dinner at (someone's place) / dinner of (used before a noun to indicate the type or host of a dinner)
additional_notes: Often appears as 'dîner chez' for 'dine at someone's home' or 'dîner de + noun' to specify the kind of dinner (e.g. 'dîner de gala' = gala dinner). Alone, 'dîner de' is incomplete and needs a noun or name after it. 'Dîner' is both a noun (dinner) and a verb (to have dinner).
target_language_example: Nous allons au dîner de gala ce soir.
native_language_example: We're going to the gala dinner tonight.

meaning: appears to be a fragment: 'dîner' = 'dinner' (noun) or 'to have dinner' (verb); 'est' = 'is' (3rd person singular of être).
additional_notes: As given, 'dîner est' is not a complete, correct French phrase on its own. Likely you saw 'dîner' and 'est' next to each other in a sentence (for example: 'Le dîner est prêt' = 'Dinner is ready' or 'Il est temps de dîner' = 'It's time to have dinner'). Use 'dîner' as a noun (le dîner) or as a verb (dîner: to have dinner). 'Est' is the present tense of être (to be) for il/elle/on.
target_language_example: Le dîner est prêt.
native_language_example: Dinner is ready.

meaning: Likely a mistake or typo; not a standard French phrase. 'Dîner' means 'to have dinner' or 'dinner'.
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'dîner ce'. It may come from a typo, truncation, or incorrect word order. Useful related forms: 'dîner' (noun/verb), 'ce soir' (this evening). For example, 'dîner ce soir' = 'have dinner this evening'. If you meant 'dîner chez' (eat at someone's place), note the preposition 'chez' (not 'ce').
target_language_example: Veux-tu dîner ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to have dinner tonight?

meaning: part of a construction meaning 'had to do something' (past obligation: devoir + infinitive).
additional_notes: This appears to be a fragment: the full pattern is 'avoir dû + faire quelque chose' or 'dû + infinitive' after a past participle (e.g. 'J'ai dû partir' = 'I had to leave'). 'Dû' is the past participle of devoir. Use 'dû' with an auxiliary (usually avoir) to express a past obligation. 'Faire quelque' is incomplete — the common phrase is 'faire quelque chose' ('to do something').
target_language_example: J'ai dû faire quelque chose pour aider.
native_language_example: I had to do something to help.

meaning: 'should have told me (it)'.
additional_notes: This is the perfect conditional of devoir + object pronouns: 'aurais dû' (you should have) + 'me' (to me) + 'le' (it/that). Used to express that someone ought to have told the speaker something in the past. In natural speech you will usually see the full form 'tu aurais dû me le dire' or 'vous auriez dû me le dire.'
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have told me that earlier.

meaning: 'owed/should have to us' or part of compound verbs meaning 'had to us' / 'should have (done) to us' (past participle + indirect object pronoun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the past participle dû (from devoir) followed by the indirect object pronoun nous. Devoir in the past tense (avoir dû) can mean 'had to' / 'must have' or, in conditional past (aurait dû / aurait dû), 'should have (done)'. The pronoun nous means 'to us' or 'us' and refers to the indirect object. Word order: past participle + pronoun often appears when the pronoun follows the verb (as in compound tenses with infinitives or in some constructions). Examples above show meanings like 'he should have returned it to us', 'they must have spotted us', 'you should have told us'.
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû nous prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have warned us earlier.

meaning: should have (to) you
additional_notes: This is the past participle dû (from devoir) followed by the clitic pronoun t' (te) attached to a verb that follows: e.g. J'aurais dû t'appeler = I should have called you. In English you use 'should have' + past participle. The construction expresses regret or obligation not met. The literal sense 'owed you' can appear in other contexts (e.g. quelqu'un a dû t'apporter = someone must have brought you), so pay attention to context: in conditional perfect (j'aurais dû) it means 'should have'.
target_language_example: J'aurais dû t'aider hier.
native_language_example: I should have helped you yesterday.

meaning: literally 'owed you it' — combination of past participle dû (from devoir: to owe / to have to) + indirect object vous (to you) + direct object le (it). Not a fixed standalone phrase; appears inside larger sentences (often with auxiliary or different word order).
additional_notes: This sequence is compositional and uncommon as an isolated fragment because French places object pronouns before the verb and agreement/auxiliary choices matter. Examples where this exact sequence can appear include reported or elliptical contexts (e.g., after an auxiliary or in perf. constructions with inversion of typical order in poetry/archaic style) or in clipped writing. More natural alternatives in full sentences: «Je vous le devais», «Je vous l'ai dû» (rare/awkward), «Il vous le devait». Be careful with word order and agreement: object pronouns normally precede the verb; when using passé composé with avoir, past participle agreement may be required if direct object precedes the verb.
target_language_example: Il a dit que cela m'était dû vous le, mais la formulation est maladroite.
native_language_example: He said that it was owed to me you it, but the wording is awkward.

meaning: of (an) attitude; relating to attitude
additional_notes: This is the contraction of de + attitude (de attitude → d’attitude). It appears in contexts describing something that concerns or comes from an attitude (e.g. 'manque d’attitude' = lack of attitude). Use when attaching adjectives or nouns to 'attitude' (gender is feminine). Pronunciation: [da.ti.tyd].
target_language_example: Son manque d’attitude m’a surpris.
native_language_example: His lack of attitude surprised me.

meaning: of her / from her / about her (contraction of de + elle; indicates possession, origin, source, or that something concerns a female person or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Contraction of de + elle. Used to show possession (though possessive pronouns like 'son/sa/ses' or structures like 'à elle' and 'le sien/la sienne' are often preferred), indicate origin or source, or to mean 'about her' after verbs like 'parler de'. Can sound literary or emphatic in some contexts; spoken French often uses it in phrases such as 'parler d’elle' or 'venir d’elle'. The exact sense depends on context.
target_language_example: Il a appris la nouvelle d’elle hier soir.
native_language_example: He learned the news about her last night.

meaning: email; an electronic message sent or received via the internet.
additional_notes: Commonly used in French as both a noun and verb (envoyer un e-mail). Pronunciation often like English. Alternative French words: courriel (more formal/Canadian) or mél. Used with articles: un e-mail, l'e-mail. Plural can be e-mails.
target_language_example: Je t'ai envoyé un e-mail avec les informations.
native_language_example: I sent you an email with the information.

meaning: fresh water (not salt water).
additional_notes: Used to describe bodies of water (rivers, lakes) or animals that live in non-salty water. Opposite: eau salée or eau de mer (sea water). Common in biological and geographic contexts.
target_language_example: Ces poissons ne supportent pas l'eau douce.
native_language_example: These fish cannot tolerate fresh water.

meaning: 'personal effect' or 'personal possession' (an item belonging to a person).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's belongings or possessions (often in contexts like travel, luggage, police reports, estates). Can be pluralized as "effets personnels" to mean "personal belongings." Not commonly used to describe emotions—it's about physical items.
target_language_example: Un policier a retrouvé un effet personnel près du lieu de l'accident.
native_language_example: A police officer found a personal effect near the scene of the accident.

meaning: 'the effect that' or 'the impression that' (what something causes or how it makes someone feel).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the effect, impression or feeling produced by something. Often follows verbs like 'savoir', 'faire' or expressions like 'ça me fait' (it makes me feel). Common in everyday speech to describe emotional or physical reactions and social impressions.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas l'effet que ça lui fera.
native_language_example: I don't know the effect that will have on him/her.

meaning: side effect (an unintended effect, especially of a drug or action).
additional_notes: Commonly used in medical contexts to describe unwanted or secondary consequences of a treatment or medication. Can also be used figuratively for indirect, unintended results of actions or policies.
target_language_example: Un effet secondaire fréquent de ce médicament est la somnolence.
native_language_example: A common side effect of this medicine is drowsiness.

meaning: well
additional_notes: A filler or discourse marker used to start a response, show hesitation, introduce a conclusion, or move the conversation forward. Tone and context change the nuance (surprise, resignation, reflection). Very common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Eh bien, d'accord — commençons tout de suite.
native_language_example: Well, all right — let's start right away.

meaning: herself (emphatic/reflexive).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize 'she' (contrast or focus) or as a reflexive pronoun meaning 'she did it herself'. Can appear alone for emphasis ('Elle-même.' = 'She herself.'). Agreement: 'elle-même' (singular feminine); plural would be 'elles-mêmes'. Often follows the verb or subject.
target_language_example: Elle a réparé la porte elle-même.
native_language_example: She repaired the door herself.

meaning: she demanded / she insisted (that she be allowed to see...)
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of exiger: 'to demand' or 'to insist on'. Often followed by 'de' + infinitive (e.g. 'exiger de voir...') or by a clause introduced with 'que' + subjunctive. Indicates a strong, sometimes formal or forceful, request.
target_language_example: Elle a exigé de parler au responsable immédiatement.
native_language_example: She demanded to speak to the person in charge immediately.

meaning: This combination is ungrammatical in French; likely a mistake. Correct forms are "elle a acheté" (she bought) or "elle achetait" (she was buying / used to buy).
additional_notes: In French, the past participle "acheté" must be used with an auxiliary verb. The most common past tense is the passé composé, formed with the present of "avoir": "elle a acheté" = "she bought" (or "she has bought"). For an imperfect (ongoing or habitual past) use "elle achetait". If a direct object precedes the verb, agreement rules apply (e.g. "les pommes qu'elle a achetées"). "Elle acheté" without an auxiliary is not correct and should be corrected in writing or speech.
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* Elle acheté la robe — on devrait dire « elle a acheté la robe ».
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* She bought the dress — one should say "she bought the dress" using the correct auxiliary.

meaning: This is not a correct French phrase; likely a mistake. Possible intended forms include «elle est arrivée» ('she arrived'/'she has arrived') or «elle arrive» ('she is arriving').
additional_notes: In French, verbs must be conjugated and many compound tenses require an auxiliary verb. The past participle 'arrivée' must agree in gender/number with the subject when used with the auxiliary être (elle est arrivée). Standing alone, 'elle arrivée' is ungrammatical because the auxiliary 'est' (or another conjugated form) is missing. Use 'être' as the auxiliary for verbs of movement like arriver.
target_language_example: Je croyais qu'elle arrivée hier, mais en fait elle est encore en route.
native_language_example: I thought she arrived yesterday, but actually she is still on her way.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; simply the subject pronoun 'elle' (she) followed immediately by the contraction 'au' (à + le, 'to the'/'at the'). On its own this sequence is incomplete and uncommon; it typically appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'elle au cinéma' if a word is omitted) or as 'elle, au...' in spoken hesitation.
additional_notes: Treat 'elle' and 'au' as separate words for learners. 'elle' = she; 'au' = à + le, used before masculine singular nouns (e.g. 'au bureau' = at the office). The two words together without intervening words are rare and usually indicate omitted words, a pause, or a transcription/typo. Example contexts where the sequence appears: 'Elle, au...' (she, um...), or in clipped written forms where punctuation is omitted.
target_language_example: Elle, au début, ne comprenait pas.
native_language_example: She, at the beginning, didn't understand.

meaning: 'she/it too' or 'also her'.
additional_notes: Used to add that a female person (elle) or a feminine noun is included in what was said. Can mean 'she too' (also she) or, when referring to a feminine noun, 'it too'. Often follows the subject or clause it relates to. In questions the order can invert (Vient-elle aussi ? = Is she coming too?).
target_language_example: Marie est invitée, et elle aussi viendra.
native_language_example: Marie is invited, and she will come too.

meaning: Not a grammatical French phrase as written; appears to be a word sequence missing the copula (est). Literally reads "she beautiful."
additional_notes: Uncommon and nonstandard — you should say "elle est belle" to mean "she is beautiful." If encountered in informal writing, it is probably a typo or omission of the verb. In poetry or stylized captions someone might deliberately drop the verb for effect (e.g., short social-media caption), but this is not standard grammar.
target_language_example: Elle belle, elle sourit dans la lumière.
native_language_example: She beautiful, she smiles in the light. (Nonstandard/stylized — correct French would be "Elle est belle, elle sourit dans la lumière.")

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'she (is) good/well' or part of a larger expression.
additional_notes: On its own, 'elle bien' is ungrammatical in standard French because an adjective or adverb normally requires a verb (e.g. 'Elle est bien' = 'She is well/OK', 'Elle va bien' = 'She is doing well'). 'Elle bien' might appear only as an incomplete fragment in casual speech, poetry, song lyrics, or as a transcription/typographical error. To express complete ideas, use 'Elle est bien', 'Elle va bien', 'Elle est bonne' (for 'she is good' in some senses) or 'Elle est douée' (for 'she is talented').
target_language_example: « Elle bien » n'a aucun sens isolé dans cette phrase.
native_language_example: "Elle bien" has no standalone meaning in this sentence.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; it is the sequence 'elle' (she) immediately followed by 'chez' (at the home/place of). This sequence is incomplete and ungrammatical on its own because 'chez' requires a following noun or name (e.g. 'chez Marie', 'chez le médecin').
additional_notes: 'Elle chez' does occur as a literal sequence only in contexts where punctuation or additional words separate them (e.g. in transcriptions, quotes, or elliptical speech), but in normal sentences you must include a verb or a noun after 'chez' (e.g. 'Elle est chez moi', 'Elle est chez Marie'). Avoid writing 'elle chez' as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: …et elle chez Marie, elle a trouvé la lettre.
native_language_example: …and she, at Marie's, found the letter.

meaning: 'she began' or 'she started'.
additional_notes: Third-person singular past historic (commença) or passé simple form of commencer; in spoken French, the passé composé (elle a commencé) is more common. Use to describe a completed action in the past. Can be followed by an infinitive (elle commença à parler) or a noun/phrase (elle commença son discours).
target_language_example: Elle commença à lire la lettre à voix haute.
native_language_example: She began to read the letter out loud.

meaning: Used in questions to ask whether something (feminine) is correct or right.
additional_notes: The phrase appears in the structure '... est-elle correcte ?' where 'elle' is the subject pronoun referring back to a feminine noun (la réponse, la traduction, la phrase, la montre, etc.). In spoken and written French, you can also ask 'Est-ce que c'est correct ?' or 'C'est correct ?' For a masculine noun use 'est-il correct ?' or simply 'correcte' agrees in gender (correcte for feminine, correct for masculine).
target_language_example: Cette phrase est-elle correcte ?
native_language_example: Is this sentence correct?

meaning: Not a fixed phrase in French; literally 'she in' — typically appears as two separate words ('elle' + 'dans') within a larger sentence. It is not an idiom by itself and its sense depends on the surrounding words (e.g., 'elle dans ce rôle' = 'her in this role').
additional_notes: Do not use 'elle dans' as a standalone expression. You'll see it when 'elle' (she) is followed by 'dans' (in/inside/within) as part of a clause. Sometimes a comma is inserted ('elle, dans...') to mark a pause or contrast, but the meaning always depends on context. Check the rest of the sentence to translate or interpret correctly.
target_language_example: Je parle d'elle dans la réunion — elle dans cette équipe a beaucoup d'expérience.
native_language_example: I'm talking about her in the meeting — her in that team has a lot of experience.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; typically a fragment where 'elle' (she/it) is immediately followed by the preposition 'de' as part of a larger construction (possessive, origin, partitive, etc.). By itself it has no independent meaning.
additional_notes: 'Elle de' usually appears only as the start of a longer expression (e.g., 'elle de Paris', 'elle de mon amie') or in colloquial/elliptical speech. If you encounter it, read the surrounding words to understand the intended structure. It is compositional (meaning derived from its parts) and can be translated literally by combining 'she/it' and 'of/from' when context makes that sensible.
target_language_example: Elle de la bande a toujours une histoire à raconter.
native_language_example: She from the group always has a story to tell.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a mistaken or ill-formed sequence. 'elle' = she/it (feminine); 'des' = plural indefinite article ('some') or contraction of de + les.
additional_notes: This sequence does not form an established expression. If you encounter 'elle des' in running text, it's probably a typo, a mis-segmentation (end of one word plus start of another), or missing verbs/prepositions. Possible intended forms include 'elle a des...' (she has some...), 'elle des...' as part of a larger phrase where words were split, or dialectal/colloquial elisions in speech that were transcribed incorrectly. Always check surrounding context to determine the intended structure.
target_language_example: Elle des enfants jouent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: She some children are playing in the garden. (incorrect/ill-formed — likely intended: 'Elle a des enfants qui jouent dans le jardin' or 'Des enfants jouent dans le jardin.')

meaning: she gives; it gives (feminine subject).
additional_notes: Third-person singular present of donner. Used when the subject is a feminine noun or 'elle' (she). Can mean 'she gives' (action of giving) or 'it gives' when referring to a feminine noun (e.g., la machine donne). Context (direct object, indirect object) clarifies what is being given. Conjugation: je donne, tu donnes, il/elle donne, nous donnons, vous donnez, ils/elles donnent.
target_language_example: Elle donne son temps aux enfants du quartier.
native_language_example: She gives her time to the neighborhood children.

meaning: literally “she already”; indicates that a female subject has already done or experienced something (elliptical without a verb)
additional_notes: This is the pronoun 'elle' followed by the adverb 'déjà'. In standard French, 'déjà' normally follows the verb or appears elsewhere in the clause (e.g. "elle est déjà partie", "elle a déjà vu ça"). The sequence 'elle déjà' by itself is elliptical or colloquial and typically requires more context or an implied verb to be grammatical in full sentences (e.g. as a clipped reply: 'Elle, déjà?' meaning 'Her — already?'). Use with care: in most full sentences you should place 'déjà' after the verb.
target_language_example: — Elle déjà ? — Oui, elle est partie.
native_language_example: — Her, already? — Yes, she has left.

meaning: 'she' + pronoun 'en' (replaces 'de' + noun or quantity); means 'she of it/them' or 'she has/of them' depending on context.
additional_notes: Combines the subject pronoun elle (she) with the unstressed pronoun en. En replaces a noun introduced by de (e.g. 'de la farine', 'des enfants') or a quantity (e.g. 'trois', 'beaucoup'). Position: en usually comes immediately before the verb (Elle en veut. Elle en a trois.). In compound tenses with an auxiliary (elle en a pris), en still precedes the auxiliary. Translate depending on context: 'she has some', 'she wants one/more of them', 'she of it/them.'
target_language_example: Elle en a acheté deux.
native_language_example: She bought two of them.

meaning: 'she' + part of the expression 'être en train (de)' meaning 'she is in the process (of) / she is ...ing'.
additional_notes: This sequence is incomplete on its own. The correct expression is usually "elle est en train (de) + infinitive" = "she is in the process of [doing something]". In quick spoken French some speakers may drop the 'est' (e.g. familiarly heard as "elle en train de..."), but standard written French requires the verb "est." Do not use "elle en train" alone; include the verb and the infinitive (or keep it as part of a larger clause).
target_language_example: On a dit qu'elle en train de partir, mais c'était mal formulé.
native_language_example: They said she was about to leave, but it was poorly phrased.

meaning: Likely a mistaken/incomplete form of "elle est en train de" meaning "she is in the process of / she is (doing)...".
additional_notes: The correct full phrase is "elle est en train de + infinitive" and it emphasises an action currently in progress (similar to "she is ...ing" in English). "Elle en train de" without "est" is ungrammatical; avoid omitting the auxiliary "est". Use "être en train de" for ongoing actions: "je suis en train de lire" = "I am reading (right now)".
target_language_example: (Incorrect) Elle en train de préparer le dîner. — Correct: Elle est en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: (Incorrect) She in process of preparing dinner. — Correct: She is preparing dinner (right now).

meaning: 'she again' or 'her again' (literal); not a common fixed phrase by itself, usually appears in fragments or needs reordering in full sentences.
additional_notes: The sequence 'elle encore' is uncommon as a standalone fixed expression in French. In natural speech it may appear in short fragments or rhetorical questions (e.g. « Elle encore ? ») to mean 'Her again?' but standard phrasing often uses 'Encore elle ?' or full sentences like 'Elle est encore là' ('She is still here'). Avoid using 'elle encore' in formal writing; prefer complete sentences or correct word order.
target_language_example: Elle encore ? Je n'y crois pas.
native_language_example: Her again? I don't believe it.

meaning: she is in / she is (in a state or location)
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman's current location, state, condition, or involvement. Followed by a noun, adjective + noun, prepositional phrase, or adverbial phrase (e.g., en déplacement, en excellente condition, en haut, en relation avec). Not all combinations are idiomatic (e.g., 'en destruction' is unusual). Context determines exact translation: 'en' often corresponds to 'in' or 'undergoing' depending on the phrase.
target_language_example: Elle est en congé cette semaine.
native_language_example: She is on leave this week.

meaning: she is on the (masculine singular noun follows)
additional_notes: A simple phrase meaning 'she is on the…' used before a masculine singular noun (le). It is just the subject pronoun + être + preposition + definite article. Common in literal contexts (e.g. elle est sur le canapé) or in descriptive phrases. Make sure the noun after 'le' is masculine and singular; if feminine use 'elle est sur la', if plural 'elle est sur les'.
target_language_example: Elle est sur le canapé.
native_language_example: She is on the sofa.

meaning: This combination is not a standard fixed phrase in French; it reads literally as 'she and' (or 'it and' when referring to a feminine noun) and needs more words to form a complete idea.
additional_notes: You will not usually see 'elle et' alone — it's just the pronoun elle ('she' or 'it' for feminine nouns) followed by the conjunction et ('and'). It must be followed by another noun, clause or adjective to make sense: e.g. 'elle et moi' (she and I), 'elle et sa sœur' (she and her sister), or in embedded clauses 'elle est...' (note: 'et' vs 'est' are different words). Be careful not to confuse 'et' (and) with 'est' (is).
target_language_example: Elle et sa sœur viennent ce soir.
native_language_example: She and her sister are coming tonight.

meaning: she demanded (formal/literary past tense).
additional_notes: Elle exigea is the passé simple (literary past) of exiger used with 'elle' — means 'she demanded' or 'she insisted on'. Commonly followed by de + infinitive (e.g. de voir...). In spoken and informal written French, the passé composé (elle a exigé) is used instead. Used in formal, narrative or written contexts.
target_language_example: Elle exigea une explication immédiate.
native_language_example: She demanded an immediate explanation.

additional_notes: The sequence 'elle faire' is not a grammatically correct, standalone French phrase. Standard French requires the verb be properly conjugated to agree with the subject pronoun 'elle' (e.g. 'elle fait' = 'she does/makes'). You might see 'elle' next to an infinitive in larger constructions (for example in reported speech or with certain verbs: « Je veux la voir faire »), but 'elle faire' taken alone is ungrammatical. If you intended a different structure ('elle fait', inversion, or cleft forms like 'c'est elle qui fait'), use the appropriate conjugation or phrasing.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vue: elle faire la vaisselle était surprenant. (This is intentionally ungrammatical to show 'elle faire' appearing as written, but correct French would be «je l'ai vue faire la vaisselle» or «elle faisait la vaisselle».)
native_language_example: I saw her: 'elle faire' the dishes was surprising. (This sentence is ungrammatical in French; proper forms would be provided in the note.)

meaning: she's doing (that) there / what is she doing there (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal components: elle = she, fait = does/makes, là = there. Alone, 'elle fait là' is incomplete and depends on intonation and context. As a neutral statement it can mean 'she's doing (something) there' when followed by more info (e.g. 'elle fait là un gâteau' is uncommon; you'd normally say 'elle fait un gâteau là-bas'). More commonly in spoken French you'll hear fragments like 'Elle fait quoi, là ?' = 'What is she doing now/there?' or 'Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait, là ?' for asking about someone's current action. Informal speech often places 'là' for emphasis: 'Il arrive là' = 'He's coming now/there'.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait là ?
native_language_example: What is she doing there?

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a mistake. A grammatically correct expression would include a verb, e.g. "elle est grande" (she is tall).
additional_notes: "Elle grande" by itself is ungrammatical in standard French because a subject plus adjective normally requires a verb or another linking structure. It could appear as a fragment, poetic omission, or transcription error. For learners, use the full phrase with the appropriate verb (elle est, elle devient, elle paraît, etc.).
target_language_example: (Incorrect/fragment) « Elle grande », écrit sur une note, sans verbe.
native_language_example: (Incorrect/fragment) "She tall," written on a note, without a verb.

meaning: she is here / her here (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literally "she here". Often used in very short, informal contexts (captions, notes, replies) to indicate a female person is present; more complete spoken forms are "elle est ici" or "elle est là". Without the verb it sounds clipped and is uncommon in formal writing. Context determines whether it's understood as a sentence fragment meaning "she is here" or as a label like "her: here".
target_language_example: Elle ici, pas lui.
native_language_example: Her here, not him.

meaning: 'she' (subject) + 'her' (direct object pronoun): she (does something to) her.
additional_notes: This is a sequence of two pronouns: elle = 'she' (subject) and la = feminine singular direct object pronoun meaning 'her' or 'it' (feminine). It appears in sentences where a female subject acts on a feminine person or a feminine noun. Word order: subject (elle) before verb, and the object pronoun (la) usually appears before the verb in simple tenses (Elle la déteste). In compound tenses the object pronoun still precedes the auxiliary (Elle l'a vue). 'La' can also refer to a feminine thing (la lettre → la).
target_language_example: Elle la conseille souvent.
native_language_example: She advises her often.

meaning: literally 'she/it at night' — combination of pronoun (elle) + time expression (la nuit).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the pronoun 'elle' (she or it) followed by the time expression 'la nuit' (at night). Depending on context, 'elle' can mean 'she' (a person) or 'it' (a feminine noun, e.g. la lune). Word order matters: 'elle la nuit' appears in sentences like questions with inversion (Pourquoi la lune brille-t-elle la nuit ?) or statements indicating presence/actions at night (avec elle la nuit dernière = with her last night). For beginners: recognize 'la nuit' = 'at night' and 'elle' = 'she/it'.
target_language_example: La lampe s'allume toute seule, on la voit bien elle la nuit.
native_language_example: The lamp lights up by itself, you can see it well at night.

meaning: she it
additional_notes: This is the combination of the subject pronoun elle (she) plus a direct object clitic le (him/it). In natural English you'd usually translate according to context as “she him” or “she it,” often rendered more smoothly as “she [verb] him/it” (e.g. elle le voit = she sees him/it). The object pronoun le comes before the verb in French (elle le cherche). If the verb is compound (passé composé), the pronoun still goes before the auxiliary (elle le a vu → elle l'a vu).
target_language_example: Elle le regarde tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She watches him/it every evening.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase. As written, it is likely a mistake or fragment: 'elle' = 'she' and 'loin' = 'far', but they require a linking verb or preposition (e.g. 'elle est loin', 'loin d'elle').
additional_notes: 'elle loin' by itself is ungrammatical and does not occur in correct French. Common correct alternatives: 'elle est loin' (she is far), 'loin d'elle' (far from her). If you see 'elle loin' in writing, it is probably a typo or omission.
target_language_example: Elle loin — phrase incorrecte : on doit dire « elle est loin ».
native_language_example: Elle loin — incorrect phrase: you must say "elle est loin."

meaning: that one (feminine) / she over there (emphatic)
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize a specific female person or a feminine noun (object) nearby or previously mentioned. Tends to be informal/spoken. Can be used alone (e.g. Elle là! — There she is/That one!) or inside a sentence to contrast with others (e.g. Pas elle là, l'autre — Not that one, the other). Tone and gesture (pointing) often accompany it.
target_language_example: Regarde elle là, elle attend depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: Look at her over there, she's been waiting a long time.

meaning: intended to convey 'she was born' but ungrammatical as written
additional_notes: The correct French is "elle est née" (for a woman). "Née" is the past participle of naître and must be used with the auxiliary verb être. In some contexts, "née" alone appears before a maiden name (e.g. "Marie, née Dupont"). Agreement: né (m), née (f), nés (pl m or mixed), nées (pl f). The sequence "elle née" without "est" is not grammatical in standard French and should be avoided.
target_language_example: Elle née (incorrect) — correct: Elle est née à Paris en 1990.
native_language_example: She was born (incorrect phrase shown: "Elle née") — correct: She was born in Paris in 1990.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase; likely a mistake or fragment. Probably intended as "elle est partie" (she left/has left) or part of a participial phrase like "elle, partie..."
additional_notes: By itself, "elle partie" is ungrammatical. Common corrections: use the auxiliary verb: "elle est partie" for the passé composé. In some written fragments or notes you might see "elle, partie tôt, ..." where commas and context make "partie" a past participle modifying "elle"; then the verb appears elsewhere. The past participle "partie" agrees in gender/number with "elle" (feminine singular). If encountered in informal speech or quick notes, the speaker likely omitted "est" or punctuation.
target_language_example: Elle partie, la maison était vide.
native_language_example: With her gone, the house was empty.

meaning: Not a complete grammatical phrase by itself; a fragment meaning 'she/it not' used in informal spoken French when the 'ne' and/or verb are omitted or in elliptical contexts.
additional_notes: Standard French negation wraps the verb with 'ne ... pas' (e.g. 'elle ne vient pas'). In casual speech the 'ne' is often dropped and verbs may be omitted in fragments, producing sequences like 'elle pas' in dialogue, notes, subtitles, or childlike speech. Alone, 'elle pas' is ungrammatical in formal writing and should be avoided; include the verb and preferably 'ne' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Elle pas contente.
native_language_example: She is not happy. (colloquial/elliptical)

meaning: 'she' + past participle 'passed' (from verb passer) appearing when 'elle' is subject and passer is in a compound tense or construction, e.g. in questions or statements meaning 'where did she go?', 'how did she go/turn out?', or 'she went/was passed'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the sequence of subject pronoun 'elle' followed by the past participle 'passée' (agreeing in gender) when used with the auxiliary être (e.g. Où est‑elle passée ?). Common uses: asking where someone went (Où est‑elle passée ? / Par où est‑elle passée ? / Où est‑elle passée alors ?), asking how an event went when reflexive (Comment s'est‑elle passée ?), or noting that she went unnoticed (elle est passée inaperçue). Word order and auxiliary (être) are required in compound tenses; the past participle agrees in gender with 'elle'.
target_language_example: Mais où est-elle passée ?
native_language_example: But where did she go?

meaning: 'she thinks' or 'she believes'
additional_notes: Simple present of the verb penser (to think). Used to report someone's opinion, belief, or thought. Can introduce a clause with que (elle pense que...) or an infinitive (elle pense partir). Pronunciation: [ɛl pɑ̃s].
target_language_example: Elle pense que le film est intéressant.
native_language_example: She thinks the movie is interesting.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; simply the subject pronoun 'elle' ('she') followed immediately by the preposition 'pour' ('for', 'to', 'in order to') when they appear adjacent in a sentence.
additional_notes: This combination is not a standard multi-word expression in French. 'Elle' is a subject pronoun; 'pour' is a preposition or subordinator. They can appear next to each other across certain constructions (often when punctuation, inversion, or an embedded clause causes adjacency), but a verb or noun normally follows 'pour'. Example uses with adjacency are rare and often part of a larger structure. The two words are compositional and can be translated literally as 'she for' but natural English will rephrase (e.g., 'for her', 'she is to', 'she in order to').
target_language_example: On a dit elle pour l'entretien, mais finalement elle est venue plus tôt.
native_language_example: They said 'she for the interview', but in the end she came earlier.

meaning: This is not grammatically correct French; likely an error. Possible intended forms: 'elle prend' (she takes/is taking), 'elle a pris' (she took/has taken) or 'elle prit' (she took — literary passé simple).
additional_notes: 'Prendre' (to take) requires correct conjugation and, for compound past, the auxiliary 'avoir'. 'Elle pris' mixes subject 'elle' with an incorrect verb form: 'pris' is the past participle (used with 'avoir' as in 'elle a pris') or looks like a mistaken present/past ending. In passé simple the correct third-person singular is 'prit' (one t), not 'pris'. If you encounter 'elle pris' it is almost certainly a typo or learner error; correct to 'elle prend', 'elle a pris' or 'elle prit' depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle pris la parole, mais son français était hésitant.
native_language_example: She took the floor, but her French was hesitant.

meaning: she smelled (bad)
additional_notes: This is the past historic (passé simple) form of the verb puer (to stink) for elle, or more commonly it's the feminine third-person singular in the passé simple used in literary/written French: elle pu = 'she stank'/'she smelled (bad)'. In spoken French, the passé composé (elle a pué) or present (elle pue) is more common. Context determines whether it refers to a person, animal or thing having a bad smell. Note: puer is informal/neutral; calling someone that is rude.
target_language_example: Après la tempête, elle pu et tout le monde a fermé les fenêtres.
native_language_example: After the storm, she stank and everyone closed the windows.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'she that he' or part of a relative clause (e.g. 'she whom he...').
additional_notes: This sequence is not an idiomatic multi-word expression in French. It looks like a fragment from a sentence where 'elle' (she/it) is followed by a relative clause introduced by 'que' with subject 'il' (he/it). Example contexts: 'elle que je connais' (she whom I know) or 'la maison qu'il a achetée' (the house that he bought). In correct French the relative pronoun agrees with the antecedent and word order matters: 'elle que...' is uncommon — you would more often see 'celle qu'il...' (the one that he...) or 'la femme qu'il...' (the woman whom he...).
target_language_example: Celle qu'il a vue est partie.
native_language_example: The one that he saw has left.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase in French; literally 'she who' or 'she that' when used in relative clauses (rare/awkward).
additional_notes: French normally uses relative pronouns like « qui », « que », « dont » after a noun or pronoun. 'Elle que' can occur in informal speech or poetic/expressive contexts to mean 'she who...' but is uncommon and often ungrammatical in standard prose. More natural alternatives: « celle qui » (the one who) or simply « elle » plus a clause with « qui/que ». Example: « celle qui » = 'the one who'; do not use 'elle que' to say 'the woman that...'.
target_language_example: Celle qui partira en premier sera prête; on ne dit pas *elle que partira*.
native_language_example: Use 'celle qui' (the one who) instead of '*elle que*'.

meaning: she who / the one (feminine) who
additional_notes: Combination of the pronoun 'elle' (she/it for feminine nouns) and the relative pronoun 'qui' (who/which). Used to introduce a relative clause describing a feminine person or a feminine noun previously mentioned. In spoken French you may also hear 'c'est elle qui...' to emphasize that she is the one who did something.
target_language_example: C'est elle qui a préparé le dîner.
native_language_example: She is the one who prepared dinner.

meaning: she (is the one) who has / who did (used to emphasize that she is the person who performed an action).
additional_notes: Used in cleft sentences (C'est... qui/que) to emphasize the subject: 'C'est elle qui a...' = 'She is the one who...'. Follows with a past participle or verb phrase (often passé composé). Common in spoken and written French to point out or confirm who did something.
target_language_example: C'est elle qui a envoyé la lettre.
native_language_example: She is the one who sent the letter.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct independent French phrase; it is ungrammatical because a conjugated verb is missing. It likely reflects a fragment of a correct expression such as "elle est rentrée" (she returned/has come home) or confusion with the noun phrase "la rentrée" (the start of the school year).
additional_notes:
As written, "elle rentrée" omits the auxiliary verb (usually "est") required with the past participle "rentrée" when speaking about a feminine subject. Correct alternatives include:
- "elle est rentrée" = she returned / she came home (passé composé with être).
- "elle rentre" = she returns / she is coming home (present tense).
- "la rentrée" = the return / start of the school year (noun).
If you see "elle rentrée" in informal writing, it is likely a typo or an elision where the writer omitted "est".
target_language_example: Elle rentrée (erreur typographique dans le texte) signale qu'il manque le verbe auxiliaire.
native_language_example: "Elle rentrée" (typographical error in the text) indicates that the auxiliary verb is missing.

meaning: 'she does' / 'she is' used to contradict or emphasize in response to a negative statement about a female person.
additional_notes: The particle si is used in French to contradict a negative question or negative assertion (English equivalents: 'Yes, she does/is', 'actually she does', 'on the contrary, she...'). 'Elle si' typically appears in replies or in contrastive structures and may be followed by a verb or clause: 'Elle, si ...' or as a short reply 'Elle si.' Tone and context determine emphasis. Not idiomatic to translate word-for-word in all contexts.
target_language_example: — Tu dis qu'elle ne comprend rien ? — Elle, si, elle comprend très bien.
native_language_example: — You say she understands nothing? — She does, actually; she understands very well.

meaning: contraction of 'elle t'' used before a verb: 'she (to) you...' — 'she [verb] you' or 'did she [verb] you?'.
additional_notes: This is 'elle' (she) + the clitic object pronoun 'te' reduced to 't'' before a vowel or mute h, followed by a past participle or verb (e.g. a dit, a aimé, attend, adore). It represents 'she' as the subject and 'you' as the direct or indirect object depending on the verb. In spoken and informal written French the apostrophe appears (t') when the verb begins with a vowel: elle t'a (she told you), elle t'aime (she loves you). Word order and meaning depend on the verb: elle t'a quitté = 'she left you'; elle t'en a parlé = 'she talked to you about it'.
target_language_example: Elle t'a envoyé un message hier.
native_language_example: She sent you a message yesterday.

meaning: Not a correct fixed French phrase; appears to be two separate words ('elle' = she; 'ta' = your - feminine singular) or a typo/missing apostrophe for 'elle t'a' or 'elle a'.
additional_notes: 'Elle' is the 3rd-person singular subject pronoun meaning 'she' (or 'it' for feminine nouns). 'Ta' is the feminine singular possessive adjective meaning 'your' (informal). They are not normally adjacent as a fixed expression. Common intended forms: 'elle a' (she has) or 'elle t'a' (contraction of 'elle te a' → 'she has to you' used in contexts like 'elle t'a dit' = 'she told you'). If you see 'elle ta' written without an apostrophe, it's likely a typo or spacing error. Literal translation of the two words in sequence would be 'she your', which is ungrammatical in English.
target_language_example: Elle ta voiture est garée devant la maison. (incorrect/colloquial writing)
native_language_example: She your car is parked in front of the house. (grammatically incorrect in English; intended: 'Her car is parked in front of the house.')

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; taken word-for-word it means "she always."
additional_notes: This combination by itself is ungrammatical as a standalone fixed phrase. In French, 'toujours' must be used with a verb or adjective (e.g. 'elle est toujours...' or 'elle ... toujours ...'). Possible correct uses include 'elle est toujours en retard' (she is always late) or 'elle arrive toujours' (she always arrives). 'Toujours' can mean 'always' or 'still' depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle toujours ne suffit pas ; il faut un verbe ou un adjectif.
native_language_example: "Elle toujours" is not sufficient; you need a verb or an adjective.

meaning: she finds / she thinks (that).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: from the verb trouver = to find. In context 'elle trouve + noun' = 'she finds (something)'. With a clause ('elle trouve que...') it means 'she thinks / she finds that...'. Commonly used in everyday speech. Pronunciation: [ɛl tʁuv].
target_language_example: Elle trouve ses clés sous le canapé.
native_language_example: She finds her keys under the sofa.

meaning: Not a valid grammatical French phrase; a fragment combining 'elle' (she) and 'un' (a/one) that does not occur together in standard French.
additional_notes: 'Elle' is a third-person singular feminine subject pronoun ('she' or 'it' for feminine nouns). 'Un' is the masculine indefinite article or numeral 'one'. They cannot form a standalone phrase 'elle un'. Possible corrections depending on intended meaning: - 'elle a un...' (she has a...) - 'elle en a un' (she has one of them) - 'elle et un(e)' is not a standard construction; use 'elle et lui/elle et moi' etc. The fragment 'elle un' might appear across word boundaries in speech or transcription errors but is ungrammatical by itself.
target_language_example: Elle un — fragment non grammatical.
native_language_example: "Elle un" — ungrammatical fragment.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase — ungrammatical as written. Likely a typo, mistaken word order, or missing verb/punctuation. Possible intended readings include "la vôtre" (yours, feminine), "elle est la vôtre" (she/it is yours), or a miswritten pair like "est votre" or "et votre".
additional_notes: "Elle votre" by itself is incorrect in French. If encountered, check context for a missing verb (e.g., "elle est la vôtre"), a missing article/pronoun (e.g., replace with "la vôtre"), or a typographical error (e.g., "est votre" or "et votre"). Use "la vôtre" to mean "yours" referring to a feminine noun, or "elle est la vôtre" to say "she/it is yours."
target_language_example: — Elle votre? Non — elle est la vôtre.
native_language_example: — "Elle votre?" No — she is yours.

meaning: she really / she truly (emphatic)
additional_notes: This is the pronoun 'elle' followed by the adverb 'vraiment'. In standard French, 'vraiment' usually follows the verb or precedes an adjective/adverb, so the sequence 'elle vraiment' typically appears only in clipped, spoken fragments (e.g. 'Elle, vraiment…' to introduce surprise, criticism, or emphasis). It is compositional and can be translated literally, but isolated 'elle vraiment' is uncommon in full sentences.
target_language_example: Elle, vraiment, je ne la comprends pas.
native_language_example: Her, really, I don't understand her.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; a sequence of the pronoun 'elle' (she/it) followed by the preposition 'à' (to/at) that is incomplete on its own. It typically appears as part of a larger, grammatical phrase (e.g. 'elle à [quelque chose]' is often an error for 'elle a [quelque chose]' or part of 'elle est à [lieu/personne]').
additional_notes: On its own 'elle à' is usually ungrammatical. Common confusions: 'elle a' (without accent) means 'she has' — note the different spelling and pronunciation from 'à' (with accent) meaning 'to/at'. If you see 'elle à' in writing, it may be a typo for 'elle a', or it may be followed by a noun or clause where 'à' functions as a preposition (e.g. 'elle à la maison' is incorrect — correct: 'elle est à la maison').
target_language_example: Dans la phrase manuscrite, on lit « elle à » suivi d’un mot manquant.
native_language_example: In the handwritten sentence, one reads "elle à" followed by a missing word.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase — likely a fragment combining 'elle' (she/it feminine) with 'à la' (to the/at the/in the style of); interpretation depends on context and punctuation.
additional_notes: This sequence is usually not a single idiomatic expression. Possibilities: • 'elle a la...' (with verb a = has) is common but spelled without accent on 'a'. • 'elle à la...' (with accent on à) can occur in larger structures like 'Elle, à la maison, ...' (She, at home, ...) or in poetic/elliptical contexts but is not a grammatical unit by itself. Check whether the intended phrase uses 'a' (avoir) or 'à' (preposition).
target_language_example: Elle à la maison, attendra jusqu'à midi.
native_language_example: She, at home, will wait until noon.

meaning: intended meaning: she is
additional_notes: This is not a standard French phrase. It combines the subject pronoun elle ("she," or sometimes "it" for a feminine noun) with the infinitive être ("to be"). In normal French, "she is" is expressed as elle est. The example sentence below is intentionally meta-linguistic so it can contain the exact term elle être.
target_language_example: L’expression « elle être » n’est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: The expression "elle être" is not correct in French.

meaning: themselves (feminine plural reflexive/emphatic pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action is done by the women/them (feminine group) or reflexively. Can follow a verb or preposition: 'elles l'ont fait elles-mêmes' (they did it themselves). Contracts with pronouns in object position (e.g., 'parler d'elles-mêmes' = 'talk about themselves').
target_language_example: Elles l'ont préparé elles-mêmes.
native_language_example: They prepared it themselves.

meaning: 'they say' (incorrect/unnatural form in French)
additional_notes: This phrase is not grammatically correct in standard French. The subject pronoun elles (they, feminine) requires the third-person plural form of the verb dire, which is disent (elles disent) in the present tense. 'Elles dit' may appear as a spelling or typing error, or as a nonstandard form produced by learners; it should be avoided. In reported speech with a singular feminine subject use elle dit; for a plural feminine subject use elles disent.
target_language_example: *Elles dit* que tout va bien. (incorrect — should be «Elles disent que tout va bien.»)
native_language_example: *They says* that everything is fine. (incorrect — should be "They say that everything is fine.")

meaning: they (feminine) to him/her
additional_notes: Combination of the subject pronoun elles (they, all-female or feminine group) and the indirect object pronoun lui (to him / to her). Used in contexts where a feminine plural subject performs an action that benefits or is directed toward a single person (lui). In English this often becomes 'they give him/her', 'they tell him/her', etc.; the verb needed in the sentence determines the full translation. Word order: subject (elles) + verb + indirect object pronoun (lui) before the verb in simple tenses (e.g., Elles lui parlent). In affirmative imperative, the object pronoun follows the verb and changes (e.g., Parlez-lui).
target_language_example: Elles lui expliquent le problème.
native_language_example: They explain the problem to him/her.

meaning: ‘all of them’ referring to a group of females (they all).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that every member of a female group shares a quality or status. Often appears after a verb in questions or statements: 'Sont-elles toutes...' = 'Are they all...'. 'Elles toutes' can be reordered as 'toutes elles' (more emphatic) or 'toutes' placed before a noun (toutes les filles). Pronoun 'elles' makes it feminine plural.
target_language_example: Sont-elles toutes prêtes pour le départ ?
native_language_example: Are they all ready to leave?

meaning: to kiss (someone or something) / to embrace (figuratively); followed by a feminine noun or pronoun (la = her/it/the).
additional_notes: Embrasser means 'to kiss' or sometimes 'to embrace' in a figurative sense. When you see 'embrasser la' it is the verb plus the feminine direct object article/pronoun (la = her/it/the). You will usually find a noun or pronoun after it (e.g. 'embrasser la fille' or 'l'embrasser' contracted). Note that context decides whether it's a literal kiss or a figurative one (e.g. 'embrasser la cause' = embrace the cause).
target_language_example: Il va embrasser la fille sous le porche.
native_language_example: He is going to kiss the girl under the porch.

meaning: kissed a / embraced a (masculine noun follows).
additional_notes: Past participle 'embrassé' (masculine singular) of the verb 'embrasser' meaning 'to kiss' or 'to hug/embrace'. 'Embrassé un' will be followed by a masculine noun (e.g. 'embrassé un ami', 'embrassé un inconnu'). For feminine objects/someone use 'embrassée une'. Context determines whether it means a kiss (romantic) or a hug; specify person or object after the phrase. Example uses: 'Il a embrassé un ami' (He kissed/ hugged a friend).
target_language_example: Il a embrassé un ami pour le remercier.
native_language_example: He kissed/ hugged a friend to thank him.

meaning: take (someone) to (a place).
additional_notes: From the verb emmener (to take someone). Used when someone is bringing another person to a destination. The object is a person (often expressed with a pronoun: le, la, l', vous, etc.). Common with places: à l'hôpital, à l'école, à la gare. If talking about taking oneself, use emmener vs. amener (regional/nuance) — both mean to bring/take someone; conduire is used for driving. Followed by à + place or a person.
target_language_example: Je l'emmène à la gare demain matin.
native_language_example: I'm taking him/her to the station tomorrow morning.

meaning: carried away by; overcome by (an emotion) or taken/transported by (a vehicle or current).
additional_notes: Used after a past participle or adjective to indicate being strongly influenced or physically carried off. Common contexts: emotions (emporté par la colère = overcome by anger), enthusiasm (emporté par son élan = carried away by his momentum), or physical movement (emporté par le courant = swept away by the current). Often followed by 'la/ le/ les' + noun or a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Il a été emporté par le courant.
native_language_example: He was swept away by the current.

meaning: fingerprint (the unique pattern on a fingertip); also used for biometric fingerprint
additional_notes: Commonly used in contexts of identification, security, police, or unlocking devices (e.g., téléphone à empreinte digitale). 'Empreinte' alone can mean 'imprint' or 'footprint'; 'empreinte digitale' specifically refers to fingerprints. Plural: empreintes digitales.
target_language_example: Le policier a relevé une empreinte digitale sur la porte.
native_language_example: The police officer lifted a fingerprint from the door.

meaning: to borrow (some amount of something, often money) — used with 'de' + noun (e.g. 'emprunter de l'argent').
additional_notes: Used when you take something temporarily. With a specific lender, French more commonly uses 'emprunter quelque chose à quelqu'un' or 'de' + noun for the thing borrowed. Examples: 'Hé, je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?' (Can I borrow some money from you?), 'J'ai besoin d'emprunter de l'argent.' When asking informally, 'Je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?' is common.
target_language_example: Hé, je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?
native_language_example: Hey, can I borrow some money from you?

meaning: to borrow (a ...).
additional_notes: Used when asking to take something temporarily from someone. Conjugate the verb (emprunter) as needed and change the noun after 'un' to the item: e.g. 'emprunter un stylo' = borrow a pen. When the item is specified with a pronoun use forms like 't'emprunter' (borrow from you) or 'vous l'emprunter' (borrow it from you).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux emprunter un chargeur, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I borrow a charger, please?

meaning: 'a snack' (small bite between meals).
additional_notes: Common noun meaning a light food taken between meals. Often used in spoken and written French. Can be singular or plural (des en-cas). Usually unstressed; may appear with verbs like prendre, préparer. Hyphenated: en-cas.
target_language_example: Je te prépare un petit en-cas pour la route.
native_language_example: I'll make you a little snack for the road.

meaning: as a friend; in a friendly way (offering advice or help rather than hostility)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the speaker's friendly intentions or that a comment is meant kindly — often said before giving criticism or advice. Common in phrases like "Je te parle en ami" (I'm speaking to you as a friend). Not idiomatic to use literally with an article (not "en un ami").
target_language_example: Je te parle en ami : écoute ce que je dis.
native_language_example: I'm speaking to you as a friend: listen to what I say.

meaning: back; backwards; back (movement) or back (to a previous state).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical movement toward the back (Mets ta tête en arrière = tilt your head back) or figuratively to go back to a previous point/state (revenir en arrière = go back/undo). Can appear in commands (En arrière toute! = Reverse! / All back!) or in phrases like revenir en arrière (to go back).
target_language_example: Si tu veux annuler, tu peux revenir en arrière.
native_language_example: If you want to cancel, you can go back.

meaning: 'meanwhile' or 'for the time being' (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens during a wait or as a temporary measure. Often followed by a clause or comma + phrase. Can be used alone as a discourse marker ('In the meantime').
target_language_example: En attendant la réparation, prenez le bus.
native_language_example: In the meantime, take the bus while the repair is done.

meaning: 'while waiting for' or 'until (something happens)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with the subjunctive when referring to an event or action that is expected or anticipated. Equivalent to 'while waiting for' or 'until' in English. Commonly followed by a verb (e.g. 'en attendant que + subjunctive'). Can also be used without 'que' as 'en attendant + noun' (e.g. 'en attendant le bus').
target_language_example: En attendant que le train arrive, nous lisons.
native_language_example: While waiting for the train to arrive, we are reading.

meaning: 'waiting' or 'on hold' (in a state of waiting)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is waiting or put on hold. Common in phone contexts (être mis en attente = put on hold) and in formal contexts (a request, application or process pending). Can be used alone as a brief status: "En attente."
target_language_example: Votre commande est en attente de vérification.
native_language_example: Your order is waiting for verification.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typographical error or mis-segmentation (possibly meant 'en' or 'au' separately).
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'en au'. 'en' and 'au' are common prepositions/articles: 'en' can mean 'in', 'by', or indicate duration/means; 'au' is the contraction of 'à le' meaning 'to the'/'at the'/'in the' for masculine singular nouns. If you saw 'en au' in text, check for a typo (e.g., 'en août' = in August, or 'en' + 'au' belonging to different clauses).
target_language_example:
Incorrect: *Je vais en au magasin.*
Correct alternatives: "Je vais au magasin." or "Je suis en ville."
native_language_example:
Incorrect: *I'm going en au the store.*
Correct: "I'm going to the store." or "I'm in town."

meaning: 'under no circumstances' or 'in no case'.
additional_notes: Used to strongly forbid or rule out something. Often placed at the start of a sentence (En aucun cas, ...), after a verb with 'ne' (tu ne dois en aucun cas ...), or alone for emphasis. It's formal/neutral — common in both spoken and written French to give a firm prohibition.
target_language_example: Tu ne dois en aucun cas partager ton mot de passe.
native_language_example: You must under no circumstances share your password.

meaning: in no way; not at all; in no manner
additional_notes: Used to deny any connection, possibility, or manner. Often appears in negative constructions (similar to 'en aucune façon' or 'd'aucune manière'). Formal or emphatic; in spoken French you might hear 'en aucune façon' or simply 'pas du tout'. Can be used alone as a short emphatic response.
target_language_example: Je ne suis impliqué en aucune manière dans cette affaire.
native_language_example: I am not involved in this matter in any way.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase (likely a typographical error or fragment).
additional_notes: The sequence 'en aux' does not form a recognized multiword expression in French. It could result from a typo, missing words, or be a fragment combining the preposition 'en' with the plural definite article 'aux' (which itself is a contraction of 'à + les'). If you saw it in a sentence, check the surrounding words — possible intended forms include 'en' + noun (e.g. 'en ville') or 'aux' + noun (e.g. 'aux États-Unis'), or expressions like 'en cours', 'en aux' is not used as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Incorrect/fragment: « Il est en aux ... » → likely incorrect; correct: « Il est aux États-Unis. »
native_language_example: Incorrect/fragment: 'He is en aux ...' → likely incorrect; correct: 'He is in the United States.'

meaning: early; ahead of time.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something arrives or happens before the expected time. Commonly follows a time expression (e.g. 'dix minutes en avance'). Can refer to people, trains, events. Opposite: 'en retard' (late).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé en avance pour la réunion.
native_language_example: I arrived early for the meeting.

meaning: forward; ahead; in front (movement or position).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement toward the front or the position ahead. Can be used literally (physically leaning or moving forward) or figuratively/idiomatically as an encouragement (e.g., "En avant, cow-boy!" = "Go ahead, cowboy!/Move forward!"). Common in commands and directions. Pair with verbs like aller, avancer, regarder, or se pencher.
target_language_example: Penche-toi un peu en avant pour que je voie.
native_language_example: Lean forward a little so I can see.

meaning: 'full speed ahead' or 'forward at full power' (command to move forward at maximum speed)
additional_notes: A nautical/military-style command used to order all engines or units to go forward at full power. Often appears as an imperative exclamation. Literal words: en (in), avant (forward), toute (all), so it is compositional. Not common in casual conversation; more formal or technical (ships, machinery, vehicles).
target_language_example: En avant toute ! On met toutes les machines en marche.
native_language_example: Full speed ahead! Start all the engines.

meaning: downstairs
additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower location or level (physically downstairs or below a reference point). Commonly used alone (Je suis en bas) or with verbs (aller en bas, porter en bas). Can also mean 'down' in a general sense (Là, en bas = down there).
target_language_example: Je descends, je te retrouve en bas.
native_language_example: I'm coming down, I'll meet you downstairs.

meaning: down/downwards at the bottom of; below (location).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located lower down, at the bottom of a slope, street, building, etc. Commonly followed by a place (la rue, la colline, l'escalier). Can mean 'down the street' or 'at the bottom of the street' in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il y a un café en bas de la rue.
native_language_example: There is a cafe down the street / at the bottom of the street.

meaning: in style; in a grand/good way; spectacularly (often used about endings or departures).
