additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a striking, impressive, or stylish manner — especially 'partir en beauté' (to leave/finish on a high note). Can be exclamatory on its own. Not slang; idiomatic but fairly transparent.
target_language_example: Il veut partir en beauté en faisant un dernier discours.
native_language_example: He wants to leave on a high note by giving one last speech.

meaning: for the better; in a good way
additional_notes: Used to indicate improvement or a positive direction/result. Can stand alone (En bien.) or appear in phrases like 'en bien pire' (= by far worse, ironically using 'bien' as intensifier) and 'aller/changer en bien' (= to change for the better). Also appears in 'en bien des' meaning 'many' (literally 'in many'), which is a different fixed expression — be careful: 'en bien des théories' means 'in many theories' not 'many good theories'.
target_language_example: J'espère que la situation évoluera en bien.
native_language_example: I hope the situation will change for the better.

meaning: in good (friendly) terms; on good terms (with someone).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase "être en bons termes (avec quelqu'un)" meaning to have a friendly or cordial relationship. Use with a person or group (avec + name/pronoun). The adjective agrees in gender/number with the subject (en bon terme is not used; common forms: en bons termes, en bonnes termes rarely used — standard: en bons termes).
target_language_example: Nous sommes en bons termes avec nos voisins.
native_language_example: We are on good terms with our neighbors.

meaning: by the (sea/shore) / on the (seaside) — indicates location at the edge of something (often the sea).
additional_notes: Often appears as en bord de + noun (e.g. en bord de mer, en bord de lac) to mean 'on/at the shore of' or 'by the ...'. Common in descriptions of houses, villages, or places located at the water's edge. Informal register is neutral; preposition en + bord is fixed in these expressions.
target_language_example: Ils ont acheté un appartement en bord de mer.
native_language_example: They bought an apartment by the sea.

meaning: made of concrete; (figurative) rock-solid, very strong or reliable
additional_notes: Literally describes something constructed from concrete (e.g., a floor, wall). Commonly used figuratively to mean 'foolproof', 'undeniable' or 'hard/unchanging' (an alibi en béton = a rock‑solid alibi; un cœur en béton = a hard/stone heart). Context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Son explication était en béton, personne n'a pu la contredire.
native_language_example: His explanation was rock-solid; no one could contradict it.

meaning: 'secretly' or 'on the sly'.
additional_notes: Used to describe actions done in secret, hidden from others. Can imply secrecy because of disapproval, surprise, or privacy. Common with people (rencontrer quelqu'un en cachette), actions (partir en cachette), or observations (regarder en cachette).
target_language_example: Ils se sont rencontrés en cachette pendant des semaines.
native_language_example: They met secretly for weeks.

meaning: 'in case of' or 'in the event of' (used to introduce a possible situation, contingency, or condition, typically followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used before a noun to warn about, prepare for, or state responsibility regarding a specific situation. Often followed by a noun: en cas de pluie, en cas d'urgence, en cas de problème. Not normally used to introduce a full clause—use 'si' for clauses. Can appear in formal and informal contexts depending on register and sentence.
target_language_example: En cas de pluie, la fête sera déplacée à l'intérieur.
native_language_example: In case of rain, the party will be moved indoors.

meaning: in question; being accused, challenged, or implicated.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like mettre/remettre/mettre en cause to mean 'to call into question,' 'to challenge,' 'to accuse,' or 'to involve/implicate' someone or something. Context decides nuance: can mean 'to doubt someone's ability/authority' (challenge) or 'to implicate/accuse' (legal). Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: On ne doit pas mettre en cause sa réputation sans preuves.
native_language_example: We must not call his reputation into question without proof.

meaning: on the run; fleeing (usually from the police or authorities).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has escaped custody or is avoiding arrest. Common in news and everyday speech. Often followed by agent (ex.: 'un tueur en cavale') or used as 'être en cavale' = to be on the run. Slightly dramatic but neutral; not slang.
target_language_example: Ils ont dit qu'il était en cavale depuis trois jours.
native_language_example: They said he has been on the run for three days.

meaning: in this
additional_notes: Used before a demonstrative noun phrase, usually followed by a relative word (e.g. 'en ce qui concerne') or a noun/adjective to mean 'in this' or 'in that' context. Common in fixed expressions: 'en ce qui concerne' (as for/regarding), 'en ce moment' (at the moment) — note that in 'en ce moment' the full phrase is 'en ce moment' meaning 'right now'. Must agree with the noun that follows in terms of meaning but not in grammatical gender/number (ce is neutral here).
target_language_example: En ce qui concerne ton projet, je peux aider.
native_language_example: As for your project, I can help.

meaning: right now
additional_notes: Used to indicate the present time or current situation. Can describe something happening now (temporary) or a current trend/period. Equivalent to 'en ce moment-même' (emphatic).
target_language_example: Je suis un peu débordé en ce moment.
native_language_example: I'm a bit overwhelmed at the moment.

meaning: at that time; in those days.
additional_notes: Refers to a past period being described or remembered. Often used to contrast past and present (nostalgic or descriptive). Can be placed at the start or end of a sentence. Equivalent to 'à cette époque-là'.
target_language_example: En ce temps-là, on vivait sans téléphone portable.
native_language_example: In those days, we lived without mobile phones.

meaning: regarding; as for; concerning
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or aspect being talked about. Formal/neutral register and very common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'en ce qui concerne toi/lui/ce projet'). Can be replaced in more informal contexts by 'pour ce qui est de' or simply 'pour' or 'quant à'.
target_language_example: En ce qui concerne le délai, nous avons besoin de deux semaines.
native_language_example: Regarding the deadline, we need two weeks.

meaning: 'as far as I'm concerned' / 'regarding me'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal opinion, position, or feelings about a topic. Complete phrase in examples is 'en ce qui me concerne' (formal). Often shortened in speech to 'pour moi' or 'en ce qui me regarde', but 'en ce qui me concerne' is common in both spoken and written French. Followed by a comma and a clause stating your view.
target_language_example: En ce qui me concerne, je préfère rester ici.
native_language_example: As far as I'm concerned, I'd rather stay here.

meaning: in person; physically present (literally 'in flesh and bone').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is physically present rather than only known by voice, photo, message, or online. Often used after meeting someone you've previously known only remotely or from descriptions. Formality: neutral; can be used in both polite and casual contexts. Gender agreement affects verbs/adjectives (e.g., rencontré / rencontrée) but the phrase itself is fixed.
target_language_example: Je suis si heureux de te voir en chair et en os !
native_language_example: I'm so happy to see you in person!

meaning: 'in charge of' / 'responsible for'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has responsibility or oversight for a person, group, task, place, or project. Followed by a noun (e.g., en charge de la classe, en charge du secteur). Formal and neutral; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je suis en charge de l'organisation de la réunion.
native_language_example: I am in charge of organizing the meeting.

meaning: on the way / en route / along the way.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a destination (Il est en chemin = he's on the way). It can also mean 'along the way' for something that happened during a trip (quelque chose en chemin). Common in short replies: 'En chemin.' = 'On my/our way.'
target_language_example: Je suis en chemin, j'arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I'm on my way; I'll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: angry
additional_notes: Used to describe someone feeling anger. Typically used with être (être en colère) or with reflexive se mettre en colère (to get angry). Can be followed by a preposition + object (en colère contre/avec quelqu'un or en colère à propos de quelque chose).
target_language_example: Il est en colère contre son frère.
native_language_example: He is angry with his brother.

meaning: 'in how much (time)' — asks about the duration needed for something.
additional_notes: Used to ask how long something will take. Always followed by a time expression (e.g., temps, semaines, jours, minutes) or a verb phrase implying arrival/completion. Common constructions: "En combien de temps... ?" (How long does it take / will it take?) or shortened to "En combien de temps ?" as a follow-up question.
target_language_example: En combien de temps peux-tu finir ce rapport ?
native_language_example: How long will it take you to finish this report?

meaning: in common; shared (between people or groups).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is shared or mutual (e.g., interests, traits, decisions). Common constructions: 'avoir quelque chose en commun' (to have something in common) and 'pris en commun' (made jointly). Can follow nouns (des intérêts en commun) or appear after 'avoir'.
target_language_example: Nous avons beaucoup d'amis en commun.
native_language_example: We have many friends in common.

meaning: in the company of; with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are with someone or accompanied by someone. Formal/neutral tone. Can refer to people or animals. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., en compagnie de mes amis, en compagnie de lui).
target_language_example: Je suis en compagnie de mes collègues ce soir.
native_language_example: I am in the company of my colleagues tonight.

meaning: with full knowledge / knowingly / being fully informed
additional_notes: Used to say someone acted with awareness of the facts or consequences. Often translates as “knowingly,” “with full knowledge,” or “informedly.” Common in formal and neutral registers. Can be used alone as a short reply (meaning “I know” or “I did it knowingly”).
target_language_example: Il a signé le contrat en connaissance de cause.
native_language_example: He signed the contract with full knowledge (knowingly).

meaning: in a romantic relationship; as a couple.
additional_notes: Used to say two people are romantically together. Can describe a relationship status (être en couple = to be in a relationship). Often contrasts with 'célibataire' (single). Not necessarily married. Common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Ils sont en couple depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: They have been a couple for two years.

meaning: in progress; ongoing; currently happening.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is happening now or underway (a process, project, investigation, transmission, etc.). Common in formal and everyday contexts. Often follows the noun (l'enquête est en cours) or appears alone as a short status message (En cours.).
target_language_example: Le dépannage est en cours, ça devrait être réglé bientôt.
native_language_example: The repair is in progress; it should be fixed soon.

meaning: in the process of; during (an action or event).
additional_notes: Used to say something is currently happening or ongoing (en cours de + noun/verb infinitive) or to indicate 'during' when referring to a class or session (en cours de français = during French class). Common with verbs: en cours de construction / en cours de réparation. Not used for finished actions.
target_language_example: Le rapport est en cours de rédaction.
native_language_example: The report is being written / is in the process of being written.

meaning: 'in danger' or 'at risk'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is threatened, unsafe, or at risk of harm. Common in both literal (physical danger) and figurative (financial, legal, etc.) contexts. Usually follows the verb être (être en danger) or verbs implying a state (se retrouver en danger, mettre quelqu'un en danger).
target_language_example: Les voyageurs sont en danger à cause de la tempête.
native_language_example: The travelers are in danger because of the storm.

meaning: outside of; away from; not involved in.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location outside something (en dehors de la maison = outside the house) or figurative exclusion (stay out of my business). It is followed by de + noun. Can mean 'except' in some contexts when used as 'en dehors de'.
target_language_example: Restez en dehors de cette affaire.
native_language_example: Stay out of this matter.

meaning: outside of; apart from; not involved in.
additional_notes: Common prepositional phrase. Can mean physically outside (outside of a place), figuratively apart from or except for (apart from), or to say someone is not involved in something (leave someone out). Context determines translation: 'outside of' (physical), 'apart from/except' (exclusion), or 'not involved in' (avoid involvement). Often followed by a noun or pronoun.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi en dehors de cette dispute.
native_language_example: Leave me out of this argument.

meaning: under; below; beneath (physically or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both for physical position (under/beneath) and for comparative measures (below a value, below average). Followed by a noun, number, or article + noun. Can be interchangeable with 'sous' in many contexts (e.g. 'sous zéro' vs 'en dessous de zéro'), but 'en dessous de' is common before a specific value or phrase.
target_language_example: Le chat dort en dessous de la table.
native_language_example: The cat sleeps under the table.

meaning: 'in trouble' or 'having difficulties' (can be general or specific, e.g. financial, practical, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is experiencing problems or struggling. Can refer to short-term trouble (e.g. in danger, needing help) or ongoing difficulties (e.g. financial hardship). Context clarifies the type of difficulty. Common in everyday and formal registers.
target_language_example: Elle est en difficulté avec ses paiements ce mois-ci.
native_language_example: She is having difficulties with her payments this month.

meaning: 'live' (as in live broadcast: happening now, not recorded).
additional_notes: Used to say something is being broadcast or shown in real time (TV, radio, streaming). Commonly placed before a noun (en direct à la télé) or alone to indicate current live coverage. Can also be 'en direct de' + location or person.
target_language_example: La conférence est diffusée en direct sur Internet.
native_language_example: The conference is being broadcast live on the Internet.

meaning: quietly; secretly; on the sly.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to describe doing something discreetly or leaving without being noticed. Often used with verbs like 'filer', 'partir', 'sortir' or 'se tirer'. Conveys mild secrecy or stealth rather than malicious intent.
target_language_example: Il est parti en douce avant que personne ne le voie.
native_language_example: He left quietly before anyone saw him.

meaning: gently; softly; smoothly.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do something gently, slowly, or carefully. Can describe actions (do it gently), processes (happen smoothly), or manners (in a gentle way). Common in spoken French: Allez-y en douceur = Go gently / take it easy. Not slang.
target_language_example: Parle-lui en douceur, il est encore fragile.
native_language_example: Speak to him gently; he is still fragile.

meaning: in the end; ultimately; all in all.
additional_notes: Used to summarize or draw a final conclusion after considering facts or a story. Similar to 'finalement' or 'en fin de compte' but slightly more formal. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: En définitive, il a décidé de refuser l'offre.
native_language_example: In the end, he decided to turn down the offer.

meaning: despite; in spite of (followed by a noun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: Formal connective used to introduce a contrast: it means that something happens although there is an obstacle or contrary fact. It is followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase (e.g., en dépit de la pluie, en dépit de ses efforts). Synonyms: malgré, malgré que + subjunctive (different structure).
target_language_example: En dépit de la fatigue, elle continua à travailler.
native_language_example: Despite the fatigue, she kept working.

meaning: in detail; thoroughly; with all the specifics.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is described, explained, or examined thoroughly. Can follow verbs like décrire, expliquer, discuter, raconter. Often used with un peu (un peu plus en détail) to ask for a bit more explanation.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me l'expliquer en détail, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in detail, please?

meaning: indeed / in fact (used to confirm, agree, or introduce support/explanation).
additional_notes: Used to confirm or reinforce a statement, agree with someone, or introduce an explanation. Can appear at the start of a sentence (En effet, ...) or after the verb/phrase (..., en effet.). Tone is neutral and common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En effet, c'est exactement ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: Indeed, that's exactly what I meant.

meaning: in her / in it (feminine) — used to refer back to a feminine noun or to say 'in her' figuratively
additional_notes: A combination of the preposition 'en' and the feminine pronoun 'elle'. 'En' can mean 'in', 'inside', 'about', or indicate a quality/state when used with pronouns. Use 'en elle' when referring to a feminine noun (e.g., la boîte → en elle = 'in it') or when speaking about a woman ('in her' or 'within her'). Context determines whether it means physical location ('inside her/it') or a more abstract sense ('in her character/essence').
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose d'intéressant en elle.
native_language_example: There is something interesting in her.

meaning: completely; in full; whole (with emphasis on completeness).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is done or applies to the whole/entire thing, from start to finish. Common with verbs like lire, remplir, manger, détruire. Can be used alone as a short question ("En entier ?") to ask if something is complete. Equivalent to "complètement" or "tout entier" in many contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai regardé la série en entier ce week-end.
native_language_example: I watched the whole series over the weekend.

meaning: opposite; across (from).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something or someone located directly opposite or across from another place or person. Commonly followed by 'de' + noun (en face de la maison) or used alone when context makes the reference clear. Can also be used in expressions meaning 'right in front of' or 'in the presence of' (informal/emphatic).
target_language_example: Le café est en face de la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: The café is opposite the library.

meaning: across from; opposite (facing something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate location directly opposite something (often with buildings, people, streets). Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'en face de la gare', 'en face de chez moi'). You can also say 'en face' alone if context is clear. Not formal/slang; literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Le café est en face de l'école.
native_language_example: The café is across from the school.

meaning: actually
additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, emphasize or add new information; often appears at the start of a sentence or clause. Can soften or contrast what was said before ("actually/in fact"). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: En fait, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Actually, I can't come tonight.

meaning: with family; as a family (doing something together).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an activity done together with family members. Common with verbs of going or spending time (aller, passer, camper, dîner, voyager). Neutral register. Gender/number of speaker affects other words but not this phrase.
target_language_example: Nous partons en famille ce week-end.
native_language_example: We're going as a family this weekend.

meaning: in favor of; supporting or for (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to express support, approval, or agreement with a proposal, person, plan, or idea. Followed by a noun or pronoun (en faveur de + X). Common in both formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Nous sommes en faveur de cette réforme.
native_language_example: We are in favor of this reform.

meaning: 'on fire' (burning).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is burning. Can describe buildings, vehicles, or places. Not idiomatic here — literal fire. Also used figuratively in informal contexts (e.g., someone 'on fire' meaning performing very well), but examples show literal use.
target_language_example: La voiture est en feu, appelle les pompiers !
native_language_example: The car is on fire, call the firefighters!

meaning: in single file; one behind the other.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or things arranged in a single line (one after another). Common in contexts like walking, marching, or vehicles on a narrow path. Often follows verbs: marcher en file, ranger en file. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Les élèves marchent en file dans le couloir.
native_language_example: The students walk in single file in the hallway.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase in French on its own; usually appears as part of longer sequences like 'en fin de...' or as a mistaken split of 'enfin'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'en fin' is incomplete or nonstandard. Common related forms: - 'enfin' (one word): means 'finally', 'well', 'in short', or used to correct oneself. Example: 'Enfin, je suis prêt.' - 'en fin de ...' (two words + de + noun): a formal/written pattern meaning 'at the end of ...' (e.g., 'en fin de journée'); but 'à la fin de ...' is more common in speech. 'En fin' by itself may appear in fixed phrases or administrative language but is not recommended as a standalone expression for learners.
target_language_example: En fin de journée, nous avons relu les notes.
native_language_example: At the end of the day, we reviewed the notes.

meaning: 'in the end' / 'ultimately' / 'all things considered'.
additional_notes: Used to summarize or give the final outcome or conclusion after considering everything. Common in spoken and written French to introduce a conclusion or final judgment.
target_language_example: En fin de compte, tout s'est bien passé.
native_language_example: In the end, everything went well.

meaning: in the act (doing something wrong) — caught red-handed.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase en flagrant délit (caught in the act/ red-handed). Alone, en flagrant is short for en flagrant délit and implies being caught while committing an offense or wrongdoing. Common in news/legal contexts. Use with délit for full expression.
target_language_example: Il a été arrêté en flagrant (délit).
native_language_example: He was arrested in the act (caught red-handed).

meaning: 'sharply' or 'skyrocketing' (very quickly and steeply upward)
additional_notes: Used adverbially to describe something that rises very quickly or steeply (prices, figures, emotions, movement). Often translated as "skyrocketing," "soaring," or "shooting up." Can apply to physical movement (someone rising quickly) or abstract increases (prices, rates, flows).
target_language_example: Les ventes ont monté en flèche après la publicité.
native_language_example: Sales shot up after the advertisement.

meaning: depending on; based on; according to
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something varies or is determined by another factor. Followed by a noun or pronoun (en fonction de + quelque chose). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Les horaires sont adaptés en fonction de la demande.
native_language_example: The schedules are adapted depending on demand.

meaning: in shape / in good shape; (also) in the shape of (when describing form).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) As an adjective phrase meaning physically fit, well, or energetic: Je suis en forme = I'm in good shape/feeling well. 2) As part of a construction en forme de + noun to describe the shape of an object: un gâteau en forme de cœur = a cake in the shape of a heart. Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Après le jogging, je me sens en forme.
native_language_example: After the jog, I feel in shape / I feel great.

meaning: 'to warn' (to caution someone) or an imperative 'watch out/guard!' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used two main ways: as a verb phrase 'mettre en garde (contre)' meaning 'to warn/caution (against)'; and as an interjection 'En garde !' meaning 'Watch out!' or the fencing command 'On guard!'. Context decides sense. Commonly followed by 'contre' when warning about something. Literal components ('in guard') don't directly explain the idiom in all uses.
target_language_example: Il m'a mis en garde contre les vols dans le quartier.
native_language_example: He warned me about thefts in the neighborhood.

meaning: 'basically' / 'roughly' or 'in large pieces/large (when describing items)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase with two main uses: 1) colloquial discourse marker meaning 'basically', 'roughly speaking', or 'in short' to summarize or simplify an idea (very frequent in conversation). 2) literal descriptive use meaning 'large' or 'in large chunks' (e.g., 'en gros flocons' = large flakes). Context determines which sense is meant. Informal but widely used. Can be translated literally as 'in large'.
target_language_example: En gros, il faut trois heures pour y aller.
native_language_example: Basically, it takes three hours to get there.

meaning: as a kind of / as a form of / by way of
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate that something is being presented or used in the capacity of that noun (often followed by 'de' or another noun phrase: 'en guise de...'). Formal and neutral register; common in written and spoken French to mean 'as' or 'in the form of'.
target_language_example: Il a offert un livre en guise de remerciement.
native_language_example: He gave a book as a token of thanks.

meaning: 'as' or 'in the form of; used as' (to indicate something used to serve the role of something else).
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing is being used or presented as something else (often temporarily or symbolically). Common with nouns: en guise de + noun. Can be translated as "as," "as a," "in lieu of," or "by way of." Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a posé une caisse en guise de siège.
native_language_example: He used a crate as a seat.

meaning: 'in general' / 'generally' (to speak about what is usually true)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement or common tendency. Often placed at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma in written French. Can be interchangeable with 'généralement'.
target_language_example: En général, je prends du thé le matin.
native_language_example: Generally, I have tea in the morning.

meaning: 'rising' or 'on the rise' (prices, rates, value going up).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is increasing (prices, currency, rates, etc.). Often follows the noun (Le prix est en hausse). Opposite: «en baisse» (falling). Can be used in present, past (étaient en hausse) and with articles as needed.
target_language_example: Les loyers sont en hausse cette année.
native_language_example: Rents are on the rise this year.

meaning: up; upstairs; above (indicating a higher place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location at a higher position or floor. Can be alone ('en haut') or with modifiers like 'tout en haut' (at the very top). Common with verbs of movement (monter, grimper) and with être to say someone is upstairs or up somewhere.
target_language_example: Elle est en haut, dans sa chambre.
native_language_example: She is upstairs, in her room.

meaning: 'at the top of' or 'above' (location on or above something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position at the upper part of something (a building, page, list, etc.). Often followed by a noun: en haut de la page, en haut de la montagne. Can also be used without 'de' as 'en haut' meaning 'upstairs' or 'above'.
target_language_example: Il y a un drapeau en haut de la tour.
native_language_example: There is a flag at the top of the tower.

meaning: at stake; involved; in play.
additional_notes: Used to say what is at risk or what is involved in a situation. Often follows a noun (e.g. "beaucoup de choses en jeu") or appears in fixed expressions like "la vie est en jeu". Also used in phrases meaning 'to come into play' with verbs like "entrer en jeu" (you come into the situation).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup d'enjeu(s) en jeu dans ce projet.
native_language_example: There is a lot at stake in this project.

meaning: 'in the air' / 'up in the air' — literal; idiomatic uses include 'up' (arms raised), 'ruined/thrown away', and sexual slang 'have sex'.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically in the air or raised (e.g., bras en l'air = arms up). Idiomatic meanings depend on context: 1) sexual slang: s'envoyer en l'air = have casual sex; 2) spoil/ruin: foutre/mettre en l'air = mess up or destroy something; 3) informal expression for being flustered or awkward (la queue en l'air = disordered/embarrassed in context). Register varies: literal uses are neutral; the sexual meaning is informal/slang and can be crude; verbs with en l'air (foutre en l'air, mettre en l'air) are informal and can be strong.
target_language_example: Ils ont les bras en l'air pendant la photo.
native_language_example: They have their arms in the air during the photo.

meaning: literally 'in the' or 'into the' (feminine singular); used when 'en' is followed by a feminine definite article in fixed expressions or older/poetic structures.
additional_notes: In modern French, 'en' usually replaces a feminine noun introduced by 'de' (e.g. 'j'en ai' = 'I have some of it') and does not combine with 'la'. The sequence 'en la' can appear in fixed expressions, poetic/literary language, or when 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in' followed by the definite article 'la' (e.g. 'en la ville' — though standard modern French uses 'dans la ville' or simply 'en ville'). More commonly you will see 'dans la', 'en' alone, or 'à la'. Avoid using 'en la' in everyday spoken French unless quoting a set phrase or reading older/literary text.
target_language_example: Dans un texte ancien on peut lire « en la maison », mais aujourd'hui on dira « dans la maison ».
native_language_example: In an old text you might read "en la maison," but today you'd say "dans la maison."

meaning: Not a correct combination in standard French; 'en' and 'le' do not appear together as separate consecutive words. One of them is usually absorbed into a contraction (du, au) or one replaces the other as a pronoun.
additional_notes:
In French, the preposition 'en' does not combine with the definite article 'le'. Common corrections: 
- Use 'du' (de + le) for 'of the'/'from the' with masculine singular nouns.
- Use 'au' (à + le) for 'to the'/'at the' with masculine singular nouns.
- Use the pronoun 'en' alone to replace a noun introduced by 'de' (e.g. 'J'en veux').
- Use the direct object pronoun 'le' alone to replace a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'Je le vois').
If you encounter 'en le' in text, it is almost always an error (often from literal translation or mistaken insertion). In rare fixed expressions or poetry you might see unusual word order, but this is nonstandard.
target_language_example: Incorrect: *Il insiste en le faisant→* (non standard) — Correct: Il insiste en le faisant (error) should be: Il insiste en le faisant is wrong; correct forms: Il insiste en le faisant (replace with "en faisant cela" or "il insiste à le faire" → standard: Il insiste pour le faire / Il insiste à le faire).
native_language_example: Incorrect: *He insists in doing it* translated literally as 'Il insiste en le faisant' is incorrect — use 'Il insiste pour le faire' or 'Il insiste à le faire' depending on context.

meaning: 'at large' / 'free' / 'free-range' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can mean physically free (not confined) or legally free (not imprisoned). In agriculture, used to describe animals raised free-range: 'poulets élevés en liberté' = free-range chickens. In legal contexts, 'en liberté conditionnelle' = on parole / released on condition. Often followed by 'conditionnelle' for 'on parole'.
target_language_example: Après sa peine, il est sorti et est resté en liberté.
native_language_example: After his sentence, he got out and remained free.

meaning: 'in place' or 'instead of' (formal; usually appears in the fixed phrase 'en lieu et place de').
additional_notes: Rarely used alone; most often found in the legal/formal expression 'en lieu et place de' meaning 'in place of' or 'instead of'. Can be followed by 'de' + noun/pronoun. In everyday speech French speakers prefer 'à la place de' or 'au lieu de'.
target_language_example: Le conseiller a été nommé en lieu et place du directeur.
native_language_example: The advisor was appointed in place of the director.

meaning: in a safe place; somewhere safe
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or object is kept somewhere safe or protected. Often appears with verbs like être (to be) or mettre (to put). Formal/neutral phrasing; more common spoken alternatives: en sécurité, en lieu sûr (slightly formal) or en lieu sûr can be shortened to 'en sécurité' for everyday use.
target_language_example: J'ai mis les documents importants en lieu sûr.
native_language_example: I put the important documents in a safe place.

meaning: 'online' or 'in a line/queue' depending on context.
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) digital/connected: 'online' (connected to the internet, using a website/service, or in a call). Example: "Je suis en ligne" = I'm online / I'm on the line. 2) physical arrangement: 'in a line' or 'in a queue' (people standing one after another). Context and verbs tell you which meaning. Common collocations: 'être en ligne' (be online / be on the phone), 'faire une demande en ligne' (apply online), 'rester en ligne' (stay on the line).
target_language_example: Je fais mes courses en ligne ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm doing my shopping online tonight.

meaning: in a bad way; speaking ill (of someone).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed expression 'parler (de quelqu'un) en mal' meaning 'to speak ill of someone' or 'talk negatively about someone'. Often appears in negative imperatives or moral advice (e.g. 'Ne parle jamais des autres en mal'). Not commonly used alone except in short responses like 'En mal ?' (meaning 'Badly? / In what way?').
target_language_example: Ne parle jamais des autres en mal.
native_language_example: Never speak ill of others.

meaning: to be suffering from / to have a longing or ache for (often followed by a noun)
additional_notes: Used to express a lack, longing, craving or physical/psychological suffering for something. Common constructions: 'en mal de' + noun (en mal d'amour, en mal de vivre, en mal de compagnie). Tone can be literary or slightly formal; often describes an ongoing state (not a one-time desire).
target_language_example: Depuis son départ, elle est en mal de compagnie.
native_language_example: Since he left, she has been longing for company.

meaning: 'running' / 'in operation' / 'in motion' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used for machines or devices to mean 'turned on' or 'operating' (e.g. 'La machine est en marche' = the machine is on). For vehicles or people it can mean 'in motion' / 'walking' / 'on the move' (e.g. 'train en marche' = moving train; 'Ils sont en marche' = they are on the move). Not idiomatic for planned actions (use 'en marche' can also imply something has started).
target_language_example: La télévision est en marche, tu peux mettre le film.
native_language_example: The TV is on, you can put on the movie.

meaning: with regard to; in the field of; concerning
additional_notes: Used to specify a topic, domain, or subject area. Often followed by a noun phrase (en matière de + [nom]). Formal/neutral register; common in written and spoken French to point to expertise, rules, or aspects of a subject.
target_language_example: En matière de santé, il faut écouter les médecins.
native_language_example: With regard to health, you should listen to doctors.

meaning: 'able to' or 'in a position to' (often followed by 'de' + infinitive: en mesure de ...).
additional_notes: Usually appears as the fixed phrase 'en mesure de + infinitive' meaning 'able to' or 'capable of'. Formal/register: neutral to formal. Common in written and spoken French. Do not confuse with 'à mesure' or 'en train de'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes en mesure de commencer le projet demain.
native_language_example: We are able to start the project tomorrow.

meaning: able to; in a position to; capable of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone is (or will be) able or in a position to do something. Common with pouvoir/être (e.g., 'être en mesure de', 'pouvoir être en mesure de'). Slightly more formal than just 'pouvoir'.
target_language_example: Je serai bientôt en mesure de signer le contrat.
native_language_example: I will soon be able to sign the contract.

meaning: in a better way; an improvement (compared to something else).
additional_notes: Used to compare or describe something as improved or better. Often appears after a verb or phrase (e.g., « faire en mieux ») or in contrast to a previous state. It's informal/neutral and idiomatic: literal word-for-word translation is possible but context matters. Commonly used in comparisons like « C'est encore en mieux » (It's even better).
target_language_example: Cette version est en mieux que la précédente.
native_language_example: This version is better than the previous one.

meaning: very quickly; in no time
additional_notes: Informal idiomatic expression meaning something will happen extremely fast. Literally 'in less than two' (understood as 'two moments/instants'). Commonly used in spoken French to reassure that an action will be done quickly.
target_language_example: Je reviens en moins de deux.
native_language_example: I'll be back in no time.

meaning: literally 'in my' — a rare/partial sequence; not a standalone phrase in French
additional_notes: You will almost never see 'en mon' by itself in French. It can appear as part of longer expressions (for example after certain verbs or in fixed phrases) but is usually ungrammatical or incomplete on its own. More natural equivalents are 'dans mon/ma/mes' (in my) or 'en moi' (in me) depending on meaning. If you meant 'en mon absence' (in my absence) or 'à mon' (to my), use the full expression.
target_language_example: En mon absence, contactez mon collègue.
native_language_example: In my absence, contact my colleague.

meaning: 'in motion' or 'moving'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone that is moving or not stationary. Can be literal (a moving object) or figurative (busy, constantly on the move). Common in short phrases: 'Cible en mouvement' = 'moving target'.
target_language_example: La voiture est en mouvement, reste à distance.
native_language_example: The car is in motion, keep your distance.

meaning: on average; typically, on the whole.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an average value or typical amount across time or people. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence (e.g., 'En moyenne, ...' or '... en moyenne'). Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En moyenne, je marche trente minutes par jour.
native_language_example: On average, I walk thirty minutes a day.

meaning: 'at the same' (incomplete fragment; usually part of 'en même temps' = 'at the same time').
additional_notes: Alone, 'en même' is not a complete common phrase in French — it appears as part of longer expressions like 'en même temps' (at the same time) or 'en même temps que' (at the same time as). If you see 'en même' by itself it's likely truncated or part of a follow-up word. Use the full expressions for correct meaning and grammar.
target_language_example: Il a parlé et en même temps il envoyait des messages.
native_language_example: He was speaking and at the same time he was sending messages.

meaning: at the same time; meanwhile; also (to add a remark).
additional_notes: Common phrase with several close uses: 1) to say two or more actions happen simultaneously (equivalent to 'at the same time'), 2) as a short reaction or hesitation in conversation ('En même temps ?' ≈ 'Well, at the same time.../I mean...'), and 3) to introduce a contrasting or qualifying remark (similar to 'that said' or 'mind you'). Very frequent in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a étudié et travaillé en même temps pendant deux ans.
native_language_example: He studied and worked at the same time for two years.

meaning: in our (something) / within our (something).
additional_notes: A formal or literary prepositional combination meaning "in our" or "within our" used before a noun (e.g., en notre âme = in our soul). It's not common in everyday spoken French; more often you will hear "dans notre" or simply "notre". Use in set phrases or older/literary texts.
target_language_example: En notre village, les fêtes durent toute la semaine.
native_language_example: In our village, the celebrations last all week.

meaning: in / among us; within ourselves (depends on context).
additional_notes: A short prepositional phrase combining 'en' + 'nous' (us). Can mean 'in us' or 'within ourselves' (e.g. feelings, qualities inside a group or person) or 'among us'/'between us' when referring to something happening within a group. Context determines whether it's literal (inside our bodies) or figurative (in our group, in our minds). Common in sentences like «Il y a de l'espoir en nous» (There is hope in us) or «Cette décision se prend en nous» (This decision is made among us).
target_language_example: Il y a une différence en nous depuis son départ.
native_language_example: There is a difference in us since his/her departure.

meaning: made of gold; (figuratively) excellent or ideal.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say something is made of gold (literal: jewelry, objects). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., un boulot en or = a great/ideal job). In literal uses, it describes material (comme « en argent », « en acier »).
target_language_example: Elle porte un collier en or pour la fête.
native_language_example: She is wearing a gold necklace for the party.

meaning: in order; everything OK/arranged properly.
additional_notes: Used to say that things are correct, organized, functioning, or acceptable. Common in everyday and formal contexts. Can mean 'in order' (tidy/organized), 'all set', or 'everything is fine.' Often appears in phrases like 'tout est en ordre' (everything is in order).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, vérifie que tout est en ordre.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check that everything is in order.

meaning: besides; moreover; in addition
additional_notes: Used to add another point or piece of information. Formal to neutral register; common in written and spoken French. Often placed at the start of a sentence or clause and followed by a comma.
target_language_example: En outre, il faudra réparer la porte.
native_language_example: Moreover, the door will need to be repaired.

meaning: broken down; not working (for machines, vehicles, appliances).
additional_notes: Used to say a device or vehicle has stopped functioning. Commonly used with verbs like tomber (tomber en panne) or être (être en panne). Can refer to temporary failures; context indicates whether repair is needed. Not informal.
target_language_example: La photocopieuse est en panne, on doit appeler le technicien.
native_language_example: The photocopier is broken down; we must call the technician.

meaning: 'en panne' means 'broken down' or 'not working'; the extra 'en' at the end is not standard French and likely results from a typo, mishearing, or a nonstandard regional/colloquial form. If intended, it may appear in casual speech before specifying a location or state (e.g., 'en panne en haut' — but this is nonstandard).
additional_notes: Preferred and standard form is 'en panne'. The sequence 'en panne en' is not grammatically correct by itself in standard French. If you see 'en panne en', check context — it may be 'en panne, en...' followed by a clause or location, or simply a mistake. Use 'être en panne' to say something is broken. Figurative uses exist (e.g., 'en panne d'inspiration').
target_language_example: Ma voiture est en panne en bas du garage.
native_language_example: My car is broken down at the bottom of the garage.

meaning: 'in perfect (condition)' or 'as a perfect...'
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun like 'état' (en parfait état) to mean 'in perfect condition'. Can also appear in phrases like 'transformé en parfait soldat' meaning 'turned into a perfect/complete [soldier]' — there it means 'as a perfect/example of'. Usually followed by a noun; adjective agrees with the noun in gender/number (e.g. en parfait état, en parfaite condition).
target_language_example: La voiture est en parfait état après la réparation.
native_language_example: The car is in perfect condition after the repair.

meaning: 'particularly' or 'specifically'.
additional_notes: Used to single out one thing, person, place or detail among others. Can start a phrase or be inserted mid-sentence. Often followed by de/à/chez or a noun/pronoun to specify what is meant.
target_language_example: Je m'intéresse aux films, en particulier aux documentaires.
native_language_example: I'm interested in films, particularly documentaries.

meaning: partly; in part; to some extent.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true only to a certain degree or not completely. Often appears in short answers (e.g., “Oui, en partie”) and before verbs/nouns (e.g., “en partie responsable”). Formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: C'est en partie à cause du mauvais temps.
native_language_example: It's partly because of the bad weather.

meaning: 'in passing' / 'by the way' / 'while passing through' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common multi-use phrase. Can mean: 1) 'in passing' or 'incidentally' when mentioning something briefly (e.g. En passant, ... = By the way); 2) 'while passing by/through' when describing movement (en passant par = via / by way of); 3) 'as one passes' for a short action done on the way. Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: En passant, j'ai acheté du pain au marché.
native_language_example: By the way / While passing, I bought bread at the market.

meaning: 'about to' or 'on the verge of' (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone/something is very close to doing something or a situation is about to happen. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: en passe de + infinitive. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Il est en passe de réussir l'examen.
native_language_example: He is about to pass the exam.

meaning: continuously; all the time; permanently.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens without interruption or very frequently. Can mean 'constantly' (temporary ongoing action) or 'permanently' (long-term state) depending on context. Common in both formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Elle travaille en permanence sur ce projet.
native_language_example: She works on this project all the time.

meaning: in person; personally (physically present).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present or does something themselves rather than via a messenger, phone, or representative. Common in formal and informal contexts. Often follows verbs like voir, venir, présenter, or être.
target_language_example: Je veux parler au directeur en personne.
native_language_example: I want to speak to the manager in person.

meaning: in perspective; giving proper context or proportion; worth considering/likely to happen (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) to say putting something 'in perspective' — i.e., seeing it in proper context or proportion (mettre qch en perspective). 2) as a short exclamation/notice meaning a prospect or threat is looming (like 'danger en perspective' = 'danger ahead/likely'). Context tells which sense applies.
target_language_example: Pour être juste, mets cette information en perspective.
native_language_example: To be fair, put this information in perspective.

meaning: in position; in place; set up/established
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically in position) and figuratively (organized, set up, implemented). Common phrases: «être en place» (to be in place/ready), «mettre en place» (to set up/put in place). Can be imperative as instruction (e.g. «restez en place» = stay where you are).
target_language_example: Ils ont mis le nouveau système en place la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: They put the new system in place last week.

meaning: outdoors; in the open air.
additional_notes: Used to describe activities or events that take place outside rather than indoors. Common with concerts, parties, sports, walks, etc. Formal or neutral register; not slang. Often follows the verb (e.g., « passer du temps en plein air ») or modifies a noun (e.g., « un concert en plein air »).
target_language_example: Nous avons organisé un pique-nique en plein air.
native_language_example: We organized a picnic outdoors.

meaning: in addition
additional_notes: Commonly used to add information or emphasize something extra. As a sentence adverb it means 'in addition' or 'moreover' (e.g. En plus, il est sympa = 'Moreover, he's nice'). It can also appear in comparisons/quantities to mean 'additional' or 'more' (e.g. payer en plus = 'pay extra') and in the phrase 'de plus en plus' (note the order) to mean 'more and more'.
target_language_example: En plus, ils ont oublié de verrouiller la porte.
native_language_example: In addition, they forgot to lock the door.

meaning: in addition to; besides; as well as
additional_notes: Used to add something extra to what was already mentioned. Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or verb (when followed by an infinitive). Often interchangeable with 'en plus' (informal) or 'outre' (more formal) depending on context. Example 5 shows a spoken/colloquial use meaning 'one more' or 'besides'.
target_language_example: En plus de son travail, elle étudie le soir.
native_language_example: In addition to her job, she studies in the evening.

meaning: at the right moment; ready; perfectly timed (literally 'in point')
additional_notes: Rare/idiomatic. 'En point' can describe something being exactly ready or arriving at the precise moment. More common expressions with similar meaning: 'à point' (especially for cooking: perfectly done) and 'à propos' (opportune). In modern spoken French, 'à point' is used more often than 'en point'.
target_language_example: Le dîner était en point quand nous sommes arrivés.
native_language_example: Dinner was perfectly ready when we arrived.

meaning: in possession of everything / of all (it)
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone came to have all of something (often money or goods). Common in questions like "Comment êtes-vous venu en possession de tout cet argent ?" — formal/neutral tone. Verb agreement and past participle depend on subject (venir + en possession de). Can be used with different determiners (tout, tous, toutes) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Comment es-tu venu en possession de tout cet argent ?
native_language_example: How did you come into possession of all that money?

meaning: in practice; practically; actually (what happens in reality)
additional_notes: Used to contrast theory/idea with how things work in reality. Can mean 'practically' or 'as a matter of fact' depending on context. Also appears in the verb phrase 'mettre en pratique' (to put into practice/implement).
target_language_example: En pratique, cette règle est rarement respectée.
native_language_example: In practice, this rule is rarely followed.

meaning: in private; privately (not in public or in front of others).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that a conversation or information should happen away from others, one-on-one or confidentially. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can be used with verbs like parler, discuter, avoir un mot, échanger.
target_language_example: Peut-on en parler en privé après la réunion ?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it in private after the meeting?

meaning: in the presence of; while someone is present; before (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action occurs with someone present or in front of someone (often a person of authority, witnesses, or a group). Common in formal contexts (e.g., legal, official) but also used in everyday speech: en présence de + noun. Can be followed by de + person/thing or alone when context is clear.
target_language_example: Il a fait ses excuses en présence de ses collègues.
native_language_example: He apologized in the presence of his colleagues.

meaning: 'in the presence of' / 'when [someone] is present'
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action happens (or is avoided) while someone or something is present. Formal/neutral register. Often followed by a person, group, or thing (e.g., en présence de mon avocat, en présence de témoins).
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas discuter de ça en présence de mes parents.
native_language_example: I prefer not to discuss that in the presence of my parents.

meaning: 'in public' — in a place or situation where other people can see or hear you.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action happens openly, in front of others (opposite of 'en privé' or 'en privé/en privé(e)'). Common with verbs like 'parler', 'dire', 'faire', or to describe events that are visible to an audience. Can refer to physical public spaces or any situation with others present (e.g., meetings, on stage, online if others can see).
target_language_example: Ne discute pas de ça en public.
native_language_example: Don't discuss that in public.

meaning: as / in the capacity of (used to say someone's role or official status).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate the role, function or legal capacity in which someone acts. Formal register; common in written and official contexts (résumé, letters, legal texts). Often followed by a profession or title: en qualité de + noun. Do not confuse with 'en tant que' (very similar; 'en tant que' is slightly more general and more common in spoken French).
target_language_example: Je signe ce document en qualité de directeur général.
native_language_example: I sign this document as (in my capacity as) the general manager.

meaning: used to ask 'in which' or 'in what' (followed by a noun), often in formal or written questions
additional_notes: Literally 'in which'. It appears in questions like « en quel(s) + [nom] » to ask about a category, period, level, etc. Agreement: quel agrees in gender and number with the noun (en quel, en quelle, en quels, en quelles). It's more formal than simply using 'quel' in some contexts (e.g. «En quelle année avez-vous commencé?» vs «Quelle année…?»).
target_language_example: En quelle année êtes-vous né ?
native_language_example: In which year were you born?

meaning: in something; about something (rare/poetic) — literally 'in something'.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'en quelque chose' is uncommon in modern everyday French. More usual are 'en quelque sorte' (in a way), 'pour quelque chose' (for something), or 'à quelque chose' within fixed expressions. When used, it would literally mean 'in something' — often appearing inside longer phrases (e.g. 'il y a en quelque chose de...') and can sound literary or formal. Do not confuse with 'quelque chose' (something) on its own.
target_language_example: Il y a en quelque chose de mystérieux dans cette vieille maison.
native_language_example: There is something mysterious in that old house.

meaning: 'in a way' / 'sort of' / 'to some extent'.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement — indicates approximation or partial agreement. Common in speech and writing. Can often be replaced by 'en quelque mesure', 'dans une certaine mesure', or informal 'un peu'.
target_language_example: Je suis, en quelque sorte, responsable de ce projet.
native_language_example: I am, in a way, responsible for this project.

meaning: under discussion / being questioned / at issue
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that is being discussed, doubted, or challenged. Can mean 'at issue' (the main topic) or 'called into question' (doubted). Often follows the noun it refers to (le sujet en question).
target_language_example: La validité de l'étude est en question.
native_language_example: The validity of the study is in question.

meaning: in whom / in which (used to refer to trust, confidence, or qualities possessed by someone/something)
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "avoir confiance en quelqu'un" or "croire en quelqu'un" where "en" refers back to a person or thing. "Qui" is a relative pronoun meaning "who/which"; together "en qui" introduces a clause describing the person/thing referred to (e.g. "une personne en qui j'ai confiance" = "a person in whom I have confidence"). Not used alone; normally part of a larger phrase ("en qui je crois", "en qui tu peux avoir confiance").
target_language_example: C'est quelqu'un en qui tu peux avoir confiance.
native_language_example: He is someone you can trust.

meaning: 'how can I' or 'in what way can I' (start of a polite offer or question about how one can help or act)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it appears as the beginning of sentences like «En quoi puis-je vous aider?» (How can I help you?). Literally 'in what can I' — used to ask in what way you can assist, contribute, or be of use. Formal/polite when combined with inversion (puis-je).
target_language_example: En quoi puis-je vous aider aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How can I help you today?

meaning: because of; due to; on account of
additional_notes: Used to give a cause or reason for something. Formal/neutral register — common in written and spoken French. Followed by a noun or noun phrase (en raison de la pluie, en raison de sa santé).
target_language_example: Le train a été retardé en raison de la neige.
native_language_example: The train was delayed because of the snow.

meaning: 'in line' or 'in formation'; used to tell people to stand/line up in an orderly row or file.
additional_notes: Commonly used by teachers, supervisors, or leaders to organize groups (children, soldiers, etc.). Can specify formation: 'en rang deux par deux' (two by two) or 'en file indienne' (single file). Often used as an imperative: 'En rang !' (= 'Line up!').
target_language_example: Mettez-vous en rang deux par deux devant la salle.
native_language_example: Line up two by two in front of the classroom.

meaning: in relation to; related to; concerning.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is connected or relevant to something else. Often followed by avec (en rapport avec) or used alone with context. Common in formal and neutral registers. Can describe relevance, association, or a professional link.
target_language_example: Choisissez un projet en rapport avec vos intérêts.
native_language_example: Choose a project related to your interests.

meaning: late
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is late or delayed, often with être: être en retard = to be late. It can also be used with arriver: arriver en retard = to arrive late. With sur, en retard sur means behind on something.
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en retard pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late for the appointment.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct standalone French expression. It appears to combine the adjective phrase 'en retard' ('late') with the demonstrative pronoun 'ce' ('this/that'), which is ungrammatical in standard French. The intended meaning would depend on context; possible corrections include 'en retard' alone, 'ce retard' ('this/that delay'), or 'en retard de...' (e.g. 'en retard de cinq minutes').
additional_notes: 'en retard ce' as written is ungrammatical. Native speakers would not use 'en retard' immediately followed by 'ce'. If you want to point to a specific delay, use 'ce retard'. If you want to say 'late' about someone/something, use 'en retard' by itself (e.g. 'Je suis en retard'). To say 'this is late' you might say 'C'est en retard' (colloquial) or better 'C'est en retard pour...' or 'C'est en retard par rapport à...'.
target_language_example: Je suis en retard, ce n'est pas grave.
native_language_example: I'm late, that's not a problem.

meaning: 'in return' / 'as a return' (something given or done in exchange)
additional_notes: Used to indicate something given, done, or expected in exchange for another action. Common in both concrete and abstract contexts (a physical item, a favor, thanks, or reciprocation). Often appears in phrases like "rien en retour" (nothing in return) or "quelque chose en retour" (something in return).
target_language_example: Il m'a aidé, et je lui ai rendu service en retour.
native_language_example: He helped me, and I did him a favor in return.

meaning: in the background; withdrawn; apart from others.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who stays back, is reserved, or remains apart from the group or the main action. Can refer to physical distance (stay back) or to someone's social/psychological behaviour (being reserved). Common in instructions (Restez en retrait = keep back/stay back).
target_language_example: Elle est restée en retrait pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: She stayed in the background during the meeting.

meaning: 'retired' (having stopped working) or 'in retreat' (military/figurative: withdrawing).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) Referring to a person who has stopped working due to age — 'être en retraite' = to be retired. 2) Used in military/figurative contexts as part of the phrase 'battre en retraite' meaning to retreat or withdraw. Context tells you which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Après quarante ans de travail, il est enfin en retraite.
native_language_example: After forty years of work, he is finally retired.

meaning: 'in nothing' / 'not at all' (used to express absence or lack of similarity/belief/ability).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative constructions with ne...en rien to mean 'not at all' or 'in no way', and after verbs like ressembler, croire, être bon to indicate complete absence (e.g. 'ne ressemble en rien' = 'doesn't resemble at all'). Alone, 'En rien.' can be a brief reply meaning 'Not at all' or 'No problem'.
target_language_example: Elle ne s'est pas améliorée en rien depuis l'année dernière.
native_language_example: She hasn't improved at all since last year.

meaning: 'on the way' or 'along the way' (while traveling or heading somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is traveling toward a destination (en route = on the way). Can mean 'while on the way' when followed by an action (e.g., 'j'ai pris de quoi manger en route' = I grabbed something to eat on the way). Common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Nous sommes en route pour Paris; on arrive dans deux heures.
native_language_example: We are on the way to Paris; we'll arrive in two hours.

meaning: legally or administratively compliant; in order.
additional_notes: Used to say that documents, status, or procedures meet legal/official requirements (papers, permits, taxes, etc.). Common in phrases like "être en règle" (to be in order/legally compliant) or as a short reply meaning "All good/OK."
target_language_example: Avant de partir, assure-toi que tes papiers sont en règle.
native_language_example: Before leaving, make sure your papers are in order.

meaning: 'in reality' / 'actually' — introduces what is true as opposed to what was expected or said.
additional_notes: Common discourse marker used to correct, clarify, or emphasize the real situation or intention. Can appear at the start of a sentence or after a verb. Equivalent to 'actually', 'in fact', or 'as a matter of fact' in English. Neutral register.
target_language_example: En réalité, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Actually, I can't come tonight.

meaning: in reserve; kept back for later use.
additional_notes: Used to say something is held back, saved, or kept as a backup. Common with nouns like 'nouvelles', 'idées', 'plans', or with quantity (en reste). Can mean 'extra' or 'spare' that you haven't used yet.
target_language_example: J'ai quelques idées en réserve si tu veux.
native_language_example: I have a few ideas in reserve if you want.

meaning: in summary; to sum up
additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or conclusion of what was said. Can stand alone as a one-line comment. Formality: neutral — suitable in spoken and written French. Pronunciation tip: the 's' in résumé is pronounced (rez-yu-may).
target_language_example: En résumé, nous devons réduire les coûts et accélérer le calendrier.
native_language_example: In summary, we must cut costs and speed up the schedule.

meaning: secretly; in a secret way.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done privately or without others knowing. Common in spoken and written French. Can appear alone as a question (En secret?) or within a sentence (faire quelque chose en secret).
target_language_example: Ils parlent en secret de leur projet.
native_language_example: They are talking secretly about their plan.

meaning: as a sign; by way of a sign; in token (often used to indicate something symbolic or as a gesture).
additional_notes: Not a very common fixed phrase on its own. Often appears in contexts like "en signe de" (e.g. "en signe de gratitude" = "as a sign of gratitude") where it introduces the purpose of a gesture or symbol. Used before a noun to explain that something is done as a symbol or token. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Il a offert des fleurs en signe d'excuse.
native_language_example: He gave flowers as a sign of apology.

meaning: 'as a sign of' or 'as a gesture of' (used to indicate that something is done to express a feeling or message).
additional_notes: Placed before a noun phrase (often introduced by de) to indicate the purpose of an action or object as a symbolic gesture (e.g., en signe de respect, en signe de gratitude). Common in formal and neutral registers; can appear in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Il leva son chapeau en signe de respect.
native_language_example: He lifted his hat as a sign of respect.

meaning: quietly; in silence; without speaking or making noise.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something without noise or speech. Can modify verbs (manger en silence, marcher en silence) or describe a general atmosphere (être en silence). Often interchangeable with 'silencieusement' but 'en silence' is slightly more literary or neutral. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ils ont attendu en silence jusqu'à l'arrivée du professeur.
native_language_example: They waited in silence until the teacher arrived.

meaning: in itself; by itself; inherently.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has a quality or exists inherently, independent of other factors. Common in phrases like "croire en soi" (to believe in oneself) where it refers to the self. Can be used to emphasize the intrinsic nature of a thing (e.g. "intéressant en soi" = interesting in itself).
target_language_example: Cette idée est intéressante en soi, même si elle est difficile à appliquer.
native_language_example: This idea is interesting in itself, even if it's hard to apply.

meaning: 'in short', 'overall', or 'basically'.
additional_notes: Used to summarize, conclude, or restate what was just said. Can mean 'in short', 'all in all', 'basically', or 'so (then)'. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause and is followed by a comma. Neutral register; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En somme, il n'a pas tenu sa promesse.
native_language_example: In short, he didn't keep his promise.

meaning: in its/one's sound; with sound
additional_notes: Used when referring to sound belonging to something (son = sound). Usually appears in contexts like "en son nom" (in his/her name) is different—don't confuse. "En son" followed by a noun can mean "in its sound" (rare) or be part of phrases like "en son temps" (in his/her time) where "son" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/its". Without more context, the common use is the possessive: "en son temps" = "in his/her time" or "en son absence" = "in his/her absence." Be careful: French possessive "son" agrees with the noun possessed, not the possessor's gender.
target_language_example: Il a organisé la cérémonie en son absence.
native_language_example: He organized the ceremony in his absence.

meaning: 'on the surface' / 'above ground' (not underground or underwater); also 'superficially' in a figurative sense.
additional_notes: Used literally to mean located at or happening on the surface (e.g., above ground, on the water, on the exterior). Common in contexts like transport (staying above ground vs. underground), military/technical (surface launches), or reporting (surface observations). Can also be used figuratively to mean only looking at the surface (superficially).
target_language_example: Je prends le métro ou je reste en surface ?
native_language_example: Do I take the subway or do I stay above ground?

meaning: suspended, unresolved, on hold.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is paused, undecided, or left unresolved (a situation, question, plan, career, etc.). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Often follows the noun it modifies (la question est en suspens).
target_language_example: Le projet est en suspens jusqu'à la réunion.
native_language_example: The project is on hold until the meeting.

meaning: 'as' or 'in the capacity/role of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone's role, capacity, status, point of view, or the function something has. Common with professions, social roles, points of view (en tant que parent / en tant que médecin / en tant que Canadienne). Can also mean 'as' when identifying something in a particular function (connu en tant que...). Not used for simple comparisons (use 'comme' for 'like').
target_language_example: Je parle en tant que professeur, pas en tant qu'ami.
native_language_example: I speak as a teacher, not as a friend.

meaning: Not a correct standalone phrase in French; the sequence 'en te' can occur only in rare/incorrect/typo contexts or within larger words. Standard French places 'te' before 'en' when both pronouns appear (e.g. 'Je t'en parle').
additional_notes: 'en' is a clitic pronoun meaning 'of it/of them' or 'from there'; 'te' is the informal second-person object pronoun. The correct order when both occur is 'te ... en' contracted to 't'en' (e.g. 'Je t'en donne'). If you encounter 'en te' it is likely a mistake, a spaced typo inside a compound (e.g. 'en teinte' split incorrectly), or an intentional stylistic inversion rarely used in poetry or archaic texts.
target_language_example: Dans ce texte mal édité, on lit « en te » au lieu de « t'en ».
native_language_example: In this poorly edited text, one reads "en te" instead of "t'en".

meaning: on time; in time (depending on context).
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "en temps voulu" (in due time) or "à temps" vs "en temps" distinctions: "en temps" can mean 'within the needed/expected time' or 'during a period' when combined with other words (e.g. "en temps de guerre" = in times of war). For 'on time' or 'in time' alone, French speakers more commonly use "à temps" (arriver à temps = arrive on time) or "en temps utile"/"en temps voulu" for 'in due time.'
target_language_example: Il faut finir le rapport en temps pour la réunion.
native_language_example: You must finish the report in time for the meeting.

meaning: in times of
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean during a period marked by something, such as war, famine, or crisis: en temps de guerre, en temps de famine. It is a fairly fixed expression and is often translated with plural 'times' in English.
target_language_example: En temps de crise, il faut rester calme.
native_language_example: In times of crisis, you have to stay calm.

meaning: at the appropriate time / in due course
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen when the time is right or when it's necessary; polite and neutral register. Often used to reassure someone that information or action will come later — not immediately. Common in formal or everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je t'en parlerai en temps voulu.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll tell you in due course.

meaning: in (the appropriate) outfit / dressed (in uniform or specific clothing).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is wearing a particular outfit, uniform, or ready in specific clothes (e.g., en tenue de pilote, en tenue de sport). Often implies readiness for an activity or role. Can be used alone as a short statement ('En tenue.') or in commands ('Mets-toi en tenue.').
target_language_example: Il doit être en tenue pour la cérémonie.
native_language_example: He must be in uniform for the ceremony.

meaning: with regard to; in terms of; concerning
additional_notes: Used to specify the aspect, category, or perspective being considered (e.g., salary, function, shape). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by a noun or noun phrase. Equivalent to 'regarding' or 'as far as ... is concerned' in English.
target_language_example: En termes de qualité, ce produit est excellent.
native_language_example: In terms of quality, this product is excellent.

meaning: 'in theory' — according to an idea or plan, but maybe not in practice.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something should work or be true based on reasoning or rules, but may not hold in reality or practice. Often followed by a contradictory remark (e.g., 'en théorie, oui, mais...'). Can be used alone as a short answer: 'En théorie.'
target_language_example: En théorie, le plan fonctionne, mais il faudra tester.
native_language_example: In theory, the plan works, but we'll need to test it.

meaning: in your tone / in the tone of
additional_notes: Used to indicate manner or style, often referring to someone's tone of voice or the overall tone of a text/speech (e.g., 'en ton humoristique' = in a humorous tone). 'En' + noun/possessive ('ton') means 'in (your) ...', so context determines whether 'ton' is literal 'your' or part of a fixed expression. You'll most commonly see 'en' followed by a noun (en colère, en retard) or 'd'un ton' (d'un ton sec). 'En ton' by itself is less common than 'd'un ton' or 'sur un ton', but can appear in phrases like 'en ton honneur' (in your honor) where 'ton' is a possessive. Pay attention to whether 'ton' is the possessive 'your' (informal) or part of another phrase.
target_language_example: Il a parlé en ton sérieux pour expliquer la situation.
native_language_example: He spoke in a serious tone to explain the situation.

meaning: in any case / anyway / at any rate.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion, emphasize a point, or change topic; similar to 'anyway' or 'at least' in English. Can appear at the start or end of a sentence. Common in spoken and informal French but also used in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas fini, mais en tout cas j'ai bien avancé.
native_language_example: I haven't finished, but in any case I've made good progress.

meaning: in total; altogether; all told.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the total number, amount, or summary. Common in questions (Combien cela coûte en tout?) and short answers (En tout, neuf). Can appear after the noun or at end of sentence. Neutral register; very common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Nous avons vendu dix billets en tout.
native_language_example: We sold ten tickets in total.

meaning: in the process of
additional_notes: Usually used as être en train de + infinitive to emphasize that an action is happening right now or was underway at that moment. It is stronger than the simple present and often corresponds to English progressive forms like "am/is/are doing."
target_language_example: Je suis en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: I'm making dinner.

meaning: part of the expression 'être en train de ...' meaning 'in the process of (doing) ...' — here followed by 'vous' as the object (e.g. 'je suis en train de vous écouter' = 'I am listening to you').
additional_notes: The full useful chunk is 'être en train de + infinitive' which expresses an action currently in progress (equivalent to the English continuous 'be ...-ing'). 'En train de vous' is not a standalone phrase; it will be followed by a verb: e.g. 'Je suis en train de vous appeler.' Pronounce the whole structure; conjugate 'être' to match the subject (je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont).
target_language_example: Je suis en train de vous répondre.
native_language_example: I am answering you (right now).

meaning: across; lying or positioned crosswise; in someone's way
additional_notes: Used to describe something crossing or lying across a space (e.g., a bridge across a river, an object across a road) or figuratively to say someone/something is obstructing a path. Often followed by de/du/la or a noun indicating what is crossed or blocked (en travers de + noun).
target_language_example: Le canapé est posé en travers de la porte.
native_language_example: The sofa is placed across the door.
