meaning: not a standalone expression in French; 'en' + 'très' can appear together before an adjective/adverb (e.g. « en très bon état ») meaning 'in/very' depending on structure.
additional_notes: There is no fixed phrase 'en très' by itself. 'Très' means 'very' and usually directly modifies an adjective or adverb (très grand, très vite). 'En' is a preposition or pronoun and can combine with an adjective phrase (en très bon état = in very good condition). Do not use 'en très' alone; check the surrounding words. Examples of correct uses: « en très bon état », « en très peu de temps ». Avoid forms like *'Je suis en très' without a following adjective or noun phrase.
target_language_example: La voiture est en très bon état.
native_language_example: The car is in very good condition.

meaning: 'in mind' / 'ahead' / 'at the front' (depends on context).
additional_notes:
Common idiom with several uses:
- 'avoir quelque chose en tête' = to have something in mind (an idea or plan).
- 'ne te mets pas en tête de...' = don't get it into your head (don't decide/assume to do something).
- 'être en tête' / 'être en tête de [groupe/classe]' = to be in front / leading / top of the class or race. Context determines whether it's mental (in mind) or spatial/competitive (in front).
target_language_example: J'ai une petite idée en tête pour le week-end.
native_language_example: I have a little idea in mind for the weekend.

meaning: phrased element used to indicate someone/something is at the forefront of one's thoughts or intentions (literally "in head to"); typically appears in constructions like "avoir en tête à + personne/quelque chose" to mean "to have (someone/something) in mind" or "to be thinking of".
additional_notes: "En tête à" by itself is uncommon; it usually appears within a larger phrase such as "avoir en tête à [quelqu'un/quelque chose]" or in colloquial structures. Regional or spoken French may use forms like "j'ai en tête à Marie" (I have Marie in mind). Be careful: more typical expressions are "avoir en tête" or "avoir quelqu'un en tête." Literal translation into English is possible but sounds unnatural; translate contextually as "to have in mind" or "to be thinking of."
target_language_example: J'ai en tête à Marie quand j'organise la fête.
native_language_example: I have Marie in mind when I organize the party.

meaning: in one
additional_notes: Used before a noun or number to express doing something in a single unit or at the same time (e.g. en un coup = in one blow, en un seul jour = in one single day). Often appears as part of fixed expressions: en un instant (in an instant), en un coup d'œil (at a glance). Context determines whether it means "in one [thing]" or "at once".
target_language_example: Il l'a fait en un jour.
native_language_example: He did it in one day.

meaning: very quickly; in the blink of an eye
additional_notes: An idiom meaning something happens almost instantly. Used in everyday speech and writing to emphasize speed. Literally refers to the blink of an eye (clin d'œil = wink/blink). Can be used with past, present, or future tenses (e.g. 'il a disparu en un clin d'œil', 'je reviens en un clin d'œil').
target_language_example: Il a réglé le problème en un clin d'œil.
native_language_example: He fixed the problem in the blink of an eye.

meaning: in a word; briefly; to sum up in one word or phrase.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a very short summary, conclusion, or direct answer. Often followed by a single word or short phrase (e.g., «oui», «non», or an adjective). Can be used alone or rhetorically as a prompt/question.
target_language_example: En un mot, c'est parfait.
native_language_example: In a word, it's perfect.

meaning: 'in no time' / 'very quickly'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun like 'temps' (en un rien de temps) or alone in colloquial speech to mean that something happens extremely fast. Often appears as the fixed expression 'en un rien de temps' (lit. 'in a nothing of time'). Can be used to emphasize speed: 'Il a fini en un rien de (temps)'.
target_language_example: Il a réparé la voiture en un rien de temps.
native_language_example: He fixed the car in no time.

meaning: very quickly; in no time; in an instant.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say something will happen or be done extremely fast. Common in spoken and written French. You can use it with future, past or present tense verbs. Equivalent to 'in no time' or 'in a flash' in English.
target_language_example: Je reviens, je serai prêt(e) en un rien de temps.
native_language_example: I'll be back, I'll be ready in no time.

meaning: in a sense / in one sense
additional_notes: Used to introduce a partial, qualified, or limited view — you are acknowledging that something is true from one perspective but not necessarily completely. Common in written and spoken French. Can be followed by a clause with present or past tense.
target_language_example: En un sens, c'était la meilleure décision.
native_language_example: In a sense, it was the best decision.

meaning: safe and unharmed; in one piece.
additional_notes: Used to wish or hope someone (or something) returns without injury or damage. Common in everyday speech when someone is leaving or after a risky situation. Literally 'in a single piece.' Tone is caring/concerned; can be used humorously or seriously.
target_language_example: Essaie de revenir à la maison en un seul morceau.
native_language_example: Try to get back home in one piece.

meaning: 'in vain' — without success or without achieving the intended result.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or effort produced no useful result. Common in both written and spoken French. Often placed after the verb or clause (e.g., « J'ai essayé en vain », « Il est mort en vain »). Equivalent to English 'in vain' and can be used for failed attempts, wasted waiting, or futile sacrifices.
target_language_example: J'ai cherché mes clés en vain toute la matinée.
native_language_example: I searched for my keys in vain all morning.

meaning: alive
additional_notes: Used to state that a person (or sometimes an animal) is living, often following a verb like être (être en vie). Common in statements about survival or existence; negative form is « ne ... plus en vie » (no longer alive). Can be used in conditional clauses (Si tu es en vie...).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, elle était heureuse d'être encore en vie.
native_language_example: After the accident, she was happy to still be alive.

meaning: in force; currently effective (law, rule, ban, system).
additional_notes: Used to say that a law, rule, ban or regulation is active now or will start to be active. Common verbs: être en vigueur (to be in force), entrer en vigueur (to come into effect). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: La loi sera en vigueur à partir du 1er janvier.
native_language_example: The law will be in force as of January 1st.

meaning: in town
additional_notes: Used to say someone is located in a town/city (in town) or going/taken to a town/city (to town). Context determines whether it's locative (il vit en ville = he lives in town) or directional (je peux vous conduire en ville = I can drive you to town). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je vais en ville cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to town this afternoon.

meaning: 'quickly' or 'in a hurry'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something fast or hurriedly. Common in spoken French; can modify verbs (partir en vitesse = leave quickly) or be used as an imperative urging someone to hurry (Reviens ici en vitesse!).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi et finis ça en vitesse.
native_language_example: Hurry up and finish that quickly.

meaning: 'in the process of' or 'on the way to' (often followed by a noun indicating change or a gerund/participle).
additional_notes: Usually appears in expressions like "en voie de disparition" (in danger of disappearing/endangered) or "en voie d'amélioration" (improving). It describes something that is currently progressing toward a state. Often followed by "de" + noun or verb-noun (e.g. disparition, amélioration, guérison).
target_language_example: Cette espèce est en voie de disparition.
native_language_example: This species is in danger of disappearing (is endangered).

meaning: in the process of; on the way to (a change, outcome, or state).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or verb to indicate something is progressing toward a particular state or outcome. Common collocations: "en voie de disparition" (endangered/going extinct), "en voie de guérison" (recovering). Formal/neutral register; often seen in news, reports, and formal writing.
target_language_example: C'est une espèce en voie de disparition.
native_language_example: It's a species in the process of disappearing (endangered).

meaning: a formal way to say 'in your' (used before a feminine singular noun), as in 'in your [possession/opinion/etc.]'.
additional_notes: Rarely used on its own; appears in formal or written French in phrases like 'en votre nom' (in your name) or 'en votre absence' (in your absence). Matches the English structure 'in your ...' and agrees with a feminine singular noun. For masculine singular you would use 'en votre' as well because 'votre' is invariant for gender; note that 'en' can have many senses (in, on, by, during, because of) depending on context.
target_language_example: Je prends la décision en votre présence.
native_language_example: I make the decision in your presence.

meaning: 'in you' or 'about you' depending on context (literal: inside you; pronominal: referring to 'you' as object of a preposition).
additional_notes: En + object pronoun (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux) can mean 'in/inside [someone]' (physical or figurative) or be part of verbs/expressions that use 'en' to mean 'about' or 'of' when combined with a pronoun. Alone, 'en vous' is often literal ('inside you') or appears in phrases like 'en vous-même' (in yourself) or in formal constructions: 'je crois en vous' (I believe in you) — note: 'en' there is a preposition meaning 'in' + stressed pronoun, not the pronoun 'vous' object of 'en'. Pay attention to context: word order and verb determine whether it’s literal, figurative, or part of a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Je crois en vous.
native_language_example: I believe in you.

meaning: 'in real life' / 'for real' / 'actually' (used to contrast reality with appearance or expectation)
additional_notes: Casual spoken expression. Used to say that something should be seen, experienced, or is true in reality (not just in photos, online, or in theory). Can mean 'actually' when reacting (En vrai ?) to express surprise or doubt. Common in conversation and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Tu devrais le rencontrer en vrai, il est très sympa.
native_language_example: You should meet him in real life, he's very nice.

meaning: 'in sight' / 'visible' / 'in view' (can also mean 'within sight or prospect')
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something can be seen or is nearby/approaching (e.g. «Chasseurs en vue!»). Also used figuratively to mean 'in prospect' or 'about/approaching' (e.g. «en vue de» = 'in sight of' or 'near'). Common in everyday and written French. Context determines whether it's literal (visible) or more figurative (expected/near).
target_language_example: Il y a un bateau en vue au loin.
native_language_example: There is a boat in sight in the distance.

meaning: with the aim of; in order to; with a view to
additional_notes: Used to introduce the purpose or intention of an action. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (en vue de + nom / en vue de + infinitif). Formal/neutral register; common in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Ils organisent une réunion en vue de préparer le projet.
native_language_example: They are holding a meeting in order to prepare the project.

meaning: 'in truth', 'actually', or 'to tell the truth'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank statement or to correct/clarify what was said. Can be placed at the start or end of a sentence. More formal or literary than casual phrases like «en fait» or «à vrai dire».
target_language_example: En vérité, je n'ai pas compris la question.
native_language_example: Actually, I didn't understand the question.

meaning: of (the) age to / old enough to
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone has reached a certain age to do something (often followed by an infinitive or a specified age). Commonly appears as 'en âge de + infinitive' (e.g., 'en âge de voter') or 'en âge de + nombre' (less common). Formal/neutral phrasing.
target_language_example: Il est en âge de commencer l'école.
native_language_example: He is old enough to start school.

meaning: in exchange; as compensation or in return
additional_notes: Used to indicate something given or done in return for something else. Can be followed by de + noun (en échange de) to specify what is exchanged, or used alone in questions/answers (Qu'est-ce que tu veux en échange ?). Common in both everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Tu m'aides à déménager, et moi je te rends service en échange.
native_language_example: You help me move, and I'll do you a favor in return.

meaning: 'in a condition' / 'in working order' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to describe the condition of something. With verbs like remettre (remettre en état) it means 'repair' or 'restore to working order'. Alone (laisser en état) it can mean 'leave as is' or 'leave in that condition'—context decides whether positive (working) or neutral (current state).
target_language_example: Il faut remettre la voiture en état avant le voyage.
native_language_example: We need to get the car back into working order before the trip.

meaning: 'in a condition/state to' or 'able to' (followed by an infinitive or noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's or something's physical, legal or functional condition. Often followed by an infinitive (en état de + infinitive) meaning 'able/capable of doing' or by a noun (en état de + noun) meaning 'in a (specified) condition'. Can be used for people, objects or legal/mental states (e.g., en état de légitime défense).
target_language_example: Après le repos, il est en état de reprendre le travail.
native_language_example: After resting, he is able to resume work.

meaning: working; operational; in working order.
additional_notes: Used to say that a machine, device, system — or sometimes a person (informally) — is functioning and can be used. Often follows être (être en état de marche). Can be used short as a standalone sentence: "En état de marche."
target_language_example: Le vélo n'était pas en état de marche après la tempête, mais je l'ai réparé.
native_language_example: The bike wasn't in working order after the storm, but I fixed it.

meaning: a short sequence appearing in sentences with 'en' (pronoun) + verb + partitive/article; by itself it has no fixed meaning—it's part of constructions like 'en a de...' or 'n'en a de...' used with quantities or expressions.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase. 'En' is a pronoun that replaces 'de' + noun (amounts, quantities, 'of it/them'). 'en a de' occurs when 'en' (object) is followed by the verb 'avoir' (a) and then 'de' introducing more detail: e.g. 'Il en a de la chance' (colloquial/emphatic) or in clipped spoken forms. Beginner learners should learn 'en' as a pronoun (e.g. 'J'en veux' = 'I want some') and watch word order: subject + en + verb. If you saw 'en a de' in text, check the full sentence—meaning depends on the noun or expression that follows.
target_language_example: Il en a de la chance, celui-là !
native_language_example: He sure is lucky, that one!

meaning: has some (of them); literally 'has of them' — used to say someone possesses some quantity of something previously mentioned
additional_notes: Built from the pronoun 'en' (replaces 'de' + noun) + verb 'avoir' + indefinite plural article 'des' (optional/colloquial). 'En' refers back to a previously mentioned thing introduced with 'de' (e.g., 'des pommes', 'des problèmes'). In natural French you will more often see 'en a' alone (e.g., 'Il en a trois') or 'il a des...' without 'en'. The sequence 'en a des' can appear in casual speech for emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'Il en a des idées' = 'He sure has ideas').
target_language_example: Elle en a des questions après le cours.
native_language_example: She has (some) questions after the class.

meaning: has it everywhere / has one of them everywhere (colloquial)
additional_notes: Idiomatic, informal phrase used to say someone or something 'has' or 'is filled with' something everywhere or in many places. Often used after a noun or pronoun: 'il en a partout' = 'he has them everywhere' or 'there's it everywhere'. Context decides what 'en' refers to (it replaces a previously mentioned object or concept).
target_language_example: Il en a partout dans la maison.
native_language_example: He has them/it all over the house.

meaning: literally 'has one that' — used to say someone/something has one (of them) that [does something or is described].
additional_notes: This is a short, colloquial fragment built with the pronoun 'en' (replacing 'of them' or 'some'), the verb 'a' (has) and 'un qui' (one that/who). It typically appears inside a larger sentence: e.g. 'Il en a un qui...' = 'He has one that...'. Use when referring back to items/people already mentioned. Not a fixed idiom on its own; you'll normally continue with a verb or description after 'qui'.
target_language_example: Elle en a un qui chante tout le temps.
native_language_example: She has one (of them) who sings all the time.

meaning: Not a standard French multi-word expression; likely a mistaken fragment combining 'en', 'ai' and an elided 'l'' (l' + following word). It does not form a correct phrase on its own and usually indicates a typo, bad spacing, or incorrect word order.
additional_notes: This sequence appears to mix three separate elements: 'en' (pronoun or preposition), 'ai' (1st person singular of 'avoir'), and 'l'' (elided definite article or object pronoun). Correct French phrases use these elements in specific orders, for example: 'je l'ai' (I have/I've got it), 'j'en ai' (I have some/of it), or combined forms like 'j'en ai l'impression' (less common) or better 'j'ai l'impression'. If you encounter 'en ai l'' in a text, it is almost certainly a typo (e.g., words misplaced or spacing wrong) and should be resolved into a standard construction such as 'je l'ai' or 'j'en ai'.
target_language_example: …j'en ai l' (typo/fragment) — intended: «j'en ai;» not grammatically complete as «en ai l'».
native_language_example: …j'en ai l' (typo/fragment) — intended: "j'en ai;" not grammatically complete as "en ai l'".

meaning: 'to come to that' / 'to get to that point/situation' (usually negative or undesirable).
additional_notes: Used with 'en' to refer back to a situation already mentioned. Often appears in expressions like "en arriver là" meaning that circumstances have reached an undesirable or extreme point. Commonly used with verbs like espérer, craindre, regretter: "J'espère ne pas en arriver là."
target_language_example: Si nous ne faisons rien, nous pourrions en arriver là.
native_language_example: If we do nothing, we could come to that (point).

meaning: to come to (a point/decision); to end up doing something; to reach the stage of
additional_notes: Used to describe reaching a stage, result, or action (often after a process, conflict, or because of circumstances). Common constructions: "en arriver à + infinitive" (to end up doing something) or "en arriver à + noun" (to reach a point/state). Tone is generally neutral but can imply inevitability or reluctance.
target_language_example: Après des mois de désaccord, nous en arriverons à signer un compromis si personne ne cède.
native_language_example: After months of disagreement, we will end up signing a compromise if nobody gives in.

meaning: 'to have had enough' / 'to be fed up with' (to be tired of something).
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun 'en' to refer back to something already mentioned (of it/them). Conjugate 'avoir' normally (j'en ai assez, tu en as assez, il en a assez, nous en avons assez). Can express both 'I've had enough' (finished tolerating) and 'there's enough of something' depending on context; here it commonly means 'to be fed up with' or 'to be tired of'.
target_language_example: Il commence à en avoir assez de lire: il en a assez.
native_language_example: He's starting to be fed up with reading: he's had enough.

meaning: to be fed up (with something); to have had enough.
additional_notes: Used to express annoyance, frustration, or exhaustion with a situation or person. Commonly followed by de + noun/verb (e.g. 'en avoir marre de...') or used alone when context is clear. Informal; interchangeable with 'en avoir assez' or 'en avoir ras-le-bol'.
target_language_example: En avoir marre de ce bruit constant, il fallait partir.
native_language_example: To be fed up with this constant noise, we had to leave.

meaning: to choose some of them / to choose from them (the pronoun en = 'of it/them').
additional_notes: en is a pronoun that replaces a noun introduced by de (quantity or part of a group). en choisir means 'to choose (some) of them' or 'to choose from it/them.' The exact English translation depends on context and any quantity: e.g. 'en choisir un' = 'to choose one of them.' Commonly used after verbs: Je vais en choisir trois. If no noun follows, en implies previously mentioned items.
target_language_example: Parmi ces livres, je vais en choisir deux.
native_language_example: From these books, I'm going to choose two of them.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo or fragment. On its own it has no fixed meaning.
additional_notes: In French, 'en' and 'de' are common prepositions/articles that often appear together in longer constructions (e.g. 'en train de', 'en + noun + de', or 'se débarrasser de'). But the two-word sequence 'en de' by itself is not a grammatical phrase. If you saw 'en de' in text, check for a missing or following word (for example 'en train de' = 'in the process of', 'en raison de' = 'because of', or 'une bouteille en de plastique' would be incorrect — correct would be 'en plastique' or 'de plastique'). If you meant a different phrase, try the full expression.
target_language_example: Incorrect: Il est en de manger. — Use: Il est en train de manger.
native_language_example: Incorrect: He is en de eat. — Use: He is in the process of eating.

meaning: in two; into two pieces; in two parts
additional_notes: Used to indicate something is split, broken, or divided into two. Often appears with verbs like casser, couper, partager (e.g. 'casser en deux', 'couper en deux'). Can describe physical division (an object broken in two) or figurative division (a plan in two).
target_language_example: Il a coupé la pomme en deux.
native_language_example: He cut the apple in two.

meaning: to say a lot about something; to reveal much (about a situation, person, etc.).
additional_notes: Idiom used to indicate that something is very telling or revealing. Often appears in constructions like «cela en dit long» (that says a lot) or «ça en dit long sur…» (that tells you a lot about…). Use to comment on a situation that exposes character, motives, quality, problems, etc.
target_language_example: Cette panne répétée en dit long sur la qualité de ce produit.
native_language_example: This repeated breakdown says a lot about the quality of this product.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a mistaken or truncated combination (e.g. 'j'en dois' = 'I owe (of it)' or 'tu en dois' = 'you owe some').
additional_notes: Alone, 'en dois' is not a common set phrase. It can appear when the pronoun 'en' (meaning 'of it/of them' or 'some') is combined with the verb 'devoir' (to owe / must) in the second person singular 'tu dois' or first person singular 'je dois', but word order in French puts the pronoun before the conjugated verb: e.g. 'j'en dois' (I owe some of it) or 'tu en dois' (you owe some). More frequently, 'devoir' with 'en' appears in contexts like 'j'en dois X euros' (I owe X euros of it) or 'tu en dois parler' is incorrect — the correct is 'tu dois en parler' (you must talk about it). If you meant 'en dois' as 'I must' / 'you must', note that the pronoun 'en' is optional and changes meaning; without 'en' use 'je dois / tu dois'.
target_language_example: Tu en dois encore dix euros au club.
native_language_example: You still owe ten euros of it to the club.

meaning: to do with it
additional_notes: Commonly used with the pronoun en (replacing 'of it' / 'of them'). Depending on context: (1) with a noun implied, 'm'en faire un' = 'make myself one' or 'have one made'; (2) as a question 'Qu'est-ce qu'il veut en faire ?' = 'What does he want to do with it/them?' or 'What does he want to make of it/them?' Use depends on the verb and the thing referred to by en.
target_language_example: Tu as une part de gâteau — que veux-tu en faire ?
native_language_example: You have a piece of cake — what do you want to do with it?

meaning: Not a standard or idiomatic French expression. Likely a mistaken word order or typo. It does not have an accepted meaning in French as written.
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'en faire ce' is not used in French. Possible intended alternatives include:
- « en faire » (e.g. « N'en fais pas » = "Don't make a fuss about it"),
- « en faire autant » (to do the same),
- « en faire cas » is incorrect — use « en tenir compte » for "take into account." 
If you encountered 'en faire ce' in a text, check for missing or misplaced words (e.g., 'en faire ceci' or 'faire ce ...'), or the writer may have meant 'en faire' followed by another clause.
target_language_example: (usage incorrect) *Je ne sais pas quoi en faire ce* — incorrect and ungrammatical.
native_language_example: (incorrect) "I don't know what to do with it this" — ungrammatical/incorrect in English as well.

meaning: 'to put an end to (something)' or 'to be done with (something) / finish with (something)'
additional_notes: Used with 'avec' + noun (en finir avec X) to mean 'to stop/put an end to X' or 'to be finished with X'. Can also be used alone or in ellipsis to mean 'finish/bring to an end' (often emphatic). Depending on context it can mean ending a situation, stopping a habit, or resolving an affair. Not informal; fairly neutral.
target_language_example: Il faut en finir avec ce dossier une bonne fois pour toutes.
native_language_example: We must put an end to this file once and for all.

meaning: to impress; to look striking or flashy (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal expression used about people, clothes, objects or situations that make a strong visual or stylish impression. Common in the fixed phrase "ça en jette" (that looks great/that's impressive). Can appear after a subject (e.g., "ça en jette") or with a noun phrase: "Il en jette, ce costume."
target_language_example: Ça en jette, ce costume — il en jette vraiment.
native_language_example: That costume is really impressive — it really makes an impression.

meaning: to put some/any of it; used with the pronoun 'en' to indicate quantity (to add/put some of something).
additional_notes: This is a verb phrase combining the pronoun 'en' (which replaces a noun introduced earlier with de) and the verb 'mettre' (to put/add). Context determines nuance: literal use = 'to put/add some (of it)'; idiomatic use = 'to overdo it' or 'to show off' (e.g. «Il en met beaucoup»). The past participle does not agree with 'en'. 'En' usually precedes the verb: 'j'en mets', 'tu en mettras', 'il en a mis'.
target_language_example: Tu veux que j'en mette un peu dans la soupe ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to put a little of it in the soup?

meaning: you're welcome
additional_notes: Short form of the polite response 'je vous en prie' or 'je t'en prie' used after someone says 'merci'. Polite and slightly formal — can be used with friends as well. Literally relates to 'I beg you' but functions as 'you're welcome'.
target_language_example:
— Merci pour ton aide !
— Je t'en prie.
native_language_example:
— Thanks for your help!
— You're welcome.

meaning: used to mean 'remind (someone) of it/them' or 'recall it/them' (often in constructions like « ça me rappelle... » or « ça m'en rappelle »).
additional_notes: Alone, 'en rappelle' is not a standalone fixed phrase; it appears as part of verbs with the pronoun 'en' + 'rappelle' (1st/3rd person singular present of rappeler). 'En' replaces a thing or quantity introduced earlier (of it/them/about it). Common patterns: « Ça me rappelle... » (that reminds me...), « Tu m'en rappelles quelqu'un » (you remind me of someone), or « Rappelle-m'en » (remind me of it/them). For beginners: remember that 'rappeler' can be reflexive or use object pronouns; word order matters (imperative: Rappelle-moi / Rappelle-m'en).
target_language_example: Ça m'en rappelle un autre film que j'ai vu l'an dernier.
native_language_example: That reminds me of another film I saw last year.

meaning: 'to realize' or 'to become aware of' (literally: 'to render oneself of it').
additional_notes: Common reflexive construction: se rendre compte de + thing. In spoken phrases like "Je m'en rends compte" the "en" replaces a previously mentioned idea or situation (equivalent to English 'of it' / 'about it'). Conjugate se rendre compte: je me rends compte, tu te rends compte, il/elle se rend compte, nous nous rendons compte, vous vous rendez compte, ils/elles se rendent compte. Use "m'en rends" only inside a full conjugated phrase (je m'en rends compte).
target_language_example: Je m'en rends compte seulement maintenant.
native_language_example: I only realize it now.

meaning: to stop at / to remain at that point (often figurative: to leave matters as they are).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the pronoun 'en' referring back to something already mentioned (e.g., a decision, an argument, a situation). 'En rester là' = to leave it at that. Can express that nothing more happens or that you won't pursue something further. Often appears in constructions like 'on en reste là' or 'j'en reste là'.
target_language_example: Je préfère en rester là pour l'instant.
native_language_example: I prefer to leave it at that for now.

meaning: 'to leave it at that' / 'to stop here' (to not continue or pursue something further)
additional_notes: Used to propose or insist that a discussion, action, or dispute should stop and not be continued. Common in phrases like "On peut en rester là" (we can leave it at that), negated forms to refuse stopping ("On ne va pas en rester là"), or as a question to seek agreement. The pronoun "en" refers back to the matter previously mentioned.
target_language_example: On peut en rester là.
native_language_example: We can leave it at that.

meaning: 'to come back' (literal) or idiomatic 'to return to a topic' / 'to be stunned' depending on context.
additional_notes: Has several uses: 1) literal: 'revenir de/à un endroit' — to come back from a place (example 1). 2) discourse: 'pour en revenir (à...)' — to return to a previous topic in conversation (example 2). 3) idiomatic colloquial: 'tu vas pas en revenir' — you're going to be shocked/amazed (equivalent to 'you won't believe it') (example 4). Choose meaning from context.
target_language_example: Pour en revenir à notre sujet, il faut finir le rapport.
native_language_example: To return to our topic, we must finish the report.

meaning: to get out of it / to manage / to cope (with a situation).
additional_notes: Often used with 's'en sortir' (reflexive) to mean 'to manage' or 'to cope' with a difficulty. In sentences like 'm'en sortir' or 't'en sortir', the 'en' refers back to the situation, problem, or trouble mentioned earlier. Can be encouraging (Tu vas t'en sortir) or factual (Je m'en suis sorti).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tu vas t'en sortir.
native_language_example: Don't worry, you'll manage.

meaning: 'remember it' (part of the reflexive verb se souvenir + pronoun en).
additional_notes: En souvenez appears in questions or statements as part of 'vous vous en souvenez' meaning 'do you remember it/about it?'. 'Se souvenir de' means 'to remember'; when the thing remembered is introduced by 'de' or previously mentioned, the pronoun 'en' replaces it: 'vous vous en souvenez' = 'you remember it/of it'. This form is formal/plural (vous). For informal singular use: 'tu t'en souviens?'.
target_language_example: Vous vous en souvenez encore?
native_language_example: Do you still remember it?

meaning: 'I will remember it' (future tense, first person singular in a reflexive construction with 'se souvenir de')
additional_notes: The full phrase is usually 'je m'en souviendrai' = 'I will remember it' or 'I will remember that'. 'Se souvenir de' means 'to remember (something)'; 'en' replaces the thing remembered (of it/about it). Used to express lasting memory or gratitude. Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Je m'en souviendrai toujours.
native_language_example: I will always remember it.

meaning: 'am/is/are ... of it' — part of expressions using the pronoun 'en' + verb 'être' to refer back to something already mentioned (feelings, certainty, gratitude, etc.).
additional_notes: En replaces a previously mentioned thing, idea, or situation introduced with de (or implied). Combined with être (suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont), it expresses states about that thing: feelings (J'en suis content = I'm happy about it), certainty (J'en suis sûr = I'm sure of it), gratitude (Je vous en suis reconnaissant = I'm grateful to you for it). Word order: subject + en + form of être + adjective/participle. If negative, place 'en' before the verb (Je n'en suis pas sûr).
target_language_example: Il a changé d'avis, et j'en suis surpris.
native_language_example: He changed his mind, and I'm surprised about it.

meaning: 'as' or 'in the capacity of' (used to indicate a role, function, or status).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'en tant que' + noun (e.g. en tant que professeur = as a teacher). It introduces the role or perspective from which something is said or done. Can also be followed by a past participle in formal constructions (less common). Not a complete phrase by itself—usually used with 'que' or followed by a role/description.
target_language_example: En tant que parent, je m'inquiète pour l'avenir.
native_language_example: As a parent, I worry about the future.

meaning: is/are at stake; concerns; depends on (something important)
additional_notes: Used in expressions like « il en va de » or « il en va de même ». Often appears as part of a larger phrase meaning that something is important for or affects someone/something (e.g. « il en va de la sécurité » = security is at stake). Literally built from pronoun en + verb aller + de. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Il en va de la réputation de l'entreprise.
native_language_example: The company's reputation is at stake.

target_language_multi_word_term: ne t'en va pas / t'en va pas
meaning: 'don't go' (informal, to one person).
additional_notes: This is the negative imperative of s'en aller (to go away/leave) used with the familiar tu form. The full form is ne t'en va pas; in spoken, casual French people often drop the 'ne' and may contract 'tu' to 't''. Use with friends, family, or children. 'S'en aller' requires the pronoun 'en' before the verb when speaking of leaving (itself often referring to leaving a place or situation).
target_language_example: Ne t'en va pas, attends-moi ici.
native_language_example: Don't go, wait for me here.

meaning: Here is/are (there's/there are) — used to present, point out or react to someone/something.
additional_notes: Informal idiomatic phrase often used to draw attention to a person or thing just mentioned or seen. Can mean 'here's another one', 'what a ...!', or simply 'there you go.' Tone depends on context and intonation: neutral when presenting (En voilà un extrait — Here's an excerpt), surprised or critical when commenting (En voilà un couillon — What a fool). Often followed by a noun or phrase.
target_language_example: En voilà un qui sait parler.
native_language_example: Here's one who knows how to speak.

meaning: to hold a grudge (against); to be angry with or resent someone
additional_notes: Commonly used as "en vouloir à quelqu'un" meaning to be upset with or resent someone. Literally composed of "en" + "vouloir" but not literal in meaning. Often appears in negative constructions (e.g. "je ne t'en veux pas" = "I'm not mad at you"). Use with a person as indirect object introduced by à (à quelqu'un).
target_language_example: Je t'en veux encore pour ce qui s'est passé hier.
native_language_example: I still hold a grudge against you for what happened yesterday.

meaning: used as part of constructions like 'en être à' to indicate a point, stage, count or amount reached in a sequence or process (English: 'at' or 'up to' in contexts like 'at the Xth stage' or 'we're at X').
additional_notes: Never used alone; appears in fixed expressions such as 'en être à' (e.g. 'J'en suis à trois tentatives', 'On en était à discuter...'). Common in spoken and written French to report progress, counts or stages. The literal components 'en' and 'à' don't convey the full meaning separately here; the phrase is semi-fixed and idiomatic.
target_language_example: On en était à en à trois tentatives quand il est arrivé.
native_language_example: We were at three attempts when he arrived.

meaning: be part of it
additional_notes: Here, en refers back to a group, plan, event, or activity already understood from context. en être is used to say that someone is involved, included, or participating.
target_language_example: Si vous organisez le voyage, j'aimerais en être.
native_language_example: If you're organizing the trip, I'd like to be part of it.

meaning: 'be so (about something)'.
additional_notes: Used after a question word (Comment, Pourquoi) to ask how someone can be so sure/confident/ certain about something previously mentioned (en = about it). 'Être si' modifies degree (so). Agreement in gender/number affects 'sûr/sûre' (or other adjectives). Common in questions: 'Comment peux-tu en être si sûr ?' = 'How can you be so sure about that?'.
target_language_example: Comment peux-tu en être si certain ?
native_language_example: How can you be so certain about that?

meaning: to be so (about it); to be so affected by that (e.g., so proud, so surprised, so tired)
additional_notes: This construction uses 'en' to refer back to a previously mentioned situation or thing (equivalent to 'about it' or 'of it') and 'être tellement' to intensify the state. It is typically followed by an adjective or past participle: 'J'en être tellement...' is not grammatically correct — the proper conjugation places the verb: e.g. 'J'en suis tellement fier.' However, the multi-word chunk 'en être tellement' appears within full conjugated forms like 'j'en être tellement' only when giving the bare infinitive or quoted fragment. Common in spoken and written French. Word order in actual sentences: 'J'en suis tellement...' or 'On en est tellement...'.
target_language_example: On en être tellement fiers qu'on en a parlé toute la soirée.
native_language_example: We were so proud about it that we talked about it all evening.

meaning: still well; still a lot / even quite (depending on context)
additional_notes: This short phrase combines 'encore' (still/yet/more) and 'bien' (well/very). Alone 'encore bien' is somewhat uncommon as a fixed phrase; its meaning depends on context and intonation. It can mean 'still well' (e.g., someone is still doing well) or reinforce quantity/degree similar to 'encore + adverb' = 'even/still quite'. Listen to context to decide whether it modifies a verb (encore bien dormi = still slept well) or a quantity (il y en a encore bien = there are still plenty).
target_language_example: Il travaille encore bien malgré la fatigue.
native_language_example: He is still working well despite the fatigue.

meaning: 'encore' = again/still; 'ce' = this/it — together they are not a fixed phrase; meaning depends on context (usually 'again this...' or 'still this...').
additional_notes: This is not an established fixed expression in French. You will sometimes see 'encore ce...' at the start of a clause to complain or emphasize repetition: e.g. 'Encore ce problème !' = 'This problem again!' or 'Encore ce bruit...' = 'That noise again...'. More commonly speakers use 'encore' with verbs (encore une fois, encore + verb) or with demonstratives as in examples above. Pay attention to word order and punctuation: it often appears as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Encore ce froid, ça devient pénible.
native_language_example: This cold again, it's getting annoying.

meaning: depends on context: 'more of' / 'still have' / part of adverb 'encore' + preposition 'de'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase with one meaning — it's the adverb 'encore' used before 'de' (or 'de' + noun) in several contexts: 1) 'encore de' + noun can mean 'more (of)' or 'even more (of)' (e.g. 'plus encore de réfugiés' = 'even more refugees'); 2) after verbs, 'encore de' often appears in questions or statements meaning 'still recovering from' or 'still have' (e.g. 'te remets-tu encore de…' = 'are you still recovering from…'); 3) in casual spoken French, 'y a encore de...' = 'there is still some...' (e.g. 'Y a encore de la peinture' = 'There is still paint.'). Use the full sentence to determine which sense applies.
target_language_example: Il reste encore de la soupe si tu veux.
native_language_example: There is still some soup left if you want.

meaning: 'still in the process of' or 'still (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Used before a verb (often with 'de' + infinitive: 'encore en train de ...') or before a présent participle to say that an action is ongoing and hasn't finished. Common in spoken and written French. Equivalent to English 'still doing' or 'still in the middle of'.
target_language_example: Je suis encore en train de finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I'm still in the process of finishing my homework.

meaning: a short linking phrase meaning 'still and' or 'again and' used to add another point—rare and stylistically marked
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common fixed expression on its own. 'Encore' means 'again', 'still', or 'more', and followed by 'et' ('and') it can introduce an additional (often contrasting or reinforcing) idea in literary or emphatic contexts: e.g. «Encore, et...». In everyday spoken French speakers more often use 'et encore' (meaning 'and still' / 'and moreover') or other connectors (comme, de plus, en plus). Be careful: 'encore et toujours' ('still and always') is a more natural phrase.
target_language_example: Il était en retard, encore et, pour ne rien arranger, la pluie a commencé.
native_language_example: He was late, and furthermore, to make matters worse, it started to rain.

meaning: again and again; repeatedly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action happens many times or continuously. Can be used with verbs (Elle le frappa encore et encore) or alone for emphasis (Encore et encore). Often interchangeable with 'à plusieurs reprises' or 'toujours'.
target_language_example: Il répète la même erreur encore et encore.
native_language_example: He repeats the same mistake again and again.

meaning: to do something again; to still be doing something (depending on context)
additional_notes: Depends on context and word order. 'Encore' before a verb generally means 'still' (ongoing action): e.g. 'Il travaille encore' = 'He is still working'. When 'encore' appears with an infinitive like 'encore faire', it can mean 'to do again' (similar to 'refaire') or indicate continuing to do something. This exact sequence ('encore faire') is less frequent than alternatives such as 'refaire' or 'encore une fois'. Pay attention to tense and placement to resolve meaning.
target_language_example: Je vais encore faire la même erreur si je n'y prête pas attention.
native_language_example: I will do the same mistake again if I don't pay attention.

meaning: 'still the' or 'again the' (literal combination of encore + definite article le).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's simply the adverb 'encore' ('still', 'again', 'more') followed by the masculine singular definite article 'le'. It appears in sentences like 'encore le même problème' (still the same problem) or 'encore le train en retard' (the train is late again). Use depends on the noun that follows ('le' agrees with a masculine singular noun).
target_language_example: C'est encore le même problème.
native_language_example: It's still the same problem.

meaning: 'me again' — nonstandard/fractured French where an English speaker inserts the English object pronoun 'me' after 'encore'; intended to mean 'moi encore' or 'encore moi'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not standard French. In correct French, use 'encore moi' or 'moi encore' instead of 'encore me'. 'Encore me' may appear in bilingual speech, informal writing by English speakers, or as a literal calque from English. Avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Désolé, encore me avec une autre question.
native_language_example: Sorry, me again with another question.

meaning: even less / much less / let alone
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is even less likely or possible than what was just mentioned. Often follows a negative clause (ne... pas / je n'avais pas) or a comparison. Equivalent to English 'let alone' or 'much less.' Can be placed after the first idea: 'Il ne peut pas X, encore moins Y.'
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas d'argent pour un café, encore moins pour un dîner au restaurant.
native_language_example: I don't have money for a coffee, let alone for a dinner at a restaurant.

meaning: 'even more' or 'more still' (to increase degree or intensity).
additional_notes: Used to strengthen a comparison or add emphasis. Can appear before or after the element it modifies (e.g., encore plus intéressant / Vous pourriez gagner encore plus). Common in everyday and written French.
target_language_example: Avec de la pratique, tu seras encore plus à l'aise.
native_language_example: With practice, you'll be even more comfortable.

meaning: literally 'still/again for' — used to indicate duration remaining or additional amount for something (e.g. 'still for' or 'for another').
additional_notes: 'Encore' means 'still', 'yet', or 'again'. When followed by 'pour' + a time or amount, 'encore pour' expresses how much time or quantity remains (e.g. 'encore pour 10 minutes' = 'for another 10 minutes'). It's not a fixed idiom on its own; you will usually see it as part of a longer phrase: 'encore pour X' or 'encore pour que...' In spoken French you may also hear 'il reste encore' instead of 'encore pour'.
target_language_example: Le film dure encore pour dix minutes.
native_language_example: The movie still runs for ten more minutes.

meaning: although / even though (expresses concession) or 'still that' in some contexts
additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession or to express surprise/doubt. In formal written French, 'encore que' often means 'although' and is followed by the subjunctive: "encore que ce soit...". In everyday speech, 'encore' + 'que' can appear in phrases like "tu veux encore que... ?" meaning "do you still want me to...?/Do you expect me to...?/Are you asking me again to...?" Context decides whether it's concessive ('although') or part of an expression meaning 'still that'.
target_language_example: Encore que ce soit difficile, je vais essayer.
native_language_example: Although it's difficult, I'll try.

meaning: a short, informal way to mean 'still some' or 'some more' (used before a noun or number)
additional_notes: Often used in spoken French before a quantity or noun to say there remains an additional amount (e.g. 'encore quelque chose', 'encore quelques'). Note that the more standard forms are 'encore un/une', 'encore des', or 'encore quelques' depending on number and gender. 'Encore quelque' by itself is incomplete and will usually be followed by a noun or number (e.g. 'encore quelque chose' or 'encore quelques minutes').
target_language_example: Tu veux encore quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Do you want something else to drink?

meaning: 'still your' or 'again your' — literal combination of encore (still/again) + ta (your, feminine singular).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase in French; it's simply the adverb encore followed by the possessive adjective ta. You will see encore used with verbs/adjectives (e.g. encore là, encore fatigué) to mean 'still' or 'again'. Ta is the informal singular 'your' used before a feminine noun (ta maison, ta sœur). Use together when referring to something feminine that is 'still' or 'again' belonging to 'you' (tu). Example: "encore ta valise" = "your suitcase again" or "your suitcase still here."
target_language_example: C'est encore ta robe sur la chaise ?
native_language_example: Is that your dress still on the chair?

meaning: one more
additional_notes: Common phrase used before a countable noun to request or mention an additional item or occurrence (e.g. encore un café = one more coffee). Can also be used with masculine singular nouns or numbers: 'encore une' for feminine nouns. Used in requests (Encore un, s'il vous plaît) or statements (Il en veut encore un).
target_language_example: Encore un, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: One more, please.

meaning: 'once again' / 'one more time' — to ask or state that something should be repeated.
additional_notes: Used to request or indicate repetition (of an action, statement, event) or to emphasize regret/ frustration when repeating something. Can appear at the start of a sentence as an interjection (e.g., 'Encore une fois, désolé !') or after a verb/object (e.g., 'Je te le demande encore une fois.').
target_language_example: Peux-tu répéter la phrase encore une fois ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat the sentence one more time?

meaning: literally 'again you' — used to express surprise, annoyance or recognition when someone appears again (e.g. 'you again').
additional_notes: This phrase combines encore ('again/still') and vous (formal/plural 'you'). Common in spoken French as an exclamation: 'Encore vous !' = 'You again!' Tone can be annoyed, surprised, or resigned depending on context. Use with vous for formal/neutral situations or when addressing more than one person; with a friend you'd more likely hear 'encore toi !'. Not a fixed idiom beyond this straightforward meaning.
target_language_example: Ah, encore vous... je pensais que vous étiez partis.
native_language_example: Oh, you again... I thought you had left.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase; a sequence where 'encore' (still/again/again more) appears adjacent to the clitic pronoun 'y' (there/to it). Its meaning depends on sentence context: typically 'still there', 'again there', or 'again to it'.
additional_notes: The exact sequence 'encore y' is uncommon as an isolated chunk because French clitic pronouns normally appear immediately before the verb, so word order often splits or reorders these elements (e.g., 'Il y est encore', 'J'y retourne encore'). 'Encore' can modify time (still), repetition (again), or quantity (more). 'Y' replaces a prepositional phrase introduced by 'à' or indicates a location. To interpret 'encore y' correctly, read the whole clause and adjust pronoun placement if needed; in spoken or poetic contexts you might encounter 'encore y' straddling a break or punctuation.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas encore y aller.
native_language_example: I don't want to go there again yet.

meaning: used to add a final contrasting remark meaning 'and that's still...' / 'at least that's...'.
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase often used to append a qualifying or mitigating comment after a statement. It can introduce something slightly positive or a consolation compared with what was just said (similar to 'at least' or 'still' in English). Common in spoken French. Depending on context, it may follow a negative or critical remark to point out one redeeming aspect.
target_language_example: Il ne sait pas cuisiner, encore ça il est bon pour le dessert.
native_language_example: He can't cook, but at least he's good with dessert.

meaning: 'at the place of' or 'place in/on the ...' (used when followed by a noun or location)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it's the noun endroit (place) followed by the preposition au (a contraction of à + le). It appears before a masculine singular noun: endroit au marché, endroit au bord de la mer (more naturally: endroit au bord de la mer). In many contexts French speakers would simply say 'à' + location (à la plage, au parc) or use 'endroit' with de (endroit de/à) depending on structure. Use 'endroit au' only when the following word is a masculine singular noun and you mean 'place at the ...'.
target_language_example: C'est un endroit au bord du lac.
native_language_example: It's a place on the shore of the lake.

meaning: in the right place at the right time
additional_notes: Used to describe being present where something important or lucky happens. Equivalent to English idiom; can refer to a fortunate coincidence or timely presence. Often used in conversational contexts to explain why someone benefited from an event.
target_language_example: Il était à l'endroit au bon moment et a trouvé le portefeuille perdu.
native_language_example: He was in the right place at the right time and found the lost wallet.

meaning: 'endroit' = place, spot; 'me' = me (object pronoun).
additional_notes: This looks like two words but is not a set phrase in French. 'Endroit' means a place or location. 'Me' is the unstressed direct or indirect object pronoun meaning 'me' (to me / me). In natural French they usually do not appear together as 'endroit me'—word order and prepositions are needed (e.g. 'un endroit pour moi', 'cet endroit me plaît', 'donne-moi l'endroit'). Use a preposition (à, pour) or put the pronoun before the verb.
target_language_example: Cet endroit me plaît beaucoup.
native_language_example: I really like this place.

meaning: such a place / a place like that (usually with disapproval or surprise).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a place just mentioned or pointed to, often expressing surprise, disapproval, or disbelief about being there or who would be there. Common in questions: Que fais-tu dans un endroit pareil ? — What are you doing in a place like that? Can be informal; tone matters (critical or incredulous).
target_language_example: Pourquoi es-tu allé dans un endroit pareil ?
native_language_example: Why did you go to a place like that?

meaning: 'place to' or 'place for' (used when followed by an infinitive to indicate a place where something is done).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before an infinitive: endroit à + infinitive = 'a place to (do something)'. Often used with verbs like aller (un endroit à visiter), trouver (un endroit à louer), or chercher (un endroit à manger). The structure is compositional: endroit = place, à = to/for. Use un/une before endroit when needed (un endroit à visiter).
target_language_example: Connais-tu un endroit à visiter près d'ici ?
native_language_example: Do you know a place to visit near here?

meaning: child of / child belonging to (used informally or dialectally to indicate possession or association)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom in standard French. Standard usage for possession is 'l'enfant de ...'. 'enfant à' occurs in regional or colloquial speech (e.g. 'l'enfant à Marie' = 'Marie's child') and in descriptive phrases like 'enfant à charge' (dependent child) where 'à' begins a complement.
target_language_example: L'enfant à Pierre attend devant la porte.
native_language_example: Pierre's child is waiting in front of the door.

meaning: 'child of' or 'son/daughter of' (indicates parentage or origin)
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate whose child someone is or to express origin/association (e.g. 'un enfant de Paris' = a child from Paris). If used literally for biological parentage, follow with the parent(s) or place. Not a fixed idiom—meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: C'est un enfant de Marie.
native_language_example: He/She is a child of Marie.

meaning: 'the child is' — third-person statement describing a child.
additional_notes: This combines the noun 'enfant' (child) and the verb 'est' (is, from être). It's used to describe a child's state, behavior, condition, or characteristic. In normal French you would often say 'Cet enfant est...' (This child is...) or 'Mon enfant est...' (My child is...). Word order is noun + être + adjective or complement.
target_language_example: Mon enfant est gentil et curieux.
native_language_example: My child is kind and curious.

meaning: a spoiled child (someone who is overly pampered and behaves entitled).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person (often a child) who expects special treatment, complains, or misbehaves because they get what they want. Can be literal (an actual child) or figurative (an adult behaving childishly). Often used reproachfully.
target_language_example: Ne sois pas un enfant gâté — partage ton jouet.
native_language_example: Don't be a spoiled child — share your toy.

meaning: 'no child' / 'not any child' (used to say that not a single child should ...).
additional_notes: Aucun ... ne is a negative construction meaning 'no/none' when referring to people or things. It is followed by a verb with 'ne' before the verb and often nothing after (the second negative word is 'aucun'). When used before a noun it agrees in gender/number: aucun enfant (masculine singular). Often translated as 'no child' or 'not any child' and used to make strong general statements.
target_language_example: Aucun enfant ne doit être puni sans raison.
native_language_example: No child should be punished without reason.

meaning: Not a fixed French phrase; appears to be two words meaning 'child can' (enfant = child, peut = can/may).
additional_notes: This is not a standard multi-word expression. It's simply the noun 'enfant' (child) followed by the verb 'peut' (3rd-person singular of pouvoir). It would appear in a sentence like 'L'enfant peut...' ('The child can...'). You must include an article or subject determiner (l', un, cet, etc.) or change word order for correct French. Example completions: 'L'enfant peut venir.' 'Un enfant peut apprendre.'
target_language_example: L'enfant peut jouer dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The child can play in the garden.

meaning: an only child (a child with no siblings).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who has no brothers or sisters. Gender agreement appears in surrounding words (e.g., 'un enfant unique' for a male, 'une enfant unique' or more commonly 'une fille unique' for a female). Commonly asked in questions about family.
target_language_example: Je suis enfant unique, je n'ai pas de frères ni de sœurs.
native_language_example: I am an only child; I don't have any brothers or sisters.

meaning: 'child of' or 'child at' — used to indicate a child belonging to or associated with someone/something (often followed by a name, place or descriptor).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase in French; it's the noun enfant followed by the preposition à. Its exact meaning depends on what follows: e.g. enfant à Marie (Marie’s child), enfant à l'école (child at school), enfant à besoins spéciaux (child with special needs). Word order and articles matter (un enfant à Marie vs. l'enfant de Marie — de is more common to indicate possession). Use «de» for clear possession (l'enfant de Paul = Paul's child). «enfant à» appears in contexts like describing affiliation, location, or function.
target_language_example: Elle est un enfant à besoins spéciaux dans cette école.
native_language_example: She is a child with special needs at that school.

meaning: 'children at' or 'children in/of the' (part of a larger phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself — it's the beginning of a noun phrase where 'enfants' (children) is followed by a preposition + article contraction (e.g. 'au' = à + le). Expect a location, age group, event or role to follow: for example 'enfants au parc' (children at the park) or 'enfants au primaire' (children in primary school). Grammar note: 'au' = 'à' + 'le' and is used before masculine singular nouns. If the noun is feminine use 'à la', plural use 'aux'.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup d'enfants au parc cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: There are a lot of children at the park this afternoon.

meaning: "children in" (a fragment) — not a complete phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This sequence is incomplete in French. 'Enfants en' usually appears before a noun or adjective that describes the group, for example 'enfants en bas âge' (young children) or 'enfants en difficulté' (children in difficulty). You should expect another word after 'en' (a noun phrase introduced by 'en' or an adjective). Do not use 'enfants en' by itself.
target_language_example: Des enfants en bas âge jouent dans le parc.
native_language_example: Young children are playing in the park.

meaning: 'children and' — simply the word enfants followed by et (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the plural noun enfants (children) followed by the conjunction et (and). You will see this when listing items (e.g. 'enfants et parents' = 'children and parents'). Pay attention to agreement of adjectives that follow and to liaison: in casual speech, a consonant sound may link to a following vowel (les enfants et les adultes → [lez‿ɑ̃fɑ̃ e le.z‿adylt]).
target_language_example: Les enfants et les parents sont invités à la fête.
native_language_example: The children and the parents are invited to the party.

meaning: in order to; so as to (used before an infinitive to express purpose)
additional_notes: Formal/neutral phrasing for expressing purpose. More common alternatives are "afin de" and "pour" + infinitive. "enfin de" is less frequent and can sound literary or slightly old-fashioned; make sure it's followed by an infinitive (e.g., "enfin de terminer"). Do not confuse with the interjection "enfin!" (meaning "finally!" or "come on!").
target_language_example: Il parle doucement enfin de se faire comprendre.
native_language_example: He speaks quietly in order to be understood.

meaning: 'finally' or 'at last' with a demonstrative/clarifying nuance (literally 'finally there' or 'finally that').
additional_notes: enfin alone commonly means 'finally' or 'well' and is frequent in spoken French. When followed by là (written with accent for 'there'), as in 'enfin là', it adds a locational or demonstrative nuance meaning 'finally there' or can be used to clarify/correct a previous statement ('well, actually...'). Note spelling: la (without accent) is the definite article 'the'; là (with accent) means 'there'. In casual speech 'enfin là' may be reduced and sound like 'enfin la' — watch context and pronunciation.
target_language_example: Il est enfin la, celui dont je t'ai parlé.
native_language_example: He is finally there, the one I told you about.

meaning: 'broke' or 'violated' (as in 'broke the' or 'violated the' — used with rules, laws, etc.)
additional_notes: Past participle form of 'enfreindre' (il/elle a enfreint). Commonly used with 'les' + noun (e.g., les règles, la loi). Means to disobey, break, or violate something formal (rules, laws, regulations). Use with avoir in compound past: 'a enfreint'.
target_language_example: Il a enfreint les règles et a reçu une sanction.
native_language_example: He broke the rules and received a penalty.

meaning: 'enemies of' — indicates who or what someone is an enemy of.
additional_notes: A simple possession/relationship construction: ennemis (plural noun) + de + noun/pronoun. Used to say that someone or something opposes another person, group, idea, or thing. Can refer to literal enemies (people at war) or figurative/ideological opponents. Word order: ennemis de + X (e.g., ennemis de la liberté).
target_language_example: Ils sont les ennemis de la paix.
native_language_example: They are the enemies of peace.

meaning: taught the (something) — past participle + definite article; part of a past passive or compound construction referring to teaching.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence: 'enseigné' is the past participle of 'enseigner' (to teach) and 'le' is the masculine singular definite article or direct object pronoun. It appears in contexts like 'a été enseigné le cours' (was taught the course) or 'il l'a enseigné' (he taught it) where word order and auxiliaries change meaning. Pay attention to agreement when used with être (e.g. 'les cours ont été enseignés') and to whether 'le' is an article ('le cours') or a pronoun ('je l'ai enseigné' → 'I taught it').
target_language_example: Le professeur a enseigné le cours d'histoire hier.
native_language_example: The teacher taught the history class yesterday.

meaning: 'together at' or 'together with' (followed by a noun introduced by au = à + le).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but the combination of ensemble (together) + au (contraction of à + le). It's used when saying that people or things are together at or with a masculine singular place or thing: e.g. "ensemble au parc" = together at the park. Remember agreement/contracted forms: use "ensemble à la" before feminine singular, "ensemble aux" before plural, and simply "ensemble" can stand alone.
target_language_example: Nous sommes ensemble au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: We are together at the cinema tonight.

meaning: together in / all together in (used to say people/things are located or acting together inside something).
additional_notes: Used when describing people or objects being together within a place or situation. Often followed by a noun or phrase indicating the location or context (e.g., "ensemble dans la même pièce", "ensemble dans ce projet"). Can also appear in sentences like "nous sommes ensemble dans cette épreuve" meaning "we're all in this (situation) together."
target_language_example: Nous sommes ensemble dans ce projet.
native_language_example: We are all together in this project.

meaning: together in/with (used before a material, color, or descriptor to mean 'made of' or 'in' when describing a set or outfit).
additional_notes: Common in fashion/context descriptions: 'ensemble en laine' = 'an outfit made of wool'; 'ensemble en bleu' = 'a coordinated outfit in blue'. It links 'ensemble' (set/outfit) with the material or characteristic introduced by 'en'. Not used alone; needs a noun or adjective after 'en'.
target_language_example: Elle porte un bel ensemble en lin pour l'été.
native_language_example: She is wearing a lovely linen outfit for the summer.

meaning: 'together for' or 'as a set for' (depends on context); often introduces purpose or indicates items grouped for something.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiomatic phrase on its own. 'Ensemble' means 'together' or 'set', and 'pour' means 'for'. Combined, they can appear in different constructions: e.g. 'travailler ensemble pour...' (work together for [a goal]) or 'un ensemble pour bébé' (a set for a baby). Pay attention to context to know whether it means 'together to/for' (action + purpose) or 'a set intended for' (noun phrase).
target_language_example: Ils travaillent ensemble pour protéger la forêt.
native_language_example: They are working together to protect the forest.

meaning: together with; along with; plus (used to indicate accompaniment or addition).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to mean 'together with' or 'along with' someone/something. Common in expressions like "ensemble à la maison" (together at home) or when listing items grouped together. Pay attention to agreement/context—often appears simply as "ensemble" (together) or in constructions like "être ensemble à" (to be together at). Not a fixed idiom on its own; its meaning depends on the words that follow.
target_language_example: Nous sommes ensemble à la fête ce soir.
native_language_example: We are together at the party tonight.

meaning: together to (a feminine singular place or event).
additional_notes: Combines ensemble (together) + à la (to the [feminine singular noun]). Use when saying that people went or worked together to a specific feminine place: à la bibliothèque, à la plage, à la ferme. Agreement in past participle follows standard rules (e.g., nous sommes allés/allées depending on gender). For masculine or mixed places use 'ensemble au' (à + le) or 'ensemble aux' for plural.
target_language_example: Nous sommes allés ensemble à la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: We went together to the library.

meaning: to hear/understand that (used when reporting what you heard or think you heard)
additional_notes: Literally from entendre (to hear) + ce (that/it). Often used to report information someone heard or to check what was understood. Can appear in expressions like «entendre ce que…» (to hear/understand what…) or in constructions such as «entendre dire que…» (to hear it said that). In everyday French, entendre can refer both to physical hearing and to grasping/learning news. The fixed sequence 'entendre ce' is typically followed by a relative clause (e.g. «entendre ce que…») or by an indirect report.
target_language_example: Il paraît que tu as entendu ce que j'ai dit — mais tu n'as pas l'air d'avoir entendu ce que je voulais vraiment dire.
native_language_example: It seems you heard what I said — but you don't seem to have heard what I really meant.

meaning: to hear about (someone/something); to learn or be told of.
additional_notes: Used when referring to hearing news or information about a person, event, or situation. Often appears with a noun or pronoun introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'entendre de lui', 'entendre de cette affaire'). Common in expressions like 'j'ai entendu dire' (I heard that / I was told). Note: 'entendre' alone means 'to hear' (sound); 'entendre de' focuses on hearing about or being informed of something.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu de bonnes nouvelles de ton projet.
native_language_example: I heard some good news about your project.

meaning: to hear voices (i.e., perceive speech or voices when no one is present); often used to describe auditory hallucinations.
additional_notes: Used to describe experiencing auditory hallucinations (hearing voices). Common in medical, psychological, or everyday descriptions of someone hearing things that aren't there. Not idiomatic — it literally means "to hear voices." Can be used in both clinical and informal contexts, but be sensitive: it refers to a symptom and can be stigmatizing if used carelessly.
target_language_example: Il a commencé à entendre des voix pendant les nuits d'insomnie.
native_language_example: He began to hear voices during sleepless nights.

meaning: to hear (someone) say; to hear that (something is said/rumored).
additional_notes: Used to report information heard from others or rumors. Often followed by a clause introduced with que (entendre dire que...) or by an infinitive (entendre dire + infinitive) and can imply secondhand or unconfirmed information: 'I heard that...'.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu dire qu'ils vont déménager l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: I heard that they're going to move next year.

meaning: to hear (someone) say that; to hear that (used to report information heard from others, often as hearsay).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information learned indirectly. Construction: entendre dire que + clause. Often signals the speaker is reporting what they've heard rather than asserting firsthand knowledge. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu dire que le cinéma va fermer cet été.
native_language_example: I heard that the cinema is going to close this summer.

meaning: 'to hear the' (followed by a plural noun or clause).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb entendre ('to hear') followed by the plural definite article les. It appears in contexts describing perceiving sounds or hearing statements/things. In natural sentences the infinitive + article form typically appears after another verb (e.g., pouvoir entendre les, vouloir entendre les, faire entendre les) or in reported constructions (e.g., entendre les + noun/phrase). The phrase must be completed by a plural noun or clause. Conjugate entendre as needed in full sentences (j'entends, tu entends, il entend, etc.).
target_language_example: Je peux entendre les voitures qui passent.
native_language_example: I can hear the cars passing.

meaning: hear about
additional_notes: Used in two related ways: 1) as 'entendre parler de' meaning 'to hear about' someone or something (e.g. 'Vous avez dû entendre parler de moi' = 'You must have heard about me'). 2) in negative constructions 'ne pas vouloir en entendre parler' meaning 'to not want to hear about it/that' (to refuse to discuss or consider something). The pronoun 'en' or the preposition 'de' often appears before the thing referred to.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus en entendre parler.
native_language_example: I don't want to hear about it anymore.

meaning: 'to hear about' (to hear someone mention or talk about something/someone).
additional_notes: Used when you become aware of something because someone mentioned it or you heard others discuss it. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. entendre parler de quelqu'un / de quelque chose). Can be used in various tenses: J'ai entendu parler de, Tu entendras parler de, Nous entendons parler de. Not the same as 'entendre' meaning 'to hear' alone — this phrase has the idiomatic sense 'to hear about'.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu parler de ce film, mais je ne l'ai pas encore vu.
native_language_example: I heard about that movie, but I haven't seen it yet.

meaning: to hear you (familiar) — literally 'to hear your...'; used when hearing what someone says or will say
additional_notes: This is the verb entendre (to hear) followed by a possessive adjective (ta = your, feminine singular). Alone, 'entendre ta' is incomplete: it's usually followed by a noun (e.g. 'entendre ta voix' = to hear your voice) or appears in spoken fragments like 'J'adore t'entendre' or 'Je vais entendre ta proposition'. In casual speech the pronoun may combine: 't'entendre' (to hear you). Use 'entendre te' only in special constructions; typical spoken form is 't'entendre'.
target_language_example: J'aimerais entendre ta chanson demain.
native_language_example: I'd like to hear your song tomorrow.

meaning: 'do you hear/understand (something)'; used to ask if someone hears or understands what is being said
additional_notes: This looks like part of a question using the verb entendre (to hear or to understand) plus quelque (some/any). On its own it is incomplete and uncommon; you'd normally see full phrases like «Tu entends quelque chose ?» (Do you hear something?) or «Tu entends ?» (Do you hear/understand?). For asking if someone understands, French speakers more often use «Tu comprends ?». For hearing, use entendre with quelque chose or rien: «Tu entends quelque chose ? / Tu n'entends rien ?».
target_language_example: Tu entends quelque chose dehors ?
native_language_example: Do you hear something outside?

meaning: 'heard what' — used to ask or state whether someone heard something that was said.
additional_notes: Often appears in questions or statements about whether a specific remark was heard (As-tu entendu ce que... / J'ai entendu ce que...). It can be followed by a clause introduced by "je/tu/il/elle/on/il a dit...". Common in both formal and informal contexts. Literal translation: "heard what".
target_language_example: As-tu entendu ce que Marie a annoncé ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what Marie announced?

meaning: 'heard what I' — an incomplete fragment typically appearing inside questions or confirmations about whether someone heard what the speaker said; not a standalone sentence.
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment. In French you normally need an auxiliary verb before entendu (e.g. «Tu as entendu…») or to complete the clause after «ce que je» (e.g. «ce que je viens de dire»). The fragment might appear in spoken corrections or repetitions like «Entendu ce que je… ?» though that exact ordering is uncommon; more natural full forms are «Tu as entendu ce que je (disais) ?» or «Vous avez entendu ce que je viens de dire ?». Entendu is the past participle of entendre (to hear).
target_language_example: Tu as entendu ce que je ? (fragment used in hesitant speech)
native_language_example: Did you hear what I (said)?

meaning: heard (some) bangs/noise (usually blows, shots or knocks).
additional_notes: Literal: 'heard blows' or 'heard knocks'. Used to report hearing loud, sudden sounds (gunshots, knocks on a door, banging). Context tells whether it's violent (coups, coups de feu) or just knocks. Often part of a past-tense report: J'ai entendu des coups = I heard banging/knocks/shots.
target_language_example: Hier soir, j'ai entendu des coups à la porte.
native_language_example: Last night I heard knocks at the door.

meaning: heard a (single) knock or shot; heard a sound once
additional_notes: Literal: 'entendre' = to hear, 'un coup' = a blow/knock/shot/sound. Commonly used to say you heard one occurrence of a noise (e.g., a knock at the door, a gunshot, a sudden sound). Context determines which English word to use (knock, bang, shot). Not an idiom — literal and compositional.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu un coup à la porte.
native_language_example: I heard a knock at the door.

meaning: heard a (sudden) sound of / heard a blow (often followed by a noun: e.g. 'entendu un coup de feu' = heard a gunshot)
additional_notes: Phrase is a sequence: 'entendu' (past participle of 'entendre' = to hear) + 'un coup de' (literally 'a hit/strike of' used to form compounds like 'un coup de feu' = gunshot, 'un coup de klaxon' = honk). It usually appears with a following noun that specifies the sound or action. Without the noun it feels incomplete in French.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu un coup de tonnerre cette nuit.
native_language_example: I heard a clap of thunder last night.

meaning: heard a (feminine noun) — past participle 'entendu' + indefinite article 'une'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: entendu (heard) followed by une (a/an feminine). It appears in sentences like «J'ai entendu une chanson» (I heard a song). The past participle may agree in certain compound tenses with a preceding direct object, but with the auxiliary avoir it usually stays 'entendu'. Useful for constructing simple past statements about hearing something feminine in French.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu une histoire intéressante.
native_language_example: I heard an interesting story.

meaning: 'among other things' or 'among others' (used to indicate one item in a larger list)
additional_notes: Used to mention one or several examples while implying there are more.
