Can introduce examples within a sentence (often followed by a noun) or stand alone as a short response meaning 'among other things' / 'among others'. Formality: neutral — appropriate in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a travaillé sur des romans, des essais, entre autres.
native_language_example: He worked on novels, essays, among other things.

meaning: between me / among me (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used with 'entre' to indicate a position or relationship involving the speaker. With people it means 'between me and [someone]' (e.g., a choice or relationship). With physical position it means 'between me and you/another person' (e.g., someone/something located in the space separating the speaker and another). In some sentences you will see 'entre moi et...' to show 'between me and...'.
target_language_example: Garde ce secret entre moi et toi.
native_language_example: Keep this secret between you and me.

meaning: 'between us' — used literally or to introduce a confidential remark (like 'between you and me').
additional_notes: Can be literal (describing a relationship or distance between people) or idiomatic to signal secrecy/intimacy: used to share a private opinion or fact not meant for others. Tone can be casual; often placed at start of sentence.
target_language_example: Entre nous, je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I'm not sure that's a good idea.

meaning: in parentheses; placed inside parentheses (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (to put text between parentheses: ( )) and figuratively to add a side comment or remark. In English this corresponds to 'in parentheses' or 'by the way' when used as an aside. Can precede a comment: "Entre parenthèses, ..." meaning 'as an aside'.
target_language_example: Entre parenthèses, il a oublié de fermer la fenêtre.
native_language_example: As an aside, he forgot to close the window.

meaning: between one / among one (literal); typically part of a larger expression (not normally used alone).
additional_notes: Alone, 'entre un' is unusual in French; you will most often see 'entre' followed by two items (e.g. 'entre A et B') or numeric ranges ('entre un et deux'). If you see 'entre un' it usually continues with 'et' + another number or item (e.g. 'entre un et trois'). It can also appear inside phrases like 'entre un...' meaning 'somewhere between one...' The phrase by itself is not a complete expression.
target_language_example: Il y a entre un et deux kilomètres jusqu'au village.
native_language_example: There are between one and two kilometers to the village.

meaning: 'to come into play' / 'to become relevant or start to take effect'.
additional_notes: Used when a factor, person or element begins to have an influence on a situation or process. Common in both spoken and written French. Can be followed by nouns (e.g., 'un facteur') or used impersonally ('... entre en jeu').
target_language_example: Quand le budget est serré, la créativité va entrer en jeu.
native_language_example: When the budget is tight, creativity is going to come into play.

meaning: to enter (data, a number, a value) — i.e., to type or input something into a form, field, or device.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a direct object for what is being entered (e.g., entrer le code, entrer la date). Often used for keyboards, forms, machines, or computer fields. If referring to entering a place, use 'entrer dans' or 'entrer à' instead ('entrer le' is specific to entering data/values). Imperative form often appears as 'Entrez le ...' in instructions.
target_language_example: Veuillez entrer le code PIN avant de continuer.
native_language_example: Please enter the PIN code before continuing.

meaning: 'entered' or 'went into' (masculine singular subject) followed by 'au' (to the/at the).
additional_notes: Entré is the past participle of entrer and must agree in gender/number with the subject when used with être (e.g., il est entré, elle est entrée, ils sont entrés). 'Au' is the contraction of 'à le' and precedes a masculine singular noun (e.g., au bureau, au magasin). Together 'entré au' appears in sentences like 'Il est entré au bureau' = 'He entered the office.' For feminine subjects use 'entrée au' (but note some speakers prefer 'dans le' for 'into the').
target_language_example: Il est entré au musée cet après-midi.
native_language_example: He entered the museum this afternoon.

meaning: 'entered into' or 'went into' (masculine singular past participle + preposition 'en')
additional_notes: This is the past participle of entrer (entré) followed by the preposition en. It often appears as part of a compound verb phrase describing entering a place, a period, a state, or starting something (e.g., entré en ville, entré en guerre, entré en fonction). Agreement of 'entré' depends on the subject when used with être (il est entré, elle est entrée). Here 'entré en' is masculine singular form; for feminine use 'entrée en'.
target_language_example: Il est entré en ville ce matin.
native_language_example: He entered the town this morning.

meaning: 'came into possession' or 'took possession' (obtained ownership or control of something).
additional_notes: Used to describe when someone acquires ownership, control or physical possession of an item, property, funds, etc. Often appears in formal or legal contexts (e.g., property, inheritance, delivery). Can refer to a past event: 'être entré en possession' = 'has come into possession'.
target_language_example: Il est entré en possession de la maison après le règlement de la succession.
native_language_example: He came into possession of the house after the estate was settled.

meaning: 'came into possession of' / 'obtained' (how someone got something).
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone acquired or came to own an object. Formal/neutral register; often appears in questions about origin, ownership, or provenance (e.g., paintings, documents). Can be used with être in passé composé: «vous êtes entré en possession de…».
target_language_example: Comment es-tu entré en possession de ce tableau ?
native_language_example: How did you come into possession of this painting?

meaning: 'how did you come into possession of' / 'how did you obtain (something)'
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone acquired or obtained an object (often a valuable item like a painting). Formal/register can be slightly formal; often used in legal, journalistic, or polite contexts. The structure: entrer en possession de + noun (entrer is conjugated to agree with subject).
target_language_example: Comment es-tu entrée en possession de ce tableau ?
native_language_example: How did you come into possession of this painting?

meaning: send the (you — informal singular or imperative); 'send' + direct plural object (les).
additional_notes: Form of the verb envoyer. In imperatives: 'Envoie les ...' = 'Send the ...' (spoken to one person informally). In statements: appears as 'je vous envoie les ...' (I send/send you) or 'que ... vous envoie les ...' (subjunctive). 'Les' is the plural direct object pronoun/article 'the' or a neutral plural object. Subject and tense change meaning (envoie = 1st person present 'j'envoie' or 3rd person/subjunctive 'qu'il/elle envoie', but alone 'envoie' is the 2nd person singular imperative or 3rd person singular indicative). Context determines whether 'les' refers to children, data, forms, etc.
target_language_example: Envoie les invitations avant vendredi.
native_language_example: Send the invitations before Friday.

meaning: 'to send by' or 'to send via' (followed by the method or channel).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the means or channel used to send something: envoyer par + (nom du moyen). Common continuations: envoyer par e‑mail, envoyer par SMS, envoyer par la poste, envoyer par courrier, envoyer par transporteur. When indicating a recipient, French more often uses envoyer quelque chose à quelqu'un. 'Par' here marks the method, route or intermediary.
target_language_example: Je veux envoyer par la poste ce colis demain.
native_language_example: I want to send this package by post tomorrow.

meaning: sent by / dispatched from (used to indicate who sent something or who someone represents).
additional_notes: Envoyé de is the past participle 'envoyé' (sent) followed by 'de' (by/from). Commonly appears in formal contexts: to say an item (email, letter, package) was sent by someone (envoyé de Marie) or to introduce someone as a representative of an organization (envoyé de l'ambassade = envoy of the embassy). For email headers, you may also see «envoyé de» to show the sending device or app. Use the right article after de when naming an organization (de + le → du; de + la stays de la; de + les → des).
target_language_example: Ce message a été envoyé de la mairie.
native_language_example: This message was sent by the town hall.

meaning: sent on (a specific date) / sent the
additional_notes: Commonly appears in formal or administrative contexts (emails, letters, invoices) to indicate the date something was sent: 'envoyé le + date'. It is the past participle 'envoyé' (sent) followed by the definite article 'le' introducing the date. If the subject is feminine plural (e.g. 'les lettres envoyées le...'), agreement may change ('envoyée(s)').
target_language_example: Courrier envoyé le 12 mars 2026.
native_language_example: Mail sent on March 12, 2026.

meaning: sent his/her/its (something).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle envoyé (sent) plus a possessive object pronoun son (his/its). In French you would more commonly see envoyé followed by a noun (envoyé son message) or envoyé + direct object pronoun (l'a envoyé). 'envoyé son' by itself is incomplete and needs a noun (son + noun) — e.g. envoyé son courrier = 'sent his mail'.
target_language_example: Il a envoyé son CV hier.
native_language_example: He sent his résumé yesterday.

meaning: sent a card (e.g., greeting card, post card).
additional_notes: Past participle phrase using envoyer (to send). Commonly used when saying someone sent a physical or digital card for a birthday, holiday, thank-you, etc. You can change the subject or tense: J'ai envoyé une carte (I sent a card), Il/Elle m'a envoyé une carte (He/She sent me a card).
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai envoyé une carte pour l'anniversaire de ma tante.
native_language_example: Yesterday I sent a card for my aunt's birthday.

meaning: sent a (holiday) card / sent a card of (something).
additional_notes: This is the past participle form used in perfect tense (avoir + envoyé) followed by the object 'une carte de ...' (e.g. 'carte de Noël' = Christmas card). In questions or statements the auxiliary (avez-vous, as-tu, a) changes. Replace 'Noël' with other occasions (Naissance, Vœux, Remerciement) to specify card type.
target_language_example: Je t'ai envoyé une carte de vœux la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I sent you a greeting card last week.

meaning: a mistake in (something) / an error on (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an error concerns a particular item, person, date, amount, etc. Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (erreur à la date, erreur à votre facture, erreur à son nom). In many contexts French speakers prefer 'erreur sur' (error on/about) — both are used, but 'erreur sur' is more frequent for items or subjects; 'erreur à' appears often with things like 'erreur à la saisie' or legal/administrative phrases. Use context to choose 'à' vs 'sur'.
target_language_example: Il y a une erreur à votre facture.
native_language_example: There is an error on your bill.

meaning: 'errors of' / 'mistakes in' (used before a noun)
additional_notes: This is the plural noun 'erreurs' (errors) followed by the preposition 'de' linking to the thing in which the errors occur: erreurs de calcul, erreurs de jugement, erreurs de frappe, etc. It must be completed by a noun or gerund/infinitive phrase (erreurs de compréhension, erreurs de conjugaison). In English it usually corresponds to 'errors in' or 'mistakes of'.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup d'erreurs de frappe dans ce document.
native_language_example: There are many typing errors in this document.

meaning: This appears to be a mistaken or ungrammatical French phrase; likely attempts at either "tu es allé trop loin" (you went/acted too far) or "c'est allé trop loin" (it went too far).
additional_notes:
As written, "es allé trop" is not correct French. Possible intended meanings:
- "Tu es allé trop loin" = "You went too far" (saying someone exceeded a limit). Use with tu/il/elle/etc. and agree past participle when needed.
- "C'est allé trop loin" = "It went too far" (a situation escalated beyond acceptable limits).
If you meant "you went too far" speaking to one person informally, use "tu es allé trop loin" (male) or "tu es allée trop loin" (female). For formal/plural "vous êtes allé/allée/allés/allées trop loin" depending on gender/number.
If you meant "it went too far," use "ça a été / c'est allé trop loin"; the most natural is "ça a été trop loin" or "c'est allé trop loin."
target_language_example: Tu es allé trop loin en le critiquant devant tout le monde.
native_language_example: You went too far criticizing him in front of everyone.

meaning: are made
additional_notes: Not usually a standalone fixed expression. It combines es (from être, used with tu) and fait ('made' or 'done'). The exact meaning depends on context; for example, in tu es fait pour..., it means 'you're made/cut out for...'.
target_language_example: Tu es fait pour ce métier.
native_language_example: You're cut out for this job.

meaning: 'are you ...ing' (part of the present progressive construction 'es-tu en train de ...')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions using the progressive structure 'être en train de + infinitive' to mean 'to be in the middle of doing something'. In questions invert the subject: 'Qu'es-tu en train de faire ?' = 'What are you doing?'. You will usually see the full phrase 'es-tu en train de'.
target_language_example: Qu'es-tu en train de préparer ?
native_language_example: What are you preparing?

meaning: are enough
additional_notes: This is the second-person singular (tu) form of être (tu es) followed by assez. It means 'you are enough' or 'you are sufficient' depending on context. 'Assez' can also mean 'enough' when modifying verbs/adjectives (e.g. 'assez grand' = 'big enough'). This phrase is compositional and can be translated literally. It is neutral/register-appropriate.
target_language_example: Tu es assez pour moi.
native_language_example: You are enough for me.

meaning: you are tall enough / you are big enough
additional_notes: This is the informal second-person singular (tu) form with the verb être (es) + assez (enough) + grand (tall/big). Use to say someone or something has sufficient size or height. Can apply to physical size or figurative 'ready'/'sufficient' when paired with adjectives. For formal or plural 'you', use 'êtes assez grand' (vous).
target_language_example: Tu es assez grand pour monter sur cette attraction.
native_language_example: You are tall enough to go on this ride.

meaning: are also
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb 'es' (2nd-person singular of 'être' = 'you are') and 'aussi' ('also/too'). It commonly appears in responses or statements meaning 'you are also' or 'are you also...'. Word order: 'tu es aussi...' (you are also ...) — note that in informal spoken French 'tu en es aussi sûr' uses 'en' and changes meaning ('are you that sure of it too'). Be careful: some example sentences show nonstandard word order or grammar (e.g., 'tu es aussi un cousin ?' = 'are you a cousin too?').
target_language_example: Tu es aussi fatigué ?
native_language_example: Are you tired too?

additional_notes: This sequence "es avec" is not a standard fixed French phrase. It looks like two separate words that could appear next to each other only in specific contexts: "es" is the second-person singular present of the verb être (tu es = you are) or an error for "est" (he/she/it is). "avec" means "with." Together they do not form a meaningful idiom; if they appear adjacent in writing it is likely an error, part of quoted speech, or the result of punctuation/word boundary issues.
target_language_example: Tu es avec moi ?
native_language_example: Are you with me?

meaning: 'are' + adverb/adjective intensifier (you are .../you are really ...).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'es' (you are) with adverbs like 'bien' used to qualify or intensify the adjective or phrase that follows. Depending on context, 'bien' can mean 'very', 'really', 'quite', or simply 'well'. Examples: 'Tu es bien habillée' = 'You are well/very dressed' (i.e. nicely dressed); 'Tu es bien le seul' = 'You really are the only one.' Word order: subject tu + es + bien + adjective/noun/phrase.
target_language_example: Tu es bien courageux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You are really brave today.

meaning: 'you are the one' (feminine) — identifies a specific woman or girl as the person referred to.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to or about a female person to single her out as the one who fits a description or role. 'Celle' is a demonstrative pronoun (feminine singular). In spoken French you often hear 'tu es celle que...' or 'tu es celle-là.' For a male you would use 'celui'.
target_language_example: Tu es celle que j'attendais depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: You are the one I've been waiting for.

meaning: is the one (is the one who/that)
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the verb form 'es' (2nd-person singular of être: 'you are') with the demonstrative pronoun 'celui' ('the one' / 'the one who/that'). It appears in sentences like 'Tu es celui qui...' ('You are the one who...') or in comparisons: 'Tu es celui que je cherche' ('You are the one I’m looking for'). 'Celui' must agree or be completed by de/qui/que/à + relative element when needed (e.g. celui qui, celui que, celui de). For 3rd-person singular 'is the one', use 'est celui'.
target_language_example: Tu es celui qui comprend.
native_language_example: You are the one who understands.

meaning: Not a valid standalone French phrase; likely a mistaken combination of two separate words (no independent meaning).
additional_notes:
There is no correct French expression 'es chez' by itself. It likely arises from a typo or mis-segmentation of two words:
- 'es' is the second-person singular present of être ('tu es' = 'you are').
- 'chez' is a preposition meaning 'at the home/place of' or used to indicate someone's place ('chez moi' = 'at my place').
These two do not combine directly without a subject: correct sequences are, for example, 'tu es chez moi' (you are at my place) or 'il/elle est chez...' (he/she is at ...). If you see 'es chez' alone, check the surrounding words for a missing subject (tu) or for a verb form that should be 'est chez' (il/elle/on est chez...).
target_language_example: Tu es chez moi ce soir ? — Oui, j'es chez toi après le travail.
native_language_example: Are you at my place tonight? — Yes, I'm at your place after work.

meaning: are like
additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern tu es comme... meaning you are like.... Here es is the tu form of être, and comme introduces a comparison.
target_language_example: Tu es comme ta mère.
native_language_example: You are like your mother.

meaning: 'is from the' or 'belongs to the' (literal: 'is of the')
additional_notes: This is a short sequence in Spanish (not French) combining the verb 'es' (he/she/it is) with the preposition 'de' and the definite article 'la'. It appears before a feminine noun/place: e.g. 'Ella es de la ciudad' (she is from the city) or in possessive senses like 'La decisión es de la directora' (the decision belongs to the director). In many cases native speakers would more naturally say 'es de' + place or 'es de la' + feminine noun. Watch for contractions in Spanish: 'de el' becomes 'del', but 'de la' stays separate. This phrase is compositional and literal.
target_language_example: La casa es de la familia García.
native_language_example: The house belongs to the García family.

meaning: are (you) proud
additional_notes: Used to say someone is proud (of themselves, someone, or something). 'es' is the second-person singular of 'être' (tu es). In spoken/informal French 'tu es' often becomes 't'es'. The adjective 'fière' agrees in gender (feminine). For a male speaker or referring to a male, use 'fièr' or more commonly spelled 'fier' (e.g., 'tu es fier'). Common constructions: 'tu es fière de toi' (are you proud of yourself) or 'tu es fière de X' (are you proud of X).
target_language_example: Tu es fière de ce que tu as accompli ?
native_language_example: Are you proud of what you accomplished?

meaning: 'are one (of)'.
additional_notes: Used in phrases like "Tu es l'un d'eux / d'entre eux / des nôtres / des leurs" to say "You are one of them/one of us/one of theirs." The full common patterns are "Tu es l'un d'eux", "Tu es l'un d'entre eux" or "Tu es l'un des nôtres/leurs." The fragment "es l'un" alone appears only as part of these constructions and always follows the subject (tu es...).
target_language_example: Tu es l'un des membres de l'équipe.
native_language_example: You are one of the members of the team.

meaning: it is the
additional_notes: Common Spanish phrase (not French) used to state or identify something using a feminine noun that follows. 'Es' = 'is' (from ser); 'la' = feminine definite article 'the'. Used before a feminine singular noun or to identify time expressions (e.g., 'Es la una' = 'It's one o'clock').
target_language_example: Es la casa de María.
native_language_example: It's María's house.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a fragment or mistaken attempt combining the verb form 'es' (2nd-person singular of être) with the possessive 'mon' and adjective 'meilleur'. It does not form a grammatical sentence by itself.
additional_notes:
'es mon meilleur' is ungrammatical because a subject pronoun (tu) is required before 'es', and when saying 'the best' in general French uses the definite article ('le/la') rather than a possessive alone. Possible correct alternatives depending on intended meaning:
- 'Tu es le meilleur.' — 'You are the best.'
- 'Tu es mon meilleur ami.' — 'You are my best friend.'
- 'C'est mon meilleur.' — 'He's/It's my best (one).'
If someone wrote 'es mon meilleur' in informal notes, they probably omitted the subject pronoun ('tu') and/or misused the article. Use 'tu es' for 'you are', and 'mon/ma' only before a noun (mon meilleur ami / ma meilleure amie) or use 'le/la meilleur(e)' for a general superlative.
target_language_example: (Fragment) ...tu es mon meilleur... — colloquial clipped speech where the subject pronoun 'tu' is omitted in writing, but spoken would be 'tu es mon meilleur'.
native_language_example: (Fragment) ...you are my best... — an incomplete fragment in English, mirroring the ungrammatical French fragment.

meaning: rare/incorrect sequence; likely a typo or fragment — not a standard French phrase
additional_notes: There is no common French phrase 'es où'. It may result from a typo or mis-splitting of words such as 'est où' (meaning 'is where') or 'es' (second-person singular of être: 'you are') followed by 'où' ('where').
target_language_example: Tu es où ?
native_language_example: Where are you?

meaning: are more
additional_notes: Usually appears after tu: tu es plus... = "you are more...". It is used to make comparisons, often before an adjective or expression, and may be followed by que for "than".
target_language_example: Tu es plus patient que moi.
native_language_example: You are more patient than me.

meaning: Not a standard French multi-word expression; likely a typo, mis-segmentation, or fragment (possibly from 'est qui', 'c'est qui', or from Spanish 'es que').
additional_notes: In modern French, 'es' is the 2nd-person singular present of 'être' (tu es = you are) and normally precedes an adjective or complement, not 'qui'. 'Est qui' (he/she/it is who) appears in constructions like 'C'est lui qui...'. 'Es qui' together is not grammatically correct in standard French; if you see it, check whether the intended phrase was 'est qui', 'c'est qui', or Spanish 'es que' (common spoken connector meaning 'it's that').
target_language_example: Si tu es qui tu dis être, montre-le.
native_language_example: If you are who you say you are, prove it.

meaning: you are alone
additional_notes: This looks like an incorrect or nonstandard form. Standard French is "es seul(e)" only when using the verb être with the second person singular (tu es) followed by the adjective seul/seule: "tu es seul" (you are alone) for a male speaker or "tu es seule" for a female speaker. Without "tu" the standalone phrase "es seul" is not grammatically complete. In writing/speech you'd normally include the subject (tu) or use the polite/ plural form "vous êtes seul(e)/(s)" or the impersonal "il/elle est seul(e)".
target_language_example: Tu es seul ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you alone tonight?

meaning: are his/her
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone expression, but a fragment you may see inside a sentence, especially after tu. Here, es is the tu form of être (“are”), and son usually means “his” or “her” before a singular noun. Son agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner, so son can mean either “his” or “her.”
target_language_example: Tu es son meilleur ami.
native_language_example: You are his/her best friend.

meaning: is on the
additional_notes: This appears to be a sequence combining a verb form (es = tú/tu? Actually 'es' is 2nd-person singular of 'ser' in Spanish, but in French 'es' is 2nd-person singular of être) with the preposition phrase 'sur le' ('on the'). In standard French, 'es sur le' would occur when addressing 'tu' with the verb être ('tu es') followed by 'sur le' + masculine noun: e.g. 'tu es sur le canapé' → 'you are on the couch'. Use 'tu es' (you are) + 'sur le/la/les' depending on the noun. For third person singular use 'il/elle est sur le...'.
target_language_example: Tu es sur le canapé.
native_language_example: You are on the couch.

meaning: Are you sure that...?/You sure that's...?
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of "(Tu) es sûr que c'..." or "T'es sûr que c'..." used to ask or check someone's certainty about a fact or situation. Often followed by "est/était" + a clause or a demonstrative (ici, là, ça, lui, etc.). "T'es" is the informal contraction of "tu es." Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: T'es sûr que c'est là?
native_language_example: Are you sure that's there?

meaning: 'are you sure that you' (used to ask someone if they are certain about doing or wanting something)
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase; usually appears as 'T'es sûr que tu...' (contraction of 'Tu es'). Used to check someone's certainty or confirm a decision. Followed by an infinitive (veux faire) or a clause (es d'attaque). Can be softened with 'vraiment' or made negative: 'Tu es sûr que tu ne veux rien ?'.
target_language_example: T'es sûr que tu veux y aller tout seul ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to go there alone?

meaning: 'are you sure that you' (feminine speaker addressing someone informally)
additional_notes: This is the second-person singular informal question form using a feminine speaker (sûre). It appears in yes/no questions asking for confirmation about the other person's intentions, wishes, or abilities. If a male speaker uses it, they'd say "es sûr que tu". In formal or plural "you" use "êtes sûr(e) que vous". Often followed by a verb or pronoun (e.g. "tu veux...", "tu en es capable").
target_language_example: Tu es sûre que tu veux vraiment y aller ?
native_language_example: Are you sure that you really want to go?

meaning: 'are still in' or 'is still in' (depending on subject) — indicates continuing state/location inside something or during a time period when used with the verb être (conjugated).
additional_notes: This sequence is not an independent fixed phrase; it appears as part of constructions with être + toujours + en + noun/gerund/time expression. Example structures: 'tu es toujours en retard' (you are still late), 'il est toujours en réunion' (he is still in a meeting), or 'nous sommes toujours en train de...' (we are still in the process of...). Adjust the être conjugation to match the subject (je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont). The form 'es toujours en' specifically corresponds to the second-person singular (tu) or appears inside questions/relative clauses where 'es' is used. Tone: neutral.
target_language_example: Tu es toujours en retard ce matin.
native_language_example: You are still late this morning.

meaning: 'you are completely/entirely' or 'you are very' (used before adjectives to intensify them)
additional_notes: In these examples, 'tout' is an adverb meaning 'completely', 'entirely' or a general intensifier equivalent to 'very' or 'all over' depending on context. It comes directly after the verb 'es' (from 'tu es') and modifies the adjective that follows (tu es tout rouge = you're all red / completely red). With adjectives that describe appearance, condition or emotion, 'tout' strengthens the adjective. Be aware: pronunciation and agreement can vary in spoken French (e.g., 'tout' can sound like /tu/).
target_language_example: Tu es tout trempé après la pluie.
native_language_example: You're completely soaked after the rain.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment with no standalone meaning.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard French expression. It appears to combine parts of different phrases: 'es' (2nd-person singular of 'être' — tu es = you are), 'tout' (all/entirely/very), and 'ce' (this/that/it). Possible intended corrections include 'c'est tout' (that's all), 'ce n'est pas tout' (that's not all), or 'tu es tout...' (you are very/entirely...). If you encounter 'es tout ce' in text, check for typos, missing words, or nonstandard word order.
target_language_example: Tu es tout ce que j'espérais.
native_language_example: You are everything I hoped for.

meaning: 'you are everything that' / 'you are all that...'
additional_notes: Used in romantic or emphatic statements: subject (tu) + es tout ce que + clause (je veux / j'ai / j'ai toujours voulu, etc.). It introduces what the person represents or provides for the speaker (everything the speaker has, wants, sees, hoped for). Literal components are meaningful but the whole phrase functions as a fixed expression in these contexts.
target_language_example: Tu es tout ce que je désire.
native_language_example: You are everything that I desire.

meaning: are a
additional_notes: Used with tu: es is the tu form of être (“to be”), and un is the masculine singular indefinite article. It is followed by a masculine singular noun, as in tu es un idiot. For a feminine noun, use es une.
target_language_example: Tu es un bon ami.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: 'are a' (second-person singular 'you are' + indefinite article 'a')
additional_notes: Form is part of the verb être (tu es) + the indefinite article un/une used to say someone is something (profession, group, characteristic). In spoken French 'tu es' often contracts to 't'es' and in informal speech 't'en es un' appears (t' + en + es + un) meaning 'are you one of them' or 'you are one of...' depending on context. Use with a noun: 'Tu es un menteur' = 'You are a liar.'
target_language_example: Tu es un bon professeur.
native_language_example: You are a good teacher.

meaning: are mine
additional_notes: Informal expression meaning someone or something belongs to the speaker or is claimed by them (often said playfully or possessively about a person). Usually used with tu/es/t'es depending on formality and contraction: "tu es à moi" = "you are mine"; "t'es à moi" is contracted spoken French. Can sound possessive — use carefully.
target_language_example: Tu es à moi, ne t'en va pas.
native_language_example: You are mine, don't go.

meaning: kind of
additional_notes: Often used before a noun (or insult) to mean 'kind of' or 'type of'. In informal or vulgar speech it can add contempt or emphasis (e.g., 'espèce de connard' = 'you kind of asshole' → 'you bloody asshole'). Here it's used in a vulgar, insulting phrase. Not typically translated word-for-word in English; translate to natural English (often 'you' + insult or 'that kind of').
target_language_example: Espèce de menteur !
native_language_example: You liar! / You kind of liar!

meaning: 'hopes not to' or 'hope(s) not to' (part of a negative phrase using 'espérer' with 'ne ... pas' or another negative particle)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the beginning of a negative clause with the verb espérer (to hope). In French negatives, espère is followed by an infinitive or a full clause: e.g. « J'espère ne pas être en retard » (I hope not to be late) or « J'espère qu'il ne viendra pas » (I hope that he will not come). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: « J'espère pas » instead of « J'espère ne pas ». Use the full negative for formal writing.
target_language_example: J'espère ne pas déranger.
native_language_example: I hope not to disturb.

meaning: 'hopes for' or 'is hoping for' (expresses wishing or wanting something to happen).
additional_notes: In French, the verb is normally used without 'pour' when followed by a verb or clause: j'espère que... (I hope that...) or j'espère + infinitive (j'espère réussir). 'Espère pour' can appear before a noun phrase to mean 'hopes for (someone/something)', but it's less common than simply 'espère' with a complement or 'a de l'espoir pour' in some contexts. For beginners, use 'j'espère que...' or 'j'espère + infinitive' for 'I hope...'.
target_language_example: J'espère pour toi que tout ira bien.
native_language_example: I hope for you that everything will be fine.

meaning: I hope that it/this is...
additional_notes: Used to express hope about something specific introduced by 'c'est' (it/this is). Commonly followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or clause (e.g. 'clair', 'la bonne taille', 'vrai'). Informal omission of 'ne' in negative contexts is common (e.g. 'J'espère que c'est pas...' instead of '...n'est pas...').
target_language_example: J'espère que c'est agréable là-bas.
native_language_example: I hope that it's pleasant there.

meaning: 'hopes that this/that' (beginning of a clause expressing hope about something).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own; it's the start of a sentence where the subject (il/elle/on/je/nous/etc.) or context supplies who hopes and what 'ce' refers to (ce + être/ça + verb). More common forms: 'j'espère que' (I hope that) or 'on espère que' (one/people hope that). 'Ce' often appears as 'ce que' or 'ce sera' depending on the clause. Use with a full clause afterward: 'J'espère que ce sera possible.'
target_language_example: J'espère que ce projet aboutira.
native_language_example: I hope that this project will succeed.

meaning: 'hope that it/he/she/they... not' — start of a negative clause expressing hope (short for "j'espère que ce n'..." or "on espère que ce n'...")
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a sentence where someone expresses hope that something is not the case. The contraction "ce n'" appears before a vowel sound (e.g. "ce n'est pas", "ce n'arrive pas"). You will usually see the full phrase like "J'espère que ce n'est pas grave." Common subjects: "j'", "on", "nous" + "espère"/"espérons". Use it to say you hope something negative does NOT happen or is NOT true.
target_language_example: J'espère que ce n'est pas trop tard.
native_language_example: I hope that it isn't too late.

meaning: 'I hope that...' (used to begin a clause expressing the speaker's hope about themselves or their actions)
additional_notes: This is the verb espérer (to hope) followed by que and the subject je. It introduces a subordinate clause describing what the speaker hopes will happen or be true. In spoken French, espérer + que is common; the tense after que follows normal sequence-of-tense rules (present: espère que je réussirai — I hope that I will succeed). Contractions or inversion aren't used here (you wouldn't say *espère m'*).
target_language_example: J'espère que je réussirai l'examen.
native_language_example: I hope that I will pass the exam.

meaning: 'I hope that you...' or 'I hope that...' (followed by a clause about 'tu')
additional_notes: Colloquial contracted form of "J'espère que tu..." where "tu" is shortened to "t'" before a verb starting with a vowel or in informal speech: e.g. "J'espère que t'as" = "J'espère que tu as". Used in spoken/informal contexts. The full sentence often begins with "J'espère que..." (I hope that...).
target_language_example: J'espère que t'as compris ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: I hope that you understood what I meant.

meaning: 'I was hoping that you...' (polite/formal way to express a past hope about someone's action or knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hoped-for situation in the past (or an unrealized expectation). Often followed by a subordinate clause with verbs in present, imperfect, conditional, or subjunctive depending on nuance and formality. Common in polite requests or to express disappointment/surprise. The subject is "vous" (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: J'espérais que vous pourriez m'aider avec ce document.
native_language_example: I was hoping that you could help me with this document.

meaning: don't try (do not attempt) — informal imperative
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'n'essaie pas' or 'ne ... pas essayer' used in spoken French to tell someone not to attempt something. Often used alone as a short warning or refusal (equivalent to 'don't even try' or 'don't try that'). Tone can be blunt; register = informal. With pronouns it may appear as 't'essaie pas' (regional/very informal) but standard written form is 'n'essaie pas' or 'ne t'essaie pas' depending on structure.
target_language_example: Essaie pas de tricher pendant l'examen.
native_language_example: Don't try to cheat during the exam.

meaning: to try (something) — 'essayer' = to try; with a direct object 'le' = it/the (masculine) item
additional_notes: Used when trying or testing a specific masculine noun (physical object, option, method). In speech you would replace 'le' with the appropriate direct object pronoun (le/la/les) or the actual noun: essayer la robe, essayer ce stylo, l'essayer (to try it). Conjugate 'essayer' normally (j'essaie/tu essaies/il essaie/nous essayons...).
target_language_example: Je vais essayer le pantalon avant de l'acheter.
native_language_example: I'll try the trousers on before buying them.

meaning: Not a correct fixed phrase in French; likely an incomplete or ungrammatical sequence. 'essayer' means 'to try' and normally appears with 'de' + infinitive (essayer de faire) or with a direct object (essayer quelque chose = try something). 'quelque' by itself requires a noun (e.g., 'quelque chose').
additional_notes:
As written, 'essayer quelque' is incomplete and should not be used. Correct patterns include:
- essayer de + infinitive (essayer de comprendre = to try to understand)
- essayer + direct object (essayer quelque chose, essayer une robe)
- 'quelque' needs a noun or must form 'quelque chose' to mean 'something'. If you see 'essayer quelque' it is probably a mistake or an unfinished phrase.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas dire « essayer quelque » tout seul ; il faut dire par exemple « essayer quelque chose ».
native_language_example: I can't say "essayer quelque" by itself; you must say for example "essayer quelque chose".

meaning: to keep trying; to always try
additional_notes: Combines the verb essayer (to try) with toujours (always). This exact word order (essayer toujours) is uncommon in natural French; speakers more often say "essayer encore et encore", "continuer d'essayer" or place "toujours" before the verb as in "toujours essayer" depending on context. Conjugate essayer with the subject (j'essaie / nous essayons).
target_language_example: Il faut essayer toujours, même si c'est difficile.
native_language_example: You must try always, even if it's difficult.

meaning: to try on (an item of clothing or footwear).
additional_notes: Used when testing clothing, shoes, or accessories in a shop or at home to check fit or look. 'Essayer' on its own means 'to try'; when followed by a noun with the indefinite article (un/une), it usually means 'to try on' that specific item. For other senses of 'try' (attempt), use 'essayer de + infinitive' (e.g. 'essayer de comprendre').
target_language_example: Je vais essayer un pantalon avant de l'acheter.
native_language_example: I'll try on a pair of trousers before buying them.

meaning: to try to see / to try and find out (whether something is possible or true).
additional_notes: A colloquial combination of essayer (to try) + voir (to see). Used to indicate attempting something to check the result or find out information. Often used in spoken French like "Je vais essayer voir" meaning "I'll try and see." It's slightly informal; in careful speech you'd say "essayer de voir" or simply "voir" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vais essayer voir si la porte est fermée.
native_language_example: I'll try and see if the door is locked.

meaning: tried to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone tried to do something. This is the past form of essayer de, as in j'ai essayé d'appeler. The apostrophe is used before a vowel or silent h; before a consonant, it is essayé de.
target_language_example: J'ai essayé d'expliquer la situation.
native_language_example: I tried to explain the situation.

meaning: 'tried to (do) you' — part of the expression 'essayer de + infinitive' with the clitic pronoun 't'' (short for 'te') before an infinitive beginning with a vowel sound (e.g. essayé de t'aider = tried to help you).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself but a fragment showing: 'essayer de' = 'to try to (do something)', and 't'' is the unstressed object pronoun 'te' (you) placed before a verb that begins with a vowel sound or mute h. In spoken and informal written French, pronouns often attach like this before verbs (te + aider → t'aider). The full structure is usually: [subject] + a/ai/avais/etc. + essayé de + t' + [infinitive].
target_language_example: Il a essayé de t'aider quand tu étais tombé.
native_language_example: He tried to help you when you fell.

meaning: 'arrived/ happened this' (used to point to something that occurred at a specific recent time, often followed by a time word like 'matin' — e.g. "est arrivé ce matin" = "arrived/happened this morning").
additional_notes: This sequence combines the verb arriver (to arrive/happen) in the passé composé (il est arrivé) or the impersonal c'est arrivé and the demonstrative 'ce' used with a time noun (ce matin, ce soir, ce week-end). Common patterns: "Il est arrivé ce matin" (He arrived this morning), "C'est arrivé ce matin" (It happened this morning). Not idiomatic on its own; 'ce' must be followed by a time expression. Can refer to people (arriver) or events (arriver/happen).
target_language_example: Le colis est arrivé ce matin.
native_language_example: The package arrived this morning.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; appears to be nonstandard word order of "il est arrivé" (he/it has arrived / he/it arrived). Could occur in inversion for questions as "Est-il arrivé ?" or in unusual/poetic word order, but as written "est arrivé il" is not typical in modern French.
additional_notes: Correct standard order for a statement is "il est arrivé". For a yes/no question use inversion with a hyphen: "Est-il arrivé ?". The sequence "est arrivé il" might appear in poetic or archaic contexts or as an error; avoid using it in written or spoken contemporary French unless intentionally stylistic. Literal translation: "is arrived he" (unnatural word order in English).
target_language_example: Est arrivé il ce matin ?
native_language_example: Has he arrived this morning?

meaning: This phrase is incomplete/incorrect as written; likely a fragment of 'est arrivé quelque chose' meaning 'something happened' or 'there has been something that happened'.
additional_notes: As provided, 'est arrivé quelque' is not a correct standalone French expression. Two likely intended forms: 1) 'Il est arrivé quelque chose' or 'Quelque chose est arrivé' — both mean 'something happened' or 'something has occurred'. 2) 'Quelque ... est arrivé' could begin a sentence like 'Quelque chose est arrivé' (Something happened) or 'Quelqu'un est arrivé' (Someone arrived). For beginners: use 'Quelque chose est arrivé' (Something happened) or the very common impersonal 'Il s'est passé quelque chose' (Something happened).
target_language_example: Il est arrivé quelque chose pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Something happened during the meeting.

meaning: '(she) arrived by/while/in' — used to say how someone arrived or in what state/manner (feminine subject).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of arriver for a feminine singular subject (elle est arrivée) followed by en + noun or gerund to indicate means, manner, or condition: en voiture (by car), en courant (running), en retard (late). For a masculine subject use est arrivé; plural subjects use sont arrivés/arrivées. 'En' often means 'by' (transport) or 'while/in' (manner or state).
target_language_example: Elle est arrivée en vélo ce matin.
native_language_example: She arrived by bike this morning.

meaning: 'is known' (incorrect combination: singular 'est' with plural 'connus'); intended meaning 'is known' or 'are known' depending on agreement
additional_notes: This entry shows the sequence est + connus. Grammatically, est is third-person singular of être (he/she/it is) while connus is the masculine plural past participle of connaître (known). The combination 'est connus' is therefore ungrammatical in standard French because subject-verb agreement is inconsistent. Correct alternatives: 'est connu' (singular masculine), 'est connue' (singular feminine), 'sont connus' (plural masculine or mixed), 'sont connues' (plural feminine). 'Connu' can mean 'known' or 'well-known/famous' depending on context.
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* Le chanteur est connus par tout le public.
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* The singer is known by the entire audience.

meaning: This sequence is ungrammatical in standard French. It appears to combine the feminine past participle form 'est partie' with the masculine pronoun 'il'. In correct French, subject and past-participle agreement must match: use 'elle est partie' (she has left) or 'il est parti' (he has left).
additional_notes: 'Est partie' is the third-person singular passé composé of partir with a feminine subject. It must agree in gender and number with the subject when conjugated with être. Placing 'il' after 'est partie' (as in 'est partie il') is not grammatical; the subject pronoun normally precedes the verb ('Il est parti' or 'Elle est partie'). Possible contexts where such a sequence might appear are rare (e.g., in dislocated or poetic structures, or as a clipped excerpt), but it's not standard usage.
target_language_example: ...elle est partie, il ne restait personne.
native_language_example: ...she had left, there was no one left.

meaning: 'left/she left ... ago' — used with a time expression introduced by "il y a" to say someone left that amount of time ago (feminine singular subject).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé with être as auxiliary for a feminine singular subject (être + past participle partie) followed by the time expression introduced by "il y a" (meaning "... ago"). Adjust subject and past participle agreement as needed (e.g. "Il est parti il y a..." for masculine). Common in spoken and written French to indicate when someone left.
target_language_example: Elle est partie il y a deux heures.
native_language_example: She left two hours ago.

meaning: a colloquial contraction meaning "isn't already" (negative + 'already')
additional_notes: This sequence is informal and nonstandard in writing. It combines the verb est (is) with the negative particle pas and already (déjà). Standard French would be « n'est pas déjà ». In spoken, casual French speakers often drop the written 'ne' and sometimes alter word order: "il est pas déjà" = "he isn't already..." Use in conversation, not formal writing.
target_language_example: Il est pas déjà parti ?
native_language_example: Hasn't he already left?

meaning: 'did not happen' (informal spoken form of "ne s'est pas passé")
additional_notes: This is a colloquial, contracted way to say "ne s'est pas passé" (itself the passive reflexive of "se passer" = "to happen" or "to take place"). Used to describe events that did not occur or did not happen as expected. In careful or written French include the full negative "ne ... pas" and the reflexive pronoun: "ça ne s'est pas passé comme prévu."
target_language_example: Ça s'est pas passé comme prévu.
native_language_example: It didn't happen as planned.

meaning: 'didn't come' (feminine subject) — informal/colloquial negation
additional_notes: This is a colloquial spoken form of the negative past: standard written form is "n'est pas venue" or in speech often "elle n'est pas venue" (she didn't come). Here 'venue' is the past participle of venir and agrees with a feminine subject. In casual spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped, producing "est pas venue". Use the full form in writing or formal speech.
target_language_example: Elle est pas venue à la fête hier.
native_language_example: She didn't come to the party yesterday.

meaning: went
additional_notes: Passé composé of passer used with être. Depending on context, it can mean 'went,' 'passed/went by,' or 'came by/stopped by.' In expressions like le pire est passé, it means 'is over.' In the reflexive form s'est passé, it means 'happened.'
target_language_example: Le train est passé il y a cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The train passed five minutes ago.

meaning: has passed the / went past the (third-person singular passé composé of 'passer' followed by the definite article 'le', commonly used with dates or specific masculine nouns)
additional_notes: This form is the third-person singular of 'passer' in the passé composé (être + passé) when the subject is singular and uses 'être' as auxiliary (e.g., 'La date est passée'). When followed by 'le' it typically precedes a specific day/date or a masculine noun introduced by 'le' (e.g., 'est passé le 10 mars'). Agreement: past participle 'passé' agrees in gender and number with the subject only when 'être' is the auxiliary (e.g., 'La date est passée' vs 'Le train est passé'). In the fixed sequence 'est passé le' the past participle is masculine singular ('passé'); context may require 'passée' if subject is feminine, which would not match 'est passé le'. Use carefully: often you'll see 'est passée le' or 'est passé le' depending on subject gender and what follows. This entry focuses on the literal sequence 'est passé le' as used before masculine nouns/dates.
target_language_example: Le train est passé le quai à midi.
native_language_example: The train passed the platform at noon.

meaning: has been through/was here (just) — indicates someone or something passed by or stopped here recently.
additional_notes: Literal: 'is passed there'. Used to report that a person, vehicle, or event went by or stopped at a place. Context often clarifies timing (recent) and subject. Can be used about people ('Il est passé là') or things ('Le bus est passé là'). Informal everyday phrasing; you may also hear variations like 'est passé par ici' or 'est passé par là'.
target_language_example: Il est passé là ce matin pour déposer le colis.
native_language_example: He stopped by here this morning to drop off the package.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment or error (no clear meaning).
additional_notes:
This sequence is not a correct or complete expression in French. It looks like a fragment combining the verb être/être passé and the determinative 'quelque' (meaning 'some' or 'a little'), but as written it doesn't form a grammatical phrase. Possible intended forms and meanings:
- "est passé" = "has passed" / "went by" (third-person singular, passé composé of passer) — e.g. "Il est passé" = "He passed by".
- "est passé quelque chose" is incorrect; to say "something happened to someone" you'd use "il s'est passé quelque chose" = "something happened".
- "quelque" needs to modify a noun (quelque chose = something; quelque part = somewhere; quelquefois = sometimes).
If you saw this in writing or speech, check for typos or missing words (e.g., "il est passé" or "il s'est passé quelque chose").
target_language_example: Il s'est passé quelque chose d'étrange hier soir.
native_language_example: Something strange happened last night.

meaning: 'did ... go' / 'how was your ...' (asking how an event or period went)
additional_notes: This sequence appears in the familiar question pattern «Comment s'est passée ta ... ?» (How did your ... go? / How was your ...?). Use with a noun for a time period or event (journée, nuit, soirée, visite, réunion, etc.). Informal/familiar register (tu). For polite/formal use, say «Comment s'est passée votre ... ?» or «Comment s'est passée votre journée ?»
target_language_example: Comment s'est passée ta réunion ce matin ?
native_language_example: How did your meeting go this morning?

meaning: 'has come out of his/her/their' (literal) — used to say someone has come out of a place or state
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it looks like part of a sentence using the passé composé (est sortie) with a feminine singular subject or a feminine noun (sortie agrees with a feminine subject when using être) plus "de son" (of his/her/its). For example: "Elle est sortie de son appartement" = "She came out of her apartment." Pay attention to agreement: for a masculine singular subject you'd use "est sorti de son", for plural subjects "sont sortis/sorties de leurs." "Son" agrees with the following noun (son appartement = his/her apartment).
target_language_example: Elle est sortie de son bureau à midi.
native_language_example: She came out of her office at noon.

meaning: literally 'fell by'; used in contexts like 'fell by (somewhere)' or 'happened to come by/into' (often in passive or pronominal constructions).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the auxiliary 'est' (être) + past participle 'tombé' (fallen) + preposition 'par'. It appears in sentences like 'Il est tombé par hasard' (he happened to come across/it happened by chance) or in locative phrases 'Il est tombé par la fenêtre' (he fell out of/by the window). Alone, 'est tombé par' is incomplete and needs more words (e.g., 'par hasard', 'par la fenêtre', 'par ici'). For beginners: look for the full expression that follows 'par' to know the meaning (chance, location, route, etc.).
target_language_example: Il est tombé par hasard sur ce vieux journal.
native_language_example: He happened to come across that old newspaper.

meaning: 'has fallen in love' (feminine singular, passé composé)
additional_notes: Used to say a female subject fell in love. Literally 'fell in love'. In passé composé the auxiliary être is used, so past participle 'tombée' agrees in gender/number with the subject (tombé/tombée/tombés/tombées). To make it masculine use 'est tombé amoureux'. Can be followed by 'de' + person (est tombée amoureuse de lui) or used alone with context.
target_language_example: Elle est tombée amoureuse de son collègue.
native_language_example: She has fallen in love with her colleague.

meaning: 'is written' (third-person singular, passive or descriptive)
additional_notes: Form of the verb écrire (to write) in the present indicative passive/descriptive construction: il/elle/on est écrit can mean 'it is written' (something is written somewhere) or be used in impersonal/abstract senses (e.g., «Il est écrit dans le contrat…» = 'It is written in the contract…'). Context determines whether it's describing a physical inscription or citing a text. Not used for 'is writing' (that's 'écrit' as present participle with être in progressive, but French typically uses 'est en train d'écrire' for 'is writing').
target_language_example: Il est écrit dans le manuel que vous devez porter un casque.
native_language_example: It is written in the manual that you must wear a helmet.

meaning: is it
additional_notes: Literally means "is it/that." It can be used directly before an adjective or noun in simple yes/no questions: "Est-ce correct ?" It also appears inside common question patterns like "qu'est-ce que" and "où est-ce que," where it helps form a question rather than being translated word-for-word every time.
target_language_example: Est-ce normal ?
native_language_example: Is it normal?

meaning: 'what (is it) that she ... to you' — beginning of a question asking what a female subject did/said/gave you.
additional_notes: This is the contracted spoken form of the question starter "qu'est-ce qu'elle t'..." followed by a verb and an object pronoun (t' = te). Used to ask informally what a woman/she said, did, gave, etc. In writing you may also see the full form "Qu'est-ce qu'elle t'a ... ?" The t' stands for "te" (to you). Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle t'a expliqué hier ?
native_language_example: What did she explain to you yesterday?

meaning: 'what did he ... to/for you' (question starter meaning 'what did he [do/say/give] you')
additional_notes: This is the spoken/question form combining est-ce que + il + te + a (past auxiliary). Commonly appears as Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a... followed by a past participle or verb (dit, demandé, donné, montré, pris, raconté, fait faire). Use to ask what someone said, did, gave, showed, etc., to you. Informal to neutral register; 't'' is the contracted form of 'te'.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a expliqué hier ?
native_language_example: What did he explain to you yesterday?

meaning: A spoken question phrase meaning 'did we/one/they have' or 'what have we/one/they' (used to ask about something that happened or was missed).
additional_notes: Combines the question marker 'est-ce que' (spoken 'est-ce qu'') with 'on' (informal 'we' / impersonal 'one' / sometimes 'they') and the auxiliary 'a' (has). Often appears in spoken or informal French to form questions about past events (with a past participle) or to ask 'what is/was there' in colloquial contexts. The exact English translation depends on context: 'What did we miss/forget/find/ever laugh about?' Pronunciation and contraction are common: 'Qu'est-ce qu'on a...?'
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on a raté pendant mon absence ?
native_language_example: What did we miss while I was gone?

meaning: do/does ...?
additional_notes: used at the beginning of a sentence to form a neutral yes/no question. Very common in everyday French. It does not translate literally in natural English; the English wording depends on the verb, such as 'do/does', 'is/are', 'can', or 'would'.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu viens avec nous ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us?

meaning: 'est-ce que' = question marker (introduces yes/no questions); 'tout le' begins phrases meaning 'everyone' when followed by 'monde' or 'tout le monde'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears when asking questions about a group: 'Est-ce que' introduces a question, and 'tout le monde' means 'everyone' or 'everybody'. Beginners can treat 'Est-ce que tout le monde...' as a fixed starter: 'Est-ce que tout le monde ... ?' = 'Is everyone ...?' or 'Does everybody ...?'. Word order stays the same in spoken and written French. If not followed by 'monde', 'tout le' may require a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'tout le monde' is most common).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tout le monde est prêt ?
native_language_example: Is everyone ready?

meaning: 'what do you have in...' (used to ask what someone is holding or what's in/inside something or someone's body/mind).
additional_notes: This combines the question marker 'est-ce que' + 'tu as' (you have) + 'dans' (in). It's used to form direct questions about what is inside or what someone has (physically or figuratively). The full question typically adds a noun: e.g. 'Qu'est-ce que tu as dans la main ?' For more natural spoken French, 'Qu'est-ce que' is often used instead of 'Est-ce que tu as...'; word order can vary (e.g. 'Qu'est-ce que tu as dans ton sac ?').
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as dans ton sac ?
native_language_example: What do you have in your bag?

meaning: 'are you trying to' (used to ask what someone is attempting to do/say)
additional_notes: Common question form. 'Est-ce que' is a neutral way to form yes/no questions; here followed by 'tu essaies de' + infinitive or phrase. Can be used to ask about actions (faire), intentions (prouver), or implied meanings (dire, me dire). In spoken French 'tu essaies de' may be shortened (Tu essaies de...?) and word order can change: 'Qu'est-ce que tu essaies de + infinitive?'
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu essaies de m'aider ou de m'embêter ?
native_language_example: Are you trying to help me or annoy me?

meaning: 'what are you doing in/at' (used to ask what someone is doing in a place)
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside the common question pattern "Qu'est-ce que tu fais à [lieu]?" Literally: "What is it that you do at/in [place]?" Use with a city or location to ask someone's activity, purpose, or reason for being there. Formality: neutral, used in spoken and written French. For other subjects: replace "tu" with "vous" (formal/plural) or a name/pronoun (e.g. "qu'est-ce qu'il/elle fait à...").
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais à Lyon ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are you doing in Lyon this weekend?

meaning: 'what are you doing' (informal, surprised or annoyed)
additional_notes: Uses the verb 'ficher' in an informal sense meaning 'to do' or 'to be up to' (similar to 'faire' or colloquial 'foutre'). Common in surprised, irritated, or confrontational questions like "What are you doing here?" or "What are you doing at this time?" Tone can be rude depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Mais qu'est-ce que tu fiches ici à cette heure ?
native_language_example: But what are you doing here at this hour?

meaning: 'who/what (is it) that...' used in questions to ask about the subject.
additional_notes: Used in spoken and neutral French to form subject questions. Combined with 'qui' for people (Qui est-ce qui...?) or 'qu'est-ce qui' for things/events (Qu'est-ce qui...?). It asks 'who/what performed or caused something' and requires a verb after the phrase. Often used when the speaker expects the answer to be the subject (not the object).
target_language_example: Qui est-ce qui a laissé la porte ouverte ?
native_language_example: Who left the door open?

meaning: is he
additional_notes: Question form of être with il, used in subject-verb inversion. It is common in formal writing and careful speech, and can also repeat a noun subject: Tom est-il... ? = Is Tom... ?
target_language_example: Ce film est-il intéressant ?
native_language_example: Is this movie interesting?

meaning: used in negative question tags: 'isn't it/ he isn't/ isn't he' (literally 'is he not').
additional_notes: This form appears when inverting subject and verb in a negative question (n'est-il pas / est-il pas). More commonly written as "n'est-il pas" in formal French; colloquially you may also hear "c'est pas" or "n'est-ce pas" for 'isn't it?'. Used to seek confirmation or express surprise. Word order changes depending on the subject (est-elle pas? / sont-ils pas?).
target_language_example: Ce film n'est-il pas intéressant ?
native_language_example: Isn't this movie interesting?

meaning: 'is thus' / 'is like that' — indicates that something is the case or is that way.
additional_notes: Formal/neutral phrase used to state a situation or to conclude an explanation. Often appears in phrases like "C'est ainsi" (That's how it is) or in written/academic contexts: "Il en est ainsi" (It is thus/It is the case). Can sound a bit formal when used alone.
target_language_example: Il en est ainsi depuis des années.
native_language_example: It has been like that for years.

meaning: 'is such that' / 'is thus that' — used to introduce a result, explanation, or characteristic.
additional_notes: Formal/literary expression. Often appears in written French to present a consequence, a reason, or to describe how something is. It can link a subject to a clause that explains or qualifies it. In everyday spoken French, simpler alternatives like "c'est pourquoi", "ainsi", or "est-ce que" (in questions) are more common.
target_language_example: Sa décision est ainsi que tout le monde a compris pourquoi il partait.
native_language_example: His decision is such that everyone understood why he was leaving.

meaning: is quite/pretty rich; has a fair amount of money or resources
additional_notes: A simple descriptive phrase: 'est' (is) + 'assez' (quite/enough) + 'riche' (rich). Used to say someone or something has a considerable amount of wealth or resources, or to soften the adjective (not extremely rich, but fairly so). Context determines whether it describes money, resources, or richness in another sense (e.g., a sauce can be 'riche').
target_language_example: Elle est assez riche pour acheter une maison.
native_language_example: She is quite rich enough to buy a house.

meaning: 'is at the end' or 'is at the tip/edge' (literally), often meaning someone/something is exhausted, fed up, or a situation has reached its limit
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'être au bout' + de + noun = to be at the end of something (e.g., time, rope, patience). Common idiomatic uses: 'être au bout du rouleau' = to be exhausted (physically or mentally); 'être au bout de sa patience' = to have run out of patience / be fed up. Context determines whether it refers to a physical end (tip/edge) or a figurative limit.
target_language_example: Après trois nuits blanches, il est au bout.
native_language_example: After three sleepless nights, he is exhausted.

meaning: 'is also what' (literal phrase used to equate or identify something as also being something else)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom in French; it's a literal sequence of words combining the verb être (est), the adverb aussi (also), and the relative phrase ce que (what/that which). You might see it in sentences like « X est aussi ce que Y … » to say 'X is also what Y…' or to add that something is also the thing described. Word order and context are important; often a comma or continuation follows. For many situations a more natural phrasing would be « est aussi » followed by a noun/adjective or « est ce que » used separately in questions. Be careful: 'est ce que' (with spaces) is a question marker, different from 'est ce que' used here as part of a clause.
target_language_example: Son rôle est aussi ce que nous attendions : un leader calme.
native_language_example: His role is also what we expected: a calm leader.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'is also what I...'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common standalone expression in French. It looks like part of a sentence: est (is) + aussi (also) + ce que je (what I...). In full sentences it would be completed by a verb or clause, for example: «C'est aussi ce que je pense» (That's also what I think) or «Il est aussi ce que je voulais» (He/it is also what I wanted). Beginners should not use this fragment alone — learn complete phrases like «C'est aussi ce que je pense.»
target_language_example: C'est aussi ce que je pense.
native_language_example: That's also what I think.

meaning: 'is also my' (used to say something belongs to or relates to the speaker as well)
additional_notes: This is a short sequence combining the verb être (est = 'is'), the adverb aussi ('also/too'), and the possessive mon ('my'). It appears inside a sentence (e.g. 'Ceci est aussi mon livre' = 'This is also my book'). Word order is fixed: 'est' follows the subject, 'aussi' typically comes before the possessive or adjective. Ensure agreement of the noun after the possessive (mon is used before masculine singular nouns and before feminine nouns that begin with a vowel sound).
target_language_example: Ce stylo est aussi mon stylo.
native_language_example: This pen is also my pen.

meaning: is different / is something else
additional_notes: Literally 'is other'; used to say that something is different, distinct, or another thing. Often appears in phrases like 'ce n'est pas X, c'est autre chose' (that's not X, it's something else). Alone 'est autre' is somewhat formal or literary and not commonly used by itself in everyday spoken French; more natural: 'est différent(e)' or 'est autre chose'.
target_language_example: Ce problème est autre que celui dont nous avons parlé.
native_language_example: This problem is different from the one we talked about.

meaning: 'is something else' or 'is another matter'
additional_notes: Used to say that something is different, separate, or of a different nature — often to contrast two things (e.g., A is X, but B est autre chose). Common in spoken and written French to downplay or distinguish a point. Typically follows the noun or clause being contrasted.
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est cher, mais la qualité du service est autre chose.
native_language_example: This restaurant is expensive, but the quality of the service is something else.

meaning: is at the (plural or feminine place); 'être' + 'à' + 'les' contracted
additional_notes: This is the verb être (est) followed by the contracted preposition 'aux' (à + les). Use before a plural noun to say something or someone is at/on/in a place: il/elle est aux [pl. place]. Example: 'Elle est aux États-Unis' = 'She is in the United States.' Not a fixed phrase—just a grammatical combination. For singular masculine use 'est au' (à + le), for singular feminine 'est à la', and for vowel-starting nouns 'est à l\''.
target_language_example: Il est aux bureaux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is at the offices today.

meaning: Not a standard standalone French phrase; a fragment that may occur when the words 'est' (is), 'bien' (indeed/well), and 'ce' (this/it) appear together in a larger sentence. It does not form a fixed expression by itself.
additional_notes: Avoid using 'est bien ce' alone. In grammatical French the demonstrative 'ce' normally appears before the verb as in 'c'est bien' or with cleft/inverted structures; sequences producing 'est bien ce' are typically parts of longer clauses (e.g., after a relative clause or in reported speech) or result from unusual word order and may sound awkward. Use complete, standard alternatives like 'C'est bien' (That's good/That's right) or reorder the clause to place 'ce' correctly.
target_language_example: Il est vrai que, dans ce contexte, est bien ce qui motive la décision.
native_language_example: It is true that, in this context, is indeed what motivates the decision.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; looks like part of a sentence meaning 'is indeed what I.../is really what I...'.
additional_notes: This word sequence is not a common idiom by itself. It appears to combine the verb 'est' (is), the adverb 'bien' (indeed/well), and a relative clause starter 'ce que je' (what I...). In natural French you would usually see it as part of a larger sentence, for example 'C'est bien ce que je pensais' ('That is indeed what I thought') or 'Il est bien ce que je croyais' (less common; better: 'Il est bien ce que je croyais qu'il était'). Beginners should learn the component parts separately: 'est' (3rd-person singular of être), 'bien' (indeed/well), and 'ce que je' (what I...).
target_language_example: C'est bien ce que je pensais.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I thought.

meaning: is fine/as it is; is good the way (it) is.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is acceptable, suitable, or okay as it currently is. Often follows a noun or clause (e.g., 'C'est bien comme ça' = 'That's fine like that'). Alone 'est bien comme' is not a complete sentence; more natural forms include 'c'est bien comme ça' or 'il est bien comme ça.' Tone is neutral; can be used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: C'est bien comme ça, tu peux le laisser.
native_language_example: That's fine as it is, you can leave it.

meaning: 'is good for' or 'is suitable for' (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something benefits, suits, or is appropriate for a person, purpose, or situation. Often follows a subject (e.g., 'Ce médicament est bien pour la toux' = 'This medicine is good for a cough'). Can be followed by a noun or an infinitive phrase introduced with 'pour' (e.g., 'pour dormir').
target_language_example: Ce livre est bien pour les débutants.
native_language_example: This book is good for beginners.

meaning: 'it is good that' (expresses approval or that something is good/reassuring).
additional_notes: Used to comment on a situation or fact: souvent suivi d'une proposition subordonnée introduite par 'que' (e.g. « c'est bien que... », mais on peut aussi entendre « est bien que » dans des phrases plus longues). More common and standard form is 'c'est bien que'. It expresses approval, relief, or that something is a good thing. Can be used with indicative or subjunctive depending on speaker's attitude (opinion, emotion, necessity → subjunctive).
target_language_example: C'est bien que tu viennes ce soir.
native_language_example: It's good that you're coming tonight.

meaning: 'it is good that you' / 'it's good that you...'
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause expressing approval or that something is good because someone does or will do something. It is typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g. « est bien que tu viennes ») when the speaker expresses opinion or emotion about an action. In everyday speech speakers may also use the indicative in casual contexts, but the grammatically correct form for many verbs of opinion requires the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Il est bien que tu sois venu pour aider.
native_language_example: It's good that you came to help.

meaning: 'it's good that you are' / 'it's good that you have' (introducing a positive comment about someone's arrival, return, or presence; followed by the subjunctive)
additional_notes: This phrase is commonly used with the subjunctive form of 'être' (sois) plus a past participle (rentré, revenu, venu/venue) to express relief or approval that someone has come/returned/arrived. The subject in the clause is 'tu' (you, informal). The full sentence often begins with 'C'est bien que...' (It's good that...). Gender of past participle (venu/venue) must agree with the person when using être in compound tenses.
target_language_example: C'est bien que tu sois arrivé sain et sauf.
native_language_example: It's good that you arrived safe and sound.

meaning: 'that's right' / 'that's correct' (affirming something)
additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with a statement, similar to 'c'est bien ça' which is the more common full form. Alone 'est bien ça' is less frequent and usually appears after a subject or in elliptical speech (e.g. 'Oui, est bien ça' is informal/colloquial). Use 'c'est bien ça' in standard speech to mean 'that's correct.'
target_language_example: — Tu as rendez-vous à 14h ? — Oui, c'est bien ça.
native_language_example: — You have an appointment at 2 pm? — Yes, that's correct.

meaning: 'is soon' or 'will be soon' (indicates something will happen/arrive in the near future).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb être (est = 'is') + bientôt ('soon'). Used to say that something exists or will occur shortly. More commonly used with verbs of motion or events (e.g. 'il est bientôt là' or better 'il arrivera bientôt'); native speakers often prefer future tense or impersonal constructions (e.g. 'ça va bientôt arriver', 'arrivera bientôt').
target_language_example: Le train est bientôt en gare.
native_language_example: The train will be at the station soon.

meaning: 'it's good to be' (used to state that being something/somewhere is a good thing)
additional_notes: This construction combines the impersonal adjective bon with an infinitive verb introduced by d' + être. It's somewhat formal/literary and not the most common spoken way to express this idea (French speakers often say 'il est bon de...' or 'c'est bien d'être...'). Use 'est bon d'être' when describing a general advantage or positive state. Ensure the subject and context make clear what 'être' refers to.
target_language_example: Pour la santé, il est bon d'être actif chaque jour.
native_language_example: For your health, it's good to be active every day.

meaning: 'it is good for you to' / 'it's good that you...'
additional_notes: This looks like a fragment of a larger sentence (e.g. «Il est bon de te voir»). Common full structure: «Il est bon de + infinitive» (It's good to ...). When addressed to someone with 'te' the speaker is referring to the person informally (tu). Use 'Il est bon de te...' before an infinitive or substitute with 'C'est bien de te...' in everyday speech. Formal version: 'Il est bon de vous...' for 'vous'.
target_language_example: Il est bon de te voir heureux.
native_language_example: It's good to see you happy.

meaning: is good for you / it is good to you (literal phrasing rarely used)
additional_notes: This exact sequence ('est bon de vous') is unusual in French on its own. You might see 'il est bon de vous voir' (it is good to see you) or 'c'est bon pour vous' (it's good for you). 'Est bon de + infinitive' can be a formal way to say 'it is good to (do something)', often introduced with 'il' or 'c'est'. When addressing someone directly, French prefers constructions like 'ça vous convient' (does that suit you?) or 'c'est bon pour vous'.
target_language_example: Il est bon de vous voir après tout ce temps.
native_language_example: It is good to see you after all this time.

meaning: is it
additional_notes: Standard French normally writes this as « est-ce » with a hyphen. The spelling « est ce » is a common informal or mistaken variant in typing. On its own, it can mean "is it?" or "is this?", but learners most often encounter it in the question pattern « est-ce que ».
target_language_example: est ce vrai ?
native_language_example: Is it true?

meaning: Not a correct or standard French phrase; likely a mistaken combination of 'est-ce que' and 'dont'.
additional_notes: There is no standard French phrase 'est ce dont'. Learners may be trying to combine the question starter 'est-ce que' (used to form yes/no or content questions) with the relative pronoun 'dont' (meaning 'of which', 'whose', or 'about which'). Use them separately: • 'Est-ce que...' introduces a question (e.g. 'Est-ce que tu viens ?' = 'Are you coming?'). • 'Dont' links clauses to show possession or relation (e.g. 'Le livre dont je t'ai parlé' = 'The book I told you about').
