additional_notes: Used to tell someone that it is their turn to do something (play, speak, act). More common and grammatically complete as « c'est ton tour ». The form « est ton tour » without the initial 'c'' is not standard in writing; learners should use « c'est ton tour ». Pronunciation: [se tɔ̃ tuʁ].
target_language_example: C'est ton tour de choisir un film.
native_language_example: It's your turn to choose a movie.

meaning: 'is always like' or 'is always as if'
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something that consistently behaves or seems a certain way. Often followed by a noun, adjective, clause introduced by que, or by an infinitive (depending on context). Common in spoken and written French. Example structures: "Il est toujours comme ça" (He is always like that) or "Elle est toujours comme si elle savait tout" (She is always as if she knew everything).
target_language_example: Il est toujours comme ça quand il est fatigué.
native_language_example: He is always like that when he's tired.

meaning: a mistaken or nonstandard combination; likely intended as "on est tous" meaning "we are all"
additional_notes: Native French speakers say "on est tous" or "nous sommes tous" to mean "we are all." The form "est tous" (est = he/it is) together with "tous" is ungrammatical unless part of a larger clause (e.g., "il est tous..." is incorrect). In the example sentences, the intended phrase is "on est tous" (colloquial "we are all"). Use "on est tous" in spoken French; use "nous sommes tous" in more formal contexts. "Tous" agrees in meaning with "all/everyone."
target_language_example: On est tous fatigués après la randonnée.
native_language_example: We are all tired after the hike.

meaning: not a standalone phrase in French; likely part of a larger expression (e.g. 'c'est tout le...' or 'il est tout le...')
additional_notes: You won't find 'est tout le' used by itself. It's the verb 'est' (is) followed by 'tout le' (all the / the whole) and normally appears inside longer phrases like 'c'est tout le...' (that's all the...) or 'il est tout le...' (he is the whole/entire... — rare). Pay attention to contractions: 'tout le' can become 'tout l'' before a vowel (e.g. 'tout l'univers'). For beginners, learn full expressions rather than this fragment.
target_language_example: C'est tout le mérite de son travail.
native_language_example: That's the whole merit of his work.

meaning: 'is all we/they/one ...' or 'that's all (we/they) ...'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing available or the entirety of what someone has. 'On' is a general/colloquial subject meaning 'we', 'they' or 'one' depending on context. The phrase often appears as 'C'est tout ce qu'on a' = 'That's all we have.' Can be used with different verbs after 'on' (e.g. 'on mange' = 'we eat').
target_language_example: C'est tout ce qu'on a pour dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: That's all we have for dinner tonight.

meaning: 'is everything to' / 'means everything to (someone)'
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is extremely important to someone. Usually appears as "X est tout pour Y" or with a pronoun: "Il/Elle est tout pour moi" = "He/She is everything to me." Not a fixed idiom beyond the literal components; word order and pronouns matter. Common in heartfelt or emphatic statements.
target_language_example: Elle est tout pour lui.
native_language_example: She is everything to him.

meaning: 'is completely' or 'is entirely' (emphasis before an adjective or verb phrase)
additional_notes: This is a combination of the verb is (est) + tout à, used to emphasize that someone or something is fully in a state or fully doing something. It typically appears before an adjective or an infinitive: e.g. « Il est tout à fait raisonnable » (he is completely reasonable) or « Elle est tout à écouter » (she is completely absorbed in listening). Commonly the fuller phrase is « tout à fait » (completely) or « tout à » followed by an infinitive to mean 'completely/fully (doing)'.
target_language_example: Il est tout à fait prêt pour le voyage.
native_language_example: He is completely ready for the trip.

meaning: 'it's too early' (to do something or for something to happen).
additional_notes: Used to say that the time is not yet appropriate for an action or event. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., pour + infinitive) or by a clause. Can be used literally (time of day) or figuratively (not ready, premature).
target_language_example: Il est trop tôt pour décider maintenant.
native_language_example: It's too early to decide now.

meaning: is very kind / that's very kind (of someone).
additional_notes: Used to thank or acknowledge someone's kindness or a polite offer. Often appears as set phrases: "C'est très aimable de ta/votre part" or "C'est très aimable à toi/vous". Polite and slightly formal — appropriate in most social situations. Can be followed by the person: de ta part (informal) / de votre part (formal).
target_language_example: C'est très aimable de votre part de m'aider.
native_language_example: That's very kind of you to help me.

meaning: is very fashionable / very 'in' (trendy)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is very fashionable or trendy. Often followed by a noun or adjective describing the trendy thing (e.g., style, vogue). More common in informal speech and advertising. You may also see simply 'être en' or 'être à la mode' for similar meanings.
target_language_example: Cette marque est très en cette saison.
native_language_example: This brand is very in this season.

meaning: 'is very kind of' (used to say someone is kind for doing something).
additional_notes: Used after a subject or impersonal construction to comment on someone's kindness regarding an action. Common structure: [Person] est très gentil de + infinitive (e.g. Il est très gentil de m'aider). Often used to thank or compliment; equivalent to English 'it's very kind of (someone) to...'.
target_language_example: Il est très gentil de m'avoir aidé hier.
native_language_example: He is very kind of to have helped me yesterday.

meaning: is very kind of (someone) to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to thank or compliment someone for a kind action or thought. In French the structure is 'C'est très gentil à + [person] (de + verb...)' — e.g. 'C'est très gentil à toi de m'aider.' The phrase agrees with the person being praised (toi, vous, lui, etc.). Polite formulas often use 'vous'.
target_language_example: C'est très gentil à toi de m'avoir aidé.
native_language_example: It's very kind of you to have helped me.

meaning: is early (it is early).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb être (est = is) + tôt (early). Used to say that the time of day is early or that something is happening earlier than usual. Commonly appears in sentences like «Il est tôt» (It's early) or with a subject: «Il est encore tôt» (It's still early).
target_language_example: Il est tôt pour partir.
native_language_example: It is early to leave.

meaning: is a good/kind person; is brave (colloquial, often meaning 'nice' or 'honest').
additional_notes: In French, 'brave' as an adjective before a noun often means 'good', 'decent' or 'kind' (not necessarily courageous). The construction 'est un brave' typically appears in descriptions like 'il est un brave homme' or in spoken French shortened to 'c'est un brave' meaning 'he's a good man' or 'he's a decent fellow'. Alone ('est un brave') without the noun is uncommon; you'll usually see 'c'est un brave' or 'il est brave' (meaning courageous). Use 'brave' before a noun to mean 'good/kind' (informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: C'est un brave homme; il aide toujours ses voisins.
native_language_example: He's a good man; he always helps his neighbors.

meaning: 'is a start' or 'is a beginning'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the first step or an initial progress toward a goal. Often follows a statement about an action or result: "C'est un début" is the full phrase meaning "That's a start." Here 'est un début' is the verb phrase 'is a start.'
target_language_example: Apprendre dix mots par jour est un début.
native_language_example: Learning ten words a day is a start.

meaning: 'is a big step' (i.e., represents significant progress or an important move)
additional_notes: Used to say that something marks important progress or a major advance. Often appears in sentences describing achievements, reforms, discoveries, or improvements: e.g., 'C'est un grand pas pour...' French grammar: 'est' is the third-person singular of être; the full phrase is usually part of a larger sentence (subject + 'est un grand pas').
target_language_example: Cette réforme est un grand pas vers l'égalité.
native_language_example: This reform is a big step toward equality.

meaning: 'is an honor to' / 'it is an honor to'.
additional_notes: Used to express that doing something or being given something is a privilege. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g. « est un honneur de vous rencontrer ») or a noun phrase. Formal and polite; common in speeches, letters, and introductions.
target_language_example: C'est un honneur de vous rencontrer aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It is an honor to meet you today.

meaning: it's an honor to (you/meet/serve you/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to politely express that something (meeting, knowing, serving someone) is an honor. Often appears as part of the fixed phrase "C'est un honneur de vous..." followed by an infinitive (avoir, connaître, rencontrer, servir). Formal and polite — common in speeches, introductions, or respectful conversation.
target_language_example: C'est un honneur de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It's an honor to meet you.

meaning: 'it's a pleasure to (meet/receive) you' or 'it's a pleasure to (do something) for you'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase "C'est un plaisir de vous..." followed by an infinitive (recevoir, rencontrer, aider, etc.). A polite, formal expression used when meeting someone or when hosting/assisting them. Translate depending on the verb that follows: e.g. "C'est un plaisir de vous rencontrer" = "It's a pleasure to meet you."
target_language_example: C'est un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It's a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: is a thing / is something (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal phrase using 'truc' (thing/something). Often used to downplay, be vague, or say something is hard to describe (e.g., 'C'est un truc compliqué' = 'It's a complicated thing'). In full sentences you'd normally see 'C'est un truc...' rather than just 'est un truc'.
target_language_example: C'est un truc qui arrive parfois.
native_language_example: It's a thing that happens sometimes.

meaning: is a thing/way of (informal) — used to describe something as characteristic of or typical for someone/something
additional_notes: Colloquial: 'truc' = 'thing' (informal). 'Est un truc de' is used to say that something is a kind of thing, habit, style, or characteristic behavior (often followed by a noun or a possessive phrase). It can express that something is typical of a person, group, or situation: e.g. 'C'est un truc de jeunes' = 'It's a young people's thing.' Not formal; more spoken French.
target_language_example: C'est un truc de famille, on se retrouve tous les dimanches.
native_language_example: It's a family thing; we all get together every Sunday.

meaning: is a (female) friend
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a female friend. 'Est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). If the friend is male, use 'est un ami'. For plural: 'sont des ami·e·s' or 'sont des amies' (female group). In spoken French, the indefinite article may be dropped in some contexts after professions or roles, but with 'amie' the article is normally kept.
target_language_example: Marie est une amie de longue date.
native_language_example: Marie is a long-time friend.

meaning: 'is a chance' or 'is lucky' (depends on context)
additional_notes: This short phrase literally means 'is a chance'. Alone it is uncommon; you will more often see related expressions such as "c'est une chance" (it's lucky / that's fortunate) or "il est une chance" rarely in poetic contexts. If used after a noun, it can mean that something 'is an opportunity' or 'is a chance' (e.g. "Ceci est une chance pour toi" = "This is an opportunity for you"). Pay attention to subject: the typical everyday phrase to say "that's lucky" is "c'est une chance."
target_language_example: C'est une chance de te rencontrer aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It's a chance/opportunity to meet you today.

meaning: 'is a loss' / 'is a waste' (it is something lost or wasted)
additional_notes: Literal phrase: est (is) + une perte (a loss). Commonly used to describe something that results in a loss (time, money, opportunity) or that is unfortunate/wasteful. Can be followed by a noun or used after que/c'est: «C'est une perte» = 'It's a loss/waste.' Context determines whether it means financial loss, wasted effort, or missed opportunity.
target_language_example: Pour lui, ce projet est une perte de temps.
native_language_example: For him, this project is a waste of time.

meaning: 'is a waste of' or 'is a loss of' (used to say something is useless or causes loss)
additional_notes: Used to describe that something results in waste, loss, or is not worth the effort/time. Commonly followed by a noun (temps, argent, énergie) or an infinitive clause (e.g., 'est une perte de temps de...'). Tone can be neutral or negative depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est une perte de temps de regarder ce film si tu n'aimes pas le genre.
native_language_example: It's a waste of time to watch that movie if you don't like the genre.

meaning: 'is an evening' or 'is a party/event (evening)' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb être (est = is) with 'une soirée' (an evening, a get-together or party). Alone it is not a fixed idiom — it appears in sentences like «C'est une soirée…» or «Cette fête est une soirée spéciale». In spoken French, 'une soirée' often means a social event or party happening in the evening. Make sure the subject matches: for 'it is an evening/party' you would normally say 'C'est une soirée.'
target_language_example: C'est une soirée très amusante.
native_language_example: It's a very fun evening/party.

meaning: is a great (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to praise something or someone: 'est une super' is followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g. 'est une super idée', 'est une super prof'). Informal but common in spoken French. You must add the feminine noun after the phrase; for masculine nouns use 'est un super'.
target_language_example: C'est une ville qui est une super découverte pour les touristes.
native_language_example: It's a city that's a great find for tourists.

meaning: came
additional_notes: passé composé of venir (“to come”), formed with être. It is used for a completed past action. The past participle agrees with the subject: est venue (feminine), sont venus / sont venues (plural).
target_language_example: Mon père est venu ce matin.
native_language_example: My father came this morning.

meaning: 'it is vital that' / 'it is essential that' (expresses necessity/importance).
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive mood after 'que' (e.g., que + subjunctive). Formal/neutral register. Same structure as other impersonal expressions like 'il faut que' or 'il est important que'. Agree the rest of sentence for gender/number as needed (present participles/participles may change).
target_language_example: Il est vital que nous finissions ce projet à temps.
native_language_example: It is vital that we finish this project on time.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase; likely a mistaken word order for «êtes-vous» (are you) or part of a longer phrase where «est» belongs to a different subject (e.g. «Il est, vous…»).
additional_notes: This sequence is almost always an error. «est» is 3rd-person singular of être (he/she/it is); «vous» is 2nd-person pronoun, so they do not form a grammatical pair. Correct alternatives for questions: - Inversion: «Êtes-vous… ?» (formal/neutral) - «Est-ce que vous… ?» + verb (neutral) If you encounter «est vous» in writing, check for a typo or mispunctuation; it should usually be corrected to one of the forms above.
target_language_example: Il est, vous dites, trop tard ?
native_language_example: He is, you say, too late?

meaning: Not a standard French phrase (likely a word order mistake); no fixed meaning.
additional_notes:
This combination is not grammatically correct in French. A learner might have meant one of these correct forms:
- "est-ce que vous... ?" (used to form yes/no questions: "Are you...? / Do you...?")
- "êtes-vous... ?" (inversion for formal questions: "Are you...?")
- "c'est vous le/la..." ("are you the..."—colloquial, but would normally be "c'est vous qui..." or "vous êtes le/la...")
If you encounter "est vous le" in writing or speech, it's likely an error; choose the appropriate correct form above depending on whether you need a question or a statement.
target_language_example: *est vous le* — incorrect sequence as in: «Pourquoi est vous le plus rapide?» (incorrect; should be «Pourquoi êtes-vous le plus rapide ?»).
native_language_example: *est vous le* — incorrect sequence as in: "Why est you the fastest?" (incorrect; should be "Why are you the fastest?").

meaning: Not a correct French expression; likely a mistaken word order. Possibly intended to be either «est-ce que» (question particle) or «êtes-vous» (inversion of être for 'are you').
additional_notes:
The exact string 'est vous que' is ungrammatical in French and should not be used. Common correct alternatives:
- 'est-ce que' (used to introduce yes/no questions): e.g. 'Est-ce que vous venez ?' = 'Are you coming?'
- 'êtes-vous' (inversion for formal questions with the verb 'être'): e.g. 'Êtes-vous prêt ?' = 'Are you ready?'
Beginners should learn 'est-ce que' as the easiest spoken question form and 'êtes-vous' for formal/written inversion. The example below shows the mistaken phrase in context to illustrate that it is incorrect and how it might appear in learners' writing or speech.
target_language_example: *est vous que* n'est pas correct en français ; on dira plutôt «est-ce que» ou «êtes-vous».
native_language_example: "est vous que" is not correct in French; say "est-ce que" or "êtes-vous" instead.

meaning: 'est' + 'vous' + 'que je' — not a correct or natural French phrase; likely a mistaken word order with no fixed meaning.
additional_notes:
This sequence mixes the 3rd-person singular verb 'est' (être), the pronoun 'vous', and the connector 'que je'. It is ungrammatical in French and should not be used. Closest correct patterns include:
- « est-ce que vous... ? » — question starter meaning 'do/does you...?' or 'is it that you...?' (e.g. « Est-ce que vous parlez anglais ? »)
- « êtes-vous... ? » — inversion for formal questions (e.g. « Êtes-vous prêt ? »)
- « que je... » — begins a subordinate clause meaning 'that I...' (e.g. « Je pense que je peux venir. »)
If you intended a question beginning with 'do you...' use 'Est-ce que vous...' or inversion 'Êtes-vous...'.
target_language_example: *est vous que je* ne se dit pas en français et doit être évité.
native_language_example: *est vous que je* is not said in French and should be avoided.

meaning: a word order used in relative or cleft-like constructions: 'it/this/that is you who...'/ 'you are the one who...'
additional_notes: This sequence appears when emphasising the subject with a structure like 'C'est vous qui...' or in reported clauses where 'vous' is the subject of a verb introduced by 'qui'. By itself 'est vous qui' is ungrammatical at the start of a sentence; you will usually see it inside a larger phrase (e.g. 'C'est vous qui décidez.'). In spoken French the full form 'C'est vous qui...' is common to emphasize who does something.
target_language_example: C'est vous qui décidez du programme.
native_language_example: It's you who decides the program. / You are the one who decides the program.

meaning: This is an incomplete fragment rather than a grammatical fixed phrase. It appears to be part of constructions like "C'est vous qui l'..." or "Est-ce vous qui l'...", meaning respectively "It is you who (it) ..." or "Is it you who (it) ...", where "l'" begins a following verb or pronoun that starts with a vowel.
additional_notes:
Alone, "est vous qui l'" is ungrammatical. Common full forms:
- "C'est vous qui l'avez fait." = "It is you who did it." (emphatic statement)
- "Est-ce vous qui l'avez fait ?" = "Is it you who did it?" (question)
The apostrophe "l'" is the elided form of "le" or "la" (direct object) or the start of a verb/pronoun beginning with a vowel. To be correct, include the initial element (C' or Est-ce) and complete the following word after "l'".
target_language_example: Est-ce vous qui l'avez fait ?
native_language_example: Is it you who did it?

meaning: Fragment — likely part of a sentence meaning 'it/that is you who ... me' or 'is it you who ... me'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself. It appears to be a clipped fragment (with m' beginning a verb or pronoun like m'entends, m'a, m'as, m'appelle). In full sentences you'd see constructions like « C'est vous qui m'appelez ? » (Is it you who is calling me?) or « C'est vous qui m'avez aidé » (You are the one who helped me). The core pattern is « C'est + (ce) + pronoun + qui + ... » to emphasize the subject: 'It's you who...'.
target_language_example: C'est vous qui m'appelez ?
native_language_example: Is it you who is calling me?

meaning: a structure meaning 'it is/was you who ... me' (used to emphasize that the other person performed an action toward the speaker).
additional_notes: This appears inside the cleft construction C'est vous qui m'avez + past participle. Use to emphasize or identify the person responsible for an action affecting the speaker (called a cleft sentence). The verb agrees with the relative pronoun 'qui' and typically is in the tense needed (here passé composé: m'avez + past participle). In spoken French you may also hear 'c'est vous qui m'avez...' contracted to 'c'est vous qui m'avez...' with same meaning. Replace 'm'' with other object pronouns as needed (te, le, lui, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est vous qui m'avez aidé quand j'avais besoin.
native_language_example: It was you who helped me when I needed it.

meaning: 'this/that is true' (unusual, nonstandard word order in French)
additional_notes: Standard French word order places the subject 'ce' before the verb: 'ce est vrai', which is contracted to 'c'est vrai' in normal speech and writing. The sequence 'est vrai ce' is not used in contemporary standard French and would generally be considered poetic inversion, archaic, or simply an error. Teach learners to use 'c'est vrai' for 'it's true' and 'c'est vrai que...' to introduce a clause ('it's true that...').
target_language_example: Est vrai ce que tu dis ?
native_language_example: Is what you say true?

meaning: 'it is true that' (used to concede or confirm a point).
additional_notes: A short form of "il est vrai que" used before a clause to admit, confirm, or acknowledge something. Common in spoken and written French. When followed by a vowel or silent h, the contraction "qu'" is used (e.g. "est vrai qu'il..."). Can introduce a concession (similar to "admittedly" or "it's true that" in English).
target_language_example: Il est vrai qu'il fait froid aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It is true that it's cold today.

meaning: 'is really this/that' (literal fragment; not a fixed standalone phrase)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed expression by itself. It can appear inside sentences where est (is) is the verb, vraiment (really) is an adverb, and ce functions as a demonstrative pronoun or part of a demonstrative construction. Grammatically it is usually part of a larger structure (e.g., « est vraiment ce que... », « est vraiment ce dont... »). In many cases the clearer idiomatic forms are « c'est vraiment... » or « est vraiment + adjective ». Use with care: word order and punctuation (e.g., « Est-ce... ? » for questions) often change the surface form.
target_language_example: Il est vraiment ce que tu décris, mais je reste sceptique.
native_language_example: He is really what you describe, but I'm still skeptical.

meaning: is really what / is truly what (used to identify or emphasize what something is)
additional_notes: This sequence combines the verb est (is) + adverb vraiment (really) + the relative/neutral phrase ce que (what/that which). It’s not a fixed idiom by itself but a common word order used to stress that something truly corresponds to or equals something else (often followed by a clause). You will often see similar patterns like «c'est vraiment ce que…» or «il est vraiment ce que…».
target_language_example: Ce film est vraiment ce que j'attendais : émouvant et bien réalisé.
native_language_example: This movie is really what I expected: moving and well made.

meaning: is caused by / is because of
additional_notes: This phrase is not a standard fixed expression in French. More common forms to express causation are "est à cause de" (is caused by) or "est à l'origine de" (is the origin of). Alone, "est à cause" is incomplete — it needs the preposition "de" and a noun or pronoun after it: e.g. "Le retard est à cause de la neige" (colloquial) or better: "Le retard est dû à la neige." For beginners, prefer "dû à" or "à cause de" to say "because of / due to."
target_language_example: Le problème est à cause d'une erreur de configuration. (less natural) → Mieux: Le problème est dû à une erreur de configuration.
native_language_example: The problem is caused by a configuration error. → Better: The problem is due to a configuration error.

meaning: 'is because of' or 'is due to'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the reason or cause of something. Grammatically, French more commonly uses "c'est à cause de" or "est dû(e) à" rather than "est à cause de" on its own; you will often see the full form "C'est à cause de..." to mean "It's because of...". Followed by a noun or noun phrase (not a clause) introduced by "de."
target_language_example: C'est à cause de la pluie que le match a été annulé.
native_language_example: It's because of the rain that the match was cancelled.

meaning: 'is up to' / 'depends on' (used to indicate responsibility, choice, or that something belongs to someone/something)
additional_notes: The exact sequence « est à ce » is uncommon and often results from a split or misplacement of words (native speakers typically say « c'est à... », « il/elle est à... » or « est à + noun/pronoun »). When it appears, it may be part of a larger construction like « il est à ce que... » (formal/rare) or a clumsy rephrasing of « c'est à... ». Use with caution; prefer standard alternatives such as « C'est à toi », « Cela dépend de » or « Il/elle appartient à ».
target_language_example: Il est à ce projet de définir les priorités, mais il hésite.
native_language_example: It is up to this project to define the priorities, but it hesitates.

meaning: it's my turn / it's up to me to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate responsibility or turn: someone says that a task or action belongs to them. Often appears in constructions like « c'est à moi de + infinitive » or after a verb with être: « c'est à moi de décider » / « c'est à moi ». The exact short form « est à moi de » appears as part of a larger clause (e.g. « Maintenant, c'est à moi de parler. »).
target_language_example: Maintenant, c'est à moi de parler.
native_language_example: Now it's my turn to speak.

meaning: Literally 'is to me that' — not a standard fixed French phrase; typically a non-idiomatic or incorrect sequence. Could arise from a mistaken combination of 'est à moi' ('is mine') and a following 'que' introducing a clause.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common or grammatical fixed expression by itself. Possible intentions: 1) to say 'c'est à moi' ('it's mine' / 'it's my turn'); 2) part of a longer, grammatically corrected clause (e.g. 'La maison est à moi, ce que j'ai acheté' is incorrect — correct forms: 'La maison est à moi, je l'ai achetée' or 'La maison, que j'ai achetée, est à moi'). For learners, prefer 'C'est à moi' for possession or 'C'est à moi de + infinitive' for 'it's my turn to...'.
target_language_example: La chaise est à moi que j'ai achetée l'année dernière. (non standard — mieux : La chaise est à moi ; je l'ai achetée l'année dernière.)
native_language_example: The chair is mine that I bought last year. (non-standard — better: The chair is mine; I bought it last year.)

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to be a misordered or incorrect sequence (literally: 'is to me that you'). It likely combines 'est à moi' ('is mine') and 'que tu' ('that you') but as written it is ungrammatical.
additional_notes: This string is not a common or correct French expression. Possible intended corrections: 'c'est à moi' or 'il est à moi' for 'it's mine'; 'que tu ...' must introduce a subordinate clause (e.g. 'que tu viennes'). Do not use 'est à moi que tu' as written. If encountered in speech or text, ask the speaker/writer to clarify.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas question que tu prennes ce jouet — il est à moi que tu le veuilles ou non.
native_language_example: It's out of the question that you take that toy — it's mine whether you want it or not.

meaning: 'belongs to my' or 'is mine' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence where est (is) + à (to/belongs to) + mon (my). It's used before a masculine singular noun to say something belongs to the speaker: [object] est à mon [nom] or more commonly est à moi. Native speakers usually say 'est à moi' instead of 'est à mon' unless followed by a specific noun ('est à mon frère'). If you see 'est à mon' alone, it's incomplete — you need the noun that follows (e.g. 'est à mon frère').
target_language_example: Ce livre est à mon frère.
native_language_example: This book belongs to my brother.

meaning: 'is about' or 'is approximately'
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself in French; it looks like part of a larger expression such as "est à peu près" (meaning "is about/approximately"). On its own, "est à peu" would be incomplete and uncommon. For learners, remember the full expression "à peu près" = "approximately" and use "est à peu près" to say "is about/roughly".
target_language_example: La réunion est à peu près terminée.
native_language_example: The meeting is about/roughly finished.

meaning: 'is about' or 'concerns' (describes the subject of something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a text, talk, film, discussion, etc., deals with a particular topic. It is the verb être + prepositional phrase à propos de. Commonly used in written and spoken French. Can appear with different subjects: « Ce livre est à propos de... », « La réunion est à propos de... »
target_language_example: Le documentaire est à propos de la protection des océans.
native_language_example: The documentary is about protecting the oceans.

meaning: is in his/her/its place; is where it/they should be.
additional_notes: Used with a noun that indicates possession (sa = his/her/its) to say someone or something is in the correct place or position. Agreement: 'sa' is feminine singular (sa place). The full phrase appears in sentences like 'Il est à sa place' (He is in his place) or 'Tout est à sa place' (Everything is where it belongs). Context determines whether 'sa' refers to his, her, or its.
target_language_example: La chaise est à sa place dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: The chair is in its place in the kitchen.

meaning: it's your turn / it's up to you (to do something)
additional_notes: Used to say that responsibility, choice, or the next action belongs to the person addressed. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause: « C'est à toi de décider » or « C'est à toi de jouer ». The full common form is « c'est à toi de ». In spoken French the leading « c' » may be dropped in writing only when context already provides it, but learners should use « c'est à toi de ».
target_language_example: C'est à toi de parler maintenant.
native_language_example: It's your turn to speak now.

meaning: it's up to you / it's your turn to
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has responsibility, choice, or the next turn. Commonly appears as 'C'est à vous de...' (with the contraction C'est). Followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase: 'C'est à vous de décider' = 'It's up to you to decide.' Polite when addressing someone (e.g. a customer or guest) and also used in casual contexts.
target_language_example: C'est à vous de choisir le film.
native_language_example: It's up to you to choose the movie.

meaning: 'it's up to you that' / 'it's for you that' (used to emphasize that something belongs to or is decided by you)
additional_notes: This phrase is a marked, somewhat formal or emphatic construction used to stress that responsibility, possession or a decision concerns the person addressed. It often appears in sentences contrasting others (e.g., « Ce n'est pas à moi, c'est à vous que revient la décision »). In everyday speech speakers more commonly use simpler forms like « c'est à vous » or « c'est vous qui… ». Use « est à vous que » when you want to strongly emphasize the object/role belongs to or is the responsibility of 'you'.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas à moi, c'est à vous que revient la responsabilité.
native_language_example: It's not up to me; it's you who are responsible.

meaning: used in formal/literary French to emphasize that something belongs to or concerns you (lit. "it is to you that I...").
additional_notes: This is a formal or literary construction that puts emphasis on the indirect object or beneficiary. It often appears in clauses where the speaker wants to stress 'to you' (vous) as the person affected: e.g. "C'est à vous que je pense" = "It is you I am thinking of." In everyday spoken French, the same idea is usually expressed more simply (e.g. "C'est toi que je cherche" / "Je pense à toi"). Word order: C'est + à + person + que + (clause).
target_language_example: C'est à vous que je pense chaque fois que je réussis.
native_language_example: It is you I think of every time I succeed.

meaning: literally 'is at this/that' — used to indicate that something belongs to, is due to, or is the responsibility of something/someone (context-dependent); this specific short phrase is uncommon alone and usually part of a larger expression.
additional_notes: Alone, 'est à ça' is not a common fixed expression in French; you'll more often see forms like 'ça tient à...' (it is due to...), 'c'est à ça que...' (that's what.../that's why...), or 'est à moi/à toi' (belongs to me/you). If you encounter 'est à ça' in a sentence, check the surrounding words: it may be an informal or clipped part of 'c'est à ça que' or similar. Do not use 'est à ça' by itself in standard French.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas grave — ce n'est pas à toi que ça est à ça.
native_language_example: This sentence is awkward — 'est à ça' should be part of a fuller expression.

meaning: used to introduce what something is for / to explain the purpose or reason (≈ 'that's what... is for' or 'that's why...').
additional_notes: This construction appears in sentences like «C'est à ça que sert.../C'est à ça que ça sert» or «C'est à ça que je pensais». On its own 'est à ça que' is part of a larger clause and usually follows 'c'est' (or another subject + être). It links the subject to the purpose, function, or intended referent. Common patterns: 'C'est à ça que sert X' (That's what X is for) and 'C'est à ça que je pensais' (That's what I was thinking).
target_language_example: C'est à ça que sert ce logiciel.
native_language_example: That's what this software is for.

meaning: Non-standard or mistaken form aiming to mimic 'est-ce qu'il' (the correct question marker). It is not grammatically correct in French; speakers should use 'est-ce qu'il' instead.
additional_notes: Likely a misspelling or mishearing of 'est-ce qu'il'. Avoid using 'est ça qu'il' in writing or formal speech. In casual speech, people sometimes contract 'est-ce que' to 'est-ce qu'' (written est-ce qu'il), but replacing 'ce' with 'ça' is incorrect. The phrase does not function as a proper question marker and may confuse native speakers.
target_language_example: Est ça qu'il vient ce soir ?
native_language_example: (Incorrect) Is that he coming tonight? — Correct form: "Est-ce qu'il vient ce soir ?" meaning "Is he coming tonight?"

meaning: colloquial/emphatic structure used in questions or statements (similar to 'is it that...' or 'is that...')
additional_notes: This sequence is informal and often appears in spoken French to add emphasis or to form a question. It usually follows a noun, pronoun or phrase and can be part of constructions like 'C'est ça que...' (That's what...) or in abbreviated speech 'Est-ce ça que...'. Alone as 'est ça que' it is not a standard neutral written form; learners will more commonly encounter 'C'est ça ?' (Is that so?) or 'Est-ce que...' for questions.
target_language_example: C'est ça que tu veux ?
native_language_example: Is that what you want?

meaning: Not a correct or grammatical French expression; likely a mistaken word order when trying to form questions or emphasize 'that' (e.g., mixing up 'Est-ce que je...' and 'C'est ça que je...').
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'est ça que je' is ungrammatical in standard French. For questions use 'Est-ce que je...' (Est-ce que je peux venir ? = Can I come?). To say 'That's what I...' use 'C'est ça que je...' (colloquial) or more formally 'C'est ce que je...'. If you see 'est ça que je' in speech or writing, it's usually an error or a transcription of someone hesitating; correct alternatives depend on intended meaning.
target_language_example: C'est ça que je voulais dire, pas 'est ça que je'.
native_language_example: That's what I meant, not 'est ça que je'.

meaning: Not a correct or standard French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment combining 'est‑ce que' and 'c'est… que'. It does not form a grammatical question or statement by itself.
additional_notes: Do not use 'est ça que tu' as written. Learners often confuse: 1) 'Est‑ce que tu…' — neutral way to ask yes/no questions (e.g. 'Est‑ce que tu viens ?' = 'Are you coming?'), and 2) 'C'est… que tu…' — cleft structure for emphasis (e.g. 'C'est toi que je veux.' = 'It's you that I want.'). If you want a simple question, use 'Est‑ce que tu...'. If you want to emphasize a constituent, use 'C'est... que tu...'.
target_language_example: (Incorrect) «Est ça que tu viens ?» — incorrect; should be «Est‑ce que tu viens ?»
native_language_example: (Incorrect) "Is that that you are coming?" — the correct form is "Are you coming?"

meaning: 'is that what you want?' (colloquial, slightly ungrammatical phrasing)
additional_notes: This phrase is an informal, conversational way to ask if something is what the other person wants. Standard, grammatically correct forms are "est-ce que tu veux ça ?" or "c'est ce que tu veux ?". You may hear "est ça que tu veux" in casual spoken French or regional speech. Use the standard forms in writing or formal speech.
target_language_example: Tu veux rester ici, est ça que tu veux ?
native_language_example: You want to stay here — is that what you want?

meaning: 'it's that which' or 'is that which' (used in spoken/colloquial French to emphasize or clarify what/which).
additional_notes: This sequence is informal and typically appears in spoken French when the speaker is clarifying or emphasizing the subject or cause: e.g. « C'est ça qui... » (That's what/that's the thing that...). As written here, without the initial C', 'est ça qui' is incomplete; the common full form is « C'est ça qui... ». It introduces a relative clause explaining what causes something or what is being talked about. Often followed by a verb: « C'est ça qui m'énerve. »
target_language_example: C'est ça qui m'énerve, il n'écoute jamais.
native_language_example: That's what annoys me — he never listens.

meaning: used in spoken French to emphasize or confirm something (roughly 'that's what it is' / 'that's the thing')
additional_notes: This sequence is informal and conversational. It's a spoken emphatic construction combining 'c'est'/'est' + 'ça' + 'qui est' to underline or confirm a fact already mentioned. Depending on context, speakers may say 'c'est ça qui est...' or simply 'c'est ça'. Alone, 'est ça qui est' without 'c'' (as in 'c'est') is uncommon in standard written French. Use in casual speech to point to or stress the thing you mean.
target_language_example: C'est ça qui est important, pas le reste.
native_language_example: That's what's important, not the rest.

meaning: and (he/she/it) + past action — used to link two past actions (auxiliary 'avoir' in passé composé).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the third-person singular of the auxiliary verb 'avoir' (a). It commonly appears before a past participle to form the passé composé (e.g., «et a vu», «et a retrouvé»). Use it to join two actions performed by the same subject. Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar for passé composé.
target_language_example: Elle a fini son travail et a quitté la pièce.
native_language_example: She finished her work and left the room.

meaning: 'and thus' / 'and so' (connects a result or continuation)
additional_notes: Used to link ideas, showing a result, conclusion or continuation. Formality: neutral — can be used in spoken and written French, though 'et donc' or just 'ainsi' may be more common in conversation. Often appears before a clause that summarizes or follows from what was said.
target_language_example: Il a travaillé tard, et ainsi il a fini le projet à temps.
native_language_example: He worked late, and thus he finished the project on time.

meaning: 'and so on' / 'and so forth' — indicates a continuation of a list or sequence.
additional_notes: Used to finish a list when you don't want to name every item. Can appear at the end of a sentence or alone as a short comment. Formal and neutral; interchangeable with 'etc.' or 'et cetera' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Il collectionne des timbres, des cartes postales, des pièces de monnaie, et ainsi de suite.
native_language_example: He collects stamps, postcards, coins, and so on.

meaning: 'and go' — the conjunction et (and) followed by the infinitive aller (to go).
additional_notes: Very literal combination: used when linking actions or clauses where the next action is 'to go'. Depending on context, it can mean 'and (to) go', 'and go (there)', or be part of idiomatic structures (e.g. «aller et venir»). As written, it's simply 'and go' and requires context (subject, place, tense) to form a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Je prends mon sac et aller au marché n'était plus possible.
native_language_example: I take my bag and going to the market was no longer possible.

meaning: 'so?' / 'and then?' — a short phrase to ask what follows, to challenge something, or to move a conversation on.
additional_notes: Used to ask what happens next (neutral) or to challenge/brush off someone's point (often with a slightly confrontational or dismissive tone). Can be followed by a question (Et alors?) or used to continue a narrative (Et alors, ...). Tone and context determine whether it's curious, impatient, or dismissive.
target_language_example: Tu m'as dit que tu partais. Et alors, qu'est-ce que tu veux faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: You told me you're leaving. So? / And then, what do you want to do now?

meaning: 'and then' or 'what's next/after that'.
additional_notes: Used to link events in sequence (and then) or to ask/press for what happens next (so? what now?). Context determines whether it's neutral (narrating) or slightly impatient when used as a question. Can be followed by a clause or used alone as a prompt.
target_language_example: J'ai fini mes devoirs, et après je vais regarder un film.
native_language_example: I finished my homework, and then I'm going to watch a movie.

meaning: 'and sit' (imperative plural or formal — from 'asseoir')
additional_notes: Combination of 'et' (and) + 'asseyez' which is the imperative form of 'asseoir' for vous or for plural subject (vous asseyez → "asseyez-vous"). By itself 'et asseyez' is likely part of a larger instruction like 'entrez et asseyez-vous' or a colloquial shortened form of 'et asseyez-vous'. In spoken French speakers often omit reflexive pronouns in hurried speech, but standard written/formal French uses 'asseyez-vous'. Use 'assieds-toi' for informal singular.
target_language_example: Entrez, et asseyez-vous, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Come in, and sit down, please.

meaning: 'and to the' or 'and at the' (contraction of et + au).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction et (and) with the contraction au (à + le). Used when linking two elements where the second begins with 'au' (à + le). You will see it in phrases like « X et au Y » but it's more common inside longer sentences (e.g. « et au cinéma » = 'and at/to the cinema'). Make sure the noun after au is masculine singular. Not a standalone idiom.
target_language_example: Nous allons au parc et au cinéma demain.
native_language_example: We are going to the park and to the cinema tomorrow.

meaning: 'and with' — used to add another person, thing, circumstance, or detail.
additional_notes: A simple combination of conjunctions: et = 'and', avec = 'with'. Used to introduce an additional item or condition (people, objects, causes, manners). Can appear in conversational questions (Et avec...?) meaning 'And what about...?' or 'And (how about) ...?'.
target_language_example: Et avec Marie, qu'est‑ce qu'on fait ?
native_language_example: And with Marie, what do we do?

meaning: and a lot / and many / and much (adds emphasis or quantity)
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun, adjective, verb phrase or clause to add emphasis on quantity or degree (similar to 'and a lot' or 'and much' in English). Can follow numbers (e.g., '10 et beaucoup' = '10 and more than that') but this usage is informal. Context determines whether it means 'many' (countable), 'much' (uncountable) or 'a lot' (general emphasis).
target_language_example: Il travaille tard, et beaucoup.
native_language_example: He works late, and a lot.

meaning: 'and white' (literal); used when listing colors or describing something as white in addition to something else
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the adjective 'blanc' (white). It appears in lists or compound descriptions: e.g. 'noir et blanc' = 'black and white'. Make sure to agree 'blanc' for gender/number when needed: 'blanche' (feminine), 'blancs/blanches' (plural).
target_language_example: La photo est en noir et blanc.
native_language_example: The photo is in black and white.

meaning: and that's fine / and okay (used to close a remark or move on)
additional_notes: "et bon" is an informal, conversational filler used to wrap up a point, soften a transition, or indicate acceptance. It can be similar to English "anyway," "well then," or "so," depending on context. Often spoken; tone and intonation matter. Not a fixed grammatical construction — native speakers may also say "bon" alone.
target_language_example: Il est en retard, et bon, on commence sans lui.
native_language_example: He's late, and anyway, we'll start without him.

meaning: and this/that
additional_notes: Used to introduce or call attention to something previously mentioned or present in the situation. Can be neutral factual ('and this...') or colloquial to ask 'and what about...' / 'what about...'. Tone depends on context and intonation. Often followed by a noun or clause.
target_language_example: Et ce projet, tu en penses quoi ?
native_language_example: And what about this project, what do you think?

meaning: 'and what' or 'and that which' (links to a clause or question).
additional_notes: Used to connect ideas, often before a clause introduced by que (ce que) or in questions. Can appear in sentences like «Et ce que... ?» to add another item or to ask 'and what about...?' It combines et (and) + ce que (what/that which).
target_language_example: Tu veux du thé, du café, et ce que je t'ai préparé ?
native_language_example: Do you want tea, coffee, and what I prepared for you?

meaning: and that
additional_notes: A linking phrase used to add information or emphasize a result; often follows a clause and can introduce a summary, consequence, or clarification. In English it usually translates as 'and that' or 'and this' — sometimes it is omitted in natural English. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a oublié son passeport, et cela complique notre voyage.
native_language_example: He forgot his passport, and that complicates our trip.

meaning: 'and each' or 'and every'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction et (and) with the distributive adjective chaque (each/every). Used before a singular noun to mean 'and each' or 'and every' when listing or adding items. Word order: et + chaque + noun. Not a fixed idiom — simply two common words used together.
target_language_example: Nous avons des stylos et chaque étudiant a un cahier.
native_language_example: We have pens and each student has a notebook.

meaning: and at/with (someone's place, business, or regarding someone).
additional_notes: Combines 'et' (and) with 'chez' (at/at the home of, with, or regarding someone's establishment). Used when listing places or people: e.g. 'chez Marie' (at Marie's) or 'chez le médecin' (at the doctor's). You will often see 'et chez' in phrases that connect multiple locations or owners: 'chez Paul et chez Marie' = 'at Paul's and at Marie's'. 'Chez' is followed by a noun or proper name; no article is needed with a proper name but is used with common nouns ('chez le médecin').
target_language_example: Je passe chez Paul et chez Marie cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I'll stop by Paul's and Marie's this afternoon.

meaning: 'and how true/indeed!' — an emphatic agreement or strong affirmation (often exclamatory).
additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with a preceding statement or to add emphasis. Equivalent to English responses like "you bet!", "absolutely!", "no kidding!", or "tell me about it!". Typically appears alone or after the statement it emphasizes (e.g., « Il fait chaud. » — « Et combien ! »). Informal but common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: — Cette fête était incroyable. — Et combien !
native_language_example: — That party was amazing. — You bet!

meaning: 'and how many' / 'and how much (of)' — used to ask about quantity after another question or statement.
additional_notes: Commonly used to add a follow-up question about quantity or amount. 'Combien de' asks 'how many' (countable) or 'how much' (with uncountable nouns); 'et' simply links it to what was just said. Can begin a standalone question or be attached to a previous clause: e.g. 'Tu as des pommes, et combien de?' is informal/colloquial — more natural: 'Et combien en as-tu ?' or 'Et combien de... ?' followed by a noun: 'Et combien de personnes ?'.
target_language_example: Tu as acheté des livres, et combien de ?
native_language_example: You bought books — and how many?

meaning: and as / and like (used to introduce a comparison, explanation, or example)
additional_notes: 'Et comme' combines 'et' (and) with 'comme' (as/like). It often links two clauses where the second gives a reason, example, comparison, or consequence: 'and since' or 'and as' in English. In speech it can be followed by a clause or a noun phrase. Context decides whether it means 'and as,' 'and since,' or 'and like.'
target_language_example: Il a oublié ses clés, et comme il pleuvait, il est resté chez lui.
native_language_example: He forgot his keys, and since it was raining, he stayed home.

meaning: 'and how' (used to ask for more information or clarification).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase to follow up or shift the topic to ask how something is done, how someone is, or for clarification. Often starts a question and can be slightly informal depending on tone. In English it often maps to 'and how?', 'how about...', or 'and how is it for you?'.
target_language_example: Et comment tu t'organises pour le weekend ?
native_language_example: And how are you organizing yourself for the weekend?

meaning: 'and how about you?' — a polite way to ask someone their opinion, feelings, or situation in return.
additional_notes: Used in conversation to return a question to the other person. Often follows a statement about yourself (e.g., J'aime le film, et comment vous ?). More common variations: « et vous ? », « et toi ? » (informal). « Et comment vous » is slightly more formal/polite because of 'vous' and can sound conversational; it may be followed by a verb or noun depending on context (e.g., « Et comment vous trouvez le film ? » or simply « Et comment vous ? »).
target_language_example: J'ai passé une bonne journée, et comment vous ?
native_language_example: I had a good day, and how about you?

meaning: and of
additional_notes: Contraction of et + de before a vowel or mute h (et de → et d'). Used to join two elements where the second begins with de followed by a vowel: e.g. "et d'amour" (and of love) or "et d'heure" (and of hour). In many contexts in English the de is part of a prepositional phrase translated as "of" or "from"; sometimes the whole phrase is better rendered simply as "and" depending on idiomatic English. Pay attention to elision: only used when the following word begins with a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Il parle de musique et d'art.
native_language_example: He talks about music and art.

meaning: 'and in' — the conjunction 'and' followed by the preposition 'in'.
additional_notes: Used when linking two clauses or items where the second begins with 'dans' (in/inside/within). Common in sentences like 'il y a... et dans...' or when adding another point: 'Il est entré et dans la pièce, il a...'. Often appears as part of longer phrases (et dans ce cas = 'and in that case'). Pronunciation: [e] [dɑ̃].
target_language_example: Il a apporté le gâteau, et dans la boîte il y avait des bougies.
native_language_example: He brought the cake, and in the box there were candles.

meaning: and (some)
additional_notes: A combination of et (and) + des (the plural indefinite article 'some' or simply plural marker). Used to join two noun phrases when the second is plural or unspecified quantity. In many contexts it simply means 'and' before a plural noun (e.g. et des couvertures = and blankets). Not an idiom — grammatical construction.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté des pommes et des oranges.
native_language_example: She bought apples and oranges.

meaning: 'and to say' or 'and say' (links an action to speaking); also used to report what someone said.
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'et' (and) + 'dire' (to say). Often appears in reported speech or when adding a comment: e.g. « Il est venu et dire... » (colloquial/elliptical) or more properly « Il est venu et a dit ... ». Alone 'et dire' can be part of expressions like « et dire que... » meaning 'and to think that...' or 'can you believe that...'. Use 'et dire que...' to introduce surprise, contrast, or regret about a fact.
target_language_example: Et dire que j'avais refusé cette offre !
native_language_example: And to think that I had refused that offer!

meaning: and must / and has to
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction et (and) + doit (3rd person singular present of devoir). Used when adding an obligation, necessity, or expectation about someone/something already mentioned. subject for doit must be clear from context (e.g., il/elle/on or a noun previously stated).
target_language_example: Il a fini son travail et doit partir maintenant.
native_language_example: He finished his work and must leave now.

meaning: and gives / and yields (from donner — to give).
additional_notes: Commonly used as the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the verb 'donne' (3rd person singular present of donner) or imperative/formal 2nd person. Context determines subject: 'il/elle donne' (he/she gives) or in recipes/formulas 'et donne' can mean 'and yields' (e.g., 'mélangez... et donne une sauce' — and it yields a sauce). Also appears in spoken instructions: 'Ajoute X et donne Y.'
target_language_example: Elle mélange la farine et donne une pâte lisse.
native_language_example: She mixes the flour and yields a smooth dough.

meaning: 'and the' (masculine singular) — the conjunction 'et' + the contracted article 'du' (de + le).
additional_notes: Used to join two nouns or noun phrases where the second begins with 'du' (de + le). 'Du' is the masculine singular partitive or the contraction of 'de' + 'le' (of the). Context decides translation: sometimes 'du' means 'of the' (possession or origin) and sometimes 'some' (partitive). Example sentences show both uses (possession: 'Fils du Gondor'; partitive/combined lists: 'la neige et du givre').
target_language_example: Nous parlons du projet et du calendrier.
native_language_example: We are talking about the project and the schedule.

meaning: 'and she' / 'and it' (used to add information about a previously mentioned feminine noun or person)
additional_notes: A simple conjunction + pronoun: et = 'and'; elle = 'she' or 'it' for feminine nouns. Used to continue a sentence by adding another detail about a feminine person or thing already mentioned. Depending on context it can mean 'and she...' (referring to a woman/person) or 'and it...' (referring to a feminine noun like 'la situation'). Pronoun agrees in gender (elle = feminine).
target_language_example: La situation est difficile, et elle change tous les jours.
native_language_example: The situation is difficult, and it changes every day.

meaning: and also; and in (when followed by a noun introduced by the preposition en).
additional_notes: Two uses shown: 1) informal/emphatic 'et en plus' = 'and moreover/also'. 2) 'et en' can join two prepositional phrases starting with en (e.g. 'en bois et en pierre' = 'made of wood and of stone'). When 'et en plus' is used, it's a connector meaning 'besides/what's more'.
target_language_example: La table est en bois et en métal.
native_language_example: The table is made of wood and metal.

meaning: and in good (health); used to say someone is healthy or well.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'en bonne santé' meaning 'in good health'. 'Et en bonne' is the connective form used after listing qualities (e.g., 'jeune et en bonne santé' = 'young and healthy'). Use with nouns referring to people or animals. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Elle est grande et en bonne santé.
native_language_example: She is tall and in good health.

meaning: and again / and also / moreover (used to add something more).
additional_notes: Common filler phrase used to add another item, to indicate 'and also' or 'and again'. Context determines nuance: listing items (and another), asking for more (and some more), or adding a qualifying comment (moreover / besides). Can be short/elliptical (e.g. 'Et encore.' meaning 'and that's not all' or 'and more').
target_language_example: Donne-moi du pain, du fromage, et encore du jambon.
native_language_example: Give me bread, cheese, and also some ham.

meaning: 'and children' — used to list children after mentioning parents or other family members.
additional_notes: This phrase appears after a list of people to add their children (e.g., "Jean, Marie et enfants"). It is not typically used alone; you'll usually see it after names or family roles (père, mère, etc.). In formal writing, you might see "et leurs enfants" (and their children) to be clearer. Pronunciation: /e ɑ̃fɑ̃/.
target_language_example: Marie, Paul et enfants viendront ce soir.
native_language_example: Marie, Paul and children will come tonight.

meaning: 'and do' or 'and make' (literal connector + verb form).
additional_notes: Et = 'and'. Faire = 'to do' or 'to make'. Together they often appear when listing actions (e.g., 'préparer, nettoyer et faire...' = 'prepare, clean and do/make...') or in idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'dire et faire' = 'say and do'). The exact translation depends on context and what follows 'faire' (object or infinitive phrase).
target_language_example: Il faut acheter du pain, cuire le rôti et faire la sauce.
native_language_example: We need to buy bread, roast the meat and make the sauce.

meaning: 'and wife' (used to add mention of a man's wife)
additional_notes: Often follows a man's name or title to indicate his wife (e.g., "Monsieur Dupont et femme" on an invitation or list). It's a formal/old-fashioned formula seen in written contexts (invitations, notices, genealogies). It literally means "and wife." In everyday speech people usually say "et sa femme" (and his wife) or use the wife's name.
target_language_example: M. Martin et femme assisteront à la cérémonie.
native_language_example: Mr. Martin and wife will attend the ceremony.

meaning: 'and windows' — the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the noun 'fenêtres' (windows).
additional_notes: This is simply a phrase combining the conjunction et (and) with the plural noun fenêtres (windows). You will most often see et used to join words or phrases (e.g., portes et fenêtres = doors and windows). Pronunciation: et [e], fenêtres [fə.nɛtʁ].
target_language_example: Les portes et fenêtres sont neuves.
native_language_example: The doors and windows are new.

meaning: and close (imperative plural/formal or polite command).
additional_notes: Combination of 'et' (and) + imperative verb 'fermez' (from fermer). Used to give a short sequence of commands: do X and then close. 'Fermez' is the imperative for vous (or plural). Context determines whether it's polite singular (vous) or addressing multiple people. Common in instructions: 'Enlevez vos chaussures et fermez la porte.'
target_language_example: Mettez la clé sur la table et fermez la porte.
native_language_example: Put the key on the table and close the door.

meaning: and French (used to add 'French' to a list or description).
additional_notes: 'et' means 'and'. 'français' can be an adjective (French) or a noun (the French language or a French person, masculine form). Together 'et français' appears when adding 'French' after another item: e.g. 'anglais et français' = 'English and French'. Make sure agreement: for feminine noun use 'française' (e.g. 'et française').
target_language_example: Il parle anglais et français.
native_language_example: He speaks English and French.

meaning: 'and happy' (the conjunction 'and' + adjective 'happy').
additional_notes: Simply combines et (and) with the adjective heureux (happy). Agreement: heureux is masculine singular; use heureuse for feminine singular, heureux for plural (masc. or mixed), and heureuses for feminine plural. Common in phrases like «sain et heureux» (healthy and happy) or «vivre et heureux» (to live and be happy).
target_language_example: Il est riche et heureux.
native_language_example: He is rich and happy.

meaning: 'and here' — used to add information about the current place, moment, or situation.
additional_notes: A simple conjunction + adverb phrase. Common in spoken and written French to link a previous idea to what follows about the present location, moment, or context. Can introduce a new point, contrast, or consequence (e.g. et ici, on fait autrement = and here we do it differently).
target_language_example: J'ai expliqué la théorie, et ici on va passer à la pratique.
native_language_example: I explained the theory, and here we're going to move on to practice.

meaning: and he
additional_notes: A simple coordinating phrase: et = and; il = he / it. Used to join clauses or actions performed by a male person or a masculine noun. Context determines whether il means 'he' (person) or 'it' (thing). Common in narrative and spoken instructions. Pronunciation and grammar: no special idiom — subject pronoun follows 'et'.
target_language_example: Il a son sac, et il part maintenant.
native_language_example: He has his bag, and he leaves now.

meaning: and I
additional_notes: A common fragment meaning "and I ...". Here, je becomes j' before a word starting with a vowel or silent h: for example, et j'arrive, et j'habite. It is not a fixed expression on its own, but the start of a larger clause.
target_language_example: Elle part maintenant, et j'arrive dans une heure.
native_language_example: She is leaving now, and I’m arriving in an hour.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; literally 'and day'.
additional_notes: This combination is not a common standalone expression in French. 'Et' means 'and' and 'jour' means 'day'. You may encounter 'et jour' inside larger phrases or across line breaks (e.g., at the end of a line: '... et\njour') or within expressions like 'de jour et de nuit' (by day and by night) or as part of longer forms such as 'et jours' when pluralized by mistake. Do not use 'et jour' by itself as a fixed idiom; prefer complete expressions like 'tous les jours' or 'de jour en jour'.
target_language_example: Le texte affichait «et jour» à cause d'un retour à la ligne mal placé.
native_language_example: The text showed "et jour" because of a misplaced line break.

meaning: and that's all / and that's fair / and exactly (depends on context)
additional_notes: Short phrase of two words. Meaning depends on context and intonation: 1) to close a statement meaning "and that's all" or "and that's it" (similar to "et voilà" or "c'est tout"); 2) to confirm fairness or correctness meaning "and fair" or "and right" (less common); 3) used after an adjective/adverb to mean "and exactly" (colloquial). Often informal and depends on surrounding sentence for precise sense. Not a fixed idiom with a single translation.
target_language_example: J'ai payé ma part, et juste.
native_language_example: I paid my share, and that's it.

meaning: and the night; used in the expression 'le jour et la nuit' to mean 'day and night' or to compare two things as completely different.
additional_notes: Most common in the fixed expression 'le jour et la nuit' (literally 'the day and the night'). Used literally to speak about day and night, and idiomatically to say two things are total opposites (English: 'like night and day' or 'day and night'). Can appear in comparisons: 'a et b, c'est le jour et la nuit.'
target_language_example: Leurs opinions sont le jour et la nuit.
native_language_example: Their opinions are like night and day.

meaning: and it
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: et means "and," and le here is the direct object pronoun placed before the next verb. It refers back to a masculine singular thing or a male person. Before a vowel or mute h, le usually becomes l’.
target_language_example: Il prend le verre et le pose sur la table.
native_language_example: He picks up the glass and puts it on the table.

meaning: and their
additional_notes: Combination of conjunction 'et' (and) + possessive adjective 'leur' (their, used for plural possessor). 'Leur' agrees with the thing possessed (always invariable), not with the owners. Use before a noun: 'et leur maison' = 'and their house.' Can also appear before a verb as indirect object: 'et leur dire' = 'and tell them.'
target_language_example: Elle a préparé le repas et leur a apporté des assiettes.
native_language_example: She prepared the meal and brought them plates.

meaning: and then / and now (used to introduce the next point, reaction, or consequence).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to move a story or argument forward, show surprise, introduce a consequence or what happens next. Tone depends on context: can be neutral (and then), questioning (and then what?), or emphatic (and now...). Often appears at sentence start. Not idiomatic in a fixed way—meaning comes from context.
target_language_example: Et là, je découvre que j'ai oublié mon passeport.
native_language_example: And then, I discover that I forgot my passport.

meaning: 'and vegetables' (used to add vegetables to a list)
additional_notes: A fragment consisting of the conjunction et ('and') followed by légumes ('vegetables'). You'll most often see it in lists or menu descriptions (e.g. 'viande et légumes' = 'meat and vegetables'). Not a fixed idiom—just the ordinary way to join 'vegetables' with another item.
target_language_example: Poulet et légumes, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Chicken and vegetables, please.

meaning: literally "and my" — the conjunction "and" followed by the feminine singular possessive "my".
additional_notes: Used to connect another item that belongs to the speaker (feminine noun). "Ma" agrees with a singular feminine noun (ma valise, ma nièce). If the next word begins with a vowel or mute h, spoken French often uses "mon" instead (mon amie) for ease of pronunciation, even though the noun is feminine. Example sentences show "et ma" linking possessions, family members, abstract concepts, or blessings.
target_language_example: Il a pris sa guitare et ma vieille montre.
native_language_example: He took his guitar and my old watch.

meaning: 'and eat' — the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the infinitive 'manger' (to eat).
additional_notes: Used to link actions or items where 'to eat' is one of them. Common in lists or when expressing intentions (e.g., "faire les courses et manger" = "do the shopping and eat"). Grammar: 'manger' stays in the infinitive after verbs that require an infinitive (e.g., vouloir, pouvoir) or after nouns when listing activities.
target_language_example: On va au parc et manger quelque chose après ?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the park and eat something afterwards?

meaning: 'and me' — English words appearing inside French text; not a standard French phrase
additional_notes: This is not standard French. It appears to be the English conjunction 'and' followed by the English pronoun 'me'. In French, 'and me' would normally be 'et moi' (or 'et moi aussi' for 'me too'). If you encounter 'et me' in French writing, it is likely a typo, code-switching, or part of an English quotation.
target_language_example: Il a dit et me que je devais partir, ce qui montre un mélange d'anglais et de français.
native_language_example: He said 'and me' that I had to leave, which shows a mix of English and French.

meaning: 'and thanks' or used to add a brief 'thanks' at the end of a sentence
additional_notes: Literally 'and thanks'. Often added informally after a statement or request to express gratitude or to soften a comment. Can be used alone as a short way to say 'and thank you' (e.g., at end of an email or list). Tone depends on context — can be polite, casual, or sometimes slightly ironic if used abruptly.
target_language_example: Je prends le café noir, et merci.
native_language_example: I'll have black coffee, and thanks.

meaning: 'and gentlemen' (used when addressing or listing men after others)
additional_notes: A simple conjunction + noun phrase: 'et' = 'and', 'messieurs' = plural of 'monsieur' (gentlemen/sirs). Often appears in formal addresses or when adding male audience members after mentioning others (e.g., 'mesdames et messieurs' = 'ladies and gentlemen'). By itself 'et messieurs' is not a fixed idiom; it usually follows another group (e.g., 'mesdames et messieurs').
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, bienvenue à la conférence.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the conference.

meaning: This phrase is ungrammatical in French; it incorrectly mixes the plural verb 'sommes' (we are) with the stressed pronoun 'moi' (me). Likely intended meanings and corrections include 'Et moi, je suis dans la...' (And me, I am in the...) or 'Et nous sommes dans la...' (And we are in the...).
additional_notes: The sequence 'et moi sommes dans la' is incorrect because 'moi' cannot be the subject of the verb 'sommes'. To correct: use 'je suis' if the speaker means 'I am' and wants emphasis ('Et moi, je suis...'), or use 'nous sommes' if the speaker means 'we are' ('Et nous sommes...'). The comma after 'Et moi' (Et moi, je...) is common to mark the topicalization/emphasis. If you need an object/place after 'dans la', complete with a noun (e.g., 'cuisine', 'maison').
target_language_example: Et moi sommes dans la — (incorrect: ungrammatical sequence as written).
native_language_example: And me are in the — (incorrect: ungrammatical as written).

meaning: we (someone + me) are the same (used with âge = 'the same age').
additional_notes: This pattern appears when saying 'X and I are the same ...' (usually 'du même âge' = 'the same age'). Grammatically, use 'X et moi sommes' when X is a subject with 'moi' (even though 'moi' is a stressed pronoun); for 'tu' use 'toi et moi sommes'. If the phrase ends with a noun/adjective, include that word (e.g. 'du même âge', 'de la même taille').
target_language_example: Marie et moi sommes du même âge.
native_language_example: Marie and I are the same age.

meaning: and my
additional_notes: Literally 'and my'. Often appears in larger phrases (e.g., 'et mon frère' = 'and my brother') or as a colloquial elliptic remark meaning 'and mine' when responding to someone (context determines whether it means 'my [noun]' or 'mine'). Not a fixed idiom by itself—its meaning depends on the noun that follows or the omitted noun in casual replies.
target_language_example: Elle a un chien et mon chat est timide.
native_language_example: She has a dog and my cat is shy.

meaning: and to die / and die (literal meaning); often used in lists or expressions about dying or consequences.
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction 'et' (and) + the infinitive 'mourir' (to die). You will see it in phrases like «vivre et mourir» (to live and die) or in sentences listing actions or consequences. Usage is literal unless part of a fixed expression or poetic phrasing. Regular grammar: keep verb in infinitive after certain verbs or prepositions.
target_language_example: Il veut voyager, vivre et mourir en paix.
native_language_example: He wants to travel, live and die in peace.

meaning: and by / and through (used to link an action with an agent, instrument, cause, or means).
additional_notes: A combination of the conjunction et (and) + the preposition par (by). Used to add information: 'and by...' or 'and through...'. Common in formal/written contexts (e.g., legal, administrative, or descriptive phrases) and in compound expressions: 'réalisé par' (made by) → 'et par' can link another agent or means. Do not confuse with the single word 'et' or the separable phrase 'par et'.
target_language_example: Le rapport a été rédigé par Marie et par Paul.
native_language_example: The report was written by Marie and by Paul.

meaning: and not / and no (used to negate or exclude something)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in spoken and written French to add a negative element after a previous clause or list. Often used with ne (e.g. «ne ... pas») or alone in colloquial speech to mean “and not” when contrasting items: «je veux ça et pas ça» = “I want this and not that.” In fast speech it can replace a longer negative phrase. Be careful: alone it does not form a complete negation without context (you often need the verb or preceding ne).
target_language_example: Je prends le café et pas le thé.
native_language_example: I'll have coffee and not tea.

meaning: 'and passes' or 'and goes by' (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'et' (and) followed by the verb 'passer' in the 3rd person singular present ('il/elle passe') or the imperative/infinitive forms in some contexts. Alone, 'et passe' isn't a fixed phrase — its meaning depends on the clause: e.g. 'et passe' can mean 'and passes (by/away/time)' or be part of commands like 'et passe!' in informal speech. Pay attention to the subject or surrounding words to know whether it means someone/something passes, time passes, or a directive.
target_language_example: Le train arrive à 8 h et passe à 8 h 05.
native_language_example: The train arrives at 8 and passes at 8:05.

meaning: 'and during' or 'and while' (used to link two actions or to add a time-related comment).
additional_notes: Combines conjunction et (and) with pendant (during/while). Used to add another point about what happens at the same time or to introduce a contrasting time-related remark. Common in spoken and written French: e.g. 'Il travaille, et pendant ce temps...' (He works, and meanwhile...). Often followed by 'que', 'ce temps', or a time expression: 'et pendant ce temps-là', 'et pendant que...'.
target_language_example: Je prépare le dîner, et pendant ce temps le chat dort.
native_language_example: I'm making dinner, and meanwhile the cat is sleeping.

meaning: and no one / and nobody (used to add 'no one' after a list or statement)
additional_notes: 'et personne' is a short phrase combining 'et' (and) + 'personne' (no one). In negative contexts, French often places 'personne' after the verb (e.g. 'je ne vois personne' = I see no one). When used after a list or clause, 'et personne' emphasizes that nobody else is included. It's not an idiom—just the conjunction plus the pronoun. Watch word order: in full negative sentences use 'ne ... personne' around the verb; 'et personne' is typically used to append 'and nobody' in a simpler structure.
target_language_example: Il y avait des étudiants, des professeurs, et personne d'autre.
native_language_example: There were students, teachers, and nobody else.

meaning: and more / and (comparative) — used to add another item or to form comparisons (… and more; … and even more).
additional_notes: Often appears in comparative structures with 'plus' repeated (e.g. 'plus ... plus ...' = 'the more ... the more ...'). Can also join adjectives or nouns ('chaudes et sèches' -> 'hot and dry'; 'plus chaudes et plus sèches' -> 'hotter and drier'). In many contexts 'et plus' simply means 'and more' or links two comparative elements. Not an idiom; literal components keep their meaning.
target_language_example: Plus tu étudies, et plus tu progresses.
native_language_example: The more you study, the more you progress.

meaning: 'and for' — used to add someone/something as the recipient, beneficiary, or topic in addition to what was just mentioned.
additional_notes: Commonly follows a previous mention to ask about or include another person, thing, or perspective. Can introduce who benefits from something (e.g., 'for the people') or ask about someone's situation ("Et pour Mario ?" = "What about Mario?"). In many contexts it functions like English 'and (what about)'.
target_language_example: Nous avons des croissants pour toi, et pour Paul aussi.
native_language_example: We have croissants for you, and for Paul too.

meaning: 'and take' or 'and to take' (the conjunction et + the verb prendre).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but simply the conjunction et ('and') followed by the infinitive or conjugated form of prendre ('to take'). Usage depends on context: it can join actions (e.g. «faire X et prendre Y») or introduce a second verb after another verb/modal expression (e.g. «vouloir et prendre» is rare).
