additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common phrase faits l'un pour l'autre, meaning two people/things are perfect for each other. It is usually used for couples or perfectly matched pairs. You will rarely see 'faits l'un pour' alone; include 'l'autre' to complete the expression. Agreement: faits (masculine plural) can change to faites if referring to feminine plural (faites l'une pour l'autre is uncommon).
target_language_example: Ils sont faits l'un pour l'autre.
native_language_example: They are made for each other.

meaning: 'needed to do' / 'had to do' (impersonal/passive sense often: 'it was necessary to do')
additional_notes: Commonly appears as "il fallait faire" or in contractions in spoken/written French. Used to say that an action was necessary or the right thing to do. In sentences like "C'est ce qu'il fallait faire," it means "That's what needed to be done" or "That was the right thing to do." The form changes with tense (imparfait: fallait, passé composé/perfect uses être/avoir + fallu).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il fallait faire un constat.
native_language_example: After the accident, it was necessary to make a report.

meaning: to have to; to be necessary that
additional_notes: Usually appears in conjugated forms such as il faut que or il va falloir que, followed by a subjunctive verb. It expresses necessity, obligation, or something that needs to be done.
target_language_example: Il va falloir que tu finisses tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to finish your homework.

meaning: I have to
additional_notes: This is a dictionary-style fragment rather than a complete standalone expression. In normal French, falloir is impersonal and is usually conjugated as il faut, so the usual full pattern is il faut que je + subjunctive verb.
target_language_example: On dit « il faut que je parte », pas « falloir que je parte ».
native_language_example: You say “il faut que I leave,” not “falloir que I leave.”

meaning: you will have to
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of il va falloir que tu / il faudra que tu. Used to tell someone they will need to do something (obligation or necessity). Often appears without the subject 'il' in casual speech: "va falloir que tu...". Followed by a verb in the subjunctive or (colloquially) the infinitive or indicative in casual speech.
target_language_example: Va falloir que tu m'appelles demain.
native_language_example: You're going to have to call me tomorrow.

meaning: 'had to' + subordinate clause (expressing necessity or obligation in the past)
additional_notes: Part of the impersonal expression il a fallu que (or il fallait que) + subjunctive/infinite structure. Use il a fallu que + subject + verb to say that something had to happen or someone had to do something. In spoken French the past form il a fallu que is very common; after il a fallu que, the verb is usually in the past or present subjunctive if the clause refers to a specific past action (e.g. il a fallu que je parte → il a fallu que je parte). For general past habitual necessity use il fallait que. 'Falloir' is impersonal (only used with il).
target_language_example: Il a fallu que je parte tôt pour attraper le train.
native_language_example: I had to leave early to catch the train.

meaning: 'took three' (used with time expressions: it took three ... / I needed three ...)
additional_notes: This is the past participle construction of the impersonal verb 'il falloir' (il a fallu) plus a time expression. It expresses how much time was required: Il a fallu trois jours = It took three days. The subject is impersonal (il). Use with verbs like 'avoir besoin' in English but always impersonal in French. Common patterns: 'Il a fallu + duration', 'Il m'a fallu + duration' (meaning 'I needed ...' or 'it took me ...').
target_language_example: Il m'a fallu trois heures pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: It took me three hours to finish the project.

meaning: 'the family has' (third-person singular present of avoir used with 'famille')
additional_notes: This is the noun 'famille' (family) followed by the verb 'a' (has). In French, 'famille' is singular, so verbs and agreements are in singular form: la famille a fait..., toute la famille est/ a.... It can express possession ('la famille a une maison') or form compound tenses ('la famille a vécu' = the family has lived / the family lived'). In questions with inversion or est-ce que, the verb still agrees with the singular noun: 'Ta famille a-t-elle...?'
target_language_example: Ma famille a acheté une maison à la campagne.
native_language_example: My family has bought a house in the countryside.

meaning: 'family of' / 'a group of related (things or people)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate membership in a family, group, category or lineage. Common with animals/plants (une famille de chiens), products (une famille de produits), or figurative groups (la famille de langues). Can precede a noun or be part of a larger phrase (la famille de mon mari). When referring to a person's relatives, use 'la famille de X' to mean 'X's family'.
target_language_example: Il étudie la famille de langues romanes.
native_language_example: He studies the family of Romance languages.

meaning: 'family and' — the phrase 'famille et ...' is simply the word 'famille' followed by 'et' (and) to connect it to another noun or pronoun (e.g. 'ma famille et moi' = 'my family and I').
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's the conjunction et ('and') used after famille. Common constructions: 'ma famille et moi' (my family and I), 'ta famille et tes amis' (your family and your friends), or 'sa famille et ses amis'. Word order is the same as in English. Be careful with agreement/pronouns after 'et' (use the correct pronoun: moi, toi, lui/elle, nous, etc.).
target_language_example: Ma famille et moi partons en vacances demain.
native_language_example: My family and I are leaving on vacation tomorrow.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone French expression; literally 'family for' and only meaningful within a larger phrase or sentence — you must check context to know the intended sense.
additional_notes: The sequence 'famille pour' is compositional (made of 'famille' = family and 'pour' = for) but is not a common fixed idiom in French. It typically appears as part of longer constructions (e.g., 'une famille pour l'adoption' or 'programme pour la famille') where word order and agreement determine meaning. Beginners should learn 'famille' and 'pour' separately and prefer complete, natural phrases such as 'pour la famille' (for the family) or 'une famille de...' (a family of...).
target_language_example: Nous cherchons une famille pour l'enfant.
native_language_example: We are looking for a family for the child.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; likely a mistaken split of 'famille' (family) and a reflexive pronoun 'se' beginning a verb (e.g. 'la famille se réunit').
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'famille se' by itself. In French, 'famille' is a noun (family). 'Se' is a reflexive pronoun that must accompany a verb (se réunir, se composer, se souvenir). Examples you may see like 'la famille se réunit' (the family meets) or 'la famille se compose de...' (the family is composed of...) combine the two words but they are separate parts of speech. If you encountered 'famille se' in text, check the following word: it's almost certainly the start of a reflexive verb phrase.
target_language_example: La famille se réunit chaque dimanche.
native_language_example: The family gets together every Sunday.

meaning: 'the family is' or 'the family goes' (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun 'famille' + the verb 'aller' in the 3rd person singular. Most commonly used to say how the family is doing (famille va bien = the family is well) or to indicate movement/destination (famille va en Italie = the family goes/is going to Italy). Use context to determine whether it means 'is/are doing' (health/state) or 'go/goes' (movement).
target_language_example: Ma famille va bien après la nouvelle.
native_language_example: My family is doing well after the news.

meaning: used with a noun to mean 'a family of/with' or indicate a type/class of family characterized by something (often followed by an adjective or noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'famille' followed by the preposition 'à' to link to a characteristic, function, or possession (e.g. 'famille à revenus modestes' = 'a family with modest incomes', 'famille à trois enfants' = 'a family with three children'). Word order and articles may vary (often 'une famille à...' or 'la famille à...').
target_language_example: Ils viennent d'une famille à revenus modestes.
native_language_example: They come from a family with modest incomes.

meaning: literally 'family was'; used when describing a family's state, situation, or composition in the past.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence of a noun (famille) + the imperfect/past of être (was). It appears in sentences like 'La famille était heureuse' (The family was happy) or 'La famille était composée de cinq personnes' (The family was made up of five people). Choose the correct tense (imparfait, passé composé, etc.) depending on the time and aspect you want to express.
target_language_example: La famille était réunie pour les fêtes.
native_language_example: The family was together for the holidays.

meaning: do some
additional_notes: fasse is the present subjunctive of faire. You often see it after que in expressions like il faut que... or elle veut que.... With des + plural noun, it means doing or making something plural, like des efforts, des copies, or des discours. In some expressions, English uses a different verb, for example faire des études often means to study.
target_language_example: Le professeur veut qu'elle fasse des exercices supplémentaires.
native_language_example: The teacher wants her to do some extra exercises.

meaning: tired for / tired of (informal/uncommon phrasing); usually you say 'fatigué de' instead.
additional_notes: The usual preposition with 'fatigué' to express being tired of something is 'de' (fatigué de). 'Fatigué pour' is not standard to mean 'tired of' and may appear in incorrect usage or regional/informal speech. 'Fatigué pour' can sometimes occur when followed by an infinitive to mean 'tired to (do something)', but standard French uses 'trop fatigué pour' + infinitive (e.g. 'trop fatigué pour sortir'). Use 'fatigué de' + noun/verb-ing equivalent (fatigué de marcher) and 'trop fatigué pour' + infinitive for 'too tired to...'.
target_language_example: Je suis trop fatigué pour sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out tonight.

meaning: miscarriage (loss of a pregnancy).
additional_notes: Refers to a spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb. Common medical term; used in both everyday and clinical contexts. 'Faire une fausse couche' = to have a miscarriage. Can be a sensitive topic—use gently.
target_language_example: Elle a fait une fausse couche au deuxième trimestre.
native_language_example: She had a miscarriage in the second trimester.

meaning: 'I absolutely must' / 'I really need to' (introduces something the speaker must do).
additional_notes: Colloquial shortened form of «Il faut absolument que je…». Used to express a strong necessity or urgent obligation to do something. Followed by a verb in the subjunctive (formal) or by an infinitive in informal speech (e.g. «Il faut absolument que je lui parle» or «Il faut absolument que je parte»). Common in spoken French. Can be directed at others (te, lui) as in the examples.
target_language_example: Il faut absolument que je termine ce rapport aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I absolutely must finish this report today.

meaning: you need to press (or one must press)
additional_notes: Informal, contracted form of il faut appuyer. Used to say that pressing (a button, spot, etc.) is necessary. Common in spoken French; context determines whether 'appuyer' means press (a button), lean/press against, or stress/emphasize. For polite instructions, use Il faut appuyer sur + object (e.g. sur le bouton).
target_language_example: Pour ouvrir la porte, faut appuyer sur le bouton rouge.
native_language_example: To open the door, you need to press the red button.

meaning: colloquial short form of 'il faut bien' — 'one must / you have to / it's necessary (and reasonable)'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of 'il faut bien'. Used to state a necessity, an explanation or a pragmatic justification (often resigned or matter-of-fact). Can introduce an action that seems obvious, unavoidable, or acceptable. Tone can be casual, slightly defensive, or ironic depending on context.
target_language_example: Faut bien prendre un peu de repos après cette semaine.
native_language_example: You have to take a bit of rest after this week.

meaning: 'need to' or 'must' used with the pronoun en (meaning 'of it' / 'of them' / 'some').
additional_notes: This is an informal/colloquial contraction of il faut / il me faut / il nous faut + en. 'En' replaces a noun introduced earlier (some/of it/of them). The full forms are il faut en (faire), il me faut en (acheter), il nous faut en (parler), etc. Use with appropriate subject pronoun: il me faut = I need, il nous faut = we need. In spoken French, people often drop 'il'.
target_language_example: Il me faut en acheter deux pour la fête.
native_language_example: I need to buy two of them for the party.

meaning: Not a correct fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'one must do something' or 'need to do something'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard, complete expression. In spoken French you might hear parts like 'il faut' (it is necessary) + 'faire quelque chose' (to do something). The correct full phrase for 'you/we/one must do something' is 'il faut faire quelque chose.' 'Quelque' alone is an adjective and must be followed by 'chose' to mean 'something' (or by a plural noun meaning 'some').
target_language_example: Il faut faire quelque chose avant qu'il ne soit trop tard.
native_language_example: We must do something before it's too late.

meaning: 'must never' or 'should never' (colloquial, contracted form of il ne faut jamais)
additional_notes: Informal spoken French often drops the subject and the 'ne' in negation. 'Faut jamais' is a shortened form of 'il ne faut jamais' and is used to give strong prohibitions or advice: 'you must never...' / 'one must never...'. Because it's missing 'il' and 'ne', it's casual and more common in conversation than in formal writing. To make it complete in standard French, use 'il ne faut jamais...'.
target_language_example: Faut jamais oublier ton passeport quand tu voyages.
native_language_example: You must never forget your passport when you travel.

meaning: 'one must eat in order to' / 'you have to eat to...'
additional_notes: Colloquial shortcut of il faut manger pour + infinitive — used to say that eating is necessary for some purpose (e.g. to have energy, to survive, to work). Often heard in spoken French without the subject (il). In full form: il faut manger pour + verb/noun. Can be followed by an explanation (pour tenir la journée, pour vivre, pour travailler).
target_language_example: Faut manger pour avoir de l'énergie le matin.
native_language_example: You have to eat to have energy in the morning.

meaning: 'one must put' / 'you must put' (colloquial contraction of il faut mettre)
additional_notes: Informal spoken French: 'faut' is the shortened form of 'il faut' (it is necessary). Combined with an infinitive or with 'mettre' followed by a noun, it expresses necessity to put/place/insert something. Context determines whether it's impersonal ('one must') or a directive ('you must'). Can be followed by an infinitive (faut mettre + infinitive) or a direct object (faut mettre + la clé).
target_language_example: Faut mettre la ceinture avant de démarrer la voiture.
native_language_example: You must put on the seatbelt before starting the car.

meaning: 'one must go up' / 'you have to go up' (from il faut monter)
additional_notes: Short for il faut monter. il faut = 'it is necessary' / 'one must' and monter = 'to go up', 'to climb', or 'to board' depending on context (stairs, hill, vehicle). Often used to give necessity or instruction. Subject is impersonal (il), so the meaning can be general (one must) or directed at the listener (you have to).
target_language_example: Il faut monter les escaliers pour arriver au musée.
native_language_example: You have to go up the stairs to get to the museum.

meaning: part of informal phrasing meaning ‘we must’ or ‘we need to’ (from il faut + nous).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase in standard French but appears when il faut (it is necessary) is combined with a pronoun or clause referring to 'us'—e.g. «Il nous faut...» (we need / we must). In spoken, hurried French you might hear parts like «faut nous…» when someone omits the subject: «Faut nous dépêcher» (colloquial for «Il faut que nous nous dépêchions» or «Nous devons nous dépêcher»). Use the full forms for formal writing: «Il nous faut…» or «Il faut que nous…».
target_language_example: Il faut nous dépêcher si on veut attraper le train.
native_language_example: We need to hurry if we want to catch the train.

meaning: one must think / you have to think (about something)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of il faut penser (à). Used to say that someone should remember or consider something. Often followed by à + noun/verb (penser à faire = remember to do). Informal spoken register; subject is impersonal (il).
target_language_example: Faut penser à appeler la banque demain.
native_language_example: You have to remember to call the bank tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'is needed for' or 'is necessary for' when the impersonal construction il faut is followed by pour to indicate purpose or the thing required.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase but the sequence il faut + ... + pour or il faut + pour + noun in contexts where 'faut' (from il faut) and 'pour' appear adjacent in the sentence. Common pattern: "Il faut + noun + pour + ..." or "Il faut + infinitive + pour + ..." The sequence 'faut pour' specifically appears when words between 'il' and 'pour' are omitted or in casual clipped forms (e.g. in reported fragments or spoken shortcuts). Register: neutral. Grammar tip: do not use 'faut pour' without the impersonal subject 'il' and appropriate complements; the full construction is typically 'Il faut ... pour ...'.
target_language_example: Il faut pour réussir de la persévérance et du travail.
native_language_example: It takes perseverance and work to succeed.

meaning: need to take / must take (lit. 'it is necessary to take')
additional_notes: This is a colloquial contraction of il faut prendre or il me faut prendre (depending on context). It expresses necessity or obligation to 'take' something (photos, a day off, someone's temperature, a decision, risks, etc.). Subject/indirect object before faut (e.g. il me faut = I need) indicates who needs it. With il faut (impersonal) it's general necessity: il faut prendre = one/you must take. Use with infinitive or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Il me faut prendre rendez-vous chez le médecin.
native_language_example: I need to make an appointment with the doctor.

meaning: short for "il faut qu'elle" — "she must" / "she has to" (expresses necessity or obligation).
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken contraction of "il faut que" followed by "elle". Used to say that something is necessary for or that someone (she) must do something: "faut qu'elle parte" = "she must leave." In standard written French you would normally use "il faut qu'elle..." and include the subjunctive after it (e.g. "il faut qu'elle parte"). In casual speech the subject "il" is often dropped and verbs may be simplified.
target_language_example: Faut qu'elle vienne ce soir.
native_language_example: She has to come tonight.

meaning: 'it's necessary that' (colloquial start of the phrase 'il faut que...')
additional_notes: This is not a complete standard phrase by itself. It appears to be an informal or clipped version of the impersonal structure "il faut que..." used to express necessity or obligation followed by a subordinate clause with the subjunctive. In natural French you will usually hear or read the full form "il faut que" (e.g. "Il faut que tu viennes"). "Faut que" (dropping the initial "il") is common in spoken, informal French. "Faut que ce" would only appear when the following words continue the clause (e.g. "Faut que ce soit prêt").
target_language_example: Faut que ce soit prêt avant midi.
native_language_example: It needs to be ready before noon.

meaning: 'I need to know' or 'it's necessary that I know'.
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of il faut que je sache. Used to express a necessity or urgency to obtain information. Common in spoken and written French. Followed by a clause introduced by que (what, where, how, etc.) or used alone for emphasis. Literal components are compositional but the phrase functions as a fixed expression meaning 'I must know' or 'I need to know'.
target_language_example: Il faut que je sache qui a pris mes clés.
native_language_example: I need to know who took my keys.

meaning: 'we must' / 'it is necessary that we...'
additional_notes: Shortened form of Il faut que nous + subjunctive. Used to express necessity or obligation for 'we' (nous). In spoken French, Il is often dropped: "Faut que nous..." or more commonly "Il faut qu'on..." Remember the verb after must be in the subjunctive (commencement: commencions, faire: fassions, parler: parlions, penser: pensions).
target_language_example: Il faut que nous parlions de ce projet demain.
native_language_example: We must talk about this project tomorrow.

meaning: 'you must go there' (colloquial / shortened form of Il faut que tu y ailles).
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken contraction of Il faut que tu y ailles / Il faut que tu y retournes. 'Il faut que' expresses necessity or obligation ('you must' / 'you need to'). The pronoun y stands for a place already mentioned (there). In full formal speech say: Il faut que tu y ailles. In commands, native speakers often drop 'Il' and shorten verbs in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu y ailles maintenant, le bus part dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: You must go there now; the bus leaves in five minutes.

meaning: 'you/one must always' or 'it's always necessary to' (colloquial contraction of il faut toujours)
additional_notes: This is a shortened, spoken form of il faut toujours. Il faut = 'it is necessary' (impersonal). With toujours it means 'always' or 'still' depending on context. Common in speech: "Il faut toujours..." → "Faut toujours..." Dropping il is informal; use full form in writing or formal speech. Followed by an infinitive or a clause introduced by que.
target_language_example: Faut toujours vérifier les freins avant de partir.
native_language_example: You should always check the brakes before leaving.

meaning: colloquial contraction of the impersonal construction 'il vous faut' — 'you need' or 'you must' (impersonal verb falloir with indirect object pronoun).
additional_notes: Not a standard written form; appears in informal or rapid speech where the initial 'il' is dropped: 'faut vous' corresponds to spoken 'il vous faut'. Use with an infinitive or a noun: e.g. 'faut vous y prendre tôt' (you need to start early) or 'faut vous un permis' in casual speech. Prefer full written form 'il vous faut' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Faut vous votre passeport pour entrer ?
native_language_example: You need your passport to enter?

meaning: short, informal way of saying "il faut y [aller/penser/aller voir/etc.]" — "one must / it's necessary to [do something there]" (often part of spoken phrases)
additional_notes: This is a clipped, colloquial combination heard in spoken French where 'faut' = spoken short for 'il faut' (it's necessary) and 'y' = there/to it. By itself it's incomplete and depends on context or a following verb or phrase (e.g. « faut y aller » = we must go there). Use in casual conversation; not standard written French.
target_language_example: On est en retard, faut y aller.
native_language_example: We're late, we have to go (there).

meaning: 'need more' (expresses that more of something is required).
additional_notes: Used impersonal with il faut + davantage + de + noun. Equivalent to 'we/you/I need more [something]' depending on context (often translated as 'more ... is needed' or 'we need more ...'). Formal/neutral register. Use 'davantage' before a noun introduced by 'de' (davantage de).
target_language_example: Il nous faut davantage de temps pour finir.
native_language_example: We need more time to finish.

meaning: (incorrect/variant form) Intended to represent 'faute de', which means 'for lack of' or 'due to a lack of'. 'faut de' by itself is not standard French; the correct expression is 'faute de'.
additional_notes: The correct phrase is 'faute de' (with an e). 'Faut de' is a nonstandard or misspelt form and should be avoided in writing and formal speech. If you encounter 'faut de' it is likely a typo, mishearing, or dialectal error. Use 'faute de' followed by a noun or infinitive to indicate that something was done because of the absence or lack of something (e.g., 'Faute de preuves...' or 'Faute de mieux...').
target_language_example: On a dit qu'il partira, mais faute de confirmation, rien n'est encore certain.
native_language_example: They said he would leave, but for lack of confirmation, nothing is certain yet.

meaning: not a standalone fixed phrase; appears as part of constructions with falloir + de + definite article (e.g. 'il faut de la...') meaning 'one needs some / there is a need for some'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears when using the impersonal verb 'il faut' (it is necessary/one must) followed by 'de' + the feminine singular partitive article 'la' (or before a feminine noun): 'il faut de la patience' = 'you need some patience'. 'Faut de la' by itself is informal/elliptical (dropping 'il') and would be heard in spoken French: 'Faut de la patience' (colloquial for 'Il faut de la patience'). Use 'il faut' in writing. The partitive 'de la' indicates an unspecified quantity of a feminine noun. For masculine nouns use 'du' (il faut du temps).
target_language_example: Il faut de la patience pour apprendre une langue.
native_language_example: You need some patience to learn a language.

meaning: 'is needed here' or 'one must (here)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but the sequence faut + ici appears when the impersonal il is omitted in informal speech or in notes. It derives from il faut (one must / it is necessary) + ici (here). To be a complete sentence in standard French you normally include il and add an infinitive or clause: Il faut attendre ici. Omitting il (faut ici) is common in spoken, colloquial, or telegraphic contexts (e.g., signs, notes, text messages).
target_language_example: Faut ici patienter jusqu'à la fin du concert.
native_language_example: One must wait here until the end of the concert.

meaning: it's necessary to (do) it
additional_notes: Informal contraction of il faut + le (or il faut le + verb infinitive / phrase). Used in spoken French to mean 'one must do it' or 'it's necessary to do it.' The subject 'il' is impersonal; the following verb or clause is usually implied or stated earlier. In many cases you will hear just faut + (object/pronoun) in casual speech. Example uses: «Faut le faire» = 'You/one must do it.'
target_language_example: Faut le faire maintenant.
native_language_example: We/You have to do it now.

meaning: 'for lack of' or 'for want of' (because there is no ...)
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done because something else is lacking or unavailable. Followed by a noun or an infinitive (faute de + noun / faute de + infinitive). Different from the single word 'faute' meaning 'mistake' (see example 2).
target_language_example: Faute de trouver les étoiles, il vole mon peigne.
native_language_example: For lack of finding the stars, he steals my comb.

meaning: wheelchair (literally: 'rolling armchair')
additional_notes: Common term for a mobility chair used by people who cannot walk or have difficulty walking. Used for both manual and electric wheelchairs. The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally. Feminine noun phrase: un fauteuil roulant / le fauteuil roulant.
target_language_example: Il a besoin d'un fauteuil roulant après l'accident.
native_language_example: He needs a wheelchair after the accident.

meaning: in favor of; as a kindness from (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate support for someone/something (in favor of) or to indicate that something is done as a kindness/benefit from a person or institution. Context determines translation: 'en faveur de' is the more common fixed expression meaning 'in favor of' (supporting). 'faveur de' can also appear in formal phrases like 'à la faveur de' meaning 'thanks to' or 'because of'.
target_language_example: Je vote en faveur de cette proposition.
native_language_example: I vote in favor of this proposal.

meaning: in favor of the (feminine noun that follows); expressing support or preference for something
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a prepositional expression meaning 'in favor of the...' and must be followed by a feminine noun (e.g. la loi, la proposition). The full expression is often 'en faveur de la' (in favor of the). On its own 'faveur de la' is incomplete; learners should use 'en faveur de la' or 'la faveur de la' depending on context. 'La faveur de la' can mean 'the favor of the...' (e.g. la faveur de la reine = the queen's favor).
target_language_example: Elle a voté en faveur de la proposition.
native_language_example: She voted in favor of the proposal.

meaning: a manner of speaking; a way of saying (often meaning 'figuratively' or 'that's just a figure of speech').
additional_notes: Used to refer to how something is said (tone, style) or to downplay a literal meaning: "C'était une façon de parler" = "I wasn't being literal." Can introduce a figurative expression (similar to "so to speak" / "in a manner of speaking"). Also used to ask about someone's speaking style ("sa façon de parler").
target_language_example: Je dis ça, façon de parler, parce que je suis surpris.
native_language_example: I say that, so to speak, because I'm surprised.

meaning: 'woman with' or 'woman who has' (introduces possession, characteristic, purpose, or association)
additional_notes: This phrase is not a standalone expression; it's the start of a noun phrase using the preposition 'à' after 'femme' to indicate possession, characteristic, purpose, or association (e.g. femme à enfants — woman with children; femme à poigne — a strong/forceful woman). You need a noun or adjective after 'à' to complete the idea. The exact translation depends on what follows.
target_language_example: Elle est une femme à poigne.
native_language_example: She is a woman with a strong hand / She is a forceful woman.

meaning: housewife; a woman who manages the home and does not work outside the home.
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman whose main occupation is running the household and often caring for children. Neutral term but can feel old-fashioned in some contexts; alternatives include « mère au foyer » (stay-at-home mother) when emphasizing childcare. Agreement: 'femme' is feminine singular.
target_language_example: Je suis femme au foyer et je m'occupe des enfants.
native_language_example: I am a housewife and I take care of the children.

meaning: 'woman with' — the phrase combines 'femme' (woman) + 'avec' (with) and is used to describe a woman who has/possesses or is accompanied by something or someone.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun 'femme' followed by the preposition 'avec'. It must be completed by whatever follows (e.g., 'femme avec un chien' = 'woman with a dog', or 'femme avec de l'expérience' = 'woman with experience'). Remember French word order: 'femme avec' + noun/adjective/phrase. Agreement and articles are still required (un/une, de, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est la femme avec le chapeau rouge.
native_language_example: That's the woman with the red hat.

meaning: a woman like (someone) / a woman such as
additional_notes: Literally 'woman like'. Used to compare or give an example (e.g., 'une femme comme elle' = 'a woman like her'). By itself 'femme comme' is incomplete; normally followed by a pronoun, name, or clause (une femme comme toi, une femme comme ma mère). Word order: adjective/comparison after the noun. Common in everyday and neutral speech.
target_language_example: Il veut une femme comme sa sœur.
native_language_example: He wants a woman like his sister.

meaning: 'woman in' (literal combination of 'femme' + preposition 'dans').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's simply the noun 'femme' (woman) followed by the preposition 'dans' (in). It will normally be completed by a location or context (e.g., "une femme dans la rue" = a woman in the street; "la femme dans ce livre" = the woman in this book). Pay attention to articles and agreement: "la femme dans le parc", "une femme dans son bureau". It's compositional and translates literally.
target_language_example: Une femme dans la cuisine prépare le dîner.
native_language_example: A woman in the kitchen is preparing dinner.

meaning: maid; chambermaid (hotel or household staff who cleans/serves).
additional_notes: Refers to a female domestic worker who cleans rooms, helps guests, or serves tea. Common in formal or hotel contexts. Literal components: femme (woman) + de chambre (of the room), so the phrase is compositional and can be translated literally as 'woman of the room.' Use 'femme de chambre' for one female maid; plural is 'femmes de chambre' or colloquially 'les femmes de chambre'.
target_language_example: La femme de chambre vous apportera des serviettes propres.
native_language_example: The maid will bring you clean towels.

meaning: housekeeper; cleaner; cleaning lady.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman whose job is to clean houses, offices, hotels, etc. Can describe a professional cleaner or someone employed part-time to do cleaning. In spoken English, 'cleaner' or 'housekeeper' are common equivalents. If referring to a male, French can use 'homme de ménage' or simply 'personne de ménage'.
target_language_example: La femme de ménage passe tous les mardis matin.
native_language_example: The cleaner comes every Tuesday morning.

meaning: 'woman in' — used before a noun to describe a woman wearing or associated with something (e.g. femme en robe = woman in a dress).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common structure: 'femme en + [clothing/material/role]'. It describes what a woman is wearing or the material she is in (e.g. en robe, en jean, en manteau) or sometimes her role when followed by a profession (less common). Choose the noun or adjective after 'en' appropriately (usually a feminine noun or an invariable expression).
target_language_example: La femme en rouge traverse la rue.
native_language_example: The woman in red is crossing the street.

meaning: the woman is
additional_notes: This is simply the noun femme (woman) followed by the third-person singular present of être (est). It functions as the start of a sentence or clause: e.g. « La femme est grande » = “the woman is tall.” Alone, without determiners (le/la/une), it sounds incomplete in French; include an article or adjective to form a natural sentence.
target_language_example: La femme est contente.
native_language_example: The woman is happy.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to be a fragment meaning 'woman is in' (e.g. 'the woman is in [the room]')
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'femme est en' is not a common standalone phrase. It looks like a literal combination of 'femme' (woman) + 'est' (is) + 'en' (in/into/while), and would normally require an article or context (e.g. 'La femme est en réunion' or 'La femme est en ville'). For correct, natural sentences, include the article ('la' or 'une') and complete the prepositional phrase after 'en'.
target_language_example: La femme est en réunion.
native_language_example: The woman is in a meeting.

meaning: a phrase pattern meaning 'the woman is a/an…' or 'my/your wife is a/an…' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a grammatical sequence: 'femme' (woman or wife) + the verb 'est' (is) + the indefinite article 'une' + a noun or adjective. Context determines whether 'femme' means 'woman' (a woman in general) or 'femme' as 'wife' (ma/ta femme). The noun that follows completes the description: e.g. 'prostituée' (prostitute), 'bonne cuisinière' (a good cook), 'bonne directrice' (a good director). Useful for making simple descriptions: 'Cette femme est une...'; 'Ma femme est une...'; 'Est-ce que ta femme est une...'.
target_language_example: Ma femme est une excellente professeur.
native_language_example: My wife is an excellent teacher.

meaning: This combination isn't a fixed phrase; it's simply the word 'femme' (woman) followed by the conjunction 'et' (and) and the partitive/article 'des' (some/of the).
additional_notes: Not a set expression. You'll see 'femme et des' only as part of a larger sentence, e.g. listing things about a woman and some other items (femme et des enfants — a woman and some children). Pay attention to agreement and article use: 'des' can be the plural indefinite article ('some') or the contraction of 'de + les' in some contexts. For natural sentences, words around this sequence determine meaning.
target_language_example: Il y a une femme et des enfants dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There is a woman and some children in the garden.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; literally 'woman and two'.
additional_notes: This combination is not a common idiom. Taken literally, 'femme' = woman and 'deux' = two. It could appear in a fragment of a sentence (e.g., listing items or people: «une femme et deux hommes» = 'a woman and two men'). Alone, it is incomplete and sounds unnatural. If you meant 'femme et deux enfants' or similar, include the noun after 'deux'.
target_language_example: Il y avait une femme et deux enfants dans la salle d'attente.
native_language_example: There was a woman and two children in the waiting room.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; likely a typo or word-order error. As written it pairs the feminine noun 'femme' with the masculine definite article 'le', which is ungrammatical. It could appear in mistaken written fragments or transcriptions.
additional_notes: Correct form for 'the woman' is 'la femme'. You may also see 'femme-le' with a hyphen only if 'le' is a clitic pronoun attached to an imperative verb (e.g. 'Fais-le'), but that construction does not apply to the noun 'femme'. If encountering 'femme le' in a text, it is almost certainly an error and should be corrected or clarified.
target_language_example: *femme le* (ungrammatical fragment — likely meant 'la femme')
native_language_example: 'femme le' (an ungrammatical fragment — likely meant 'la femme')

meaning: that woman / the woman there (used to point out or refer to a specific woman)
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression combining femme (woman) with là (there/that) to indicate a particular woman nearby or previously mentioned. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation: can mean 'that woman' (slightly dismissive or emphatic) or simply 'the woman over there.' Not a fixed idiom; it's compositional and common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Tu vois la femme là, près de la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Do you see that woman by the window?

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken sequence (e.g., intended 'femme de...' or 'femme, me...' ).
additional_notes:
This exact two-word sequence 'femme me' does not form a normal expression in French. Possible intended forms:
- 'femme de ...' (woman of/of the) as in 'femme de chambre' (chambermaid), 'femme de ménage' (cleaning woman).
- 'la femme me ...' as part of a sentence where 'me' is an object pronoun: e.g. 'La femme me parle' (The woman speaks to me). In that case words are separate: 'femme' (noun) + 'me' (indirect/direct object pronoun meaning 'me').
If you saw 'femme me' in text, check for a missing word or punctuation. For learners: remember that object pronouns (me, te, le, la, lui, etc.) typically come before the verb (La femme me voit = The woman sees me).
target_language_example: La femme me parle tous les matins.
native_language_example: The woman talks to me every morning.

meaning: "femme" = woman; "ne" = part of negative construction (not).
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words that normally don't form a fixed phrase. 'Femme' means 'woman'. 'Ne' is the first particle of the standard French negation (ne...pas, ne...jamais, etc.) and must be paired with a second part (usually 'pas') to express 'not'. You will not say 'femme ne' by itself in natural French; likely you will see 'une femme' (a woman) or a negative sentence like 'la femme ne ... pas' (the woman does not ...).
target_language_example: La femme ne comprend pas la question.
native_language_example: The woman does not understand the question.

meaning: 'woman for' (literal) — not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely part of a larger phrase such as 'femme pour [quelque chose]' or a mistranscription.
additional_notes: Alone, 'femme pour' is incomplete and uncommon. 'Femme' = woman; 'pour' = for. In French you'd normally see 'femme de' or 'femme pour' only within a full context (e.g., 'une femme pour travailler' — 'a woman to work' — but more natural is 'une femme qui travaille' or 'une femme pour ce poste'). If you encountered 'femme pour' in text, look for the rest of the phrase after 'pour' that explains purpose or intended role. Avoid using 'femme pour' by itself.
target_language_example: Nous cherchons une femme pour ce poste.
native_language_example: We are looking for a woman for this position.

meaning: 'femme se' is not a correct or complete French expression on its own.
additional_notes: This sequence likely results from a mistaken split of words or missing context. In French, 'femme' means 'woman' and 'se' is a reflexive pronoun used before a verb (e.g. 'elle se lave' = 'she washes herself'). You will never use 'femme se' alone; instead you might see constructions like 'la femme se lève' (the woman gets up) or 'une femme se sent' (a woman feels). If you intended a common phrase, check for the verb that follows 'se' (e.g. 'femme se marier' -> 'une femme se marie' = 'a woman gets married').
target_language_example: La femme se repose après le travail.
native_language_example: The woman rests after work.

meaning: This is not a standalone French phrase; it looks like two words 'femme' (woman) + 'très' (very) but is incomplete.
additional_notes: In French, the adverb 'très' (very) normally comes before an adjective or another adverb, not directly after a noun. If you want to say 'a very [adjective] woman', use 'une femme très + adjective' (e.g. 'une femme très intelligente'). If you intended 'very woman' in English (which isn't grammatical), French would not use 'femme très' either. If you meant 'very feminine' use 'très femme' in some contexts (colloquial) but it's uncommon. 'Femme très' by itself should be completed with an adjective to make sense.
target_language_example: C'est une femme très courageuse.
native_language_example: She is a very courageous woman.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken word order (correct: "la femme vous..." or "vous, femme...") or part of a larger phrase.
additional_notes: Alone, "femme vous" is ungrammatical in standard French. French word order normally places the subject before the verb (e.g., "la femme vous voit" = "the woman sees you") or uses pronoun before the verb (e.g., "vous, femme..." for emphasis). If you meant to address a woman politely, use "Madame" or "vous, madame". If it appears in a longer sentence, check word order and articles (la/une) or verbs.
target_language_example: La femme vous attend au café.
native_language_example: The woman is waiting for you at the café.

meaning: literally 'woman at/of' — not a fixed phrase by itself; used as part of expressions like 'femme à (quelque chose)' or 'femme à (quelqu'un)' to indicate a woman's relation, role, characteristic, or possession.
additional_notes: Alone, 'femme à' is incomplete and needs more words (a noun or name) to form a meaningful phrase: for example 'la femme à Paul' (Paul's wife; colloquial), 'femme à barbe' (bearded woman), or 'femme d'affaires' (businesswoman — note different structure). In spoken French, 'la femme à Paul' is informal/regional; the standard would be 'la femme de Paul' or 'l'épouse de Paul'. Use 'à' after 'femme' mainly in set expressions or certain regional/colloquial constructions.
target_language_example: C'est la femme à Paul, elle travaille au marché.
native_language_example: That's Paul's wife; she works at the market.

meaning: 'women of' — a part of a larger phrase that links 'women' to something (possession, origin, characteristic, role).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it must be followed by a noun or phrase (e.g. femmes de chambre, femmes de science, femmes de la région). It uses the plural noun 'femmes' (women) plus the preposition 'de' (of, from, about, with). Context determines the best English translation: 'of', 'from', 'for', or sometimes 'women who...'.
target_language_example: Les femmes de la ville participent au festival.
native_language_example: The women of the town are participating in the festival.

meaning: women and children (the women and the children)
additional_notes: A common fixed expression used to refer to both groups together (e.g., in evacuation, priority, or general statements). 'Les' is the definite article repeated for both nouns but can also appear once: 'les femmes et enfants' is possible in spoken/written French. Used in contexts like 'women and children first' or asking about exits or boarding for those groups.
target_language_example: Les femmes et les enfants doivent sortir en premier.
native_language_example: The women and the children must go out first.

meaning: Please (literally: 'I beg you') — used to politely request someone to do something (here: close/open the window).
additional_notes: The full polite phrase appears as '... , je te prie' (informal) or '... , je vous prie' (formal/plural). It follows an imperative or a polite question: 'Peux-tu fermer la fenêtre, je te prie ?' = 'Could you close the window, please?'. It's a bit formal/old-fashioned but still used to add politeness. Use 'je vous prie' for strangers, elders or formal situations; 'je te prie' with friends/family.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous fermer la fenêtre, je vous prie ?
native_language_example: Could you close the window, please?

meaning: a window (of) — used in expressions like 'fenêtre de temps' or 'fenêtre de tir' to mean a time/opportunity window
additional_notes: Fenêtre means 'window'. When followed by 'de + noun' it forms a compound meaning 'window of [something]' (a period, an opportunity, a viewing pane, or a gap). Common in contexts like scheduling (une fenêtre de temps), transport (une fenêtre d'arrivée), or photography/observation (fenêtre d'observation). Use 'de' or the contraction 'd'' before a vowel. Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Nous avons une petite fenêtre de temps demain matin.
native_language_example: We have a small window of time tomorrow morning.

meaning: Not a standard French multiword term; likely a typo, mis-segmentation, or non-French fragment. It has no established meaning as a fixed expression in French.
additional_notes:
Possible explanations:
- Could be a misspelling or mis-segmentation (e.g. 'fer' = 'iron' (noun) and 'est' = 'is' (verb), but together 'fer est' is not grammatical in standard French). 
- If you encountered it in a sentence, it may be two separate words that should not be adjacent (e.g. 'le fer est...' meaning 'the iron is...' where 'fer' is a noun and 'est' is the verb 'is'); in that case the phrase can appear but only as part of a larger grammatical sentence. 
- Could be an OCR/typing error for forms like 'ferme' (farm/close) or 'faut est' (incorrect) or 'faire est' (incorrect). Provide the original sentence for accurate identification.
target_language_example: Le fer est un métal essentiel dans l'alimentation humaine.
native_language_example: Iron is an essential metal in human nutrition.

meaning: 'will do' as part of expressions meaning 'will do what (is necessary/possible)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "faire ce qu'il faut" (do what is necessary), "faire ce qu'on peut" (do what we can). Here 'fera ce' is the future of 'faire' + demonstrative 'ce' and requires a following clause (e.g. 'fera ce qu'il faut'). It does not stand alone; translate according to the full expression (e.g. 'will do what is necessary', 'will do what we can').
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, on fera ce qu'il faut.
native_language_example: Don't worry, we'll do what is necessary.

meaning: will do some
additional_notes: A fragment of the future tense of faire ('to do/make') plus du. It usually needs a noun after it, such as fera du yoga ('will do yoga'), fera du bruit ('will make noise'), or fera du bien ('will do good / will be good for'). Not usually used on its own.
target_language_example: Demain, elle fera du yoga.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, she'll do yoga.

meaning: I'll do what you (tell/want).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a common structure meaning 'I will do what you say/want.' It uses the future tense (ferai) and is completed by verbs like 'dis', 'me diras', 'veux', 'voudras'. Often used to reassure or to promise to follow someone's wishes or instructions.
target_language_example: Je ferai ce que tu veux demain.
native_language_example: I'll do what you want tomorrow.

meaning: I will do what you (formal/plural) ... (I will do as you ask/say/want).
additional_notes: This phrase begins a sentence meaning 'I will do what you ...' followed by a verb or phrase (e.g. demandez, dites, voulez). 'Ferai' is the future tense of 'faire' (je ferai = I will do). 'Vous' here is the polite or plural 'you'. Commonly completed as 'je ferai ce que vous demandez/dites/voulez/me direz.'
target_language_example: Je ferai ce que vous demandez demain.
native_language_example: I will do what you ask tomorrow.

meaning: I'll do everything (that)... / I will do whatever is necessary.
additional_notes: This phrase introduces a promise or strong willingness to do all that is required; it's usually followed by a clause starting with que (que + verb) or qui (qui + être). Common in expressions like "Je ferai tout ce que tu veux" or "Je ferai tout ce qui est nécessaire." Tone is neutral — can be formal or informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce que tu me demanderas pour que le projet réussisse.
native_language_example: I'll do everything you ask me to so that the project succeeds.

target_language_multi_word_term: ferai tout ce que je (peux / pourrai / pense être juste)
meaning: I'll do everything I can / I'll do whatever I (think is right).
additional_notes: Common way to promise or emphasize effort/commitment. Often completed with verbs like peux, pourrai, pense être juste, or other infinitives. Use peux (present) for immediate ability, pourrai (future) to stress future ability. Tone can be strong (vow, reassurance) depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce que je peux pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I'll do everything I can to help you.

meaning: 'I will do everything that' / 'I will do whatever (is needed) that...'
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause meaning the speaker will do everything necessary or everything that is required/asked. It uses the future tense of faire (je ferai). Usually followed by a subordinate clause introduced by que or followed directly by a verb phrase (e.g. '...est nécessaire', '...pour t'aider', '...se passe'). Common in promises or assurances.
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce qui est nécessaire pour réussir.
native_language_example: I will do everything that is necessary to succeed.

meaning: you would do better (to)
additional_notes: Commonly used to give advice or a recommendation — often followed by 'de' + infinitive (e.g. 'ferais mieux de partir'). In spoken French, corresponds to a mild/strong suggestion depending on context and tone. The subject can change (je ferais mieux = I'd be better off), but most example uses are second person 'tu ferais mieux' giving advice to someone else.
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de téléphoner avant d'y aller.
native_language_example: You'd be better off calling before you go.

meaning: 'would do better not to' (a conditional suggestion to avoid doing something).
additional_notes: This is part of the common construction « tu ferais mieux de ne pas... » or « il ferait mieux de ne pas... » used to give advice or a warning in the conditional. It is followed by an infinitive (often with pas): ferais mieux de ne pas + infinitive. Polite/stronger than a direct order. The fragment 'ferais mieux de ne' by itself is incomplete; include 'pas' and a verb to form the full negated suggestion.
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de ne pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: You would do better not to go out tonight.

meaning: 'would do anything' (would do whatever it takes).
additional_notes: Expressions with 'ferais n'importe quoi' mean someone is willing to do anything (often to help or please someone). The full phrase is 'ferais n'importe quoi' or 'ferais n'importe quoi pour...' Using just 'ferais n'importe' is informal/elliptical; include 'quoi' in neutral speech. Conveys strong willingness, sometimes exaggeration. Verb is conditional of 'faire' (je ferais = I would do).
target_language_example: Je ferais n'importe quoi pour te protéger.
native_language_example: I would do anything to protect you.

meaning: would not do (someone) any harm / would not hurt / wouldn't be harmful; also used in expressions like 'wouldn't hurt to' (do something).
additional_notes: This is the negative conditional form of 'faire' plus 'de' used in idiomatic phrases. Often appears as 'ne ... ferait pas de mal (à ...)' meaning 'it wouldn't hurt (someone)' or 'wouldn't be a bad thing'. Can express that something would be harmless or that doing something would be beneficial (e.g. 'Un peu de café ne me ferait pas de mal' = 'A little coffee wouldn't hurt me' i.e. would help). In casual speech the 'ne' is sometimes dropped: 'ça ne te ferait pas de mal' → 'ça te ferait pas de mal'.
target_language_example: Une pause ne te ferait pas de mal.
native_language_example: A break wouldn't hurt you.

meaning: 'would do a' (conditional of faire + indefinite article)
additional_notes: ferait is the conditional form of faire (to do/make). Followed by une + noun it means 'would do/make a...' Used for hypothetical or polite requests (Il vous ferait une fleur? — Would he do you a favor?) or to express what would happen or who would do something. Structure: [subject] ferait une + [noun].
target_language_example: Elle me ferait une faveur si je la lui demandais.
native_language_example: She would do me a favor if I asked her.

meaning: close the
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say that you close or shut something: fermer le portail, fermer le coffre. With some objects, English may use a different verb, for example fermer le robinet is usually 'turn off the tap/faucet.'
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de fermer le frigo.
native_language_example: Don't forget to close the fridge.

meaning: to close one's eyes; idiomatically, to ignore or pretend not to notice something (to look the other way, turn a blind eye).
additional_notes: Literally 'to close the eyes.' Used both literally (physically closing one's eyes) and figuratively to ask someone to overlook, ignore, or be lenient about a fault or problem. Context and wording (e.g., adding 'là‑dessus' or 'pour cette fois') clarify the figurative sense.
target_language_example: Pourrais-tu fermer les yeux là‑dessus pour cette fois ?
native_language_example: Could you turn a blind eye to that this time?

meaning: an informal, blunt way to tell someone to 'shut your (…)', usually 'shut your mouth' or 'shut up'.
additional_notes: A colloquial contraction of fermer ta bouche (shut your mouth). Used in spoken French, often sharp or rude. Usually completed by the noun (bouche) or left hanging for effect: fermer ta gueule (more vulgar) or fermer ta bouche (less vulgar). Tone matters—can be offensive. Not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: Fermer ta et écoute—je parle.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen—I'm talking.

meaning: to lock (with a key).
additional_notes: Used when a door, window, box, etc., is secured using a key. Often interchangeable with "verrouiller" (to lock) but "fermer à clef" emphasizes using a key. Commonly used in everyday situations (e.g., fermer la porte à clef).
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de fermer à clef la porte en partant.
native_language_example: Don't forget to lock the door with the key when you leave.

meaning: 'to lock' (to lock something with a key).
additional_notes: Used for locking doors, windows, cabinets, etc., with a key. Commonly appears as "fermer la porte à clé" (to lock the door). The construction uses 'à clé' to indicate using a key. You can also say 'verrouiller' for 'to lock' (more general) or 'déverrouiller' / 'ouvrir à clé' for 'to unlock'.
target_language_example: Assure-toi de fermer à clé la porte avant de partir.
native_language_example: Make sure to lock the door with the key before leaving.

meaning: zipper; the fastening with teeth and a slider used on clothes, bags, etc.
additional_notes: Common Canadian French term (also used in France); in France you may also hear «fermeture Éclair» (brand) or simply «zip»/«fermeture à glissière». Used for clothing, bags, tents. Agreement: feminine noun phrase (une fermeture éclair).
target_language_example: La fermeture éclair de ma veste est cassée.
native_language_example: The zipper on my jacket is broken.

meaning: 'fire at' or 'shoot at' (to open fire on someone/something).
additional_notes: Used when talking about shooting or opening fire with a weapon: 'feu à' is usually followed by the target (e.g. 'feu à la voiture'). In written/formal registers you may also see 'ouvrir le feu sur' or simply 'tirer sur'. Not to be confused with 'feu' meaning traffic light. Note the preposition is 'à' (with accent).
target_language_example: Les soldats ont donné feu à l'ennemi. — ou dans une formulation plus littérale : ils ont donné 'feu à' l'ennemi.
native_language_example: The soldiers opened fire on the enemy.

meaning: 'fire of' or 'light/beam/flash from' depending on context; often used in compound expressions (e.g. feu de camp = campfire, feu de signalisation = traffic light, feu de détresse = distress light).
additional_notes: feu literally means 'fire' and feu de is used to form many fixed expressions where the second noun specifies the type or purpose of the fire/light/ignition. In some contexts 'feu' refers to a traffic signal (feu rouge/vert) or a shooting/attack ('feu!' = 'fire!'). The literal translation often works but the full expression should be learned as a phrase (feu de camp ≠ 'fire of camp' in natural English; it's 'campfire').
target_language_example: Nous avons allumé un feu de camp ce soir.
native_language_example: We lit a campfire tonight.

meaning: campfire; an outdoor fire used for warmth, cooking, or social gathering while camping
additional_notes: Common, literal phrase. Used for fires made at a campsite, on a beach, or outdoors. Can refer to both the physical fire and the social activity around it. Watch local regulations—building a feu de camp may be restricted in some areas.
target_language_example: Le soir, nous nous sommes assis autour du feu de camp pour chanter.
native_language_example: In the evening we sat around the campfire to sing.

meaning: 'the fire/traffic light is' — combination of noun 'feu' (fire or traffic light) + verb 'être' (to be).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but simply the noun 'feu' followed by the verb 'est' (he/it is). 'Feu' can mean a fire (flame) or a traffic light; context tells which. Useful adjectives after 'feu est' include chaud (hot), rouge/vert/jaune (traffic-light colors), and éteint/allumé (off/on for lights or fire).
target_language_example: Le feu est vert, nous pouvons avancer.
native_language_example: The traffic light is green, we can go forward.

meaning: traffic light showing red; red traffic light (stop signal).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a red traffic signal that requires vehicles to stop. Can be used in directions (e.g., 'after the red light') or in contexts about traffic violations (e.g., 'running a red light').
target_language_example: Attends au feu rouge avant de traverser.
native_language_example: Wait at the red light before crossing.

meaning: 'green light' — permission to go ahead; approval to proceed.
additional_notes: Used both literally (traffic signal: the green light allowing pedestrians or vehicles to go) and figuratively (authorization, official approval to start an action or project). Common in spoken and written French. Can be used alone as a short expression (e.g., «Feu vert.»).
target_language_example: On attend le feu vert pour lancer le projet.
native_language_example: We're waiting for the green light to start the project.

meaning: to set fire to (something feminine) / to burn down.
additional_notes: Phrase is part of the construction mettre le feu à + [noun] meaning 'to set fire to' or 'to burn' (often intentionally). Here 'la' is the feminine definite article before a feminine noun: e.g. 'mettre le feu à la grange' = set fire to the barn. Use 'au' for masculine singular (mettre le feu au hangar) and 'aux' for plural. This is not a casual expression; it often implies arson or deliberate burning in examples.
target_language_example: Ils ont mis le feu à la maison abandonnée.
native_language_example: They set fire to the abandoned house.

meaning: the leaves of / the sheets of (literal part of a noun phrase: 'feuilles' + 'des' meaning 'of the' or plural possessive).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the start of a noun phrase: 'feuilles' (plural of 'feuille' = leaf, sheet) followed by the partitive/genitive article 'des' (contraction of 'de + les' = 'of the' or plural indefinite 'some'). The exact translation depends on context: 'feuilles des arbres' = 'leaves of the trees'; 'feuilles des cahiers' = 'sheets of the notebooks'. Watch word order: in French the noun 'feuilles' comes before 'des' when 'des' is part of a following noun group that it modifies (often you'll see 'les feuilles des arbres' or just 'feuilles d'arbre' in other constructions).
target_language_example: Les feuilles des arbres tombent en automne.
native_language_example: The leaves of the trees fall in autumn.

meaning: 'the leaves are' or 'the leaves (verb...)' — 'feuilles' (leaves) + 'sont' (are).
additional_notes: A simple noun + verb (être) combination used to describe the state or action of leaves. 'Sont' is the 3rd person plural present form of être (to be). In the examples it describes colors or a past action when used with past participles (e.g. 'sont devenues', 'sont tombées') — note agreement of past participle with plural feminine 'feuilles' when using compound tenses with être. Use 'les feuilles sont...' to say 'the leaves are...' and follow with an adjective, past participle, or location.
target_language_example: Les feuilles sont encore vertes.
native_language_example: The leaves are still green.

meaning: An informal/colloquial misspelling or play on words — likely intended as 'fiché' (recorded/registered) or 'fais chier' (vulgar). On its own 'fiche le' has no standard meaning in French.
additional_notes: No standard phrase 'fiche le' exists in French. It may appear as a typo, as two separate words ('fiche' = card/form, 'le' = the), or in regional/slang contexts as a mistaken transcription of 'fiché' (past participle of 'ficher' meaning 'to record/label') or of a vulgar expression when spoken quickly. Do not use this as a set phrase. If you saw it in writing, check context: could be 'fiche le dossier' (incorrect; correct: 'fiche le dossier' still incorrect — proper forms: 'fiche le dossier' would be nonstandard) or simply 'fiche' + article 'le'.
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est une erreur — 'fiche le' n'a pas de sens ici.
native_language_example: I think it's a mistake — 'fiche le' doesn't make sense here.

meaning: 'leave someone alone' or 'let someone be'.
additional_notes: Informal (milder than 'foutre la paix'). Used to tell someone to stop bothering or disturbing another person. Can be directed at someone (Il me fiche la paix) or used imperatively (Fiche-moi la paix !). More polite alternatives: 'laisse-moi tranquille' or 'laissez-moi tranquille'.
target_language_example: Il me fiche la paix quand je travaille.
native_language_example: He leaves me alone when I work.

meaning: to leave quickly; to get out of here (colloquial, strong)
additional_notes: Informal/slang expression used to tell someone to go away or to describe leaving in a hurry. Often stronger than simplement "partir" and can be rude depending on tone/context. Variants: "ficher le camp d'ici", "fous le camp" (more vulgar).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux qu'on fiche le camp avant qu'il n'arrive.
native_language_example: We'd better get out of here before he arrives.

meaning: wire (metal wire, usually iron or steel).
additional_notes: Refers to a thin, flexible strand of metal (often iron/steel). Commonly used for fencing (fil de fer barbelé = barbed wire), crafting, repairs. Not idiomatic here—literal physical material. Can appear with articles/quantities: du fil de fer (some wire), un fil de fer (a wire).
target_language_example: Je vais acheter du fil de fer pour réparer la clôture.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy some wire to fix the fence.

meaning: 'red wire' (literally); used literally to refer to a red electrical/connecting wire
additional_notes: Used when talking about actual wires (electrical, in models, or in devices) — e.g., when cutting or connecting wires. Not an idiomatic 'common thread' here (that idiomatic meaning exists in French too but contexts and examples provided are clearly literal). Useful in instructions and emergency situations (e.g., 'Cut the red wire').
target_language_example: Ne touche pas aux autres fils, coupe seulement le fil rouge.
native_language_example: Don't touch the other wires, cut only the red wire.

meaning: 'single file' (one behind the other).
additional_notes: Used to describe people or animals walking in a single line, one after another. Common in instructions (e.g., teachers to students). Usually preceded by 'en' (en file indienne). Literal components 'file' (line) and 'indienne' (Indian) — the expression is idiomatic but understandable.
target_language_example: Mettez-vous en file indienne pour entrer dans la classe.
native_language_example: Line up in single file to enter the classroom.

meaning: A way to address or refer to 'your/my daughter' followed by 'you' — often used to direct a comment or question to the person or about the person.
additional_notes: This pattern shows two parts: a noun (fille/ta fille/ma fille) followed by a vocative or subject pronoun (tu). It can be used to address the daughter directly (Ma fille, tu devrais...) or to comment about someone’s daughter to that person (Ta fille, tu y as pensé?). The comma and intonation matter in speech. Equivalent English patterns: “My daughter, you should…”, “If you want to marry my daughter, you must…”.
target_language_example: Ma fille, tu m'écoutes quand je parle ?
native_language_example: My daughter, are you listening to me?

meaning: 'girl at' or 'girl with' (incomplete chunk used before a noun or place).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the start of a noun phrase like «fille au chien» (girl with the dog) or «fille au café» (girl at the café). In French, au = à + le and means 'at the' or 'to the' (masculine singular) or can indicate possession/association ('with the') in some contexts. You will normally see «fille au» followed immediately by a masculine noun.
target_language_example: La fille au manteau rouge attend le bus.
native_language_example: The girl with the red coat is waiting for the bus.

meaning: literally 'girl had' — the past-imperfect form meaning 'the girl had' or 'the girl was (having)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words: fille (girl) + avait (imparfait of avoir). Used to describe states or actions in the past (imperfect). Context determines translation: 'avait' can mean possession ('had') or part of a description ('was ...ing' when combined with another verb in progressive sense in English). Example: La fille avait six ans = The girl was six years old / The girl had six years.
target_language_example: La fille avait beaucoup de jouets quand elle était petite.
native_language_example: The girl had a lot of toys when she was little.

meaning: 'girl with' — used to describe a girl who has or is accompanied by something or someone
additional_notes: This is simply the noun fille (girl) followed by the preposition avec (with). It appears in descriptions like "la fille avec les cheveux rouges" (the girl with red hair) or "la fille avec moi" (the girl with me). Word order: noun + avec + object. Not a fixed expression; meaning comes from the parts.
target_language_example: La fille avec le sac rouge est ma sœur.
native_language_example: The girl with the red bag is my sister.

meaning: 'girl in' or 'daughter in' — literal combination of fille + dans; not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression in French. It simply pairs the noun fille (girl/daughter) with the preposition dans (in/inside/within). You will normally see it as part of a longer phrase, e.g. "la fille dans la maison" (the girl in the house) or "une fille dans la foule" (a girl in the crowd). Pay attention to articles and agreement: "la/une fille dans...". If you meant 'son/daughter-in-law' or other family relations, different words are used (belle-fille = daughter/in-law).
target_language_example: La fille dans le jardin joue avec le chien.
native_language_example: The girl in the garden is playing with the dog.

meaning: 'girl in' — a fragment used before a noun or adjective to describe a girl who is in/doing something (in + noun/adjective).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase in French; it's usually the start of a larger phrase such as fille en colère (girl who is angry), fille en or (girl in gold), or fille en vacances (girl on holiday). You will almost always see it followed by a noun, an adjective, or a phrase that completes the idea. Pay attention to gender/number agreement in the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: C'est la fille en rouge qui gagne le concours.
native_language_example: It's the girl in red who wins the contest.

meaning: literally 'girl is' — combination of noun 'fille' (girl/daughter) + verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'fille' followed by the third-person singular of être ('est'). Used when describing or stating something about a girl or daughter (e.g. 'La fille est intelligente' = 'The girl is intelligent'). Pay attention to articles (la/une) and adjective agreement (feminine).
target_language_example: La fille est très gentille.
native_language_example: The girl is very kind.

meaning: This combination by itself has no fixed meaning in French.
additional_notes: ‘fille’ means 'girl' or 'daughter'. 'et' means 'and'. Together, 'fille et' is just two words that need more context (e.g. 'fille et garçon' = 'girl and boy', or 'fille et mère' = 'daughter and mother'). Do not use 'fille et' alone as a phrase — add the second noun or phrase after 'et' to complete the idea. Pronunciation: fille [fij], et [e].
target_language_example: La fille et le garçon jouent au parc.
native_language_example: The girl and the boy are playing in the park.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete fragment (could be 'fille de' or 'fille, me...' or an anglicism).
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'fille me' does not form a correct or common French expression. 'Fille' means 'girl' or 'daughter'. If you meant 'fais-moi' (do/make me) or 'file-moi' (give me — informal), those are different verbs. Possible intended phrases:
- 'ma fille' = my daughter
- 'une fille me plaît' (correct order: 'une fille me plaît') = a girl pleases me / I like a girl
- 'fais-moi' (imperative of 'faire') = make/do me or 'do for me'
- 'file‑moi' (informal imperative of 'filer') = give me / hand me (slang)
If you can provide the full sentence or context, I can give the correct phrase and translation.
target_language_example: Une fille me parle dans la rue. (example showing correct order: subject 'une fille' + verb 'me')
native_language_example: A girl is talking to me on the street.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment. 'fille' = girl/daughter; 'ne' is the first part of negation (ne ... pas).
additional_notes: This combination by itself is incomplete and ungrammatical. In French, negation requires both 'ne' (or 'n’' before a vowel) and a second particle such as 'pas', 'jamais', 'plus', etc. Example correct uses: 'La fille ne parle pas' (The girl does not speak) or 'La fille n'est pas là' (The girl is not here). If you saw 'fille ne' in text it probably belongs to a larger sentence where 'ne' begins a negation referring to 'fille'.
target_language_example: La fille ne mange pas.
native_language_example: The girl does not eat.

meaning: literally 'girl for' — not a standalone French phrase; likely part of a larger expression (e.g., 'fille pour mariage', 'fille pour le rôle').
additional_notes: By itself, 'fille pour' is incomplete. 'Fille' means 'girl' or 'daughter' and 'pour' means 'for' or 'to'. In French, 'fille pour' must be followed by a noun or verb to form a meaningful phrase (examples: 'fille pour mariage' = 'girl for marriage' or 'fille pour le rôle' = 'girl for the role'). Do not use 'fille pour' alone — provide the object or purpose after 'pour'.
target_language_example: Ils cherchent une fille pour le rôle principal.
native_language_example: They are looking for a girl for the lead role.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken split of words (e.g. 'fille se...' would be part of a sentence meaning 'the girl ...' followed by a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This is not an independent multiword expression. In French, 'fille' means 'girl' and 'se' is a reflexive pronoun used before a verb (e.g. 'se laver' = 'to wash oneself'). Together they only appear as part of a larger clause: 'La fille se lave' = 'The girl washes (herself)'. Do not use 'fille se' alone.
target_language_example: La fille se promène dans le parc.
native_language_example: The girl is walking in the park.

meaning: literally 'girl very' — not a fixed phrase; 'très' is the adverb 'very' and modifies an adjective or adverb that would follow (e.g. 'une fille très gentille' = 'a very kind girl').
additional_notes: By itself 'fille très' is incomplete in French. 'Très' must modify an adjective or another adverb: structure is usually 'une fille très + adjective' (feminine noun + 'très' + adjective). Make sure the adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun (e.g. 'très jolie', 'très intelligentes').
target_language_example: C'est une fille très intelligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent girl.

meaning: an only daughter (one and only female child in the family).
additional_notes: Used to say a woman or girl has no sisters and is the only daughter of her parents. Often preceded by an article or pronoun (je suis fille unique / elle est votre fille unique). Can refer to someone's status in the family; not formal or slang.
target_language_example: Elle est fille unique, mais elle a deux frères.
native_language_example: She is an only daughter, but she has two brothers.

meaning: 'the girl goes' or 'the girl is going' (simple present or near future in spoken French).
additional_notes: This is the subject (fille = girl) + verb (va = goes/is going) form of the verb aller. Alone, 'fille va' is not a complete natural sentence in French — you'd normally include an article or pronoun (e.g. 'la fille va' = the girl goes) or add a destination/infinitive (e.g. 'La fille va à l'école' or 'La fille va partir'). In spoken French you often hear 'elle va' rather than repeating 'la fille'.
target_language_example: La fille va à l'école tous les matins.
native_language_example: The girl goes to school every morning.

meaning: literally 'girl/daughter of' — used to indicate a girl's relationship to someone or something (possession, belonging or origin).
additional_notes: This is the start of a possessive or descriptive phrase: 'fille de' is more common for 'daughter of', but in informal spoken French you may hear 'la fille à + name' (especially in some regional varieties) instead of 'la fille de + name'. Example: 'la fille à Marc' = 'Marc's daughter'. Also used in expressions like 'la fille à sa mère' meaning 'the girl like her mother'. Be careful: standard written French prefers 'de'.
target_language_example: C'est la fille à Sophie.
native_language_example: She's Sophie's daughter.

meaning: 'daughters of' or 'girls of' (possession/relationship)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that the girls/daughters belong to or are related to someone or something. Often followed by a noun or name: e.g. 'les filles de Marie' = Marie's daughters. Can also appear in phrases like 'des filles de la rue' (girls of the street). In spoken French, possessive structures may vary (e.g. 'les filles à Marie' in some regional/colloquial uses), but 'filles de' is the standard written form. Remember to include the definite/indefinite article as needed (les filles de, des filles de, une fille de).
target_language_example: Les filles de Paul sont très sympathiques.
native_language_example: Paul's daughters are very friendly.

meaning: girls/daughters of (the) — used to say someone belongs to or is associated with someone or something (plural feminine).
additional_notes: ‘filles’ is the plural feminine noun for 'girl' or 'daughter'. 'du' is the contraction of 'de + le' (of the/the) and agrees in gender/number with the possessed noun, not with 'filles'.
