additional_notes: Used when indicating the thing or quantity gained with the preposition de: gagner de l'argent, gagner de la confiance, gagner de précieuses minutes. When a specific numeral directly follows gagner, de can be omitted (gagner 10 €). Context determines exact English rendering (to win, to earn, to gain). The phrase alone is not idiomatic without the following noun or quantity.
target_language_example: Il a réussi à gagner de précieuses minutes pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He managed to gain precious minutes during the meeting.

meaning: to save time; to make something take less time
additional_notes: Used when an action or tool reduces the amount of time needed. Common in everyday and formal speech. Often appears with faire (faire gagner du temps) to mean 'to help someone save time' or with ça/ça nous/te to say 'this saves (us/you) time.'
target_language_example: Un raccourci clavier peut te faire gagner du temps.
native_language_example: A keyboard shortcut can save you time.

meaning: to make progress; to gain ground or become more influential or successful
additional_notes: Used both literally (e.g., erosion or territory) and figuratively (an idea, movement, product, or candidate becoming more popular or successful). Commonly followed by 'sur' + object (gagner du terrain sur la concurrence) or used alone with context (ce mouvement gagne du terrain).
target_language_example: Le mouvement commence à gagner du terrain dans les régions rurales.
native_language_example: The movement is beginning to gain ground in rural areas.

meaning: to win the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: Gagner means 'to win' or 'to earn'. When followed by le, it introduces a specific masculine singular thing being won (e.g. gagner le match, gagner le prix). You must include the noun after 'le' (or use a contraction: gagner l' before a vowel). For feminine nouns use 'gagner la' and for plural 'gagner les'. Can also mean 'to gain' in contexts like 'gagner le temps' (gain time).
target_language_example: Il espère gagner le match demain.
native_language_example: He hopes to win the match tomorrow.

meaning: to earn/win my (followed by a noun); 'gagner' = to earn/win, 'ma' = my (feminine singular).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a combination of the verb gagner and the possessive adjective ma. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'gagner ma vie' = to earn my living). Context determines whether gagner means 'to earn' (money, a living) or 'to win' (a prize, a game).
target_language_example: Je dois gagner ma vie pour payer le loyer.
native_language_example: I need to earn my living to pay the rent.

meaning: to earn a living / to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone earns money to pay for living expenses. Common in everyday speech. Often followed by mention of a job or situation (e.g., 'Que fait ton père pour gagner sa vie ?'). Can be used impersonally ('Il faut gagner sa vie') or reflexively about difficulties ('difficile de gagner sa vie').
target_language_example: Elle travaille comme secrétaire pour gagner sa vie.
native_language_example: She works as a secretary to earn her living.

meaning: earned/won a lot (of money, points, etc.)
additional_notes: Compound of the past participle gagné (from gagner: to win, to earn, to gain) and beaucoup (a lot). Context decides whether it means 'earned' (salary, money), 'won' (a prize, a game), or 'gained' (experience, weight). It's used after a subject with an auxiliary (e.g., J'ai gagné beaucoup).
target_language_example: J'ai gagné beaucoup d'argent cette année.
native_language_example: I earned/won a lot of money this year.

meaning: won first (place) / won the first (one)
additional_notes: Phrase combines the past participle 'gagné' (won) with 'le premier' (the first). Context determines whether it means 'won first place' (e.g. in a race) or 'won the first [round/item]'. It is not a fixed idiom — it's simply a short phrase you would use in a sentence (e.g. 'Il a gagné le premier prix' or 'Elle a gagné le premier match'). Make sure to include the noun if needed ('prix', 'match', 'tour') for clarity.
target_language_example: Elle a gagné le premier prix du concours.
native_language_example: She won the first prize in the contest.

meaning: won a (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: The verb gagner (past participle gagné) here is used in the past tense (often as part of passé composé: 'a gagné') meaning 'won' or 'earned'. 'Un' is the indefinite article for a masculine singular noun that follows (e.g. un prix, un million). Use 'a gagné' for 'he/she/it won' and change the article/gender as needed (une for feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Il a gagné un prix la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: He won a prize last week.

meaning: won (something) at; gained by/through (context-dependent).
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'gagné' plus the preposition 'à'. It can be used to say someone 'won at' a game or competition (e.g. gagné à la loterie → won in the lottery), or that something was 'gained/benefited by' a particular action when followed by a verb or noun (context determines exact translation). Watch for other verbs/structures: 'avoir gagné à' (to have benefited from) vs. 'gagner à' (to win at).
target_language_example: Il a gagné à la loterie la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: He won the lottery last week.

meaning: a kid associated with or characterized by (colloquial). Used to indicate a child/youngster who has or belongs to something or someone (e.g., 'the kid with/at/of ...' or 'a ... kid').
additional_notes: Gamin (masculine) = kid, youngster, street child (informal). When followed by à + noun it often describes association, possession, or characteristic (e.g., 'le gamin à la casquette' = the kid with the cap). Informal and conversational; more common in spoken French. Use la gamine à for the feminine. For origin, 'gamin de' or 'gamin de la rue' is often preferred. Articles and agreement follow normal rules.
target_language_example: Regarde le gamin à côté qui joue au ballon.
native_language_example: Look at the kid next to us who's playing with the ball.

meaning: wardrobe; clothes collection; closet for clothes.
additional_notes: Refers to a person's clothing collection or the piece of furniture where clothes are stored. Commonly used to talk about your outfits, style, or a wardrobe change. Can be used in singular/plural (les garde-robes) but often in singular to mean 'one's wardrobe'.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté une nouvelle garde-robe pour l'été.
native_language_example: She bought a new wardrobe for the summer.

meaning: bodyguard (a person who protects someone).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a security person who protects someone from physical danger. Can be singular masculine or feminine: un garde du corps / une garde du corps. Often used with possessives (mon garde du corps).
target_language_example: Elle a engagé un garde du corps pour les déplacements.
native_language_example: She hired a bodyguard for travel.

meaning: police custody; being held by the police for questioning.
additional_notes: Refers to the period when a suspect is detained by police for investigation and questioning (before possible charge or release). Common in legal/police contexts; not the same as prison or long-term detention. Often used with verbs like 'être placé en garde à vue' (to be placed in custody) or simply 'être en garde à vue'.
target_language_example: Il a été placé en garde à vue pour être interrogé.
native_language_example: He was placed in police custody for questioning.

meaning: 'keep my' or 'hold on to my' (first-person singular: to keep, maintain, or keep possession of something).
additional_notes: Built from the verb garde (from garder: to keep, to keep hold of, to maintain) + the possessive mon (my). Used in many contexts: keeping calm (garder son calme), keeping a secret, physically keeping an object, or maintaining an agreement/position. The verb changes with subject (je garde, tu gardes, il/elle garde). For idiomatic phrases like garder son calme or garder un secret, the possessive may be son/sa depending on the noun's gender.
target_language_example: Je garde mon calme pendant l'entretien.
native_language_example: I keep my calm during the interview.

meaning: to keep an eye on; to watch or monitor someone/something.
additional_notes: Informal everyday expression used to say you will monitor or watch for something (safety, progress, trouble). Often appears as garder un œil (on), garder l'œil sur, or garder les yeux ouverts. Can be followed by an object: garder l'œil sur la voiture / garder l'œil sur les enfants. Similar to surveiller but slightly lighter/colloquial.
target_language_example: Je vais garder l'œil sur la voiture pendant que tu fais les courses.
native_language_example: I'll keep an eye on the car while you do the shopping.

meaning: to stay on course; to keep going in the right direction (figurative: maintain direction or momentum).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean maintaining a plan, strategy, or steady progress despite difficulties. Can apply to projects, teams, personal goals, or organizations. Literal imagery comes from sailing/navigation (keep the heading).
target_language_example: Malgré les difficultés, il faut garder le cap sur nos objectifs.
native_language_example: Despite the difficulties, we must stay on course with our goals.

meaning: to keep silent; to remain quiet (not speak).
additional_notes: Used to say someone stays quiet or refuses to speak. Can be literal (be quiet) or figurative (keep a secret, refuse to comment). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Pendant l'heure d'examen, il faut garder le silence.
native_language_example: During the exam hour, you must keep silent.

meaning: to (get) to the station by (a mode of transport).
additional_notes: Used to say how someone goes or travels to the train station. The pattern is 'aller/venir/rejoindre la gare en + [moyen de transport]' (e.g., en voiture, en bus, en taxi). Not a fixed idiom—it's the noun 'gare' + preposition 'en' introducing the transport method.
target_language_example: Nous allons à la gare en bus.
native_language_example: We're going to the station by bus.

meaning: 'the station is' (used to describe the train/bus station's state or location).
additional_notes: Gare = station (usually train station). 'est' is the third-person singular of être (to be). Together they start simple sentences like 'La gare est ...' to describe location (in the center, before the bridge, between towns) or condition/state (closed, under repair). Often followed by prepositions (dans, en, à, entre) or adjectives/past participles (fermée, en réparation).
target_language_example: La gare est fermée aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The station is closed today.

meaning: used to indicate traveling to/from the station 'by' a particular means (e.g. by bus, by taxi).
additional_notes: The preposition 'par' here means 'by' or 'via' when specifying the mode or route of travel (par le bus, par taxi). More commonly in French you may also see 'en' for transport (en bus, en taxi) or 'par le train' when emphasizing via/through. 'Gare par' appears in phrases like 'aller à la gare par le bus' = 'go to the station by bus.'
target_language_example: Je vais à la gare par le métro.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station by subway.

meaning: to (go) to the train station to do something / at the station in order to…
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's just the noun gare (train station) followed by the preposition pour + infinitive or pronoun, meaning you went to the station for a purpose (e.g. to meet someone, to say goodbye). In examples the structure is often 'aller à la gare pour + verb' or 'aller à la gare pour + pronoun' (with an implicit verb like 'voir' or 'dire au revoir').
target_language_example: Il est allé à la gare pour accueillir sa sœur.
native_language_example: He went to the station to welcome his sister.

meaning: 'guy/guys from' or 'boy of' (used to indicate a person/people associated with a place, group, or quality)
additional_notes: Gars is an informal word for 'guy' or 'lad' (masculine). 'Gars de' is followed by a noun to show origin, affiliation, or a characteristic (e.g. gars de la ville, gars de l'équipe). Because 'gars' is plural in form when meaning 'guys', context and articles determine singular/plural. Use 'un gars' for 'a guy' or simply 'les gars' for 'the guys'. Informal register; commonly used in speech.
target_language_example: C'est un gars de Paris.
native_language_example: He's a guy from Paris.

meaning: 'boy of' or 'boy from' (literally) — used to indicate possession, origin, job role, or relationship when followed by a noun.
additional_notes: This is the noun 'garçon' (boy) followed by the preposition 'de' (of/from). It must be completed by another noun or phrase (e.g., garçon de café, garçon de l'école, garçon de la ville). Common fixed expressions: 'garçon de café' (waiter), 'garçon de course' (errand boy). Word order and articles matter: 'garçon du village' = boy from the village; 'garçon de la boutique' = boy of the shop. Not idiomatic by itself — you need the following noun.
target_language_example: Il travaille comme garçon de café dans ce bistrot.
native_language_example: He works as a café waiter in that bistro.

meaning: literally 'boy of the' — used as the start of a noun phrase meaning 'the boy from/of the…' (e.g. 'the boy from the countryside/forest' or 'a boy saved from the…' when followed by a noun like 'noyade').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the beginning of a phrase where 'garçon' (boy) is linked to a following noun introduced by the article 'la' (feminine). Meaning depends on the noun that follows: e.g. 'garçon de la campagne' = 'boy from the countryside'; in sentences like 'sauver le garçon de la noyade', 'de la' introduces the danger or cause ('from drowning'). Word order and articles matter (de la = of the/from the, feminine).
target_language_example: Ils ont retrouvé le garçon de la forêt sain et sauf.
native_language_example: They found the boy from the forest safe and sound.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; literally 'boy is'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a set expression in French. It would appear when 'garçon' (boy or waiter) is the subject of a sentence followed by the verb être (to be). For example: 'Le garçon est grand.' (The boy is tall.) Alone, 'garçon est' is incomplete and needs adjectives, nouns, or clauses to finish the sentence. 'Garçon' can also mean 'waiter' in a restaurant context (le garçon/ le garçon de café).
target_language_example: Le garçon est content de jouer au parc.
native_language_example: The boy is happy to play in the park.

meaning: 'tomboy' — a girl who behaves or dresses in ways traditionally associated with boys.
additional_notes: Used to describe a girl who prefers activities, clothing, or behavior stereotypically considered masculine (e.g., rough play, sports). It can be neutral or affectionate, but context and tone matter. Literal translation is 'boy missed/failed', which doesn't convey the actual meaning in English.
target_language_example: Ma nièce est un vrai garçon manqué : elle adore grimper aux arbres.
native_language_example: My niece is a real tomboy: she loves climbing trees.

meaning: This combination is not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken split. 'garçon' means 'boy' or 'waiter' and 'ne' is the first part of the negation 'ne ... pas'.
additional_notes: You will not see 'garçon ne' used as a fixed expression. Possible intended uses: 1) 'Le garçon ne ... pas' — the boy does not ... (complete the negation with a verb and 'pas'); 2) 'Garçon!' used alone to call a waiter (informal and can be rude). Remember that everyday spoken French often drops the 'ne' and uses only 'pas' for negation (Le garçon ne vient pas → Le garçon vient pas).
target_language_example: Le garçon ne comprend pas la question.
native_language_example: The boy does not understand the question.

meaning: literally 'boy or a/one' — not a standard fixed phrase; looks like a fragment comparing or listing 'garçon' (boy) with 'une' (feminine indefinite article).
additional_notes: This is not a normal multiword expression in French. It appears to be a fragment or mistaken combination: 'garçon' (masculine noun, 'boy' or 'waiter') and 'une' (feminine indefinite article 'a'/'an'). In correct sentences you would use either a matching article and noun (e.g. 'un garçon' = a boy) or contrast genders explicitly (e.g. 'un garçon ou une fille' = a boy or a girl). Beginners should not use 'garçon ou une' as-is.
target_language_example: Un garçon ou une fille ?
native_language_example: A boy or a girl?

meaning: the boy (subject) + reflexive marker 'se' used with a reflexive verb (e.g. 'the boy (himself) ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words together: 'garçon' (boy) and the reflexive pronoun 'se' used before a reflexive verb (se déshabiller, se noyer, se perdre, se promener). In sentences the verb follows 'se' and agrees with the subject. For a female subject use 'fille' instead of 'garçon'. In spoken French 'se' can contract in certain tenses (e.g. il s'est).
target_language_example: Le garçon se lave les mains.
native_language_example: The boy washes his hands.

meaning: 'parked there' (appearance of the past participle 'garé' before the feminine definite article 'la' when the participle and article appear adjacently in a phrase — see notes).
additional_notes: 'Garé' is the past participle of garer (to park). When used as an adjective it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: garé (m. sing.), garée (f. sing.), garés (m. pl.), garées (f. pl.). The exact sequence 'garé la' can occur in spoken or written French when word order or punctuation brings the past participle directly before the feminine article (for example in a reduced clause or after a pause): e.g. 'La moto, garé la, est à réparer.' (colloquial/marked). More standard phrasing places the participle after the noun: 'la voiture garée là'. Note that 'là' (there) indicates location; 'garé la' itself mixes a masculine-form participle with the feminine article and so is nonstandard or the result of elision/colloquial speech unless context forces the masculine form. Use standard agreement (garée la) for grammatically correct feminine nouns.
target_language_example: La moto, garé la, n’a plus de frein.
native_language_example: The motorcycle, parked there, no longer has any brakes.

meaning: 'to the left at' or 'left onto' (used when indicating a left turn onto or at a specific place)
additional_notes: Used in directions: 'gauche au' typically appears where 'gauche' (left) is followed by a preposition+article like 'au' to indicate location ('à' + 'le'). Less common as a standalone phrase; more idiomatic alternatives include 'tournez à gauche' or 'à gauche, au/à la/aux + [lieu]'. Contexts: 'gauche au prochain feu' = 'left at the next light' or 'gauche au carrefour' = 'left at the junction.'
target_language_example: Tournez gauche au prochain feu.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next traffic light.

meaning: a colloquial filler meaning 'like' or 'kind of' used before verbs or clauses to soften/hedge what you say.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Often used the same way as 'genre' alone or 'comme' to introduce an example, rephrase or hesitation. Common structures: 'genre + [clause]' (e.g. 'Genre, j'étais en retard.') or 'genre à + infinitive' (used less frequently) — more typical is 'genre + que' or 'genre + verb'. Avoid in formal writing. Tone: casual, conversational; can signal approximation, hesitation or an example.
target_language_example: Il m'a dit ça, genre à me faire culpabiliser.
native_language_example: He told me that, like trying to make me feel guilty.

meaning: 'people at' or 'people in/with' (a fragment; not a complete fixed phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression in French. 'Gens' means 'people' and is often followed by a preposition + article (e.g. 'gens au', 'gens à la', 'gens du') when specifying location, context, or possession. 'Au' is the contraction of 'à le' (to/at the/of the). You will usually see 'gens au' as part of a larger phrase like 'des gens au travail' (people at work) or 'des gens au pouvoir' (people in power). For correct grammar, 'des gens' (some people) is common; 'les gens au...' or 'des gens au...' are typical structures.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens au marché aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are people at the market today.

meaning: 'people with' (used to describe people who have or share something)
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun or a relative clause (e.g., gens avec des enfants; gens avec qui je travaille). 'Gens' is plural and informal to neutral; use 'les gens' for 'the people'. In many contexts you may need a preposition or article after 'avec' (avec des, avec le/la, avec qui).
target_language_example: Des gens avec des chiens se sont rassemblés au parc.
native_language_example: People with dogs gathered in the park.

meaning: people in / people who are in (a place or group)
additional_notes: Used to refer to people located inside or belonging to a specific place, area, group or context. 'Gens' is a plural noun (informal alternative to 'personnes'); 'dans' means 'in' and is followed by a location or group (la vallée, le monde, la maison, cette salle). Word order: 'gens dans + [place]'. Can be replaced by 'personnes dans' for a more formal tone.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de gens dans le parc aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the park today.

meaning: used to describe people characterized by something (people who are ...).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of a longer phrase: "des gens en colère" (people who are angry), "des gens en retard" (people who are late). "Gens" means "people"; "en" links to an adjective or noun phrase that follows and describes their state or condition. In many cases you will see articles or adjectives around it (des gens en bonne santé). Informal and neutral contexts; word order and agreement follow normal French rules.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens en colère dans la rue.
native_language_example: There are people who are angry in the street.

meaning: 'people and' — a fragment, not a complete phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression in French. "Gens" means "people" and "et" means "and". You will normally see "gens et" only as part of a longer phrase (e.g. "gens et choses", "gens et familles") or in lists ("les gens et les animaux"). Alone it is incomplete and should be followed by another word or phrase. "Gens" is invariable in form (use "des gens", "quelques gens").
target_language_example: Des gens et des animaux traversaient le village.
native_language_example: People and animals were crossing the village.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French sequence — likely a typo or non-native construction. 'Gens' means 'people' and must be used with appropriate articles or relative pronouns; 'me' is an object pronoun meaning 'me'. Together 'gens me' does not form a correct phrase in French.
additional_notes: 'gens' normally appears as 'des gens', 'les gens', or followed by 'qui'/'de' etc. The object pronoun 'me' follows a verb (e.g. 'ils me voient'). If you intended to say 'people who ... me' use 'des gens qui me ...' (e.g. 'des gens qui me comprennent'). If you meant 'they (people) me' you need a verb and subject pronoun (e.g. 'ils me...' or 'les gens me...'+verb). The sequence 'gens me' on its own is ungrammatical and likely a typing mistake.
target_language_example: Des gens qui me comprennent m'aident.
native_language_example: People who understand me help me.

meaning: This sequence by itself is not a standard French phrase; 'gens' means 'people' and 'ne' is the first part of negation (usually paired with 'pas', 'plus', 'jamais', etc.).
additional_notes: You will not see 'gens ne' alone in correct modern French. 'Gens' (people) is a plural noun that normally appears with verbs or adjectives: e.g. 'Les gens sont contents.' Negation in French is typically formed with 'ne ... pas' (or other second particles) around the verb: e.g. 'Les gens ne comprennent pas.' If you encounter 'gens ne' in older texts, poetry, or incorrectly written sentences, it's likely an incomplete negation where the second negation word is missing or placed elsewhere. Remember to place 'ne' before the conjugated verb and the negative partner (pas, plus, jamais, etc.) after it.
target_language_example: Les gens ne savent pas toujours quoi dire.
native_language_example: People do not always know what to say.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French multiword phrase; likely a word order mistake or truncation. It does not occur as a fixed expression in French.
additional_notes:
Possible intended corrections depending on context:
- 'les gens' = 'people' (general noun).
- 'nous, les gens...' = 'we, the people...' (requires 'les').
- 'les gens nous...' as part of a clause: e.g. 'Les gens nous aident' = 'People help us.'
- 'gens qui nous...' for relative clauses: 'les gens qui nous aiment' = 'the people who love us.'
If you see 'gens nous' in a text, check for missing articles or verbs; it is not correct as written.
target_language_example: Les gens nous regardent quand nous passons.
native_language_example: People watch us when we walk by.

meaning: 'people that you' (used to introduce a clause about people related to 'you').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a fragment combining gens (people) + relative clause introduced by que + the subject tu. It appears in sentences like «les gens que tu connais» = 'the people that you know'. Use with determiners (les, tous, ces, etc.) and appropriate verb forms after 'tu'. In spoken French you may also hear «les gens qu'tu...» with elision.
target_language_example: Ce sont les gens que tu connais depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: These are the people that you have known for a long time.

meaning: 'people who' or 'people that'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people characterized by what follows (a clause). Often appears in spoken French as part of phrases like "les gens que" or "des gens qui/que"; note that "qui" is more common as the relative pronoun for people when it is the subject of the clause (les gens qui habitent ici). "Que" is used when the people are the direct object of the verb in the relative clause (les gens que j'ai rencontrés).
target_language_example: Ce sont des gens que j'admire beaucoup.
native_language_example: These are people that I admire a lot.

meaning: Not a complete fixed phrase on its own; looks like part of a sentence meaning 'people are in/doing (something)'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'Gens' means 'people' (often preceded by 'les' or another determiner: 'les gens'), 'sont' is the third-person plural of 'être' ('are'), and 'en' is a preposition/pronominal particle with several uses (in, of it/them, about it, in/at). Together 'les gens sont en...' appears when describing how people are (e.g., 'les gens sont en colère' = 'people are angry') or where/what state they are in (e.g., 'les gens sont en ville' = 'people are in town', or 'les gens sont en train de...' = 'people are in the process of...'). Make sure to include the definite article 'les' or another determiner in normal speech: 'gens sont en' by itself is incomplete.
target_language_example: Les gens sont en colère contre la décision.
native_language_example: People are angry about the decision.

meaning: people are (in the process of) ...
additional_notes: This is part of the progressive construction 'les/des gens sont en train de + infinitive' used to say that people are currently doing something. Use 'les gens' (the people) or 'des gens' (some people). You can omit 'en train' and still be correct ('les gens jouent'), but 'être en train de' emphasizes the action is happening right now.
target_language_example: Des gens sont en train de préparer le repas.
native_language_example: Some people are preparing the meal right now.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; likely a typo, mishearing, or mis-segmentation of other words (for example 'gens de', 'je t' + verb, or dialectal/phonetic forms).
additional_notes:
The sequence 'gens te' does not occur as a valid multi-word unit in standard French. Possible explanations:
- Typo for 'gens de' (people of) as in 'les gens de la ville'.
- Mis-segmentation where 'te' belongs to a nearby verb (e.g. 'je te' + verb) or a contraction like 't'en'.
- A transcription of spoken French where liaison or elision created ambiguous spacing.
If you provide the original sentence or context, a correct reconstruction and translation can be given.
target_language_example: (This exact sequence is ungrammatical; shown here only as requested) Les gens te regardent, mais la phrase est incorrecte.
native_language_example: The people watch you, but the sentence is incorrect.

meaning: 'people who' (used before a relative clause or infinitive phrase to describe a group of people with a characteristic or activity)
additional_notes: Used in expressions like "des gens à qui parler" or "des gens à aider". Often appears as "des gens à + infinitive" or "des gens à + qui/que" to specify people suitable for or in need of something. It requires a determiner (e.g., des, les, ces) before "gens": "des gens à inviter", "les gens à qui je pense". Not a fixed idiom by itself—it’s compositional and depends on the following words to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Je cherche des gens à aider ce week-end.
native_language_example: I'm looking for people to help this weekend.

meaning: kind/nice of you (to ...).
additional_notes: Used to thank or compliment someone's action; often appears as « gentil de votre part » (lit. 'kind of your part'). Followed by an infinitive or just used alone. Polite/formal phrasing (vous form). In spoken French you may also hear the shorter « gentil de ta part » (informal).
target_language_example: C'est vraiment gentil de votre part de m'avoir aidé.
native_language_example: It's really kind of you to have helped me.

meaning: life jacket; personal flotation device worn to keep someone afloat in water.
additional_notes: Used for safety on boats, during water sports, or in emergencies. Can be mandatory by law in many situations. Plural: gilets de sauvetage. Synonym often simply gilet (in nautical context) or gilet de flottaison.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas ton gilet de sauvetage avant de monter à bord.
native_language_example: Don't forget your life jacket before boarding.

meaning: literally 'life jackets of' or '... life jackets' (part of the phrase 'gilets de sauvetage' = life jackets).
additional_notes: This phrase by itself is incomplete; it's typically followed by a noun (most commonly 'sauvetage' to form 'gilets de sauvetage' = life jackets). Used in safety contexts (boats, planes). In French you generally say 'gilet(s) de sauvetage' (singular/plural) or simply 'gilet(s)' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Vérifiez où sont les gilets de sauvetage avant de partir.
native_language_example: Check where the life jackets are before leaving.

meaning: 'the ice is' — simple present phrase used to describe the state or quality of ice (or ice cream in some contexts).
additional_notes: glace = 'ice' or 'ice cream' depending on context. When followed by est (3rd person singular of être) it describes the condition of the ice/ice cream (e.g., safety, firmness, taste). Pay attention to context: 'la glace est solide' (the ice is solid — frozen water) vs 'cette glace est bonne' (this ice cream is good).
target_language_example: La glace est encore gelée, attends avant de marcher dessus.
native_language_example: The ice is still frozen, wait before walking on it.

meaning: 'government of' or 'the government of (something/someone)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate which government you mean (e.g. government of a country, region, or a particular leader). Typically followed by a noun: gouvernement de la France, gouvernement du Québec, gouvernement de coalition. In English you often translate it as 'the government of ...' or simply '... government' (e.g. the French government).
target_language_example: Le gouvernement de la France a annoncé de nouvelles mesures.
native_language_example: The government of France announced new measures.

meaning: This exact sequence is not a set phrase in French; it's simply the noun 'goût' (taste) followed by the verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: You will not find 'goût est' as an independent expression. It appears when describing something about taste: e.g. 'Le goût est sucré' (The taste is sweet) or in clauses like 'Le goût, c'est...' (As for the taste, it is...). For beginners it's more useful to learn 'le goût' (taste) and basic copula sentences with 'est' (is).
target_language_example: Le goût est trop salé pour moi.
native_language_example: The taste is too salty for me.

meaning: not much / little (of importance or quantity)
additional_notes: Used mostly in negative or limiting contexts (often after ne... pas or alone as a short reply) to mean 'not much' or 'not very useful'. Common in spoken French. It can refer to quantity ('there isn't much left') or significance/usefulness ('it doesn't help much'). Often appears as 'pas grand-chose' or without 'pas' in casual replies.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas grand-chose dans le frigo.
native_language_example: I don't have much in the fridge.

meaning: literally 'big of' — not a standalone phrase; appears as part of expressions like 'grand de quelque chose' (meaning 'tall/large for' or 'big compared to') or in fixed expressions (e.g. 'grand de taille').
additional_notes: On its own, 'grand de' is incomplete. 'Grand' is an adjective meaning 'big, tall, great' and is often followed by a noun or a prepositional phrase. When you see 'de' after 'grand' it usually introduces a comparison, a measure, origin, or a complement (e.g. 'grand de taille', 'grand de ce pays', or in constructions like 'il est grand de coeur'—poetic). For beginner learners, learn complete expressions instead (e.g. 'grand pour son âge' = 'big/ tall for his age').
target_language_example: Il est grand pour son âge, pas « grand de » tout seul.
native_language_example: He is tall for his age, not 'grand de' by itself.

meaning: 'big day' — an important or special day (e.g., wedding, graduation, major event).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a significant, often anticipated occasion. Can be general ('C'est un grand jour') or specific ('le grand jour est arrivé'). Equivalent to English "the big day." Tone is neutral; suitable in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Le grand jour approche : je me marie la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: The big day is coming: I'm getting married next week.

meaning: a big/important day for (someone or something)
additional_notes: Used to say that a particular day is important, memorable or significant for a person, group, or event. Often follows the noun or pronoun it refers to: 'C'est un grand jour pour elle.' Can be used for celebrations, milestones, firsts, or major changes.
target_language_example: C'est un grand jour pour notre équipe.
native_language_example: This is a big day for our team.

meaning: a large book; literally 'big book'.
additional_notes: Common, literal phrase used to describe the physical size of a book (big/tall). Not an idiom here. Context determines meaning — could also refer to an important ledger/accounting book in specific contexts (e.g., 'le grand livre' in accounting), but in these example sentences it simply describes size.
target_language_example: Il y a un grand livre sur la table.
native_language_example: There is a large book on the table.

meaning: 'department store' — a large shop selling many different kinds of goods.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for big, multi-department retail stores (like Macy's or Galeries Lafayette). Used with definite/indefinite articles (le grand magasin, un grand magasin). Can also refer to the food court or restaurant area inside (On mangera au grand magasin = We'll eat at the department store).
target_language_example: Je vais au grand magasin pour acheter un manteau.
native_language_example: I'm going to the department store to buy a coat.

meaning: a big thank you; many thanks
additional_notes: An informal/friendly way to express strong gratitude. Often used alone ('Grand merci !') or before/after a brief reason: 'Grand merci pour ton aide.' Slightly more emphatic than 'merci' but less formal than 'merci beaucoup.'
target_language_example: Grand merci pour ton aide aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: A big thank you for your help today.

meaning: wide open; fully open (often describing a door, window, or space).
additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase. Commonly placed after the noun (e.g. la porte grand ouverte), though in everyday speech people also say 'grandes ouvertes' when plural. It emphasizes that something is completely open. Not idiomatic — means exactly what the words suggest.
target_language_example: La fenêtre est grand ouverte pour laisser entrer l'air.
native_language_example: The window is wide open to let the air in.

meaning: too big/large for (something or someone); 'big enough for' in some contexts.
additional_notes: Used with 'pour' + person or purpose/place to say something is too large or (with modifiers like 'assez' or context) large enough. Common in descriptions of clothing, objects, or size relative to a person/age. Word order: adjective 'grand' before 'pour' phrase (grand pour + noun/pronoun).
target_language_example: Ce manteau est trop grand pour moi.
native_language_example: This coat is too big for me.

meaning: not standard on its own; appears as part of a comparative phrase meaning 'bigger/more than the...'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a complete fixed expression by itself. It's part of comparative structures using 'plus grand que les...' (more/bigger than the...) or 'plus grand que' followed by a plural noun (les = the). Alone 'grand que les' is ungrammatical; learners should use 'plus grand que les...' or 'aussi grand que les...' depending on the comparison. Example patterns: 'plus grand que les autres' (bigger than the others), 'plus grand que les enfants' (taller than the children).
target_language_example: Mon sac est plus grand que les leurs.
native_language_example: My bag is bigger than theirs.

meaning: 'about time' or 'it's high time' (used to say something should happen soon or finally happen)
additional_notes: Often used impersonally with il est grand temps de + infinitive (Il est grand temps de partir = It's about time to leave / We should leave now). Conveys urgency or that something is overdue. Not literal (doesn't refer to weather or big time).
target_language_example: Il est grand temps de finir ce projet.
native_language_example: It's about time to finish this project.

meaning: 'it's high time' / 'it's about time' (used to say something should happen now)
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive in French (e.g. que + subjunctive). Expresses that something is overdue and should happen immediately. Polite or neutral; can be used in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il est grand temps que tu arrêtes de fumer.
native_language_example: It's high time you stopped smoking.

meaning: 'big screen' — the cinema/movie screen; used to refer to movies or appearing in films.
additional_notes: Refers to cinema/theatrical films as opposed to TV or small screens. Common phrases: 'sur le grand écran' or simply 'sur grand écran' (without article) to mean 'in cinemas' or 'on the big screen.' Can also mean 'to appear in a movie' (e.g., become a film star).
target_language_example: Elle rêvait de jouer un rôle sur le grand écran.
native_language_example: She dreamed of playing a role on the big screen.

meaning: grandmother is / grandmother has (followed by an adjective or past participle).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'grand-mère' (grandmother) plus the verb 'être' (to be) in the present tense. It appears before adjectives (e.g. 'devenue vieille' — has become old) or past participles used in passive or perfect senses (e.g. 'décédée' — has died). In English you may need to translate as 'my/our grandmother is…', 'has…', or 'died' depending on context. Add a possessive (ma, notre) when specifying which grandmother.
target_language_example: Ma grand-mère est décédée hier soir.
native_language_example: My grandmother died last night.

meaning: 'grandfather is' or 'my/your/his/her grandfather is/was' (subject + verb form)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun 'grand-père' (grandfather) followed by the verb 'être' (to be). In examples it appears with third-person singular 'est' (present) to say where someone is, what happened (with past participle or context), or to introduce information about the grandfather. For past events speakers often use 'est mort' (has died) or 'est venu' (has come) — note French sometimes uses passé composé (il est venu, il est mort) formed with être for certain verbs. Replace 'grand-père' with a possessive to specify whose grandfather (mon, ton, son, etc.).
target_language_example: Mon grand-père est vétérinaire.
native_language_example: My grandfather is a veterinarian.

meaning: a loudmouth; someone who talks too much or speaks bluntly.
additional_notes: Informal and somewhat rude. Literally 'big mouth' (gueule = mouth, often coarse). Used to describe a person who boasts, interrupts, or speaks loudly and offensively. Can be directed at someone (insult) or used descriptively.
target_language_example: Il est toujours en train de parler — c’est une vraie grande gueule.
native_language_example: He's always talking — he's a real loudmouth.

meaning: an adult; a grown-up (literally 'big person')
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to an adult or someone mature. Can be used literally to mean a tall/large person (see examples 1–2) or figuratively to mean an adult/grown-up (examples 3–5). Context tells which meaning is intended. Polite/formal when addressing adults as 'Vous êtes une grande personne.'
target_language_example: Je suis une grande personne maintenant.
native_language_example: I am a grown-up now.

meaning: ‘bigger than that one’ (feminine singular comparison using a pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to compare feminine nouns. 'Plus grande que celle...' means 'larger/bigger than that one' — 'celle' is a feminine demonstrative pronoun replacing a previously mentioned noun (celle-ci / celle-là). If the noun is masculine use 'celui'; for plural use 'ceux' or 'celles'. Commonly appears as 'plus grande que celle-ci' (than this one) or 'plus grande que celle-là' (than that one).
target_language_example: Sa valise est plus grande que celle de Marie.
native_language_example: Her suitcase is bigger than Marie's.

meaning: 'Ferris wheel' (large amusement-park wheel with passenger cabins).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to the large rotating wheel at fairs, amusement parks or city attractions. Masculine noun phrase (la grande roue is standard). Can be used literally (the ride) or in contexts like videos/photos of it.
target_language_example: Nous avons pris des photos depuis la grande roue.
native_language_example: We took photos from the Ferris wheel.

meaning: Ancient Greek (the classical language of Greece).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical form of the Greek language used in antiquity (Homer, classical Athens). Often appears as a school subject (faire/étudier le grec ancien). Not to be confused with 'grec moderne' (Modern Greek).
target_language_example: Elle étudie le grec ancien à l'université.
native_language_example: She studies Ancient Greek at university.

meaning: good common sense; practical sense or sound judgment.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's practical intelligence or a simple, sensible approach to problems. Often applied to people or decisions that are down-to-earth and pragmatic. Similar to English 'common sense' or 'good sense' but with an emphasis on robustness ('gros' = big/strong). Not slang; can modify personne (un homme de gros bon sens) or action (une décision de gros bon sens).
target_language_example: C'est une femme de gros bon sens; elle sait prendre des décisions sensées.
native_language_example: She has good common sense; she knows how to make sensible decisions.

meaning: 'big arms' literally; informally 'muscular guy' or 'tough guy' (can be used mockingly or to address/describe someone strong or a bully)
additional_notes: Can be literal (Tom a de gros bras = Tom has big/strong arms) or idiomatic/informal when used to call someone 'tough guy' or 'muscle' (often teasing or critical: « Hé, les gros bras ! »). Tone depends on context — can be playful, admiring, or sarcastic. Masculine plural form often used vocatively.
target_language_example: Arrête de jouer les gros bras, on n'a pas besoin de toi.
native_language_example: Stop acting like a tough guy, we don't need you.

meaning: big/large dog
additional_notes: Simple adjective + noun: gros modifies chien to mean physically large (can also imply 'fat' in some contexts). Used in everyday speech. Agreement: gros (m./sing.) becomes grosse for feminine (une grosse chienne).
target_language_example: Le gros chien dort dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The big dog is sleeping in the garden.

meaning: 'the jackpot' or 'the big prize' (the main prize in a lottery/contest).
additional_notes: Used to talk about winning the biggest prize (lottery, raffle, game, promotion). Can be literal (a large prize) or figurative (hitting a major success). Common expression: 'tirer le gros lot' = to win the jackpot.
target_language_example: Ils ont tiré le gros lot au tirage au sort hier.
native_language_example: They won the jackpot in yesterday's draw.

meaning: 'swear word' or 'bad word'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to rude, offensive, or taboo words (vulgar language). Often used in plural (des gros mots). Can be used euphemistically when avoiding saying the actual word. Common in everyday speech and in conversations about language with children.
target_language_example: Ne dis pas de gros mots devant les enfants.
native_language_example: Don't say swear words in front of the children.

meaning: big toe.
additional_notes: Refers specifically to the largest toe on the foot (the one next to the foot's inner edge). Common in medical or everyday contexts (moving, injury, pain). Pronunciation tip: 'gros' sounds like /ɡʁo/ and 'orteil' like /ɔʁ.tɛj/.
target_language_example: Je me suis cogné le gros orteil contre la table.
native_language_example: I stubbed my big toe on the table.

meaning: 'big fish' — literally a large fish; idiomatically: an important person / big catch or a big problem/opportunity.
additional_notes: Usually literal when talking about fishing or size (un gros poisson = a large fish). Can be used figuratively to mean an important person, a major catch (e.g., in crime or business), or a bigger issue/opportunity (similar to 'a bigger fish to fry'). Context tells whether it's literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Nous devons attraper ce gros poisson avant la fin de la journée.
native_language_example: We need to catch that big fish before the end of the day.

meaning: insult meaning 'big lump' used like 'fat/huge slob' or 'idiot/jerk' (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive. Literally 'big pile' or 'big lump', but used as an insult similar to 'you big oaf' or stronger 'you piece of shit' depending on context. Often combined with 'de merde' to be more insulting. Use only in strong informal contexts (angry speech) — avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ne m'appelle pas gros tas de merde !
native_language_example: Don't call me you big piece of shit!

meaning: headline (a big, prominent title on a page or article).
additional_notes: Used for the main, attention-grabbing title of a newspaper article, web article, poster, etc. Can also mean a large-font title in design/layout. Not idiomatic — literal use of gros (big) + titre (title).
target_language_example: Le gros titre du journal parlait de la grève.
native_language_example: The newspaper's headline was about the strike.

meaning: insult: 'big cow' used to call someone stupid, mean, or nasty.
additional_notes: A rude, offensive expression in French. Literally means "big/ fat cow," but used as an insult toward a person (often implying cruelty, clumsiness, or unpleasantness). Can be shouted or said angrily. Avoid using in polite company; it can be strong, especially toward women. Tone and context determine severity; in casual teasing among friends it may be less harsh, but generally not appropriate for formal situations or with strangers.
target_language_example: Ne l'appelle pas une grosse vache, ce n'est pas gentil.
native_language_example: Don't call her a 'big cow,' that's not nice.

meaning: blood type (blood group).
additional_notes: Refers to a person's blood classification (A, B, AB, O and Rh factor: positif/négatif). Commonly used in medical contexts and when donating/receiving blood. You can answer with e.g. "A positif" / "O négatif" or ask "Quel est votre groupe sanguin ?"
target_language_example: Mon groupe sanguin est O négatif.
native_language_example: My blood type is O negative.

meaning: because of; thanks to (used to indicate cause or positive reason).
additional_notes: Used to attribute a cause or reason, often with a positive connotation (something good happened). Followed by a noun or pronoun. Can be used neutrally but usually implies gratitude or a beneficial cause. For negative causes, French prefers 'à cause de'.
target_language_example: J'ai réussi l'examen grâce à mes révisions.
native_language_example: I passed the exam thanks to my studying.

meaning: 'war on' or 'campaign against' (indicates a struggle, campaign or policy directed at something)
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate a fight, campaign or policy targeting that noun (e.g. 'la guerre à la drogue' = 'the war on drugs'). Often appears alongside 'guerre contre' — 'contre' is more literal while 'à' is common in set phrases and headlines. Typically followed by a definite article or noun phrase; note the accent on 'à'.
target_language_example: Le titre du journal parlait d'une guerre à la pollution.
native_language_example: The newspaper headline spoke of a war on pollution.

meaning: civil war — an armed conflict within a single country between organized groups or factions.
additional_notes: Used to describe internal wars (historical or fictional) inside a state, region, organization, or even metaphorically in smaller groups. Can refer to well-known events (e.g., la guerre civile américaine) or imagined/conflictual situations (e.g., within a community, section, or 'empire' in fiction).
target_language_example: La guerre civile a duré plusieurs années et a dévasté le pays.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years and devastated the country.

meaning: 'war of' or 'war for' — used to form phrases describing a specific kind of war or conflict (e.g. guerre de Sécession, guerre de religion).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of a compound noun meaning 'war of/for ...'. It is followed by a noun or noun phrase that specifies the cause, place, period, or type of the war. Agreement and articles may appear after it (la guerre de l'information, la guerre du Vietnam).
target_language_example: La guerre de Sécession a marqué l'histoire des États-Unis.
native_language_example: The Civil War marked United States history.

meaning: the Vietnam War (the armed conflict in Vietnam, mainly 1955–1975).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical war in Vietnam. Capitalization: in French it's usually written 'guerre du Vietnam' (only 'Vietnam' capitalized). Common in contexts about history, politics, veterans, protests. Can be used with verbs like 'être opposé à', 'mourir pendant', 'manifester contre'.
target_language_example: Il a étudié la guerre du Vietnam en cours d'histoire.
native_language_example: He studied the Vietnam War in history class.

meaning: 'hangover' (after drinking too much alcohol).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Literally 'mouth of wood' but means the physical symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue) after excessive drinking. Common in spoken French: J'ai la gueule de bois = I'm hungover. Use in casual contexts; avoid in very formal writing.
target_language_example: Après la fête, il avait la gueule de bois toute la journée.
native_language_example: After the party, he was hungover all day.

meaning: tour guide; a person who leads and informs tourists.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (job/profession) who shows visitors around sights and provides information. Can be used with articles and job titles: 'être guide touristique' (to be a tour guide) or 'un/une guide touristique'.
target_language_example: Il travaille comme guide touristique à Paris.
native_language_example: He works as a tour guide in Paris.

meaning: as a / in the form of (used to indicate purpose or role — often in the fixed expression 'à la guise de' or influenced by 'en guise de')
additional_notes: Rare on its own; usually appears in the expression 'en guise de' meaning 'as' or 'in place of'. Used to say something is serving as or acting like something else (e.g., 'en guise de réponse' = 'as a response'). Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a utilisé un vieux cahier en guise de carnet.
native_language_example: He used an old notebook as a notebook / as a makeshift notebook.

meaning: 'cake with' (used before a flavor or ingredient, e.g. gâteau au chocolat = chocolate cake).
additional_notes: Used to describe the main flavor or ingredient of a cake. Follows gâteau (masculine) so au = à + le. For plural or feminine ingredients the form changes (gâteau à la, gâteau aux). Common collocations: gâteau au chocolat, gâteau au citron, gâteau aux pommes.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un gâteau au citron pour l'anniversaire.
native_language_example: I would like a lemon cake for the birthday.

meaning: 'cake of' or 'cake made with/containing' — used to specify the type or main ingredient/flavor of a cake (e.g. gâteau de chocolat = chocolate cake).
additional_notes: This is a common construction where 'gâteau' (cake) is followed by 'de' and a noun to indicate flavor, filling, or what the cake is made from. You will often see forms like 'gâteau au chocolat' (more idiomatic for chocolate cake), 'gâteau de pommes' (apple cake) or 'gâteau de mariage' (wedding cake). Use 'au/aux' when referring to a flavored cake (au chocolat, aux noix) and 'de' when indicating composition, origin, or a descriptive noun (gâteau de mariage, gâteau de riz).
target_language_example: J'ai préparé un gâteau de pommes pour le dessert.
native_language_example: I made an apple cake for dessert.

meaning: cake for (someone or something); indicates the recipient or purpose of a cake.
additional_notes: Combine gâteau (cake) with pour + noun/pronoun to say who the cake is for or its occasion (e.g., gâteau pour Marie, gâteau pour l'anniversaire). Common in everyday speech and formal contexts. Remember to include the appropriate article or name after pour: "un gâteau pour toi", "un gâteau pour mon père".
target_language_example: J'ai acheté un gâteau pour ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: I bought a cake for your birthday.

meaning: a genius at / great skill in (someone who is exceptionally good at something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has exceptional talent or knack for a particular area. Typically followed by a noun (génie de la cuisine) or an infinitive/activity (génie pour résoudre des problèmes). Often used in praise. 'Génie' is a noun; the preposition 'de' links the talent to the field.
target_language_example: C'est un génie de la photographie.
native_language_example: He's a genius at photography.

meaning: kind/generous of (someone) to do something — used to comment on someone's generosity.
additional_notes: Typically appears in the fixed expression "C'est [très] généreux de + (pronoun/noun) + part" or "de votre/sa part." It literally points out that an action or offer is generous coming from that person. Common in polite responses to offers or compliments. Use the appropriate pronoun (ma part, ta part, sa part, votre part) to indicate whose generosity you mean.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment généreux de votre part de m'aider.
native_language_example: It's really generous of you to help me.

meaning: lives just/only a short distance away (at/from).
additional_notes: Used with a person or place: 'Il/Elle habite juste à...' + location (often followed by a street name, neighbourhood, town, or distance). 'Juste' here emphasizes that the place is very close or only a small distance away. Can be followed by 'côté', 'coin', a preposition (e.g. 'à côté de', 'à 5 minutes'), or a specific address.
target_language_example: Elle habite juste à côté, on peut y aller à pied.
native_language_example: She lives just next door; we can walk there.

meaning: usually the / typically the
additional_notes: Habituellement means 'usually' or 'normally'. Paired with the definite article le, it will be followed by a masculine singular noun or a time expression (e.g. habituellement le lundi = usually on Mondays). Common in statements about routines or what normally happens. Word order is adverb + article + noun/time.
target_language_example: Habituellement le dimanche, nous allons au marché.
native_language_example: Usually on Sundays, we go to the market.

meaning: to shrug (one's shoulders); indicate indifference, uncertainty, or lack of an answer.
additional_notes: Used to describe the gesture of raising the shoulders. Often used literally (Il a haussé les épaules) or figuratively to indicate not knowing or not caring. Common in descriptions and spoken replies. The reflexive form se hausser les épaules is uncommon; typically use hauser les épaules with a subject.
target_language_example: Il a haussé les épaules quand je lui ai demandé, en haussant les épaules.
native_language_example: When I asked him, he shrugged his shoulders.

meaning: high-end; top quality; premium.
additional_notes: Used to describe products, services or places that are of superior quality or luxury (hotels, restaurants, goods). Often placed after the noun (un hôtel haut de gamme) but can appear alone as a label. Not slang.
target_language_example: Nous avons choisi un restaurant haut de gamme pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We chose a high-end restaurant for his birthday.

meaning: top of / upper part of (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate the upper part or top of something (e.g. 'le haut de la page' = the top of the page). Often appears in fixed phrases like 'haut de gamme' (high-end) or 'haut de la robe'. 'Haut' here is a noun/adjective; word order and articles may change (le haut de, le haut du).
target_language_example: Regarde en haut de l'étagère.
native_language_example: Look at the top of the shelf.

meaning: the top of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used as part of a noun phrase to indicate the upper part or top surface of something whose noun is feminine (e.g. la table → le haut de la table). Often followed immediately by a feminine noun. For masculine nouns you would use "haut du" (contraction of "de le").
target_language_example: Le chat est assis sur le haut de la chaise.
native_language_example: The cat is sitting on the top of the chair.

meaning: 'haut et' by itself is not a fixed phrase in French; it usually appears as part of longer expressions (e.g. 'haut et fort') meaning 'loudly' or 'clearly'.
additional_notes: As written, 'haut et' is incomplete. You will see 'haut et fort' (literally 'high and strong') meaning 'out loud', 'loudly' or 'clearly' (e.g. 'dire quelque chose haut et fort' = 'say something out loud and clearly'). Context matters: don't use 'haut et' alone. Other compounds: 'haut et court' (less common) or adjectives joined by 'et' follow the same pattern.
target_language_example: Il a dit son opinion haut et fort.
native_language_example: He said his opinion out loud and clearly.

meaning: high-ranking; well-placed (influence or position).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who holds a high position or has strong influence (e.g., a senior official, executive, or someone with connections). Often appears after a noun: un fonctionnaire haut placé, une source haut placée. Agreement: when used as an adjective before a noun it follows normal gender/number rules (haut placé → haute placée, hauts placés, hautes placées).
target_language_example: Il a obtenu des informations auprès d'une source haut placée.
native_language_example: He obtained information from a high-ranking source.

meaning: aloud; in a loud voice (spoken out loud).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is spoken so others can hear (e.g., reading, declaring, speaking up). Often appears as 'à haute voix' meaning 'out loud'. Without 'à' it can still describe tone (a 'haute voix'—a loud voice) but the common expression is 'à haute voix'.
target_language_example: Elle lit le poème à haute voix.
native_language_example: She reads the poem aloud.

meaning: 'ups and downs' — good and bad moments or fluctuations.
additional_notes: Used to describe variable situations, relationships, moods, or fortunes. More common form in French is "des hauts et des bas" or simply "hauts et bas" (without "des" before the first word). Can be used in both personal and general contexts.
target_language_example: Notre relation a connu des hauts et des bas, mais nous sommes toujours ensemble.
native_language_example: Our relationship has had its ups and downs, but we're still together.

meaning: literally 'hour arrives' — not a standard fixed French phrase; likely a mistaken or truncated form. Could be part of expressions like «l'heure arrive» ('the time/moment is coming') or an incorrect omission of the article/auxiliary.
additional_notes: As written, 'heure arrive' is grammatically incomplete in French. Use a full form such as «l'heure arrive» (poetic/informal) or «l'heure est arrivée» / «le moment est arrivé» for clarity. 'Heure arrive' might appear in notes, headlines, or telegram-style writing where articles are dropped, but it's not recommended for normal speech or writing.
target_language_example: L'heure arrive bientôt, préparez-vous.
native_language_example: The time is coming soon, get ready.

meaning: 'what time did you' (used in questions with 'à quelle' — 'À quelle heure as-tu ... ?')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the question pattern 'À quelle heure as-tu ... ?' meaning 'At what time did you ...?' It's used with the passé composé (as-tu + past participle) to ask when an action happened. Informal spoken questions may drop inversion and use 'tu as ... à quelle heure ?' instead.
target_language_example: À quelle heure as-tu acheté le billet ?
native_language_example: What time did you buy the ticket?

meaning: '(at) what time did you...?' (part of the question 'À quelle heure avez-vous...')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common question pattern 'À quelle heure avez-vous + past participle' (passé composé) to ask when someone did something in the past. Full form is 'À quelle heure avez-vous [fait X] ?' You can replace 'avez-vous' with 'as-tu' (informal singular) or 'avez-vous' stays for formal/plural. The phrase requires a verb in the past participle after it (e.g. fermé, quitté, entendu).
target_language_example: À quelle heure avez-vous mangé hier soir ?
native_language_example: What time did you eat last night?

meaning: 'hour begins' or 'the hour starts' (literal); used to indicate the beginning of a period of time or event, though in natural French it typically appears with an article or within a larger phrase.
additional_notes: This is compositional (heure + commence). On its own "heure commence" is uncommon without an article or context; native speakers usually say "l'heure commence", "Ça commence à [heure]", or "L'événement commence à [heure]". "Heure commence" might appear in telegraphic, abbreviated, or poetic contexts but is not standard as a standalone phrase in everyday speech.
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence la réunion ? — L'heure commence à neuf heures.
native_language_example: At what time does the meeting start? — The hour starts at nine o'clock.

meaning: literally 'hour begins the'; not a fixed phrase — appears as part of fuller constructions to indicate when something starts (e.g. « l'heure commence le ... » meaning 'the hour starts on/...')
additional_notes: This is not an independent, idiomatic expression in French. You will usually see it within a larger sentence such as «L'heure commence le [jour/date]» or «L'heure à laquelle cela commence le [jour]». For time use «à [heure]» (Ça commence à 19h). For day/date use «le [jour/date]» (Ça commence le lundi). Beginners should prefer full, natural phrases rather than the bare fragment.
target_language_example: L'heure commence le lundi à 19h.
native_language_example: The hour starts on Monday at 7 PM.

meaning: time to go; time to leave.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the moment when someone should or must leave (for school, work, an appointment, etc.). Often appears with possessives (mon/ton/son heure d'aller) or in questions/announcements (C'est l'heure d'aller). Common in everyday speech about schedules and routines.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure d'aller; prépare ton sac.
native_language_example: It's time to go; pack your bag.

meaning: 'time to' (do something) / 'hour of' (a period of time)
additional_notes: Used in two common patterns: 1) C'est l'heure de + infinitive/noun = 'it's time to ...' or 'it's time for ...' (e.g., C'est l'heure de partir = It's time to leave). 2) [une] heure de + noun or retard = 'one hour of ...' or 'one hour late' (e.g., une heure de retard = one hour delay/one hour late). Context determines whether it means 'time to' or 'an hour of'.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de manger; nous avons une heure de trajet.
native_language_example: It's time to eat; we have an hour of travel.

meaning: 'moment of glory' — a brief time when someone is praised, successful or in the spotlight.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short, often celebratory or triumphant period when someone receives attention or admiration. Common in informal and formal contexts. Comparable to English 'moment of glory' or 'time to shine.'
target_language_example: Allez, montre ce que tu sais — c'est ton heure de gloire !
native_language_example: Come on, show what you can do — it's your moment of glory!

meaning: 'the hour of the' or part of time expressions like 'at the time of the...'
additional_notes: This fragment appears in time or schedule phrases (heure de la réunion, heure de la classe). It must be completed by a noun; alone it is incomplete. Use 'heure de' + noun to express the time of an event. When referring to a specific clock time, use 'à' or 'il est' (e.g. 'à 14h').
target_language_example: L'heure de la réunion est vendredi à 10 h.
native_language_example: The time of the meeting is Friday at 10 a.m.

meaning: a time during the night; an hour that falls at night (e.g., 'o'clock at night').
additional_notes: Used to specify that a given hour occurs at night. Often follows a numeral (une heure de la nuit, trois heures de la nuit). Can emphasize nighttime as opposed to morning or afternoon.
target_language_example: Nous sommes à l'heure de la nuit où les rues deviennent silencieuses.
native_language_example: We are at the hour of the night when the streets become quiet.

meaning: rush hour; peak traffic time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the times of day when roads, public transport, or services are busiest (typically morning and evening commutes). Can be singular or plural: heures de pointe. Often used with aller, éviter, prendre, or être coincé dans (être coincé dans les bouchons).
target_language_example: Évite l'heure de pointe si tu peux, les trains sont toujours pleins.
native_language_example: Avoid rush hour if you can; the trains are always full.

meaning: not a standalone phrase; appears as part of expressions like "il est l'heure de se [verbe]" meaning "it's time to [verb]".
additional_notes: You will not use "heure de se" alone. It combines "il est l'heure de" (it's time to) with a reflexive verb (se réveiller, se préparer, se coucher, etc.). Structure: "Il est l'heure de se + infinitive". The reflexive pronoun stays with the infinitive (se). Common in everyday speech to tell someone it's time to do something for themselves.
target_language_example: Il est l'heure de se préparer pour l'école.
native_language_example: It's time to get ready for school.

meaning: 'what time should I' or 'at what time must I'.
additional_notes: Combines the question phrase 'À quelle heure' (at what time) with 'dois-je' (should I / must I). Used to ask when the speaker is expected to do something (arrive, be picked up, check in, etc.). In full questions include the verb or action (e.g., 'À quelle heure dois-je venir ?'). Polite and neutral register.
target_language_example: À quelle heure dois-je arriver à l'aéroport ?
native_language_example: What time should I arrive at the airport?

meaning: the time for (something); it's time to (do/eat) [masculine noun follows].
additional_notes: Used to say it's the time for a particular activity or meal. 'Heure' (feminine) + 'du' = de + le, so 'du' is used before masculine nouns (le dîner, le déjeuner, le thé, le dodo, le dessert). For feminine nouns use 'de la' (e.g. l'heure de la sieste) and for plural use 'des'. Often appears in expressions like 'C'est l'heure du + noun' or 'C'est bientôt l'heure du...'.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure du goûter.
native_language_example: It's snack time.

meaning: literally 'hour is' — the words appear in time-related constructions (e.g., in phrases like 'l'heure est venue' or 'l'heure est grave') and within the standard time-telling pattern 'il est [heure]'.
additional_notes: The two words 'heure est' do not form a standalone phrase in everyday speech; they appear together in fixed expressions (e.g., 'l'heure est grave' = 'the time is serious' / 'this is a serious moment') or as part of larger constructions. For telling the time, French uses 'il est + [heure]' (note word order differs: 'il est huit heures' rather than 'heure est huit'). Beginners should learn both the fixed expressions and the regular time structure.
target_language_example: L'heure est venue de partir.
native_language_example: The time has come to leave.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase. 'heure est le' is a fragment reflecting the words for 'hour', 'is', and the definite article 'the' but it does not occur in that order in standard French; the correct question is 'Quelle heure est‑il ?' and statements use 'Il est [heure]'.
additional_notes: 'heure est le' should not be used as written. If you want to ask the time, say 'Quelle heure est‑il ?' (formal/neutral) or 'Il est quelle heure ?' (informal). To state the time, use 'Il est + [nombre] heure(s)' (e.g. 'Il est trois heures'). The fragment could appear only inside a larger incorrect word order or transcription error.
target_language_example: (incorrect fragment) heure est le
native_language_example: (incorrect fragment) hour is the

meaning: literal connector used when telling time: 'heure et' = 'hour and' (as in 'hour and minutes').
additional_notes: Used when stating the hour followed by minutes: 'heure(s) et [minutes]'. Use 'une heure' for 1 o'clock, 'heures' for 2+. Common phrases: 'heure et quart' ( :15), 'heure et demie' ( :30), 'heure et dix' ( :10). In casual speech the 'et' may be omitted in some contexts (e.g. 'trois heures quinze'), but 'heure et' remains a standard structure. Agreement: 'une heure et' not 'une heures et'.
target_language_example: Il est une heure et quart.
native_language_example: It is one fifteen (1:15).

meaning: 'heure il' is not a standard fixed phrase in French; it is most likely a fragment resulting from word order or punctuation (for example when part of 'Quelle heure il est' or 'heure, il ...').
additional_notes: The sequence 'heure il' by itself does not form an idiomatic expression. Common correct constructions for asking/telling the time are 'Quelle heure est‑il ?' or 'Il est [heure]'. If you encounter 'heure il' in running text, it is usually due to missing punctuation or reordering (e.g., 'À cette heure, il...' or an informal inversion 'Quelle heure il est ?').
target_language_example: À cette heure il n'est plus possible de réserver.
native_language_example: At this hour it is no longer possible to make a reservation.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; likely a mistaken word order or typo (should be 'l'heure', 'à l'heure' or 'le + [day/date]').
additional_notes: 'Heure' is feminine so it contracts with 'la' to form 'l'heure'. You say 'à [heure]' or 'à + l'heure' for times (e.g. 'à 14 heures', 'à l'heure'). 'Le' is used before days or dates (e.g. 'le lundi', 'le 5 mai') but not directly before 'heure' in normal French. If you see 'heure le' in text, it's almost always an error, a typo, or the result of word reordering in speech or editing. To correct, determine whether the intended phrase was 'l'heure', 'à l'heure', or 'à + [nombre] heure(s)'.
target_language_example: Cette phrase contient une erreur : « heure le » n'est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: This sentence contains an error: "heure le" is not correct in French.

meaning: at the time when / the moment when
additional_notes: Usually appears with the definite article as « l'heure où » meaning 'the time when' or 'the moment when'. It introduces a clause that describes when something happens. Use with verbs in the following clause. In speech the elision (l') is common, but the lexeme 'heure ou' as two words can appear in exercises or quoted fragments.
target_language_example: Nous avons discuté de l'heure ou il fallait décider.
native_language_example: We discussed the time when we had to decide.

meaning: 'what time ... leaves/departs' (literally: 'what time leaves')
additional_notes: Used in questions with 'À quelle' to ask the departure time of a vehicle (train, plane, bus). The full phrase is 'À quelle heure part ... ?'. 'Part' is from the verb partir (to leave). Common in travel contexts.
target_language_example: À quelle heure part le bus pour la gare ?
native_language_example: What time does the bus to the station leave?

meaning: This sequence is not a correct or standard French phrase. It appears to be a typo or misordered words (possible intended phrases include 'à partir de (l')heure', 'heure par heure', or 'à part le ...').
additional_notes: There is no standard usage 'heure part le'. Depending on intent: use 'à partir de (heure)' to mean 'from (time)'; 'heure par heure' for 'hour by hour'; or 'à part le ...' to mean 'except the ...'. If you provide context, a correct alternative can be suggested. The example below deliberately uses the exact sequence 'heure part le' to reflect the literal (incorrect) input but is not grammatical French.
target_language_example: *heure part le* n'apparaît pas dans les dictionnaires et n'est pas une expression correcte en français.
native_language_example: '*heure part le* does not appear in dictionaries and is not a correct expression in French.'

meaning: literally 'hour for' — used to indicate the time for something (e.g. a scheduled time or duration); commonly appears in phrases like "heure pour + infinitive" or "heure pour + activity."
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's a combination of "heure" (hour/time) and the preposition "pour" (for). You'll see it in contexts like "l'heure pour partir" (the time to leave) or "une heure pour étudier" (one hour for studying). Depending on context, it can indicate a scheduled time, a deadline, or the amount of time allocated. Use gender/number as needed (une heure, des heures).
target_language_example: C'est l'heure pour partir si tu veux arriver à l'heure.
native_language_example: It's time to leave if you want to arrive on time.

meaning: literally 'hour that he/it' — a fragment used within time expressions (e.g. 'l'heure qu'il est' = 'the time it is' / 'what time it is').
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it appears inside larger expressions about time. The common full expression is 'l'heure qu'il est' meaning 'the current time' or 'what time it is'. You will also see 'l'heure qu'il était' (the time it was). Alone, 'heure qu'il' needs surrounding words to make sense.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas l'heure qu'il est.
native_language_example: I don't know what time it is.

meaning: literally 'hour that'; used in time expressions to mean 'the time when' or 'the hour at which'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; appears in phrases like 'l'heure que' or 'à l'heure que' to introduce the time something happens (similar to 'the time when' or 'at the moment that'). Often followed by a clause or a specific time. Depending on context, simpler alternatives like 'quand' (when) or 'à l'heure où' (at the time when) are more common.
target_language_example: L'heure que tu arrives, on aura déjà commencé.
native_language_example: By the time you arrive, we'll have already started.

meaning: No standard meaning — likely a typo or mishearing (probably 'heure' + pronoun or 'à l'heure').
additional_notes: The sequence 'heure te' does not form a correct French phrase. It may be the result of a typo or two words run together. Possible intended phrases: • 'à l'heure' (on time) • 'heure t.' as an abbreviation (rare) • 'heure de...' (hour of / time to...). If you can provide the original sentence or context, I can identify the correct phrase and give translations and examples.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous donner la phrase complète contenant « heure te » ?
native_language_example: Can you provide the full sentence containing 'heure te'?

meaning: Not a standard or recognized French multi-word expression; likely a typo, mishearing, or incorrectly ordered words. It has no established meaning in French.
additional_notes: Possible explanations: 1) Typo or word order error — maybe intended 'ton heure' ('your time' or 'your moment'). 2) Misheard phrase — could be part of a longer expression or names (e.g., 'heure tonique' is not standard). Without context, treat it as nonstandard. Use 'ton heure' for the meaning 'your time' or 'your moment'.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas l'expression « heure ton » dans cette phrase.
native_language_example: I don't understand the expression "heure ton" in this sentence.

meaning: "heure tu" is not a standard French phrase; likely a typo or misordering.
additional_notes:
There is no common French expression 'heure tu'. Possible intended forms:
- 'À quelle heure tu...' (informal) or 'À quelle heure...' meaning 'what time...'.
