target_language_example: Ils sont faits l'un pour l'autre.
native_language_example: They are made for each other.

meaning: the banana (fruit); also used informally to mean 'a big smile' or 'great mood' (avoir la banane = to be grinning).
additional_notes: Primary literal meaning: the fruit. Informally, French speakers say 'avoir la banane' to mean 'to have a huge grin' or to be in high spirits. Context tells which meaning applies. Use 'la banane' alone usually refers to the fruit; the idiomatic sense commonly appears in the verb phrase 'avoir la banane'.
target_language_example: Après le spectacle, il avait la banane toute la soirée.
native_language_example: After the show, he had a huge grin all evening.

meaning: the bar; can refer to a physical bar/rod, a bar in sports (e.g. high jump), or the bar as a legal profession/bench (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Common noun with several meanings depending on context. Can mean: 1) a metal rod or horizontal bar (la barre d'appui, la barre de fer), 2) a bar in gymnastics or sports (saut à la perche — la barre), 3) the legal profession or the courtroom bench (passer le barreau / être au barre), 4) figuratively a standard or threshold (fixer la barre). Articles and expressions: 'à la barre' (at the bar/in the dock or giving testimony), 'passer la barre' (get past the barrier/threshold). Gender is feminine: la barre.
target_language_example: Il a passé la barre et a réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: He passed the bar and passed the exam.

meaning: the beautiful one / the beauty (feminine); also used idiomatically to refer to a prize, the best, or a girlfriend/wife in familiar contexts.
additional_notes: Literally 'the beautiful (feminine)'. Used before a feminine noun (la belle maison = the beautiful house) or as a noun phrase meaning 'the beauty' or 'the lovely (woman)'. In informal speech it can be affectionate (La belle arrive = the lovely one is arriving) or ironic (regarding something impressive: Quelle belle idée!). Context matters: without a noun, 'la belle' usually refers to a woman or to something praised. Not a fixed idiom by itself; often part of expressions like 'la belle et le clochard' (the Beauty and the Tramp) or in titles.
target_language_example: Regarde la belle — elle porte une robe rouge.
native_language_example: Look at the beauty — she's wearing a red dress.

meaning: porridge; a soft, often mushy food made by boiling cereals or other ingredients.
additional_notes: Used for soft, easily swallowed foods (rice porridge, oatmeal, baby food). Can be savory or sweet. Often implies a smooth, mushy texture. In informal contexts, can also mean something ruined or turned into a mess (e.g., 'faire de la bouillie' = to mess up or make mush of something).
target_language_example: Chaque matin, je prépare de la bouillie d'avoine avec du miel.
native_language_example: Every morning I make oatmeal porridge with honey.

meaning: the chance/opportunity to (do something); the likelihood of
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or a noun to express having the possibility/opportunity to do something or the probability of something happening. Context determines whether it means 'opportunity' ('a chance to...') or 'probability' ('the chance of...'). Common structure: 'avoir la chance de + infinitive' (to be lucky to / have the opportunity to).
target_language_example: J'ai la chance de voyager cet été.
native_language_example: I have the chance/opportunity to travel this summer.

meaning: 'the chance to...'/ 'the opportunity to...'
additional_notes: This is a truncated/informal fragment of a phrase you might hear in spoken French where the verb or infinitive following t' (te) is omitted in examples. It comes from "la chance de te + [infinitive]" (or contracted "la chance de t' + [infinitive]") meaning the opportunity to do something. Commonly used with verbs: voir, rencontrer, parler, etc. Example: "J'ai la chance de t'avoir" = "I have the luck/opportunity to have you" (i.e. I'm lucky to have you).
target_language_example: J'ai la chance de t'avoir rencontré.
native_language_example: I have the chance to have met you. / I'm lucky to have met you.

meaning: 'the chance/opportunity to (do) something for you' or 'the chance of you' (depends on context)
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it usually appears inside a larger sentence such as "la chance de vous aider" (the chance to help you) or "la chance de vous rencontrer" (the chance to meet you). "La chance" means luck or opportunity; when followed by "de + infinitive" it means "the opportunity to...". With a direct object pronoun like "vous" the structure can be "la chance de vous + infinitive" (to you/for you) or "la chance de vous + past-participle" in some expressions. Pay attention to word order: French often uses "la chance de" + verb, not "chance to you."
target_language_example: Merci de me donner la chance de vous aider.
native_language_example: Thank you for giving me the chance to help you.

meaning: a crude, vulgar way to refer to (a) person as "an idiot"—using the feminine article and noun; strong insult.
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive. 'Con' is a vulgar noun/adjective meaning 'stupid' or 'idiot'. The feminine form is 'conne' (spoken /kɔ̃/), but some speakers may use 'la con' colloquially to point to a (female) idiot; written use is uncommon and marked. Avoid in polite or formal contexts.
target_language_example: Regarde la con qui a pris ma place !
native_language_example: Look at the idiot who took my seat!

meaning: 'the cream' — literal dairy cream; also used figuratively to mean 'the best' or 'the cream of the crop'.
additional_notes: Can refer to dairy cream (la crème fraîche, la crème liquide). In expressions it often means 'the best' (e.g., «la crème de la crème» = the very best). Context tells whether it's literal or figurative. Feminine noun (la).
target_language_example: Elle ajoute de la crème au café.
native_language_example: She adds cream to the coffee.

meaning: 'the dozen' — a group of twelve (commonly used to refer to twelve items).
additional_notes: Used to refer to twelve of something (e.g., une douzaine d'œufs, une douzaine de viennoiseries). Can be used literally; in informal contexts it may imply 'a lot' but that's less common. Plural when counting multiple dozens: des douzaines.
target_language_example: Je veux la douzaine d'œufs, pas seulement six.
native_language_example: I want the dozen of eggs, not just six.

meaning: 'the way' or 'the manner' (how something is done).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the manner, method or style of doing something. Often followed by 'dont', 'de', 'de faire', or a clause: la façon dont/ la façon de + infinitive. Can be used in formal and informal contexts. Plural: les façons.
target_language_example: J'aime la façon dont tu expliques les choses.
native_language_example: I like the way you explain things.

meaning: 'time' or 'occasion' (an occurrence); also used to indicate simultaneity in expressions like 'à la fois' (at the same time).
additional_notes: Often used after a number (une fois, deux fois) or in fixed phrases (la première fois, la dernière fois). Context decides if it denotes a single occurrence or simultaneity. Common in expressions: 'à la fois' (both/at the same time), 'toutes les fois' (every time).
target_language_example: La première fois que je l'ai rencontré, c'était à Paris.
native_language_example: The first time I met him, it was in Paris.

meaning: to the party with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say going/being present at a party accompanied by someone. 'Avec' means 'with' and is followed by the person (moi, toi, lui, Tom...). The phrase itself is not idiomatic—it's just the noun 'la fête' + preposition 'avec'. You can change 'la fête' to other events (le concert, la réunion) the same way.
target_language_example: Je voudrais aller à la fête avec mes amis.
native_language_example: I would like to go to the party with my friends.

meaning: Not a grammatically correct standalone French phrase; appears to be a mistaken word order or fragment. It may be part of longer, correct expressions such as «la fête, c'est…» (the party is…) or «la fête ce soir» (the party [is] tonight).
additional_notes: As written, 'la fête ce' doesn't occur in standard French by itself. Likely causes: omitted punctuation or words (e.g., missing 's'' in 'c'est' or missing following time expression). Correct possibilities include: 1) «La fête, c'est…» to introduce a comment about the party. 2) «La fête ce soir» or «La fête, c'est ce soir» to indicate time. If you encounter 'ce' immediately after a noun, check for 'c'est' (subject + 'c'' + 'est') or a time phrase starting with 'ce' (ce soir, ce week-end).
target_language_example: La fête ce soir, c'est annulée — non, je voulais dire : la fête ce soir.
native_language_example: The party tonight is canceled — no, I meant: the party tonight.

meaning: A polite phrase used when asking to be let off/left at the train station (literally: 'drop me at the station, please').
additional_notes: This construction appears in requests like "Descendez-moi à la gare, je vous prie" or informal "Descends-moi à la gare, je te prie." "Je vous prie/je te prie" is a polite way to say "please." "Largue-moi à la gare" is informal/slang (larguer = drop/leave someone). Also used literally in narration: "En sortant de la gare, je vis…" where "la gare" simply means "the station." Context decides whether it's a request (imperative + me) or a location in a sentence.
target_language_example: Descends-moi à la gare, je te prie — je dois attraper le train de 18h.
native_language_example: Drop me off at the station, please — I need to catch the 6 pm train.

meaning: to (be) at the station / to arrive at the station (with a time expression).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun la gare (the station) with the preposition à when indicating arrival or presence at a place and often used with a time: arriver à la gare à 7 heures = arrive at the station at 7. For beginners: use 'être à la gare' (to be at the station) or 'arriver à la gare' (to arrive at the station). The second 'à' before a time marks when (à cinq heures).
target_language_example: Je serai à la gare à six heures.
native_language_example: I will be at the station at six o'clock.

meaning: the big / the tall (feminine singular); used before a feminine noun or as a noun phrase meaning 'the big one' (feminine).
additional_notes: Formed from the feminine definite article la + the adjective grande. Use la grande before a feminine singular noun: la grande maison (the big house). Alone, la grande can mean 'the big one' referring to a feminine noun mentioned earlier (e.g., la grande, pas la petite). Remember adjective-noun order: the adjective usually follows the noun in French, but grande precedes a noun only when used in certain fixed expressions or for emphasis; more commonly you say une grande maison (a big house).
target_language_example: Je prends la grande assiette, pas la petite.
native_language_example: I'll take the big plate, not the small one.

meaning: 'the guitar and' (literal fragment)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it's a literal combination of the feminine singular noun la guitare (the guitar) followed by the conjunction et (and). You will usually see it as part of a longer sentence listing things (e.g., «la guitare et le piano» = the guitar and the piano). Do not use it alone as a full expression.
target_language_example: La guitare et le piano sont dans le salon.
native_language_example: The guitar and the piano are in the living room.

meaning: height; the measurement from bottom to top or altitude/level.
additional_notes: Used for physical height (la hauteur d'une table, d'un immeuble), for altitude (la hauteur d'une montagne) and figuratively for level/standard (être à la hauteur = to be up to the task). Definite article la is normally used; context determines whether it's a concrete measurement or abstract idea.
target_language_example: La hauteur de cette table est de 75 cm.
native_language_example: The height of this table is 75 cm.

meaning: 'the height of' or 'the amount/level of' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Usually used to indicate physical height (la hauteur de la porte) or an abstract level/amount (la hauteur des dépenses). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Can also appear in measurements (la hauteur est de 2 mètres).
target_language_example: La hauteur de cet arbre est impressionnante.
native_language_example: The height of this tree is impressive.

meaning: 'haste' or 'eagerness' (a feeling of wanting something quickly).
additional_notes: A feminine abstract noun. Commonly used in expressions like «être/avoir la hâte de + infinitive» meaning to be eager or impatient to do something. Not used for physical speed (use 'rapidité' or 'vitesse' for that). Often appears in formal or literary contexts; in everyday spoken French people often say «avoir hâte de + infinitive» (without the article).
target_language_example: J'ai la hâte de te revoir.
native_language_example: I am eager to see you again.

meaning: 'the lottery' (a game of chance where people buy tickets to win money or prizes).
additional_notes: Used for national/state lotteries or any raffle-style game. Can refer to both the institution ('the lottery') and the event/draw. In conversation it often appears with verbs like jouer à la loterie (to play the lottery), gagner à la loterie (to win the lottery), or acheter un billet de loterie (to buy a lottery ticket).
target_language_example: Elle a gagné gros à la loterie la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: She won big in the lottery last week.

meaning: flattery; sucking up to someone (noun, usually informal)
additional_notes: Informal/slang. Literally from the verb 'lécher' (to lick); used to describe insincere praise or behavior intended to gain favor. Often appears in expressions like 'faire la lèche' or 'faire de la lèche' (to flatter, to brownnose). Can be used sarcastically: 'Arrête la lèche.'
target_language_example: Il fait la lèche au patron pour obtenir une promotion.
native_language_example: He's sucking up to the boss to get a promotion.

meaning: the light (feminine noun) — refers to something light in weight or intensity
additional_notes: La légère combines the feminine definite article 'la' with the adjective 'légère' used as a noun (nominalized adjective). It can refer to a light object, a slight feeling, or a minor/brief thing depending on context. Without context it is ambiguous; you will often see it in phrases like 'la légère brise' (the light breeze) or nominalized in poetic/colloquial uses: 'la légère' = 'the light one' (feminine). Agreement is feminine singular.
target_language_example: J'ai pris la légère couverture parce qu'il ne fait pas très froid.
native_language_example: I took the light blanket because it's not very cold.

meaning: 'the house with' (phrase used to describe a house that has something)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the article + noun + preposition used to introduce a feature of a house (e.g. la maison avec un jardin = the house with a garden). You will usually complete the phrase with a noun or clause: la maison avec piscine, la maison avec trois chambres, la maison avec vue sur la mer, etc. Watch agreement and word order: adjectives or descriptive phrases follow the noun.
target_language_example: Nous cherchons la maison avec un grand jardin.
native_language_example: We are looking for the house with a large garden.

meaning: Not a standard French expression; likely a typo, misordering, or fragment (possibly intended as 'c'est la maison' or 'la maison de ...').
additional_notes: The sequence 'la maison ce' is not grammatical in French as written. Possible causes: missing punctuation, swapped words, or omitted words ('la maison, ce ...' as the start of a sentence meaning 'the house, this ...', or intended 'c'est la maison' = 'it's the house', or 'la maison de ...' = 'the house of ...'). If encountered in text, check context for a missing comma, verb, or preposition. Teach beginners correct alternatives: use 'c'est' before a noun phrase to identify, and 'de' to show possession.
target_language_example: La maison ce n'est pas à moi.
native_language_example: The house, it is not mine.

meaning: 'the house tomorrow' (literal phrase: refers to 'the house' at a time tomorrow).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun phrase 'la maison' (the house) followed by the adverb 'demain' (tomorrow). It could appear in a short answer or fragment to indicate location or plan (e.g. 'Je serai à la maison demain' = 'I'll be at home tomorrow'). By itself it's not a complete sentence in French; learners should add a verb or context. Word order is the same as in English.
target_language_example: Je serai à la maison demain.
native_language_example: I'll be at home tomorrow.

meaning: "the house in" (incomplete fragment; needs more words to form a full phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. In French, 'la maison' means 'the house' and 'en' is a pronoun or preposition meaning 'in', 'of it/them', or 'from there' depending on context. 'La maison en' would typically be followed by a noun, adjective, or relative clause (e.g. 'la maison en bois' = 'the wooden house') or appears in constructions with 'en' replacing a noun introduced earlier (e.g. 'la maison en est proche' — less common). As given, it is most likely the start of a descriptive phrase such as 'la maison en bois', 'la maison en face', or 'la maison en ruine.'
target_language_example: La maison en bois près du lac est à vendre.
native_language_example: The wooden house near the lake is for sale.

meaning: This looks like 'the house and' — not a standard fixed French phrase on its own.
additional_notes: Likely a fragment: 'la maison' = 'the house' and 'et' = 'and'. In French, they are separate words used to connect nouns or phrases (e.g., 'la maison et le jardin' = 'the house and the garden'). As given, 'la maison et' is incomplete and should be followed by another element. Use articles and agreement as in English: 'la' for feminine singular nouns.
target_language_example: La maison et le jardin sont grands.
native_language_example: The house and the garden are big.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely an error or fragment. It appears to be the feminine noun phrase 'la maison' ('the house') immediately followed by the masculine article 'le', which is ungrammatical without context.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'la maison le' does not form a correct standalone expression in French. Possible explanations: - Typo or transcription error (an extra 'le'). - Fragment of a longer sentence where punctuation separates items (e.g., 'la maison, le jardin et le garage'). - Part of reported speech or a headline missing punctuation. To correct, either remove the stray 'le' or supply the noun that 'le' should modify (e.g., 'la maison le garage' -> 'la maison et le garage' or 'la maison, le garage').
target_language_example: La maison le long du canal a été rénovée.
native_language_example: The house along the canal has been renovated.

meaning: 'the house' + 'rather than' — used to prefer the house over something else
additional_notes: This is the short sequence combining the noun la maison (the house/home) with the comparative phrase plutôt que (rather than). It's not a fixed idiom by itself; you will usually see it inside a larger sentence to express preference or choice (e.g. je préfère rester à la maison plutôt que sortir). Pay attention to word order: plutôt que is followed by a verb or noun phrase representing what is being rejected.
target_language_example: Je reste à la maison plutôt que d'aller au cinéma.
native_language_example: I'm staying at home rather than going to the cinema.

meaning: at home rather than (doing something); preferring to stay home instead of doing another action
additional_notes: Used to express a preference for being at home instead of doing some alternative action. Usually followed by an infinitive verb describing the action avoided (e.g. 'la maison plutôt que de sortir' = 'home rather than go out'). Word order: 'plutôt que de' introduces the alternative action. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je suis resté à la maison plutôt que de sortir avec eux.
native_language_example: I stayed at home rather than go out with them.

meaning: This exact string is not a correct or grammatical French phrase; it likely reflects a word-order or omission error. Possible intended phrases are "toute la maison" (the whole/entire house) or "la maison toute seule" (the house by itself).
additional_notes: "La maison toute la" is ungrammatical in French because the determiner and modifier order is wrong; "toute" as a determiner/adjective should precede the noun ("toute la maison") or be followed by an adjective like "seule" ("la maison toute seule"). If you need to express "the whole house," use "toute la maison." If you mean "the house by itself/alone," use "la maison toute seule." The provided target-language example below deliberately includes the exact ungrammatical sequence to show how it might appear in error; do not use this form in correct French.
target_language_example: Il a écrit par erreur « la maison toute la » dans sa note, mais c’est incorrect.
native_language_example: He mistakenly wrote "la maison toute la" in his note, but it is incorrect.

meaning: at someone's mercy; in a helpless position under someone's control or power.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or thing is completely dependent on someone/something and cannot resist. Often appears in expressions like «être à la merci de quelqu'un/quelque chose» (to be at someone's/ something's mercy). Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Après la panne, nous étions à la merci du mauvais temps.
native_language_example: After the breakdown, we were at the mercy of the bad weather.

meaning: fashion; style; what's fashionable or trendy.
additional_notes: Used to talk about fashion, trends, or something being in style. Can refer to clothing, tastes, or popular practices. Common expressions: 'à la mode' (in fashion/trendy) and 'être à la mode' (to be fashionable).
target_language_example: Cette robe est très à la mode cette saison.
native_language_example: This dress is very fashionable this season.

meaning: the music is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase used to describe the music (followed by an adjective, a mood, a location, etc.). Common in sentences like "La musique est forte" (The music is loud) or "La musique est relaxante" (The music is relaxing). Use it to talk about characteristics or states of music. Contraction with "est" does not occur (you always keep both words).
target_language_example: La musique est trop forte dans ce café.
native_language_example: The music is too loud in this café.

meaning: swimming (the activity or sport).
additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the act of swimming or the sport of swimming. Used to talk about swimming in general (faire de la nage is less common than nager or faire de la natation). Often appears in contexts like 'la nage synchronisée' (synchronized swimming) or when contrasting different swimming styles (la nage libre = freestyle).
target_language_example: La nage m'aide à rester en forme.
native_language_example: Swimming helps me stay fit.

meaning: 'food and' — the phrase 'la nourriture' (food) followed by 'et' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the noun 'la nourriture' plus the conjunction 'et' to join another item (e.g. 'la nourriture et des couvertures'). Use 'de la nourriture' for unspecified quantity (some food). Watch agreement: 'nourriture' is feminine singular. Common in lists of supplies or donations.
target_language_example: Ils ont apporté de la nourriture et des vêtements.
native_language_example: They brought food and clothes.

meaning: the page (a sheet, a page in a book or on a website).
additional_notes: Used for a physical page (in a book, notebook) or a web page. Definite article 'la' makes it specific: 'la page' = the page. For 'a page' use 'une page'. Can also appear in expressions like 'tourner la page' (to move on). Pronunciation note: the final 'e' in 'page' is pronounced /paʒ/.
target_language_example: Tourne la page et continue.
native_language_example: Turn the page and keep going.

meaning: 'the share', 'the portion' or 'the part' (a portion of something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a portion, share or slice of something (money, food, responsibility, etc.). Appears in expressions like "prendre sa part" (to take one's share), "donner la part" (to give the share) or "faire sa part" (to do one's part). Feminine singular; exact translation depends on context (portion, share, role).
target_language_example: Il ne reste plus que la part de Marie dans le frigo.
native_language_example: Only Marie's share remains in the fridge.

meaning: the share/portion of (someone or something); someone's share of
additional_notes: Used to indicate a portion, share or role that belongs to someone or something (e.g. la part de marché = market share; la part de responsabilité = the share of responsibility). Often followed by a noun or a person introduced by de (la part de Paul). Can be used in literal (a piece/portion) and figurative senses (responsibility, blame, influence).
target_language_example: Quelle est la part de chacun dans ce projet ?
native_language_example: What is each person's share in this project?

meaning: the watermelon (fruit).
additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the large green-and-red summer fruit with sweet flesh. Used like any regular noun: le/la depending on gender (here la). Plural: les pastèques. Common in everyday speech and markets.
target_language_example: La pastèque est très sucrée cette saison.
native_language_example: The watermelon is very sweet this season.

meaning: 'perfection' or 'complete excellence'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the state of being perfect or an ideal example. Can be used literally (e.g., an object or performance is flawless) or more loosely/ironically. Feminine noun phrase (la). Common collocations: 'atteindre la perfection' (to reach perfection), 'presque la perfection' (almost perfection).
target_language_example: Son gâteau était la perfection.
native_language_example: Her cake was perfection.

meaning: 'pity' or 'compassion' (a feeling of sorrow and desire to help someone in distress).
additional_notes: Used to talk about sympathy or compassion; also used in expressions of contempt or disappointment (e.g., « Quelle pitié ! »). Commonly appears in phrases like « avoir pitié de quelqu'un » (to feel pity for someone) and « montrer de la pitié » (to show pity).
target_language_example: Il a montré la pitié qu'il ressentait pour les victimes.
native_language_example: He showed the pity he felt for the victims.

meaning: the most (feminine singular); used to form superlatives (e.g. 'the most beautiful').
additional_notes: La plus is the feminine singular form of 'le plus' used before adjectives or adverbs that modify a feminine singular noun (or to agree with a feminine subject). For masculine nouns or general neutral statements use 'le plus'; for plural use 'les plus'. It can mean 'the most' (superlative) or be part of comparative constructions (e.g. 'plus ... que' = 'more ... than'). Word order: 'la plus' typically comes before the adjective (la plus belle).
target_language_example: C'est la plus grande maison du quartier.
native_language_example: It's the biggest house in the neighborhood.

meaning: hiking; a hike or long walk in nature.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about recreational walking in the countryside, mountains, or forests. Can refer to the activity (faire de la randonnée), a specific hike (une randonnée), or long-distance treks. Often paired with gear words (chaussures de randonnée, sentier).
target_language_example: Nous allons faire la randonnée demain matin dans les Alpes.
native_language_example: We're going to do the hike tomorrow morning in the Alps.

meaning: the room for/of (used before a noun phrase introduced by à, but incomplete on its own).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the beginning of compound names like "la salle à manger" (dining room) or "la salle à boire" (rare). You will always need the following word(s) to know which room is meant. Remember the full expressions are feminine singular: la salle à manger, la salle à jouer, etc.
target_language_example: Nous déjeunons dans la salle à manger.
native_language_example: We have lunch in the dining room.

meaning: silk (the fabric or material).
additional_notes: Feminine noun. Used to talk about the material (fabric, thread) or things made from it (silk clothing). Often appears without an article when used in general sense (e.g., « porter soie » less common), but normally you say « la soie » for 'silk' as a specific substance. Plural (les soies) is rarely used except in technical contexts (e.g., hairs/bristles described as 'soies').
target_language_example: Elle porte une robe en la soie pour la cérémonie.
native_language_example: She is wearing a silk dress for the ceremony.

meaning: witchcraft; sorcery; the practice of magic.
additional_notes: Used to describe supernatural magic, occult practices, or figuratively to express that something seems mysterious or inexplicable (e.g., "It's like witchcraft"). Often uncountable in French when speaking generally: "de la sorcellerie."
target_language_example: Ce mécanisme fonctionne sans explication — on dirait de la sorcellerie.
native_language_example: This mechanism works without explanation — it looks like witchcraft.

meaning: 'the kind' / 'the sort' / 'that kind' (referring to a kind, type, or manner)
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases such as «une sorte de» or «de la sorte»; when used alone as «la sorte» it typically refers back to a previously mentioned kind or situation (e.g. «de la sorte» = 'in that way'). Can be neutral or slightly formal depending on context. Not usually used in isolation without context.
target_language_example: La sorte de gâteau dont tu parlais n'est pas celle que j'aime, mais la sorte aux pommes est délicieuse.
native_language_example: The kind of cake you were talking about is not the one I like, but the apple kind is delicious.

meaning: slang for 'the car' (informal); in some regions can also mean 'tire' or 'candy' (colloquial).
additional_notes: This is an informal, regional slang term. In France, 'la bagnole' or 'la caisse' are more common for 'the car'; 'la tire' meaning 'car' is used in Quebec and some informal contexts. 'Tire' (without article) in standard French usually means 'tire' (as in wheel) is 'pneu' — 'tire' is English. 'Tire' can also be slang for 'money' or an old word for 'candy' in some dialects; because usage varies by region, prefer 'la voiture' (standard) for 'the car' in formal situations.
target_language_example: Tu prends la tire ce soir pour aller au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Are you taking the car tonight to go to the cinema?

meaning: the falling/arrival of (used to talk about the start or arrival of a time of day or a phenomenon, e.g. 'la tombée de la nuit' = 'nightfall')
additional_notes: This is a set phrase used with a specific noun (most commonly 'la tombée de la nuit' — nightfall). It describes the onset or descent of something (light, night, dusk). It is usually followed by a time- or phenomenon-word introduced by 'la' (feminine). Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous partirons à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We will leave at nightfall.

meaning: the train (the long trailing part of a dress, robe, or garment); can also mean a literal trail or something that drags/ trails behind.
additional_notes: Most often used for the long trailing portion of a wedding dress or ceremonial robe (la traîne d'une robe). Feminine noun. Pronounced [la tʁɛn]. Context determines whether it's sartorial (dress train) or literal (something trailing behind).
target_language_example: La mariée portait la traîne de sa robe avec grâce.
native_language_example: The bride wore the train of her dress gracefully.

meaning: 'the head of' or 'the head to/for' used as part of a larger phrase (often followed by a noun or pronoun).
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete fixed expression by itself; it appears as part of phrases like "donner la tête à" or constructions where "tête" takes a complement introduced by "à" (e.g. "la tête aux enfants", "la tête aux nuages"). You will usually see a full phrase such as "avoir la tête à quelque chose" (to be in the mood for something) or "donner la tête à" (rare). Pay attention to the verb and the words that follow — they determine the exact meaning. "La tête" can mean the physical head or be idiomatic (mind, mood, attention).
target_language_example: Il n'a pas la tête aux devoirs aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He doesn't have his mind (head) on his homework today.

meaning: from head to toe; completely, entirely (describing the whole body or something covering/affecting the whole person).
additional_notes: Literally 'the head to the feet'. Used to describe something that affects or covers the entire body (clothing, illness, feeling). Equivalent to English 'head to toe' or 'from head to foot'. Can modify verbs or adjectives: e.g. 'habillé(e) la tête aux pieds' = 'dressed from head to toe'.
target_language_example: Elle était habillée la tête aux pieds de noir.
native_language_example: She was dressed head to toe in black.

meaning: the old woman; the old (female) one.
additional_notes: Literally 'the old (female)'. Used to refer to an older woman or, colloquially, 'the old lady' (e.g., someone's wife) depending on context and tone. Can be neutral or slightly familiar/rude depending on context and intonation. If followed by a noun (e.g. 'la vieille maison') it means 'the old (feminine) [noun]'.
target_language_example: La vieille du village raconte des histoires.
native_language_example: The old woman from the village tells stories.

meaning: vodka (the alcoholic drink) — feminine noun with definite article.
additional_notes: Used to refer to vodka in general or a specific bottle/glass: la vodka. In French the word is feminine (la). Can be used with partitive or quantities: de la vodka, un verre de vodka, une bouteille de vodka. Pronunciation: [la vɔd.ka].
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de la vodka, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I would like a glass of vodka, please.

meaning: 'the view' or 'sight' (what you can see; also the sense of sight in some contexts).
additional_notes: Commonly used for a scenic view (e.g. la vue sur la mer = the view of the sea) or to refer to vision (perdre la vue = to lose one's sight). Often used with prepositions: avoir la vue sur, profiter de la vue, une vue panoramique. Feminine gender (la).
target_language_example: Depuis le balcon, la vue sur la ville est magnifique.
native_language_example: From the balcony, the view of the city is magnificent.

meaning: This sequence is not a standard standalone French phrase; it combines the feminine definite article 'la' and the contraction 'au' ('à le') and most often results from a typo, mis-segmentation, or informal speech where words run together.
additional_notes: In correct French 'la au' (without accent on 'la') is uncommon. Possibilities: (1) It's a typo for 'là au' (with accent on 'là'), meaning 'there at the...'; (2) it's a mis-segmentation of two separate words 'la' + 'au' occurring nearby but belonging to different parts of the sentence; (3) confusion between 'la' and 'là'. If you meant 'là au', it is used colloquially before a place phrase: e.g. 'là au fond'. Remember 'au' = 'à le' (before masculine singular nouns) and does not normally follow the feminine 'la' directly.
target_language_example: La au marché, il y a un stand de légumes.
native_language_example: The at the market, there is a vegetable stall. (This sentence illustrates a mistaken or nonstandard sequence 'la au' rather than correct French.)

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a mistaken separation of 'là' + 'avec' meaning 'there with' or 'la' (feminine direct object) + 'avec' ('with').
additional_notes:
As written, 'la avec' is not a common or correct fixed expression. Possible intended forms:
- 'là, avec' (là = there) used to mean 'there, with...' (e.g., pointing out location or accompaniment).
- 'la' (feminine direct object pronoun) normally appears before the verb (e.g., 'je la vois' = 'I see her'); it would not be followed directly by 'avec'.
If you mean 'there with', use 'là avec' (with accent on là) and include context: e.g., 'Elle est là avec moi.' If you meant 'with her', say 'avec elle.' Beginners should be careful about spacing and accents: 'là' (there) vs 'la' (the or her/it as pronoun).
target_language_example: Je vois la avec son chien.
native_language_example: I see her there with her dog. (Note: sentence is nonstandard; correct forms are 'Je la vois avec son chien.' or 'Je vois là, avec son chien.')

meaning: well, properly (with 'la' = her/it).
additional_notes: Combines the object pronoun 'la' (her/it, feminine) with the adverb 'bien' (well). Used after a verb to tell someone to do something to her/it properly or carefully (e.g., Regarde-la bien = Look at her carefully). Word order: verb + object pronoun + adverb. Polite/plural form uses 'la' with plural verb forms (e.g., Tenez-la bien / Traitez-la bien).
target_language_example: Salue-la bien de ma part.
native_language_example: Give her my best regards. (Literally: Greet her well on my behalf.)

meaning: 'la' (her/it - feminine direct object pronoun) + 'dans' (in/into); used to mean 'put her/it in' or 'into it/her'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (meaning 'her' or 'it' for a feminine noun) followed by the preposition 'dans' ('in/into'). Word order in spoken/written French can place the object pronoun before the verb (e.g. 'mets-la dans...') or attached to an imperative with a hyphen. In examples here 'la' refers to a feminine thing or person (depending on context) and 'dans' introduces the container/location. Adjust pronouns for gender/number (le, les, lui, etc.).
target_language_example: Mets-la dans la boîte.
native_language_example: Put it/her in the box.

meaning: a short, colloquial filler used before mentioning something specific (like 'the one with...'); often used in conversation to refer informally to a particular person or thing.
additional_notes: Informal and spoken. 'La de' is typically followed by a descriptive phrase: e.g. « la de la pharmacie » or « la de lundi ». It contracts/echoes structures like « celle de » or « la [chose] de » and can vary by region. Avoid in formal writing. Context is required to know the referent — it's a demonstrative shorthand ('the one of/with...').
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de la de la réunion ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the one from the meeting?

meaning: Not a standard single French phrase; as written it is likely a typo, misordering, or an incorrect separation of words (examples: 'là en', 'la' + 'en', or 'l'en').
additional_notes:
'la en' does not form a correct or common expression in French. Possible intended readings:
- 'là en' (with accent) can begin phrases like 'là en bas' (down there) or 'là en haut' (up there).
- 'la' (feminine definite article or direct object pronoun) followed by 'en' (a pronoun meaning 'of it/of them' or 'from there') should usually be ordered and contracted according to French pronoun rules (for example, 'je la comprends' or 'j'en veux'), not written 'la en'.
- 'l'en' (contraction of 'le/ la' + 'en') is rare and occurs only in specific fixed or literary contexts.
Learners should verify source text and correct spacing/accents; do not write 'la en' in standard French.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu sais pourquoi la en parle comme ça ?
native_language_example: Do you know why she talks about it like that?

meaning: Bring/let her in (object pronoun + infinitive).
additional_notes: This appears to be the combination of the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (her/it) placed before an infinitive 'entrer' (to enter). In standard written French the pronoun comes before the infinitive only when another verb governs it: e.g. 'Fais-la entrer' = 'Make/bring her enter' or more naturally 'Let her in' / 'Bring her in'. In polite/formal commands use 'Faites-la entrer, s'il vous plaît.' For negative commands with an infinitive, the pronoun still precedes the infinitive: 'Ne la faites pas entrer.' Note: 'la entrer' by itself is not a standalone phrase — it always appears as part of a verb phrase (imperative or with another conjugated verb).
target_language_example: Faites-la entrer, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please let her in.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; most likely an incorrect spacing or typo. Could represent the two separate words 'la' (feminine definite article or object pronoun) and 'et' (and) occurring adjacent in a sentence, but they do not form an idiomatic multi-word unit.
additional_notes: 'la et' as written is not a recognized French expression. Possible intended forms: - 'là et' (with accent) where 'là' = 'there' and 'et' = 'and' (still not a fixed phrase). - Two separate words 'la' + 'et' appearing together across a phrase boundary (e.g., end of one clause and start of another). Treat as compositional literal words rather than an idiom. If you meant another word (e.g., 'lâcheté', 'laet'), provide the correct spelling or context.
target_language_example: Je vois la et je la reconnais quand même.
native_language_example: I see her and I recognize her anyway.

meaning: to make her (do something) / to get her to (do something).
additional_notes: A construction using the causative verb 'faire' + object pronoun 'la' (her). 'Faire' + infinitive means 'to cause/make/get someone to do something'. Word order: subject + faire + object pronoun + infinitive (e.g. Nous l'avons fait partir). In the example, 'la faire aller dormir' = 'get her to go to sleep'. Pronoun 'la' stands for a feminine singular person or noun. Replace with le, les, etc. as needed.
target_language_example: Je vais la faire parler au téléphone.
native_language_example: I'll get her to speak on the phone.

meaning: 'shut up' (tell someone to be quiet).
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat rude. Literally 'to close it' (la = it, referring to the mouth). Commonly used in spoken French to tell someone to stop talking. Use with caution; can be offensive in formal situations.
target_language_example: Il ferait mieux de la fermer pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He'd better shut up during the meeting.

meaning: 'to play it' / 'to act/handle a situation in a certain way' (informal conversational use)
additional_notes: Used with a direct object pronoun (la, le) to mean 'to play it' literally or figuratively: how to approach, perform, present, or handle something. Common in expressions like « la jouer serrée » (play it tight/keep things guarded) or « la jouer clean » (play it clean/ play fair). Tone can be neutral or blunt; in informal contexts it may be used with slang/insults. The verb jouer keeps its normal meanings (play, act), so the phrase is compositional.
target_language_example: On va la jouer tranquille et éviter les risques.
native_language_example: We'll play it safe and avoid risks.

meaning: A combination of object pronouns: 'la' (her/it, feminine direct object) + 'lui' (to him/to her, indirect object). It can appear in constructions like 'donner la lui' in older or regional French, but in modern standard French the order and forms differ (see notes).
additional_notes: In contemporary standard French, you will almost never see 'la lui' directly next to each other in neutral word order because when both direct and indirect object pronouns are used, the usual order is: me/te/se/nous/vous > le/la/les > lui/leur > y > en. So 'give it to him' is 'donne-le-lui' (hyphens in imperative) or 'je le lui donne.' Written as separate words only in very old, poetic, or dialectal usages. Be careful: 'la' can also be a feminine definite article ('the'), and 'lui' can be tonic (stressed) pronoun meaning 'him' — context matters. For beginners, learn the standard pronoun order and use forms like 'je la lui donne' (I give it to him/her) or 'donne-le-lui' (imperative: give it to him/her).
target_language_example: Je la lui donne demain.
native_language_example: I will give it to him/her tomorrow.

meaning: there (emphatic; points out something nearby or just mentioned)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to emphasize location or presence of something: like 'there' or 'right there' in English. Often accompanies a gesture (pointing) or used to draw attention to something just mentioned. Common in conversational French (e.g., « Regarde la là! »). Not used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Regarde la là, c'est ma voiture.
native_language_example: Look over there, that's my car.

meaning: to bring her back / to take her home (bring someone back to a place).
additional_notes: La ramener is the colloquial use of ramener + object pronoun la (her/it). Depending on context it can mean 'bring her back' (return someone to a location) or 'take her home'. It's common in spoken French. If the object is masculine use le (le ramener); plural use les. Ramener comes from ramener (to bring back).
target_language_example: Tu peux la ramener chez elle ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you bring her back to her place tonight?

meaning: literally 'want her/it' — second person singular informal (tu) + direct object pronoun 'la' (feminine).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's a combination of the object pronoun 'la' (meaning 'her' or 'it' for a feminine noun) placed before the verb 'veux' (the present tense of vouloir for 'tu' as in 'tu veux'). In correct standard word order you would say 'tu la veux' (Do you want it/her?) or in an informal clipped context someone might say just 'La veux ?' as an elliptical question, but written French usually includes the subject: 'Tu la veux ?'. In negative or compound tenses, placement changes (e.g., 'Tu ne la veux pas.' / 'Je ne l'ai pas voulue.').
target_language_example: Tu la veux ou tu la laisses ?
native_language_example: Do you want it/her or will you leave it?

meaning: There she is / here she is (feminine), or 'there it is' for a feminine noun; used to point someone or something out.
additional_notes: Common spoken expression used when someone or something (usually feminine) appears or is pointed out. Can be used literally (spotting a woman, girl, or a feminine noun like 'voiture') or playfully/ironically (e.g. calling someone 'la belle' or 'Cendrillon'). Often accompanied by surprise, relief, or mild reproach. Tone and context determine nuance.
target_language_example: La voilà qui sort de la voiture.
native_language_example: There she is getting out of the car.

meaning: there (over) / right there (nearby).
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression used to point out a location or to emphasize something close by: 'la' = there, 'à' adds emphasis or direction. Often contracted in speech and used with gestures: e.g. « là, à gauche » or « la, à côté »; can also appear as 'là, à' separated by a comma. Not a fixed grammatical phrase — context and intonation determine exact sense.
target_language_example: Regarde la à côté de la porte.
native_language_example: Look right there next to the door.

meaning: the Cavalry; (also) the cavalry unit or a place name (La Cavalerie).
additional_notes: Capitalized 'La Cavalerie' is often a proper noun — the name of a town in southern France (in Aveyron) — or the name of a military unit. Lowercase 'la cavalerie' refers to cavalry (soldiers on horseback). Context (capitalization, article, geography or military) tells you which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Nous visiterons La Cavalerie pendant notre voyage en Aveyron.
native_language_example: We will visit La Cavalerie during our trip to Aveyron.

meaning: the conception; the idea or the moment of conception (also a proper name: place/Marian title).
additional_notes: Capitalized as 'La Conception' can be a proper noun (e.g., name of a town, church, or the Marian title 'Immaculate Conception'). In lowercase 'la conception' commonly means 'the act of conceiving' (pregnancy) or 'the design/creation of an idea or project'. Context tells whether it's biological, creative, or a place/name.
target_language_example: La conception du projet a pris plusieurs mois.
native_language_example: The conception/design of the project took several months.

meaning: The La Défense district in Paris (major business/commercial district); can also mean 'defense' in general depending on context.
additional_notes: When capitalized and preceded by 'la', La Défense refers to the large business district west of Paris (offices, métro/RER station, landmarks). In spoken French, 'la Défense' can be used in phone or travel contexts to mean the La Défense station or area (e.g., 'Passez-moi la Défense' = put someone through to a line/office at La Défense). Lowercase 'défense' without 'La' means defense (military/protection).
target_language_example: Je travaille dans un cabinet à La Défense.
native_language_example: I work at a firm in La Défense.

meaning: 'may the Force be (with you)'.
additional_notes: A truncated version of the famous sci‑fi blessing "Que la Force soit avec toi / avec vous" (from Star Wars). Alone, "la Force soit" is incomplete in French; native speakers would say the full phrase. Used jokingly or playfully to wish someone luck or support, often among fans. "Force" here is capitalized when referring to the Star Wars concept.
target_language_example: Que la Force soit avec toi pour ton examen !
native_language_example: May the Force be with you for your exam!

meaning: the barn (feminine singular) — 'la Grange' can also be a proper name (e.g., a place, restaurant, or surname).
additional_notes: As a common noun, 'la grange' means 'the barn' (a building for farm animals or hay). Capitalized as 'La Grange' it often appears as a place name, business name, or family name; in that case treat it as a proper noun and translate according to context. Feminine noun: une grange / la grange. Pronunciation note: the 'g' is hard (like in 'go').
target_language_example: Ils ont réparé la grange avant l'hiver.
native_language_example: They repaired the barn before winter.

meaning: 'fishing' (the activity) OR 'peach' (the fruit) depending on context; informally can mean 'energy' or 'pep'.
additional_notes: Primary meanings: 1) la pêche = fishing (activity). 2) la pêche = the peach (fruit). Colloquially, avoir la pêche / être en pleine pêche means to be energetic, in high spirits (similar to 'to be full of energy'). Context (capitalization not significant in French) and articles help: parler de la pêche (talking about fishing) vs. manger une pêche (eat a peach).
target_language_example: Ce week-end, je vais à la pêche; j'espère revenir avec du poisson.
native_language_example: This weekend I'm going fishing; I hope to come back with some fish.

meaning: 'the Queen' (the female monarch or a queen as a figurehead).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a reigning female monarch or to the queen consort in contexts like formal speech, chants, toasts, or exclamations (e.g., 'Vive la Reine!'). Capitalization (La Reine) is common when referring to a specific sovereign. Can also be used more generally to speak about 'a queen' in a story or conversation.
target_language_example: Vive la Reine et son règne !
native_language_example: Long live the Queen and her reign!

meaning: 'the ... room for' (part of a construction indicating the purpose or occupant of a room)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of expressions like "la chambre à coucher" (bedroom), "la chambre à louer" (room for rent), or "la chambre à manger" (dining room — note: correct is "la salle à manger" but some learners may see "chambre à" in creative compounds). In French, "à" after a noun often introduces purpose, function, or what the room is for. You will usually see another word after "à" to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Nous avons visité la chambre à coucher de l'appartement.
native_language_example: We visited the apartment's bedroom.

meaning: the farm; can also be used colloquially to tell someone to 'shut up' (short for «ta ferme» / «la ferme» as an interjection).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: 'la ferme' = 'the farm' (a place where animals/plants are raised). Context determines meaning. As an interjection, 'La ferme !' is informal and rude — equivalent to 'Shut up!' or 'Be quiet!' Can appear in sentences like 'Vous venez de la ferme ?' (Are you from the farm?) or 'Les chevaux sont dans la ferme.' (The horses are in the farm).
target_language_example: Arrête de parler et la ferme, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop talking and shut up, please.

meaning: 'time' or 'occasion' (an occurrence); also used to indicate simultaneity in expressions like 'à la fois' (at the same time).
additional_notes: Often used after a number (une fois, deux fois) or in fixed phrases (la première fois, la dernière fois). Context decides if it denotes a single occurrence or simultaneity. Common in expressions: 'à la fois' (both/at the same time), 'toutes les fois' (every time).
target_language_example: La première fois que je l'ai rencontré, c'était à Paris.
native_language_example: The first time I met him, it was in Paris.

meaning: 'the face/mouth of' or (colloquial) 'the look/appearance of' / used in insults like 'la gueule de...'
additional_notes: Gueule is an informal, somewhat coarse word meaning 'mouth' or 'face' (often for animals or in rude speech about people). 'La gueule de...' can be used literally ('the mouth of...') or colloquially to comment on someone's appearance or to introduce an insult ('la gueule de ce type' = 'look at that guy's face' / 'that guy's ugly mug'). Avoid in formal contexts. Female form and possessives follow normal rules (la gueule du chien, la gueule de ce mec).
target_language_example: Regarde la gueule de ce chien, il a l'air fatigué.
native_language_example: Look at that dog's face, it looks tired.

meaning: shame; embarrassment; disgrace.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a feeling of personal embarrassment (avoir honte), an action that brings disgrace on someone or a group (être la honte de...), or an exclamation to express strong embarrassment ('La honte!' or 'Rien que la honte!'). Can be used as a noun (la honte) or in expressions (me fous pas la honte = don't embarrass me).
target_language_example: Ne me fous pas la honte devant mes amis.
native_language_example: Don't embarrass me in front of my friends.

meaning: the pretty (feminine singular) — used before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: La is the feminine definite article 'the'. Jolie is an adjective meaning 'pretty' or 'nice'. Together they must agree with a feminine singular noun that follows: e.g. la jolie maison (the pretty house), la jolie femme (the pretty woman). In speech you may also hear l' jolie only before a vowel-starting adjective + noun, but more correctly l' is used before a vowel sound (l'amie jolie). Placement: in French the adjective usually follows the noun, but some common short adjectives (including joli(e)) can come before the noun. Example forms: le joli (masculine), les jolies (feminine plural).
target_language_example: La jolie fleur sent très bon.
native_language_example: The pretty flower smells very good.

meaning: 'the day has' (used as the start of a past-tense comment about how the day was).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the structure 'La journée a été...' followed by an adjective (longue, rude, épuisante, belle, bonne) to describe how the day went. 'La journée a' by itself is incomplete — it needs a past participle (été) and a complement. Useful for asking or stating how someone's day was: 'La journée a été bonne ?' = 'Was the day good?'.
target_language_example: La journée a été stressante, mais maintenant je me détends.
native_language_example: The day was stressful, but now I'm relaxing.

meaning: 'the ... language' used in superlative/questions (part of the construction: « quelle/quel est la langue la plus ... »).
additional_notes: This appears as part of superlative questions about languages: «Quelle est la langue la plus + adjective?» (Which language is the most ...?). Grammatically, use quelle (feminine) with langue (f.), or quel with masculine nouns. The second «la» is the definite article used in the superlative construction «la plus» (the most). In correct phrasing, you usually see: «Quelle est la langue la plus difficile au monde?» or shortened focus: «Quelle langue est la plus difficile?» Both are natural. Remember agreement: adjective after plus must agree with langue.
target_language_example: Quelle est la langue la plus parlée au monde?
native_language_example: Which language is the most spoken in the world?

meaning: part of the expression 'la main dans le sac' meaning 'caught in the act' (literally 'the hand in the bag').
additional_notes: By itself 'la main dans le' is incomplete — it's the beginning of the idiom 'la main dans le sac' (to be caught red-handed). Use the full expression when saying someone was caught doing something wrong. Literal image: someone's hand is inside a bag (caught stealing).
target_language_example: Il a été pris la main dans le sac en train de voler.
native_language_example: He was caught red-handed stealing.

meaning: to raise one's hand to ask (a question).
additional_notes: Used to describe the action of raising a hand (in class, a meeting, etc.) with the purpose of asking a question. In examples given the full verb phrase is usually 'lever la main pour poser (une question)'. 'Lever la main' is the core expression; 'pour poser' specifies the intention. Common in classroom contexts.
target_language_example: Il a levé la main pour poser une question pendant le cours.
native_language_example: He raised his hand to ask a question during class.

meaning: This exact form is incorrect in standard French; likely a mistaken mix of 'la majeure' (feminine) or 'le majeur' (masculine).
additional_notes:
There is no common French phrase 'la majeur'. Possible intended forms:
- 'la majeure' (feminine adjective or noun): e.g. 'la majeure partie' = 'the majority' or in music 'la majeure' (major, as in interval/third) when agreeing with a feminine noun.
- 'le majeur' (masculine noun): can mean 'the thumb' (in anatomy) or 'the major' in rank, or 'majeur' as adjective 'adult' => 'le majeur' (the adult male). Spellings and agreement matter: 'majeure/majeur'.
For beginners: learn 'la majeure partie' = 'the majority' and 'majeur/majeure' as adjective meaning 'adult' or 'major'.
target_language_example: La majeure partie des étudiants a réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: The majority of the students passed the exam.

meaning: 'the majority' or 'the greater part' (of something).
additional_notes: Often used in the fixed expression 'la majeure partie (de)' meaning 'the majority of' or 'most of'. Followed by a noun introduced by 'de' (la majeure partie de + noun). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: La majeure partie de la journée, il a travaillé dehors.
native_language_example: Most of the day, he worked outside.

meaning: a bad habit
additional_notes: Used to talk about a repeated behaviour that is considered negative or unhealthy (smoking, biting nails, procrastination). Often used with verbs like avoir (avoir la mauvaise habitude de...), prendre (prendre une mauvaise habitude) or perdre (se débarrasser d'une mauvaise habitude).
target_language_example: J'ai la mauvaise habitude de vérifier mon téléphone la nuit.
native_language_example: I have the bad habit of checking my phone at night.

meaning: the best
additional_notes: Usually this is written as standard French la meilleure, with an extra -e to match the feminine article la. It means the feminine form of “the best,” as in la meilleure option (“the best option”).
target_language_example: C'est la meilleure idée.
native_language_example: It's the best idea.

meaning: swimming (the activity or sport).
additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the act of swimming or the sport of swimming. Used to talk about swimming in general (faire de la nage is less common than nager or faire de la natation). Often appears in contexts like 'la nage synchronisée' (synchronized swimming) or when contrasting different swimming styles (la nage libre = freestyle).
target_language_example: La nage m'aide à rester en forme.
native_language_example: Swimming helps me stay fit.

meaning: 'the news of' or 'news about'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce information or a report concerning someone or something. Often followed by a person, event, or situation (e.g., la nouvelle de son succès, la nouvelle de l'accident). Can be used in formal and neutral contexts. Not to be confused with 'la nouvelle' meaning 'short story' when used alone.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu la nouvelle de sa promotion hier.
native_language_example: I heard the news of his/her promotion yesterday.

meaning: 'the piece of' or 'the room of' depending on context; used as part of a longer phrase.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase — "la pièce de" needs a noun or name after it. It can mean "the piece of (something)" (e.g., la pièce de monnaie = the coin) or start a possessive construction with 'de' (e.g., la pièce de théâtre = the play/literary piece). It can also be used when talking about a room owned or used by someone if followed by a person (less common: la pièce de la maison = the room of the house). Choose the meaning based on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: La pièce de monnaie que j'ai trouvée est vieille.
native_language_example: The coin that I found is old.

meaning: the full (feminine noun phrase) — 'pleine' = full; 'la' = the (feminine).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the feminine singular definite article + adjective 'pleine'. It must agree with a feminine noun that follows or is understood from context (e.g. la pleine lune = the full moon; la pleine conscience = full awareness). On its own 'la pleine' is usually followed by a noun (or part of a noun phrase) and cannot stand alone unless context makes the noun clear. 'Plein'/'pleine' means 'full' or 'filled'.
target_language_example: La pleine lune éclaire la nuit.
native_language_example: The full moon lights up the night.

meaning: most
additional_notes: Used to indicate the majority of a group or amount. Frequently appears as "la plupart de" or "la plupart d'" followed by a noun or pronoun (la plupart d'entre vous = most of you). Can be followed by a verb when referring to most of someone's time/life (la plupart de sa vie).
target_language_example: La plupart des étudiants ont réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: Most of the students passed the exam.

meaning: most people
additional_notes: Used to talk about the majority of people in general. Can be followed by verbs or adjectives. Tone depends on the rest of the sentence (neutral, positive, or negative). Often contracted in speech to "la plupart" when context is clear.
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment les jours ensoleillés.
native_language_example: Most people like sunny days.

meaning: 'most of' (used in the expression 'la plupart du temps' = 'most of the time')
additional_notes: Literally 'the majority of'. Commonly appears in the fixed phrase 'la plupart du temps' meaning 'most of the time' or 'usually'. Can be followed by different nouns (la plupart des gens = most people), but with 'temps' the partitive 'du' (de + le) is used: 'la plupart du temps'.
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the bus to go to work.

meaning: most of the time; usually
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens frequently or generally. Can appear at the start or within a sentence. Equivalent to 'usually' or 'generally' in English.
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the bus to get to work.

meaning: on the tips of the toes; tiptoe (position or movement).
additional_notes: Used to describe standing or moving on the very front of the feet (toes). Common in dance (e.g., ballet) and everyday contexts to indicate quiet, careful movement. Can be singular in expression: 'sur la pointe des pieds' = 'on tiptoe' or 'quietly/on tiptoe'.
target_language_example: Elle est entrée dans la chambre sur la pointe des pieds.
native_language_example: She entered the room on tiptoe.

meaning: 'the apple into' (used with a verb of cutting or dividing to mean splitting the apple into parts)
additional_notes: This phrase fragment appears before a measure or number (e.g. "en deux" = into two). In the examples the full expression is "couper la pomme en deux" = to cut/split the apple into two pieces. The preposition "en" + number/measure indicates the resulting number/size (en deux, en quatre, en morceaux, en tranches). You will normally see the complete phrase (la pomme en deux / en morceaux).
target_language_example: Elle veut couper la pomme en quartiers.
native_language_example: She wants to cut the apple into quarters.

meaning: 'please' (polite request added after an imperative or question; literally 'I beg you').
additional_notes: This is a polite formula often added after a command or question to soften it. Full phrase is "je vous prie" (formal). In spoken French you may hear just "je vous en prie" in replies, but after imperatives/questions it's usually "je vous prie" or simply "s'il vous plaît". Use with verbs: "Fermez la porte, je vous prie." It's formal/polite and suitable in respectful situations.
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: the door of / the ...'s door (possessive construction, followed by a vowel/h or elided noun).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a possessive or descriptive phrase using la porte de, contracted before a vowel or muted h (de + vowel/h → d'). It must be completed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. la porte d'entrée, la porte d'ami, la porte d'Isabelle). In English it corresponds to "the door of..." or "...'s door." You will rarely use la porte d' alone — always complete it (unless trailing off).
target_language_example: La porte d'entrée est verrouillée.
native_language_example: The front door is locked.

meaning: This exact sequence is not idiomatic French; it appears to be a word-order or duplication mistake. Likely intended forms include «la porte ouverte» (the open door) or «la porte est ouverte» (the door is open).
additional_notes: 'La porte ouverte la' is not standard French. It may result from repeating the definite article or misplacing words. Use 'la porte ouverte' to describe a noun phrase (the open door), 'la porte est ouverte' for a complete sentence (the door is open), or 'laisser la porte ouverte' to say someone leaves the door open. If you encounter 'la ... la' at the end of a phrase, check for transcription errors or spoken dialect features.
target_language_example: Je crois que tu as laissé la porte ouverte la, regarde — elle claque avec le vent.
native_language_example: I think you left the door open there, look — it slams in the wind.

meaning: the door left open at night / leaving the door open during the night
additional_notes: Used to refer to the state of a door being left open during the night (often implying a security or comfort issue). Commonly appears in questions about who left the door open. You can replace «la nuit» with a specific night (e.g. «la nuit dernière», «la nuit passée») to indicate which night.
target_language_example: Tu as laissé la porte ouverte la nuit dernière?
native_language_example: Did you leave the door open last night?

meaning: 'the first time that we' (introduces a clause describing the first occasion when we did something)
additional_notes: Used to begin a clause telling when something happened for the first time. Followed by a verb in the past (passé composé, imparfait, plus-que-parfait) or another tense depending on context. Commonly appears in stories or recollections. The phrase can be shortened to "la première fois" when the rest of the clause is clear from context.
target_language_example: La première fois que nous sommes allés en France, nous avons visité Paris.
native_language_example: The first time that we went to France, we visited Paris.

la première fois que nous nous

target_language_multi_word_term: la première fois que nous nous
meaning: 'the first time that we (verb... )' — introduces a memory of a first occasion involving both speakers.
additional_notes: Used to start a clause recalling a first shared experience (commonly followed by a reflexive verb like 'sommes rencontrés', 'nous sommes vus', etc.). Agreement (rencontrés/rencontrées) matches the group's gender(s). Often appears with verbs of remembering: 'se rappeler', 'se souvenir de'.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de la première fois que nous nous sommes parlés.
native_language_example: I remember the first time that we spoke.

meaning: right away; at the very first moment; first thing (in the morning)
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to mean 'immediately' or 'as soon as possible' (e.g., Je m'en occupe la première heure = I'll take care of it right away). Can also be literal: 'the first hour' (e.g., schedule). Context (spoken vs. written) determines whether it's idiomatic or literal. Common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Je t'appelle la première heure demain matin.
native_language_example: I'll call you first thing tomorrow morning / right away tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'the whore' or a strong swear word meaning 'the f***ing (woman)' — very vulgar.
additional_notes: La putain is a highly offensive term in French. Literally 'the whore', it's used to insult someone, to swear in anger, or in expressions like "putain" (without the article) meaning 'damn' or 'fuck'. Do not use in polite conversation. If used to refer to a person, it is derogatory and insulting. In spoken French, people more often say just "putain" as an expletive.
target_language_example: Ne l'appelle pas la putain, ce n'est pas acceptable.
native_language_example: Don't call her 'the whore', that's not acceptable.

meaning: a river named/associated with (used in place names: 'the river of...').
additional_notes: This construction appears in some French place names or geographic descriptions where 'à' links the river to a person, family, or feature (e.g. 'la rivière à Pierre' = 'Pierre's River' or 'the river at Pierre'). It's more common in regional or historical toponymy (especially in Quebec and some older French usages) than in everyday French. In standard modern French you more often see 'la rivière de...' or 'la rivière du/de la ...'.
target_language_example: Nous allons pêcher à la rivière à Jacques ce week-end.
native_language_example: We're going fishing at Jacques's River this weekend.

meaning: the room for/of (used before a noun phrase introduced by à, but incomplete on its own).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the beginning of compound names like "la salle à manger" (dining room) or "la salle à boire" (rare). You will always need the following word(s) to know which room is meant. Remember the full expressions are feminine singular: la salle à manger, la salle à jouer, etc.
target_language_example: Nous déjeunons dans la salle à manger.
native_language_example: We have lunch in the dining room.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; literally 'health is more'. Likely an incorrect, incomplete, or context-dependent fragment rather than a complete idiom.
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a common standalone expression. 'La santé' = health; 'est' = is; 'plus' can mean 'more' or (with 'ne') 'no longer'. Without surrounding context or grammatical markers, the phrase is ambiguous and usually incorrect as a complete sentence. Possible intended sentences using the same words: - 'La santé est plus importante que l'argent.' (Health is more important than money.) - 'La santé est plus fragile qu'on ne le croit.' (Health is more fragile than one thinks.) - 'La santé est plus qu'une absence de maladie.' (Health is more than the absence of disease.) If you meant 'no longer,' you would normally write 'n'est plus' (e.g., 'Il n'est plus en bonne santé').
target_language_example: La santé est plus importante que l'argent.
native_language_example: Health is more important than money.

meaning: the sister (female sibling) or a nun (in religious contexts).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a female sibling. In religious contexts, especially in church-related texts or when capitalized, it can mean 'a nun' or a sister in a religious order. The definite article 'la' makes it specific: 'the sister'. To say 'my sister' use 'ma sœur'. Pronunciation: [la sœʁ].
target_language_example: La sœur de Marie est médecin.
native_language_example: Marie's sister is a doctor.

meaning: the falling/setting (often used for 'the fall' of night — 'the onset of' something, e.g. 'la tombée de la nuit' = nightfall).
additional_notes: Often appears in fixed expressions like «la tombée de la nuit» (nightfall) or «la tombée du jour» (dusk). It is a feminine noun derived from the verb tomber (to fall). Used to talk about the moment when something 'falls' into place or begins (most commonly day → night).
target_language_example: Nous partons avant la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We leave before nightfall.

meaning: the falling of / the onset of (used with times or things that 'fall' or begin, e.g. la tombée de la nuit = the onset of night).
additional_notes: Often used in fixed expressions like "la tombée de la nuit" (dusk/nightfall) or "la tombée du jour" (dusk). It conveys the idea of something descending or beginning (light, night, silence). It is followed by a noun and translated as "the onset/coming/fall of" in English. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous partirons à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We will leave at nightfall.

meaning: with head held high; confidently, proudly
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to act confidently or to describe doing something without shame or embarrassment. Common in commands (Garde la tête haute) and statements (rentrer la tête haute). Literal components are understandable (tête = head, haute = high), so it's compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Après l'entretien, elle est repartie la tête haute.
native_language_example: After the interview, she left with her head held high.

meaning: 'the head that' or 'the head which' (literal fragment used to introduce a relative clause about 'la tête')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a fragment: la tête (the head) followed by qui (who/which) begins a relative clause describing the head. In natural speech you normally see it as part of a full sentence (e.g. la tête qui tourne = the head that is spinning / feeling dizzy). Useful to recognize when reading or listening so you can connect the noun with the following clause.
target_language_example: J'ai la tête qui tourne après la montagne russe.
native_language_example: My head is spinning after the roller coaster.

meaning: 'the cow' (literal) — also an exclamation like 'wow'/'oh my!'
additional_notes: Literally means the female cow. Commonly used in spoken French as an informal interjection (Oh la vache !) to express surprise, astonishment, annoyance or admiration — similar to 'wow', 'jeez', or 'oh my goodness' in English. In a literal context it refers to the animal (e.g. donner du lait, traire). Tone and context tell you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: La vache donne du lait chaque matin.
native_language_example: The cow gives milk every morning.

meaning: This sequence is not a standard French phrase; likely a mistake or fragment (for example, an extra repeated article).
additional_notes: In French, 'la ville' means 'the city' or 'the town'. Seeing 'la' twice — 'la ville la' — is almost always an error, an incomplete sentence, or colloquial/regional speech where a final 'la' can be an emphatic filler. For correct usage use 'la ville' alone. If you meant possession or specification use 'de la ville' (of the city) or 'la ville de...' (the city of...).
target_language_example: Je visite la ville la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: I'm visiting the city next week.

meaning: the city where I (was/was born, live, etc.).
additional_notes: A relative expression combining 'la ville' (the city) + 'où' (where) + a verb with 'je'. Use it to point to a specific city connected to the speaker (birthplace, residence, memories). 'Où' introduces a clause of place and is followed by a verb (e.g. 'suis né', 'vis', 'ai grandi'). Agreement (né/née) depends on the speaker's gender when using past participles.
target_language_example: La ville où je vis est tranquille.
native_language_example: The city where I live is peaceful.

meaning: is very unsatisfactory; leaves much to be desired.
additional_notes: Used in the fixed expression 'laisser beaucoup à désirer' meaning something is disappointing or not good enough. Usually follows the subject (Ce rapport laisse beaucoup à désirer). You can also say simply 'laisse à désirer' (without 'beaucoup') — 'beaucoup' intensifies the criticism. Formal register-neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: La qualité du repas laisse beaucoup à désirer.
native_language_example: The quality of the meal leaves much to be desired.

meaning: leave that / stop that (imperative: tell someone to stop or leave something alone).
additional_notes: Informal command made of laisser (to leave/let) + demonstrative ce. Commonly used to tell someone to stop doing something or to leave an object/situation alone: 'Laisse ça' is more frequent than 'laisse ce' before a noun (which would become 'laisse ce ...'). Alone, 'laisse ce' is often followed by a noun (e.g. 'laisse ce livre') or used in speech as 'laisse, ce...' to mean 'forget it' or 'never mind' when followed by an explanation. Tone can be sharp depending on context.
target_language_example: Laisse ce livre, il est abîmé.
native_language_example: Leave that book, it's damaged.

meaning: 'leave my' or 'let my' (imperative + possessive beginning).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself: "laisse" is the imperative of laisser (to leave/let) and "mon" is the masculine singular possessive (my). It typically appears at the start of commands like "Laisse mon sac!" (Leave my bag alone!) or in spoken contractions: "Laisse mon..." followed by a noun. In casual speech you may also hear "laisse-moi" (leave me / let me) which is different ("moi" = me).
target_language_example: Laisse mon sac, s'il te plaît.
