meaning: Used to single out or contrast a person and introduce a comment about them — roughly 'as for him/her' or 'him, that...'.
additional_notes: Informal conversational expression. 'Lui' is a disjunctive (stressed) pronoun; 'ça' adds emphasis or starts the ensuing remark. Often followed by a clause about habits, preferences, or character. Word order is fixed: 'lui ça' at the start of the comment. Tone can be positive or negative depending on context.
target_language_example: Lui, ça le fatigue de voyager autant.
native_language_example: As for him, traveling that much tires him.

meaning: 'to shed light on' / 'to make clear' when used as part of expressions like 'faire la lumière au/ sur' (note: 'au' appears when followed by a masculine noun introduced with 'à' in some constructions)
additional_notes: On its own 'lumière au' is not a standalone idiom; it appears inside larger phrases such as 'donner/mettre/faire la lumière au + [masculine noun]' or more commonly 'faire la lumière sur + [quelque chose]'. When 'au' appears it results from the contraction of 'à le' and links 'lumière' to a masculine noun (e.g. 'faire la lumière au témoin'). Use with care: 'faire la lumière sur' is more frequent for 'shed light on'.
target_language_example: Le détective a fait la lumière au témoin avant l'audience.
native_language_example: The detective shed light on (or clarified things for) the witness before the hearing.

meaning: light of / light from (used to indicate the source or type of light).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun to describe the origin, color, quality or metaphorical sense of light (e.g. lumière du soleil, lumière de la lune, lumière de la lampe). Can be literal (physical light) or figurative (a new perspective: «à la lumière de» meaning "in light of"). When used in the idiomatic phrase «à la lumière de», it means "in light of" or "considering".
target_language_example: La lumière de la lune éclaire le jardin.
native_language_example: The light of the moon lights the garden.

meaning: literally 'light is' — not a fixed phrase in French; appears as part of a sentence (e.g. 'la lumière est...').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase. In French you will often see 'la lumière est' or 'la lumière est ...' followed by an adjective or clause to describe the light (e.g. 'la lumière est forte', 'la lumière est douce', 'la lumière est arrivée'). Always include the article (la/une) or context. Use 'lumière' (feminine noun) with appropriate agreement: 'la lumière est belle.'
target_language_example: La lumière est belle ce matin.
native_language_example: The light is beautiful this morning.

meaning: literally 'Monday and' — used to link 'Monday' with what follows (part of a sentence), not a fixed phrase.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the day 'lundi' followed by the conjunction 'et' ('and'). In the example sentences it connects two clauses: 'came on Monday' and 'left the next day'. You will rarely learn 'lundi et' as a standalone chunk — instead learn 'le lundi' (on Monday) and the conjunction 'et' separately. Note the article 'le' before weekdays is common to mean 'on Monday'.
target_language_example: Il est arrivé le lundi et est reparti mardi.
native_language_example: He arrived on Monday and left on Tuesday.

meaning: on Monday at (followed by a time or place).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to specify when something will happen: 'lundi à 14h' = 'on Monday at 2 pm', or 'lundi à la maison' = 'on Monday at the house'. In spoken French times are often given with 'à' plus the hour. If you only want to say 'on Monday' without adding time/place, use 'lundi' alone.
target_language_example: Rendez-vous lundi à 9h au bureau.
native_language_example: Meeting on Monday at 9 at the office.

meaning: used as the first part of compound expressions referring to a period or a relation involving the moon (e.g., 'lune de miel' = honeymoon) or figurative uses ('lune de...').
additional_notes: Alone 'lune' means 'moon'. The fragment 'lune de' isn't a standalone phrase: it appears at the start of compounds or expressions (most common: 'lune de miel' = honeymoon). When you see 'lune de' expect a noun after 'de' that completes the expression. Not idiomatic by itself.
target_language_example: Ils viennent de rentrer de leur lune de miel.
native_language_example: They just came back from their honeymoon.

meaning: honeymoon
additional_notes: Used to refer to the vacation or period right after a wedding. Can also be used metaphorically for a short, idyllic period after a new beginning (e.g., a 'honeymoon' phase). Always feminine singular: 'la lune de miel' or 'une lune de miel.'
target_language_example: Ils partent en lune de miel en Grèce après le mariage.
native_language_example: They're going on their honeymoon to Greece after the wedding.

meaning: part of a phrase that introduces the type or purpose of glasses (e.g. lunettes de soleil = sunglasses; lunettes de lecture = reading glasses).
additional_notes: Lunettes means 'glasses' or 'spectacles'. When followed by de + noun, it specifies the kind or function: 'de soleil' (for sun), 'de lecture' (for reading), 'de protection' (for protection). Remember to include the article when needed: 'des lunettes de soleil' or 'une paire de lunettes de lecture'.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une paire de lunettes de soleil.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of sunglasses.

meaning: sunglasses (eye-wear that protects from the sun).
additional_notes: Plural in French (always used in the plural form). 'Lunettes' = 'glasses'; adding 'de soleil' specifies sunglasses. Used like other plural nouns: mes lunettes de soleil, tes lunettes de soleil. Can be worn for style or eye protection.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté de nouvelles lunettes de soleil pour les vacances.
native_language_example: I bought new sunglasses for the holiday.

meaning: black sunglasses / black eyeglasses (depending on context).
additional_notes: Typically refers to dark-colored glasses. In everyday use, 'lunettes noires' most often means sunglasses (to protect from the sun) but can also mean black-framed eyeglasses. Use context: daytime/outdoor = sunglasses; indoors/night or about frames = black eyeglasses.
target_language_example: Elle porte des lunettes noires quand il fait soleil.
native_language_example: She wears black sunglasses when it's sunny.

meaning: 'there/then, we' — a sequence used to introduce what 'we' did or will do at that time or place
additional_notes: The phrase combines là (there/then/at that point) with nous (we). Depending on context, là can indicate a location (there), a moment in time (then/that night), or a discourse marker (and then). It's used to set the scene or point to a specific moment/place before saying what 'we' did or will do. Punctuation and intonation matter: 'là, nous...' often translates as 'and then we...' or 'at that time we...'.
target_language_example: Là, nous avons décidé de partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: At that moment, we decided to leave immediately.

meaning: over there
additional_notes: Used to point to a place that is away from the speaker, often farther away than just là. It can refer to a physical place or a more general distant location.
target_language_example: Je vois la gare là-bas.
native_language_example: I can see the station over there.

meaning: in there
additional_notes: Used to refer to a place or container that is inside or in an interior space. Common in spoken French; can point to location ('there inside') or to people/things located inside. Often used with gestures or context. Can be contracted in casual speech (y'a quelqu'un là-dedans?).
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu'un là-dedans ?
native_language_example: Is there someone in there?

meaning: about that / on that / on it (refers back to something just mentioned)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a topic, object, or matter mentioned earlier. Can mean 'about that' (discussing a subject) or 'on that'/'on it' (working on, placing something). Often follows the thing it refers to (e.g. 'J'ai lu un article là‑dessus' = 'I read an article about that'). Can also begin a sentence to introduce a conclusion or limitation ('Là‑dessus, nous ne pouvons pas aider' = 'On that point we can't help').
target_language_example: J'ai lu un article là‑dessus.
native_language_example: I read an article about that.

meaning: up there
additional_notes: Indicates a location higher than the speaker (physically above or at a higher place). Can refer to something above in the same building (upstairs), on a hill/roof, or more figuratively (e.g., 'up there' in the sky). Context decides whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Il y a un oiseau là-haut dans l'arbre.
native_language_example: There is a bird up there in the tree.

meaning: Not a standard French multi-word phrase. Likely a mistaken sequence produced by a typo, a missing apostrophe (should be 'l'a'), or an improper separation of words ('là' + 'a' used separately). 'là' = there/here; 'a' = third-person singular of 'avoir' (has).
additional_notes:
Written as 'là a' (with a space and no apostrophe) is non-idiomatic. Possible intended forms:
- Typo for 'l'a' (contraction of 'le/la' + 'a') as in 'Il l'a vu' = 'He saw it' — note the apostrophe.
- Two separate words 'là' and 'a' used in different parts of a sentence, but they would normally not appear adjacent without punctuation (e.g. 'Là, à côté, ...').
Beginners: treat 'là' and 'a' separately and watch for the contraction 'l'' + verb. Avoid writing 'là a' as a unit.
target_language_example: Il pense que là a été la première fois.
native_language_example: He thinks that there was the first time.

meaning: 'there at the' or 'over at the' (combination of là + au)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but the sequence of adverb là ('there') followed by the contracted preposition au (à + le, 'to/at the'). Common in spoken and written French when pointing to or specifying a location: e.g. « Là au fond de la salle, il y a une fenêtre. » Word order and agreement follow normal rules (au = à + le). Depending on context, là can emphasize location ('right there') or serve as a discourse marker ('well, ...').
target_language_example: Là au fond de la salle, il y a une fenêtre.
native_language_example: There at the back of the room, there is a window.

meaning: there with / here with (indicates being together with someone or something at a place).
additional_notes: Combination of là (there/here/at that place) + avec (with). Used to say someone or something is at a place together with someone/something else. Context determines whether là means 'there' or 'here' (often spoken as 'là' to point). Common in spoken French: e.g. « Il est là avec moi » = 'He is here with me.'
target_language_example: Elle est là avec ses amis.
native_language_example: She is there with her friends.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; typically a sequence of the adverb 'là' plus the demonstrative 'ce' used in spoken French to draw attention or begin a comment (often with a pause or comma). It signals 'now/then, this/that' before continuing.
additional_notes: Written as 'là ce' without punctuation is unusual; more natural is 'là, ce...' with a pause. Do not treat it as a single grammatical unit — learn 'là' and 'ce' separately. 'Là' can mean 'there', 'here', or colloquially 'now/then'; 'ce' is the neutral demonstrative pronoun/adjective. Example usages often include a following clause: e.g. 'Là ce, ...' appears only in rapid speech or transcriptions and is better rendered as 'Là, ce que...'
target_language_example: Là ce que je veux dire, c'est que tu devrais appeler avant de venir.
native_language_example: What I mean is that you should call before coming.

meaning: a combination used to point to something specific ('there' + 'what/that which'); often appears in phrases like « c'est là ce que... » meaning 'that is what...'.
additional_notes: Rare as an isolated fixed phrase; it combines 'là' (there / here / that) with 'ce que' (what / that which). You'll usually see it inside larger structures: e.g. « C'est là ce que je voulais dire » = 'That's what I meant.' Word order and context determine nuance (emphasis on 'that').
target_language_example: C'est là ce que je voulais te montrer.
native_language_example: That's what I wanted to show you.

meaning: 'there' + 'what you' (fragment used in sentences like "voilà ce que tu..." or "c'est là ce que tu...")
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence of words that can appear in different contexts. Often appears in constructions like "voilà ce que tu..." (here/this is what you...) or "c'est là ce que tu..." (that's what you...). Alone it is incomplete and needs a verb or rest of the clause. The pronoun "tu" is the familiar singular 'you'.
target_language_example: Voilà ce que tu dois faire.
native_language_example: Here's what you must do.

meaning: a fragment meaning 'there/that which you...' used to introduce what someone does or feels (incomplete phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed expression by itself; it's a sequence that can appear in sentences like « C'est là ce que vous voulez ? » or « Voilà là ce que vous demandiez. » In natural French you'd more often hear complete forms such as « c'est ce que vous... », « voilà ce que vous... », or « est-ce là ce que vous... ». Use it only as part of a full sentence; it points to 'that' (là/voilà) and introduces what 'you' (vous) do, want, said, etc.
target_language_example: Est-ce là ce que vous cherchiez ?
native_language_example: Is that what you were looking for?

meaning: 'there in' or 'over there in' — points to a location or moment (informal spoken usage).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a combination of 'là' (there/then) and 'dans' (in/within). Used to indicate a place ('là, dans la cuisine' = 'there, in the kitchen') or a time/period ('là dans une semaine' = 'there in a week' i.e. 'in about a week'). Often appears with a pause or comma: 'là, dans...'. Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the words that follow. Useful in casual speech.
target_language_example: Tu vois la boîte là dans le coin ?
native_language_example: Do you see the box over there in the corner?

meaning: in five (minutes) / in five (units) — indicates something will happen five units from now (usually minutes).
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken French with an implied time unit (often minutes): e.g. « J'arrive là dans cinq » means 'I'll be there in five (minutes)'. The noun for the unit is often omitted in casual speech. Can also be followed by a full expression like « là dans cinq minutes ». "Là" adds immediacy ("right now/in a moment").
target_language_example: Attends, j'arrive là dans cinq.
native_language_example: Wait, I'll be there in five (minutes).

meaning: 'there in a' or 'over there in a' (phrase fragment used to point to something located inside/within one [feminine noun])
additional_notes: This is a sequence of words rather than a fixed idiom; you will usually see it followed by a feminine noun (une) and describes something located 'there' inside or 'over there in a ...'. Context determines exact translation (e.g., là dans une boîte = 'there in a box'). It's conversational and common in spoken French when pointing something out. It is not a standalone sentence and typically appears as part of a larger clause.
target_language_example: Regarde là dans une boîte, il y a des photos.
native_language_example: Look there in a box, there are some photos.

meaning: A sequence where là (demonstrative/locative) is followed by de to refer back to or specify something previously mentioned or pointed out — roughly ‘that ... of’ / ‘there ... from’ depending on context. It is not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on surrounding words and syntax.
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written French when singling out or linking an item to its source/attribute: e.g. 'la maison là de mon oncle' (that house of my uncle) or 'le goût là de ce fromage' (that taste of this cheese). Usage and punctuation vary; in many cases you may see 'là' separated from 'de' by the noun it modifies. Not always translatable literally into English; consider rephrasing (e.g. 'that ... from/of').
target_language_example: Tu vois la photo là de Marie ?
native_language_example: Do you see that picture of Marie?

meaning: 'there' + 'in/on' — a short spoken sequence used to point to a place, time or situation before continuing the sentence; often marks attention or contrast and is followed immediately by another word or phrase beginning with 'en' (e.g. 'en ce moment', 'en bas')
additional_notes: Informal spoken sequence. 'Là' can mean 'there' or 'now' and is used to draw attention; 'en' begins the following expression. On its own 'là en' is incomplete and functions as a discourse marker or lead-in (pause/filler) to what comes next: place, time, or circumstance. Common in conversation: 'Là en bas...', 'Là en ce moment...'.
target_language_example: Là en bas, il y a un café sympa.
native_language_example: Down there, there's a nice café.

meaning: 'there is' or 'there lies' (used to point out where something is or what the main issue is).
additional_notes: Combines 'là' (there) + verb 'est' (is). Often used to emphasize location or to introduce the core point: e.g. « Là est le problème » = 'There lies the problem' / 'That's the problem.' It is grammatical but slightly formal or literary in some contexts; in everyday speech you might also hear « c'est là » or « voilà le problème ». Word order matters: 'là est' typically precedes a noun or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Là est la différence entre les deux méthodes.
native_language_example: There lies the difference between the two methods.

meaning: This exact sequence is not a standard or grammatical French phrase; it appears to be a mistaken ordering of words (likely intended as "là pour" or "est pour").
additional_notes:
"là est pour" does not occur in normal French. Possible intended components:
- "là pour" (compositional): used to indicate presence or purpose (e.g. "Je suis là pour t'aider." = "I'm here to help you").
- "est pour" (compositional): part of a clause meaning "is for" or "supports" (e.g. "Il est pour la réforme." = "He is for the reform").
If you encounter "là est pour" in written text, it is almost certainly a typo, word-order error, or fragment of a larger sentence. For learners, prefer the standard constructions "être là pour" and "être pour."
target_language_example: Dans cette phrase mal écrite, « là est pour » n'a pas de sens.
native_language_example: In this poorly written sentence, "là est pour" has no meaning.

meaning: 'there and' — not a fixed phrase; 'là' (there/then) followed by conjunction 'et' (and) used in various contexts.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiomatic expression. 'Là' can mean 'there' (place) or 'then' (time); 'et' simply means 'and'. In sentences like 'Il était assis là et fumait sa pipe.' it links two actions or descriptions: 'He was sitting there and was smoking his pipe.' In imperative location + instruction ("Mets-toi là et reste debout."), it means 'Put yourself there and...'. In 'ce soir-là et ...' the '-là' is a locative/time marker attached to a noun or adverb (ce soir-là = that evening) and 'et' still connects clauses. Because it's just two common words used together, treat them separately when learning.
target_language_example: Reste là et attends-moi cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Stay there and wait for me five minutes.

meaning: 'there' (là) + subject pronoun 'he/it' (il); in spoken French used at the start of a comment or to point to something — often functions as a discourse marker meaning 'so, well, here...' before a statement.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but the sequence adverb + pronoun. In conversation speakers use 'là', 'là il' or 'là elle' to draw attention, introduce a remark, contrast, or resume a story. The comma is often a slight pause when spoken: 'Là il...' can signal emphasis, transition, or clarification. Informal and common in everyday speech; not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Là il a dit que ce n'était pas possible, alors on est partis.
native_language_example: So he said it wasn't possible, so we left.

meaning: Part of the expression 'là il y a' meaning 'there is/there are' (used to point out or emphasize something right there).
additional_notes: By itself 'là il y' is incomplete; it appears in phrases like 'là il y a' or 'là, il y a' to indicate existence or to draw attention to something nearby. Common in spoken and written French; a pause or comma after 'là' increases emphasis (e.g. 'Là, il y a un problème.').
target_language_example: Là il y a un chat sur le balcon.
native_language_example: There is a cat on the balcony (right there).

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; most likely a mistaken juxtaposition of 'là' (there/here) and 'le' (the / him/it).
additional_notes: In French, 'là' means 'there' or 'here' and is typically used alone or in fixed forms (e.g. 'là-bas', 'voilà'). 'Le' is the masculine singular definite article or a direct object pronoun. 'Là le' does not form a correct lexicalized expression; if you encounter it it may be a transcription of hesitancy in speech (e.g. 'là, le...') or a typographical error where punctuation is missing ('là, le ...'). Grammatically, the order 'là le' can appear in casual spoken sequences before a pause but is not a standard phrase to be learned as a unit.
target_language_example: Là le, je ne sais pas quoi dire — c'était surprenant.
native_language_example: There, um, I don't know what to say — it was surprising.

meaning: 'there, there' — used like English 'there, there' to comfort someone or call attention (can be gentle/reassuring) or sometimes to tell someone to calm down.
additional_notes: Often said softly to comfort a person or animal (similar to 'there, there' in English). Can also be used to gently chide or to draw attention to something nearby when stressed. Tone and context determine meaning. Not commonly written formally; mainly spoken.
target_language_example: Là là, ça va aller, ne t'inquiète pas.
native_language_example: There, there, it'll be okay, don't worry.

meaning: here/there + we/one/you (subject) — used to introduce or comment on a situation (informal spoken link: 'so, here we...').
additional_notes: Combination of adverb là ('here' or 'there') and subject pronoun on (colloquial 'we', 'one', or 'you' depending on context). Common in spoken French to start a sentence or clause and draw attention to what follows: e.g. 'Là on fait quoi ?' = 'So, what do we do now?'. Placement: usually 'Là, on...' or 'Là on...' with a slight pause. Tone: conversational; frequently used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Là on fait quoi maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

meaning: a sequence used in spoken/written French to point to a moment/place and introduce a clause about 'I' (literally 'there that I' — often part of constructions like "c'est là que je..." meaning "that's when/where I...").
additional_notes: By itself 'là que je' is not a standalone phrase; it typically appears inside larger expressions such as "c'est là que je...", "voilà là que je...", or "là que je me rends compte...". In those contexts, 'là' (there/then) + 'que' (that) introduces a clause explaining what 'I' did, felt, or realized. Commonly used to indicate a specific moment, place, or turning point ("that's when I..." / "that's where I..."). Register: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: C'est là que je me suis rendu compte de mon erreur.
native_language_example: That's when I realized my mistake.

meaning: 'là que je l'' is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's a fragment that typically begins a clause meaning "there that I/that I ..." or "it's there that I ..." depending on context.
additional_notes: This sequence is a fragment combining là (there), que (that/which/when introducing a clause), je (I) and the start of a verb/object clitic l' (le/la/les before a vowel). You will see it inside longer sentences such as "C'est là que je l'ai vu" (It's there that I saw him/it) or "Là que je l'entends, il est parti" (colloquial word order). By itself it is incomplete; you need the rest of the clause (verb and object) to understand the meaning. Typical uses: to point out a place or moment ("it's there/then that...") or in spoken/colloquial reorderings.
target_language_example: C'est là que je l'ai rencontré.
native_language_example: That's where I met him/her/it.

meaning: 'it's there that I (have) ...' — used to point out where or when you did something (e.g. found or saw someone/something).
additional_notes: Common structure: C'est là que je l'ai + past participle (trouvé(e), vu(e), etc.). Used to emphasize the place or moment where an action occurred. The past tense is usually passé composé (je l'ai trouvé). Agreement of past participle with direct object (e.g. trouvée/voir → vue) depends on gender and position of the object pronoun 'l''.
target_language_example: C'est là que je l'ai perdue.
native_language_example: That's where I lost it.

meaning: 'there that you' — part of a clause meaning 'when/where/at the point that you...' or 'it's there that you...'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; 'là que tu' appears in sentences to introduce a relative or explanatory clause (e.g. «C'est là que tu vois...», «Là que tu arrives, ...»). Often equivalent to English 'that's where/when you...' or 'it's then that you...'. Context determines whether it refers to place (where) or time/point (when/that). Usually follows or starts a clause and is informal/neutral conversational French.
target_language_example: C'est là que tu comprends la différence.
native_language_example: That's when you understand the difference.

meaning: used to point to a place, moment, or situation: 'there that you...' → 'it's there that you... / is that where you...?'
additional_notes: Combines 'là' (there) with a relative clause introduced by 'que' plus 'vous'. Common in questions and statements to indicate location, time, or the point where something happens. Word order: 'C'est là que vous...' or 'Est-ce là que vous...?' Often translated as 'is that where you...?', 'that's where you...','or 'it's there that you...'.
target_language_example: C'est là que vous travaillez maintenant?
native_language_example: Is that where you work now?

meaning: a spoken sequence used to point to or emphasize something just mentioned (literally 'there that it') — often part of a larger phrase like « c'est là que ça... »
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; you will usually hear it inside sentences such as « C'est là que ça se complique » (That's where it gets complicated) or « C'est là que ça pose problème » (That's where the problem lies). It is colloquial and common in speech. The phrase combines « là » (there/that) + « que » (that/where) + « ça » (this/it) to point to a moment, place, or aspect previously mentioned.
target_language_example: C'est là que ça devient intéressant.
native_language_example: That's where it becomes interesting.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; appears to be two separate words: 'là' (there) and the reflexive pronoun 'se'.
additional_notes: You will almost never see 'là se' as a single idiomatic unit. 'Là' means 'there' or 'here' (depending on context). 'Se' is a reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (il se lave = he washes himself). If you encounter 'là se' it is likely part of a sentence where 'là' is an adverb and 'se' begins a reflexive verb following it, e.g. 'Là se trouve...' (There is/are ... / There lies ...). Common correct constructions: 'Là se trouve...', 'Là se cachent...', 'Là se situe...'.
target_language_example: Là se trouve la bibliothèque du village.
native_language_example: There is the village library.

meaning: 'there if' (literal), often used in spoken French to add emphasis or to set up a condition — similar to 'now if...' or 'if (you/it) is/are there' in English.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself but a common spoken sequence. 'Là' can mean 'there' or colloquially 'now'; 'si' means 'if' (or 'yes' in other contexts). Together 'là si' frequently appears at the start of a clause to introduce a condition or to emphasize a contrast (e.g. 'Là si on part tard...' → 'Now, if we leave late...'). Intonation and context determine the nuance. Informal register is common.
target_language_example: Là si on part tard, on ratera le dernier train.
native_language_example: Now, if we leave late, we'll miss the last train.

meaning: 'there for you' — used to say you'll be present or available if someone needs you.
additional_notes: Common phrase in offers of help or support. Usually follows subject + être (Je suis / Je serai) and is completed by a verb phrase introduced by 'tu' (e.g. 'tu as besoin', 'tu as besoin de parler'). Tone is friendly and reassuring. Can be used with present ('je suis là si tu...') or future ('je serai là si tu...').
target_language_example: Je suis là si tu as besoin de parler ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm here if you need to talk tonight.

meaning: Colloquial spoken phrase used to draw attention before mentioning possession: literally 'there your' or 'here your'. Often introduces a noun or points something out to the listener (familiar register).
additional_notes: Informal, conversational. 'Là' functions as an attention marker ('there'/'here') and 'ta' is the familiar feminine possessive 'your' (the following noun is feminine). Common in rapid speech: e.g. 'Là, ta clé' if feminine, though note 'clé' is feminine so 'ta clé' is correct. For masculine nouns use 'là ton'. Avoid in formal writing; use 'voici/voilà ta/ton' instead. Tone can be slightly brusque or casual depending on context.
target_language_example: —Tu l'as vu ? —Là, ta clé, elle est sur la table.
native_language_example: —Did you see it? —There, your key, it's on the table.

meaning: a colloquial/discourse filler meaning 'right now' or 'at this point' (adding emphasis).
additional_notes: Used informally in spoken French to emphasize timing or a current state: 'là' = 'there/now', 'tout' intensifies. Often appears with 'de suite' or alone as 'là' (e.g. 'là tout de suite'). On its own 'là tout' is casual and may be followed by another word (e.g. 'là tout de suite').
target_language_example: Là tout, je suis un peu fatigué.
native_language_example: Right now, I'm a bit tired.

meaning: a colloquial sequence used to emphasize 'all that' or 'everything that' (usually part of a larger phrase), often introducing what follows.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone expression; typically appears with commas and followed by que + clause (e.g. « là, tout ce que... ») or before a noun phrase. Common in informal spoken French to add emphasis or immediacy. Do not use alone—place it inside a full sentence.
target_language_example: Là tout ce que je veux, c'est du calme.
native_language_example: Right now, all I want is some peace and quiet.

meaning: 'there a' — not a fixed phrase; 'là' (there/then) followed immediately by the indefinite article 'un' (a/an) in a sentence
additional_notes: Not an idiomatic multiword expression. 'Là' can be a discourse marker ('then/there') or locative ('there'), and may be followed directly by 'un' when pointing out or specifying a single item: word order and meaning depend on context. Do not treat 'là un' as one lexical unit—translate each word separately.
target_language_example: Là un homme se tenait à la porte.
native_language_example: There a man was standing at the door.

meaning: a formal/Polite way to present or hand something to someone (literally: ‘here is yours’ or ‘here you are’).
additional_notes: Used when giving or showing an item to someone in polite or formal contexts (often in shops, restaurants, or when handing documents). It combines 'là' (here) + 'votre' (your). You might also see shorter forms like 'le voici' / 'la voici' or informal 'voilà'.
target_language_example: Voici votre ticket, et là votre table est prête.
native_language_example: Here is your ticket, and there your table is ready.

meaning: A sequence of the adverb 'là' (there/right there) immediately followed by the preposition 'à' (at/to), used to emphasize a location or moment — roughly 'right there at' or 'right at'. It is not a fixed idiom but a juxtaposition that occurs in spoken or written French to add immediacy.
additional_notes: Treat 'là' and 'à' as separate words performing their usual roles: 'là' points or emphasizes, 'à' introduces a complement. The sequence 'là à' appears in contexts like 'là à côté', 'là à l'entrée' or 'là à ce moment-là'. Avoid writing them as a single fused preposition. Formal written French may prefer punctuation or reordering (e.g., 'là, à...') but 'là à' can appear in natural speech.
target_language_example: Il se tenait là à l'entrée, sans rien dire.
native_language_example: He stood right there at the entrance, saying nothing.

meaning: to leave someone alone; to stop bothering or pestering someone.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to tell someone to stop annoying, following, or nagging you. Common in spoken, familiar contexts (friends, family). Can be stronger or more colloquial than 'laisse-moi tranquille' depending on tone. Literally 'let go of the bunch' (of grapes), which has no literal meaning in English.
target_language_example: Tu devrais lâcher la grappe à Julie, elle en a marre.
native_language_example: You should leave Julie alone, she's had enough.

meaning: gets up at (a time) / rises to (a level) — usually used with a subject (il/elle) and a time or amount.
additional_notes: Form: third-person singular of the verb se lever (se lever → il/elle se lève). When followed by à + time, it means 'gets up at' (e.g. Il se lève à 7 h). It can also be used transitively in other contexts (e.g. 'la marée se lève' — 'the tide rises'), but 'lève à' as presented is most likely 'gets up at'. Use reflexive pronoun (je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève).
target_language_example: Il se lève à sept heures tous les matins.
native_language_example: He gets up at seven every morning.

meaning: 'self-defense' (justified use of force to protect oneself or others).
additional_notes: Legal term used when someone uses force because they reasonably believe it is necessary to prevent harm. Often used in court contexts (plaider la légitime défense). Can describe both physical actions and the legal justification for them.
target_language_example: Il a agi en légitime défense quand il a repoussé l'assaillant.
native_language_example: He acted in self-defense when he pushed the attacker away.

meaning: 'the vegetables are' (third-person plural of être with légumes).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'légumes' (vegetables) followed by the verb 'sont' (are). It's not an idiom—used to describe a state or quality of vegetables (e.g., 'Les légumes sont frais' = 'The vegetables are fresh'). Remember French requires the definite article: 'Les légumes sont...' rather than just 'Légumes sont...' unless in a headline or note.
target_language_example: Les légumes sont prêts à être cuisinés.
native_language_example: The vegetables are ready to be cooked.

meaning: the makings/qualities of (someone); having the potential or right stuff for something.
additional_notes: Used idiomatically with 'avoir l’étoffe de/ d’un/une + profession/role' to say someone has the qualities, talent, or potential to become that. Similar to English 'have the makings of' or 'have the right stuff.' Often followed by a profession or role.
target_language_example: Il a l’étoffe d’un bon leader.
native_language_example: He has the makings of a good leader.

meaning: has the makings of / is cut out to be (someone)
additional_notes: Used to say someone has the qualities, character, or potential to become a certain type of person (often followed by a profession or role). Formal/neutral register. Structure: l'étoffe d'un/une + [article] + [profession/role].
target_language_example: Elle a l’étoffe d’une bonne cheffe.
native_language_example: She has the makings of a good chef.

meaning: told me to (do something) for/about you; literally 'told me to you' but functions as '[someone] told me to give/bring/ask something to you'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment typically followed by a verb or object (e.g. 'm'a dit de vous donner ça' = 'told me to give this to you'). 'M'' is the clitic for 'me' (to/for me), and 'a dit' is the passé composé of 'dire' (to tell). It indicates that a third person instructed the speaker to do something involving 'vous' (you/formal or plural). Common in polite or formal contexts. Can be used with named subjects (Elle, Il, On, M. X).
target_language_example: Le directeur m'a dit de vous apporter les documents.
native_language_example: The director told me to bring you the documents.

meaning: to me
additional_notes: Contraction of me + a before a vowel. In these examples, it appears in the pattern m'a l'air / ça m'a l'air..., which means something like 'seems to me' or 'looks ... to me.' In other contexts, m'a can also simply be part of a verb phrase, as in il m'a vu ('he saw me').
target_language_example: Ça m'a l'air facile.
native_language_example: That seems easy to me.

meaning: 'you have never (to me)' — contracted spoken form of 'tu ne m'as jamais ...' (you have never ... me).
additional_notes: This is the informal/conversational contracted form appearing in sentences with 'tu' + passé composé and the negation 'ne ... jamais' (never). The full form is 'tu ne m'as jamais ...' meaning 'you have never ... me' (e.g., helped me, told me). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'tu m'as jamais ...' or written colloquially 'tu m'as jamais...' but in correct written French include 'ne'. Use with verbs in past (passé composé) addressed to 'tu'.
target_language_example: Tu ne m'as jamais prévenu de ce problème.
native_language_example: You have never warned me about this problem.

meaning: 'didn't me' as part of the colloquial contracted form of 'tu ne m'as pas...' (you didn't [to me]... / you haven't [to me]...).
additional_notes: Informal, spoken contraction dropping the ne: 'tu (ne) m'as pas ...' = 'you didn't/you haven't (to me) ...'. Used when someone didn't tell, hear, or listen to the speaker. In writing or formal speech use the full negative 'tu ne m'as pas...'. The 'm'' is the indirect/direct object pronoun meaning 'me'.
target_language_example: Tu m'as pas dit que tu venais ?
native_language_example: You didn't tell me you were coming?

meaning: 'you seem to me' / 'you look (to me)'.
additional_notes: Contraction of 'me' + 'as' in the expression 'tu me donnes l'air' or more directly from 'tu m'as l'air' (colloquial). Used to say how someone appears to the speaker (mood, health, character). Often followed by an adjective or a phrase introduced by 'de' or 'en' (e.g. 'en forme', 'd'aller bien', 'd'un garçon aimé'). This form is spoken/colloquial — in careful writing you'd more often see 'tu as l'air' or 'tu me donnes l'air'.
target_language_example: Tu m'as l'air fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You seem tired to me today.

meaning: to go away / to leave (oneself).
additional_notes: Used to say you will leave a place or situation. It's the pronominal form of 'aller' with the clitic 'en' and the reflexive pronoun 'me' contracted: 'm'en aller' = 'me en aller'. Common in spoken and written French. Often appears with verbs like devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir + infinitive (Je dois m'en aller = I have to leave).
target_language_example: Il est tard, je dois m'en aller.
native_language_example: It's late, I have to leave.

meaning: I'll take care of it myself / I'll handle it myself.
additional_notes: Combination of se occuper de (s'occuper de) with 'en' (refers to the thing/topic already mentioned) and 'moi-même' for emphasis. Used to say you will personally deal with something. Common in spoken and written French. Word order: Je vais m'en occuper moi-même (or Je m'en occupe moi-même).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je m'en occuper moi-même.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll take care of it myself.

meaning: short for 'me est' used in passive or impersonal constructions meaning 'to me' (e.g. 'happened to me', 'occurred to me').
additional_notes: m'est is the contraction of 'me est' (me + est) and appears in expressions like 'ça m'est arrivé' (that happened to me) or 'ça m'est venu' (it came to me). It's used when the verb is in the third person (est/arrivé/venu) and the indirect object is 'me'. In English this often translates as 'to me' or 'it occurred to me'. The form changes with the person (me → m', te → t', lui/leur unchanged).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, ça m'est passé par la tête.
native_language_example: Suddenly, it occurred to me.

meaning: 'my maid' or 'my female housekeeper' (familiar/old-fashioned).
additional_notes: Literally 'my good (woman)'. Used to refer to a female domestic worker (housemaid). This expression is somewhat old-fashioned and can sound familiar or condescending today; modern French more often uses 'ma femme de ménage', 'ma gouvernante' (formal), or 'la femme de ménage'. Context matters: in historical texts or novels you may see 'ma bonne' used by employers. Not possessive in a sexual sense — it indicates employment/relationship, not affection. If speaking politely, avoid unless quoting older usage.
target_language_example: Quand j'étais enfant, ma bonne m'a appris à faire le lit.
native_language_example: When I was a child, my maid taught me how to make the bed.

meaning: 'my ...' as the start of a phrase referring to a mailbox or a company's box (requires completion, e.g. 'ma boîte aux lettres' = my mailbox or 'ma boîte aux lettres électroniques' informal for my inbox)
additional_notes: This fragment is incomplete by itself — it typically begins a compound noun: 'boîte aux lettres' (mailbox), 'boîte aux lettres électroniques' (email inbox) or less commonly fixed expressions. Don't use 'ma boîte aux' alone in speech or writing; always complete it with the second element (e.g. 'lettres', 'annonces'). In informal French, 'ma boîte' alone can mean 'my company' or 'my workplace'.
target_language_example: Je vais vérifier ma boîte aux lettres.
native_language_example: I'm going to check my mailbox.

meaning: 'well', 'indeed', or 'honestly' — a mild expression used to emphasize what you say (like 'well, to be honest' or 'indeed').
additional_notes: A conversational, slightly old-fashioned or literary interjection. Often used to soften or emphasize a statement, express mild surprise, acceptance, or personal opinion. Tone can be neutral, resigned, or approving depending on context. Not strongly informal/slang, but not formal either.
target_language_example: Ma foi, je ne m'attendais pas à ça.
native_language_example: Well, I didn't expect that.

meaning: 'my word' — a promise or assurance (I give you my word).
additional_notes: Used to swear that what you say is true or to promise you'll do something. Can appear in phrases like "donner sa parole" (to give one's word) and "c'est ma parole contre la tienne" (it's my word against yours). Formal or neutral — appropriate in many contexts.
target_language_example: Je te donne ma parole que je serai là demain.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I'll be there tomorrow.

meaning: 'my little one' — a familiar, affectionate way to address a girl, young woman, or someone close (like 'sweetie' or 'kiddo').
additional_notes: Used as a term of endearment or encouragement. Tone and meaning depend on context and relationship: can be affectionate (to a child, friend, partner) or playful. When spoken alone ('Ma petite.'), it can serve as a gentle address or to get attention. Not typically formal; avoid with strangers or in professional settings unless the relationship allows familiarity.
target_language_example: Allez, ma petite, tu peux y arriver !
native_language_example: Come on, sweetie, you can do it!

meaning: literally 'my more' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment (e.g. start of 'ma plus grande peur' = 'my biggest fear')
additional_notes: By itself 'ma plus' is incomplete in French. 'Ma' is the feminine singular possessive 'my'; 'plus' can mean 'more' or be part of superlative constructions (often followed by an adjective and a noun: 'ma plus grande...', 'ma plus belle...') or used with verbs to mean 'no longer' (with ne). Beginners will most often see 'ma plus' when forming a feminine superlative: 'ma plus grande peur' = 'my biggest fear'.
target_language_example: Ma plus grande réussite a été d'apprendre une nouvelle langue.
native_language_example: My greatest achievement was learning a new language.

meaning: my apple (literally) — 'pomme' = apple; used to indicate possession of an apple
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: ma (my, feminine noun) + pomme (apple). Use ma before feminine singular nouns. Can be used literally ('my apple') or in childish/emphatic exclamations (e.g., 'Ma pomme !') but there is no common idiomatic meaning beyond the literal in standard French.
target_language_example: Il a mangé ma pomme sans me demander.
native_language_example: He ate my apple without asking me.

meaning: coffee machine; coffee maker.
additional_notes: Refers to a device that brews coffee (in offices, homes, cafés). Common everyday noun. Can be used in casual complaints about it breaking (e.g. "la machine à café déconne").
target_language_example: La machine à café est dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: The coffee machine is in the kitchen.

meaning: washing machine (appliance for doing laundry).
additional_notes: Common household appliance. Used to ask about location, features or usability. In casual speech you may also hear simply "la machine" when context is clear.
target_language_example: La machine à laver est dans la buanderie.
native_language_example: The washing machine is in the laundry room.

meaning: a machine used to rewind or wind (something); a winding/rewinding machine.
additional_notes: Literally 'machine to wind/rewind'. Often followed by what it winds (e.g., machine à remonter les bobines). Can refer to devices that rewind film, tape, clocks (remonter une montre = wind a watch) or industrial winding machines. Not commonly used alone without context; specify what is being wound if unclear.
target_language_example: La machine à remonter reconstitue les bobines de film après projection.
native_language_example: The winding machine rewinds the film reels after projection.

meaning: part of the phrase 'machine à remonter le temps' — 'time machine' (literally: 'machine to wind back time').
additional_notes: Alone this fragment is incomplete in French; the full idiom is 'machine à remonter le temps' meaning a device that lets you travel back in time (fictional). 'Remonter' here means 'to go back up' or 'to wind back' and 'le temps' = 'time'. You will rarely see just 'machine à remonter le' by itself — always include the final word(s).
target_language_example: Ils ont inventé une machine à remonter le temps dans le roman.
native_language_example: They invented a time machine in the novel.

meaning: typewriter (a mechanical or electromechanical device for writing).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a physical typewriter (not a computer or printer). In modern French it can sound a bit old-fashioned because typewriters are less common today; people might instead say 'ordinateur' for a computer or 'imprimante' for a printer. Used with verbs like 'utiliser', 'emprunter', 'trouver'.
target_language_example: Puis-je emprunter votre machine à écrire pour une heure ?
native_language_example: May I borrow your typewriter for an hour?

meaning: swimsuit; bathing suit (garment for swimming).
additional_notes: Used for both men's and women's swimwear in general. Can refer to one-piece or two-piece swimsuits, trunks, or swim briefs depending on context. Plural is "maillots de bain." Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas ton maillot de bain pour la piscine.
native_language_example: Don't forget your swimsuit for the pool.

meaning: 'hand in the' — a fragment used in expressions where 'main' (hand) is part of a phrase (e.g. 'mettre la main dans le sac').
additional_notes: By itself 'main dans le' is incomplete; it appears as the beginning of fixed expressions or verbs with 'main' as the noun. Common full phrases include: 'mettre la main dans le sac' (to be caught in the act), 'avoir la main sur' (to have control over), or 'la main dans la main' (hand in hand). Check the complete expression to know the idiomatic meaning.
target_language_example: Ils marchaient la main dans la main dans le parc.
native_language_example: They were walking hand in hand in the park.

meaning: Not a standalone fixed phrase; 'main' (hand) plus preposition 'en' typically begins a longer expression. On its own it's incomplete and likely a fragment of constructions like 'main en l'air' (non‑idiomatic — prefer 'mains en l'air') or part of other phrases where 'en' governs a complement.
additional_notes: Alone, 'main en' is incorrect or incomplete in standard French. It may appear in texts as the start of a longer locution or because of a typographical split (e.g., line break). Use the full idiom instead ('mains en l'air' for 'hands up', 'main en...' will need completion).
target_language_example: Il a levé la main en l'air.
native_language_example: He raised his hand in the air.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase on its own; likely part of a larger expression (e.g. "la main est ...") or a mistake. Literally means "hand is."
additional_notes: Alone, "main est" is unusual in French. "Main" = hand; "est" = is (third-person singular of être) or east (as a noun/adjective, spelled 'est' for the cardinal direction). Common correct uses include: "La main est..." (The hand is...), "main-d'œuvre" (workforce), or direction "à l'est" (to the east). If you meant the direction 'east', use 'est' alone or 'à l'est'. If you meant 'my hand is...' use 'ma main est...'.
target_language_example: Ma main est froide.
native_language_example: My hand is cold.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase — it's the word 'main' (hand) followed by a conjunction or verb in examples; 'main' means 'hand'.
additional_notes: The input 'main et' is not a standard multiword expression in French. In the example sentences, 'main' appears in different constructions: as a direct object (prendre la main), after verbs (tendit sa main), in commands (Levez la main), in reflexive/reciprocal contexts (On se tient la main) and in the idiom 'reprends ta vie en main' (take your life in hand = take control of your life). Learn 'main' (feminine noun) and common phrases with it rather than 'main et' specifically.
target_language_example: Reprends ta vie en main et avance.
native_language_example: Take control of your life and move forward.

meaning: 'hand for' (literal); usually appears as part of longer phrases (e.g. "une main pour..." meaning "a hand to/for..." — i.e. help or function).
additional_notes: On its own, 'main pour' is not a complete idiomatic phrase in French. 'Main' = hand; 'pour' = for/to. You will most often see 'main' followed by 'pour' within expressions like "une main pour aider" (a hand to help) or in constructs such as "donner la main pour..." (to lend a hand for...). For beginner learners, treat it as the literal combination 'hand' + 'for' and expect a noun or verb after it. Remember that to say 'to lend a hand' French commonly uses "donner un coup de main" (idiomatic).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'une main pour porter ces sacs.
native_language_example: I need a hand to carry these bags.

meaning: hand to set down / hand for placing (used to indicate a hand offered or positioned to put something down)
additional_notes: Literal phrase composed of main (hand) + pour poser (for placing/setting down). It can describe a hand used to steady, take, or set an item down — for example, when asking someone to give you 'a hand to put this on the table' or describing a designated hand position. This is not a fixed idiom; its meaning depends on context and is best used with clarified object (e.g. 'une main pour poser le vase').
target_language_example: Donne-moi une main pour poser la boîte sur l'étagère.
native_language_example: Give me a hand to put the box on the shelf.

meaning: hand to place a (feminine noun) / (used to indicate using the hand to put down or set something)
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it combines 'main' (hand) with the infinitive 'poser' (to place/put down) and the indefinite article 'une' for a feminine noun. In context you would finish with the object: e.g. 'main pour poser une tasse' (a hand to place a cup). Useful when describing a gesture or asking for a free hand to set something down. Word order and gender matter: 'une' signals the object is feminine. For a masculine object use 'un' (main pour poser un...).
target_language_example: Donne-moi ta main pour poser une tasse sur la table.
native_language_example: Give me your hand to place a cup on the table.

meaning: 'but' or 'however' (informal/colloquial).
additional_notes: A spoken colloquial contraction of 'mais si' used to contradict a negative statement or to insist (equivalent to English 'yes it is!' / 'on the contrary'). Used mainly in rapid speech and informal contexts. Example: someone says 'Il n'a pas faim' and you reply 'Main si!' to mean 'Yes he is!'. Spelling in standard French is 'mais si'.
target_language_example: Main si il veut venir, il viendra.
native_language_example: But yes he wants to come, he will come.

meaning: literally 'hand on his/her/its' — used to describe placing a hand on someone or something (e.g. hand on his shoulder).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the phrase 'la main' or 'mettre/poser la main' + 'sur' + a possessive (son/sa/ses). Use appropriate verb tense (mettre, poser, avoir mis) and agree possessive with the thing touched (son épaule = his/her shoulder). Common in physical descriptions (touching gently) and in set phrases like 'mettre la main sur' meaning 'to get hold of' or 'to lay hands on' (can be literal or figurative).
target_language_example: Elle posa sa main sur son bras pour le rassurer.
native_language_example: She placed her hand on his arm to reassure him.

meaning: used in phrases like «donner la main à» or «mettre la main à» meaning 'to give a hand to' / 'to take part in' / 'to help with'.
additional_notes: By itself 'main à' is not a complete expression; it appears in fixed verbs/phrases: - «mettre la main à (quelque chose)» = to pitch in, to help with a task; - «donner la main à (quelqu'un)» = to give one's hand (literally) or to help/support someone; - «tenir la main à» = to hold someone's hand (literal or figurative). Use with an object (quelque chose / quelqu'un).
target_language_example: Je vais mettre la main à la préparation du repas.
native_language_example: I'll help with preparing the meal.

meaning: front hands; the hands placed at the front (literal).
additional_notes: This is a literal, descriptive phrase made of mains (hands) + avant (front). It could be used in contexts like describing the position of hands on a bicycle, horse reins, a car steering wheel, or in exercise instructions (e.g., 'place your front hands'). Not a fixed idiom — meaning depends on context. Use article or possessive for natural phrases (les mains avant, ses mains avant).
target_language_example: Placez vos mains avant sur le guidon.
native_language_example: Place your front hands on the handlebars.

meaning: literal fragment meaning 'hands before the' — not a complete fixed phrase by itself; typically part of instructions like placing hands in front of something (e.g. 'mains avant les yeux').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'mains' = hands, 'avant' = before/in front of (often temporal; for physical placement 'devant' is more common), 'les' = the (plural). Expect a noun to follow (e.g. 'mains avant les yeux'). In natural French for physical position, prefer 'mains devant les...'. Keep article agreement with the plural noun that follows.
target_language_example: Placez les mains avant les yeux pour bloquer la lumière.
native_language_example: Place your hands before the eyes to block the light.

meaning: 'hands of' (the plural possessive/part of a noun phrase meaning 'the hands of...')
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the start of a noun phrase meaning 'the hands of (someone/something)'. In French, mains is feminine plural (les mains). 'des' here can be the contraction of 'de + les' meaning 'of the' (e.g. les mains des enfants = the hands of the children) or the indefinite article 'des' (some) depending on context. You will usually see it inside a longer phrase: mains des + noun. Word order: 'les mains de Marie' or 'les mains des enfants'.
target_language_example: Les mains des enfants sont sales après le jeu.
native_language_example: The children's hands are dirty after playing.

meaning: with bare hands; without any tools or weapons
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something using only their hands (no gloves, tools, weapons). Common in contexts like fighting ('se battre à mains nues'), catching something, or handling objects directly. Plural 'mains' is required; 'nues' agrees in gender/number. Can be used literally or figuratively (e.g., unable to act 'les mains nues' implies unarmed/unassisted).
target_language_example: Il a attrapé le chat à mains nues.
native_language_example: He grabbed the cat with his bare hands.

meaning: 'empty-handed' (having nothing in your hands; often used figuratively for coming away with nothing)
additional_notes: Literally 'hands empty'. Used to describe someone who has no objects in their hands or, figuratively, someone who obtained nothing (e.g., left an event or negotiation without any results). Can be used after a verb (e.g., 'rester mains vides', 'partir mains vides').
target_language_example: Il est rentré chez lui les mains vides après l'entretien.
native_language_example: He went home empty-handed after the interview.

meaning: now at / right now at (used before a time or place)
additional_notes: This is the phrase maintenant (now) followed by the preposition au (à + le). It appears before a specific time, place or event introduced by a masculine noun (e.g., au cinéma = at the cinema, au travail = at work). In many contexts you'd say simplement "maintenant" or "en ce moment"; use "maintenant au" when pointing to something happening now at a particular location or time: "maintenant au théâtre" = "now at the theater."
target_language_example: Il passe maintenant au cinéma près de chez nous.
native_language_example: It's playing now at the cinema near our home.

meaning: Shortened spoken form of "maintenant, c'..." used to start a sentence meaning "now, it/that..." or "now, it's..."
additional_notes: This is an informal, conversational contraction where "c'" stands for "c'" in front of a vowel (short for "ce" or "c'est"). You will commonly hear it in speech: e.g. "Maintenant c'est trop tard" → "Maintenant c' est trop tard" often becomes "Maintenant c'est..." or clipped to "Maintenant c'..." in rapid speech. Use the full written forms ("maintenant, c'est" or "maintenant ce") in formal writing.
target_language_example: Maintenant c'est à toi de décider.
native_language_example: Now it's your turn to decide.

meaning: 'now it's' — used to introduce a current situation or to contrast with before (now it's ...).
additional_notes: Literally 'now it is'. Often starts a sentence that describes the current state, a change, or a conclusion (e.g. 'Maintenant c'est plus simple' = 'Now it's easier'). In spoken French you may hear contractions or different word order, but the phrase itself is neutral and common. Followed by a noun phrase, adjective, or clause.
target_language_example: Maintenant c'est plus clair.
native_language_example: Now it's clearer.

meaning: 'now in' or 'now at' — used to introduce what is happening now in a place, time period, or situation
additional_notes: This is a combination of maintenant (now) + dans (in/within). It often appears when describing what is happening currently inside a specific location or time frame: e.g. "maintenant dans la salle" (now in the room) or "maintenant, dans ce chapitre" (now, in this chapter). Be careful: depending on word order and punctuation, you may more commonly see "maintenant, dans..." (with a comma) or simply "maintenant" followed by a location introduced by "dans."
target_language_example: Maintenant dans la cuisine, on prépare le dîner.
native_language_example: Now in the kitchen, they are preparing dinner.

meaning: "now in" (literal). Used to begin a phrase meaning 'now in [a place/state/subject]' or to introduce a clause (e.g. 'now, in...'). The two-word sequence typically requires following words to be natural.
additional_notes: Maintenant = 'now'. En is a versatile preposition/pronoun (in, on, by, of it, about it, while ...-ing). "Maintenant en" appears when immediately followed by a place, topic phrase, or clause (e.g., "Maintenant en France...", "Maintenant en parlant...", "Maintenant en ce qui concerne..."). Avoid using "maintenant en" alone without what comes next.
target_language_example: Maintenant en France, on porte souvent des masques lors des pics épidémiques.
native_language_example: Now in France, people often wear masks during epidemic peaks.

meaning: 'now and' — the adverb maintenant ('now') followed by the conjunction et ('and'), used to link 'now' with another element in a sequence or list.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; it's a compositional sequence. Often uncommon as a standalone collocation in French, because 'et maintenant' (with et before maintenant) is more frequent. 'Maintenant et' can appear in lists or paired temporal expressions (e.g. 'hier, maintenant et demain') or in poetic/emphatic structures.
target_language_example: Nous parlons du passé, maintenant et du futur.
native_language_example: We talk about the past, now and the future.

meaning: 'now he/it' or 'now, he/it...'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the sequence of the adverb maintenant ('now') followed by the subject pronoun il ('he' or impersonal 'it'). Usage depends on the sentence: e.g. 'Maintenant il arrive' = 'Now he is arriving' or 'Maintenant il faut...' (more commonly 'Il faut maintenant...') for 'now it is necessary...'. Word order can vary in French; beginners will more often hear 'maintenant' at the start of a sentence followed by the subject.
target_language_example: Maintenant il parle plus doucement.
native_language_example: Now he speaks more quietly.

meaning: 'now I' — the beginning of a clause meaning 'now I ...' or 'now that I ...'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; it's the adverb 'maintenant' (now) followed by subject pronoun 'je' (I). Appears at the start of sentences to indicate a change in time, a new conclusion, or a contrast: e.g. maintenant je fais ceci (now I do this) or maintenant je comprends (now I understand). Word order is literal.
target_language_example: Maintenant je sais quoi faire.
native_language_example: Now I know what to do.

meaning: now (followed by a masculine noun or clause) — literally 'now the'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the adverb 'maintenant' ('now') followed by the definite article 'le' before a masculine noun or part of a clause (e.g. 'maintenant le problème...' or 'maintenant le film commence'). In spoken French you may also hear 'maintenant que' ('now that') when introducing a clause. Use 'maintenant la' for feminine nouns, 'maintenant les' for plural.
target_language_example: Maintenant le film commence, éteins ton téléphone.
native_language_example: Now the movie is starting, turn off your phone.

meaning: 'now we' (literal combination of 'maintenant' = now and 'nous' = we).
additional_notes: This is simply the words 'maintenant' (now) + 'nous' (we). By itself it's not a fixed idiom; it can begin or appear within a sentence like "maintenant nous..." to mean "now we..." followed by an action or statement (e.g. "maintenant nous partons" = "now we are leaving"). In standard writing, a comma is often used after 'Maintenant' when it introduces a clause, but in casual or poetic contexts the comma may be omitted.
target_language_example: Maintenant nous partons pour la gare.
native_language_example: Now we are leaving for the station.

meaning: now we / now one (informal spoken start of a sentence meaning 'now, we...' or 'so now...')
additional_notes: A spoken conversational phrase used to introduce what someone (we/one) will do or what happens next. 'On' often replaces 'nous' (we) in everyday French and can also mean 'one' or 'people' in general. Depending on context, it can mean 'we', 'people', or be vague. It commonly appears at the start of a sentence: 'Maintenant on...' = 'Now we're going to...' or 'So now one...'.
target_language_example: Maintenant on y va, il ne faut pas traîner.
native_language_example: Now we're going, we mustn't linger.

meaning: 'now that' (introduces a reason or new situation that changes something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact or change of circumstances that explains or justifies what follows. Often placed at the start of a clause: 'Maintenant que + [clause], ...'. Equivalent to English 'now that' or 'since' (in the causal sense).
target_language_example: Maintenant que tu as fini tes devoirs, tu peux sortir.
native_language_example: Now that you've finished your homework, you can go out.

meaning: now everything / everything now (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom in French; it's simply the words 'maintenant' (now) + 'tout' (everything/all). Meaning depends on sentence word order and context. It can appear in phrases like 'maintenant, tout est prêt' (now everything is ready) or 'tout maintenant?' (everything now?). Watch punctuation and word order: 'tout maintenant' emphasizes doing everything immediately; 'maintenant tout' is less common alone and usually part of a larger clause (e.g. 'Maintenant tout est clair').
target_language_example: Maintenant tout est prêt pour la fête.
native_language_example: Now everything is ready for the party.

meaning: 'now you' — part of a sentence meaning 'now you (do something)' or 'and now you...'
additional_notes: Literally 'now you'. Used to introduce what the other person does or experiences next. It must be followed by a verb or clause (e.g. 'maintenant tu peux', 'maintenant tu sais'). Common in spoken and written French to signal a change or next action/state.
target_language_example: Maintenant tu peux partir.
native_language_example: Now you can leave.

meaning: 'now you' — the adverb maintenant (now) followed by the pronoun vous (you).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; normally maintenant is followed by a verb or used with punctuation when addressing someone directly. In written French, include a comma when speaking to someone: "Maintenant, vous..." Often appears in contexts like "Maintenant vous..." followed by a verb or question. Use appropriate intonation in speech.
target_language_example: Maintenant vous êtes prêts ?
native_language_example: Now, are you ready?

meaning: 'now at' or 'now (located) at' — used to indicate the current time or place where something/someone is.
additional_notes: A combination of maintenant (now) + preposition à (at/to). Used to say where or when something is now. Often followed by a time, place, or verb in structures like "maintenant à + [lieu]" (now at [place]) or in conversational phrases like "maintenant, à..." to start a comment. Not a fixed idiom — treat as compositional.
target_language_example: Il est maintenant à la maison.
native_language_example: He is now at home.

meaning: 'now that' or 'now (this/that)' depending on context
additional_notes: This sequence pairs maintenant ('now') with pronoun/demonstrative ça ('that/this'). Alone it is fragmentary and its exact translation depends on the rest of the sentence. Common uses: 'maintenant ça...' to introduce a new point or consequence ('now that...'), or in spoken French to emphasize a contrast or change ('and now that...'). In conversation it may sound informal. Don't use it by itself without finishing the idea.
target_language_example: Maintenant ça change tout.
native_language_example: Now that changes everything.

meaning: 'the mayor has' (maire = mayor; a = has)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short sequence: maire (noun) + a (third-person singular of avoir). It appears in sentences like "Le maire a annoncé..." = "The mayor has/announced..." or more naturally in English, "The mayor announced..." Use 'le maire a' or 'la maire a' depending on context; often 'le maire' is used. This sequence is grammatical rather than idiomatic.
target_language_example: Le maire a signé le document ce matin.
native_language_example: The mayor signed the document this morning.

meaning: 'come on' (used to encourage, urge, or express mild surprise/doubt)
additional_notes: Informal expression. Often used to push someone to do something, to show disbelief, or to urge agreement—similar to English 'oh, come on' or 'go on'. Tone depends on context and intonation: friendly encouragement, mild impatience, or incredulity. Frequently followed by a verb or used alone in conversation.
target_language_example: Allez, viens on y va, il ne reste plus beaucoup de temps — mais allez !
native_language_example: Come on, come with me, there's not much time left — oh, come on!

meaning: 'but then' / 'well then' — used to react, draw a conclusion, express surprise or to press for clarification.
additional_notes: Common discourse marker. Depending on context and intonation it can mean 'well then' (moving the conversation forward), 'but then...' (contradiction or conclusion), or express surprise/strong reaction (like 'what?!'). Often followed by a question. Not formal or slang — neutral conversational.
target_language_example: Mais alors, que fait-on maintenant ?
native_language_example: Well then, what do we do now?

meaning: 'but to the' or 'but at the' (fragment used before a masculine singular noun or before certain contractions)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the combination of the conjunction mais ('but') + the preposition à + the masculine singular definite article le, which contracts to au. You'll typically see 'mais au' at the start of a clause introducing a contrast about a masculine noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'mais au contraire', 'mais au travail'). It must be completed by a noun, noun phrase, or clause. Pronunciation: [mɛ o].
target_language_example: Il aime voyager, mais au travail il est très sérieux.
native_language_example: He likes to travel, but at work he is very serious.

meaning: 'but rather' / 'but indeed' (used to correct or strengthen a previous statement).
additional_notes: Used to contrast or correct what was just said (often replacing a wrong idea) or to reinforce a point. Common patterns: 'ce n'est pas X, mais bien Y' = 'it's not X, but rather Y', or 'mais bien' placed after a pause to emphasize agreement ('Oui, mais bien sûr'—here 'bien' intensifies). Formality: neutral; appears in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas un problème, mais bien une opportunité.
native_language_example: It's not a problem, but rather an opportunity.

meaning: Of course; certainly; (often used to express obvious agreement or mild sarcasm).
additional_notes: Common phrase for strong affirmation. Can be neutral (friendly agreement) or sarcastic/irritated depending on tone and context. Often appears with que oui/que si for extra emphasis: "Mais bien sûr que oui." Use in spoken and informal written French; simple and frequent.
target_language_example: Mais bien sûr que oui, je viendrai à la fête.
native_language_example: Of course I will come to the party.

meaning: anyway / well / oh well (softens or concedes a point)
additional_notes: Informal conversational filler used to downplay, concede, or move on from something just said. Often follows a remark to indicate resignation, mild disagreement, or acceptance. Tone depends on context and intonation (can be short: 'Mais bon.' or in a sentence: 'Ouais, mais bon.').
target_language_example: Il fait froid, mais bon, on peut quand même y aller.
native_language_example: It's cold, but oh well, we can still go.

meaning: but this
additional_notes: A short combination used to add contrast or introduce clarification about something just mentioned. Often followed by a clause (e.g. « mais ce que... », « mais ce n'est pas... »). On its own it is usually part of a larger phrase rather than a complete expression. Tone depends on context — can soften a contradiction or emphasize a correction.
target_language_example: Je pensais que c'était prêt, mais ce n'est pas encore fini.
native_language_example: I thought it was ready, but it's not finished yet.

meaning: but in / however, in (used to contrast and introduce a location, time, or context)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction mais (but) with the preposition dans (in). Used to contrast a previous statement and then specify a place, time, situation, or context. Depending on sentence rhythm, it may be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause introduced by a noun phrase (e.g., « mais dans ce cas », « mais dans la rue », « mais dans mon expérience »). Not an idiom—meaning is literal.
target_language_example: Je suis d'accord, mais dans ce quartier il y a beaucoup de bruit.
native_language_example: I agree, but in this neighborhood there is a lot of noise.

meaning: but (only) / except (for) — introduces a limitation or contrast, often meaning 'but not more than' or 'except for'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to contrast quantities or conditions. When followed by a number or quantity, it can mean 'no more than' or 'only' (e.g. «mais de 10» = 'more than 10' — note: 'mais de' alone without context often appears in negative or contrasting sentences). It can also appear in contrasts like «Il n'y a pas de problème, mais de la fatigue» (but rather fatigue). Context determines exact nuance. Not idiomatic/slang.
target_language_example: Je voulais venir, mais de la pluie m'a arrêté.
native_language_example: I wanted to come, but the rain stopped me.

meaning: 'but' + plural partitive/indefinite article (e.g. 'but some' or 'but...'), used to contrast then introduce plural nouns or expressions
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction mais ('but') followed by des, which can be the plural indefinite article ('some') or the contraction of de + les. Common in sentences like «Je veux venir, mais des questions restent» (rare) or more naturally «Je veux venir, mais il y a des questions». In many cases word order or additional words are required in natural speech (e.g. 'mais il y a des...' or 'mais des fois...'). Not a fixed idiom—just two words that often appear together when contrasting and then mentioning plural items or general quantities.
target_language_example: J'aimerais aider, mais des problèmes persistent.
native_language_example: I'd like to help, but some problems persist.

meaning: 'but still' / 'but then' — used to add another point, emphasise something, or press for more information.
additional_notes: Commonly used in conversation to introduce an additional objection, reinforce a contrast, or ask for clarification/further detail. Can mean 'however' when adding a stronger point (e.g., "Il est sympa, mais encore..." = "He's nice, but there's more to say"). Often appears alone as a prompt: "Mais encore ?" meaning "And then? / What else?" Tone and context determine whether it's mild, impatient, or persuasive.
target_language_example: Tu as fini le projet, mais encore, il faut vérifier les chiffres.
native_language_example: You finished the project, but still, we need to check the numbers.

meaning: 'but is' (combination of conjunction 'mais' = 'but' and verb 'est' = 'is').
additional_notes: This is simply the sequence of the conjunction 'mais' followed by the third-person singular of 'être' ('est'). It appears in sentences like 'mais est-ce que...' or 'mais est...' as part of a larger clause: e.g. 'Il est fatigué, mais est motivé.' Note that in natural French you often need punctuation or additional words (comma, pronoun, or inversion) for clarity: 'mais il est...' or 'mais est-ce que...'
target_language_example: Il n'est pas riche, mais est heureux.
native_language_example: He isn't rich, but is happy.

meaning: 'but here' — used to contrast a previous statement with what's true in the current place or situation.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction mais (but) with ici (here). Used to introduce a contrast focused on the current location, moment, or situation. Can start a clause: "Mais ici, ..." Common in spoken and written French. Tone depends on context — can be neutral, corrective, or emphatic.
target_language_example: Je pensais que ce serait tranquille, mais ici c'est bruyant.
native_language_example: I thought it would be quiet, but here it's noisy.

meaning: but I
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast, objection, or correction. j' is the shortened form of je before a vowel or silent h, so you commonly see forms like mais j'ai, mais j'aime, mais j'habite.
target_language_example: Mais j'aime bien ce film.
native_language_example: But I really like this movie.

meaning: short spoken form of 'mais je te...' used before a verb or object (means 'but I ... you' or 'but I ... you...'), often part of a sentence like 'mais je t'aime' or 'mais je t'ai dit'.
additional_notes: This is an informal, contracted fragment you hear in spoken French when 'te' (the object pronoun 'you') is elided before a vowel or mute h: 'je te' → 'je t''. It always needs the rest of the verb or phrase to make sense (e.g. 'mais je t'aime' = 'but I love you'; 'mais je t'ai dit' = 'but I told you'). Not a standalone phrase; appears in casual speech and writing that reproduces speech.
target_language_example: Mais je t'ai déjà dit de venir tôt.
native_language_example: But I already told you to come early.

meaning: but (there/that); used to contrast, correct, or add emphasis about a situation or place
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction mais (but) with the demonstrative/adverb là (there/that/then). Common in spoken French to introduce a contrast or stronger comment about something just mentioned — e.g. 'mais la' can mean 'but as for that,' 'but now,' or 'but in that case.' Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Je comprends ton idée, mais la, ça ne marche pas.
native_language_example: I understand your idea, but as for that, it doesn't work.

meaning: but the
additional_notes: A simple combination of the conjunction mais (but) plus the definite article le (the). Used when contrasting or qualifying a noun introduced by le. In conversation it can start a clause: "mais le problème..." = "but the problem...". Nothing idiomatic here — treat as two words used together. Word order and gender/number of the article must agree with the noun (le → la, les as needed).
target_language_example: Je veux venir, mais le train est en retard.
native_language_example: I want to come, but the train is late.
