additional_notes: This phrase is an informal, colloquial grouping seen when the speaker asks someone else to allow them to speak with a third person. The full standard form is usually Laisse/Laissez-moi lui parler or Laissez-moi lui parler seul à seul. Use laisse-moi (tu) for informal singular, laissez-moi (vous) for formal or plural. 'Lui' can mean 'him' or 'her' depending on context.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi lui parler avant que tu partes.
native_language_example: Let me talk to him/her before you leave.

meaning: me (used to emphasize or point to oneself, often conversational).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Moi là' adds emphasis or signals 'as for me' / 'me here' — used to contrast, to insist, or to draw attention to the speaker. Tone and context matter; it can sound casual, slightly defensive, or expressive. Not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Moi là, je préfère rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: Me, I prefer to stay home tonight.

meaning: 'me' / 'to me' — shows both stressed and unstressed forms of the first-person singular object placed together for contrast or clarification.
additional_notes: French distinguishes an unstressed clitic 'me' used before a verb (e.g. 'Il me voit' = He sees me) and a stressed/emphatic form 'moi' used after prepositions, in short answers, or for emphasis (e.g. 'C'est pour moi ?' or 'Moi, je préfère...'). The sequence 'moi me' can appear in spoken or written French when a speaker contrasts or clarifies roles (e.g. 'Moi, me, ça m'est égal' — 'As for me, I don't care'), or in emphatic constructions where both forms are used together. They are not interchangeable in all positions: use 'me' as the clitic before a verb and 'moi' for emphasis or after prepositions.
target_language_example: Moi me demande si c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Me wonders if it's a good idea.

meaning: Informal emphatic sequence used by a speaker to single out themselves before mentioning something that belongs to them or expresses their stance (like 'as for me, my...').
additional_notes: Colloquial, spoken French; used to contrast the speaker with others or to introduce a personal possession, opinion or preference. Often followed by a noun or a short noun phrase (moi mon téléphone, moi mon avis) or a clause. Tone is informal and conversational; generally avoided in formal writing.
target_language_example: Moi mon avis, c'est qu'il faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: As for me, my opinion is that we should leave now.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase. 'Moi' means 'me' (stressed/emphatic pronoun) and 'ne' is the first element of negation. When adjacent they occur in emphatic or colloquial constructions, e.g. 'Moi ne...' to contrast or refuse, though standard written French usually inserts a subject pronoun after a topicalized 'moi' (e.g. 'Moi, je ne...').
additional_notes: 'Moi ne' by itself is uncommon in neutral written French; you'll more often see 'Moi, je ne...'. In informal speech and some literary registers, 'Moi ne...' can appear (often followed by omission or elision) to place emphasis or form a contrast. 'Ne' must be paired with a negative word (pas, plus, jamais, etc.) to complete the negation.
target_language_example: Moi ne veux pas y aller.
native_language_example: Me, I don't want to go there.

meaning: me neither / neither do I (used to disagree or say you also don't).
additional_notes: Used to express that the speaker also does not do or feel what was just stated. Commonly follows a negative statement by someone else. Informal to neutral; pronunciation often links words (mwa nɔ̃). Can replace 'moi non plus' when context makes meaning clear, but 'moi non plus' is more emphatic and grammatically complete in some cases.
target_language_example:
— Je n'aime pas le café.
— Moi non.
native_language_example:
— I don't like coffee.
— Me neither.

meaning: used to contrast the speaker ('me') with a group ('us') — to emphasize difference in opinion, responsibility, action, or perspective (literally 'me us').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a short sequence that can appear in spoken or written French to contrast an individual's position with that of a group. Often set off by a pause or punctuation (e.g. « Moi, nous... » or « Moi nous... » depending on style). Meaning depends on context and intonation; may be part of a larger sentence such as a contrast between personal stance and the group's stance.
target_language_example: Moi nous, on n'est pas d'accord sur ce point.
native_language_example: Me, we don't agree on that point.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'me, I...' used to introduce your own situation or opinion (often followed by a contrasting statement).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Moi où...' (also heard as 'moi, où...') is used to bring up how something affects you or what you think, often before saying you are different from others or giving your own experience: e.g. 'Moi, où j'habite...' or 'Moi où je travaille...' It functions like 'as for me' or 'me, I...' in English. Expect it in conversation; not appropriate for formal writing.
target_language_example: Moi où j'habite, on ne fait pas ça.
native_language_example: As for me, where I live, we don't do that.

meaning: Not a fixed French phrase; a spoken fragment combining 'moi' (me / as for me) with 'où elle' (where she). Often used in informal speech to contrast the speaker with another person and typically needs a continuation to be complete (e.g. 'Moi, où elle...').
additional_notes: This construction is colloquial and appears in dialogue as a truncated contrast: the speaker starts to contrast their situation or opinion with that of 'elle' ('her'). It may be punctuated with pauses or commas: 'Moi, où elle...' and is followed by a contrasting clause or left implied. It is not idiomatic as a standalone fixed expression.
target_language_example: Moi où elle, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Me, whereas she, I prefer to stay home.

meaning: Literally 'me where is' — not a standard fixed phrase. Typically a fragment used informally when the speaker refers to themselves ('moi') then begins a question ('où est...'), e.g. to ask where something is for them or to ask 'where am I' in an incomplete way.
additional_notes: This sequence is not an established idiom; it appears as a spoken fragment and is grammatically incomplete on its own. Natural alternatives: "Où suis‑je ?" (Where am I?), "Moi, où est [quelque chose] ?" (As for me, where is [something]?). In writing, include the noun or finish the question for clarity. Tone: informal when used in speech.
target_language_example: Moi où est mon sac ?
native_language_example: Me, where is my bag?

meaning: A colloquial spoken sequence used to contrast the speaker with someone else, roughly 'as for me — where he...'. Often begins a sentence fragment that contrasts the speaker's attitude or situation with that of 'il' (he).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a fragmentary structure: 'moi' (as for me) followed immediately by 'où il' (where he/when he/if he), usually completed by a clause. In speech the comma after 'moi' may be dropped, producing the exact sequence 'moi où il'. Informal and primarily spoken; common in regional or conversational register.
target_language_example: Moi où il est, je m'en fiche.
native_language_example: As for me — where he is, I don't care.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase — a sequence of three separate words: 'moi' (me/I, used for emphasis), 'où' (where), 'se' (reflexive pronoun used with a verb). On its own it is incomplete and not idiomatic; it would normally appear as part of a larger clause (e.g. « Moi, où se trouve… »).
additional_notes: This is not a set expression in French. The three words can appear adjacent in speech or writing when someone begins a question or clause that involves the speaker and a reflexive/impersonal construction. Correct and common structures include: « Moi, où se trouve… ? » (Me — where is…?) or « Moi, où se gare la voiture ? » (Me — where does the car park?) but the bare sequence 'moi où se' without a following verb is incomplete. Pay attention to word order: 'où se' is typically followed by a verb (e.g. trouve, situe, gare).
target_language_example: Moi où se trouve ce document ?
native_language_example: Me — where is this document?

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; a fragment combining 'moi' (me / as for me) + 'où' (where) + 'tu' (you). Often appears in informal speech as the start of a contrastive question or remark: 'Me — where you...?' and requires completion.
additional_notes: This is not a standard set phrase. It is compositional: 'moi' used contrastively ('as for me'), followed by 'où tu' introducing a question about the other person's location or action. In natural French you would normally complete the sentence (e.g. « Moi, où tu es ? » or « Moi où tu vas ? »). Without completion it sounds like an interrupted sentence or colloquial speech. Use in spoken, informal contexts.
target_language_example: Moi où tu es, je te rejoins tout de suite.
native_language_example: Me — where you are, I'll join you right away.

meaning: Not a standard French fixed phrase; a sequence of words that by themselves is ungrammatical or nonsensical in normal usage. Could appear as a mistaken fragment or in colloquial/emphatic speech only within a larger sentence (e.g., 'Moi, où vous...?' as a clipped question meaning 'Me — where you...?' but this is rare and ambiguous).
additional_notes:
Avoid using 'moi où vous' as a standalone expression. Possible intended alternatives depending on context:
- 'Moi, où... ?' (As for me, where...?)
- 'Où êtes‑vous ?' or 'Où es‑tu ?' (Where are you?)
- 'Moi et vous' (Me and you)
If used informally for emphasis in conversation, a speaker might pause and say 'Moi, où vous...' before completing the thought, but this is colloquial and elliptical, not a fixed idiom.
target_language_example: Moi, où vous... où est-ce que je dois aller ?
native_language_example: Me — where you... where am I supposed to go?

meaning: 'as for me' or 'me, personally' (used to introduce your own opinion or to contrast your stance).
additional_notes: This sequence is typically part of spoken colloquial constructions and is incomplete on its own; it's usually followed immediately by words like 'contre', 'rapport', 'hasard' or a clause (e.g. 'moi par contre', 'moi par rapport à'). Written forms often include a comma after 'Moi' when used to contrast: 'Moi, par contre,...'. Alone 'moi par' without what follows sounds clipped or unfinished in natural French.
target_language_example: Moi par rapport à ça, je suis sceptique.
native_language_example: Me, regarding that, I'm skeptical.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase; likely a literal or childlike attempt to say "I speak" or "me speak" (correct: "je parle").
additional_notes: This combination is ungrammatical in standard French. French places subject pronouns before verbs (je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous, ils/elles). "Moi" is a tonic pronoun used for emphasis or after prepositions (e.g. "C'est moi" = "It's me") and cannot serve as the simple subject before a verb. If you want to emphasize the subject, use "Moi, je parle..." The sequence "moi parler" can appear inside larger informal or erroneous utterances (child speech, direct literal translations) but is not correct by itself.
target_language_example: Moi parler, ce n'est pas correct — il faut dire « je parle ».
native_language_example: "Me speak" is not correct — you should say "I speak."

meaning: me (not); I don't — used colloquially to contradict or exclude oneself.
additional_notes: Informal, spoken expression used to disagree or say that something doesn't apply to the speaker. Often appears alone or before a verb omitted by context (e.g. « Moi pas. » = "Not me."). In full sentences speakers usually say "Moi, non" or use a conjugated verb with negation ("Moi, je ne ... pas").
target_language_example: Moi pas, je n'aime pas le poisson.
native_language_example: Not me, I don't like fish.

meaning: 'me pay' — a nonstandard, colloquial sequence used to indicate the speaker will pay (or should pay); often a simplified or emphatic form found in casual speech or childlike/learner speech.
additional_notes: Not standard French grammar. Native speakers typically say 'c'est moi qui paie', 'moi, je paie' or 'je paie'. 'Moi payer' can appear in truncated or emphatic speech, in written dialogue imitating children or learners, or in errors by non-native speakers. Use cautiously — in most contexts it sounds ungrammatical or informal.
target_language_example: — Qui paie ? — Moi payer !
native_language_example: — Who's paying? — Me pay! (intended: I'll pay!)

meaning: 'please me' or 'do me a favor' (used in commands: 'Fais-moi plaisir' = 'Do me a favor/please me')
additional_notes: Common in imperatives: 'Fais-moi plaisir' (informal singular), 'Faites-moi plaisir' (formal/plural). It asks the listener to do something for the speaker, sometimes gently pleading or requesting compliance. Not a standalone phrase — usually follows an imperative verb (fais-/faites-/rends-). Tone can be polite, pleading, or slightly impatient depending on context.
target_language_example: Fais-moi plaisir et arrête de t'inquiéter.
native_language_example: Do me a favor and stop worrying.

meaning: me neither / neither do I (used to agree negatively with someone)
additional_notes: Informal spoken response used to agree with a negative statement about oneself. Equivalent to "moi non plus", which is the standard form. "Moi plus" is a colloquial, shortened or mistaken variant and might be understood in casual contexts, but prefer "moi non plus" in writing or formal speech.
target_language_example:
— Je n'aime pas les araignées.
— Moi plus.
native_language_example:
— I don't like spiders.
— Me neither.

meaning: used informally to introduce your personal opinion, preference or stance: 'as for me' / 'for me'.
additional_notes: 'Moi pour' is a spoken sequence where 'moi' (me/for me) is followed by 'pour' to highlight what concerns you. It is informal and often part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'Moi pour le dessert...'). More standard alternatives include 'pour ma part' or 'moi, je...'. Not a fixed idiom but a colloquial connector.
target_language_example: Moi pour le dîner, je prends une soupe.
native_language_example: As for me for dinner, I'll have a soup.

meaning: 'me, why' — used to ask why something applies to the speaker or to express surprise/defensiveness about being blamed or included.
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase where 'moi' (me) is followed by 'pourquoi' (why). Often appears alone or in short replies: e.g. someone accuses or asks the speaker to do something and the speaker replies 'moi pourquoi' meaning 'Why me?' or 'Why would I (do that)?'. Tone can be defensive, surprised, incredulous, or dismissive. Equivalent in meaning to 'Pourquoi moi ?' but with casual stress on 'moi'.
target_language_example: Ils veulent que je paye la facture. — Moi pourquoi ?
native_language_example: They want me to pay the bill. — Why me?

meaning: 'me — why you...' (colloquial/informal fragment used to express surprise, indignation, or to challenge someone — literally 'me, why you...')
additional_notes: Not a fixed grammatical phrase but a spoken fragment used in casual conversation. It pairs 'moi' (me/I) with 'pourquoi tu' (why you/why do you) to react when someone blames, questions, or accuses the speaker. Often the remainder of the sentence is omitted; intonation and context convey the full meaning. Use in informal speech or social media; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: — Tu m'accuses de mentir ? — Moi pourquoi tu ?
native_language_example: — You're accusing me of lying? — Me? Why you?

meaning: Not a standard, grammatical French phrase; literally the stressed pronoun 'moi' ('me') followed by the infinitive 'prendre' ('to take').
additional_notes: The sequence 'moi prendre' does not function as an independent expression in French. 'Moi' is the disjunctive (stressed) pronoun used for emphasis or after prepositions (e.g., 'C'est moi', 'pour moi'). 'Prendre' is the infinitive 'to take'. You might encounter these two words adjacent in fragments or colloquial speech when parts of a sentence are omitted (e.g., elliptical answers or notes), but they must be integrated into a grammatical structure to be correct: for example 'Il va me prendre' (He is going to take me) or 'Moi, je prends' (Me, I take). Do not use 'moi prendre' as a standalone phrase in formal writing or speech; it will sound ungrammatical.
target_language_example: Si tu veux jouer, moi prendre, ça me va.
native_language_example: If you want to play, me take (me taking), that's fine by me.

meaning: used in colloquial/emphatic constructions to mean 'as for me' or 'me, who/that...' — often introduces a contrast or a clause about the speaker
additional_notes: Appears mainly in spoken/informal French. Usually follows a pause or comma: « Moi, que... ». Can introduce a relative clause emphasizing the speaker's position or action (contrast/emphasis). Its exact function depends on context; not a fixed idiom by itself.
target_language_example: Moi que je travaille tard, je n'ai pas le temps de sortir le soir.
native_language_example: As for me — I work late, I don't have time to go out in the evening.

meaning: A colloquial fragment used to contrast the speaker with the addressee — roughly 'me, you...' or 'as for me compared with you'. Often introduces the speaker's reaction or position contrasted with what the other person does or is.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a spoken-conversation pattern using the stressed pronoun 'moi' plus a clause introduced by 'que' referring to 'tu'. Typically informal; often appears with pauses or commas (e.g. « Moi, que tu... ») and is followed by a clause expressing the speaker's attitude or consequence. Translation depends on context (e.g. 'as for me,' 'me — if you...').
target_language_example: Moi que tu fasses ça, je ne suis pas d'accord.
native_language_example: Me — if you do that, I don't agree.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; appears to be two separate words 'moi' (me/I) and 'quel' (which/what). Together they do not form a common or grammatical expression in standard French.
additional_notes:
Likely a typo, misordering, or fragment. Possible related/correct forms:
- 'Moi, quel...' (rare/poetic) could begin an emphatic clause: 'Moi, quel...' → 'As for me, what a...'.
- 'Mais quel...' (common) means 'But what a...'.
- Use 'Moi, je...' to emphasize the subject ('As for me, I...').
Avoid using 'moi quel' by itself in standard speech or writing; if you see it, check for missing punctuation, a typo, or omitted words.
target_language_example: Moi quel enthousiasme j'ai vu hier !
native_language_example: As for me, what enthusiasm I saw yesterday!

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; an unlikely sequence of two separate elements: 'moi' (me/I) and 'quel est' (which is/what is). It can appear together in informal or truncated speech when the speaker self-references and immediately asks a question, but it's not a conventional set phrase.
additional_notes: 'moi quel est' should not be used as a single grammatical chunk. If used, it will usually occur across a pause or punctuation (e.g. "Moi, quel est..." or "Et moi, quel est...") to contrast the speaker with others or to ask about something that pertains to the speaker. Prefer more natural constructions such as "Et moi ? Quel est... ?" or "Moi, quel est mon... ?"
target_language_example: Moi quel est ton problème, sérieusement ?
native_language_example: Me — what is your problem, seriously?

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete combination. Individually, 'moi' = 'me / I' and 'quelque' = 'some / a few / somewhat'.
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence 'moi quelque' does not occur in standard French as a fixed expression. It may appear as part of an interrupted utterance or a mistaken fusion of words (e.g., someone starting 'Moi, quelque...' before completing a sentence such as 'Moi, quelque chose...'). Don't use 'moi quelque' by itself in formal writing or speech. Learn the components separately: 'moi' is a stressed pronoun used for emphasis (Moi, je veux partir = Me, I want to leave). 'quelque' is an adjective or adverb appearing in phrases like 'quelque chose' (something), 'quelques' (a few), or 'quelquefois' (sometimes).
target_language_example: Moi quelque... je ne sais pas comment répondre.
native_language_example: Me, well... I don't know how to answer.

meaning: "me something" — not a standard fixed phrase in French; looks like a literal combination of 'moi' (me) + 'quelque chose' (something).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common standalone expression in French. If you want to say 'something for me' you'd say 'quelque chose pour moi' or 'donne-moi quelque chose' for 'give me something.' 'Moi quelque chose' might appear in informal speech as a clipped fragment (e.g. starting a sentence: 'Moi, quelque chose m'inquiète' — 'Me, something worries me'), but by itself it is ambiguous and ungrammatical as a complete phrase.
target_language_example: Donne-moi quelque chose à manger, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me something to eat, please.

meaning: a phrase used to introduce a comment about yourself in relation to someone else (literally: 'me who to him/her') — often part of a larger clause like 'moi qui lui ...' meaning 'as for me, who ... to him/her' or 'I, who ... for him/her'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed standalone expression; it's typically the start of a relative or contrasted clause: 'Moi, qui lui ...' or 'Moi qui lui avais dit ...'. It emphasizes the speaker's role or contrast (e.g. surprise, reproach or explanation). In English it often translates as 'I, who ...' or 'Me, who ...'. You will usually see it followed by a verb and more information. It is compositional and literal but sounds formal or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Moi qui lui avais conseillé de venir, je suis déçu qu'il ait refusé.
native_language_example: I, who had advised him to come, am disappointed that he refused.

meaning: 'me, you know' — a casual, emphatic tag used to stress the speaker's point or reaction
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Moi quoi' is often added at the end of a sentence to emphasize the speaker's feeling, surprise, annoyance, or to contrast themselves with others. Tone and context determine the exact nuance (e.g., 'I, what?' / 'As for me, obviously'). It is similar to adding 'you know' or 'I mean' in English, or stressing 'me, though' in conversation.
target_language_example: Ils ont tous dit non, et moi quoi ?
native_language_example: They all said no, and me, what? (What about me?)

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'what can I do?' or 'what am I supposed to do?'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Used as a resigned or defensive response when someone asks what you should do, or to show you have no control over a situation. Structure: 'moi, quoi, faire' — often with commas or intonation. Similar to 'que veux-tu que je fasse ?' but more casual and ungrammatical.
target_language_example: On me reproche tout le temps, moi quoi faire ?
native_language_example: They blame me all the time — what can I do?

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French sequence; appears to be a word-order error. Literally reads 'me/to me watch' but is not used in natural French.
additional_notes:
This sequence is unidiomatic. In French, stressed pronoun 'moi' is not placed directly before an infinitive or conjugated verb to mark the object. Possible correct alternatives depending on intended meaning:
- 'Look at me' (imperative familiar): 'regarde-moi' or (formal/plural) 'regardez-moi'.
- 'I watch' (present tense): 'je regarde'.
- 'for me to watch' (subordinate clause): 'pour que je regarde' or 'que je regarde'.
If you see 'moi regarder' in learner speech, it's likely a literal transfer from English word order. Avoid using 'moi regarder' and learn proper pronoun placement (object pronouns before conjugated verbs: 'tu me regardes'; after affirmative imperatives: 'regarde-moi').
target_language_example: C'est juste moi regarder ce film, pas toi.
native_language_example: It's just me watching this movie, not you.

meaning: 'me' + 'to return / to go home' used informally to indicate the speaker is going home or coming in (often elliptical and nonstandard)
additional_notes: This is not a standard grammatical phrase in French. It likely appears in very casual speech, text messages or transcribed speech where subjects and verb forms are compressed or ungrammatical (e.g., instead of the full sentence 'Moi, je rentre' or 'Je rentre'). Use the normal forms 'Je rentre' (I'm going home / I'm coming back) or 'Moi, je rentre' for emphasis. 'Rentrer' means to go back home or to come back in. The sequence 'moi rentrer' omits the conjugated subject verb agreement and is informal/nonstandard.
target_language_example: (Message) Moi rentrer 18h.
native_language_example: (Message) Me — coming back at 6 PM.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to be a mistaken word order or an incomplete fragment. Could be intended as 'moi, réfléchir' (meaning 'as for me, to think/reflect') or part of imperatives like 'laisse-moi réfléchir' ('let me think').
additional_notes:
The sequence 'moi réfléchir' by itself is ungrammatical in French. Common correct alternatives:
- 'Moi, je réfléchis...' — 'As for me, I am thinking...'
- 'Laisse-moi réfléchir' / 'Laissez-moi réfléchir' — 'Let me think.'
- 'Je vais réfléchir' — 'I'll think about it.'
If you want to emphasize the speaker before a verb, use 'Moi, je...' followed by a conjugated verb. 'Se réfléchir' exists but means 'to be reflected' (rare) and isn't used with 'moi réfléchir.'
target_language_example: Moi, réfléchir n'est pas correct; dis plutôt «Moi, je réfléchis» ou «laisse-moi réfléchir».
native_language_example: 'Moi, réfléchir' is not correct; say instead 'Moi, je réfléchis' or 'laisse-moi réfléchir.'

meaning: literally 'me to settle' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'me (to) pay/settle' or emphasising that the speaker will take care of the bill or the problem ('I'll handle it').
additional_notes: This is not a common set phrase in French on its own. It looks like an object pronoun 'moi' followed by the infinitive 'régler' and would normally appear in a larger sentence (e.g. 'C'est moi qui vais régler' or 'Laisse-moi régler' / 'Moi, je règle') meaning 'I'll pay' or 'Let me handle it.' For beginners: use full, common alternatives instead of 'moi régler' fragments — e.g. 'Laisse-moi régler' (Let me pay/handle), 'Je règle' (I'll pay), 'C'est moi qui règle' (I'll take care of it).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi régler l'addition, c'est pour moi.
native_language_example: Let me pay the bill, it's on me.

meaning: 'me' (stressed moi) followed by an elided reflexive clitic 's'' — an incomplete or colloquial fragment where 'moi' is followed by a contracted 'se' before a vowel-starting verb; not a standard standalone expression.
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon as an isolated unit. It typically appears in clipped or colloquial speech where the speaker starts with the stressed pronoun 'moi' then immediately begins a reflexive verb with elision (e.g., 'moi s'amuser...' as an informal fragment). In careful speech one would say 'moi, je m'amuse...' or use the full reflexive form 'se + verb'. Treat 'moi s'' as an incomplete fragment that will normally be followed by a vowel-initial verb.
target_language_example: Moi s'amuser, pas question !
native_language_example: Me having fun? No way!

meaning: Not a standard or idiomatic French phrase; likely a typo, transcription error, or nonstandard/dialectal usage. It has no accepted meaning in standard French as written.
additional_notes:
Possible intended corrections depending on context:
- 'mon service' = my shift / my service / my department.
- 'à mon service' = at my service / working for me.
- 'moi, s'il vous plaît' or 'pour moi, s'il vous plaît' = me, please (when ordering).
If you encountered 'moi service' in text or speech, provide the full sentence or context for a precise correction. It could also be a name, brand, or foreign insertion rather than French.
target_language_example: «Je n’ai jamais vu 'moi service' utilisé en français standard : 'moi service' semble être une erreur.»
native_language_example: "I have never seen 'moi service' used in standard French: 'moi service' appears to be an error."

meaning: Informal fragment used to contrast with a previous negative or differing statement — roughly 'as for me, that (is different)' or 'I, on the other hand, do/feel that'.
additional_notes: Casual spoken French. Often appears after someone expresses dislike or a negative reaction; the speaker uses this to indicate their opposite reaction. Commonly followed by a verb or clause that may be omitted if understood (e.g. 'moi si ça me plaît'). Alone, 'moi si ça' is a fragment and not a complete sentence; learners will more frequently hear 'moi si' or 'moi, si...'
target_language_example: Tu n'aimes pas la pluie ? Moi si ça m'apaise.
native_language_example: You don't like the rain? Me, on the other hand, the rain soothes me.

meaning: This phrase is incorrect in French; it mixes a stressed pronoun 'moi' with a verb form 'sommes' that only agrees with 'nous'. It should be replaced by a grammatically correct form such as 'nous sommes dans' (we are in) or 'moi, je suis dans' (me, I am in) depending on meaning.
additional_notes:
'Moi' is a tonic (stressed) pronoun and cannot serve as the subject that governs the verb form 'sommes'. 'Sommes' is the first-person plural of 'être' and only matches 'nous'. If you encounter 'moi sommes dans', treat it as an error and use one of the correct alternatives below:
- Nous sommes dans... = We are in...
- Moi, je suis dans... = Me, I am in... (emphatic)
- On est dans... = We're in (colloquial)
If the intent was to emphasise the subject while keeping plural, use 'nous' plus a stressed pronoun: 'Nous, on est dans...' or 'Nous, nous sommes dans...'.
target_language_example: (incorrect) Moi sommes dans la voiture.
native_language_example: (incorrect) Me are in the car. — Intended: We are in the car / I am in the car (emphatic).

target_language_multi_word_term: moi et ... sommes dans la même
meaning: We (X and I) are in the same (class/place).
additional_notes: Used to say that you and another person are in the same group, class, team, etc. Structure: [Name/Pronoun] et moi sommes dans la même + [noun]. Note that when you mention people together in French, the other person usually comes before 'moi' (e.g. 'Elle et moi'). The verb agrees in the first-person plural (sommes). Common nouns: 'classe', 'équipe', 'promotion', 'ville', etc.
target_language_example: Paul et moi sommes dans la même équipe.
native_language_example: Paul and I are on the same team.

meaning: 'you and I are...' (used to say two people are something together)
additional_notes: The correct French phrase in the example sentences is "Toi et moi sommes..." or "Sheila et moi sommes..." — it means "X and I are..." (we are). Use "et" to join the two subjects. The verb agrees with the plural subject (sommes = first-person plural "we are"). Common pattern: "X et moi sommes + adjective/noun."
target_language_example: Toi et moi sommes de bons collègues.
native_language_example: You and I are good colleagues.

meaning: This sequence is not correct French; it mixes singular and plural pronouns/verb forms and has no standard meaning.
additional_notes:
Likely an incorrect combination. Possible intended corrections:
- "nous sommes du même avis" = "we are of the same opinion." 
- "on est du même avis" = informal "we're of the same mind." 
- "moi, je suis du même avis" = "I agree / I'm of the same opinion." 
The provided term cannot be used in correct French; replace with one of the corrected phrases depending on whether you mean "I" (moi/je) or "we" (nous/on).
target_language_example: *Incorrect usage*: « moi sommes du même » n'est pas correct : « moi sommes du même avis » -> incorrect.
native_language_example: *Incorrect usage*: "moi sommes du même" is not correct: "moi sommes du même avis" -> incorrect.

meaning: Not a fixed French phrase; a sequence of two separate words that can appear next to each other in speech or writing. 'moi' is the disjunctive (stressed) pronoun meaning 'me' or 'myself'; 'son' is the third-person singular possessive adjective meaning 'his', 'her', or 'its' depending on context.
additional_notes: This entry treats 'moi son' as two independent words that may occur adjacent (for example in conversational fragments or transcribed speech) but do not form an idiomatic expression. 'Moi' is used for emphasis, after prepositions, or alone (e.g., 'C'est moi', 'Pour moi'). 'Son' precedes a noun and agrees with that noun (e.g., 'son livre' can mean 'his book' or 'her book' depending on the possessor). Be careful: 'son' agrees with the possessed noun (gender/number), not the possessor's gender. In natural sentences you will usually find a noun after 'son' — isolated 'moi son' is uncommon outside clipped speech or errors.
target_language_example: C'est moi son voisin qui l'a entendu.
native_language_example: I'm his/her neighbor who heard it.

meaning: 'me' used after a preposition (as in 'on me', 'to me', or 'kiss me') — part of phrases like 'crois-moi sur parole' (believe me), 'embrassez-moi sur la bouche' (kiss me on the mouth).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the stressed/tonic object pronoun 'moi' followed by the preposition 'sur' in various expressions. 'Moi' is used instead of 'me' after prepositions or for emphasis. Examples from the sentences: 'Crois-moi sur parole' = 'believe me on my word', 'Embrassez-moi sur la bouche' = 'kiss me on the mouth', 'Tape-moi sur la gueule' = crude/informal 'hit me in the face'. Register varies by phrase — some are polite, others vulgar.
target_language_example: Fais-moi confiance, crois-moi sur parole.
native_language_example: Trust me, believe me on my word.

meaning: Not a correct or grammatical French phrase; it appears to be a scrambled/mistaken sequence of pronouns and verb parts and has no clear meaning as written.
additional_notes:
This string mixes stressed pronoun 'moi', indirect object pronoun 'te', verb 'dire' and part of 'quelque' incorrectly. Possible intended correct phrases include:
- « me dire quelque chose » (to tell me something)
- « te dire quelque chose » (to tell you something)
- « moi, te dire quelque chose... » could be an informal, spoken attempt to emphasize the speaker before continuing, but it should be completed and is not standard. For learners: use the clitic object pronouns (me, te, le/la, nous, vous, leur) before the verb (e.g. « Peux-tu me dire quelque chose ? »).
target_language_example: Moi te dire quelque... ce n'est pas correct en français parlé standard.
native_language_example: "Moi te dire quelque..." is not correct in standard spoken French.

meaning: let me introduce you (to someone).
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase "Laisse-moi te présenter..." (Let me introduce you...). Use to offer to introduce the person you're speaking to. If introducing someone to a third party, include "à" + person/group: "te présenter à ma famille". Polite alternative: "Permettez-moi de vous présenter" or "Laissez-moi vous présenter" (formal).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi te présenter mon ami, Julien.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my friend, Julien.

meaning: A colloquial, confrontational expression used to introduce a dismissive or contrasting stance toward what the other person offers or says; roughly 'As for your.../Me, your...' and typically followed (explicitly or elliptically) by a noun (e.g. conseils, histoires).
additional_notes: Informal/slang; spoken rather than standard written French. Often appears at the start of a sentence to signal dismissal, skepticism, or indifference. Usually requires a noun after 'tes' (tes conseils, tes histoires), but can be left elliptical for effect. Regional usage possible.
target_language_example: Moi tes, je m'en fiche.
native_language_example: Me, your stuff—I don't care.

meaning: a sequence of words that can appear together in sentences meaning 'me' (moi) followed by 'every' or 'all the' (tous les); not a fixed phrase by itself.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiomatic expression. It simply shows the pronoun 'moi' (me) followed by the determiners 'tous les' (all/the every) in nearby words of example sentences. Depending on word order and context, 'moi' can be the indirect or stressed pronoun ('to me', 'me' for emphasis) and 'tous les' modifies a plural noun (tous les détails = all the details; tous les soirs = every evening). They do not form a compound meaning together.
target_language_example: Donne-moi tous les documents.
native_language_example: Give me all the documents.

meaning: used colloquially to introduce one's own perspective or situation—similar to 'moi aussi' or 'quant à moi' (informal, contrastive).
additional_notes: Often spoken with a pause or slight emphasis (e.g. 'Moi... tout, ...') and used to add a personal comment, preference, or reaction. More casual than 'moi aussi' and not typical in formal writing. Depending on intonation and context, it can mean 'as for me' or 'me, on the other hand'.
target_language_example: Moi tout, je trouve que c'est trop cher.
native_language_example: As for me, I find it too expensive.

meaning: colloquial/emphatic phrase meaning 'as for me' or 'me, ...' used to introduce a personal stance or contrast
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Used to emphasize the speaker's opinion or situation, often at the start of a clause: 'Moi tout de...' can be followed by a verb or statement. Variant of 'moi' with added emphasis; may be regional. Equivalent in standard French: 'moi, ...' or 'quant à moi, ...'.
target_language_example: Moi tout de, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: As for me, I prefer to stay home.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to be a fragment. Most likely a mistaken or truncated sequence (e.g. intended: « moi, tout ce que... » meaning "me, all that/whatever..." or part of « pour moi, tout ça »).
additional_notes:
As written, "moi tout ce" is not a common standalone expression. It will typically occur as part of a longer construction such as:
- « moi, tout ce que... » (introducing what concerns the speaker): « Moi, tout ce que je veux, c'est... »
- or as a misordered/truncated piece of « pour moi, tout ça » / « tout ça pour moi ». If you see "moi tout ce" in informal text or speech, it is likely missing punctuation or words. Prefer learning the fuller, grammatical phrases above.
target_language_example: Moi tout ce que j'entends, c'est du bruit.
native_language_example: Me, all I hear is noise.

meaning: Me, relaxed / I'm fine (calm).
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to state that the speaker is calm, unbothered, or not worried. Often used alone or in short replies: "Moi tranquille." Tone is casual; commonly contrasts the speaker's calm with others' concern. Not appropriate for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Moi tranquille, je n'ai pas de souci pour l'examen.
native_language_example: Me, I'm chill; I have no worries about the exam.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; the words are 'moi' (me/I) + infinitive 'travailler' (to work). It appears as a fragment, a mistaken literal translation, or shorthand. It does not form a correct sentence on its own.
additional_notes: Use 'je travaille' for 'I work' (subject + conjugated verb). To emphasize contrast you can say 'Moi, je travaille' (which includes both 'moi' and a conjugated verb). If you encounter 'moi travailler' it may be from non-native speech, a note, or an unfinished thought. Avoid using it as a standalone sentence.
target_language_example: (Informal note) Moi travailler — besoin d'argent.
native_language_example: (Informal note) Me work — need money.

meaning: me, a/an ...?
additional_notes: Usually appears in the emphatic pattern « moi, un/une + noun ? » to express surprise, denial, or disbelief, as in « Moi, un menteur ? » = « Me, a liar? » In standard French, a comma is normally written after « moi »; the punctuation is omitted here only to match the requested term exactly. « un » changes to « une » before feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Et moi un professeur ? Pas encore !
native_language_example: And me, a teacher? Not yet!

meaning: Informal spoken fragment meaning 'for me, one of [that]' — used to request or order a single item for the speaker (e.g., a drink), typically followed by the item.
additional_notes: Colloquial and elliptical: speakers often drop surrounding words and complete the phrase with the item (e.g., 'moi un coup de blanc' = 'I'll have a glass of white wine'). Common in cafés, bars, markets or among friends. Not appropriate in formal registers. The phrase is incomplete on its own and depends on context to specify the item.
target_language_example: Moi un coup de rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of red (wine), please.

meaning: me, a little (used to signal limited agreement, involvement or feeling)
additional_notes: Colloquial short phrase used in spoken French to indicate that you personally share something only to a small extent. Often occurs as a brief response or parenthetical remark: "Moi, un peu" or condensed in quick speech as "moi un peu". Informal; tone and context determine nuance (slight agreement, mild feeling, small amount).
target_language_example: — Tu aimes le sport ? — moi un peu
native_language_example: — Do you like sports? — me, a little

meaning: 'me' + 'a little (of)' — not a fixed phrase; a spoken fragment used when the speaker emphasizes themselves and asks for/mentions a small amount of something.
additional_notes: Not a set expression. Appears in informal spoken French where speaker contrasts or personalizes a request or preference: moi (as for me) + un peu de (a little of). It must be followed by a noun or understood context (e.g., un peu d'eau, un peu de pain). Often used with a pause or comma: «Moi, un peu de...». Register: colloquial/informal.
target_language_example: Moi un peu de pain, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Me, a little bread, please.

meaning: literally 'me a cup' — an informal, clipped way to indicate you want a cup for yourself (e.g., of coffee or tea). It omits the verb and relies on context to be interpreted as a request.
additional_notes: Very colloquial; can sound abrupt or childlike if used alone. Common in fast, familiar speech where verbs are dropped: context supplies 'donne', 'apporte' or 'je voudrais'. For polite or complete forms use: «Donne-moi une tasse», «Apporte-moi une tasse», «Une tasse pour moi, s'il vous plaît.»
target_language_example: — Qui veut du café ? — Moi une tasse, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: — Who wants coffee? — Me, a cup, please.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; incorrect word order. The correct forms are "je viens" (I come / I'm coming) or the emphatic/contrasted "moi, je viens" (me, I'm coming).
additional_notes: French subject pronouns normally precede the verb (je viens). "Moi venir" is ungrammatical as a standalone phrase and likely a literal transfer from another language. Emphasis with "moi" requires a clause: "Moi, je viens..." For beginners, use "je viens" for neutral statements and "Moi, je viens" to contrast or emphasize. Avoid using "moi venir".
target_language_example: Moi venir n'est pas correct en français.
native_language_example: "Moi venir" is not correct in French.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely two words used together meaning 'me, quickly' or 'quickly to me' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a common idiomatic expression. It can appear in informal spoken or written contexts where someone asks to be given or involved quickly: e.g. 'Donne-moi vite...' (give me quickly...) or as a clipped response like 'Moi, vite!' meaning 'Me — quickly!' without a verb. Alone, it is ambiguous and depends on surrounding words. For beginners: prefer full phrases such as 'Donne-moi vite' (give me quickly), 'Viens vite' (come quickly), or 'Dépêche-toi' (hurry up).
target_language_example: Donne-moi vite le sac, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me the bag quickly, please.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning something like 'let me see' or 'let me think'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Used as a hesitation or thinking phrase before answering or checking something. Similar to 'laisse voir', 'voyons' or 'attends voir'. Not grammatically standard — more of a casual interjection. Use in informal conversations; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Moi voir ce… il me semble que le rendez‑vous est à 14h.
native_language_example: Let me see… I think the appointment is at 2 PM.

meaning: A nonstandard or regional sequence of pronouns likely intended to mean 'moi, vous' ('me, you') or an emphatic/colloquial pronoun cluster — not standard French.
additional_notes: This exact form 'moi vos' is not standard French. It may appear in transcriptions of rapid speech, regional dialects, or errors and probably represents either (1) two separate pronouns said together ('moi, vous' = 'me, you') or (2) a misspelling of 'moi, vous autres' / 'moi, vous' used for emphasis. In standard French, pronouns are used in specific orders (e.g. 'tu et moi' = 'you and I', or object pronouns like 'vous me' in fixed structures). Do not use 'moi vos' in formal writing; instead use 'moi, vous', 'toi et moi', or the grammatically correct pronoun sequence for the intended meaning.
target_language_example: Toi et moi, pas 'moi vos' — dis plutôt 'toi et moi'.
native_language_example: You and me, not 'moi vos' — say 'toi et moi' instead.

meaning: 'we (want)' used after pronouns like 'elle et moi' or 'le chef et moi' — literally the verb vouloir conjugated for 'nous' placed after 'moi' as part of a subject like 'X et moi voulons'.
additional_notes: French subject with 'X et moi' (X and I) uses the first-person plural verb form (nous). In spoken and written French you often see 'X et moi' followed by the verb conjugated for nous: e.g. 'Elle et moi voulons...' = 'She and I want...'. Do not say 'moi veux' — the verb must match 'nous' (voulons). This pattern is compositional and not informal.
target_language_example: Mon frère et moi voulons visiter Paris cet été.
native_language_example: My brother and I want to visit Paris this summer.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; most likely a fragment, a punctuation-dependent sequence, or a mistaken word order. It can appear in spoken or written French when the speaker pauses or omits words (e.g. 'Moi, vous…' to contrast with the listener, or as part of a larger construction like 'moi vous dis' in colloquial speech).
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'moi vous' without punctuation is uncommon as a standalone expression. Possible interpretations:
- 'Moi, vous…' (with a pause/comma): the speaker contrasts themselves with 'you' and will continue, equivalent to 'As for me, you...'.
- In fast or colloquial speech, parts of verbs/pronouns may be dropped so 'moi vous' could appear in transcriptions but is not grammatically complete.
- Incorrect word order: the correct phrases are 'Et vous?' (And you?) or 'Moi, je vous...' (As for me, I you...).
Learner tips: use 'Et vous?' (formal) or 'Et toi?' (informal) to ask 'And you?'; use 'Moi, je...' to emphasize the subject 'I'.
target_language_example: Moi vous, je ne comprends pas pourquoi vous partez.
native_language_example: Me — you, I don't understand why you're leaving.

meaning: 'let me help you' (part of the polite phrase "laissez-moi vous aider").
additional_notes: Usually appears in the set phrase "Laissez-moi vous aider" (or the contracted "Laissez-moi vous aider !") to offer assistance politely. "Laissez-moi" = "let me"; "vous" = formal or plural you; "aider" = to help. Use "te" instead of "vous" for informal singular (Laisse-moi t'aider).
target_language_example: Laissez-moi vous aider à porter ces sacs.
native_language_example: Let me help you carry these bags.

meaning: A colloquial spoken fragment used to introduce what the speaker would (or would not) tell the listener; roughly 'let me tell you' or 'as for me, to tell you'. Often part of a larger clause rather than a standalone fixed expression.
additional_notes: Informal, commonly found in spoken/familiar registers. Usually appears embedded in larger phrases (e.g. « ça, moi vous dire… » or « moi vous dire que… ») and may omit grammatical elements for emphasis. Not a fixed idiom on its own; word order differs from standard written French (standard: « moi, je vous dis » or « je peux vous dire »). Tone can be emphatic or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Ça, moi vous dire, je n'en ai aucune idée.
native_language_example: That, let me tell you, I have no idea about it.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French multi-word expression; appears to be a fragment mixing stressed or object pronouns and an infinitive, e.g. 'me you give' or 'I you give' but incorrect as written.
additional_notes: This sequence is ungrammatical in standard French. Possible intended meanings depend on correction: 'me donner' (to give me), 'vous donner' (to give you), or a construction with stressed pronouns for emphasis like 'moi, vous donner...' within a larger clause. Object pronouns precede the verb (Il me donne = He gives me). If you want to say 'Can you give it to me?' say «Peux-tu me le donner ?». If emphasizing the subject 'me' in colloquial speech you might hear isolated stressed pronouns, but 'moi vous donner' alone is not a correct sentence.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu veux que moi vous donner ce document ? (erroné/fragment — non standard)
native_language_example: Do you want me to give you this document? (incorrect/fragment — nonstandard)

meaning: 'let me explain (to you)'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in the common polite request Laissez-moi vous expliquer = "Let me explain to you". Laissez-moi (let me) + vous expliquer (to explain to you). Used to offer or begin an explanation; can be shortened to "Laissez-moi expliquer" or simply "Laissez-moi" in context. Formal/polite due to "vous"; use "te" in informal situations (Laisse-moi t'expliquer).
target_language_example: Laissez-moi vous expliquer ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: Let me explain to you what happened.

meaning: 'let me show you' (request/offering to demonstrate or point something out).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase Laissez-moi vous montrer or Permettez-moi de vous montrer. Used to offer to demonstrate, explain, or point out something. In full French the verb is usually preceded by laissez/permets/je vais (Laissez-moi vous montrer... / Permettez-moi de vous montrer... / Je vais vous montrer...). Formal polite form uses laissez-moi (or Permettez-moi de...) + infinitive. Use with objects or clauses: comment, où, quelque chose, un exemple, etc.
target_language_example: Laissez-moi vous montrer un exemple rapide.
native_language_example: Let me show you a quick example.

meaning: Not a standard French fixed phrase; appears to be a fragment meaning roughly 'me (to) ask you' or 'for me to ask you' when words are misordered or incomplete.
additional_notes: This sequence is not correct as an independent expression in French. It likely results from incorrect word order or omission of verbs/pronouns. Correct alternatives include: "me poser (une question)" = 'to ask me (a question)', "vous poser (une question)" = 'to ask you (a question)'. If you intend 'for me to ask you (something)', a full sentence would be: "Pour que je vous pose la question..." or "Que je vous pose la question...". Avoid using 'moi vous poser' by itself.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous voulez que ce soit moi vous poser la question ?
native_language_example: Do you want it to be me to ask you the question?

meaning: literally 'me check' — not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or colloquial fragment meaning 'let me check' or 'I'll check'.
additional_notes: This combination is not a standard fixed phrase in French. The usual ways to say 'let me check' or 'I'll check' are «laisse-moi vérifier», «je vais vérifier», or «je vérifie». 'Moi vérifier' might appear in casual speech as a truncated or incorrect form (for example from non-native speakers or in instant messages), but avoid using it in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi vérifier avant de te répondre.
native_language_example: Let me check before I answer you.

meaning: 'me' (colloquial emphatic); used to insist that something applies to or concerns the speaker
additional_notes: Informal, regional/colloquial. "Moi, y..." or simply "moi y" appears in some spoken French varieties (especially in parts of northern France and Belgium) to emphasize the speaker or to introduce their position/opinion or reaction. It often functions like English "as for me" or "me, I..." and may be followed by a verb or comment. Not standard in formal writing; avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Moi y, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Me, I prefer to stay home.

meaning: 'It's my turn to go' / 'I should go' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Informal, regional/colloquial expression. Often used to say you are the one who should go or take action next (e.g. enter, leave, speak, or do something). Structure: 'moi' emphasizes the speaker; 'y' refers to the place/action; 'aller' is the infinitive. You might also hear more standard alternatives like 'c'est à moi d'y aller' or 'je dois y aller'.
target_language_example: Bon, moi y aller, j'ai encore du travail.
native_language_example: Well, I should go, I still have work.

meaning: Let me think about it / let me reflect on that.
additional_notes: A colloquial/neutral way to ask for time to consider something. Usually appears in the phrase 'Laisse-moi y réfléchir' (informal singular) or 'Laissez-moi y réfléchir' (formal/plural). 'Y' replaces a thing or situation already mentioned (about it). You can add time qualifiers: 'un peu', 'plus longtemps'.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi y réfléchir avant de répondre.
native_language_example: Let me think about it before answering.

meaning: as for me / me, (in my case)
additional_notes: Colloquial way to introduce one's own opinion, situation or reaction. Often used at the start of a clause: "Moi à ..." followed by a verb phrase or a statement (e.g. "Moi à ta place..." or "Moi à la maison..." ). More common in spoken or regional French; the version with a comma ("Moi, à ...") is standard, but the form without the comma ("moi à") appears in informal transcripts and speech. Can express contrast or personal stance.
target_language_example: Moi à ta place, je ne dirais rien.
native_language_example: As for me, in your place I wouldn't say anything.

meaning: Not a correct or grammatical French phrase; likely a mistaken combination of the stressed pronoun 'moi' with 'à' + 'le' (which should contract to 'au').
additional_notes: This sequence is ungrammatical. In French, 'à' + 'le' contracts to 'au' before a masculine noun. Pronouns like 'moi' are used in constructions such as 'à moi' (to me) or as a stressed pronoun after a comma or preposition, but 'moi à le' never occurs. Possible intended corrections include: 'à moi' (to me / mine), 'au + noun' (à + le + noun) or reordering to 'moi, à lui/à elle' when contrasting persons. Beginners should learn contractions (à + le = au) and proper pronoun placement.
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* "moi à le" — cette suite n'est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* "moi à le" — this sequence is not correct in French.

meaning: Not a standard grammatical French phrase; a literal juxtaposition of 'moi' (me/I) and the infinitive/verb form 'être' (to be / to exist).
additional_notes: This combination is ungrammatical in standard French as a standalone clause. French uses subject pronouns (je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous, ils/elles) before conjugated verbs: e.g. 'je suis' = 'I am'. 'Moi' is used for contrast or emphasis (e.g. 'moi, je suis d'accord' = 'me, I agree') or after prepositions (e.g. 'pour moi' = 'for me'). You might encounter 'moi être' in literal glosses, child speech, or non-native/creative usages, but it should be avoided in standard French. To express 'I am,' use 'je suis'; to say 'to be me' use 'être moi' within a larger infinitive construction (e.g. 'personne ne veut être moi' = 'nobody wants to be me').
target_language_example: Dans sa citation maladroite, il a écrit « moi être convaincu », ce qui n'est pas correct.
native_language_example: In his awkward quote, he wrote 'moi être convinced', which is not correct.

meaning: 'the slightest idea who' (used when you don't know who someone is)
additional_notes: Usually appears in negative contexts with verbs like 'avoir' or 'n'avoir ... aucune' (e.g. 'je n'ai pas la moindre idée de qui...'). It emphasizes complete lack of knowledge about a person's identity. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas la moindre idée de qui a appelé.
native_language_example: I don't have the slightest idea who called.

moindre idée de qui ferait une

target_language_multi_word_term: moindre idée de qui ferait une
meaning: any idea who would do (something like that).
additional_notes: Used in questions to express surprise or incredulity about who might do a certain (usually bad or surprising) action. Often appears as 'As-tu la moindre idée de qui ferait une telle chose ?' or with formal 'Avez-vous'. 'La moindre idée' = 'the slightest idea'.
target_language_example: As-tu la moindre idée de qui ferait une telle chose ?
native_language_example: Do you have the slightest idea who would do such a thing?

meaning: 'at least, not' — used together as 'du moins, pas ...' to introduce a restriction or exception (literally 'at least, not ...').
additional_notes: Du moins = 'at least' or 'well, at least' to soften or qualify a previous statement. When followed by pas + phrase it specifies something that is excluded. Common in spoken and written French to hedge or limit a claim (e.g. 'Du moins, pas encore' = 'At least, not yet'). Word order: 'Du moins, pas ...' + element being negated.
target_language_example: Je vais y aller demain. Du moins, pas avant midi.
native_language_example: I'll go tomorrow. At least, not before noon.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; a sequence of the words 'moins' (less/fewer) and 'ce' (this/it) that can occur accidentally or across word boundaries. It is typically not meaningful on its own and often indicates a fragment, a typo, or two separate words belonging to different parts of a sentence.
additional_notes: Use 'moins' and 'ce' separately: 'moins' = less/fewer; 'ce' = this/it. Common correct expressions include 'à moins que' (unless) and constructions like 'moins ce que...' are incorrect — the correct link is usually 'ce que' or 'moins que'. If you see 'moins ce' together, it's likely a split across clauses (e.g. 'moins, ce...') or an error. This entry treats 'moins ce' as a non-standard sequence rather than a phrase to be memorized.
target_language_example: Il y a moins ce soir, ce comportement m'inquiète.
native_language_example: There is less tonight, this behavior worries me.

meaning: literally 'minus two times'; used to indicate 'subtract twice' or 'two times less' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom—its meaning depends on context. In arithmetic or instructions it can mean 'subtract two times' (do the subtraction twice) or 'minus twice' (−2×). In everyday French, 'deux fois moins' is the more common way to say 'two times less' or 'half as much' is usually expressed as 'deux fois moins' or better 'la moitié'. Be careful: word order matters ('deux fois moins' vs 'moins deux fois'). Without context, the phrase is uncommon.
target_language_example: Si tu retires moins deux fois, tu changes le résultat.
native_language_example: If you subtract minus two times, you change the result.

meaning: less than (followed by a noun phrase introduced by 'de' + article), often part of expressions like 'moins du temps' or 'moins du moitié' (note: usually appears as 'moins de' + definite article contracted to 'du').
additional_notes: Formed from 'moins de' (less than) + the contraction 'du' = 'de' + 'le'. Use when 'de' is followed by the masculine singular definite article 'le' (e.g. 'moins du temps prévu' = 'less than the scheduled time'). In many cases learners see 'moins de' without an article; use 'moins du' only when a specific masculine noun preceded by 'le' is intended. Example: 'Il a moins du courage que tu penses' is less common than 'Il a moins de courage que tu penses' — native speakers often prefer 'moins de' unless referring to a specific known noun preceded by 'le.'
target_language_example: Nous avons moins du budget prévu pour ce projet.
native_language_example: We have less than the planned budget for this project.

meaning: less in / less by (used in comparisons or quantities; uncommon as a fixed phrase)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common fixed expression in French on its own. It can appear when 'moins' (less) is followed by a preposition phrase starting with 'en' (e.g. 'moins en hiver', 'moins en quantité'), or in constructions like 'il y en a moins' where 'en' is a pronoun referring to a previously mentioned quantity. If you see 'moins en' it usually belongs to a larger phrase — check the surrounding words to understand whether 'en' is a pronoun ('there/of it') or a preposition ('in').
target_language_example: On utilise moins de chauffage en été, donc on dépense moins en énergie.
native_language_example: We use less heating in summer, so we spend less on energy.

meaning: literally 'minus the' — used in calculations or to indicate subtraction; also appears in constructions like 'à moins le' in casual speech but standard French uses 'à moins que' for 'unless'.
additional_notes: Most commonly 'moins le' appears in arithmetic or when subtracting something: e.g. 'dix moins le prix' (ten minus the price). It can also occur when followed by a noun: 'moins le temps' (less the time), but this is less common than using 'moins de' for 'less of'. Do not confuse with the conditional conjunction 'à moins que' (unless). For indicating 'unless', use 'à moins que (ne)...' rather than 'moins le'.
target_language_example: Vingt euros moins le coupon = dix-huit euros.
native_language_example: Twenty euros minus the coupon = eighteen euros.

meaning: literally 'the less one' — used to start comparative clauses meaning 'the less (someone) ...' or 'the fewer (we) ...'
additional_notes: Appears in comparative constructions like 'moins on [verb], mieux c'est' (the less one ..., the better). Often followed by a verb and completed by a contrasting clause introduced by 'mieux', 'plus', etc. Can refer to people in general (on = one/we/people). 'On' is informal/neutral and common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Moins on en parle, mieux c'est.
native_language_example: The less we talk about it, the better.

meaning: 'the less you' (start of a comparative clause)
additional_notes: Used in comparative constructions that pair 'moins' with 'tu' to mean 'the less you...'. Usually part of a larger structure like 'moins tu fais X, moins Y...' or 'moins tu sais, moins...' Often followed by a verb. English equivalent: 'the less you...'.
target_language_example: Moins tu manges tôt, moins tu auras faim le matin.
native_language_example: The less you eat early, the less hungry you'll be in the morning.

meaning: minus one; one less than (used in numbers or to indicate subtraction).
additional_notes: Used in arithmetic or when describing a count reduced by one (e.g., 'trois moins un = deux'). Also used idiomatically in time expressions in spoken French to say 'one to' the hour: e.g. 'il est huit heures moins dix' = 'it's ten to eight'. In such time expressions 'moins' subtracts minutes from the next hour. Pronunciation and usage are the same as the separate word 'moins' followed by the number 'un'.
target_language_example: Il est six heures moins une.
native_language_example: It's one to six (5:59, or one minute before six).

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely an incorrect word order. 'mois' = month, 'le' = the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: This sequence does not form a grammatical expression in French. The correct order for 'the month' is 'le mois'. If you encounter 'mois le' in text, it is probably a typo or a transcription error (e.g., words swapped during editing). Related correct phrases: 'le mois' (the month), 'ce mois' (this month), 'le mois prochain' (next month).
target_language_example: Dans la phrase, 'mois le' semble être une erreur de frappe et devrait être 'le mois'.
native_language_example: In the sentence, 'mois le' appears to be a typing error and should be 'le mois'.

meaning: literally 'month(s) more' — used in time expressions to mean 'plus X months' or 'X months more/longer'.
additional_notes: Often appears after a number to say how many months are added or remain (e.g., 'trois mois plus' = 'three months more'). In French normally you'd say 'trois mois de plus' or 'trois mois de plus/encore' or place 'plus' before a quantity in some constructions ('plus d'un mois' = 'more than a month'). 'mois plus' by itself is incomplete and mostly occurs as part of larger phrases (e.g., 'un mois plus tard' = 'one month later').
target_language_example: Il est parti un mois plus tard.
native_language_example: He left one month later.

meaning: month(s) that / since (depends on context) — often part of expressions indicating a number of months or a point in time relative to months.
additional_notes: Alone, 'mois que' is not a fixed phrase; it's typically used inside larger expressions. It can appear in comparisons or time expressions, for example: 'Il y a deux mois que...' (it's been two months since...) or 'le mois que vient' (the coming month). Word order and surrounding words determine the exact meaning: with a number + 'que' it often indicates duration ('depuis' meaning), while with adjectives or other qualifiers it links to 'month' as a noun.
target_language_example: Il y a trois mois que j'attends cette réponse.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for that answer for three months.

meaning: 'a (short) time with' or 'a moment with' (refers to spending some time together or having a brief interaction with someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about spending time with someone or having a brief occasion/interaction. Often appears in expressions like "passer un moment avec" (to spend time with) or "un moment avec toi" (a moment with you). Can be followed by a person, activity, or thing. Not a fixed idiom on its own; usually part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: J'aimerais passer un moment avec toi ce soir.
native_language_example: I'd like to spend some time with you tonight.

meaning: a (short) moment of; a time for (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a brief period or point in time, often followed by an infinitive or a noun (e.g. moment de réfléchir, moment de détente). Common in phrases like 'un moment de' (a moment of ...). Can indicate a specific occasion or a short break.
target_language_example: Donne-moi un moment de réflexion, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a moment to think, please.

meaning: literally 'time/moment is' — not a standalone fixed phrase in French; likely part of a larger expression (e.g. 'le moment est venu' = 'the time has come').
additional_notes: On its own, 'moment est' is incomplete and uncommon. You will typically see 'moment' followed by a verb or expression (le moment est venu, c'est le moment, au bon moment). Do not use 'moment est' alone; use a full phrase to express timing or that the right time has arrived.
target_language_example: Le moment est venu de partir.
native_language_example: The time has come to leave.

meaning: 'the moment' or 'the time' (a specific point or short period). Note: standard French word order is "le moment"; "moment le" is nonstandard and occurs only in poetic, emphatic, or inverted structures.
additional_notes: In everyday French the phrase is "le moment" (with the article before the noun). "Moment le" is not standard and appears rarely for stylistic inversion, poetic effect, or in archaic constructions. Avoid using it in normal speech. Gender is masculine. Can appear inside longer expressions when inversion is used: e.g., "Moment, le voilà" (poetic/informal) or in fixed poetic word order.
target_language_example: Moment le plus sombre, il trouva la force de sourire.
native_language_example: At the darkest moment, he found the strength to smile.

meaning: at the moment when / the moment that
additional_notes: Used to introduce the time when something happens. 'Moment que' is less common and can sound incomplete or informal in many contexts; 'au moment où' is the standard phrasing. 'Moment que' may appear in some regional or spoken uses and in fixed expressions, but learners should usually prefer 'au moment où' or 'au même moment que'.
target_language_example: Il est arrivé au moment que la réunion commençait.
native_language_example: He arrived at the moment that the meeting was starting.

meaning: when the time comes; at the appropriate moment
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future time when something will happen or be decided. Often appears in phrases like "le moment venu" (when the time comes). Formal to neutral register; common in speech and writing. Can be followed by an infinitive or a clause: "Le moment venu, nous en parlerons."
target_language_example: Le moment venu, je te dirai la vérité.
native_language_example: When the time comes, I'll tell you the truth.

meaning: a (pleasant) time doing something; an occasion spent doing X.
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (moment à + verb) to say someone spent time doing an activity. Often appears as "passer un moment à + inf." meaning "to spend time (pleasantly) doing..." Can be neutral or positive depending on adjectives (agréable, bon).
target_language_example: J'ai passé un bon moment à lire cet article.
native_language_example: I had a good time reading that article.

meaning: my God
additional_notes: An exclamation used to express surprise, shock, dismay, admiration, or strong emotion. Can be religious but is commonly used as a general interjection in everyday speech. Register ranges from neutral to informal; avoid in very formal or secular contexts if you want to be strictly neutral.
target_language_example: Mon Dieu, je n'avais pas vu ça venir !
native_language_example: Oh my God, I didn't see that coming!

meaning: an expletive meaning 'no way', 'yeah right', or a rude expression of disbelief; literally 'my ass'.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to show strong disbelief, insult, frustration, or to tell someone off. Can appear alone (Mon cul ! / Mon cul, ouais !) or inside phrases (Bouger mon cul ! = 'Move my ass!' meaning 'get moving' or expressing refusal depending on tone). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Mon cul, je vais te croire.
native_language_example: Yeah right, I'm going to believe you.

meaning: my taste / to my liking (used in expressions like 'à mon goût' = 'to my taste').
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase 'à mon goût' meaning 'in my opinion' or 'as I like it' (often used to say something is too much, not enough, or just right for someone). Common in subjective comments about food, style, volume, etc. Example sentences often omit 'à' informally ('Pas assez à mon goût' or 'Pas mon goût' in casual speech).
target_language_example: Ce plat est trop salé à mon goût.
native_language_example: This dish is too salty for my taste.

meaning: 'my prohibition' or 'my ban' — indicating that the speaker forbade something.
additional_notes: Used to say someone did something despite the speaker's order or rule. Interdiction is a noun meaning 'ban' or 'prohibition'; mon shows possession ('my'). Grammar note: the agreement in the example sentences (venu/venue/venus/venues) is because the past participle of venir agrees with the subject when used with être in the passé composé.
target_language_example: Il est parti malgré mon interdiction.
native_language_example: He left despite my prohibition.

meaning: 'my ...' used when starting a full name or a phrase like 'my name of' (incomplete phrase); often appears in constructions like «mon nom de famille» (my family name) or «mon nom de scène» (my stage name).
additional_notes: By itself, 'mon nom de' is incomplete in French and needs a following noun (e.g. famille, jeune fille, scène) to complete the idea. Common full phrases: «mon nom de famille» (my family/last name), «mon nom de jeune fille» (my maiden name), «mon nom de scène» (my stage name). Use 'mon' because the speaker is male or generic; women also use 'mon' with 'nom' because 'nom' is masculine. If you want to say 'my name is ...' use «je m'appelle ...» or «mon nom est ...».
target_language_example: Mon nom de famille est Martin.
native_language_example: My family name is Martin.

meaning: 'my dish' or 'my meal' (literally 'my plate')
additional_notes: Used to refer to a dish, meal, or plate that belongs to or was chosen by the speaker. Context determines whether it means a prepared dish (e.g. from a menu), a meal on a plate, or a favorite dish. The possessive 'mon' is used even if the noun is feminine in casual speech only when followed by a vowel sound (e.g. 'mon amie'); for 'plat' (masculine) 'mon' is the correct possessive.
target_language_example: C'est mon plat préféré au restaurant.
native_language_example: This is my favorite dish at the restaurant.

meaning: 'my point' (as in 'the point I make' or 'my argument')
additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker's argument, opinion, or main point in a conversation. Often appears in phrases like "mon point de vue" (my point of view) or when emphasizing what you are trying to say: e.g. «Voici mon point.» It can sound slightly formal depending on context; alone it rarely replaces fuller phrases like "mon avis" or "ma remarque."
target_language_example: Mon point, c'est que nous devons partir maintenant.
native_language_example: My point is that we need to leave now.

meaning: 'my point of' — the start of a phrase meaning the speaker's viewpoint about a specific aspect (usually completed by a noun or phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's typically followed by a noun or expression (e.g. 'mon point de vue' = 'my point of view'). Alone it can sound unfinished. Use 'mon point de vue' for 'my point of view' or 'mon point de départ' for 'my starting point'.
target_language_example: Mon point de vue, c'est que nous devons attendre.
native_language_example: My point of view is that we should wait.

meaning: a friendly informal address meaning 'my mate', 'pal', or 'old friend' (like 'buddy').
additional_notes: Used between acquaintances or friends, usually among men but can be used more widely. Informal and familiar; tone can be affectionate or casual. Literally means 'my old (one)' but functions as a vocative. Can be replaced by 'mon pote' or 'mon ami' in similar contexts.
target_language_example: Salut mon vieux, ça fait plaisir de te voir.
native_language_example: Hi buddy, it's great to see you.

meaning: 'yeah right' / 'as if!' (expresses disbelief or sarcasm); literal: 'my eye'.
additional_notes: Common informal/exclamatory phrase used to show scepticism, disbelief, or to dismiss what someone said. Often used alone or after a statement (e.g., "Du tennis, mon œil!" = "Tennis, my eye!" meaning you don't believe it). Can also be used jokingly; context and intonation determine force. The literal meaning ('my eye') is seldom intended except in medical contexts (e.g., "Mon œil a gonflé" = "My eye is swollen").
target_language_example: Tu as fini tout ce gâteau? Mon œil!
native_language_example: You finished that whole cake? Yeah right!

meaning: there are people who
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's likely part of a larger expression where monde (people/world) is the subject and a (from avoir) begins a verb phrase (e.g., "y a" as in "il y a" or "le monde a" meaning "people have"). Possible interpretations: 1) "le monde a..." = "people have..." (completing with a noun/clause), 2) spoken/colloquial "y a" contracted after monde in conversation (less common). You will usually see it inside a full sentence (e.g., "Le monde a changé" = "The world/people have changed").
target_language_example: Le monde a beaucoup changé ces dernières années.
native_language_example: People/the world have changed a lot in recent years.

meaning: the world laughed / everyone laughed (past tense)
additional_notes: This is a short past-tense phrase: 'monde' = 'world' or 'people/everyone', 'a' = third-person singular of avoir used in passé composé, and 'ri' = past participle of 'rire' (to laugh). It implies that lots of people laughed or that everyone laughed. In natural French you'd usually add 'Le' (Le monde a ri) or use a subject (Tout le monde a ri).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a ri de sa blague.
native_language_example: Everyone laughed at his joke.

meaning: "the world has been" (literal) — likely part of a larger sentence; not a standalone phrase.
additional_notes: This is not an independent fixed expression in French. It combines monde (world/people) + a été (has been) and needs more words to form a complete idea (e.g., « le monde a été surpris » = "the world was/has been surprised"). In many contexts monde can mean "the world" or informally "people/everyone" (le monde). Use a complete clause after "a été" to show what happened or how something was. "A été" is the passé composé of être (to be).
target_language_example: Le monde a été choqué par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: The world was shocked by the news.

meaning: 'the world needs' or 'people need' (literal: 'world needs')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'monde a besoin' usually appears inside a sentence like 'Le monde a besoin de...' meaning 'The world needs...'. In spoken French the article 'le' is often included: 'Le monde a besoin de paix.' It can also be used more generally to mean 'people need' or 'society needs.' Don't forget the preposition 'de' before the noun or infinitive that follows (e.g. 'de paix', 'de changer').
target_language_example: Le monde a besoin de plus de compassion.
native_language_example: The world needs more compassion.

meaning: '(the) world/people need(s) (something)'; commonly used in the phrase 'tout le monde a besoin de' meaning 'everyone needs'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'tout le monde a besoin de' (everybody needs). Use 'de' before an infinitive verb or before a noun. When followed by a pronoun, pronoun placement and contraction rules apply (e.g. 'en a besoin' = 'needs it').
