Note that 'le monde' is grammatically singular, but 'tout le monde' behaves like 'everyone' and takes third-person singular verbs. Be careful: 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' is ungrammatical — correct is 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' is commonly replaced by 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' only in colloquial speech; more proper: 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' → better: 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' (prefer rephrasing: 'Tout le monde doit le faire' or use object pronoun placement 'Tout le monde a besoin de le faire' is generally avoided).
target_language_example: Le monde a besoin de toi.
native_language_example: The world/people need you.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'people have some' or 'the world has some'.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed expression in French. It looks like a word group where monde = 'world' or 'people' and a des = 'has some' (a + des is not grammatically correct together: correct would be 'a des' only after monde: 'le monde a des...' meaning 'the world/people have...'). You will usually see 'le monde a' (the world has) or 'le monde a des [choses/problèmes]' (people have some [things/problems]). Without an article ('le' or 'du'), 'monde a des' alone is incomplete. Use full sentences like: 'Le monde a des problèmes' = 'The world has problems' or 'Il y a des gens' = 'There are people.'
target_language_example: Le monde a des opinions différentes sur ce sujet.
native_language_example: People have different opinions on this topic.

meaning: everyone has the right (to...) — a non-standard/colloquial phrase meaning 'people are allowed' or 'everyone is entitled to'.
additional_notes: This exact phrase is ungrammatical in standard French. Standard forms are 'tout le monde a le droit de...' or 'tout le monde a droit à...'. Often used colloquially where a speaker shortens 'tout le monde' to 'monde' in speech, but avoid this in writing. Follow with an infinitive (a le droit de + infinitive) or a noun introduced by 'à'.
target_language_example: Tout le monde a le droit de s'exprimer.
native_language_example: Everyone has the right to express themselves.

meaning: 'people are afraid' or 'everyone is scared'.
additional_notes: This phrase is an informal, conversational way to say that many people (or the general public) are frightened or worried about something. Grammatically you would normally see it as "le monde a peur" (with the article) or "tout le monde a peur" (meaning 'everyone is afraid'). Without the article it can appear in headlines or clipped speech. Use it to describe widespread fear or alarm.
target_language_example: Le monde a peur à cause de cette rumeur.
native_language_example: People are afraid because of that rumor.

meaning: 'people are afraid of' or 'the world is afraid of'
additional_notes: This phrase is used to say that many people (or people in general) are afraid of something. In French you would normally write 'le monde a peur de...' or 'les gens ont peur de...'. It precedes an infinitive or a noun: e.g. 'le monde a peur de l'avenir' (people are afraid of the future) or 'le monde a peur de perdre son travail' (people are afraid of losing their jobs).
target_language_example: Le monde a peur de l'avenir.
native_language_example: People are afraid of the future.

meaning: part of a larger expression meaning 'everyone has their…' or 'the world has its…' (used to say that people have different tastes, faults, or ways).
additional_notes: Alone 'monde a ses' is incomplete; it appears in phrases like 'le monde a ses raisons' or 'le monde a ses défauts' and is used to concede that something exists or is normal. Often translated as 'everyone has...' or 'there are...' depending on context. Common structures: 'Le monde a ses raisons' (people have their reasons), 'Le monde a ses défauts' (the world/people have their flaws).
target_language_example: Le monde a ses raisons, même si on ne les comprend pas toujours.
native_language_example: People have their reasons, even if we don't always understand them.

meaning: This sequence is not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'world has a' or words appearing out of order.
additional_notes: The words 'monde', 'a', and 'un' are common individually: 'monde' = world/people, 'a' = (he/she/it) has or present of avoir, and 'un' = a/one. Together as 'monde a un' there is no fixed idiomatic meaning in French. It may occur inside a larger correct phrase (for example 'le monde a un avis' = 'the world has an opinion') or be a typo/misaligned word order. For beginners: don't use 'monde a un' by itself. Learn the individual words and common phrases like 'le monde' (the world/people), 'il a' (he has), and 'un/une' (a/one).
target_language_example: Le monde a un rêve commun.
native_language_example: The world has a common dream.

meaning: 'the world likes' or 'people like' (literal: 'world likes')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression in French on its own. 'Monde' can mean 'people' or 'the world', and 'aime' is the third-person singular of 'aimer' (to like/love). Together they might appear in a sentence like 'Le monde aime...' meaning 'People like...' or 'Everyone likes...'. Make sure to include the definite article 'le' (Le monde aime...) when speaking generally about people.
target_language_example: Le monde aime ce film.
native_language_example: People like this movie.

meaning: people like (the)... / everyone likes (the)...
additional_notes: This looks like a fragment rather than a complete phrase. 'Monde' here means 'people' (informal/general). The usual full expressions are 'le monde aime...' or 'tout le monde aime...' ('everyone/people like...'). If you want to say 'people like the [noun]', use 'les gens aiment...' or 'tout le monde aime les ...'. Word order: subject (le monde/tout le monde/les gens) + verb (aime/aiment) + object.
target_language_example: Tout le monde aime les croissants au beurre.
native_language_example: Everyone likes butter croissants.

meaning: 'monde au' is not a standalone French phrase; it's likely part of a larger expression (e.g. 'le monde au...' or 'mettre le monde au courant').
additional_notes: You will not find 'monde au' used by itself. 'Monde' means 'world' or 'people' and 'au' is a contraction of 'à le' ('to the'/'at the'). Common expressions that include these words: 'mettre le monde au courant' (to inform people), 'le monde au pouvoir' (the world in power) — the exact meaning depends on the full phrase. If you saw 'monde au' in a sentence, look for the words before and after to identify the complete expression.
target_language_example: Il faut mettre le monde au courant de la réunion.
native_language_example: We need to inform people about the meeting.

meaning: 'people with' or 'the world with' depending on context; often part of phrases like "un monde avec..." meaning "a world with..." or used when talking about people who have/are with something/someone.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed phrase on its own. 'Monde' means 'world' or 'people' (as in 'le monde' = people/everyone). 'Avec' means 'with'. Together they appear in longer expressions (e.g. 'un monde avec peu de ressources' = 'a world with few resources'; or 'le monde avec qui je travaille' = 'the people I work with'). Pay attention to articles and connectors: 'le monde avec...' (the people with...) or 'un monde avec...' (a world with...).
target_language_example: Le monde avec qui je voyage est très sympa.
native_language_example: The people I travel with are very nice.

meaning: 'the world knows' or 'everybody knows'.
additional_notes: Combines monde (the world/people) and connaît (knows). Used to say that something is widely known or obvious to everyone. In natural French you would more often hear 'tout le monde connaît' or 'le monde sait' rather than just 'monde connaît' by itself — the given phrase appears incomplete and needs a determiner or subject ('tout le monde connaît...').
target_language_example: Tout le monde connaît cette chanson.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that song.

meaning: 'people in' or 'world in' (literal combination of monde + dans); by itself it's not a fixed phrase in French.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed expression. 'Monde' means 'people' or 'world' and 'dans' means 'in'. You will normally see them together as part of a larger phrase, e.g. 'le monde dans la rue' (the people/in the street) or 'il y a du monde dans la salle' (there are people in the room). Learners should treat 'monde' and 'dans' separately and learn common full phrases where they appear together.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde dans le parc aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the park today.

meaning: 'world of' or 'sphere of' — used to talk about someone's area, environment, or a type of world (e.g. monde de la mode = world of fashion).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to specify a domain, social circle, or setting. Common in expressions like 'le monde de l'art', 'le monde du travail', 'un monde à part'. Can be used literally (planet/people) or figuratively (sphere, industry). Often appears with definite article: 'le monde de...'.
target_language_example: Elle travaille dans le monde de la restauration.
native_language_example: She works in the world of (the) restaurant industry / in the hospitality industry.

meaning: the outside world; what's happening outside (lit. 'world outside').
additional_notes: Used to refer to the world beyond one's current place or bubble — news, society, people outside a given location or situation. Often appears in phrases like «le monde dehors» or «le monde d'en dehors». Tone is neutral; more natural: «le monde dehors» or «le monde d'en dehors».
target_language_example: Il ne sait rien du monde dehors.
native_language_example: He knows nothing about the outside world.

meaning: 'the world of' or 'the realm/field of' (used to talk about a particular area, group, industry, or way of life)
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to specify which 'world' is meant: monde des affaires (business world), monde des médias (media world), monde des artistes (artists' world). Often used to describe a social or professional sphere, sometimes with connotations about its rules or culture.
target_language_example: Il travaille dans le monde des technologies.
native_language_example: He works in the world of technology.

meaning: 'so-called' (literally 'world called'), used to describe something referred to by a particular name or label
additional_notes: 'Monde dit' is not a very common fixed phrase in French by itself. More often you will see constructions like "le monde dit X" or "ce qu'on dit être X" to mean "the so-called X" or "what is called X." It introduces a label that someone uses (sometimes with doubt or distance). Equivalent everyday French: "soi-disant" or "le soi-disant X."
target_language_example: Le monde dit "expert" n'a pas toutes les réponses.
native_language_example: The so-called "expert" doesn't have all the answers.

meaning: 'people say that' / 'the world says that' (used to report what others say)
additional_notes: Literally 'world says that'. Used informally to report general opinion or rumor (like 'they say that' or 'people say that'). Often appears in spoken French; you might also hear 'on dit que' or 'les gens disent que' for the same idea. Followed by a clause introduced by que.
target_language_example: Le monde dit que ce film est extraordinaire.
native_language_example: People say that this movie is amazing.

meaning: 'the world must' or 'people must' (literal translation of two words; not a fixed phrase)
additional_notes: This is not an established fixed expression in French by itself. It reads as the noun 'monde' (world/people) followed by the verb 'doit' (must/owes) and would need more context to form a complete idea (e.g., 'le monde doit agir' = 'the world must act', or 'le monde doit de l'argent' → uncommon; better: 'il doit de l'argent au monde' is odd). In everyday French, 'monde' often means 'people' ('tout le monde' = 'everyone'). If you mean 'people must', a natural phrasing is 'les gens doivent' or 'tout le monde doit'.
target_language_example: Tout le monde doit respecter les règles.
native_language_example: Everyone must respect the rules.

meaning: 'monde en' by itself is not a complete French phrase; 'monde' means 'world' or 'people' and 'en' is a pronoun/preposition meaning 'of it/of them' or 'in'.
additional_notes:
This sequence ('monde en') is incomplete without more words. Common constructions you may see include:
- 'le monde en général' = 'the world in general' or 'people in general'
- 'il y a du monde' / 'beaucoup de monde' (means 'there are people' / 'a lot of people') — here 'en' is not used.
- 's'en moquer' uses 'en' as a pronoun ('to not care about it').
'En' is a very common and versatile word: it can replace phrases introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'J'ai trois pommes' → 'J'en ai trois' = 'I have three of them') or indicate location ('en France' = 'in France'). 'Monde' can mean 'the world' or 'people/ crowd' depending on context. Because 'monde en' lacks context, learn full phrases where 'monde' and 'en' appear together.
target_language_example: Le monde en général s'inquiète du changement climatique.
native_language_example: People in general are worried about climate change.

meaning: the world is
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the noun monde (world; also 'people' or 'society') followed by the verb est (is). Meaning depends on context: 'ce monde est...' = 'this world is...'; 'le prénom le plus répandu dans le monde est...' = 'in the world is...'. 'Monde' can mean 'the planet', 'the world', or more abstractly 'society/people'.
target_language_example: Ce monde est trop bruyant pour moi.
native_language_example: This world is too noisy for me.

meaning: the world/people have remained / people stayed (literal); often part of a larger sentence meaning 'the world remained' or 'everyone stayed'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the sequence of words 'monde' (world/people) + 'est resté' (has/had stayed or remained). In French, 'le monde' can mean 'people' or 'everyone' in informal speech. Agreement depends on context: with 'le monde' the verb is usually singular (est resté) but sometimes plural verbs (sont restés) appear in spoken French. You will most often see this inside a fuller sentence, e.g. 'Le monde est resté chez lui' ('People stayed at home') or 'Le monde est resté silencieux' ('Everyone remained silent').
target_language_example: Le monde est resté silencieux pendant la minute.
native_language_example: Everyone remained silent for the minute.

meaning: 'the world is at' (fragment) — not a complete phrase; appears as part of expressions like "le monde est au courant" (people know) or "le monde est au travail" (people are working).
additional_notes: This string alone is not a standalone expression in French. It's the sequence "monde est au" that occurs when a noun phrase with monde (the world/people) is followed by the verb être and the preposition à/au (contraction of à + le) before another word. Common complete examples: "Le monde est au courant" (People are aware), "Le monde est au travail" (People are at work). Use the full sentence to convey meaning.
target_language_example: Le monde est au courant de la nouvelle.
native_language_example: People are aware of the news.

meaning: 'the world is happy' or 'people are happy'.
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining monde (world/people) + est (is) + heureux (happy). In French, "le monde" often means "people" or "everyone" rather than the planet. As given, this is a simple declarative sentence fragment; you'd usually say "Le monde est heureux" to mean "Everyone is happy" or "The world is happy." Use the adjective form to agree in gender/number when referring to specific people (e.g., "Les gens sont heureux").
target_language_example: Le monde est heureux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Everyone is happy today.

meaning: part of the phrase 'tout le monde est là' — 'is everybody here?' or 'is everyone here?'.
additional_notes: Usually used with 'tout' as 'tout le monde est là?' to ask if all people (everyone) are present. Common in classrooms, meetings, or gatherings. Informal-neutral; can be said with intonation for a question or written with 'Est-ce que'. Not used alone without 'tout' in most contexts.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tout le monde est là pour commencer la réunion?
native_language_example: Is everyone here to start the meeting?

meaning: 'it's a small world' (expresses surprise at an unexpected connection)
additional_notes: Used to react when you discover an unexpected link or coincidence (e.g., meeting someone you know in an unlikely place). Often appears in the fixed expression 'Quel monde petit !' or 'Le monde est petit !'. Informal-to-neutral; common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Le monde est petit : elle travaille avec mon frère !
native_language_example: It's a small world: she works with my brother!

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; literally 'world is very' — likely part of a longer sentence (e.g., 'le monde est très ...' = 'the world is very ...').
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is incomplete in French. You'll usually see it as part of a full sentence: 'Le monde est très grand' (The world is very big) or 'Le monde est très différent aujourd'hui' (The world is very different today). Remember to include an article ('le' or 'le/ce/un') and an adjective or complement after 'très'.
target_language_example: Le monde est très grand et plein de surprises.
native_language_example: The world is very big and full of surprises.

meaning: 'the world belongs to' or 'the world is (for)'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase; you will usually see it as part of a larger sentence like « le monde est à ceux qui... » meaning 'the world belongs to those who...'. It expresses possession or that something/someone has an advantage or opportunity. Not a standalone sentence; needs a subject before and a complement after.
target_language_example: Le monde est à ceux qui se lèvent tôt.
native_language_example: The world belongs to those who get up early.

meaning: 'monde' = world / people; 'et' = and. (Together they are not a fixed phrase.)
additional_notes: This is not a standard multi-word expression in French. 'Monde' means 'world' or 'people' (e.g., tout le monde = everyone). 'Et' is the conjunction 'and'. If you see 'monde et' in a sentence it will be part of a larger phrase (for example 'monde et société' = 'world and society') — you should look at the words that follow to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: Tout le monde et ses amis sont invités.
native_language_example: Everyone and their friends are invited.

meaning: literally 'made world' — not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment (e.g. monde fait de… = a world made of…)
additional_notes: This is not a common standalone expression in French. It can appear as part of a larger construction like « un monde fait de rêves » (a world made of dreams) or in poetic/descriptive language. If you saw it alone, check the full sentence — the intended meaning depends on the verb (faire) used in a past participle construction or on the noun phrase that follows. Do not use 'monde fait' by itself to mean anything idiomatic.
target_language_example: Ils ont imaginé un monde fait de solidarité et de musique.
native_language_example: They imagined a world made of solidarity and music.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo, misordering, or missing article/hyphen. Closest correct forms: «le monde» (the world/people) or «ce monde-là / le monde-là» (that world/that crowd).
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'monde la' without article or hyphen. If you see 'monde la' it is usually an error or the result of omitted punctuation (should be 'monde-là') or missing article ('le monde'). 'Monde-là' with a hyphen means 'that world' or refers to a particular group of people. Check context for correction.
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis n'intéresse pas le monde la — il faudrait écrire «le monde-là» ou «le monde» selon le sens.
native_language_example: What you say doesn't interest 'le monde la' — you should write "le monde-là" or "le monde" depending on the meaning.

meaning: "le" refers to a previously mentioned person or thing; in phrases like "tout le monde le ..." it means "everyone (him/it) ..." — i.e. everyone + object pronoun.
additional_notes: This sequence appears when the object pronoun "le" (him/it) follows "tout le monde" (everyone). In English you'd translate the whole phrase as "everyone [does/knows/hates] him/it" depending on context. The gender/meaning of "le" depends on what was mentioned earlier (masculine person or masculine noun). For a feminine referent you'd see "tout le monde la". Word order is: subject (tout le monde) + object pronoun (le) + verb.
target_language_example: Tout le monde le respecte dans le quartier.
native_language_example: Everyone respects him in the neighborhood.

meaning: everyone knows it / everybody knows (about it).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the full phrase "tout le monde le sait" meaning 'everyone knows it'. Used to state that some fact or piece of information is widely known or obvious. Can be used in statements or questions (e.g., "Est-ce que tout le monde le sait ?"). Tone is neutral and suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Tout le monde le sait déjà, alors pourquoi en parler ?
native_language_example: Everyone already knows it, so why talk about it?

meaning: 'monde' = 'world' or 'people'; 'me' = object pronoun 'me' (to/for me)
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words rather than a fixed multiword phrase. 'Monde' can mean 'the world' or informally 'people' (e.g. 'beaucoup de monde' = 'a lot of people'). 'Me' is the unstressed object pronoun meaning 'me' (before a verb: 'me voit' = 'sees me') or after a preposition as 'moi' would be used instead. Alone, 'monde me' is not a standard French phrase — you will usually see them in different positions in a sentence (e.g. 'Le monde me regarde' = 'The world is watching me').
target_language_example: Le monde me regarde.
native_language_example: The world is watching me.

meaning: 'the world dies' or 'people are dying' (literal phrasing; likely poetic or hyperbolic)
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed phrase in everyday French. Taken literally, 'monde' means 'world' or 'people' and 'meurt' is the third-person singular present of 'mourir' ('to die'). Context matters: it could be used poetically (the world is dying), hyperbolically (everyone is dying), or as a clipped fragment in speech or writing. For everyday conversation, more natural phrases are 'le monde est en train de mourir' (the world is dying) or 'les gens meurent' (people are dying).
target_language_example: À force de pollution, on dirait que le monde meurt.
native_language_example: Because of so much pollution, it feels like the world is dying.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase in French; 'monde' = 'world/people' and 'ne' is the first part of the negation 'ne ... pas' or pairs with negative pronouns like 'personne'. The sequence 'monde ne' by itself is incomplete and rarely appears as a contiguous unit in standard sentences.
additional_notes: This sequence is generally unnatural because 'ne' normally precedes a verb and a negative particle or pronoun follows/combines with it. You might encounter 'monde' and 'ne' adjacent in certain constructions (e.g. when a relative or adverbial places them next to each other), but such cases are uncommon and often sound awkward. Examples of related correct usages: 'Il n'y a pas beaucoup de monde.' (There aren't many people.) 'Personne ne vient.' (Nobody is coming.)
target_language_example: Le monde ne comprend pas toujours les choix des artistes.
native_language_example: The world does not always understand artists' choices.

meaning: 'the world cannot' / 'people cannot' (literal pieces; incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This string is not a complete, standalone phrase in French. It combines monde (the world/people) with ne...pas (negative), and would appear inside a larger sentence like «Le monde ne peut pas... » meaning 'People/the world cannot...'. Depending on context, monde can mean 'the world' or informally 'people/everyone'. Remember to include a verb after ne...pas to finish the sentence.
target_language_example: Le monde ne peut pas tout comprendre.
native_language_example: People cannot understand everything.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a word order mistake (should be 'nous' + verb or 'le monde' in a phrase).
additional_notes: The sequence 'monde nous' by itself does not form a correct or common French expression. Native speakers would usually say 'le monde' (the world/people) or 'nous' (we/us) in different positions, for example: 'Le monde nous regarde' (The world is watching us) or 'Nous, le monde...' in more complex structures. If you saw 'monde nous' in written text, it is probably a typo or part of a larger sentence where word order was broken.
target_language_example: Le monde nous regarde.
native_language_example: The world is watching us.

meaning: 'the world speaks' or 'people are talking' (literal)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed everyday phrase in French by itself. Taken literally, monde = 'world' or 'people', parle = 'speaks'. In context it could appear inside a larger sentence (e.g., 'le monde parle de...' = 'people are talking about...'). Alone, 'monde parle' sounds like a fragment and would usually need more words to be natural.
target_language_example: Le monde parle de ce film ces jours-ci.
native_language_example: People are talking about that movie these days.

meaning: 'people are talking about' or 'the world is talking about'.
additional_notes: This phrase is usually part of a larger sentence, often preceded by 'tout le' or 'le' (e.g. 'tout le monde parle de...') meaning 'everyone is talking about...'. Alone 'monde parle de' is not a complete phrase; you need a subject (e.g. 'tout le monde') and an object/topic after 'de'. It's used to say that a lot of people are discussing or that something is widely talked about.
target_language_example: Tout le monde parle de ce nouveau film.
native_language_example: Everyone is talking about that new movie.

meaning: 'people think' or 'the world thinks' (what people generally believe or say)
additional_notes: A short phrase combining monde (world/people) and pense (thinks). In natural French you'd more often see full forms like 'le monde pense que...' or 'tout le monde pense que...' to mean 'people think that...' or 'everyone thinks that...'. Alone, 'monde pense' looks like a clipped or poetic fragment. Use with a clause: 'Le monde pense que c'est fini.'
target_language_example: Le monde pense que tu as raison.
native_language_example: People think that you are right.

meaning: people think that / everyone thinks that
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial shorthand for 'le monde pense que' meaning 'people in general think that' or 'everyone thinks that'. Used to report a common opinion; tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'que'.
target_language_example: Le monde pense que c'est impossible, mais nous allons essayer.
native_language_example: People think that it's impossible, but we will try.

meaning: 'the world can' (literal) — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g. "le monde peut..." meaning "people/the world can...").
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'Monde' usually means 'world' or 'people' (as a group). 'Peut' is the third-person singular of 'pouvoir' (can/may). Together they appear where a speaker says that the world/people can do something (e.g. "Le monde peut changer"). In everyday French you'd normally see the article ('le monde peut', 'le monde peut penser') or a different subject ('les gens peuvent').
target_language_example: Le monde peut changer si nous agissons maintenant.
native_language_example: The world can change if we act now.

meaning: Not a fixed French expression; simply the sequence of the noun 'monde' (world/people) followed directly by the preposition 'pour' (for). It can appear within longer phrases or sentences but is not a standard multiword idiom by itself.
additional_notes: This sequence usually needs surrounding words to form a grammatical phrase (e.g. 'le monde pour...' or 'un monde pour...'). Depending on context, 'monde' can mean 'the world' or 'people/people present'. Example uses might be poetic or part of larger constructions ('un monde pour les enfants'). If you intended a different fixed expression, consider alternatives like 'tout le monde' (everyone) or 'pour le monde' (for the world).
target_language_example: Il rêve d'un monde pour les générations futures.
native_language_example: He dreams of a world for future generations.

meaning: 'monde' = world/people; 'que' = that/which — together they are not a fixed phrase in French.
additional_notes: This is not an established multiword expression. 'monde' often means 'people' or 'world' and is frequently used with relative pronouns (que, qui) in sentences like « les gens que... » or « le monde qui... ». Alone, 'monde que' would simply be the word 'monde' followed by the relative pronoun 'que' starting a clause (e.g. « le monde que je connais » = 'the world that I know'). Do not treat 'monde que' as a single lexical unit.
target_language_example: Le monde que j'ai rencontré en voyage était très accueillant.
native_language_example: The people/world that I met while traveling were very welcoming.

meaning: 'people are watching' or 'everyone is watching'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase in French by itself; it combines monde (people/the world) and regarde (is watching). You might hear it in contexts like «tout le monde regarde» (everybody's watching) or «le monde regarde» (people are watching / the world is watching). Use with articles or pronouns: «tout le monde regarde», «le monde regarde».
target_language_example: Le monde regarde ce match ce soir.
native_language_example: People are watching this match tonight.

meaning: 'the rest of the world' or 'the people/places remaining' (literal combination of monde + reste)
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase in French. Native speakers would normally say "le reste du monde" for 'the rest of the world' or "les gens qui restent / ceux qui restent" for 'the people who remain.' "monde reste" can appear in nonstandard, poetic, or elliptical contexts but is uncommon on its own.
target_language_example: Si le monde reste silencieux, rien ne changera.
native_language_example: If the world remains silent, nothing will change.

meaning: 'people know' or 'the world knows' (third-person present of savoir: 'monde sait' = 'people/one knows')
additional_notes: Monde means 'world' or 'people' in a general sense. Used in expressions like 'tout le monde sait' (everyone knows). Alone 'monde sait' is uncommon; native speakers usually say 'le monde sait' or 'tout le monde sait'. Use with verbs in third person singular: 'sait' is from savoir (to know).
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que Paris est belle.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that Paris is beautiful.

meaning: 'the world knows this' / 'everyone knows this' (nonstandard word order in French)
additional_notes: The phrase 'monde sait ce' is not standard French word order. Standard expressions are 'tout le monde sait ça' or 'tout le monde le sait'. The sequence 'monde sait ce' might appear in poetic, emphatic, or erroneous constructions, but it should be avoided in normal speech and writing. When translating literally, word-for-word order is possible but unnatural in French.
target_language_example: Monde sait ce que j'ai fait ? Non, bien sûr que non.
native_language_example: Does the world know what I did? No, of course not.

meaning: 'the world' (monde) + reflexive pronoun se; not a fixed phrase on its own
additional_notes: This is not a standalone French expression. It looks like the noun 'monde' (world, people) followed by the reflexive pronoun 'se' that belongs to a verb (e.g., 'le monde se demande...' = 'people wonder...'). You will not normally use 'monde se' alone; instead you'll see 'le monde se ...' or 'les gens se ...' with a verb (se sentir, se demander, se moquer, etc.).
target_language_example: Le monde se demande ce qui va se passer demain.
native_language_example: People are wondering what will happen tomorrow.

meaning: people began to / everyone started to (do something)
additional_notes: Literary or formal past-tense construction: 'se mit à' is the passé simple of 'se mettre à' (to begin to). Used to describe that a group of people (le monde) started doing something. In spoken French you would more often hear the passé composé 'le monde s'est mis à' or 'les gens ont commencé à'.
target_language_example: Le monde se mit à applaudir quand elle arriva sur scène.
native_language_example: People began to applaud when she came on stage.

meaning: 'the world seems' or 'people seem' (literal sequence: 'world seems')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's just two words that can appear together in a sentence (e.g. 'Le monde semble heureux' = 'The world seems happy') or as part of expressions like 'Il semble que le monde...' For beginner learners, treat 'monde' = 'world' or sometimes 'people/the public' and 'semble' = 'seems/appears'. Subject-verb agreement matters: 'le monde semble' (singular verb).
target_language_example: Le monde semble plus calme aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The world seems calmer today.

meaning: 'the world smiles' (literal) — likely part of a poetic or lyrical phrase meaning 'the world smiles' or 'everyone is smiling'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed everyday expression in French; it reads as a literal combination of monde (world/people) + sourit (3rd-person singular of sourire = 'smiles'). You might see it in poetry, song lyrics, headlines or creative writing to convey a mood: the world is smiling / everything seems happy. If you want to say 'people are smiling' more naturally, use 'les gens sourient.'
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, tout semble parfait, le monde sourit.
native_language_example: Today everything seems perfect, the world smiles.

meaning: 'monde sur' by itself is not a standard fixed expression in French; likely part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'le monde sur...' or 'monde sur...' as in 'le monde sur Internet').
additional_notes: You won't usually see 'monde sur' alone as a standalone phrase. It typically appears as 'le monde sur ...' or 'le monde de ...' to mean 'the world on/over ...' or to refer to people on a platform (e.g. 'le monde sur Internet' = 'people on the Internet' or 'the world on the Internet'). Choose 'sur' when meaning 'on' (location, platform); use 'de' for 'of' or belonging. For beginners: learn 'monde' = 'world' or 'people' in general, and 'sur' = 'on' or 'upon'.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde sur Internet.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people on the Internet.

meaning: 'the world on the...' (fragment; not a complete fixed phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression in French. It looks like a fragment of a sentence — for example, 'le monde sur le net' (the world on the net) or 'un monde sur le papier' (a world on paper). You will normally see 'monde' followed by a prepositional phrase (sur le/la/les + noun). Translate literally as 'world on the...'. Don't use this fragment alone; include the noun after 'le' to complete the phrase.
target_language_example: Il existe un monde sur le web que tu ne connais pas.
native_language_example: There is a world on the web that you don't know.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment (e.g. from 'le monde te...' or 'monde, tu...').
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'monde te' does not form a valid multi-word expression in French. It may appear when a sentence is split or when someone types part of a sentence such as 'le monde te regarde' ('the world is watching you') or 'monde, tu...' (addressing 'world' in poetic use). If you see 'monde te' in writing, check the surrounding words — it's probably two separate words belonging to different parts of the sentence rather than an idiom. For beginner learners: focus on learning 'monde' (world/people) and the pronoun 'te' (you, object form) separately.
target_language_example: Le monde te regarde.
native_language_example: The world is watching you.

meaning: 'the world goes' / part of expressions about how things are going (e.g. "le monde va..." as in commenting on the state of the world).
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase in French; appears as part of larger expressions (e.g. « le monde va mal », « le monde va vite »). Used to comment on the state or behavior of people/society or on how fast/slow things change. You usually need an adjective or adverb after it (mal, bien, vite, mieux, etc.).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le monde va trop vite pour moi.
native_language_example: Today, the world moves too fast for me.

meaning: 'everyone is doing well' or 'is everyone okay?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that all people (a group, audience, family, etc.) are well or okay. Commonly appears as a question (Est-ce que tout le monde va bien ?) or as a statement (Tout le monde va bien.). 'Tout le monde' means 'everyone'. 'Va bien' = 'is doing well'/'is fine'.
target_language_example: Après l'accident, elle a demandé : « Est-ce que tout le monde va bien ? »
native_language_example: After the accident, she asked, "Is everyone okay?"

meaning: 'people wanted' or 'the world wanted' (past tense of vouloir with monde as subject)
additional_notes: Monde means 'people' or 'everyone' in informal contexts. When combined with the imperfect/conditional/past tense of vouloir (wanted), 'monde voulait' appears inside a sentence where 'le monde' is the subject: e.g. «Le monde voulait...». You rarely see 'monde voulait' standing alone; include the article 'le/ tout le' or a subject pronoun in full sentences. Use it to report what many people desired or expected in the past.
target_language_example: Le monde voulait des réponses après l'accident.
native_language_example: People wanted answers after the accident.

meaning: 'people' or 'everyone' when referring to people in general (followed by a verb or comment about the listener/group).
additional_notes: The phrase 'monde vous' by itself is not a standard fixed phrase in French. More common is 'tout le monde' (everyone) or 'le monde' (people/world). If you see 'monde, vous' it might be part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'Le monde, vous le savez...' or 'Le monde vous regarde') where 'monde' is the subject 'people/the world' and 'vous' is the object 'you'. For learners, use 'tout le monde' to say 'everyone', or 'le monde' when speaking about people/the world. Word order matters: French typically places subject before object (Le monde vous regarde = The world is watching you).
target_language_example: Tout le monde vous entend.
native_language_example: Everyone can hear you.

meaning: 'people there' or 'the people there' (referring to people in a place or situation)
additional_notes: This is an informal, shortened way to refer to 'les gens qui sont là' or 'les gens à cet endroit/concernés'. You will most often see it in spoken French or casual written contexts (texts, social media). It combines 'monde' (people) with the pronoun 'y' (there/about it). Use it when pointing to people present or involved: e.g. 'Il n'y avait pas beaucoup de monde' → 'Il n'y avait pas trop de monde y' (colloquial). Not standard in formal writing.
target_language_example: Il y avait plein de monde y ce soir.
native_language_example: There were lots of people there tonight.

meaning: 'a lot of' or 'many people/things to' (used in expressions like "un monde à + infinitive/nom")
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase by itself; 'monde' means 'people' or 'world' and can be combined with prepositions (à, de, etc.) in different expressions. 'Un monde à' appears in contexts like 'un monde à voir' (a world to see) or in colloquial phrasing where 'monde' quantifies people: e.g. 'Il y avait un monde à l'extérieur' (There were many people outside). For beginners, learn common full expressions rather than 'monde à' alone.
target_language_example: Il y avait un monde à l'entrée du musée.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people at the museum entrance.

meaning: 'the change is' or 'the currency is' (depending on context)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the words monnaie (money/coin/change/currency) + est (is). You will see it inside sentences like «La monnaie est rendue» (the change is given back) or «La monnaie est européenne» (the currency is European). Use it when describing the state or identity of money or currency. Word order and meaning depend on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: La monnaie est arrivée, vous pouvez la récupérer.
native_language_example: The change has arrived, you can pick it up.

meaning: 'monsieur' (sir/Mr.) + 'est' (is) — literally 'Mr. is' or 'sir is'.
additional_notes: This is simply the two-word sequence formed by the noun monsieur and the verb est (third-person singular of être). On its own it is not a complete natural phrase in French; it would need more words to make sense (e.g. "Monsieur est malade" = "Mr. is sick" or better "The gentleman is sick"). Use monsieur to address or refer to a man (Monsieur Dupont = Mr. Dupont).
target_language_example: Monsieur est arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: Mr. arrived late.

meaning: 'sir' or 'Mr.' used before a title or word starting with a vowel (contracted form of "monsieur le/la").
additional_notes: This is the spoken/written contraction of "monsieur le" (or sometimes "monsieur la") used before a vowel or mute h: e.g. "monsieur l'avocat" → "monsieur l'avocat" (no extra change in spelling). In formal address, you often see "Monsieur le Président" or in less formal contexts "monsieur le directeur"; before a vowel speakers/writers may write or pronounce "monsieur l'". Capitalize "Monsieur" when used as a title. Use masculine "monsieur" for men; it is not interchangeable with "madame".
target_language_example: Monsieur l'inspecteur, puis-je vous parler ?
native_language_example: Mr. Inspector, may I speak with you?

meaning: 'puts up' or 'raises it' / 'he/she/it climbs it' depending on context
additional_notes: monte is the third-person singular (il/elle/on) or the imperative (tu) of monter. 'monte le' can mean either an action of raising or mounting an object ('puts up the...') or physically going up/onto something ('climbs it') depending on the verb sense and context. With a direct object like 'le' it usually means 'puts up/assembles/raises it' (e.g. monter un meuble = to assemble a piece of furniture) when used transitively. As an imperative (tu), 'Monte-le !' means 'Climb it!' or 'Take it up!' Tone and context determine the meaning. Watch word order and pronoun placement in spoken French: object pronouns normally attach after the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative imperative (Monte-le !) but precede the verb in declarative sentences (Il le monte.).
target_language_example: Il monte le meuble en une heure.
native_language_example: He assembles the piece of furniture in an hour.

meaning: Come up here / go up there (informal imperative).
additional_notes: Imperative of 'monter' (to go up, to climb) combined with 'là' (there/here depending on context). Used to tell someone to move upward or to come to the speaker's position (e.g., come up to the stage, come upstairs, or 'come here' if speaker is above). Informal; tone depends on context and intonation. Can be used with family, friends, or to instruct someone physically.
target_language_example: Monte là, j'ai quelque chose à te montrer.
native_language_example: Come up here, I have something to show you.

meaning: 'to stand guard' or 'to keep watch'
additional_notes: Used when someone takes a position to watch over a place, person, or thing (military, security, or informal contexts). Can refer to a scheduled shift of guarding. Verb phrase: monter la garde (infinitive).
target_language_example: Ce soir, Paul va monter la garde devant la porte.
native_language_example: Tonight, Paul is going to stand guard in front of the door.

meaning: to go to someone's head; to make someone arrogant, overly confident, or dizzy (literally: 'rise to the head').
additional_notes: Used when something (success, praise, alcohol, power, etc.) causes a person to become conceited, overly confident, or disoriented. Can also describe physical dizziness (e.g., from alcohol or heat). Often structured as 'Ça lui est monté à la tête', 'Quelque chose lui est monté à la tête', or with 'lui monter à la tête' + noun or clause: 'L'alcool lui a monté à la tête.'
target_language_example: La gloire lui est montée à la tête et il a commencé à ignorer ses amis.
native_language_example: Fame went to his head and he started ignoring his friends.

meaning: 'shows (to)' or used in noun phrases to mean '... with/for' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the verb 'montrer' conjugated in the present tense (il/elle montre à... = he/she shows to...). 'Montrer' takes a direct object (what is shown) and 'à' introduces the person. It can also occur in fixed noun phrases (e.g. montre à gousset = pocket watch) where 'à' links the noun to a specification. Note orthography: accent on 'à'.
target_language_example: Il montre à son ami la montre à gousset.
native_language_example: He shows his friend the pocket watch.

meaning: 'show it' or 'show him' (informal singular command) — imperative of 'montrer' + masculine direct object pronoun 'le'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in the affirmative imperative when addressing one person informally: correct written form is hyphenated as 'Montre-le !'. In normal declarative sentences object pronouns come before the verb (e.g. 'Il le montre'). Depending on context 'le' refers to a masculine noun or a male person. Tone is informal; for formal/plural use 'Montrez-le !'.
target_language_example: Montre le livre à Paul — montrez-le !
native_language_example: Show the book to Paul — show it!

meaning: to show how (something is done); to demonstrate how it works
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to demonstrate a method, process, or how to use something. Often followed by a verb or understood object (e.g. 'montrer comment ça marche' — show how it works). Alone, it can be colloquial/truncated; native speakers more often say the full phrase like 'montrer comment ça marche' or 'montrer comment on fait'.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me montrer comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Can you show me how this works?

meaning: 'to show someone' when followed by an indirect object (incomplete as written)
additional_notes: 'Montrer quelque' by itself is not a complete French expression. 'Montrer' means 'to show' and normally takes a direct object (what is shown) and, if specifying the person shown, uses 'à' before the person: montrer quelque chose à quelqu'un. The fragment 'montrer quelque' could appear in contexts where 'quelque' begins a longer phrase (e.g., 'montrer quelque attention'), or in colloquial/elliptical speech, but on its own it's incomplete and should be completed (e.g., 'montrer quelqu'un' to present someone, or 'montrer quelque chose à quelqu'un').
target_language_example: Je vais montrer quelque chose à ma sœur, pas simplement montrer quelque.
native_language_example: I'll show something to my sister, not just show someone.

meaning: 'to show a/an' (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Montrer = to show. The phrase 'montrer un' is not a fixed idiom by itself but simply the verb plus the indefinite article 'un' used before a masculine noun (e.g. montrer un livre, montrer un problème). Use 'montrer une' before feminine nouns and 'montrer des' for plural. Commonly followed by a direct object or by 'à' + person (montrer un document à quelqu'un).
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer un exemple.
native_language_example: I'll show you an example.

meaning: 'I will show you the' (future tense, singular/plural object follows)
additional_notes: montrerai = first-person singular future of montrer (to show). la is the feminine singular definite article ('the') used before a feminine noun (la bibliothèque, la ville, la peur, la rue). Combine with indirect object pronouns (te, vous) to mean 'I will show you the...'. Word order: Je (te) montrerai la + noun.
target_language_example: Je te montrerai la place demain.
native_language_example: I'll show you the square tomorrow.

meaning: gone up to / increased to; got on (a vehicle) to; went up to (a place) — exact meaning depends on context and syntax
additional_notes: Monté is the past participle of monter. With à + number it usually means 'rose to' or 'increased to' (e.g., les prix sont montés à 10 €). With à + place or vehicle it can mean 'got on/into' or indicate direction/arrival (il est monté à Paris — he went up to Paris; elle est montée à bord — she got on board). Auxiliary (être vs. avoir), agreement, and broader context determine nuance. The phrase must appear exactly as "monté à" (masculine singular form) in the sentence to match this entry.
target_language_example: Il est monté à l'étage et a frappé à la porte après être monté à l'étage.
native_language_example: He went up to the floor and knocked on the door after having gone up to the floor.

meaning: 'make fun of' or 'mock (someone) for (something)'.
additional_notes: Form appears as part of the verb se moquer de (to make fun of). The full conjugated reflexive form normally appears (je me moque de, il se moque de), but the sequence 'moques de' can occur in contexts like questions or emphatic structures mirroring the 2nd person singular (tu te moques de...) shortened in dialogue or transcription. Use de before the thing or person being mocked. Note: standalone 'moquer de' without the reflexive pronoun is uncommon; prefer 'se moquer de'.
target_language_example: Tu te moques de moi? — Tu moques de moi? (colloquial shortening)
native_language_example: Are you making fun of me? — Are you making fun of me? (colloquial shortening)

target_language_multi_word_term: te moques de moi / te moques de moi ? (tu te moques de moi)
meaning: 'are you making fun of me?' or 'you are making fun of me.' (to mock or make fun of someone).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb se moquer de + person. Used to say someone is mocking, teasing, or not taking you seriously. In questions it expresses surprise or offense: "Tu te moques de moi ?" = "Are you kidding me?" In statements: "Tu te moques de moi." = "You're making fun of me." Common in informal spoken French. The full infinitive form is se moquer de.
target_language_example: Oh non, tu te moques de moi ?
native_language_example: Oh no, are you kidding me?

meaning: 'bitten by' (passive voice)
additional_notes: Used in the passive construction with être (e.g. 'a été mordu par') to say someone/something was bitten by an animal or insect. 'Mordu' is the past participle of 'mordre' (to bite). Can describe literal bites; in some contexts it can be used figuratively (e.g. 'mordu de' means 'crazy about', but that is a different construction).
target_language_example: Elle a été mordu par un chien pendant sa promenade.
native_language_example: She was bitten by a dog during her walk.

meaning: 'dead to' or 'death to' (used in phrases expressing hatred or condemnation, often followed by a noun)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; 'mort au' appears in slogans or exclamations like 'mort au roi' (death to the king) or in historical/revolutionary contexts. It literally means 'death to' and is used to call for the death or downfall of someone or something. Strong/violent expression — avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ils criaient «Mort au tyran!» pendant la manifestation.
native_language_example: They shouted "Death to the tyrant!" during the protest.

meaning: the death of my (followed by a family member or close person).
additional_notes: A fixed phrase fragment used before a noun to say 'the death of my ...' (e.g., père, maître). 'Mon' agrees with the possessor (my) and the noun that follows provides the person who died. In full sentences you'll see it as part of 'la mort de mon père / maître'.
target_language_example: Après la mort de mon frère, j'ai changé de ville.
native_language_example: After the death of my brother, I moved to another city.

meaning: literally 'stillborn' or 'born dead' (describes a baby born without signs of life).
additional_notes: The correct French form is normally hyphenated as "mort-né" (or "mort-née" for a female). Written as two words ('mort ne') is nonstandard and may result from typographical omission of the hyphen or of the accent; the meaning and usage remain the same — a formal/medical term describing an infant born without life. Commonly used adjectivally (un bébé mort-né). Do not confuse with separate words "mort" (dead) and "né" (born) in other contexts.
target_language_example: Le bébé a été déclaré mort ne à l'arrivée à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: The baby was declared stillborn upon arrival at the hospital.

meaning: 'starving' or 'very hungry'.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning extremely hungry (can be used literally for animals/people or figuratively). Often used without an article: Je suis mort de faim. Not literally 'dead' — it's hyperbolic. Common in everyday speech (neutral to informal).
target_language_example: Je suis mort de faim.
native_language_example: I'm starving.

meaning: 'dying of laughter' — very funny / I'm cracking up (used to say something is extremely funny).
additional_notes: Informal expression often used in speech, messages, or social media. Literally means 'dead from laughing' but functions like English hyperbolic phrases: 'LOL', 'I'm dying (of laughter)', or 'hilarious'. Can appear alone (« Mort de rire ! ») or after a comment (« Il a raconté une blague, mort de rire. »).
target_language_example: J'ai vu la vidéo — mort de rire !
native_language_example: I saw the video — I'm cracking up!

meaning: 'dead in' or 'dead inside' depending on context; often part of a phrase describing where or how someone/something died or is emotionally numb.
additional_notes: Literally, mort = dead and dans = in. 'mort dans' usually appears inside longer expressions (e.g. mort dans un accident = died in an accident; mort dans ses bras = died in his/her arms). It can also be used figuratively (mort dans) to suggest being 'dead inside' when followed by an emotional state, but that usage is less common and more informal. Pay attention to tense and agreement with the subject (e.g. il est mort dans..., elle est morte dans...).
target_language_example: Il est mort dans un accident de voiture.
native_language_example: He died in a car accident.

meaning: 'dead from' or 'dead of' (used to indicate cause or circumstance of death).
additional_notes: Often follows a noun or phrase describing cause, manner, or context (e.g. 'mort en bas âge' — 'died at a young age', or 'mort en mer' — 'died at sea'). Can appear in formal, written contexts such as reports, obituaries, historical accounts. The preposition after 'mort' can vary (mort de, mort par, mort en) depending on the nuance: 'mort de' often indicates cause ('mort de maladie'), 'mort en' often indicates location, circumstance, period, or state ('mort en prison', 'mort en 1918').
target_language_example: Il est mort en mer pendant la tempête.
native_language_example: He died at sea during the storm.

meaning: 'mort il' is not a standard French phrase; it is the sequence of the adjective 'mort' (dead) followed by the pronoun 'il' (he) and usually appears only as part of a larger sentence or as a punctuation-separated fragment.
additional_notes: By itself, 'mort il' is ungrammatical in standard French word order. Typical correct forms are 'il est mort' (he is dead) or 'mort, il...' when 'mort' is used as a past participle/adjective in a stylistic or parenthetical clause with punctuation. 'Mort il' might appear in poetic, archaic, or transcribed speech contexts, or as a result of punctuation (e.g., 'Mort, il...') but should not be treated as a fixed expression. For learners: use 'il est mort' for 'he is dead', or 'mort' after a noun (e.g., 'un mort').
target_language_example: Mort il ne savait plus quoi dire.
native_language_example: Dead, he no longer knew what to say.

meaning: Not a grammatical or standard French multi-word expression. It appears to be a mistaken word order combining 'mort' (dead/death) and the existential 'il y (a)', so it likely reflects a typo or nonstandard construction. Context may indicate the speaker meant 'il y a un mort' (there is one dead person) or part of 'il y a mort d'homme' (a literary idiom).
additional_notes:
As written, 'mort il y' is ungrammatical. Common correct alternatives:
- 'il y a un mort' = 'there is one dead person' or 'one person has died'.
- 'il y a des morts' = 'there are dead people' / 'there are casualties'.
- 'il y a eu un mort' = 'there was one death'.
- 'il y a mort d'homme' (literary) = 'a serious matter involving death' (rare).
If you encounter 'mort il y' in a text, treat it as an error and reorder or ask the speaker for clarification.
target_language_example: Mort il y... — cette inversion est incorrecte dans la phrase telle quelle.
native_language_example: Mort il y... — this inversion is incorrect in the sentence as written.

meaning: dead for / died for (someone or something); indicates the cause or purpose of someone's death (often 'died for' as in sacrifice).
additional_notes: Used after être (il est mort pour...) to say someone died for a cause, person, or country. Can express literal sacrifice ('died for his country') or theological concept ('died so that...'). With subjunctive vs indicative in subordinate clause: 'mort pour que nous vivions' (subjunctive) is more standard when expressing purpose; 'mort pour que nous puissions vivre' uses modality ('can').
target_language_example: Il est mort pour sa famille.
native_language_example: He died for his family.

meaning: dead because of / killed by (used to indicate cause or agent of death)
additional_notes: Used after 'mort' (past participle of 'mourir') to specify cause ('mort à la suite d'un accident') or agent ('mort à la guerre', 'mort à l'arme blanche'). More commonly French uses 'mort de' for causes (mort de maladie) and 'tué par' or 'mort aux mains de' for agents; 'mort à' appears in set phrases (e.g. 'mort à la guerre') or older/literary contexts. Pay attention to articles and prepositions: 'mort à' + definite noun is possible, but for illnesses 'mort de' is more natural.
target_language_example: Il est mort à la guerre en 1916.
native_language_example: He died in/was killed in the war in 1916.

meaning: 'dead since' (indicates how long ago a feminine person or feminine noun ceased to be alive or in use)
additional_notes: Used after the verb être (e.g., Elle est morte depuis...) to state the duration since death. 'Morte' agrees in gender/number: use 'mort' for masculine, 'mortes'/'morts' for plural as appropriate. Can apply to non-human feminine nouns (e.g., 'une langue morte depuis...'). The time expression that follows (des mois, huit ans, des siècles) indicates the elapsed time since death.
target_language_example: Elle est morte depuis des mois.
native_language_example: She has been dead for months.

meaning: died (X time) ago — used to say someone (feminine) died a certain time ago
additional_notes: Combine 'morte' (past participle of 'mourir' for a female subject) with 'il y a' + time expression to indicate how long ago she died. For a male use 'mort il y a'. For plural feminine use 'mortes il y a'. Example structure: «Elle est morte il y a trois ans.»
target_language_example: Ma grand‑mère est morte il y a cinq ans.
native_language_example: My grandmother died five years ago.

meaning: 'word with' (literal) — used to say a word together with someone or to indicate a word that contains/has something
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom in French by itself. Literally 'mot avec' combines 'mot' (word) + 'avec' (with). It can appear in phrases like 'un mot avec quelqu'un' (a word with someone — meaning a short private talk) or 'un mot avec X' meaning 'a word containing X' depending on context. For beginner learners, note that you usually need more words to make the idea clear (e.g. 'dire un mot avec quelqu'un', 'un mot avec un accent').
target_language_example: Je voudrais avoir un mot avec vous après la réunion.
native_language_example: I'd like to have a word with you after the meeting.

meaning: password (a secret word or phrase used to access an account or service).
additional_notes: Used for online accounts, devices, or any protected access. Common verbs: entrer (to enter), changer (to change), modifier (to modify), oublier (to forget). Often plural: mots de passe. Formal and neutral term.
target_language_example: Veuillez entrer votre mot de passe pour vous connecter.
native_language_example: Please enter your password to log in.

meaning: a way of speaking; the wording or phrasing used (how something is said).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's choice of words or the particular expression/wording used to describe something. Often appears in phrases like "selon le mot" or "lui donner le mot juste" but "mot dire" by itself is uncommon in modern French; learners may encounter it in fixed expressions or older texts. If you mean "dire un mot" (to say a word / to say a few words) or "mot d'ordre" (slogan/order word), choose the correct phrase instead.
target_language_example: Le mot dire de ce rapport change la perception du problème.
native_language_example: The wording of this report changes the perception of the problem.

meaning: 'word' + verb 'is' (simple declarative: 'this/that word is...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's just the noun mot (word) followed by the verb est (is). You'll see it in sentences that describe a particular word: Ce mot est… (This word is…). Use ce mot est for 'this/that word is...'.
target_language_example: Ce mot est difficile à retenir.
native_language_example: This word is hard to remember.

meaning: 'word for word' — literally translating each word.
additional_notes: Used to describe a literal, exact translation that follows the original word order and vocabulary. Often warned against because it can sound unnatural or change the meaning; can be used as an instruction (e.g., "translate word for word") or a description of a translation method.
target_language_example: Ne traduis pas ce texte mot à mot, cela sonnerait bizarre.
native_language_example: Don't translate this text word for word; it would sound odd.

meaning: literally 'engine of' — used to say the engine, motor, or driving force behind something (often followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun to describe a machine's motor (moteur de voiture, moteur de bateau) or metaphorically as the driving force/cause (le moteur de la croissance). Followed by de + noun. Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Le moteur de la voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: The car's engine is broken down.

meaning: search engine (website or tool used to search the web or a database).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to web search engines like Google, Bing, etc., but can also mean any tool that searches a database. Used in questions about preference or performance. Plural: moteurs de recherche.
target_language_example: Quel moteur de recherche préfères-tu pour chercher des infos ?
native_language_example: Which search engine do you prefer for looking up information?

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'engine not...' (moteur = engine, ne = part of negation).
additional_notes: This combination is not a complete expression on its own. In French, negation around a verb uses 'ne ... pas' (or other negatives) so you might see 'le moteur ne démarre pas' (the engine does not start). Alone, 'moteur ne' is just the noun 'moteur' followed by the first part of a negation and is incomplete. For beginners: learn full negative structures (ne + verb + pas/plus/jamais, etc.) and common phrases about engines (le moteur démarre, le moteur tourne, le moteur est en panne).
target_language_example: Le moteur ne démarre pas.
native_language_example: The engine does not start.

meaning: crossword puzzle(s).
additional_notes: Refers to the activity or printed puzzles made of a grid with clues. Often used in plural in French (faire des mots croisés = to do crosswords). Common in newspapers and magazines.
target_language_example: Elle aime faire les mots croisés chaque matin.
native_language_example: She likes to do the crossword puzzles every morning.

meaning: a phrase used before specifying a category or language (literally 'words in...') — e.g. 'les mots en anglais' = 'the words in English'.
additional_notes: Usually appears before a language, topic or form to indicate 'words in [language/topic]' or 'words starting with/containing [letters]' depending on context. Not a fixed idiom by itself; requires completion (e.g. 'mots en anglais', 'mots en -tion'). Common in headings, search filters or classroom contexts.
target_language_example: Cherche des mots en français pour l'activité.
native_language_example: Look for words in French for the activity.

meaning: 'words and' — simply the noun 'mots' (words) followed by the conjunction 'et' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's just two common words next to each other. You will normally see 'mots et' as part of a larger expression (e.g. 'mots et expressions', 'mots et phrases'). 'Mots' is plural of 'mot' and 'et' means 'and'. Pronunciation: /mo e/.
target_language_example: Des mots et des images aident à comprendre le texte.
native_language_example: Words and images help to understand the text.

meaning: literally 'words but' — used in contrasts like 'words (but) ...' to contrast words with something else (meaning, facts, phrases).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun 'mots' (words) followed by 'mais' (but) to set up a contrast. You'll often see full phrases like 'pas des mots mais des faits' ('not words but deeds') or 'je comprends les mots mais pas le sens' ('I understand the words but not the meaning'). Use it when opposing 'words' to another concept.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas des mots mais des actions qui comptent.
native_language_example: It's not words but actions that matter.

meaning: 'words' + negative particle — used to start clauses meaning 'words cannot...' or 'words do not...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the noun 'mots' (words) followed by the negative particle 'ne' beginning a negation with a verb later in the clause (often with 'peuvent', 'peuvent pas', 'sont pas', or 'pourraient'). In spoken French the 'ne' is often followed by 'pas', 'plus', or omitted in informal speech (e.g. «Les mots (ne) peuvent pas…»). Use it to say that words are unable to do something (express, describe, soothe, etc.).
target_language_example: Les mots ne peuvent pas décrire ce que je ressens.
native_language_example: Words cannot describe what I feel.

meaning: 'words (to someone)' — used when saying words directed at someone (often followed by a person or body part).
additional_notes: Common construction: 'dire des mots à quelqu'un' or 'murmurer des mots à quelqu'un/à son oreille'. 'Deux mots à dire' is an idiom meaning 'a few words to say' (often to correct or warn). The phrase needs a complement: who receives the words (à + personne) or the body part (à son oreille).
target_language_example: J'ai deux mots à lui dire avant qu'il parte.
native_language_example: I have a couple of words to say to him before he leaves.

meaning: 'to starve' (literally: to die of hunger); used both literally and figuratively.
additional_notes: Can be literal (someone will die from lack of food) or figurative (I'm starving / extremely hungry; or emphatic refusal: I'd rather starve than...). In everyday spoken French, people often say J'ai faim / J'ai trop faim for 'I'm hungry' rather than mourir de faim, which is stronger or dramatic. Conjugate like a regular verb phrase (mourir) + de faim.
target_language_example: J'ai tellement marché que je pourrais mourir de faim.
native_language_example: I walked so much I could starve / I'm starving.

meaning: 'movements of' or 'motion(s) of' — a phrase used to indicate the actions, motions, or changes related to something
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun to describe types or groups of movements (e.g. mouvements de protestation, mouvements de danse, mouvements de prix). Use with a specific noun to say 'movements of/for/related to X'. Grammatically, 'mouvements' is plural; the preposition 'de' links to the noun that follows. Can be part of formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Les mouvements de la mer sont puissants aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The movements of the sea are powerful today.

meaning: means of transport; method or vehicle used to travel or move goods.
additional_notes: Used to refer generally to any way of traveling (car, bus, train, bike, plane, etc.) or to transport goods. Can be singular (a means) or plural (moyens de transport). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Quel moyen de transport prends-tu pour aller au travail ?
native_language_example: Which means of transport do you take to get to work?

meaning: the wall is (…)
additional_notes: A short phrase combining mur (wall) and est (is). 'Est' is the third-person singular of être (to be). By itself 'mur est' is not a complete sentence in most contexts — you will usually add an adjective, location, or clause after it (e.g. 'Le mur est blanc', 'Le mur est à gauche'). Useful for describing a wall's state, color, or position.
target_language_example: Le mur est blanc.
native_language_example: The wall is white.

meaning: 'walls of' (used to indicate possession or characteristic: the walls belonging to something)
additional_notes: Literal prepositional phrase: murs = walls (plural), de = of/from. Commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g. murs de la maison, murs de pierre). Can also appear in fixed expressions (murs de verre, murs porteurs). Grammar: de links the walls to what they belong to or are made of.
target_language_example: Les murs de la maison sont blancs.
native_language_example: The walls of the house are white.

meaning: classical music (Western art music tradition).
additional_notes: Refers to the Western classical music tradition (baroque, classical, romantic, modern orchestral and chamber music, etc.). Used with partitive article de la/du or as a topic: écouter de la musique classique, être passionné de musique classique. Not specific to any one composer or piece.
target_language_example: J'aime écouter de la musique classique en travaillant.
native_language_example: I like to listen to classical music while working.

meaning: 'music of' or 'music for' (used to specify the type, origin or purpose of music)
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to indicate whose music, what kind of music, or music for something (e.g. musique de film = film music / soundtrack; musique de chambre = chamber music; musique de fête = music for a party). Word order: musique + de + noun. Can also appear in titles and descriptions.
target_language_example: J'aime la musique de film moderne.
native_language_example: I like modern film music.

meaning: 'to the museum by (transport)'; the pattern 'au musée en + [vehicle]' means going to the museum using a particular mode of transport.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'au/au(x)/à la musée' (here 'au musée') + 'en' + mode of transport (en taxi, en bus, en voiture, en métro). Use 'en' with most vehicles (en taxi, en bus, en voiture, en avion). For bikes and small vehicles you may see 'à vélo' or 'à pied' (on foot). Verb choice varies (aller, venir, se rendre, être allé(e), etc.).
target_language_example: Ils vont au musée en métro.
native_language_example: They are going to the museum by subway.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase — looks like two separate words: 'mère' (mother) and the verb 'a' (has/has got).
additional_notes: This is not a set expression. In French, 'mère' means 'mother' and 'a' is the third-person singular of 'avoir' (to have). Together they appear in sentences like 'La mère a...' ('The mother has...') or in possessive contexts ('La mère a une voiture' = 'The mother has a car'). For a possessive construction meaning 'mother's', French usually uses 'de' + noun (la voiture de la mère) or possessive adjectives (sa mère = his/her mother) rather than putting 'mère a' directly before a noun. Watch word order: subject + verb (La mère a ...).
target_language_example: La mère a trois enfants.
native_language_example: The mother has three children.

meaning: literally 'mother loves' — a simple subject-verb fragment meaning 'mother loves' or 'mom loves'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own in many contexts; it's the subject (mère) + present-tense verb (aime). You would usually add an object or complement: e.g. 'ma mère aime le chocolat' (my mother loves chocolate). 'Mère' is somewhat formal — more commonly 'maman' for 'mom'. Verb 'aime' is the 3rd-person singular of 'aimer' (to like/love).
target_language_example: Ma mère aime lire le soir.
native_language_example: My mother likes to read in the evening.

meaning: Not a standalone phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'mother in' as part of a larger expression (e.g. 'mère de' or 'mère dans la foule').
additional_notes: « mère dans » by itself is not a fixed multiword expression in French. You will usually see the noun mère followed by a preposition (mère de = mother of; mère de famille = mother of the family) or followed by a location introduced by dans (la mère dans la cuisine = the mother in the kitchen). If you encountered 'mère dans' in a sentence, read the surrounding words: the meaning depends on the noun or phrase that follows. For learners, treat it as the noun 'mère' (mother) plus the preposition 'dans' (in/inside/within).
target_language_example: La mère dans la cuisine prépare le dîner.
native_language_example: The mother in the kitchen is preparing dinner.

meaning: 'mother in' — not a standalone phrase in French; appears as part of larger expressions (e.g. mère-en-? or mère de ...).
additional_notes: On its own, 'mère en' is incomplete and not used as a fixed phrase. You will normally see 'mère' (mother) followed by a preposition or adjective (mère de, mère adoptive, mère célibataire) or as part of hyphenated compounds (mère-grand). If you saw 'mère en' in text, check the surrounding words — for example 'mère en pleurs' (mother in tears) or 'mère en colère' (mother who is angry).
target_language_example: La mère en colère a parlé au directeur.
native_language_example: The angry mother spoke to the principal.

meaning: mother is
additional_notes: This is simply the phrase "mère est" (mother + is). It appears when describing something about someone's mother (e.g. "your mother is aware", "your mother is at home") or in sentences where "mère" functions as the subject (sometimes without a possessive pronoun in contexts like addressing a family member: "Mère est malade"). Also note "vaisseau-mère" is a compound meaning "mothership" (not related to a human mother). Use a possessive (ma/ta/votre) when specifying whose mother: « votre mère est… », « ma mère est… ».
target_language_example: Ma mère est en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: My mother is on vacation this week.

meaning: "mother is in" (literal fragment; unfinished phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete French expression on its own; it's a fragment meaning "mother is in" followed by a location or state (e.g. "mère est en réunion" = "mother is in a meeting" or "mère est en ville" = "mother is in town"). You will normally see it completed with a noun introduced by en (en réunion, en train de..., en ville, en vacances) or with an adjective/state (en forme). Use it only as part of a full sentence.
target_language_example: Ma mère est en réunion jusqu'à 15h.
native_language_example: My mother is in a meeting until 3 PM.

meaning: 'mother is in the middle of' (doing something) — indicates an action currently in progress.
additional_notes: This is part of the progressive construction 'être en train de + infinitive' meaning 'to be doing (something) right now'. In the examples it's used with 'ma mère' or 'mère' to say 'my mother is (currently) preparing...'. You would normally include the full phrase 'ma mère est en train de...' or 'elle est en train de...'.
target_language_example: Ma mère est en train de lire un livre.
native_language_example: My mother is reading a book (right now).

meaning: 'the mother belongs to' or 'the mother is at/with' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; a sequence of words that requires context. 'Est à' often expresses possession or association (e.g., 'La maison est à ma mère' = 'The house belongs to my mother') or location with appropriate articles/pronouns. Alone, 'mère est à' is incomplete and must be followed by a noun, pronoun, or place. Word order and articles matter in full sentences (e.g., 'La mère est à l'hôpital' = 'The mother is at the hospital').
target_language_example: La mère est à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: The mother is at the hospital.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself; likely part of a sentence meaning "mother is at the..." (e.g. "mère est à la maison" = "mother is at the house/home").
additional_notes: This string isn't a standalone idiom in French — it's the beginning of a clause: "mère est à la + [place]". You will usually see a location word after "à la" (la maison, la porte, la cuisine, etc.). Remember: use "à la" before feminine singular places (la maison, la porte); use "au" before masculine singular (au travail), and "aux" before plural (aux urgences). Verbal subject can be "ma mère" (my mother) or just "mère" in some headlines/notes.
target_language_example: Ma mère est à la maison.
native_language_example: My mother is at home.

meaning: Not a standard French multi-word phrase; appears to be an incorrect or incomplete fragment. 'mère' means 'mother' and should be followed by a verb, possessive, preposition, or other words; 'le' is a masculine definite article and normally does not follow 'mère'.
additional_notes: 'mère le' as written is ungrammatical in French. Possible causes: typo, mis-segmentation (e.g., part of 'mère-là' or 'la mère le...'), or a fragment from a larger construction (e.g., 'mère, le...' with a comma). If encountered, check the surrounding text for correction. Correct alternatives include 'ma mère', 'la mère de...', or 'ma mère est...'.
target_language_example: Il y avait une phrase mal tapée dans le texte : « mère le » ne veut rien dire ici.
