You might see 'pas' and 'et' adjacent by chance when words from different clauses meet (e.g. 'pas' ending one clause and 'et' starting the next) or due to transcription/punctuation issues. If you encounter 'pas et' in text, check for a missing punctuation mark or for words omitted. Possible intended expressions include 'pas de' (no/none), 'ne... pas' (negation), or 'pas encore' (not yet).
target_language_example: Il n'est pas et il ne veut pas venir.
native_language_example: He is not, and he doesn't want to come.

meaning: negation of performing a single action or making a single thing — literally 'not to do a (feminine singular noun)' and typically appears as part of a larger clause (e.g., 'pas faire une erreur' = 'not to make a mistake').
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone idiom; it combines the negation 'pas' with the verb 'faire' and the indefinite article 'une'. In standard French the full negative usually includes 'ne' (ne pas faire une ...), but in spoken/casual French 'ne' is often dropped, producing 'pas faire une ...'. You'll normally need a subject and an object or complement to complete the sentence. Be careful with verb conjugation and register (use 'ne' in formal writing).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux pas faire une erreur ici.
native_language_example: It's better not to make a mistake here.

meaning: 'not finish' or 'not end' (negation of finir)
additional_notes: Used with an auxiliary (ne... pas) or informal 'pas' after a verb to negate finishing/ending something or to express a fear/wish that a situation will not end a certain way. In speech the 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. 'Je veux pas...'). Can mean 'not finish' (complete) or 'not end up' (result/ending).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas finir comme ça.
native_language_example: I don't want to end up like that.

meaning: not French; not typical of French language/culture
additional_notes: Used to say something is not French (either not from France or not typical of French people/ways). Context decides whether it refers to language (not in French) or to nationality/cultural traits. Can be used alone as a brief comment (e.g. "Ce n'est pas français") or after a noun/adjective phrase.
target_language_example: Ce plat n'est pas français, il vient d'Italie.
native_language_example: This dish is not French; it comes from Italy.

meaning: not much / not very (big/important); used to downplay size, amount, or importance
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "pas grand-chose" (not much) or before adjectives/nouns to minimize something: e.g. "Ce n'est pas grand (chose)" or "Il n'y a pas grand monde" (there aren't many people). Informal to neutral register. Context determines whether it refers to size, quantity, or importance.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas grand monde au café aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There aren't many people at the café today.

meaning: 'not fair' or 'unfair'.
additional_notes: Used to express that something is unfair, unjust, or not right. Can modify a situation, decision, or behavior: e.g. C'est pas juste (It's not fair). Informal spoken French often drops the 'ne' (ne... pas). Can be followed by anything judged unfair: personne, décision, vie, etc.
target_language_example: C'est pas juste que tu partes si tôt.
native_language_example: It's not fair that you're leaving so early.

meaning: 'not there' or 'not here' (negative phrase combining 'pas' and 'là' — often written without accent in informal contexts as 'la').
additional_notes: Used in negative contexts to indicate absence: standard form is «il n'est pas là»; in speech the 'ne' is often dropped, yielding «il est pas là». Watch for ambiguity: 'la' without accent can also be the feminine definite article 'la' — context and presence of 'pas' or a preceding verb help disambiguate. In careful writing use 'là' (with accent) for 'there'.
target_language_example: Il est pas la.
native_language_example: He isn't here.

meaning: 'not allowed' or 'didn't let (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Combination of 'pas' (negation) + past participle 'laissé' from laisser (to let/allow/leave). Used in negative sentences: e.g. 'il ne m'a pas laissé' = 'he didn't let me'/'he didn't allow me'. Often appears with a subject and an infinitive or direct object: 'ne ... pas laissé + infinitive' (didn't allow to do) or 'ne ... pas laissé + noun' (didn't leave/abandon). In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped, leaving 'pas laissé' as in 'Il m'a pas laissé'.
target_language_example: Il ne m'a pas laissé sortir hier soir.
native_language_example: He didn't let me go out last night.

meaning: not it
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: pas makes the verb negative, and le is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him." In standard French, this usually appears as part of ne ... pas le + verb, as in ne pas le faire ("not do it"). In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: je veux pas le savoir.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas le croire.
native_language_example: I can't believe it.

meaning: not theirs / not their (something)
additional_notes: Combination of the negation 'pas' with the possessive pronoun/adjective 'leur' (their). Depends on context: 'pas leur' can negate ownership ('Ce n'est pas leur voiture' = 'That is not their car') or reject an action attributed to them ('Ce n'est pas leur faute' = 'It is not their fault'). In spoken French you may also hear 'pas à eux' to emphasize 'not theirs'. Remember word order: 'pas' appears after the verb in negation (ne ... pas) unless 'ne' is dropped in informal speech.
target_language_example: Ce sac n'est pas leur.
native_language_example: That bag is not theirs.

meaning: 'not read' (negation of 'lu', the past participle of 'lire').
additional_notes: Used in spoken and written French to say someone did not read something. Often appears in contracted spoken forms: 't'as pas lu' (tu as pas lu) instead of the standard negation 'tu n'as pas lu'. It requires an auxiliary (avoir) in passé composé: 'tu n'as pas lu le journal'. 'Pas lu' by itself is not a complete verb phrase — include the subject and auxiliary or an object to be clear.
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas lu ce message ?
native_language_example: You haven't read this message?

meaning: 'not him' or 'not to him' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can mean 'not him' (identifying a person who is not the one) or be part of a negative construction with an indirect object pronoun ('ne ... pas lui' = 'not to him' / 'won't be for him' / 'won't be possible to him'). Word order and surrounding words determine meaning. In spoken French, the initial 'ne' is often dropped (C'est pas lui).
target_language_example: Ce n'était pas lui qui a appelé.
native_language_example: It wasn't him who called.

meaning: quite a lot / not bad (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common, versatile phrase. Literally 'not bad'. Used praiseably to mean 'not bad' or 'pretty good' (e.g., C'est pas mal = That's not bad). Can also mean 'quite a lot' or 'a fair amount' in questions or statements (e.g., Ça fait pas mal ? = Does that make quite a difference?/Is that a lot?). In casual speech the 'ne' is dropped: 'pas mal' instead of 'ne ... pas mal'.
target_language_example: C'est pas mal, ton dessin.
native_language_example: Your drawing is not bad.

meaning: quite a lot of / many / a fair amount of
additional_notes: Informal-to-neutral expression used to indicate a considerable quantity or number. Often used before a noun (pas mal de + noun). Can be used with countable or uncountable nouns. Tone is conversational but acceptable in writing; not very formal. Equivalent to 'beaucoup de' but slightly less emphatic or more colloquial.
target_language_example: Il y a pas mal de gens au marché aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are quite a lot of people at the market today.

meaning: quite a lot of things / many things
additional_notes: Informal-to-neutral expression meaning 'a good number of things' or 'many things'. Used both in positive sentences (we talked about many interesting things) and to say something explains a lot. Can modify nouns: 'pas mal de + noun'. Tone is casual but common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il y avait pas mal de choses à voir au musée.
native_language_example: There were quite a lot of things to see at the museum.

meaning: 'not me' (fragment of a negative construction)
additional_notes: Not a standalone, standard French phrase. 'pas' is the negation particle and 'me' is the object pronoun; they appear together only as parts of a negative clause (typically surrounding the verb: «ne ... pas» with 'me' before the verb: «ne me ... pas»). In colloquial speech the 'ne' is often dropped, producing structures like «me rappelle pas» or fragments such as «pas me» in spoken replies, but 'pas me' alone is unusual in written French. Use complete negative constructions for clarity: «je ne me souviens pas», «ce n'est pas moi».
target_language_example: Tu veux que je le fasse? — Pas me, je suis occupé.
native_language_example: You want me to do it? — Not me, I'm busy.

meaning: 'not to put' or 'not to put on' (negation of mettre)
additional_notes: Pas mettre is the negated form of the verb mettre (to put, to put on). In French negation, pas is placed after the conjugated auxiliary or main verb (ne ... pas). In spoken or informal French, the ne is often omitted, so you may hear or see phrases like 'je pas mettre' in very casual speech or note-taking, but the correct full form is 'ne pas mettre' when used in infinitive constructions (e.g. 'Il faut ne pas mettre' → better: 'Il ne faut pas mettre'). Common uses: 'mettre' can mean to put/place something, to put on (clothes), to turn on (an appliance). The phrase 'ne pas mettre' expresses not doing those actions.
target_language_example: Ne pas mettre les mains dans la boîte.
native_language_example: Do not put your hands in the box.

meaning: 'not me' or 'definitely not I'.
additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility or exclude oneself. Common in spoken French; can be standalone (short answer) or part of a sentence. Informal contractions like "c'était pas moi" are very common in speech. Emphatic forms often place a pronoun before or after for contrast: "toi, pas moi" (you, not me).
target_language_example: Ce bruit? Pas moi, je dormais.
native_language_example: That noise? Not me, I was sleeping.

meaning: not my (—); indicates something does not belong to me or is not my responsibility/choice
additional_notes: Usually appears before a noun (pas mon/ma/mes) to deny ownership or association: e.g. 'pas mon problème' = 'not my problem'. In spoken French you may also hear 'c'est pas mon...' used to shrug off responsibility. Be careful with gender/number: mon (m. or before vowel), ma (f.), mes (pl.).
target_language_example: C'est pas mon problème.
native_language_example: That's not my problem.

meaning: not just any / not just anything (used to qualify a noun or action as specific or special)
additional_notes: Often appears before a noun or phrase to stress that something is particular, specific, or of importance (e.g. pas n'importe quel/quelle). Common constructions: pas n'importe qui, pas n'importe quoi, pas n'importe quel/quelle + noun. It negates a vague or random option and implies selectivity or seriousness.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas n'importe quelle voiture, c'est une voiture de sport.
native_language_example: This isn't just any car; it's a sports car.

meaning: 'pas' is the basic negation word 'not' used with 'ne' (ne ... pas = not).
additional_notes: In standard French the negation is formed as 'ne ... pas' surrounding the verb. The sequence 'pas ne' is not the normal word order and is generally ungrammatical for negating a verb; however it can appear in emphatic or archaic constructions, in certain fixed expressions, or when 'pas' modifies a noun phrase preceding 'ne' (rare). In modern spoken French 'ne' is often dropped and only 'pas' is used (Je ne sais pas → Je sais pas). 'Pas' also means 'step' in other contexts. Learners should learn the canonical 'ne ... pas' pattern for negation; encountering 'pas ne' is unusual and typically not recommended for learners to use.
target_language_example: Pas ne saurais-je dire pourquoi cela est arrivé.
native_language_example: I cannot say why that happened.

meaning: 'not not' — used to soften or correct a negative, often meaning 'not exactly' / 'not really' or to add emphasis (colloquial).
additional_notes: Rare as a standalone pair; 'pas non' appears in spoken French to nuance or contradict a previous negative statement (e.g., 'Ce n'est pas non plus...' or as a clipped response). Context determines meaning: it can mean 'not exactly', 'not really', or serve as an emphatic negative reply. Avoid using it in formal writing; prefer clearer phrases like 'pas vraiment', 'pas exactement', or 'ce n'est pas le cas'.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas non plus une mauvaise idée.
native_language_example: It's not exactly a bad idea either.

meaning: 'not ours' (negation + possessive)
additional_notes: Combines 'pas' (negation) with the possessive adjective 'notre' (our). Used to say that something does not belong to us or is not our responsibility/choice. In natural French you'd usually see it in a fuller phrase, e.g. 'Ce n'est pas notre voiture' or with contraction 'pas le nôtre' when replacing a noun: 'Ce n'est pas le nôtre.' Pay attention to gender/number: notre (singular before noun), nos (plural), and le nôtre/la nôtre/les nôtres when replacing a noun.
target_language_example: Ce stylo n'est pas notre.
native_language_example: This pen is not ours.

meaning: 'not us' or 'none of us'.
additional_notes: Negative phrase: pas negates the subject nous (we/us). Used to say that something does not apply to the speaker and others. In spoken French you may also hear "ce n'est pas nous" or simply "nous pas" in informal structures. Word order usually: « ce n'est pas nous », « pas nous » can be used alone as a brief reply.
target_language_example: Ce bruit? Pas nous, on était au cinéma.
native_language_example: That noise? Not us, we were at the cinema.

meaning: 'not necessary that' / 'it's not necessary that...'
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not required or doesn't need to happen. Often appears in constructions with il n'est pas nécessaire que + subjunctive (e.g. il n'est pas nécessaire que tu viennes). In spoken or shortened contexts you may see just pas nécessaire (informal). When a subject follows, French typically uses a full phrase (il n'est) before pas nécessaire que.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas nécessaire que tu m'attendes.
native_language_example: It's not necessary that you wait for me.

meaning: 'not or' — literally 'not or' but this combination is not a standard fixed phrase in French; it may appear in structures like 'pas ou...' when negating alternatives or in informal/fragmented speech.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'pas ou' is unusual as a standalone phrase. In French negation, 'pas' is used with 'ne' (often dropped in speech) to make negative statements (e.g. 'je ne veux pas'). 'Ou' means 'or'. You might see 'pas ou' inside longer constructions such as 'pas ou ...' when someone is listing options to exclude (e.g. 'pas ou trop' is nonstandard). More commonly alternatives are negated with constructions like 'ni... ni...' (neither... nor...) or 'pas... mais...' (not... but...). Avoid using 'pas ou' as a fixed expression; check the full sentence context.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas ou l'autre; c'est un choix différent.
native_language_example: It's not this or the other; it's a different choice.

meaning: not open the (feminine noun) — a negative construction used when saying someone cannot or will not open something (la + feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the negative pattern "ne ... pas + ouvrir + la" (or colloquially without "ne"). The feminine article "la" indicates the object is feminine (e.g. la boîte, la fenêtre). Use "ne...pas" for formal negatives; in spoken French people often drop "ne": "Tu peux pas ouvrir la fenêtre ?" Conjugate the verb (peux, peut, pouvons) and place object after the verb.
target_language_example: Elle ne veut pas ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to open the door.

meaning: not where / don't know where (used in negative questions or statements about location)
additional_notes: Appears as part of negation with savoir or connaître (e.g., je ne sais pas où = I don't know where). Often used in questions asking if someone knows where something or someone is (Tu ne sais pas où...?/Tu saurais pas où...?). In spoken French, the full 'ne' is frequently dropped (Tu sais pas où?). Use 'où' for location or direction; for time use 'quand'.
target_language_example: Tu ne sais pas où est la bibliothèque ?
native_language_example: You don't know where the library is?

meaning: 'not where you' — fragment used in sentences to negate location related to 'you'
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's a fragment that appears inside a larger sentence, typically after a verb or clause (e.g., 'ce n'est pas où tu penses' = 'it's not where you think'). It combines 'pas' (negation) with 'où' (where) and 'tu' (you). Word order and presence of other words are important. For full sentences, include a verb or demonstrative (ce, c', etc.).
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas où tu crois.
native_language_example: It's not where you think.

meaning: 'not by' or 'not per' (used to negate a measure, rate, or method introduced by 'par')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but simply the negation 'pas' followed by the preposition 'par'. It appears when you negate phrases that would normally use 'par' to indicate rate, means, distribution, or agent (e.g. 'par jour', 'par personne', 'par la poste'). Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar. Depending on context, you might also see 'ne ... pas' around the verb rather than 'pas' directly before 'par' (e.g. 'Il n'est pas envoyé par la poste').
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas par personne, mais par groupe.
native_language_example: It's not per person, but per group.

meaning: 'not because' (used to negate a causal idea)
additional_notes: Rarely appears alone as "pas parce"; usually part of a longer phrase like "pas parce que..." (not because that...) or "pas parce de..." is incorrect. Use "pas parce que" to say that something is not the reason for something else. In spoken French, you may also hear "pas parce que..." followed by an explanation or contrast. Remember to include the conjunction "que" when introducing a clause: "pas parce que + [clause]".
target_language_example: Je suis venu, pas parce que tu m'as invité, mais pour voir la ville.
native_language_example: I came not because you invited me, but to see the city.

meaning: 'don't cry' (a short, direct negative command or comment).
additional_notes: A concise negative phrase combining 'pas' (not) with the infinitive 'pleurer' (to cry). It can be used as a command (spoken to someone) or as a remark (e.g., telling someone not to complain or to stop crying). Tone depends on context — can be gentle, firm, or dismissive. For a polite command use 'ne pleure pas' (tu) or 'ne pleurez pas' (vous).
target_language_example: Allez, pas pleurer — on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Come on, don't cry — we'll find a solution.

meaning: not to wear / not to carry (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literally 'not carry' or 'not wear'. 'Porter' can mean 'to wear' (clothes), 'to carry' (an object), or 'to bear' (a responsibility). 'Pas' is the negation particle used with 'ne' in standard written French (e.g. 'ne pas porter'), but in spoken informal French 'ne' is often dropped in casual speech (e.g. 'je pas porter' is nonstandard). For correct standard negation, use 'ne ... pas' (e.g. 'Je ne porte pas de chapeau'). This entry shows the multi-word combination 'pas porter' as it appears within negation.
target_language_example: Je dis que je ne veux pas porter ce sac.
native_language_example: I say that I don't want to carry this bag.

meaning: not why; (used to deny/explain that something is not the reason)
additional_notes: Rare as an isolated phrase. Often appears inside a longer sentence to say that something is not the reason (e.g. 'Ce n'est pas pourquoi...' or '...n'est pas pourquoi'). English equivalents: 'not the reason' or 'that's not why'. You will commonly see the full negative construction with subject and verb: 'Ce n'est pas pourquoi...' or 'Ce n'est pas la raison pour laquelle...'.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas pourquoi je suis venu.
native_language_example: That's not why I came.

meaning: 'not ready' (plural, masculine or mixed groups).
additional_notes: Used after a conjugated être (ils ne sont pas prêts, nous ne sommes pas prêts, etc.). For feminine plural use pas prêtes. Can refer to people or things (e.g., plans) when plural. Common negative construction: ne ... pas + adjective; in informal speech the 'ne' is often dropped (Ils sont pas prêts).
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas prêts.
native_language_example: They are not ready.

meaning: 'could not' (negation of 'pouvoir' in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was unable to do something in the past. Formed with ne ... pas + avoir (a) + past participle 'pu' (from pouvoir). In speech, the 'ne' is often dropped: Elle n'a pas pu → Elle a pas pu or Elle n'a pas pu (formal). Followed by an infinitive or action: pas pu venir, pas pu faire, pas pu marcher.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas pu venir hier soir.
native_language_example: I couldn't come last night.

meaning: 'not that' or the negation part of 'not that' in subordinate clauses (short for "ne ... pas que" or used in spoken negation before 'que')
additional_notes: In French spoken and written negative sentences, 'pas qu'' appears when negating verbs that introduce a subordinate clause with 'que' (or when 'ne' is dropped in informal speech). Often you see full forms like "je ne crois pas que..." or the spoken contraction "je crois pas qu'...". It does not stand alone; it must be followed by a clause starting with 'que' (or 'qu'' before a vowel). Used to express doubt, denial, or to negate a fact. Remember that subjunctive is often required after 'je ne crois pas que' in formal writing/speaking.
target_language_example: Je crois pas qu'elle vienne ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't think that she'll come tonight.

meaning: 'not when' (used to negate a time clause)
additional_notes: Literally 'not when'. Used to negate or contradict a temporal clause introduced by quand (when). Often appears in longer sentences, e.g. to say that something does not happen at a certain time. In spoken French it may be replaced by other constructions (e.g. 'ce n'est pas quand...' or 'pas le/la/les fois où...') depending on context. Pay attention to sentence structure: negation surrounds the verb (ne...pas) in formal writing, but 'pas quand' can appear in informal fragments.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas quand tu veux, mais quand nous sommes prêts.
native_language_example: It's not when you want, but when we are ready.

meaning: not that
additional_notes: This sequence is usually part of a larger negative structure rather than a fixed expression by itself. After a verb, *ne ... pas que* introduces a clause: *je ne savais pas que...* = 'I didn't know that...'. In *il n'y a pas que...*, it means 'not only' or 'not just'.
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas que ce serait si difficile.
native_language_example: I didn't think it would be so difficult.

meaning: not that I... / it's not that I...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a qualification or objection starting with 'it's not that I...' followed by a verb beginning with 'j'' (je) — often continues with a verb (e.g. 'pas que j'aie', 'pas que j'veuille'). Common in spoken and written French to soften a statement or explain a motive. The full phrase is usually 'ce n'est pas que je...' or simply 'pas que je...' and may contract to 'pas que j'' before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas que j'aie peur, mais je préfère attendre.
native_language_example: It's not that I'm afraid, but I prefer to wait.

meaning: not only / not just (colloquial, used to say something isn't limited to the mentioned thing or place)
additional_notes: Informal spoken sequence. Often appears within a larger negation (e.g. « ce n'est pas que là… ») or as a clipped remark in conversation. 'la' may be written 'là' to mean 'there' or 'that', but in rapid speech the accent is often omitted. Use in careful writing prefers full constructions like « Ce n'est pas seulement là que... ».
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas que la, on peut trouver du travail ailleurs aussi.
native_language_example: It's not just there; you can find work elsewhere too.

meaning: not that we / it's not that we
additional_notes: A short phrase used to contradict or soften a statement by specifying that the reason or situation is not because of 'us' (nous). Often appears in longer sentences (e.g. « ce n'est pas que nous ... ») to introduce an explanation or contrast. Tone is neutral; can be used in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas que nous ne voulions pas venir, mais nous avons un empêchement.
native_language_example: It's not that we didn't want to come, but we have a conflict.

meaning: not you / it's not that you (are)...
additional_notes: Used to exclude 'you' from a statement or to start a contrast (often part of a longer sentence). Can appear in informal and neutral contexts. Depending on context, it may be followed by a clause (e.g. 'pas que vous soyez...' = 'not that you are...') or used in a short reply to exclude the listener ('Ce n'est pas que vous' = 'It's not you'). Tone and the rest of the sentence determine the nuance.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas que vous soyez en tort, mais il faut changer la procédure.
native_language_example: It's not that you are at fault, but we need to change the procedure.

meaning: not something / not anything (used to negate the idea of 'something')
additional_notes: This phrase combines the negation word pas with 'quelque chose' (something). In natural French, full negation is usually formed with 'ne ... pas': 'ne ... pas quelque chose' is uncommon. More common alternatives: 'pas quelque chose' can appear in emphatic or clipped speech, but learners should use 'rien' for 'nothing' (e.g. 'ce n'est pas quelque chose' = 'it's not something' while 'ce n'est rien' = 'it's nothing'). Remember spoken French often drops 'ne'.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas quelque chose de grave.
native_language_example: It's not something serious.

meaning: No way / absolutely not (used to refuse something strongly).
additional_notes: Used in informal and neutral contexts to refuse or forbid an action. Often appears as 'Pas question de + infinitive' (No way of + verb) or 'Il n'est pas question que + subjunctive' (It is out of the question that...). In spoken French 'Il n'est pas' is frequently shortened to 'Il est pas' or omitted entirely: 'Pas question...'.
target_language_example: Pas question d'ouvrir la porte ce soir.
native_language_example: No way I'm opening the door tonight.

meaning: 'not who' (literal sequence) — not a fixed idiom; typically appears as part of a negation where 'pas' (not) and 'qui' (who/that) end up adjacent in the sentence.
additional_notes: By itself 'pas qui' is not an established multi-word expression in French. 'Pas' is the negation particle and 'qui' is a relative or interrogative pronoun. They can appear next to each other in constructions like 'ce n'est pas qui...' or when 'pas' closes a negation and 'qui' begins a relative clause (e.g. 'Ce n'est pas qui...'). Learn 'pas' and 'qui' separately; seeing them together usually reflects sentence structure rather than a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas qui a dit ça, c'était quelqu'un d'autre.
native_language_example: It's not who said that; it was someone else.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; a sequence of words that can appear in larger grammatical contexts. Literally 'step/negation who/that is' (depending on sense of 'pas'). Often a fragment or result of word order in a clause, e.g. part of 'qui n'est pas' if words are reordered or in elliptical speech.
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is uncommon as a set phrase. 'Pas' is primarily the negation particle ('not') but can also mean 'step'. 'Qui est' means 'who/which is'. If you encounter 'pas qui est' it is likely a fragment, typo, or part of a clause where words have been split for emphasis or in poetry. For standard negation with a relative clause use 'qui n'est pas' ('which is not'). Literal translation of the sequence is possible but context-dependent.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas qui est responsable ; c'est plutôt le système.
native_language_example: It is not who is responsible; it is rather the system.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct or meaningful phrase in French.
additional_notes:
The words 'pas', 'qui' and 'je' are all common French words ('not/step', 'who/that', 'I'), but together as 'pas qui je' they do not form a grammatical expression. Possible intended phrases include: 'pas que je...' (meaning 'not that I...'), 'pas qui' rarely used alone, or 'qui je suis' ('who I am'). If you encounter 'pas qui je' in text, it's likely a typo, word order mistake, or fragment. Learn correct alternatives depending on intent: 
- 'Pas que je...' + clause (e.g. 'Ce n'est pas que je veuille...') = 'It's not that I want...'
- 'qui je suis' = 'who I am' (used in 'savoir qui je suis').
- 'je ne... pas' = standard negation (e.g. 'Je ne sais pas' = 'I don't know').
target_language_example: Correct alternatives: "Ce n'est pas que je veuille partir." or "Je ne sais pas qui je suis."
native_language_example: Correct alternatives: "It's not that I want to leave." or "I don't know who I am."

meaning: not a standalone phrase; usually part of a larger expression (e.g. 'je ne sais pas quoi' = 'I don't know what').
additional_notes: You won't use 'pas quoi' alone. It appears when 'pas' (negation) comes before a question word like 'quoi' inside a larger clause: 'je ne sais pas quoi dire' (I don't know what to say). In spoken French, subject/auxiliary can be dropped: 'Je sais pas quoi dire.'
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi répondre.
native_language_example: I don't know what to answer.

meaning: not looked at / didn't watch (past participle negated).
additional_notes: This is the negation of the past participle 'regardé' (from regarder). In spoken and written French you'd normally see it in a sentence with an auxiliary verb (ne ... pas) or as part of a short negative reply: e.g. 'Je n'ai pas regardé' = 'I didn't watch/look at'. Often the 'ne' is dropped in casual speech/writing: 'J'ai pas regardé.' Use depending on formality.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas regardé le film hier soir.
native_language_example: I didn't watch the movie last night.

meaning: didn't answer (to); did not reply to
additional_notes: Negative past participle construction: 'pas' negates the verb 'répondu' (past participle of répondre). Usually appears with a subject and an indirect object introduced by 'à' (e.g. 'Je n'ai pas répondu à son message' = I didn't reply to his message). Word order often: subject + ne/n' + auxiliary (avoir) + pas + répondu + à + object. In spoken French, 'ne' is often dropped: 'J'ai pas répondu à...'
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas répondu à ton e‑mail hier.
native_language_example: I didn't reply to your email yesterday.

meaning: haven't answered my (…)
additional_notes: This is a fragment used to say someone did not reply to the speaker's question or message. It combines negation (ne ... pas) + past participle (répondu) + indirect object introduced by à and a possessive (ma = my, feminine noun follows). In full: «Tu n'as pas répondu à ma question.» Informal spoken forms often drop 'ne' (T'as pas répondu à ma...). Use 'mon' before masculine nouns (pas répondu à mon...), 'mes' for plural, 'vos'/'votre' for formal/plural.
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas répondu à ma question hier.
native_language_example: You didn't answer my question yesterday.

meaning: not to wake (someone) up
additional_notes: A negated form using 'pas' with the verb réveiller (to wake [someone]). Typically appears within a full negative construction with 'ne' (Ne ... pas) but in spoken or informal French the 'ne' is often omitted. Commonly used with object pronouns or explicit objects: e.g. 'Ne le réveille pas' = 'Don't wake him.' Ensure correct agreement and placement of pronouns when used.
target_language_example: Il faut absolument pas réveiller le bébé pendant la sieste.
native_language_example: You must absolutely not wake the baby during the nap.

meaning: Not a standard fixed expression; likely a fragment (pas + possessive 'sa') meaning 'not his/her/its' or part of a negation like 'ne ... pas sa ...' but by itself it's incomplete.
additional_notes: This is not a common standalone phrase in French. 'Pas' is the particle used in negation (with 'ne': 'ne ... pas' = not). 'Sa' is a feminine singular possessive adjective meaning 'his/her/its' (before a feminine noun). Together they may appear in a sentence as part of a longer structure (e.g. 'Ce n'est pas sa faute' = 'It's not his/her fault'). Do not use 'pas sa' alone; include the noun after 'sa' and the negation context for a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas sa décision.
native_language_example: That is not his/her decision.

meaning: 'pas' + reflexive pronoun 'se' — not a fixed phrase; these two words can appear together when describing negation involving a reflexive verb, but they are not adjacent in correct standard word order.
additional_notes: 'Pas se' is not a standalone expression. In standard French negation with reflexive verbs, the structure is: subject + ne + reflexive pronoun + verb + pas (e.g. 'Il ne se lave pas'). The sequence 'pas se' can appear in nonstandard or poetic word orders, in ellipsis, or when 'pas' belongs to a preceding clause and 'se' begins the next (e.g. in coordinated sentences), but learners should not treat 'pas se' as a single unit. In spoken French, 'ne' is often dropped: 'Il se lave pas.'
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas se rendre compte — (nonstandard; correct: "Je ne me suis pas rendu compte").
native_language_example: I did not realize — (nonstandard phrasing shown; correct: "I did not realize").

meaning: 'not trust' or 'not rely on' (used with à: ne pas se fier à ...).
additional_notes: Negative form of the reflexive verb se fier (à) meaning 'to trust' or 'to rely on'. Typically appears as "ne pas se fier à" + noun/pronoun. Common in warnings or advice: "Il ne faut pas se fier à..." = "Don't trust/...". Use à before the person/thing you don't trust (se fier à quelqu'un/quelque chose).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas se fier aux apparences.
native_language_example: Don't trust appearances.

meaning: not alone; not by herself (feminine).
additional_notes: Used to say someone (female) is not alone or not the only one. Often appears in contexts like "elle n'est pas seule" (she is not alone) or as part of a larger phrase. Alone, 'pas seule' without 'ne' is informal/elliptical; grammatically complete negative is 'n'est pas seule' or 'elle n'est pas seule'. 'Seule' agrees with a feminine subject; for a man use 'pas seul'.
target_language_example: Elle n'est pas seule ce soir.
native_language_example: She is not alone tonight.

meaning: Not so fast; slow down; hold on.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down, stop, or take things one at a time. Can be literal (walking/running) or figurative (rushing through actions or conclusions). Common in spoken French and can be followed by a name or phrase: "Pas si vite, [name]!"
target_language_example: Pas si vite — attends, vérifie d'abord.
native_language_example: Not so fast — wait, check first.

meaning: colloquial contracted sequence used in spoken negatives involving the clitic 'te' (roughly 'not you' or part of 'don't... you')
additional_notes: Informal, contracted spoken form: 'pas' (negation) appears next to a clitic pronoun that has been elided as 't'' (from 'te'). It is not a standalone phrase and typically appears inside larger colloquial constructions (e.g. after inversion or with clitic placement: "T'en vas pas" → often heard as "Pas t'en vas" in some emphatic or regional usages). Avoid in formal writing; use standard negation with 'ne...pas' and full pronouns. Meaning depends on context and word order.
target_language_example: Pas t'as intérêt à revenir ici.
native_language_example: You better not come back here. / You have no business coming back here.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase; a sequence of three words that can appear together in negative sentences where 'pas' negates the verb and 'te' and 'le' are object pronouns (indirect and direct). It appears in fragments of sentences like 'je ne te le dis pas' or in colloquial speech 'je te le dis pas'.
additional_notes: 'Pas te le' by itself is not grammatical as an independent expression; word order in full sentences is subject + ne (often dropped in speech) + indirect object pronoun (te) + direct object pronoun (le) + verb + pas. In compound tenses, pronouns precede the auxiliary. In spoken French 'ne' is commonly omitted, producing sequences like 'je te le dis pas' where 'pas te le' might appear across a clause boundary only in nonstandard orders or for emphasis but is still not an independent idiom.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas te le dire, alors pas te le demande pas.
native_language_example: I don't want to tell you, so don't ask me for it.

meaning: 'not you' — used to exclude or check if someone isn't included.
additional_notes: Literal: 'not you'. Common in short replies or questions to exclude the listener, express surprise that someone else is chosen, or to ask why the listener isn't included. Tone depends on context and intonation (can be neutral, surprised, hurt, or accusatory). Often used alone or with question words: 'Et pas toi ?' = 'And not you?'.
target_language_example: Pourquoi eux et pas toi ?
native_language_example: Why them and not you?

meaning: 'not your' (negation + possessive), used when saying something does not belong to or is not appropriate for 'you'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but simply the word 'pas' (negation) followed by the possessive adjective 'ton' (your, familiar). Context and word order matter: in a sentence you'd normally have a verb or noun before/after (e.g. 'Ce n'est pas ton livre' = 'This is not your book'). Alone, 'pas ton' is uncommon without surrounding words. 'Ton' is informal/familiar singular; use 'votre' for formal or plural.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas ton problème.
native_language_example: That's not your problem.

meaning: Don't touch (it) / Hands off.
additional_notes: Informal, strong command used to tell someone not to touch or interfere with something or someone. Often followed by the object (à + noun) or used alone as an interjection. Tone can be protective or angry.
target_language_example: Pas touche à mon téléphone !
native_language_example: Don't touch my phone!

meaning: 'not all' or 'not entirely'
additional_notes: Used to negate 'tout' (everything/all). Often appears in phrases like 'pas tout à fait' (not quite) or 'pas tout le monde' (not everyone). Alone, 'pas tout' is informal/elliptical and may need context; usually followed by more words (e.g., 'pas tout de suite' = not right away).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas tout expliquer maintenant.
native_language_example: I can't explain everything right now.

meaning: not completely / not entirely (usually part of a larger phrase, e.g. 'pas tout à fait' = 'not quite')
additional_notes: This fragment by itself is incomplete in French and typically appears inside fuller expressions (most commonly 'pas tout à fait'). It negates completeness or entirety. Don't use 'pas tout à' alone — use the full phrase (e.g. 'pas tout à fait', 'pas tout à fait sûr', 'pas tout à fait prêt').
target_language_example: Il n'est pas tout à fait prêt.
native_language_example: He is not quite ready.

meaning: 'not too early' or more commonly 'about time' / 'it's about time' (used to say something happened later than expected).
additional_notes: Literally 'not too early'. Often used informally to comment that something finally happened after a delay (similar to 'it's about time' or 'finally'). Can also be used more literally to say something shouldn't be done too early. Tone depends on context; often mildly impatient or relieved.
target_language_example: Ah, tu arrives enfin — pas trop tôt !
native_language_example: Ah, you're finally here — it's about time!

meaning: 'not find' or 'can't find' (the negation 'pas' paired with the verb trouver)
additional_notes: This is the negation built with 'pas' and the verb 'trouver'. Standard written French uses ne ... pas (e.g. je ne trouve pas), but in informal speech the 'ne' is often dropped, producing forms like 'je pas trouver' only in certain colloquial constructions or fragments — however, 'pas trouver' should generally appear within a full clause (e.g. 'je ne pas trouver' is ungrammatical; correct would be 'je ne trouve pas' or colloquially 'je trouve pas'). Use 'pas trouver' as the sequence of words when quoting or discussing the negation, or in reduced/informal speech fragments: 'pas trouver mes clés'.
target_language_example: Je dis « pas trouver mes clés » quand je parle vite.
native_language_example: I say 'can't find my keys' when I speak quickly.

meaning: not to kill / can't kill (negation with the verb tuer)
additional_notes: pas is the negation particle used with verbs (ne ... pas). In spoken French, the 'ne' is often dropped, so you hear 'tu peux pas' instead of 'tu ne peux pas'. 'Pas tuer' by itself isn't a fixed phrase — it's just the verb 'tuer' (to kill) negated. Can be used literally (kill a person or animal) or figuratively (e.g. 'you can't kill an idea').
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas tuer une idée.
native_language_example: You can't kill an idea.

meaning: not one
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there are zero of something. It is often followed by a singular noun: pas un livre = not a single book. In a full negative sentence, standard French usually also includes ne before the verb.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas un euro sur moi.
native_language_example: I don't have a single euro on me.

meaning: not a good (one); indicates someone/something is not good at/for something
additional_notes: Used to negate that someone or something is 'a good' [noun/role/thing]. Appears before a noun (un/une) and an adjective or noun like 'danseur', 'nageur', 'amant', 'moment'. In English: 'not a good [X]'. Can modify people, activities or objects. Word order: ne ... pas un bon + noun (or pas un bon + noun phrase).
target_language_example: Il n'est pas un bon professeur.
native_language_example: He is not a good teacher.

meaning: 'not see' (negation with the verb voir)
additional_notes: This is the negative form combining 'pas' (not) with the verb 'voir' (to see). In standard French, negation usually requires 'ne' before the verb: 'ne ... pas voir' or more commonly 'ne pas voir' when used with an infinitive (e.g. 'ne pas voir'). In spoken and informal French, the 'ne' is often dropped, leaving 'pas voir' in contexts like 'Je peux pas voir' (I can't see). Use with verbs conjugated or with an infinitive as appropriate. Example contexts: inability to see physically, not wanting to see, or failing to notice.
target_language_example: Je peux pas voir sans mes lunettes.
native_language_example: I can't see without my glasses.

meaning: not your / not yours (negation before a possessive), used to say something does not belong to or concern the person addressed
additional_notes: 'Pas' is the negation particle 'not' and 'votre' is the formal/plural possessive 'your'. Together they appear in contexts like "Ce n'est pas votre sac" (That is not your bag) or in replies: "Pas votre problème" (Not your problem). Remember French standard negation uses ne ... pas; in spoken/informal French 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. "C'est pas votre livre"). Use 'votre' for vous (formal you or plural). For informal singular use 'ton'/'ta'.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas votre siège, monsieur.
native_language_example: That is not your seat, sir.

meaning: 'not you' or used in polite negative constructions meaning 'aren't you' / 'you don't' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Direct combination of 'pas' (not) + 'vous' (you, formal/plural). Often appears in short answers or in questions after inversion/est-ce que, e.g. «Et vous?» vs. «Pas vous?» to ask 'Not you?' or 'Aren't you?'. Can be used to politely exclude or negate someone: «Ce n'est pas vous» = 'It's not you.' Context and intonation determine whether it's a question or statement.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas vous sur la photo?
native_language_example: Isn't that you in the photo?

meaning: A non-standalone fragment made of three words: 'pas' (not), 'vous' (you), and 'y' (there/to it). It typically appears only as part of a larger sentence or fixed expression; by itself it does not form a standard French phrase. It can occur when words are split by negation or inversion in longer constructions (e.g. 'Ne vous y fiez pas', 'Vous n'y êtes pas').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase. If you encounter 'pas vous y' in text, it usually reflects word order within a larger clause where negation or clitic placement has been split (often in spoken or poetic rearrangements). Possible related full expressions include 'Ne vous y fiez pas' (don't trust it), 'Vous n'y êtes pas' (you're not right / not on the right track), or clauses like 'Ce n'est pas vous y...' only as part of a longer structure. Translation depends on the surrounding words; do not translate the fragment literally.
target_language_example: Ne dites pas : « pas vous y », mais « ne vous y fiez pas » si vous voulez dire « don't trust it ».
native_language_example: Do not say: "pas vous y", but "ne vous y fiez pas" if you mean "don't trust it".

meaning: 'not travel' or 'cannot travel' (negation of voyager).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the verb voyager (to travel) with negation. In French negation is often formed with ne ... pas around the verb: je ne peux pas voyager = I cannot travel / I can't travel. Spoken French sometimes drops the 'ne' (e.g. je peux pas voyager). Use appropriate conjugation for different subjects (je ne peux pas, tu ne peux pas, il/elle/on ne peut pas, nous ne pouvons pas, vous ne pouvez pas, ils/elles ne peuvent pas).
target_language_example: Nous ne pouvons pas voyager cet été à cause des restrictions.
native_language_example: We cannot travel this summer because of the restrictions.

meaning: 'pas' + 'y' is not a fixed phrase; it results from negation ('pas') appearing together with the pronoun 'y' in a sentence (e.g. spoken variants like 'y a pas' or informal orderings where 'pas' follows the verb and 'y' precedes it). It signals negation involving a locative or 'à' complement replaced by 'y'.
additional_notes: You will not find 'pas y' as a standalone fixed expression in standard written French. In standard word order, the negation surrounds the verb with 'ne ... pas' and the pronoun 'y' normally precedes the verb (e.g. 'Il n'y a pas de pain'). In informal/spoken French, 'ne' is frequently dropped and word order can surface as 'y a pas' or 'il y a pas', which contains the adjacent sequence 'y' then 'pas'. The sequence 'pas y' (with that exact order) is rare in standard French; when it occurs it is typically across clause boundaries or in altered word order in speech or in imperative constructions with clitics. Use with caution: prefer standard 'Il n'y a pas...' for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Y a pas, y a pas — c'est pas y qui décide.
native_language_example: There's none, there's none — it's not him who decides.

meaning: not because (of); used to deny a reason
additional_notes: Used to say that something did not happen for a particular reason. Often appears in phrases like « ce n'est pas à cause de… » or « pas à cause de moi » to refute a cause. It is negative (pas) + à cause (de).
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas à cause de toi si j'ai raté le train.
native_language_example: It's not because of you that I missed the train.

meaning: 'step by step' or 'gradually'.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something slowly, carefully, or progressively. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Common in instructions, encouragement, or reflections about progress.
target_language_example: On va résoudre ce problème pas à pas.
native_language_example: We'll solve this problem step by step.

meaning: was not
additional_notes: Combination of the negation particle pas with the past participle été (from être). Used in compound tenses (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, etc.) with auxiliary avoir or être to form negative past statements: e.g. 'n'a pas été' = 'has not been' or 'was not'. By itself 'pas été' is incomplete — you will usually see it with an auxiliary verb and possibly a subject (je n'ai pas été, il n'a pas été, elle n'avait pas été).
target_language_example: Il n'a pas été invité à la réunion.
native_language_example: He was not invited to the meeting.

meaning: not to be in (a certain state, condition, place or mood) — used as part of the negative construction 'ne pas être en + [nom/adjectif]'.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed idiom; it appears in negative sentences with 'ne' (often omitted in speech) followed by 'pas être en ...'. Common combinations: 'ne pas être en forme', 'ne pas être en colère', 'ne pas être en vacances', 'ne pas être en mesure', 'ne pas être en retard'. The phrase is compositional: meaning derives from its parts. Can be translated literally into English as 'not to be in ...'.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas être en retard, mais aujourd'hui il ne va pas être en forme.
native_language_example: One mustn't be late, but today he will not be in good shape.

meaning: 'no problem' / 'no worries' / 'it's fine'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say that something is not an issue. Common in spoken and informal contexts but also acceptable in neutral situations. Can respond to a request, confirm agreement, or say you can handle something.
target_language_example: Tu peux m'aider cet après‑midi ? — Pas de problème.
native_language_example: Can you help me this afternoon? — No problem.

meaning: no problem; don't worry; it's okay.
additional_notes: Informal, friendly phrase used to reassure someone or to say that something is not an issue. Equivalent to "no worries" or "no problem" in English. Commonly used alone or after a statement (e.g., "Pas de souci, je m'en occupe.").
target_language_example: Pas de souci, je peux t'aider ce soir.
native_language_example: No problem, I can help you tonight.

meaning: 'not for' or 'not in favor of'
additional_notes: Used to negate a phrase that would normally take 'pour' (for). Often appears before a noun, verb or clause to say something is not intended for, suitable for, or in support of someone/something. Context matters: it can mean 'not meant for', 'not in favor of', or 'not because of'. For stronger negation with verbs, French usually uses 'pas' with 'être' or another verb (e.g., 'je ne suis pas pour').
target_language_example: Ce cadeau n'est pas pour toi.
native_language_example: This gift is not for you.

meaning: 'what is happening in' (used in questions: Que se passe-t-il dans ... ? = What's happening in ...?)
additional_notes: This appears inside the common question formula "Que se passe-t-il dans + [place/thing] ?". Literally: "What happens it in...", but in natural English: "What's happening in..." or "What's going on in...". Use to ask about events, situations, or someone's thoughts (e.g. "dans sa tête"). Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Que se passe-t-il dans la rue ?
native_language_example: What's happening in the street?

meaning: 'happen with' or 'be going on with' (used in questions/statements about what is occurring concerning someone or something).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase "Qu'est-ce qui se passe avec... ?" meaning "What's going on with... ?" Used to ask about someone's situation, condition, or events involving a person or thing. Passe is from the verb se passer (to happen); avec means with. The verb agrees with qu' (impersonal construction: "Qu'est-ce qui se passe...").
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui se passe avec ton ordinateur ?
native_language_example: What's going on with your computer?

meaning: 'passe des' is not a standalone fixed expression; it's the 3rd-person singular present (or imperative-like conjugation in some contexts) of the verb 'passer' followed by the partitive/article 'des' plus a noun. Depending on context it can mean 'passes (some)...', 'is passing (some)...', or be part of constructions meaning 'spends (time)', 'takes (exams)', 'hands over (objects)', etc.
additional_notes: This sequence must be read as part of a larger clause: 'passe' is a conjugated verb form and 'des' is the partitive/indefinite plural article. Examples of meanings vary with the noun that follows: 'passe des vacances' (spends holidays), 'passe des examens' (takes exams), 'passe des objets' (passes/hand over objects). Pay attention to subject agreement (je passe, tu passes, il/elle passe, nous passons...). The literal translation 'passes of' is usually not idiomatic in English; translate according to the full phrase.
target_language_example: Il passe des livres à ses collègues chaque semaine.
native_language_example: He passes some books to his colleagues every week.

meaning: something happens / things happen (informal phrasing)
additional_notes: This phrase is a casual way to say that events or occurrences are taking place. It often appears in contexts like "il se passe des choses" (there are things happening) or as part of spoken expressions. On its own "passe des choses" is not a complete standard sentence; learners will most often hear the full form with a subject and the reflexive verb: "Il se passe des choses."
target_language_example: Il se passe des choses intéressantes en ville ce week-end.
native_language_example: There are interesting things happening in town this weekend.

meaning: 'passes between' or 'goes between' (something passes through or in the space separating two things).
additional_notes: Literally from the verb passer + preposition entre. Used when something moves through or in the gap/space separating two objects or people. Context determines tense and subject (e.g. 'il passe entre', 'ça passe entre'). Can also be used figuratively (a detail 'passes between' two events). Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional.
target_language_example: La corde passe entre les deux poteaux.
native_language_example: The rope passes between the two posts.

meaning: a casual way to tell someone to come over or drop by (come here / come over).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Often used to invite someone to come to the speaker's location or to ask someone to move closer: e.g. 'Passe là' ≈ 'come over here' or 'come here for a moment'. Could appear as 'passe donc là', 'viens passe là' depending on region. Not a fixed formal phrase; context and tone matter. If used with a specific object, it can mean 'pass that over here' (hand it to me), but isolated 'passe là' usually means 'come here' or 'bring it here'.
target_language_example: Hé, passe là un instant, j'ai quelque chose à te montrer.
native_language_example: Hey, come over here for a moment, I have something to show you.

meaning: Not a correct or natural French phrase. Likely a mistaken word order for the imperative with an object pronoun ('passe-moi' meaning 'pass me' or 'give me') or a typo produced by literal translation from English.
additional_notes: French places object pronouns after the verb with a hyphen in affirmative imperatives: 'passe-moi' (informal singular). In other constructions the pronoun precedes the verb: 'il me passe' or 'tu me passes'. If you encounter 'passe me' it is almost always an error (typo, mistranslation, or nonstandard spacing).
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* «passe me le sel» — this is wrong; correct form is «passe-moi le sel».
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* "pass me the salt" — (analogous mistaken literal word order).

meaning: have a
additional_notes: Commonly appears in different constructions: 'il se passe un ...' = 'there is/there is happening a ...' (something is happening); 'passer un bon moment/bon week-end' = 'to spend/have a good time, to have a good weekend'; 'Passe un ...' used as an imperative (informal) = 'Have a ...' (e.g. Passe un agréable Noël = Have a pleasant Christmas). The exact English verb (have, spend, happen) depends on context.
target_language_example: Passe un bon voyage !
native_language_example: Have a good trip!

meaning: something happens / there's something going on (informal)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase. 'Il se passe un truc' or 'Y a un truc qui se passe' means 'something is happening' or 'there's something odd/interesting going on.' 'Truc' is a vague word meaning 'thing' and can be used when you don't specify details. Often used to express surprise, suspicion, or to introduce an unexplained event.
target_language_example: Il se passe un truc bizarre dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: Something strange is happening in this neighborhood.

meaning: move on (to something/someone else), switch topic or partner
additional_notes: This is an informal fragment often seen in phrases like "passer à autre chose" (move on to something else) or "passer à autre chose/à autre chose". On its own "passe à autre" is incomplete; you normally add "chose" (something) or a noun. Used when changing subject, activity, or partner. Common in spoken French: "On passe à autre chose ?" = "Shall we move on?"
target_language_example: On passe à autre chose, d'accord ?
native_language_example: Let's move on to something else, okay?

meaning: to spend a lot (of time) / to happen a lot (depending on context)
additional_notes: Depends on context: most often used with time (passer beaucoup de temps = to spend a lot of time). Can also describe frequency with an event or feeling (quelque chose passe beaucoup = it happens or appears a lot) but that use is less common. Usually needs an object (de temps, à + infinitive, or avec quelqu'un) or further context to be natural.
target_language_example: Je passe beaucoup de temps ici.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time here.

meaning: to place an order (for goods or services).
additional_notes: Commonly used when ordering in shops, restaurants, online, or by phone. Conjugate passer as needed (e.g., je passe commande, nous avons passé commande). Often followed by what is being ordered (passer commande de + item) or by a direct object.
target_language_example: Je vais passer commande d'une nouvelle imprimante aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm going to place an order for a new printer today.

meaning: to go from; to change from one state/thing to another; to move past (by amount).
additional_notes: Used to describe a change or transition (e.g., passer de A à B = go from A to B) or to indicate skipping/omitting something in informal contexts. Can also be used with quantities: passer de X à Y (increase/decrease). Requires preposition 'à' when specifying the target (passer de... à...).
target_language_example: Il faut parfois passer de l'idée à l'action.
native_language_example: Sometimes you have to go from idea to action.

meaning: to move on from this / to stop being in this state (context-dependent)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed idiom by itself; it combines the verb 'passer' (to pass, to go through, to move on) with the prepositional phrase 'de ce' (of/from this). Meaning depends on the full sentence: e.g. 'passer de ce stade' = 'move on from this stage', 'passer de ce sentiment' = 'get past this feeling'. You'll usually see it followed by a noun or phrase that specifies what is being left behind. Use context to determine tense and exact translation.
target_language_example: Il doit passer de ce ressentiment pour avancer.
native_language_example: He needs to get past this resentment to move forward.

meaning: to go past or pass in front of (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used when moving so that you go by the front of a place or person. Can refer to walking, driving, or being located in front of something briefly. Also used figuratively (e.g., 'to pass someone' in a race or ranking) depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous allons passer devant le musée en revenant.
native_language_example: We'll pass in front of the museum on the way back.

meaning: to go from (something) — used when indicating a change from one state/thing to another (followed by a noun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: A contraction of 'passer de' + definite article 'le' (du = de + le). Often appears before a masculine singular noun: 'passer du froid au chaud' (to go from cold to warm). It can express physical movement, a transition in time, change of state, or switching topics. Requires an object (what you're moving from). For feminine nouns you'd see 'passer de la' (or 'de l'' before a vowel).
target_language_example: Il a dû passer du chômage à un emploi stable pour subvenir aux besoins de sa famille.
native_language_example: He had to go from unemployment to a steady job to provide for his family.

meaning: to have a good time; to enjoy oneself (informal, incomplete phrase usually followed by a noun like 'temps')
additional_notes: On its own 'passer du bon' is not a complete fixed expression in French — learners will more often hear 'passer du bon temps', 'passer un bon moment', or 's'amuser'. 'Passer' + time expressions means to spend or have time; 'du bon' qualifies that the time is good/enjoyable. Mostly used in casual spoken French. When using 'passer du bon', include the noun that follows (e.g. 'temps').
target_language_example: Ils aiment passer du bon temps ensemble le week-end.
native_language_example: They like to have a good time together on weekends.

meaning: to spread the word; to tell people / pass on a message.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to inform others or pass along a short message. Commonly used in commands or reports (Fais/Faites passer le mot = 'Spread the word'). Can be followed by a recipient (Je lui ai fait passer le mot = I passed the message to him). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Fais passer le mot à tout le monde.
native_language_example: Spread the word to everyone.

meaning: to pass the time; to kill time (do something to make time go by).
additional_notes: Used to describe activities done to occupy oneself while waiting or to make time feel shorter. Neutral register; can mean harmless, casual activities (reading, watching TV, chatting). Often appears in questions (Que fais-tu pour passer le temps ?) or short phrases (Pour passer le temps).
target_language_example: Je regarde des vidéos pour passer le temps.
native_language_example: I watch videos to pass the time.

meaning: to come to mind; to occur to (someone).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say that a thought, idea or possibility briefly appears in someone's mind. Often used impersonally with constructions like 'il m'est/te/leur/etc. passé par la tête' or in colloquial speech 'ça m'a/te/etc. passé par la tête'. Can describe fleeting or sudden thoughts.
target_language_example: Il m'est passé par la tête de passer par la tête cette idée.
native_language_example: The idea of passing through my mind came to me.

meaning: to spend more (time) / to pass more (time) — used to say someone spends more time doing something
additional_notes: Formed from the verb passer + adverb plus. In context it usually means 'to spend more (time)' (e.g. passer plus de temps à faire quelque chose). You normally need de + noun or à + verb after: «passer plus de temps», «passer plus de temps à étudier». Alone, 'passer plus' is incomplete and should be followed by what is being spent or done. 'Plus' here means 'more'.
target_language_example: Je vais passer plus de temps à apprendre le français cette année.
native_language_example: I will spend more time learning French this year.

meaning: 'to spend (time) doing something' or 'to pass something along' depending on context; here 'passer' + indefinite object pronoun 'quelque' often begins expressions like 'passer quelque temps' (to spend some time).
additional_notes: Alone 'passer' is a very common verb with many meanings (to pass, to spend time, to go by, to hand over, to take a test, etc.). 'Quelque' means 'some' or 'a few' and usually appears before a noun (quelque chose, quelque part, quelque temps). The combination 'passer quelque' by itself is incomplete and must be followed by a noun: e.g. 'passer quelque temps' (spend some time), 'passer quelque chose' (to pass/hand over something). For beginners, learn fixed phrases: 'passer du temps' / 'passer du temps à + infinitive' (to spend time doing...), 'passer quelque chose à quelqu'un' (to pass something to someone).
target_language_example: Nous allons passer quelque temps à la campagne cet été.
native_language_example: We are going to spend some time in the countryside this summer.

meaning: to pass something (to someone), to hand something over; also to spend (time) doing something or to take (an exam) depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase is versatile. Most commonly it means 'to pass/hand something' (passer quelque chose à quelqu'un). With 'du temps' it means 'to spend time' (passer du temps). With 'un examen' in some varieties it can mean 'to take an exam' (passer un examen). Context and any added words (à, pour, du temps, un examen, etc.) determine the exact sense. Verb is transitive; include the object after 'passer'.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me passer quelque chose sur la table ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me something from the table?

meaning: to make a few (phone) calls; to call a few people.
additional_notes: Short for "passer quelques coups de fil". Used when you want to say you'll place a few telephone calls. Common in spoken French. Can take "de fil" (singular) or colloquial plural "de fils", but "de fil" is standard. Often followed by "de fil" explicitly, but understood from context if omitted.
target_language_example: Je vais passer quelques coups de fil cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'll make a few phone calls this afternoon.

meaning: to make a quick call or do something briefly (often 'passer un coup de fil' = to give someone a quick phone call).
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete by itself and usually needs a complement: most commonly 'passer un coup de fil' (make a quick phone call) or 'passer un coup de balai' (give a quick sweep). Used to indicate a short, casual action. Informal in everyday speech when shortened to 'passer un coup' to mean 'give someone a quick call.'
target_language_example: Je vais passer un coup de fil à Marie tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'll give Marie a quick call right away.

meaning: to spend or go through (a period of time or an event); to experience or have (something).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (une + noun). Common constructions: passer une nuit/soirée/journée/bonne journée/bonne soirée = to spend/have a (night/evening/day). Can also mean to let something go by (J'ai vu passer une souris = I saw a mouse run by) or to undergo an event (passer une audition = to take/attend an audition). Context determines whether it means 'spend', 'have', 'go by', or 'take'.
target_language_example: Nous allons passer une semaine tranquille à la campagne.
native_language_example: We are going to spend a quiet week in the countryside.

meaning: to move on; to get past something and focus on something else.
additional_notes: Used when telling someone (or oneself) to stop dwelling on a situation, problem, relationship, or emotion and start focusing on something new. Common in everyday speech. Often followed by context or nothing: e.g. 'passer à autre chose' (move on) or 'passer à autre chose dans la vie'.
target_language_example: Après cette dispute, il vaut mieux passer à autre chose.
native_language_example: After that argument, it's better to move on.

meaning: 'to miss' or 'to fail to take advantage of' (an opportunity); can also mean 'to pass by' something without noticing it.
additional_notes: Common idiom. Often used with chance/opportunity/occasion (une occasion, une chance, l'amour, etc.) to say you missed it. Can be literal (pass by something) but most often idiomatic: passer à côté de quelque chose = ne pas profiter de, rater. Typical constructions: passer à côté de + noun. Context tells whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Il a passé à côté d'une grande opportunité en refusant le poste.
native_language_example: He missed a great opportunity by refusing the job.

meaning: to hand/ pass that (to someone) or to let that go; context-dependent phrase using 'passer' + 'ça'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on context. Often used when handing something over: 'Tu peux me passer ça ?' = 'Can you pass that to me?' It can also mean 'let that go' or 'move on from that' in informal uses, but that sense usually appears in longer expressions (e.g. 'passer ça sous silence' = 'let that pass/keep it quiet'). Pay attention to tone and surrounding words to know whether it's literal (physically passing an object) or figurative.
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer ça, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass that to me, please?

meaning: would happen (in questions) — literally 'would happen it' (formal inversion).
additional_notes: Used in hypothetical questions with the impersonal verb se passer (to happen). Formed by conditional tense + subject-verb inversion for questions (Que se passerait-il ? = What would happen?). Common in hypothetical or speculative situations. Equivalent informal word order: Qu'est-ce qui se passerait ?
target_language_example: Que se passerait-il si on supprimait les voitures du centre-ville ?
native_language_example: What would happen if we removed cars from the city center?

meaning: pass (something) to
additional_notes: Used as an imperative or polite request (vous form) meaning to hand something to someone or to convey/send something (a greeting, a message, news). Followed by the direct object: a physical object (le journal), a greeting (le bonjour), a message (le mot) or a phrase (le secteur au peigne fin = sweep the area thoroughly). In spoken requests you may also hear 'passe-moi' (tu form) for informal situations.
target_language_example: Passez le sel, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

meaning: literally 'past this' — used to refer to something beyond a certain point or time (often followed by a noun or moment).
additional_notes: Rare as an isolated pair; typically appears in phrases like 'passé ce point', 'passé ce soir', or 'passé ce stade' to mean 'after this point/time' or 'beyond this stage'. Can also appear in more formal/written contexts. Remember word order: 'passé' (past) + demonstrative 'ce' (this). When referring to people or plural nouns, forms change (ex.: 'passé cet âge', 'passés ces moments').
target_language_example: Passé ce point, il n'y a plus de signal.
native_language_example: After this point, there is no more signal.

meaning: 'passed into' / 'went into' (movement from one place/state into another), or 'appeared in' (used with events/media).
additional_notes: Commonly a compound of the past participle passé + preposition dans. Use with verbs of movement (e.g., Il est passé dans la rue = He went through/along the street) or to say something entered a place or period (Le bateau est passé dans le port). It can also mean 'appeared in' when talking about media or events (Son nom est passé dans les journaux = His name appeared in the newspapers). Context and the verb/subject decide whether it describes physical movement, entry into a state/time, or appearing/being mentioned.
target_language_example: Il est passé dans la rue à toute vitesse.
native_language_example: He passed through the street at full speed.

meaning: been here (past participle used to say someone 'passed by' or 'visited here').
additional_notes: Literally 'passed here'. Often used in spoken French to say that someone stopped by or passed by a place (e.g., Il est passé ici = He was here/He stopped by). Context decides whether it means 'came by', 'was here' or 'dropped in briefly'. If referring to an action you did, use je suis passé(e) ici. With a direct object it can mean 'showed' or 'spent' in different contexts, but most commonly it describes physically passing by a location.
target_language_example: Il est passé ici ce matin pour déposer le colis.
native_language_example: He stopped by here this morning to drop off the package.

meaning: 'to spend' (time) + definite article (feminine noun), as in 'spent the (day/night)'.
additional_notes: Passer (quelque chose) + la + [période] = to spend (that period). In examples, 'passé la journée', 'passé la nuit' mean 'spent the day/night'. The verb agrees with subject (J'ai passé, Il a passé). The article 'la' matches a feminine time-word (la journée, la nuit). For other periods you may see 'le' (le matin), 'la' (l'après-midi sometimes 'l'après-midi'), or no article with plurals.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé la soirée au restaurant.
native_language_example: We spent the evening at the restaurant.

meaning: literally 'passed where'; used to ask or say where someone/something passed by or went by (informal spoken French).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle passé with the question word où. Often found in casual spoken questions like « Il est passé où ? » meaning 'Where did he go?' or 'Where has he been?' Depending on context it can mean 'where did [someone/something] pass by?' or simply 'where did [they/it] go?'. In standard written French you'd more often hear « Où est-il passé ? »
target_language_example: Le bus est passé où ? Je l'ai raté.
native_language_example: Where did the bus go? I missed it.

meaning: Used in speech to ask 'what happened?' or 'what's wrong?' (informal, surprised or pressing).
additional_notes: Colloquial fragment often heard in spoken French. It's a shortened, more abrupt form of 'Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ?' or 'Qu'est-ce qui t'est passé ?' depending on context. Used to demand an explanation when something unexpected or negative occurs. Tone can be blunt or concerned; not formal. You may also hear 'c'est passé quoi ?' or simply 'quoi ?' in similar casual contexts.
target_language_example: Tu as l'air choqué — passé quoi ?
native_language_example: You look shocked — what happened?

meaning: 'spent' or 'took' (used with a noun to say someone spent time doing something, took an exam, celebrated an event, or physically moved a body part).
additional_notes: A construction using the past participle passé + a possessive (son/sa/ses) + noun. Meaning depends on the noun: e.g. passé son permis = took (and passed) his/her driving test; passé son enfance = spent his/her childhood; passé son bras = put/placed his/her arm; passé son tour = skipped his/her turn; passé son anniversaire = spent his/her birthday. Context and the following noun determine translation. Gender/number of the possessive changes with the noun (son/sa/ses).
target_language_example: Il a passé son diplôme l'année dernière.
native_language_example: He took his diploma (completed his degree) last year.

meaning: 'past your' or 'beyond your' (literal), often appears as part of expressions like "passé ton/ta/tes ..." meaning something that has passed or is beyond someone's reach/ability; not a fixed standalone phrase.
additional_notes: On its own, 'passé ton' is incomplete in French; you normally need a noun or context (e.g. "c'est passé ton âge", "c'est passé ton niveau") or a verb form (e.g. "il t'est passé" in other constructions). It literally combines the past participle/adjective 'passé' (past/passed) with the possessive 'ton' (your). Useful to recognize inside longer phrases but don't use it alone.
target_language_example: Ce concert est passé ton âge — choisis quelque chose de plus adapté.
native_language_example: This concert is past your age — pick something more appropriate.

meaning: spent/ended up spending three (units of time).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (jours, semaines, mois, heures, ans) to say someone spent three of those units doing something. Common structure: passé + number + time unit (here 'trois'). In these examples 'passé' is the past participle of 'passer' and indicates duration experienced. Often followed by a prepositional phrase: en/à/derrière + noun (e.g. en mer, à Islamabad, en plein air, derrière les barreaux).
target_language_example: Elle a passé trois semaines à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: She spent three weeks learning French.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase in French; literally 'passed very' — typically appears as part of a larger clause (e.g. with an adjective or adverb following) to indicate how something went or how quickly it passed.
additional_notes: On its own 'passé très' is incomplete and uncommon; you will normally see 'passé' (past participle) and 'très' (adverb) separated by word order depending on the construction: e.g. 'ça s'est très bien passé' or 'c'est passé très vite'. If you must reproduce 'passé très' exactly, it may occur in informal or elliptical contexts, but it usually requires further words to be grammatical. Word order tips: with pronominal verbs the adverb often appears between auxiliary and past participle ('s'est très bien passé'); in non-pronominal constructions the adverb can follow the past participle ('passé très vite').
target_language_example: Le concert est passé très mal, selon lui, donc il a dit : « passé très », mais c'était incomplet.
native_language_example: The concert went very badly, according to him, so he said: "passé très", but it was incomplete.

meaning: 'had a very' (used with experiences: had a very good time, had a very good Christmas, etc.)
additional_notes: Common construction: passé (past participle of 'passer') + un/une + adjective phrase. Often used to describe having spent or experienced something (un bon moment, un bon Noël, une bonne soirée). In English you usually translate as 'had a very…' or 'spent a very…' depending on context. Verb agreement: 'passé' used with avoir (no gender agreement) unless used with être in other senses.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé un très bon week-end en famille.
native_language_example: We had a very nice weekend with family.

meaning: 'moved on to', 'switched to', or 'came over to' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Form is the past participle passé followed by the preposition à.
