additional_notes: Common in questions to request specifics. Often followed by verbs like vouloir, savoir, apprendre, étudier. Can be shortened to 'quelque chose de particulier' or simply 'quelque chose' if less specific. Formal: same structure with 'vous'. Word order: 'Y a-t-il quelque chose en particulier que ... ?' or 'Est-ce qu'il y a quelque chose en particulier que ... ?'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose en particulier que tu voudrais apprendre cette année ?
native_language_example: Is there something in particular that you would like to learn this year?

meaning: 'something is' — the phrase begins a sentence stating a quality or fact about 'something'.
additional_notes: quelque chose means 'something'. When followed by est (3rd-person singular of être), it forms 'something is ...'. Use est for describing or giving information about an unspecified thing. In spoken French you may also hear 'y a quelque chose qui est...' or 'il y a quelque chose' instead of starting with 'quelque chose est.'
target_language_example: Quelque chose est étrange ici.
native_language_example: Something is strange here.

meaning: 'something' — used to refer to an unspecified thing; when followed by 'vous' in speech it may start a question or phrase addressing the listener (e.g. 'quelque chose, vous...?').
additional_notes: The core phrase is 'quelque chose' meaning 'something'. It can appear alone or in sentences (Je veux quelque chose = I want something). The fragment 'quelque chose vous' by itself is incomplete in French; in spoken or informal questions you might hear constructions like 'Quelque chose, vous?' or 'Quelque chose vous gêne?' meaning 'Is something wrong with you?' or 'Does something bother you?'. For beginners focus on 'quelque chose' as the standard expression for 'something'.
target_language_example: Quelque chose vous inquiète ?
native_language_example: Is something worrying you?

meaning: A fragment of a longer expression meaning 'something about this/that' or 'something to this...' — incomplete on its own and requires additional words to be grammatical (e.g. 'quelque chose à ce sujet').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself. Typically appears as part of constructions like 'quelque chose à ce sujet' (something about that/this) or 'quelque chose à ce propos'. It cannot stand alone; must be completed with a noun (sujet/propos) or clause. Commonly used in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose à ce sujet qui m'inquiète.
native_language_example: There is something about this that worries me.

meaning: something in the style of / something like (followed by a noun or expression)
additional_notes: This fragment is used before a noun or adjective to say 'something like' or 'something in the ... way/style'. It is often completed by a noun or descriptive phrase (e.g. 'quelque chose à la mode', 'quelque chose à la maison'). Informal spoken French may shorten or vary the structure (e.g. 'un truc à la...'). Make sure the rest of the sentence provides what it's 'à la'.
target_language_example: On veut quelque chose à la française pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We want something French-style for dinner.

meaning: somewhere
additional_notes: Common adverbial expression meaning 'in/at some place' — often vague. Can mean a physical location ('somewhere over there'), or figurative/unspecified location ('somewhere in the world', 'somehow'). When used in questions it asks if someone/something is present in an unspecified place. Pairing with words like 'là', 'par', or 'dans' is frequent (e.g. 'quelque part là', 'quelque part par là‑dessus').
target_language_example: Ils vivent quelque part près de la côte.
native_language_example: They live somewhere near the coast.

meaning: somewhere near / around (a place or time); indicates an approximate location or point in time
additional_notes: This is a variant/informal combination of 'quelque part' (somewhere) with 'par' used to indicate 'around' or 'about' a point (often in spoken or regional French). It can be followed by a noun or a time expression: e.g. 'quelque part par ici' (somewhere around here) or 'quelque part par trois heures' (around three o'clock). Use more standard phrases like 'quelque part', 'vers', or 'aux environs de' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu quelque part par ici cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I saw him somewhere around here this afternoon.

meaning: some time / a while (an unspecified period of time)
additional_notes: Used to indicate an indefinite, often short-to-moderate amount of time. Can appear after 'il y a' or 'ça fait' to mean 'some time ago' or 'it's been some time that...'. Can also be used on its own as a brief expression meaning 'a while'.
target_language_example: Ça fait quelque temps que je n'ai pas vu Marie.
native_language_example: It's been a while since I saw Marie.

meaning: some (feminine plural pronoun): a few of them.
additional_notes: Used as a pronoun replacing a feminine plural noun previously mentioned or indicated (e.g., 'quelques-unes de ces pommes' → some of them). Agreement is feminine plural; masculine form is 'quelques-uns'. Often used alone in short answers.
target_language_example: Tu veux des fraises ? — Oui, je prendrai quelques-unes.
native_language_example: Do you want any strawberries? — Yes, I'll take a few of them.

meaning: 'some (of them)' or 'a few (of them)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified small number of people or things previously mentioned or implied. Often used with the pronoun en (J'en ai quelques-uns) or after de/ces/celui-ci (quelques-uns de ces livres). Agreement: when referring to people, verb can be plural (Quelques-uns étaient...). Can stand alone as a short answer ("Quelques-uns.").
target_language_example: J'en prendrai quelques-uns.
native_language_example: I'll take a few (of them).

meaning: Not standard French; likely a mistake or typo. Native speakers would normally use "quelques" + plural noun (e.g. "quelques cas") or the plural noun "casses" if referring to breaks/crashes. "quelques casse" (singular "casse" after "quelques") is grammatically incorrect.
additional_notes:
Possible interpretations:
1) Typo for "quelques cas" = "some cases".
2) Intended as "quelques casses" (plural of "casse") meaning "a few breaks/crashes/robberies" depending on context, but uncommon.
3) If seen in informal writing/speech, treat as an error and correct to "quelques" + plural noun. "Quelques" always requires a plural noun form.
Use caution: "casse" as a noun can mean "breakage", "crash", or colloquially "deal"/"robbery" in certain phrases, so choose the correct plural meaning "casses" when appropriate.
target_language_example: Il y a quelques casse dans le magasin après la manifestation. (usage non standard / possiblement une faute — mieux: «quelques casses» ou «quelques dégâts»)
native_language_example: There are a few breakages in the store after the demonstration. (nonstandard usage — better: "quelques casses" or "some damages")

meaning: a few days (later/more); used as part of a time expression (e.g. 'a few days later' or 'a few more days')
additional_notes: Incomplete on its own — usually appears as 'quelques jours plus tard' (a few days later) or 'quelques jours de plus' (a few more days). Without the following word, context determines whether it means 'later' or 'more'. Use the full phrase for clarity.
target_language_example: Quelques jours plus tard, elle a reçu une réponse.
native_language_example: A few days later, she received an answer.

meaning: a few minutes later / a few more minutes
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and written French to indicate that something happens a short time after a previously mentioned moment. Often appears as 'quelques minutes plus tard' (a more complete form). Alone, 'quelques minutes plus' is usually followed by a time-adverb like 'tard' or used in a phrase indicating 'more' time (e.g., 'quelques minutes plus' de discussion). For beginners, prefer the full form 'quelques minutes plus tard' = 'a few minutes later.'
target_language_example: Nous avons attendu, et quelques minutes plus tard il est arrivé.
native_language_example: We waited, and a few minutes later he arrived.

quels sont les aliments que tu manges

target_language_multi_word_term: quels sont les aliments que tu manges
meaning: 'Which foods do you eat' / 'What foods do you eat'
additional_notes: A polite, neutral question asking someone to list foods they eat. 'Quels' agrees with the plural 'aliments'. You can change 'tu' to 'vous' for formal/plural (Quels sont les aliments que vous mangez). Often followed by context (avec des baguettes, avec du vin, etc.).
target_language_example: Quels sont les aliments que tu manges habituellement avec du fromage ?
native_language_example: Which foods do you usually eat with cheese?

quels sont les aliments que vous mangez

target_language_multi_word_term: quels sont les aliments que vous mangez
meaning: 'what foods do you eat' (polite/formal plural or singular polite)
additional_notes: A formal/polite question asking which foods someone typically eats. 'Quels' agrees with 'aliments' (masculine plural). 'Vous' can be singular polite or plural. Often followed by adverbs like 'habituellement' or context (avec des baguettes, avec du vin rouge, etc.). You can make it informal by using 'tu' instead of 'vous': 'quels sont les aliments que tu manges'.
target_language_example: Quels sont les aliments que vous mangez habituellement au petit-déjeuner ?
native_language_example: What foods do you usually eat for breakfast?

meaning: Not a standard standalone French phrase; appears when the word 'question' is followed by the preposition 'à' (written 'à' with accent) meaning 'to' or 'for' — used to introduce who the question is directed to or the topic (e.g. 'la question à...').
additional_notes: In correct French the preposition must be written 'à' (with grave accent). 'question a' (without accent) is orthographically incorrect and can be ambiguous. The entry shows the sequence 'question a' as requested, but in real use write 'question à'.
target_language_example: La question à résoudre est importante.
native_language_example: The question to solve is important.

meaning: a matter of (a) point; used to refer to a specific detail or issue (often formal or administrative).
additional_notes: This phrase is not a very common fixed expression in everyday French. It can be used to point to a particular issue, item, or technical point under discussion (similar to 'a point about' or 'a matter of'). Depending on context, it may appear in formal/procedural language (e.g., 'une question de point d'ordre' = a point of order). If you see it alone, check surrounding words to understand the exact nuance.
target_language_example: C'est une question de point technique à clarifier avant de signer.
native_language_example: It's a technical point to clarify before signing.

meaning: literally 'question of point of' — not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to combine elements ('question de' and 'point de') and would normally be rephrased. If encountered, it likely signals an awkward or incorrect construction and should be replaced by 'question de ...' or 'le point de ...' depending on intended meaning.
additional_notes: This sequence is not idiomatic as written. Native speakers would rarely say 'question de point de' by itself. Use 'une question de [nom]' (une question de principe), 'la question de [quelque chose]' (la question de l'argent), or 'le point de [infinitive/nom]' (le point de départ, le point de vue). If you see 'question de point de' it may be a mistaken repetition or partial clipping of a longer phrase and should be rewritten for clarity.
target_language_example: La formulation 'question de point de' dans cette phrase semble incorrecte : 'C'est une question de point de vue', pas 'question de point de'.
native_language_example: The wording 'question de point de' in that sentence seems incorrect: 'C'est une question de point de vue,' not 'question de point de.'

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; usually results from an incorrect word order or an incomplete negative construction. 'Ne' is the first adverb of negation and must be paired with a second element (e.g. 'pas', 'plus', 'jamais') and placed around a verb. 'Question' is a noun; the sequence 'question ne' on its own is ungrammatical unless part of a larger structure (e.g. 'la question ne ... pas').
additional_notes: If you encounter 'question ne' in a sentence, check for a verb following 'ne' (e.g. 'la question ne se pose pas') or for other surrounding words. Correct patterns include 'la question ne ... pas' (the question does not ...), 'la question de' (the question of/about), or 'se poser la question' (to ask oneself the question). This entry preserves the exact two-word sequence for identification but it is not an idiom.
target_language_example: La question ne se pose pas dans ce contexte.
native_language_example: The question does not arise in this context.

meaning: a question aimed at or about (someone or something); 'question for' (used before mentioning the person/topic the question is directed to).
additional_notes: Used when specifying who or what the question is directed to: 'une question pour Marie' = a question for Marie. Often followed by a person (name/pronoun) or a purpose/topic introduced by a noun or infinitive. In English you usually say 'a question for...' or 'a question about...'; choose 'pour' when you mean the question is intended for someone or to obtain something.
target_language_example: J'ai une question pour toi à propos du projet.
native_language_example: I have a question for you about the project.

meaning: literally 'question that' — not a standard fixed phrase in French; could appear when introducing a clause about a question (e.g. «la question que...» = 'the question that...').
additional_notes: Alone, 'question que' is incomplete and uncommon. More natural forms are 'la question que...' or 'la question de savoir si...' depending on meaning. Use 'la question que' to introduce a relative clause that describes the question (e.g. la question que tu poses). To say 'the question of whether...' use 'la question de savoir si...'.
target_language_example: La question que tu poses est importante.
native_language_example: The question that you are asking is important.

meaning: a question directed to (someone) — 'a question for' or 'a question to'.
additional_notes: Used when specifying the person who is being asked: 'une question à + personne'. Often appears in phrases like 'poser une question à quelqu'un' (to ask someone a question) or 'une question à vous' (a question for you). The preposition à links the question to its addressee. Word order: 'une question à Marie' = 'a question for Marie'.
target_language_example: J'ai une question à te poser.
native_language_example: I have a question to ask you.

meaning: 'the question was' (past description: introducing what a question asked or what the issue turned out to be)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the simple combination of 'question' (noun) and 'était' (imperfect of 'être'). You'll see it in sentences like 'La question était de savoir...' or 'La question était : comment...'. It introduces what the question/issue consisted of in the past. Use 'la question est' for present, and 'la question sera' for future.
target_language_example: La question était de trouver une solution rapide.
native_language_example: The question was to find a quick solution.

meaning: 'questions to' or 'questions for' (followed by a person or body)
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a construction where 'questions' (plural) is followed by 'au' (contraction of à + le) and then a noun: e.g. 'questions au professeur' = questions for/to the teacher. Use 'aux' for plural recipients (à + les) and 'à la/à l'' for feminine or vowel-starting nouns: 'questions à la directrice', 'questions à l'équipe'.
target_language_example: J'ai des questions au professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I have questions for the teacher after class.

meaning: questions in the style of / questions about (used before a noun or phrase to indicate the type or style of questions)
additional_notes: This phrase is usually followed by a noun or noun phrase that describes the kind of questions (e.g. "questions à la française" = questions in the French style, or "questions à la volée" = off-the-cuff questions). It literally means "questions in the ...". Context determines whether it refers to style, topic, or manner. Not a complete fixed phrase on its own—needs a following word.
target_language_example: Nous avons eu des questions à la fin de la présentation.
native_language_example: We had questions at the end of the presentation.

meaning: questions for you / questions to ask you
additional_notes: Used when saying you have questions directed at the listener (formal/plural 'vous'). Commonly appears in phrases like 'J'ai des questions à vous poser' (I have questions to ask you). Polite/formal; if speaking informally to one person, use 'des questions à te poser'.
target_language_example: J'ai quelques questions à vous poser avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have a few questions to ask you before leaving.

meaning: who have
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. It is the relative pronoun qui followed by ai ("have," 1st person singular). You often see it in sentences like c'est moi qui ai..., where qui refers to moi, so the verb stays in the 1st person: c'est moi qui ai oublié = "I'm the one who forgot." English usually translates the whole structure more naturally, not word for word.
target_language_example: C'est moi qui ai oublié les clés.
native_language_example: I'm the one who forgot the keys.

meaning: 'who owns this' or 'to whom does this belong?'
additional_notes: Used to ask who is the owner of an object. The full question is usually formed as "À qui appartient ce/ce/ces + noun ?" or with inversion: "À qui appartient ce vélo ?" In spoken French, you may also hear "C'est à qui, ce... ?" or simpler "À qui est... ?"
target_language_example: À qui appartient ce sac ?
native_language_example: Who owns this bag?

meaning: 'who/which would arrive' or 'that would happen/occur' (conditional)
additional_notes: Form: relative pronoun + conditional of arriver. Used to introduce a hypothetical or conditional clause describing a person, thing, or event that would arrive or happen. Context often determines whether it refers to arrival (arriver) literally or to an event occurring. Can appear in sentences like: « Si ... , qui arriverait ? » or « Une situation qui arriverait rarement. »
target_language_example: C'est une situation qui arriverait seulement en cas d'urgence.
native_language_example: It's a situation that would happen only in case of emergency.

meaning: Contraction used in casual speech/writing before a vowel or 'h' to start a clause like 'qui est/qui a' (e.g. 'qui c'est...' = 'who is...').
additional_notes: This form is an informal, clipped spoken/written contraction where 'c'' stands for 'c'' (short for 'ce' or 'c'' as in 'c'est') following 'qui'. You will see it in casual conversation or transcriptions: e.g. 'qui c'est?' (colloquial for 'qui est-ce? / who is it?') or 'qui c'a dit ça?' (very casual contraction of 'qui a dit ça?'). Not standard in formal writing. Use full forms ('qui est', 'qui a', 'qui est-ce') in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Qui c'est qui vient ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who is coming tonight?

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a mistake, typo, or fragment of a larger expression (for example 'qui est-ce' or 'qu'est-ce que').
additional_notes: Alone, 'qui ce' is ungrammatical and not used in standard French. If encountered, check for missing words or incorrect word order. Do not use 'qui ce' as an independent expression; it usually signals an editing error.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas pourquoi il a écrit « qui ce » tout seul dans le texte.
native_language_example: I don't know why he wrote "qui ce" by itself in the text.

meaning: 'who that' or 'who/which (that)'.
additional_notes: Rare and formal in modern spoken French. Combines qui (who/which) with cela (that) — often appears in literary or legal contexts to point back to a person or thing mentioned: e.g. « la personne qui cela regarde » = 'the person to whom that relates'. In everyday French, speakers prefer constructions like « qui » alone, « auquel/à qui », or « cela qui » depending on structure.
target_language_example: La décision concerne la personne qui cela regarde.
native_language_example: The decision concerns the person whom that relates to.

meaning: that/which matters to (someone); that counts for
additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or valued by a person or group. Follows a noun or clause (ce qui compte pour moi = what matters to me). Common in expressions about priorities, feelings or criteria.
target_language_example: Ce qui compte pour elle, c'est la confiance.
native_language_example: What matters to her is trust.

meaning: 'which concerns' or 'that relates to'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or subject being referred to. Common in written and formal contexts (reports, articles, emails). Can be followed by a noun or clause: e.g. "le dossier qui concerne la sécurité" or "les questions qui concernent le budget". Often interchangeable with "concernant" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Voici le document qui concerne votre demande.
native_language_example: Here is the document that concerns/relates to your request.

meaning: 'which of' or 'who of' (used to ask/select from a group)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to ask which person or thing from a set. Often appears in questions like "Qui de vous... ?" (Which of you...?) or "Qui de ces livres est le tien ?" Sometimes followed by a relative clause. Note: not a fixed idiom—it's simply the interrogative pronoun 'qui' combined with the preposition 'de'.
target_language_example: Qui de vous veut venir avec moi ?
native_language_example: Which of you wants to come with me?

meaning: "who must" with 'dois' being the 1st or 2nd person singular present of devoir; used when the understood subject of 'dois' is je (I) or tu (you). In many contexts this sequence is incomplete and requires surrounding words to clarify who 'qui' refers to.
additional_notes: 'Qui' is a relative pronoun meaning 'who' or 'that'. 'Dois' is the present-tense form of devoir for je (I) and tu (you). The sequence 'qui dois' occurs when the relative pronoun refers to a person about whom the speaker is expressing obligation in the 1st or 2nd person perspective (often in colloquial or elliptical constructions). It is less common than 'qui doit' (3rd person) because relative clauses normally agree with a 3rd-person antecedent; use 'qui dois' only when context makes the 1st/2nd-person subject clear. For other subjects use: il/elle/on doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils/elles doivent.
target_language_example: C'est toi qui dois décider maintenant.
native_language_example: It's you who must decide now.

meaning: 'who she' — a colloquial/tabletop phrase used to single out or clarify a female person previously mentioned; functions as a brief question or confirmation (e.g. 'Who, her?').
additional_notes: Literally 'who she'. In standard written French you'd usually use 'qui' alone or a different structure (e.g. 'celle qui', 'la personne qui'). 'qui elle' appears mainly in spoken or informal contexts, often with intonation or punctuation: 'Qui elle ?' or embedded in a sentence for emphasis ('Tu parles de qui elle ?').
target_language_example: Tu parles de qui elle ? — Je parle de Marie.
native_language_example: Who are you talking about, her? — I'm talking about Marie.

meaning: who are
additional_notes: Usually appears in a full question such as « qui es-tu ? » meaning « who are you? ». Here « es » is the « tu » form of « être » (to be).
target_language_example: Qui es-tu ?
native_language_example: Who are you?

meaning: 'who are you' (informal singular; asking someone's identity or who they are)
additional_notes: Used to ask a person's identity or to prompt self-reflection (e.g., 'Who are you when no one is watching?'). Word order 'qui es-tu' is informal/standard spoken French; in very formal contexts you might hear 'qui êtes-vous' (formal/plural). Contractions or intonation can change emphasis (e.g., 'Toi, qui es-tu ?' stresses 'you').
target_language_example: Qui es-tu vraiment, derrière ce masque ?
native_language_example: Who are you really, behind that mask?

meaning: 'who tries' or 'who is trying'.
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun 'qui' (who) with the verb 'essayer' in the present tense (essaie) for il/elle/on. Used to describe a person (or thing) performing an attempt or effort. Can also appear in questions or embedded clauses: 'la personne qui essaie' = 'the person who is trying'.
target_language_example: C'est l'élève qui essaie le plus en classe.
native_language_example: He/She is the student who tries the most in class.

meaning: 'which/is good' or 'who is good' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Literally 'who/which is good'. 'Qui' can mean 'who' (people) or 'which/that' (things). Use depending on whether it refers to a person or a thing: e.g. 'un ami qui est bon' (a friend who is good/kind/skillful) or 'un gâteau qui est bon' (a cake that is good/tasty). Adjective 'bon' must agree in gender/number when expanded in a sentence (bonne, bons, bonnes). Commonly used in simple descriptions; meaning of 'bon' varies by context (good, kind, tasty, suitable).
target_language_example: C'est un professeur qui est bon avec les enfants.
native_language_example: He is a teacher who is good with children.

meaning: 'which is' or 'that is' (followed by origin, date, quantity, price, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a detail about something (origin, ownership, date, measurement, price, etc.). Often appears in phrases like "qui est de + [origine/date/montant]". It literally combines the relative pronoun "qui" (who/which) with the verb "être" (to be). Context determines the exact translation (which/that/which is).
target_language_example: La voiture qui est de mon frère est rouge.
native_language_example: The car that is my brother's is red.

meaning: 'what is right' or 'what is fair/just'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the morally right or fair action/thing in context. Commonly appears in phrases like «faire ce qui est juste» (do what is right) or «c'est ce qui est juste» (that's what is right). Not about correctness (juste can mean 'correct' or 'fair') — here it usually means morally right or appropriate.
target_language_example: Il hésite, mais il finira par faire ce qui est juste.
native_language_example: He hesitates, but he'll end up doing what is right.

meaning: that/which belongs to me (mine).
additional_notes: A relative clause meaning 'that/which is mine' or 'that belongs to me'. Used to describe a person or object owned by or associated with the speaker. Formal or neutral; you can also say 'qui est à moi' for emphasis, but more common short forms are 'le mien / la mienne / les miens / les miennes' or simply 'à moi' in spoken French.
target_language_example: Voici le stylo qui est à moi.
native_language_example: Here is the pen that belongs to me.

meaning: 'who (you) do/are doing' — nonstandard or ungrammatical combination in French; mixes subject/object 'qui' with 2nd-person singular verb 'fais'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not correct in standard French by itself. Possible intended forms: 'qui fait' (who does/is doing — 3rd person), 'qui fais-tu ?' (rare/informal inversion asking 'who do you do' — generally ungrammatical or context-dependent), or part of a clause like 'Qui fais-tu entrer ?' (Who are you letting in?). If you encounter 'qui fais' check the full sentence and the intended subject. Avoid using 'qui fais' alone.
target_language_example: Dis-moi, qui fais entrer ce soir ?
native_language_example: Tell me, who are you letting in tonight?

meaning: 'who/which makes/causes (something to be)'; often part of a phrase meaning 'which makes someone/something [do/be] ...'.
additional_notes: This construction combines the relative pronoun 'qui' (who/which) with the verb 'faire' (to make/do) followed by 'de' and another noun or infinitive. It often expresses causation or results (e.g., 'qui fait de lui un expert' = 'which makes him an expert') or forms causative structures (e.g., 'qui fait de parler...' is less common than 'qui le/la fait ...'). Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar: 'qui' refers back to a person or thing and the verb agrees with that antecedent. Common patterns: 'qui fait de + noun' (which makes ... into ...) and 'faire de quelqu'un/quelque chose + noun'.
target_language_example: C'est une expérience qui fait de toi un meilleur médecin.
native_language_example: It's an experience that makes you a better doctor.

meaning: "who he" or "who it" (rare/ungrammatical in isolation)
additional_notes: The sequence 'qui il' is not a standard fixed phrase in French. Alone it usually appears as part of a larger clause (e.g. 'qui, il…' as spoken hesitation) or in informal/clipped speech. In correct written French, 'qui' (who/that) is followed by a verb or subject pronoun depending on the structure: use 'qui est' (who is), 'qui il est' only appears in reported spoken fragments ("qui il est, je ne sais pas" is nonstandard). For 'who he is' the correct full forms are 'qui il est' in colloquial speech but more formally 'qui il est' is acceptable in subordinate clauses; better: 'qui il est' as part of 'je sais qui il est' (I know who he is).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui il est.
native_language_example: I don't know who he is.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase; appears to be an ungrammatical fragment or typo combining 'qui' (who/that) + 'il' (he) + an initial apostrophe of a clitic 's'' (short for 'se' or part of 's'il'). It does not occur as a standard expression and cannot stand alone.
additional_notes: Likely causes: a typing error (e.g., intended 'qui s'' as in 'qui s'appelle'), mistaken word order (should be 'qui il est' for 'who he is'), or split contraction (e.g., 's'il' = 'si il' but correctly written 's'il'). If you encounter 'qui il s'' in text, check for missing or misordered words. Correct alternatives include 'qui s'' + verb (qui s'appelle), 'qui il est' (who he is), or 's'il' in conditional clauses.
target_language_example: *Unusable/illustrative* — Ce passage contient la suite de caractères « qui il s' » qui est clairement une faute : « qui il s' » n'est pas grammatical.
native_language_example: *Unusable/illustrative* — This passage contains the character sequence "qui il s'" which is clearly an error: "qui il s'" is not grammatical.

meaning: 'who I' (rarely used as a standalone phrase in French)
additional_notes: This sequence can appear inside larger clauses (e.g. 'qui je suis' = 'who I am' or 'qui je pensais' = 'who I thought [it was]'). By itself, 'qui je' is incomplete and not used alone. Remember French word order: relative pronoun 'qui' often introduces a clause and is followed by a verb, not a subject pronoun. More natural phrases include 'qui je suis' (who I am) or 'que je' (that I) depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Tu sais qui je suis ?
native_language_example: Do you know who I am?

meaning: 'who plays' (used to describe someone playing a musical instrument); introduces the instrument with 'de' (plays [an instrument])
additional_notes: Used to describe someone playing a musical instrument: 'qui joue de + instrument' (e.g. qui joue de la guitare). The verb jouer is followed by 'de' (not 'à') with most instruments in French. For sports or games French uses 'jouer à' (e.g. jouer au tennis). 'Qui joue de' commonly appears in questions or relative clauses: Qui joue de quel instrument? / La personne qui joue de la flûte. Remember to contract definite articles: de + le = du; de + la remains de la; de + les = des.
target_language_example: Qui joue de la guitare dans ce groupe ?
native_language_example: Who plays the guitar in this band?

meaning: 'who (you) have/has it' — part of a question/statement identifying the person who did something to 'it' (object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'qui' (who) + 'l'' (direct object pronoun 'it' or 'him/her') + 'as' (2nd person singular of 'avoir'). It appears in sentences like 'C'est toi qui l'as fait venir ?' meaning 'Are you the one who brought it?' The verb that follows (fait, trouvÃ©, Ã©crit, etc.) often appears after this clause, and past participle agreement may change if the object is feminine (e.g. 'faite', 'Ã©crite') when the object precedes the verb and agrees with a preceding direct object. Used to ask or confirm who performed an action involving 'it'.
target_language_example: C'est toi qui l'as cassée ?
native_language_example: Are you the one who broke it?

meaning: who/that (it/him)
additional_notes: Combination of relative pronoun qui + direct object pronoun le. Used when referring back to a person or thing (qui = who/that) while also including a pronoun le (it/him) that would normally be the object of a verb. Appears in constructions like "la personne qui le sait" (the person who knows it) or after verbs when le refers to a previously mentioned masculine noun or idea. Word order and agreement follow standard French pronoun rules.
target_language_example: La vidéo qui le montre est en ligne.
native_language_example: The video that shows it is online.

meaning: 'who/which that' + 'to them' (relative pronoun + indirect object pronoun).
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun qui (subject: who/which/that) with the indirect object pronoun leur (to them). Used when the relative clause has qui as subject and the verb takes an indirect object referring to 'them'. English often uses 'who/which ... to them' or 'who/which ... for them'. Example structure: [noun] + qui + [verb] + leur + [complement].
target_language_example: Les enfants qui leur parlent sont leurs voisins.
native_language_example: The children who speak to them are their neighbors.

meaning: 'who' (as subject) + 'to him/her'; used to refer to the person who does something to or for someone else.
additional_notes: Qui introduces the person performing an action (relative or interrogative). Lui is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him' or 'to her'. In relative clauses (C'est moi qui lui ai appris ça) qui marks the subject; in questions (Qui lui a dit ça?) it asks 'who told him/her'. Word order and verb agreement follow standard French rules (verb agrees with the relative subject).
target_language_example: C'est Paul qui lui a donné le livre.
native_language_example: It's Paul who gave him/her the book.

meaning: not a standalone phrase; looks like part of a clause meaning 'that I ... to him/her' (relative 'who/that' + indirect object + verb 'ai').
additional_notes: This sequence is not an independent expression. It combines: 'qui' (who/that), 'lui' (to him/to her as an indirect object or 'him/her' as indirect object pronoun), and 'ai' (first-person singular present of 'avoir' — 'I have'). In French it appears inside a sentence like 'qui lui ai donné' ('that I gave to him/her') or 'qui lui ai parlé' ('that I spoke to him/her'). You will rarely see 'qui lui ai' alone; it must be followed by a past participle or other verb phrase.
target_language_example: C'est le livre qui lui ai donné hier.
native_language_example: That's the book that I gave to him/her yesterday.

meaning: 'that/which is to him/her' or 'that belongs to him/her' (literal: 'which to him/her is')
additional_notes: This is a short fragment rather than a complete phrase; it commonly appears inside larger clauses: e.g. «la lettre qui lui est adressée» (the letter that is addressed to him/her) or «la maison qui lui est propre» (the house that belongs to him/her). Qui = 'which/that' (relative pronoun referring to a thing or person previously mentioned). Lui = indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him' or 'to her' depending on context. Est = third-person singular of être ('is'). Word order is fixed: relative pronoun + indirect object pronoun + verb. Gender/number agreement may affect surrounding words, but not qui/lui/est themselves.
target_language_example: Voici le cadeau qui lui est destiné.
native_language_example: Here is the gift that is intended for him/her.

meaning: 'who (you) have me' — part of a spoken/clipped clause meaning 'who made me' or 'who ... me' when followed by a past participle; literally 'who you have me'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a fragment: 'qui' (who) + 'm'' (me, object pronoun) + 'as' (you have, 2nd person singular of avoir). It appears in spoken or written contexts as part of sentences like 'qui m'as dit...' (who told me...), 'qui m'as donné...' (who gave me...). The contracted 'm'' is used before a vowel sound. In formal writing you may see the same structure without contraction if preceding word ends with a consonant (e.g., 'qui me as' is incorrect — always 'm'as' before a vowel sound).
target_language_example: Qui m'as dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: Who told me the truth?

meaning: 'that concerns me' / 'as far as I'm concerned' / 'which is about me'
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that affects or is relevant to the speaker. Can introduce a clause or phrase specifying what matters to the speaker. Equivalent to 'as for me' or 'as far as I'm concerned' in English when used to give an opinion or indicate relevance.
target_language_example: Pour ce qui me concerne, je préfère rester ici.
native_language_example: As far as I'm concerned, I prefer to stay here.

meaning: that has (to) me / that happened to me (used in relative clauses with subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to describe something or someone that affects the speaker. Typically appears with verbs like arriver (arrived/happened) and requires the subjunctive (soit). Common in phrases like "la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée" = "the best thing that has happened to me." Can be shortened in casual speech (e.g., "qui m'est arrivée" uses indicative and is more direct).
target_language_example: Il est la meilleure décision qui me soit arrivée.
native_language_example: He is the best decision that has happened to me.

meaning: that happened/occurred to me (subjunctive relative clause).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to introduce a relative clause in the subjunctive (often after expressions like 'la pire chose' or 'la meilleure expérience') to describe something that happened to the speaker. The subjunctive 'soit' expresses subjectivity, doubt or evaluation about the event. Word order: 'la pire chose qui me soit arrivée' = 'the worst thing that happened to me.'
target_language_example: C'est la meilleure décision qui me soit arrivée.
native_language_example: It's the best decision that has happened to me.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom on its own; it's the sequence of the relative pronoun 'qui' (who/which/that) followed by the subject pronoun 'on' (one/we/they). It can appear in speech or nonstandard constructions but is uncommon in standard written French because contractions or different relative pronouns are normally used (e.g., 'qu'on', 'que l'on', or 'qui + verb' when 'qui' is the subject).
additional_notes: 'Qui on' by itself is not a standalone phrase. In standard French, when 'on' is the subject of a relative clause, the contracted form 'qu'on' (from 'que on') is used after a direct-object relative 'que'. When 'qui' is correct as relative subject, it typically precedes a verb (e.g., 'qui on voit' is nonstandard; prefer 'qu'on voit' or 'que l'on voit'). You may encounter 'qui on' in casual speech or in mistaken/careless writing, or in constructions where 'qui' refers to something and 'on' begins the following clause (e.g., in speech ellipsis).
target_language_example: C'est quelqu'un qui on dit très généreux.
native_language_example: He's someone whom people say is very generous.

meaning: 'who speaks' / 'that speaks' (relative clause) or 'who is speaking' (question)
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) as a relative clause meaning 'who/that speaks' (e.g. un guide qui parle le français = a guide who speaks French). 2) in questions about the speaker: 'À qui parle-t-elle ?' = 'To whom is she speaking?'. Also appears in idiomatic expressions like 'Voilà qui parle à mon âme' meaning 'That speaks to my soul' (i.e. that resonates with me). The verb that follows must agree with the subject (qui + verb).
target_language_example: Je cherche quelqu'un qui parle anglais.
native_language_example: I'm looking for someone who speaks English.

meaning: 'who thinks' or 'that thinks' (relative clause)
additional_notes: Used as a relative phrase introduced by qui to describe a person or thing that thinks or believes something. It often appears in sentences like «la personne qui pense…» or «quelqu'un qui pense que…». Remember word order: qui (subject) + verb (pense). Can refer to mental activity (penser) or to an opinion (penser que…).
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu'un qui pense que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: There is someone who thinks it's a good idea.

meaning: 'and what's more' / 'moreover' (used to add information)
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the expression "qui plus est" meaning "moreover" or "what's more"—a somewhat formal or literary connector. By itself "qui plus" is incomplete; learners will most often encounter the full phrase "qui plus est." It introduces an additional point that strengthens or adds to what was just said.
target_language_example: Il a réussi son examen, qui plus est avec une excellente note.
native_language_example: He passed his exam, and what's more with an excellent grade.

meaning: moreover; what's more; furthermore.
additional_notes: Used to add an extra, often stronger or surprising point. It is slightly formal or neutral — common in written and spoken French. It usually follows a clause and is followed by a comma. Can introduce an additional fact that reinforces the previous statement.
target_language_example: Il a raté le train et, qui plus est, oublié son portefeuille.
native_language_example: He missed the train and, what's more, forgot his wallet.

meaning: 'whoever' or 'whomever' (introduces an indefinite person)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning 'no matter who' or 'whoever'. Typically followed by a subject and verb (e.g. 'qui que tu sois' = 'whoever you are'). In formal written French it often requires the subjunctive verb (sois, soyez, soit). Common in expressions like 'Qui que tu sois' or 'Qui que vous soyez'.
target_language_example: Qui que tu sois, tu es le bienvenu ici.
native_language_example: Whoever you are, you are welcome here.

meaning: anyone, anybody (used after questions or negatives)
additional_notes: Used after questions or negatives to mean 'anyone' without specifying identity. Often appears in questions like «Y a-t-il qui que ce soit…?», or after verbs: «Je ne connais qui que ce soit» (rare). Formal/neutral; word order often places it after the verb or preposition. Equivalent in positive statements is usually not used (use quelqu'un).
target_language_example: Y a-t-il qui que ce soit dans la maison ?
native_language_example: Is there anyone in the house?

meaning: Not a correct or natural French phrase; likely a mistaken concatenation of 'qui que ce soit' ('whoever') and 'est' ('is').
additional_notes: Do not use 'qui que ce soit est' as a single fixed phrase. In French, 'qui que ce soit' already means 'whoever' or 'anyone' and must be followed by a verb or clause appropriate to the sentence (e.g. 'Qui que ce soit vient...'). In contexts meaning 'whoever is ...' you would say 'qui que ce soit + verb' (e.g. 'Qui que ce soit intéressé...') or use 'quiconque est...' in more formal registers. The sequence 'qui que ce soit est' can appear in speech only if 'est' starts a following clause that should instead be linked differently (e.g. better: 'qui que ce soit, il est...' is awkward). Avoid using 'qui que ce soit est' as written; rewrite the sentence so 'est' is the main verb of a clause headed by 'qui que ce soit' or replace with 'quiconque est'.
target_language_example: Cette formulation « qui que ce soit est » n’est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: The phrasing "qui que ce soit est" is not correct in French.

meaning: who/which had
additional_notes: Combination of relative pronoun 'qui' (who/which) + reflexive past perfect (plus-que-parfait) or past perfect (depending on context) of a pronominal verb: 's'' (se) + était (auxiliary être in imperfect). Used to introduce a clause describing someone/something that had previously done or been something. Followed by a past participle: e.g. 'qui s'était réveillé', 'qui s'était arrêté'. English equivalent often uses 'who had' or 'which had'.
target_language_example: La voiture qui s'était arrêtée fumait encore.
native_language_example: The car that had stopped was still smoking.

meaning: 'who knows' — expresses uncertainty or possibility.
additional_notes: Used to suggest that something is unknown or unpredictable; can introduce a question (Qui sait ce qui s'est passé ?) or appear alone/at the end of a sentence to mean 'who knows' or 'maybe' (Tu devrais, qui sait ?). Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Qui sait si elle acceptera l'invitation ?
native_language_example: Who knows if she'll accept the invitation?

meaning: 'what is happening in' or 'what takes place in' (used to ask about events or states inside/within something).
additional_notes: Used in questions or relative clauses to refer to events, situations or processes occurring inside a place, a person's mind, or in a more abstract context (e.g. the world). Commonly appears in: «Qu'est-ce qui se passe dans... ?» (What's happening in...?) or «tout ce qui se passe dans...» (everything that happens in...).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui se passe dans ce quartier la nuit ?
native_language_example: What's happening in this neighborhood at night?

meaning: 'what is happening between' (used to ask or refer to events/relations involving two or more people)
additional_notes: Used to talk about situations, conflicts, or relationships involving people. Often appears in questions (Qu'est-ce qui se passe entre vous ?) or statements referring to private matters (Ce qui se passe entre X et Y). Can be formal or neutral; context determines tone. The literal parts are compositional, but the whole is an idiomatic way to say 'what is happening between (them/you/us)'.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce qui se passe entre toi et ton frère.
native_language_example: I want to know what is happening between you and your brother.

meaning: 'what is happening there' or 'what's going on there'.
additional_notes: A colloquial fragment used to ask about events or situations at a place. Often appears in questions introduced by "Qu'est-ce qui se passe là ?" (What's happening there?). Can be used in spoken French; the pronoun "là" can be omitted or replaced by a specific place (e.g. "qui se passe ici", "qui se passe au bureau").
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui se passe là ?
native_language_example: What's going on there?

meaning: 'who took you' or 'who got you' (literally: who has taken you).
additional_notes: This is a short clause using 'qui' (who) + passé composé of 'prendre' (t'a pris = te a pris → 'has taken you'/'took you'). Often appears inside a larger sentence or question: e.g. 'C'est qui t'a pris ?' or 'Je ne sais pas qui t'a pris.' Depending on context it can mean physically taking someone, hiring/choosing someone ('who took you on'), or figuratively 'who made you...'. Pronunciation: the t' is the object pronoun 'te' contracted before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui t'a pris pour ce poste.
native_language_example: I don't know who took you for that position.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; appears to be a mistaken or broken sequence (likely from 'qui t'ai...' as part of a larger verb phrase such as 'que je t'ai...' or 'qui t'a...').
additional_notes:
You will not find 'qui t'ai' as an independent expression in correct French. It looks like a fragment resulting from a contraction or a typo. Possibilities:
- 'qui t'a' = 'who/that has you' or 'who/that gave you' (from 'qui t'a donné...').
- 'que je t'ai' = 'that I have (to) you' or 'that I gave you' (from 'que je t'ai dit', 'que je t'ai donné').
If you see 'qui t'ai' in writing, check the surrounding words: it is almost certainly missing a letter (e.g., 'qui t'a') or split across words (e.g., 'que je t'ai').
target_language_example: Je pense que tu voulais écrire 'que je t'ai dit' plutôt que 'qui t'ai'.
native_language_example: I think you meant to write 'que je t'ai dit' rather than 'qui t'ai'.

meaning: who/that brings you (or leads you) — used to describe the person or thing that causes you to come or to be somewhere
additional_notes: Qui = who/that; t' = te (you, object). Can refer to a person or a reason/situation that 'brings' you somewhere (physically or figuratively). Context determines whether it's literal (someone brings you) or figurative (something leads you to do or feel something). Contraction t' appears before a vowel sound. Common in relative clauses: « la personne qui t'amène » or « ce qui t'amène ici ? »
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui t'amène ici aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: What brings you here today?

meaning: who you are (informal, contracted spoken form of "qui tu es").
additional_notes: This is a colloquial contraction used in spoken French: "qui t'es" = "qui tu es". It appears when asking someone's identity or emphasizing who someone is (e.g., "Qui t'es, toi?" = "Who are you?" or "Who do you think you are?"). In written French, use the full form "qui tu es" or the more standard "qui es-tu?" for questions. Tone can be neutral or confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: Eh bien, qui t'es, toi, pour me dire ça ?
native_language_example: So, who are you to tell me that?

meaning: 'that takes you' or 'who takes you' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literal components: qui (who/that) + te (you, object) + prend (takes). Used when describing someone or something that 'takes' or 'seizes' you, or figuratively when an emotion/feeling 'takes' you (e.g., 'une faiblesse qui te prend'). In conversation it often appears inside a larger clause (e.g., 'c'est qui te prend ?', 'qui te prend comme ça ?') and meaning depends on surrounding words. Not a fixed idiom by itself.
target_language_example: Il y a une panique qui te prend parfois la nuit.
native_language_example: There is a panic that takes you sometimes at night.

meaning: 'who (you) work' — part of a question or relative clause using the formal/plural 'vous' form of 'travailler'.
additional_notes: Comprised of the relative pronoun 'qui' (who) plus the verb 'travaillez' (2nd-person plural/formal of travailler). Used when referring to people you (formal) or you all work with: e.g. 'Les personnes qui travaillez ici...' is ungrammatical in French — correct order is 'Vous qui travaillez...' or in relative clauses use 'qui travaillent' for third-person plural. Common in questions: 'Qui travaillez-vous ?' = 'Who do you work (for/with)?' Note word order: in questions with 'vous' the verb follows the pronoun (inversion) 'Qui travaillez-vous ?' or more naturally 'Vous travaillez avec qui ?'.
target_language_example: Qui travaillez-vous dans cette entreprise ?
native_language_example: Who do you work (for) in this company?

meaning: 'who you' — not a standard standalone French phrase; a sequence of words that can appear inside larger constructions
additional_notes: Alone, 'qui tu' is not a correct standalone phrase in standard French. 'Qui' means 'who' and 'tu' means 'you', but normal question forms require inversion or est-ce que: 'Qui es-tu ?' or 'Qui est-ce que tu es ?' In relative or emphatic contexts you might see 'toi qui...' (you who...) or colloquial/poetic orders where 'qui tu' appears inside a longer sentence (often nonstandard). Use caution: 'qui tu' by itself is ungrammatical in standard written French.
target_language_example: Toi qui tu parles si fort, baisse la voix.
native_language_example: You who speak so loudly, lower your voice.

meaning: 'who (do) you ... me' — part of expressions like 'pour qui tu me prends ?' or 'à qui tu me fais penser ?' used to ask who the other person thinks you are or who you make them think of.
additional_notes: This sequence isn't a fixed phrase by itself but appears in idiomatic questions. Common constructions: 'Pour qui tu me prends ?' = 'Who do you take me for?' (challenging/offended tone). 'À qui tu me fais penser ?' / 'Tu sais à qui tu me fais penser ?' = 'Who do I remind you of?' or 'Do you know who I make you think of?'. Informal spoken word order often omits inversion ('tu sais...?' instead of 'sais-tu...?').
target_language_example: Pour qui tu me prends, pour un imbécile ?
native_language_example: Who do you think I am, an idiot?

meaning: Intended to mean "who goes" but nonstandard/incorrect in French; likely a misspelling or confusion between "qui va" (who goes) and "tu vas" (you go).
additional_notes: "qui vas" is not correct in standard French. The correct interrogative is "qui va ?" for "who is going?" "qui vas" could result from mistakenly combining "qui" with the 2nd-person singular conjugation "vas" (which belongs to "tu"). Avoid using "qui vas" in written or spoken French; native speakers will correct it to "qui va" or reinterpret the sentence depending on context.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, qui vas ici aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who goes here today?

meaning: "which means" or "that means" (used to explain or define something).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a definition, clarification, or paraphrase of a word, phrase, or situation. It literally translates as "which wants to say," but functions the same as English "which means" or "that is to say." Can introduce a synonym, explanation, or consequence.
target_language_example: Il a dit « je suis crevé », qui veut dire qu'il est très fatigué.
native_language_example: He said "I'm exhausted," which means he is very tired.

meaning: intended as 'who wants' but nonstandard/incorrect in standard French
additional_notes: This form is generally incorrect for standard French. Correct forms: «qui veut» (3rd person singular: 'who wants') or, when addressing someone directly, «qui veux-tu ?» / «qui est-ce que tu veux ?» (2nd person singular: 'who do you want?'). «qui veux» (with -s) can appear in informal speech only if the subject 'tu' is omitted or in mistakes; avoid in formal writing and speech.
target_language_example: Qui veux-tu inviter ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who do you want to invite tonight?

meaning: 'who/that has just (done something)' — part of the recent past construction with a reflexive verb
additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb in the recent past (venir de + infinitive) when the subject is described by a relative clause. Example structure: [noun] qui vient de se + [infinitive]. It means the action happened a very short time ago. Remember to keep the infinitive form after 'venir de'. Agreement of past participle is not used here because the construction uses the infinitive (e.g., 'qui vient de se laver' = 'who has just washed (themselves)').
target_language_example: La fille qui vient de se réveiller est encore fatiguée.
native_language_example: The girl who has just woken up is still tired.

meaning: 'alertness' or 'vigilance' (usually used in the expression être sur le qui-vive / être sur ses qui-vives meaning 'to be on the alert').
additional_notes: Rarely used alone in modern spoken French; most commonly appears in the fixed expression être sur le qui-vive or être sur ses qui-vives. Formal or literary register; found in writing, news, or formal speech. Plural form 'les qui-vives' or 'ses qui-vives' is common in usage.
target_language_example: Il est toujours sur le qui-vive depuis la tentative d'effraction.
native_language_example: He has been constantly on the alert since the attempted break-in.

meaning: 'who's there' or 'look who's here' (used to point out someone's arrival or presence).
additional_notes: Informal/exclamatory phrase used when you notice someone arriving or present; often preceded by words like 'tiens', 'mais', 'regarde/ regardez'. Equivalent to 'look who it is' or 'well, look who's here.' Not a literal composition of the words — it's an idiomatic expression used to draw attention to a person.
target_language_example: Tiens, qui voilà — Paul et Sophie !
native_language_example: Well, look who's here — Paul and Sophie!

meaning: who brings you / that brings you (to a place or situation).
additional_notes: Literally 'who brings you.' Used to describe a person or thing that leads, brings, or causes you to arrive somewhere or be in a certain situation. Can refer to physically bringing someone (e.g., to an event) or figuratively (e.g., what leads you to a conclusion). Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: La voiture qui vous amène est déjà arrivée.
native_language_example: The car that brings you has already arrived.

meaning: 'whatever you want' / 'whatever pleases you'
additional_notes: Informal idiom used after a verb like faire, prendre, boire, dire to mean 'do/take/say/drink whatever you like' or 'anything you want'. Literally 'that sings to you' — i.e. that appeals to you. Often used in familiar contexts to give freedom of choice.
target_language_example: Choisissez le dessert qui vous chante.
native_language_example: Choose whatever dessert you want.

meaning: 'that/which is to you' or 'that/which is for you' (often part of a larger phrase)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in longer constructions like "qui vous est destiné(e)" (which is intended for you) or "qui vous est utile" (which is useful to you). "Qui" is a relative pronoun meaning "that/which/who." "Vous" is the polite or plural "you." "Est" is the third-person singular of "être" (to be). Alone, "qui vous est" is incomplete and needs a past participle, adjective, or noun phrase to finish the idea.
target_language_example: Voici le document qui vous est destiné.
native_language_example: Here is the document that is intended for you.

meaning: 'that makes you' / 'that causes you to' (followed by an action, feeling, or state)
additional_notes: A relative clause beginning with qui (that/who) + indirect object vous. It introduces something or someone that causes, gives, or produces an effect on 'you'. Often followed by a noun (e.g. 'qui vous fait plaisir') or a verb phrase introduced by a noun phrase (e.g. 'une chose qui vous fait rire'). Not a complete sentence by itself; fits into larger sentences.
target_language_example: C'est un film qui vous fait réfléchir.
native_language_example: It's a film that makes you think.

meaning: 'who are you' (formal or plural)
additional_notes: Formal or polite form of asking someone's identity. Used with vous (formal singular or plural). Often used in introductions or when asking who someone is; can be preceded by 'pardon' for politeness. In informal situations with friends or family use 'qui es-tu'.
target_language_example: Pardon, qui êtes-vous et que faites-vous ici ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who are you and what are you doing here?

meaning: 'whoever has' or 'anyone who has' (introduces an indefinite subject with the auxiliary verb a).
additional_notes: Quiconque = 'whoever' / 'anyone who'. In these examples it's followed by the auxiliary verb a (third-person singular of avoir) because the main verb is in compound tenses (e.g., a pensé, a dit, a entendu). It can introduce a statement (Quiconque a pensé...) or a question (Quiconque a-t-il...?) — note that in polite/written French questions are often formed with inversion (a-t-il). In everyday spoken French you might instead hear 'Quelqu'un a...' or 'Quelqu'un a-t-il...?' Quiconque is slightly formal/neutral; not slang.
target_language_example: Quiconque a vu le chien doit appeler son propriétaire.
native_language_example: Anyone who has seen the dog must call its owner.

meaning: 'whoever is' or 'anyone who is'.
additional_notes: Literary/formal construction: 'quiconque' means 'whoever' or 'anyone who' and is often followed by a verb (e.g. 'quiconque est…'). Used in formal writing, laws, or emphatic statements. In spoken French, people more often use 'n'importe qui' or 'qui que ce soit'.
target_language_example: Quiconque est responsable devra en répondre.
native_language_example: Anyone who is responsible will have to answer for it.

meaning: fifteen days; commonly used to mean two weeks.
additional_notes: Can mean a period of 15 days or, more commonly in everyday French, 'in two weeks' or 'every two weeks' depending on context. When used alone it can indicate the length of time (e.g., 'Quinze jours.' = 'Two weeks.'). Usage examples: 'dans quinze jours' = 'in two weeks'; 'tous les quinze jours' = 'every two weeks/fortnight'.
target_language_example: On part en vacances dans quinze jours.
native_language_example: We're leaving on vacation in two weeks.

target_language_multi_word_term: ne ... pas des yeux / ne le/la quitte pas des yeux
meaning: 'not take one's eyes off (someone/something)'; to watch closely
additional_notes: Used to say someone watches or follows someone/something closely without looking away. Common structure: (ne) + (le/la/les) + quitte + pas + des yeux. In spoken French the initial 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. «Le quitte pas des yeux»). 'Des yeux' is idiomatic here and should not be translated word-for-word as 'of eyes' in English.
target_language_example: Ne le quitte pas des yeux pendant qu'il traverse la rue.
native_language_example: Don't take your eyes off him while he crosses the street.

meaning: 'to leave your' or 'to quit your' (followed by a noun, e.g. house, job, account)
additional_notes: quitter is a transitive verb meaning to leave, to quit or to abandon. When followed by a possessive like votre (your), it introduces the thing being left: quitter votre maison (leave your house), quitter votre travail (quit your job), quitter votre compte (log out/close your account). Use the infinitive or a conjugated form of quitter appropriately (e.g. Je vais quitter votre... is unusual — more natural: Je vais quitter ma/mon...). Note that 'votre' is the formal/plural 'your'. For informal singular use 'ton'/'ta'.
target_language_example: Elle a décidé de quitter votre entreprise.
native_language_example: She decided to leave your company.

meaning: 'what' or 'what about' used to ask or introduce a topic/possibility
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or expressions like "Quoi de neuf ?" (What's new?) or "Quoi de prévu ?" (What is planned?). It can introduce a subject, ask for information, or suggest an option. Often followed by a noun, adjective, or past participle. Informal to neutral register depending on the phrase.
target_language_example: Quoi de neuf chez toi ?
native_language_example: What's new with you?

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment where 'quoi' (what) is followed by 'a' (has). It appears in informal speech or in clauses but is generally ungrammatical as a standalone question form. Often replaced by 'Qu'est-ce qui a...' or 'Qu'est-ce que...' in correct written French.
additional_notes: 'Quoi a' can occur inside speech fragments or mistaken/elliptical constructions (e.g., '...quoi a dit?') but is not a recommended phrase. Use proper interrogative structures: 'Qu'est-ce qui a...?' for subject questions and 'Qu'est-ce que...?' for object questions. In casual speech, 'quoi' may appear alone as 'Quoi?' to mean 'What?' and then be followed by a verb in continuation, which can produce sequences like 'quoi a' in transcriptions of spoken dialogue.
target_language_example: — Quoi a-t-il dit ? — Rien.
native_language_example: — What did he say? — Nothing.

meaning: 'what do you (have/need/be) ...?' — part of questions asking 'what' with inversion
additional_notes: Usually appears after a preposition like 'de' (e.g. 'De quoi as-tu besoin ?') or in questions about feelings or possessions ('De quoi as-tu peur ?'). It's the inversion (formal/literary/neutral) word order: question word 'quoi' + subject 'tu' (with verb before or after depending on full phrase). In spoken French, you will more often hear 'Tu as besoin de quoi ?' or 'Qu'est-ce que tu as besoin ?' is less common; instead use 'De quoi as-tu besoin ?' or 'Tu as besoin de quoi ?' for informal speech.
target_language_example: De quoi as-tu besoin pour étudier ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you need to study tonight?

meaning: 'what' + 'to the/at the' — part of colloquial expressions; often used in spoken French as a filler or in questions like 'quoi, au...?'
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed idiom by itself. It appears when quoi ('what') is followed by the contraction au (à + le) in a sentence (e.g. 'Quoi au menu ?' – 'What on the menu?'). In casual speech, 'quoi' is also used as a filler at the end of sentences ('C'est compliqué, quoi'), but that usage does not combine with 'au'. Check the full sentence to understand the meaning.
target_language_example: Quoi au programme ce soir ?
native_language_example: What's on the agenda tonight?

meaning: 'what with' or 'what...with' — used to ask or clarify what to have/put/bring with something (colloquial/informal fragment).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination of 'quoi' (what) + 'avec' (with). It appears in spoken French when someone asks what to accompany or combine with something: e.g. 'Quoi avec ça ?' = 'What with that?' or 'What should go with that?'. Often used alone as a short question. Word order can vary: 'Avec quoi ?' is more standard and neutral; 'Quoi avec ?' is more casual and occurs in conversation.
target_language_example: Tu prends du fromage — quoi avec ?
native_language_example: You're getting cheese — what with it?

meaning: 'what's the point' / 'what good is it' (expresses futility or uselessness)
additional_notes: Used to express that something is pointless or useless. Often appears in rhetorical questions or short exclamations: «À quoi bon…?» is the full form meaning "to what good…?" Colloquial/poetic; common in spoken and written French. Can be followed by an infinitive or a clause (À quoi bon essayer ? / Quoi bon insister ?).
target_language_example: À quoi bon continuer si personne n'écoute ?
native_language_example: What's the point of continuing if no one is listening?

meaning: 'what' used informally in spoken French as the start of a question or exclamation where 'c'' is a contraction (often of 'c'est' or 'ça').
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial fragment heard in everyday speech. 'Quoi c'' is typically followed by a verb or phrase (e.g. 'Quoi c'est pas vrai ?' contracted in rapid speech to 'Quoi c' pas vrai ?') and is incomplete alone; it reproduces spoken contractions and should be avoided in formal writing. Tone can be surprised, disbelieving, or interrogative depending on context.
target_language_example: Quoi c' pas vrai ?
native_language_example: What, that's not true?

meaning: colloquial/informal way to say 'what is it' or 'what's that' (often ungrammatical or regional).
additional_notes: This sequence is not standard French; the normal question is 'qu'est-ce que c'est ?' or 'c'est quoi ?'. 'Quoi c'est' may appear in fast speech, regional varieties, or in informal writing where word order is mixed. Avoid in formal contexts. Use to ask for identification or clarification ('What is that?').
target_language_example: Quoi c'est que ce bruit ?
native_language_example: What is that noise?

meaning: what in / what (is) in — used to ask or refer to the content or cause inside something (informal, often part of a larger phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase on its own; 'quoi' (what) followed by 'dans' (in) appears when asking about what is inside or what is happening within something: e.g. 'Quoi dans la boîte?' or in spoken French it may be part of a clause like 'Tu mets quoi dans le sac ?' (What are you putting in the bag?). Word order and context matter — more natural forms are 'Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans...' or 'Qu'est-ce qu'on met dans...'.
target_language_example: Tu mets quoi dans ton sandwich ?
native_language_example: What are you putting in your sandwich?

meaning: 'what's new?' — a casual greeting asking what's up or what's new.
additional_notes: Informal, used to ask how someone is or to start a conversation. Equivalent to 'What's up?' or 'What's new?' in English. Common with friends, colleagues, or casually addressing someone; not appropriate for very formal situations. Can be followed by a name or title (e.g., 'quoi de neuf, chef?').
target_language_example: Salut Marc, quoi de neuf ?
native_language_example: Hi Marc, what's new?

meaning: 'what' (colloquial/familiar — tag use), often used to ask for clarification, express surprise, or echo something about someone
additional_notes: Informal, spoken French. 'Quoi' can be used alone as a question word (like 'what?') or combined with a subject pronoun (quoi + elle) to mean 'what about her' or 'what did she [do/say]?' depending on intonation and context. Common in casual conversation; not standard in formal or written French. In neutral/written contexts use 'Qu'est-ce qu'elle... ?' or 'Que fait-elle ?'.
target_language_example: — Elle a dit non ? — Quoi elle ?
native_language_example: — She said no? — What, her?

meaning: 'what about it' / 'what of it' — used in spoken French as part of questions or short responses when asking or dismissing something previously mentioned.
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken combination often found in questions like « Et quoi, en ? » or within clauses such as « Quoi, en faire ? ». Alone it's fragmentary; native speakers usually include it in a larger phrase (e.g. « Et quoi, on fait quoi de ça ? »). It can express curiosity, challenge, or dismissal depending on intonation and context. Not a fixed idiom by itself but a common pairing of the interrogative quoi with the preposition/en referring back to something already mentioned.
target_language_example: Tu n'as plus de travail, et quoi, on fait quoi en ?
native_language_example: You don't have a job anymore — so what, what are we supposed to do about it?

meaning: what to do
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what action should be taken. Appears in statements, questions, and subordinate clauses after verbs like savoir (to know) or se demander (to wonder). Often follows expressions like "je ne sais pas" (I don't know) and can be used with or without prepositions (e.g., "quoi faire de..." meaning "what to do with...").
target_language_example: Je me demande quoi faire ce week-end.
native_language_example: I wonder what to do this weekend.

meaning: 'what yesterday' (not a standard fixed phrase) — typically a clipped or surprised reaction meaning 'What, yesterday?' or 'About yesterday?'.
additional_notes: Not a conventional fixed expression in French. 'Quoi' = 'what' and 'hier' = 'yesterday'. When used together, it appears in informal spoken or written contexts as a fragmented question or reaction; punctuation and intonation are important: e.g. 'Quoi hier ?' Use sparingly in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Quoi hier ? Tu as vraiment fait ça hier ?
native_language_example: What, yesterday? You really did that yesterday?

meaning: "what (is it) that he/it" or a colloquial chunk used in questions/expressions (depends on context)
additional_notes: Alone 'quoi' = 'what'. 'Il' = 'he/it' or impersonal 'it'. 'Quoi il' is not a standard fixed phrase; it appears inside casual spoken questions or relative clauses (e.g. « Quoi, il part ? » = "What, is he leaving?" or in constructions like « Je sais pas quoi il veut » = "I don't know what he wants"). Word order can vary in spoken French; in careful written French you'd usually say « ce qu'il » (e.g. « ce qu'il veut ») or « quoi ? » as a short question.
target_language_example: Je sais pas quoi il veut manger.
native_language_example: I don't know what he wants to eat.

meaning: "what he/it is" — a nonstandard, colloquial sequence reflecting spoken word order or interruption (not correct for formal written French)
additional_notes: This sequence is not standard French word order for embedded clauses. Standard forms are "ce qu'il est" for embedded meaning (e.g. "Je sais ce qu'il est") or "Quoi ? Il est... ?" when expressing surprise in speech. "quoi il est" can appear in informal oral contexts where the speaker runs words together or is interrupted. Avoid it in formal writing; use standard alternatives instead.
target_language_example: Je me demande quoi il est en train de préparer.
native_language_example: I wonder what he is preparing.

meaning: 'what it is about' or 'what this concerns'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the subject, cause, or content of something. Often appears in questions or statements introduced by verbs like 'savoir', 'dire', 'voir' and polite formulas ('Puis-je savoir...'). The full structure is 'de quoi il s'agit' (or in inversion/question form 'de quoi s'agit-il ?'). In casual speech you may also hear 'c'est de quoi?' but 'de quoi il s'agit' is common in statements.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous m'expliquer de quoi il s'agit ?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me what it is about?

meaning: 'what I have' (used in questions/clauses like 'de quoi j'ai...' = 'what I look like / what I need / what I want')
additional_notes: Appears in the construction 'de quoi j'ai + noun/verb' or 'de quoi j'ai l'air' and is used to ask or state what someone possesses, needs, wants, or appears to be. Common patterns: 'De quoi j'ai l'air ?' (How do I look? / What do I look like?), 'Tu sais de quoi j'ai besoin ?' (Do you know what I need?). Informal spoken French often drops inversion: 'De quoi j'ai l'air ?' instead of 'De quoi ai-je l'air ?'.
target_language_example: Tu sais de quoi j'ai peur ?
native_language_example: Do you know what I'm afraid of?

meaning: 'what I' (rare/informal; typically appears in spoken fragments or as filler)
additional_notes: Not a standard fixed phrase. In French, 'quoi' means 'what' and 'je' means 'I'. The sequence 'quoi je' usually appears in casual spoken French as a filler or in interrupted/fragmented speech (e.g. '...quoi je...' = '...like, I...') and is not used as a grammatically complete unit in formal writing. In standard questions or statements you would use 'ce que je', 'que je' or reorder words ('qu'est-ce que je...').
target_language_example: Il m'a répondu, quoi je n'ai rien compris.
native_language_example: He answered me, like I didn't understand anything.

meaning: 'what I think' (literal phrase) — not the standard neutral phrasing in French
additional_notes: This combination mirrors English word order but is not the usual way to say 'what I think' in French. Native speakers normally say 'ce que je pense' or use opinion phrases like 'à mon avis' or 'selon moi'. 'Quoi je pense' can appear in colloquial or emphatic speech as a fragment (e.g. 'Quoi, je pense... ?' meaning 'What — I think...?' or in casual questioning), but on its own it is generally ungrammatical in neutral written French.
target_language_example: Quoi, je pense que c'est une mauvaise idée ?
native_language_example: What — I think that's a bad idea?

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; usually a fragment where 'quoi' (what) is followed by the article/pronoun 'le'. It appears only as part of a larger phrase or colloquial interjection (e.g. 'quoi, le...?' meaning 'what, the...?' or as a segmentation inside a sentence).
additional_notes: Do not treat 'quoi le' as a single lexical item. It is compositional: 'quoi' and 'le' function separately. You may encounter it in informal speech or writing (often with a comma: 'Quoi, le... ?') or as part of a clause ('...quoi le...'). If seen, read the surrounding sentence to understand the meaning. Learning the separate uses of 'quoi' and 'le' is recommended.
target_language_example: Quoi le problème ?
native_language_example: What, the problem?/What is the problem?

meaning: 'quoi m'' is not a standalone standard phrase; it looks like the word 'quoi' followed by a contracted pronoun beginning with m- (e.g. m', short for me, me+verb) — typically part of a larger expression, not used alone.
additional_notes: This fragment appears when 'quoi' (what/which) is directly followed by a verb or pronoun that starts with 'm' and is contracted with an apostrophe (for example: 'm'' = me or 'm'' = me + verb e.g. 'm'a' in informal speech). Alone it has no fixed meaning; you will see it inside sentences like 'Tu sais quoi m'a dit...' (You know what he told me...) or in informal colloquial endings '...quoi, ma' becomes 'quoi m'' before a vowel. For beginners: learn 'quoi' by itself (what) and learn contractions like 'm'' = me (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Tu sais quoi m'a dit ton frère ?
native_language_example: Do you know what your brother told me?

meaning: colloquial fragment meaning 'so what (to me)' or 'what of it (for me)' — used to dismiss something or express indifference
additional_notes: Informal/slang fragment. 'm'en' is contraction of 'm'en fiche' / 'm'en fous' (I don't care). Typically incomplete on its own and appears in spoken French (e.g., 'quoi m'en ?' or embedded in larger utterances). Avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: — Il dit que c'est grave. — Quoi m'en ? Je m'en fiche.
native_language_example: — He says it's serious. — So what? I don't care.

meaning: 'what we' (fragment) or conversational filler sequence where 'quoi' interrupts or precedes 'nous'; not a fixed idiom on its own
additional_notes: Not a standard fixed phrase. 'Quoi' normally means 'what' or acts as a filler; when followed by 'nous' it typically appears in spoken/informal contexts to restart or emphasize a clause (e.g. '...quoi, nous...'). For formal/written French prefer 'ce que nous', 'que nous' or restructure (e.g. 'ce que nous faisons'). The sequence can be part of constructions like 'tu sais quoi, nous...' but written examples may insert punctuation or pauses: '...quoi, nous...'.
target_language_example: Quoi nous, on pourrait essayer encore une fois.
native_language_example: What, us? We could try one more time.

meaning: 'what' (informal/filler), used in casual speech to introduce or emphasize a comment — often equivalent to 'you know' or 'like' after a statement.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed phrase; it's an informal spoken combination where 'quoi' acts as a filler and 'on' is the impersonal/colloquial 'we' or 'people' (often meaning 'you' or 'one'). You will hear it in relaxed conversation: e.g. 'C'est nul, quoi on s'ennuie' or appended to the end of a sentence as emphasis ('Il est bizarre, quoi, on sait pas pourquoi'). Avoid in formal writing. Pronounced quickly: /kwa ɔ̃/.
target_language_example: Il est parti sans prévenir, quoi on ne comprend pas.
native_language_example: He left without warning, you know, we don't understand.
