target_language_example: Parfois, je dis que je vais rendre visite de temps en à mes voisins, même si j'ajoute toujours la personne après 'à' dans la phrase complète.
native_language_example: Sometimes I say I'll visit from time to time my neighbors, though I always add the person after 'à' in the complete sentence.

meaning: (literal) you return/give back to work; (intended) you go back to work / return to work — phrase as written is non‑standard and likely a confusion of rendre vs. retourner/revenir.
additional_notes: As written, 'rends au travail' uses the verb rendre (to return/give back) in the 2nd person singular present (tu rends) without an explicit subject. This is unusual for meaning 'go back to work'. Native speakers would usually say 'Retourne au travail', 'Reviens au travail' or use the reflexive imperative 'Rends-toi au travail' is not idiomatic. 'Rends au travail' can also be part of a longer sentence where 'rends' has an object (e.g., 'rends le dossier au travail' — return the file to the office), in which case the phrase is grammatical but then 'au travail' marks destination for the object, not the subject.
target_language_example: Tu rends au travail les clés que tu as prises hier ?
native_language_example: Are you returning the keys you took yesterday to the office?

meaning: you return (something) to / give back to (someone) — 2nd person singular of rendre + preposition à
additional_notes: "Rends à" appears when the verb rendre (to return/give back/make) is followed by the preposition à (to) and addressed to tu (present tense or imperative). Common in sentences like "Rends à Marie le livre" (Return the book to Marie) or "Rends à ton frère ce que tu lui as pris". Note that word order can vary: object can come before or after the recipient; pronouns may replace nouns (e.g., "rends-le à Marie").
target_language_example: Rends à Marie le livre que tu as emprunté.
native_language_example: Return to Marie the book you borrowed.

meaning: 'made/caused (something) + the' or part of a past participle construction meaning 'returned the' / 'rendered the' depending on context
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the past participle 'rendu' (from rendre: to give back, to render, to make) followed by the definite article 'le'. It appears in different constructions, for example: "il a rendu le livre" (he returned the book), or in passive/compound structures like "rendu le résultat" (the result rendered/produced). Meaning depends on the verb tense and sentence: 'rendu le' can mean 'returned the...', 'made the...', or 'rendered the...'. Watch for agreement: 'rendu' agrees in gender/number when used with être in passive voice (e.g., "rendue"/"rendus"/"rendues").
target_language_example: Elle a rendu le dossier au client hier.
native_language_example: She returned the file to the client yesterday.

meaning: to return to the (feminine) / to go back to the
additional_notes: Used before a feminine place or institution introduced by la (e.g. la maison, la fac, la maison de retraite). Means to go back/return to that place. Context determines tense/person (rentrer → to come/return home/to a place). If the place is masculine use rentrer au; plural use rentrer aux.
target_language_example: Je vais rentrer à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to return to the house/home tonight.

meaning: entered into / bumped into / came back into (depending on context).
additional_notes: Past participle of rentrer + preposition dans. Can mean: 1) to enter a place (Je suis rentré dans ma chambre = I went/returned into my room), 2) to collide with something (Je suis rentré dans un poteau = I ran into/bumped into a pole), or 3) to enroll/enter institutionally in some contexts (rentrer dans une école = to enter/join a school). Context determines whether it's physical entry, accidental collision, or figurative/official entry. Uses être as auxiliary with intransitive sense (movement) when referring to re-entering or returning; when used transitively in collision sense it can take avoir in some constructions (but common usage uses être for movement). Agreement of past participle applies when auxiliary is être.
target_language_example: Mon fils est rentré dans ma chambre.
native_language_example: My son came back into my room.

meaning: 'to enter/come back into' or 'to return to' (used with a following place, state, or mode).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or noun phrase introduced directly after en. Can mean physically entering or returning into a place (rentré en Algérie, rentré en bus = returned by bus), or entering a state or role (rentré en scène = came back on stage; rentré en moi-même = withdrew into myself). In contexts like "rentré en sang" it means to return in that condition (i.e. covered in blood). Choose the English translation based on whether the following word names a place, means of transport, state, or condition.
target_language_example: Je suis rentré en bus hier soir.
native_language_example: I returned by bus last night.

meaning: returned to
additional_notes: From the verb rentrer (to return/go back in). Used with a place or time: 'rentré à Paris' = returned to Paris; 'rentré à 22h' = came back at 10 pm. Requires agreement in compound tenses when used with être (elle est rentrée). If followed by a noun of place, use the preposition à for cities or locations that take à (rentré à la maison / à Paris).
target_language_example: Il est rentré à la maison tard hier soir.
native_language_example: He returned home late last night.

meaning: to start over / begin again from scratch.
additional_notes: Used when you want to abandon previous progress or plans and begin anew. Common in everyday conversation. Often follows verbs like 'vouloir', 'devoir' or appears as a suggestion/question. Equivalent to 'start from zero' or 'start over.'
target_language_example: On va repartir à zéro et refaire le plan.
native_language_example: We'll start over and redo the plan.

meaning: 'meal of' or 'meal with' (used to describe what a meal consists of or the occasion of a meal)
additional_notes: repas means 'meal'. When followed by a noun introduced by de, it describes the content, purpose or type of the meal: e.g. 'repas de fête' (celebratory meal), 'repas de famille' (family meal), 'repas de midi' (midday/lunch meal). Can also appear in phrases like 'un repas de trois plats' (a three-course meal). The exact English preposition may be 'of', 'with', or omitted depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous organisons un repas de famille dimanche.
native_language_example: We are having a family meal on Sunday.

meaning: 'repas' = meal, 'est' = is. Together they form the sequence 'repas est' which by itself is not a fixed phrase — it would appear inside a sentence like "Le repas est prêt" (The meal is ready).
additional_notes: This is not a multiword idiom; it's simply the noun repas (meal) followed by the verb être in the 3rd person singular (est = is). You will normally see it as part of a full sentence: Le repas est..., Un repas est..., Ce repas est.... Remember to agree adjectives with repas (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Le repas est prêt.
native_language_example: The meal is ready.

meaning: the meal / mealtime (the noun 'repas' preceded by the definite article 'le', meaning 'the meal').
additional_notes: 'Le repas' is used to refer to a specific meal or meals in general. French requires the article when speaking about meals in the abstract or about a particular meal. You can specify the type of meal (le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner, le dîner) or use 'le repas' for a meal in general.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, repas le est prévu pour midi.
native_language_example: Today, the meal is scheduled for noon.

meaning: to postpone (something feminine) / to put off the (feminine) [e.g. la réunion].
additional_notes: Reporter is a transitive verb meaning 'to postpone' or 'to defer'. The direct object follows (here 'la' = 'the' for a feminine noun like 'réunion'). You can change 'la' to other articles/pronouns (reporter la réunion, reporter le rendez-vous, reporter ça). Common construction: reporter + direct object + (à + time) to indicate the new time: Reporter la réunion à demain = postpone the meeting until tomorrow.
target_language_example: Peut-on reporter la réunion à vendredi ?
native_language_example: Can we postpone the meeting until Friday?

meaning: 'rest in peace' (a wish for the dead to be at peace).
additional_notes: Used when speaking about someone who has died. Can be said directly to the deceased (Repose en paix) or as a wish (Qu'elle/qu'il repose en paix). Formal or neutral tone; common in obituaries, condolences, prayers. Not usually used for living people.
target_language_example: Qu'il repose en paix après tant de souffrance.
native_language_example: May he rest in peace after so much suffering.

meaning: to put down or place (something) again; to rest something (on a surface) or temporarily set aside; depending on context can also mean to ask or pose again (e.g., reposer une question).
additional_notes: Depends on context and the noun that follows. Common with concrete objects (reposer un livre, reposer un appareil) meaning 'to lay/put back down'. With abstract nouns (reposer une question) it means 'to ask again' or 'to pose again'. For beginners, treat it primarily as 'to put/lay something back down' when followed by a tangible object.
target_language_example: Je vais reposer un livre sur la table.
native_language_example: I'm going to put a book back on the table.

meaning: to respect the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: This is the verb respecter followed by the definite article le (the). It means to show respect for, to comply with, or to observe something masculine: e.g. respecter le règlement (to follow the rules), respecter le choix de quelqu'un (to respect someone's choice). Conjugate respecter as needed and keep le before a masculine noun; if the noun begins with a vowel or mute h, use l' (respecter l') and for feminine nouns use la/les (respecter la, respecter les).
target_language_example: Il faut respecter le règlement de l'école.
native_language_example: You must respect the school's rules.

meaning: to obey/follow the (rules of a) code (e.g., 'respecter le code de la route' = obey traffic laws).
additional_notes: Used with a specific code after 'de' (most commonly 'de la route' = traffic laws). Means to comply with rules or regulations. Common in obligations/advice: devoir/should + respecter. Conjugate respecter as usual (respecte, respectez, etc.).
target_language_example: Il faut respecter le code de la route pour éviter les amendes.
native_language_example: You must obey the traffic laws to avoid fines.

meaning: you/it look(s) more and more / resemble(s) more and more
additional_notes: From the verb ressembler (to resemble, to look like) + 'de plus en plus' (more and more). Used to say someone or something is becoming increasingly similar to someone/something else. Conjugation depends on subject (tu ressembles, il/elle ressemble, ça ressemble, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu ressembles de plus en plus à ton frère.
native_language_example: You look more and more like your brother.

meaning: 'feel it' — imperative or present-tense informal/neutral form using the verb ressentir + feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (refers to a feminine noun like la douleur, la chaleur)
additional_notes: From ressentir (to feel). 'Ressens la' can appear as an affirmative imperative addressing 'tu' (command: 'feel it') or as informal spoken word order where object pronoun follows the verb for emphasis; standard declarative order is 'tu la ressens' or 'je la ressens'. 'La' is a feminine direct object pronoun meaning 'it'. Use when the thing felt is feminine (e.g., la douleur, la chaleur, la tension).
target_language_example: Ressens la, cette chaleur sur ta peau.
native_language_example: Feel it, that warmth on your skin.

meaning: 'feel for' or 'feel about' (have feelings toward someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing after 'pour' to indicate emotions or feelings directed toward them (love, affection, sympathy, etc.). Common in phrases like 'ce que je ressens pour toi' or 'ce que tu ressens pour moi'. Appears in conjugated forms (je ressens, tu ressens, il/elle ressent). Often found in romantic or emotional contexts but can express any directed feeling.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je ressens pour toi.
native_language_example: You know what I feel for you.

meaning: 'fast food' (the industry or type of food/service).
additional_notes: Used to talk about fast-food restaurants or the fast-food industry in general. Can refer to the food itself (cheap, quickly prepared meals) or to places that serve it. Common in formal and neutral contexts; not slang.
target_language_example: Je préfère éviter la restauration rapide pour des raisons de santé.
native_language_example: I prefer to avoid fast food for health reasons.

meaning: 'the rest of the' or 'the remainder of the' (followed by a noun beginning with a vowel or mute h).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the remaining part of something. 'Reste de' contracts with the definite article: before a vowel or mute h you often see 'reste de l'' + noun (e.g. l'argent, l'équipe). For consonant-starting nouns you'd say 'le reste du' (masc) or 'le reste de la' (fem). Can refer to people (the rest of the team/crew) or things (the rest of the money).
target_language_example: Avec le reste de l'argent, nous avons payé la facture.
native_language_example: With the rest of the money, we paid the bill.

meaning: 'the rest of his/her' (the remaining part of someone's life, sentence, time, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to talk about the remainder belonging to a person (sa = his/her depending on the noun's gender). Commonly followed by a noun like vie (life), phrase (sentence/phrase), journée (day). 'Reste de sa vie' = 'the rest of his/her life.'
target_language_example: Elle a passé le reste de sa vie à enseigner.
native_language_example: She spent the rest of her life teaching.

meaning: 'the rest of your' or 'the remainder of your'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains of something belonging to 'vous' (your). 'Reste' can mean remaining portion (food, time, people, life, etc.). 'Votre' is the formal/plural 'your'. Agreement: if the noun after is feminine and requires adjectives, adjust accordingly (e.g. 'le reste de votre vie', 'le reste de vos amis'). Common in questions about leftover food, remaining members of a group, or the remainder of a period of time.
target_language_example: Garde le reste de votre gâteau pour demain.
native_language_example: Keep the rest of your cake for tomorrow.

meaning: 'the rest of' or 'the remaining (plural)'.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to refer to the remainder of a group or quantity (reste des + noun). Equivalent to 'the rest of the...' or 'the remaining (items)'. Common in everyday and written French. Word order: 'le reste des affaires' = 'the rest of the things'.
target_language_example: Donne-moi le reste des pièces, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me the rest of the coins, please.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'the rest is' or 'what remains is'.
additional_notes: This combination appears to be a fragment, not a fixed multiword expression. In correct French you'd say 'le reste est...' (the rest is...) or 'il reste' (there remains / there is left). Use 'le reste est' before an adjective or clause to describe what remains, or 'il reste' to say something is left/remaining. Example: 'Le reste est à vous.' / 'Il reste trois pommes.'
target_language_example: Le reste est à nettoyer après la fête.
native_language_example: The rest is to be cleaned after the party.

meaning: 'there remains a lot' or 'there is still a lot (left)'
additional_notes: Phrase is composed of the verb rester (to remain/to be left) in third person singular (reste) plus beaucoup (a lot). It's used to say that a large quantity or amount is still present or available. To match subject you may see forms like il reste beaucoup (there remains a lot) or il y reste beaucoup (less common). Can be followed by a noun or nothing (implying amount).
target_language_example: Il reste beaucoup de pain pour demain.
native_language_example: There is a lot of bread left for tomorrow.

meaning: 'how many/much is left' or 'how much remains'
additional_notes: Used to ask how many items or how much quantity remains of something. Often appears in questions: (Il) reste combien de + noun? Informal everyday phrasing. Can be used with countable nouns (combien de pommes) or uncountable (combien de pain / combien d'argent). Word order: 'Il reste combien de X ?' or 'Combien de X reste-t-il ?' Both are common; the first is more casual.
target_language_example: Il reste combien de biscuits ?
native_language_example: How many cookies are left?

meaning: the remainder of / remaining (part of something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate what is left of something (e.g., le reste de la journée = the rest of the day). Can refer to time, quantity, people, objects, etc. Often contracted in speech but written as two words. Commonly followed by de + definite article (du/de la/des) when specifying a particular thing.
target_language_example: Je vais dormir le reste de la soirée.
native_language_example: I'll sleep for the rest of the evening.

meaning: 'the rest of' (masculine singular) — used before a masculine noun to mean the remaining part of something.
additional_notes: Formed from the noun 'reste' (remainder) + definite article 'du' (de + le). Use before masculine singular nouns: 'le reste du gâteau' = the rest of the cake. For feminine nouns use 'reste de la' (or 'reste de l'' before a vowel). Can be used with time expressions: 'le reste du soir' = the rest of the evening. Often appears with 'le' as in 'le reste du...'.
target_language_example: Je vais manger le reste du pain.
native_language_example: I'm going to eat the rest of the bread.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'remains and' or 'stay and' depending on context.
additional_notes: This looks like two words: 'reste' (verb or noun) and conjunction 'et' (and). By itself it is not a common multiword expression in French. 'Reste' can be the 3rd-person singular of rester (he/she/it remains/stays) or the noun 'the rest'. Paired with 'et' it usually continues a sentence (e.g. 'reste et...' = 'remains and...'). For beginners: treat as separate words—use 'reste' or 'reste de'/'le reste' for 'the rest', and 'reste' + infinitive or subject for 'remains/stays'.
target_language_example: Il reste et attend que tu reviennes.
native_language_example: He stays and waits for you to come back.

meaning: 'don't stay' or 'don't remain' (informal spoken negative imperative or present-tense negation).
additional_notes: A contraction of the negative form 'ne reste pas' often heard in spoken French; 'ne' is frequently dropped in casual speech/writing: 'reste pas là' = 'don't stay there'. Can be used as an imperative (telling someone not to stay) or as present-tense negation (Nous on reste pas longtemps = 'we don't stay long'). Use the full 'ne ... pas' in formal contexts. Often followed by a place or manner (là, sous la pluie) or by a duration (longtemps).
target_language_example: Reste pas dehors, il fait froid.
native_language_example: Don't stay outside, it's cold.

meaning: there is little left / remains only a small amount
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb rester (to remain) with peu (little). Used to say that only a small quantity, amount, time, etc., remains. Context determines what 'little' refers to (time, food, money, etc.). Often followed by a noun or a clause: il ne reste peu de..., or in spoken French you'd more commonly hear il reste peu / il n'en reste que peu.
target_language_example: Il reste peu de pain, achète-en s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: There is little bread left; please buy some.

meaning: 'remains for' / 'is left for' (indicating what is still available, needed, or remaining for something)
additional_notes: Used with quantities, time, tasks or people: it indicates what is left or still needed/available with respect to something. Often followed by a noun or infinitive (e.g. 'reste pour aujourd'hui', 'reste pour finir'). Can appear in impersonal constructions ('Il reste pour...') or with a subject ('Il me reste pour payer...').
target_language_example: Il reste pour terminer le projet deux jours.
native_language_example: There remain two days to finish the project.

meaning: remains a / is still a (used to say something continues to be a particular thing).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'rester' (to remain/stay) with an indefinite article + noun. Used to state that something continues to have a certain status or quality (e.g., 'reste un mystère' = 'remains a mystery'). Can be followed by a noun or adjective. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Pour le public, cela reste un mystère.
native_language_example: For the public, that remains a mystery.

meaning: 'to stay between' / 'to remain just between (us)'; used to ask or say that something should be kept private among a small group.
additional_notes: Commonly used with nous (rester entre nous) or entre toi et moi. It means 'keep this confidential' or 'don't tell others.' Polite/neutral register. Often followed by the people involved (nous, vous, toi et moi).
target_language_example: Garde ça, s'il te plaît — ça doit rester entre nous.
native_language_example: Keep this, please — it has to stay between us.

meaning: Not a correct or complete French phrase as written; appears to be a mistaken word order. Individually: 'rester' = to stay, 'ici' = here, 'ce' = this/that. Possible intended meanings include 'stay here' (rester ici) or 'to stay here is/that' (rester ici + clause).
additional_notes: 'rester ici ce' is ungrammatical in French. Correct alternatives depend on intent: 'Reste ici' (informal imperative), 'Restez ici' (formal/plural imperative), 'Rester ici est...' (To stay here is ...), or 'Reste ici, ce sera mieux' (Stay here, it will be better). The word 'ce' cannot follow 'rester ici' directly without a clause or modification.
target_language_example: Rester ici ce sera difficile si la tempête continue.
native_language_example: To stay here will be difficult if the storm continues.

meaning: to remain a/one (literal: 'to remain one') — used when rester is followed by the indefinite article un and a noun; not a fixed idiom by itself but a compositional sequence (e.g., rester un mystère).
additional_notes: Not a common standalone phrase. 'Rester un' will always be completed by a noun (or noun phrase): rester un ami, rester un mystère, rester un problème. Context determines meaning. Pay attention to gender/number (un vs. une, des) and tense/agreement of rester.
target_language_example: Après toutes ces années, il va rester un ami fidèle.
native_language_example: After all these years, he will remain a faithful friend.

meaning: to remain for / to be left to (a feminine noun) — depending on context, it can mean something is still to be done or that responsibility/decision belongs to someone/something feminine
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the combination of the verb construction 'rester à' with the feminine definite article 'la' before a noun (e.g. 'rester à la mairie'). Meaning depends on what follows: 'rester à la + noun' often conveys that something remains for or is up to that entity (the entity is grammatically feminine). Can introduce an infinitive with 'de' after: 'rester à la X de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Il reste à la direction de confirmer les détails.
native_language_example: It remains for the management to confirm the details.

meaning: (you) stay with / (he/she) stays with (depending on form) — literal meaning 'remain with' or 'stay with'
additional_notes: Derived from the verb rester (to stay) combined with the preposition avec (with). 'Restes avec' is the second-person singular present indicative (tu restes avec) or could appear in contexts like questions (Pourquoi restes-tu avec...?) and descriptions (Tu restes avec lui?). For the imperative 'stay' with tu, use 'reste' (without -s): 'Reste avec moi.' Watch agreement: for il/elle/on use 'reste', for nous 'restons', for vous 'restez', for ils/elles 'restent'.
target_language_example: Pourquoi restes avec lui si tu n'es pas heureux ?
native_language_example: Why do you stay with him if you are not happy?

meaning: stay at / remain on (followed by a place or a device)
additional_notes: Imperative form of 'rester' (vous). 'Restez au' is followed by a masculine singular article + noun beginning with a consonant sound (e.g. 'restez au bureau') or by a contraction such as 'au téléphone' (stay on the phone). Common in instructions or requests: 'restez au chaud' (stay warm) would be unusual—more natural is 'restez au + noun' for locations or 'restez sur' for devices/positions. Remember to adjust for gender/number: 'restez à la', 'restez aux', or 'restez sur' when appropriate.
target_language_example: Restez au téléphone, je vous transfère.
native_language_example: Stay on the phone, I'll transfer you.

meaning: stayed in; remained inside (past participle + preposition).
additional_notes: Literally 'stayed in' — 'resté' is the past participle of 'rester' (to stay/remain) and agrees in gender/number with the subject when used with être (e.g., 'restée', 'restés'). 'Dans' means 'in' and is followed by a place or situation (e.g., 'resté dans la maison', 'resté dans son rôle'). Used to describe remaining physically inside a place or staying within a state/role. Note: when the subject is feminine or plural, the past participle must agree (elle est restée dans..., ils sont restés dans...).
target_language_example: Il est resté dans la maison pendant l'orage.
native_language_example: He stayed in the house during the storm.

meaning: 'stayed in' or 'remained in' (past participle of rester + preposition en).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (resté) to say someone or something stayed or remained in a state, place, clothing, or condition introduced by en. Common constructions: 'être resté en [lieu]' (rested in a place), 'resté en [vêtement]' (stayed wearing), or figurative uses like 'resté en colère' (remained angry). Subject agrees with resté when used with être in compound tenses: e.g. elle est restée en chemise. If no context, 'en' requires a following noun or phrase.
target_language_example: Il est resté en ville pour le week-end.
native_language_example: He stayed in town for the weekend.

meaning: 'delay in' or 'lateness to' (followed by a noun indicating where or what).
additional_notes: Used to say there is a delay or someone is late for something. It is typically followed by a noun with the definite article contracted: 'au' = 'à le' (masculine singular). Common contexts: transport (retard au train), appointments (retard au rendez-vous), or delays in schedules (retard au planning). If the following noun is feminine use 'à la' (retard à la).
target_language_example: Il y a un retard au train de 20 minutes.
native_language_example: There is a 20-minute delay for the train.

meaning: This is not a correct French word order; likely a mistaken inversion of 'ce retard' (this/that delay) or confusion with another structure. 'retard ce' as written is ungrammatical in standard French.
additional_notes: French places demonstratives before nouns: 'ce retard' = 'this/that delay'. If you encounter 'retard ce' in writing or speech, it's a word-order error or typo. To express the idea correctly, use 'ce retard' or rephrase (e.g., 'ce retard est dû à...').
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais vu un retard ce flagrant dans ma carrière.
native_language_example: I've never seen such a blatant delay in my career.

meaning: delay in (doing) / late in (doing) — used to indicate being late or having a delay regarding something
additional_notes: Often appears as 'avoir du retard en [matière/activité]' (to be behind in a subject/activity) or 'retard de/à' depending on context. 'Retard en' is followed by a noun (e.g., 'retard en informatique') or by a gerund/infinitive phrase in some constructions. Common in contexts like work, school, transport, or projects. For describing lateness to an appointment, 'en retard' (without 'en') is more common: 'Je suis en retard.'
target_language_example: Elle a du retard en maths ce semestre.
native_language_example: She is behind in math this semester.

meaning: delay in (doing) — used to indicate being late or a delay in relation to something.
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'avoir du retard pour' or 'être en retard pour' + activity/event (e.g. un rendez-vous, un train, une livraison). 'Retard' is a noun meaning 'delay' or 'lateness'; 'pour' introduces the thing affected by the delay. Commonly used with verbs like avoir, être, prendre du retard, or with time expressions.
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai du retard pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late for the appointment.

meaning: 'delay for the' or 'delay of the' (used before a noun or time expression)
additional_notes: This fragment appears before a noun or time expression to indicate a delay related to that thing (e.g., retard pour le train = delay for the train). It's not a complete fixed phrase by itself; you must finish with the noun: 'retard pour le vol', 'retard pour le rendez-vous', etc. Use appropriate article (le/la/les) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Il y a un retard pour le train de 18h.
native_language_example: There is a delay for the 6 p.m. train.

meaning: behind schedule on; delay in (something)
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something is late or delayed with respect to a task, schedule, payment, project, etc. Often appears as 'avoir du retard sur [quelque chose]' or 'être en retard sur [quelque chose]'. Use 'sur' to specify what you're behind on. Can be followed by a noun or an infinitive verb (e.g. 'sur le projet', 'sur la livraison').
target_language_example: Nous avons du retard sur le projet à cause des fournisseurs.
native_language_example: We are behind schedule on the project because of the suppliers.

meaning: delay in (something) — indicates that something is late or delayed with respect to a specific event, time, or place
additional_notes: Commonly used with a noun or infinitive after 'à' to specify what is delayed (e.g., 'retard à l'arrivée' — delay in arrival, or 'retard à payer' — delay in paying). Also used with verbs in expressions like 'retard à + infinitive' less often; more frequent structures are 'retard de + noun' or 'être en retard à + place/event'. For beginners, remember 'en retard' = 'late'; 'retard' (noun) + 'à' points to what the delay concerns.
target_language_example: Il y a un retard à l'arrivée du train.
native_language_example: There is a delay in the train's arrival.

meaning: delay because of / late due to
additional_notes: Used to explain the reason for a delay or being late. Typically followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'retard à cause du trafic', 'retard à cause de la neige'). When referring to a person being late, you can use 'en retard à cause de...'. Common alternatives: 'à cause de' with the appropriate article ('à cause du/de la/des').
target_language_example: Le train a eu un retard à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: The train had a delay because of the snow.

meaning: delay in (something) — used before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or mute h (the phrase will finish the noun, e.g. «retard à l'arrivée» = delay in the arrival).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself: "retard à l'" is the beginning of expressions like "retard à l'arrivée" (delay in arrival) or "retard à l'allumage" (delay in ignition/start). The contraction "l'" stands for the definite article "la" or "le" before a vowel; here it usually represents "la" + vowel (feminine noun) or occasionally "le" if the noun is masculine but elided. Use with a specific noun that follows. Common in timetables, transport updates, or technical contexts.
target_language_example: Il y a un retard à l'arrivée du vol 342.
native_language_example: There is a delay in the arrival of flight 342.

meaning: to hold back (one's) — used with emotions or bodily reactions (e.g. tears, laughter).
additional_notes: Common construction: retenir + possesive (ses, ses larmes / son rire). Means to stop oneself from showing or expressing something. Often appears in past tenses (ne put / ne pouvait retenir ses larmes). Use with verbs or nouns like larmes, sanglots, rires, mots.
target_language_example: Il n'a pas réussi à retenir ses rires.
native_language_example: He couldn't hold back his laughter.

meaning: to hold one's breath (physically); figuratively, to wait anxiously or be in suspense
additional_notes: Can be used literally (to stop breathing temporarily) or figuratively to indicate anxious waiting or expectation. Common negated phrase: 'ne pas retenir son souffle' (don't hold your breath — i.e., don't expect it). Tense and subject agree normally: je retiens, nous retenions, ils ont retenu, etc.
target_language_example: Nous avons dû retenir son souffle en attendant les résultats.
native_language_example: We had to hold our breath while waiting for the results.

meaning: remove this (object) / take this away
additional_notes: Imperative form using the verb retirer (to remove, take away) followed by a demonstrative pronoun ce (this/that). Used to tell someone to remove or take away a specific item or element. In spoken French, people might also say "enlève ça" (colloquial) or "retire ça"; "retire ce" is normally followed by a noun (e.g. "retire ce livre") or used with a demonstrative pronoun as "retire ça". Polite form: "Retirez ceci/ça, s'il vous plaît."
target_language_example: Retire ce manteau du lit, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Take this coat off the bed, please.

meaning: removed/took off his/her (something); withdrew (a request) — past tense.
additional_notes: Retiré is the past participle of retirer. With a possessive (sa), it usually means 'took off' when referring to clothing or accessories (e.g., sa chemise, sa ceinture). With abstract nouns like "sa demande" it means 'withdrew' or 'cancelled' (a request, application). Gender of the possessor is shown by the possessive (sa = his/her for a feminine noun that follows). Context tells whether it's physical removal or withdrawing an action.
target_language_example: Il a retiré sa veste avant d'entrer.
native_language_example: He took off his jacket before going in.

meaning: removed his/her (something).
additional_notes: Past participle form of retirer (to remove) combined with a possessive (ses = his/her/its, plural). Used to say someone took off or removed multiple items they owned (glasses, clothes, gloves). Context determines gender of subject (il/elle). For present tense use 'retire ses' or other conjugations.
target_language_example: Il a retiré ses chaussures en entrant.
native_language_example: He removed his shoes when entering.

meaning: fast-forward; advance forward (in media/playback) or figuratively 'moving forward again'
additional_notes: Commonly used in the context of audio/video players to mean 'fast-forward' or 'skip ahead'. It contrasts with 'retour arrière' (rewind). Can also be used figuratively to say returning to a forward movement, but primary use is technical. In commands or buttons you may also see 'avance rapide' or simply '>>'.
target_language_example: Appuie sur le bouton 'retour avant' pour avancer de 30 secondes.
native_language_example: Press the 'fast-forward' button to skip ahead 30 seconds.

meaning: back in; return to (a place or point in time).
additional_notes: Combines 'retour' (return) with the preposition 'dans' (in/into). Used to indicate going back into a location, a previous state, or returning to a moment in time (e.g., 'retour dans la maison', 'retour dans le passé'). Often appears in contexts like 'retour dans la ville' or 'retour dans X minutes'. If followed by a time expression, it can mean 'in' (after) — be careful: 'de retour dans une heure' = 'back in an hour.'
target_language_example: Nous faisons un retour dans le village cet été.
native_language_example: We're returning to the village this summer.

meaning: back in a (female noun) / return to a (female noun) — used when saying you will be back at or returning to a place or situation (where the following word is feminine).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short phrase composed of retour (noun) + dans une (into a/ in a — feminine). You will usually see it followed by a feminine noun: e.g. "retour dans une heure" (back in an hour — heure is feminine), "retour dans une semaine" (back in a week). For masculine nouns use "retour dans un". Often used in signs or short messages to indicate temporary absence and when someone will return.
target_language_example: Retour dans une heure, je reviens.
native_language_example: Back in an hour, I'll be back.

meaning: 'return to' or 'back to' (indicates going back to a place, state, or topic).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun or pronoun to say someone/something goes back to a place, a previous state, or resumes a topic. Can appear in phrases like "retour à la normale" (return to normal) or "retour à la maison" (return home). If used with verbs, French often uses "retourner" or "revenir" instead (e.g. "retourner à la maison" or "revenir à la discussion").
target_language_example: Après la pause, il y a un retour à la normale.
native_language_example: After the break, there is a return to normal.

meaning: back to the (feminine noun); return to the (feminine noun)
additional_notes: A fixed phrase used before a feminine noun to indicate returning or going back to something or a state. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (la maison, la normale, la vie). If the noun is masculine use 'retour au' (à + le → au). Can also be used figuratively (retour à la normale = back to normal).
target_language_example: Après les vacances, c'est le retour à la routine.
native_language_example: After the holidays, it's back to the routine.

meaning: back to square one; back to the starting point (after a setback).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when a plan or effort fails and you must start over. Often used in informal and neutral contexts. Literally 'return to the start square' (like a board game).
target_language_example: Après l'échec du projet, c'est un retour à la case départ.
native_language_example: After the project's failure, it's back to square one.

meaning: Not a grammatical or standard French phrase as written; likely a mistaken word order or fragment. It may appear when text is split or when the noun 'retraite' and pronoun 'il' occur next to each other in a larger sentence (e.g., 'retraite, il...' or as a transcription error).
additional_notes: Use correct forms such as «il prend sa retraite», «il part à la retraite», or «la retraite d'il» (rare/incorrect) should be avoided. If you encounter 'retraite il' in running text, check for missing punctuation or inversion (e.g., 'retraite, il...' meaning 'retirement, he...').
target_language_example: Après la retraite il est parti vivre au nord.
native_language_example: After retirement he went to live in the north.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase. This sequence appears to be a mistaken word order or typo (possibly the user meant «il y a retraite», «il y a une retraite», or simply «retraite»).
additional_notes:
The exact string «retraite il y» is incorrect in French grammar and does not occur in standard usage. Possible intended corrections:
- «retraite» — means "retirement" (le fait de cesser une activité professionnelle) or "retreat" (lieu ou période de retrait, souvent pour méditation ou repos).
- «il y a une retraite» — "there is a retreat" (more natural than «il y a retraite»).
- «une retraite a lieu» — "a retreat is taking place." 
If you provide the intended meaning, a correct phrase and natural examples can be given.
target_language_example: La note sur la porte disait «retraite il y», ce qui semble être une erreur.
native_language_example: The note on the door said "retraite il y," which appears to be a mistake.

meaning: 'meet (each other) at' — used to suggest meeting someone at a specific place.
additional_notes: Form of the pronominal verb se retrouver (to meet or meet up). In conversation French people often shorten to "On se retrouve au..." to propose a meeting spot. Followed by a place (le bassin, le bureau, le motel, etc.). Can be used with times: "On se retrouve au café à 18h ?" The literal components are understandable (retrouver = find/meet, au = at the), so it's compositional.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au café à 18h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the café at 6 pm?

meaning: find/meet (him/her/it) there; meet up there
additional_notes: Compound of the verb retrouver (to find, to meet again) + là (there). Used when asking someone to meet or say they will meet/find someone or something at a specific place: e.g. «Je te retrouve là» = 'I'll meet you there.' Context determines whether it means 'find' (locate) or 'meet' (come together). Informal and common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je te retrouve là à 18h devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: I'll meet you there at 6 PM in front of the cinema.

meaning: is/are located at; meets at (depending on context)
additional_notes: Formed from the verb retrouver. When used with a place, 'retrouver quelqu'un à' means 'to meet someone at' or 'to find someone/thing at' (e.g. Je retrouve Paul à la gare = I meet Paul at the station). When used impersonally with a noun or pronoun subject ('ça se retrouve à...') it can mean 'is found/occurs at' or 'results in'. The exact sense depends on context and the sentence's subject and object.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à midi devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: We'll meet at noon in front of the cinema.

meaning: I'll meet you at the (place). / to meet someone at a location.
additional_notes: From the verb se retrouver or retrouver (to meet/meet up). Commonly used to arrange meeting places: 'Je te/vous retrouve à la voiture' = 'I'll meet you at the car.' Can be used with 'à la/au/à l'' + place (feminine/masculine/vowel). Informal to neutral; use 'on se retrouve' for 'let's meet' or 'je te retrouve' for 'I'll meet you'.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la cafétéria à midi.
native_language_example: Let's meet at the cafeteria at noon.

meaning: to find/get back my (female person or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Retrouver means 'to find again' or 'to reunite with' depending on context. 'Ma' is the feminine singular possessive ('my'). Use 'retrouver mon' before masculine nouns starting with a consonant, and 'retrouver mes' for plural. Common uses: retrouver ma famille (reunite with my family), retrouver ma vie (get my life back).
target_language_example: Je dois retrouver ma mère.
native_language_example: I need to find my mother.

meaning: 'to come back from' (a place) or 'to recover from' (an illness/shock).
additional_notes: Primary meaning is physical: to return from a location (Il revient de Paris = He came back from Paris / He's back from Paris). It also commonly means to recover from something non-physical (J'en reviens = I'm over it / I've recovered from it) or to be back after an illness/experience (Elle revient d'une longue maladie = She is recovering from a long illness). Context determines translation. Use être or avoir in compound tenses depending on sense: with movement it generally forms with être (Il est revenu de voyage), while figurative or pronoun constructions often use avoir (Elle en revient).
target_language_example: Il revient de Paris.
native_language_example: He is coming back from Paris.

meaning: to come back here / return here (informal, emphatic)
additional_notes: Colloquial and slightly redundant: revenir = 'to come back' and ici/ là both indicate location. Combining ici and là is casual and emphasizes the speaker's demand that someone return to this spot (e.g., 'come back here now'). More standard forms are revenir ici or revenir là. Often used with imperative (reviens/revenez) or in constructions like devoir revenir ici là. Pronunciation and register: informal, used in speech.
target_language_example: Il va falloir revenir ici là si tu veux finir le travail.
native_language_example: You will have to come back here if you want to finish the work.

meaning: 'to come back here next week' (part of a question about returning next week).
additional_notes: This phrase combines revenir (to come back), ici (here) and la semaine (usually followed by prochaine to mean 'next week'). In natural French you typically say "revenir ici la semaine prochaine" or ask with inversion/est-ce que/tu vas... The fragment here can be used to form questions: "Vas-tu revenir ici la semaine prochaine ?" or "Allez-vous revenir ici la semaine prochaine ?"
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu vas revenir ici la semaine prochaine ?
native_language_example: Are you coming back here next week?

meaning: 'revenir plus' is not a common standalone fixed phrase; literally 'to come back more' or part of expressions meaning 'come back later/earlier' or indicating negation when used with 'ne' ('no longer return'). It’s usually part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'revenir plus tard', 'ne revient plus').
additional_notes: On its own 'revenir plus' is incomplete and uncommon. 'Revenir' = to come back/return. 'Plus' can mean 'more' (as in 'revenir plus tôt' = return earlier/more early) or, in negative constructions with 'ne', 'no longer' (e.g. 'il ne revient plus' = he no longer returns). To interpret it, check surrounding words and verb conjugation. For polite imperatives use 'revenez plus tard' (formal/plural) or 'reviens plus tard' (informal/singular).
target_language_example: Il a dit qu'il allait revenir plus tard, mais il n'est jamais revenu — on ne peut pas simplement écrire 'revenir plus' sans contexte.
native_language_example: He said he would come back later, but he never returned — you can't just write 'revenir plus' without context.

meaning: 'to go back on' or 'to revisit/withdraw (a statement or decision)'; also 'to return to (a place)'.
additional_notes: Used in two main senses: 1) figurative: revenir sur + noun = reconsider, retract or change a previous statement or decision (e.g. revenir sur une décision / une déclaration). 2) literal: revenir sur + lieu = come back/return to a place (often used with 'Terre' for returning to Earth). Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Après réflexion, je dois revenir sur ma décision.
native_language_example: After thinking it over, I must go back on my decision.

meaning: to return to (a place) or to regain (consciousness); 'come back' or 'return'.
additional_notes: Often followed by a place (revenir à la maison = come back home) or by 'lui' meaning regain consciousness (revenir à lui). Can be used with times (revenir à cinq heures = come back at five). Common, neutral register. Conjugate revenir (il revient, il est revenu) and use preposition à before places/objects when needed.
target_language_example: Elle va revenir à la maison demain matin.
native_language_example: She will come back home tomorrow morning.

meaning: to return to the (feminine noun) / to go back to a topic, place, condition or state that is expressed by a feminine noun
additional_notes: Formed from revenir (to return) + à la (to the, feminine singular). Use 'revenir au' for masculine singular and 'revenir aux' for plural. Can be literal (physically returning) or figurative (returning to a subject, habit, situation). Verb must be conjugated appropriately for subject (e.g., je reviens, nous revenons).
target_language_example: Nous devons revenir à la normale après la tempête.
native_language_example: We need to return to normal after the storm.

meaning: returned for / came back in order to (someone or something).
additional_notes: Uses the past participle 'revenu/revenue' with auxiliary être (je suis revenue). 'Pour' introduces the purpose or beneficiary: 'pour toi' = for you; 'pour demander pardon' = in order to ask forgiveness. Gender and number must agree with the subject (revenu, revenue, revenus, revenues). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle est revenue pour t'aider.
native_language_example: She came back to help you.

meaning: 'may see each other again' or 'might meet again'.
additional_notes: Combination of 'se revoir' (to see each other again) in the future tense ('reverra' = he/she/one/ nous? actually 'on' or 'il/elle' future) plus 'peut‑être' (maybe). Used to express uncertainty about meeting again. Common in farewells or reflecting on future contact. Can be used with different subjects (on, nous, tu, vous) — here 'on se reverra peut‑être' = 'we might meet again.'
target_language_example: On se reverra peut-être cet été si tu viens en ville.
native_language_example: We might see each other again this summer if you come to town.

meaning: won't come back / will not return.
additional_notes: Informal spoken negation of 'ne reviendra pas' (future tense). In everyday French, the 'ne' is often dropped in speech and casual writing: 'il reviendra pas' = 'il ne reviendra pas'. Use to say someone or something will not return. Can refer to people, vehicles, events, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, elle reviendra pas — c'est définitif.
native_language_example: Don't worry, she won't come back — it's final.

meaning: 'come back' + time connector 'as soon as' (part of the phrase meaning "come back as soon as...").
additional_notes: reviens is the imperative (tu) or present indicative of revenir (to come back). dès means 'as soon as' or 'from'. Together they appear at the start of an instruction: "reviens dès que..." = "come back as soon as..." On its own, 'reviens dès' is incomplete and normally followed by 'que' + clause or a time expression (e.g. dès que possible, dès demain).
target_language_example: Reviens dès que tu as terminé.
native_language_example: Come back as soon as you have finished.

meaning: 'don't come back anymore' / 'don't return (anymore)'
additional_notes: Imperative form using 'revenir' (to come back/return) with 'plus' meaning 'anymore' or 'no longer'. Often used in commands or strong refusals: 'Ne reviens plus' = 'don't come back (again)'. Commonly strengthened by 'jamais' (never): 'Ne reviens plus jamais' = 'never come back'.
target_language_example: Ne reviens plus chez moi, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don't come back to my place anymore, please.

meaning: I/you/he/she/it comes back completely; 'revenir tout' isn't a common fixed phrase — likely part of a larger sentence meaning 'come back all (of it)' or 'come back completely'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'reviens tout' is unusual in French. It looks like the verb revenir (to come back) followed by the adverb/quantifier 'tout' (all/completely). Context matters: e.g. 'Il revient tout seul' (he comes back by himself) vs. 'Ça revient tout de suite' (that comes back/right away) — but 'reviens tout' would typically need more words (e.g. 'reviens tout de suite' = 'come back right away' or 'ça revient tout' as part of 'ça revient tout le temps' = 'that happens all the time'). For a beginner: don't memorize 'reviens tout' as a fixed expression; learn 'reviens' (come back / return (imperative or present)) and 'tout' (all/every/very/completely) and watch for full phrases like 'reviens tout de suite' (come back right away) or 'reviens tout seul' (come back alone).
target_language_example: Reviens tout de suite, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come back right away, please.

meaning: part of the phrase 'reviens tout de suite' or 'reviens tout de...' meaning 'come back immediately' or 'come back from (something)'; by itself it's incomplete
additional_notes: This sequence 'reviens tout de' is not a complete fixed phrase on its own in French — it's usually the start of a longer expression such as 'reviens tout de suite' (come back immediately) or 'reviens tout de X' when followed by a place or action. 'Reviens' is the imperative/form of 'revenir' (to come back / return) used to tell someone to return. If you encounter 'reviens tout de' alone in text, check the rest of the sentence: it's likely truncated. For polite requests, use 'reviens' + 's'il te plaît' or 'revenez' (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Reviens tout de suite, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come back right away, please.

meaning: to see (someone/something) again; to review or revise (something) — here with a masculine singular object following 'le'.
additional_notes: ‘Revoir’ can mean both 'see again' (meet again) and 'review/revise'. When followed by 'le' it points to a specific masculine noun previously mentioned (e.g. 'revoir le plan' = review the plan; 'revoir le professeur' would be uncommon — you'd normally say 'revoir le prof' or 'revoir le professeur' for 'see the teacher again'). Context determines whether it means meet again or review. In spoken French the object may be contracted (revoir + le + noun stays separate), and for feminine objects use 'la' (revoir la) or plural 'les' (revoir les).
target_language_example: Je dois revoir le rapport avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I need to review the report before the meeting.

meaning: you receive some / you get some (informal singular 'tu' form).
additional_notes: 'Reçois' is the 2nd-person singular present of 'recevoir' (tu reçois). Paired with 'des' it introduces an unspecified plural quantity (some). Often followed by a noun: 'tu reçois des messages' = 'you receive some messages.' In polite/formal contexts use 'recevez des' (vous).
target_language_example: Tu reçois des lettres chaque semaine ?
native_language_example: Do you receive any letters every week?

meaning: 'received it' (feminine direct object pronoun 'la' = it/her)
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'reçu' (from recevoir = to receive) used with the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' after it. In spoken or informal French you might see or hear 'reçu la' to mean 'received it/her' referring to a feminine object (la lettre, la commande, etc.). In standard written French the object pronoun usually appears before the verb (je l'ai reçue). Note agreement: when the direct object pronoun precedes the past participle, the participle agrees in gender/number (reçue). If the pronoun follows (as in some informal speech), you may still hear 'reçu la' without written agreement.
target_language_example: Tu as reçu la lettre ? — Oui, j'ai reçu la hier.
native_language_example: Did you receive the letter? — Yes, I received it yesterday.

meaning: 'received my' (feminine object) — short for "j'ai reçu ma..."
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's typically part of a sentence like "J'ai reçu ma commande" (I received my order) or a message fragment (e.g. in chat) meaning "I received my [item]". "Reçu" is the past participle of "recevoir"; when used with avoir it doesn't agree with the subject but can agree with a preceding direct object. "Ma" is the feminine singular possessive adjective (my).
target_language_example: J'ai reçu ma lettre ce matin.
native_language_example: I received my letter this morning.

meaning: was shot in (body part).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was hit by a bullet in a specific body part. Often followed by a noun indicating the location (la poitrine, la tête, la jambe). Grammatically, recevoir une balle = to receive/get a bullet (i.e., to be shot). Common in news or narratives; can be literal (gunshot) and is not idiomatic.
target_language_example: Il a reçu une balle dans la jambe pendant l'attaque.
native_language_example: He was shot in the leg during the attack.

meaning: rich in / full of (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: ‘Riche du’ is a combination of the adjective riche (rich) and the preposition du (de + le). It is used before a noun to say something contains or has a lot of something: riche du + noun. In many contexts French prefers 'riche en' (riche en vitamines, riche en histoire). 'Riche du' is used when the noun is introduced by the definite article (du = de + le) or to emphasize what someone/something is 'rich with' in a figurative or specific sense (e.g., riche du patrimoine, riche du soutien du public). Check whether the noun needs an article; if not, use 'riche en'.
target_language_example: La région est riche du patrimoine architectural.
native_language_example: The region is rich in architectural heritage.

meaning: 'are rich' or 'are wealthy' (the adjective 'riches' following the verb 'sont', third-person plural of être)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a compositional sequence: 'sont' (they are) + plural adjective 'riches' (rich/wealthy). It appears when describing plural subjects: e.g., 'Les voisins sont riches.' Ensure correct adjective agreement with plural subjects. Tone: neutral; can appear in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Les voisins riches sont souvent enviés.
native_language_example: The rich neighbors are often envied.

meaning: 'nothing in' or 'nothing inside' (literally); used to say there is nothing in/inside something or that someone has no feeling/interest in something when followed by a noun.
additional_notes: Literal use: 'rien dans le sac' = nothing in the bag. Idiomatic/colloquial uses occur in contexts like 'rien dans la tête' (nothing in the head = someone who knows nothing or is empty-headed) or 'rien dans le ventre' (nothing in the stomach). In spoken French, 'rien' is often followed directly by a noun with 'dans' to specify location or domain. Remember word order: 'rien' + 'dans' + noun. To negate possession/ability you may see other constructions (e.g., 'il n'y a rien dans...').
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien dans la boîte.
native_language_example: There is nothing in the box.

meaning: 'nothing like that' / 'there's nothing like (it)' (used to say something is unmatched or that something like that won't happen again).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is unparalleled, impossible, or will not happen again. Can stand alone as a short comment ('Rien de tel.') meaning 'Nothing like that' or 'That's the best/just what you need' depending on context (e.g. 'Rien de tel pour oublier les ennuis' = 'Nothing like that to forget your worries' meaning 'There's nothing better than that'). Often appears in negative constructions (rien de tel ne se reproduira).
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, une bonne douche — rien de tel.
native_language_example: After a long day, a good shower — there's nothing like it.

meaning: 'nothing of' or 'nothing to' (part of expressions like 'rien du tout').
additional_notes: On its own 'rien du' is incomplete and normally appears before another word (e.g. 'rien du tout' = 'nothing at all', 'rien du tout à voir' = 'nothing to do with it'). Use 'rien' for 'nothing'; when combined with 'du' it links to a following noun or set phrase. Common complete forms: 'rien du tout' (nothing at all), 'rien du tout à voir' (nothing to see/relate).
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien du tout à faire ici.
native_language_example: There is absolutely nothing to do here.

meaning: 'nothing at all' or 'not... at all'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total absence of something. Often appears with negation (ne ... rien du tout) meaning 'not ... at all' or alone as a strong 'nothing' (e.g., plus rien du tout = nothing left at all). Informal to neutral register; common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien du tout à déclarer.
native_language_example: I have absolutely nothing to declare.

meaning: 'nothing to' or 'nothing in' (depends on context) — used when negating something combined with a following noun or phrase
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'rien' means 'nothing' and is usually followed by a preposition or article (e.g. rien en commun, rien en moi). Alone 'rien en' will require more words to complete the idea. Common patterns: 'rien en commun' (nothing in common), 'rien en moi' (nothing in me), 'rien en retour' (nothing in return). Remember that 'rien' is used with ne...rien for full negation (Je ne vois rien = I see nothing). In informal speech the 'ne' is often dropped.
target_language_example: Nous n'avons rien en commun.
native_language_example: We have nothing in common.

meaning: 'nothing' + conjunction fragment (incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: On its own, 'rien et' is not a complete fixed phrase in French — it's usually the start of a longer construction (e.g. poetic or emphatic sequences) or a fragment from a larger sentence. Avoid using 'rien et' alone in normal conversation. Use 'rien' for 'nothing' and combine with proper connectors when needed: 'rien d'autre' (nothing else), 'rien ni personne' (neither anything nor anyone).
target_language_example: Il ne resta rien et tout fut oublié.
native_language_example: Nothing remained and everything was forgotten.

meaning: 'rien' = nothing; 'me' = to/for me. Together they appear in constructions such as "rien me" when followed by a verb or within a clause (often with the negative particle 'ne'), conveying that nothing affects or does something to the speaker (e.g. "nothing surprises me", "nothing matters to me").
additional_notes:
By itself 'rien me' is incomplete in French and normally occurs inside a larger clause. Common correct patterns:
- "Rien ne me..." + verb (subject 'rien' with negation particle 'ne') → e.g. "Rien ne me surprend." 
- In spoken or informal contexts, 'ne' is sometimes dropped: "Rien me fait peur."
- 'Rien me' can also appear when 'rien' is object: e.g. "Tu ne me dis rien." Note word order and presence/absence of 'ne'.
target_language_example: Rien me fait peur.
native_language_example: Nothing scares me.

meaning: ‘nothing would make me’ or 'nothing would (cause) me to...'
additional_notes: This is the start of a conditional phrase using 'rendre' in a causative sense (e.g. rendre + adjective or noun: rendre heureux = make (someone) happy). 'Rien ne me rendrait ...' means 'nothing would make me ...' and is usually completed by an adjective or verb in the infinitive (e.g. 'rien ne me rendrait heureux', 'rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que...'). It's used to express that no thing/event could cause the speaker to feel or do something. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de te revoir.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than seeing you again.

rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse

target_language_multi_word_term: rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse
meaning: 'Nothing would make me happier' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Expression used to say that nothing would give the speaker greater happiness than the thing that follows (usually introduced with 'que de' + infinitive, or 'que' + clause). The adjective 'heureuse' agrees with a female speaker; a male speaker would say 'heureux'. Can be followed by 'te', 'vous', etc., to specify whom the speaker would like to see happy.
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de te voir réussir.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than seeing you succeed.

meaning: 'only', 'just', or 'nothing but' (emphasis or restriction).
additional_notes: Used to limit or emphasize that there's nothing else besides what's mentioned. Can indicate exclusivity ('only us'), surprise/annoyance ('just pills!'), or purpose ('just for you'). Common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause.
target_language_example: Il y avait rien que des feuilles par terre.
native_language_example: There was nothing but leaves on the ground.

meaning: An exclamation meaning 'really?', 'is that so?', or to show surprise/irony about something notable.
additional_notes: Used to react to a statement or fact—can express surprise, disbelief, mild sarcasm, or emphasize that something is impressive or excessive. Tone and context determine whether it's positive (wow, impressive) or skeptical (you don't say). Often spoken alone or with punctuation (Rien que ça ? / Rien que ça !).
target_language_example: Tu as couru dix kilomètres ce matin ? Rien que ça ?
native_language_example: You ran ten kilometers this morning? Really?

meaning: 'nothing that' / 'nothing which' (used to introduce a relative clause after 'rien')
additional_notes: Combines the pronoun 'rien' (nothing) with the relative pronoun 'qui' (who/which/that). Used when referring to 'nothing' that does something: e.g. 'Il n'y a rien qui...' Note the negative structure: often appears with ne...pas or il n'y a. If the verb requires 'que' instead of 'qui' (object), use 'rien que' or 'rien que je...' depending on function.
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien qui m'intéresse dans ce magasin.
native_language_example: There is nothing that interests me in that store.

meaning: 'nothing to you' or part of a phrase meaning 'nothing (for) you' — typically appears as words 'rien' and the indirect object pronoun 'te' within larger sentences (e.g. "ça ne te fait rien"). Alone it is not a fixed idiom.
additional_notes: Alone, "rien te" is not a complete or common fixed phrase; in natural French the order often includes "ne" (e.g. "rien ne te...") or appears in constructions like "ça ne te fait rien". Learn full expressions rather than the isolated pair. "Te" is the familiar second-person singular indirect object pronoun (to/for you).
target_language_example: Ça ne te fait rien ? Rien te choque ? (informal speech might compress elements, but 'rien te' appears when speaking quickly)
native_language_example: Does it not bother you? Nothing shocks you?

meaning: 'nothing' used in constructions where 'rien' and 'vous' appear adjacent in spoken or elided forms (often part of larger phrases like 'rien ne vous...' or in short replies such as 'Rien, vous ?').
additional_notes: The literal words 'rien vous' rarely form a standalone grammatical unit; they usually occur when 'rien' (nothing) is followed by the pronoun 'vous' in a larger clause (e.g. 'rien ne vous empêche...'). In casual speech the 'ne' is often omitted, producing sequences like 'rien vous empêche...'. 'Rien, vous ?' is a short reply meaning 'Nothing, and you?'.
target_language_example: Rien vous empêche-t-il d'essayer ?
native_language_example: Nothing prevents you from trying?

meaning: 'nothing about it' or 'do nothing about it' (used after a verb with 'y' referring to a situation/place/thing).
additional_notes: This structure appears in negative sentences with 'ne ... rien' plus the pronoun 'y' (referring to a situation, place, or thing). It means that nothing can be done regarding that matter. Word order: subject + (ne) + verb + rien + y + faire/accomplir. Common in expressions like 'On ne peut rien y faire' = 'There is nothing we can do about it.'
target_language_example: Désolé, on ne peut rien y changer.
native_language_example: Sorry, there's nothing we can change about it.

meaning: 'nothing to do' / 'has no business (here)' / expression meaning 'no way' or 'it's hopeless' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'nothing to do'. Used in several ways: 1) To say someone has no reason/role/place somewhere: "Elle n'a rien à faire ici" = "She has no business being here." 2) As a short exclamation meaning 'no way', 'it's impossible', or 'doesn't work': "Rien à faire !" = 'No luck' or 'Nothing helps.' 3) In threats/commands to mean 'there's no chance' or 'it won't be allowed': "Si tu te présentes sans, rien à faire !" = 'If you show up without it, it's pointless/no chance.' Tone depends on context; common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Tu n'as rien à faire dans cette réunion si tu n'es pas membre.
native_language_example: You have no business in that meeting if you're not a member.

meaning: 'don't care at all' / 'couldn't care less' (very strong, vulgar)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar — 'foutre' is a strong swear verb here. Used to express total indifference or contempt. Can stand alone as an exclamation or take an object introduced by de/du (e.g., 'rien à foutre de ça' = 'don't give a damn about that'). Avoid in polite or formal contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai reçu des critiques, mais j'ai rien à foutre.
native_language_example: I got criticism, but I couldn't care less.

meaning: part of a larger expression meaning 'nothing to (do with) ...' or 'nothing at ...' (incomplete fragment).
additional_notes: On its own 'rien à la' is not a complete phrase in French; it looks like the beginning of expressions such as 'rien à la maison' (nothing at home), 'rien à la télé' (nothing on TV), or 'rien à voir' (nothing to do with / nothing to see). Learners will usually encounter 'rien à' followed by a noun, a verb (infinitive) or 'voir'. Pay attention to the rest of the sentence to get the full meaning.
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien à la télé ce soir.
native_language_example: There is nothing on TV tonight.

meaning: 'nothing to do with' / 'has nothing to do with it'
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is unrelated to a situation or topic. Common in answers or to deny involvement. Often appears in negative constructions (ne ... rien à voir) and can be followed by 'avec' or 'là-dedans' to specify with what it's unrelated.
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis n'a rien à voir avec le problème.
native_language_example: What you're saying has nothing to do with the problem.

meaning: to laugh at (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate laughing directed toward a person, action, situation, or idea. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (rire de quelqu'un, rire de quelque chose) or a verb in infinitive (rire de faire quelque chose). Can be neutral (laugh in amusement) or negative (make fun of). To express 'laugh with' you'd use 'rire avec'. Context and intonation determine whether it's playful or mocking.
target_language_example: Ils aiment rire de ses blagues.
native_language_example: They like to laugh at his jokes.

meaning: to risk one's life; to put one's life in danger for someone or something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a person or cause after "pour" (e.g. "pour le sauver") to say someone endangered themselves to help/protect. The literal verb is "risquer" + direct object (sa vie). It's not idiomatic slang; a strong, serious expression.
target_language_example: Il a risqué sa vie pour sauver son frère.
native_language_example: He risked his life to save his brother.

meaning: 'rivière' = river; 'est' = is / east (depends on context).
additional_notes: Alone, 'rivière' means 'river' (a flowing body of fresh water). 'Est' can be either the verb 'être' in third person singular ('is') or the cardinal direction 'east' depending on context. However, the two-word sequence 'rivière est' is uncommon by itself — you'd more often see phrases like 'la rivière est...' (the river is...) or 'la rivière Est' (the East River, using a capital letter) or 'rive est' (east bank). Be careful with capitalization and context to know whether 'est' is a verb or a direction.
target_language_example: La rivière est très large après la pluie.
native_language_example: The river is very wide after the rain.

meaning: used in place names to mean 'river of' or 'river at' (introduces the following name or feature)
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase in everyday speech; appears in geographic names (e.g., Rivière-à-Pierre, Rivière-à-Claude) where à links 'rivière' to a proper name or feature. In English this corresponds to 'River of/at X' or simply 'X River' depending on convention. The preposition à here is part of the fixed place name and follows French place-name conventions.
target_language_example: La carte indique une rivière à proximité du village.
native_language_example: The map shows a river near the village.

meaning: a river named with the pattern 'rivière à la ...' (literally 'river of the/at the ...'), used in place names
additional_notes: Often appears in Canadian (Quebec) or French place names: 'rivière à la ...' followed by a descriptive noun (e.g. 'rivière à la Tortue' = 'Turtle River'). The construction is part of a proper name, not a general grammatical phrase. When translating, keep it as 'River' + name (e.g. 'Rivière à la Pierre' → 'Pierre River' or 'River of the Stone').
target_language_example: Nous avons fait du canoë sur la rivière à la Tortue.
native_language_example: We went canoeing on the Rivière à la Tortue (Turtle River).

meaning: white rice (cooked or uncooked).
additional_notes: Common food term. Used when choosing between types of rice (e.g., white vs. brown). Can refer to plain steamed rice or rice porridge (gruau de riz blanc). Gender: masculine (le riz). Pronunciation: 'ree blahn'.
target_language_example: Je préfère le riz blanc avec ce plat.
native_language_example: I prefer white rice with this dish.

meaning: evening dress; formal gown (worn for evening events).
additional_notes: Refers to a formal dress worn to evening occasions (balls, galas, formal dinners). Often implies long or elegant attire. Singular 'robe de soirée', plural 'robes de soirée'. Commonly used in contexts describing formal dress codes.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté une nouvelle robe de soirée pour le mariage.
native_language_example: She bought a new evening dress for the wedding.

meaning: Used to say a dress looks good on someone (literally: 'the dress suits you').
additional_notes: Common phrase structure: 'Cette robe te va...' + adjective/phrase (à la perfection, à merveille, à ravir, très bien). 'Te' is the indirect object pronoun for 'you' (informal singular). For formal/plural 'you' use 'vous' (e.g. 'Cette robe vous va très bien'). The verb 'aller' in this construction means 'to suit' or 'to fit' (both appearance and fit).
target_language_example: Cette robe te va très bien, elle met tes yeux en valeur.
native_language_example: That dress looks great on you; it brings out your eyes.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase as written. It combines the noun 'robe' (dress) and the pronoun 'vous' (you/formal you), but this exact sequence is ungrammatical or incomplete in normal French.
additional_notes: Possible explanations: a typo or omitted preposition/possessive (correct forms include 'une robe pour vous' = a dress for you, 'votre robe' = your dress). As written, 'robe vous' could appear in a fragment of speech or poetry but is not a conventional multi-word expression. Use corrected forms for clear communication.
target_language_example: Répétez après moi: «robe vous» — ceci n'est pas une phrase correcte.
native_language_example: Repeat after me: "robe vous" — this is not a correct phrase.

meaning: a dress for (someone) / a dress to (someone) — indicates a dress given, sent, bought for a person or comparison 'robe à' in contexts with 'à' meaning 'for' or comparison.
additional_notes: When followed by a person (avec un pronom ou un nom), 'robe à [quelqu'un]' means a dress intended for or given to that person (Il a acheté une robe à sa fille = He bought a dress for his daughter). With verbs like acheter, offrir, envoyer, it marks the indirect object. In the last example, 'Je préfère cette robe à celle-ci', 'à' expresses comparison (prefer X to Y). 'Robe à' is not an indivisible fixed phrase; meaning depends on context and the word after 'à'.
target_language_example: Elle a cousu une robe à sa sœur pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: She sewed a dress for her sister for her birthday.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo or mis-segmentation (maybe 'roi' = king and 'ne' = negation particle).
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'roi ne' does not form a valid multiword expression in French. If you see it, it's probably an error: either 'roi' (king) should stand alone, or 'ne' should be part of a negation (e.g. 'ne ... pas'). Example corrections: 'le roi' (the king), 'le roi ne veut pas' (the king does not want).
target_language_example: Le roi ne veut pas partir.
native_language_example: The king does not want to leave.

meaning: 'the king was' (simple past description).
additional_notes: Combines roi (king) + était (imperfect of être = 'was'). Used to describe a past state, habitual action, or background information. Remember that était is the imparfait tense, not the passé composé — it's for ongoing or repeated past situations, descriptions, or context.
target_language_example: Le roi était vieux et sage.
native_language_example: The king was old and wise.

meaning: 'this/that novel is' or simply 'the novel is' (subject + être).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'roman' (novel) followed by the verb 'est' (is). It appears in simple descriptive sentences: Ce roman est... (This novel is...), Le roman est... (The novel is...). Use to describe qualities (difficile, ennuyeux, long) or to give information about a novel (basé sur...). Word order is noun + être + adjective or past participle.
target_language_example: Ce roman est très intéressant et bien écrit.
native_language_example: This novel is very interesting and well written.

meaning: spare tire (the extra wheel kept in a car for emergencies).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the temporary replacement wheel stored in a vehicle (often in the trunk). Common in everyday conversation about cars; can be singular or plural (roues de secours).
target_language_example: Il faut vérifier la pression de la roue de secours.
native_language_example: You should check the pressure of the spare tire.

meaning: 'red is' (literal — not a standard fixed phrase in French)
additional_notes: This combination is simply the adjective 'rouge' (red) followed by the verb 'est' (is). On its own it doesn't form a common idiomatic expression; it could appear in a sentence like 'La pomme rouge est mûre' ('The red apple is ripe'), where 'rouge' describes a noun and 'est' links to a complement. Beginners will more often see 'rouge' used before a noun (la voiture rouge) and 'est' as the third-person singular of 'être' (il/elle est = he/she/it is).
target_language_example: La robe rouge est jolie.
native_language_example: The red dress is pretty.

meaning: the red one; 'red' as a noun (the color red) when the adjective is nominalized with the definite article.
additional_notes: Used when distinguishing colors or choosing between options. The article 'le' turns the adjective 'rouge' into a noun meaning 'the red (one)' or 'red' as a color. Common in questions and lists: 'le rouge, le bleu ou le jaune ?'
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu préfères le rouge, le bleu ou le jaune ?
native_language_example: Do you prefer the red one, the blue one, or the yellow one?

meaning: literally 'road of' or 'route to'; used to indicate the road, route or direction related to a place or thing (e.g. la route de Paris = the road to/for Paris, la route de campagne = the country road).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a place name or noun to describe which road, route, or way is being referred to.
