additional_notes: Combines the verb 'savoir' (to know) in the present tense with 'toujours' (still/always). In negative sentences 'ne ... pas' often surrounds the verb: 'Je ne le sais toujours pas' = 'I still don't know it.' In affirmative sentences it can mean 'I still know' or 'I always know' depending on context. Use appropriate subject (je sais, tu sais, il sait...).
target_language_example: Je ne le sais toujours pas.
native_language_example: I still don't know it.

meaning: Not a standalone phrase; 'sais' is the 1st/2nd person singular of 'savoir' (to know) and 'très' means 'very'.
additional_notes: These two words may appear next to each other in a sentence (e.g., "tu sais très bien" = "you know very well"). By themselves they don't form an independent expression. Pay attention to subject pronouns: je sais (I know), tu sais (you know), il/elle sait (he/she knows). 'Très' modifies adjectives or adverbs (very).
target_language_example: Tu sais très bien où aller.
native_language_example: You know very well where to go.

meaning: 'I know very well (that)...' — used before 'que' or 'ce que' to say you are fully aware of something.
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular of 'savoir' (je sais) + 'très bien' (very well) followed by 'ce' as part of 'ce que' or 'ce qu''. It emphasizes certainty or clear knowledge about what follows (actions, facts, intentions). Common in spoken and written French. English equivalents: 'I know very well what...' or 'I know perfectly well that...'.
target_language_example: Je sais très bien ce que tu attends de moi.
native_language_example: I know very well what you expect of me.

meaning: 'know (you) to what' — the start of a question or clause meaning "(you) know to what/which..." or "do you know how/what..."
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a fragment: typically appears in sentences like «Tu sais à quel point...», «Tu sais à quel âge...», or in reported questions «Je ne sais pas à quel moment...». It combines the verb savoir (tu sais / je sais) with the preposition à and the interrogative quel (which/what + noun). Use it to ask or refer to 'to what extent', 'at what time/age', 'which ...', etc.
target_language_example: Tu sais à quel âge on commence les cours de piano?
native_language_example: Do you know at what age people start piano lessons?

meaning: 'do you know what I'm (thinking/was thinking)?' (part of a question or statement about what someone thinks)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions or statements like "Tu sais à quoi je pense ?" (Do you know what I'm thinking?) or "Tu sais à quoi je pensais ?" (Do you know what I was thinking?). It requires subject and verb agreement: usually as part of "Tu sais à quoi je pense/pensais" or in a statement "tu sais à quoi je pense" and in questions often with rising intonation. Use pense (present) for current thoughts and pensais (imperfect) for past thoughts. Not a fixed idiom—compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Tu sais à quoi je pensais hier soir ?
native_language_example: Do you know what I was thinking last night?

meaning: the season of (the ... season)
additional_notes: Used to talk about a particular time of year associated with something (flowers, allergies, hunting, etc.). Follows with a noun (usually plural) or a noun phrase: "la saison des fleurs", "la saison des allergies". Equivalent to English "the ... season". Use definite article (la/le/les) as needed: "la saison des fruits" = the fruit season.
target_language_example: En automne, c'est la saison des récoltes.
native_language_example: In autumn, it's the harvest season.

meaning: the rainy season (period of year with frequent rain).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the time of year when rainfall is heavy or frequent in a particular region (also called 'wet season' in English). Often used with verbs like commencer/débute, finir/terminer. Not idiomatic—literal meaning is clear.
target_language_example: La saison des pluies commence en mai chez nous.
native_language_example: The rainy season starts in May where we live.

meaning: 'knows how to play' (used with musical instruments).
additional_notes: Used to say someone can play a musical instrument. Structure: (subject) sait jouer de + le/la/les + instrument. For instruments that use definite articles (la guitare, le piano, la batterie). In English we say 'play the guitar' or simply 'play guitar' — French requires the article after 'de'.
target_language_example: Elle sait jouer de la guitare depuis son enfance.
native_language_example: She has known how to play the guitar since childhood.

meaning: 'knows where she (is)'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb savoir (sait = he/she/it knows) + question word où (where) + pronoun elle (she). The auxiliary verb être (est) indicating 'is' is often included after elle in full sentences (e.g. 'sait où elle est'). The fragment 'sait où elle' can appear in longer clauses or in speech where the final verb is implied or repeated. Make sure to use correct subject agreement for savoir: je sais, tu sais, il/elle sait, nous savons, vous savez, ils/elles savent.
target_language_example: Personne ne sait où elle est.
native_language_example: Nobody knows where she is.

meaning: 'knows who you (are)'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete sentence in French; a full sentence would be 'Il sait qui tu es' (He knows who you are) or 'Elle sait qui tu es'. 'Sait' is the 3rd-person singular of 'savoir' (to know). Use 'tu es' for 'you are' (informal singular).
target_language_example: Il sait qui tu es.
native_language_example: He knows who you are.

meaning: really knows / truly knows
additional_notes: Used after a subject (e.g., personne ne) to emphasize that someone does not truly know something or that the truth is uncertain. Common in negative sentences: "Personne ne sait vraiment..." It can also be used in questions or affirmative sentences to stress certainty. 'Vraiment' intensifies 'sait'.
target_language_example: Personne ne sait vraiment la vérité.
native_language_example: Nobody really knows the truth.

meaning: 'minimum wage' — the lowest legal hourly or monthly pay employers must provide.
additional_notes: Used to talk about legally mandated lowest pay level in a country or region. Can refer to hourly, monthly, or annual amounts depending on context. Often preceded by a definite article (le salaire minimum) or numbers (ex: soit environ...).
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a augmenté le salaire minimum cette année.
native_language_example: The government raised the minimum wage this year.

meaning: 'dirty son' used as an insult meaning 'you nasty/rotten son' or 'you bastard' (insulting someone, often angrily).
additional_notes: Literal translation is 'dirty son', but in French 'sale' before a noun intensifies the insult (like 'dirty' or 'filthy' in English). It's vulgar/insulting; use only in strong informal contexts or when quoting. Can be directed at a man (fils = son) but functions like a general insulting phrase similar to 'sale type' or 'sale con' depending on tone. Not appropriate in polite company.
target_language_example: Ne parle pas comme ça à ta mère, sale fils !
native_language_example: Don't talk to your mother like that, you filthy son!

meaning: waiting room (a place where people wait for an appointment or service).
additional_notes: Used for places like doctor's offices, train stations, clinics, offices. Always feminine singular: 'la salle d'attente'. To say 'in the waiting room' use 'dans la salle d'attente' or 'à la salle d'attente'. Plural: 'salles d'attente'.
target_language_example: J'attends le médecin dans la salle d'attente.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for the doctor in the waiting room.

meaning: bathroom (room with bath/shower, sink; sometimes toilet).
additional_notes: Refers to the room for washing and bathing. In some contexts the toilet (WC) is separate — French homes often have a 'salle de bain' (bath/shower + sink) and a separate 'toilettes' or 'WC'. Commonly used when asking to use the bathroom or describing its location.
target_language_example: Je peux utiliser votre salle de bain ?
native_language_example: Can I use your bathroom?

meaning: 'bathroom' (room with bath/shower, sink; may include toilet)
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for the room where you bathe or shower and usually wash up. In some contexts a separate 'toilet' (WC) may exist; if you specifically mean a room with only a toilet, use 'toilettes' or 'WC'. Used both in signs and everyday speech (e.g., 'La salle de bains' or 'Je peux utiliser votre salle de bains ?').
target_language_example: Je vais nettoyer la salle de bains cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to clean the bathroom this afternoon.

meaning: classroom (a room where classes are held).
additional_notes: Common, neutral term used for any room used for teaching in schools. Usually feminine singular: 'la salle de classe'. Often used with possessives (ma/ta/notre) or adjectives (grande, propre, petite).
target_language_example: La salle de classe est prête pour les élèves.
native_language_example: The classroom is ready for the students.

meaning: control room (a room where systems, machines, or operations are monitored and managed).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a dedicated room for overseeing equipment, operations, security, or broadcasting (e.g., in factories, power plants, TV studios, airports). Often preceded by an article: la salle de contrôle, une salle de contrôle. Pronunciation tip: 'salle' sounds like /sal/; the phrase is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Les techniciens travaillent dans la salle de contrôle.
native_language_example: The technicians work in the control room.

meaning: meeting room; a room where people meet to discuss or hold meetings.
additional_notes: Commonly used in offices, hotels, schools, or community centers. Can refer to a formal conference room or a smaller meeting space. 'Salle' = room, 'réunion' = meeting — literal, compositional phrase. Plural: salles de réunion.
target_language_example: La réunion aura lieu dans la salle de réunion au deuxième étage.
native_language_example: The meeting will take place in the meeting room on the second floor.

meaning: part of compound nouns meaning 'room for' or 'room with' (used before a noun like manger, coucher, bain).
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase by itself — 'salle' means 'room' and 'à' here links to the intended use or function. It appears in compounds like 'salle à manger' (dining room), 'salle à coucher' (bedroom, though 'chambre' is more common), or 'salle à manger/salle à manger' (dining room). In modern usage some fixed expressions are more common (e.g. 'salle de bain' instead of 'salle à bain'). Use with a noun immediately after: 'salle à + noun'.
target_language_example: Nous avons une salle à manger lumineuse.
native_language_example: We have a bright dining room.

meaning: dining room (the room where people eat).
additional_notes: Common household noun. Used with articles: la salle à manger, une salle à manger. Typical prepositions: dans la salle à manger (in the dining room), sur la table de la salle à manger (on the dining-room table).
target_language_example: Nous dînons dans la salle à manger ce soir.
native_language_example: We're eating in the dining room tonight.

meaning: 'hi, (you) ...' used to greet a group, often followed by a noun or name (e.g. salut les amis = hi friends).
additional_notes: Informal greeting. 'Salut' alone means 'hi' or 'bye'. When followed by 'les' it usually precedes a group identifier (amis, gars, filles, etc.) or can be used on its own as a casual 'hi everyone' in spoken French. Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Salut les amis, on va au café ?
native_language_example: Hi everyone/Hi friends, shall we go to the café?

meaning: calmness and self-control, especially in a difficult or dangerous situation; composure.
additional_notes: Used to describe keeping or losing composure under stress. Often appears in expressions like garder son sang-froid (keep your cool) or perdre son sang-froid (lose one's temper). Can describe a person (un homme de sang-froid) or an action done calmly (abattu de sang-froid = shot in cold blood). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Malgré la panique, elle a gardé son sang-froid.
native_language_example: Despite the panic, she kept her cool.

meaning: blood in (something) — used to say there is blood inside or mixed with a body fluid or location
additional_notes: Followed by a noun indicating where the blood is found (e.g., selles, urine, yeux). Common in medical contexts to report symptoms. Use possessive or definite article as needed: « du sang dans mes selles » (blood in my stool) or « du sang dans l'urine » (blood in the urine).
target_language_example: Il y a du sang dans mes urines.
native_language_example: There is blood in my urine.

meaning: This exact phrase is not a standard French expression; likely a fragment meaning 'blood is' (sang = blood, est = is).
additional_notes: The words are valid separately: 'sang' means 'blood' (noun, masculine) and 'est' is the third-person singular of 'être' ('is'). However, 'sang est' together without context is ungrammatical as a standalone phrase in French. You would normally see 'le sang est...' (the blood is...) or a verb form with a subject before 'est' (e.g. 'Il est...'). If you meant a different phrase (e.g. 'sans est' is wrong too), check spelling or provide full sentence context.
target_language_example: Le sang est chaud après une blessure.
native_language_example: The blood is warm after an injury.

meaning: literally 'blood on the' — part of a phrase referring to blood on something
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a fragment: sang (blood) + sur les (on the, plural). You'll normally see it inside a longer expression (e.g. 'du sang sur les mains' or 'du sang sur les murs'). Alone it doesn't form a complete idiom. 'Sur les' is the plural definite preposition 'on the'.
target_language_example: Il y a du sang sur les murs après l'accident.
native_language_example: There is blood on the walls after the accident.

meaning: homeless (used as an adjective or noun meaning a person without a home).
additional_notes: Literally 'without home'. Can be used as an adjective (une personne sans-abri) or as a noun (un sans-abri, des sans-abri). Neutral/formal registers; not slang. Plural is invariable in hyphenated form (des sans-abri). Often preceded by an article or possessive.
target_language_example: Il y a plusieurs sans-abri dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are several homeless people in this neighborhood.

meaning: flawless; without mistakes; perfect (often used as a noun: 'a perfect result').
additional_notes: Used as an adjective or noun. As an adjective it describes something without errors (un travail sans-faute). As a noun it can mean 'a perfect score' or 'no mistakes' (faire un sans-faute = make no mistakes). Common in formal and everyday contexts to praise performance or plans.
target_language_example: Elle a réussi l'exposé sans-faute.
native_language_example: She gave a flawless presentation.

meaning: constantly / all the time; without stopping
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens repeatedly or continuously. Can mean 'constantly', 'nonstop', or 'all the time' depending on context. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il se plaint sans arrêt depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: He has been complaining nonstop since this morning.

meaning: 'without any doubt' — definitely / undoubtedly / certainly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize certainty. Can start a sentence (as a sentence adverb) or appear before a noun/verb phrase. Equivalent to 'sans doute' but stronger. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Sans aucun doute, elle remportera le concours.
native_language_example: Without any doubt, she will win the contest.

meaning: 'no kidding' / 'you're kidding' / 'seriously' (used to show surprise, irony, or to ask if someone is serious).
additional_notes: Informal phrase. Can express genuine surprise ("No kidding?"), mild sarcasm or irony ("No kidding, Sherlock"), or be used to urge seriousness ("Come on, seriously!"). Tone and context determine if it's sincere or sarcastic. Often used alone or followed by a short comment.
target_language_example: Sans blague, tu as gagné la loterie ?
native_language_example: No kidding, you won the lottery?

meaning: 'constantly' or 'without stopping' (continuously, all the time).
additional_notes: Used to describe actions or states that happen continuously or repeatedly with little or no interruption. Can be translated as 'constantly', 'nonstop', 'all the time' or 'ceaselessly'. Works with both ongoing actions (Il neigeait sans cesse) and repeated behaviors (Il se vante sans cesse). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Elle téléphone à sa mère sans cesse.
native_language_example: She calls her mother constantly.

meaning: without saying that; not to mention the fact that
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point or emphasize something obvious/unspoken. Often appears in the middle of a sentence to introduce an additional remark that reinforces or adds to what was just said. Equivalent to English 'not to mention' or 'needless to say' depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a raté le train, sans dire que son téléphone était en panne.
native_language_example: He missed the train, not to mention that his phone was dead.

meaning: probably; without doubt (used to express likelihood or strong probability)
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase. Typically placed before a verb or phrase (e.g., «c'est sans doute…», «il connaît sans doute…») or alone for emphasis. Often translated as 'probably' or 'no doubt.' Can be followed by 'que' + clause, but can also stand alone. Slightly more formal than very casual equivalents like 'probablement' or 'sans aucun doute' (the latter is stronger: 'without any doubt').
target_language_example: Il viendra sans doute demain.
native_language_example: He will probably come tomorrow.

meaning: without delay; immediately
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do something right away or to describe an action that happens immediately. Formal or neutral tone; common in instructions, commands, reports. Can be used with imperative verbs or to describe how someone acted.
target_language_example: Répondez à ce message sans délai.
native_language_example: Reply to this message without delay.

meaning: without her / without it (feminine).
additional_notes: Literal prepositional phrase: 'sans' means 'without' and 'elle' is the feminine third-person singular pronoun. Used to say someone or something feminine is absent or not included. Context decides whether it refers to a person (she/her) or a feminine noun (e.g., la ville → 'sans elle' = 'without it').
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas partir sans elle.
native_language_example: I can't leave without her.

meaning: 'without exception' or 'no exceptions'
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something applies to everyone or everything mentioned — there are no exceptions. Common in short responses (e.g., to confirm that every item/person is included). Formality: neutral; can be used in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Tous les employés, sans exception, doivent assister.
native_language_example: All employees, without exception, must attend.

meaning: without doing (something); without making (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is done 'without' performing an action. Usually followed by an infinitive verb: 'sans faire + [infinitive]'. Common in written and spoken French. Can also appear before a noun when implying 'without making' (e.g. 'sans faire de bruit' = 'without making noise').
target_language_example: Il est parti sans faire de bruit.
native_language_example: He left without making a noise.

meaning: definitely / without fail; be sure to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to insist that something must happen or be done; equivalent to 'for sure' or 'no excuses'. Common in commands or promises. Tone can be firm but not necessarily rude. Literally 'without mistake'.
target_language_example: Tu dois venir sans faute demain matin.
native_language_example: You must come tomorrow morning without fail.

meaning: polite refusal or downplaying; 'no thanks' / 'don't bother' / 'it's nothing special'.
additional_notes: Common informal-to-neutral phrase used to refuse offers politely or to modestly downplay a compliment or invitation. Tone and context determine meaning: often equivalent to 'no thanks' (declining something) or 'don't make a fuss'/'it's nothing' (minimizing). Can be used alone or with merci. Not rude but casual; you may hear it in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Non merci, sans façon.
native_language_example: No thanks, I don't need that.

meaning: 'endless' or 'never-ending'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that has no end or seems to continue indefinitely. Can be literal (something truly endless) or figurative (an ongoing process, repetitive action). Often placed after the noun (la guerre sans fin) or before as a short phrase (Sans fin.).
target_language_example: Cette tâche semble sans fin.
native_language_example: This task seems endless.

meaning: not interesting; of no interest; pointless.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that does not hold attention, is boring, or is irrelevant/useless in a given context. Can be used as a full sentence (Sans intérêt.) or follow nouns (un argument sans intérêt). Tone is neutral to slightly dismissive. Not idiomatic — literal meaning matches the English phrase.
target_language_example: Ce film est sans intérêt, on peut partir.
native_language_example: This movie is not interesting; we can leave.

meaning: without the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Combine the preposition sans (without) with the definite article le. Used before masculine singular nouns: e.g. sans le sel, sans le guide. In spoken French, articles sometimes contract or are omitted in particular expressions, but standard written form keeps both words. For feminine use say «sans la», for plural «sans les», and for indefinite use often «sans un/une» is possible.
target_language_example: Il est parti sans le parapluie.
native_language_example: He left without the umbrella.

meaning: penniless; having no money.
additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning to be broke. Used to describe someone who has no or very little money. Common in spoken and written French. Literal words: 'without the penny' but it's idiomatic.
target_language_example: Après la faillite, il était sans le sou.
native_language_example: After the bankruptcy, he was penniless.

meaning: 'without my' (feminine singular possessive)
additional_notes: Combination of the preposition 'sans' (without) + the possessive adjective 'ma' (my, used before feminine singular nouns). Use before a feminine noun: e.g. 'sans ma carte' = 'without my card'. Note that spoken French often contracts or changes word order, but 'sans ma' remains two separate words. For masculine nouns use 'sans mon', for plural use 'sans mes'.
target_language_example: Je suis parti sans ma valise.
native_language_example: I left without my suitcase.

meaning: speechless; without words (literally 'without word')
additional_notes: Used to describe being so surprised, shocked, moved, or stunned that one has no words. Often appears in expressions like «rester sans mot» (to be left speechless). Can be followed by «devant» + noun (e.g. «sans mot devant tant de beauté») or used alone: «Je suis sans mot.»
target_language_example: Je suis resté sans mot devant la scène.
native_language_example: I was left speechless in front of the scene.

meaning: without saying a word; silently.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone leaving, departing, or acting without speaking or explaining — often implies abruptness or silence. It's a fixed expression (not formal or slang). Can be used with verbs of leaving or disappearance.
target_language_example: Elle est partie sans mot dire.
native_language_example: She left without saying a word.

meaning: without even saying (used to emphasize that someone didn't say something expected, e.g. 'without even saying goodbye').
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a short phrase or word (e.g. 'au revoir', 'bonjour'). Used to emphasize surprise or disappointment that the expected speech did not occur. Structure: 'sans même' + infinitive (dire). 'Sans même' can be used with other verbs: 'sans même regarder', 'sans même répondre'.
target_language_example: Elle est partie sans même dire merci.
native_language_example: She left without even saying thank you.

meaning: without us
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or applies excluding the speaker and their group. Can be literal (physically without) or figurative (not involving/including us). Often appears in everyday conversation and writing. Pronunciation: [sɑ̃ nu].
target_language_example: Ils commencent la réunion sans nous.
native_language_example: They start the meeting without us.

meaning: without thinking; instinctively, automatically.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without deliberate thought or reflection (equivalent to 'without thinking' or 'without considering'). Can describe quick actions or remarks made instinctively. Often followed by a verb (e.g. 'il a réagi sans penser').
target_language_example: Elle a répondu sans penser et l'a regretté ensuite.
native_language_example: She answered without thinking and regretted it afterward.

meaning: 'without problem' — meaning 'no problem', 'no trouble', or 'easily'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is easy, possible, or causes no difficulty. Can be a short reply equivalent to 'no problem' or 'you're welcome' in informal speech. Neutral register — appropriate in most contexts.
target_language_example: Je peux t'aider sans problème.
native_language_example: I can help you, no problem.

meaning: 'no hard feelings' or 'no grudges'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you hold no grudge after an argument, mistake, or awkward situation. Can be said sincerely or lightheartedly. Common in spoken and written French; often used alone as a short phrase. Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: D'accord, tu as pris ma place — sans rancune ?
native_language_example: Okay, you took my seat — no hard feelings?

meaning: 'without you' (informal/colloquial contraction of 'sans toi')
additional_notes: This is not standard written French. It appears in casual speech or informal writing where 'toi' (you, object form) is reduced to 'te' after 'sans'—but grammatically 'sans' takes the disjunctive pronoun 'toi' (sans toi). Use 'sans toi' in formal writing. You may hear 'sans te' in fast spoken phrases (e.g., 'J'ai fait ça sans te demander') meaning 'I did that without asking you,' though many speakers would instead say 'sans te le dire' or 'sans te demander.'
target_language_example: Il est parti sans te prévenir.
native_language_example: He left without warning you.

meaning: without your (plural or familiar) — used before a plural/familiar noun.
additional_notes: Combines the preposition sans (without) + the possessive tes (your, used for plural or familiar objects). Use tes when the thing belongs to the person you address and is plural (tes lunettes, tes conseils, tes clés, tes copains). Common in everyday spoken and written French. Note: tes is second-person singular familiar (tu) possession; for formal/plural you would use vos (sans vos).
target_language_example: Sans tes lunettes, tu ne vois pas bien le tableau.
native_language_example: Without your glasses, you can't see the board well.

meaning: without tone; lacking tone or intonation (literal) / without your tone (colloquial, depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'sans' = without and 'ton' = tone or your (informal possessive). Alone, 'sans ton' is unusual without context. It can mean 'without tone' (e.g., speaking without vocal intonation or a lack of color/tone in art) or, if followed by a noun like 'avis' (sans ton avis), could be interpreted as 'without your...' though standard French would use 'sans ton + noun'. Be careful: 'ton' can also be the informal possessive 'your' (tu). For 'without you' you would say 'sans toi'.
target_language_example: Il a répondu sans ton, presque plat et monotone.
native_language_example: He answered without tone, almost flat and monotone.

meaning: 'without a' or 'without any' (used before a masculine singular noun or in fixed expressions like 'sans un bruit' = 'without a sound').
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'sans' (without) + 'un' (a). Common in French to mean 'without a/any' before a noun; often used in set phrases (e.g. 'sans un bruit' = 'without a sound', 'sans un mot' = 'without a word'). Context determines whether it feels indefinite ('without any') or literal ('without a').
target_language_example: Il est parti sans un adieu.
native_language_example: He left without a goodbye.

meaning: 'shamelessly' or 'without shame/embarrassment'.
additional_notes: Used to describe actions done openly without guilt, modesty, or embarrassment. Often modifies verbs (e.g., 'faire quelque chose sans vergogne'). Can be critical or disapproving. Formality: neutral to slightly literary; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il mentait sans vergogne devant tout le monde.
native_language_example: He lied shamelessly in front of everyone.

meaning: 'speechless' or 'unable to speak' (because of shock, surprise, amazement, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to describe being so surprised, shocked, amazed, or stunned that you cannot speak. Common in both singular and plural (tout le monde était sans voix). Can be used in present, past (je suis resté sans voix), or with verbs like rester/laisser. Not literal (not about lacking a voice).
target_language_example: À la vue du cadeau, je suis resté sans voix.
native_language_example: At the sight of the gift, I was left speechless.

meaning: without that; otherwise / apart from that (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'without that'. Can mean 'without that (thing/person)' when talking about removing or excluding something. In conversational French it is also used like 'sinon' or 'otherwise' to introduce a consequence or alternative: e.g. 'Sans ça, ça ira' = 'Other than that, it'll be fine.' Context determines whether it's literal (excluding an object) or transitional (meaning 'otherwise').
target_language_example: J'ai tout préparé, sans ça on ne peut pas partir.
native_language_example: I prepared everything; otherwise we can't leave.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment (literally 'health is').
additional_notes: This string 'santé est' is not a common multi-word expression in French. Alone it reads as the noun 'santé' (health) followed by the verb 'est' (is) and would normally be part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'La santé est importante' — 'Health is important'). If you encounter it, check the surrounding words — it's probably an incomplete clause or a typo.
target_language_example: La santé est importante pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Health is important for everyone.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; literally 'health is more' or 'health is greater'. Interpreted word-by-word: 'santé' = 'health', 'est' = 'is', 'plus' = 'more' (or 'no longer' in negative contexts).
additional_notes: This sequence on its own is uncommon and sounds unnatural without additional words. A learner will more often see phrases like 'la santé est importante' (health is important) or comparative constructions such as 'la santé est plus importante que...' (health is more important than...). Be careful: 'plus' without negation means 'more'; with negation ('ne...plus') it means 'no longer'. If you must use these words together, include context (e.g. 'La santé est plus importante que l’argent').
target_language_example: La santé est plus importante que l’argent.
native_language_example: Health is more important than money.

meaning: literally 'health and' — a fragment used when listing 'health and ...' (e.g., 'santé et bien-être'); not a standalone phrase.
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself. You'll see 'santé et' as the first part of compound terms or headings (santé et sécurité, santé et bien-être, santé et prévention). Translate the whole phrase (health and safety, health and well-being). Do not use 'santé et' alone in a sentence.
target_language_example: santé et sécurité au travail
native_language_example: health and safety at work

meaning: 'fir of' / 'fir tree of' — a partial phrase used before a noun to describe something made from or related to a fir tree (e.g., sapin de Noël = Christmas tree).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; sapin means 'fir' or 'fir tree'. In French compounds it commonly appears as 'sapin de Noël' (Christmas tree) or 'sapin de ...' to indicate origin/material/association. Use with a following noun (e.g., 'sapin de Noël', 'sapin de montagne').
target_language_example: Nous avons acheté un sapin de Noël en vente ce week-end.
native_language_example: We bought a Christmas tree on sale this weekend.

meaning: Christmas tree.
additional_notes: Refers to the decorated tree used at Christmas. Can mean a real fir/tree or an artificial one. Commonly used with verbs like installer/monter (set up), décorer, acheter. Noël is capitalized.
target_language_example: Nous avons acheté un sapin de Noël et nous l'avons décoré ce week-end.
native_language_example: We bought a Christmas tree and decorated it this weekend.

meaning: except the / except for the (feminine singular noun following).
additional_notes: Sauf means 'except' or 'except for'. When followed by a feminine singular noun or a feminine noun phrase, you'll often see 'sauf la' (e.g. 'sauf la pluie', 'sauf la première forme'). Use 'sauf le' for masculine singular, 'sauf les' for plural. Can be used with abstract nouns (la peur) or concrete items. Word order: 'tout est ... sauf la ...' or 'on avait tout prévu sauf la pluie.'
target_language_example: Ils ont tout mangé sauf la salade.
native_language_example: They ate everything except the salad.

meaning: but / except that (introduces a contrast or objection)
additional_notes: Used to contrast a previous statement, to point out an exception, problem, or correction. Often spoken and common in conversation. Can be followed by a full clause or a short interjection (e.g., "Sauf que quoi ?" = "But what?" or "Except that what?").
target_language_example: Je voulais accepter son aide, sauf que je ne voulais pas dépendre de lui.
native_language_example: I wanted to accept his help, but I didn't want to depend on him.

meaning: 'unless' or 'except if'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception or condition that cancels the previous statement. Equivalent to 'unless' in English; often placed before a clause. Can be followed by a subject and verb (e.g. 'sauf si tu viens').
target_language_example: Je viendrai au dîner, sauf si je tombe malade.
native_language_example: I'll come to dinner unless I get sick.

meaning: except one / except for one
additional_notes: Used to exclude a single person or thing from a general statement. 'Sauf' means 'except' or 'except for'; when followed by 'un' it specifies that only one is excluded. Word order: 'sauf un' usually comes after the noun or clause it modifies (e.g., 'Tous sont venus, sauf un.').
target_language_example: Ils ont tous répondu, sauf un.
native_language_example: They all replied, except one.

meaning: polite formula meaning 'with all due respect' (used before disagreeing or giving a contrary opinion).
additional_notes: Used to soften disagreement or criticism; often placed at the start of a sentence. Formal/polite register. Can be used alone as a brief preface. Less common in very casual speech.
target_language_example: Sauf votre respect, je pense que ce n'est pas la meilleure solution.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I think that's not the best solution.

meaning: to be obvious; to stand out (visually or noticeably).
additional_notes: Used to say that something immediately catches attention or is easy to notice. Often appears in impersonal constructions like "ça saute aux yeux" ("it's obvious") or with past tense "ça lui a sauté aux yeux" ("it struck him/her"). Literal image: "to jump to the eyes."
target_language_example: Ça saute aux yeux que le tableau n'a pas été retouché.
native_language_example: It's obvious that the painting wasn't retouched.

meaning: past participle 'sauté' (from sauter = to jump/skip) used with 'par' to indicate the agent in a passive construction or to indicate something was skipped/omitted by someone — e.g. '...was jumped by', '...was skipped by'. Context determines whether it means physically jumped over, omitted, or figuratively bypassed. Remember past participle agreement when used with être.
additional_notes: 'Sauté par' is compositional: 'sauté' + 'par'. It commonly appears in passive voice (La porte a été sautée par le voleur) or in contexts meaning 'skipped/omitted by' (Une étape a été sautée par l'équipe). Agreement: when the past participle is used with être, it agrees in gender and number with the subject (sauté, sautée, sautés, sautées). With avoir, agreement depends on preceding direct object. Register: neutral; can be used in both formal and informal contexts depending on overall sentence.
target_language_example: Une étape importante a été sautée par l'équipe.
native_language_example: An important step was skipped by the team.

meaning: 'to save the' (masculine singular direct object)
additional_notes: This is the verb sauver (to save, rescue) followed by the definite article le, used before a masculine singular noun: sauver le chien (to save the dog), sauver le projet (to save the project). Conjugate sauver as needed: il sauve le..., nous avons sauvé le... If the noun begins with a vowel or mute h, le becomes l' (sauver l'arbre).
target_language_example: Ils veulent sauver le village.
native_language_example: They want to save the village.

meaning: saved the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'sauvé' (saved) followed by the definite article 'le' and a masculine noun. It appears in sentences describing someone rescuing or preserving someone/something. In spoken French you might hear the passé composé with 'avoir' (Il a sauvé...). The object after 'le' is typically a person or thing being rescued (le garçon, le roi, le vaisseau).
target_language_example: Elle a sauvé le chat coincé dans l'arbre.
native_language_example: She saved the cat stuck in the tree.

meaning: 'I/you/he/she didn't know that you...' (colloquial/incomplete clause)
additional_notes: This phrase is an informal fragment using the imperfect tense negative (ne is often dropped in speech). It appears mid-sentence to express surprise or new information about the person addressed (vous). Context needed to complete the idea (e.g. 'je ne savais pas que vous étiez là' = I didn't know you were here). In spoken French, speakers often omit 'je' and the 'ne'.
target_language_example: Je ne savais pas que vous étiez médecin.
native_language_example: I didn't know that you were a doctor.

meaning: 'I knew that it/this/that...' (past tense: I knew that ...).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form of 'savoir' (tu/je savais) plus 'que' and the contracted 'c'' from 'ce' before a vowel (c'était = it/that was). Common in sentences expressing that someone already suspected or was certain about something in the past. Contraction 'c'' is used before verbs starting with a vowel or mute h (c'était, c'est, c'était). Replace subject (je/tu/il...) as needed: 'Je savais que c'était...' = 'I knew that it was...'; 'Comment tu savais que c'était moi ?' = 'How did you know it was me?'.
target_language_example: Je savais que c'était dangereux, mais je l'ai fait quand même.
native_language_example: I knew that it was dangerous, but I did it anyway.

meaning: part of a sentence meaning 'did (you) know that this/that...'; from 'savoir que ce...' used to introduce information someone might already know or be surprised by
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's a fragment combining the verb 'savais' (you knew / did you know) with 'que ce' ('that this/that'). You'll usually see it in full sentences like 'Tu savais que ce film est basé sur une histoire vraie ?' or in questions 'Savais-tu que ce... ?' For formal written French use 'savais-vous' (vous) or 'saviez-vous' in questions. Word order can change: 'Savais-tu que...' (inversion) or 'Tu savais que...?' (informal).
target_language_example: Tu savais que ce livre a été adapté au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Did you know that this book was adapted into a movie?

meaning: knew who
additional_notes: A past-tense phrase: 'savais' is the imperfect of 'savoir' (I knew / you knew depending on subject). In examples here it pairs with 'qui' to mean 'knew who (someone was / someone was looking for)'. Context determines the subject (je savais = I knew; tu savais = you knew). Commonly followed by a clause introduced by a verb (e.g. cherchait/cherchaient/étiez).
target_language_example: Je savais qui avait la clé.
native_language_example: I knew who had the key.

meaning: didn't know / didn't know how to (past).
additional_notes: Informal negative past of savoir (imparfait + pas). Used to say someone lacked knowledge or ability in the past, or didn't know what to do/say. Can be followed by an infinitive (savait pas nager), a subordinate question (savait pas quoi dire), or a clause. In written/neuter register you may see "ne savait pas" (full negation) rather than dropping "ne"; dropping "ne" is common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Il ne savait pas conduire quand il a acheté la voiture.
native_language_example: He didn't know how to drive when he bought the car.

meaning: 'you know well' or a polite/insisting way to say 'you know' (formal/plural).
additional_notes: From the verb savoir (to know). 'Savez' is the 2nd-person plural/formal present (vous savez). 'Savez bien' is used to emphasize that the listener is already aware of something or to remind them — equivalent to 'you do know'/'as you know'. Often appears in conversations or arguments. With a single person in informal speech, use 'sais bien' (tu sais bien).
target_language_example: Vous savez bien que je n'ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: You know very well that I don't have the time.

meaning: 'do you know what we/one/they ...' — used to introduce a question or suggestion about what to do or what is said.
additional_notes: Short for 'savez-vous ce que l'on ...' or 'tu sais ce qu'on ...'. 'On' is an impersonal or familiar subject that often means 'we', 'people', or 'they' depending on context. This phrase commonly starts questions like 'savez ce qu'on devrait faire ?' (do you know what we should do?) or statements like 'Vous savez ce qu'on dit.' (you know what people say). Formal version: 'savez-vous ce que l'on ...'.
target_language_example: Savez ce qu'on doit faire ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you know what we should do tonight?

meaning: 'do you know what it is' (short for 'savez ce que c'est')
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used to ask if someone recognizes or understands something. Often contracted in speech to 'savez ce que c'est' or shortened further ('savez ce que c'...') before a pause. Can be used as a tag question ('vous savez ce que c'est, non?') or in past tense ('vous savez ce que c'était?'). Useful for pointing at things or checking shared knowledge.
target_language_example: Vous savez ce que c'est, un code rouge?
native_language_example: Do you know what it is, a red code?

meaning: You know what I... / Do you know what I... (used to introduce something the speaker will say about themselves).
additional_notes: A conversational opener meaning “Do you know what I…” or “You know what I…”. Often appears as 'Vous savez ce que j'ai…', 'Vous savez ce que j'aime…' etc. Common in spoken or informal contexts to draw attention before telling a story, opinion, discovery, or personal fact. The full form requires a verb after 'j'' (j'ai, j'aime, j'aimerais, etc.). 'Vous' can be replaced by 'tu' in informal speech: 'Tu sais ce que j'ai…'.
target_language_example: Vous savez ce que j'ai découvert hier ?
native_language_example: You know what I discovered yesterday?

meaning: literally 'know what you' — used to start a clause meaning 'you know what (you) ...' or in questions/remarks 'do you know what you are/are saying/are doing?'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the start of sentences like «vous savez ce que vous faites/sayez» meaning 'you know what you're doing/ saying'. Often used in questions to challenge or ask for confirmation. Word order may change in casual speech (e.g., «vous savez ce que vous dites?»). It requires a verb or clause after it (faites, dites, demandez, rappelez, êtes...).
target_language_example: Vous savez ce que vous faites quand vous touchez ce bouton?
native_language_example: Do you know what you're doing when you touch that button?

meaning: do you know what that/it (means/does/implies)?
additional_notes: This is a spoken/informal fragment used in questions: full forms often add verbs like "veut dire", "signifie", "fait", or "implique" (e.g. "Vous savez ce que ça veut dire ?"). Polite/formal version uses "Savez-vous" instead of "Vous savez". "ça" refers to something just mentioned (that/it).
target_language_example: Vous savez ce que ça veut dire ?
native_language_example: Do you know what that means?

meaning: do you know what
additional_notes: A conversational phrase using the 2nd-person plural/formal form of 'savoir' (savez) followed by 'ce qui' ('what' / 'that which'). Often appears in questions: 'Vous savez ce qui... ?' meaning 'Do you know what...?' In spoken French the subject 'vous' may be dropped when context is clear (e.g. 'Savez ce qui s'est passé ?'). Use 'sais ce qui' with 'tu' for informal singular: 'Tu sais ce qui... ?'.
target_language_example: Savez ce qui se passe ici ?
native_language_example: Do you know what is happening here?

meaning: do you know how (to...)
additional_notes: From the verb savoir (to know) + comment (how). Used in questions (savez comment...?) to ask if someone knows how to do something. In informal speech the tu form (sais comment) or inverted/est-ce que forms may be used. Can also appear without an explicit verb afterward when context makes the action clear: "Savez comment?" meaning "Do you know how?"
target_language_example: Savez comment utiliser cette application ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to use this app?

meaning: 'do you know what' or 'do you know about what' (used to ask if someone knows about something, to introduce information, or rhetorically before giving news).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as part of questions like « vous savez de quoi je parle ? » or to preface a statement. Ensure pronoun/verb agreement: « vous savez » (formal/plural) vs « tu sais » (informal/singular). Can be used rhetorically: « Savez de quoi ? » to prompt explanation. Often followed by « je parle » or a clause explaining the topic.
target_language_example: Savez de quoi je parle ?
native_language_example: Do you know what I'm talking about?

meaning: do you know where
additional_notes: Informal spoken short form of a question using the verb savoir (vous form) + où. Often appears at the start or middle of a question: « Savez où est la gare ? » = « Do you know where the train station is? ». In casual speech speakers may drop the subject or rearrange word order (e.g. « Vous savez où… ? »). Use intonation or a question mark to indicate it's a question.
target_language_example: Savez où se trouve la pharmacie ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the pharmacy is?

meaning: 'do you know where one/we/they' or more naturally 'do you know where (we/one/they) ...?'
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase built from the verb savoir (savez = you know, formal/plural) + où (where) + on (one/we/people). Common in questions: 'Savez où on peut acheter ça ?' = 'Do you know where we can buy that?' 'On' is often used instead of 'nous' in spoken French. Depending on context, 'savez' can be polite (vous form) or plural.
target_language_example: Savez où on prend le bus pour la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where we catch the bus to the station?

meaning: you know that I
additional_notes: This is part of the expression formed with the verb savoir (vous savez / tu sais) + que + subject pronoun + verb. Alone 'savez que je' is incomplete; common uses: 'vous savez que je...' (you know that I...), or in a question 'vous savez que je... ?' (do you know that I...?). 'Savez' is the second-person plural/formal present form of 'savoir'. For informal singular use, say 'tu sais que je...'.
target_language_example: Vous savez que je peux vous aider.
native_language_example: You know that I can help you.

meaning: literally “know that you”; used as part of the verb savoir with the pronoun vous — commonly appears in sentences/questions like “Savez que vous ...” or in inverted/question form “Savez-vous que ...?” to mean “Do you know that you ...?” or in statements when reordered as “Vous savez que ...”
additional_notes: This exact word sequence (savez que vous) is less common in standard neutral word order because French usually places the pronoun adjacent to the verb (e.g., savez-vous) or uses Vous savez que ... When encountered, it may appear in longer sentences or spoken registers where que introduces a clause and vous is the subject of a following verb. It reflects the verb savoir (to know) with second-person plural/polite singular (vous).
target_language_example: Il faudrait que vous sachiez, mais savez que vous n’êtes pas seul ?
native_language_example: You should know, but do you know that you are not alone?

meaning: know-it-all
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who acts as if they know everything. Often used informally and can be pejorative. Literally from 'savoir' (to know) + 'tout' (everything). Can appear after a noun (un/une) as 'un/une savez-tout' but more common is 'monsieur/madame je-sais-tout' or 'un/une qui sait tout'.
target_language_example: Ne sois pas un savez tout, laisse les autres parler.
native_language_example: Don't be a know-it-all, let others speak.

meaning: 'do you know what' (start of a question: ask if someone knows what something is or what will happen).
additional_notes: This is the informal/question form using the verb savoir (vous form). It often begins a question like "Savez à quoi/à quoi ça sert?" or "Savez à quoi il pense?" In spoken French you may also hear "tu sais à quoi" (informal singular) or the inversion "Savez-vous à quoi..." (more formal). Followed by a clause introduced by "à quoi" (what for/what) or by "ça sert", "il sert", etc.
target_language_example: Savez à quoi sert cette machine ?
native_language_example: Do you know what this machine is for?

meaning: know what I
additional_notes: This is a clipped beginning of phrases like «savoir ce que j'ai…», «savoir ce que j'en pense…». It means 'to know what I…' and is followed by a verb or object (e.g. ai fait, ai vu, en pense). Used in questions: «Tu veux savoir ce que j'ai fait ?» = 'Do you want to know what I did?'. In spoken French the final vowel/consonant after j' depends on the following word (j'ai, j'en).
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir ce que j'ai dit ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know what I said?

meaning: to find out what (is/has) happened; to know what the situation is
additional_notes: Used to express wanting to learn the facts or the state of something. Often followed by past participle or another verb (e.g., « arrivé ») to ask what happened. Common in questions and statements of curiosity or concern.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce qui est arrivé hier soir.
native_language_example: I want to find out what happened last night.

meaning: 'to know how much' or 'to know how many' (to want or have the information about an amount or number).
additional_notes: Used when asking or stating that someone wants/has information about a quantity (amount, price) or number of items. Context determines whether it means 'how much' (amount/price) or 'how many' (count). Common in questions: «Je voudrais savoir combien ça coûte» (I would like to know how much it costs) or «Je veux savoir combien vous êtes» (I want to know how many of you there are).
target_language_example: Je voudrais savoir combien ça coûte avant d'acheter.
native_language_example: I would like to know how much it costs before buying.

meaning: to know how I (do/know/feel/etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase begins questions or clauses asking someone if they want to know the way something is done or the speaker's state or reason (e.g. how I know, how I got them, how I feel). The verb after 'je' changes the exact meaning: 'savoir comment je le sais' = how I know it; 'savoir comment je me sens' = how I feel. Common in spoken and written French for introducing an explanation.
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir comment je l'ai appris ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know how I learned it?

meaning: to know about (something) / to have heard of or have information concerning someone or something.
additional_notes: savoir is the verb 'to know' (facts, information, how to do something). The sequence 'savoir de' is less common as a standalone fixed phrase than constructions like 'savoir que', 'savoir de quoi', or 'savoir parler'. When 'savoir' is followed by 'de' it usually introduces a noun phrase meaning 'to know about' or 'to have heard of' (e.g. 'savoir de lui', 'savoir de cette affaire'). In many cases French prefers 'savoir quelque chose', 'savoir que...', 'en savoir sur...', or 'avoir entendu parler de...' depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais savoir de cette affaire avant de prendre une décision.
native_language_example: I would like to know about this matter before making a decision.

meaning: to be grateful to someone for something; to appreciate (someone doing something).
additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal expression used to indicate gratitude or to make a courteous request. Commonly used in constructions like «je vous saurais gré de + infinitive» (I would be grateful if you would...). Emphasizes appreciation more than casual thanks; appropriate in formal letters or requests.
target_language_example: Je sais gré à Pierre de son aide.
native_language_example: I am grateful to Pierre for his help.

meaning: 'to know more' or 'to find out more'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with the preposition en or sur: 'en savoir plus (sur...)' = to learn more about (something). Often appears in questions or invitations (e.g. 'Tu veux en savoir plus ?') and in short phrases like 'Pour en savoir plus' (For more information).
target_language_example: Si tu veux en savoir plus, demande-lui.
native_language_example: If you want to know more, ask him/her.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete form (possibly intended: 'savoir quelque chose' = 'to know something' or 's'en savoir plus' etc.).
additional_notes: There is no common French expression 'savoir quelque' by itself. Beginners probably mean 'savoir quelque chose' (to know something) or constructions like 'quelque chose' (something) combined with 'savoir' as a verb: 'savoir quelque chose'. If you see 'savoir' followed by 'quelque', check whether 'quelque' is followed by a noun (e.g. 'quelque chose', 'quelque part') or whether the speaker meant 'savoir que' (to know that).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir quelque chose sur ton voyage.
native_language_example: I want to know something about your trip.

meaning: literally 'to know who I...' — an incomplete phrase used when starting a clause about someone's identity or role
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression; it's the beginning of a clause (e.g. «savoir qui je suis», «savoir qui je suis vraiment»). You need a verb or complement after it (most commonly 'suis'). Alone it is incomplete and will sound unfinished. Typical use: 'faire savoir qui je suis' (to make who I am known) or 'savoir qui je suis' (to know who I am).
target_language_example: Elle veut savoir qui je suis.
native_language_example: She wants to know who I am.

meaning: to know who (has/had) you — used as part of phrases like "know who helped you" or "know who called you"
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete sentence on its own; it's the beginning of clauses such as "savoir qui vous a appelé" (to know who called you) or "savoir qui vous a aidé" (to know who helped you). The auxiliary verb following "a" (usually a past participle) determines tense and meaning. Formality is neutral.
target_language_example: Je voudrais savoir qui vous a appelé hier soir.
native_language_example: I would like to know who called you last night.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; literally 'to know a' but incomplete — likely a fragment missing a noun or clause.
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'savoir une' by itself. 'Savoir' (to know) is usually followed by a clause (savoir que...), an infinitive (savoir + infinitive = to know how to...), or a full noun phrase (savoir une chose). If you encounter 'savoir une' in text, it's probably truncated or a typo. For learners, prefer patterns like 'savoir que...' (to know that...), 'savoir + infinitive' (to know how to ...), and use 'connaître' for familiarity with people/places.
target_language_example: Il ne suffit pas de savoir une chose, il faut aussi la comprendre.
native_language_example: It is not enough to know one thing, you must also understand it.

meaning: to know how to handle a situation; to be skillful or tactful in a particular context (socially or practically)
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's ability, tact, or practical skill. Often followed by a context (e.g., avec les enfants, en cuisine) or used alone. Literal parts: 'savoir' = to know, 'y' = there/it, 'faire' = to do — the phrase is idiomatic as a whole.
target_language_example: Elle sait y faire en public.
native_language_example: She knows how to handle herself in public.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; 'savoir' (to know) can appear before the preposition 'à' when followed by a complement (e.g. savoir à qui, savoir à quoi). 'savoir à' alone is incomplete and should be completed by a question word or noun phrase.
additional_notes: Use 'savoir' to mean 'to know' (facts, information, or how to do something). It commonly combines with other words: - savoir que + clause = to know that - savoir comment/quoi/pourquoi = to know how/what/why - savoir + infinitive = to know how to (faire) - savoir à qui / à quoi / à quel point = to know to whom / what / to what extent. The sequence 'savoir à' must be followed by a complement; by itself it is not a complete expression.
target_language_example: Je voudrais savoir à qui s'adresse cette lettre avant de répondre.
native_language_example: I would like to know to whom this letter is addressed before replying.

meaning: we all know the (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: Literally 'we know all the...' Used before a noun to say that something is commonly known by everyone. It’s the plural first-person present of 'savoir' + 'tous les' (masculine plural). You will usually see it with a masculine plural noun after it: e.g. 'savons tous les risques'. For feminine or mixed groups you might see 'nous savons tous' or 'nous savons toutes les' depending on agreement and structure. In casual speech 'on sait tous' can also be used.
target_language_example: Nous savons tous les conséquences de cette décision.
native_language_example: We all know the consequences of this decision.

meaning: science fiction (genre: stories about imagined future science, technology, space, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a noun (feminine: la science-fiction). Can refer to the genre in books, films, TV. Often shortened to 'SF' in writing or speech. Pronounced like English but written with a hyphen in French.
target_language_example: Elle adore la science-fiction et regarde des films futuristes.
native_language_example: She loves science fiction and watches futuristic movies.

meaning: 'scene of' or 'scene from' (used to refer to a specific part/scene of something, often a film, play or event).
additional_notes: Usually appears before a noun to indicate which scene is being talked about (scène du film = scene from the film; scène du crime = scene of the crime). The article that follows can change (scène du, de la, des) depending on the gender/number of the noun. Common collocations: "la scène du film", "la scène du crime", "la scène du spectacle."
target_language_example: Regarde la scène du film où ils se retrouvent.
native_language_example: Look at the scene from the movie where they meet again.

meaning: 'to leave' / 'to go away' (informal)
additional_notes: Colloquial pronominal verb used to say someone leaves or escapes quickly. Often implies leaving abruptly, sneaking off, or leaving to avoid something. Conjugates like a regular pronominal verb (je me barre, il s'est barré). Tone can be rude or familiar depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vais me barrer avant que ça dégénère.
native_language_example: I'm going to take off before this gets out of hand.

meaning: to brush (one's own teeth, hair, etc.) — a reflexive verb meaning to groom oneself
additional_notes: Used with a body part introduced by a definite article (e.g., se brosser les dents, se brosser les cheveux). Conjugated reflexively (je me brosse, tu te brosses, il/elle se brosse, nous nous brossons, vous vous brossez, ils/elles se brossent). Common collocations: se brosser les dents, se brosser les cheveux. Can be preceded by verbs or expressions (commencer à se brosser, devoir se brosser, savoir comment se brosser).
target_language_example: Il sait comment se brosser les dents.
native_language_example: He knows how to brush his teeth.

meaning: to break (oneself); used for accidentally fracturing or seriously injuring a body part (e.g., se casser la jambe = to break one's leg). Informally can also mean 'to leave' or 'to get hurt' in exclamations.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb. Commonly followed by a definite article + body part (se casser la jambe, le bras, la cheville, etc.). The informal 'to leave' sense (Il s'est cassé) is common in spoken French. Context determines whether it refers to a physical injury or leaving.
target_language_example: Comment a-t-il pu se casser ?
native_language_example: How could he have broken himself? / How could he have hurt himself?

meaning: 'to say to oneself' or 'to tell oneself' (to think or consider internally); also used impersonally/passively as 'it is said' or 'people say'.
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: subject directs thought or remark at themselves (e.g., 'Je me dis...'). In impersonal/passive-like uses, 'Il se dit que...' means 'People say that...' or 'It is said that...'. Common in spoken and written French. Can be followed by a clause ('se dire que...') or an infinitive ('se dire de...') depending on context.
target_language_example: Parfois, il aime se dire qu'il a fait le bon choix.
native_language_example: Sometimes he likes to tell himself that he made the right choice.

meaning: is said in (a language or expression); is expressed as
additional_notes: Used to indicate how something is expressed or named in a particular language or form. Often follows a noun or phrase: « X se dit en + langue » (X is said/translated in [language] as...). Common in questions and explanations: « Comment se dit... en français ? ». Formality: neutral/common.
target_language_example: Le mot « ordinateur » se dit en français.
native_language_example: The word "ordinateur" is said in French.

meaning: to give oneself / to make oneself (do something) — used reflexively to mean to put in effort, to allow oneself, or to arrange/meet (depending on context).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb with several senses: 1) se donner les moyens de = to give oneself the means / to do what is necessary (make an effort) to achieve something; 2) se donner rendez-vous = to arrange to meet (literally 'give oneself a meeting'); 3) can also mean to allow oneself (se donner du temps = allow oneself time). Context determines meaning. Commonly followed by a noun (les moyens) or rendez-vous, or by an infinitive/prepositional phrase.
target_language_example: Il était satisfait de se donner tous les moyens de réussir dans la vie.
native_language_example: He was satisfied to give himself every means to succeed in life.

meaning: to get ... done to oneself
additional_notes: Often used as se faire + infinitive to mean that something happens to the subject, often something unwanted: se faire filmer = get filmed, se faire écraser = get run over, se faire enfermer = get locked up. With a noun phrase, it can mean doing something to yourself: se faire du mal = hurt yourself.
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas se faire arrêter.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to get arrested.

meaning: 'to get (something) cut' — to have someone cut something for you (often hair, clothes, or a service performed by another).
additional_notes: Pronominal construction indicating that the subject receives an action carried out by someone else. Commonly used for haircuts (se faire couper les cheveux), having fabric cut, or more generally to have a service done by another person. Use with a direct object: se faire couper + les cheveux / la robe / quelque chose. The tense and person of 'faire' determine timing and agreement (e.g., Je me fais couper les cheveux = I'm getting my hair cut).
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux cet après‑midi; je préfère me faire couper par ce coiffeur.
native_language_example: I'm going to get my hair cut this afternoon; I prefer to have this hairdresser cut it for me.

meaning: to get/earn/prepare oneself some (something); to give oneself (something) — used with a noun to indicate acquiring, experiencing, or making something for oneself
additional_notes: A pronominal construction: 'se faire' + article + noun (des = plural indefinite) often means 'to get/earn/receive' (e.g., se faire des amis = to make friends), 'to treat oneself to' or 'to cause oneself' depending on context. The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows. Conjugate 'se' to match the subject (e.g., je me fais, ils se font). 'Se faire des' requires a plural noun after 'des'.
target_language_example: Ils aiment se faire des amis quand ils voyagent.
native_language_example: They like to make friends when they travel.

meaning: 'to get late' (the hour becomes late; used impersonally)
additional_notes: Used impersonally, typically with il or ça (Il se fait tard / Ça se fait tard). Common in spoken and written French to indicate that the time is getting late and it may be time to leave or stop an activity.
target_language_example: Il se fait tard, il se fait tard; il faut y aller.
native_language_example: It's getting late, it's getting late; we need to go.

meaning: 'worries' (literally: 'makes oneself some' — used in 'se faire du souci' = to worry)
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive expression 'se faire du souci' (often conjugated: je me fais, il/elle se fait, nous nous faisons) meaning 'to worry' or 'to be worried about.' Commonly followed by 'pour' or 'à propos de' + person or subject. Use with 'pour' (pour sa santé) or 'à son sujet' (about him/her).
target_language_example: Il se fait du souci pour son examen.
native_language_example: He is worried about his exam.

meaning: 'the fact is that' / 'it so happens that' (used to introduce a fact or explanation).
additional_notes: This fixed phrase often appears in written or spoken French to point out a reason, explanation or surprising fact: «Ce qui se fait, c'est que...». It usually follows a neutral clause and introduces what follows as a fact. It is slightly formal/neutral rather than very casual. It can be part of longer constructions (e.g. «Il se fait que...», «Il se fait que, malheureusement,...»).
target_language_example: Il se fait que j'ai déjà pris un rendez-vous ce jour-là.
native_language_example: It so happens that I already made an appointment that day.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation or fact about what someone does/experiences (≈ 'the thing is that you' / 'it happens that you')
additional_notes: This is a colloquial, somewhat emphatic construction often used in spoken French to present a reason, a surprising fact, or to correct/clarify. It usually appears in contexts like « ce qui se fait, c'est que tu... » or more simply « il se fait que tu... », though the full common phrasing is « il se fait que... » (it happens/it so happens that...). Alone as written, 'se fait que tu' is fragmentary — expect surrounding words (subject or impersonal 'il') in natural speech. Use it to introduce what follows as a current situation or unexpected reality.
target_language_example: Il se fait que tu es la seule personne qui peut nous aider.
native_language_example: It so happens that you are the only person who can help us.

meaning: to not care about; to make fun of / to mock (informal).
additional_notes: Informal and coarse. Depending on context it can mean either 'not care about' (e.g., se foutre de quelque chose = to not give a damn about something) or 'to make fun of / mock' (e.g., se foutre de quelqu'un = to laugh at or ridicule someone). Avoid in formal situations. Appears in conjugated forms like je m'en fous, il s'en fout, or ils se foutent de. Tone and meaning depend on construction and context.
target_language_example: Ils se foutent de ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: They don't care about what you say.

meaning: a short pronoun combination used before a verb or noun phrase; usually part of reflexive or pronominal constructions (literally 'to oneself it/her' or 'to oneself it/them'), often requires more words to show full meaning.
additional_notes: ‘se’ is the reflexive/reciprocal pronoun for il/elle/on/ils/elles and formal you (se). ‘la’ is a direct object pronoun (her/it/that, feminine). Alone 'se la' is incomplete — it appears as part of phrases like 'se la raconter' (to brag), 'se la péter' (informal: to show off), or before a verb: 'se la faire' (to get/beat someone). Meaning depends entirely on the verb or phrase that follows. Register can be informal with idiomatic verbs (e.g., 'se la péter').
target_language_example: Il aime se la raconter devant ses amis.
native_language_example: He likes to brag about it in front of his friends.

meaning: to wash one's hands.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase used to indicate that the subject performs the action on themselves (washing their own hands). Common in instructions, obligations, hygiene contexts and everyday actions. Conjugate the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous/se) to match the subject and adjust auxiliary (être) in compound tenses: e.g., Il/Elle s'est lavé(e) les mains.
target_language_example: Il faut se laver les mains !
native_language_example: You must wash your hands!

meaning: a combination of the reflexive pronoun 'se' + masculine singular direct object pronoun 'le' used before a verb (e.g. 'se le ...') meaning 'to (something) it/himself/herself' or 'to (something) oneself' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's a sequence of two pronouns that appear before a verb in French when both a reflexive pronoun (se) and a masculine singular direct object pronoun (le) are needed. Word order: pronouns come before the conjugated verb (or before an infinitive). In spoken/written French, se + le often becomes 'se le' (e.g. 'il se le demande' is incorrect—correct is 'il se le demande' is rare; more common patterns are 'se le + inf.' like 'je vais me le acheter' → note that with conjugated verbs + infinitive the reflexive pronoun changes to 'me/te/nous/vous' to match subject). Remember that 'se' changes to 's",
target_language_example: Il va se le prendre demain.
native_language_example: He is going to take it for himself tomorrow.

meaning: 'gets up at' (for people) or 'rises at' (for the sun/moon/etc.).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb 'se lever' = to get up / to rise. Use 'se lève à + time' to say when someone gets out of bed or when a celestial body rises. Conjugate 'se lever' to match the subject (je me lève, tu te lèves, il/elle se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils/elles se lèvent). Note spelling change: the stem vowel è appears in all singular and third-person plural forms (je me lève, tu te lèves, il/elle se lève, ils/elles se lèvent).
target_language_example: Elle se lève à sept heures du matin.
native_language_example: She gets up at seven o'clock in the morning.

meaning: to begin (to)
additional_notes: A pronominal verb used with different complements to mean 'start doing something' (se mettre à + infinitive) or 'position oneself'/'get into a state' (se mettre + noun/adjective). Common patterns: se mettre à + infinitive = 'begin to ...'; se mettre + noun/adjective = 'place/put oneself' or 'become (in a state)'. Use the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) that matches the subject.
target_language_example: Il est temps de se mettre à étudier sérieusement.
native_language_example: It's time to start studying seriously.

meaning: to begin to (do something); to start (doing something).
additional_notes: Common pronominal verb phrase used with an infinitive: se mettre à + infinitive = 'to start to [verb]'. Can indicate a deliberate start (Elle s'est mise à étudier) or a change of state (Il s'est mis à pleuvoir = it began to rain). Conjugate 'se mettre' appropriately and keep the infinitive after 'à'.
target_language_example: Il vient de se mettre à neiger.
native_language_example: It has just started to snow.

meaning: to do without (someone/something); to not need or not care about
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: se passer de + [quelque chose/quelqu'un]. In many contexts you will see forms like "il/elle se passe de" meaning "he/she/it does without". With pronouns referring to the thing omitted, use "s'en passer" (e.g., "je m'en passe"). Agreement: the preposition is "de"; when the following article is plural/contracted it becomes "des" (se passe des + [plural noun]). The expression can be neutral or indicate preference/indifference. Watch for register: common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il se passe des vieilles habitudes quand il veut progresser.
native_language_example: He does without old habits when he wants to progress.

meaning: 'a ... happens' or 'is happening (an event)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the pronominal verb construction 'se passer' used impersonally to say that something happens or takes place. Structure: 'Il se passe un + noun' or 'Il se passe quelque chose' = 'There is/There happens a ...'. In spoken French the subject 'Il' is often present: 'Il se passe un événement' or shortened in fast speech, but the full impersonal form normally includes 'il'. Use to describe occurrences or events.
target_language_example: Il se passe un problème avec la connexion.
native_language_example: There is a problem happening with the connection.

meaning: happen; take place
additional_notes: Often used for events or situations. With subjects like ça, quelque chose, or qu'est-ce qui, it usually means "to happen" or "to occur." It can also describe how something goes or unfolds, depending on context.
target_language_example: Quelque chose vient de se passer.
native_language_example: Something just happened.

meaning: to do without; to be able (or not) to go without something or someone.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun introduced by de (se passer de quelque chose / de quelqu'un). Can express necessity (cannot do without: ne pas pouvoir se passer de) or dismissiveness (can easily do without). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Example contexts: personal needs, services, habits. Conjugates reflexively (je me passe de, tu te passes de, il/elle se passe de, nous nous passons de, vous vous passez de, ils/elles se passent de).
target_language_example: Les gens modernes ne peuvent se passer de voitures.
native_language_example: Modern people cannot do without cars.

meaning: to happen (with 'quelque' as part of the construction 'se passer quelque chose' = 'something happens')
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself in French. The usual expression is 'se passer quelque chose' or 'il se passe quelque chose' meaning 'something happens' or 'something is happening'. The direct object (quelque chose, un accident, un problème) follows 'se passer'. Often used impersonally with 'il' (Il se passe...). Do not drop the final 'chose' if you mean 'something'—'se passer quelque' alone is incomplete in normal usage; here 'se passer quelque' is shown as the stem of that construction.
target_language_example: Il se passer quelque chose d'étrange ce soir.
native_language_example: There will happen something strange tonight. (There will be something strange happening tonight.)

meaning: to complain (about something or someone).
additional_notes: Pronominal verb: always appears with a reflexive pronoun (je me plains, tu te plains, il/elle se plaint, nous nous plaignons, vous vous plaignez, ils/elles se plaignent). Can be followed by de + noun or que + clause to indicate what one complains about (se plaindre de quelque chose / se plaindre que ...). Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., customer service).
target_language_example: Il ne fait que se plaindre de son travail.
native_language_example: He does nothing but complain about his job.

meaning: 'to be' or 'to feel' (used to describe someone's state or condition); can also mean 'to fare' or 'to do' (how someone is doing).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used to talk about health, mood, or general condition. Common constructions: "se porter bien/mal" (to be well/ill), "se porter mieux" (to get better). Often appears with an adverb or adjective. Conjugate with the subject (e.g., "je me porte", "il se porte"). Not used for carrying objects (use "porter" without se). Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Se porter bien est important après une maladie ; je veux me porter mieux.
native_language_example: Being well is important after an illness; I want to get better.

meaning: to be possible (rare, formal/literary; reflexive construction used to indicate that something can or cannot happen)
additional_notes: Very uncommon in modern spoken French. More typical alternatives: pouvoir (il peut), cela se peut, être possible. 'Se pouvoir' occurs in fixed or archaic phrases (e.g. « ça ne se peut pas ») and in literary/registered contexts. Use with caution—learners will rarely need it.
target_language_example: Il ne se peut pas que cela se pouvoir ainsi.
native_language_example: It cannot be that this can be so.
