meaning: 'to take' (reflexive) — part of many idiomatic constructions with varied meanings depending on context (e.g. to consider oneself, to get/hit oneself, to be fooled, to get carried away, to end up).
additional_notes: A flexible reflexive form of prendre used only within larger expressions or constructions. Meaning depends on what follows or context: se prendre pour (to consider oneself/pretend to be), se prendre une claque (to get slapped), se prendre au jeu (to get carried away), se prendre (quelque chose) (to get/receive something). Conjugates like prendre but with reflexive pronouns: je me prends, tu te prends, il/elle se prend, nous nous prenons, vous vous prenez, ils/elles se prennent. Alone it is often incomplete; check the rest of the phrase to determine sense.
target_language_example: Il va se prendre une surprise s'il pense que tout est facile.
native_language_example: He will get a surprise if he thinks everything is easy.

meaning: 'to remember' or 'to recall' (reflexive form).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object or with 'de' + noun/pronoun (both are common in speech: se rappeler quelque chose or se rappeler de quelque chose). Indicates the act of bringing something back to mind. Conjugates like a reflexive verb (je me rappelle, il se rappelle). Context and preposition use can vary by region and register.
target_language_example: Il a des difficultés à se rappeler les noms.
native_language_example: He has difficulty remembering names.

meaning: 'to go' or 'to get to' (to travel/arrive somewhere); also 'to surrender' or 'to give oneself up' in another sense.
additional_notes: Common pronominal verb with two main uses: 1) movement: se rendre (à/au/à la/chez) + place = to go/ travel/ get to a place (e.g., se rendre au travail, se rendre à Boston). 2) surrender: se rendre = to give oneself up/surrender (used in military, police or informal contexts). The presence of a destination preposition (à/au/à la/chez) usually indicates the movement meaning; context and tone determine the surrender meaning. Conjugates with reflexive pronouns (je me rends, tu te rends, il/elle se rend, nous nous rendons, vous vous rendez, ils/elles se rendent) and past participle agrees when used pronominally with être (elle s'est rendue).
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à Boston ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get to Boston?

meaning: to stick together, support one another (especially in difficult times).
additional_notes: Idiomatic reflexive expression meaning to unite and help each other. Used for friends, family, coworkers, or communities facing challenges. Not literal (you don't actually squeeze elbows). Often appears with phrases like il faut / c'est le moment de / on doit.
target_language_example: C'est le moment de se serrer les coudes.
native_language_example: It's time to stick together.

meaning: 'to use' (something) or 'to make use of' (also 'to help oneself to' in certain contexts).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb construction: se servir de + noun. Use de before the thing being used (je me sers de mon téléphone). Can also mean 'to help oneself to' (e.g. «Servez‑vous» = 'Help yourself'). Conjugates like servir but reflexive: je me sers, tu te sers, il/elle se sert, nous nous servons, vous vous servez, ils/elles se servent.
target_language_example: Elle aime se servir de son téléphone pour prendre des notes.
native_language_example: She likes to use her phone to take notes.

meaning: to remember; to recall (something).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb: used with de when followed by a noun or pronoun (se souvenir de quelque chose / de quelqu'un). Conjugated with être in compound tenses (e.g., je me suis souvenu(e)). Commonly followed by an object introduced by de (je me souviens de toi). Can be followed by an infinitive to mean 'remember to' in negative or certain contexts (e.g., souviens‑toi de fermer la porte).
target_language_example: Il éprouve des difficultés à se souvenir des noms.
native_language_example: He has difficulty remembering names.

meaning: 'where is my...?' (used to ask the location of something you own)
additional_notes: This is the combination of the reflexive verb se trouver (to be located) and a possessive mon (my). In questions you can invert or use 'Où est mon...' instead; both are natural. Use mon before masculine singular nouns (or before any singular noun starting with a vowel sound). To ask about someone, word order is the same: 'Où se trouve mon ami ?' Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Où se trouve mon portefeuille ?
native_language_example: Where is my wallet?

meaning: to be located; to be found
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone or something is: se trouver quelque part = to be / be found somewhere. With a noun object, it can also mean to find or get something for oneself, as in se trouver un travail or se trouver un appartement. In the location sense, it is usually not translated literally as 'to find oneself'.
target_language_example: Mon livre doit se trouver quelque part dans la chambre.
native_language_example: My book must be somewhere in the room.

meaning: 'see each other at' or 'meet at' (used to say where you'll meet someone).
additional_notes: Common informal way to say you'll meet someone at a place or time. Often used in the impersonal/plural form "On se voit à..." meaning "We'll see each other/See you at..." Can be followed by a location (l'école, la réunion) or a time expression (mon retour). Verb is reflexive (se voir = to see each other).
target_language_example: On se voit à la gare à 18 heures.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the station at 6 PM.

meaning: to shake one's head (usually to say 'no' or show disapproval).
additional_notes: Common physical gesture: moving the head from side to side. Can indicate refusal, disagreement, disbelief, or disapproval. Use with subject: je secoue la tête, il a secoué la tête. For nodding 'yes' use 'hocher la tête'.
target_language_example: Elle secoue la tête quand elle n'est pas d'accord.
native_language_example: She shakes her head when she disagrees.

meaning: in/within (the) heart, center, or midst of; used to indicate membership or location inside something (often figurative).
additional_notes: Sein (masculine) literally means 'breast' or 'bosom' and is used figuratively in expressions like 'au sein de' to mean 'within' or 'at the heart of' an organization, family, group, institution, etc. It is followed by 'de' + noun (e.g. 'au sein de la communauté'). Common fixed form: 'au sein de' (in/within). Formal/register: neutral to formal; not slang.
target_language_example: Au sein de l'entreprise, elle dirige le département marketing.
native_language_example: Within the company, she heads the marketing department.

meaning: a (rare or poetic) expression meaning 'salt is' or used in fixed phrases referring to salt; literally 'salt is'.
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'sel' (salt) followed by the verb 'est' (is). Not a common standalone fixed phrase in modern everyday French; you will mainly encounter 'sel est' inside literary, poetic, or descriptive sentences (e.g., 'Le sel est essentiel' — 'Salt is essential') or in longer constructions. For everyday use, say complete sentences like 'Le sel est ici' or 'Il y a du sel.'
target_language_example: Le sel est sur la table.
native_language_example: The salt is on the table.

meaning: week of (used to indicate the week during/starting on which something happens)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or date to specify which week is meant: semaine de + noun/date. Common in schedules, announcements, or to say 'the week of Monday/June 5th'. You will often see it followed by a day (semaine du 5 juin) or an event (semaine de vacances). In spoken French, 'la semaine du...' is also very common (literally 'the week of...').
target_language_example: La semaine de rentrée commence le 2 septembre.
native_language_example: The week of the new term begins on September 2.

meaning: used to indicate a rate or frequency '... per week' or to specify a week 'week of...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common combination: 'semaine à' often appears in expressions like 'trois fois par semaine' or 'une semaine à Paris' (a week in Paris). When used to express rate, English usually uses 'per week' or '/week' (e.g. '10 euros la semaine' or '10 euros par semaine'). When used to specify duration/location, it can mean 'week at' or 'week of' depending on context: 'une semaine à la campagne' = 'a week in the countryside.' Pay attention to surrounding words to know whether it means frequency (per week) or location/duration.
target_language_example: Je passe une semaine à Lyon cet été.
native_language_example: I'm spending a week in Lyon this summer.

meaning: 'it seemed that' or 'seemed like'.
additional_notes: Used to express an impression, appearance, or belief about something (often with impersonal il + semblait que). Can be followed by a clause introduced by que. When referring to the speaker's impression use 'Il me semblait que...' ('It seemed to me that...'). The verb 'sembler' is regular and here in the imperfect tense ('semblait').
target_language_example: Il me semblait que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: It seemed to me that you had already left.

meaning: 'seems' followed by a state or condition introduced by en (e.g., 'seems in ...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the verb sembler ('to seem') used with the preposition en + a noun or present participle to describe being in a certain state (e.g. 'semble en colère', 'semble en train de...'). Common structures: 'semble en + noun' (seems in a state of...), 'semble en train de + infinitive' (seems to be in the process of...). Use context to determine the following word(s).
target_language_example: Il semble en colère après la réunion.
native_language_example: He seems angry after the meeting.

meaning: 'seems to' used with ne to form a negated seeming (often followed by pas + infinitive or pas + que).
additional_notes: You won't usually see 'semble ne' alone; it's part of a larger construction like 'il semble ne pas...' or 'cela semble ne pas...' meaning 'it seems not to...'. In modern spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. 'il semble pas...'), but in written or formal French you may find the full negative: 'il semble ne pas comprendre' = 'he seems not to understand'. 'Sembler' is followed by an infinitive or by 'que' + clause.
target_language_example: Il semble ne pas comprendre la question.
native_language_example: He seems not to understand the question.

meaning: 'it seems that the...' (start of a clause expressing appearance or likelihood)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself — it's the verb 'sembler' (to seem) followed by 'que' and a definite article for a feminine noun ('la'). It introduces a statement about how something appears or seems. In full sentences you will usually see a subject after 'que' (e.g. 'semble que la situation...' or, more commonly, 'il semble que la...'). Native speakers often use 'il semble que...' rather than omitting 'il'.
target_language_example: Il semble que la réunion ait été annulée.
native_language_example: It seems that the meeting was canceled.

meaning: seems that everything / it seems like everything
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete phrase; you'd normally see it in sentences like "il semble que tout..." (it seems that everything...) or "on dirait que tout...". Use "il semble que" + clause to mean "it seems that..." and follow with a verb or noun phrase (e.g. "il semble que tout est prêt"). "Tout" means "everything/everyone" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il semble que tout soit prêt pour la réunion.
native_language_example: It seems that everything is ready for the meeting.

meaning: 'it seems that all the / it seems like the whole...'
additional_notes: This looks like an incomplete fragment rather than a fixed phrase. It combines the verb 'sembler' (to seem) + 'que' (that) + 'tout le...' (all the / the whole...). You will usually see a complete sentence like 'Il semble que tout le monde...' (It seems that everyone...) or 'Il semble que tout le projet...' (It seems that the whole project...). Remember to include a subject (e.g. 'il' or a noun) and finish 'tout le...' with an appropriate noun (monde, projet, monde, personnel, etc.).
target_language_example: Il semble que tout le monde soit déjà parti.
native_language_example: It seems that everyone has already left.

meaning: 'it seems that you' / 'you seem to...'
additional_notes: A shortened phrase often used in spoken or written French to introduce an observation about someone. Grammatically it's part of a construction with 'sembler' (to seem). In full sentences you'll usually see 'il semble que tu...' (it seems that you...) or simply 'tu sembles...' (you seem). After 'semble que tu' the verb that follows is in the indicative in everyday speech, though with impersonal 'il semble que' some speakers use the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Il semble que tu sois fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It seems that you are tired today.

meaning: 'it seems that you' / 'you seem to...'
additional_notes: Combination of the verb sembler (to seem) + que + subject pronoun vous. Used to introduce an observation or impression about the person addressed (formal you or plural you). Often followed by an adjective, a clause, or an infinitive: e.g. "il semble que vous soyez..." (subjunctive after impersonal constructions) or "il semble que vous ayez...". In everyday speech you may also hear "on dirait que vous...". Formal register when using "vous"; use "tu" for informal singular.
target_language_example: Il semble que vous ayez besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: It seems that you need help.

meaning: 'seems a' / 'appears a' (used before an adjective or noun phrase meaning someone/something appears to be ...)
additional_notes: Formed from the verb sembler (to seem/appear) plus the indefinite article un. In many examples the article is followed by an adjective (e.g., 'un peu fatigué' = 'a little tired') or a noun phrase. More commonly you will see 'semble' used with adjectives without 'un' (e.g., 'Il semble fatigué'), but 'semble un peu ...' is a frequent pattern to soften a judgement ('seems a little ...'). Use with subject pronouns: 'Il semble un peu ...', 'Ça me semble ...'.
target_language_example: Cette décision me semble un peu risquée.
native_language_example: This decision seems a little risky to me.

meaning: 'common sense' (basic practical judgment or good sense).
additional_notes: Used to refer to practical, everyday judgment that most people are expected to have. Often appears in negative constructions (manquer de sens commun / être dépourvu de sens commun) to criticize someone's poor judgment. Can be used generally (Le sens commun) or about a person.
target_language_example: Il lui manque du sens commun quand il traverse sans regarder.
native_language_example: He lacks common sense when he crosses without looking.

meaning: the meaning of this/that (thing); 'sens' = meaning, 'de ce' = of this/that
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the meaning or sense of something mentioned (a word, gesture, paragraph, etc.). 'Ce' agrees with a masculine demonstrative noun (le mot, le geste, le paragraphe). For feminine nouns you'd say 'sens de cette…'. Common in questions: 'Quel est le sens de ce… ?' or statements: 'Je ne crois pas que tu comprennes le sens de ce mot.'
target_language_example: Quel est le sens de ce geste ?
native_language_example: What is the meaning of this gesture?

meaning: the meaning of this/that (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what something (a feminine noun) means or signifies. 'Sens' = meaning, direction, or sense depending on context; here it refers to 'meaning'. 'Cette' agrees with a feminine noun (cette image, cette phrase, cette lettre). Use 'le sens de ce' before masculine nouns (ce livre).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas le sens de cette phrase.
native_language_example: I don't understand the meaning of this sentence.

meaning: a sense of humor; the ability to appreciate or express humor.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's capacity to find things funny or to make others laugh. Can be positive (Il a un grand sens de l'humour) or ironic/critical (Vous avez un curieux sens de l'humour). Often used with verbs like avoir (avoir le sens de l'humour) or in questions (Où est ton sens de l'humour ?) to suggest someone is not being funny.
target_language_example: Elle n'a pas le sens de l'humour quand on plaisante.
native_language_example: She doesn't have a sense of humor when we joke.

meaning: 'sense like' or 'meaning like' — a non-fixed, marginal combination used when someone informally links the notion of 'sens' (meaning/direction) with 'comme' (like/as) to introduce an example or comparison. Rare in standard French; sounds colloquial or clipped.
additional_notes: Not a standard fixed phrase. More idiomatic alternatives: «dans le sens de», «au sens de», «comme» or «dans ce sens». Occurs when a speaker is hesitating or making an on-the-fly comparison (e.g., «sens, comme…»). Prefer standard options in formal writing or when clarity is needed.
target_language_example: Je parle du sens comme tu l'as expliqué tout à l'heure.
native_language_example: I mean the sense/meaning like you explained it earlier.

meaning: 'sens comme un' is not a common fixed phrase; it appears to be part of a larger construction combining "sens" (sense) and a simile introduced by "comme un" (like a). It would be used when comparing how something makes sense in the manner of someone or something (e.g. "ça a du sens comme un..."), but this exact sequence is unusual in isolation. Prefer established alternatives such as "avoir du sens pour quelqu'un" (to make sense to someone) or phrasing with "comme" attached to a full clause.
additional_notes: Not an idiom by itself; typically incomplete and grammatically odd alone. Native speakers rarely use the bare string "sens comme un"; you'll usually see "ça a du sens, comme un..." or "ça a du sens pour..." If you need to express "it makes sense to me/you/him," use "Ça a du sens pour moi/toi/lui" or "Ça me paraît logique."
target_language_example: Sa remarque a sens comme un avertissement : on doit y prêter attention.
native_language_example: His remark makes sense like a warning: we must pay attention to it.

meaning: 'sense/direction in' — not a fixed phrase by itself; typically appears as part of larger constructions indicating direction, orientation, or meaning within something (e.g. 'dans le sens de', 'le sens dans lequel').
additional_notes: Alone 'sens dans' is rarely used; native speakers use it inside longer phrases. 'Sens' = direction/meaning; 'dans' = in/inside. Use when specifying the sense or direction located within or inside something (e.g. 'le sens dans lequel', 'le sens dans la phrase').
target_language_example: Le sens dans lequel la flèche pointe est évident : sens dans la direction nord.
native_language_example: The direction in which the arrow points is obvious: sense in the northward direction.

meaning: I feel sorry/I'm sorry for (someone or something).
additional_notes: This phrase is a conjugated form of the verb 'sentir' in the first person singular present ('je sens') combined with 'désolé pour' meaning 'sorry for'. Alone 'sens désolé pour' without the subject 'je' is incomplete in French; you will normally say 'Je suis désolé pour...' (I am sorry for...) or 'Je me sens désolé pour...' (I feel sorry for...). Use 'désolé pour' to express regret or sympathy toward a person or situation.
target_language_example: Je me sens désolé pour toi après ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: I feel sorry for you after what happened.

meaning: Not a standard standalone French phrase; appears to combine 'sens' (from 'sentir' or 'se sentir') with 'désolée' (feminine 'sorry'). Intended meaning: 'I feel sorry' or 'I am sorry' when spoken by a female speaker, but the correct full forms are 'je suis désolée' or 'je me sens désolée'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'sens désolée' is incomplete and ungrammatical in standard French. If the speaker wants to say 'I am sorry' use 'je suis désolée' (female) or 'je suis désolé' (male). If the speaker wants to say 'I feel sorry' or 'I feel remorseful' use 'je me sens désolée'. In informal speech fragments can occur, but avoid using 'sens désolée' by itself in writing or polite conversation.
target_language_example: Je me sens désolée de ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: I feel sorry about what happened.

meaning: 'feel now' or 'I now feel' (indicates a change to the current feeling/state)
additional_notes: Used to say that one's feelings or state have changed compared with before. 'Sens' is from the verb 'se sentir' (to feel) in the first person singular ('je me sens'). 'Désormais' means 'from now on' or 'now/anymore' and emphasizes the new situation. Common in sentences like 'Je me sens désormais...' followed by an adjective (en sécurité, en confiance, sûr(e) de moi, etc.).
target_language_example: Je me sens désormais plus calme.
native_language_example: I now feel calmer.

target_language_multi_word_term: se sentir en / me sens en
meaning: 'to feel (in a certain state)'. Used with adjectives/nouns introduced by en (e.g. en sécurité, en forme).
additional_notes: This is the reflexive verb se sentir followed by en + noun/adjective phrase to describe how someone feels: physical or emotional states (en sécurité, en forme, en confiance...). Use the appropriate reflexive pronoun (je me sens, tu te sens, il se sent...). Not all adjectives require en (e.g. je me sens heureux), but many common states use en + noun/adjective. In the example 'Comment tu te sens en toi-même ?' the meaning is 'How do you feel about yourself/inside?'.
target_language_example: Je me sens en confiance quand je parle en public.
native_language_example: I feel confident when I speak in public.

meaning: 'right sense' / 'correct understanding' — the correct interpretation, feeling, or sense of something
additional_notes: Used to say someone has the correct sense, feeling, or judgment about a situation, idea, tone, or nuance. Often appears in contexts like literature, criticism, teaching, or everyday judgment: avoir le sens juste de (quelque chose) = to have the right sense/feel for something. Not an idiom; literal components (sens = sense/direction, juste = right/correct) help understand it.
target_language_example: Elle a un sens juste de la mesure lorsqu'elle parle des problèmes sociaux.
native_language_example: She has the right sense of proportion when she talks about social issues.

meaning: 'I feel it' or 'I sense it' when the subject 'je' is omitted in conversational speech; technically part of 'je le sens' or could appear in imperative with hyphen ('sens-le' = 'smell it')
additional_notes: The sequence 'sens le' by itself is non-standard as a complete sentence. In French, the pronoun typically precedes the verb ('je le sens'). 'Sens le' can appear in speech when the subject is dropped (colloquial transcription) or as two words if a speaker separates imperative with no hyphen, though standard imperative uses a hyphen: 'sens-le'. Context determines meaning: either 'I feel it' (je le sens) or an informal command 'smell it' (sens-le).
target_language_example: (colloquial) — Sens le : je le sens depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: (colloquial) — I feel it: I've been feeling it since this morning.

meaning: rather means / in the sense of... (used to correct or specify the meaning you intended)
additional_notes: Often used to correct or refine what you just said: you say one thing, then add 'sens plutôt' plus the clearer phrase. It can appear as 'dans le sens plutôt de...' or simply 'sens plutôt' in spoken French. Common in informal and neutral speech to soften or clarify a statement.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas en colère, sens plutôt déçu.
native_language_example: I'm not angry, rather disappointed.

meaning: contraction of 'sens que' appearing before a vowel/apostrophe; usually part of phrases meaning 'meaning that' or 'sense that'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the word sens (meaning 'sense' or 'direction') followed by que with elision before a vowel (qu'). It appears in contexts like 'au sens qu\'...' (in the sense that...) or 'dans le sens qu\'...' (in the sense that...). Use to introduce an explanation or clarify meaning. Example structure: 'au sens qu\' + clause. Not common on its own without surrounding words.
target_language_example: Dans le sens qu'il l'entend, c'est correct.
native_language_example: In the sense that he understands it, that's correct.

meaning: 'I feel that we/people will...' (expression of a present feeling or intuition about a future event involving 'on' = we/people/one).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like s'entendre, s'amuser, se marrer to express a gut feeling or expectation about how things will go. 'Je sens' = 'I feel/I have a sense'; 'qu'on' contracts 'que' + 'on' (we/people/one). Often followed by 'va' + infinitive to talk about a future occurrence (e.g., 'je sens qu'on va s'entendre' = I feel we'll get along). Informal to neutral register depending on the verb (e.g., 'se marrer' is more informal).
target_language_example: Je sens qu'on va bien s'amuser ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have a feeling we'll have a great time this weekend.

meaning: 'some sense' or 'a kind of sense' (rare/unnatural phrase)
additional_notes: This exact sequence "sens quelque" is not a standard fixed expression in French and is likely a fragment, inversion, or typo. Native speakers would use alternatives depending on meaning: "quelque sens" ('some sense'), "un certain sens" ('a certain sense' / 'in a certain way'), or "dans le sens de" ('in the sense of' / 'in the direction of'). If you encounter "sens quelque" in writing, treat it as nonstandard and consult context — it may be part of a longer phrase where words were reordered (e.g., poetic inversion) or an editorial error.
target_language_example: Cette tournure — « sens quelque » — paraît étrangère au français courant.
native_language_example: This phrase — "sens quelque" — feels foreign to everyday French.

meaning: 'feel so' — used to intensify how someone feels (e.g. 'I feel so good').
additional_notes: Used after a reflexive verb se + sentir (je me sens) to strengthen the adjective that follows (bien, seul, stupide, etc.). In correct French the order is usually 'je me sens si + adjective'. Be careful: 'tu sens si bon' is incorrect — for smelling good you'd say 'tu sens si bon' is colloquial/awkward; better: 'tu sens tellement bon' or 'tu sens si bon' is uncommon; for 'you smell good' use 'tu sens bon' or 'tu sens très bon'. 'Si' here means 'so' (degree), not 'if'.
target_language_example: Je me sens si heureux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel so happy today.

meaning: 'feel so' or 'feel very' (used after 'je me sens')
additional_notes: Typically appears as 'je me sens tellement ...' where 'tellement' intensifies an adjective or adverb describing how someone feels (bien, mal, mieux, jolie, stupide, etc.). Use with reflexive verb 'se sentir' (je me sens, tu te sens…). 'Tellement' = 'so/very' and emphasizes degree or emotion.
target_language_example: Je me sens tellement fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

meaning: 'feel always' — used with 'je/tu/il se' etc. to say you always feel a certain way (e.g. 'I always feel...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the verb se sentir (me sens = I feel) plus toujours (always). Use with an adjective: Je me sens toujours fatigué(e). Remember to agree the adjective in gender and number (fatigué for masculine, fatiguée for feminine). For other subjects change the reflexive pronoun: Tu te sens toujours..., Il/Elle se sent toujours..., Nous nous sentons toujours..., Ils/Elles se sentent toujours....
target_language_example: Je me sens toujours content après une promenade.
native_language_example: I always feel happy after a walk.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistake or mishearing (no clear meaning).
additional_notes: This combination does not appear in normal French. It might be a typo or a misheard fragment of another phrase such as "sans tout" (still unusual), "sens" (sense/direction) + "tout" (all/everything) used separately, or part of a larger expression (e.g., "sans tout dire" or "sens de tout"). If you encountered it in speech or writing, check the surrounding context or ask the speaker for clarification.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas « sens tout » — peux-tu répéter ou préciser ?
native_language_example: I don't understand "sens tout" — can you repeat or clarify?

meaning: 'very (in the sense of)'; used to intensify a noun or adjective when describing the specific sense or meaning of something.
additional_notes: This combination is not a fixed idiom on its own; it typically appears inside a larger phrase like "au sens très strict" or "dans le sens très large" to qualify the meaning (sens) being discussed. Use it to emphasize the degree or strictness of the 'sense' or 'meaning' you're referring to. It's compositional and formal-ish; you will mostly see it in written or careful spoken French.
target_language_example: On utilise ce mot dans un sens très large ici.
native_language_example: We use this word in a very broad sense here.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; likely a typo, misordering, or fragment. Possible intended forms include 'un sens' (a meaning/direction) or 'sens unique' (one-way).
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'sens un' in French. It should generally be rewritten (e.g. 'un sens' or 'sens unique') depending on meaning. The phrase as written may appear in poetry or wordplay but is not standard. If encountered in text, check for typographical errors or inverted word order.
target_language_example: Dans ce vers, l'auteur joue sur les mots et écrit « sens un » pour provoquer l'étrangeté.
native_language_example: In this verse, the author plays with words and writes "sens un" to create strangeness.

meaning: 'will feel better' (informal future, 2nd person singular)
additional_notes: This is the future tense of 'se sentir' (to feel) used with 'tu' (you). It expresses reassurance or expectation that someone's physical or emotional state will improve. Often appears with time words (demain, après) or conditions (si...). In spoken French the subject pronoun 'tu' is usually included: 'tu te sentiras mieux.'
target_language_example: Tu te sentiras mieux si tu te reposes.
native_language_example: You will feel better if you rest.

meaning: 'will soon be of' or 'will soon be' (used before a noun/phrase to indicate something will soon belong to or become something)
additional_notes: This is a short sequence: 'sera' is the future tense of 'être' (to be). 'Bientôt' means 'soon'. 'De' introduces what follows (often a noun, possession, origin, or a clause). You will typically see it inside a larger sentence (e.g. 'Il sera bientôt de retour' — he will be back soon, where 'de' may be part of a fixed expression). Alone it is incomplete; pay attention to the word that follows 'de' to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: La maison sera bientôt de nouveau disponible.
native_language_example: The house will soon be available again.

meaning: 'will be better' (future tense of 'être' + 'mieux').
additional_notes: Used to say that something will be better or preferable in the future. 'Sera' is the third-person singular future of être (to be). 'Mieux' means 'better' (adverb or comparative). Commonly appears in phrases like « ce sera mieux » (that will be better) or « tu seras mieux » (you will be better/feel better).
target_language_example: Ce sera mieux demain.
native_language_example: It will be better tomorrow.

meaning: will be too
additional_notes: compositional phrase: sera is the future of être ('will be') and trop means 'too' or 'too much'. It is often followed by an adjective or adverb, as in ce sera trop cher ('it will be too expensive').
target_language_example: Ce sera trop difficile pour eux.
native_language_example: It will be too difficult for them.

meaning: 'will be a' (future tense + indefinite article)
additional_notes: Combines the future tense of être (sera = he/she/it/one will be) with the indefinite article un (a). Used to say that someone or something will become or be regarded as a particular thing or quality in the future (Ce sera un honneur = It will be an honor). Agreement: 'un' changes to 'une' for feminine nouns (ce sera une bonne idée).
target_language_example: Ce sera un bon souvenir.
native_language_example: It will be a good memory.

meaning: 'When I grow up, I want...' (used to introduce what someone wants to be/do in the future).
additional_notes: Literally built from 'Quand/Lorsque je serai grand' ('when I will be big') + 'je veux' ('I want'). Commonly used by children to state future ambitions. In natural French you usually say 'Quand je serai grand, je voudrai' less often; however 'je veux' is frequently used in spoken or simple sentences. You can replace 'grand' with 'âgé' or use 'être' + profession/role.
target_language_example: Quand je serai grand, je veux devenir médecin.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to become a doctor.

meaning: I'll be there in (a) ... — used to tell someone when you'll arrive, followed by a time unit.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the future tense (je serai = I will be) + 'là' (there) + 'dans' (in) + 'une' (a/an) before a time expression (minute, heure, demi-heure, seconde, etc.). Replace 'une' with the correct article/number when needed (e.g. 'dans 10 minutes', 'dans une heure', 'dans une demi-heure'). Common for short waiting times.
target_language_example: Je serai là dans une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I'll be there in half an hour.

meaning: when you are grown up
additional_notes: Second-person singular future of être + grand; used to talk about something that will happen or be allowed once the person is an adult (or older). Common in questions about future plans (Que feras-tu quand tu seras grand ?) or in conditional/permission contexts (Tu pourras... quand tu seras grand). Can be used figuratively for 'older/mature'.
target_language_example: Quand tu seras grand, tu pourras choisir ta carrière.
native_language_example: When you are grown up, you will be able to choose your career.

meaning: will never be again (you will never ... again)
additional_notes: This string combines future tense of être (tu seras) with 'plus jamais' meaning 'never again'. Normally you'd see a subject (tu/il/elle/on) before 'seras' or use 'ne ... plus jamais' for full negation. 'Plus jamais' on its own emphasizes 'never ever again'. Example contexts: promises, warnings, strong statements about the future.
target_language_example: Tu ne seras plus jamais seule.
native_language_example: You will never be alone again.

meaning: 'will be (in)'. (Future tense of 'être' + preposition 'en' meaning 'in' or part of a phrase like 'en sécurité' = 'will be safe')
additional_notes: This is the second-person plural (vous) future form of être (vous serez) followed by en. Often appears in set phrases such as 'en sécurité' (safe) or 'en retard' (late). Alone 'serez en' needs a following noun or adjective phrase (e.g. 'serez en sécurité', 'serez en mesure de...'). Use with vous (formal you or plural you).
target_language_example: Vous serez en sécurité pendant votre voyage.
native_language_example: You will be safe during your trip.

meaning: will be released (passive future tense)
additional_notes: Passive construction: être (au futur simple) + participe passé 'libérés' (agreeing in gender/number with the subject). Used to say that people or things will be freed or set free in the future. Subject usually plural (e.g., 'les otages'). You can change tense/person by conjugating 'être' (je serai libéré, il sera libéré, nous serons libérés).
target_language_example: Les prisonniers seront libérés la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: The prisoners will be released next week.

meaning: 'will not be' (negative future tense of être or other verbs in third-person plural)
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial contraction of the future negative construction 'ne ... pas' with a third-person plural verb (ils/elles seront pas). In written or formal French, the full form is 'ne seront pas'. Used to say that 'they' or 'things' will not be something in the future. Can appear with other verbs in the future (e.g. 'ne seront pas' or colloquially 'seront pas').
target_language_example: Ils seront pas prêts demain.
native_language_example: They will not be ready tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; literally 'snake is'.
additional_notes: This exact two-word string is not a fixed expression in French. If you meant 'le serpent est...' it would simply be the start of a sentence meaning 'the snake is...'. Check whether you intended: • 'serpent' (snake) on its own, • 'serpent est' as part of a longer sentence (e.g. 'Le serpent est venimeux' = 'The snake is venomous'), or • a different phrase like 'serpent à sonnettes' (rattlesnake) or an idiom such as 'être une serpente' (rare/dated). For beginners: use 'le serpent' for 'the snake' and conjugate être (est) to describe it: 'Le serpent est grand.'
target_language_example: Le serpent est dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The snake is in the garden.

meaning: to shake someone's hand; to give a handshake.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression for greeting, agreement, or formality. Used with indirect object (serrer la main de quelqu'un) or with reflexive/reciprocal forms (se serrer la main = to shake each other's hands). Can be polite or formal (Veuillez vous serrer la main = Please shake hands).
target_language_example: Il a refusé de leur serrer la main.
native_language_example: He refused to shake their hands.

meaning: to grit one's teeth; to endure something painful or difficult without complaining.
additional_notes: Literally 'to tighten the teeth.' Used when someone suppresses pain, frustration, or discomfort and keeps going. Can be used for physical pain or for tolerating unpleasant situations. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle a dû serrer les dents pendant toute la réunion.
native_language_example: She had to grit her teeth throughout the meeting.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase. Appears to be the adjective/past participle 'serré' followed immediately by the feminine direct-object pronoun 'la' (her/it), which in correct French would normally be contracted or reordered (see notes). On its own it suggests 'tight/held/squeezed her/it' but is not standard surface word order.
additional_notes: This sequence is typically ungrammatical in standard French as written: object pronouns normally precede the verb (e.g. 'je l'ai serrée') or attach to an imperative (e.g. 'serre-la' written with a hyphen). If intended as adjective + noun, agreement and order differ ('la robe est serrée'). If intended as verb + pronoun in affirmative imperative, write 'serre-la' (with hyphen). If intended after a past participle, the pronoun precedes the auxiliary: 'Je l'ai serrée.'
target_language_example: Serre-la vite, elle est serrée.
native_language_example: Hold her/it quickly, it's tight.

meaning: 'secret service' or 'intelligence service/agency' (a government organization that gathers intelligence and conducts covert operations).
additional_notes: Used to refer to secret/intelligence services (e.g., domestic security, foreign intelligence, spy agency). Often used in plural (les services secrets) when speaking generally, but can be singular to refer to a specific service. Not necessarily the proper name of an organization (e.g., la CIA).
target_language_example: Le service secret a intercepté des communications suspectes pendant l'enquête.
native_language_example: The secret service intercepted suspicious communications during the investigation.

meaning: 'to serve a' (followed by a noun) — used when serving someone something (food, drink, a document, a purpose, etc.)
additional_notes: Servir is a versatile verb. With the indefinite article 'un' it literally means 'to serve a/one (something)'. You will usually see it followed by a noun: servir un café (to serve a coffee), servir un but (to serve a purpose), servir un document (to serve a document). Conjugate servir according to the subject (je sers, tu sers, il sert, nous servons, vous servez, ils servent). If talking about serving someone directly, use 'servir quelqu'un' (servir le client).
target_language_example: Le serveur va servir un café au client.
native_language_example: The waiter is going to serve a coffee to the customer.

meaning: literally 'his/her fingers in' — used with a verb (faire courir, passer) to mean to run/passage of one's fingers through (hair).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of actions like 'faire courir ses doigts dans ses cheveux' or 'passer ses doigts dans ses cheveux' meaning to run one's fingers through one's hair. It's a physical, neutral expression describing touching or combing hair with fingers. The possessive 'ses' agrees with the subject (ses doigts = his/her fingers). Use with verbs like 'faire courir', 'passer', 'mettre' + 'dans' + the body part (cheveux).
target_language_example: Elle passa ses doigts dans ses cheveux en soupirant.
native_language_example: She ran her fingers through her hair, sighing.

meaning: 'alone at' or 'alone in/of' (used before a location, time, or role)
additional_notes: Combines 'seul' (alone) with the preposition 'au' (a + le). Used when saying someone is alone at/in a masculine singular place or situation: e.g. 'seul au bureau' = alone at the office. Word order: 'seul au + [place/role/time]'. If the noun is feminine use 'seule à' (seule à la maison). If plural, use 'seuls aux' or 'seules aux'.
target_language_example: Il est seul au bureau aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is alone at the office today.

meaning: completely alone; feeling utterly isolated (emotionally or physically).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is totally alone or feels isolated — often emotional. Can be literal (no one else present) or figurative (feeling nobody understands you). Common in expressions like « je me sens seul au monde » (I feel completely alone).
target_language_example: Après la dispute, je me sentais seul au monde.
native_language_example: After the argument, I felt completely alone.

meaning: alone and / only and (literal combination of 'seul' + 'et').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom in French by itself — it's simply the adjective/alone/only (seul) followed by the conjunction 'and' (et). You will usually see 'seul' used alone (seul, seule, seuls, seules) to mean 'alone' or 'only'. If you find 'seul et' in a sentence, read it as two separate words: 'seul' describes something and 'et' links it to the next element. Pay attention to gender/number of 'seul'.
target_language_example: Il est seul et fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He is alone and tired after the trip.

meaning: Not a standard fixed expression in French; most often a mistaken sequence. Speakers intend either "seul" (alone/only) or "seulement que" / "ce n'est que" depending on context.
additional_notes: The sequence "seul que" is not a common or grammatically standard collocation. You might encounter it in non-native or erroneous usage. Correct alternatives include: "seul" + noun/adjective (Je suis seul), "seulement" (only), or the idiom "ce n'est que" (it is only). In some cases writers mistakenly write "seul que" where they mean "seul qui" (the only one who) or "seulement que."
target_language_example: Il est seul que je connaisse parmi eux.
native_language_example: He is the only one that I know among them.

meaning: 'the only one who' or 'the only ... that/which'.
additional_notes: Used to single out one person or thing among others when followed by a relative clause introduced by qui. Often appears with a definite article for natural usage (le seul qui / la seule qui), but 'seul qui' can occur in literary, elliptical, or emphatic contexts. Ensure gender/number agreement when used attributively: seul (m. sing.), seule (f. sing.), seuls/seules (pl.).
target_language_example: Il est seul qui puisse résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: He is the only one who can solve this problem.

meaning: 'alone on' or 'alone at' (indicating being the only person in a place or on something)
additional_notes: Seul is an adjective meaning 'alone' or 'only'. When followed by a preposition like sur ('on') it describes being the only one located on/at a surface, platform, page, team, etc. Word order: seul agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (seul, seule, seuls, seules). In many contexts French speakers might say "tout seul sur..." for emphasis. Context will determine the best English preposition (on/at/in).
target_language_example: Il est seul sur la scène.
native_language_example: He is alone on the stage.

meaning: alone at the (feminine noun) — used before a feminine place or thing to say someone is the only one there or doing something there.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the adjective 'seul' ('alone' / 'only') followed by the preposition 'à' and the feminine singular article 'la' plus a noun (e.g. 'seul à la maison'). Use 'seul au' before masculine nouns and 'seul aux' before plural nouns. Agreement: if the subject is feminine, use 'seule' (e.g. 'seule à la fête'). Often translated as 'the only one at' or 'alone at'.
target_language_example: Il était seul à la réunion.
native_language_example: He was the only one at the meeting.

meaning: not a standard French phrase; likely an incorrect combination—correct forms are « seul » (alone) or « seul à + infinitive » (the only one to ...).
additional_notes:
The exact sequence « seul à le » is ungrammatical in French. Common correct patterns:
- « seul » = alone, by oneself (adjective or pronoun). Example: « Je suis seul. »
- « le seul » = the only (followed by a noun): « le seul problème ». 
- « seul à + infinitive » = the only one to (do something): « Il est seul à comprendre. »
If you meant 'the only one to [do something] it', use « le seul à le + infinitive » only when a direct object pronoun is required: e.g. « Il est le seul à le savoir » (He is the only one to know it). Note word order: include « le » (the) before « seul » when specifying 'the only (one)'.
target_language_example: Il est le seul à le savoir.
native_language_example: He is the only one to know it.

meaning: alone together; one-on-one (private, between two people).
additional_notes: Used to say that two people will speak privately, without others present. Similar to English 'one-on-one' or 'alone together'. Often used before or during a request to speak privately: Je veux parler seul à seul avec toi. Can be used as a short command/statement: 'Seul à seul.'
target_language_example: Peux-tu rester dehors ? Je dois parler à Marc seul à seul.
native_language_example: Can you stay outside? I need to speak to Marc one-on-one.

meaning: alone in / alone at (feminine singular) — used before a noun or phrase introduced by 'en' to say a woman/thing is alone in or by means of something
additional_notes: Seule is the feminine singular form of 'seul' (alone). 'Seule en' appears before nouns or clauses introduced by 'en' (e.g., 'seule en ville', 'seule en France') or before a gerund/phrase using 'en' to indicate location, condition, or means. Make sure the subject is feminine singular (elle, la femme, la fille, etc.). For masculine singular use 'seul en'.
target_language_example: Elle est seule en ville ce soir.
native_language_example: She is alone in town tonight.

meaning: 'only the' (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Combines 'seule' (feminine form of 'seul' = only/alone) with the definite article 'la'. Used before a feminine singular noun to mean 'only the' or to emphasize that only that particular thing/person applies. Word order: adjective usually follows the noun in French, but with 'seul/seule' it can come before for emphasis (e.g., 'seule la solution' = 'only the solution').
target_language_example: Seule la musique m'aide à me détendre.
native_language_example: Only the music helps me relax.

seule à ne pas être invitée

target_language_multi_word_term: seule à ne pas être invitée
meaning: the only one who was not invited
additional_notes: Used to describe a person (usually feminine singular) who is the only one excluded from an invitation list or event. 'Seule' agrees with a feminine subject; for a masculine subject use 'seul à ne pas être invité'. The full structure often follows the subject: e.g., 'Elle était seule à ne pas être invitée.'
target_language_example: Marie s'est sentie blessée d'être seule à ne pas être invitée à la fête.
native_language_example: Marie felt hurt to be the only one who wasn't invited to the party.

meaning: 'only this' or 'just this' (used to limit or emphasize a single thing)
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'seulement' (only/just) with the demonstrative 'ce' (this/it). It is not a fixed idiom — context matters and you may more commonly see 'seulement ça', 'seulement ceci' or 'juste ça' depending on register. 'Ce' is neutral and often needs a verb or noun after it (e.g. 'seulement ce livre'). Alone, 'seulement ce' can sound incomplete in French.
target_language_example: Je veux seulement ce livre, pas les autres.
native_language_example: I only want this book, not the others.

meaning: only (used before a noun or quantity introduced by 'de').
additional_notes: Often appears when qualifying a noun or amount with 'de' (e.g. 'seulement de l'eau', 'seulement de trois personnes'). In many contexts French uses 'seulement' alone (seulement + verb/adverb) or 'seulement' + noun with an article; 'seulement de' specifically occurs before 'de' that introduces a following noun phrase (especially after quantities or negations). Word order: 'seulement' comes before 'de'. Not always required — check whether the sentence uses an article or a quantity that requires 'de'.
target_language_example: Il y a seulement de l'eau dans la bouteille.
native_language_example: There is only water in the bottle.

meaning: literally 'only he/it' or 'only that'; not a fixed standalone phrase but can appear within sentences to restrict or contrast the subject or as part of a clause.
additional_notes: As written, 'seulement il' can occur in two main ways: 1) directly before a verb to restrict the subject ('Seulement il sait la vérité' = 'Only he knows the truth'), though more natural variants include 'Seul lui' or 'Il seul' depending on emphasis; 2) with a pause/comma ('Seulement, il...') where 'seulement' functions as an introductory adverb meaning 'however' or 'but' — note that punctuation changes meaning. Beginners should watch word order and register: 'seulement' commonly appears before the word it restricts ('seulement moi', 'seulement lui') or as a sentence adverb ('Seulement, ...').
target_language_example: Seulement il sait la vérité sur ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: Only he knows the truth about what happened.

meaning: 'only I' or 'it's just me' (used to emphasize that the speaker alone does something or feels something)
additional_notes: This is simply the adverb 'seulement' (only/just) placed before the subject pronoun 'je'. It emphasizes that the action/opinion/feeling applies to the speaker alone. In natural French you'd more often hear 'moi seulement', 'seulement moi', or 'c'est seulement moi' depending on context, or 'seulement' placed elsewhere (e.g. 'Je suis seulement fatigué'). 'Seulement je' can sound slightly formal or marked and is less common in everyday speech when standing alone at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Seulement je pense que ce projet est risqué.
native_language_example: Only I think this project is risky.

meaning: 'only the' (masculine singular) or 'just the' — used to limit or emphasize a noun that follows.
additional_notes: Seulement means 'only' or 'just'. When it appears before the definite article 'le' it modifies a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'seulement le temps', 'seulement le ticket'). In speech you might also hear 'seulement' after the noun ('le temps seulement'), which is equally correct but slightly different emphasis. Remember to match the article/gender: use 'seulement la' for feminine nouns and 'seulement les' for plurals.
target_language_example: J'ai seulement le livre sur la table.
native_language_example: I only have the book on the table.

meaning: 'only him' or 'just him'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is the only person (male) involved or concerned. Placement can vary: often follows the noun or pronoun it restricts. For feminine referent use 'seulement elle'. Can also appear as 'rien que lui' or 'seullement lui' (less common spelling).
target_language_example: C'est seulement lui qui peut réparer la voiture.
native_language_example: He's the only one who can fix the car.

meaning: only us / just us
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something concerns or involves no one else but the speaker and others included in 'nous' (we/us). Can appear in phrases like 'C'est seulement nous' (it's only us) or 'Ils voient seulement nous' (they see only us) though word order often places 'seulement' before the element it modifies (e.g. 'nous seulement' is less common). In speech, context or stress determines whether it means 'only we' (subject) or 'only us' (object).
target_language_example: C'est seulement nous qui avons la clé.
native_language_example: It's only us who have the key.

meaning: 'only' or 'just' + 'you' (object pronoun) — used to say the action is limited to the person 'you'.
additional_notes: seulement = 'only/just'. te is the unstressed direct or indirect object pronoun for 'you' (singular, familiar). Together they often appear after a verb (e.g. Je veux seulement te parler = I just want to talk to you). Word order: verb + (seulement) + te. The tense of the verb can change (veux, voulais, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux seulement te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want to tell you the truth.

meaning: 'only you' (literal word-by-word: 'only you')
additional_notes: This exact word order "seulement tu" is unusual in standard French and often sounds marked or ungrammatical. Native speakers normally say "seulement toi" (with the stressed pronoun) or "toi seul/ toi seule" for emphasis. "Seulement tu" might appear in poetic, dialectal, or colloquial emphatic contexts, or as a mistaken inversion. Prefer "seulement toi" or "toi seul/ toi seule" in natural speech.
target_language_example: Dans cette histoire, seulement tu comprends ce que je veux dire.
native_language_example: In this story, only you understand what I mean.

meaning: only one (feminine) / just one
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean 'only one' or 'just one'. 'Seulement' can also mean 'only' in other positions; when specifying a masculine noun use 'seulement un'. Agreement depends on the noun that follows (une + feminine noun).
target_language_example: Il y a seulement une chaise dans la pièce.
native_language_example: There is only one chair in the room.

meaning: so/so much that; to the extent that; (in negative context) 'that much' or 'that well'.
additional_notes: Has two main uses: 1) as a conjunction meaning 'so... that' to introduce a result (Il faisait chaud, si bien que nous sommes partis). 2) in conversational/negative contexts as a comment about degree, often in shortened questions or negatives meaning 'that much/that well' (Je ne le connais pas si bien que ça = I don't know him that well). Tone can be neutral or informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Je l'apprécie, mais pas si bien que ça.
native_language_example: I like him, but not that much / not that well.

meaning: 'so happy' or 'very happy'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong happiness. 'Si' here means 'so' (intensifier). Commonly followed by 'de' + infinitive/nom (content de vous voir), 'pour' + quelqu'un (happy for someone), or 'que' + subjunctive (content que tu sois venu). Can be used alone as an exclamation: 'Je suis si content.'
target_language_example: Je suis si content pour toi, tu as réussi l'examen !
native_language_example: I'm so happy for you, you passed the exam!

meaning: 'si' ('if'/'whether') followed directly by the pronoun 'en' when they appear together across a clause boundary or in spoken sequences (e.g., in subordinate clauses: "Je me demande si en..." or hesitation: "Si en... ?"); not a fixed idiom by itself but a compositional sequence.
additional_notes: 'Si' is a conjunction introducing conditional or indirect questions; 'en' is a pronoun meaning 'of it/of them' or a prepositional adverb meaning 'from there'. The sequence 'si en' occurs when 'si' precedes a clause that begins with 'en' (often before a verb or subject pronoun). It is more common in spoken or informal contexts when 'en' refers back to something mentioned earlier (e.g., « Je me demande si en reste. »). Word order: 'en' normally comes before the verb (on en a, il en reste).
target_language_example: Je me demande si en reste pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: I wonder if there is any left for everyone.

meaning: 'so proud' (feminine singular)
additional_notes: si = 'so' (intensifier). fière is the feminine form of 'fier' (proud). Used before adjectives to emphasize degree. Match gender/number with the person or thing described: 'si fier' (masculine), 'si fières' (feminine plural), etc. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle est si fière de sa fille.
native_language_example: She is so proud of her daughter.

meaning: 'so proud of' (used before a noun or pronoun)
additional_notes: Used to express a strong degree of pride about someone or something. Fière agrees in gender with the speaker or subject: 'fière' for feminine, 'fier' for masculine. Commonly followed by 'de' + noun, pronoun, or infinitive (e.g. 'si fière de toi', 'si fier de son fils', 'si fière d'avoir...').
target_language_example: Je suis si fière de toi pour ton examen.
native_language_example: I am so proud of you for your exam.

meaning: 'so happy to' (used by a female speaker)
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb or clause to say you are very happy about something. 'Si' intensifies 'heureuse' (very). Because 'heureuse' is the feminine form, the speaker is female (male speakers would say 'si heureux de'). Followed by 'de' plus an infinitive or 'de' + clause (e.g., 'de te voir', 'de savoir que…').
target_language_example: Je suis si heureuse de te voir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am so happy to see you today.

meaning: so interesting (feminine singular)
additional_notes: si = 'so' or 'that' used to intensify an adjective. Intensity agrees with the noun's gender and number: si intéressant (m.), si intéressante (f.), si intéressants (pl. m.), si intéressantes (pl. f.). Often used to express surprise or emphasis (e.g., C'est si intéressant !).
target_language_example: La conférence était si intéressante que je n'ai pas vu le temps passer.
native_language_example: The lecture was so interesting that I didn't notice the time passing.

meaning: so little / so few (to a small extent).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a small amount, degree, or extent. Placed before nouns (si peu de ...) or before adjectives/adverbs (si peu photogénique / si peu sûrs) to mean 'so little' or 'so hardly'. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Nous savons si peu de choses sur ce sujet.
native_language_example: We know so little about this subject.

meaning: if only (expressing a wish or regret).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish, regret, or longing for something that is not (or may not be) true. Often followed by a clause in the imperfect, conditional, or past conditional depending on time and likelihood. Can be used alone as a short exclamation: «Si seulement!»
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais partir demain.
native_language_example: If only I could leave tomorrow.

meaning: as if it were yesterday; used to say something feels very recent
additional_notes: This phrase is a conditional expression often used to describe memories or events that feel very fresh — as though they happened just yesterday. It can appear in sentences like 'On dirait que c'était hier' (It feels like it was yesterday) or as part of a longer clause. Tone is neutral and suitable for spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de cette chanson comme si c'était hier.
native_language_example: I remember that song as if it were yesterday.

meaning: 'if this' or 'if that' (literal: conditional 'if' + demonstrative 'this/that')
additional_notes: Combination of the conditional conjunction si ('if') and the demonstrative ce ('this/that'). It appears in sentences like «Si ce n'est pas…» ('If it's not…') or «Si ce que tu dis est vrai…» ('If what you say is true…'). Often part of longer structures; by itself it's incomplete and requires the rest of the clause. Pronunciation: [si sə].
target_language_example: Si ce que tu dis est vrai, nous devons agir.
native_language_example: If what you say is true, we must act.

meaning: if it is not / unless / except if
additional_notes: Commonly used in conditional phrases. Can introduce a negative condition (if it is not the case) or make an exception (except if). Often followed by pas (not) or que (only). Equivalent to English 'if it isn't', 'unless', or 'except that'.
target_language_example: Je viendrai, si ce n'est que je suis malade.
native_language_example: I'll come, unless I am sick.

meaning: as if nothing had happened / as if nothing were wrong
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something acting as though an event, problem, or awkward situation did not occur. Often follows a description of the event and sets up a contrast (e.g. 'il a continué, si de rien n'était' = he carried on as if nothing had happened). Formality: neutral; common in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il est rentré chez lui si de rien n'était.
native_language_example: After the accident, he went home as if nothing had happened.

meaning: so/that being the case; if that's the case.
additional_notes: Formal/literary expression used to introduce a conclusion or consequence based on what was just stated. Equivalent to 'dans ce cas' or 'si c'est le cas'. You may see it in written or formal spoken French; less common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Si fait, nous devrons organiser une réunion urgente.
native_language_example: If that's the case, we will need to organize an urgent meeting.

meaning: if he; if it
additional_notes: This sequence is usually written as « s'il » in standard French, because « si » + « il » normally contracts. The phrase is compositional: « si » means 'if' (and sometimes 'whether' depending on context), and « il » can mean 'he' or 'it'.
target_language_example: On partira ensemble si il vient demain.
native_language_example: We'll leave together if he comes tomorrow.

meaning: if I
additional_notes: si j' is si + je, with je shortened before a vowel or silent h: si j'ai, si j'habite, si j'étais. It usually introduces a condition ('if I'), but after verbs like se demander it can also mean 'whether I'.
target_language_example: Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
native_language_example: If I have time, I'll come.

meaning: 'if ever' / 'in case (that)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conditional or hypothetical situation; often adds emphasis or a sense of precaution (English: 'if ever', 'if by any chance', 'in case'). Common in spoken and written French. Can appear alone at the start of a sentence or inside one. Not formal/slang—neutral.
target_language_example: Si jamais tu as besoin d'aide, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If ever you need help, call me. (In case you need help, call me.)

meaning: a polite hedge: 'if I may say (so)' or 'so to speak'.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a remark, show modesty, or indicate the speaker is aware the phrasing may be imperfect. Common in formal or polite contexts but also in everyday speech. Equivalent to 'if you will' or 'so to speak'.
target_language_example: C'est, si je puis dire, une solution élégante.
native_language_example: It is, if I may say so, an elegant solution.

meaning: a polite formula meaning 'if I may' or 'if I may be allowed to (say)'.
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce an opinion, suggestion, or question. Often followed by permettre (e.g. 'si je puis me permettre') and usually appears at the start of a sentence. Formal/polite register; can be omitted in casual speech. English equivalents: 'if I may', 'if I may say so', or 'with your permission'.
target_language_example: Si je puis me permettre, je vous conseillerais de relire ce paragraphe.
native_language_example: If I may, I would advise you to reread this paragraph.

meaning: 'if the' (feminine noun follows) — conditional 'if' + definite article 'la'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the conditional conjunction si followed by the feminine singular definite article la. It appears when you conditionally refer to a specific feminine noun: e.g. si la voiture, si la porte, si la situation. Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar. Pronunciation often links the sounds: [si la].
target_language_example: Si la porte est fermée, frappez avant d'entrer.
native_language_example: If the door is closed, knock before entering.

meaning: 'if the' (conditional conjunction + definite article)
additional_notes: Combines the conditional conjunction si (if) with the masculine singular definite article le (the). Used to introduce a conditional clause referring to a specific masculine noun. Word order: si + le + noun. Note that si can also mean 'whether' in some contexts, but with le it normally means 'if the...'.
target_language_example: Si le train est en retard, j'arriverai en retard.
native_language_example: If the train is late, I will arrive late.

meaning: 'if my' (conditional phrase used before a noun/pronoun, e.g. 'if my...')
additional_notes: Si mon is the combination of the conditional 'si' (if) + the possessive adjective 'mon' (my). It introduces a hypothetical condition referring to something that belongs to the speaker. In natural French, you'd usually see it followed by a noun (si mon frère, si mon travail) or by a subject and verb with the noun implied. For spoken or informal contexts, contractions or rephrasing may occur (e.g., 'si j'ai mon…' for 'if I have my…').
target_language_example: Si mon téléphone est mort, je ne peux pas appeler.
native_language_example: If my phone is dead, I can't call.

meaning: 'if necessary' / 'if needed'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something will be done only if required. Can appear at start of a sentence (Si nécessaire, ...), inline (faire X si nécessaire), or alone as a short response meaning 'if needed' or 'if necessary.' Formality: neutral — suitable for both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je t'appellerai si nécessaire.
native_language_example: I'll call you if necessary.

meaning: 'if so' or 'if yes' (used to refer back to a previously mentioned condition or question).
additional_notes: Often follows a clause or question already stated. Commonly used in written or formal contexts to mean 'in that case' or 'if the answer is yes.' It pairs with 'si non' (= 'if not'). Example usage: 'Confirmez votre présence et, si oui, indiquez le nombre de personnes.'
target_language_example: Avez-vous un passeport valide ? Si oui, veuillez le présenter.
native_language_example: Do you have a valid passport? If so, please present it.

meaning: if yes or (not a standard set phrase) — appears to be part of a longer question like "si oui ou non" meaning "if yes or not / whether or not".
additional_notes: Alone, "si oui ou" is incomplete and uncommon. The usual expression is "si oui ou non" (or simply "oui ou non") meaning "yes or no" / "whether or not." You will encounter "si oui" to mean "if so/if yes" and "ou non" to mean "or not." Use the full forms: "si oui, si non" or "si oui ou non."
target_language_example: Dis‑moi si oui ou non tu veux venir.
native_language_example: Tell me whether or not you want to come.

meaning: if possible; preferably
additional_notes: Used to add a polite preference or wish — softens a request or condition. Often follows a time, quantity, or description (e.g., "dès demain, si possible" = "tomorrow, if possible" or "preferably tomorrow"). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me rappeler ce soir, si possible ?
native_language_example: Can you call me back tonight, if possible?

meaning: if some / if any (introductory fragment used before a noun or expression meaning 'some' or 'any')
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself in French; 'si' (if) can be followed by 'quelque' (some/any) in constructions like 'si quelque chose' (if something) or 'si quelque personne' (if any person), though more common is 'si quelqu'un' or 'si quelque chose' using the fused forms. Alone, 'si quelque' is an incomplete fragment and learners will usually see it as part of longer expressions. Use 'si quelqu'un' for 'if someone' and 'si quelque chose' for 'if something'.
target_language_example: Si quelque chose change, je te préviendrai.
native_language_example: If something changes, I'll let you know.

meaning: not a standard/fixed French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete fragment (possibly intended as 'si quoi que ce soit' meaning 'if anything' or 'if anything at all').
additional_notes:
As written, 'si quoi que' is not a correct or complete expression in French. Beginner learners encountering this should check for the full phrase 'si quoi que ce soit' (or more commonly 'si jamais' / 's'il y a quelque chose') which means 'if anything' or 'if there is anything at all'. Use the complete forms below instead:
- 'si quoi que ce soit' (formal/written) → 'if anything/if there is anything'
- 'si jamais' (spoken) → 'if ever/if anything'
- 's'il y a quelque chose' → 'if there is something'.
Common structure: 'si quoi que ce soit' often appears in polite offers or warnings: 'Appelez-moi si quoi que ce soit ne va pas' (better: 'Appelez-moi si quelque chose ne va pas' or 'Appelez-moi si jamais il y a un problème').
target_language_example: Appelez-moi si quoi que ce soit ne va pas. (better: Appelez-moi si quelque chose ne va pas.)
native_language_example: Call me if anything is wrong. (better: Call me if something is wrong.)

meaning: if nothing / if not anything
additional_notes: Rarely used on its own; typically appears in longer phrases like «si rien n'est fait» (if nothing is done) or in colloquial speech with subject/verb following. In standard French, negative constructions usually include «ne» (e.g. «si rien n'est fait») but in spoken French the «ne» is often dropped («si rien n'est fait» → «si rien n'est fait» still keeps ne; casual: «s'il n'y a rien» instead of «si rien»). Use with care — prefer complete structures like «si rien n'est fait», «si rien ne change», or «s'il n'y a rien».
target_language_example: Si rien n'est fait, la situation va empirer.
native_language_example: If nothing is done, the situation will get worse.

meaning: 'if nothing (does)...' — start of a conditional clause meaning 'in case nothing...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conditional idea when followed by a verb (e.g. si rien ne change = if nothing changes). It requires a verb after 'ne' (often part of the negative 'ne ... rien' construction). In spoken French, the 'ne' is frequently dropped: 'si rien ne change' → 'si rien change'.
target_language_example: Si rien ne bouge, on part demain.
native_language_example: If nothing moves/changes, we'll leave tomorrow.

meaning: if his/her/its sound; if the sound
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction 'si' (if) followed by the noun 'son' (sound/his/her/its depending on context). Without context, it can mean either 'if (the) sound...' or 'if his/her/its...' (son as possessive) followed by a noun omitted here. Pay attention to pronunciation: 'son' (sound) [sɔ̃] and 'son' (possessive 'his/her/its') are spelled the same but pronounced [sɔ̃] as well — they are homographs. In spoken French, meaning comes from the words that follow. For example, 'si son' + noun usually uses 'son' as a possessive (son chien = his/her dog), while 'si le son' or 'si un son' indicates 'the sound' or 'a sound.'
target_language_example: Si son téléphone sonne, dis-lui que j'arrive.
native_language_example: If his/her phone rings, tell him/her I'm coming.

meaning: 'if your' (conditional + possessive), used to introduce a condition about something belonging to 'you' (singular, informal).
additional_notes: Combines 'si' (if) with the possessive adjective 'ton' (your, masculine singular noun). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (or noun phrase) that 'ton' modifies: e.g. 'si ton train arrive' or 'si ton frère vient'. In speech or informal writing you may also see 'si tu' + verb constructions instead (e.g. 'si tu veux...'). Not a fixed phrase—just a common short sequence in conditional sentences.
target_language_example: Si ton sac est prêt, on peut partir.
native_language_example: If your bag is ready, we can leave.

meaning: 'if all' or 'if everything' (literal); used as part of conditional phrases like "si tout..." meaning "if all [things/people]..."
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed expression. It normally appears at the start of a condition: e.g. "si tout va bien" (if everything is going well), "si tout le monde" (if everyone...). You will rarely use "si tout" alone in speech — it's followed by more words to complete the idea. Pay attention to the rest of the clause to know whether it refers to 'everything' (tout) or 'everyone' (tout le monde).
target_language_example: Si tout se passe bien, nous partirons demain.
native_language_example: If everything goes well, we'll leave tomorrow.

si tu as besoin de quoi

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as besoin de quoi
meaning: 'if you need anything' (informal, short for 'si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit')
additional_notes: Used to offer help or availability. Informal and conversational; often followed by an instruction (e.g. 'appelle', 'viens me voir'). Full formal version: 'si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit'. Can be used alone as a reassurance: 'Si tu as besoin de quoi, dis-le.'
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

meaning: This phrase as written is incomplete; likely the start of a conditional clause meaning 'if you have some/any' or 'if you have something'.
additional_notes: In French, 'si' means 'if'. 'tu as' = 'you have'. 'quelque' is an adjective meaning 'some' but must be followed by a noun (quelque chose = something; quelques + plural noun = some/several). Common complete phrases: 'si tu as quelque chose' (if you have something), 'si tu as quelques minutes' (if you have a few minutes). As written, do not use alone—finish the phrase with a noun or 'chose'.
target_language_example: Si tu as quelque chose à ajouter, dis-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you have something to add, say it now.

meaning: used to show doubt, mild disagreement, or to accept someone's statement reluctantly ('if you say so').
additional_notes: A common conversational phrase. Can be neutral acceptance, polite doubt, or ironic/skeptical depending on tone and context. Often short and dismissive. Use with friends or in informal situations; tone conveys meaning more than grammar.
target_language_example: D'accord, si tu le dis, mais je ne suis pas convaincu.
native_language_example: Alright, if you say so, but I'm not convinced.

meaning: 'if a' — the conditional phrase 'si' (if) followed by the indefinite article 'un' (a/an).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but simply the combination of the conjunction si and the article un (masculine singular). It appears when you start a conditional clause about a single countable masculine noun: e.g. si un ami, si un problème, si un client. Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar. In many contexts si + un may be followed by que or a verb: si un ami vient..., si un problème se produit....
target_language_example: Si un ami vient, dis‑le moi.
native_language_example: If a friend comes, tell me.

meaning: if your (singular formal or plural).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction si (if) + the possessive adjective votre (your, formal or plural). Used to introduce a condition relating to something that belongs to or is associated with the person(s) addressed. Remember to follow with a noun: si votre nom, si votre voiture, etc. For informal singular 'your' use ton/ta/tes instead of votre.
target_language_example: Si votre passeport est expiré, vous ne pouvez pas voyager.
native_language_example: If your passport is expired, you cannot travel.

si vous avez besoin de quoi

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de quoi
meaning: if you need anything / if you need something
additional_notes: A polite, slightly informal way to offer help. Often used at the end of a conversation or message. It can be shortened to "si vous avez besoin" or made more colloquial with "si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit". The literal words mean "if you have need of what," but the sense is "if you need anything." Use "vous" for formal/plural and "tu" for informal/singular.
target_language_example: N'hésitez pas à me contacter si vous avez besoin de quoi.
native_language_example: Don't hesitate to contact me if you need anything.

si vous avez besoin de quoi que

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de quoi que
meaning: if you need anything (at all).
additional_notes: Commonly completed as "si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit" — a polite offer of help. Used in formal and neutral contexts (vous form). Often followed by suggested contact methods (appeler, envoyer un courriel, etc.). Literal elements: 'si' = if, 'vous avez besoin de' = you need, 'quoi que ce soit' = anything at all.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelez le bureau.
native_language_example: If you need anything at all, call the office.

meaning: literally 'is hers/his/its' — the sequence combines the feminine singular possessive pronoun 'sienne' (meaning 'hers' or 'its' when referring to a feminine noun) and the verb 'est' (third-person singular of 'être', 'is').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a short grammatical sequence; 'sienne' normally follows the definite article ('la sienne') when standing alone as a possessive pronoun: e.g. 'La voiture sienne est neuve' is uncommon — more natural: 'La voiture est la sienne.'
