(morning)', or 'often on the...'; used to specify a frequent occurrence tied to a noun or time expression. Word order: adverb before the noun/article. Common in phrases like 'souvent le week-end' or 'souvent le matin'.
target_language_example: Je vais souvent le matin au parc.
native_language_example: I often go to the park in the morning.

meaning: 'often for' — used to say something happens frequently for a given reason, purpose, or duration
additional_notes: This is the combination of the adverb 'souvent' (often) followed by the preposition 'pour' (for). You'll see it when a speaker describes something that happens frequently 'for' a particular reason, purpose, or time period: e.g. 'souvent pour X'. It's compositional and literal: translate 'souvent' → 'often' and 'pour' → 'for'. Make sure the rest of the sentence clarifies what follows 'pour' (a reason, a purpose, or a duration).
target_language_example: Ils viennent souvent pour les concerts.
native_language_example: They often come for the concerts.

meaning: often a / often one (used when describing frequency followed by a feminine noun)
additional_notes: Combination of adverb 'souvent' (often) and the feminine indefinite article 'une'. Used before a feminine noun: e.g. 'souvent une erreur' = 'often an error'. Not a fixed idiom—just a common word sequence. Word order: 'souvent' usually comes before the noun phrase or before the verb depending on sentence; when describing frequency of a noun, you can say 'C'est souvent une...' or 'Il y a souvent une...'.
target_language_example: Il y a souvent une solution simple.
native_language_example: There is often a simple solution.

meaning: will remember (about/of)
additional_notes: Future tense of se souvenir de (to remember). Used with a subject (je, tu, il...) and followed by the thing or person remembered introduced by de. English translations often use 'will remember' + direct object or 'remember' + preposition 'of'/'about'. Can express remembering people, moments, feelings, etc.
target_language_example: Je me souviendrai de cette soirée toute ma vie.
native_language_example: I will remember that evening my whole life.

meaning: 'remember (something/someone)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir de (je me souviens de, tu te souviens de, etc.). In speech the de often contracts before a vowel or is written d'. Use 'tu te souviens de...' to ask 'do you remember...?' and follow with a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g. d'elle, d'autre chose, de ce jour).
target_language_example: Tu te souviens d'où nous étions allés?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we went?

meaning: 'remember (that)...' — used to recall a fact or something someone said.
additional_notes: This is based on the reflexive verb se souvenir de + clause. In speech you'd usually say "souviens-toi que..." (informal singular) or "souvenez-vous que..." (formal/plural). With a clause, you can use "souviens de ce que...", but more common is "souviens-toi que...". Followed by a verb or clause that describes what to remember.
target_language_example: Souviens de ce que je t'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: Remember what I told you yesterday.

meaning: a fragment from the reflexive verb se souvenir de meaning 'remember (her/it)' or 'remind yourself of (her/it)' when referring to a feminine noun or a feminine pronoun represented by 'la'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own; it's a piece of a reflexive construction (se souvenir de). In full sentences you'll see the reflexive pronoun before the verb (je me souviens de la ...). 'La' can refer to a feminine noun or a previously mentioned feminine person or thing. Often speakers use d'elle, de ça, de lui, or a noun instead of 'la' for clarity. Watch agreement and word order: je me souviens de la photo / je me souviens d'elle.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de la chanson que tu chantais.
native_language_example: I remember the song you used to sing.

meaning: remember my/remember that relates to my (someone or something).
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir de (to remember). In full sentences you say Je me souviens de mon père (I remember my father) or Tu te souviens de mon frère ? (Do you remember my brother?). Use the correct reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) to match the subject and adjust the noun that follows (mon/ma/mes) for possession. Often followed by a person, name, or thing. Common in questions and statements.
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de mon professeur de français ?
native_language_example: Do you remember my French teacher?

meaning: 'remember his/her/its' (used to say you recall something belonging to or about someone)
additional_notes: Form comes from the reflexive verb se souvenir de + possessive (son). Use with je/tu/il etc. plus the appropriate possessive: 'son' = his/her/its (masculine or general). The English subject (I/you) is explicit in French (je me souviens, tu te souviens). Commonly followed by a noun (visage, nom, anniversaire, numéro) or a clause introduced by que.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de son nom.
native_language_example: I remember his/her name.

meaning: 'remember (something)' — abbreviated form of se souvenir de + masculine singular or unstressed noun/pronoun (tu te souviens du film).
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir de (to remember). In speech and writing you'll see forms like je me souviens du, tu te souviens du, il/elle se souvient du, etc. Use 'du' = de + le before masculine singular nouns; use 'de la', 'de l'' or 'des' for other genders/numbers, or 'de' + a pronoun (e.g. te souviens-tu de...). The past participle and tense follow the reflexive construction (often with être in compound tenses).
target_language_example: Tu te souviens du jour où nous nous sommes rencontrés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the day we met?

meaning: 'don't remember (of/about)'.
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial negative form of se souvenir de (to remember). In full formal form you'd say "ne me/te/se/etc. souviens pas de" or with ne...pas around the verb: "je ne me souviens pas de..." The phrase is followed by a person or thing introduced by de (de lui, de ça, de cet endroit). Use reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nous, vous) depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Je ne me souviens pas de ton visage.
native_language_example: I don't remember your face.

meaning: no longer remember; don't remember anymore
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir (to remember) plus 'plus' meaning 'no longer' or 'anymore' after a negative construction (often with ne). In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped, so 'Je (ne) me souviens plus' means 'I don't remember anymore.' Can be used with or without an object: 'de l'air' / 'de toi', or alone ('Tu ne te souviens plus ?').
target_language_example: Je ne me souviens plus de son nom.
native_language_example: I don't remember his/her name anymore.

meaning: Not a standalone phrase; likely part of 'je me souviens très...' meaning 'I remember very...' (followed by an adjective or adverb).
additional_notes: The words 'souviens' (from se souvenir) and 'très' (very) do not form an independent fixed expression. 'Souviens' appears in conjugated forms like 'je me souviens' (I remember). 'Très' is an adverb meaning 'very' and modifies adjectives or adverbs, not the verb directly. Common correct uses: 'Je me souviens très bien' = 'I remember very well', or 'Je me souviens très clairement' = 'I remember very clearly.'
target_language_example: Je me souviens très bien de cette journée.
native_language_example: I remember that day very well.

meaning: Likely a misspelling or fragment; probably intended 'spectacle' (a show, performance) or the phrase 'spectacle à' as part of 'spectacle à [quelque chose]' meaning 'show at/for'.
additional_notes: There are no example sentences provided. In French, 'spectacle' means 'show', 'performance' or 'event'. It is usually followed by a preposition when specifying location or purpose: e.g. 'spectacle à Paris' (show in Paris), 'spectacle à thème' (themed show). If you saw 'spectacle a' without accent on 'à', it may be a typo for 'spectacle à' (à = 'at'/'to'/'for') or simply the word 'spectacle' followed by the verb 'a' (has), as in 'le spectacle a commencé' ('the show has started'). Check the context to decide which is intended.
target_language_example: Le spectacle a commencé à 20 heures.
native_language_example: The show started at 8 p.m.

meaning: 'the show is' (literal: 'spectacle is')
additional_notes: This looks like two words where 'spectacle' means 'show' or 'performance' and 'est' is the third-person singular of 'être' ('is'). On its own this fragment is incomplete — you'd normally see it inside a full sentence (e.g. 'Le spectacle est annulé' = 'The show is cancelled'). Not an idiom; literal composition matches the English word order.
target_language_example: Le spectacle est prêt à commencer.
native_language_example: The show is ready to start.

meaning: gas station; petrol station.
additional_notes: Common term for a place where you buy fuel for vehicles and often find a convenience store, pumps, and sometimes a service bay. Used in everyday speech and on signs. In Canada you may also hear 'station-service'.
target_language_example: Je vais à la station essence pour faire le plein.
native_language_example: I'm going to the gas station to fill up.

meaning: ballpoint pen; a pen that uses a small rotating ball to dispense ink.
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a ballpoint pen in French. Used when specifying the pen type (as opposed to fountain pen = "stylo plume" or felt-tip = "feutre"/"stylos marqueur"). "À" here indicates the pen has a ball (bille).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo à bille pour signer ce document.
native_language_example: I need a ballpoint pen to sign this document.

meaning: 'knew that I...' (past participle 'su' + conjunction 'que' + subject 'j'' as in 'j'étais') — used in questions like 'How did you know that I...?'
additional_notes: This fragment appears in spoken/written questions: Comment (as-/t-)as-tu su que j'... / Comment avez-vous su que j'... / Comment tu as su que j'... It combines the past participle su (from savoir = to know) with que + the start of a subordinate clause about the speaker (j'), e.g. j'étais. English equivalent: 'How did you know that I...?' Contractions like t'as (tu as) and the drop of vowels (j') are common in speech. Use 'su que je...' in full when not eliding the vowel.
target_language_example: Comment as-tu su que j'étais venu ?
native_language_example: How did you know that I had come?

meaning: southwest (direction or region).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the compass direction or a region located to the southwest. Can be used with articles and prepositions (au sud-ouest de..., dans le sud-ouest de...) or alone as a label/direction. Hyphenated in French. Pronounced like 'soo-dwɛst'.
target_language_example: Le vent vient du sud-ouest.
native_language_example: The wind is coming from the southwest.

meaning: 'south of' (used to indicate the southern part of or located south of something).
additional_notes: Used before a place name or noun to say that something is situated to the south of that place (e.g. "le sud de la France" = the south of France). Can also mean the southern region of a larger area. Remember to use the appropriate article with country/region names when required (le sud du Canada, le sud de la France).
target_language_example: Nous passons nos vacances dans le sud de la France.
native_language_example: We spend our holidays in the south of France.

meaning: enough times; sufficiently often
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been done or should be done a sufficient number of times. Often follows a verb (e.g., "faire suffisamment de fois") or appears in constructions like "assez de fois". "Suffisamment" is more formal than "assez" but both are common. Countable context: refers to repeated occurrences.
target_language_example: J'ai répété l'exercice suffisamment de fois pour le maîtriser.
native_language_example: I repeated the exercise enough times to master it.

meaning: literally 'am bought' — passive form meaning 'have been bought' (first person singular).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé passive-like construction using 'être' + past participle 'acheté'. More naturally, French uses 'j'ai acheté' (I bought / I have bought) when the subject is the buyer. 'Je suis acheté' would mean someone bought me (I was purchased) and is rarely used except in literal contexts (e.g., objects, animals) or figuratively (e.g., 'I'm bought' meaning corrupted). For completed action about buying something you did, use 'j'ai acheté'.
target_language_example: Je suis acheté par une entreprise étrangère.
native_language_example: I have been bought by a foreign company.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct French phrase; it looks like a mistaken combination of words meaning something like 'am bought a' or 'was bought a'.
additional_notes:
Likely a typo or word-order error. In French, the auxiliary verb for the perfect tense of acheter is avoir (j'ai acheté), not être (suis). Possible corrections depending on intended meaning:
- 'j'ai acheté une ...' = 'I bought a ...'
- 'je me suis acheté une ...' = 'I bought myself a ...' (reflexive construction)
- 'a été acheté(e) une ...' = 'a ... was bought' (passive)
The sequence 'suis acheté une' as written is ungrammatical and should not be used.
target_language_example: (Incorrect:) *suis acheté une* — cette suite de mots n'est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: (Incorrect:) *suis acheté une* — this sequence of words is not correct in French.

meaning: I went (to) — used with a reflexive infinitive: 'I went to [do something for myself]'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of 'aller' + a reflexive pronoun and an infinitive (aller + se + infinitive). It expresses that the speaker went somewhere in order to do an action for themselves (e.g., se promener = go for a walk, se faire vacciner = get vaccinated). In English you usually say 'I went to [do something]' or 'I went and [did something]'. The reflexive 'me' agrees with the subject 'je'.
target_language_example: Je suis allé me coucher tôt hier soir.
native_language_example: I went to bed early last night.

meaning: 'I had fun' or 'I enjoyed myself' (past tense, first person singular with reflexive verb se amuser).
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé of the reflexive verb se amuser: Je me suis amusé(e). Use me/te/se/nous/vous + être (suis/es/est/sommes/êtes/sont) + amusé. The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject when the reflexive pronoun is a direct object: Je me suis amusé (m) / Je me suis amusée (f). Also used in exclamations (Que je me suis amusé !) to emphasize how much fun you had.
target_language_example: Je me suis amusée à la fête hier soir.
native_language_example: I had fun at the party last night.

meaning: I arrived at the (feminine place).
additional_notes: First-person singular past tense of arriver (être arrivé): 'je suis arrivé(e)'. 'À la' is the feminine singular form of 'at the' used before feminine place nouns (la gare, la maison, la fête). If the speaker is female, write 'je suis arrivée'. Can be followed by a specific place or time expression.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la gare hier soir.
native_language_example: I arrived at the train station last night.

meaning: 'I am stopped' or 'I have been arrested' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present of the verb phrase être arrêté. It can mean either you are physically stopped (e.g., a car, a process) or that you have been arrested by police. Context (topic, surrounding words) tells which meaning is intended. For 'I have been arrested' the passive/agent sense is common: 'Je suis arrêté par la police.' For 'stopped' as in a vehicle: 'Je suis arrêté au feu' (I'm stopped at the light).
target_language_example: Je suis arrêté par la police.
native_language_example: I have been arrested by the police.

meaning: am sitting
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular past (passé composé) of se asseoir used in examples where the speaker says they sat down or are seated. In French you usually say "je me suis assis(e)" (with reflexive pronoun and agreement with gender: add -e for feminine). In casual present descriptions someone might also say "je suis assis(e)" to mean "I am sitting". Context determines whether it's a completed action (I sat down) or a state (I am seated).
target_language_example: Je me suis assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I sat down near the window.

meaning: 'am/is/was sitting on' or part of 'to sit (oneself) on'—from the reflexive verb s'asseoir + preposition sur.
additional_notes: Derived from the reflexive verb s'asseoir (to sit down). In context you will usually see it with a reflexive pronoun (je me suis assis(e) sur, il s'est assis sur) or following a subject (je suis assis(e) sur for state). Use sur to indicate the surface or object being sat on (canapé, sol, banc, rocher). Be mindful of past-participle agreement when using passé composé with a preceding reflexive pronoun: je me suis assis (masc) / je me suis assise (fem).
target_language_example: Je me suis assis sur le canapé à côté de lui.
native_language_example: I sat down on the couch next to him.

meaning: 'am/was seated' (feminine singular, past participle used with 'être' in passé composé).
additional_notes: From the verb 's'asseoir' (to sit). In the passé composé with 'être' the past participle agrees with the subject: 'je me suis assise' (I sat / I have sat — said by a woman). Without reflexive pronoun it can be 'je suis assis(e)' for present ('I am seated'). Used to say where someone sat or that they sat down. For a male speaker use 'suis assis'.
target_language_example: Je me suis assise sur la chaise près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I sat down on the chair by the window.

meaning: 'I fought' or 'I struggled' (past tense, reflexive: I fought myself / I fought on my own).
additional_notes: From the verb se battre (to fight/struggle). In the passé composé with être: Je me suis battu(e). Can mean: physically fought someone (Je me suis battu avec X), fought hard/struggled (Je me suis battu de toutes mes forces), or fought for a cause/person (Je me suis battu pour toi). Remember the past participle agrees in gender with the subject when using être (battu → battue for a female speaker).
target_language_example: Je me suis battu pour obtenir cette bourse.
native_language_example: I fought to get that scholarship.

meaning: I am injured
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive past (je me suis blessé) used to say you were injured or hurt yourself. In present tense 'je suis blessé(e)' means 'I am injured' (add -e for feminine). With 'me suis' it's passé composé (I got injured / I hurt myself). Commonly followed by where or how (au genou, avec un couteau, en faisant ça).
target_language_example: Je me suis blessé en tombant du vélo.
native_language_example: I hurt myself when I fell off the bike.

meaning: 'I burned (myself)' — past tense (passé composé) of se brûler: to burn oneself.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) to say you accidentally burned a body part. In examples it's 'je me suis brûlé(e)' (add -e if speaker is female). Common constructions: 'se brûler la langue', 'se brûler le doigt', 'se brûler à + object' (se brûler à la jambe). Often followed by the body part introduced by definite article (le/la) rather than possessive.
target_language_example: Je me suis brûlée en retirant la casserole du four.
native_language_example: I burned myself when taking the pan out of the oven.

meaning: 'am/was hidden' or 'hid myself' (first person singular, passé composé or present passive form depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the auxiliary 'suis' (être) with the past participle 'caché' and most often appears in the reflexive form 'je me suis caché' meaning 'I hid myself' (I hid). Alone 'suis caché' can also be present passive ('I am hidden') if used with a subject (e.g. 'je suis caché' = 'I am hidden'). In spoken French, context and reflexive pronoun determine whether it's reflexive (I hid myself) or passive (I am hidden). Agreement: with a female speaker, write 'je me suis cachée'.
target_language_example: Je me suis caché derrière l'armoire.
native_language_example: I hid behind the wardrobe.

meaning: I'm broke (I have no money).
additional_notes: Informal expression using the adjective 'cassé' (broken) to mean 'broke' about money. Usually said in the first person with 'je suis cassé' or contracted 'suis cassé' in casual speech. Common in spoken French; context makes clear it refers to lack of money, not a physical object.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce week-end, je suis cassé.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out this weekend, I'm broke.

meaning: 'I went to bed' (perfect tense of 'se coucher')
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé: 'je me suis couché(e)' = 'I went to bed' or 'I lay down'. Use 'me' for 'I'; add -e if speaker is female (je me suis couchée). Can be modified by time expressions (tard, tôt, à minuit).
target_language_example: Je me suis couché à minuit hier.
native_language_example: I went to bed at midnight yesterday.

meaning: I am cut off / I got cut off (e.g., phone call, power).
additional_notes: Literal: past participle 'coupé' with être (suis). Commonly used to say you've been disconnected (on the phone) or lost power. Context determines tense: 'je suis coupé' is present passive/state (I am cut off); to report a recent disconnection speakers often say 'j'ai été coupé' or 'on m'a coupé' for more natural phrasing. Informal in everyday speech when reporting a dropped call: 'Je suis coupé' or more commonly 'On m'a coupé' / 'J'ai été coupé'.
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis coupé — je rappelle tout de suite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm cut off — I'll call back right away.

meaning: 'I told myself that...' (used to report a thought or idea you had).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the reflexive past construction je me suis dit que. Use it to say you thought or told yourself something. Common in spoken and written French to introduce a suggestion, idea, or reflection. Structure: Subject + me/te/se + être (conjugated) + dit + que + clause. English equivalents: "I thought that...", "I told myself that..."
target_language_example: Je me suis dit que ce serait une bonne idée de téléphoner.
native_language_example: I told myself that it would be a good idea to call.

meaning: 'I managed' or 'I got by' (I handled it, often by myself or resourcefully).
additional_notes: This is the past form of se débrouiller (je me suis débrouillé / je me suis débrouillée). It means to manage, cope, or get by — often implying you found a solution on your own or made do with limited resources. Use with je me suis débrouillé (masculine) or je me suis débrouillée (feminine). Can be followed by what you managed to do (e.g., pour + infinitive) or used alone to mean 'I managed.'
target_language_example: Je me suis débrouillé pour trouver un appartement.
native_language_example: I managed to find an apartment.

meaning: 'I am determined' or 'I have decided' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal components: 'suis' = 'am' (1st person singular of être), 'décidé' = 'decided' or 'determined'. Alone, 'je suis décidé' means 'I am determined' (firm in my intention). In some contexts, French speakers more often say 'j'ai décidé' + infinitive to mean 'I decided to...' (I made the decision). Use 'je suis décidé' to emphasize personal resolve; use 'j'ai décidé de...' to state a decision you made.
target_language_example: Je suis décidé à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I am determined to learn French.

meaning: 'I hurried' or 'I rushed' (past tense: je me suis dépêché = I hurried myself / I rushed).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of the pronominal verb se dépêcher (to hurry). Often used with me/te/se/nous/vous + être auxiliary: je me suis dépêché(e). Add -e for feminine speaker (dépêchée). Commonly followed by a reason (pour/ne pas...) or an action achieved.
target_language_example: Je me suis dépêché pour arriver à l'heure.
native_language_example: I hurried to arrive on time.

meaning: 'I am asleep in' / 'I am asleep while (in the middle of)' — depends on context; literally 'I am asleep in/while'.
additional_notes: This string is not an independent fixed expression; it combines the verb être in first person singular ('je suis') + the past participle 'endormi' (asleep) and the preposition 'en' which introduces the circumstance (time, activity, material, or state) during which the speaker is asleep: e.g. 'je suis endormi en classe' (I am asleep in class), 'je suis endormi en réunion' (I am asleep during the meeting), or 'je suis endormi en plein jour' (I am asleep in broad daylight). To express the action of falling asleep, French more commonly uses 'je m'endors en...'. Use 'je suis endormi en...' to describe the state of being asleep in a particular situation.
target_language_example: Je suis endormi en classe pendant la conférence.
native_language_example: I am asleep in class during the lecture.

meaning: 'I fell asleep' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of the pronominal verb s'endormir (to fall asleep). The full form is 'je me suis endormie' (female speaker) or 'je me suis endormi' (male speaker). Used to say that you fell asleep (often accidentally or at a specific moment). In questions the reflexive pronoun and auxiliary invert or use est-ce que: 'Est-ce que je me suis endormie ?'.
target_language_example: Je me suis endormie tout de suite devant le film.
native_language_example: I fell asleep right away during the movie.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment or typo (e.g. 'je me suis fait une...' or 'je suis fait...' ).
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'suis fait une' is not correct by itself. Common related constructions: 'je me suis fait une...' (colloquial reflexive + past participle with 'faire' meaning 'have/get someone do something' or 'treat myself to a...'), or 'je suis fait' (informal: 'I'm done/ruined/beat' or 'I'm made' depending on context). If you meant 'je me suis fait une idée' = 'I formed an idea', or 'je me suis fait une faveur' = 'I treated myself to a favor'. Ask for the full sentence if unsure.
target_language_example: Je me suis fait une idée de la situation.
native_language_example: I formed an idea of the situation.

meaning: 'am/was parked' (part of the reflexive past tense of garer: se garer).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb se garer. In present: je me gare (I park myself / I park). In passé composé: je me suis garé(e) = I parked / I stopped the car and parked. Agree past participle with subject gender when using être as auxiliary (je me suis garé [m] / garée [f]). Commonly followed by location (au parking, dans la rue, devant la maison).
target_language_example: Je me suis garée devant l'immeuble.
native_language_example: I parked in front of the building.

meaning: I am imagined / I was imagined (passive of 'imaginer')
additional_notes: Suis imaginé is the first-person singular passive form using the present indicative of 'être' + past participle 'imaginé'. It is uncommon in everyday French — speakers more often use active forms (Je m'imagine) or different tenses (j'ai été imaginé). Context matters: it can mean 'I am imagined' (present passive) or, with intonation/context, refer to a past passive idea. More natural alternatives: 'je m'imagine' (I imagine myself), 'on m'a imaginé' or 'j'ai été imaginé' (I was imagined/created).
target_language_example: Je sais que dans ce conte, je suis imaginé comme un héros courageux.
native_language_example: I know that in this tale I am imagined as a brave hero.

meaning: 'I imagined that' (used with 'je me' → 'je me suis imaginé que')
additional_notes: This construction is reflexive and normally appears as 'je me suis imaginé que...' meaning 'I pictured/assumed/thought that...'. It often expresses a personal assumption or a mental picture (sometimes mistaken). In spoken/written French you may also see 'je m'imaginais que' (imperfect) for ongoing or habitual imagining, or 'je me suis imaginé' for a specific past moment. Use with subject pronoun (je, tu, il/elle, nous, etc.) and adjust past participle agreement when necessary (rare with 'imaginer' reflexive).
target_language_example: Je me suis imaginé que tu arriverais plus tôt.
native_language_example: I imagined that you would arrive earlier.

meaning: 'am left' or 'is left' (passive construction using être + laissé)
additional_notes: This is part of a passive or causative construction: the verb 'laisser' (to leave/let) is used with the auxiliary être (here 'suis' = I am) to indicate that someone is left/allowed/left behind. Without context, 'suis laissé' usually begins a passive clause (e.g. 'Je suis laissé seul' = 'I am left alone') or can appear in perfect tenses with être (e.g. 'Je suis laissé tomber' = 'I am/was let down' or 'I got dropped' depending on context). Word order and tense must match the subject (je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, etc.).
target_language_example: Je suis laissé seul quand ils partent.
native_language_example: I am left alone when they leave.

meaning: 'I washed (myself)' — past participle form used with reflexive verb 'se laver' in the passé composé
additional_notes: This appears as part of the reflexive passé composé: subject + reflexive pronoun + auxiliary (être) + past participle. For je: 'Je me suis lavé(e)'. The past participle agrees in gender and number with the reflexive direct object when appropriate (e.g. je me suis lavé (m.), je me suis lavée (f.)). Common uses: "les cheveux", "les pieds", or alone to mean 'I washed (myself)'.
target_language_example: Je me suis lavée ce matin avant de partir.
native_language_example: I washed myself this morning before leaving.

meaning: 'I am up' or 'I got up' (first-person singular of être + past participle 'levé')
additional_notes: Literally 'am up' — used with être in compound tenses or as a state: "je suis levé(e)" can mean 'I am up' (I'm out of bed) or 'I have gotten up' depending on context. Add (e) if the speaker is female: levé -> levée. More common alternatives: "je me suis levé(e)" (I got up) uses the reflexive verb 'se lever'.
target_language_example: Je suis levé depuis six heures.
native_language_example: I've been up since six o'clock.

meaning: 'am feeling unwell' or 'am in a bad way' (first-person singular of 'être' + adverb 'mal').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but part of sentences like 'Je suis mal' or 'Je suis mal au ventre'. Alone it sounds incomplete in French; native speakers usually say 'Je suis mal' to mean 'I'm feeling sick/unwell' or 'I'm in trouble' depending on context. More common/complete forms: 'Je suis malade' (I'm sick) or 'Je me sens mal' (I feel unwell).
target_language_example: Je suis mal depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: I've been feeling unwell since this morning.

meaning: am married
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive passé composé 'je me suis marié(e)' meaning either the current marital state ('I am married') or the completed action of marrying ('I got married'). With context it can emphasize the event (got married) or the state (am married). Remember to add (e) for a female speaker: je me suis mariée. Often used with details (avec quelqu'un, ici, de nouveau).
target_language_example: Je me suis marié l'été dernier avec Marie.
native_language_example: I got married last summer to Marie.

meaning: 'am put' / 'have been put' (passive construction with être + mis)
additional_notes: Literally the present tense of être (suis) + past participle mis (from mettre). Appears in passive or resultative phrases like « je suis mis en difficulté » (I am put/placed in difficulty) or in reflexive/impersonal constructions. More commonly you will see other forms (est mis, sommes mis) depending on the subject. Use it to say someone/something is placed, put, or made to be in a state. Pronunciation: /sɥi mi/.
target_language_example: Je suis mis en garde contre cette erreur.
native_language_example: I am warned against this mistake.

meaning: 'am made to' / 'have been put to' (passive construction: feminine singular)
additional_notes: This is part of a passive or causative expression using the verb 'mettre' in the past participle 'mise' (feminine) with 'être' (suis = I am). Usually appears in sentences like 'Je suis mise à l'écart' (I am put aside) or 'Je suis mise à travailler' (I am made to work). The exact meaning depends on the rest of the sentence. Because 'mise' is feminine, the speaker (or the noun it refers to) is feminine. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Je suis mise à l'écart depuis la réunion.
native_language_example: I have been put aside since the meeting.

meaning: 'am/was taking care of' or 'dealt with' (part of the reflexive construction 's'occuper de').
additional_notes: This appears as part of the reflexive past construction 'je me suis occupé de...' using auxiliary 'être' (agree 'occupé' with subject gender: occupé/occupée). It means to look after someone or to handle a task/problem. Neutral register; common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Je me suis occupé de ce problème hier.
native_language_example: I took care of this problem yesterday.

meaning: I left/I've gone to (somewhere) — first-person singular past (être + partir) followed by a preposition 'à'.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of partir for 'je' (je suis parti / je suis partie). Use 'suis parti à' before a place introduced with 'à' (e.g., à Paris, à la maison). If the speaker is female, write 'je suis partie à' (extra -e). In spoken French you may also hear the present 'je pars à' for 'I'm leaving for...'.
target_language_example: Je suis parti à Paris la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I left for Paris last week.

meaning: am not
additional_notes: Usually heard in informal French as part of je suis pas..., with ne dropped instead of standard je ne suis pas.... It can also appear in negative compound tenses with être, like je (n')y suis pas allé ('I didn't go there'). In tu ne me suis pas ?, suis is a different verb: suivre ('to follow').
target_language_example: Je suis pas sûr.
native_language_example: I'm not sure.

meaning: I am/was lost in (physically or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronoun (je me suis perdu) to say you got lost. Can be literal (lost in snow, a maze, a city) or figurative (lost in someone's world, thoughts, a book). Tense and subject change as usual: je me suis perdu (past), je suis perdu (present). Include preposition 'dans' + place or abstract noun.
target_language_example: Je me suis perdu dans la ville hier soir.
native_language_example: I got lost in the city last night.

meaning: I am busy / I am occupied (literally: 'am taken').
additional_notes: Formed from the verb 'être' (suis) + past participle 'pris' of 'prendre'. Commonly used to say you're busy or unavailable (e.g., 'Je suis pris' = I'm tied up / I can't do it now). Can also mean 'I was caught' or 'I'm captured' in other contexts depending on context and tense, but as 'suis pris' present it usually expresses being occupied. Use polite alternatives like 'je suis occupé(e)' if unsure.
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis pris cet après-midi, peut-on se voir demain ?
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm busy this afternoon; can we meet tomorrow?

meaning: I rushed / I hurried (lit. 'I rushed myself').
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb 'se précipiter' meaning to hurry or rush somewhere, often suddenly or urgently. Commonly used with motion verbs/places (dehors, en bas, à la maison, hors de). In English you can translate as 'I rushed out', 'I hurried down', etc. Conjugation: je me suis précipité (passé composé, masculine speaker); feminine adds -e (je me suis précipitée).
target_language_example: Je me suis précipité dehors quand j'ai entendu le bruit.
native_language_example: I rushed outside when I heard the noise.

meaning: 'I prepared (myself / something)' or 'I got ready.'
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular past formed with the pronominal verb se préparer (je me suis préparé). It can mean 'I got myself ready' (dressed, left, prepared oneself) or 'I prepared something for myself' when followed by an object (e.g., je me suis préparé un sandwich). Context and presence of an object determine whether it's reflexive (got ready) or means 'prepared for oneself' (made something). Remember agreement: if the subject is feminine, use préparée (je me suis préparée).
target_language_example: Je me suis préparé un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: I made myself a coffee before leaving.

meaning: 'I presented myself' / 'I introduced myself' or 'I showed up' (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular past (passé composé) of the pronominal verb se présenter. It can mean to introduce oneself (Je me suis présenté = I introduced myself) or to appear/show up/attend (Je me suis présenté à la réunion = I showed up/attended the meeting). Context (direct object or à + place/person) determines the meaning. Use with a role after 'comme' to say you introduced yourself as someone (e.g., comme maire).
target_language_example: Je me suis présenté à la porte et j'ai attendu qu'on m'ouvre.
native_language_example: I showed up at the door and waited for someone to open it.

meaning: 'I surrendered' / 'I realized' / 'I went' (depends on reflexive or passive use).
additional_notes: This form appears in different constructions with different meanings because of the past participle rendu and reflexive pronoun me. 1) With reflexive 'je me suis rendu' + à (Je me suis rendu au marché) = 'I went/returned to' or 'I went to' (formal) — literally 'I rendered myself to' (can sound slightly formal). 2) With 'je me suis rendu compte (que...)' = 'I realized' or 'I became aware that...'. 3) In passive/reflexive sense 'je me suis rendu' can mean 'I surrendered' (as in giving up) when context implies surrendering. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Je me suis rendu compte que j'avais oublié mes clés.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my keys.

meaning: I returned/I've returned to (someone's place) / I came back home to (someone's house).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a short past statement using the passé composé with the verb rentrer (Être/avoir + rentré). 'Suis rentré(e) chez' literally means 'am/was returned to [someone's place]'. You must add a possessor or person after 'chez' (e.g. chez moi, chez lui, chez mes parents). Include agreement of 'rentré' with subject if using être (e.g. 'suis rentré' for a male speaker, 'suis rentrée' for a female speaker). Common in spoken French: 'Je suis rentré(e) chez moi' = 'I went back home.'
target_language_example: Je suis rentré chez mes parents hier soir.
native_language_example: I returned to my parents' house last night.

meaning: I returned/I've come back to (a place) — first-person singular, passé composé of 'rentrer' with a following place introduced by 'à'.
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular passé composé form: 'je suis rentré(e) à ...' (use 'rentrée' if the speaker is female). 'Rentrer' uses être as auxiliary when indicating movement back to a place. The place that follows is introduced with 'à' for towns, home, or buildings (e.g., 'à Paris', 'à la maison'). If specifying entering a building or 'home', speakers often say 'je suis rentré(e) chez moi' instead of 'à moi'.
target_language_example: Je suis rentré à la maison à dix heures.
native_language_example: I came back home at ten o'clock.

meaning: I stayed at (someone's place) / I stayed home (chez + pronoun).
additional_notes: Uses the past participle resté with être (passé composé of rester). 'Chez' means 'at the home/place of' and is followed by a person or a possessive pronoun (chez moi = at my place/home). Typical structure: subject + suis resté(e) + chez + (moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/etc.). If the speaker is female, use suis restée.
target_language_example: Hier soir, je suis resté chez ma sœur.
native_language_example: Last night, I stayed at my sister's place.

meaning: I stayed at the (feminine place) / I remained at the (feminine place).
additional_notes: First-person singular past (passé composé or passé simple/compound sense) of rester + preposition à + feminine definite article la. Used before a feminine noun indicating a location (e.g., la maison, la gare, la soirée). Context determines tense: often used in spoken French as part of 'je suis resté(e) à la...' (note agreement: add -e for feminine speaker: je suis restée).
target_language_example: Je suis resté à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: I stayed at the house all day.

meaning: I find myself / I ended up (in a place or situation); literally 'am found' (passive/ pronominal use of retrouver)
additional_notes: Often used with a location or situation to say that the speaker 'ended up' somewhere or 'found themselves' doing/being something. It is the first-person singular present of être + retrouvé (past participle) used in a pronominal/passive sense — commonly appears as 'je me suis retrouvé' (I found myself / I ended up). Without the reflexive 'me' ('je suis retrouvé'), it can mean 'I was found' (passive). Context determines whether it's reflexive (ended up) or passive (was found).
target_language_example: Je me suis retrouvé seul au café après la réunion.
native_language_example: I ended up alone in the café after the meeting.

meaning: 'am awake' (I am awake).
additional_notes: First-person singular of être + past participle réveillé used as an adjective: 'je suis réveillé(e)' means 'I am awake' (add -e if speaker is feminine). Without the subject pronoun 'je' the phrase 'suis réveillé' is incomplete in standard writing but may appear in spoken or poetic ellipsis. To say 'I woke up' (an action) use 'je me suis réveillé(e)'.
target_language_example: Je suis réveillée depuis six heures.
native_language_example: I have been awake since six o'clock.

meaning: ‘am/was awakened at’ (used to say what time you woke up or were woken up).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular form of the passive/reflective construction with réveiller: je suis réveillé à + heure (present or past participle used adjectivally). More commonly speakers say Je me suis réveillé à + time (I woke up at ...). Je suis réveillé à can describe a current state ('I am awake at...') but for past action use Je me suis réveillé à. Include the time after à: e.g. à 7 h, à 7 heures du matin.
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé à 7 heures ce matin.
native_language_example: I woke up at 7 o'clock this morning.

meaning: 'I woke up' (feminine, past tense — first person singular).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of se réveiller (reflexive verb). 'Je me suis réveillée' uses the auxiliary être and agrees in gender with a feminine speaker (réveillé for masculine). It means the moment of waking up. If speaker is male, say 'je me suis réveillé.'
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillée à six heures ce matin.
native_language_example: I woke up at six o'clock this morning.

meaning: 'I feel' (with a past participle sense: literally 'am felt' — uncommon/awkward phrasing in French)
additional_notes: This sequence combines the first-person singular of être in the present ('suis') with the past participle 'senti' (from 'sentir'). On its own 'suis senti' is unusual: French speakers normally say 'je me sens' + adjective (je me sens bien), 'je me suis senti(e)' for 'I felt' (past), or 'je suis senti(e) [par quelqu'un]' rarely when passive (I was felt). Without 'je' and with no reflexive pronoun, 'suis senti' is likely an incomplete or incorrect fragment. Use 'je me sens' (I feel [now]) or 'je me suis senti(e)' (I felt) in most contexts.
target_language_example: Je me sens fatigué; hier, je me suis senti très inquiet.
native_language_example: I feel tired; yesterday, I felt very worried.

meaning: 'served myself' or 'used (for oneself)', depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of the reflexive verb se servir. It can mean 'to use' (Je me suis servi de = I used/used the help of) or 'to serve oneself' (Je me suis servi un verre = I helped myself to a drink). The reflexive pronoun me indicates the subject did the action to/for themselves. With de + noun or avec + noun it means 'used (something)'. With a direct object (un verre, une tasse) it means 'helped myself to'.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je me suis servi de ta loupe pour lire.
native_language_example: Tonight, I used your magnifying glass to read.

meaning: a form of 'tomber' (to fall) used with 'en' + noun/gerund to mean 'fell into' a state or 'fell while' doing something.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of tomber (je suis tombé) followed by 'en'. Common patterns: 'tomber en' + noun = 'fall into' a state (e.g. tomber en amour = fall in love; often colloquial), and 'tomber en' + present participle/gerund-like phrase or direction = 'fall while' or 'fall ...' (e.g. tomber en courant = fall while running). You will also see 'tomber' with prepositions like 'sur', 'dans', 'de', 'à', 'contre' for other meanings. Gender agreement: if speaker is female, use 'tombée' (je suis tombée en...).
target_language_example: Je suis tombé en pleurant quand j'ai vu la nouvelle.
native_language_example: I fell into tears when I saw the news.

meaning: am still
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of "je suis toujours...". "suis" is the "I am" form of être, and "toujours" can mean either "still" or "always" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je suis toujours ici.
native_language_example: I'm still here.

meaning: 'I was mistaken' / 'I made a mistake' (refers to being wrong about something).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of "se tromper" (to be mistaken / to make a mistake). Literally contains the auxiliary verb (être) and the past participle "trompé"; the full phrase in sentences is usually "je me suis trompé(e)". Use to admit an error or that you were wrong about a person, fact, opinion, etc. Add (e) for feminine speaker: "je me suis trompée."
target_language_example: Je me suis trompé en pensant que la réunion était demain.
native_language_example: I was mistaken in thinking the meeting was tomorrow.

meaning: I was mistaken about / I got the wrong (one).
additional_notes: This is the first-person passé composé of 'se tromper de' + noun: used to say you chose or identified the wrong person, place, date, number, etc. Common pattern: 'Je me suis trompé de + [nom]' (or 'de + infinitive' for wrong action). Adjust gender: a woman would say 'Je me suis trompée de...'.
target_language_example: Je me suis trompé de bus, celui-ci va dans la mauvaise direction.
native_language_example: I got the wrong bus; this one goes the wrong way.

meaning: I was wrong / I made a mistake (female speaker).
additional_notes: First-person singular passé composé of 'se tromper' used by a female speaker (agreements: 'trompée' with final -e). Common to admit an error, e.g. wrong queue, wrong assumption, or apologizing. With male speaker it would be 'me suis trompé'. Often appears with 'je me suis trompée' or shorter 'je me suis trompée.'
target_language_example: Je me suis trompée de train, le prochain part dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I was wrong about the train; the next one leaves in ten minutes.

meaning: 'I came (here) to (do something to/for you)'.
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence meaning the speaker arrived with the purpose of doing something for or to 'you' (informal singular tu). It's built from the past tense of 'venir' (je suis venu) + 'pour' (in order to) + the clitic 'te' (you). The full action follows (e.g. donner, parler, sauver). Use 'venue' if the speaker is feminine (je suis venue).
target_language_example: Je suis venu pour te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I came to tell you the truth.

meaning: 'I came to (you) ...' — used to introduce the purpose of coming to someone (spoken by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Literally 'am come you'. This is part of the structure 'Je suis venu(e) vous + [infinitive]' or 'Je suis venu(e) vous voir' meaning 'I came to tell you / to see you / to give you...'. The past participle 'venu' agrees in gender and number with the subject: a woman says 'venue', a man would say 'venu'. 'Vous' is the formal or plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Je suis venue vous apporter un message.
native_language_example: I came to bring you a message.

meaning: I am really good/well (feeling, doing fine).
additional_notes: Informal phrase built from the verb être (je suis) + vraiment bien. Used to say you feel good, are doing fine, or are comfortable in a situation. In full sentence you'd normally include the subject 'je' (Je suis vraiment bien) unless context already makes it clear. Can refer to physical well-being, mood, or satisfaction with a situation (e.g., a job, a place).
target_language_example: En vacances, je suis vraiment bien ici.
native_language_example: On vacation, I feel really good here.

meaning: 'I fainted' or 'I passed out' (first person past: je me suis évanoui).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of the pronominal verb s'évanouir (to faint). It describes losing consciousness temporarily. Use with je me suis évanoui(e) — add final -e if the speaker is female. Common contexts: heat, shock, injury, exhaustion. Formal/neutral tone.
target_language_example: Après avoir vu le sang, je me suis évanouie.
native_language_example: After seeing the blood, I fainted.

meaning: I am allergic (to ...).
additional_notes: Used to state an allergy to something. In French you say 'je suis allergique à/aux/au + [substance]' depending on gender/number: 'à' + le = au (au lait), 'à' + les = aux (aux arachides). When speaking about a general allergy to a category, use the definite article. Can be followed by 'de' in some constructions but most common is 'être allergique à'.
target_language_example: Je suis allergique aux fraises, je ne peux pas en manger.
native_language_example: I am allergic to strawberries; I can't eat them.

meaning: 'am/is/are well' or 'am/are/is (here/right)'; used to say you're fine, comfortable, located, or certain.
additional_notes: Depends on context and subject (je suis bien, tu es bien, il/elle est bien). Can mean: 1) I'm fine/well (state of health or mood); 2) I'm comfortable/ content (happy with situation); 3) I am indeed located at/about a place (asking/confirming location: "Je suis bien à la poste ?"); 4) I'm sure/determined (je suis bien décidé = I'm determined). Tone and intonation matter: as a short reply, it can mean "No, I'm fine" or "Yes, I'm okay."
target_language_example: Je suis bien ici, merci.
native_language_example: I'm fine here, thanks.

meaning: am good
additional_notes: literally 'am good.' Used to talk about ability or quality. With en or à + a subject or thing, it often means 'good at' (je suis bon en maths, je suis bon à ça). Before a noun, usually with un/une, it means 'a good ...' (je suis un bon nageur). A female speaker would usually say je suis bonne.
target_language_example: Je suis bon en français.
native_language_example: I'm good at French.

meaning: 'I am happy to' or 'I'm glad to'.
additional_notes: Used after the subject 'Je' as part of 'Je suis content d' + infinitive' to express pleasure about an action or situation. If speaker is female, use 'Je suis contente d'' (with an extra 'e'). The contraction d' appears before a vowel or silent h (d'avoir, d'entendre).
target_language_example: Je suis content d'apprendre la nouvelle.
native_language_example: I'm glad to hear the news.

meaning: 'I am happy that...' (short for je suis content que...)
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present of être + content que + subjunctive clause. It expresses that the speaker is pleased about something. In writing, qu' is used before a vowel (qu' + [verb/clause]). With a female speaker use 'je suis contente que...'. The verb in the following clause normally takes the subjunctive (e.g. je suis content que tu viennes).
target_language_example: Je suis content qu'il puisse venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm happy that he can come tonight.

meaning: 'I'm glad that you...' (expresses the speaker's happiness about something the other person does or is).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of être + adjective (Je suis content(e)) followed by que + subject (tu) + verb in the subjunctive when referring to feelings about actions/states. Use sois (subjunctive) for most verbs after que. Choose contente if speaker is female. Common for expressing emotion about someone else's action or state.
target_language_example: Je suis content que tu sois venu.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you came.

meaning: I'm glad that you... / I'm happy that you... (used to express pleasure about something someone did).
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular of 'être content' followed by 'que' + subjunctive or past subjunctive. Use it to express that you are pleased about someone's action or presence. The verb after 'que vous' must be in the subjunctive (present subjunctive for current/ongoing actions: 'vous soyez'; past subjunctive for completed actions: 'vous ayez/ayez pu' or 'vous soyez venu(s)'). Agreement: if the subject 'vous' is plural, past participle may take a plural ending (venus). Pronunciation tip: the 's' in 'suis' is silent in casual speech—says like 'swee' /sɥi/.
target_language_example: Je suis content que vous ayez pu venir.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you were able to come.

meaning: 'I'm glad that you...' (used to express happiness about what someone did or did).
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular of 'être content(e) que' followed by 'vous' + verb in the subjunctive (or past subjunctive for actions completed). Use 'contente' if the speaker is female, 'content' if male. Commonly followed by verbs like 'ayez appelé', 'ayez pu venir', or 'soyez venu(e)'. It's a polite/formal way to express gratitude or relief to one or more people (or to a single person you address formally).
target_language_example: Je suis contente que vous ayez accepté mon invitation.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you accepted my invitation.

meaning: am in a
additional_notes: A fragment combining the first-person singular present of être (je suis) with dans un (in a). It appears in sentences like «Je suis dans un restaurant» (I am in a restaurant) or «Je suis dans un mauvais mood» (I'm in a bad mood). For beginners: remember to include the subject pronoun je before suis. The indefinite article (un/une) must agree in gender with the noun that follows (un for masculine nouns, une for feminine).
target_language_example: Je suis dans un parc.
native_language_example: I am in a park.

meaning: 'I'm sorry for' or 'I'm sorry to (do/have done)'.
additional_notes: Used to apologize. Usually follows the subject 'je' as in 'je suis désolé de...' and is followed by an infinitive (de + verb) or a past infinitive (de + avoir + past participle) to explain the reason. Polite and common in both formal and informal situations; use 'désolée' if the speaker is female. You can also say 'je suis désolé(e)' alone to express regret without specifying why.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de t'avoir oublié.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for having forgotten you.

meaning: 'I'm sorry for' (used by a female speaker) or 'sorry to...'
additional_notes: Used to apologize and introduce the reason (infinitive or clause). 'Suis désolée' is first-person singular feminine; a male speaker would say 'je suis désolé de'. Often followed by an infinitive (de + verb) or a past infinitive (de + avoir + past participle) to explain what you're sorry for.
target_language_example: Je suis désolée de vous avoir fait attendre.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for making you wait.

meaning: 'I am determined' (I have made a firm decision or resolution).
additional_notes: First-person singular of être + déterminé. Used to express strong will or resolve to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g. « je suis déterminé à réussir »). Tone is neutral to strong; suitable in formal and informal contexts. Determiné can also mean 'determined' in the sense of 'decisive' or 'resolute' when describing someone's character.
target_language_example: Je suis déterminé à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I am determined to learn French.

meaning: am/are/is in favor (of); support
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular (je) or used after other subjects with être (e.g., 'je suis en faveur de...', 'elle est en faveur de...') followed by 'de' + noun or infinitive to indicate support for something. Formal/neutral register. Common alternatives: 'je soutiens' or 'je suis pour'.
target_language_example: Je suis en faveur de réduire les déchets plastiques.
native_language_example: I am in favor of reducing plastic waste.

meaning: am still
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a sentence with je, as in je suis encore... = i am still.... Here suis is the 1st-person singular form of être, and encore most often means still in this pattern.
target_language_example: Je suis encore à la maison.
native_language_example: I'm still at home.

meaning: I'm still in / I'm still at (a place or situation).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of être (je suis) followed by encore en, used to say you are still in a place, still in the middle of an activity, or still in a particular state. It must be completed by a noun or gerund/participle phrase (e.g. 'suis encore en réunion', 'suis encore en train de travailler', 'suis encore en France'). In spoken French the subject pronoun 'je' is often included: 'je suis encore en...'.
target_language_example: Je suis encore en train de finir le rapport.
native_language_example: I'm still finishing the report.

meaning: 'I am happy that' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Used by a female speaker to express happiness about something that happened or that someone did; followed by a clause in the subjunctive (e.g. que vous ayez pu venir, que vous soyez venu(e)). For a male speaker, use "suis heureux que". Can be shortened in speech to "je suis contente que" (also common).
target_language_example: Je suis heureuse que tu aies trouvé un emploi.
native_language_example: I am happy that you found a job.

meaning: 'I am happy that you...' (feminine speaker)
additional_notes: Used by a female speaker to say she is happy about something the listener does or a situation concerning them. Followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., ailles, sois, viennes) in many cases — though with certain verbs or tenses the indicative may appear. To address a male speaker, use "suis heureux que tu". For plural/formal 'you' use "suis heureuse que vous".
target_language_example: Je suis heureuse que tu sois là.
native_language_example: I am happy that you are here.

meaning: I'm happy to (see/hear) you; I'm glad that you ... (familiar singular 'you').
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase using the verb 'être' (je suis) + 'heureux/heureuse de' + infinitive or clause starting with a pronoun. 'Te' is the familiar singular object pronoun (you). Common completions: 'te voir' (to see you), 'te l'entendre dire' (to hear you say it). Use 'heureuse' if the speaker is female.
target_language_example: Je suis heureux de te rencontrer.
native_language_example: I'm happy to meet you.

meaning: 'I am happy to (you)...' — part of phrases meaning 'I am happy to see/know/meet you' or 'I'm glad that...'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in polite or formal sentences when the speaker expresses happiness about something concerning the listener (seeing, hearing, having someone on board, etc.). Complete sentences normally include a verb or clause after 'de vous' (e.g. 'voir', 'revoir', 'entendre dire', 'avoir à bord', 'trouver en bonne santé'). Use 'heureuse' if the speaker is female: 'je suis heureuse de vous...'.
target_language_example: Je suis heureux de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: I am happy to meet you.

meaning: 'I'm glad that you...' or 'I'm happy that you...'
additional_notes: This is the first part of the sentence used to express gladness about something the other person did or a state they are in. It requires the subjunctive after 'que' (e.g. 'tu sois', 'tu aies', depending on the verb). Gender of past participle/agreement appears in examples ('venu' vs 'venue'). Commonly used in polite or emotional contexts.
target_language_example: Je suis heureux que tu aies réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you passed the exam.

meaning: am here
additional_notes: Usually appears with a subject pronoun, most often je suis ici = 'I am here'. It is literal and straightforward. In time expressions like ça fait huit ans que je suis ici, French uses the present tense where English often says 'have been here'.
target_language_example: Je suis ici pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I'm here to help you.

meaning: am the most
additional_notes: Context-dependent. "suis" is the first-person singular of être (to be) or suivre (to follow) when conjugated as 'je suis'. Paired with "le plus" it most commonly means "I am the most" (e.g., je suis le plus patient = I am the most patient). If coming from suivre (less common: "je suis le plus" as part of a longer phrase like "je suis le plus jeune" vs. "je suis le plus" can also be start of 'I follow the most' in contexts where 'suis' is 'follow' but this requires object/clarification). Use with an adjective: je suis le plus + adjective = I am the most + adjective.
target_language_example: Je suis le plus rapide de l'équipe.
native_language_example: I am the fastest in the team.

meaning: 'I'm here in' or 'I'm located in' (followed by a place or situation).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'être' in the 1st person singular present ('je suis') with 'là' (here) and 'dans' (in). In natural French you normally say 'je suis là, dans...' or 'je suis dans...' depending on emphasis. 'Je suis là dans la salle' emphasizes 'here' then specifies where; 'je suis dans la salle' is the simpler form. Use with a noun or phrase after 'dans' to indicate location or context.
target_language_example: Je suis là dans la cuisine si tu veux me parler.
native_language_example: I'm here in the kitchen if you want to talk to me.

meaning: 'I am a doctor.' (first-person singular present of être + noun)
additional_notes: This is the simple, direct way to say you are a doctor. 'Suis' is the 'je' form of the verb être (to be). In spoken French the subject pronoun 'je' is normally included: 'Je suis médecin.' You can change the profession noun as needed: 'Je suis professeur.'
target_language_example: Je suis médecin et je travaille à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: I am a doctor and I work at the hospital.

meaning: 'am neither' (used in constructions like 'je ne suis ni ... ni ...' = 'I am neither ... nor ...')
additional_notes: Rarely appears alone as 'suis ni' — it is part of the negative correlative structure 'ne ... ni ... ni' meaning 'neither ... nor'. In full form with a subject and 'ne' it becomes 'je ne suis ni fatigué ni malade' (I am neither tired nor sick). Spoken French often drops the 'ne': 'je suis ni...' (colloquial/informal).
target_language_example: Je ne suis ni prêt ni sûr.
native_language_example: I am neither ready nor sure.

meaning: informal contraction meaning 'I am not at' or 'I'm not in/aware of' depending on context (short for 'je ne suis pas au/à...').
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken fragment where the subject pronoun je is often dropped and the negation ne is omitted (colloquial French). It must be completed by a location, situation or expression after 'au' (e.g., 'au courant' = aware, 'au travail' = work). Example full phrases: 'Je ne suis pas au courant' (I'm not aware), 'Je suis pas au travail' (I'm not at work).
target_language_example: Je suis pas au courant de ce changement.
native_language_example: I'm not aware of this change.

meaning: shortened/informal part of a negative phrase meaning 'I am not (from/of)' or 'I'm not the kind of...'
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the informal, contracted spoken form of 'je ne suis pas du...' used in casual conversation. It commonly appears in expressions like 'je suis pas du tout' (I'm not at all) or 'je ne suis pas du genre' / 'je suis pas du genre' (I'm not the type to...). In informal speech the 'je' and 'ne' are often dropped: 'suis pas du' = 'je ne suis pas du'. Always check the rest of the sentence to know whether it means 'from' (du = de + le) or 'the type of'.
target_language_example: Je suis pas du genre à me plaindre.
native_language_example: I'm not the type to complain.

meaning: I'm not more / I'm no more (used to downplay or refuse something).
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of "je ne suis pas plus" or answer fragment after a clause: e.g. "Je suis pas plus content que toi" (I'm no more happy than you). Often used in spoken French without the initial "je" (suis pas plus...). Can express 'not especially' or 'not more than' and is informal. Context determines whether it compares quantity/degree or rejects an offer/request.
target_language_example: Franchement, je suis pas plus intéressé par ce film.
native_language_example: Honestly, I'm not any more interested in that movie.

meaning: '(I) am not sure that' (expressing doubt about a clause).
additional_notes: This is the colloquial, shortened form of « je ne suis pas sûr que ». It introduces a subordinate clause and is often followed by the subjunctive in formal written French (e.g., que Tom soit...). In spoken French people frequently drop the initial 'je ne' and sometimes the 'ne' in the verb, so 'suis pas sûr que' is common in conversation. Use with a subject (je) implied if the full phrase is omitted.
target_language_example: Je suis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I'm not sure that it's a good idea.

meaning: informal way to say "(I) am not your..." (shortened from "je ne suis pas ton...").
additional_notes: Common spoken contraction where the subject pronoun "je" and the negation particle "ne" are dropped or reduced. Used before a noun (ami, ennemi, frère, etc.) to deny a relationship or role. Tone can be neutral or strong/insulting depending on context and words added. For polite or formal speech, use the full form: "Je ne suis pas ton..."
target_language_example: Je suis pas ton ami, alors respecte mes choix.
native_language_example: I'm not your friend, so respect my choices.

meaning: colloquial/informal start of a phrase meaning 'I'm not in the mood for...' or 'I'm not up to...'
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken fragment. It uses the contracted spoken form of 'je ne suis pas' (often just 'je suis pas' or dropped 'je') followed by 'à la' + noun or verb phrase to express lack of readiness, ability, mood, or willingness for something (e.g. 'suis pas à la fête' = 'I'm not in the party mood', or 'suis pas à la... aujourd'hui' = 'I'm not up for it today'). You will usually hear it in speech, often without the subject pronoun (e.g. 'Je suis pas à la'). Add the rest of the sentence to make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Je suis pas à la fête ce soir, désolé.
native_language_example: I'm not in the party mood tonight, sorry.

meaning: am maybe
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of être (suis) plus peut-être (maybe). Used when the speaker is uncertain about a state or identity: "I might be..." In natural English you would usually say "I might be" or "I may be" rather than a literal "am maybe." Context often completes the phrase (e.g. "suis peut-être fatigué" → "I might be tired").
target_language_example: Je suis peut-être fatigué.
native_language_example: I might be tired.

meaning: 'I am no longer a...' (negation + identity: 'I'm no longer a/an...')
additional_notes: This is part of the present-tense first-person form 'je ne suis plus un/une ...' used to say you are no longer something (child, kid, stranger, etc.). 'Plus' here means 'no longer'. Remember to include 'ne' for formal writing/construction, though in speech French speakers often drop 'ne' (Je suis plus un → colloquial). Choose 'un' or 'une' to match the noun's gender. Can be followed by a noun or short description.
target_language_example: Je ne suis plus un étudiant, je travaille maintenant.
native_language_example: I'm no longer a student; I work now.

meaning: used in phrases like "je ne suis que le..." to mean "I'm only the..." or "I'm just the..."
additional_notes: Appears in the fixed expression "je ne suis que + noun" meaning "I'm merely/only [a/the]..." It downplays the speaker's role or importance. Common translations: "I'm just the messenger," "I'm only the translator," "I'm only the sheriff." The literal words individually are compositional, but the phrase functions as a set expression in context.
target_language_example: Je ne suis que le traducteur; ne m'en voulez pas si le sens change.
native_language_example: I'm just the translator; don't blame me if the meaning changes.

meaning: 'I am delighted to' (female speaker).
additional_notes: Used by a woman (ravie = feminine form) to express pleasure about meeting someone, helping, hearing news, or doing something. Followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., faire, voir, rencontrer) or by que/relative clauses. Male speakers would say 'suis ravi de'. Common polite phrase in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Je suis ravie de faire votre connaissance.
native_language_example: I am delighted to meet you.

meaning: 'I am delighted/glad that' (expressing pleasure about something).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or pleasure about a situation; subject is typically first person singular (je suis ravie — feminine speaker). If a male speaker, use 'suis ravi que'. Followed by a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' and then the subjunctive for many verbs (e.g. que tu sois, que vous ayez) when the clause expresses emotion, doubt, desire, or possibility.
target_language_example: Je suis ravie que tu aies pu venir.
native_language_example: I am delighted that you were able to come.

meaning: 'I am grateful to you for your...'
additional_notes: This is the first part of the full sentence 'Je te suis reconnaissant pour ta...' used to express thanks for a specific quality, action or thing someone provided. The complete phrase normally begins with 'Je' and includes the indirect object pronoun ('te' for 'to you', 'vous' for formal/plural). Use the appropriate possessive after 'ta' (ta = your, feminine singular noun). For masculine nouns use 'ton' (Je te suis reconnaissant pour ton aide). A feminine speaker might say 'Je te suis reconnaissante pour ta...' (agreeing 'reconnaissant(e)').
target_language_example: Je te suis reconnaissant pour ta patience.
native_language_example: I am grateful to you for your patience.

meaning: literally 'am without' — first-person singular of 'être sans' (to be without).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the present tense 'je suis' (I am) followed by 'sans' (without). You will usually see it as part of a full sentence: 'Je suis sans...' meaning 'I am without...' or 'I'm lacking...' It must be followed by a noun or phrase (e.g. 'argent', 'voiture', 'idée'). In spoken French people more often say 'je n'ai pas' + noun (I don't have) instead of 'je suis sans'.
target_language_example: Je suis sans argent jusqu'à la fin du mois.
native_language_example: I am without money until the end of the month.

meaning: 'am/are/is so happy to' (expressing strong happiness about doing or experiencing something).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'être' (je suis, tu es, il/elle est...) followed by 'si heureux/heureuse de' + infinitive or a clause. 'Si' here intensifies the adjective (so/very). Use 'heureux' for masculine speakers and 'heureuse' for feminine. Formality is neutral; 'vous' vs 'te' changes formality or number.
target_language_example: Je suis si heureux de t'aider aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am so happy to help you today.

meaning: 'am/are/is under' (literal: to be under something) — used with expressions like 'suis sous pression' or 'suis sous le feu'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the verb être (conjugated: je suis, tu es, il/elle est...) + 'sous' (under). Common in sentences like 'je suis sous pression' (I'm under pressure) or 'nous sommes sous contrat' (we are under contract). Remember to conjugate être appropriately for the subject (je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont). 'Sous' is followed by a noun or noun phrase; you cannot follow it directly with an adjective without a noun.
target_language_example: Je suis sous pression cette semaine.
native_language_example: I am under pressure this week.

meaning: 'I am often' or 'I often am' (first-person singular of être + 'often').
additional_notes: This is the verb être (to be) in the present first-person singular (je suis) followed by the adverb souvent (often). It expresses frequency about a state or condition of the speaker: e.g. 'Je suis souvent fatigué' = 'I am often tired.' In natural sentences you usually include the subject pronoun je before 'suis souvent'.
target_language_example: Je suis souvent en retard le matin.
native_language_example: I am often late in the morning.

meaning: I am surprised to (see/learn that)...
additional_notes: Used with verbs or infinitives introduced by 'de' to express surprise about an action or fact. Formality: neutral. You can change subject pronoun (Je suis surpris(e) de..., Nous sommes surpris de...). If addressing formally use 'vous' in the continuation: e.g. «Je suis surpris de vous voir.» Remember to add (e) for feminine speaker: 'surprise'.
target_language_example: Je suis surpris de te voir ici.
native_language_example: I am surprised to see you here.

meaning: 'I am surprised to (see/meet/learn) you' — the start of a sentence meaning 'I am surprised to...' directed at 'you' (informal).
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own; it's the beginning of a clause using the verb 'être' in the first person singular (je suis) followed by 'surpris(e) de' + infinitive or a clause with 'te' (the informal object 'you'). Usually appears as 'Je suis surpris de te voir', 'Je suis surpris de te retrouver ici', or 'Je suis surpris de te dire que...'. If speaking formally or to a woman, adjust gender: 'Je suis surprise de te...'.
target_language_example: Je suis surpris de te voir ici ce matin.
native_language_example: I am surprised to see you here this morning.

meaning: 'I'm sure that you' (polite/formal) or 'I'm sure you' when addressing someone formally or in plural.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular phrase 'Je suis sûr que vous...' meaning the speaker is confident about what follows. In full form it is usually 'Je suis sûr que vous...' or 'Je suis sûr(e) que vous...' (add -e if speaker is female). Use 'sûr' for certainty; 'sûr(e)' must agree with the speaker's gender. For informal singular 'you' (tu) say 'Je suis sûr que tu...'.
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que vous réussirez cet examen.
native_language_example: I'm sure that you will pass this exam.

meaning: 'am very interested' (first person singular).
additional_notes: This is the verb être (suis) + adjective phrase très intéressé, used to say you are very interested in something. It must match the speaker's gender in writing/spoken agreement: a male speaker would say "je suis très intéressé", a female speaker would commonly say "je suis très intéressée" (adds -e). Often followed by de/à + noun or infinitive: "je suis très intéressé par ce poste" or "je suis très intéressé à en savoir plus" (more naturally: "intéressé à" is less common than "intéressé par" or "intéressé de" depending on context).
target_language_example: Je suis très intéressé par ce poste.
native_language_example: I am very interested in this position.

meaning: 'I am an old' (used before a masculine noun to mean 'old' in age or longtime/familiarity).
additional_notes: The phrase combines the verb suis (I am) + un vieil, where vieil is the shortened form of vieux used before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h (e.g. vieil ami, vieil homme). It can mean "old" (age) or "longtime"/"old (longstanding)" as in "an old friend". If the noun begins with a consonant, use "vieux" (e.g. un vieux copain).
target_language_example: Je suis un vieil ami de la famille.
native_language_example: I am an old friend of the family.

meaning: 'am one of' — fragment of 'je suis un de...' used to indicate belonging to a group or category.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present of être without the subject pronoun (je). Beginners should include the pronoun: 'je suis un de...' or more commonly 'je fais partie de...' / 'je suis l'un(e) de...'. 'un de' is followed by a noun phrase (often with a possessive: 'un de mes amis'). The fragment 'suis un de' may appear in casual speech after a pause or as part of a larger sentence but is not a complete sentence by itself.
target_language_example: Je suis un de ceux qui préfèrent travailler tôt le matin.
native_language_example: I am one of those who prefer to work early in the morning.

meaning: am your
additional_notes: Usually appears after je: je suis votre... = "I am your...". Suis is the je form of être ("to be"), and votre means "your" when speaking to one person formally or to more than one person. It is normally followed by a noun, as in je suis votre guide.
target_language_example: Je suis votre guide pour aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am your guide for today.

meaning: I'm at your service / I'll be with you (shortly).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you'll attend to them soon or that you are available to help. Common in customer/service contexts or polite conversation. In short responses like 'Je suis à vous' it can mean 'I am yours' (polite/figurative: at your disposal). Often followed by time expressions: 'dans un instant', 'tout de suite'.
target_language_example: Je suis à vous dans une minute, monsieur.
native_language_example: I'll be with you in a minute, sir.

meaning: follows a (masculine) — as in 'follows a [noun]'.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'suivre' (il/elle/on suit) + the indefinite article 'un'. It literally means 'follows a' and is used before a masculine singular noun. Commonly appears in sentences like 'Il suit un cours' (He is taking/attending a course) or 'Elle suit un régime' (She is following a diet). Context determines whether 'follow' means physically follow, attend/take, or adhere to (a rule, plan, diet, etc.).
target_language_example: Elle suit un cours de français.
