native_language_example: She is taking a French class.

meaning: to follow the (masculine singular noun); to keep up with the
additional_notes: ‘Suivre’ means ‘to follow’ or ‘to take (a course)’. When combined with the definite article ‘le’ it introduces a masculine singular noun (e.g., suivre le cours = to take/follow the class). Context determines nuance: physical following (follow someone/the path), keeping up with (news, progress), or attending/taking (a course). Conjugate ‘suivre’ as needed (je suis, tu suis, il suit, nous suivons...).
target_language_example: Je vais suivre le cours de français cet été.
native_language_example: I will take/follow the French course this summer.

meaning: to follow its course; to proceed as expected or naturally (an event, process, situation).
additional_notes: Used about events or processes that continue without interference. Can imply letting things happen without intervening. Similar to 'prendre son cours' or English 'let it take its course.' Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Après les discussions, nous avons décidé de laisser la situation suivre son cours.
native_language_example: After the discussions, we decided to let the situation take its course.

meaning: 'subject of this' or 'topic of this'.
additional_notes: Rarely used as a fixed phrase on its own; you will more often see 'le sujet de ce [document/texte/cours]' or phrasing like 'le sujet de cette conversation' to mean 'the subject/topic of this'. Make sure to include the appropriate article (le/la/les) and noun that follows (e.g. 'le sujet de ce texte').
target_language_example: Le sujet de ce texte est l'environnement.
native_language_example: The subject of this text is the environment.

meaning: 'subject of the' (feminine noun) — used before a feminine noun to say what something is about
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the start of a noun phrase: sujet de la + [feminine noun]. Use 'sujet du' before masculine nouns (sujet du projet), and 'sujet des' for plural (sujet des élèves). Common in contexts like discussions, essays, presentations: le sujet de la conférence, le sujet de la discussion.
target_language_example: Le sujet de la présentation est l'énergie solaire.
native_language_example: The subject of the presentation is solar energy.

meaning: 'the subject of your...' (used to refer to the topic or matter belonging to someone)
additional_notes: This is a fragment: usually followed by a noun (e.g. 'sujet de votre email', 'sujet de votre message', 'sujet de votre conversation'). It literally means 'subject of your...' and is used to specify possession (votre = your). Formal or neutral register. Make sure the noun that follows agrees in meaning but not in gender/number (votre is invariant for singular formal/plural).
target_language_example: Le sujet de votre email doit être clair et précis.
native_language_example: The subject of your email must be clear and precise.

meaning: about; concerning (used before a plural noun introduced by de + les → des).
additional_notes: Formed from 'au sujet de' (about/concerning). When the noun is plural and uses the article 'les', 'de + les' becomes 'des', so you'll see 'au sujet des' or 'au sujet de' + noun. Common in formal and neutral contexts to introduce the topic being discussed or asked about.
target_language_example: Nous avons parlé au sujet des projets pour l'été.
native_language_example: We talked about the plans for the summer.

meaning: very; really (informal intensifier placed before an adjective or noun phrase)
additional_notes: Colloquial: 'super' is used as an intensifier meaning 'very' or 'really'. When followed by 'de' it often appears in expressions like 'super de ...' before a noun or to link to another element (though more common patterns are 'super + adjective' or 'super + noun' without 'de'). In everyday speech you will more often hear 'super + adjective' (e.g. 'super bon') or 'super de + noun' in some regional or emphatic uses. Use in informal contexts.
target_language_example: C'est super de ta part.
native_language_example: That's really nice of you.

meaning: 'I suppose that we/one/they...' or 'I guess that...'.
additional_notes: Common spoken expression using the verb supposer + que with the contracted subject on (short for 'on'). On can mean 'we', 'one', or informal 'they/people' depending on context. Often used to express a tentative assumption or mild guess. In more formal writing you'd see 'suppose que nous' or 'je suppose que...'. The negative may appear as 'je suppose qu'on ne...' or colloquially 'je suppose qu'on n' / 'je suppose qu'on a pas' (spoken omission of 'ne').
target_language_example: Je suppose qu'on finira vers huit heures.
native_language_example: I suppose we'll finish around eight o'clock.

meaning: I suppose that it/that is... (expressing a guess or assumption).
additional_notes: A shortened form of "je suppose que c'est..." used to express a tentative assumption or mild certainty. Common in spoken and written French. Can be followed by adjectives, nouns, or clauses (e.g., "c'est bon", "c'est le cas", "c'est vrai"). Often used with "je" but can appear with other subjects ("on suppose que c'..."). Tone is neutral; not particularly formal or informal.
target_language_example: Je suppose que c'est la bonne clé.
native_language_example: I suppose that's the right key.

meaning: 'I suppose that I' / 'I assume that I' (used to introduce a personal assumption or opinion)
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular form of the verb 'supposer' + que. It introduces a guess, assumption, or tentative opinion about something you (the speaker) might do or think. In spoken French you may also hear 'je suppose que' with the subject repeated; 'suppose que je' may appear inside a sentence (e.g. 'Tu suppose que je...') but most commonly you'll use 'je suppose que...' to start a sentence. Use it to soften statements or to express uncertainty.
target_language_example: Je suppose que je devrais partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I suppose that I should leave now.

meaning: 'I suppose that we' / 'I guess that we'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal assumption or tentative conclusion about what 'we' (nous) do, feel, or should do. Followed by a verb phrase in various tenses or moods (devoir, pouvoir, être, etc.). Equivalent to 'I suppose we...' or 'I guess we...' in English; slightly formal/neutral.
target_language_example: Je suppose que nous devrions partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I suppose that we should leave now.

meaning: you suppose / you assume (that)...
additional_notes: This is the second-person plural (or formal singular) present of the verb supposer followed by que. It introduces what someone thinks or assumes about a situation. In spoken French you may also hear 'supposons que vous' (let's suppose that you) or the informal singular 'supposes que tu' rarely; for informal direct address use 'vous' as formal or plural. Common structures: 'Je suppose que vous...' (I suppose that you...), 'Suppose que vous...' (Imagine/suppose that you...).
target_language_example: Je suppose que vous connaissez la ville.
native_language_example: I suppose that you know the city.

meaning: immediately; right away; at once.
additional_notes: Adverbial phrase meaning to do something without delay. Slightly formal or literary in tone but still used in spoken French. Synonyms: tout de suite, immédiatement. Often used after verbs (Je veux le voir sur-le-champ).
target_language_example: Répare ça sur-le-champ, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Fix that right away, please.

meaning: based on; on the basis of
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is founded on specific information, criteria, documents, data, or principles. Formal or neutral register (often seen in written or bureaucratic contexts). More commonly in French you might see "sur la base de" (with the article) or alternatives like "à partir de" or "en se basant sur."
target_language_example: La décision a été prise sur base des rapports reçus.
native_language_example: The decision was made based on the reports received.

meaning: on that
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) literal/prepositional: 'sur' + demonstrative to mean 'about/on that' (e.g. parler sur ce que... = about that). 2) discourse formula used to close or move on: 'sur ce' = 'with that' or 'on that note' / 'having said that' (often followed by a result or action, e.g. 'Sur ce, il s'en alla' = 'With that, he left'). Can appear in set phrases like 'parier sur ce' (bet on that) or 'revenir sur ce que...' (return to/withdraw/clarify what was said).
target_language_example: Sur ce, je te laisse réfléchir.
native_language_example: With that, I'll let you think about it.

meaning: confident about; sure of
additional_notes: Used after être (être sûr(e) de) to indicate certainty regarding something. Agreement: sûr becomes sûre for feminine subjects and may take plural (sûrs/sûres). Common constructions: 'être sûr de + noun/infinitive/que...' Note: in standard French the fixed phrase is 'sûr de' with circumflex; casual writing/speech sometimes omits diacritics ('sur de').
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sur de cette décision.
native_language_example: I am not sure of this decision.

meaning: over/for long (distances) — part of the phrase 'sur de longues distances' meaning 'for long distances' or 'over long distances'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears before a noun (typically 'distances') to indicate extent or duration across a large length/area. Common complete phrase: 'sur de longues distances' = 'over long distances' or 'for long distances'. Used with verbs like marcher, voler, transporter. Agreement (habitué/habituée) depends on the subject, not on this phrase.
target_language_example: Les migrateurs voyagent sur de longues distances chaque année.
native_language_example: Migratory birds travel over long distances every year.

meaning: on the right track; heading in the correct direction (figurative).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say someone or something is making progress or moving toward a good outcome. Can refer to plans, projects, learning, behaviour, etc. Often used with verbs like être, mettre, guider, or continuer (e.g. 'être sur la bonne voie', 'mettre quelqu'un sur la bonne voie').
target_language_example: Ton projet est sur la bonne voie, continue comme ça.
native_language_example: Your project is on the right track, keep it up.

meaning: on tiptoe; quiet/very lightly on the balls of the feet.
additional_notes: Used to describe walking or entering quietly and lightly, often to avoid making noise or to be stealthy. Can be literal (physically on your toes) or figurative (doing something discreetly).
target_language_example: Il entra dans la chambre sur la pointe des pieds pour ne pas réveiller le bébé.
native_language_example: He entered the room on tiptoe so as not to wake the baby.

meaning: 'immediately' or 'right away'.
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to mean 'at once' or 'without delay' (equivalent to English 'immediately' or 'right now'). Not to be confused with the literal sense 'on the field' — context decides meaning. Formal and common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Si tu veux partir, fais-le sur le champ.
native_language_example: If you want to leave, do it immediately.

meaning: because of; attributed to; charged to (an account).
additional_notes: Can mean 'attribute something to' (e.g. blame or cause: «mettre sur le compte de» = 'attribute to') or a literal accounting sense 'charge to the account of' (e.g. expenses). Context determines whether it's figurative (cause/blame) or financial. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Elle a mis son échec sur le compte de la malchance.
native_language_example: She attributed her failure to bad luck.

meaning: immediately; directly involved; on the case (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common idiom with two main uses: 1) To say someone was killed 'sur le coup' = 'instantly' or 'on the spot' (adverb of time). 2) To say a person or group is 'sur le coup' = 'on the case' or 'handling/involved with' (responsibility/attention). Context determines whether it means 'immediately' or 'working on it.'
target_language_example: La brigade est sur le coup depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: The team has been on the case since this morning.

meaning: on the side/slope of (a hill, mountain, building, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to describe something located on the side or slope of a natural feature (hill, mountain) or sometimes a large object; implies being positioned partway up or along the side rather than on top. Common in geographic descriptions.
target_language_example: Le village est construit sur le flanc de la montagne.
native_language_example: The village is built on the side of the mountain.

meaning: in the moment; at the time (then).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's reaction, impression, or decision at the time something happened (often implying their view may have changed later). Common in spoken and written French. Can appear at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Sur le moment, je n'ai pas réalisé mon erreur.
native_language_example: At the time, I didn't realize my mistake.

meaning: literally 'on the paper'; idiomatically 'in theory' or 'on paper' (i.e., according to documents or plans, maybe not in reality).
additional_notes: Used both literally (something drawn or written on paper) and figuratively to mean 'in theory' or 'according to the documents/plan'—often implying a contrast with reality. Context tells which meaning; short standalone 'Sur le papier.' usually means 'On paper / In theory.'
target_language_example: Sur le papier, ce projet fonctionne, mais en pratique il y a des problèmes.
native_language_example: On paper, this project works, but in practice there are problems.

meaning: about to; on the verge of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone was/ is/ will be just about to do something. Can refer to the very recent past, present, or immediate future depending on tense: e.g. 'il était sur le point de partir' (he was about to leave) or 'je suis sur le point de partir' (I'm about to leave).
target_language_example: J'étais sur le point de partir quand tu as téléphoné.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

meaning: 'about to' (followed by an infinitive reflexive verb) — indicates an action is imminent
additional_notes: Used before a reflexive infinitive (se + verb) to say someone/something is about to do something. Structure: sur le point de se + [infinitive]. Often used in both spoken and written French. Example: Il est sur le point de se réveiller = He is about to wake up. Note the agreement: 'sur le point de' does not change for gender/number of the subject.
target_language_example: Elle est sur le point de se coucher.
native_language_example: She is about to go to bed.

meaning: 'on the bridge' or idiomatically 'on duty / available / ready to help'.
additional_notes: Literally means 'on the bridge' (physically on a bridge). Frequently used idiomatically to mean someone is present, ready, or working/available to help (similar to 'all hands on deck' or 'everyone on duty'). Context determines meaning: in a physical sense (meeting point or location) it means 'on the bridge'; in workplace or emergency contexts it means 'on duty / mobilized'.
target_language_example: On a besoin de tout le monde sur le pont pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We need everyone on deck / available to finish the project.

meaning: on the alert; watchful; on guard.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to be attentive and ready to react. Used for people or groups (soldiers, guards, friends) and often appears in imperative or descriptive contexts. Not literal: 'qui-vive' comes from older French meaning 'living who' but today the whole phrase means 'alert'.
target_language_example: Restez sur le qui-vive si vous entendez un bruit étrange.
native_language_example: Stay on the alert if you hear a strange noise.

meaning: on the ground; in the field; at the site (physically present).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present at a location (e.g., a field, a worksite, a conflict zone, a sports pitch). Can mean 'in practice' or 'in real-life conditions' vs. 'in theory' when used metaphorically (e.g., 'sur le terrain, c'est différent'). Common in journalism ('reporter sur le terrain') and sports ('sur le terrain' = on the pitch).
target_language_example: Le médecin travaille chaque semaine sur le terrain dans les villages.
native_language_example: The doctor works every week on the ground in the villages.

meaning: 'custom-made' or 'made to measure' (tailored to specific needs).
additional_notes: Used to describe clothing, objects, services or solutions made or adapted specifically for a person or purpose. Can be used alone as a short answer (= 'custom-made'). Common in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Ils veulent une étagère sur mesure pour le salon.
native_language_example: They want a custom-made shelf for the living room.

meaning: on the orders of; by order of (someone in authority).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action was carried out because someone—often an official, superior, or authority—ordered it. Common in formal, administrative, legal, police, military, medical, and workplace contexts. Typically followed by a person or title introduced by de (e.g., sur ordre de la police, sur ordre du maire).
target_language_example: L'accès a été fermé sur ordre de la direction.
native_language_example: Access was closed on the orders of management.

meaning: on site; there; at the location (immediately/physically present).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at the place in question or that something will be done/understood once at the location. Can mean 'on the spot' or 'there and then'. Context decides whether it refers to being present ('we'll be there') or doing/understanding something once present ('you'll see/understand once you're there').
target_language_example: Nous serons sur place vers midi.
native_language_example: We will be on site / there around noon.

meaning: 'on which' or 'about which' (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Combination of preposition sur (on/about) + interrogative adjective quelle (which, feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun to ask which one (on which / about which). Word order: sur quelle + noun (e.g. sur quelle page). Can also appear in indirect questions (Je me demande sur quelle table il a mis le livre).
target_language_example: Sur quelle table as-tu posé le vase ?
native_language_example: On which table did you put the vase?

meaning: 'on whom' or 'who' in expressions meaning 'depending on' / 'relying on' / 'about whom' (used after preposition 'sur').
additional_notes: Literally 'on whom'. Used in several contexts: to ask who is the target of an action (Sur qui tirez-vous? — Who are you shooting at?), to indicate reliance or dependence (compter sur quelqu'un — to count on someone), or to wonder who will be affected or chosen (sur qui ça va retomber / tomber — who it will fall on; sur qui on pourrait tomber — who we might run into). After 'sur', use 'qui' when referring to people. Meaning depends on the verb: translate as 'on whom', 'who', 'who to', 'who you can count on', etc.
target_language_example: Choisis bien, pense à sur qui tu peux compter en cas de problème.
native_language_example: Choose carefully, think about who you can count on if there's a problem.

meaning: on top of; above all; especially (depends on context).
additional_notes: Sur tout by itself is not a very common fixed phrase in French; its meaning depends on context and surrounding words. It can be the preposition sur + tout (e.g. 'sur tout le monde' = 'on top of everyone' or 'above everyone') or an emphatic combination meaning 'above all' when used as 'surtout' (note: 'surtout' is the usual single-word form meaning 'above all' / 'especially'). Be careful: 'sur tout' (two words) is usually literal (on/over everything) or part of a larger phrase, while 'surtout' (one word) is the adverb meaning 'especially'/'above all.'
target_language_example: Il a posé des fleurs sur tout le meuble.
native_language_example: He put flowers all over the piece of furniture.

meaning: literally 'on/onto an old' — used in 'tomber sur un vieil ami' meaning 'to run into an old (longtime) friend'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in phrases like 'tomber sur un vieil ami' (to run into/meet unexpectedly an old friend). 'Vieil' is the masculine form of 'vieux' used before a vowel sound (vieil ami). 'Sur' here is part of the verb phrase 'tomber sur' meaning 'to come across/encounter'. Do not translate word-for-word; 'tomber sur' = 'to run into' or 'to come across'.
target_language_example: Hier, je suis tombé sur un vieil collègue au marché.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old colleague at the market.

meaning: about that; on that (used after certain verbs or expressions)
additional_notes: Informal contraction of 'sur ça' is not a fixed idiom on its own in French — context matters. Alone, 'sur' + 'ça' literally means 'on that' or 'about that'. Often appears in phrases like 'je ne suis pas d'accord sur ça' (I'm not in agreement about that) or in spoken/colloquial speech as part of 'et sur ça...' meaning 'and about that...'. Native speakers more commonly use 'à propos de ça', 'sur ce', or 'pour ça' depending on the intended meaning. Use 'sur ça' in simple spoken contexts to refer back to something just mentioned.
target_language_example: On n'a pas encore décidé sur ça.
native_language_example: We haven't decided about that yet.

meaning: being tapped / wiretapped / under surveillance (phone or line).
additional_notes: Used to say a phone, line, or person is being monitored by authorities or someone else listening in. Common in police/legal contexts but also in informal speech when suspecting eavesdropping. Can refer to electronic surveillance (calls, messages).
target_language_example: Je crois que ma ligne est sur écoute.
native_language_example: I think my line is tapped.

meaning: 'surprised to see/meet/know you' (part of a phrase meaning 'surprised to... you')
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it appears as the beginning of constructions like "surpris de te voir" (surprised to see you) or "surpris de te retrouver" (surprised to find you). te is the informal singular object pronoun (you). Use "vous" instead of "te" for formal or plural you: "surpris de vous voir." Verb agreement: surpris (m.) / surprise (f.).
target_language_example: Je suis surpris de te voir ici.
native_language_example: I'm surprised to see you here.

meaning: 'watch your' or 'mind your' (used to tell someone to control something about themselves, here 'langage' = language/words).
additional_notes: Imperative phrase: 'surveille' is the singular familiar (tu) command of 'surveiller' (to watch/monitor). Commonly followed by a noun: e.g. 'surveille ton langage' = 'mind your language' (don’t use rude words). Used to warn or scold someone; can be blunt or rude depending on tone. If addressing more than one person or formally, use 'surveillez votre'.
target_language_example: Surveille ton ton quand tu parles à ta grand-mère.
native_language_example: Mind your tone when you speak to your grandmother.

meaning: Represents the pattern 'suspecter + [person]' — to suspect someone (of doing something); to think someone may be guilty or responsible.
additional_notes: This entry shows the syntactic pattern 'suspecter' followed directly by the person (the direct object). In full sentences, the thing suspected is usually expressed with 'de' + infinitive or with a noun: 'suspecter quelqu'un de + infinitive/noun'. The bare pattern 'suspect a' is a notational representation of that construction (a = someone).
target_language_example: Je suspect a depuis qu'il a menti.
native_language_example: I suspect him since he lied.

meaning: 'solar system' — the Sun and the objects that orbit it (planets, moons, asteroids, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to our Solar System or to any star's system of orbiting bodies. Always masculine in French (le système solaire). Common in scientific and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Notre système solaire comprend huit planètes.
native_language_example: Our solar system includes eight planets.

meaning: 'skipped' or 'cut' (as in skipping classes) — past participle used with direct object plural
additional_notes: From the verb sécher (familier) meaning to skip or miss something intentionally, especially classes (sécher les cours). 'Séché les' is the past participle 'séché' followed by a plural direct object (les + noun implied). It's informal. Use with auxiliary avoir: J'ai séché les cours. Not used for accidental absences. Can also mean 'dried' in literal contexts (sécher = to dry), but that sense is neutral and different.
target_language_example: Il a séché les cours hier matin.
native_language_example: He skipped classes yesterday morning.

meaning: security/safety with (used to say someone or something provides safety or confidence)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it's the noun 'sécurité' followed by the preposition 'avec'. You will typically see it in phrases like "avoir/en ressentir de la sécurité avec quelqu'un" (to feel safe with someone) or "la sécurité avec cet équipement" (the safety provided by this equipment). Word order and context determine the exact English translation (e.g. 'feel safe with', 'safety with', 'security in').
target_language_example: Je me sens en sécurité avec toi.
native_language_example: I feel safe with you.

meaning: 'safety in' or 'security in' (used to talk about safety/security within a place, situation, or system).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a common combination: sécurité (safety/security) + preposition dans (in/inside). It appears in phrases like "sécurité dans le travail" (safety at work), "sécurité dans la rue" (safety in the street) or "sécurité dans l'entreprise" (security within the company). Choose the noun after "dans" to specify the place or context. For formal contexts, sécurité can mean physical safety or data/security depending on context.
target_language_example: La sécurité dans le quartier s'est améliorée.
native_language_example: Safety in the neighborhood has improved.

meaning: 'security of' or 'safety of' (used before a noun to indicate protection, safety, or security relating to that thing)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the preposition phrase formed by sécurité (security/safety) + de (of). It appears before a noun or noun phrase: sécurité de l'information (information security), sécurité de la route (road safety). Agreement and articles follow normal rules (de + le → du, de + les → des).
target_language_example: La sécurité de l'information est essentielle pour notre entreprise.
native_language_example: The security of information is essential for our company.

meaning: This sequence by itself has no fixed meaning in French; it looks like two words ('sécurité' = 'security/safety' and 'est' = 'is') that would be part of a larger sentence.
additional_notes: You will not see 'sécurité est' used alone as a phrase. 'Sécurité' can mean 'safety' or 'security' depending on context. 'Est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). Together they appear inside sentences like 'La sécurité est importante' (Safety is important) or 'La sécurité est assurée' (Security is ensured). To use them correctly, include an article or subject before 'sécurité' and a complement after 'est'.
target_language_example: La sécurité est essentielle sur ce chantier.
native_language_example: Safety is essential on this construction site.

meaning: 'safety/security there' — used to point out that a place or situation is safe or secure
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'sécurité' (safety/security) and 'là' (there). Can be used in spoken French to reassure someone about a location or situation: short, colloquial phrasing often heard in conversations or messages. Context and intonation determine whether it refers to physical safety, data/security, or general reassurance. Not an idiom; simply a composition of two common words.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, la sécurité là est bonne.
native_language_example: Don't worry, the security there is good.

meaning: stayed in (spend time lodging in a place, often a hotel or country).
additional_notes: Past participle form of séjourner + preposition dans. Used to say someone stayed somewhere (hotel, country, town). Common with avoir in compound past (elle a séjourné). Can describe short or longer stays; neutral/register, suitable for travel contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai déjà séjourné dans ce petit hôtel près de la plage.
native_language_example: I have already stayed in that small hotel near the beach.

meaning: seriously (about); used to indicate taking something seriously or being serious about doing something.
additional_notes: Often appears before an infinitive or noun to stress seriousness or real commitment (e.g. "sérieusement à travailler", "sérieusement à la tâche"). It is less common as a fixed phrase than simply "sérieusement"; context will determine whether it links to an action (être sérieux à faire quelque chose) or describes attitude toward a subject. Use it to emphasize genuine intent or earnestness.
target_language_example: Il se met sérieusement à étudier pour l'examen.
native_language_example: He is getting serious about studying for the exam.

meaning: 'sure of that' or 'certain of that'.
additional_notes: Used to express certainty about something just mentioned or implied. Often appears in phrases like 'Je suis sûr de ce que...' (I'm sure of what...) or 'Es-tu sûr de ce?' (Are you sure of that?). Be careful: 'sûr' must agree in gender/number (sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres) when used as an adjective referring to a noun; 'sûr de' before a clause or pronoun stays the same aside from agreement with the speaker (e.g., 'Je suis sûre de ce' if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Es-tu sûr de ce que tu dis ?
native_language_example: Are you sure of what you're saying?

meaning: 'sure/ certain (that) not to' — used to ask or confirm that someone is certain about not doing or not having something.
additional_notes: Appears in questions or confirmations: 'Tu es sûr de ne pas... ?' = 'Are you sure you don't...?' Often followed by an infinitive (vouloir venir, avoir été suivi, aller) or a verb phrase. Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French. Note the structure: sûr (agreeing in gender/number if needed) + de + ne + infinitive/verb phrase.
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de ne pas vouloir venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you don't want to come with us?

meaning: 'sure that' (introduces a clause expressing certainty).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase; it is part of larger structures like "être sûr que" (to be sure that). Alone, "sûr que ce" is incomplete — normally you will see "je suis sûr que ce..." or "tu es sûr que ce..." followed by a clause. Use it to state certainty about something. Pay attention to agreement (sûr/sûre) with the subject's gender.
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que ce film va te plaire.
native_language_example: I'm sure that this movie will please you.

meaning: 'sure that I...' — the start of a clause meaning you are certain about something you (I) will do or think
additional_notes: This is a fragment often seen before a verb starting with a vowel, e.g. 'sûr que j'arrive' (informal speech) or in spoken/written contexts where the rest of the sentence follows. In standard French you'd more commonly see 'je suis sûr(e) que...' (I am sure that...) or simply 'sûr que...' as a colloquial shortened form meaning 'of course' or 'sure that...'. Pay attention to agreement: 'sûr' becomes 'sûre' for feminine subjects when used after 'je suis'.
target_language_example: Sûr que j'y vais, ne t'inquiète pas.
native_language_example: Sure that I'm going, don't worry.

meaning: short, informal fragment meaning 'sure that I (do) / sure I will (do) it'—incomplete clause used in speech
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself. It appears to be a clipped spoken fragment where 'sûr' = 'sure' and 'j'en' is the start of a clause with 'en' (meaning 'of it' / 'about it' / 'from it') — e.g. from phrases like 'sûr que j'en prends' ('sure I'll take some of it') or 'sûr que j'en viendrai' (colloquial). Very informal and context-dependent; the rest of the clause is usually omitted because the meaning is clear from context. Avoid using this fragment in formal writing. Pronounced with casual speech; the 'u' in 'sûr' often sounds like [syʁ].
target_language_example: Tu veux du café ? — Sûr que j'en veux.
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee? — Sure, I do want some.

meaning: 'of course I.../sure that I... (used to assert something about oneself)'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment used in spoken French. When completed it becomes phrases like "Bien sûr que je l'ai fait" (Of course I did it) or "Bien sûr que je l'aime" (Of course I love him/her/it). "Bien sûr" adds emphasis ("of course"), while "sûr que" can introduce a statement of certainty. "je l'" is the beginning of a verb or object with the pronoun "le/la/les" elided before a vowel (e.g. "je l'ai", "je l'aime"). Very common in casual and formal speech.
target_language_example: Bien sûr que je l'ai dit.
native_language_example: Of course I said it.

meaning: 'sure that I (it/him)' — part of a sentence meaning 'I'm sure that I ... it/him.'
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete phrase. 'Sûr' (masculine) means 'sure' or 'certain'. In full sentences you usually see 'je suis sûr que je le...' or in feminine 'je suis sûre que...'. The 'le' is a direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'him' and follows the subject only in spoken fragments; in correct written French the structure is 'Je suis sûr(e) que je le + verb'. Informal speech often drops 'suis' and uses contractions: 'Sûr que je le ferai' is heard but grammatically you should say 'Je suis sûr que je le ferai.'
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que je le ferai demain.
native_language_example: I'm sure that I will do it tomorrow.

meaning: 'sure that I ...' (fragment used to start a clause expressing certainty about oneself)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it's a fragment you might see inside a sentence such as "Je suis sûr que je me trompe" (I'm sure that I'm wrong) or "Sûr que je me suis trompé" (Sure that I made a mistake). In spoken French the leading "Je suis" or context is often present; "sûr que" introduces a clause expressing certainty. Watch word order and reflexive verbs when completing the clause (e.g. "je me suis" for past reflexive).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que je me suis trompé.
native_language_example: I'm sure that I made a mistake.

meaning: "I'm sure that..." — expresses certainty. It literally inverts the usual French order (normal: "je suis sûr que...").
additional_notes: This inverted order is archaic, poetic, or used for emphasis; uncommon in everyday speech. Match gender: "sûr" (masculine speaker) or "sûre" (feminine). In standard prose/speech prefer "je suis sûr(e) que...". Include the conjunction "que" before the clause. The phrase as given places the adjective before the subject for stylistic effect.
target_language_example: Sûr que je suis, je reviendrai quoi qu'il arrive.
native_language_example: Sure that I am, I will return no matter what happens.

meaning: Are you sure that... (spoken, feminine singular 'sure')
additional_notes: This is the feminine form (sûre) used when addressing or referring to a woman or when using the feminine subject. The phrase is typically followed by 'est' or another verb beginning with a vowel/consonant, often contracted as "c'" + verb (e.g. c'est, c'était). Informal/colloquial spoken examples often use "T'es sûre que..." for "Tu es sûre que..." and "Vous êtes sûre que..." when politely speaking to a woman. For a male speaker/address, use "sûr que c'..." or "sûr(e)" depending on context.
target_language_example: T'es sûre que c'est la bonne clé ?
native_language_example: Are you sure that's the right key?

meaning: 'my/your/someone's sister has' — the noun sœur (sister) followed by the auxiliary verb a (has) used to form the passé composé or to indicate possession/action in present perfect-like contexts.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common word sequence: sœur (sister) + a (3rd person singular of avoir). Depending on context, a + past participle forms the passé composé (e.g. «Ma sœur a emmené…» = 'My sister took…/has taken…'). It can also mean 'has' when followed by a noun (possession). The subject can be replaced (ma/ta/votre/sa sœur). Watch agreement rules: past participle may agree with a preceding direct object; with être verbs use être instead of avoir.
target_language_example: Sa sœur a fini ses devoirs hier soir.
native_language_example: His/Her sister finished her homework last night.

meaning: “(my/your/her/etc.) sister is…” — the subject 'sœur' (sister) followed by the verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common short chunk showing how to describe someone's sister. Replace the possessive (ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur) to match the owner. 'Sœur' is feminine; adjectives and articles must agree (une sœur intelligente, ma sœur est contente).
target_language_example: Ma sœur est professeure de français.
native_language_example: My sister is a French teacher.

meaning: This looks like two words 'sœur' (sister) + 'et' (and); not a fixed phrase on its own — usually part of a longer phrase (e.g. 'sœur et frère' = 'sister and brother').
additional_notes: Not a standalone idiom. 'Sœur' means 'sister' and 'et' means 'and'. In French they are used just like their English equivalents to join nouns or phrases. Ensure agreement in context (e.g. possessives: 'ma sœur et mon frère'). If you see 'sœur et' it will be followed by another word. Pronunciation: sœur [sœʁ], et [e].
target_language_example: Ma sœur et mon ami viennent ce soir.
native_language_example: My sister and my friend are coming tonight.

meaning: 'sœur' = sister; 'se' = reflexive pronoun (herself/oneself).
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words that normally don't form a fixed multiword expression. 'Sœur' is a noun meaning 'sister'. 'Se' is the third-person singular/plural reflexive pronoun used before a verb (e.g. 'elle se lave' = 'she washes herself'). You will rarely see 'sœur se' together unless followed by a verb (e.g. 'ma sœur se promène' = 'my sister is taking a walk').
target_language_example: Ma sœur se réveille tôt le matin.
native_language_example: My sister wakes up early in the morning.

meaning: 'is there/are there (any) ...' in questions (inversion with 'il' and part of 'y a-t-il d'autres...')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in inverted yes/no or information questions with 'y a-t-il' (from 'il y a') plus 'd'' before a plural or partitive noun (often in 'd'autres' = 'other(s)'). It asks whether there exist/are any of something. In spoken French you often hear the non-inverted 'y a-t-il' pronounced like 'y a-t-il' or the informal 'est-ce qu'il y a'. 'd'' is the contraction of 'de' before a vowel. Use with nouns: 'Y a-t-il d'autres questions ?' = 'Are there any other questions?'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il d'autres livres dans la valise ?
native_language_example: Are there any other books in the suitcase?

meaning: a linking sequence appearing in inverted questions where '-t-il' follows a verb (or 'y a-t-il') and is immediately followed by a location phrase beginning with 'dans la' — used in formal/neutral questions to ask if someone/something is in a place (e.g. 'is there/are there in the...').
additional_notes: This structure arises from subject-verb inversion for questions. The '-t-' is an epenthetic sound inserted for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (or in 'y a-t-il'). 't-il' itself is not a standalone word; it combines with the preceding verb. 'dans la' begins a feminine singular location phrase. Use in neutral or formal questions; register is not informal. The meaning depends on the full question (e.g. 'y a-t-il dans la...' = 'is there in the...').
target_language_example: Combien de garçons y a-t-il dans la pièce ?
native_language_example: How many boys are there in the room?

meaning: 'are there still any' (used in questions to ask whether something still exists or is available)
additional_notes: This is part of the inversion question form with 'y a-t-il' (literally 'is there') plus 'encore' (still) and the plural indefinite article 'des'. Used to ask about the continued existence or availability of plural things or people. In spoken French, you may also hear 'est-ce qu'il y a encore des...' or the shorter 'y a-t-il encore des...' The phrase requires a plural noun after 'des'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il encore des places pour le concert ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are there still any seats for the concert tonight?

meaning: short question form: 'was there a / did there exist a / did someone have a ...' (used to ask whether something happened or existed).
additional_notes: This form appears in inverted yes/no questions with il (often after adding a question word like 'y' or 'a'). 'Y a-t-il eu un ... ?' = 'Was there a ...?' or 'Did there occur a ...?'. 'A-t-il eu un reçu ?' asks whether he received a receipt (literally 'Has he had a receipt?'). Use with events (procès, scandale, tremblement de terre) or possessions/occurrences. Formal/neutral register; inversion is common in written and spoken questions.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il eu un problème hier soir ?
native_language_example: Was there a problem last night?

meaning: A word order used in questions: 'will/does/is ... us' (inversion with 'il' + object 'nous').
additional_notes: This sequence appears in formal or neutral written/spoken questions where the subject pronoun 'il' is inverted with the verb (va-t-il, cela va-t-il, que va-t-il, etc.), and 'nous' is the object (us). The '-t-' is a liaison vowel inserted for pronunciation when the verb form ends with a vowel (e.g. va + il → va-t-il). Equivalent in English: 'will/does/is it ... us?' or 'what will happen to us?'.
target_language_example: Cela va-t-il nous inquiéter ?
native_language_example: Will that worry us?

meaning: 'Is there something (that is)...' — used to ask whether something of a certain kind exists or is available.
additional_notes: This phrase appears within the question form 'Y a-t-il quelque chose de + adjective?' or 'Y a-t-il quelque chose de + adjective + ici/au menu...'. 'Y a-t-il' is the inversion question form of 'il y a' (there is/are). The structure asks if there exists something with a particular quality (e.g. nouveau, pas cher). Often contracted in speech to 'y a-t-il' pronounced quickly; in informal speech people may say 'est-ce qu'il y a quelque chose de...'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose de végétarien au menu ?
native_language_example: Is there something vegetarian on the menu?

t-il quelque chose de particulier que

target_language_multi_word_term: t-il quelque chose de particulier que
meaning: 'Is there anything in particular that...?' (used to ask if someone wants/needs a specific thing/activity).
additional_notes: This phrase is usually used as part of the question starter 'Y a-t-il quelque chose de particulier que...' or the informal 'Y a-t-il' contracted to 'Y a-t-il' / 'Y a'. It asks whether there is any specific item, preference, or request. Follow with an infinitive or a clause (e.g. 'tu veuilles boire', 'vous vouliez manger'). Use 'tu' for informal singular and 'vous' for formal or plural. Can be shortened in speech: 'Tu veux quelque chose de particulier?'
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose de particulier que tu voudrais manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is there anything in particular you would like to eat tonight?

meaning: 'Is there something that you...?' (used to ask if the other person has something to say or do)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions introduced by 'Y a-t-il' (Is there) and followed by a clause with 'que tu' + verb (often in the subjunctive: veuilles/voudrais que tu fasses). Commonly used to ask if someone wants to say or tell something. Formal/written style uses 'Y a-t-il'; in spoken French people often say 'Est-ce qu'il y a' or simply 'Tu as quelque chose à...'. The verb following 'que tu' may be in subjunctive after expressions like 'vouloir que'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose que tu veuilles me dire ?
native_language_example: Is there something you want to tell me?

meaning: 'is there something that...?' (used to ask if some thing or factor exists that causes or explains something)
additional_notes: This is part of the question form 'Y a-t-il quelque chose qui...?' — literally 'Is there something that...?' Used to ask whether any specific thing/situation exists (e.g. that worsens pain, that is wrong). Formal/polite; can be used with tu/vous in rest of sentence. Often contracted in speech to 'y a-t-il...' or 'est-ce qu'il y a...'. Followed by a verb clause describing what the 'something' would do.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quelque chose qui rende la machine bruyante ?
native_language_example: Is there something that makes the machine noisy?

meaning: 'what will happen' (used in questions: Que va-t-il se passer ? = What will happen?)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the impersonal question structure 'Que va-t-il se passer...?' or 'Que va-t-il arriver...?' It uses inversion (va-t-il) for formal/neutral questions. You can also say 'Qu'est-ce qui va se passer ?' which is more common in spoken French. Use to ask about future events or outcomes.
target_language_example: Que va-t-il se passer ce soir ?
native_language_example: What will happen tonight?

meaning: 'is there a problem' (used in questions)
additional_notes: This phrase is the inversion question form using 'il' as an impersonal subject with 'y a' (there is). More commonly heard as 'Y a-t-il un problème ?' in spoken and written French. Use to ask if something is wrong, if there's an issue, or if someone should be concerned. Can be followed by details (avec ceci, entre vous deux, dont je devrais être au courant).
target_language_example: Y a-t-il un problème avec la commande ?
native_language_example: Is there a problem with the order?

meaning: Is there a phone? (used in questions: 'Y a-t-il un téléphone ?')
additional_notes: This appears in the inverted formal question form 'Y a-t-il...' meaning 'Is there...?' which is common in written or neutral spoken French. 'Y' = 'there' (il y a = there is/are). You will usually see the full phrase 'Y a-t-il un téléphone ?' when asking whether a phone exists or is available somewhere. Informal spoken alternatives: 'Il y a un téléphone ?' or 'Y a-t-il un téléphone dans le coin ?'.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il un téléphone près d'ici ?
native_language_example: Is there a phone near here?

meaning: 'is there another' (used in questions)
additional_notes: This fragment appears inside the inversion question form 'Y a-t-il une autre...' meaning 'Is there another...?' It asks if an additional option/thing exists (issue, solution, exit). 'Y a-t-il' = 'Is there' or 'Are there'. Use with a noun: 'Y a-t-il une autre + [noun] ?'. Formal/neutral register; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il une autre option disponible ?
native_language_example: Is there another option available?

meaning: appears to be a fragment meaning 'told you something' or 'said something to you' (informal, contracted).
additional_notes: This is not a complete standard French phrase by itself. It looks like a contraction of 't'a dit quelque chose' (he/she/it told you something) with 'quelque chose' shortened or missing. In spoken/informal French people often contract words: 'il t'a dit' = 'he told you'. To say 'said something to you' properly use 't'a dit quelque chose' or 't'a dit ça'.
target_language_example: Il t'a dit quelque chose à propos du rendez‑vous ?
native_language_example: Did he tell you something about the appointment?

meaning: contraction of 'tu n'as pas' meaning 'you don't have' or in some contexts part of negation 'you didn't' (informal spoken French).
additional_notes: 't'a pas' is an informal, spoken contraction combining 'tu' + 'as' with the negation part 'pas'. It's commonly used in casual conversation and in many dialects. It can mean 'you don't have' (tu n'as pas) or be part of perfect tense negation after 'tu as' (tu n'as pas + past participle) depending on context. In writing, use the full 'tu n'as pas' for standard/formal French.
target_language_example: T'a pas de stylo ?
native_language_example: You don't have a pen?

meaning: I've brought you a/one (something).
additional_notes: A short form of 'je t'ai apporté un/une ...' used when telling someone you brought them something. 'T'' is the object pronoun for 'toi' (you). Use 'un' for masculine nouns and 'une' for feminine nouns. Can be followed by a noun (cadeau, livre, truc) or a vague word (quelque chose, truc).
target_language_example: Je t'ai apporté un gâteau.
native_language_example: I brought you a cake.

meaning: 'I told you (that)...' used to introduce what was said or described.
additional_notes: Contraction of 'je t'ai dit' + 'ce (que/qui...)'. Common in spoken and written French. Followed by 'que' to introduce a clause ('ce que' = what/that which) or 'qui' for persons/events ('ce qui' = what/that which (subject)). The full phrase is usually 'Je t'ai dit ce que...' or 'Je t'ai dit ce qui...'.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit ce que j'ai vu hier.
native_language_example: I told you what I saw yesterday.

meaning: have you
additional_notes: contraction of te + ai. te becomes t' before a vowel. It usually appears after je or j' in phrases like je t'ai..., often in the passé composé: je t'ai vu = I saw you / I've seen you. It is not usually used by itself, and the full sentence often translates with simple past in English.
target_language_example: Je t'ai vu ce matin.
native_language_example: I saw you this morning.

meaning: 'have loved you since' (short for je t'aime depuis ...).
additional_notes: This is the contracted form used in spoken or informal French where the subject and object pronoun are combined (je t'aime depuis = I have loved you since). It is followed by a time expression indicating when the love began (e.g. 'toujours', 'l'enfance', '2010'). Context often makes clear the missing subject pronoun (je).
target_language_example: Je t'aime depuis notre première rencontre.
native_language_example: I have loved you since our first meeting.

meaning: This is not a standalone phrase in French; it's a fragment meaning 'you love (you) and' when appearing in a sentence (t' = te, aime = love, et = and).
additional_notes: t'aime et is a combination of t' (short for te, object 'you'), aime (2nd/3rd person singular of aimer) and et (and). It cannot be used alone — it will appear inside a larger sentence (e.g. 'Je t'aime et...' = 'I love you and...'). Watch pronunciation: t' is linked to the verb (je t'aime pronounced [ʒə tɛm]).
target_language_example: Je t'aime et je veux passer ma vie avec toi.
native_language_example: I love you and I want to spend my life with you.

meaning: 'I'll call you as soon as' or 'I'll call you once...'
additional_notes: Common spoken shortening of Je t'appelle dès que. Used to tell someone you will call them immediately after a specific event happens (e.g. when you arrive, when you have news). The que is often included (dès que) but can be dropped in casual speech. t' is the object pronoun for 'te' (you, informal).
target_language_example: Je t'appelle dès que j'arrive.
native_language_example: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

meaning: Contraction of 'tu as' + preposition 'dans' — used informally to say 'you have ... in/within' or to ask if someone has something in/at a place or time.
additional_notes: T'as is the colloquial spoken contraction of 'tu as' (you have). When followed by 'dans' it introduces what someone has inside/within or indicates possession at a location or time (e.g. 't'as dans le sac' = 'you have in the bag' — more natural as part of a full sentence: 'Qu'est-ce que t'as dans le sac ?'). This form is informal and common in speech; in writing or formal contexts use 'tu as dans'. Exact meaning depends on context and sentence completion. Pronunciation and usage vary regionally; avoid in formal registers.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que t'as dans le sac ?
native_language_example: What do you have in the bag?

meaning: short for "tu as dans le..." — literally 'you have in the...' used idiomatically to mean 'what do you have inside/what are you capable of'.
additional_notes: Informal contraction: "t'as" = "tu as". Common expressions: "ce que t'as dans le ventre" (what you've got in you / what you're capable of), "ce que t'as dans le crâne" (what's in your head / your ideas). Used to challenge someone or ask about abilities, thoughts, feelings, or something inside a container/body. Usually spoken; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Allez, montre ce que t'as dans le ventre !
native_language_example: Come on, show what you've got!

meaning: I had told you not to... (used to report a past instruction to refrain from something).
additional_notes: Contraction of 'je t'avais dit de ne...' or 'je vous avais dit de ne...' depending on context. Used to remind or reproach someone about a past warning or instruction not to do something. In full form it is usually followed by 'pas' plus an infinitive: 'je t'avais dit de ne pas venir'. In spoken French 'je' is often dropped and 't'avais dit de ne' signals informal, familiar speech.
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit de ne pas ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: I had told you not to open the door.

meaning: I had told you that I... (intro to a clause reporting something speaker had previously said)
additional_notes: Contraction of 'tu avais dit que je...'. Used to remind someone of what the speaker had already told them. Often followed by a past action (j'avais croisé), a future-in-the-past (je reviendrais / je viendrais / je le ferais) or a present-state verb (je me tenais informée). Common in spoken French; 't'' is informal spoken contraction of 'te'.
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit que je viendrais te voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: I had told you that I would come see you this weekend.

meaning: please; you're welcome; go ahead (polite/request or polite response).
additional_notes: Very common, versatile polite expression. Used to make a request more polite (equivalent to 'please' or 'I beg you') or as a polite response meaning 'you're welcome' or 'don't mention it'. Context and intonation determine the sense. Contraction of 'je t'en prie' (I beg you).
target_language_example: Dis-le-moi maintenant, je t'en prie.
native_language_example: Tell me now, please.

meaning: Contraction of «tu en es» — asks or states where someone stands regarding something (progress, state, degree). Equivalent to “where are you at (with it)?” or “how far along are you?”
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken French. 't'en' = 'tu en'. Often used in questions like «Tu t'en es où ?» or statements «Tu t'en es content ?» depending on context; may refer to progress, emotional state, realization, etc. Can be followed by an adjective, noun phrase, clause, or a prepositional phrase. Informal; more common in conversation than in formal writing.
target_language_example: Tu t'en suis où, avec ce projet ?
native_language_example: Where are you at with this project?

meaning: 'you are at' (informal spoken) — contraction of 'tu es au'.
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction used in speech and informal writing. 'Tu es' becomes 't'es'. 'Au' is the contraction of 'à le' and requires a masculine singular noun following (e.g. 't'es au boulot' = 'you are at work'). Often used to ask or tell someone's location or situation: 'T'es au café ?' 'T'es au courant ?' (note: in that idiom 'au' is part of 'au courant').
target_language_example: T'es au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you at the cinema tonight?

meaning: short for "ne t'inquiète pas" — "don't worry" (to you, informal).
additional_notes: Informal contraction used in speech and casual writing. Often appears as "t'inquiète pas" or simply "t'inquiète" to reassure someone. Used with tu (singular familiar). Equivalent to English "don't worry" or "no worries." For polite/formal situations use "ne vous inquiétez pas."
target_language_example: T'inquiète, tout va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything will be fine.

meaning: your big / your tall (familiar) — feminine or used before a feminine noun; often part of informal speech or nicknames (e.g. 'ta grande sœur' = 'your big sister').
additional_notes: Ta is the familiar singular possessive 'your' used before a feminine noun. Grande is the adjective 'big/large/tall' (feminine form). Alone, 'ta grande' is incomplete and would normally be followed by a feminine noun (ta grande maison, ta grande sœur). In casual speech it can appear in clipped phrases or nicknames (e.g. 'ta grande' meaning 'your big one'), but without context it sounds informal and vague.
target_language_example: Ta grande sœur habite près d'ici.
native_language_example: Your big sister lives near here.

meaning: 'shut up' (very rude/strong)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Literally 'your maw/mouth' but used as an order to be silent. Only use with close friends in coarse joking contexts or avoid entirely in polite conversation. Stronger than 'tais-toi' or 'ferme-la'.
target_language_example: Ferme ta gueule et écoute.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen.

meaning: your mother
additional_notes: A direct way to say "your mother" when speaking to one person you address as tu. For formal speech or when speaking to several people, French uses votre mère instead.
target_language_example: Ta mère arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: Your mother is arriving in ten minutes.

meaning: 'your plus' or 'your plus one' (depends on context) — literally 'your more/plus'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed common phrase on its own; meaning depends on context. 'Ta' is the familiar singular possessive 'your' (before a feminine noun). 'Plus' can mean 'more', 'plus', or serve in expressions like 'être en plus' (to be extra) or in arithmetic. In conversational French, 'ta plus' might appear in constructions like 'ta plus belle' (your most beautiful) with an omitted noun, or in casual contexts where 'plus' functions as a noun (e.g. 'ton plus' meaning 'your advantage/asset'). Without more context, avoid using 'ta plus' alone — include the noun or verb phrase it's modifying.
target_language_example: Ta plus grande qualité, c'est ta patience.
native_language_example: Your greatest quality is your patience.

meaning: at the table of / on the table of (contraction of 'table à le' which is actually ungrammatical; likely a mistaken fragment).
additional_notes: This exact phrase 'table au' is not a standard fixed expression in French by itself. It looks like the contraction 'au' = 'à le' or 'à + le' used after a noun: e.g., 'la table au fond' (the table at the back) is colloquial shorthand for 'la table qui est au fond'. More commonly you will see 'à la table de...' (at the table of...) or 'la table au fond' (the table in the back). Be careful: 'table à' (followed by an activity, e.g. 'table à manger') or 'à table!' (time to eat) are correct uses. If you intended 'à la table' (at the table) or 'la table au fond' (the table at the back), use those full forms.
target_language_example: La table au fond est réservée.
native_language_example: The table at the back is reserved.

meaning: ‘table with’ — used to say something is on the table or an action involving the table together with something/someone.
additional_notes: This is a combination of the noun 'table' and the preposition 'avec' (with). It appears in different structures: (1) describing something on or touching the table ('ramasser les grains de sucre sur la table avec son doigt' — using his finger on the table), (2) indicating an instrument used on the table ('essuyer la table avec un torchon' — wipe the table with a cloth), and (3) sharing the table with someone ('partager cette table avec toi' — share this table with you). The meaning depends on the verb and context; 'avec' introduces the person or thing accompanying or used.
target_language_example: Je nettoie la table avec une éponge.
native_language_example: I'm cleaning the table with a sponge.

meaning: 'table in' (literal); not a common fixed phrase — likely part of a larger expression such as "mettre/poser quelque chose sur la table dans..." or used in contexts like "table dans un article" meaning 'table in (a document)'.
additional_notes: Alone, "table dans" is not a standard fixed expression in French. You will typically see the noun "table" followed by a prepositional phrase (e.g. "la table dans la cuisine" = "the table in the kitchen") or the verb phrases that include "table" (e.g. "mettre sur la table"). If you encountered "table dans" inside technical or editorial contexts, it can mean 'table in [a document/section]' (e.g. "table dans l'article" = "table in the article"). Watch the surrounding words to understand the intended meaning. For beginner learners, treat it as the noun "table" + preposition "dans" ('in/inside'), used compositionally.
target_language_example: La table dans la cuisine est en bois.
native_language_example: The table in the kitchen is made of wood.

meaning: 'table of' or 'table for' — the start of a noun phrase meaning a table belonging to or used for something (e.g. table de cuisine = kitchen table).
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it's the preposition de after the noun table. It introduces what the table is for, what it belongs to, or what it contains. You will normally see it followed by a noun (table de nuit, table de jardin, table de conférence). Pronunciation: [tabl də].
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une table de jardin.
native_language_example: I bought a garden table.

meaning: Ambiguous or incomplete phrase as written. Could be a typo for 'tableau à' (preposition 'à' with accent) beginning a longer phrase, or 'tableau A' (capital A) meaning a table/chart/figure labeled A. Without context it's unclear.
additional_notes:
Two main possibilities:
- 'tableau à' (with accent) is the start of constructions like 'tableau à double entrée' (two-way table) or 'tableau à remplir' (table to fill in). In that case 'à' is the preposition 'to/for/with' and the phrase must be completed.
- 'tableau A' (capital letter) can mean 'table/figure A' or 'painting A' when items are labeled. The written form 'tableau a' (lowercase a without accent) is likely a typographical error and can be confused with the verb 'a' (has). Check context and accents/capitalization.
Learner tip: 'a' (no accent) is the verb 'has' (il a), while 'à' (accent) is a preposition. Capitalization also changes meaning when letters are used as labels.
target_language_example: Le professeur a montré le tableau a pendant la présentation, mais c'était clairement une faute : il voulait dire 'tableau A' ou 'tableau à compléter'.
native_language_example: The teacher showed 'tableau a' during the presentation, but it was clearly a mistake: he meant 'tableau A' or 'tableau à compléter'.

meaning: 'table of' or 'board of' — used to indicate something belonging to or related to a table/board (e.g. table of contents, board of directors).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common noun + preposition combination. The meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g. 'tableau de bord' = dashboard, 'tableau de prix' = price table, 'tableau de contenu(s)' = table of contents). In many cases it corresponds directly to English 'table of', 'chart of', or 'board of'.
target_language_example: Consultez le tableau de bord pour voir l'état du système.
native_language_example: Check the dashboard to see the system status.

meaning: freckle (a small brownish spot on the skin, often from sun exposure).
additional_notes: Singular form is 'tache de rousseur' (a freckle). Plural is 'taches de rousseur' (freckles). Often used to describe small brown spots on the face or arms. Pronunciation tip: 'tâche' can be confused with 'tâche' (task) — here it's 'tache' without circumflex in modern spelling but pronounced the same. Can be used descriptively (Elle a une tache de rousseur) or collectively (Il a des taches de rousseur).
target_language_example: Elle a une petite tache de rousseur sur le nez.
native_language_example: She has a small freckle on her nose.

meaning: 'size is' — used to state or ask about the size of something.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the noun taille (size) and the verb être (est = is). Common in statements (Cette taille est trop petite) and in questions using De quelle taille est...? (What size is...?). Use tu/vous depending on formality. Not an idiom; it's literal.
target_language_example: De quelle taille est ta veste ?
native_language_example: What size is your jacket?

meaning: 'how tall' or 'how big' (asking for size or height).
additional_notes: Used in questions with Quelle taille fait + subject to ask about someone's height or the size/area/length of an object/place. Context determines whether it means height (person) or size/dimensions (room, park). Can be followed by a person, object, or impersonal 'il' for a thing (Quelle taille fait-il ?). Typical answers give a measurement (e.g., 'Il fait 1,80 m.' or 'Elle fait 50 m².').
target_language_example: Quelle taille fait ta valise ?
native_language_example: How big is your suitcase?

meaning: 'while', 'whereas', or 'as' (shows contrast or simultaneous actions).
additional_notes: Used to link two clauses. Can indicate contrast (similar to 'whereas') or simultaneous actions (similar to 'while'/'as') depending on context. Formality: neutral; common in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Il lisait le journal, tandis que je préparais le dîner.
native_language_example: He was reading the newspaper while I was making dinner.

meaning: so many things; so much to do/so much about something.
additional_notes: Used to express a large quantity or multitude of items, tasks, or matters. Can refer to concrete objects or abstract matters (ideas, problems, things to do). Often used alone for emphasis (e.g., "Tant de choses.").
target_language_example: Il reste tant de choses à voir dans cette ville.
native_language_example: There are so many things left to see in this city.

meaning: 'all the better' / 'that's good' (expressing relief or approval).
additional_notes: Used to react positively to news or a situation — expresses that the outcome is preferable or will be beneficial. Can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on tone. Often stands alone or followed by a prepositional phrase (pour + pronoun).
target_language_example: Tant mieux si tu peux venir.
native_language_example: All the better if you can come.

meaning: 'too bad' / 'oh well' — expresses resignation or that you accept an unfortunate outcome.
additional_notes: Used to show resignation, indifference, or that you give up trying to change a situation. Can be mild ('oh well') or a bit sharper ('serves you right' in context 2). Often stands alone or followed by 'pour + noun/pronoun' (e.g. 'tant pis pour toi').
target_language_example: Ils ont vendu les billets ? Tant pis, on ira une autre fois.
native_language_example: They sold the tickets? Oh well, we'll go another time.

meaning: as long as
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a condition or time span. Primary meaning is 'as long as' (conditional: 'provided that' / 'while the condition holds'). Can also mean 'while' for simultaneous actions. In informal contexts, in expressions like 'tant que vous y êtes' it can mean 'while you're at it' or 'since you're doing that'. Not to be confused with 'autant que' (as much as).
target_language_example: Tant que tu travailles dur, tu progresseras.
native_language_example: As long as you work hard, you'll improve.

meaning: even a little; to any extent
additional_notes: A formal/literary expression used to say 'even slightly' or 'in the slightest'. Often appears in negative or conditional contexts (e.g. 'si tant soit peu' = 'if even a little'). Use in spoken French is less common than in written or formal registers.
target_language_example: Si tu pouvais m'aider, ne serait-ce que tant soit peu, ce serait apprécié.
native_language_example: If you could help me, even a little, it would be appreciated.

meaning: 'aunt of' or 'aunt to' (used to indicate a familial relationship, often dialectal or emphatic)
additional_notes: Standard French normally uses 'la tante de ...' or possessive forms ('ma tante', 'la tante de Marie'). 'tante à' appears in some regional/dialectal or informal spoken uses (e.g. 'tante à moi') for emphasis. Avoid in formal writing; prefer 'tante de'.
target_language_example: C'est la tante à moi qui habite ici.
native_language_example: She's my aunt who lives here.

meaning: 'aunt is' — the subject noun 'tante' (aunt) followed by the verb 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the noun 'tante' (female relative) plus the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). Used to describe your aunt's location, condition, age, profession, or state. Remember that possessive adjectives change with the possessor: ta tante (your, informal singular), ma tante (my), sa tante (his/her). Word order is the same as English: 'tante est ...'.
target_language_example: Ma tante est professeur à Lyon.
native_language_example: My aunt is a teacher in Lyon.

meaning: hits/strikes on the (plural) — literally 'hits on the'.
additional_notes: This is the verb tape (from taper/taper sur) + preposition sur + plural article les. It appears before a plural noun: e.g. "tape sur les touches" = "hits the keys." 'Taper sur' can mean physically hit, tap repeatedly, or figuratively criticize/attack. Choose meaning from context. Conjugate tape for il/elle/ça (present) or use other forms for different subjects.
target_language_example: Il tape sur les touches du clavier.
native_language_example: He hits the keys of the keyboard.

meaning: to get on someone's nerves; to annoy or irritate someone
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Used when someone or something repeatedly annoys or frustrates you. Commonly used in spoken French: "Ça me tape sur les nerfs" = "It annoys me." Can be followed by a person (Il me tape sur les nerfs) or a thing/situation (Le bruit me tape sur les nerfs).
target_language_example: Ça me tape vraiment sur les nerfs quand tu répètes la même histoire.
native_language_example: It really gets on my nerves when you repeat the same story.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatically correct French expression; most likely a word order error or fragment.
additional_notes: There is no common French phrase 'tard ce'. 'Tard' means 'late' (usually an adverb: Il est tard) and 'ce' is a demonstrative (this/that) or pronoun. If you encounter 'tard ce' in text, it's probably a mistake, a typo, or part of a larger misordered phrase. Correct alternatives: 'Il est tard' (It's late), 'si tard' / 'aussi tard' (so late), 'ce soir-là' (that evening), or 'à ce moment-là' (at that moment).
target_language_example: *Tard ce* n'est pas une expression correcte en français écrit.
native_language_example: 'Tard ce' is not a correct expression in written French.

meaning: late in (a period of time) — used to say something happens late during a particular time span (e.g., late in the evening, late in the year).
additional_notes: Followed by a time expression (e.g., la soirée, la nuit, l'année). Equivalent to 'late in the ...' in English. Commonly used to specify when during a larger period something occurs. Can be followed by definite article + noun (tard dans la nuit) or a possessive/time word (tard dans l'après‑midi).
target_language_example: Nous sommes arrivés tard dans la soirée.
native_language_example: We arrived late in the evening.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a word order error. 'tard' means 'late' and usually follows the verb or comes at end of clause (e.g. «Je suis parti tard»).
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'tard le'. If you see 'le tard' or 'tard le' it is probably incorrect or part of a longer structure (e.g. 'le plus tard possible' = 'as late as possible'). Correct positions: 'tard' after the verb or at the end: «Il est arrivé tard», «Ne viens pas trop tard». Use 'tard' with time expressions: «tard le soir» can appear in informal speech to mean 'late in the evening', but more natural is 'tard le soir' → 'late in the evening' (note the article 'le' pairs with 'soir', not directly with 'tard').
target_language_example: Il est arrivé tard le soir.
native_language_example: He arrived late in the evening.

meaning: late to (do something) — indicates being late for an action or event.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or noun phrase with preposition à to say someone is late to do something or late for something. More commonly you'll see just 'tard' alone (Il est tard = It's late) or 'en retard' (être en retard à/au/chez + noun). 'Tard à' appears in phrases like 'tard à arriver' (late to arrive) but 'en retard' is often preferred in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il est tard à partir ce matin.
native_language_example: He was late to leave this morning.

meaning: a cup of tea
additional_notes: A common and literal phrase used to refer to one serving of tea in a cup. Can be used literally (drinking tea) or idiomatically as an invitation to visit/chat (e.g. "come up for a cup of tea"). Note article/number agreement: une tasse de thé (feminine).
target_language_example: Veux-tu encore une tasse de thé ?
native_language_example: Would you like another cup of tea?

meaning: to get/find you a (something) — informal way to offer to find or get someone an item or solution
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of a sentence meaning "(I will) get/find you a [noun]". Common in spoken French: the subject (je) is often omitted and the verb chercher (to look for/get) is used with an indirect object pronoun te (to you). You must add a noun after un/une (e.g., 'te chercher un verre', 'te chercher un taxi'). Tone is informal/friendly.
target_language_example: Je peux te chercher un taxi si tu veux.
native_language_example: I can get you a taxi if you want.

meaning: 'to ask you something' (incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete French expression on its own. It looks like part of a sentence where the speaker will continue with what they want to ask (quelque chose = something) or specify the question. The typical complete forms are « te demander quelque chose » (to ask you something) or « te demander de + infinitive » (to ask you to do something). The pronoun te is the familiar singular 'you'. Use tu-form conversations.
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander quelque chose : peux-tu m'aider demain ?
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you something: can you help me tomorrow?

meaning: to tell you that / to tell you what
additional_notes: Fragment often appears in sentences like «Je vais te dire ce que...» (I'll tell you what...) or «Je peux te dire ce qui s'est passé» (I can tell you what happened). It is not a complete clause by itself; usually followed by «que», «qui», or a clause explaining what is being told. Informal and neutral registers both use it. Pronoun order: te (informal you) comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce qui s'est passé hier.
native_language_example: I'll tell you what happened yesterday.

meaning: 'to tell you what/that...' (used to introduce what someone will be told)
additional_notes: Common phrase structure: subject + (aller/venir/vouloir) + te dire ce que + clause. It introduces the content of what will be told to 'te' (you, informal). 'Te' is the informal singular object pronoun; use 'vous dire ce que' for formal or plural. The following clause can be in any tense (present, past, future).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que j'ai vu hier.
native_language_example: I'll tell you what I saw yesterday.

meaning: the beginning of a clause meaning 'to tell you what I...' (incomplete fragment)
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase — you need to finish the sentence with a verb or clause (e.g. 'te dire ce que je pense', 'te dire ce que je veux'). 'Te' is the informal singular 'you' (object), 'dire' = 'to tell', and 'ce que je' starts a relative clause 'what I...'. Common in spoken and written French when addressing someone directly. To be polite or formal, use 'vous' instead of 'te'.
target_language_example: Je veux te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I want to tell you what I think.

meaning: 'to tell you the' (part of the phrase 'te dire la vérité' = 'to tell you the truth')
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the sequence 'te dire' (to tell you) followed by a definite noun (here 'la vérité'). 'Te' is the informal singular object pronoun (you). You'll most often see it in sentences like 'te dire la vérité' (to tell you the truth). In formal situations use 'vous' instead of 'te' (e.g. 'vous dire la vérité').
target_language_example: Je dois te dire la vérité maintenant.
native_language_example: I must tell you the truth now.

meaning: to tell you something / to say something to you
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase in French; it normally appears as part of a larger clause like «je voulais te dire quelque chose» (I wanted to tell you something) or «il faut que je te dise quelque chose». «Te» is the informal singular object pronoun 'to you'. Use «vous» for formal/plural. The verb can be conjugated (dire → dis, dire, dirai, dise) and the word «quelque» is usually followed by «chose» (something) or another noun.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire quelque chose avant de partir.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you something before leaving.

meaning: to tell you a (something) — the start of a phrase meaning 'to tell you a [thing/comment]' (informal/colloquial spoken French).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the beginning of expressions like «te dire une chose» or casual constructions «je vais te dire une/te dire un truc» meaning 'I'll tell you something'. Often used in speech before giving news, a comment, or a secret. In many contexts speakers shorten it to «te dire un truc» or «te dire quelque chose». When using, finish with a noun (une chose, un truc, une vérité, etc.) or add the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire une chose : arrête de t'inquiéter.
native_language_example: I'll tell you one thing: stop worrying.

meaning: I give you a (masculine singular) ... / I'll give you a ...
