Often used in legal, economic or formal contexts (e.g., 'un bien immobilier' = a real estate property). When used alone, context determines singular/plural sense; the plural is 'des biens'.
target_language_example: Cet appartement est un bien de famille.
native_language_example: This apartment is a family property.

meaning: a (simple) man of / a fellow of — used to describe a person associated with something (often informal or familiar).
additional_notes: Bonhomme literally means 'good man' or 'fellow'. The construction 'un bonhomme de + noun' is colloquial and used to characterize someone by a trait, role or thing they are linked to (e.g. 'un bonhomme de neige' = a snowman; 'un bonhomme de chantier' could mean a construction worker/fellow on site). It is more common in spoken/familiar French and sometimes humorous. Not all combinations are standard — some are set expressions (bonhomme de neige), others are creative.
target_language_example: C'est un bonhomme de théâtre, il adore monter sur scène.
native_language_example: He's a theatre fellow; he loves getting on stage.

meaning: a ... office / an office of ... (used to describe a specific office belonging to an organization or a person)
additional_notes: Follow 'un bureau de' with a noun indicating the organization, service, department, profession or person (e.g. un bureau de poste, un bureau de médecin, un bureau de direction). In many contexts French uses 'le bureau de' (the office of) or 'un bureau de' (an office of). For specific locations you may also see 'un bureau à' or simply 'le bureau' depending on phrasing. Use the appropriate article (un/le) and agreement for the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Nous avons rendez-vous dans un bureau de poste du centre-ville.
native_language_example: We have an appointment at a post office in downtown.

meaning: a (large) house, estate or building of — (literally: 'a castle of') used to describe type or ownership/production (e.g., wine).
additional_notes: Literally 'a castle of'. In modern French 'château' can mean a castle, a large country house, or a winery/estate (especially for wine: 'un château de Bordeaux'). 'Un château de' is followed by a noun indicating material, origin, purpose or possession (e.g. 'un château de sable' = a sandcastle; 'un château de famille' = a family estate; 'un château de Bourgogne' used in wine names). For beginners: watch context — it doesn't always mean a medieval fortress.
target_language_example: Ils ont construit un château de sable sur la plage.
native_language_example: They built a sandcastle on the beach.

meaning: a quick (usually affectionate or knowing) gesture; short form used before certain words (most commonly 'œil' = 'eye')
additional_notes: This is an abbreviated form of 'un clin d’œil' (a wink). In French you often see 'un clin d’' followed by a noun starting with a vowel (especially 'œil') or used in fixed expressions. Alone it is incomplete; native speakers typically finish the phrase (e.g., 'un clin d’œil') or use it in contexts where the rest is understood. It implies a brief, playful or knowing action.
target_language_example: Elle m’a fait un clin d’œil en passant.
native_language_example: She gave me a wink as she passed.

meaning: part of a larger expression meaning 'an account at' or 'an account with' (used before a financial institution or service).
additional_notes: This fragment by itself is incomplete: French normally uses 'un compte à' in phrases like 'un compte à la poste' (an account at the post office) or 'un compte à [nom de la banque]'. More common is 'un compte chez' (with a person or company) or 'un compte à la banque / au Crédit Agricole'. Pay attention to the article that follows (à + le = au, à + la = à la).
target_language_example: J'ai ouvert un compte à la banque ce matin.
native_language_example: I opened an account at the bank this morning.

meaning: a hit
additional_notes: Basic meaning is 'a hit' or 'a blow'. Depending on context, it can also mean one attempt or one go (en un coup = 'in one go'). In the casual expression boire un coup, it means 'have a drink'.
target_language_example: On va boire un coup après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a drink after work?

meaning: a quick
additional_notes: This is a truncated form used before a noun beginning with a vowel or mute h (e.g. un coup d'état, un coup d'œil, un coup d'accélérateur). It often conveys the idea of a brief action, attempt, or sudden occurrence (a quick look, a sudden push, a blow/attempt). In many fixed expressions the full meaning is idiomatic (e.g. un coup d'état = a coup). The apostrophe indicates the elision of de before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Donne-moi un coup d'œil par ici.
native_language_example: Give me a quick look over here.

un coup de pied dans les

target_language_multi_word_term: un coup de pied dans les
meaning: 'a kick in the' (literal); often the start of the expression 'un coup de pied dans les [something]' meaning a forceful kick into/against something or figuratively 'a blow to the...'
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase — you normally complete it with a body part or object (e.g. 'un coup de pied dans les dents' = 'a kick in the teeth') or a noun ('un coup de pied dans les portes'). Used literally for physical kicking and figuratively to describe a severe setback or insult. Grammar: 'coup' is masculine, and the whole construction uses 'de' after 'coup' plus the preposition 'dans' before the plural noun ('les').
target_language_example: Il a reçu un coup de pied dans les jambes pendant le match.
native_language_example: He got a kick in the legs during the match.

meaning: one of
additional_notes: Used to indicate a single member of a group (un de + plural noun or un de + relative clause). Often followed by a plural noun (un de mes amis) or a clause (un de ceux qui...). In spoken French the article and preposition are separate words but together mean 'one of'.
target_language_example: C'est un de mes livres préférés.
native_language_example: It's one of my favorite books.

meaning: sometime / one of these days (at an unspecified time in the future)
additional_notes: Informal, idiomatic phrase used to suggest that something will happen at an indefinite future time. Can be used for invitations (Come visit us sometime), warnings or threats (I'll do it to you one of these days), or vague plans. Tone depends on context and intonation—can be friendly or menacing.
target_language_example: Viens me voir un de ces jours, on prendra un café.
native_language_example: Come see me sometime, we'll have a coffee.

meaning: one of
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say 'one of' a group (e.g., un des livres = one of the books). If followed by 'les' it contracts to "un des" stays the same in writing but pronunciation connects; with de + definite article combinations (du, de la, des) be careful — 'un des' is separate words meaning 'one of the'. Commonly appears as 'un des + [plural noun]'.
target_language_example: C'est un des meilleurs films que j'ai vus.
native_language_example: It's one of the best films I've seen.

meaning: an odd/strange person; a funny guy (depending on context)
additional_notes: Can mean 'a strange/odd person' (neutral/slightly negative) or informally 'a funny guy' (amusing). Often followed by de + noun (e.g., 'un drôle de type' = 'a strange fellow'). Alone, 'un drôle' is colloquial and can imply surprise or mild disapproval. Gender changes: 'une drôle' for feminine. Common in expressions 'un drôle de...' meaning 'a strange...'.
target_language_example: C'est un drôle de voisin : il parle tout seul.
native_language_example: He's a strange neighbour: he talks to himself.

meaning: a French person (a man) or a French language speaker; can also mean 'a Frenchman'.
additional_notes: The phrase uses the indefinite article + nationality. It usually refers to a male person from France or a male native speaker of French. To refer to a woman, use « une Française ». To refer to the French language in general, use « le français » (no article 'un'). Context determines whether it means 'a French person' (nationality) or 'a French speaker'.
target_language_example: J'ai rencontré un Français au café.
native_language_example: I met a Frenchman at the café.

meaning: a big thank you; many thanks.
additional_notes: Informal to neutral expression used to warmly thank someone or a group. Often used in spoken and written French (emails, messages, speeches). You can add 'à tous' (to everyone) or specify the reason with 'pour…'. Tone is grateful and emphatic.
target_language_example: Un grand merci pour votre aide précieuse.
native_language_example: A big thank you for your valuable help.

meaning: a large number of; many
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate 'many' or 'a large number of' people or things. More formal than just «beaucoup de». Followed by a plural noun and verb agreement is plural (e.g., «Un grand nombre de personnes ont…»).
target_language_example: Un grand nombre de touristes visitent la ville chaque été.
native_language_example: A large number of tourists visit the city every summer.

meaning: 'a man of the' (start of a longer phrase) — incomplete by itself; would be followed by a plural noun with definite article or appear in comparative/idiomatic constructions.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase. In French, the more common patterns are «un homme de + [singular noun/adjective]» or «un des hommes» (one of the men). The sequence «un homme des» can occur before a plural noun introduced by the definite article (e.g. «un homme des plus célèbres») or in emphatic/comparative constructions (e.g. «un homme des plus aimables»). Such uses are relatively formal and less frequent; speakers often prefer alternatives. Beginners should not treat «un homme des» as a complete phrase but recognize it as the beginning of a longer expression.
target_language_example: C'est un homme des plus respectés dans sa profession.
native_language_example: He is a man of the most respected in his profession.

meaning: 'a man or...' (used to ask whether someone is a man or a woman)
additional_notes: Typically appears in the question pattern "un homme ou une femme ?" to ask someone's gender (male or female). Often followed by "une femme"; standalone fragment "Un homme ou une femme ?" is natural in spoken or written questions. Use polite/full forms: "Est-ce un homme ou une femme ?" or "La victime était-elle un homme ou une femme ?"
target_language_example: C'est un homme ou une femme ?
native_language_example: Is it a man or a woman?

meaning: a decent (person); an honest person (used with a noun to mean 'a respectable/solid…').
additional_notes: Rare and somewhat formal or literary as a standalone phrase. In French you usually say honnête (adj) before a noun (un homme honnête) or honnêtement (adv). 'Un honnête' by itself can appear in older or literary texts as a shorthand for 'un honnête homme' (a gentleman/man of integrity) or to mean 'a decent sort of person.' Not common in everyday spoken French.
target_language_example: Ce village est plein d'honnêtes gens, mais rares sont «un honnête» sans défaut.
native_language_example: This village is full of decent people, but few are 'an honest one' without fault.

meaning: a disadvantage to / a drawback of (doing) something
additional_notes: Used to introduce the negative aspect or downside of an action or situation. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'à + infinitive') or by a noun/verb phrase introduced with 'de' depending on structure: 'un inconvénient à + infinitive' or 'un inconvénient de + noun/infinitive'. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Un inconvénient à accepter ce poste est le long trajet quotidien.
native_language_example: A drawback to accepting this job is the long daily commute.

meaning: a disadvantage/objection to this (or to that); a problem with this
additional_notes: Used to point out a drawback, objection or problem related to something just mentioned. Often followed by an infinitive or clause explaining the objection (e.g. « un inconvénient à ce projet est que... », or in more natural phrasing « l'inconvénient de ceci »). In everyday speech you may also hear « le problème, c'est que... » or simply « un inconvénient » without « à ce ». Formal register.
target_language_example: Un inconvénient à ce plan est qu'il coûte trop cher.
native_language_example: A drawback to this plan is that it costs too much.

meaning: 'an objection to the fact that' / 'a problem with someone doing something'.
additional_notes: Used to express that one has an objection, problem or disadvantage with a proposed action or situation (often followed by a subjunctive clause: 'à ce que + subjunctive'). Common in polite or formal contexts: e.g. 'Y a-t-il un inconvénient à ce que vous partiez maintenant ?' = 'Is there any objection to you leaving now?'.
target_language_example: Est-ce qu'il y a un inconvénient à ce que je fume ici ?
native_language_example: Is there any objection to my smoking here?

meaning: one day
additional_notes: In these examples, it means at an unspecified time in the future: 'one day' or 'someday.' It can also literally mean 'one day' as a time unit depending on context.
target_language_example: Un jour, j'irai à Paris.
native_language_example: One day, I'll go to Paris.

meaning: 'in a day or two' / 'one day or two' (indicates an approximate short time span)
additional_notes: Used with a number (often 'un') + 'jour(s) ou (deux)' to mean 'about one or two days' or 'in a day or two'. It expresses approximation or a short delay. Can be used with verbs in present or future to indicate when something will happen or how long someone will stay. Common everyday expression.
target_language_example: Je reviendrai dans un jour ou deux.
native_language_example: I'll come back in a day or two.

meaning: every (number) day(s); e.g. "un jour sur deux" = every other day.
additional_notes: Used with a number after it (un jour sur deux, un jour sur trois, etc.) to express a repeating frequency: one day in N days. Equivalent to "tous les deux jours" for "un jour sur deux". Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport un jour sur trois.
native_language_example: I exercise every three days.

meaning: 'a pain', 'an ache', 'a harm' or 'an evil' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can refer to physical pain (e.g. un mal de tête = a headache), an abstract problem or harm (un mal social = a social ill), or general difficulty. Often appears in fixed phrases (avoir un mal, faire du mal). Meaning depends on nouns or verbs around it. Gender is masculine (un).
target_language_example: J'ai un mal de dos depuis hier.
native_language_example: I have a backache since yesterday.

meaning: a lot; a great amount; (colloquial) loads, tons.
additional_notes: Informal/slang expression meaning 'a lot' or 'a large amount' used in spoken French. Can modify nouns (un max de travail = a ton of work) or be used alone as an exclamation (Un max ! = Awesome / That's a lot). Often used in casual contexts; register is colloquial. Can imply gaining/earning a lot when used with verbs like 'se faire' (se faire un max de blé = make a lot of money).
target_language_example: J'ai un max de devoirs ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have a ton of homework this weekend.

meaning: a lie told enough times (i.e. 'a lie sufficiently' — used to say that repeating a lie makes people believe it).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences like 'Si on raconte un mensonge suffisamment de fois...' meaning 'If a lie is told often enough...'. 'Suffisamment' modifies how often the lie is told (sufficiently/often enough). In natural English you'd say 'a lie told often enough' or 'a lie repeated enough times'. The construction is compositional: 'un mensonge' = 'a lie', 'suffisamment' = 'sufficiently/enough'.
target_language_example: Si tu racontes un mensonge suffisamment de fois, les gens finiront par y croire.
native_language_example: If you tell a lie enough times, people will end up believing it.

meaning: in a moment; any time now (something will happen very soon).
additional_notes: Used to say that an event is expected to occur very soon, often implying unpredictability (could happen at any moment). Common in spoken French. Can be followed by an action or a clause: e.g. «Il va arriver un moment à l'autre» = 'He'll arrive any moment now.'
target_language_example: Le train partira un moment à l'autre, dépêchons-nous.
native_language_example: The train will leave any moment now, let's hurry.

meaning: 'a step forward' (literally: a step in/forward).
additional_notes: Commonly used with directions like 'avant' (forward) or 'arrière' (back). Literally describes a physical small movement — 'faire un pas en avant' = to take a step forward. Can also be used figuratively (progress, improvement). In examples the phrase appears as 'un pas en avant' meaning one step forward.
target_language_example: Elle a fait un pas en avant pour mieux voir.
native_language_example: She took a step forward to see better.

meaning: Not a complete phrase on its own — seen as the start of expressions meaning 'a little something' or 'a small...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression in French. It appears as the beginning of phrases like «un petit quelque chose» (a little something) or in informal speech as part of «un petit quelque chose en plus» (a little something extra). Do not use 'un petit quelque' alone; include the rest of the expression (e.g. 'quelque chose').
target_language_example: J'ai préparé un petit quelque chose pour ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: I prepared a little something for your birthday.

meaning: 'a little' or 'a small (one)' — diminutive/qualifier used before nouns or to soften requests.
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to mean 'a small' (un petit chien = a small dog) or before an action/object to mean 'a little' (prendre un petit verre). Can also be used to soften statements or requests (Un petit conseil ? = A little piece of advice?). Context determines whether it refers to physical size, quantity, or is simply a softening/diminutive expression.
target_language_example: Je veux un petit gâteau, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want a small cake, please.

meaning: a little
additional_notes: Used to mean a small amount or degree. Very common with adjectives and adverbs to mean 'slightly' or 'somewhat' (for example, un peu dingue = 'a little crazy'). It can also be used with verbs: Je parle un peu français = 'I speak a little French.' Before a noun, it usually becomes un peu de + noun.
target_language_example: Je suis un peu fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm a little tired today.

meaning: a little of
additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about a small amount of something, especially uncountable nouns or abstract ideas: un peu de bière, un peu de courage, un peu de bon sens. In everyday speech, it can also sound like a suggestion, offer, or encouragement depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un peu de café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I would like a little coffee, please.

meaning: a little time / a bit of time
additional_notes: Used to request or describe a small amount of time (short pause, extra minutes, or time saved). Common in requests (Donnez-moi un peu de temps) and when talking about saving time. Can be used with verbs like donner, avoir, gagner, économiser.
target_language_example: Donnez-moi un peu de temps pour finir ce rapport.
native_language_example: Give me a little time to finish this report.

meaning: not a fixed expression; likely 'un peu' (a little) followed by a definite article 'le' before a noun or phrase
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'un peu le' is not a standalone fixed phrase. It typically appears when 'un peu' (a little, slightly) directly precedes a masculine singular noun or a noun phrase with the article 'le', or in colloquial speech before an adjective + noun: e.g. 'un peu le stress' (a bit of stress) or 'un peu le problème' (a bit of the problem). In many cases you'd see 'un peu de' instead (un peu de pain = a little bread). Use 'un peu le' when the noun is specific/definite (the...), or in informal/emphatic constructions.
target_language_example: J'ai un peu le trac avant le spectacle.
native_language_example: I'm a bit nervous before the show.

meaning: 'to be close to' or 'to be near (death)'; literally 'one foot in (the grave)'.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone is very close to dying or in very bad health. Often completed as "un pied dans la tombe" (one foot in the grave). Can be used literally for danger/near-death or figuratively for being near the end of something. Tone can be dramatic or humorous depending on context.
target_language_example: Après cet accident, il a presque un pied dans la tombe.
native_language_example: After that accident, he almost has one foot in the grave.

meaning: part of the idiom "avoir un pied dans la tombe" — to be near death or very close to dying.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the idiom "avoir un pied dans la tombe" (literally “to have one foot in the grave”). Used to describe someone who is very old, very ill, or in a situation likely to cause death. It is figurative and common in spoken and written French. You will usually see the full phrase; the provided fragment "un pied dans la" should be completed by "tombe" to convey the meaning.
target_language_example: Il a déjà un pied dans la tombe.
native_language_example: He's already got one foot in the grave.

meaning: an extra; an added benefit; a plus (something additional or advantageous).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an additional feature, advantage, or bonus. Can be used as a noun: 'C'est un plus' = 'That's a plus/that's a bonus.' Often informal to neutral register. Common in spoken and written French to value something positive added to a situation or object.
target_language_example: Avoir une terrasse, c'est un plus pour cet appartement.
native_language_example: Having a terrace is a plus for this apartment.

meaning: a little, a bit; literally 'a hair'.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to indicate a small amount or slight degree (positive or negative). Can be literal when talking about an actual hair, but most often figurative: un poil trop grand = a tad too big; tu n’as pas changé d’un poil = you haven't changed at all. Often appears in colloquial spoken French.
target_language_example: Il est un poil en retard, mais rien de grave.
native_language_example: He's a bit late, but nothing serious.

meaning: Not a correct standalone French phrase. Likely a mistake: 'porte' is a feminine noun (une porte) meaning 'a door', or it appears as the first element in compounds like 'un porte‑monnaie' (a wallet) where 'porte-' means 'holder for'.
additional_notes: Do not use 'un porte' alone. Use 'une porte' for 'a door', or use the proper compound with 'porte-' (e.g. 'un porte‑monnaie', 'un porte‑clé', 'un porte‑serviette'). 'Un porte' would be grammatical only inside a larger compound or as a typographical/utterance error. 'Porte' is feminine and a cognate of English 'port' in some senses but not identical; choose the correct gender and form.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas dire « un porte » quand on parle d'une porte : on dira « une porte ».
native_language_example: You should not say "un porte" when talking about a door: you would say "une porte".

meaning: a first (one); an initial (one).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to mean 'a first' or 'an initial' instance of something (e.g., un premier pas = a first step). Often appears in phrases like 'un premier essai', 'un premier rendez-vous'. Can also be used alone to refer to 'a first [one]' when context supplies the noun. Agreement: 'premier' becomes 'première' before feminine nouns.
target_language_example: C'était un premier pas important.
native_language_example: That was an important first step.

meaning: 'a damn' / 'a f***ing' used as a swear intensifier before a noun (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very vulgar. 'Putain' here is used like an intensifier placed before a noun to show strong emotion (anger, contempt, surprise). Often translated as 'f***ing' or 'damn' in English. It can be standalone (putain!) or combined with articles as in examples. Avoid in polite/formal situations.
target_language_example: C'est un putain de problème.
native_language_example: This is a f***ing problem.

meaning: a father for / a father to (someone or something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone is a father figure or the biological/social father of someone or something. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. un père pour cet enfant, un père pour moi). Context determines whether it's literal (biological father) or figurative (father figure, guardian). Can appear in constructions like "être un père pour [quelqu'un]" meaning "to be a father to [someone]".
target_language_example: Il est un père pour ses neveux depuis que leur père est parti.
native_language_example: He has been a father to his nephews since their father left.

meaning: 'a quarter of' (used before a noun or time expression)
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun starting with a vowel sound (written with the apostrophe): un quart d'heure (15 minutes), un quart de litre (a quarter of a litre). For time, French also uses « et quart » after the hour (e.g. trois heures et quart = 3:15). The part after d' can be a noun (un quart d'heure) or a quantity (un quart d'un kilo).
target_language_example: J'ai bu un quart d'un litre d'eau.
native_language_example: I drank a quarter of a litre of water.

meaning: a very small amount; nothing (informal, dismissive).
additional_notes: Used in French to downplay something—either to say 'just a little' or to say 'it's nothing' (no problem). Context determines whether it means a tiny amount (un peu) or 'it doesn't matter.' Common in expressions like « ce n'est pas un rien » (it's not nothing). Tone is informal to neutral.
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide — c'était un rien.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — it was nothing.

meaning: very little time; in almost no time
additional_notes: Informal expression meaning a very short amount of time—similar to 'in no time' or 'in a flash' in English. Often used with verbs to say something will happen quickly. Can be used with 'en' as in 'en un rien de temps'.
target_language_example: Il a réparé la voiture en un rien de temps.
native_language_example: He fixed the car in no time.

meaning: a person without (used before a noun to mean 'someone lacking' something)
additional_notes: Literally 'a without'. Typically appears as 'un sans‑X' (often hyphenated) to denote someone deprived of X (e.g., 'un sans‑papiers', 'un sans‑abri'). 'Un sans' by itself is rare and sounds incomplete unless context supplies the missing noun; it can be used colloquially if the noun is understood from prior discourse.
target_language_example: Après la tempête, il a aidé un sans (il savait que la personne avait perdu sa maison).
native_language_example: After the storm, he helped a person without (he knew the person had lost their home).

meaning: in one piece; as a single piece; whole (not broken).
additional_notes: Used to say something remains intact or is done/served as a single piece. Can describe physical objects (an object that wasn't broken) or food served whole (e.g., cake, bread). Context determines whether it's equivalent to 'one piece' or 'in one go' (e.g., eating something in a single bite).
target_language_example: Heureusement, la statue est arrivée un seul morceau.
native_language_example: Luckily, the statue arrived in one piece.

meaning: 'such a' or 'so' (used before an adjective or noun to intensify).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize degree or quality. Often appears in phrases like « un si bon repas » (such a good meal) or in exclamations « Un si petit village ! ». Can be followed by an adjective + noun or occasionally an adjectival phrase. Not used alone; it's different from the conjunction si ('if' or 'so') and from the monosyllable 'si' meaning 'yes' in replies to negatives. Context determines nuance: 'such a' (emphasis) or 'so' (intensity).
target_language_example: C'était un si beau coucher de soleil.
native_language_example: It was such a beautiful sunset.

meaning: a sigh of (followed by an emotion or reaction, e.g. relief, fatigue).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone making a single audible exhale that expresses an emotion. Common collocations: un soupir de soulagement (a sigh of relief), un soupir de fatigue (a sigh of tiredness), un soupir d'exaspération (a sigh of exasperation). Usually followed by a noun naming the emotion or reaction. Often used in past tenses: poussa/poussé un soupir de...
target_language_example: Après l'examen, elle poussa un soupir de joie.
native_language_example: After the exam, she let out a sigh of joy.

meaning: a lot of; loads of; many.
additional_notes: Informal/neutral expression meaning 'many' or 'a large quantity of'. Used before a noun (un tas de + noun). Can be used with countable or uncountable nouns. Slightly colloquial but common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: J'ai un tas de livres à lire.
native_language_example: I have a lot of books to read.

meaning: such a
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the type or degree of something: 'such a' (followed by a noun) or simply 'such' (before a noun phrase). Can express admiration, surprise, disapproval, or intensity depending on context. In negative contexts (example 5) it can mean 'such a guy' with a negative connotation. Often followed by adjectives or nouns (un tel + noun).
target_language_example: Je n'avais jamais vu un tel spectacle.
native_language_example: I had never seen such a spectacle.

meaning: a whole, an entirety; the whole thing
additional_notes: Used to refer to something considered as a single complete unit or the totality of parts. Often appears in expressions like "le tout" (the whole) or "dans son ensemble". Can be used abstractly (the whole concept) or literally (the entire object). Context determines whether definite article is used: "le tout" = the whole; "un tout" = a whole or an entire entity among others.
target_language_example: Ce petit meuble forme un tout avec la décoration de la pièce.
native_language_example: This small piece of furniture forms a whole with the room's decor.

meaning: “something that I…” — introduces a thing the speaker doesn't understand/know or must do; often followed by a verb in the negative (e.g. comprends pas).
additional_notes: Informal, conversational. Truc is vague: 'thing' or 'something'. Common in questions/statements expressing lack of understanding or knowledge (Il y a un truc que je comprends pas = There's something I don't understand). Often appears with colloquial contractions: 'y a' (il y a) and 'pige pas' (don't get).
target_language_example: Il y a un truc que je ne comprends pas dans cet exercice.
native_language_example: There's something I don't understand in this exercise.

meaning: a glass of (used before a noun starting with a vowel or mute h).
additional_notes: Common phrase to order or talk about a drink or a measure of liquid (un verre d'eau, un verre de vin). The apostrophe is used before a vowel sound: un verre d'orange (un verre de jus d'orange), un verre d'eau. For consonant-starting nouns use "un verre de". Often used when ordering or serving beverages.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a glass of water, please.

meaning: 'one in' or 'one inside' (literal), often part of larger expressions like 'un dans l'autre' or used when counting 'one in [a group]'.
additional_notes: By itself 'un dans' is not a complete fixed phrase in French; it is usually the words 'un' (one/a) followed by the preposition 'dans' (in/inside) and appears inside fuller sentences: e.g. 'un dans chaque boîte' (one in each box), 'un dans l'autre' (one into the other). Use depends on context and needs surrounding words to form a natural expression.
target_language_example: Mets un dans chaque poche.
native_language_example: Put one in each pocket.

meaning: sometime soon / one of these days (at an unspecified near-future time)
additional_notes: Informal expression used to suggest doing something in the near future without fixing a date. Equivalent to 'one of these days' or 'sometime soon' in English. Often used with verbs like 'sortir', 'se voir', 'faire', or with plans that are casual and not scheduled. Can be used alone as a casual suggestion: « On devrait se voir, un de ces quatre. »
target_language_example: On ira prendre un café, un de ces quatre.
native_language_example: We'll go for a coffee one of these days.

meaning: 'one of the' (used before a noun starting with a vowel sound; contraction of "un de le/ la" in some informal contexts or dialects)
additional_notes: This form is not standard written French. In standard French you would say "un de + plural/noun" (e.g. "un de mes amis") or use the partitive/article: "un/des". "Un de l'" may appear in casual speech as a contraction before a vowel (e.g. "un de l'équipe" intended as 'one of the team'), but it's considered colloquial or regionally influenced. Prefer standard alternatives: "un de + (definite article)" becomes "un de l' + noun" only when the noun is introduced by the definite article ("un de l'équipe" = one of the team) — still informal. For clarity, use: "un membre de l'équipe" or "un(e) des..."
target_language_example: Il y a un de l'équipe qui parle français.
native_language_example: There is one of the team who speaks French.

meaning: one by one; individually, in sequence
additional_notes: Used to say that actions or items are handled singly, one after another. Often interchangeable with "un à un". Common in both spoken and written French. Can introduce a sequence (e.g. "Ils sont sortis un par un").
target_language_example: Les invités sont entrés un par un.
native_language_example: The guests entered one by one.

meaning: 'one that' / 'a ... that' (introduces a specific item/person among others)
additional_notes: Used to pick out or refer to one item or person from a group, followed by a relative clause introduced by qui. Often appears with y en a/il y en a/avez-vous un to ask if there exists one with a particular property. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Vous avez un qui fonctionne sans pile ?
native_language_example: Do you have one that works without a battery?

meaning: one at a time; one by one; per (when counting or distributing).
additional_notes: Used to indicate items or actions done individually or distributed singly. Often appears in contexts like "un à un" (one by one) or before verbs/nouns to mean 'one each' (e.g. "Donne-leur un à un" = give them one each / one at a time). Alone, "un à" usually combines with another word (number, noun, or repetition) and is not commonly used isolated in formal writing.
target_language_example: Donne les bonbons un à un.
native_language_example: Give the candies one at a time.

meaning: a weapon for (doing something) — introduces the purpose or type of weapon (usually followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it’s the start of expressions like «une arme à feu» (a firearm) or «une arme à longue portée» (a long-range weapon). The preposition à links the noun 'arme' to its function, characteristic, or the object it uses. In many cases the full construction is 'une arme à + noun'.
target_language_example: Il possède une arme à feu.
native_language_example: He owns a firearm.

meaning: somewhere else; another place (rare/poetic phrasing)
additional_notes: Literally 'another part/place.' Native speakers typically use 'ailleurs' for 'elsewhere' or 'un autre endroit/lieu' for 'another place.' 'Une autre part' is grammatically possible but uncommon and can sound poetic, regional, or archaising. Use 'ailleurs' in most everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Je sens que mon cœur est une autre part, comme s'il appartenait à une autre part du monde.
native_language_example: I feel as if my heart is elsewhere, as if it belonged to another part of the world.

meaning: a wound caused by (used with a following cause, e.g. 'une blessure par balle' = a gunshot wound).
additional_notes: Phrase is used with a noun that names the cause or instrument (balle = bullet, arme blanche = bladed weapon, brûlure = burn, etc.). Common in medical, legal, and news contexts. When specifying cause of death use 'd'une blessure par...' or 'mort(e) d'une blessure par...'.
target_language_example: Il a survécu à une blessure par balle au bras.
native_language_example: He survived a gunshot wound to the arm.

meaning: a (metaphorical) bubble of — used to compare something to a fragile, temporary, or delicate thing (often 'bulle de savon' = soap bubble).
additional_notes: Usually appears in similes or metaphors (e.g. une bulle de savon). Means fragility, short-lived nature, or being isolated/insulated. Common structure: 'comme/pareille à/ressembler à une bulle de (savon)'. Not a fixed idiom on its own — often completed by 'savon' or used in figurative expressions.
target_language_example: Leur bonheur semblait être une bulle de savon, belle mais fragile.
native_language_example: Their happiness seemed like a soap bubble, beautiful but fragile.

meaning: to some extent; to a certain degree
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limited or partial degree — not absolute. Common in formal and neutral registers. Can qualify statements (e.g., 'Cela a aidé, dans une certaine mesure.'). Often followed by context explaining the limitation.
target_language_example: Il a, dans une certaine mesure, raison.
native_language_example: He is, to some extent, right.

meaning: a room shared with his (used when specifying that someone shares a room with a male person or with someone referred to by masculine possessive) — often part of phrases meaning 'to share a room with someone'.
additional_notes: This phrase is typically followed by a noun referring to the person (e.g. frère, colocataire) and uses the masculine singular possessive 'son'. Depending on context you may need ma/ta/sa/nos/etc. The verb is usually 'partager' or constructions like 'a dû partager' / 'lui a fallu partager'.
target_language_example: Il a dû partager une chambre avec son frère.
native_language_example: He had to share a room with his brother.

meaning: a sudden craving or desire (colloquial, often for food); a whim or fancy
additional_notes: Informal expression used to describe a sudden urge or passing fancy. Often followed by 'de' + noun (e.g. une chic de chocolat). Mostly regional/colloquial — not standard in all French varieties. Can also appear as 'avoir une chic' meaning 'to have a craving'.
target_language_example: J'ai eu une chic de glace ce soir.
native_language_example: I had a sudden craving for ice cream tonight.

meaning: not a fixed expression by itself; appears as part of longer phrases like "une chose en particulier" (one thing in particular) or "une chose en plus" (one more thing).
additional_notes: Alone, "une chose en" is incomplete and will be followed by another word (often an adjective, adverb, or prepositional phrase). Common completions: "une chose en particulier" (one thing in particular), "une chose en plus" (one more thing), "une chose en moins" (one thing less). Use the full phrase for clear meaning.
target_language_example: Il y a une chose en particulier que je veux dire.
native_language_example: There is one thing in particular that I want to say.

meaning: 'a ... thing' or 'a ...-style thing' — used before a noun or adjective to describe something in a vague or imprecise way (often followed by a noun or description).
additional_notes: This is an informal, colloquial fragment rather than a fixed phrase. It appears when a speaker hesitates or gives a vague description: e.g. « une chose à la... » then they specify (une chose à la mode, une chose à la maison, une chose à la main). Often it's completed immediately (à la + noun = 'in the style of' or 'like'), or followed by an adjective to mean 'a kind of thing'. Alone it sounds unfinished. Useful in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: C'est une chose à la mode, tout le monde en parle.
native_language_example: It's a trendy kind of thing; everyone is talking about it.

meaning: not a fixed phrase by itself; likely 'a conclusion if...' — 'une conclusion' means 'a conclusion' and 'si' means 'if' or 'so'.
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words rather than a standard multiword expression. 'Une conclusion' = 'a conclusion' (feminine noun). 'Si' can mean 'if' (subordinate clause) or 'so/very' depending on context. Together, 'une conclusion si' would typically be followed by an adjective or clause (e.g. 'une conclusion si hâtive' = 'such a hasty conclusion' or 'une conclusion si logique' = 'a conclusion so logical'). It is not an idiom. Watch gender/number agreement (une conclusion, des conclusions).
target_language_example: Ne tire pas une conclusion si hâtive sans vérifier les faits.
native_language_example: Don't draw such a hasty conclusion without checking the facts.

meaning: 'one of the most' (used to say something is among the top/most ...)
additional_notes: Used before an adjective to indicate that the noun is among the highest degree within a group (e.g. one of the most beautiful, one of the largest). Followed by an adjective and often by a complement like 'au monde', 'de France', etc. Agreement: adjective agrees with the noun (gender/number).
target_language_example: Cette plage est une des plus belles du pays.
native_language_example: This beach is one of the most beautiful in the country.

meaning: once
additional_notes: Usually refers to a single occasion. It can also appear in storytelling to mean something like 'once' or 'one day' (for example, Il était une fois... = 'Once upon a time...'). In the longer expression une fois que, it means 'once/when' followed by a clause.
target_language_example: Je suis allé à Paris une fois.
native_language_example: I went to Paris once.

meaning: 'once again' or 'one more time' (used in expressions like «une fois de plus»).
additional_notes: The fragment 'une fois de' is not normally used alone; it appears in fixed expressions such as «une fois de plus» (once again/one more time) or «une fois de trop» (one time too many). Use the full expression. It indicates repetition or an additional occurrence. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Il est arrivé en retard une fois de plus.
native_language_example: He arrived late once again.

meaning: literally “one time for”; a fragment that appears in idioms (e.g. "une bonne fois pour toutes") used to mean finally/once and for all. By itself it's uncommon and usually incomplete.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase. Learners should prefer full expressions like "une fois" (once) or "une bonne fois pour toutes" (once and for all). "Une fois pour" will typically be followed by other words; using it alone can sound unfinished.
target_language_example: Il faut régler ça une fois pour, pas à chaque réunion.
native_language_example: We need to settle this once for (good), not at every meeting.

meaning: once and for all; finally, so it's settled permanently.
additional_notes: Use to say that something will be done now to end a problem or settle an issue permanently. Often used before or after an imperative or statement for emphasis. Tone can be firm or exasperated. Equivalent to 'for good' or 'finally' in English.
target_language_example: On va parler et régler ça une fois pour toutes.
native_language_example: We'll talk and settle this once and for all.

meaning: once a / one time a (rare/formal literary phrasing)
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed everyday phrase in modern spoken French. It may appear in literary or formal contexts as part of a larger expression (e.g., "une fois un homme..." = "once a man..."), equivalent to English "once a..." or "once upon a time, a...". In casual speech, speakers more often say "il était une fois" for fairy-tale openings or use simple past/imparfait constructions. Watch word order: "une fois" alone can also mean "once" (as in "once you..." = "une fois que...").
target_language_example: Une fois un voyageur entra dans le village et demanda de l'eau.
native_language_example: Once a traveler entered the village and asked for water.

meaning: a young (female); short for 'une jeune fille' or 'une jeune femme' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally 'a young (one)'. In everyday French, 'jeune' is an adjective meaning 'young'. Used as a noun phrase 'une jeune' is informal and elliptical — speakers often shorten 'une jeune fille' (a young girl) or 'une jeune femme' (a young woman) to 'une jeune' when the head noun is understood. Context tells whether it refers to a girl or young woman. Not complete as a standalone formal phrase in writing.
target_language_example: Une jeune est entrée dans le café, regardant autour d'elle.
native_language_example: A young woman/ girl walked into the café, looking around.

meaning: a time machine (literally: a machine to go back/upward in time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a device that allows one to travel back in time. Often completed as 'une machine à remonter le temps'. 'Remonter' here means 'go back/up' in time (not physical upward movement). Common in fiction and hypothetical speech.
target_language_example: Si j'avais une machine à remonter le temps, je changerais une erreur.
native_language_example: If I had a time machine, I would change a mistake.

meaning: a minute
additional_notes: Literally means 'a minute.' It can refer to a short amount of time, or be used on its own to ask someone to wait briefly.
target_language_example: Attends une minute, j'arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I'm coming.

meaning: in a minute; any moment now (something expected to happen very soon).
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen imminently or could change at any moment. Slightly informal; often used when waiting for an event (e.g., arrival, start, change). Can be followed by a verb or stand alone in context.
target_language_example: Il va arriver une minute à l'autre.
native_language_example: He will arrive any minute now.

meaning: a bet; a stake (money placed on a game, competition, or gamble).
additional_notes: Commonly used in gambling contexts (poker, horse racing, casino) and metaphorically for any financial or figurative 'stake'. Often appears in phrases like "faire une mise" (to place a bet) or "la mise minimale" (the minimum bet). Note that "mise" alone can also appear in other compounds with different meanings (e.g. "mise en place", "mise à jour").
target_language_example: Il a fait une mise sur le cheval numéro 4.
native_language_example: He placed a bet on horse number 4.

meaning: a new pair (of...)
additional_notes: Used before a noun that comes in pairs (chaussures, gants, lunettes, chaussettes, etc.). In French 'paire' is feminine: 'une paire'. 'Nouvelle' agrees in gender with 'paire' (feminine). To complete the idea, add 'de' + item: une nouvelle paire de chaussures = a new pair of shoes.
target_language_example: Elle veut acheter une nouvelle paire de chaussettes.
native_language_example: She wants to buy a new pair of socks.

meaning: a spoken/colloquial contraction of 'une ou deux' meaning 'one or (one) or two' / used when hesitating between one option and another (rare).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard fixed phrase. On its own 'une ou' is incomplete in writing and usually part of a longer expression like 'une ou deux' (one or two) or 'une ou l'autre' (one or the other). In fast speech speakers may say 'une ou' when trailing off or hesitating before continuing. For learners, prefer the full forms 'une ou deux', 'une ou l'autre', or simply 'ou' for 'or'.
target_language_example: Je prendrai une ou deux pommes, je ne sais pas encore.
native_language_example: I'll take one or two apples, I don't know yet.

meaning: 'a loss' or 'a waste' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common noun meaning loss (of money, people, items, weight, etc.) or waste (time/opportunity). Used with possessives or quantities: une perte de 10 kg, une perte d'argent. Can also mean casualty (e.g., military losses). Plural is des pertes.
target_language_example: La société a enregistré une perte financière cette année.
native_language_example: The company recorded a financial loss this year.

meaning: a fear; a feeling of being afraid.
additional_notes: Common, general noun used to talk about fear in French. Can be used in expressions like avoir peur (to be afraid) or donner la peur (to scare someone). With adjectives or complements: une peur bleue (very intense fear), une peur de ... (fear of ...). Article 'une' makes it singular and feminine.
target_language_example: J'ai eu une peur en voyant ce chien.
native_language_example: I got a fright when I saw that dog.

meaning: 'a [piece/room/coin] of' — beginning of a phrase meaning 'a piece of' or 'a room of' depending on context (followed by a word starting with a vowel or mute h).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the feminine indefinite noun 'une pièce' followed by the contraction d' (de) before a vowel. 'Pièce' has several meanings: a room (une pièce de la maison), a coin (une pièce de monnaie), a play/drama (une pièce de théâtre), or a piece/part (une pièce d'identité — an identity document). After d' you expect a noun or descriptor starting with a vowel/mute h (e.g. d'identité, d'eau, d'occasion).
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé une pièce d'identité dans la rue.
native_language_example: I found an identity document on the street.

meaning: for some reason / if, for any reason, that were to happen.
additional_notes: A formal/neutral phrase used to introduce a hypothetical or unexpected possibility. Built from 'pour une raison quelconque' (for some/any reason) plus 'cela' (that/it). Common in conditional sentences: 'Si, pour une raison quelconque, cela arrivait...' = 'If, for some reason, that happened...'. You can shorten it to 'pour une raison quelconque' or more simply 'pour une raison quelconque, si...' In everyday speech people often say 'pour une raison quelconque' or more colloquially 'pour une raison quelconque' → 'pour une raison quelconque' (no strong slang).
target_language_example: Si, pour une raison quelconque, cela devait arriver, avertis-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If, for some reason, that were to happen, warn me immediately.

meaning: an attempt / a try
additional_notes: Used to describe an effort or attempt to do something. Often followed by 'de' + verb (une tentative de faire quelque chose) or a noun (une tentative de suicide). Can be formal or neutral. In contexts like 'tentative de suicide' or 'tentative de noyade' it refers to a suicide attempt or attempted drowning.
target_language_example: Elle a fait une tentative de réparer la voiture.
native_language_example: She made an attempt to fix the car.

meaning: A sequence of two words that can appear together in a sentence (uns = masculine plural indefinite article used in some dialects/contexts; les = definite plural article), but 'uns' is not standard French — likely a typo or from another language; in standard French these two words don't form a fixed phrase.
additional_notes: In standard French, 'uns' is not commonly used as a standalone word; the normal indefinite plural article is 'des'. 'Les' is the definite plural article ('the'). If you see 'uns les' it is probably a mistake, a typo, or comes from a dialect/older text. Possible intended phrases: 'un, les...' (e.g. 'un... les...'), 'des les' is incorrect (should be 'des' or 'les'), or it could be from German ('uns' = 'us') accidentally mixed in. For learners: don't memorize 'uns les' as a phrase — learn 'des' (some) and 'les' (the) instead.
target_language_example: Incorrect: *Uns les enfants jouent dans le parc.* — correct: "Les enfants jouent dans le parc."
native_language_example: Incorrect: *Uns les children play in the park.* — correct: "The children are playing in the park."

meaning: in urgent need of / it is urgent to (do something).
additional_notes: Usually appears with an infinitive (urgent de + infinitive) or followed by a noun introduced by 'avoir' (avoir besoin urgent de). More common constructions: 'il est urgent de + infinitive' (it is urgent to...), 'avoir/être urgent' with 'de' is less common alone. Use 'il est urgent de...' to say something must be done quickly.
target_language_example: Il est urgent de prendre des mesures.
native_language_example: It is urgent to take measures.

meaning: 'to use the' (masculine singular object)
additional_notes: Combines the verb utiliser (to use) with the definite article le (the). It must agree with the gender/number of the noun: utiliser la (fem. sing.), utiliser les (pl.), utiliser l' (before vowel). Common in instructions or sentences describing using an object or tool.
target_language_example: Tu peux utiliser le couteau pour couper le pain.
native_language_example: You can use the knife to cut the bread.

meaning: 'to use the' (plural).
additional_notes: Combines the verb utiliser (to use) with the plural definite article les. Followed by a plural noun or plural concept. Can be used for tangible items (les livres, les toilettes) or abstract things (les données, les gens). Polite forms for requests often use je peux/ puis‑je + utiliser les. Watch word order: question forms may invert or use est‑ce que. Not idiomatic—literal composition.
target_language_example: Je vais utiliser les livres de la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: I am going to use the library books.

meaning: used (followed by plural noun); 'utilisé' = used, 'des' = some/any (plural article).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: the past participle 'utilisé' (masculine singular) plus the plural indefinite article 'des' before a plural noun (e.g., « utilisé des outils » = used some tools). Agreement: if the subject is plural, you may see 'utilisés' instead of 'utilisé'. In negative or formal contexts 'des' can change to 'de' (e.g., « n'a pas utilisé de … »).
target_language_example: Il a utilisé des outils anciens pour réparer la porte.
native_language_example: He used some old tools to repair the door.

meaning: 'screw off' / 'get lost' (very rude)
additional_notes: Very vulgar imperative phrase. Literally 'go shit' but used to tell someone to go away angrily. Strongly informal and offensive; avoid in polite company. Often appears in extended insults (e.g. "va te faire chier", "va te faire foutre").
target_language_example: Il lui a crié "va chier" après la dispute.
native_language_example: He shouted "screw off" at him after the argument.

meaning: 'is going to do the' (used before a masculine noun or activity introduced by definite article)
additional_notes: This is the present near-future construction with aller + infinitive followed by a direct noun phrase introduced by the definite article (le). In French you often say «va faire le ménage», «va faire le plein», «va faire le pont» etc. Depending on context, it can be an instruction (Imperative: «Va faire le...») or a statement about someone's future action («Il va faire le...»). Note: word order and gender matter (use la for feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Va faire le ménage, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Go do the housework, please.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'is going to do something' or part of 'va faire quelque chose' ('is going to do something').
additional_notes: Alone 'va faire quelque' is incomplete and uncommon. The correct full phrase is 'va faire quelque chose' (informal) meaning 'is going to do something'. 'Va' is the 3rd-person singular or imperative of 'aller' used as near-future ('is going to'). 'Faire' means 'to do/make'. 'Quelque' must be followed by 'chose' (something) or an adjective + noun (e.g. 'quelque chose', 'quelque chose de bien'). Do not use 'va faire quelque' by itself in standard French.
target_language_example: Il va faire quelque chose pour réparer la porte.
native_language_example: He is going to do something to fix the door.

meaning: 'never' in negative spoken French (colloquial); used after a verb to mean 'doesn't ever' or 'will never'.
additional_notes: This is an informal, colloquial contraction of the negative construction ne ... jamais where the ne is dropped (common in spoken French): e.g. 'Il ne va jamais' → spoken 'Il va jamais'. Use in casual conversation; avoid in formal writing. Typically appears after a conjugated verb (va = 3rd person singular of aller, but the pattern applies to other verbs: 'fais jamais' etc.).
target_language_example: Il va jamais venir.
native_language_example: He will never come.

meaning: 'go (and) take/look' (as in 'go take a look')
additional_notes: Common conversational construction with the verb jeter + an object like 'un œil' or 'un coup d'œil' to mean 'take a look'. Often uses 'aller' (va/ on va) + infinitive to indicate a near-future action ('we're going to...') or an imperative 'va jeter...' meaning 'go take.../go have a look'. The object can be omitted in casual speech ('On va jeter un oeil' = 'We'll go have a look').
target_language_example: Va jeter un œil à la fenêtre, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Go take a look at the window, please.

meaning: colloquial contraction meaning 'doesn't ... at all' or 'won't ... anything' (negation with 'ne' omitted)
additional_notes: Informal spoken French where the subject-verb 'va' (from 'aller' or as dummy verb) appears with 'rien' (nothing) and the 'ne' is dropped: e.g. 'Il va rien comprendre' = 'He won't understand anything.' Common in everyday speech in many regions. It is not standard written French; the grammatical form in standard French is 'ne ... rien' (e.g. 'Il ne va rien comprendre').
target_language_example: Elle va rien dire si tu ne poses pas la question.
native_language_example: She won't say anything if you don't ask the question.

meaning: 'will' + 'there' (part of future/periphrastic constructions meaning 'will [do it/there/etc.]') — used in spoken/familiar French to form future actions referring to something already mentioned or to 'there'.
additional_notes: This is the verb aller (il/elle/on va) + the pronoun y. In context it often appears in periphrastic future constructions (on va y + infinitive) meaning 'we/one will [do it/think about it/reflect on it]' or to indicate movement/existence toward a place ('va y venir' = 'will come there'). 'Y' replaces a place or a previously mentioned idea ('about it', 'there'). In written French you may see "on va y réfléchir" (we will think about it). Pronunciation in speech often links them closely.
target_language_example: On va y répondre demain.
native_language_example: We'll respond to it tomorrow.

meaning: 'is going to be in' or 'will be in' (future construction + preposition 'en').
additional_notes: This is part of the near-future tense using aller + infinitive (va être = 'is going to be'). When followed by 'en' it introduces a state, location (in), time period, or a way of doing something depending on the context (e.g. 'va être en retard' = will be late, 'va être en France' = will be in France, 'va être en colère' = will be angry). You normally need additional words after 'en' to complete the idea. Informal spoken French often uses 'va être' for near future; for plural subjects use 'vont être'.
target_language_example: Elle va être en retard si elle ne part pas maintenant.
native_language_example: She is going to be late if she doesn't leave now.

meaning: is going to be a (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Combination of the near-future construction 'aller + infinitive' (ça va être = it is going to be) followed by the indefinite article 'une'. Used before a feminine noun or an expression treated as feminine (une journée, une bataille, une nuit). Common in spoken and written French to describe upcoming events, conditions, or qualities. Replace 'une' with 'un' for masculine nouns (ça va être un...).
target_language_example: Ça va être une journée chargée.
native_language_example: It's going to be a busy day.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo, mis-segmentation, or two separate words from different parts of a sentence (possible intended phrases include 'ça va', 'vas-y', or 'va, ce...').
additional_notes: There is no common expression 'va ce' in French. It may appear in a mistaken transcription where 'va' (go/verb) and 'ce' (this/that/demonstrative) are adjacent but belong to different syntactic roles. Examples of possible corrections: 'ça va' (How are you?/It's okay), 'vas-y' (Go ahead), or a clause started by 'va, ce...' (rare and usually part of a longer phrase). Verify the source text and punctuation before translating.
target_language_example: Va ce que tu veux, mais explique-toi.
native_language_example: Do what you want, but explain yourself.

meaning: literally 'goes like' — used to compare how something suits, fits, or behaves (often followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Used when describing how something 'goes' with something else (e.g., a color goes with an outfit) or how a situation is unfolding compared to something else. Common patterns: 'Ça va comme ...' or 'X va comme Y' (X suits/works with Y). Not a fixed idiom on its own — usually appears inside a larger sentence. Choose verb form 'va' (third-person singular of 'aller') to match a singular subject.
target_language_example: Cette robe va comme un gant avec tes chaussures.
native_language_example: That dress goes like a glove with your shoes.

meaning: 'fits like a' or 'suits like a' (used to compare how well something fits or suits someone or something)
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: 'va comme un...' is followed by a noun to say that something fits/suits someone in the same way as that noun. Often completed by a phrase like 'va comme un gant' (fits like a glove) or 'va comme un sac' (suits like a sack — negative). Alone it's incomplete and needs the rest of the expression.
target_language_example: Cette robe va comme un gant.
native_language_example: That dress fits like a glove.

meaning: 'how's it going?' (informal spoken greeting, short for "ça va ?" / "ça va, comment ?")
additional_notes: This is an informal, colloquial way to ask how someone is doing, often heard in casual spoken French. It may be a regional or rapid-speech contraction and is not standard written French. Use with friends or peers, not in formal situations. Typical alternatives: "Ça va ?", "Comment ça va ?"
target_language_example: Salut ! Va comment aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Hi! How's it going today?

meaning: it is the same / likewise / applies likewise
additional_notes: Used to say that the same situation, rule or comment also applies to something else. Often used in formal or neutral contexts. Can appear as 'il en va de même' (the full idiom) meaning 'the same goes for...'.
target_language_example: Il en va de même pour les étudiants internationaux.
native_language_example: The same goes for international students.

meaning: “the same goes for” or “this is also true for”.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that what was just said also applies to someone or something else. Often appears in the fixed expression "il en va de même pour" (literally "it goes the same for") and is common in both formal and neutral registers. Use to add a parallel point: "Il en va de même pour X" = "X is the same/also affected."
target_language_example: Il en va de même pour les étudiants qui habitent loin.
native_language_example: The same goes for students who live far away.

meaning: imperative 'go (and) + them' — tells someone to go to/for/see a group or people/objects (informal singular 'tu' form).
additional_notes: A combination of the imperative of 'aller' (va) used with the object pronoun 'les' (them). 'Va les...' is informal and directed at one person (tu). The exact meaning depends on the verb context that follows or is implied: e.g. 'va les chercher' = go fetch them, 'va les rejoindre' = go join them, 'va les voir' = go see them. When 'les' refers to people, it's equivalent to 'them'; for objects it means 'them' (plural). In spoken French you may also hear 'vas-y' instead of 'va' before other verbs.
target_language_example: Va les appeler tout de suite.
native_language_example: Go call them right away.

meaning: A casual, regional or familiar way to address someone (like 'come on, man' or 'go on, mate') — depends on context; 'va' is the imperative of 'aller', and 'mon' is a familiar address (short for 'mon vieux' or 'mon pote').
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed expression in formal French; it appears in colloquial or regional speech as two separate words: 'va' (imperative 'go' or an interjection meaning 'come on') followed by 'mon' (a familiar vocative meaning 'my [man]' or 'mate'). It can soften commands or express surprise, encouragement, or mild reproach depending on tone. Register: informal. Usage varies by region and speaker; you may hear forms like 'allez, mon', 'va, mon vieux', or simply 'va, mon'.
target_language_example: Allez, va mon, tu peux le faire !
native_language_example: Come on, man, you can do it!

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; appears to be a mistaken juxtaposition of 'va' (go / he/she goes) and 'notre' (our). It does not form a correct fixed expression on its own.
additional_notes: This sequence does not form a correct phrase in French because 'notre' is a possessive adjective that must be followed by a noun, not by a verb. Possible intended forms: 'va à notre...' (go to our...), 'va nous...' (imperative + object pronoun, though the correct clitic order is 'va nous ...' in informal speech but more commonly written with infinitive: 'va nous aider' is colloquial), or 'va-t-il/va-tu...' (questions). If you see 'va notre' in text, it's likely a typo or missing word(s). 'va' can be either the informal imperative 'go' (tu form) or the third-person singular present 'goes'.
target_language_example: Il va notre chemin n'est pas le même.
native_language_example: He goes; our path is not the same. (This sentence is ungrammatical/awkward in French and shows 'va notre' appearing but results from incorrect phrasing.)

meaning: 'is wrong with' or 'doesn't work with' (used after 'quelque chose' or 'ça').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the negative construction 'ne ... pas avec' after words like 'quelque chose' or 'ça' to say that something is wrong with or doesn't fit/agree with another thing. In spoken French 'ne' is often dropped: 'ça va pas avec...' or 'il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas avec...'. Can mean 'is malfunctioning' (a device) or 'doesn't match/go well with' (an object or idea) depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas avec mon téléphone.
native_language_example: There is something wrong with my phone.

meaning: literally 'goes without'; used to say something works/continues or happens despite the absence of something
additional_notes: Composed of the verb aller/aller (va) + sans (without). Often appears in phrases like 'ça va sans dire' (that goes without saying) or 'va sans dire que...' — meaning 'it's obvious/needs no saying'. On its own 'va sans' is not commonly used; it's usually part of fixed expressions. Use with impersonal constructions (ça/il) or followed by an infinitive/que clause in set phrases.
target_language_example: Ça va sans dire que tu seras invité.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that you will be invited.

meaning: a very strong vulgar insult: 'go fuck yourself' (literally 'go get yourself fucked in the ass').
additional_notes: Extremely offensive and vulgar. Used to express hatred, anger, or to insult someone; can be directed at someone casually among very close friends in crude contexts but generally not acceptable in polite company. Contains homophobic and sexual violence connotations; avoid using. Grammatically imperative (va = go) + reflexive te + infinitive faire enculer.
target_language_example: Il m'a traité de menteur et je lui ai répondu : « Va te faire enculer ! »
native_language_example: He called me a liar and I answered him, "Go fuck yourself!"

meaning: Go f*** yourself (very rude insult; tell someone to get lost angrily).
additional_notes: Strongly vulgar and offensive. Used to express extreme anger, rejection, or contempt. Do not use in polite conversation. Literally means 'go make yourself f***ed,' but functions like the English phrase 'go f*** yourself' or 'fuck off.' Can be directed at someone (tu form).
target_language_example: Non—va te faire foutre, je ne t'aiderai pas.
native_language_example: No—go f*** yourself, I won't help you.

meaning: 'go away' / 'get lost' (rude; literally 'go have yourself seen')
additional_notes: A strong, insulting way to tell someone to go away. Commonly used in informal and angry contexts. Equivalent in English to 'get lost,' 'sod off,' or 'go to hell' depending on tone. You can add 'ailleurs' (elsewhere) to emphasize 'go away somewhere else.' Avoid using in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: Non, va te faire voir — je ne veux pas en parler.
native_language_example: No, go away — I don't want to talk about it.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase as written; likely a misspelling, misordering, or fragment of another phrase.
additional_notes:
'Va ton' by itself is not correct French. Possible intended forms include:
- 'va-t'en' (go away) — imperative 'va' + enclitic 't'en' (written with hyphens and an apostrophe).
- 'vas-y' (go ahead) — informal imperative 'vas' + pronoun 'y'.
- 'va ton chemin' could appear as a nonstandard/informal attempt to say 'suis ton chemin' (follow your path) or 'va de ton côté' (go your own way), but 'va ton' alone is incomplete. If you encounter 'va ton' in text or speech, check surrounding words or ask the speaker for clarification.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire par « va ton », peux-tu répéter ?
native_language_example: I don't understand what you mean by "va ton", can you repeat?

meaning: '(we/he/she) goes all' — part of the phrase 'on y va tous' meaning 'we all go' or 'we're all going'.
additional_notes: Alone 'va' is the third-person singular of aller (il/elle/on va) or the imperative 'go'. 'Tous' means 'all' or 'everyone'. In spoken French you'll often see 'on y va tous' or 'on va tous' to mean 'let's all go' or 'we're all going'. Word order can be 'on y va tous' or 'on va tous'; 'y' means 'there'. Use 'tous' (plural) after the verb when referring to people (agrees in pronunciation: 'tous' after a verb is usually pronounced [tu]).
target_language_example: On y va tous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we all going there tonight?

meaning: 'is too...' or 'goes too...' (indicates that something is excessive or goes too far)
additional_notes: Commonly used after a subject to say that something is excessive, unreasonable, or goes beyond limits. Often followed by an adjective, a verb in infinitive, or a clause: il va trop loin (he goes too far), ça va trop vite (it's going too fast), ça va trop te coûter (that will cost you too much). Informal spoken register is frequent. Contraction with subject: 'ça va trop' or 'il va trop'.
target_language_example: Il va trop loin avec ses critiques.
native_language_example: He is going too far with his criticism.

meaning: 'is/are doing very' or 'goes very' — used to say something is going or behaving to a high degree (often followed by an adjective or adverb).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'ça va très bien' (that's going very well) or 'il va très vite' (he/it goes very fast). 'Va' is the 3rd-person singular of 'aller' (to go, to be doing). The subject can be 'ça', 'il', 'elle', or a noun; 'très' intensifies the adjective or adverb that follows. Not a standalone phrase—needs an adjective/adverb after it.
target_language_example: Ça va très bien aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Things are going very well today.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a misspelling or misordering (possibly meant: « va, votre ... » or « allez-vous » / « va pour »).
additional_notes:
As written, 'va votre' does not form a correct or common expression in French. Possible intended forms:
- « allez-vous » (formal/plural 'do you go' / inversion for questions) or « vas-tu » (informal 'do you go').
- « va pour » (informal, means 'okay, agreed' or 'let it be so').
- could be a mistaken separation of 'votre' (your) after a verb, e.g. 'va votre chemin' (incorrect) instead of 'allez votre chemin' (still odd). If you saw 'va votre' in text, check surrounding words or consider it a typo. For learners: study correct verb forms (aller) and pronouns: 'je vais', 'tu vas', 'il/elle va', 'nous allons', 'vous allez', 'ils/elles vont'.
target_language_example: Il va falloir vérifier le mot — 'va votre' n'est pas correct.
native_language_example: We should check the word — 'va votre' is not correct.

meaning: Not a correct or standard French expression as written; it appears to be the demonstrative 'cette' (this/that) and the noun 'vacances' (holidays/vacation) in the wrong order. In natural French, use 'ces vacances' (these holidays) or restructure the sentence so 'cette' modifies a singular feminine noun (e.g. 'cette période de vacances').
additional_notes: 'Vacances' is typically plural in French, so 'cette vacances' is ungrammatical. If you mean 'these holidays' use 'ces vacances'. If you want to keep 'cette', use a singular noun: 'cette vacance' is very rare; prefer 'cette période de vacances' or 'cette semaine de vacances'. The sequence 'vacances cette' might appear in some poetic or inverted structures but is nonstandard and will be understood as incorrect by native speakers.
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas vacances cette année, je préfère rester chez moi.
native_language_example: I don't like holidays this year; I prefer to stay at home.

meaning: 'vacation/holiday of' or '...’s vacation' (used to introduce the type, time, or possessive of holidays)
additional_notes: Often appears before a noun to specify when or whose holidays: e.g. vacances d'été (summer holidays), vacances de Noël (Christmas holidays), vacances de printemps (spring break), vacances de mon frère (my brother's holidays). In French, vacances is plural and usually used with de or d' to link to another word. Use de + definite article when needed: les vacances de Noël or les vacances du professeur.
target_language_example: Les vacances de Noël sont toujours chargées.
native_language_example: The Christmas holidays are always busy.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken fragment meaning 'the cows (to) us' or a typo.
additional_notes:
This combination is not idiomatic in French. 'Vaches' is the plural noun 'cows'. 'Nous' is the first‑person plural object or subject pronoun ('we' or 'us'). Together they do not form a fixed expression. Possible intended forms:
- 'les vaches nous...' followed by a verb (e.g. 'les vaches nous regardent' = 'the cows are looking at us').
- 'vache' appears in idioms (e.g. 'quelle vache!' informal, 'quel salaud' tone) but 'vaches nous' by itself is incorrect. If you saw this in a sentence, check for missing words or typos.
target_language_example: Les vaches nous regardent depuis le pré.
native_language_example: The cows are watching us from the field.

meaning: 'I'm going to go (and) [do something to/for myself]' — part of a future proche construction with a reflexive verb (je vais aller me ...).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when using the near future (aller + infinitive) combined with a reflexive infinitive. The full pattern is: subject + vais/va/allons/etc. + aller + me/te/se/nous/vous + infinitive. It literally means 'I am going to go to [do something to/for myself]'. Often used for actions you will do for yourself (e.g., 'je vais aller me coucher' = I'm going to go to bed). In casual speech the first 'aller' (to go) + another verb can sound repetitive but is grammatical when indicating motion + reflexive action.
target_language_example: Je vais aller me reposer cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to go rest this afternoon.

meaning: I am going to go to (somewhere or do something).
additional_notes: Present tense of 'aller' (je vais) + infinitive 'aller' + preposition 'à'. Often used to express near future with motion toward a place: 'Je vais aller à la plage' = 'I'm going to go to the beach.' Unusual to use two 'aller' verbs in many contexts; more common is 'je vais aller' (I will go) or simply 'j'irai' (future tense). Use 'à' before locations or activities that take the preposition 'à'.
target_language_example: Je vais aller à la bibliothèque cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'm going to go to the library this afternoon.

meaning: 'I'm going to call the... (female noun)'.
additional_notes: This is the near-future construction using 'aller' + infinitive (je vais appeler = I'm going to call). 'La' is the feminine definite article that agrees with the noun that follows (e.g. la police, la sécurité). For a masculine noun use 'le' (je vais appeler le...); for plural use 'les'. Common in urgent contexts (threat to call police/security).
target_language_example: Je vais appeler la mairie pour demander des informations.
native_language_example: I'm going to call the town hall to ask for information.

meaning: am fine
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of je vais bien to say how you are feeling or doing. French often uses aller here where English uses be or do. With other subjects, the verb changes: tu vas bien, il/elle va bien, nous allons bien, etc.
target_language_example: Je vais bien, merci.
native_language_example: I'm fine, thank you.

meaning: I'm going to get/fetch it (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Vais chercher la is the short form of 'je vais chercher la ...' used before a feminine noun (la + noun). It indicates going to fetch, get, or bring something or someone. In speech the subject 'je' is often dropped in casual contexts. Use 'le' for masculine nouns, 'les' for plural. Can also be used with people (e.g., 'je vais chercher la police' meaning 'I'm going to call/get the police' in some contexts).
target_language_example: Je vais chercher la clé, j'arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'm going to get the key, I'll be right back.

meaning: I'm going to get the...
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase using the near-future construction 'aller + infinitive' (here: 'je vais chercher' = 'I'm going to fetch/get'). Followed by a masculine singular noun with the definite article 'le' (e.g. 'le café', 'le camion', 'le chat'). Use to say you'll go bring or pick up something or someone. For feminine nouns use 'la' (je vais chercher la...); for plural use 'les' (je vais chercher les...).
target_language_example: Je vais chercher le livre à la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: I'm going to get the book from the library.

meaning: I'm going to get/fetch my ... (male possessor).
