target_language_example: Je veux leur téléphoner ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to call them tonight.

meaning: 'want to read' (first or second person singular of vouloir + lire).
additional_notes: Combines the present tense of vouloir (je veux, tu veux) with the verb lire (to read). Use to express desire to read something or to ask if someone wants to read. Conjugation changes with subject: je veux lire, tu veux lire, il/elle veut lire, nous voulons lire, vous voulez lire, ils veulent lire. Can be followed by a direct object (un livre, le courrier) or by clauses (lire que...).
target_language_example: Je veux lire ce roman ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to read this novel this weekend.

meaning: want to eat (some/of) — expresses desire to eat part of or some quantity of something; typically followed by a partitive article (du/de la/des) or a noun phrase.
additional_notes: This is the construction with vouloir (e.g. je veux, tu veux) + manger + de. Often requires a partitive/article or a following noun: "Je veux manger du gâteau." If left alone as "veux manger de" it feels incomplete and is usually followed by what you want to eat (e.g. "veux manger de la tarte"). For politeness, prefer "j'aimerais manger" or "je voudrais manger" in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Tu veux manger de la soupe ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat some soup tonight?

meaning: This is not a correct French phrase; it appears to be a fragment meaning 'want to eat some' but is ungrammatical.
additional_notes: The correct ways to express 'want to eat some' in French depend on subject and context: e.g. 'Je veux manger quelque chose' (I want to eat something), 'Je veux manger un peu' (I want to eat a little), or 'Je veux manger quelque chose à manger' is redundant. 'Quelque' by itself is an adjective and must be followed by a noun (quelque chose = something; quelquefois = sometimes). If you mean 'do you want to eat something?' use 'Tu veux manger quelque chose ?' or more politely 'Voulez-vous manger quelque chose ?'.
target_language_example: Je veux manger quelque chose avant de partir.
native_language_example: I want to eat something before leaving.

meaning: 'want to tell me this' (fragment)
additional_notes: This is not a complete, standard French phrase by itself — it's a fragment you'd see inside a sentence, for example: «Tu veux me dire ce que tu penses ?» or «Qu'est‑ce que tu veux me dire ?». The more natural full forms are «tu veux me dire ça», «tu veux me dire ceci», or «tu veux me dire ce que…». Use with a clause or a demonstrative (ça/ceci) to be grammatical.
target_language_example: Tu veux me dire ce que tu as vu ?
native_language_example: Do you want to tell me what you saw?

meaning: 'I want my' (fragment).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself — it combines veux (1st/2nd/3rd person singular of vouloir in present) and mon (my). In natural French you'd normally say "je veux mon..." to mean "I want my..." or use the correct subject/verb agreement: "tu veux mon..." (you want my...) or "il/elle veut mon..." (he/she wants my...). Make sure to include the subject pronoun (je, tu, il/elle) and finish the sentence with the object (e.g. "je veux mon livre").
target_language_example: Je veux mon livre.
native_language_example: I want my book.

meaning: 'even want' or 'want even to' — used to emphasize desire (often in contrast or to show surprise/refusal).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the verb vouloir (veux) plus the adverb même. 'Même' adds emphasis: it can intensify a desire ('I even want...'), highlight contrast ('I don't even want...'), or express surprise. Context and word order matter (e.g. 'je ne veux même pas' = 'I don't even want to'). Contraction and agreement follow normal grammar (veux is 1st/2nd person singular of vouloir).
target_language_example: Je ne veux même pas y penser.
native_language_example: I don't even want to think about it.

meaning: 'want us' or 'you/he/she wants us' depending on subject
additional_notes: This is not a complete standalone phrase — it's the verb vouloir (veux) followed by the pronoun nous. Meaning depends on the subject: 'je veux nous' is ungrammatical; 'tu veux nous…' means 'you want us…'; 'il/elle veut nous…' would use 'veut' (not 'veux'). With 'veux-nous' (hyphen) it can appear in informal commands (tu veux-nous ? is rare). More common constructions: 'tu veux que nous ...' (you want us to ...), 'il veut nous aider' (he wants to help us). Pay attention to subject-verb agreement and word order: direct object pronoun normally precedes the verb (il nous veut is rare/means something different); typical: 'il veut nous inviter' or 'il veut nous voir'.
target_language_example: Tu veux nous aider ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to help us tonight?

meaning: 'I want to speak to my...' (used before a feminine family member or partner).
additional_notes: This phrase is the stem of sentences where the speaker says they want to talk to a specific female person (ma + noun). You must add the feminine noun after 'ma' (ma mère, ma fille, ma copine, ma femme). For masculine nouns use 'veux parler à mon'. 'Je veux parler à...' is a direct, neutral way to request to speak with someone; polite contexts may use 'Je voudrais parler à...' or 'Puis-je parler à...'.
target_language_example: Je veux parler à ma mère tout de suite.
native_language_example: I want to speak to my mother right away.

meaning: 'I want to speak to my...' (used before a masculine singular family member or male person).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase for expressing desire to speak with someone. 'Veux' is the familiar/conjugated form of 'vouloir' (je veux = I want). 'Parler à' means 'to speak to'. 'Mon' is the masculine singular possessive used before masculine nouns (mon frère, mon fils) and also used before feminine nouns that begin with a vowel (ma amie → mon amie). In formal contexts you might use 'Je voudrais parler à mon...' (I would like to speak to my...).
target_language_example: Je veux parler à mon médecin.
native_language_example: I want to speak to my doctor.

meaning: 'don't want to' + partitive/quantity expression (colloquial/contracted)
additional_notes: This is an informal, contracted sequence where 'veux pas' is the negated form of 'vouloir' (to want) used in speech instead of 'ne veux pas'. The 'en' pronoun refers back to something introduced earlier and replaces expressions introduced by 'de' (quantity, partitive, or 'of it/them'). Together, 'veux pas en' means 'don't want any of it' or 'don't want any (of them/of that)'. You will often see it in spoken French: e.g. 'Je veux pas en prendre' = 'I don't want to take any (of it/them)'.
target_language_example: Non merci, je veux pas en prendre.
native_language_example: No thanks, I don't want any (of it).

meaning: 'I don't want that' (informal, contracted form)
additional_notes: Colloquial/contracted negative: subject + 'veux pas' is an informal way to say 'ne veux pas' (I do not want). 'Ça' means 'that' or 'this' depending on context. Common in spoken French; avoid in formal writing where 'je ne veux pas ça' is preferred. Depending on tone, can be blunt—use politely with 's'il te plaît' or 's'il vous plaît'.
target_language_example: Je veux pas ça, merci.
native_language_example: I don't want that, thanks.

meaning: 'want to spend (time) at' or 'want to move from' depending on context
additional_notes: This fragment combines the verb vouloir (veux = you/ I want in familiar speech) + passer + the partitive article du (de + le). It appears in larger phrases like "je veux passer du temps" (I want to spend time) or "je veux passer du statut X au statut Y" (I want to move from X to Y). You need the rest of the sentence to know the meaning: often followed by temps (time), temps à + verb (time doing something), or a noun indicating a state/place. Conjugation: veux is singular (je veux, tu veux).
target_language_example: Je veux passer du temps avec mes amis ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to spend time with my friends this weekend.

meaning: 'want to spend time' (with someone or doing something).
additional_notes: A common phrase using the verb vouloir (veux = I/you informal want). Followed by an activity or a person: 'passer du temps avec quelqu'un' = spend time with someone; 'passer du temps à + infinitive' = spend time (doing) something. Conjugate veux to correspond to the subject (je veux, tu veux, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux passer du temps avec toi ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to spend time with you this weekend.

meaning: 'want to pay' (I/you/he/she/they want to pay depending on subject)
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir (to want) in the present tense with the infinitive payer (to pay). You must match veux to the correct subject: je veux (I want), tu veux (you want). In isolation 'veux payer' is informal — subject is often omitted in casual speech but make sure context shows who wants to pay. Commonly used when offering to pay a bill, a meal, etc.
target_language_example: Je veux payer l'addition.
native_language_example: I want to pay the bill.

meaning: want no more / want more (depends on context) — literally 'want more of' or 'don't want any more of'.
additional_notes: This phrase uses 'veux' (want) + 'plus de'. 'Plus de' can mean either 'more of' (a desire for additional quantity) or 'no more of' (when paired with a negation: 'ne ... plus de'). Context and presence of 'ne' or tone determine the meaning. Examples: 'Je veux plus de temps.' = I want more time. 'Je ne veux plus de ça.' = I don't want that anymore. After 'veux plus de' you usually add a noun or an object (no verb).
target_language_example: Je veux plus de patience avec lui.
native_language_example: I want more patience with him.

meaning: want no longer to (you) / don't want to (see) you anymore
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word order in negative/nonstandard sentences: je ne veux plus te voir = I don't want to see you anymore. In informal speech people sometimes drop the ne and say Je veux plus te voir to mean the same. The verb (veux) must agree with the subject and is followed by an infinitive and the object pronoun te (e.g. te voir). Use ne ... plus for formal negation; dropping ne is common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus te parler.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to you anymore.

meaning: 'want for' — literal combination of the verb vouloir (to want) + preposition pour (for); not an established fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: Not an idiomatic unit by itself. It can occur when vouloir is followed by a clause or noun introduced by pour (e.g. expressing purpose or beneficiary). More common constructions: vouloir + infinitive (je veux partir) or vouloir que + subjunctive (je veux que tu viennes). Whenever you see 'veux pour' you need surrounding context to know whether 'pour' indicates purpose, beneficiary, or part of another phrase.
target_language_example: Je veux pour toi ce qui est meilleur.
native_language_example: I want for you what is best.

meaning: want to be able to / want to have the ability to
additional_notes: Combination of the verb vouloir (veux = I/you form) + pouvoir (to be able to). Used to express a desire to have the ability or permission to do something. In sentences it will be conjugated to match the subject (e.g. je veux pouvoir, tu veux pouvoir, il/elle veut pouvoir). Often followed by an infinitive verb: vouloir pouvoir + infinitive.
target_language_example: Je veux pouvoir voyager sans inquiétude.
native_language_example: I want to be able to travel without worry.

meaning: 'I want to take' or 'you want to take' depending on subject (veut/veux = want + prendre = to take).
additional_notes: This is the verb vouloir (to want) + infinitive prendre (to take). Conjugation changes with subject: je veux prendre (I want to take), tu veux prendre (you want to take), il/elle veut prendre, nous voulons prendre, etc. Can mean 'take' in many senses: take an object, take (have) something (e.g. a coffee), take retirement/pension, or bring something along. Literal translation is possible. Not idiomatic on its own—meaning depends on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Je veux prendre un café, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want to have/take a coffee, please.

meaning: 'want that this/that...'; a fragment combining 'veux que' with the demonstrative pronoun 'ce', used when the speaker wants a situation or thing (referred to by 'ce') to be a certain way — still triggers subjunctive or is part of constructions like 'veux que ce soit...'.
additional_notes: Because 'ce' is a neutral demonstrative, 'veux que ce' typically appears in the longer phrase 'veux que ce soit...' (I want that this/that be...), which requires the subjunctive ('soit'). It can introduce statements about situations or facts rather than a specific person (compare 'veux que tu...' for a person). Not used alone; must be completed by a verb (often 'être') and the subjunctive mood.
target_language_example: Je veux que ce soit prêt pour demain.
native_language_example: I want that this/it be ready for tomorrow (I want it to be ready for tomorrow).

meaning: do you want me to…
additional_notes: Common spoken fragment of the structure « tu veux que j' + subjunctive/infinitive », used to ask or confirm whether the other person wants the speaker to do something. In French, after « veux que » the verb normally takes the subjunctive (e.g. « que j'aille »). In casual speech the object or rest of the verb phrase may be shortened (hence the trailing apostrophe). Use to offer help, ask permission, or check instructions.
target_language_example: Tu veux que j'aille le chercher ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to go get it?

meaning: You want me to (do something) — used to ask or report someone's request for the speaker to perform an action.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a subordinate clause with 'vouloir que' + subjunctive (or infinitive-like constructions in casual speech). In the examples, m' is the reflexive clitic (me) that attaches to verbs starting with a vowel (m'en aille, m'en charge, m'excuse, m'occupe). Common in questions: 'Tu veux que je...' = 'Do you want me to...?' Use it when someone asks whether they should do something for you.
target_language_example: Tu veux que je m'occupe de la réservation ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to take care of the booking?

meaning: 'want that my' — start of a clause expressing desire about something belonging to the speaker.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the beginning of a subordinate clause: veux que + subject (here mon + noun) or more commonly veux que + subject + verb. In correct French you usually say "je veux que mon..." followed by a verb (subjunctive mood) or a noun phrase: e.g. «Je veux que mon frère vienne» (I want my brother to come) or «Je veux que mon chien soit heureux». "Mon" must be followed by a noun (mon frère, mon ami, mon téléphone). Remember that after "veux que" the verb describing the action generally takes the subjunctive (qu'il vienne, qu'elle soit), but when simply stating possession or wanting an object, you can use direct object: "Je veux mon livre."
target_language_example: Je veux que mon frère vienne ce soir.
native_language_example: I want my brother to come tonight.

meaning: 'I want/us to' — expresses the speaker's desire that we (including the speaker and others) do or be something.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb vouloir in the first person singular (je veux) + que + nous + subjunctive or present tense depending on context. It introduces a wish, request, or desire about actions or states involving 'us' (including the speaker). In French, the verb after 'que' often takes the subjunctive when expressing desire (e.g., que nous fassions, que nous soyons). Useful for talking about what you want for your group or relationship.
target_language_example: Je veux que nous partions ensemble demain.
native_language_example: I want us to leave together tomorrow.

meaning: 'want everything' or 'want that everything' (incomplete fragment — usually part of a larger sentence)
additional_notes: This is not a complete grammatical phrase by itself in French. It combines veux que (subjunctive trigger: 'want that') with tout ('everything' or 'all'). In correct sentences you'd usually see: «Je veux que tout [subjunctive clause]» (I want everything to...) or «Je veux tout» (I want everything). When followed by a clause, the verb in that clause must be in the subjunctive: e.g. «Je veux que tout soit prêt.»
target_language_example: Je veux que tout soit prêt pour demain.
native_language_example: I want everything to be ready for tomorrow.

meaning: wants that everyone/the whole (followed by a noun or clause)
additional_notes: This fragment combines the verb vouloir (veux) with que (that) and tout le (the whole/the entire). It's not a complete phrase by itself—you'll usually see it in longer sentences like "je veux que tout le monde..." (I want everyone...) or "je veux que tout le projet soit terminé" (I want the whole project to be finished). After "veux que" use the subjunctive for verbs (e.g., "je veux que tu viennes"). "Tout le" must agree with the noun it modifies (tout le / toute la / tous les / toutes les).
target_language_example: Je veux que tout le monde vienne.
native_language_example: I want everyone to come.

meaning: want that (something happens); expresses a desire for a specific outcome
additional_notes: A colloquial fragment: often part of a larger sentence (e.g., «Je veux que ça marche» = I want that to work). After "veux que" the verb describing the desired action is normally in the subjunctive (e.g., «Je veux que tu viennes»). When followed by "ça" it usually refers to a situation or thing previously mentioned. Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je veux que ça se passe bien.
native_language_example: I want that to go well.

meaning: want something / would like something
additional_notes: Informal first-person or second-person form of vouloir + 'quelque chose' (something). Commonly used to express desire or request: "Je veux quelque chose" = I want something. To be polite, learners should use "je voudrais quelque chose" or add "s'il vous plaît". Can appear with nouns, infinitives, or more specific objects (e.g. "veux quelque chose à boire").
target_language_example: Je veux quelque chose à manger, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want something to eat, please.

meaning: 'want to go/return to (a place)'.
additional_notes: Form is imperative/first-person conversational: 'je veux rentrer à...' (I want to go back/return to...) or in questions/short replies someone might say 'veux rentrer à...' when quoting or reporting. 'Rentrer' means to return/ go back (home or to a place). Followed by a place introduced by à (a city, town, or someone's home): 'rentrer à Paris', 'rentrer à la maison' (note: 'à la maison' uses 'à' but commonly 'rentrer chez moi' for returning to someone's home). Conjugate 'vouloir' for different subjects: je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, etc.
target_language_example: Je veux rentrer à la maison maintenant.
native_language_example: I want to go back home now.

meaning: want(s) to go back/return to (a feminine place) — 'I/you/he/she want(s) to return to the [place]'.
additional_notes: This is part of a sentence: 'rentrer' = to return/go back home or to a place. 'À la' is the feminine singular preposition 'to the' (before a feminine noun): e.g. à la maison, à la gare. Conjugate the subject pronoun before 'veux' (je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut). Often followed by a place: 'je veux rentrer à la maison.'
target_language_example: Je veux rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I want to go back home.

meaning: 'I want to return' or 'I want to go back'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir (to want) in the first person singular (veux) with retourner (to return/go back). Used to express desire to go back to a place or to go back in time/steps (e.g., 'retrace steps' or 'go back'). If you mean 'to return something' (to give back), French often uses rendre instead. For polite requests, use Je voudrais retourner or Je veux retourner + infinitive when speaking strongly.
target_language_example: Je veux retourner à la maison.
native_language_example: I want to return/go back home.

meaning: "want to laugh" (literally) — often used colloquially to express disbelief, surprise, or that something is ridiculous (similar to "you're kidding" or "no way").
additional_notes: Literally the present tense of 'vouloir' + 'rire' (to want to laugh). Alone 'veux rire ?' can be said as a short, informal reaction meaning "are you kidding me?" or "you've got to be joking." In full sentences it simply means someone wants to laugh (e.g., «Je veux rire» = "I want to laugh"). Tone and context determine whether it's literal or idiomatic. Informal in idiomatic use.
target_language_example: Tu as oublié notre rendez-vous ? Veux rire !
native_language_example: You forgot our meeting? Are you kidding!

meaning: 'want to know' (part of the phrase meaning 'want to know that/what')
additional_notes: This sequence appears when someone says they 'want to know' something and is usually followed by a clause introduced by 'que' (that) or 'qui/quoi/comment/etc.' (who/what/how). The full phrase is typically 'je veux savoir ce que...' (I want to know what...) or 'je veux savoir si...' (I want to know if...). Alone, 'veux savoir ce' is incomplete and needs the rest of the clause.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think.

meaning: 'want to know what I...' — start of a question or statement meaning someone wants to know something about the speaker (thoughts, feelings, intentions, actions).
additional_notes: This phrase is the combination of veux savoir (want to know) + ce que je (what I...). It usually appears in questions (Tu veux savoir ce que je...?) or statements (Je veux savoir ce que je peux faire...). Fill in the verb after 'je' to complete the idea (pense, ressens, veux, peux faire, etc.). Use 'tu' or 'je' depending on subject: 'Tu veux savoir ce que je...' = 'Do you want to know what I...?'
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir ce que je pense ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know what I think?

meaning: 'I want to know what you...'
additional_notes: A common phrase starter used to ask about another person's thoughts, knowledge, intentions or meaning. It needs a verb after 'tu' (e.g. penses, sais, veux dire). Grammatically the full phrase is 'Je veux savoir ce que tu ...' (I want to know what you ...). Can be used politely when softened (e.g. «J'aimerais savoir…»).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses de ce film.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think of this movie.

meaning: 'I want to know what you...'.
additional_notes: This phrase begins a polite or neutral request to learn another person's opinion, action, feelings, or intention. In full sentences you normally include a verb after 'vous' (e.g. 'pensez', 'faites', 'voulez dire'). For formal or plural 'you' use 'vous'; for informal singular use 'tu' (je veux savoir ce que tu ...). You can soften it with 'j'aimerais savoir ce que vous...' for a more polite tone.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que vous en pensez.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think about it.

meaning: I want to know where you (...)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a sentence expressing a desire to learn a location or source related to the person addressed. It's followed by a verb (past, present, or future) or an infinitive (e.g., as entendu, habites, prévois de vivre). Use 'Je veux savoir où tu...' to ask about where someone lives, heard something, plans to live, etc. Politer alternatives: 'J'aimerais savoir où tu...' or 'Pourrais-tu me dire où tu...'.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir où tu vas cet été.
native_language_example: I want to know where you are going this summer.

meaning: 'I want to know who you...' or 'I want to know who (did something) to you/for you'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the verb vouloir ('veux' = I want) + savoir (to know) + qui (who) + vous (you). It begins a question/report of wanting to know the identity of a person related to the listener. The rest of the sentence supplies the action: e.g. 'qui vous a dit ça' (who told you that), 'qui vous a envoyé' (who sent you), or 'qui vous êtes' (who you are). Use appropriate past participle agreement and pronoun placement. In spoken French you might also hear 'je veux savoir qui t'a…' (informal singular).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui vous a aidé.
native_language_example: I want to know who helped you.

meaning: 'want to know' followed by a prepositional question (about time, person, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase vouloir savoir + preposition à used when asking for specific information introduced by à (e.g. à quelle heure, à qui, à quel endroit). In English: "I want to know at what time...", "I want to know who..." The full clause often includes a question word (quelle, qui, où) after à. You can replace veux by other forms (je veux, il veut, nous voulons).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir à quel moment tu arrives.
native_language_example: I want to know at what time you arrive.

meaning: 'want to join you' or 'want to get in touch with you' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the informal 1st‑person singular of vouloir + te joindre. 'Joindre' can mean 'to join' (join a group, meet up) or 'to reach/get in touch with' (call or contact someone). With 'te' it addresses 'you' (singular, informal). Context decides whether it's about meeting up (Je veux te joindre au café) or contacting (Je veux te joindre par téléphone).
target_language_example: Je veux te joindre demain pour en parler.
native_language_example: I want to get in touch with you tomorrow to talk about it.

meaning: appears to be an incomplete phrase meaning "(I) want to show you something"
additional_notes: This string is not a correct full French sentence as written. The natural, complete expression is «je veux te montrer quelque chose» (I want to show you something). Sometimes speakers drop words in casual speech or make typos; always include "je" (or another subject) and finish with «quelque chose» for 'something'. Use «tu veux me montrer quelque chose?» for the question 'do you want to show me something?'.
target_language_example: Je veux te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: I want to show you something.

meaning: literally 'want your' — incomplete fragment; not a standalone phrase
additional_notes: This is not a complete or standard French expression by itself. It looks like the verb vouloir in the 1st or 2nd person singular (veux = 'I want' or 'you want' in informal 2nd person) followed by the possessive adjective 'ton' ('your' for a masculine singular noun). You need a noun after 'ton' to make a grammatical phrase (e.g. 'je veux ton stylo' = 'I want your pen'). Without a noun, it will sound unfinished or like a typo. In spoken French, 'tu veux ton...' can start a question or request but must be completed.
target_language_example: Je veux ton livre quand tu auras fini.
native_language_example: I want your book when you are finished.

meaning: 'still want' or 'always want' (depending on context) — present tense of vouloir (to want) with toujours (still/always).
additional_notes: Two-word sequence: veux = 1st/2nd person singular present of vouloir (je veux = I want, tu veux = you want). Toujours usually means 'always' or 'still' — context decides whether it means continual desire ('always want') or continuing to want something ('still want'). Common in sentences like "Tu veux toujours venir ?" (Do you still want to come?) or "Il veut toujours des sucreries" (He always wants sweets). Contraction with pronouns remains normal (e.g., "Je veux toujours" = "I still want" or "I always want").
target_language_example: Tu veux toujours venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you still want to come with us?

meaning: 'want all' or 'want everyone' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence: veux is the 1st/2nd person singular of vouloir (to want). 'tous' can mean 'all' (masculine plural) or 'everyone'. Meaning depends on the noun or pronoun that follows or the context. Remember word order and agreement: 'je veux tous' usually needs an object or clarifier (e.g. 'je veux tous les livres' = I want all the books; 'je veux tous' alone can be used informally to mean 'I want everyone' if referring to people already mentioned). If referring to people directly, 'tous' may be replaced by 'tout le monde' (everyone).
target_language_example: Je veux tous les gâteaux.
native_language_example: I want all the cakes.

meaning: 'want to find' (first or second person singular form with infinitive 'trouver').
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir (to want) in the present tense (je veux = I want, tu veux = you want) with the infinitive trouver (to find). Use with a subject: "Je veux trouver..." (I want to find...) or "Tu veux trouver..." (You want to find...). Common in everyday requests or statements about intentions. To make polite requests, use "je voudrais trouver" or add qualifiers (e.g., "je veux trouver un livre" = I want to find a book).
target_language_example: Je veux trouver un appartement près du travail.
native_language_example: I want to find an apartment near work.

meaning: 'do you want' (informal, singular 'tu' form)
additional_notes: This is the inversion question form used with tu, but written here without the hyphen as requested: veux tu + infinitive/noun to ask someone (you, informal) if they want something or would like to do something. In spoken French, speakers often use 'tu veux' (no inversion) with rising intonation. The hyphenated form 'veux-tu' is standard in formal/written questions; the unhyphenated 'veux tu' may appear in casual writing or when spacing is inconsistent. Use 'veux tu' in polite offers or direct questions; when following inversion rules in standard writing, prefer 'veux-tu'.
target_language_example: Veux tu un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: want to live in (somewhere).
additional_notes: Common construction: subject + veux/veux (conjugated vouloir) + vivre + dans + place (city, country, apartment, neighborhood). Use veux with je (je veux). For other subjects, conjugate vouloir (tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, etc.). Can refer to a desire to live in a physical location or a particular situation/condition when followed by an abstract noun.
target_language_example: Je veux vivre dans une grande ville.
native_language_example: I want to live in a big city.

meaning: 'I want to see your' (informal singular 'your').
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir in the first person singular (je veux) + voir (to see) + the possessive adjective ta (your, feminine singular). Used when the speaker wants to see something belonging to or associated with 'tu' (one person). Ta is used before feminine nouns (maison, maman, mère, patronne, photo). In spoken French the subject pronoun je is often included (Je veux voir ta...) but the phrase shown is the verb phrase part. Polite/formal alternatives: "Je voudrais voir votre..." or "J'aimerais voir votre..."
target_language_example: Je veux voir ta photo.
native_language_example: I want to see your photo.

meaning: 'want your' — 'veux' is the verb 'vouloir' (to want) in the 1st/2nd person singular or formal 2nd person plural form; 'votre' is the formal/plural possessive 'your'.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'veux votre' is not a complete phrase on its own; it would appear inside a sentence like 'Je veux votre aide' (I want your help) or in a question 'Vous voulez votre reçu ?' (Do you want your receipt?). Note: 'veux' (I/you informal want) pairs with 'je' (je veux) or 'tu' (tu veux). For formal/plural 'you' use 'voulez' (vous voulez). When addressing someone formally or multiple people, combine 'vous' + 'voulez' and 'votre' (your). Make sure subject and verb agree: 'Je veux votre...' (I want your...), 'Tu veux ton...' (You informal want your...), 'Vous voulez votre...' (You formal/plural want your...).
target_language_example: Je veux votre avis, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want your opinion, please.

meaning: Incomplete/probably incorrect fragment—intended to mean 'I want to show you something.'
additional_notes: This phrase as written is not grammatically correct in French. The correct full sentence is «Je veux vous montrer quelque chose.» (formal or polite) or «Je veux te montrer quelque chose.» (informal). Alternatives: «Je voudrais vous montrer quelque chose.» is more polite. Use «quelque chose» for 'something.' Ensure subject pronoun (je) and the object word 'chose' are included.
target_language_example: Je veux vous montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: I want to show you something.

meaning: I want to ask you (pose to you).
additional_notes: A common way to say 'I want to ask you' formally/politely in French. 'Vouloir vous poser une question' literally means 'to want to pose/put a question to you.' Use 'vous' for formal or plural 'you'; with friends use 'te' (Je veux te poser une question). Often followed by 'une question', 'des questions', or a qualifier (simple, rapide, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux vous poser une question importante.
native_language_example: I want to ask you an important question.

meaning: Do you really want me to... ? (asks if the speaker should do something)
additional_notes: Used to question whether the other person truly expects or desires the speaker to perform an action. Often expresses surprise, hesitation, disbelief, or reluctance. Followed by an infinitive (faire, partir, répondre, être, venir, etc.). Common in spoken and informal contexts but also neutral.
target_language_example: Tu veux vraiment que je t'aide ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you really want me to help you tonight?

meaning: 'veux' = want (1st/2nd person singular present of vouloir); 'à' is a preposition — together they are not a fixed phrase with a single meaning but occur when vouloir is followed by 'à' in specific, often rare or idiomatic, constructions (e.g., vouloir à quelqu'un = to bear a grudge against someone).
additional_notes: Not a standard inseparable multi-word phrase. Two main uses: 1) vouloir à quelqu'un — idiomatic: to hold something against someone / to bear a grudge (e.g., Il me veut à cause de ça = He holds it against me). 2) vouloir + à + infinitive is generally not used to mean 'want to' (use vouloir + infinitive instead). For learners: expect 'je veux' + infinitive for 'I want to ...' and 'vouloir que + subj.' for 'want that ...'. The form 'veux à' on its own will normally appear only in contexts like 'tu me veux à?' or 'il me veut à'? within the idiom 'vouloir à quelqu'un'.
target_language_example: Tu me veux à cause de ce que j'ai dit ?
native_language_example: Do you hold it against me because of what I said?

meaning: 'want to be sure' or 'want to make sure'.
additional_notes: Polite/direct expression using the verb vouloir (veux = I/you informal) + être certain (to be sure). Use to express a desire for certainty or confirmation. If speaking formally to one person, use "veux-vous être certain" is not correct — use "voulez-vous être certain" for 'do you want to be sure?' For first person: "je veux être certain(e)". Add "que" + clause to specify what you want to be sure of (e.g. "je veux être certain que..." = 'I want to be sure that...').
target_language_example: Je veux être certain que la porte est fermée.
native_language_example: I want to be sure that the door is locked.

meaning: 'want to be the' (first/second/third, best, etc.)
additional_notes: Built from the verb vouloir (to want) + être (to be) + definite article + noun/ordinal. Used to express a desire to occupy a particular role, position, rank, or quality (e.g., le premier, le meilleur, le chat). Change the article/gender as needed: je veux être la (feminine) or je veux être un/une (indefinite). For polite requests or softer wishes, use je voudrais être or j'aimerais être.
target_language_example: Je veux être le professeur de cette classe.
native_language_example: I want to be the teacher of this class.

meaning: 'I want to be a' (feminine singular).
additional_notes: A common phrase for expressing a desire to become or to be something (female speaker or referring to a feminine noun). 'Veux' is the 1st or 2nd person singular of vouloir: Je veux (I want), Tu veux (you want). Use 'un' for masculine nouns (Je veux être un médecin) and 'une' for feminine nouns (Je veux être une médecin is possible but often 'médecin' is masculine in usage; choose the correct noun gender). To form other persons, change the verb (Nous voulons être...).
target_language_example: Je veux être une artiste célèbre.
native_language_example: I want to be a famous artist.

meaning: 'life in' or 'life at' (used to describe someone's life in a particular place or situation)
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own; usually appears as part of larger expressions like "la vie à la campagne" or "sa vie à Paris". The preposition à indicates location or context. In writing, ensure the accent on à is included; without the accent ('a') it would be the verb avoir ('has'). Remember to include the article or possessive (la, sa, ma, etc.) before vie when needed.
target_language_example: Sa vie à Paris est pleine de surprises.
native_language_example: His life in Paris is full of surprises.

meaning: 'life in' (used before a masculine singular place or title introduced by 'au')
additional_notes: Used to talk about life in a country, city, or under/with someone (e.g. a leader). 'Au' is the contraction of 'à le' and appears before masculine nouns: 'au Japon', 'au Caire', 'au Royaume-Uni' (note: Royaume-Uni is masculine), or in set phrases like 'vie au Seigneur' to mean long life to someone. For feminine places use 'en' (vie en France).
target_language_example: La vie au Canada est tranquille.
native_language_example: Life in Canada is peaceful.

meaning: 'to live with' (literally) — used to say someone lives with another person or lives with a situation/condition.
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase vivre avec (infinitive) in a shortened form: vie (noun 'life') + avec is less common alone; more commonly you use vivre avec (je vis avec, elle vit avec) to mean 'to live with' someone or 'to live with' a situation (e.g., a disability, a problem). If you see 'vie avec' it may appear in phrases like 'la vie avec...' meaning 'life with...' (La vie avec un chien = life with a dog). Use vivre (conjugated) for full sentences.
target_language_example: La vie avec trois enfants est très animée.
native_language_example: Life with three children is very busy.

meaning: 'life like' or 'live like' — used to compare or describe the way someone lives (usually appears in larger phrases, e.g. vivre comme...).
additional_notes: On its own 'vie comme' is not a complete phrase in French. 'Vie' is a noun (life) and 'comme' means 'like' or 'as'. More commonly you will see the verb 'vivre' (to live) in expressions such as 'vivre comme...' (to live like...). Use 'vie comme' when talking about 'a life like ...' (une vie comme...) or in constructions describing the type of life: 'une vie comme les autres' (a life like the others).
target_language_example: Elle rêve d'une vie comme celle de sa sœur.
native_language_example: She dreams of a life like her sister's.

meaning: 'life begins' (used to say when real/enjoyable life starts)
additional_notes: Often used in phrases like "La vie commence après..." or "La vie commence à..." to humorously or seriously indicate the moment when life feels meaningful or enjoyable (after coffee, at forty, when paying taxes, etc.). Common in fixed expression structure: La vie commence + (après/à/quand) + phrase.
target_language_example: La vie commence après une bonne nuit de sommeil.
native_language_example: Life begins after a good night's sleep.

meaning: 'life of' (the beginning of a noun phrase like vie d'étudiant, meaning 'student life')
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own — it's the start of a compound noun meaning 'the life of...' followed by a noun that begins with a vowel or mute h (h muet), hence the elision: vie d' + noun. Common uses: vie d'étudiant (student life), vie d'artiste (artist's life), vie d'adulte (adult life). Pay attention to the following noun to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: La vie d'étudiant est souvent pleine de découvertes.
native_language_example: Student life is often full of discoveries.

meaning: 'life in' (used to talk about someone's life or life situation in a place or condition).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of phrases like 'la vie dans la ville' (life in the city) or 'ma vie dans ce pays' (my life in this country). 'Vie' is a noun (life) and 'dans' is a preposition (in/inside). Use with a definite article or possessive: 'la vie dans ce quartier', 'ma vie dans cette maison'.
target_language_example: Sa vie dans le village était tranquille.
native_language_example: His life in the village was peaceful.

meaning: 'life of' (the ...'s life) — part of a phrase meaning the life or everyday life of a person or group
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of constructions like « la vie des enfants » (the life of children) or « la vie des gens » (people's lives). In French, vie (life) is feminine: la vie des + plural noun means 'the life(s) of the ...'. Be careful: you need a noun after des (the plural partitive/possessive), and context determines whether it's 'the life of' or 'the lives of'.
target_language_example: La vie des étudiants est parfois stressante.
native_language_example: Students' lives are sometimes stressful.

meaning: 'life ahead' — used to say someone has their whole life in front of them / lots of time ahead.
additional_notes: Usually appears in phrases like «(toute) la vie devant toi/elle/nous/vous» to comfort or encourage, meaning the person still has plenty of time or opportunities. Common in spoken and written French. Pronouns agree (devant moi/toi/elle/nous/vous).
target_language_example: Tu viens d'avoir ton diplôme — tu as toute la vie devant toi.
native_language_example: You just graduated — you have your whole life ahead of you.

meaning: literally 'life in' — used as the start of phrases describing the way of life, living conditions, or existence in a given context (requires a following noun or adjective).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; 'vie en' appears before a noun or adjective to describe a type or manner of life: e.g. 'vie en ville' (life in the city), 'vie en commun' (living together / communal life), 'vie en couple' (life as a couple). Use it like 'vie en + [noun/adjective]'. The preposition 'en' choice affects meaning (compare 'vie à la campagne' = life in the countryside).
target_language_example: La vie en ville est souvent plus rapide que la vie à la campagne.
native_language_example: Life in the city is often faster than life in the countryside.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely an incorrect fragment meaning 'life is in...' or part of a larger expression (e.g. « la vie est en ... »).
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a common or complete French phrase by itself. You may see it as part of a longer sentence such as « la vie est en marche », « la vie est en train de changer », or poetic uses like « la vie est en mouvement ». For beginners: don't memorize 'vie est en' alone — learn complete expressions (e.g. « la vie est belle » = 'life is beautiful', « la vie est en mouvement » = 'life is in motion').
target_language_example: La vie est en train de changer pour beaucoup de gens.
native_language_example: Life is in the process of changing for many people.

meaning: 'life and' — the phrase 'vie et' is the start of compound expressions meaning 'life and ...' (e.g. vie et mort = life and death).
additional_notes: Not a standalone expression; 'vie et' is typically followed by another noun to form a paired concept (vie et mort, vie et œuvre, vie et temps, etc.). Used in titles, literary contexts, or compound phrases to link 'life' with another idea. Watch word order: 'vie et' is followed by the second noun (often 'mort').
target_language_example: la vie et la mort sont liées
native_language_example: life and death are connected

meaning: 'life here' or 'living here' (refers to life in this place).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining vie (life) and ici (here). Can refer to the general experience, conditions, or day-to-day life in a specific location: e.g. la vie ici est calme — life here is calm. Often used with a verb (être, aimer, trouver) or as part of a longer sentence.
target_language_example: La vie ici est très différente de celle de la ville.
native_language_example: Life here is very different from that in the city.

meaning: 'vie ne' is not a standalone French phrase; likely a mistaken split of words (e.g. from 'ne ... pas' around 'vie' or part of another expression).
additional_notes: There are no common expressions 'vie ne' by itself. In French negation, 'ne' surrounds the verb (e.g. 'ne ... pas'), not the noun 'vie'. Examples you might see where these two words appear near each other: 'La vie ne vaut rien' (life is worth nothing) or 'La vie ne cesse de...' (life never stops ...). If you saw 'vie ne' in text, check surrounding words — it's probably 'vie' (life) and the negation particle 'ne' attached to a verb.
target_language_example: La vie ne tient qu'à un fil.
native_language_example: Life hangs by a thread.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a word order error (possibly intended: « la vie peut... » meaning “life can...” or « vie, peut... » in a larger sentence).
additional_notes: As written, « vie peut » is ungrammatical in French. Beginners may see it if words are accidentally split or punctuation is missing. Common correct patterns: « la vie peut … » (life can …), « il se peut que … » (it may be that …), or verb forms like « peut vivre » (can live). Check surrounding words to determine intended meaning.
target_language_example: La vie peut être belle.
native_language_example: Life can be beautiful.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase by itself; likely part of expressions meaning 'live more' or 'life plus' depending on context
additional_notes: Alone, 'vie plus' is not a common set phrase in French. It could appear as two separate words in sentences such as 'vivre plus' (to live more) if 'vie' is a form of the verb 'vivre' (subjunctive/imperative form would be 'vive', not 'vie'), or as a noun phrase like 'vie plus...' (e.g. 'vie plus riche') where 'plus' modifies 'vie' meaning 'more ... life' or 'plus de vie' (more life). Check surrounding words: the correct constructions are usually 'vivre plus' (to live more), 'plus de vie' (more life), or 'vie + comparative/adjective' (e.g. 'une vie plus riche' = a richer life).
target_language_example: Je veux une vie plus simple.
native_language_example: I want a simpler life.

meaning: private life; privacy.
additional_notes: Refers to a person's personal life, affairs, and right to privacy. Used both as a general right (avoir droit à sa vie privée) and in possessive phrases (ma vie privée). Can be used in formal contexts (e.g. company/privacy policies) and informal (te mêle pas de ma vie privée).
target_language_example: Respecte ma vie privée, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Please respect my private life / my privacy.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment meaning 'life that' or part of a clause (vie + que = 'life that').
additional_notes: This is not a common standalone expression. It looks like the noun vie ('life') followed by the conjunction que ('that' or 'which') and would normally appear as part of a larger sentence (e.g. la vie que tu veux = 'the life that you want'). Do not use 'vie que' by itself; include the rest of the clause. Word order and agreement follow normal French grammar.
target_language_example: La vie que je mène est très calme.
native_language_example: The life that I lead is very calm.

meaning: daily life; everyday life.
additional_notes: Refers to routine, everyday activities and experiences. Used to talk about someone's typical day, habits, work-life balance, or how something affects ordinary life. Can be used in both informal and formal contexts (tu/vous forms in examples).
target_language_example: Parle-moi de ta vie quotidienne au travail.
native_language_example: Tell me about your daily life at work.

meaning: real life; everyday, actual life (as opposed to fiction, imagination, or online life).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what happens in books, films, virtual/online worlds, dreams, or performances with everyday reality. Can refer to someone's real-life situation or the real world in general.
target_language_example: Dans la vie réelle, il faut souvent travailler dur pour réussir.
native_language_example: In real life, you often have to work hard to succeed.

meaning: "life devoted to" or "life spent (doing)" — used in phrases where someone's life is given to or spent on something, or in fixed expressions like wishes (e.g., "Longue vie à...").
additional_notes: Typically appears in contexts such as "passer sa vie à...", "consacrer sa vie à...", "dédier sa vie à..." or in exclamations like "Longue vie à...". After "à" you may find an infinitive (for actions) or a noun/definite phrase (for a person, cause, or thing). The exact phrase "vie à la" occurs when the article "la" precedes a feminine noun or part of a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Il a consacré toute sa vie à la science.
native_language_example: He devoted his whole life to science.

meaning: life in/of (a particular setting) — 'life in the ...' or 'life of the ...'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a way of life tied to a location or condition: e.g. la vie à la campagne (life in the countryside), la vie à la mer (life by the sea). Often followed by a noun with the definite article la. Not a fixed idiom by itself; it combines with a place or state. Can also appear in poetic or contrasting expressions (e.g. la vie à la mort).
target_language_example: La vie à la campagne lui convient parfaitement.
native_language_example: Life in the countryside suits her perfectly.

meaning: life was
additional_notes: A combination of the noun vie (life) + the imperfect of être (was). Literally 'life was'. In context it often appears with a possessive (ma/sa) or subject (la/sa) — e.g. "ma vie était..." = "my life was..." Use to describe past states or situations. Not an idiom; meaning is compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Ma vie était plus simple avant.
native_language_example: My life was simpler before.

meaning: an old/longtime friend of mine (used before a possessive expression).
additional_notes: Used in the construction 'un vieil ami à moi' (or 'une vieille amie à moi') to mean 'an old/longtime friend of mine'. The phrase literally mixes 'vieil ami' (old friend) with 'à moi' (of mine). It's colloquial but common in spoken and written French. You can replace 'à moi' with another possessor (e.g. 'à lui', 'à elle'). Use 'vieil' before masculine nouns starting with a vowel sound (vieil ami) and 'vieux ami' elsewhere (e.g. 'un vieux ami' before consonant).
target_language_example: Elle a rencontré un vieil ami à elle au marché.
native_language_example: She met an old friend of hers at the market.

meaning: 'spinster' or 'unmarried woman (old-fashioned, often pejorative)'
additional_notes: Literally 'old girl'. Used to describe a woman who has never married, usually older — the term is dated and can be derogatory. In modern usage it's often avoided; use célibataire (single) or femme non mariée for neutral terms. Can be used jokingly in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Elle est restée vieille fille toute sa vie.
native_language_example: She remained a spinster her whole life.

meaning: old town; the historic part of a town or city.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the older, often historic district of a city (narrow streets, old buildings). In French, 'vieille' agrees in gender with 'ville' (feminine). Can mean 'an old city' when used without the article (e.g. 'une vieille ville').
target_language_example: Nous avons visité la vieille ville cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We visited the old town this afternoon.

meaning: old-fashioned; from the old school (traditional, conservative).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, idea, style or method that follows older traditions or conservative ways. Can be neutral, affectionate, or mildly critical depending on tone and context. Often used as «être de la vieille école» (to be old-school).
target_language_example: Il est de la vieille école : il préfère les méthodes classiques.
native_language_example: He's old-school: he prefers classical methods.

meaning: will come to
additional_notes: Literal future of venir + à. Often used to indicate someone/something will arrive at a place or reach a point (in time, a decision, or a location). Context determines translation: 'viendra à la fête' = 'will come to the party'; 'cela viendra à un prix' = 'that will come at a cost' or 'will amount to'. If followed by an infinitive (viendra à + infinitive) it can mean 'will end up (doing)'.
target_language_example: Il viendra à la réunion demain.
native_language_example: He will come to the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: 'I just thought' (I have just had the thought).
additional_notes: Formed from venir de + infinitive to express a very recent past action. Here the speaker uses the first-person singular present (je viens de) + penser to say they just thought of something or just realized it. Common in spoken French to report a recent mental action. To be fully grammatical in isolation you'd usually say "je viens de penser"; in conversation the subject pronoun can be dropped in informal speech ("viens de penser" as a note about what you just thought).
target_language_example: Je viens de penser à appeler Marie.
native_language_example: I just thought of calling Marie.

meaning: I come from / I am from (masculine singular) — used to say where you come from or where something originates.
additional_notes:
Second person singular present of venir is 'tu viens'; 'viens du' can appear in commands or statements depending on context. However 'viens du' as written mixes 'viens' (1st/2nd person) with 'du' (of the/from the, masculine). Common uses:
- "Je viens du..." (I come from the...) uses 'viens' with 'je'.
- "Tu viens du..." (You come from the...) uses 'viens' with 'tu'.
'Du' is the contraction of 'de + le' and is used before masculine singular places or things (e.g. 'du Canada', 'du bureau'). For feminine places use 'de la' (or 'de l'' before a vowel), and for plural use 'des'.
target_language_example: Tu viens du Canada ?
native_language_example: Are you from Canada?

meaning: 'come and' — used to link two imperative actions (you come and then ...).
additional_notes: This is the 2nd person singular imperative of venir (viens) followed by 'et' ('and'). It appears in spoken instructions or invitations: 'Viens et vois' (Come and see). Often used to tell someone to do two actions in sequence or to invite them to join and do something. In some cases a comma or a pause is used in speech: 'Viens, et ...'.
target_language_example: Viens et regarde ce que j'ai trouvé.
native_language_example: Come and look at what I found.

meaning: 'are you coming or...?'/ offers a choice using 'come' (colloquial, often incomplete)
additional_notes: A short conversational phrase using the 2nd-person singular imperative of 'venir' (viens) plus 'ou' (or). It often introduces a choice or question like 'viens ou pas?' (are you coming or not?) or 'viens, ou...' trailing off to prompt a decision. It's informal and typically completed by 'pas' or another option.
target_language_example: Tu viens ou tu restes ?
native_language_example: Are you coming or are you staying?

meaning: literally 'come by' or 'come through'; often part of instructions like 'viens par ici' (come this way) or 'viens par la porte' (come in through the door).
additional_notes: Phrase consists of the verb venir (to come) followed by the preposition par. By itself 'viens par' is incomplete and needs a place or route (ici, là, la porte, chez moi, etc.). Used to indicate the route or entry point someone should use. Informal and common in spoken French when giving directions or invitations; the verb form 'viens' is the imperative familiar (tu) form of venir.
target_language_example: Viens par ici, on va entrer par la porte arrière.
native_language_example: Come this way — we'll enter through the back door.

meaning: spoken negative form of venir: "(I/you) don't come" or "(I/you) am/are not coming".
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial contraction of "ne ... pas" around the verb venir. Often used in speech and casual writing; standard form is "ne viens pas" (tu) or "je ne viens pas" (je). Context decides subject: with no subject shown, it can be part of a sentence addressing someone (tu) or reporting about oneself (je) when combined with a subject pronoun. Used for commands (Ne viens pas !) and statements (Je viens pas / Tu ne viens pas ?).
target_language_example: Je viens pas ce soir, désolé.
native_language_example: I'm not coming tonight, sorry.

meaning: 'come (here) more' or part of commands with 'plus' meaning 'no more' / 'closer' / 'earlier' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase appears in two different uses because 'plus' has multiple meanings in commands: 1) 'ne ... plus' = 'no longer / don't (do something) anymore' (negative imperative): e.g. 'Ne viens plus me voir' = 'Don't come see me anymore.' 2) In positive imperatives, 'plus' can mean 'more' or 'closer' or 'earlier' when combined with verbs: 'Viens plus près' = 'Come closer.' or 'Viens plus tôt' = 'Come earlier.' Pay attention to negation: 'Ne viens plus...' = stop doing it; 'Viens plus...' = come more/closer/earlier.
target_language_example: Ne viens plus m'embêter, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don't bother me anymore, please.

meaning: colloquial/familiar way to introduce a reason or explanation (similar to "because" or "since") in spoken French; often used in patterns like "C'est que..." or "Je viens que..." but note: "viens que" by itself is uncommon and may be a mishearing.
additional_notes: The exact phrase "viens que" is not a standard fixed expression in written French. Learners may encounter it in casual speech as part of constructions where the speaker quickly links to an explanation (e.g. "Tu comprends, viens que..."), or it can be a contraction/mishearing of "c'est que" or of verbs like "viens de" (have just) + que. Prefer standard connectors like "parce que", "car", or "puisque" for "because/since". If you hear "viens que", pay attention to context — it often precedes an explanation or is followed by a clause introduced by "que".
target_language_example: Tu sais, viens que je n'avais pas d'argent ce jour-là.
native_language_example: You know, it's because I didn't have any money that day.

meaning: come to (a place or event); an invitation or question asking someone to attend or come over.
additional_notes: Used to invite or ask if someone will attend an event or go to a location. 'Viens' is the informal singular imperative or present tense (tu) of venir. The preposition 'à' + definite article + place/event follows (à la fête, à la réunion, à la cuisine). For formal or plural address use 'venez à la'. Often shortened in speech to 'tu viens à...' meaning 'are you coming to...'.
target_language_example: Tu viens à la fête ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party tonight?

meaning: literal pieces: 'comes to see me from...' — used to say someone comes to visit you and indicates their origin or starting point.
additional_notes: This is a sequence of words rather than a fixed idiom: 'venir me voir' = 'to come see me / to visit me'. Adding 'de' usually introduces where they came from (e.g. 'vient me voir de Paris' = 'comes to see me from Paris') or can be followed by an infinitive/phrase in some contexts, but by itself 'vient me voir de' is incomplete and needs the origin/place/time. Use it when talking about someone traveling to visit you.
target_language_example: Ma sœur vient me voir de Lyon ce week‑end.
native_language_example: My sister is coming to see me from Lyon this weekend.

meaning: '(he/she/it) comes to (see) us' or 'comes to visit us'.
additional_notes: Vient is the 3rd-person singular present of venir (to come). 'Nous' is the object pronoun 'us' and follows the verb in standard word order. Often used with verbs of seeing/visiting (voir, rendre visite) or simply venir + infinitive. Context determines whether it's 'comes to see us', 'comes to visit us', or 'comes by'.
target_language_example: Il vient nous aider ce week-end.
native_language_example: He is coming to help us this weekend.

meaning: old-fashioned; traditional (often with a mildly critical tone)
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, their ideas, or behavior as out of date, conservative, or not modern. Can be mildly teasing or critical depending on tone. Agreement: when describing a feminine plural noun, use form 'vieilles jeux' is incorrect — correct adjective agreement is 'vieux' stays unchanged before masculine plural nouns, but for feminine use 'vieille(s)' (however the fixed expression is most often used with people/ideas as 'vieux jeu' for men or 'vieux jeu' applied generally). Commonly used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ses vêtements sont un peu vieux jeu, mais il s'en fiche.
native_language_example: His clothes are a bit old-fashioned, but he doesn't care.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears as the adjective 'vieux' (old) followed by the verb form 'est' (is).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a set expression. 'Vieux' must agree in gender/number with the noun it modifies (vieux, vieille, vieux, vieilles). 'Est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be) and normally follows a subject (e.g., 'Il est vieux') or is preceded by a noun in a clause (e.g., 'Le vieux est parti'). In isolation 'vieux est' is unlikely; it usually appears inside a complete sentence where word order or agreement may change. For beginners: ensure correct agreement and include the appropriate subject or noun to form a grammatical sentence.
target_language_example: Le vieux est fatigué après la longue marche.
native_language_example: The old man is tired after the long walk.

meaning: city with / city of (used when 'ville' is followed by the preposition 'à' introducing a feature, purpose, location or description).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'ville à' appears as part of longer expressions (e.g. 'ville à taille humaine', 'ville à forte population', 'ville à vocation touristique'). The preposition 'à' links 'ville' to a following noun or phrase. Ensure correct articles/adjectives and agreement in the full expression.
target_language_example: Ville à taille humaine, elle attire de nombreux nouveaux habitants.
native_language_example: A city of human scale, it attracts many new residents.

meaning: city of / town of (used to indicate a city's name or to refer to municipal authority).
additional_notes: Commonly follows the name of a place (e.g., 'la ville de Lyon' = 'the city of Lyon') or precedes a function/department when referring to municipal services (e.g., 'la ville de Paris organise...' or 'les services de la ville'). Used in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: La ville de Nantes organise un festival cet été.
native_language_example: The city of Nantes is organizing a festival this summer.

meaning: 'city of' or 'town of' (the + city/town).
additional_notes: This is the contraction of 'ville de' + definite article 'le' or 'la' when referring to a specific city: 'ville du' = 'ville de le' (used before masculine place names). It appears before a masculine singular noun: e.g. 'la ville du Havre' or in names/phrases like 'les services de la ville du Mans'. For feminine place names you would use 'ville de la' (or 'ville de' if no article).
target_language_example: Les habitants de la ville du Havre se préparent pour le festival.
native_language_example: The residents of the city of Le Havre are preparing for the festival.

meaning: the city / the town (with the definite article placed after the noun); ungrammatical in standard French except in marked contexts such as poetic inversion, dialogue imitation, errors, or regional/nonstandard speech.
additional_notes: Standard French places the definite article before the noun: "la ville" = "the city". "ville la" is not correct in normal prose or everyday speech. It may appear in poetry for stylistic inversion, in colloquial transcriptions imitating speech, in certain regional usages, or as a typographical/transcription error. Do not use "ville la" in standard writing—use "la ville" instead.
target_language_example: Ville la, on ne la reconnaît plus après les rénovations. (poetic/inverted style)
native_language_example: The city, one no longer recognizes it after the renovations.

meaning: ‘the town/city where I...’ — beginning of a relative clause locating where the speaker does something or is from.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it starts a clause that must be finished (e.g. ville où je suis né / ville où je vis). 'Ville' = city/town. 'Où' = where (relative pronoun: place or time). Use it to give the place connected to the subject 'je'. Word order: 'ville où je' + verb or past participle. Common completions: 'je vis' (I live), 'je suis né(e)' (I was born), 'j'ai grandi' (I grew up).
target_language_example: C'est la ville où je suis né.
native_language_example: This is the town where I was born.

meaning: literally 'city for' — not a fixed phrase; appears when 'ville' (city) is followed by a purpose or recipient introduced by 'pour' (for).
additional_notes: This is not an idiomatic multiword expression. You will see 'ville pour' when a noun 'ville' is followed by 'pour' plus an infinitive, noun, or pronoun to indicate purpose, use, destination, or intended recipient (e.g. 'une ville pour touristes', 'la ville pour vivre'). Make sure to read the rest of the sentence to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: C'est une ville pour les étudiants.
native_language_example: It's a city for students.

meaning: literally 'city at' or 'town with' — not a fixed phrase by itself; appears as part of larger expressions (e.g. ville à taille humaine, ville à visiter).
additional_notes: On its own, 'ville à' is incomplete in French and requires more words to form a meaningful expression. It is typically followed by a noun, adjective, infinitive or relative construction to describe a quality, purpose or location (examples: 'ville à taille humaine' = a human-scale town; 'ville à visiter' = a town to visit; 'ville à côté de Lyon' = town next to Lyon). For beginners: don't use 'ville à' by itself — always include the following word(s) that complete the phrase.
target_language_example: C'est une ville à taille humaine, agréable pour se promener.
native_language_example: It's a human-scale town, pleasant to stroll around.

meaning: 'the city was' (simple past/state description).
additional_notes: Combines ville (city/town) with était (imperfect of être = 'was'). Used to describe a past or ongoing state or background condition. In English you'd usually translate as 'the city was...' followed by an adjective or past participle. Étaient would be plural for 'les villes étaient'.
target_language_example: La ville était vivante la nuit.
native_language_example: The city was lively at night.

meaning: white wine.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to wine made from white grapes or light-colored wine. Used in drinking/restaurant contexts (e.g., ordering a glass) and comparing preferences (vin blanc vs. vin rouge = white wine vs. red wine). Pronunciation: 'van blahn'.
target_language_example: Un verre de vin blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A glass of white wine, please.

meaning: 'the wine is' (subject + verb 'être')
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'vin est' where 'vin' (wine) is the subject and 'est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). It appears in sentences that describe how wine is made (e.g., 'Le vin est fabriqué...' — 'The wine is made...'). In natural French you usually include the definite article: 'Le vin est...'.
target_language_example: Le vin est vieilli en fûts de chêne.
native_language_example: The wine is aged in oak barrels.

meaning: red wine.
additional_notes: Common phrase for wine made from red grapes. Used when ordering or talking about wine preferences. Plural form is vins rouges (but often stays as vin rouge when talking in general). Can be preceded by partitive/article (du vin rouge, un verre de vin rouge).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a glass of red wine, please.

meaning: 'wine on' (the combination of the noun vin + the preposition sur: indicates wine located on or spilled onto something)
additional_notes: This is not an idiom—it's simply the noun vin ('wine') followed by the preposition sur ('on', 'onto', 'upon'). Used to say that wine is resting on a surface (e.g. 'une bouteille de vin sur la table') or that wine has been spilled onto something (e.g. 'du vin sur sa chemise'). Word order is noun + sur; articles and determiners (du, une, le) still apply.
target_language_example: Il y a du vin sur la nappe.
native_language_example: There is wine on the tablecloth.

meaning: 'wine for' or 'wine to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used when specifying the purpose, style, or pairing of a wine (e.g., vin à table = wine for the table; vin à cuire = wine for cooking). Often followed by a noun or infinitive. This is a simple prepositional construction: vin (wine) + à (to/for).
target_language_example: Nous avons acheté du vin à cuire pour la sauce.
native_language_example: We bought cooking wine for the sauce.

meaning: twenty-five (25).
additional_notes: A cardinal number. Used for quantities, ages, dates (e.g., le vingt-cinq décembre = December 25th), money, etc. Pronounced [vɛ̃t siŋ]. In dates spoken with day + month, the article le is used: le vingt-cinq décembre. Written with a hyphen.
target_language_example: Il a vingt-cinq ans.
native_language_example: He is twenty-five years old.

meaning: the number twenty-two (22); used for time, age, dates, or counting.
additional_notes: Pronounced [vɛ̃.dø]. Used like the English 'twenty-two' for hours (e.g. vingt-deux heures = 10 p.m.), ages, calendar dates (le vingt-deux janvier = the 22nd of January), and simple counting or lists. In spoken French, numbers are often linked to the context (time, âge, date) so include the unit (heures, ans, janvier) when needed.
target_language_example: La réunion commence à vingt-deux heures.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at ten p.m. (22:00).

meaning: 'twenty-six' (the number 26).
additional_notes: Used as a cardinal number for counting, dates, ages, quantities, etc. In dates you may hear both 'le vingt-six octobre' (the 26th of October) and simply 'le vingt-six' when the month is understood. Hyphenated in modern French spelling: vingt-six.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui nous sommes le vingt-six mars.
native_language_example: Today is the twenty-sixth of March.

meaning: twenty-three (the number 23).
additional_notes: Used as a numeral for age, time (hours), measurement, counting, or standalone answers. In spoken French, hyphenated numbers from 21 to 99 use hyphens (vingt-trois). Pronunciation: [vɛ̃ twa].
target_language_example: Il a vingt-trois ans et habite à Paris.
native_language_example: He is twenty-three years old and lives in Paris.

meaning: the number 'twenty-one'.
additional_notes: Used to say the number 21. Appears in counts, ages, scores, or when calling out a number (e.g., in a game or taking a turn). In compound numbers like 81 it appears as part of 'quatre‑vingt‑un' (literally 'four‑twenty‑one' = 81). Pronunciation and liaison rules can affect sounds in connected speech.
target_language_example: J'ai vingt‑un ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

meaning: 'twenty and' — part of French numbers (used when forming numbers after 20 in some dialects/contexts).
additional_notes: In standard French, numbers 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 are formed with 'vingt-et-un', 'trente et un', etc. 'Vingt et' by itself appears as the beginning of 'vingt et un' (21). In everyday writing you will more often see the full number (vingt et un) or hyphenated (vingt-et-un). 'Vingt et' alone is not used as a standalone phrase meaning something other than the numeric construction.
target_language_example: Il a vingt et un ans.
native_language_example: He is twenty-one years old.

meaning: 'twenty-one' (the number 21).
additional_notes: Used whenever referring to the number 21. In French numbers, 'et' is used between tens and 'un' for 21, 31, 41, 51, and 61 (e.g., vingt et un, trente et un). Pronunciation: the 't' in 'et' is pronounced; the final 't' of 'vingt' is usually silent unless followed by a vowel in liaison.
target_language_example: Il y a vingt et un étudiants dans la classe.
native_language_example: There are twenty-one students in the class.

meaning: 'live your...' (informal imperative telling someone to live their life/experience something)
additional_notes: Short for the imperative tu form of vivre + a possessive: 'vis ta ...' is used in speech to encourage someone to enjoy or fully experience something (e.g. 'Vis ta vie', 'Vis ta vie à fond', 'Vis ta passion'). Often followed by a noun (vie, meilleure vie, passion, vie, vie à fond). Informal, conversational tone. You may also see 'vis ta meilleure vie' or simply 'vis ta vie.'
target_language_example: Vis ta vie et ne t'inquiète pas de ce que pensent les autres.
native_language_example: Live your life and don't worry about what others think.

meaning: 'face of' or 'look of' (used to describe someone's facial expression or appearance related to something).
additional_notes: This is the noun 'visage' (face) followed by the preposition 'de' (of). It appears in phrases like 'le visage de la peur' (the face/appearance of fear) or before a clause to comment on someone's expression: e.g. 'son visage de dégoût' (his/her face showing disgust). Often used in literary or descriptive contexts. For everyday speech, French speakers more commonly use 'le visage' alone, or expressions with 'avoir' (avoir un visage, avoir l'air) to describe looks.
target_language_example: Son visage de surprise disait tout.
native_language_example: His face of surprise said it all.

meaning: 'visit of' or 'visit by' — used to say who is visiting or what kind of visit it is.
additional_notes: Followed by a person (visite de ma tante) or an institution/event (visite de l'inspecteur, visite de chantier). Can also introduce a type of visit (visite médicale, visite guidée). In English you often translate it as 'a visit from' or 'a visit to' depending on word order; check the sentence to see if the person is the visitor or the place visited.
target_language_example: Nous attendons la visite de mes parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: We are expecting a visit from my parents this weekend.

meaning: a (brief) visit for a short time; a visit made from time to time (context-dependent).
additional_notes: This phrase is not very common on its own in French; it likely refers to a short or occasional visit. Depending on context, it could mean a brief visit ('visite de courte durée') or a visit that happens occasionally ('visite de temps en temps'). Native speakers more often say 'une visite de courte durée', 'une visite rapide' or 'une visite de temps en temps'.
target_language_example: Il a fait une visite de temps pour voir la maison avant de signer.
native_language_example: He made a short visit to see the house before signing.

meaning: part of the phrase 'de temps en temps' meaning 'from time to time' or 'occasionally'.
additional_notes: This entry shows the fragment 'visite de temps en' used with verbs like 'rendre visite' (to pay a visit). The full idiom is 'de temps en temps' and is placed after a verb or at the end of a sentence: 'Elle me rend visite de temps en temps.' = 'She visits me occasionally.' Not compositional as a fragment; the complete idiom is fixed.
target_language_example: Ils nous rendent visite de temps en temps.
native_language_example: They visit us from time to time.

meaning: 'visited — and how many times!' (an emphatic reaction expressing surprise or admiration at the number of visits)
additional_notes: Informal, emphatic expression used to respond when told someone has visited a place/person repeatedly. Combines the past participle visité with et combien (literally 'and how many'), functioning like English 'visited — and how!' Tone and context convey the emphasis; not for formal use.
target_language_example: — Il a visité Paris cet été ? — Visité et combien !
native_language_example: — He visited Paris this summer? — Visited — and how!

meaning: 'visited and how long' — used when asking which place someone visited and the duration of their stay.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'visité' (visited) with a question about duration 'combien de (temps)'. Often followed by 'temps' (time) and a subject-verb (e.g., 'es-tu resté(e)?', 'êtes-vous resté(e)(s)?'). Gender and number affect past participle agreement (resté vs restée, restés, restées). Common in informal and formal questions about travel.
target_language_example: Quel pays as-tu visité et combien de temps es-tu restée ?
native_language_example: Which country did you visit and how long did you stay?

meaning: lives on; earns a living from (something).
additional_notes: Formed from vivre de + noun: 'vivre de' means to make a living from or to depend financially on something (e.g. un écrivain qui vit de ses romans = a writer who earns a living from his novels). In spoken/written French the present 3rd-person singular is 'vit de'. Use with a noun or verb in the infinitive (vivre de + nom / vivre de + infinitif).
target_language_example: Elle vit de ses peintures.
native_language_example: She lives on / makes a living from her paintings.

meaning: 'sees the' (he/she/it sees the) — present tense of voir with definite article
additional_notes: Vit is the 3rd-person singular present form of the verb voir (to see). When followed by a definite article (le/la/les), it literally means 'he/she/it sees the ...' or 'you (formal) see the ...' depending on context. Subject (il/elle/on/ça) is often omitted in spoken/written French when context is clear. Use vit la, vit les, etc., for feminine/plural objects. Not informal or slang.
target_language_example: Il vit le chien dans le jardin.
native_language_example: He sees the dog in the garden.
