meaning: colloquial negation of 'vit' (lives) — short for 'ne vit pas' = 'doesn't live' or 'is not alive/doesn't live (somewhere)'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French where the 'ne' is dropped: 'ne ... pas' → '... pas'. Context determines meaning: with a person, it usually means 'doesn't live' (in a place) or 'is dead' (less common/ambiguous); with a thing it can mean 'doesn't last' (rare). Use in casual speech; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Il vit pas ici, il habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: He doesn't live here, he lives in Lyon.

meaning: lives for; is passionate about (someone or something).
additional_notes: From the verb vivre (vit = il/elle/on vit) + pour (for). Used to say someone 'lives for' something — i.e. that it gives their life meaning or they are very devoted to it. Can refer to a person (Il vit pour elle) or an activity/idea (Elle vit pour la musique).
target_language_example: Il vit pour son art.
native_language_example: He lives for his art.

meaning: necessary/essential that (followed by a subjunctive clause).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is crucial; it is always followed by 'que' + subjunctive (e.g., 'Il est vital que tu viennes.'). Common in formal and neutral registers. Similar to 'il est essentiel que'.
target_language_example: Il est vital que vous finissiez le projet à temps.
native_language_example: It is vital that you finish the project on time.

meaning: 'vitamin A' (a fat‑soluble vitamin important for vision, skin and immune system).
additional_notes: Used like in English to talk about the specific vitamin. Often appears with verbs like contenir (contain), être riche en (be rich in), or être toxique (be toxic) at high doses. In French the article and gender: 'la vitamine A' (feminine).
target_language_example: Les carottes sont une bonne source de vitamine A.
native_language_example: Carrots are a good source of vitamin A.

meaning: vitamin C (the nutrient).
additional_notes: Refers to the essential nutrient (ascorbic acid) found in fruits and vegetables and in supplements. Used just like in English: can talk about foods that contain it or taking it for health. In French the measure is feminine: 'la vitamine C' and you can say 'contient de la vitamine C' or 'riche en vitamine C'.
target_language_example: Je prends de la vitamine C quand je sens un rhume arriver.
native_language_example: I take vitamin C when I feel a cold coming on.

meaning: quickly and (used to link actions or qualities, often in spoken or informal French).
additional_notes: Vite means 'quickly' and et means 'and.' Together 'vite et' is simply the adverb plus conjunction and is used when listing or connecting actions or descriptions (e.g., 'vite et bien' = 'quickly and well'). On its own 'vite et' is incomplete and needs a following word or phrase. Common fixed phrase: 'vite et bien' (quickly and well).
target_language_example: Fais-le vite et bien.
native_language_example: Do it quickly and well.

meaning: quickly; in a quick, informal way.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done fast, often informally. Can modify verbs (faire quelque chose vite fait) or be used alone as a short reply meaning "quickly" or "briefly." Tone can be casual; context may imply a quick, possibly rough job rather than thorough.
target_language_example: Je vais préparer le repas vite fait.
native_language_example: I'll prepare the meal quickly.

meaning: as quickly as possible / as soon as possible
additional_notes: Often used after words like 'le' or 'aussi' as in 'le plus vite possible' or 'aussi vite que possible'. On its own 'vite possible' is informal/elliptical; learners will most commonly see the full phrase 'le plus vite possible' meaning 'as fast as possible'.
target_language_example: Fais-le le plus vite possible, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it as quickly as possible, please.

meaning: quickly for / quickly to (used before an infinitive or purpose), though this exact pairing is uncommon in French
additional_notes: Vite means "quickly." 'Pour' means "for" or "to" (introduces purpose or an infinitive). The sequence "vite pour" can appear when describing doing something quickly in order to achieve something (e.g. "Il a agi vite pour protéger..." = "He acted quickly to protect..."). However, native speakers more often place adverbs like vite before the verb ("Il a vite réagi") or use "pour" + infinitive without "vite" adjacent. Pay attention to word order and the verb form that follows.
target_language_example: Il est intervenu vite pour éteindre l'incendie.
native_language_example: He intervened quickly to put out the fire.

meaning: quickly that you / as soon as you (colloquial fragment used in speech)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standard phrase on its own; it's a sequence that can appear in spoken or informal French when someone is urging speed or describing something happening quickly related to 'tu'. Often part of longer sentences, e.g. « Fais vite que tu arrives à l'heure » (colloquial) or « Viens vite que tu voies » (regional/colloquial). In standard French you'd more commonly say « dès que tu » (as soon as you) or use an imperative + infinitive/que clause. Use with caution — it sounds informal and sometimes regional.
target_language_example: Dépêche‑toi, fais vite que tu ne rates pas le train.
native_language_example: Hurry up, be quick so you don't miss the train.

meaning: quickly to / quickly at (followed by an infinitive or noun) — indicates doing something quickly or moving quickly toward something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before an infinitive (e.g. « vite à faire ») or before a noun/place to express speed or urgency. In natural French, speakers more often say « vite, + verb » or « rapidement »; « vite à » can sound a little literary or regional depending on context. Check surrounding words to see whether it's functioning adverbially (modifying a verb) or as a direction (moving quickly toward).
target_language_example: Il s'est mis vite à travailler pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: He quickly got to work to finish the project.

meaning: quickly to the (feminine noun) / quickly at the (feminine place)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence: 'vite' (quickly) + the preposition 'à' + the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g. 'vite à la gare' would mean 'quickly to the station'). It requires a following feminine noun or expression. Word order: adverb 'vite' usually comes before the verb or before 'à + noun' when giving short instructions or comments. Pronunciation note: 'vite à la' is spoken smoothly; the 'e' in 'vite' is often reduced.
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, vite à la gare !
native_language_example: Hurry up, quickly to the station!

meaning: 'live longer' (they live longer)
additional_notes: Literal: 'vivent' = they live (from vivre), 'plus' = more/longer. Used to compare lifespans or duration: 'vivre plus longtemps' is the full phrase. Here 'vivent plus' is followed by 'longtemps' or the comparison context (e.g. 'que les hommes' = than men).
target_language_example: Les femmes vivent plus longtemps que les hommes.
native_language_example: Women live longer than men.

meaning: we live in a (…)
additional_notes: A common phrase used to describe the environment, situation or place where 'we' live. Combine with a noun (monde, pays, quartier, etc.) and often followed by an adjective: "vivons dans un monde/ un pays + adjective." Conjugation note: 'vivons' is the first-person plural (nous) form of 'vivre' (to live). To talk about 'I live in a...', use 'je vis dans un/une'.
target_language_example: Nous vivons dans un monde plein d'espoir.
native_language_example: We live in a world full of hope.

meaning: we live in a (…)
additional_notes: First-person plural present tense of vivre + preposition dans + indefinite article une. Used to say where a group including the speaker lives (a city, house, farm, etc.). Followed by a noun or noun phrase describing the place. Change article/gender/number as needed (ex: nous vivons dans un appartement; nous vivons dans le sud).
target_language_example: Nous vivons dans une petite maison près de la mer.
native_language_example: We live in a small house near the sea.

meaning: to live a (life/experience) — used before a noun like vie (life) or expérience (experience).
additional_notes: Common construction: vivre + une + [noun]. Often followed by vie (une vie) or expérience (une expérience). Means to experience or spend one's life in a certain way (to have/lead a life, or to go through an experience). Use vivre (infinitive) with appropriate subject and tense: Je veux vivre une vie heureuse = I want to live a happy life.
target_language_example: Elle espère vivre une vie pleine de voyages.
native_language_example: She hopes to live a life full of travel.

meaning: to live in the style of / to live like (someone or something)
additional_notes: This phrase is used before a noun (often with an article) to say someone lives in a certain way or adopts a particular lifestyle or cultural style: vivre à la + [noun]. English equivalents: "to live like a [noun]", "to live in the ... way/ style". Context often indicates fashion, tradition, or manner (e.g. vivre à la campagne = to live in the countryside / live country-style). If followed by an adjective or a proper noun, articles and agreements apply: vivre à la française, vivre à la mode, vivre à la John (informal).
target_language_example: Ils ont décidé de vivre à la campagne.
native_language_example: They decided to live in the countryside.

meaning: 'here is/are' used to present something (followed by a demonstrative clause)
additional_notes: voici means "here is/are." When combined with ce + [clause], as in "voici ce que...", it introduces or points to something that will be explained or shown ("here is what..." / "this is what..."). On its own, "voici ce" is incomplete; expect a relative or demonstrative clause after ce (e.g. "voici ce que je veux"). Common alternatives: voilà ce que (slightly more general or used for something further away).
target_language_example: Voici ce que j'ai trouvé pour toi.
native_language_example: Here is what I found for you.

meaning: literally 'here is to' — not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a mistaken or incomplete combination. It does not function as an independent idiom.
additional_notes: voici is used to present or show something ('here is / here are'). À is a preposition ('to', 'at', 'in', etc.). Alone, 'voici à' is not a normal collocation; if you see it, it's usually part of a larger construction (e.g. 'voici à quoi' or a typo). Always check the full sentence. Example constructions that are correct: 'voici à quoi je pense' ('here is what I'm thinking of').
target_language_example: Voici à quoi je pensais hier soir.
native_language_example: Here is what I was thinking about last night.

meaning: literally 'way is' or 'lane is' — not a standalone fixed phrase in French; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'la voie est...' meaning 'the track/lane/route is...').
additional_notes: This pair of words by itself is not an idiom. 'Voie' can mean lane (road), track (rail), way, route, or method. When followed by 'est' it simply begins a statement about the condition or state of that lane/route/way: e.g. 'La voie est libre' (the track is clear) or 'La voie est fermée' (the lane is closed). Watch articles and context: you'll usually see 'la/une/ma voie est...'.
target_language_example: La voie est fermée à cause des travaux.
native_language_example: The lane is closed because of construction.

meaning: railway; railroad track(s).
additional_notes: Refers to the tracks or the railway line used by trains. Can mean the physical tracks (the line you cross) or the railway route (a railway service). Often used with traverser (to cross) or long de (along).
target_language_example: Il traverse la voie ferrée pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: He crosses the railway track to go to work.

meaning: See this / you should see this (informal imperative/suggestion).
additional_notes: From the verb voir (to see) in subjunctive or familiar imperative-like constructions: phrases like «Il faut que tu voies ça» or «Faut que tu voies ça» mean 'you need to see this' or 'you should see this' — used to urge someone to look at or watch something (a photo, video, situation, etc.). In casual speech, subject pronouns and 'il' can be dropped: «Faut que tu voies ça.» Not a literal idiom; it's a direct request/suggestion.
target_language_example: Tu dois venir, faut que tu voies ça.
native_language_example: You have to come, you need to see this.

meaning: this is how / that's how (used to introduce an explanation or the way something is done or seen).
additional_notes: Common phrase to present a method, explanation, or opinion. Often placed at the start of a sentence to summarize or conclude: 'Voilà comment...' + clause. Tone is neutral; can be used in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Voilà comment on a résolu le problème.
native_language_example: That's how we solved the problem.

meaning: 'here is' / 'that's' used before a noun or clause to present or introduce something (often followed by a quantity, reason, or explanation).
additional_notes: Voila (voilà) is a very common French word used to present, point out, or conclude. When followed by de + noun/phrase, it often introduces a cause, a quantity, or an example: e.g. « voilà de bonnes nouvelles » (here are good news) or « Voilà de quoi réfléchir » (that's something to think about). In spoken French, voilà can be used alone as a discourse marker (e.g. 'Voilà.'). Accent on the a (voilà) is standard. Use de after voilà when linking to a noun phrase introduced by de.
target_language_example: Voilà de quoi manger pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Here is enough food for everyone.

meaning: 'here are' or 'there are' (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Voila/voilà is used to present or point out something. When followed by des + plural noun it introduces multiple items (e.g. voilà des livres = here are some/there are some books). In spoken French the accent mark is optional but standard: voilà. Can be used to draw attention or to hand things to someone.
target_language_example: Voilà des oranges pour toi.
native_language_example: Here are some oranges for you.

meaning: that's all; that's it; nothing more to say.
additional_notes: Used to conclude a statement or to downplay/finish an explanation. Can sound dismissive or final. Often follows a clause to indicate there's no deeper reason or nothing else to add (English equivalents: "that's all", "that's it"). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas menti, voilà tout.
native_language_example: I didn't lie, that's all.

meaning: here is a / there is a (introducing or presenting something feminine singular).
additional_notes: Voilà (or voilá) is used to present, show, or indicate something. When followed by a noun, it agrees with the noun's gender/number: voilà une (feminine singular), voilà un (masculine singular), voilà des (plural). Common in spoken and written French to draw attention to an object, person, idea, or example.
target_language_example: Voilà une idée intéressante.
native_language_example: Here's an interesting idea.

meaning: to check with / to look into (with someone or somewhere) — often used to suggest checking availability, asking someone, or verifying something.
additional_notes: Common in expressions like « je vais voir au service » or « vois au magasin » meaning 'I'll check with the department' or 'ask the shop'. It implies contacting or consulting a person/place for information. Often followed by a location, person, or purpose (voir au sujet de... is also possible). More formal than slang.
target_language_example: Je vais voir au bureau et je te tiens au courant.
native_language_example: I'll check with the office and let you know.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to; to discuss/arrange with (depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two senses: 1) Être/avoir quelque chose à voir avec = 'to be related to' or 'to have something to do with' (cause or relation). Example: "rien à voir avec" = 'nothing to do with.' 2) Voir avec quelqu'un = 'check with' or 'arrange with' (ask or coordinate with someone). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Je dois voir avec mon collègue avant de confirmer.
native_language_example: I need to check with my colleague before confirming.

meaning: 'see what I' — start of phrases meaning to look at or check what I (am doing/see/can do/just did).
additional_notes: This is a fragment used to introduce what the speaker is doing, has done, can do, or is seeing. It typically continues with a verb (e.g. vois, fais, peux faire, viens de faire) and is followed by an object or clause. Common uses: inviter someone to look (Viens voir ce que je fais), offer to check (Laisse-moi voir ce que je peux faire), or report perception (Vous devriez voir ce que je vois).
target_language_example: Regarde, viens voir ce que je viens de découvrir.
native_language_example: Look, come see what I just discovered.

meaning: 'to see clearly' — both literally (visually) and figuratively (to understand a situation).
additional_notes: Can be used for physical sight (e.g., after cleaning glasses) or for understanding/confusion resolution (to 'see the truth' or 'get a clear picture'). Common constructions: 'voir clair dans (quelque chose)' = understand something clearly, or 'ne pas voir clair' = not understand / be suspicious. Often followed by a direct object or an explanation clause.
target_language_example: Je commence à voir clair dans cette affaire.
native_language_example: I'm beginning to see clearly in/understand this matter.

meaning: to check on how you are / to see how you are doing
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used when someone wants to find out another person's state, progress, or reaction. Often appears in past or present (je suis venu voir comment tu allais / je viens voir comment tu vas). Can be followed by different verbs (vas, allais, vas te mettre) depending on tense and context. Polite and neutral; not slang. Use with tu for informal singular 'you'. For formal or plural use 'voir comment vous...'.
target_language_example: Je viens voir comment tu vas après ton opération.
native_language_example: I'm coming to see how you're doing after your surgery.

meaning: to see in/into; depending on context, either 'to perceive inside/within' (visual perception) or part of the verb phrase 'voir' plus a prepositional complement indicating location (to visit or meet someone in/at a place).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — compositional: 'voir' (to see/visit) + 'dans' (in/inside/within). Common uses: 1) literal perception with 'dans' indicating environment or medium (voir dans le noir = see in the dark), 2) encountering or visiting someone located in a place (te voir dans cet hôtel = to see you at/in that hotel), 3) appears in larger expressions or quotations (voir dans le monde). Context determines whether it means visual perception or meeting/visiting.
target_language_example: Est‑ce que les chats peuvent vraiment voir dans le noir ?
native_language_example: Can cats really see in the dark?

meaning: to see into my (used when describing checking inside or looking through something belonging to the speaker)
additional_notes: A short fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase; typically followed by a noun (e.g., "voir dans mon sac" = "to look inside my bag"). Used when talking about looking into or checking inside something that belongs to the speaker. For full sentences you need a verb form and object (e.g., "Je veux voir dans mon..." or "Il a regardé dans mon...").
target_language_example: Il a regardé voir dans mon sac pour trouver ses clés.
native_language_example: He looked to see in my bag to find his keys.

meaning: 'to see about' or 'to check/consider doing' (used before an infinitive or noun to indicate looking into or arranging something).
additional_notes: Used in informal and neutral contexts to say you'll check, consider, or arrange something. Often appears as "voir + de + [infinitive]" (e.g. "voir de réserver", "voir de régler") or "voir avec" when specifying a person/party to consult. Can be followed by an expression meaning 'if' (voir si) to mean 'see if'.
target_language_example: Je vais voir de réserver une table pour vendredi.
native_language_example: I'll see about reserving a table for Friday.

meaning: to look into something further; to examine more closely
additional_notes: Used to indicate investigating, checking, or reviewing something in more detail. Often appears in contexts like 'voir de plus près' (to see more closely) or 'voir de plus près ce qui se passe' (to look more closely at what's happening). Alone, 'voir de plus' may feel incomplete without a following phrase (e.g. 'près', 'tard', or an object).
target_language_example: Je vais voir de plus près ce document.
native_language_example: I'll take a closer look at this document.

meaning: Fragment of the expression 'voir de temps en temps' — used to mean 'to see (someone/something) from time to time' or 'occasionally'. On its own it is incomplete and should be completed with 'temps' (→ 'voir de temps en temps').
additional_notes: 'Voir de temps en' is not a complete phrase in French; learners should use 'de temps en temps' for 'from time to time' or the full verb phrase 'voir de temps en temps' to mean 'see occasionally'. The fragment may appear in interrupted speech or as a typo. 'De temps en temps' is neutral and common.
target_language_example: Parfois je peux voir de temps en... (je voulais dire 'voir de temps en temps').
native_language_example: Sometimes I might see (and trail off) — I meant 'see from time to time'.

meaning: to see or regard someone/something as (to consider someone to be)
additional_notes: Used to express how you perceive or judge someone or something; often followed by a noun or role (e.g., « voir quelqu'un en + nom »). Different from plain « voir » (to see/meet). Common synonyms: « considérer comme », « prendre pour ». Can be followed by articles when needed: « le voir en ami » / « la voir en leader ».
target_language_example: Je vois en toi un vrai spécialiste.
native_language_example: I see you as a true specialist.

meaning: literally 'to see and' — a fragment that is normally part of a longer expression; incomplete on its own.
additional_notes: 'Voir et' on its own is not a complete, commonly used phrase in French. It typically appears as the first part of compound expressions (e.g. 'voir et approuver', 'voir et revoir') or in stylistic repetitions. Do not use 'voir et' alone unless intentionally quoting or fragmenting a longer expression; instead use the full expression that conveys your meaning.
target_language_example: Nous devons voir et discuter ce point demain.
native_language_example: We need to see and discuss this point tomorrow.

meaning: to see/notice (there); to consider in that context
additional_notes: This short phrase combines voir (to see) with là (there/that). Depending on context it can mean literally 'see there' (drawing attention to something) or be part of a larger expression meaning 'to see it that way' or 'to consider that'. Without context, it's versatile and often appears in spoken French: e.g. « Regarde, tu peux voir là » (look, you can see it there) or « Si tu vois ça là, ... » (if you see it that way/there...).
target_language_example: Regarde par la fenêtre, tu peux voir là le jardin.
native_language_example: Look out the window, you can see the garden there.

meaning: to see where / to find out where (something is or how far something goes)
additional_notes: Commonly used in contexts like checking location, assessing progress, or figuring out next steps. Often appears in sentences such as «Je vais voir où c'en est» (I'll see how far it's come) or «Je vais voir où il habite» (I'll see/find out where he lives). Can be followed by a clause introduced by 'ça', 'il', 'c'en', or a question word (où + clause).
target_language_example: Je vais voir où se trouve la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: I'll see where the library is.

meaning: to check by / to see by (a means); to judge by
additional_notes: Used to indicate determining something using a particular method, evidence, or perspective: 'voir par + (quelque chose)' = to look at/assess something through that lens or means. Less common than alternatives like 'voir' alone or 'juger par'. Often appears in formal or written contexts (e.g. voir par le témoignage, voir par les faits).
target_language_example: On peut voir par ses actions qu'il est sérieux.
native_language_example: You can tell by his actions that he is serious.

meaning: to check/see about something; to look into (doing) something.
additional_notes: Used to say you will check, arrange, or consider something. Often followed by an infinitive or a noun: e.g. "Je vais voir pour ça" (I'll look into that) or "Je vais voir pour réserver" (I'll see about booking). Common in spoken and informal registers but acceptable in polite speech. Context decides exact translation: 'see about', 'check', 'look into', or 'try to arrange'.
target_language_example: Je vais voir pour trouver une solution.
native_language_example: I'll look into finding a solution.

meaning: to check/arrange something for someone; to take care of it (informal, often followed by the thing or person concerned).
additional_notes: A colloquial expression used when agreeing to handle or look into something on someone else's behalf. Often appears in contexts like 'Je vais voir pour le dossier' (I'll check on the file) or 'Je vois pour toi' (I'll take care of it for you). The phrase requires context to complete meaning (what you'll 'voir' and for whom).
target_language_example: Je vais voir pour le rendez-vous et je te tiens au courant.
native_language_example: I'll take care of the appointment and let you know.

meaning: 'see (me/it) when you...' — used to invite someone to visit or check something at a time that suits them
additional_notes: Common in informal and neutral contexts. Usually followed by a verb like veux, peux, voudras, souhaites, auras du temps. Can mean 'come see me when you want' or 'look/check it when you have time.' Tone depends on the verb used: veux/woudras = more casual offer; auras du temps = when you have time. The phrase is compositional (literal meaning clear) and not a false cognate.
target_language_example: Passe me voir quand tu veux.
native_language_example: Drop by to see me whenever you want.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; literally 'to see some/any' but incomplete—likely an incorrect or truncated expression.
additional_notes: This combination is not a typical multiword expression. In French, 'voir' (to see) is usually followed by a direct object (e.g. 'voir quelque chose' = 'to see something') or by a person/thing ('voir Marie', 'voir le film'). 'Quelque' by itself is an adjective meaning 'some' and must be followed by a noun (quelque chose, quelques-uns, etc.). If you encounter 'voir quelque' it is probably a mistake or part of a longer phrase that was cut off.
target_language_example: Je voudrais voir quelque chose d'intéressant.
native_language_example: I would like to see something interesting.

meaning: to see who / to check who (is/does something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when you want to find out the identity of a person or who is responsible for something. Can be literal (see who is there) or more abstract (find out who can help). Often appears in contexts like «je vais voir qui est à la porte» or «je vais voir qui peut m'aider».
target_language_example: Je vais voir qui frappe à la porte.
native_language_example: I'll see who is knocking at the door.

meaning: 'to see one's' (followed by a noun) — used when talking about someone seeing or experiencing something belonging to or affecting them
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common verbal sequence: voir (to see/experience) + son/sa/ses (possessive). The meaning depends on the noun that follows: e.g. voir son ami (to see his/her friend), voir son erreur (to realize/see one's mistake), voir son projet aboutir (to see one's project succeed). Pronoun agrees in gender/number with the possessed noun (son/sa/ses).
target_language_example: Elle va voir son frère ce soir.
native_language_example: She is going to see her brother tonight.

meaning: to check/look (something) up on; to see on (a website, map, schedule, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used when referring to finding information 'on' a source (e.g., on a website, on a map, on a schedule). Depending on context, it can mean 'to look at' or 'to check on' something. Often followed by the source introduced with 'sur' (sur le site, sur la carte, sur l'horaire) or by the thing being checked.
target_language_example: Je vais voir sur le site pour les horaires.
native_language_example: I'll check the website for the schedules.

meaning: 'to see your' (verb + possessive: voir + tes)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: voir (to see) followed by tes (your, plural or informal singular). You'll see it in sentences like "Je veux voir tes photos" (I want to see your photos) or "Tu peux voir tes messages ici" (You can see your messages here). The verb may need to be conjugated (e.g., je vois, tu vois, il/elle voit) depending on the subject. Tes is used before plural nouns (tes amis, tes livres) and is informal or neutral when addressing one person familiar; use vos for formal/plural.
target_language_example: Je veux voir tes photos de vacances.
native_language_example: I want to see your vacation photos.

meaning: to see them all / to see everything (masculine plural).
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb voir (to see) and the pronoun/adjective tous (all). Usage depends on context and grammar: 'voir tous' can appear before a noun ('voir tous les films' = to see all the films) or with a direct object pronoun implied/explicit ('je veux tous les voir' or more formally 'les voir tous'). Word order in French often places object pronouns before the verb (e.g. 'je les vois tous'). Here 'tous' agrees in gender/number with what it refers to (tous = masculine plural, toutes = feminine plural).
target_language_example: Je veux voir tous les tableaux du musée.
native_language_example: I want to see all the paintings in the museum.

meaning: to anticipate or foresee; (informal) to have enough resources/room to cope with the future
additional_notes: Primary sense: 'voir venir' means to see something coming / anticipate an event (J'aurais dû le voir venir = I should have seen it coming). Informal uses: can mean 'to leave margin/cover for the future' or 'to wait and see' depending on context (Je te passe quelques dollars, pour voir venir = I'll give you some dollars to tide you over / to have some buffer). Also appears in expressions like 'avoir de quoi voir venir' meaning 'to have enough to get by/plan ahead.'
target_language_example: Garde un peu d'argent de côté pour voir venir.
native_language_example: Keep some money aside to be prepared for what's coming.

meaning: 'to see your' (followed by a noun: e.g. see your shoes, papers, etc.)
additional_notes: Common construction using the verb voir + possessive adjective vos (plural or formal 'your'). Used when asking or stating that someone wants to look at something belonging to the other person(s). In polite requests, être + pouvoir or pourrions/ pourrions-je is often added: "Puis-je voir vos papiers ?" Vos is the formal or plural 'your'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me laisser voir vos documents, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you let me see your documents, please?

meaning: to see to; to take care of (make sure something is done).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone will handle or ensure a task. Often followed by an infinitive: voir à + infinitive (e.g., voir à réparer = make sure to repair). More formal than "s'occuper de" in some contexts. Can also be used alone: "Je vais voir à ça" = "I'll take care of that / I'll look into that."
target_language_example: Je vais voir à régler ce problème demain.
native_language_example: I'll make sure to resolve this problem tomorrow.

meaning: 'do you see' (informal/neutral question form with inversion)
additional_notes: Second-person singular of voir (to see) used in inversion questions. Common in spoken and written French to ask if someone perceives, understands, or meets someone/something. Can be literal (visually seeing) or figurative (seeing/understanding). Often appears with negatives (ne ... pas) or question words (que).
target_language_example: Vois-tu ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you see/understand what I mean?

meaning: 'see no' or 'don't see any' (negative phrase used with 'je/tu/il/elle/on' forms of voir plus 'aucune' to mean not seeing any)
additional_notes: 'Vois aucune' appears as part of a negative construction: subject + vois + aucune + noun (often spoken as 'je ne vois aucune...'). In everyday French the full negative often includes 'ne' (je ne vois aucune raison), but in informal speech the 'ne' is frequently dropped (je vois aucune raison). 'Aucune' agrees in gender with the noun it modifies (aucun for masculine). Use to mean 'not any' or 'no ... at all.'
target_language_example: Je ne vois aucune solution au problème.
native_language_example: I don't see any solution to the problem.

meaning: 'see what I mean' (used to check if someone understands your point).
additional_notes: Informal everyday phrase used after explaining something to ask if the listener understands or agrees. Often appears as 'tu vois ce que je veux dire?' or shortened to 'vois ce que je veux' in casual speech; context may drop 'tu' and 'dire'. Can be used alone or at the end of a sentence.
target_language_example: J'ai expliqué le problème deux fois, vois ce que je veux ?
native_language_example: I explained the problem twice, see what I mean?

meaning: 'see what' or 'look and find out what'
additional_notes: Informal instruction or suggestion using the verb voir (to see). Often part of a larger sentence: e.g. «Vois ce qui se passe» (see what's happening) or «Vois ce qui est dans le sac» (see what's in the bag). Can be used to tell someone to check, find out, or observe something. Depending on context, tone can be neutral (ask someone to check) or somewhat commanding.
target_language_example: Vois ce qui se passe dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: See what's happening in the kitchen.

meaning: 'do you see this' or 'do you see that' (informal spoken phrase used to draw attention to something nearby).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb 'voir' (to see) in the 2nd-person singular imperative/question form 'tu vois' plus the demonstrative 'cette' (this/that). Common in spoken French to point out or ask if someone notices a person or object. Can also be used with 'tu vois ce' (masculine singular) or 'tu vois ces' (plural). Tone and context tell whether it's a question or a prompt (e.g. 'Do you see that?').
target_language_example: Tu vois cette maison au bout de la rue ?
native_language_example: Do you see that house at the end of the street?

meaning: ‘see (someone/something) as’ — to perceive or consider someone/something in a certain way.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (me, le, la, etc.) + comme + description (un étranger, comme ça, dans la réalité). Common for expressing someone’s perception or self-image: Je le vois comme un ami / Je me vois comme ça. Often appears in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je te vois comme une personne honnête.
native_language_example: I see you as an honest person.

meaning: see (something) in (someone/something) — notice a quality, sign, or presence inside or through someone/something; or 'see you in' when arranging time/place.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb voir + preposition dans. Common uses: 1) to say you perceive or recognize a trait, emotion, or sign in someone's eyes, face, behavior, etc. (Je le vois dans ses yeux = I can see it in his eyes). 2) to indicate seeing someone in a film or medium (Tu la vois dans le film = You see her in the movie). 3) to indicate time for a meeting or appointment (Je te vois dans une heure = I'll see you in an hour). Context (pronouns, nouns following dans) determines whether 'dans' expresses location, medium, or time.
target_language_example: Je le vois dans ses yeux.
native_language_example: I can see it in his eyes.

meaning: 'see' or 'meet' (second-person singular of voir + partitive/plural article), e.g. 'you see/meet some' or 'you notice...'
additional_notes: Vois is the tu form of voir (to see). When followed by des it introduces a plural direct object (unspecified quantity): 'tu vois des...' = 'you see some...'. It can mean physically seeing, noticing, or meeting people/things depending on context. In spoken French the subject tu is often omitted in short expressions (e.g. 'Vois des gens' is unusual alone; more natural: 'Tu vois des gens' or 'Je vois des amis').
target_language_example: Tu vois des oiseaux dans le jardin ?
native_language_example: Do you see any birds in the garden?

meaning: 'don't you see (that)...' — used to ask if someone understands or notices something
additional_notes: This is a colloquial/conversational fragment from the question 'Tu ne vois pas ce qui... ?' or 'Tu vois pas ce qui... ?' It literally uses 'voir' (to see) but means 'to notice/understand' in context. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'qui' (what/that) describing the situation. In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped: 'Tu vois pas... ?'.
target_language_example: Tu ne vois pas ce qui se passe dehors ?
native_language_example: Don't you see what's happening outside?

meaning: 'don't see' or 'don't understand (what/who)' in negative expressions like "je ne vois pas de..."
additional_notes: Used in negative sentences to indicate you don't understand or can't identify the person/thing being referred to. Often appears as part of "je ne vois pas de qui/quoi..." meaning "I don't see/know who/what (you are talking about)". In everyday speech the spoken form may drop the 'ne' (Je vois pas de...).
target_language_example: Je ne vois pas de quoi tu parles.
native_language_example: I don't see/understand what you're talking about.

meaning: 'see' or 'notice' that / 'only see' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) As part of 'je vois que...' it means 'I see that...' or 'I notice that...'. 2) In negative constructions like 'je ne vois que...' it can mean 'I only see...' (limited to). Be careful: informal/colloquial uses include 'je vois que dalle' meaning 'I don't see anything' (dalle = slang for 'nothing'). Context (negation, emphasis, or exclamation) determines the sense.
target_language_example: Je vois que tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: I see that you're tired.

meaning: 'I see that you...' / 'I notice that you...'.
additional_notes: A phrase used by the speaker to comment on or point out something they observe about the listener(s). It often begins a sentence: 'Je vois que vous…' followed by a clause (verb or adjective). Can be used politely or neutrally to state an observation. Conjugation depends on subject (here 'je vois' = I see).
target_language_example: Je vois que vous avez fini le travail.
native_language_example: I see that you have finished the work.

meaning: 'see very' (literal combination), not a fixed phrase in French
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed expression in French. It looks like the verb voir (to see) followed by the adverb très (very). You might encounter it inside a sentence where the subject and object are present, e.g. "Je te vois très clairement" (I see you very clearly) or "Je vois très bien" (I see very well). Alone, "vois très" is incomplete — you usually need a subject (je/tu/il...) or an adverbial/compliment after it. Use correct word order: subject + vois + (complement) + très or subject + vois + très + (adverb/adjective) depending on sentence.
target_language_example: Je te vois très clairement.
native_language_example: I see you very clearly.

meaning: see a
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression; it is a combination of vois (from voir, "to see") and un ("a/an" or "one" in masculine form). It usually appears as part of a longer sentence, such as je vois un chat = "I see a cat." Without more context, vois can also mean "I see," "you see," or a command like "look."
target_language_example: Je vois un chat dans la rue.
native_language_example: I see a cat in the street.

meaning: 'the neighbor is' (voisin = neighbor, est = is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword phrase — it's just the noun 'voisin' (neighbor) followed by the verb 'est' (is). You will usually see 'le voisin est...' or 'ma voisine est...' with an article or possessive. Gender and number change: voisin (m.), voisine (f.), voisins (pl.). Use 'est' for il/elle/on (he/she/one is).
target_language_example: Le voisin est sympathique.
native_language_example: The neighbor is friendly.

meaning: 'sees tomorrow' (literally) — normally part of a verb phrase meaning 'will see tomorrow' or 'meets tomorrow' depending on context
additional_notes: This is the third-person singular present form of voir (voit) followed by the adverb demain. Alone it reads 'he/she/it sees tomorrow' or can mean 'will see tomorrow' in informal speech when talking about meeting someone or checking something the next day. More commonly French uses future tense (verra demain) or a construction like 'on se voit demain' (we'll see each other tomorrow). Pay attention to subject and context to understand whether it means 'see' (perceive), 'meet', or implies future action.
target_language_example: On se voit demain au café ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other tomorrow at the café?

meaning: sees later / will see (someone) later
additional_notes: Literally "sees later." Can be used to say someone will see someone/something later (e.g., Il voit plus tard = He'll see (it/him/her) later). However, without context the phrase is incomplete — often appears in sentences like «On se voit plus tard» (We’ll see each other later) or «Il verra ça plus tard» (He will see that later). Note: conjugation and subject must match (voir → voit for il/elle/on).
target_language_example: On se voit plus tard au café.
native_language_example: We'll see each other later at the café.

meaning: 'takes care of' or 'sees to (the)' (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: This is a form of the verb voir used in a construction meaning someone handles, attends to, or makes sure of something: voit à + le/la/les becomes voit à l' before a vowel. Often used like «Il voit à l'organisation» = He sees to the organization/handles the organization. More common verbs for 'take care of' include s'occuper de and s'assurer de; voit à l' is slightly formal and less frequent in spoken French.
target_language_example: Elle voit à l'installation du matériel.
native_language_example: She takes care of the installation of the equipment.

meaning: Phrase showing the noun 'voiture' (car) followed by the verb 'avoir' (to have) or 'a' as third-person singular of 'avoir' or part of other constructions (e.g. 'a l’air').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the word 'voiture' (feminine noun meaning 'car') followed by the verb form 'a' (il/elle a = he/she/it has) or part of expressions like 'a l’air' (seems). Useful patterns: 'La voiture a...' (The car has...), 'Sa voiture a deux ans' (His/her car is two years old), 'Cette voiture a l’air...' (This car seems...). Remember agreement: 'voiture' is singular, so use 'a'.
target_language_example: La voiture a un pneu crevé.
native_language_example: The car has a flat tire.

meaning: 'car with' or 'car at/on' as the beginning of a longer phrase (not a complete expression by itself).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase in French; it's the noun voiture ('car') followed by the preposition au (contraction of à + le). It usually appears as the start of a longer phrase such as 'voiture au garage' (car in the garage) or 'voiture au feu' (car at the traffic light) — though native phrasing more commonly uses 'dans la voiture', 'à la voiture' or other constructions depending on context. Beginners should treat 'voiture' (feminine noun) and remember au is used before masculine singular nouns (à + le). For a feminine noun you'd use à la (e.g. 'à la voiture' is uncommon; more natural: 'dans la voiture').
target_language_example: La voiture au garage est réparée.
native_language_example: The car at the garage is repaired.

meaning: Not a valid or grammatical French phrase; likely a mistake or word order error.
additional_notes: This combination ('voiture' + 'ce') does not occur in standard French. 'Voiture' is feminine, so demonstratives and determiners must agree: use 'cette voiture' (this car), 'la voiture' (the car), or 'une voiture' (a car). The sequence 'voiture ce' might appear in incorrect speech or as a typo. If you see 'ce' referring to a clause, the correct order would be different (e.g. 'La voiture, ce n'est pas...' or 'La voiture, ce sont...').
target_language_example: La voiture ce n'est pas en panne.
native_language_example: The car, it's not broken down.

meaning: 'car in' (literal combination); not a fixed phrase — typically appears as part of a larger expression to indicate a car is inside or within something (e.g. 'une voiture dans la rue' or 'la clé dans la voiture').
additional_notes: Not an established idiom on its own. 'Voiture' = car; 'dans' = in/inside/within. Use 'dans' to indicate being inside or within boundaries. For other spatial relations use prepositions like 'sur' (on), 'devant' (in front of), 'derrière' (behind). The exact phrase 'voiture dans' will normally be followed by a noun or clause specifying the container or location.
target_language_example: Il y a une voiture dans le garage — regarde la voiture dans l'ombre.
native_language_example: There is a car in the garage — look at the car in the shadow.

meaning: a car/belonging to — used to describe the type or owner of a car (e.g., police car, someone's car).
additional_notes: Voiture = car. 'Voiture de' is followed by a noun that specifies either the owner (voiture de Marie = Marie's car) or the type/purpose (voiture de police = police car). When indicating possession with a person, French usually uses 'la voiture de [nom]' (note the article). Word order differs from English (owner/role follows 'voiture de').
target_language_example: La voiture de mon frère est rouge.
native_language_example: My brother's car is red.

meaning: rental car; a car rented for temporary use.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a car borrowed from a rental company. Common in travel contexts (airport, agency). Can appear with determiners: une voiture de location (a rental car), la voiture de location (the rental car). In signs or documents you may see shortened forms like "voiture de location exclue" (rental car excluded).
target_language_example: Nous avons pris une voiture de location pour visiter la région.
native_language_example: We rented a car to visit the area.

meaning: literally 'car of my' — not a complete or standard phrase in French; appears to be a fragment meaning 'my car' when completed as 'la voiture de mon ...' or more simply 'ma voiture'.
additional_notes: This string is incomplete. In French you usually say 'ma voiture' (my car) to mean a car that belongs to you. You might see 'la voiture de mon père / amie / frère' to mean 'my father's / my friend's / my brother's car' — that construction needs a noun after 'mon' (e.g. 'père'). Use 'mon' before masculine singular nouns (mon père), and 'ma' before feminine nouns (ma voiture).
target_language_example: La voiture de mon frère est rouge.
native_language_example: My brother's car is red.

meaning: sports car
additional_notes: Refers to a car designed for performance, speed, and handling. Used like any noun phrase; plural is voitures de sport. Common in everyday speech and formal contexts. You can use adjectives normally: une petite voiture de sport, une nouvelle voiture de sport.
target_language_example: Il a acheté une voiture de sport rouge.
native_language_example: He bought a red sports car.

meaning: 'voiture' = car; 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in' or used to indicate material/means—together 'voiture en' is not a fixed phrase by itself.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. In French, 'voiture' means 'car' and is usually followed by a preposition to complete the idea: e.g. 'voiture en panne' (car that has broken down), 'voiture en bois' (car made of wood), 'voiture en ville' (car in town) or 'en voiture !' (informal, equivalent to 'let's go/into the car!'). You will normally see 'voiture' with adjectives or prepositional phrases; 'en' will change meaning depending on context (material, location, state, or part of idiomatic expressions).
target_language_example: La voiture en panne bloque la route.
native_language_example: The car that has broken down is blocking the road.

meaning: the car is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: voiture (car) + est (is). Used to state something about a car (condition, location, readiness, etc.). In natural French you would often include a possessive before voiture (ma/ta/sa/notre/votre) or an adjective/complement after est. Word order: [possessive] voiture est + complement. Can be used in questions with Est-ce que or inversion: Est-ce que ta voiture est neuve ?
target_language_example: Ma voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: My car is broken down.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a typo or fragment meaning 'car and...'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete or common expression in French. 'Voiture' means 'car' and 'et' means 'and'. Together they form the beginning of a compound phrase or coordination (e.g., 'voiture et moto' = 'car and motorcycle'), but 'voiture et' by itself is unfinished. If you see it in text, check for missing words after 'et' or consider that it may be a typing error. For 'the car and ...' you would continue after 'et' with another noun or clause.
target_language_example: La voiture et la moto sont garées devant la maison.
native_language_example: The car and the motorcycle are parked in front of the house.

meaning: literally 'car here' — used to refer to a car and its location (e.g., asking to stop or park the car here).
additional_notes: Common in imperatives and questions about stopping or parking: 'Arrête la voiture ici' (Stop the car here) or 'Je peux garer ma voiture ici ?' (Can I park my car here?). Use with verbs like arrêter (stop) or garer (park). Word order is normal: determiner + voiture + adverb/place (ici).
target_language_example: Arrête la voiture ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop the car here, please.

meaning: 'car' + time/condition word 'when' — not a fixed phrase; shows examples where voiture (car) appears with quand (when).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom: it's the noun voiture (car) used in sentences that also include quand (when). Useful patterns shown: 1) quand introduces a clause of time or condition (Quand il passe la prendre = when he comes to pick her up). 2) Quand can mean 'when' or 'if' in conditional sense (Pourquoi acheter... quand la vieille fonctionne = Why buy... when/if the old one still works). 3) Quand bon te semble / quand tu veux / quand vous voulez = 'whenever you like' / 'whenever you want' — polite offers. Word order: voiture stays as a noun; quand starts the temporal/conditional phrase.
target_language_example: Tu peux emprunter ma voiture quand tu veux.
native_language_example: You can borrow my car whenever you want.

meaning: literally 'car on' — not a fixed phrase; 'voiture' = car and 'sur' = on/about (preposition).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. It looks like two words that would appear together when describing position (e.g., 'la voiture sur la route' = 'the car on the road') or when beginning a phrase about a car concerning something ('une voiture sur laquelle...'). You will usually need more words after 'sur' (a noun, pronoun, or relative clause). 'Voiture' is a common noun; 'sur' is a preposition.
target_language_example: Il y a une voiture sur la route.
native_language_example: There is a car on the road.

meaning: literally 'car with' — used as part of a noun phrase to describe a car that has or is equipped with something (e.g., voiture à essence = car with gasoline/ petrol-powered car).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of constructions that specify a characteristic, purpose or fuel/type of a car. Common completions: 'voiture à essence' (petrol/gasoline car), 'voiture électrique' (electric car — note the adjective form), 'voiture à hydrogène' (hydrogen-powered car), 'voiture à quatre portes' (four-door car). Word order and agreement depend on the words that follow. Often in French the particle 'à' plus a noun describes what the car uses or is equipped with.
target_language_example: C'est une voiture à essence.
native_language_example: It's a petrol (gasoline) car.

meaning: electric car; a car powered by electricity rather than gasoline.
additional_notes: Common everyday term. 'Voiture' = car, 'électrique' = electric — so the phrase is compositional and can be translated literally. Used like any noun phrase: une voiture électrique, la voiture électrique, acheter une voiture électrique. Pronunciation tip: électrique (é-lec-trique).
target_language_example: Ils vendent une voiture électrique dans ce magasin.
native_language_example: They sell an electric car in that store.

meaning: in a low voice; quietly (speaking softly).
additional_notes: Used to describe speaking quietly or whispering so others don't hear. Often follows verbs like parler, dire, chuchoter (e.g. parler à voix basse). Common in instructions or descriptions (Il a parlé à voix basse).
target_language_example: Parle à voix basse, le bébé dort.
native_language_example: Speak in a low voice, the baby is sleeping.

meaning: 'voice of' (the voice belonging to or representing someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something expresses opinions, authority or representation for a person, group, institution or abstract idea. Often followed by a noun (le peuple, le gouvernement, le Seigneur). Common in proverbs and formal statements (e.g. "La voix du peuple..."). Not idiomatic — literal possession.
target_language_example: La voix du professeur compte dans la décision.
native_language_example: The voice of the teacher matters in the decision.

meaning: aloud; in a loud voice (spoken audibly).
additional_notes: Used to indicate speaking so others can hear — often paired with verbs like 'lire' (lire à voix haute), 'dire' (dire à voix haute) or 'parler' (parler à voix haute). Not an idiom; it's literal. In French the more common fixed form is 'à voix haute' or simply 'à haute voix' (both mean 'aloud'). 'voix haute' by itself may appear in some phrases but usually appears with 'à' or as part of a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Elle lit le texte à voix haute pour la classe.
native_language_example: She reads the text aloud for the class.

meaning: 'vol à' (with accent) — can mean 'flight to' when indicating destination, or form part of theft expressions ('theft of/at') depending on context. The unaccented 'a' is incorrect in French; correct form is 'vol à'.
additional_notes: Write 'vol à' with the accent on à. In air travel contexts use 'vol à destination de', 'vol pour', or 'vol à' + place to indicate destination. In crime/legal contexts 'vol à' followed by a noun or phrase names a type of theft (e.g., 'vol à l'étalage', 'vol à la tire'). The unaccented 'vol a' is a common typing mistake and not standard French.
target_language_example: Le panneau indique le numéro du vol a — vérifiez l'heure de départ.
native_language_example: The board shows the number of flight a — check the departure time.

meaning: 'flight to' or 'flight toward' (used before a destination) or 'flight for' in some contexts (e.g., vol à destination de).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'vol à Paris' or more properly 'vol à destination de Paris' to indicate where a plane is going. In everyday usage, French more often uses 'vol pour', 'vol à destination de' or 'vol direct' depending on nuance. 'Vol à' by itself is incomplete and usually needs a destination or phrase after it. Also note 'vol' alone can mean 'theft' — context (flight vs. theft) matters.
target_language_example: J'ai un vol à destination de Madrid demain.
native_language_example: I have a flight to Madrid tomorrow.

meaning: 'are flying in' or 'fly in' (they fly in/are flying in a place).
additional_notes: Third-person plural of the verb 'voler' (ils/elles volent) followed by the preposition 'dans' meaning 'in' or 'inside'. Commonly used to say that birds or objects are flying in/through a space (e.g. 'volent dans le ciel' = 'are flying in the sky'). Use a different preposition for other nuances (e.g. 'volent au-dessus de' = fly above).
target_language_example: Les papillons volent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The butterflies are flying in the garden.

meaning: 'are flying to' or 'fly toward' (third-person plural of voler + vers).
additional_notes: Built from the verb voler (to fly) in the present tense for ils/elles (volent) plus the preposition vers (toward/to). Used to describe groups (they) flying toward a destination or in the direction of something. Can also be used figuratively (e.g., events moving toward something). If the intended meaning is 'steal from' (voler), context or different objects are needed; here, with vers it clearly means 'fly toward.'
target_language_example: Ils volent vers Paris pour les vacances.
native_language_example: They are flying to Paris for the holidays.

meaning: thief who steals by (a certain method or in a certain place); used before a noun to describe the type of thief (e.g. voleur à la tire = pickpocket).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own: 'voleur' means 'thief' and 'à' is followed by a noun indicating the method or location (à la tire, à la roulotte, à l'étalage). Common fixed expressions include 'voleur à la tire' (pickpocket) and 'voleur à l'étalage' (shoplifter). Use with definite/indefinite articles as needed: un voleur à la tire, le voleur à l'étalage.
target_language_example: La police recherche un voleur à la tire dans le métro.
native_language_example: The police are looking for a pickpocket in the subway.

meaning: 'pickpockets' (literally: 'thieves at the pull'), i.e., thieves who steal from pockets/bags in public.
additional_notes: Used to warn about or describe people who steal wallets, phones, or other items by stealth in crowded places (on buses, trains, markets). Often appears in signs or spoken warnings: «Attention aux voleurs à la tire» = Watch out for pickpockets. The phrase is fixed; 'à la tire' specifies the method. Gender/number agreement applies to surrounding words (e.g., 'Soyez attentif/attentive(s) aux voleurs à la tire').
target_language_example: Attention aux voleurs à la tire dans le métro.
native_language_example: Watch out for pickpockets on the subway.

meaning: 'volume of' — indicates the amount, size, or quantity of something (physical volume or figurative amount).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify quantity or capacity. Can refer to physical space (le volume d'un récipient), sound level (le volume de la musique), or figurative amounts (le volume de ventes). Followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by de. For sound level specifically, French also uses 'le volume' alone (e.g. augmenter le volume).
target_language_example: Le volume de la bouteille est de 1 litre.
native_language_example: The volume of the bottle is 1 liter.

meaning: stole the / has stolen the (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: From the verb voler (to steal). 'La' is the feminine singular definite article, so 'volé la' appears before a feminine noun (la cassette, la pomme, la vedette, la bière). Context determines tense/person (e.g. 'Elle a volé la...' = she stole the...). Can also be used idiomatically (e.g. 'voler la vedette' = to steal the show).
target_language_example: Il a volé la montre de son frère.
native_language_example: He stole his brother's watch.

meaning: they are going to (do) it / they will (do) it.
additional_notes: Formed from the third-person plural of aller (vont = they go/are going) + direct object pronoun le (it/him). Used to express a near-future action or to ask if someone will do something. Gender/number of the object may change the pronoun (la, les, l'). In spoken French, future with aller is very common: Ils vont le faire = They are going to do it. Word order: subject + vont + object pronoun + verb.
target_language_example: Ils vont le finir demain.
native_language_example: They are going to finish it tomorrow.

meaning: 'shut up' (very rude, plural).
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and insulting way to tell a group to be quiet; 'vos' is the plural possessive 'your', and 'gueules' literally means 'mugs' or 'faces' (slang for mouths). Use only in strong, confrontational contexts (or when quoting/understanding profanity). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Fermez vos gueules et partez d'ici.
native_language_example: Shut up and get out of here.

meaning: Your Highness (formal address to a prince/princess or royal person).
additional_notes: Used as a very formal, respectful form of address to royalty or nobility. Always capitalized for the title in French (Altesse). Often followed by a verb or polite phrase (e.g., «je vous conseille», «je vous en prie»). Not used in casual situations.
target_language_example: Votre Altesse, permettez-moi de vous présenter notre invité.
native_language_example: Your Highness, allow me to introduce our guest.

meaning: a formal way to address someone with the title 'Excellency' (used for high officials, diplomats, bishops).
additional_notes: Very formal and honorific. Used when speaking to or about people who hold certain high-ranking positions (e.g., ambassadors, heads of state, some ecclesiastical figures). In France it is less common in everyday speech; expect it in diplomatic, ceremonial, or historical contexts. Use in spoken French only in very formal situations.
target_language_example: Votre Excellence, puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Your Excellency, may I ask you a question?

meaning: 'Your Majesty' — a formal address for a king, queen, emperor, or empress.
additional_notes: Very formal and respectful. Used when directly addressing a monarch (royal title). Capitalize 'Majesté' when used as a title. Not used for ordinary people; in modern everyday French it's rare except in historical, ceremonial, or fictional contexts (books, films, role-play).
target_language_example: Votre Majesté, permettez-moi de vous présenter le rapport.
native_language_example: Your Majesty, allow me to present the report to you.

meaning: Please (may) I have your attention? / Attention, please.
additional_notes: A polite phrase used to ask a group or person to listen or look. Common in announcements, formal settings, meetings, or when addressing an audience. Full form is « Votre attention, s'il vous plaît. » Variations: « Je peux avoir votre attention, s'il vous plaît ? », « Pourrais‑je avoir votre attention ? »
target_language_example: Votre attention, s'il vous plaît : le train partira dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Attention please: the train will depart in five minutes.

meaning: your ... card (start of a phrase before a vowel sound, e.g. 'votre carte d'identité' = your identity card)
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase: 'votre carte d'' is used when the following word begins with a vowel or mute h and is elided after 'de' (de → d'). Common completions include 'votre carte d'identité' (ID card), 'votre carte d'étudiant' (student card), or 'votre carte d'assurance'. Use 'votre' for formal or plural 'your'.
target_language_example: Puis-je voir votre carte d'identité, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see your identity card, please?

meaning: your room too / your room as well (often in comparisons like 'as ... as you can').
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'votre chambre' (your room) with 'aussi' (also/as). In the example sentences 'aussi' is used in comparisons: 'aussi ... que vous pouvez' = 'as ... as you can' (e.g., 'aussi propre que vous pouvez' = 'as clean as you can'). Alone, 'votre chambre aussi' can mean 'your room too' (adding your room to a list) or be part of a comparative structure. Word order and meaning depend on context.
target_language_example: Gardez votre chambre aussi propre que possible.
native_language_example: Keep your room as clean as possible.

meaning: Your code with me / your code (shared) with me.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a set expression in French by itself; it would be used in contexts where someone asks or says that another person’s code (e.g., PIN, passcode, access code, or a piece of programming) is being given/shared/used with the speaker. You would normally see it inside a full sentence, for example: «Pouvez-vous me donner votre code?» or «Est-ce que vous partagez votre code avec moi?» Pay attention to register and security: asking for someone’s PIN or password can be sensitive and should be done appropriately.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous partager votre code avec moi pour que je puisse accéder au dossier?
native_language_example: Can you share your code with me so I can access the folder?

meaning: 'your ... license/permit to' (the start of a phrase meaning a permit belonging to you, usually followed by an action or vehicle type)
additional_notes: This is a possessive phrase: 'votre' = your (formal or plural), 'permis' = license/permit, 'de' links to what the permit is for. Common completions: 'votre permis de conduire' (your driver's license), 'votre permis de séjour' (your residence permit), 'votre permis de travail' (your work permit). Use 'votre' for usted/formal or plural; use 'ton' for informal singular.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous montrer votre permis de conduire, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show your driver's license, please?

meaning: 'your most' or 'your plus' (depends on context) — typically used to indicate the strongest/most important quality or advantage you have.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom on its own; it usually appears as part of a longer expression like «votre plus grand atout» (your greatest asset) or «votre plus belle réussite» (your greatest achievement). Alone, 'plus' means 'more' or 'most' and modifies a following noun. Make sure a noun or adjective follows to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Parlez-moi de votre plus grand atout.
native_language_example: Tell me about your greatest asset.

meaning: 'your point' (what you mean or the main idea you are making).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's argument, opinion or the main idea they are expressing. Common in phrases like «Quel est votre point ?» (What is your point?) or in responses: «Je comprends votre point, mais…» (I understand your point, but…). Formal register uses vous; use «ton point» in informal speech with friends (though «ton point» is less common than other phrasing like «ton argument»).
target_language_example: Je comprends votre point, mais nous devons aussi considérer le coût.
native_language_example: I understand your point, but we must also consider the cost.

meaning: 'your point of' (used before a noun to say someone's perspective or area, e.g. 'votre point de vue' = 'your point of view')
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete phrase by itself — it's typically followed by a noun (most commonly 'vue' to form 'votre point de vue'). It means 'your ...' (possessive formal/plural 'your') + 'point of'. Use 'votre' for vous (formal or plural).
target_language_example: J'aimerais connaître votre point de vue sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I'd like to know your point of view on this project.

meaning: your real (masculine singular) — used before a noun to say 'your real ...'
additional_notes: This is the possessive adjective 'votre' (your, formal/plural) + the adjective 'vrai' (real/true). It must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies: 'votre vrai' before a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'votre vrai ami'). For a feminine singular noun use 'votre vraie', for plural use 'vos vrais' (masculine) or 'vos vraies' (feminine). 'Votre' is formal or used for 'you' plural; for informal singular use 'ton/ta/tes'.
target_language_example: Est-ce que c'est votre vrai passeport ?
native_language_example: Is that your real passport?

meaning: would like to speak
additional_notes: Polite conditional form of vouloir + infinitive parler. Used to express a desire or polite request (e.g., "I would like to speak to you/about something"). Common in formal or courteous contexts: "Je voudrais parler à monsieur Dupont." Can be followed by à + person or de/à propos de + topic.
target_language_example: Je voudrais parler à la responsable, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I would like to speak to the manager, please.

meaning: would like ... to
additional_notes: Usually seen as je voudrais que... to express a wish or polite request about what someone else does or what happens. It is followed by que + another clause, typically with the subjunctive: je voudrais que tu viennes = "I'd like you to come." English often translates this with "would like someone to..." rather than a literal "would like that..."
target_language_example: Je voudrais que tu viennes avec nous.
native_language_example: I'd like you to come with us.

meaning: would like to
additional_notes: This is usually an incomplete fragment, most often from je voudrais te + infinitive, such as je voudrais te parler ('I'd like to talk to you'). voudrais is a polite/softer form of vouloir ('to want'), and te means 'you' before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je voudrais te parler un moment.
native_language_example: I'd like to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: would like a
additional_notes: Used to ask for or say you want one masculine singular thing in a polite way. It comes from the conditional of vouloir. Use une with feminine nouns instead: je voudrais une table.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: would like to ... you
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a longer pattern such as je voudrais vous parler / vous montrer / vous dire. Voudrais means 'would like' (a polite form of vouloir), and vous means 'you' (formal singular or plural). In French, object pronouns like vous come before the infinitive: je voudrais vous parler = 'I would like to speak to you.'
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous aider.
native_language_example: I would like to help you.

meaning: I just wanted (that)... / I only wanted (that)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple, often explanatory wish or intention about something someone wanted to happen or for someone to know. Commonly followed by a subordinate clause with subjunctive (e.g., 'que ce soit...') or indicative (especially in spoken French: 'que tu le saches'). 'Juste' softens or minimizes the request/intent ('only', 'just').
target_language_example: Je voulais juste que tu comprennes la situation.
native_language_example: I just wanted you to understand the situation.

meaning: I just wanted to see (what)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce curiosity or intention to observe an outcome. Commonly followed by a clause like 'qui...' (what/who) plus a verb in various tenses (se passait, se passerait, arriverait). Polite/neutral; often expresses that the action was only to watch or check, not to intervene.
target_language_example: Je voulais juste voir ce qui allait se passer.
native_language_example: I just wanted to see what would happen.

meaning: 'wanted to (her/it)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect tense of vouloir (voulais = I/he/she/you(you-singular informal) wanted / was wanting) followed by the direct object pronoun la (her/it). In English this expresses a past desire or intention directed at a feminine singular person or a feminine/neutral noun (la = her/it). Context determines whether it means 'wanted to see her', 'wanted to get it (feminine)', etc. The verb that follows may be omitted in casual speech when understood from context: e.g. 'Je voulais la' plus an understood verb becomes 'Je voulais la voir' or 'Je voulais la récupérer'.
target_language_example: Je voulais la voir hier, mais elle n'était pas là.
native_language_example: I wanted to see her yesterday, but she wasn't there.

meaning: 'wanted to (do something) to/for him/her'.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect tense of vouloir (je voulais = I wanted / I was wanting) plus the indirect object pronoun lui (to him / to her). Used before an infinitive verb: Je voulais lui dire = I wanted to tell him/her. The imperfect here expresses a past desire or intention (often incomplete or background action). Pronoun lui does not show gender.
target_language_example: Je voulais lui offrir un cadeau pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: I wanted to give him/her a gift for his/her birthday.

meaning: wanted to ... me
additional_notes: A combination of voulais (“wanted” / “was wanting”) and me (“me”). Before an infinitive, me can be the object of the verb (tu voulais me dire = “you wanted to tell me”) or part of a reflexive verb (je voulais me rendre = “I wanted to go/get myself to”). French puts me before the infinitive, unlike English.
target_language_example: Je voulais me reposer un peu.
native_language_example: I wanted to rest a little.

meaning: didn't want (someone/something) to...; expresses a past desire that something not happen.
additional_notes: Informal negative past construction of vouloir + que + subjunctive (often shortened in speech: "je voulais pas que..."). Used to say you didn't want someone to do/see/be somewhere. The verb after "que" usually takes the subjunctive in full written French (e.g. "je ne voulais pas que tu sois").
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas que tu saches la vérité comme ça.
native_language_example: I didn't want you to find out the truth like that.

meaning: wanted you to
additional_notes: A sentence fragment rather than a fixed expression. It most often appears as je voulais que tu..., meaning 'I wanted you to...'. French often uses vouloir que + subjunctive where English uses 'want someone to + verb', for example: je voulais que tu viennes = 'I wanted you to come'.
target_language_example: Je voulais que tu viennes avec nous.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come with us.

meaning: 'I just wanted to' (polite, followed by an action directed at 'you').
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form vouloir (je voulais) used to make a polite or less direct request or statement: 'I just wanted to [do something to/for you].' Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (parler, poser, regarder, etc.). Can be used to soften interruptions or requests. In spoken French you may also hear 'je voulais juste vous...' (juste ~ seulement).
target_language_example: Je voulais seulement vous aider.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help you.

meaning: 'I wanted to (to) you it' → part of 'Je voulais te le dire' = 'I wanted to tell you (it)'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the verb 'voulais' (imperfect of vouloir = wanted) with the object pronouns 'te' (to you / you) and 'le' (it / him). In full sentences you'll usually see 'Je voulais te le dire' (I wanted to tell you it / I wanted to tell you) or 'Je voulais te le montrer' (I wanted to show it to you). The imperfect 'voulais' expresses a past desire or intention. Word order: subject + voulais + indirect object pronoun (te) + direct object pronoun (le) + verb (dire/montrer).
target_language_example: Je voulais te le dire avant que tu partes.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you before you left.

meaning: 'wanted a car' (imperfect past tense — she/he wanted a car).
additional_notes: Voulait is the imperfect (imparfait) form of vouloir (to want) used to describe a past, ongoing, habitual, or background desire. "Une voiture" = a car. Context and subject determine gender/number (here examples use different female/male names; verb agrees with subject). Use when describing what someone wanted in the past: e.g., childhood wishes, ongoing past desires, or polite indirect speech.
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il voulait une voiture rouge.
native_language_example: When he was young, he wanted a red car.

meaning: 'would you kindly' or 'would you please (for me)' (used to form a polite request with a clitic pronoun 'me').
additional_notes: This phrase fragment combines the polite imperative/question form 'voulez bien' with the clitic 'm'' (short for 'me') and is completed by an infinitive or verb phrase (e.g. 'voulez bien m'aider', 'voulez bien m'apporter'). It is formal/polite and used to ask someone to do something for the speaker. Written usage often appears as 'Voulez-vous bien m'...' when addressing 'vous'.
target_language_example: Voulez bien m'aider à porter ces sacs ?
native_language_example: Would you please help me carry these bags?

meaning: polite way to ask someone to allow or excuse us (literally: 'would you kindly/please allow us' or 'please excuse us').
additional_notes: Used in polite requests where the speaker asks others to excuse, allow, or give space/time to the speaker and their group. Often appears as 'Vous voulez bien nous ... ?' + verb (excuser, laisser, accorder un instant, etc.). Formal/polite register; common in spoken and written French when being courteous.
target_language_example: Vous voulez bien nous excuser un instant ?
native_language_example: Would you please excuse us for a moment?

meaning: want to do
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir (to want) with an infinitive (faire — to do/make). Used to ask or state what someone wants to do. In polite or plural/formal speech use vous voulez faire; in informal singular use tu veux faire. Word order in questions can change (Qu'est-ce que vous voulez faire? / Vous voulez faire quoi?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que vous voulez faire ce weekend ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

meaning: 'do you want to see a...' (polite/plural or formal you)
additional_notes: A common spoken phrase used to offer to show something. 'Vous' is formal or plural; structure = vous (voulez) voir (infinitive) + un/une + noun. Can be used with nouns (film, truc, bon combat). For informal singular use 'tu veux voir un...'.
target_language_example: Vous voulez voir un endroit sympa ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see a nice place?

meaning: 'whether you wanted to or not' (addressing 'you' — imperfect/subjunctive form used in set phrases)
additional_notes: Common phrase used after a verb or clause to say that something happens regardless of the person's wishes.
