Can appear before an infinitive (vraiment aller + infinitive) to mean 'really intend to' or after a pronoun/verb phrase for emphasis.
target_language_example: Tu vas vraiment aller à la réunion demain ?
native_language_example: Are you really going to go to the meeting tomorrow?

meaning: 'really need your' (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: This fragment combines 'vraiment' (really), 'besoin de' (need of), and the possessive 'ton' (your, masculine singular or before a masculine noun). It's not a complete sentence on its own — it introduces that the speaker strongly needs something that belongs to or concerns the listener (e.g., 'vraiment besoin de ton aide' = 'really need your help'). Use 'ta' before feminine singular nouns and 'tes' before plural nouns. For emphasis, 'j'ai vraiment besoin de ton...' or 'on a vraiment besoin de ton...' are common full phrases.
target_language_example: J'ai vraiment besoin de ton aide aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I really need your help today.

meaning: 'really this' — used to emphasize or question the truth of something just mentioned (informal/colloquial fragment).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it combines vraiment (really/truly) + ce (this/that/it). In natural French you will more often hear forms like 'c'est vraiment ça' (that's really it), 'vraiment?' (really?), or 'c'est vraiment ce...' followed by a noun or clause (e.g. 'c'est vraiment ce que tu veux?'). As written, 'vraiment ce' usually appears inside a larger sentence to add emphasis or disbelief and is not used alone.
target_language_example: Tu veux partir maintenant? Vraiment ce soir?
native_language_example: You want to leave now? Really tonight?

meaning: really/actually what (that) — used to question or emphasize whether something is truly as stated or felt
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or statements to check sincerity, truth, or intensity. "Vraiment" (really) modifies the clause introduced by "ce que" (what/that which). In many examples the phrase can be split: "C'est vraiment ce que tu veux ?" = "Is that really what you want?" Also used in affirmative sentences: "J'apprécie vraiment ce que tu fais." = "I really appreciate what you do."
target_language_example: Tu veux partir maintenant ? C'est vraiment ce que tu veux ?
native_language_example: You want to leave now? Is that really what you want?

meaning: a sequence where the adverb 'vraiment' (really/truly) directly precedes the preposition 'de', used to add emphasis before a noun phrase or infinitive that requires 'de' (e.g. really of / really to). Not a fixed idiom by itself but a common collocation depending on the verb/adjective construction.
additional_notes: 'Vraiment de' is compositional: it's the adverb 'vraiment' inserted before the preposition 'de' required by the following word (verbs that take 'de' + infinitive, nouns with 'de', etc.). It appears in sentences like 'vraiment de la chance', 'vraiment de quoi', or before infinitives after verbs that take 'de' (e.g. 'avoir besoin de'). The literal translation is often possible but ensure the English structure matches (e.g. 'I really need to...' or 'really some...').
target_language_example: Il y avait vraiment de la lumière dans la pièce.
native_language_example: There was really some light in the room.

meaning: 'really (some/any) / truly (some/any)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it combines 'vraiment' (really/truly) with the partitive article 'de la' used before feminine singular uncountable nouns (e.g. de la chance, de la patience). Use 'vraiment de la' when you want to emphasize the quantity or quality of something uncountable. Context is needed: you will normally see it followed by a noun (vraiment de la chance).
target_language_example: Elle a vraiment de la chance.
native_language_example: She really has some luck.

meaning: 'really some' or 'truly some' (literal), but this exact sequence is unusual by itself in French
additional_notes: Alone, 'vraiment du' is incomplete and not a fixed phrase. 'Vraiment' means 'really' or 'truly' and 'du' is the partitive article ('some') or contraction of 'de le'. You will typically see 'vraiment' followed by an adjective, verb, or a partitive phrase like 'vraiment du pain' (really some bread) in emphatic contexts, or more naturally 'vraiment' + verb/adjective (e.g. 'vraiment bon', 'vraiment utile'). For beginners: don't treat 'vraiment du' as a standalone expression; learn 'vraiment' and the uses of 'du' separately.
target_language_example: Il y avait vraiment du monde au concert.
native_language_example: There were really some people at the concert. (i.e. it was very crowded)

meaning: a sequence where vraiment (really) is followed by en (in/of it) — typically part of a larger phrase (e.g. vraiment en colère = really angry); on its own 'vraiment en' is incomplete.
additional_notes: You will almost always see 'vraiment' + an adjective or expression starting with 'en' (en colère, en retard, en forme, etc.). 'Vraiment en' shouldn't be used alone — you must complete the phrase (what the person is 'in' or 'about'). 'Vraiment' intensifies the adjective or state. Example structures: 'vraiment en colère' (really angry), 'vraiment en retard' (really late), 'vraiment en forme' (really fit/energetic).
target_language_example: Il est vraiment en colère contre son collègue.
native_language_example: He is really angry with his colleague.

meaning: literally 'really the' — not a standalone fixed phrase; 'vraiment' means 'really' and 'le' is the definite article or pronoun.
additional_notes: This is not a set expression by itself. 'Vraiment' is an adverb meaning 'really' or 'truly'. 'Le' can be the definite article (the) before a masculine noun or a neutral pronoun meaning 'it' or 'him'. You will most often see 'vraiment' followed by an adjective (vraiment bon), a verb (vraiment vouloir), or used alone for emphasis (C'est vraiment !). 'Vraiment le' can appear when 'vraiment' modifies a phrase that begins with 'le' (e.g. 'vraiment le meilleur').
target_language_example: C'est vraiment le meilleur choix.
native_language_example: This is really the best choice.

meaning: really him / truly him (emphatic reference to a specific man or person)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you are talking about that particular person (him). Context determines exact sense: it can express surprise, confirmation, or insistence (e.g. «C'est vraiment lui!» = "It's really him!" vs «Tu veux vraiment lui parler?» = "Do you really want to talk to him?"). Word order can vary: more common forms are «c'est vraiment lui», «vraiment lui?» or «vraiment, lui?» depending on intonation. Not an idiom; literal meaning from components.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment lui que j'ai vu au cinéma hier soir.
native_language_example: He's really the one I saw at the cinema last night.

meaning: 'really' + 'me' — the adverb 'vraiment' used in close proximity to the clitic pronoun 'me' to emphasize that something affects the speaker.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'vraiment' commonly modifies a verb or feeling and may appear immediately before or after clitic pronouns in spoken or emphatic contexts. Standard word order usually places clitic pronouns before the verb (e.g. 'Ça me fait vraiment plaisir'), but in casual speech or for emphasis you may hear 'vraiment me' when 'vraiment' is stressed just before the pronoun+verb sequence (e.g. 'Vraiment me faire ça !' as an exclamative). Use with care: some placements can sound colloquial or marked.
target_language_example: Vraiment me dire ça, tu n'aurais pas dû.
native_language_example: To really tell me that, you shouldn't have.

meaning: really for; genuinely in favor of or truly intended for
additional_notes: Combines 'vraiment' (really/truly) with 'pour' (for). Used to emphasize that something is truly meant for, intended for, or in favor of someone/something. Context determines whether it means 'truly intended for' (e.g. un cadeau vraiment pour toi = a gift really for you) or 'really in favor of' (e.g. je suis vraiment pour cette idée = I'm really for this idea). Word order and surrounding words matter; not a fixed idiom but a simple adverb + preposition phrase.
target_language_example: Je suis vraiment pour cette solution.
native_language_example: I'm really for this solution.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely an incomplete combination. 'vraiment' = 'really', 'quelque' = 'some' or part of 'quelque chose' ('something').
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence 'vraiment quelque' is not a common, standalone expression in French. If you see it, it's usually part of a larger phrase: for example 'vraiment quelque chose' (colloquial, emphatic: 'really something') or 'vraiment quelque chose de...' ('really something of.../really...'). More correct forms: 'vraiment quelque chose' = 'really something' (often used informally), 'quelque chose de vraiment...' = 'something really...'. Don't use 'vraiment quelque' on its own.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment quelque chose !
native_language_example: That's really something!

meaning: really sure / truly certain (about something)
additional_notes: Combination of adverb 'vraiment' (really) + adjective 'sûr' (sure). Note: 'sûr' agrees in gender and becomes 'sûre' for feminine subjects (e.g., elle est vraiment sûre). Often followed by 'de' + noun or clause (vraiment sûr de + nom / vraiment sûr que + proposition). Written accent on 'sûr' is common but sometimes omitted in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Je suis vraiment sûr de ma réponse. — Ici, 'vraiment sûr' exprime une forte certitude.
native_language_example: I am really sure of my answer.

meaning: really a / truly a (emphasis before a noun)
additional_notes: Combination of 'vraiment' (really/truly) + indefinite article 'un'. Used to emphasize that something is truly or genuinely one of a kind, often followed by a noun: 'vraiment un + noun'. In spoken French the phrase may appear with elision or focus on 'vraiment' (e.g., 'c'est vraiment un problème'). Not idiomatic as a standalone fixed phrase — it's the adverb + article construction.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment un bon film.
native_language_example: It's really a good movie.

meaning: literally 'really you'; used to emphasize or confirm that it is indeed you (or to express surprise about the person).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself — it's the adverb 'vraiment' (really/truly) combined with the pronoun 'vous' (you). Context determines meaning: can be part of a question or exclamation (e.g. « C'est vraiment vous ? » = 'Is it really you?') or used for emphasis in statements. Pronunciation and intonation are important for conveying surprise or confirmation. For polite/formal speech use 'vous'; in informal contexts you might hear 'vraiment toi'.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment vous au téléphone ?
native_language_example: Is it really you on the phone?

meaning: A non-standard juxtaposition of the adverb 'vraiment' (really) and the pronoun/adverbial 'y' (there / to it); not a fixed phrase — appears as a fragment or unusual word order rather than a correct standalone expression.
additional_notes: 'Vraiment y' by itself is uncommon in French because 'y' generally precedes the conjugated verb or attaches to an infinitive, and 'vraiment' usually modifies a verb, adjective, or clause. Correct sentences place 'y' and 'vraiment' according to standard word order (e.g. 'Il y est vraiment' or 'Je n'y crois pas vraiment'). If 'vraiment y' appears, it's likely part of a larger clause or a colloquial/incomplete fragment (e.g. 'Vraiment, y...' as a spoken hesitation). Learners should study 'vraiment' and 'y' separately and follow normal placement rules.
target_language_example: Vraiment y croire, c'est difficile pour moi.
native_language_example: To really believe it, it's difficult for me.

meaning: really at / truly in (used to emphasize location, time, or degree before a noun or verb phrase).
additional_notes: Vraiment means 'really' or 'truly' and à is a preposition ('at', 'to', 'in' depending on context). Together they can emphasize location, timing, or the intensity of an action, e.g. vraiment à la maison (really at home), vraiment à l'heure (really on time), or in some constructions before an infinitive with emphasis (less common). The exact English translation depends on the following words; you will often see 'vraiment' used alone before adjectives or verbs (vraiment triste, vraiment vouloir).
target_language_example: Il est vraiment à la maison aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is really at home today.

meaning: 'really that' — used to confirm or emphasize what was just said (colloquial).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to agree, confirm, or emphasize a point just made. Often follows a statement and functions like English 'really' or 'is that so' / 'that's really it' depending on intonation. Can be shortened to 'vraiment?' when asking for confirmation. Tone and context decide whether it's affirmation, surprise, or mild disbelief.
target_language_example: — Tu as fini le projet ? — Vraiment ça ?
native_language_example: — You finished the project? — Really?

meaning: 'given that' / 'since' (because of the fact that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or cause; similar to parce que, puisque, or étant donné que. More formal than 'parce que' in some contexts. Often placed at the start of a clause: 'Vu que + clause'.
target_language_example: Vu que tu es là, aide-moi à porter ces cartons.
native_language_example: Given that you're here, help me carry these boxes.

meaning: 'seen also' or 'also seen' — used to refer the reader to another entry or mention (similar to 'see also').
additional_notes: Commonly used in reference lists, indexes, dictionaries, or cross-references to point to related items. In everyday conversation you would rarely say 'vu aussi' by itself; instead you'll see it in written notices: e.g. 'voir aussi' is more common for 'see also'. 'Vu' is the past participle of 'voir' (to see).
target_language_example: Article consulté — vu aussi : chapitre 3 pour plus de détails.
native_language_example: Article consulted — see also: chapter 3 for more details.

meaning: 'seen with' (someone).
additional_notes: Used with the past participle of voir (vu) plus avec to say that someone was observed in the company of another person. Common in informal spoken French. Often followed by a pronoun or noun (ex: avec elle, avec Tom).
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai jamais vu avec elle.
native_language_example: I have never seen him/her with her.

meaning: seen this
additional_notes: A compositional chunk from voir. In sentences like tu as vu ce... or vous avez vu ce..., it means "have you seen/did you see this...". Here ce means "this/that" before a masculine singular noun.
target_language_example: Tu as vu ce film ?
native_language_example: Have you seen this movie?

meaning: seen what
additional_notes: This is a contracted fragment of phrases like «j'ai vu ce qu'il a fait» meaning 'I saw what he did' or questions like «vous avez vu ce qu'elle a fait ?» ('did you see what she did?'). The full form is typically «vu ce que + subject + verb». Use for referring to something observed or witnessed. The contraction "qu'" appears before a vowel sound (qu'il, qu'elle, qu'on).
target_language_example: J'ai vu ce qu'il a dit hier.
native_language_example: I saw what he said yesterday.

meaning: 'given what you' / 'seeing what you' (introduces a consequence based on what someone did or said)
additional_notes: Colloquial fragment used to start a clause: 'Vu ce que tu...' often leads to a conclusion or decision (e.g. 'vu ce que tu as dit, ...' = 'given what you said, ...'). It requires completion (past participle, action, or clause) to be grammatical. Common in spoken and informal written French.
target_language_example: Vu ce que tu as fait, je comprends ta colère.
native_language_example: Given what you did, I understand your anger.

meaning: 'seen this/that' (past participle 'vu' + demonstrative 'cet')
additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific masculine singular noun that follows (cet before vowels or mute h). 'Vu' is the past participle of 'voir' (to see). Together they mean 'seen this/that' as in 'have you seen this man?' or 'I have never seen this man.' The gender/number must match the noun: use 'vu ce' (rare), 'vues ces' etc. In spoken French you may hear contractions or different orders (e.g., 'tu as vu cet homme?').
target_language_example: Tu as déjà vu cet endroit?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this place?

meaning: 'given how' or 'considering how' / 'since'
additional_notes: Often used to introduce a reason or comment about the way something happened or the situation (similar to 'given that' or 'considering how' in English). Common in spoken and written French. Usually followed by a clause: vu comment + [subject + verb]. Can also appear as part of expressions like "Vu comment il parle, on dirait qu'il est fâché."
target_language_example: Vu comment il travaille, il va réussir l'examen.
native_language_example: Given how he works, he's going to pass the exam.

meaning: 'seen in which' or 'based on which' (used when referring to something observed within a particular context or source).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short sequence: 'vu' (past participle of voir = 'seen' or 'given') + 'dans' ('in') + an interrogative 'quel' ('which'). It appears in questions or relative clauses: e.g. asking in which document/place/source something was seen, or saying 'given in which...' when referring to a context. Word order and gender/number must agree when expanded (quel → quelle/quels/quelles). Often you'll see similar phrases like 'vu dans quel document' or 'vu dans quel contexte'.
target_language_example: Tu as vu dans quel magazine cet article est paru ?
native_language_example: Did you see in which magazine this article appeared?

meaning: seen from the (feminine) — indicates viewpoint or perspective
additional_notes: Literally 'seen from the'. Often followed by a feminine noun or noun phrase (e.g. 'vu de la rue' = 'seen from the street'). Use 'vu du' before masculine nouns and 'vu des' before plural nouns. Common in descriptions, reports, or when giving an opinion from a particular viewpoint. Agreement with past participle may be required when used with être or when the participle acts adjectivally.
target_language_example: Vu de la terrasse, le jardin paraît plus grand.
native_language_example: Seen from the terrace, the garden looks bigger.

meaning: seen/visible from my (point of view or location) — used when describing how something looks from the speaker's perspective or from their premises
additional_notes: Literally 'seen from my...'. The fragment is usually followed by a noun indicating place, angle or possession (e.g. 'vu de ma fenêtre', 'vu de ma chambre'). Not a fixed idiom on its own; it depends on the following noun to complete the meaning. Agreement: when the past participle 'vu' refers to a feminine noun, it becomes 'vue' (e.g. 'vue de ma fenêtre'), but as a fragment 'vu de ma' can appear when the speaker uses masculine or neutral phrasing or in ellipses.
target_language_example: Vu de ma terrasse, la ville semble plus calme.
native_language_example: Seen from my terrace, the city seems quieter.

meaning: seen in the process of (doing something); caught in the act of
additional_notes: Literal components: vu (past participle of voir = seen) + en train (de) (in the process of). Usually followed by an infinitive: 'vu en train de + infinitive' = seen doing something. Can be used to say someone was observed while doing a specific action. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu en train de lire ton message.
native_language_example: I saw him in the process of reading your message. / I saw him reading your message.

meaning: seen the
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. vu is the past participle of voir (“to see”), and le means “the” before a masculine singular noun. It often appears with avoir in the passé composé: tu as vu le... = “you saw/did you see the...?”
target_language_example: J'ai vu le film hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw the movie last night.

meaning: seen my
additional_notes: A combination of the past participle voir (vu) with the possessive adjective ma (my). Commonly appears in questions like «As-tu vu ma... ? / Tu as vu ma... ?» meaning “Did you see my...?” It can also appear in statements like «J'ai vu ma...», meaning “I saw my...”. Use ma before feminine singular nouns (ma femme, ma sœur, ma mère, ma fille, ma partition).
target_language_example: As-tu vu ma clé ?
native_language_example: Did you see my key?

meaning: 'seen more' or 'seen better' / 'I've seen better' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal past participle construction from voir (vu) + plus. Can appear in different contexts: 1) As part of comparisons or expressions meaning 'I've seen better' or 'that's nothing special' (often elliptical), e.g. « J'ai vu plus impressionnant » → 'I've seen more impressive (things).' 2) In past perfect senses when combined with auxiliaries or negatives, e.g. « Je n'en ai pas vu plus » → 'I didn't see any more.' Alone, 'vu plus' without surrounding words is uncommon; learners will most often encounter it inside fuller phrases. 'Plus' may mean 'more' (comparative) or 'anymore' (in negative contexts) — pronunciation and context determine meaning.
target_language_example: J'ai vu plus impressionnant que ça.
native_language_example: I've seen more impressive than that.

meaning: 'seen someone' (past participle construction used to ask if someone saw another person)
additional_notes: From the verb voir (to see). Often appears in questions with avoir: "Avez-vous vu quelqu'un ?" = "Did you see anyone/someone?" Add "d'autre" to ask "anyone else." In spoken French "vu" is the past participle, so full forms include "Tu as vu quelqu'un ?" or formal/inverted "Avez-vous vu quelqu'un ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous vu quelqu'un d'autre près de la porte ?
native_language_example: Did you see anyone else near the door?

meaning: seen/seen something like; used to introduce an example or approximation ("something like").
additional_notes: Literally 'seen something like'. Often used in spoken French to give an approximate example or to rephrase what was seen/heard: e.g. « j'ai vu quelque chose comme ça » = "I saw something like that." Can introduce a rough estimate or comparison. If used without 'vu' the phrase 'quelque chose comme' alone means 'something like'.
target_language_example: J'ai vu quelque chose comme un chat dans le jardin.
native_language_example: I saw something like a cat in the garden.

meaning: 'seen who' — used in questions to ask who (someone) saw or who did something.
additional_notes: Casual/informal spoken structure combining the past participle vu (from voir) with the question word qui. Often appears in spoken French with inversion or intonation: "T'as vu qui ?" = "Who did you see?" or "T'as vu qui a fait ça ?" = "Did you see who did that? / Who did that?" The more formal/written alternatives are "Qui as-tu vu ?" (Who did you see?) or "As-tu vu qui a fait ça ?" (Have you seen who did that?).
target_language_example: T'as vu qui au concert hier ?
native_language_example: Who did you see at the concert yesterday?

meaning: Not a valid French phrase; appears to be a mistaken or jumbled sequence of words (likely combining 'vu que', 'qui' and 'ce que').
additional_notes:
This sequence does not form a correct or recognized French expression in French. Learners should use the correct separate expressions instead:
- 'vu que' = 'given that / since' (to give a reason)
- 'qui' = relative pronoun 'who / which / that'
- 'ce que' = 'what / that which' (object form)
Do not use 'vu qui que ce'. The example below deliberately includes the incorrect sequence to show it is erroneous and should be avoided.
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* Vu qui que ce, il faut corriger la phrase.
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* Given 'vu qui que ce', the sentence needs to be corrected.

meaning: 'seen his/her/its' (past participle 'vu' + possessive 'ses' = 'saw his/her/its' referring to plural possessed items)
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb voir in the passé composé (or past participle used after avoir) and the plural possessive adjective ses (his/her/its). Use depends on the subject and context: e.g. J'ai vu ses yeux = I saw his/her eyes. French does not mark the gender of the possessor in 'ses' (it could mean his or her). 'Vu' must agree only when used with être or as an adjective after a plural direct object preceding the verb; with avoir + direct object after the verb there is no agreement (J'ai vu ses yeux → vu stays unchanged).
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai vu ses photos et elles sont magnifiques.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw his/her photos and they are beautiful.

meaning: 'seen on/at the' (masculine/feminine depends on noun that follows)
additional_notes: Past participle 'vu' (seen) + preposition 'à' + article 'la'. Used to say you saw someone/something at a place or on a medium: 'vu à la télé' = seen on TV; 'vu à la gare' would require 'vu à la gare' (gare is feminine). For masculine places/media use 'vu au' (à + le) or 'vu à l'' before a vowel. Agreement: 'vu' stays the same for masculine/direct object; for feminine singular the past participle becomes 'vue' if the direct object precedes the verb in compound tenses with avoir. In spoken French, 'télé' and 'TV' are common shortcuts.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu à la télévision hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw him on television last night.

meaning: 'seen that at' or 'saw that at' (literal); used when telling someone you saw something at a particular place or time
additional_notes: This is a casual, spoken sequence: vu (past participle of voir) + ça (that) + à (at). In natural speech you might hear 'j'ai vu ça à la télé' or 'tu as vu ça à la fête ?' It usually appears inside a larger sentence (with a subject and auxiliary), e.g. 'Je l'ai vu ça à…' Note word order: in standard writing you would normally say 'J'ai vu ça à la télé' rather than 'Vu ça à la télé' unless using a clipped, colloquial style.
target_language_example: Je l'ai vu ça à la télé hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw that on TV last night.

meaning: bicycle for / bicycle with (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines vélo (bicycle) with the preposition à. Use 1) 'vélo à + [person]' to mean 'a bicycle for [person]' (indicating the recipient or intended user). Example: 'un vélo à John' = a bicycle for John. 2) 'vélo à + [feature]' (often with a noun phrase) to describe a bicycle equipped with something: e.g. 'vélo à pignon fixe' = fixed-gear bicycle. Context determines whether 'à' shows purpose/recipient or a characteristic.
target_language_example: Ils ont acheté un vélo à leur fille pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: They bought a bicycle for their daughter for her birthday.

meaning: to check the (masculine) / to verify the (masculine).
additional_notes: This is the verb vérifier (to check/verify) followed by the masculine singular definite article le. It appears before a masculine noun or when referring to a masculine object already known (e.g. vérifier le dossier, vérifier le moteur). Use vérifier la for feminine nouns, vérifier les for plural, and vérifier + direct object without article when appropriate (vérifier ça).
target_language_example: Je vais vérifier le dossier avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I'll check the file before the meeting.

meaning: 'the truth' used in phrases to mean 'to tell the truth' / 'actually' / 'honestly'.
additional_notes: Appears in several common French expressions: "C'est la vérité" (that's the truth), "en vérité" (in truth / actually), "pour dire la vérité" or "pour te dire la vérité" (to tell the truth / honestly). Used to introduce a frank statement or correct what was said before. Not limited to first person — can refer to truth in general.
target_language_example: Pour te dire la vérité, je n'ai jamais vu ce film.
native_language_example: To tell you the truth, I've never seen that movie.

meaning: used to introduce a statement that corrects, balances, or adds nuance to what was just said (English: 'to be fair,' 'in all honesty,' or 'truth be told').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom alone; it often appears in the expression 'pour être juste/vrai, vérité à…' or in spoken corrections like 'vérité, ...' More commonly French speakers say 'pour être honnête,' 'à vrai dire,' or 'pour être juste.' 'Vérité à' by itself is rare — learners will more often encounter 'à vrai dire' (to be honest) or 'à dire la vérité' (truth be told). Use it to soften or qualify a previous statement.
target_language_example: À vrai dire, vérité à dire, je n'étais pas très préparé.
native_language_example: To be honest, truth be told, I wasn't very prepared.

meaning: clothing with/for (used before a specification, e.g. size, purpose, pattern — 'vêtements à...' = 'clothes with/for...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment: vêtements (clothes) followed by à introduces a characteristic, purpose, size, price, or feature (e.g. vêtements à manches longues = clothes with long sleeves; vêtements à vendre = clothes for sale; vêtements à la mode = fashionable clothes). You will usually see a noun, adjective, or infinitive after à. Context determines the exact translation ('with', 'for', 'to', 'at', etc.).
target_language_example: Je cherche des vêtements à manches longues pour l'hiver.
native_language_example: I'm looking for clothes with long sleeves for winter.

meaning: the yours is / yours is (referring to a feminine or general noun) — literally 'yours is...'.
additional_notes: « La vôtre » (with accent and article) is a possessive pronoun meaning 'yours' and replaces a feminine or gender-neutral noun previously mentioned. It agrees in gender/number with the thing possessed: la vôtre (feminine singular), le vôtre (masculine singular), les vôtres (plural). When followed by est, it forms a sentence like 'yours is ...'. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Comparée à la mienne, la vôtre est magnifique.
native_language_example: Compared to mine, yours is magnificent.

meaning: weekend
additional_notes: A loanword from English used in French to mean the two-day period at the end of the week (Saturday and Sunday). Can be used as a noun (un week-end) and in expressions like "à ce week-end" (see you this weekend). Pronunciation and gender: typically masculine (le/un week-end).
target_language_example: Nous partons en week-end demain.
native_language_example: We're going away for the weekend tomorrow.

meaning: 'is there/are there' or used to form yes/no questions with 'il y a' (there is/there are) in inversion
additional_notes: This is part of the inversion question form of 'il y a' (il y a → y a-t-il). The '-t-' is an inserted liaison consonant used when 'il' follows a verb that ends with a vowel (y a + il → y a-t-il) to make pronunciation and grammar correct. Used to ask about existence or occurrence: 'Y a-t-il...' = 'Is there...' / 'Are there...' It appears in formal or neutral questions; in speech people often use 'Est-ce qu'il y a...' or 'Il y a...' with rising intonation instead.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il des billets disponibles pour ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are there tickets available for tonight?

meaning: there was/were a lot (of) / there has been a lot (of)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of "il y a eu beaucoup (de)" = "there was/were a lot of" (past/events or quantities that occurred). Used to report past occurrences or quantities (people, things, events). If followed by a noun, add "de" before the noun: "beaucoup de neige". In formal writing you may see the full form "il y a eu beaucoup".
target_language_example: Il y a eu beaucoup de monde à la fête hier.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people at the party yesterday.

meaning: 'there is enough' or 'there are enough' (informal spoken French)
additional_notes: Contraction of il y a assez; common in casual speech and writing. Used to say that a quantity or situation is sufficient. Can be followed by de + noun, or used alone: "y a assez" (that's enough). In more formal contexts use "il y a assez" or "ça suffit."
target_language_example: Y a assez de chaises pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: There are enough chairs for everyone.

meaning: 'there is something/someone else' or 'there is another (thing/person)'.
additional_notes: This appears to be an informal or colloquial fragment combining 'y a' (contraction of 'il y a' = 'there is/are') with 'autre' (other). In standard French you'd usually say 'il y a autre chose' (there is something else) or 'il y a un autre/une autre' (there is another one). Alone, 'y a autre' is incomplete and would be found in casual speech or dialects; use full phrases for clear, correct French.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas là, mais y a autre personne qui peut aider.
native_language_example: He's not here, but there is another person who can help.

meaning: there is/are a lot (of)
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of "il y a beaucoup" ("there is/are a lot of"). Used before a noun or expression of quantity: e.g. "y a beaucoup de gens" = "there are a lot of people". Common in casual conversation and writing; avoid in formal contexts. Often appears as "y'a beaucoup" when the vowel is elided.
target_language_example: Y a beaucoup de monde au marché aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people at the market today.

meaning: 'there is a lot to' / 'there is much to (do/see/learn...)'.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken structure often derived from il y a + infinitive phrase: il y a beaucoup à + verb-infinitive or + noun. Used to say that many things exist or many actions are possible/needed. In speech il y a → y a (drop 'il'). Followed by an infinitive (e.g. y a beaucoup à faire) or by a noun phrase (less common).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup à découvrir dans cette ville.
native_language_example: There is a lot to discover in this city.

meaning: 'there is/are' + emphasis (colloquial spoken form of il y a, with bien adding assurance or contrast).
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction: 'il y a' → 'y a' commonly used in spoken French. Adding 'bien' gives emphasis, reassurance or contrast (e.g. 'there really is', 'there certainly are', or 'there is after all'). Used in informal speech; often followed by a noun, clause or further comment. Example contexts: defending a point ('Y a bien des gens qui...'), confirming existence ('Y a bien un problème'), or contrasting ('Y a bien une différence').
target_language_example: Y a bien un livre sur la table, je l'ai vu.
native_language_example: There really is a book on the table, I saw it.

meaning: 'there are certain' or 'there are some (specific)'.
additional_notes: This is an informal/clipped form of "il y a certaines" (there are certain...). It introduces a subset or particular items/people within a group. In spoken French, the subject "il" is often dropped, producing "y a" for "il y a". Follow with a plural noun or phrase (e.g. "y a certaines personnes", "y a certaines raisons").
target_language_example: Y a certaines personnes qui préfèrent travailler le matin.
native_language_example: There are certain people who prefer to work in the morning.

meaning: there are those (who)... / some people (who)...
additional_notes: Informal spoken French contraction of 'il y a ceux' used to introduce a group of people contrasted with others (often followed by 'qui' + verb). Common in conversation or writing that mimics speech. Equivalent to 'there are those' or 'some people' in English. Usually followed by a clause: 'y a ceux qui...' and contrasted with 'y a ceux qui...' or 'et y a les autres...'.
target_language_example: Y a ceux qui aiment la plage, et y a ceux qui préfèrent la montagne.
native_language_example: There are those who like the beach, and there are those who prefer the mountains.

meaning: there is/are more (informal, contraction of 'il y a de plus').
additional_notes: Informal spoken construction using 'y a' for 'il y a' (there is/are). 'de plus' means 'more' or 'in addition' — together they indicate that there is more (of something) or that something else exists in addition. In careful/written French you'd usually say 'il y a de plus' or better 'il y a encore' / 'de plus, ...' depending on context. Use in conversation.
target_language_example: Y a de plus des problèmes dont il faut parler.
native_language_example: There are also more problems that we need to talk about.

meaning: There are children (here/there).
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of « il y a des enfants ». Used to state that children are present or exist in a place or situation. Can be neutral or emphatic depending on intonation or punctuation. The version without the contraction, « il y a des enfants », is more formal/standard. Often used before a comment or complaint (e.g. pointing out that something is inappropriate because children are present).
target_language_example: Y a des enfants dans la salle, baisse la musique.
native_language_example: There are children in the room, turn the music down.

meaning: 'there are ten' or 'it's ten (o'clock)'
additional_notes: Colloquial/informal contraction of 'il y a dix' or part of spoken expressions. Depending on context, it can mean 'there are ten (of something)' or, in time-telling, 'il est dix heures' is standard but casual speech may use 'y a dix heures' to mean 'it's ten o'clock' (often heard in fast, informal speech). Without context, it's ambiguous — prefer the full forms ('il y a dix' or 'il est dix heures') in writing.
target_language_example: Y a dix personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are ten people in the room.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase. Appears to be a nonstandard word order mixing the colloquial contraction 'y a' (il y a = there is/are) with the pronoun 'en' (some/of it/them). In natural French the pronoun 'en' usually appears before the verb (e.g. 'y en a') or after in spoken contractions, so the exact sequence 'y a en' is ungrammatical or extremely rare.
additional_notes: Native speakers will normally say 'y en a' or 'il y en a' to mean 'there are some' or 'there is some'. 'y a en' may occur in rapid speech errors, misordered transcription, or in poetic/colloquial plays on word order, but it should not be treated as a correct fixed expression. Use 'y en a' instead.
target_language_example: Bon, y a en trop, il faut les ranger.
native_language_example: Well, there are too many of them, we have to put them away.

meaning: 'there is still one' or 'there's another one left'.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken French: 'y a' is an informal contraction of 'il y a' (there is/are). Used to say that one more item/person remains or that another instance exists. Can be followed by a noun or implied from context. Example: 'y a encore une place' = 'there's still one seat left.'
target_language_example: Y a encore une place si tu veux venir.
native_language_example: There's still one seat if you want to come.

meaning: 'there is/are about' (approximate quantity or time)
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of il y a + environ. Used to give an approximate amount or time: y a (number) / y a environ (number). Common in conversation and casual writing. Example: "y a environ 10 personnes" = "there are about 10 people." When starting a sentence you may also hear just "y a" for "il y a."
target_language_example: Y a environ dix minutes avant le train.
native_language_example: There are about ten minutes before the train.

meaning: there is/there are (colloquial), often used to point something out or emphasize presence nearby
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of il y a, sometimes combined with là for emphasis or to indicate something close in space or time (e.g. « y a là un problème » = 'there's a problem (right here)'). Common in everyday conversation and regional speech. Use il y a in formal writing.
target_language_example: Y a là un livre sur la table.
native_language_example: There's a book on the table.

meaning: there is less / there are fewer (informal spoken contraction of 'il y a moins')
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form: 'y a' is a contraction of 'il y a' (there is/there are). Use 'il y a moins' to compare quantities (e.g., 'il y a moins de monde' = 'there are fewer people'). In speech or informal writing you may see or hear 'y a moins'. Remember to include 'de' before a noun or number when needed: 'il y a moins de bruit'.
target_language_example: Y a moins de gens ici qu'hier.
native_language_example: There are fewer people here than yesterday.

meaning: colloquial contraction of 'il y a' plus 'neuf' meaning 'there are nine' or 'it's nine' (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is an informal/casual spoken form where 'il y a' is reduced to 'y a' and followed by the numeral 'neuf' (9). It can mean 'there are nine (of something)' or in time expressions 'it's nine' (Il est neuf / Il est neuf heures) when context drops 'heures'. Not standard written French; common in speech and informal writing (texts, chat).
target_language_example: Y a neuf personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are nine people in the room.

meaning: 'there is no' or 'there are no' (informal spoken form of 'il n'y a pas de')
additional_notes: This is the contracted, colloquial spoken form of 'il n'y a pas de' used before a noun beginning with a vowel or consonant (often written in speech as 'y a pas de' or 'y a pas d'' before a vowel). Use in informal conversation; in writing prefer the full form 'il n'y a pas de' or 'il n'y a pas d''. It negates existence: 'there isn't/aren't any' or 'there is no'.
target_language_example: Y a pas d'eau ici.
native_language_example: There is no water here.

meaning: 'there may be a' or 'there might be a' (informal spoken French)
additional_notes: This is a colloquial contraction of Il y a peut‑être un/une... used in speech and informal writing. 'Y a' stands for 'il y a' (there is/are). Use with a noun: 'y a peut‑être un problème' = 'there may be a problem.' For formal contexts, prefer 'Il y a peut‑être un...' or 'Il se peut qu'il y ait un...'.
target_language_example: Y a peut-être un problème avec la voiture.
native_language_example: There might be a problem with the car.

meaning: 'that's all there is' / 'that's the only thing' / 'that's what matters'
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'il n'y a que ça' or 'il n'y a que ça qui...'. Used to emphasize that something is the only option, the only thing that matters, or the only thing that will do. Common in spoken French; can appear alone as an exclamation ("Y a que ça!"). Tone can be emphatic or approving depending on context.
target_language_example: Pour eux, y a que ça qui compte.
native_language_example: For them, that's the only thing that matters.

meaning: Is there someone there? / There's someone there (depends on intonation).
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of 'Il y a quelqu'un là' or 'Il y a quelqu'un là-bas'. Used to ask if someone is present in a place or to point out that someone is there. Often contracted to 'Y a quelqu'un...' in speech. Intonation determines whether it's a question or a statement; adding a question mark or rising voice makes it a question.
target_language_example: Y a quelqu'un là-dedans ?
native_language_example: Is there anyone in there?

meaning: Is there someone at... / Is anyone at... (used when asking if someone is present at a place or available on the phone)
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of "est-ce qu'il y a quelqu'un à..." or "y a-t-il quelqu'un à...". Often followed by a place or device: e.g. "y a quelqu'un à la porte ?" (Is someone at the door?), or "y a quelqu'un à l'appareil ?" (Is anyone on the line / on the phone?). Common in everyday conversation. The contraction "y a" represents "il y a".
target_language_example: Y a quelqu'un à la porte ?
native_language_example: Is there someone at the door?

meaning: 'there is something that...' (colloquial/informal introduction to a statement about a problem or surprise)
additional_notes: This is a casual, spoken construction — short for 'il y a quelque chose que...' It introduces an observation, worry, or complaint (e.g. 'there's something that bothers me' or 'there's something strange'). Often followed by a verb or clause explaining what the 'something' is. In written or formal French use 'il y a'.
target_language_example: Y a quelque chose que je ne comprends pas dans ce dossier.
native_language_example: There’s something that I don’t understand about this file.

y a quelque chose que je

target_language_multi_word_term: y a quelque chose que je
meaning: 'there is something that I...' (start of a sentence expressing that the speaker has something to say or does/feels something)
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken-style fragment combining 'y a' (colloquial for 'il y a' = 'there is/are') with 'quelque chose que je...' ('something that I...'). It's not a complete sentence on its own — it introduces a thought the speaker will finish (e.g. 'y a quelque chose que je dois te dire' = 'there's something I must tell you'). Use 'il y a' in more formal contexts. Contractions and dropped words are common in speech.
target_language_example: Y a quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There is something I have to tell you.

y a quelque chose que vous

target_language_multi_word_term: y a quelque chose que vous
meaning: 'there is something that you...' (start of a clause)
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken-style fragment of the expression 'Il y a quelque chose que vous...' and is used to introduce that there exists something which the listener does or should do/know. In careful French you'd say 'Il y a quelque chose que vous...' followed by a verb or clause (e.g. 'Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir'). The shortened form 'y a' is very common in speech instead of 'il y a'.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir avant de partir.
native_language_example: There is something that you must know before leaving.

y a quelque chose qui ne

target_language_multi_word_term: y a quelque chose qui ne
meaning: 'there's something that doesn't...' (start of a sentence expressing that something is wrong or not as it should be)
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken French contraction of Il y a quelque chose qui ne... followed by a verb (usually with pas): e.g. Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas. Used to express that something is wrong, off, or not working. In writing, prefer the full form 'Il y a...'.
target_language_example: Y a quelque chose qui ne va pas avec la voiture.
native_language_example: There's something wrong with the car.

meaning: 'there is something to' / 'there is something worth (doing)'.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken French contraction of 'il y a'. Used to say that something exists to be done, seen, said, etc., or that there is something of interest/importance related to the following infinitive or noun. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g. 'y a quelque chose à dire') or a place/thing (e.g. 'y a quelque chose à voir').
target_language_example: Ici, y a quelque chose à visiter.
native_language_example: Here, there's something to visit / there's something worth visiting.

meaning: some time ago; a while ago
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression equivalent to 'il y a quelque temps'. Used to indicate an unspecified time in the past (not very recent). You can use it to introduce a past event without giving a date. In writing or formal speech, prefer 'il y a quelque temps.'
target_language_example: Je l'ai rencontré y a quelque temps au marché.
native_language_example: I met him a while ago at the market.

meaning: there are fifteen / it's fifteen (minutes) ago/after (colloquial spoken form of 'il y a quinze' or 'il est quinze')
additional_notes: This is an informal, contracted spoken form. In written French you'd usually see 'il y a quinze' (meaning 'there are fifteen' or 'fifteen [units] ago') or 'il est quinze heures' (it's 3 p.m.). Alone 'y a quinze' often appears in casual speech to mean 'there are fifteen (of them)' or part of a time expression like 'y a quinze minutes' = 'fifteen minutes ago'. Context determines whether it's counting items or giving a time reference. For formal speech or writing, use the full forms ('il y a quinze', 'il y a quinze minutes').
target_language_example: Y a quinze personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are fifteen people in the room.

meaning: 'there are seven' (colloquial spoken form of il y a sept)
additional_notes: Contraction of il y a sept. Common in casual spoken French and informal writing (texts, transcripts). Use il y a sept in formal contexts. It simply states the existence/number of something: 'there are seven'. Pronounced /i a sεt/ or more quickly /ja sεt/.
target_language_example: Y a sept chaises dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are seven chairs in the room.

meaning: 'there is/are only' or 'there's only'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of il y a seulement. Used to say that only a limited number/amount exists. In writing prefer 'il y a seulement'. Often followed by a number, quantity, time or noun (e.g. y a seulement un problème / y a seulement trois places).
target_language_example: Y a seulement deux places de libres.
native_language_example: There are only two spots left.

meaning: there are six / it's six o'clock (informal contracted speech)
additional_notes: This is an informal, contracted spoken form of il y a six (there are six) or c'est six heures (it's six o'clock) depending on context. In everyday spoken French, people often drop the initial 'il' and contract sounds: 'y a' = il y a (there is/are) or sometimes used like 'y'a' before a time (y a six heures) to mean 'it's six (o'clock)'. Without full sentence context, 'y a six' most commonly appears in casual speech to state a number (there are six) or mention a time. Not appropriate for formal writing.
target_language_example: Y a six personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are six people in the room.

meaning: there is/are so much; so many (colloquial contraction of 'il y a tant')
additional_notes: Informal spoken French: 'y a' is a contraction of 'il y a' (there is/are). 'tant' means 'so much' or 'so many' depending on countability. Together 'y a tant' expresses that there is a large amount or number of something, often followed by 'de' + noun or by a clause (e.g. 'y a tant de monde', 'y a tant à faire'). More common in speech than writing.
target_language_example: Y a tant de choses à dire.
native_language_example: There are so many things to say.

meaning: there are so many things (to do/say/see/etc.)
additional_notes: Informal spoken French: contraction of 'il y a tant de choses'. Used to express that many things exist or remain (often followed by clarification or left general). Common in conversation to emphasize quantity or complexity (e.g., 'Y a tant de choses à faire' = 'There are so many things to do').
target_language_example: Y a tant de choses à comprendre dans ce livre.
native_language_example: There are so many things to understand in this book.

meaning: there is/there are so much/so many (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of 'il y a tellement' used to emphasize quantity or degree (so much, so many, so + adjective). Often followed by a noun, a clause introduced by 'que', or an adjective/adverb. Common in everyday conversation; avoid in very formal writing.
target_language_example: Y a tellement de monde au marché aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are so many people at the market today.

meaning: 'there is/are always' (colloquial spoken form of il y a toujours)
additional_notes: Informal contraction of il y a toujours. Common in spoken French and informal writing. Used to say that something exists or happens continuously or repeatedly. In formal writing, use « il y a toujours ». Can be followed by a noun (y a toujours un problème) or a clause (y a toujours des gens qui...).
target_language_example: Y a toujours du monde au café le soir.
native_language_example: There are always people at the café in the evening.

meaning: there are always (some)...
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of il y a toujours des. Used to say that something exists or happens regularly/always. Followed by a plural noun: 'y a toujours des problèmes' = 'there are always problems'. In writing, prefer 'il y a toujours des'.
target_language_example: Y a toujours des gens qui posent des questions.
native_language_example: There are always people who ask questions.

meaning: informal spoken fragment meaning 'there is always some/there are always some' (incomplete phrase).
additional_notes: This is a colloquial contraction of 'il y a toujours quelque(s)...' used in spoken French before a noun or expression (e.g. 'quelque chose', 'quelqu'un', 'quelques ...'). It is incomplete on its own and must be followed by a word or phrase (e.g. 'y a toujours quelque chose' = 'there is always something'). Common in casual speech; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Y a toujours quelque chose qui cloche ici.
native_language_example: There is always something wrong here.

meaning: there is always a (there's always a ...).
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of "il y a toujours un" used in spoken French. "Y a" = "il y a" (there is/are). Followed by a noun; expresses that something (a person, thing, or situation) always exists or happens. Common in informal speech; avoid in formal writing where use full "il y a toujours un..."
target_language_example: Y a toujours un ami pour t'aider quand tu en as besoin.
native_language_example: There's always a friend to help you when you need it.

meaning: there is everything / everything is there
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of il y a tout or il y a de tout; used to say that all kinds of things or everything is present. Often spoken as "y a" (without the initial "il") in informal speech. Can introduce a list or describe a place that has everything you need. For more formal contexts use "il y a tout" or "il y a de tout."
target_language_example: Dans ce magasin, y a tout ce qu'il faut pour la cuisine.
native_language_example: In this store, there's everything you need for the kitchen.

meaning: there are three / it's been three (colloquial spoken form of "il y a trois...")
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of "il y a trois..." used in spoken French. Often followed by a time expression (e.g. "y a trois jours" = "three days ago") or a noun phrase ("y a trois personnes" = "there are three people"). Not typically used in formal written French; write the full "il y a" in formal contexts. Pronounced like /ya tʁwɑ/.
target_language_example: Y a trois personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are three people in the room.

meaning: There's too much / There are too many (colloquial contraction of il y a trop).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French: 'y a' is a contraction of 'il y a' (there is/there are). Use 'y a trop' before a noun or verb phrase to say there is too much of something or that something is done too much. In writing or formal speech prefer 'il y a trop'. You will often see it followed by a noun (y a trop de monde) or an infinitive/verb phrase (y a trop parler = too much talking).
target_language_example: Y a trop de bruit ici.
native_language_example: There's too much noise here.

meaning: 'there is/are too many' or 'there is too much' (informal spoken contraction of il y a trop de).
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of il y a trop de. Used before a noun to say there is an excessive amount/number of something. Followed by a noun (countable plural for 'too many', uncountable for 'too much'). Common in everyday conversation and informal writing; avoid in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: Y a trop de monde au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: There are too many people at the cinema tonight.

meaning: 'there is/are very' (informal spoken contraction of 'il y a très')
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken sequence where 'il y a' is contracted to 'y a' and followed by 'très' to intensify whatever follows (e.g. 'y a très peu', 'y a très longtemps'). You'll rarely hear 'y a très' standing alone; it's always followed by an adjective, adverb, or phrase. Use in casual conversation and informal writing only. The full formal form is 'il y a très...'.
target_language_example: Y a très peu de pain dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: There is very little bread in the kitchen.

meaning: there is an urgent need
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of 'il y a un besoin urgent'. 'Y a' is a contracted/informal pronunciation of 'il y a'. Use to say something requires immediate attention. Common in speech and in writing only in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Il y a un besoin urgent de médicaments dans la clinique.
native_language_example: There is an urgent need for medicine at the clinic.

meaning: There's a (female) servant / There's a maid (colloquial spoken contraction of 'il y a une bonne').
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken contraction: 'y a' = 'il y a' (there is/are). 'Une bonne' is a dated word for a female domestic worker (maid). Today 'une bonne' can sound old-fashioned or dismissive; modern terms are 'une femme de ménage' or 'une aide ménagère'. Use 'y a une bonne' only in very informal speech or when quoting older usage.
target_language_example: Dans la maison, y a une bonne qui s'occupe du ménage.
native_language_example: In the house, there's a maid who takes care of the cleaning.

meaning: 'there is one thing that' / 'there is something that'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of 'il y a une chose que'. Used to introduce a single point or thing you want to mention. Common in conversation; in writing or formal speech prefer 'il y a une chose que'. Often followed by a clause explaining the thing (que + verb).
target_language_example: Y a une chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There is one thing I must tell you.

y a une chose que je

target_language_multi_word_term: y a une chose que je
meaning: there is one thing that I / there's something that I (do/think/know/feel).
additional_notes: Short for 'Il y a une chose que je...'. Used to introduce a single important item or fact about the speaker (followed by a verb or clause). Common in both spoken and written French. Can be completed by verbs like 'dois', 'peux', 'sais', 'ressens', 'voudrais savoir', etc.
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: There is one thing I want to tell you.

meaning: there is half (an hour) — colloquial contraction meaning «il y a une demi(heure)» or sometimes «il est (une) et demie» depending on context
additional_notes: This is informal, spoken French where words are contracted: 'il y a' → 'y a' and 'demi' often short for 'demi-heure' or 'une demie' (half past). Without context it can mean 'there is half (an hour)' or be part of phrases like 'y a une demi-heure' ('half an hour ago' or 'for half an hour'). Use in casual speech; not standard written French.
target_language_example: Y a une demi-heure qu'il est parti.
native_language_example: He left half an hour ago.

meaning: 'there is a girl' (informal spoken form of "il y a une fille")
additional_notes: Common spoken French shortens "il y a" to "y a". Use to say that a girl/person is present or exists in a place or situation. In written or formal speech, use "il y a une fille." Can be followed by location (dans la chambre), a clause (qui te demande), or stand alone as an announcement.
target_language_example: Y a une fille dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: There is a girl in the kitchen.

meaning: a minute ago / just a minute ago
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of "il y a une minute" meaning 'one minute ago'. Often used in conversation to indicate something happened very recently. In fast speech "il" is dropped: "y a" = "il y a". Can be replaced with other time expressions: "y a cinq minutes" = 'five minutes ago'.
target_language_example: Il est parti y a une minute.
native_language_example: He left a minute ago.

meaning: There is a car / There's a car.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken form of 'il y a une voiture'. In casual speech French often drops the 'il' and contracts 'il y a' to 'y a'. Use in everyday conversation; avoid in formal writing. Can be followed by location or additional info: 'y a une voiture devant la maison.'
target_language_example: Y a une voiture garée devant la porte.
native_language_example: There's a car parked in front of the door.

meaning: 'there is' or 'there are' used in informal spoken French (contraction of il y a + à in some contexts).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in casual speech when speakers contract phrases: il y a (there is/are) and a (to) can appear together in informal contexts (e.g., 'y a à' = 'il y a à' meaning 'there is to' or 'one must/there is something to' before an infinitive). It's colloquial and mainly spoken; avoid in formal writing. Often heard as 'y a' (for il y a) alone. Context determines translation — sometimes simply 'there is/are', sometimes part of a construction like 'y a à + infinitive' meaning 'there is something to (do)'.
target_language_example: Y a à réfléchir avant de décider.
native_language_example: There's something to think about before deciding.

meaning: to go there
additional_notes: y replaces a place or destination already mentioned, so y aller usually means "to go there." In some common expressions like il faut y aller or allez-y, it can mean "we have to go / get going" or "go ahead."
target_language_example: On va y aller demain matin.
native_language_example: We're going there tomorrow morning.

meaning: to go all out; to give it everything (do something with maximum effort or energy).
additional_notes: Built from 'y aller' (to go for it / to start / to give something a try) plus 'tout' (all). Used to encourage putting full effort into an action. Informal, often used in spoken French. Contexts: sports, parties, trying something challenging. Note that 'y aller' alone can mean 'go ahead' or 'try it', while 'y aller tout' emphasizes doing it completely.
target_language_example: Allez, y aller tout ce soir pour le concert !
native_language_example: Come on, give it your all tonight for the concert!

meaning: to go for it; to give something a try (idiomatic).
additional_notes: This is an idiomatic expression meaning to attempt something, to take action, or to go all out. It often appears as 'y aller' (without 'à') or 'y aller à fond' (to go all in). The pronoun 'y' refers to a place or situation mentioned before. Context determines whether it's literal (to go there) or figurative (to try/attack a task).
target_language_example: Si tu veux réussir, il faut y aller à fond.
native_language_example: If you want to succeed, you have to go for it / give it your all.

meaning: there will be
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the full expression « il y aura des + plural noun », the future form of « il y a ». It is used to say that something will exist or happen in the future: « il y aura des problèmes » = « there will be problems ».
target_language_example: À la réunion, il y aura des invités importants.
native_language_example: There will be important guests at the meeting.

meaning: there was
additional_notes: Common expression 'il y avait' is the imperfect of 'il y a' and means 'there was/there were' (describing past situations or repeated/past background). 'de' here often begins a noun phrase with partitive (de la, du), indefinite (de nombreux) or is followed by a noun. Use for describing past existence or presence (weather, objects, people, conditions).
target_language_example: Avant l'accident, il y avait de la lumière dans la salle.
native_language_example: Before the accident, there was light in the room.

meaning: 'there was/were lots of' or 'there was/were plenty of'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of il y avait plein de … meaning a large quantity. Often used with nouns (count or mass). Can be followed by de + noun (de is required). Contraction: in speech people say 'y'avait plein' (y avait).
target_language_example: Hier, il y avait plein de monde au concert.
native_language_example: Yesterday, there were lots of people at the concert.

meaning: there is/are
additional_notes: Used in existential expressions, usually with impersonal il: il y a = 'there is/there are'. With other verbs, it gives meanings like 'there can be', 'there must be', or 'there will be' (for example, il peut y avoir, il doit y avoir, il va y avoir). It does not mean 'to have' in the normal possession sense. In informal speech, il is sometimes dropped: va y avoir....
target_language_example: Il va y avoir un problème si on part trop tard.
native_language_example: There will be a problem if we leave too late.

meaning: to be/there is (some amount of); indicates existence or presence of something (often followed by a noun or quantity).
additional_notes: This is a use of the impersonal construction "il y a" but with "y" placed before another verb form or in negative/questions where word order shifts (e.g., "Il peut y avoir du monde" → "There may be people"). "y avoir du" commonly appears in expressions like "il peut y avoir du..." (there may be some...), "il va y avoir du..." (there's going to be some...), or "il pourrait y avoir du...". After "du" a noun often follows ("du monde", "du bruit", "du mal"). It's not a fixed idiom by itself; consider it as part of constructions expressing existence/amount.
target_language_example: Il peut y avoir du bruit ce soir.
native_language_example: There may be some noise tonight.

meaning: a sequence combining the locative pronoun 'y', the verb 'avoir' and the quantifier 'quelque' used to express existence/possession in a context: roughly 'there is/are some' or 'to have some' (usually completed by a noun or phrase).
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone idiom; in natural French the sequence appears within larger constructions (e.g. 'il y a quelque chose', 'y avoir quelque chose à dire'). Often 'quelque' is followed by a noun or 'chose' or becomes plural 'quelques' + noun. The impersonal construction 'il y a' is the most common context. Word order in the exact sequence 'y avoir quelque' is uncommon without following words, so expect continuation (e.g. 'y avoir quelque chose').
target_language_example: Il peut y avoir quelque chose qui cloche.
native_language_example: There may be something wrong.

meaning: 'there must be another' / 'there must be another one' (used to suggest an alternative exists).
additional_notes: Common structure: Il doit y avoir un autre + noun (moyen, accès, chemin...). 'Il doit y avoir' expresses logical certainty or strong supposition ('there must be' / 'there should be'). 'Y' refers to a place or situation already mentioned; here it's idiomatic and often not translated directly into English. Used to propose that an alternative solution, route, or access exists.
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir un autre restaurant ouvert ce soir.
native_language_example: There must be another restaurant open tonight.

meaning: including; included.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something is part of a group or list. Often appears after the items being discussed (like '... , y compris X') or alone in short replies ('Vous y compris' = 'Including you'). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Nous avons invité toute la famille, y compris ma grand‑mère.
native_language_example: We invited the whole family, including my grandmother.

meaning: to believe in it / to believe that (something is true or will happen).
additional_notes: The pronoun y refers to a previously mentioned idea, event, or situation. Commonly used with verbs like croire, refuser, vouloir, réussir (t'arrives à y croire?). Can express belief (y croire) or lack of belief (ne pas y croire). Translate as 'believe it' or 'believe in it' depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais y croire, même si c'est difficile.
native_language_example: I want to believe it, even if it's hard.

meaning: gently there / take it easy with it (do something gently or slowly there)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it combines the pronoun 'y' (meaning 'there' or 'to it') with the adverb 'doucement' ('gently', 'slowly', 'quietly'). Context determines whether 'y' refers to a place, an action, or an object mentioned earlier. Common uses: telling someone to go slowly somewhere (e.g. 'Va y doucement' = 'Go there slowly') or to be gentle with something/someone ('Fais-y doucement' = 'Be gentle with it/them').
target_language_example: Fais-y doucement avec ce meuble, il est fragile.
native_language_example: Be gentle with that piece of furniture, it's fragile.

meaning: there is/there are (some)
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken contraction of 'il y en a' used to say that some of something exist or are available. Common in everyday conversation. Can be followed by a noun or nothing (implying 'some' of a previously mentioned item). Example: 'Y en a plus' = 'There's no more' (contraction of 'Il n'y en a plus').
target_language_example: Y en a encore dans le frigo.
native_language_example: There are still some in the fridge.

meaning: There are two (of them).
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken French. Contraction of 'il y en a deux' = 'there are two (of them)'. 'Y' stands for 'il y a' and 'en' replaces a previously mentioned noun (meaning 'of them' or 'of it'). Used to state quantity when the thing has already been mentioned or is understood from context.
target_language_example: Tu veux des crêpes ? — Oui, y en a deux dans la boîte.
native_language_example: Do you want some pancakes? — Yes, there are two of them in the box.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French expression; likely a sequence of the pronoun/adverb 'y' ('there' / 'to it') followed immediately by the conjunction 'et' ('and'), or a typo/split of another phrase (e.g. 'y est').
additional_notes: There is no common idiomatic phrase 'y et'. 'y' is an adverbial pronoun used for places or to replace 'à' + thing (e.g. 'j'y vais', 'j'y pense'). 'et' is the coordinating conjunction 'and'. If you encounter 'y et' in running text, it usually means two separate words serving distinct roles ('Il y et...') or a typographical error; check surrounding words. It can appear when 'y' ends a clause and 'et' begins the next: e.g. 'Il y...' + 'et...'.
target_language_example: Il y et elle qui décident de la couleur.
native_language_example: He is there and she decides the color. (Note: sentence is unusual — 'y' normally needs a verb; this example deliberately places 'y et' as written to show the sequence.)

meaning: 'does it' or 'makes it' when combined with 'y' referring to a place/situation (literal) or 'y' as a neutral pronoun (idiomatic).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the verb 'faire' (conjugated) appearing after the pronoun 'y'. 'Y' most commonly replaces a previously mentioned place (there) or a clause introduced by 'à' (to it). Context determines meaning: e.g. 'Il y fait chaud' = 'It is hot there' (faire used impersonally about weather/conditions). Or 'Il y fait attention' (nonstandard) would mean 'He pays attention to it' but normally you would say 'Il y fait attention' is uncommon — more common: 'Il y fait attention' is acceptable for some verbs; many verbs combine naturally with 'y' + faire in idioms (e.g. 's'y faire' = 'get used to it').
target_language_example: Il y fait froid en hiver.
native_language_example: It's cold there in winter.

meaning: take it easy; go slowly; calm down
additional_notes: Informal expression used to tell someone to slow down, relax, or not overdo something. Often used in spoken French (especially in some regional or familiar contexts). Equivalent to 'doucement' or 'tranquille' in meaning. Can be used as an interjection: 'Y mollo!' or within a sentence: 'Vas-y mollo.'
target_language_example: Vas-y mollo avec ce gâteau, il est délicat.
native_language_example: Take it easy with that cake, it's delicate.

meaning: to spend (time) there / to spend (time) on it; also idiomatically 'to die' in informal contexts (j'ai cru y passer = I thought I was going to die).
additional_notes: Common pronominal phrase: 'y' refers to a place or situation previously mentioned. Primary, neutral meaning: to spend time (e.g. 'y passer trois heures' = spend three hours on it/there). Informally and idiomatically, used with danger or near-death: 'j'ai cru y passer' = I thought I was done for / I thought I was going to die. Context decides meaning.
target_language_example: On ne va pas y passer toute la journée.
native_language_example: We're not going to spend the whole day on that.

meaning: 'to die there' or 'to be killed' (informal, idiomatic)
additional_notes: Used idiomatically with the pronoun y to mean 'to die' or 'to be fatally harmed' (often suddenly or in a particular place/situation). Common in spoken French. Context determines tense: e.g. «J'ai cru que j'allais y rester» = I thought I was going to die. Not literal 'to stay there.'
target_language_example: On a failli tomber du pont — j'ai cru que j'allais y rester.
native_language_example: We almost fell off the bridge — I thought I was going to die.

meaning: Not a standard fixed expression in French; a sequence of two separate words ('y' + 'sans') that may appear adjacent in a sentence but do not form an idiom together.
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon as a deliberate phrase. 'y' is an unstressed pronoun meaning 'there' or replacing à + noun (e.g. J'y pense = I think about it). 'sans' is a preposition meaning 'without' and requires a noun or pronoun (e.g. sans sucre = without sugar). If you see 'y sans' together, it usually results from word order where 'y' closes a clause and 'sans' begins the next phrase (e.g. ...y, sans ...), or from informal punctuation/typing that omits a comma. To express 'without it/there' correctly, use 'sans' + noun or stressed pronoun (e.g. sans ça, sans lui) or restructure the sentence so the pronoun placement follows French clitic rules (e.g. Je n'y suis pas allé sans lui).
target_language_example: Il y est allé, y sans billet — (incorrect or colloquial writing); correct: Il y est allé sans billet.
native_language_example: He went there, y without a ticket — (incorrect or colloquial writing); correct: He went there without a ticket.

meaning: 'we are there' or 'we've arrived / we're at that point'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'nous' and the pronoun 'y' meaning 'there' or 'at that point'. Often appears in phrases like 'nous y sommes' (we're there/at that stage) and 'nous y sommes presque' (we're almost there). Can be used literally (arrived at a place) or figuratively (reached a stage/point in a process). In questions the order can invert: 'Y sommes-nous ?' = 'Are we there yet / are we at that point?'.
target_language_example: Après des heures de travail, nous y sommes enfin.
native_language_example: After hours of work, we're finally there.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase. Likely a fragment or typo of colloquial 'y a un' (short for 'il y a un') meaning 'there is a' or 'there's a'. On its own 'y un' is ungrammatical.
additional_notes: Standard form: 'il y a' = 'there is/there are'. In informal spoken/written French people often omit 'il' and say 'y a' or 'y a un/une' (e.g. 'y a un problème'). 'y un' without the verb 'a' is incorrect. Use 'y a un' or 'il y a un' instead.
target_language_example: Y un chien dort sous la table.
native_language_example: There's a dog sleeping under the table.

meaning: Let's go, everyone / come on, (you) guys.
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to urge a group to start moving or to encourage people to go. 'On y va' = 'let's go' or 'we're off'. The tag 'les' is a casual vocative addressing a group (les enfants, les filles, les gars, les mecs). Tone depends on following noun: 'les enfants' is neutral, 'les mecs' or 'les gars' is informal. Commonly used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Allez, on y va, les amis !
native_language_example: Come on, let's go, friends!

meaning: 'to see' or 'to find' in a certain way; often used impersonally to mean 'to see anything (wrong/right) in something' or 'to find any reason/objection'.
additional_notes: This expression combines the pronoun y (there/in it) with the verb voir (to see). It's commonly used in negative or interrogative constructions like « Je n'y vois rien » (I don't see anything in it / I don't understand it) or « Tu y vois un problème ? » (Do you see a problem with that?). It can mean 'to perceive', 'to understand', or 'to find (a problem/advantage)'. Context determines whether it's literal (seeing with eyes) or figurative (finding/considering).
target_language_example: Tu veux y voir clair ? — Non, mais j'essaie d'y voir.
native_language_example: Do you want to make things clear? — No, but I'm trying to see/figure it out.

meaning: (colloquial) you are not (there) / you don't have it / you don't understand — contraction where 'y' stands for 'y/il y' (there/it) and 'êtes' is 'être' (2nd person plural or polite singular) in negative context
additional_notes: Very informal spoken French; contraction commonly heard in casual or regional speech. 'Y êtes pas' is typically used as part of a negative phrase (instead of 'vous n'êtes pas' or 'tu n'es pas'). Depending on context it can mean 'you are not there', 'you don't get it', or 'you don't have it'. Avoid in formal writing; use standard forms in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Vous y êtes pas encore, on reviendra plus tard.
native_language_example: You aren't there yet, we'll come back later.

meaning: to be there
additional_notes: y replaces a place or location already mentioned or understood from context. It is commonly used to say that someone is present at a place, will arrive there, or feels as if they are there.
target_language_example: J'aimerais y être ce soir.
native_language_example: I'd like to be there tonight.

meaning: 'eyes of' (used to describe someone's eyes or a characteristic of eyes)
additional_notes: A fragment meaning 'eyes of' that must be completed (e.g. yeux de biche = 'doe eyes', yeux de lynx = 'sharp-eyed'). Commonly appears in descriptive expressions or idioms. Use with a noun or adjective to specify whose eyes or what kind of eyes.
target_language_example: Elle a des yeux de biche.
native_language_example: She has doe-like eyes.

meaning: part of a larger phrase meaning 'the eyes of the ...' (literally 'eyes of the')
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase on its own. 'yeux' = 'eyes' and 'de la' = 'of the' (feminine singular). You'll usually see it inside expressions like 'les yeux de la ville' or 'les yeux de la mère' where it links eyes to a following feminine noun. Remember French articles must agree: 'de la' before a feminine noun, 'du' before a masculine noun, 'des' for plural.
