target_language_example: Il a lu la lettre à voix haute pour que tout le monde comprenne.
native_language_example: He read the letter aloud so everyone could understand.

meaning: as much as one wants; freely; at will
additional_notes: Used to indicate unlimited quantity or unrestricted action. In everyday contexts (e.g., buffet) it means 'all-you-can-eat' or 'as much as you like'. In military/literal contexts (e.g., 'Feu à volonté') it means 'fire at will' or 'shoot freely' (give permission to shoot whenever desired). Tone is neutral; context determines whether it's casual (buffet) or serious (shooting).
target_language_example: Au buffet, vous pouvez manger à volonté.
native_language_example: At the buffet, you can eat as much as you like.

meaning: At your command; I am ready to obey you.
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrase often used in military, hierarchical or service contexts to show readiness to follow orders. Can be addressed to one person (formal 'vous') or used as a short reply meaning 'yes, sir/ma'am' or 'I'm at your disposal.' Not casual; in everyday civilian French you might instead say "je suis à votre disposition" or "je suis là".
target_language_example: À vos ordres, lieutenant — nous partons tout de suite.
native_language_example: At your command, lieutenant — we're leaving right away.

meaning: 'in your opinion' or 'what do you think?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone's opinion politely (formal/plural vous). Can appear at the beginning or end of a question. For informal/familiar situations use 'à ton avis'.
target_language_example: À votre avis, quel musée vaut le plus le détour?
native_language_example: In your opinion, which museum is most worth visiting?

meaning: A toast meaning 'to your health' / 'cheers'.
additional_notes: Used when clinking glasses or offering a toast. Formal/polite because of 'votre' (your). You can also say 'à ta santé' (informal singular) or simply 'santé!'. Often followed by the reason for the toast (e.g., 'à votre santé et à des jours meilleurs').
target_language_example: À votre santé — que ce nouveau projet réussisse !
native_language_example: Cheers — may this new project succeed!

meaning: At your service; happy to help you / ready to serve you.
additional_notes: Polite formula used to offer help or indicate readiness to assist. Common in customer service, formal speech, or when introducing oneself. Can be used sincerely or politely as a set phrase. Formal register; use with vous (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Je suis à votre service si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: I am at your service if you have any questions.

meaning: It's your turn / it's up to you to act.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that they should take their turn or that responsibility/action now belongs to them. Common in games (your turn) and in everyday situations (it's up to you). Polite/formal when using "vous"; informal equivalent with friends is "à toi de jouer."
target_language_example: À vous de jouer — que décidez-vous ?
native_language_example: It's your turn — what do you decide?

meaning: to you and (someone/something else); part of a phrase used to address someone plus others (e.g., family).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like "à vous et à votre famille/mère" when offering wishes or rights to someone and others connected to them. It is a simple prepositional phrase: "à" (to/for) + "vous" (you) + "et" (and). Followed by the second item (e.g., "à votre famille"). Used in formal and informal contexts depending on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Bonne année à vous et à votre famille !
native_language_example: Happy New Year to you and your family!

meaning: used to emphasize that something applies specifically to you (plural or formal) or to contrast 'you' with others
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of the preposition à and the stressed pronoun vous followed by que; it appears in structures that contrast or emphasize the person addressed, e.g. "À vous que ça regarde" (as for you) or "À vous que je parle" (I'm talking to you). It's more literary or formal than casual speech; in everyday French you might instead hear "quant à vous" or simply "vous" with intonation. Context determines whether "vous" is plural or formal singular.
target_language_example: À vous que cela intéresse, la réunion commence à 18 h.
native_language_example: To you who are interested, the meeting starts at 6 PM.

meaning: "it's up to you that I..." / introduces a contrast emphasizing the speaker's action or feeling toward 'you'
additional_notes: This short sequence is not a fixed idiom; it appears inside longer sentences to contrast 'you' with someone else (e.g. « À vous, que je respecte, ... ») or to emphasize that the speaker does something specifically regarding 'you'. Beginners will more often see full structures like « Quant à vous, ... » (as for you) or « Pour vous, je... ». Alone, « à vous que je » is incomplete and needs the surrounding sentence to make sense.
target_language_example: À vous que je connais depuis toujours, je veux dire merci.
native_language_example: To you, whom I have known forever, I want to say thank you.

meaning: 'to the truth' or part of the expression 'à vrai dire' (meaning 'to tell the truth' / 'actually')
additional_notes: Alone, 'à vrai' is incomplete and not used by itself in French. You will most often see it as the start of the fixed phrase 'à vrai dire' (literally 'to tell the truth'), which means 'actually', 'to be honest', or 'frankly'. Do not use 'à vrai' on its own; use 'à vrai dire'.
target_language_example: À vrai dire, je ne suis pas sûr de la réponse.
native_language_example: Actually, I'm not sure of the answer.

meaning: to be honest / actually / truthfully.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank, corrective, or clarifying remark. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause (À vrai dire, ...). Tone can be neutral or slightly candid; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: À vrai dire, je n'aime pas ce film.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don't like that movie.

meaning: 'at sight' or 'on sight' — immediately upon seeing; shoot/attack/act as soon as something is seen.
additional_notes: Used in orders or warnings meaning 'as soon as you see it/him/her, act immediately' (often used with verbs like tirer, tuer, abattre). Common in military, hunting, or dramatic contexts. Not a literal measurement of distance here; means 'upon sight'.
target_language_example: Si un intrus entre, neutralisez-le à vue.
native_language_example: If an intruder comes in, neutralize them on sight.

meaning: a short sequence combining the preposition à with the pronoun y; used when y follows à in speech or in certain constructions (often part of larger phrases).
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase: 'à' is a preposition and 'y' is a pronoun meaning 'there' or 'to it/to them'. They can appear together when a verb or expression requires à and the pronoun y replaces a previously mentioned place or thing. In normal writing they are usually separated (à y), but in spoken French you may hear them close together. Example contexts: parler à + y (rare), penser à + y (penser à + y replaces 'penser à cela'), or construction like 'vas-y' (different: combines 'va' + 'y'). Be careful: many verbs use 'à' plus a noun, and when that noun is replaced by 'y' you keep the préposition 'à' in the sentence, not attached to 'y'.
target_language_example: Je vais penser à y répondre demain.
native_language_example: I will think about answering it tomorrow.

meaning: to write a (something) — part of a construction meaning 'to be able/willing to write a ...' or 'to agree to write a ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment appearing after verbs like 'arriver à' (manage to), 'être disposé(e) à' (be willing to), or 'être prêt(e) à' (be ready to). It must be completed by a noun (une lettre, un email, etc.). Word order: verb + à + écrire + indefinite article + noun. Gender/number of the adjective (prêt/prête) matches the person. Use 'à écrire' with other verbs infinitive the same way.
target_language_example: Es-tu prêt à écrire une lettre demain ?
native_language_example: Are you ready to write a letter tomorrow?

meaning: 'approximately' or 'about' (used in the fixed expression 'à peu près').
additional_notes: Usually appears as the fixed phrase 'à peu près' meaning 'approximately' or 'roughly'. It can modify quantities, ages, amounts, comparisons, or degree (e.g., 'à peu près autant', 'à peu près ton âge', 'à peu près ivre'). In questions it asks for an approximate amount ('À peu près combien...'). Not used alone without 'près' in standard usage.
target_language_example: Il coûte à peu près vingt euros.
native_language_example: It costs about twenty euros.

meaning: 'how old is' (used in questions: Quel âge a-t-il ? / Quel âge a-t-elle ?)
additional_notes: This is the inverted verb form with the impersonal 'a-t-' insertion used when asking someone's age with inversion for pronunciation and grammar: 'Quel âge a-t-il ?' = 'How old is he?'. The '-t-' is added between the verb 'a' (avoir) and the subject pronoun 'il' or 'elle' when the verb ends in a vowel and the subject begins with a vowel sound, to make pronunciation and inversion grammatical. You will most often see the full forms 'Quel âge a-t-il ?' or 'Quel âge a-t-elle ?' in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Quel âge a-t-elle maintenant ?
native_language_example: How old is she now?

meaning: How old is this/that ... ?
additional_notes: Used to ask the age of a thing, place, building, machine, etc. 'Quel âge' = 'what age' and 'cet' is the masculine demonstrative used before a vowel sound (cet arbre, cet avion, cet hôpital). For feminine nouns use 'cette' (Quelle âge → actually 'Quel âge' stays same), and for plural use 'quel(s) âge' with 'ces' (e.g. 'Quel âge ont ces...' or 'Ces... ont quel âge?').
target_language_example: Quel âge a cet arbre ?
native_language_example: How old is this tree?

meaning: 'How old is this...' (asks the age of a person or thing).
additional_notes: Used inside the question 'Quel âge a cette ... ?' to ask the age of a specific feminine noun introduced by 'cette' (this/that). For masculine singular use 'Quel âge a ce ... ?' or for plural 'Quel âge ont ces ... ?'. Common for people, buildings, objects, artworks, vehicles, etc.
target_language_example: Quel âge a cette maison ?
native_language_example: How old is this house?

meaning: How old is your... (informal singular 'your')
additional_notes: Use to ask someone's or something's age. 'Ta' is the familiar singular possessive for feminine nouns (e.g. femme, fille, sœur, maison, voiture). For masculine nouns use 'ton' (Quel âge a ton frère ?). Formal or plural 'your' uses 'votre' (Quel âge a votre fille ?). Word order: Quel âge a + [possessive + noun].
target_language_example: Quel âge a ta voiture ?
native_language_example: How old is your car?

meaning: How old is your... (informal 'your' singular).
additional_notes: Use before a family member or person to ask their age. 'Ton' is the familiar singular possessive used with masculine nouns (ton amie if vowel sound). For formal or plural 'your', use 'Quel âge a votre...' (formal) or 'Quel âge a votre/vos...' depending on singular/plural. If asking about someone directly, you can also say 'Quel âge a [name] ?'.
target_language_example: Quel âge a ton frère ?
native_language_example: How old is your brother?

meaning: This sequence is not a correct French phrase. It looks like two words placed together: âge (age) and avez (you have).
additional_notes: In French, âge is a noun meaning "age." Avez is the second-person plural (or polite singular) present of avoir: "you have." They do not form a fixed expression when simply put together as "âge avez." To ask someone's age or speak about age you would use correct constructions such as: "Quel âge avez-vous ?" (formal/plural) or "Quel âge as-tu ?" (informal/singular). To say "to have age" literally you use avoir + âge (e.g. "J'ai vingt ans" = I am twenty years old).
target_language_example: Quel âge avez-vous ?
native_language_example: How old are you?

meaning: How old were you when you...?
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's age at the time of a past event. Formal/plural/polite because it uses 'vous'. Followed by a past tense verb (e.g. 'avez appris', 'vous êtes marié(e)'). For informal singular use, say 'Quel âge avais-tu quand tu... ?'.
target_language_example: Quel âge aviez-vous quand vous avez déménagé en ville ?
native_language_example: How old were you when you moved to the city?

meaning: at the age of / age of
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone's age when something happened or to state how old someone/something is. Often followed by a number (âge de 20 ans) or by an infinitive to express 'at the age of [doing something]' (à l'âge de commencer — though more common: 'à l'âge de + number'). In spoken French, you may also see 'à l'âge de' instead of 'âge de' at the start of a phrase. Requires context (the article 'l'' is often used: 'à l'âge de 30 ans').
target_language_example: Il a déménagé à l'âge de 18 ans.
native_language_example: He moved at the age of 18.

meaning: used to compare ages: 'the same age as' or 'as old as'.
additional_notes: Appears in comparisons with 'le même âge que' (the same age as) or with qualifiers like 'à peu près' (about). Structure: [il/elle a] + [le même âge que] + [someone]. You can also say 'a le même âge que moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux'.
target_language_example: Elle a le même âge que moi.
native_language_example: She is the same age as me.

meaning: …years old (as old) as me; 'the same age as me'.
additional_notes: Used to compare ages: typically appears after a noun or pronoun with a comparative structure (e.g. 'Il a le même âge que moi' = 'He is the same age as me'). Can also appear in shorter informal replies: 'Moi ? J'ai 30 ans.' / 'Et toi ?' — 'J'ai le même âge que toi.' Note word order: French uses 'le même âge que...' rather than repeating 'âge que moi' alone in formal sentences.
target_language_example: Elle a le même âge que moi.
native_language_example: She is the same age as me.

meaning: older than my… (used when comparing ages; 'âgée' is feminine form).
additional_notes: This fragment appears in comparisons using 'plus ... que' (more ... than). 'âgée' agrees in gender with the person described (âgée for feminine, âgé for masculine). 'mon' is the possessive 'my' used before a masculine noun (mon père, mon frère). For a feminine noun use 'ma' (ma mère). Full structure: Subject + est + plus + adjective + que + possessor + noun. Example sentences show family comparisons.
target_language_example: Ma cousine est plus âgée que mon cousin.
native_language_example: My cousin (female) is older than my cousin (male).

meaning: it was
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase using 'ça' (it/that) + past tense of 'être' (to be). Used to describe past situations or to react to a question about how something went (e.g., "Ça a été, l'école ?" = "How was school?"). Can be followed by a noun (Ça a été un désastre) or by an adjective/short comment (Ça a été bien). Informal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Ça a été une longue journée, mais on a fini le projet.
native_language_example: It was a long day, but we finished the project.

meaning: An exclamation expressing surprise, disbelief, or amazement (like "well I'll be" / "wow").
additional_notes: Used to react to something unexpected. Tone can be amused, shocked, or impressed depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken and informal written French; often preceded by interjections (oh, eh ben, bah). Not rude.
target_language_example: Ça alors, tu as réussi à finir le projet si vite !
native_language_example: Well I'll be, you managed to finish the project so quickly!

meaning: 'that/this happen' (used in questions like "How did/ could this/that happen?")
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrased questions: Comment (ai-je / as-tu / a-t-il / etc.) pu laisser ça arriver ? Literally 'let that happen' but idiomatically means 'allow this to happen' or 'how did this happen?' Used to express surprise, regret, or blame. 'Ça' = 'this/that'; 'arriver' = 'to happen'.
target_language_example: Comment ai-je laissé ça arriver ?
native_language_example: How did I let this happen?

meaning: Not a fixed idiom by itself; the sequence 'ça au' occurs when the demonstrative 'ça' ('that/this/it') is followed by the contraction 'au' (à + le = 'to the'/'at the') as part of a larger clause.
additional_notes: There is no standalone expression 'ça au'. Treat 'ça' and 'au' separately: 'ça' is informal demonstrative pronoun; 'au' is contraction of 'à' + 'le'. The sequence appears when 'ça' is used in a clause and is immediately followed by another phrase beginning with 'au' (often separated by a comma or pause). Example contexts: « Ça au cinéma... », « Ça au travail... ». For clarity, native speakers usually insert a pause or punctuation: « Ça, au cinéma, ... » or rephrase to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Ça au cinéma, ça arrive souvent.
native_language_example: That at the cinema happens often.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone expression; it's the informal demonstrative 'ça' ('that/it') directly followed by the contracted preposition 'aux' (à + les = 'to the' / 'at the') before a noun or noun phrase. It expresses 'that/it to the...' or 'that/it at the...' depending on context and usually requires a sentence restructuring or punctuation in natural French.
additional_notes: You won't find 'ça aux' as an independent idiom. It occurs when 'ça' appears immediately before a prepositional phrase beginning with 'aux' (e.g. 'ça aux enfants...'). In speech this is common but in writing it's often clearer to use a comma ('Ça, aux enfants, ...'), rephrase with 'cela' or move the elements. 'Ça' is informal; prefer 'cela' or a different construction in formal registers.
target_language_example: Ça aux enfants, ça ne plaît pas.
native_language_example: That to the children, that is not pleasing. / Children don't like that.

meaning: it had
additional_notes: A common everyday combination of ça + avait (imperfect of avoir). Ça often means 'it', 'that', or 'this' depending on context, and is less formal than cela.
target_language_example: Ça avait l'air facile.
native_language_example: It looked easy.

meaning: a nonstandard or colloquial word order meaning 'before that' or 'previously' (standard form is 'avant ça' or 'ça, avant' in some constructions)
additional_notes: 'Ça avant' is uncommon and not standard; French normally uses 'avant ça' for 'before that'. You might hear 'ça avant' in casual speech, poetic inversion, or in emphatic/stilted constructions, but avoid using it in formal writing. When used, context and intonation determine the meaning.
target_language_example: Je te disais ça avant, mais tu ne m'écoutais pas.
native_language_example: I told you that before, but you weren't listening to me.

meaning: literally 'that/this with' — not a fixed idiom; occurs when 'ça' (this/that) is directly followed by 'avec' (with), typically in informal or clumsy phrasing and often requires reordering or punctuation in standard French.
additional_notes: Not a set phrase. In standard written French you normally separate 'ça' and 'avec' or reorder (e.g. 'Ça, avec lui...' or 'Avec lui, ça...'). Using 'ça avec' as a contiguous chunk is colloquial and can sound awkward; it may appear in rapid speech or casual writing. Prefer clearer constructions for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Je ne ferai pas ça avec toi.
native_language_example: I will not do that with you.

meaning: used in casual speech to emphasize or confirm something when embedded in longer expressions (often part of phrases like «ça va bien» or «ça me va bien»).
additional_notes: Alone, 'ça bien' is not a standard complete phrase in French and sounds clipped; it normally appears inside longer expressions. Common full forms: «ça va bien» (it's going well/I'm fine), «ça me va bien» (that suits me/it fits me well). Informal register — avoid using 'ça bien' by itself; use the full expressions instead.
target_language_example: Oui, ça bien, ça va — je t'explique.
native_language_example: Yes, that's fine, it's okay — I'll explain to you.

meaning: 'that is' or 'this is' used to emphasize or introduce something
additional_notes: Common spoken structure: ça, c'est + noun/phrase to highlight or contrast something. Often used to point out, emphasize, or contrast an item among others. Can be followed by a clause: «Ça, c'est clair.» In fast speech the comma is often omitted: «ça c'est» or reduced to «ça» plus intonation.
target_language_example: Ça c'est exactement ce que je voulais.
native_language_example: That is exactly what I wanted.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken or nonstandard sequence. 'Ça' = 'that/it'; 'ce' is a demonstrative pronoun used in structures like 'c'est'.
additional_notes: Native speakers do not usually say 'ça ce' together. If it appears, it may be a typo, a pause with a following demonstrative ('ça, ce ...'), or very informal/redundant speech for emphasis (rare and nonstandard). Learn 'ça' and 'c'est' separately instead.
target_language_example: Ça ce n'est pas correct.
native_language_example: That, that is not correct.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; likely a fragment combining 'ça' (that/it) and 'chez' (at the home/place of). It appears only as part of a larger construction (e.g. 'ça chez moi...') rather than as an independent expression.
additional_notes: You will not find 'ça chez' used alone as a stable expression. If encountered, it's almost certainly the start of a phrase where 'chez' is followed by a noun or pronoun: 'ça chez moi...', 'ça chez lui...', 'ça chez nous...'. In speech punctuation or pauses can make it look like two-word unit, but grammatically 'ça' and 'chez' serve separate functions. Use 'ça' to refer to something mentioned and 'chez' to indicate location/possession. Example patterns: 'Ça chez moi, c'est différent.' or 'Ça chez lui, ça pose problème.'
target_language_example: Ça chez moi, ça ne tient pas.
native_language_example: That, at my place, doesn't hold up.

meaning: a spoken filler used to introduce an example or to hesitate (similar to 'like' or 'you know' in English).
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial. Often appears in speech before giving an example, explanation, or when hesitating: e.g. « Il y a des choses, ça, comme... » It can combine with other words (ça, comme ça) or appear as part of a sentence fragment and is not a complete grammatical structure on its own. Not used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Il y a des choses, ça comme les retards, ça m'énerve.
native_language_example: There are things, like delays, that annoy me.

meaning: How's that? / What about that?
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to ask for someone's opinion or reaction to something just said or shown. Often appears as a short question: 'Ça comment ?' or preceded by 'Et' as 'Et ça comment ?'. Tone and context determine whether it's casual curiosity, surprise or mild challenge.
target_language_example: Ça comment ? Tu aimes ça ?
native_language_example: How's that? Do you like that?

meaning: 'that's bad' / 'that sucks' / 'that's risky' (informal)
additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to complain about something, say it's unpleasant, dangerous, or likely to go badly. Tone ranges from mild annoyance to strong disapproval depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken French; avoid in formal writing. Can refer to a situation, an object, or a plan.
target_language_example: Tu vas y aller tout seul ? Non, ça craint.
native_language_example: You're going there alone? No, that would suck / that's risky.

meaning: colloquial filler pointing to something within someone's possession or experience (literally 'that in his/her/its') — usually part of a larger phrase, not a standalone expression.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it appears when a speaker refers to 'that' (ça) being 'in' (dans) someone's thing/situation (sa). You will usually hear it in casual spoken French as part of a sentence like « Il a ça dans sa valise » (He has that in his suitcase) or « Tu as ça dans ta tête ? » (Do you have that in your head?). Pay attention to agreement: sa changes to son/ta etc. depending on the possessor and the gender/number of the possessed noun.
target_language_example: Elle a ça dans sa tête depuis des années.
native_language_example: She has that in her head for years.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase on its own; depends on context — literally 'that/it in a'. Often part of larger expressions (e.g. « mettre ça dans un tiroir » = 'put that in a drawer').
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a standalone idiom. 'Ça' = 'that/it'; 'dans' = 'in'; 'un' = 'a' (masculine). You will see it when 'ça' is the object and a masculine singular noun follows (un + noun): 'ça dans un sac', 'ça dans un carton', etc. Pay attention to the noun that follows to understand the full meaning. Word order and agreement are regular; if the noun is feminine use 'une' (e.g. 'ça dans une boîte').
target_language_example: Je mets ça dans un sac.
native_language_example: I'll put that in a bag.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; usually a fragment where "ça" (that/it) appears next to the partitive/article "de la" before a feminine noun — commonly found in colloquial speech or in transcription fragments meaning roughly "that kind of.../that (some) ..." depending on context.
additional_notes: Not a set expression to be used as-is in formal writing. Often appears as part of a larger utterance (e.g. "ça de la chance" or "c'est ça de la ...") or as a casual clipped sequence in spoken French. Interpretation depends on the surrounding sentence; sometimes reflects nonstandard word order or casual elision. Check the full sentence to determine if it's simply "ça" + "de la" + noun.
target_language_example: Tu appelles ça de la cuisine, sérieusement ? — Non, mais ça de la, c'est n'importe quoi.
native_language_example: You call that cooking, seriously? — I mean, that sort of thing is nonsense.

meaning: closer / more closely (as in 'look at that more closely').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'voir ça de plus près' meaning to examine or look at something more carefully or from up close. 'Ça' is informal 'that/this'. You can replace 'voir' with other verbs of looking/examining (regarder, étudier). Used in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Allons voir ça de plus près au musée.
native_language_example: Let's go see that more closely at the museum.

meaning: literally 'that tomorrow'; used informally to refer to 'that (thing) tomorrow' or to postpone something until tomorrow
additional_notes: This is an informal, conversational grouping of words rather than a fixed idiom. You will most often encounter 'ça demain' as part of a larger phrase or sentence like 'On fait ça demain ?' meaning 'Shall we do that tomorrow?' Standalone 'ça demain' is unusual; use complete phrases: 'On fait ça demain', 'On voit ça demain'.
target_language_example: On remet le rendez-vous — on fait ça demain ?
native_language_example: Let's move the appointment — shall we do that tomorrow?

meaning: 'ça' = 'that/it'; the fragment 'ça depuis des' is not a complete fixed phrase — it typically appears at the start of a longer expression meaning 'that for (some period) ...' or as an informal clipped sequence inside a sentence.
additional_notes: Not a standalone idiom. 'Ça' is informal pronoun meaning 'that/it'. 'Depuis' means 'since' or 'for' (duration). 'Des' is the plural partitive or contraction of 'de' + 'les' meaning 'some' or 'of the'. In natural French this fragment is usually followed by a time noun (années, mois, jours) and more context: e.g. 'ça depuis des années' or appears within longer constructions like 'Je pense à ça depuis des semaines.' Beginners should learn complete patterns rather than the fragment alone.
target_language_example: Je pense à ça depuis des semaines.
native_language_example: I've been thinking about that for weeks.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment or typo (e.g. 'ça, des...' or part of 'ça' followed directly by 'des'). By itself it has no clear standalone meaning in French.
additional_notes: This sequence does not form a common multiword expression. It can appear when 'ça' (that/it) is followed by a noun phrase introduced by the plural indefinite article 'des' without intervening punctuation or words, often due to casual speech, transcription, or a typographical error. If you encounter 'ça des' in text, check for missing punctuation or omitted words. Possible clarifications depending on context: insert a comma ('ça, des...'), add a verb ('ça, ce sont des...'), or correct to similar phrases like 'ça donne' or 'ça, c'est'.
target_language_example: Ça des problèmes? Tu veux dire 'ça, des problèmes' ?
native_language_example: "Ça des problèmes?" Do you mean "that — problems"?

meaning: that/this (thing or remark) in front of; used to say something is placed or said in the presence of someone or something.
additional_notes: Combines 'ça' (that/this) with 'devant' (in front of, before, in the presence of). Used both for physical placement (e.g., 'found that in front of my door') and for social context meaning 'in front of someone' (e.g., 'don't say that in front of him'). Tone depends on sentence; can be neutral for location or emotional/critical when referring to actions or comments made in someone's presence.
target_language_example: Ne fais pas ça devant les enfants.
native_language_example: Don't do that in front of the children.

meaning: 'that which' or 'what ... of it' (used in relative constructions after 'ça')
additional_notes: Rare/uncommon combination: 'ça' (that/it/this) + relative pronoun 'dont' (meaning 'of which' or 'whose'). Typically appears in phrases like «ça dont je t'ai parlé» = 'that which I told you about' or more naturally «ce dont je t'ai parlé». Native speakers usually prefer 'ce dont' rather than 'ça dont' in standard French. Use 'ça dont' mostly in casual speech or for emphasis, but 'ce dont' is safer for learners.
target_language_example: Ça dont je t'ai parlé est intéressant, mais on dit plus souvent «ce dont je t'ai parlé».
native_language_example: That which I told you about is interesting, but people more often say "ce dont I told you about".

meaning: 'that which I' or 'what I ... (of which I)'.
additional_notes: Not a complete, standard phrase on its own. It combines colloquial 'ça' (that/it) with the relative pronoun 'dont' (of which/about which) and subject 'je'. Standard/formal French uses 'ce dont je' rather than 'ça dont je'. 'Ça dont je' may appear in casual speech or regional/colloquial constructions but can sound awkward. Typically followed by a verb: e.g. 'ça dont je parle' = 'that which I am talking about' (more natural: 'ce dont je parle').
target_language_example: Ça dont je parle n'est pas clair.
native_language_example: That which I am talking about is not clear.

meaning: 'that again' or an exclamation meaning 'of all things!' or 'would you believe it' (expresses surprise, annoyance, or resignation about something recurring).
additional_notes: Used conversationally to react to an event or fact that happens again or is unexpected/annoying. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be neutral surprise, mild annoyance, or ironic resignation. Often appears in informal speech and combined with gestures or other words (e.g. "Ah, ça encore...", "Et ça encore!").
target_language_example: Ah, ça encore — la photocopieuse est en panne.
native_language_example: Oh, that again — the copier is broken.

meaning: that together / all of that together (spoken, colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression. Used to refer to a group of things, actions, or an overall situation as a whole. Often appears in phrases like « tout ça ensemble » or « ça, ensemble » to mean 'all that' or 'that combined'. Alone, 'ça ensemble' is colloquial and may sound incomplete; learners will more often hear 'tout ça' or 'tout ça ensemble'.
target_language_example: Tu veux garder ça ensemble ou séparer les pièces ?
native_language_example: Do you want to keep that together or separate the pieces?

meaning: 'that and' (rare/elliptical fragment); not a complete fixed phrase in French
additional_notes: Ça = 'that' or 'it' (informal). 'Ça et' by itself is not a standard fixed expression; you'll usually see 'ça et ça' (this and that) or 'ça et autre chose' (that and something else) where 'et' simply means 'and'. Alone, 'ça et' is an incomplete fragment and should be followed by another element. Use in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: Ça et ça, c'est la même chose.
native_language_example: That and that are the same thing.

meaning: Informal: 'How's it going?' or 'Everything alright?'; can also mean 'It's going well.'
additional_notes: Very informal/slang. Used to ask if someone is doing OK or if a situation is fine, similar to 'Ça va ?' or English 'How's it going?' Can also be used as a brief positive reply: 'Ça gaze.' = 'It's going well.' Mostly spoken, casual; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Salut ! Ça gaze ?
native_language_example: Hi! How's it going?

meaning: not a standard fixed French phrase; likely a mistaken or nonstandard sequence. Could appear in speech as 'ça, hier' meaning 'that, yesterday' or be an error for 'c'était hier' ('it was yesterday').
additional_notes: As written without punctuation, 'ça hier' is not common or idiomatic. If spoken with a pause ('ça, hier') it can function in a sentence to refer to 'that' and place it in time: e.g. 'Ça, hier, ...'. For correct alternatives learn: 'hier' = 'yesterday', 'c'était hier' = 'it was yesterday', 'ça, c'était hier' = 'that was yesterday'.
target_language_example: Ça hier, on n'avait pas le temps de finir.
native_language_example: That, yesterday, we didn't have time to finish.

meaning: 'that, he/it' (colloquial spoken sequence where ça is followed by il for emphasis or to introduce a comment about someone/something).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in spoken French when the speaker uses ça (that/it) and then il/elle to comment on a person or thing—often to contrast, emphasize, or topicalize (e.g., « Ça il est sympa. » meaning 'That one, he's nice.'). It's informal and more common in conversation than in formal writing. The literal words keep their normal meanings (compositional), but the combination serves pragmatic/discourse functions (emphasis, topic marking).
target_language_example: Ça il ne supporte pas la chaleur.
native_language_example: That one, he can't stand the heat.

meaning: 'it will be fine' / 'that will do' (reassurance or acceptance).
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone, say something is acceptable, or express that a situation will improve. Can mean 'that will do' when accepting an option, or 'it'll be okay' when offering comfort. Tone and context determine whether it's optimistic, resigned, or simply approving.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas pour le dîner, ça ira.
native_language_example: Don't worry about dinner, it'll be fine.

meaning: A colloquial spoken-device to emphasize or contrast a point about the speaker: 'as for that, I...' or 'that — I (do/don't)...'
additional_notes: Common in everyday spoken French. 'Ça' refers to something just mentioned; 'je' introduces the speaker's stance or reaction. Often followed by a verb or short comment (e.g. « Ça je l'accepte. »). Stress and pause often occur between 'ça' and 'je' in speech.
target_language_example: Ça je ne l'accepte pas.
native_language_example: That — I do not accept it.

meaning: short, colloquial way to mean 'that one' or 'that (feminine) thing' in spoken French (often contracted from 'ça, la' or used in regional speech).
additional_notes: Very informal and regional; usage is uncommon in standard written French. Often heard in casual spoken French when referring to a feminine noun previously mentioned or pointed out: 'ça' = that/it, 'la' = there/that (feminine). Depending on context it can mean 'that one (feminine)' or simply add emphasis. Not to be confused with 'ça la fait' or other fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Tu veux garder la robe ou vendre ça la ?
native_language_example: Do you want to keep the dress or sell that one?

meaning: That works / That's cool / It's okay (informal approval).
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression used to say something is acceptable, successful, or gives the desired effect. Tone can range from neutral approval ('that will do') to positive enthusiasm ('that's great') depending on context and intonation. Often used in casual conversation among friends.
target_language_example: Tu veux qu'on se retrouve à 18h ? — Oui, ça le fait.
native_language_example: Do you want to meet at 6? — Yes, that works.

meaning: that one / that (nearby or just-mentioned thing) — used to point out something.
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken expression used to draw attention to or specify an object or idea already in view or just mentioned. Often accompanied by a gesture (pointing) or tone. Can be shortened to just « ça »; « là » adds emphasis or indicates proximity ('that one there'). Used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Donne-moi ça là, sur la table.
native_language_example: Give me that one there, on the table.

meaning: it works
additional_notes: Common informal phrase. Literally 'that walks' but used to say something functions ('it works') or to agree/confirm a plan ('okay', 'that works'). In negative form 'ça ne marche pas' or colloquially 'ça marche pas' = 'it doesn't work' or 'that won't do.'
target_language_example: D'accord, on se retrouve à 18 h si ça marche pour toi.
native_language_example: Okay, we meet at 6 pm if that works for you.

meaning: 'it works at' or 'it runs on' (describes something functioning on/with a particular thing or at a certain rate)
additional_notes: A colloquial structure using ça marche ('it works', 'okay') followed by à + noun to specify how or with what something works (e.g. 'ça marche à l'électricité' = 'it runs on electricity', or 'ça marche à 100 km/h' = 'it runs at 100 km/h'). Common in spoken French. Can also be used metaphorically (e.g. 'ça marche à la confiance' = 'it works by/with trust').
target_language_example: Cette lampe, ça marche à piles.
native_language_example: This lamp runs on batteries.

meaning: It bites / it's biting (literal) — can also mean 'it's effective' or 'it takes' in some contexts.
additional_notes: Usually used literally about an animal or object that bites (e.g., a dog, fish, or a tool). In fishing, 'ça mord ?' asks 'Is it biting?' meaning 'are the fish biting?'. Can be used figuratively to mean something 'works' or 'has effect' (e.g., a remark that 'bites' emotionally). Informal, common in spoken French. Negative form: 'ça ne mord pas' or colloquially 'ça mord pas'.
target_language_example: Jette l'appât, regarde si ça mord.
native_language_example: Throw the bait, see if it's biting.

meaning: 'it's okay' / 'never mind' / 'it doesn't matter'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone, downplay a problem, or say that something is not important. Tone can be neutral or comforting. Common in spoken French; can replace 'ce n'est pas grave' or 'peu importe' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas grave, ça ne fait rien.
native_language_example: It's okay, it doesn't matter.

meaning: No, not that / definitely not (used to reject or disagree with something).
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression. Often used to contrast or refuse a suggestion, idea, or possibility; tone can be emphatic. It can appear alone (Ça non !) or with more words (Ça non, je ne peux pas). Similar to "pas question" or simply "non" but with extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Tu veux venir ce soir ? — Ça non, j'ai trop de travail.
native_language_example: You want to come tonight? — No way, I have too much work.

meaning: Colloquial spoken filler meaning roughly 'as for that' or 'that, we/one/people...' used to introduce or comment on a topic; typically the demonstrative 'ça' is followed by subject 'on' to shift focus or give an opinion/action about that thing.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Not a fixed lexicalized idiom but a common sequence used to emphasize or contrast: 'Ça on...' often begins a clause (e.g. 'Ça on peut le faire'). Pronunciation links the words in flow. Translates often as 'as for that' or 'that, we/you/one...'.
target_language_example: Ça on peut le faire demain.
native_language_example: As for that, we can do it tomorrow.

meaning: 'this or that' / 'this one or...' (informal, used when offering a choice or clarification).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Ça' = 'that/this' and 'ou' = 'or'. Often used alone or followed by a noun/pronoun to present options: e.g. « Tu veux ça ou ça ? » (Do you want this one or that one?). Can also appear in fragments: « Ça, ou… ? » when asking for an alternative or clarification. Not a fixed idiom—just the combination of two common words.
target_language_example: Tu prends le poulet, ça ou le poisson ?
native_language_example: Are you taking the chicken, this or the fish?

meaning: Informal spoken fragment used to ask about location or to refer back to a place/situation—depends on punctuation and context. Can mean 'Where is that?' or start a question like 'That—where (is it/are you going with it)?'
additional_notes: Colloquial; common in casual conversation. 'Ça' = 'that/it'; 'où' = 'where'. Often appears as a fragment or in shortened questions (e.g., 'Ça où ?' or embedded in speech). Avoid in formal writing; prefer full forms like 'Où est-ce que c'est ?' or 'Où est-ce que tu vas avec ça ?'. Tone/pause changes meaning: 'Ça, où ?' = 'Where is that?'; 'Ça où tu vas ?' is nonstandard/spoken for 'Where are you going with that?'.
target_language_example: Ça où ?
native_language_example: Where is that?

meaning: Not a fixed standalone expression in French; typically an incomplete sequence that appears at the boundary of clauses or when speech is elided. Its meaning depends on the full construction (e.g., 'ça, par contre', 'ça par ici'), so you must consider surrounding words to interpret it.
additional_notes: Alone, 'ça par' is incomplete and should not be treated as a set phrase. You may encounter the exact adjacent words 'ça par' in casual speech or writing when punctuation or words are omitted (e.g., 'Ça par…' before a correction or aside), or across clause boundaries ('Ça par [contre]...'). Learners should look for the full expressions that follow or precede it (par contre, par ici, par là, par hasard, etc.).
target_language_example: Ça par contre, ce n'est pas acceptable.
native_language_example: That, on the other hand, is not acceptable.

meaning: 'that because' — not a standard fixed phrase; a sequence of words that can appear informally when 'ça' refers to something and 'parce' begins 'parce que'
additional_notes: The sequence 'ça parce' by itself is not grammatically complete in French. In informal speech you might encounter it as part of a clause where 'parce' is the start of 'parce que' (often with elision or interrupted speech), e.g. 'Ça, parce...'. More natural forms: 'C'est parce que...' or 'Ça, c'est parce que...'. Use with caution — write 'parce que' in full in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ça, parce que tu l'as demandé, je vais t'aider.
native_language_example: That, because you asked for it, I'll help you.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase; an informal, incomplete combination that can appear in spoken French where 'ça' (that/it) precedes 'parce que' (‘because’). Often part of a larger clause (e.g. 'ça, parce que...') and generally understood as 'that, because...' or a colloquial shortcut for 'c'est parce que' ('it's because').
additional_notes: Not an idiomatic or grammatically complete standalone expression in standard French. You will commonly hear 'ça, c'est parce que...' or simply 'c'est parce que...' in clear speech. If used, 'ça' is typically followed by a pause or comma: 'ça, parce que...' and then a reason clause. Marked informal and conversational.
target_language_example: Ça, parce que je n'avais pas le temps, je n'ai pas pu venir.
native_language_example: That, because I didn't have the time, I couldn't come.

meaning: 'it's about' or 'it deals with' (informal), or used to ask if something 'works' or 'connects' in context.
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken French. As 'ça parle de...' it means 'it's about...' (referring to a topic). On its own, in casual speech, 'ça parle ?' can mean 'Does that make sense?' or 'Will that work?' depending on context. Tone and surrounding words determine meaning. Not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Le film, ça parle d'une amitié improbable.
native_language_example: The movie is about an unlikely friendship.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a fragment or misheard sequence (no fixed meaning).
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'ça pour ton' is not a correct or common French expression. It may come from a mishearing or from combining words that don't grammatically fit together. Possible intended forms and meanings: 
- 'ça pour toi' = 'this/that for you' (pointing something out or offering something). 
- 'c'est pour ton...' (informal contraction) as part of 'c'est pour ton ...' meaning 'it's for your...' followed by a noun (e.g. 'c'est pour ton bien' = 'it's for your own good'). 
- 'ça, pour [quelque chose]' can appear in colloquial emphatic constructions (e.g. 'ça, pour être grand, il est grand' = 'he's really tall'), but needs a correct syntax. 
If you meant a specific phrase, check the spelling or provide the full sentence.
target_language_example: C'est pour toi, pas «ça pour ton».
native_language_example: It's for you, not 'ça pour ton'.

meaning: a clipped, colloquial fragment meaning 'that (which) she' used in spoken French before a relative clause (not a complete phrase on its own).
additional_notes: This is not a standard, complete grammatical expression by itself. It looks like a contraction of 'c'est que' or a colloquial linking of 'ça' + 'que' + 'elle' and may appear in spoken, regional or emphatic speech as part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'c'est ça qu'elle a dit' → 'that's what she said'). On its own it will sound unfinished; learners will more often encounter full forms such as 'c'est ce que elle/elle a' (usually 'c'est ce qu'elle...') or 'ça, c'est elle qui...'.
target_language_example: C'est ça qu'elle a dit hier.
native_language_example: That's what she said yesterday.

meaning: 'that' or 'the fact that' (informal/casual clipped form; typically part of spoken, hesitating speech and often grammatically incomplete on its own)
additional_notes: Not a standard fixed phrase. Appears in rapid or colloquial speech when a speaker truncates fuller forms like « c'est que » or « ce qu'il ». Usually occurs inside a larger sentence and can signal hesitation or emphasis. Avoid in formal writing; prefer « c'est que », « ce que », or « ce qu'il » when appropriate.
target_language_example: Je savais pas que ça qu'il ferait ça, franchement.
native_language_example: I didn't know that he would do that, honestly.

meaning: a clipped/colloquial combination meaning 'that (which) we/one ...' or 'so that we/one ...' depending on context
additional_notes: This is an informal, spoken sequence where ça (that/it/so) is followed by qu'on (que + on). Its exact sense depends on the rest of the sentence: it can introduce a relative clause ('that we…') or a result/purpose idea ('so that we…') in casual speech. You will mostly see it in conversation, not in formal writing. Be attentive to liaison and punctuation: in careful speech writers might use « ça, qu'on… » or rephrase to « ce que l'on… » (more formal) or « ce qu'on… ».
target_language_example: On laisse la porte ouverte, ça qu'on puisse rentrer facilement.
native_language_example: We leave the door open, so that we can get in easily.

meaning: literally 'that when' — used informally in questions to ask when something will happen or to prompt someone to set a date/time.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Often appears in short questions or prompts like 'Ça, c'est quand ?' or combined with a verb/phrase: 'Le dîner, ça quand ?' — meaning 'When is the dinner?' Used to insist on wanting a time/date or to remind someone to decide. Not a fixed idiom; it's simply the demonstrative 'ça' + question word 'quand'.
target_language_example: La réunion, ça quand ?
native_language_example: The meeting — when is it?

meaning: 'that' or 'that which' when referring to something the other person did or wants (colloquial, used in questions/statements).
additional_notes: Appears inside structures like "C'est ça que tu...?" or "C'est à ça que tu...?" to point to something specific (an action, object, or reason) tied to 'tu'. Often used in spoken/colloquial French to confirm, question, or show surprise about what the other person did, wanted, or is doing. The full phrase usually begins with "C'est" or "C'est à". Not a fixed idiom by itself—meaning comes from the whole clause.
target_language_example: C'est ça que tu veux vraiment ?
native_language_example: Is that really what you want?

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a non-idiomatic fragment that could be an incorrect attempt to say 'that which you...' or a colloquial, clumsy sequence like 'ça que vous...' used informally but ungrammatically.
additional_notes: "Ça que vous" is not a common or grammatically correct full phrase in standard French. Speakers normally use "ce que vous..." for 'that which you...' or restructure the sentence (e.g. "ça, vous..." to introduce a comment). In casual speech someone might say "ça que vous..." by mistake or in clipped talk, but it is best avoided in written or formal French. Use "ce que vous..." or "ça, vous..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Ça que vous dites n'est pas clair.
native_language_example: That which you say is not clear.

meaning: a spoken/conversational fragment meaning 'that I have' or 'that I've got' (informal, often part of a larger clause)
additional_notes: This is not a complete standard written phrase but a colloquial, reduced sequence you might hear in casual speech when the speaker omits a relative pronoun or connector (e.g. instead of 'ce que j'ai' or 'ça que j'ai' used regionally). In careful French you'd more often see 'ce que j'ai' ('what I have' / 'that I have'). 'Ça que j'ai' can appear in emphatic or familiar speech: 'C'est ça que j'ai dit' → 'That's what I said' (more standard: 'C'est ce que j'ai dit'). Use in writing is rare; prefer 'ce que j'ai' or full clauses in formal contexts.
target_language_example: C'est ça que j'ai trouvé hier.
native_language_example: That's what I found yesterday.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment used in colloquial speech meaning roughly 'that that I...' or part of a clause where 'ça' = 'that/this' and 'que je' = 'that I'. It is incomplete by itself and usually continues with a verb or clause.
additional_notes: This sequence is generally a fragment rather than an idiom. You will most often encounter it inside longer colloquial sentences (e.g. for emphasis or after pauses). Prefer full, standard alternatives such as 'ce que je...' (what I...) or 'c'est que je...' (it's that I...). Using 'ça que je' alone sounds unfinished in French.
target_language_example: Tu vois ça que je t'ai montré ?
native_language_example: Do you see that which I showed you?

meaning: 'that which I... (fragment)' — an incomplete/clipped fragment, not a standard fixed phrase; likely part of a longer sentence where a verb or object is omitted after l'.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a complete or grammatical standalone expression in French. It appears to be a clipped transcription of a larger clause such as 'c'est ça que je l'ai.../je l'ai...' or 'c'est que je l'...'. In correct usage, 'ça que' often appears in emphatic structures ('c'est ça que...') and 'l' is an elision of 'le'/'la'/'lui' before a vowel and must be followed by a verb (e.g. 'l'ai', 'l'ai vu', 'lui ai dit'). Beginners should use full, grammatical forms instead of this fragment.
target_language_example: C'est ça que je l'ai dit au revoir en partant.
native_language_example: That's what I said goodbye to him/her when leaving.

meaning: literally 'that which I am' — not a standard fixed phrase; unusual and generally nonstandard in French when used alone
additional_notes: This exact sequence is uncommon. Native speakers would normally use «ce que je suis» for 'what/who I am' or «c'est que je suis...» to introduce an explanation. «Ça que je suis» might appear in emphatic colloquial speech or dialectal contexts but is best avoided in standard French.
target_language_example: Ça que je suis, tu ne le comprendras jamais.
native_language_example: That which I am, you will never understand it.

meaning: Not a complete standard phrase on its own; appears as the start of a familiar spoken clause meaning 'that which I ... you' or 'that I ... you' depending on completion.
additional_notes: This fragment is not a full, grammatical phrase by itself. In colloquial spoken French you may hear beginnings like "ça que je t'..." before a verb or clause is completed (e.g. "Ça que je t'ai dit...", "Ça que je t'parle..."), often used for emphasis or in regional/relaxed speech. For standard usage, prefer complete constructions such as "ce que je t'..." (what I ... you) or "ça que je t'ai dit" only in informal contexts. Watch for elision: "je t'..." indicates a verb beginning with a vowel (je t'ai, je t'entends, etc.).
target_language_example: Ça que je t'ai dit, c'était important.
native_language_example: What I told you, it was important.

meaning: 'that you are' — nonstandard/colloquial fragment; not a fixed phrase
additional_notes: This exact sequence ('ça que tu es') is not standard French as a standalone expression. It may appear as a fragment in casual speech or writing, often as a contracted or mistaken form of 'c'est que tu es', 'ça, que tu es...' for contrast/emphasis, or within hesitations. Native speakers would generally use 'c'est que tu es...' to introduce an explanation, or 'toi, tu es...' to emphasize the person. Avoid using 'ça que tu es' formally; treat it as a colloquial fragment or error.
target_language_example: Ça que tu es fatigué, on le voit à tes yeux.
native_language_example: That you are tired, we can see it in your eyes.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a fragment meaning roughly 'that which you (to) me' or 'that you [did/told] me' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a complete or common French expression by itself. It combines 'ça' (that/this), 'que' (that/which/that...); and 'tu me' (you me). In natural French you'd normally insert a verb or rephrase: e.g. 'c'est ce que tu m'as dit' (that's what you told me) or 'ce que tu me fais' (what you do to me). Using 'ça que tu me' alone sounds informal or unfinished; it's typically part of colloquial or emphatic speech like 'C'est ça que tu me dis ?' or 'Ça, que tu me fasses ça…'
target_language_example: C'est ça que tu me dis ?
native_language_example: Is that what you're telling me?

meaning: 'that which you want' (colloquial/informal phrasing).
additional_notes: This is an informal, somewhat nonstandard way to say 'what you want' or 'that which you want.' More common and grammatically standard alternatives are 'ce que tu veux' or 'ce que vous voulez.' 'Ça' is a familiar pronoun used in spoken French; using it with 'que' plus a verb or clause is typical in casual speech but may sound ungrammatical to some speakers.
target_language_example: Prends ça que tu veux, il n'y en aura pas pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Take whatever you want, there won't be enough for everyone.

meaning: 'this is how' / 'that's how (something happens)'.
additional_notes: Used in the fixed phrase C'est comme ça que ça se + verb to explain or comment on the way something happens or is done: 'C'est comme ça que ça se passe/termine/joue.' The structure: C'est comme ça que + ça se + [verb]. Common in spoken and written French. 'Ça' refers to the situation; 'se' is the reflexive/pronominal marker of the verb (se passer, se terminer, se jouer, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que ça se fait.
native_language_example: That's how it's done.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; likely a mistaken or incomplete combination (unusable as-is).
additional_notes:
The sequence «ça quelque» does not form a correct phrase in French. You might be thinking of similar, valid expressions such as:
- «ça ne ... pas» or «ce n'est pas» (negation)
- «quelque chose» (something) — note word order: «quelque chose» not «ça quelque»
- «ça me/te/...» followed by a verb or adjective (e.g. «ça me plaît»)
If you meant «quelque chose», it means "something." If you meant «ça» plus a determiner/pronoun, the correct structure depends on the intended meaning. Ask with the intended English meaning and I can give the right French phrase.
target_language_example: Incorrect: «ça quelque» — not used. Correct: «quelque chose» → «J'ai quelque chose à te dire.»
native_language_example: Incorrect: "ça quelque" — not used. Correct: "quelque chose" → "I have something to tell you."

meaning: not a standard French collocation; likely an incorrect, informal, or misheard sequence where speakers intended 'ce qui' or 'ça que'. It does not function as a grammatical relative pronoun in standard French.
additional_notes: Use 'ce qui' for subject relative clauses ('ce qui est important...') and 'ce que' for object relative clauses ('ce que je veux...'). 'Ça' is an informal demonstrative pronoun used in expressions like 'ça va' or in colloquial constructions ('c'est ça que...'), but 'ça qui' is generally ungrammatical. If you encounter 'ça qui' in speech, it's often a slip, a regional/dialectal pronunciation of 'ce qui', or part of an elided phrase (e.g. 'c'qui...' in rapid speech). Prefer 'ce qui' or 'ce que' in written and formal speech.
target_language_example: C'qui m'embête, c'est le bruit — prononcé familièrement comme 'ça qui' par certains locuteurs.
native_language_example: What bothers me is the noise — pronounced familiarly like 'ça qui' by some speakers.

meaning: a non-standard/colloquial way to start a relative clause similar to 'ce qui' ('that which' / 'what'); often considered incorrect in standard French.
additional_notes: Standard French uses 'ce qui' or 'ce que'. 'Ça qui est' may appear in very casual speech or regional varieties where 'ça' substitutes for 'ce', but it's generally ungrammatical in written and formal contexts—avoid it in formal writing and use 'ce qui' instead. Use 'ce qui' before a verb (ce qui est important) and 'ce que' before a clause where 'que' governs an object (ce que je veux).
target_language_example: Ça qui est difficile, c'est de trouver du temps.
native_language_example: What is difficult is finding time.

meaning: Everything's good / OK / it's working — an informal way to say 'OK' or 'all right'.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to confirm agreement, say that things are going well, or acknowledge instructions. Common in spoken French. Equivalent to 'OK', 'got it', 'sounds good', or 'all good' depending on context. Use with friends, colleagues in casual settings; avoid in very formal situations.
target_language_example: D'accord, rendez-vous à 18h ? — Ça roule !
native_language_example: Okay, meeting at 6 p.m.? — Sounds good!

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; a sequence of the demonstrative 'ça' ('that/this/it') followed immediately by the preposition 'sans' ('without') — typically a fragment that would be completed by an object or clause (e.g. 'ça sans toi...').
additional_notes: This is not a common standalone expression. In natural French you'll usually see a pause or punctuation between 'ça' and 'sans' (e.g. 'Ça, sans toi, ne marcherait pas.') or a linking word: when written without punctuation ('ça sans ...') it appears in informal speech or in truncated phrases. For learners: treat 'ça' and 'sans' as separate words and use them in full expressions (e.g. 'ça sans toi' = 'that without you').
target_language_example: Ça sans toi ne vaudrait rien.
native_language_example: That without you would be worth nothing.

meaning: used to ask 'how/why is it that...?' or 'how come...?'
additional_notes: Informal conversational phrase used to express surprise or ask for an explanation about a situation. Often appears in questions introduced by 'Comment' (Comment ça se fait que...). Followed by a clause describing the surprising fact. Equivalent to 'How/Why is it that...?' or 'How come...?'.
target_language_example: Comment ça se fait que tu n'es pas venu hier ?
native_language_example: How come you didn't come yesterday?

meaning: People would know (used to say something would already be common knowledge if it were true).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to dismiss a hypothetical claim by implying that, if it were true, everyone would already know about it. Often used sarcastically. Typical structure: respond to a supposition with « ça se saurait ». Equivalent to English 'if that were so, everyone would know' or 'we'd all know about it'.
target_language_example: Si c'était vrai, ça se saurait.
native_language_example: If that were true, everyone would know.

meaning: that (feminine) alone / that by itself (feminine).
additional_notes: Rare/incorrect as written: standard French normally uses 'ça seul' (neutral) or uses a clearly feminine pronoun or determiner ('elle seule', 'la seule') to indicate feminine agreement. 'Ça' is grammatically invariable and treating it as feminine with 'seule' is nonstandard; avoid 'ça seule' in formal writing. If encountered, it may reflect colloquial speech, a typographical error, or regional usage. Prefer 'ça seul', 'elle seule', or rephrase ('seule cette chose').
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas que ça seule décide pour nous.
native_language_example: I don't want that alone to decide for us.

meaning: a spoken emphatic expression meaning roughly 'that (indeed)' or 'well, that...'; used to emphasize or contrast a statement
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial. 'Ça si' appears in spoken French to add emphasis, contrast, or to introduce a strong opinion after a pause (similar to 'that, now...' or 'as for that...'). It usually precedes a clause or comment: e.g. « Ça, si… » or « Ça, si tu veux » and is more common in certain regional or conversational styles. Not a fixed grammatical phrase; context decides exact nuance.
target_language_example: Ça si, je n'avais jamais vu ça de ma vie.
native_language_example: That—now that—I had never seen that in my life.

meaning: that's enough
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (or oneself) that something should stop or that there is enough of something. Can be firm or polite depending on tone/context. Often used alone as an interjection. Can be followed by a noun or phrase: "une année de fête, ça suffit" = "one year of partying is enough."
target_language_example: Ça suffit, arrêtez de vous chamailler.
native_language_example: That's enough, stop bickering.

meaning: It suits you / It looks good on you; can also mean 'that fits you' or 'it's appropriate for you' (spoken).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say that clothing, a color, or a style looks good on someone (literal: 'that goes you well'). Informally it can also comment on behavior or a remark, meaning 'that suits you' or 'that's rich coming from you' depending on tone and context. Used in familiar conversation (tu).
target_language_example: Tu sais, ça te va bien, le blanc.
native_language_example: You know, white looks good on you.

meaning: 'it's going (badly)' or 'it's turning out (badly)'; can also mean 'is it working/rolling?' depending on context.
additional_notes: Common informal phrase. Often used to say a situation is turning bad (Ça tourne mal = things are going wrong). Can also be used interrogatively in contexts like filming or machines to ask if something is running/rolling (Ça tourne ? = Are we rolling? / Is it working?). Context determines meaning; in the provided examples it mainly means 'it's going/turning bad.'
target_language_example: Fais attention, si ça tourne mal, on part tout de suite.
native_language_example: Be careful, if it turns bad, we'll leave right away.

meaning: that's all; that's it (informal, emphatic)
additional_notes: Very informal spoken French. Used to sum up, dismiss something, or indicate there's nothing more to say about a topic. Similar to « et voilà » or « c'est tout ». Often contracted in speech and can sound like one phrase. Not standard in formal writing.
target_language_example: Je n'en veux plus, ça tout.
native_language_example: I don't want any more, that's it.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; typically a fragment arising when 'ça' is followed directly by 'tout le' in speech or written fragments (e.g. 'ça tout le monde...' or 'ça tout le temps...'). It is not a standalone idiom.
additional_notes: You will not find 'ça tout le' as an independent expression. It appears only as part of longer constructions and usually requires punctuation or additional words to form a grammatical phrase (e.g. 'Ça, tout le monde...' or 'Ça tout le temps...' are colloquial/elliptical). If you meant a complete phrase, use the full expression such as 'tout le monde' (everyone) or 'tout le temps' (all the time).
target_language_example: Ça tout le monde le sait n'est pas correct sans virgule; on écrira plutôt «Ça, tout le monde le sait.»
native_language_example: 'Ça tout le monde le sait' is not correct without a comma; you would write 'Ça, tout le monde le sait.'

meaning: colloquial emphasis: a spoken foregrounding structure meaning roughly 'that — you...' used to draw attention to or contrast something about the person or thing (often introducing a comment or judgment).
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. 'Ça, tu...' (often pronounced [sa ty]) is used to emphasize or contrast a point about someone or something before making a remark (e.g. 'Ça, tu... n'y vas pas!' = 'That — you shouldn't go!'). Common in conversation and regional speech; not typical in formal written French. Usually followed by a clause, exclamation, or judgment.
target_language_example: Ça tu n'y es pour rien.
native_language_example: That — you aren't to blame.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical French phrase; likely a typo, fragment, or transcript error (commonly meant: 'c'est un' or 'ça a').
additional_notes:
The sequence 'ça un' does not form a correct expression in French on its own. Possible intended corrections:
- 'c'est un' = 'it's a' or 'this is a' (identification)
- 'ça a' = 'it/that has' (verb 'avoir' with impersonal 'ça')
If you encounter 'ça un' in writing or speech, treat it as an error or missing words and ask for clarification. For learners, practice the correct forms 'c'est un' and 'ça a'.
target_language_example: (Erreur de transcription) « Il a dit: 'ça un...'? » — probablement voulu: « c'est un... »
native_language_example: (Transcription error) "He said: 'ça un...'?" — probably meant: "c'est un..."

meaning: are you okay?
additional_notes: A very common everyday expression. As a question, it can mean "are you okay?" or simply "how are things?" depending on context and tone. It is also used as an answer: "Ça va." = "I'm fine / it's going okay."
target_language_example: Salut, ça va aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Hi, how's it going today?

meaning: 'I'm fine' / 'It's going well' (response to 'How are you?').
additional_notes: Common, everyday reply to 'Ça va ?' or 'Comment ça va ?'. Can mean both personal wellbeing ('I'm fine') or that a situation is going well ('It's fine/going well'). Tone and context determine nuance; adding 'merci' is polite. Informal but widely used in neutral conversation.
target_language_example: Salut ! Ça va bien, merci.
native_language_example: Hi! I'm fine, thanks.

meaning: used to introduce a range or list: 'it ranges from...' or 'it goes from...'
additional_notes: Common in French to describe a spectrum, variety, or range of possibilities. Often followed by '...à...' (e.g. 'ça va de X à Y') or by a noun phrase listing items. Can be used in formal and informal contexts. Not to be confused with the standalone 'ça va' meaning 'how are you' or 'it's fine'.
target_language_example: Les cadeaux ça va de petits souvenirs à des objets très chers.
native_language_example: Gifts range from small souvenirs to very expensive items.

meaning: it's fine for / that's enough for / that will do for
additional_notes: Used to say something is sufficient or acceptable for a given purpose or situation. Often followed by a noun or phrase indicating what it's enough for (e.g., 'pour le moment', 'pour aujourd'hui', 'pour toi'). Tone can be neutral or slightly informal depending on context. Similar to plain 'ça va' (it's okay) but adds 'pour' to specify what it is okay for.
target_language_example: Ça va pour aujourd'hui, on reprendra demain.
native_language_example: That's enough for today; we'll pick up again tomorrow.

meaning: 'it's going very...' used to start a phrase that describes how things are going (usually followed by an adjective or adverb).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; native speakers add a word after it (e.g. bien, mal, vite, doucement) to say 'it's going very well/very badly/very fast…'. 'Ça va' alone means 'how are you?' or 'it's going' and is extremely common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Ça va très bien, merci.
native_language_example: It's going very well, thanks.

meaning: 'it was worth the' (usually completed as "ça valait le coup" = "it was worth it").
additional_notes: Commonly used with "coup" as "ça valait le coup" to say an effort, risk or action was worthwhile. Past imperfect "valait" indicates a past judgment. You may also hear "ça valait la peine" with the same meaning. Informal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Ça valait le coup d'attendre une heure pour entrer.
native_language_example: It was worth waiting an hour to get in.

meaning: Incomplete fragment; not a standard complete phrase by itself. It appears to be the beginning of expressions like 'ça veut dire quelque chose' (that means something) or 'ça veut dire quelque part' (that means somewhere), or it could be the start of 'ça veut dire quelque chose de...' (that means something ...). On its own it doesn't convey a full meaning.
additional_notes:
Teach learners that this is a partial phrase. Common complete forms:
- 'Ça veut dire...' + explanation = 'That means...'
- 'Ça veut dire quelque chose' = 'That means something.'
- 'Ça veut dire que...' = 'That means that...'
- 'Ça veut dire quelque part' = 'That means somewhere.'
Avoid using 'ça veut dire quelque' alone in written or spoken French; finish the phrase so the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Ça veut dire quelque chose, pas seulement des mots.
native_language_example: That means something, not just words.

meaning: quickly, right away (informal; contraction of il faut que ça aille vite or faire ça vite)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to say something should be done quickly or immediately. Often appears in commands or requests: faire ça vite (do that quickly), il faut que ça aille vite (it must go quickly). Alone 'ça vite' is not a complete sentence; in speech it may be slurred into phrases like 'fais ça vite' or 'va vite'.
target_language_example: Fais ça vite, on est en retard.
native_language_example: Do that quickly, we're late.

meaning: 'there' or 'it (there)' used in informal expressions (part of phrases like "ça y est").
additional_notes: On its own "ça y" is incomplete; it appears in common informal expressions such as "ça y est" (that's it; it's done) and "ça y est ?" (is it ready/done?). Alone it rarely stands by itself — learners should learn full phrases that include it. Pronounced informally as /sa i/ and used in spoken French.
target_language_example: Ça y est, j'ai fini !
native_language_example: That's it, I'm finished!

meaning: That's it / It's done / It's ready (expression of completion or that something has finally happened).
additional_notes: Used to announce that something has been completed, achieved, or has finally occurred. Can express relief, satisfaction, or realization. Common in spoken French and informal contexts but also neutral enough for general use. Often followed by an exclamation or a clause explaining what happened.
target_language_example: Ça y est, on peut partir.
native_language_example: That's it, we can leave.

meaning: colloquial/informal way to say 'see you later' or 'bye' (short for « ça, à plus » / « à plus »).
additional_notes: Very informal. Often written in chat or text messages as 'à plus' or 'a+' and pronounced /a ply/ or /a ply/; 'ça à plus' is a casual variation that may appear in speech or informal writing. Use only with friends or peers, not in formal contexts. Equivalent to English 'see you later' or 'bye'.
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller, ça à plus !
native_language_example: Okay, I have to go, see you later!

meaning: exchange of / swapping / trade of (used before a noun).
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase used to indicate that one thing is exchanged or traded for another. It is followed by a noun (e.g. échange de cadeaux, échange de vues). Common in formal and neutral contexts. Use 'un échange' as the noun plus 'de' to link to what is exchanged.
target_language_example: Un échange de cadeaux a eu lieu entre les deux familles.
native_language_example: An exchange of gifts took place between the two families.

meaning: 'escaped from' or 'got away from' (someone or something dangerous or pursuing).
additional_notes: Used with people or institutions (la police, la justice, la loi) or abstract dangers (la mort). Often appears as 'échappé à + article + noun' or 'échappé à + de' depending on gender/number (e.g. échappé à la police, échappé au danger, échappé aux autorités). It implies avoiding capture, harm, or consequence.
target_language_example: Il a échappé à la police pendant deux ans.
native_language_example: He escaped from the police for two years.

meaning: to burst out laughing; to suddenly start laughing loudly
additional_notes: Describes a sudden, often uncontrollable laugh. Common in spoken and written French. Conjugate the verb éclater (e.g., il/elle éclate de rire, nous éclatons de rire). Typically used with a subject followed by the expression éclater de rire.
target_language_example: Ils ont éclaté de rire quand il a imité le professeur.
native_language_example: They burst out laughing when he imitated the teacher.

meaning: 'to burst into tears' or 'to break down crying'.
additional_notes: Used to describe suddenly starting to cry intensely. Often implies uncontrollable sobbing. Can refer to one person or a group. Common in both written and spoken French; can carry a slightly literary or formal tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Quand elle a reçu la lettre, elle a éclaté en sanglots.
native_language_example: When she received the letter, she burst into tears.

meaning: burst of / sudden outburst of (followed by a noun), e.g. a sudden surge or explosion of something (emotion, activity, light).
additional_notes: Éclaté de is formed from the past participle éclaté (burst/split) + de. It appears before a noun to describe a sudden, intense occurrence (e.g. un éclaté de rire = a burst of laughter). Often used in fixed expressions like «un éclaté de rire», «un éclaté de lumière», or «un éclaté de colère». More common is the singular noun phrase «un éclat de...», but «éclaté de» can appear in descriptive contexts. Use with definite/indefinite article as needed: «un éclat de», «des éclats de».
target_language_example: Un éclaté de rire a rempli la salle.
native_language_example: A burst of laughter filled the room.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase. Likely a misspelling or token sequence: either 'école à' (school + preposition 'à' = 'school at/in') or 'école a' where 'a' is the verb 'avoir' (has) following a subject omitted in this fragment. As written it's ambiguous and usually indicates a typo or incomplete sentence.
additional_notes:
As written, 'école a' is not grammatical by itself. Common readings:
- 'école à' (with grave accent) requires a following complement: e.g. 'école à Paris' = 'school in Paris'.
- 'école a' (without accent) can occur in a larger sentence where 'a' is the verb avoir: e.g. 'L'école a fermé.' = 'The school has closed.'
Learners should check for context and correct the accent when the preposition 'à' is intended. The two tokens are not a fixed multi-word expression.
target_language_example: L'école a fermé tôt aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The school closed early today.

meaning: 'school of' or 'department of' — used to indicate a type of school or a field/department within an institution.
additional_notes: Followed by a noun indicating the subject, discipline, institution or style (e.g. école de musique, école de commerce, école de médecine). Can also mean 'school of thought' (école de pensée). When referring to an institution name, 'de' may contract (e.g. École nationale d'administration). In English you usually translate it as 'school of' or simply 'the [discipline] school'.
target_language_example: Il étudie à l'école de commerce de sa ville.
native_language_example: He studies at his city's business school.

meaning: language school; a school that teaches foreign languages.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a place where languages are taught (e.g., French school for foreigners, English school). Often pluralized as "écoles de langue". Can describe private language institutes as well as university language centers. Commonly followed by the language taught (école de langue française, école de langue anglaise) or by the target audience (école de langue pour étrangers).
target_language_example: Je m'inscris à une école de langue pour améliorer mon français.
native_language_example: I'm enrolling in a language school to improve my French.

meaning: language school; a school that teaches foreign languages.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an institution where languages are taught (private or public). Can mean a language institute, language center, or language department. Commonly used with verbs like 'aller', 'travailler dans', or 'étudier à'.
target_language_example: Je travaille dans une école de langues depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I have been working at a language school for two years.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase — likely a typo or incorrect word order (perhaps meant 'seconde école', 'école se...' beginning of a reflexive verb, or 'école' + pronoun 'se').
additional_notes: There is no common multi-word expression 'école se' in French. Possible explanations: 1) a typing error (e.g. intended 'école' alone or 'école se...' as the start of a sentence like 'L'école se trouve...'), 2) wrong word order for a phrase such as 'seconde école' (second school) or 'école de...'
